docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Keep the following reference handy throughout the rest of the workbook. These commands cover every technique from the chapter.

Command What It Does nmap -p 3389 -Pn <target_ip> Check if RDP port is open nmap -p 3389 -sV -Pn <target_ip> Detect RDP service and version nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption <target_ip> Enumerate RDP encryption levels nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-ntlm-info <target_ip> Extract NTLM authentication details nmap -p 3389 --script ssl-cert <target_ip> Retrieve RDP SSL/TLS certificate xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:user /p:pass /cert:ignore Connect to RDP with credentials xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:user /p:pass /cert:ignore +clipboard Connect with clipboard sharing xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:user /p:pass /cert:ignore /drive:share,/tmp/rdp_share Connect with drive redirection xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:user /p:pass /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution Connect with auto-resize hydra -l user -P wordlist.txt -t 4 -V -f rdp://<target_ip> Brute force RDP with Hydra

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text:
You can now detect, enumerate, and exploit RDP; the graphical remote access protocol. But RDP is not the only remote management service on a Windows machine. Chapter 5 introduces WinRM (Windows Remote Management), a command-line remote management protocol that runs on ports 5985 (HTTP) and 5986 (HTTPS). WinRM provides remote command execution without a graphical desktop, making it faster and stealthier than RDP. The tools change; you will use evil-winrm instead of xfreerdp: but the workflow remains the same: discover the service, enumerate what you can, and test credentials to gain access.

Where RDP gives you a visual desktop, WinRM gives you a PowerShell session. Both paths lead to full system access, but they leave different forensic footprints and are defended by different security controls. A complete penetration tester knows both.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. RDP runs on TCP port 3389 by default. Nmap reports the service name as ms-wbt-server (Microsoft Windows-Based Terminal Server), regardless of whether the server runs native Windows RDP or xrdp.

2. (1) rdp-enum-encryption: reveals which security layers (Standard RDP, TLS, CredSSP/NLA) and encryption levels (40-bit, 56-bit, 128-bit RC4, FIPS 140-1) the server supports. (2) rdp-ntlm-info: extracts NTLM authentication metadata including hostnames, domain names, and OS version without requiring credentials. (3) ssl-cert: retrieves the SSL/TLS certificate used by the RDP service, showing the subject, issuer, and validity dates.

3. The /cert:ignore flag tells xfreerdp to accept untrusted (self-signed) certificates without prompting for confirmation.

4. Test in this priority order: (1) Default credentials (admin/admin, admin/password, admin/admin123). (2) Keyboard patterns (qwerty, 123456, abc123). (3) Organizational context (FinanceCorp2024, Finance123). (4) Seasonal/date patterns (Summer2025, Welcome1).

5. The -t flag controls the number of parallel threads. A value of 4 is recommended for RDP because the TLS handshake overhead makes high thread counts unreliable and likely to trigger rate limiting.

6. The -f flag tells Hydra to stop after finding the first valid credential pair, rather than continuing to test all remaining combinations in the wordlist.

7. (1) +clipboard: enables bidirectional clipboard sharing between local and remote. (2) /drive:share,/tmp/rdp_share: maps a local directory into the remote session as a network drive. (3) /dynamic-resolution: adjusts the remote desktop resolution when you resize the window.

8. BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) is a critical vulnerability in the RDP service on Windows 7, Windows Server 2008, and Windows Server 2008 R2. It allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted requests to port 3389, without needing any credentials. It is classified as "wormable" because it can propagate automatically between vulnerable machines. RDP assessments should always include a BlueKeep check on Windows targets.

docs.title: Why WinRM Matters
docs.text:
Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is the protocol that system administrators rely on to manage Windows machines from across the network. Every enterprise environment running Windows Server likely has WinRM enabled on dozens or hundreds of hosts. When a penetration tester discovers an exposed WinRM service, they have found a direct path to remote command execution; provided they can authenticate.

FinanceCorp, like many organizations, uses WinRM to manage its Windows infrastructure. During your engagement, you will probe these services for weaknesses, test credentials, and demonstrate the impact of unauthorized remote management access.

docs.title: What Is WinRM?
docs.text:
WinRM is Microsoft's implementation of the WS-Management (Web Services-Management) protocol. The protocol uses SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) messages carried over HTTP or HTTPS to communicate with remote hosts. Two default ports handle WinRM traffic.

Port Transport Description 5985 HTTP Unencrypted WinRM communication 5986 HTTPS TLS-encrypted WinRM communication

Because WinRM rides on top of HTTP, it often blends in with normal web traffic. Firewalls and intrusion detection systems may not flag it unless they inspect traffic at the application layer. An attacker who gains valid credentials can execute commands, transfer files, and pivot deeper into the network; all through a protocol that the organization itself depends on.

docs.title: What Will You Learn?
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Detect WinRM services running on target hosts using port scanning
  • Enumerate WinRM version information and authentication configurations
  • Test credentials manually against WinRM endpoints
  • Perform automated brute-force attacks against remote management services
  • Execute commands remotely after successful authentication
  • Search for and retrieve sensitive files from compromised hosts

docs.title: Lab Progression
docs.text:
Each lab in this chapter builds on the skills from the previous one. The table below shows how the labs connect.

Exercise Title Core Skill 5.1 WinRM Service Detection Port scanning with nmap 5.2 WinRM Version and Configuration Enumeration Header analysis and script scanning 5.3 WinRM Manual Authentication Credential testing 5.4 WinRM Credential Brute Force Automated password attacks with Hydra 5.5 WinRM Command Execution Post-authentication enumeration 5.6 WinRM File Retrieval Filesystem search and data exfiltration

docs.title: Attack Flow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the progression from initial discovery to data retrieval.

graph LR
    A[Scan Ports] --> B[Enumerate Service]
    B --> C[Test Credentials]
    C --> D[Brute Force]
    D --> E[Execute Commands]
    E --> F[Retrieve Files]

Each lab represents one node in the attack chain. Skipping a step in a real engagement could mean missing critical information, so treat each exercise as a required phase of the penetration test.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following items before beginning Exercise 5.1.

  • You have access to the OpenCyberRange platform and can launch Chapter 5 lab environments
  • Your attack machine has nmap, curl, and hydra installed
  • You understand basic Linux command-line navigation (covered in Chapter 1)
  • You can open an SSH session from your attack machine using the ssh command
  • You have a text editor or note-taking tool ready to record your findings

If any of these items are missing, revisit the platform setup guide or ask your instructor before proceeding.

docs.title: Conventions Used in This Chapter
docs.text:
Command examples appear in fenced code blocks. Placeholders use angle brackets; replace <target_ip> with the actual IP address of your lab target. Flags are always wrapped in the OCR{<flag_here>} format. Never share flags outside your lab session.

Proceed to Exercise 5.1; WinRM Service Detection when you are ready.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Service detection is always the first step in any penetration test. Before you can exploit WinRM, you need to confirm that the service is running and identify which ports it listens on.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: FinanceCorp has hired your team to assess the security of their Windows infrastructure. Your project lead has assigned you a single target host suspected of running remote management services. Your first task is to scan the host, identify any WinRM endpoints, and document what you find.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Scan the target for WinRM ports (5985 and 5986)
  • Identify the service version running on open ports
  • Confirm network connectivity to the target
  • Document all detected services

docs.title: Background: How WinRM Listens on the Network
docs.text:
WinRM relies on two well-known ports to accept incoming management connections. Port 5985 handles unencrypted HTTP traffic, while port 5986 handles HTTPS traffic encrypted with TLS (Transport Layer Security). When a WinRM service is active, it registers an HTTP listener that responds to SOAP requests on these ports.

From a scanning perspective, WinRM ports behave like standard HTTP services. On a real Windows host, the server identifies itself as "Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0" because WinRM uses the Windows HTTP Server API to handle requests, and recognizing that server string is key to identifying WinRM during reconnaissance. The string appears in the HTTP Server response header, so the reliable way to read it is a header request with curl -I. An nmap version scan reads the same banner inconsistently and, against the lab endpoint, reports a generic Python http.server fingerprint instead.

In the OpenCyberRange lab environment, a WinRM simulator runs on the target host to replicate the behavior of a real Windows WinRM service. The simulator responds with the same headers and version strings you would see in a production environment.

graph LR
    A[Attacker Machine] -->|Port 5985 HTTP| B[WinRM Service]
    A -->|Port 5986 HTTPS| B
    A -->|Port 22 SSH| C[SSH Service]
    B --> D[windows-target]
    C --> D

docs.title: Tool Primer: nmap
docs.text:
Nmap (Network Mapper) is the standard tool for port scanning and service detection. The flags used in this exercise are listed below.

Flag Purpose -p Specify ports to scan (e.g., -p 5985,5986) -sV Probe open ports to determine service version -sC Run default nmap scripts against detected services -Pn Skip host discovery and treat the target as online -v Increase verbosity to show scan progress

A basic version-detection scan produces output similar to the following. The lab WinRM endpoint is backed by a lightweight HTTP server, so nmap -sV reports a Python http.server fingerprint rather than the Windows banner. Confirm the WinRM identity with a header request instead, which is covered in the walkthrough.

PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
5985/tcp open  http    SimpleHTTPServer 0.6 (Python 3.10.12)
5986/tcp open  http    SimpleHTTPServer 0.6 (Python 3.10.12)

docs.title: Step 1: Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Before scanning, confirm that you can reach the target host. Run a ping command with a limited count to avoid waiting indefinitely.

Kali - Ping the target to verify connectivity

ping -c 3 <target_ip>

You should see three reply packets. If you receive "Destination Host Unreachable" or 100% packet loss, verify that your lab environment is running and that you have the correct IP address.

docs.title: Step 2: Scan for WinRM Ports
docs.text:
Run an nmap scan targeting only the WinRM ports and SSH port. Limiting the scan to specific ports keeps it fast and focused.

Kali - Scan for WinRM and SSH ports

nmap -p 22,5985,5986 -sV <target_ip>

Review the output carefully. You should see port 5985 reported as open with an HTTP service. Against the lab endpoint, nmap fingerprints it as SimpleHTTPServer 0.6 (Python 3.10.12) rather than the Windows banner, so do not expect "Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0" from -sV here. Port 22 should show an SSH service. Record every open port, its state, and the reported service version. Step 3a confirms the WinRM banner directly with curl.

docs.title: Step 3: Run a Script Scan
docs.text:
Nmap includes scripts that can extract more detail from detected services. Run a default script scan against the WinRM ports to gather extra information.

Kali - Run default NSE scripts against WinRM ports

nmap -p 5985,5986 -sC -sV <target_ip>

Compare the output to your previous scan. Script scans may reveal additional details such as HTTP response headers, authentication methods, or redirect behavior. Note any new findings.

docs.title: Step 3a: Confirm the WinRM Banner with curl
docs.text:
The -sV scan does not surface the Windows banner against this target, so request the HTTP headers directly. The Server header is where WinRM advertises itself, and a header-only request avoids pulling the response body.

Kali - Read the HTTP Server header on port 5985

curl -I http://<target_ip>:5985

Look for a Server: Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0 line in the response. That header is the signature that identifies the endpoint as WinRM, confirming what the version scan could not.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect via SSH and Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
The target also runs an SSH service on port 22. Use the credentials provided to log in and retrieve the flag file.

Kali - Connect to the target via SSH

ssh admin@<target_ip>

When prompted for a password, enter password123. Once logged in, read the flag file.

Kali - Read the flag file

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Copy the table below into your notes and fill in each row based on your scan results.

Port State Service Version 22 5985 5986

docs.title: Step 5: Record the Flag
docs.text: The flag you retrieved from /home/admin/flag.txt follows the standard format. Record it in your notes as OCR{<flag_here>}, replacing <flag_here> with the value you found in the file.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does WinRM appear as an HTTP service in nmap scan results?
Reveal Answer

WinRM uses the Windows HTTP Server API (HTTP.sys) to handle connections. Because it communicates over HTTP/HTTPS, nmap identifies it using the standard HTTP service fingerprint rather than a custom WinRM-specific signature.

  1. What is the significance of the "Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0" version string?
Reveal Answer

The version string indicates that the service uses Microsoft's HTTP Server API version 2.0. Any service built on HTTP.sys, including WinRM, SCCM, and SSRS, may report the same string, so further enumeration is needed to confirm the exact service.

  1. Why did we also scan port 22 in addition to the WinRM ports?
Reveal Answer

Port 22 runs SSH, which provides an alternative remote access method. Identifying all remote management services on a host gives a complete picture of the attack surface and may provide fallback access if one protocol is locked down.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• WinRM listens on ports 5985 (HTTP) and 5986 (HTTPS) by default
  • The "Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0" server string identifies WinRM, but read it from the HTTP Server header with curl -I because nmap -sV does not report it reliably against the lab endpoint
  • Script scans (-sC) can reveal additional configuration details beyond basic version detection
  • Always document every open port and service during the reconnaissance phase
  • In Exercise 5.2, you will dig deeper into WinRM's configuration by analyzing HTTP headers and authentication methods

docs.title: Exercise 5.2: WinRM Version and Configuration Enumeration
Before You Begin
docs.text: In Exercise 5.1, you confirmed that WinRM is running on the target host. Now you need to learn more about how the service is configured. Enumeration; the process of extracting detailed information from a detected service; reveals authentication methods, supported protocols, and potential misconfigurations.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your FinanceCorp engagement continues. The project lead wants you to determine exactly how WinRM is configured on the target before attempting any authentication. Knowing which authentication methods are supported will shape your attack strategy for the remaining exercises.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Inspect HTTP response headers returned by the WinRM service
  • Identify supported authentication mechanisms
  • Use nmap scripts to automate header enumeration
  • Determine whether the service uses encryption

docs.title: Background: HTTP Headers and WinRM Configuration
docs.text:
Every HTTP-based service returns response headers when a client connects. These headers contain metadata about the server software, supported features, and security settings. For WinRM, the headers reveal which authentication methods the server accepts.

Common authentication methods supported by WinRM include Basic, Negotiate (NTLM/Kerberos), Kerberos, Certificate-based, and CredSSP (Credential Security Support Provider). The WWW-Authenticate header lists which methods the server will accept. A server that allows Basic authentication over unencrypted HTTP is especially dangerous because credentials travel in base64 encoding, which is trivially reversible.

The Server header confirms the underlying technology stack. A value of "Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0" confirms that the service is built on the Windows HTTP Server API, consistent with WinRM. Combined with the port number, these headers provide strong evidence that you are dealing with a WinRM endpoint.

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl
docs.text:
Curl is a command-line tool for transferring data using various protocols. In this exercise, you will use it to send HTTP requests and inspect the response headers.

Flag Purpose -I Fetch HTTP headers only (HEAD request) -s Silent mode; suppress progress bars -v Verbose mode; show full request and response --head Same as -I, sends a HEAD request

A typical header response from a WinRM endpoint looks like the following.

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Length: 0
Server: Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate
Date: Mon, 22 Feb 2026 12:00:00 GMT

The 401 status code is expected; it means the server requires authentication before granting access.

docs.title: Step 1: Fetch Headers with curl
docs.text:
Send a HEAD request to the WinRM HTTP port to retrieve the response headers without downloading any content.

Kali - Fetch WinRM HTTP response headers

curl -I http://<target_ip>:5985

Examine the output line by line. Look for the Server header to confirm the technology and the WWW-Authenticate header to identify accepted authentication methods. A 401 Unauthorized response is normal here because you have not provided credentials.

docs.title: Step 2: Use Verbose Mode for Full Detail
docs.text:
Verbose mode shows both the outgoing request and the incoming response, which helps you understand the complete HTTP exchange.

Kali - Verbose request to inspect full HTTP exchange

curl -v http://<target_ip>:5985

In the output, lines starting with > represent the request your machine sent, and lines starting with < represent the server's response. Pay attention to any authentication-related headers or cookies that appear in the response.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate Headers with nmap Scripts
docs.text:
Nmap includes an http-headers script that automates header retrieval. Run it against the WinRM port.

Kali - Enumerate headers with nmap http-headers script

nmap -p 5985 --script http-headers <target_ip>

The script output organizes the headers into a readable list. Compare the results with what you retrieved manually using curl. Both methods should return the same information, but nmap's script formats the data more cleanly for documentation.

docs.title: Step 4: Check for HTTPS on Port 5986
docs.text:
Repeat the header check against port 5986 to see if HTTPS-based WinRM is available.

Kali - Check HTTPS WinRM headers on port 5986

curl -Ik https://<target_ip>:5986

The -k flag tells curl to ignore certificate validation errors, which are common in lab environments using self-signed certificates. If the port is open, compare the authentication headers to those on port 5985. HTTPS endpoints may offer different authentication options than their HTTP counterparts.

docs.title: Step 5: Connect and Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Log in to the target via SSH using the provided credentials to collect the flag.

Kali - Connect to the target via SSH

ssh admin@<target_ip>

Enter the password password123 when prompted. Once connected, read the flag.

Kali - Read the flag file

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the headers and authentication methods you discovered by filling in the table below.

Header Value (Port 5985) Value (Port 5986) Server WWW-Authenticate Content-Length HTTP Status Code

docs.title: Step 6: Record the Flag
docs.text: Write down the flag from /home/admin/flag.txt in the format OCR{<flag_here>}.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the WinRM endpoint return a 401 status code when you connect without credentials?
Reveal Answer

The 401 Unauthorized status code indicates that the server requires authentication. WinRM does not allow anonymous access, so any request without valid credentials is rejected with a 401 response along with a WWW-Authenticate header listing acceptable methods.

  1. What risk does Basic authentication over HTTP (port 5985) pose?
Reveal Answer

Basic authentication encodes credentials in base64, which is not encryption. Anyone capturing network traffic between the client and server can decode the credentials instantly. Running Basic authentication over unencrypted HTTP exposes usernames and passwords to any attacker on the network path.

  1. How does the WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate header affect your attack planning?
Reveal Answer

The Negotiate method supports both NTLM and Kerberos authentication. Knowing the server accepts Negotiate tells you that NTLM hash-based attacks or Kerberos ticket attacks may be viable, depending on the domain configuration. It also means simple plaintext brute force may need to be adapted to handle the Negotiate handshake.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• HTTP response headers reveal the server technology and supported authentication methods
  • The WWW-Authenticate header is the most valuable piece of information during WinRM enumeration
  • A 401 response is expected and confirms that the service requires credentials
  • Both curl and nmap scripts can extract headers, giving you flexibility in your approach
  • In Exercise 5.3, you will attempt to authenticate against WinRM using known credentials

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 5.2 revealed which authentication methods the WinRM service accepts. Now you will test whether a known set of credentials can grant access to the remote management service. Manual authentication testing is a critical skill because automated tools are not always available or appropriate.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: During your FinanceCorp engagement, a colleague on the social engineering team recovered a potential username and password combination from a phishing exercise. The credentials are admin:password. Your job is to test whether these credentials grant access to the WinRM service on the target host.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand WinRM authentication methods at a conceptual level
  • Attempt manual credential testing against the target
  • Use SSH as a practical authentication method in the lab environment
  • Confirm or deny the validity of recovered credentials

docs.title: Background: WinRM Authentication Methods
docs.text:
WinRM supports several authentication mechanisms, each with different security properties. Understanding these methods helps you choose the right tool and approach for credential testing.

Method Description Security Level Basic Username and password sent in base64 encoding Low; easily decoded Negotiate Automatically selects NTLM or Kerberos Medium to High Kerberos Ticket-based authentication requiring a domain controller High Certificate Client certificate presented for identity verification High CredSSP Credential Security Support Provider; delegates credentials Medium

Basic authentication is the simplest to attack because the credentials are only base64-encoded, not encrypted. Negotiate is more common in enterprise environments and requires a multi-step handshake. In production penetration tests, tools like Evil-WinRM handle these protocols automatically.

In the OpenCyberRange lab environment, the WinRM simulator runs on a Linux container. While the WinRM ports respond with realistic headers, the practical way to test authentication and interact with the host is through SSH on port 22. The concepts remain the same; you are testing whether credentials grant remote management access.

graph LR
    A[Recovered Credentials] --> B{Authentication Attempt}
    B -->|Success| C[Remote Shell Access]
    B -->|Failure| D[Access Denied - 401]

docs.title: Tool Primer: Evil-WinRM (Conceptual)
docs.text:
Evil-WinRM is a purpose-built tool for interacting with WinRM services during penetration tests. While you will use SSH in this exercise, understanding Evil-WinRM syntax prepares you for real-world engagements.

Flag Purpose -i Target IP address -u Username -p Password -P Port number (default 5985) -S Use SSL/HTTPS (port 5986)

A typical Evil-WinRM command looks like the following.

evil-winrm -i <target_ip> -u admin -p password

A successful connection drops you into a PowerShell-like prompt on the remote host. A failed attempt returns an authentication error.

docs.title: Step 1: Attempt Authentication via curl
docs.text:
Before using SSH, try authenticating against the WinRM HTTP endpoint using curl with Basic authentication. Send a POST request with credentials embedded in the request.

Kali - Test WinRM Basic authentication with curl

curl -u admin:password http://<target_ip>:5985/wsman

The -u flag sends the username and password using HTTP Basic authentication. Examine the response code. A 401 means the credentials were rejected or the server does not accept Basic authentication. Any other response; particularly a 200 or a SOAP XML body; indicates successful authentication.

docs.title: Step 2: Test with the SSH Service
docs.text:
Since the lab environment provides SSH access for practical interaction, test the same credentials against the SSH service.

Kali - Connect to the target via SSH

ssh admin@<target_ip>

When prompted, enter the password password. Note that the password for this exercise is password, not password123 from previous labs. If the credentials are valid, you will land in a shell session on the target.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm Access and Gather Context
docs.text:
Once logged in, verify your identity and permissions. Run a few quick commands to confirm who you are and where you landed.

Target - Verify identity and gather context

whoami
id
hostname
pwd

The whoami command shows your current username. The id command reveals your user ID (UID) and group memberships. The hostname command confirms you are on the correct target. The pwd command (print working directory) shows your starting location in the filesystem.

docs.title: Step 4: Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Navigate to the flag location and read its contents.

Target - Read the flag file

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

Record the flag value before ending your session.

docs.title: Step 5: Exit the Session
docs.text:
Cleanly disconnect from the target by typing the exit command.

Target - Disconnect from the remote session

exit

Always close your sessions when you are done to avoid leaving open connections that could alert defenders.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the results of your authentication attempts in the table below.

Method Credentials Used Result (Success/Fail) curl Basic Auth admin:password SSH admin:password 
whoami output:
id output:
hostname output:

docs.title: Step 6: Record the Flag
docs.text: Write down the flag from /home/admin/flag.txt using the format OCR{<flag_here>}.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why might an organization disable Basic authentication on WinRM while leaving Negotiate enabled?
Reveal Answer

Basic authentication transmits credentials in base64, which offers no real protection. Negotiate uses NTLM or Kerberos, both of which include challenge-response mechanisms that never send the plaintext password over the network. Disabling Basic authentication reduces the risk of credential interception.

  1. In a real engagement, why would you prefer Evil-WinRM over SSH for accessing a Windows target?
Reveal Answer

Evil-WinRM provides a PowerShell session that understands Windows commands, paths, and object models. SSH on Windows is less common and may have limited functionality. Evil-WinRM also supports file upload/download and in-memory PowerShell script execution, making it a more capable post-exploitation tool.

  1. Why is it important to test credentials manually before running automated tools?
Reveal Answer

Manual testing confirms that the credentials work and that the service is reachable. Running an automated brute-force tool against a service that requires a different authentication protocol wastes time and generates unnecessary log entries. Manual verification also reduces the chance of triggering account lockout policies.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• WinRM supports multiple authentication methods, each with different security trade-offs
  • Basic authentication is the easiest to test but the least secure for the target organization
  • Manual credential testing should always precede automated attacks
  • Always record the exact credentials that grant access; password variations matter
  • In Exercise 5.4, you will use automated tools to brute-force credentials when you do not have a known password

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: In Exercise 5.3, you tested a known set of credentials manually. Real penetration tests rarely hand you working passwords. When manual testing fails, automated brute-force tools let you test thousands of password combinations in minutes. The skill here is knowing how to build a targeted wordlist and configure the tool properly.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: FinanceCorp's IT department uses a shared administrative account on several servers. Your team suspects the password is weak but does not have a confirmed value. You have been asked to run a controlled brute-force attack against the target's remote management service to discover the password. The rules of engagement allow password attacks during off-hours.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Create a custom password wordlist for the attack
  • Configure Hydra for an SSH-based brute-force attack
  • Discover the valid password through automated testing
  • Log in with the discovered credentials and capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Brute-Force Attacks and Wordlists
docs.text:
A brute-force attack systematically tests every possible password from a list until one succeeds. The quality of the wordlist determines whether the attack succeeds. A small, targeted list built from reconnaissance findings often outperforms a massive generic dictionary.

Effective wordlists include common passwords (like "password," "123456," and "qwerty"), organization-specific terms (company names, product names), and variations with numbers and special characters appended. Tools like CeWL can scrape websites to build custom wordlists, but for this exercise you will create one manually.

Brute-force attacks carry real risks in production environments. Account lockout policies may disable the target account after a set number of failed attempts. Intrusion detection systems may flag the rapid connection attempts. Always confirm that the rules of engagement permit brute-force testing and understand the lockout thresholds before launching an attack.

graph LR
    A[Build Wordlist] --> B[Configure Hydra]
    B --> C[Launch Attack]
    C --> D{Password Found?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Authenticate]
    D -->|No| F[Refine Wordlist]
    F --> B

docs.title: Tool Primer: Hydra
docs.text:
Hydra is a fast, flexible network login cracker that supports dozens of protocols including SSH, FTP, HTTP, and SMB. The flags you will use in this exercise are listed below.

Flag Purpose -l Specify a single username -P Specify a password wordlist file -t Number of parallel connection threads -V Verbose mode; show each login attempt -f Stop after the first successful login ssh:// Target protocol and address

A successful Hydra result looks like the following.

[22][ssh] host: 10.0.0.5   login: admin   password: qwerty
1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found

The output clearly shows the discovered username and password along with the port and protocol used.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Password Wordlist
docs.text:
Build a custom wordlist containing common weak passwords. Open a text editor or use the command line to create the file.

Kali - Create a custom password wordlist

cat << 'EOF' > /tmp/passwords.txt
password
password123
admin
admin123
letmein
welcome
123456
qwerty
abc123
monkey
master
dragon
login
princess
football
EOF

The file now contains 15 common passwords. In a real engagement, you would tailor the list based on intelligence gathered during reconnaissance; employee names, company terms, and patterns observed in leaked credential databases.

docs.title: Step 2: Verify the Wordlist
docs.text:
Confirm that the file was created correctly and count the entries.

Kali - Verify the wordlist contents and line count

wc -l /tmp/passwords.txt
cat /tmp/passwords.txt

You should see 15 lines. Each line contains exactly one password candidate. Make sure there are no blank lines or extra whitespace that could cause Hydra to test empty strings.

docs.title: Step 3: Launch the Brute-Force Attack
docs.text:
Run Hydra against the SSH service on the target. The command specifies the username, wordlist, thread count, and target.

Kali - Launch Hydra brute-force attack against SSH

hydra -l admin -P /tmp/passwords.txt -t 4 -V -f ssh://<target_ip>

Breaking down the command: -l admin sets the username to test, -P /tmp/passwords.txt points to your wordlist, -t 4 limits the attack to 4 parallel threads (reducing the chance of triggering lockouts), -V shows every attempt in real time, and -f tells Hydra to stop as soon as it finds a valid password.

Watch the output scroll by. Each line shows a username-password combination being tested. When Hydra finds a match, it prints a success message with the valid credentials highlighted.

docs.title: Step 4: Record the Discovered Credentials
docs.text: When Hydra finishes, note the valid username and password from the output. The discovered credentials should be admin:qwerty.

docs.title: Step 5: Authenticate with the Discovered Password
docs.text:
Log in to the target using the credentials Hydra found.

Kali - Connect with the discovered credentials

ssh admin@<target_ip>

Enter the password qwerty when prompted. A successful login confirms that the brute-force attack worked and the credentials are valid.

docs.title: Step 6: Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Read the flag file from the admin home directory.

Kali - Read the flag file

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

Record the flag value, then exit the session.

Kali - Exit the SSH session

exit

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document your brute-force attack results below.

Wordlist size:
Hydra command used:
Credentials discovered:
Number of attempts before success:
Setting Value Target IP Target Port Username Password Found Threads Used

docs.title: Step 7: Record the Flag
docs.text: Write down the flag from /home/admin/flag.txt in the format OCR{<flag_here>}.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did we limit Hydra to 4 threads instead of using the maximum?
Reveal Answer

A high thread count sends many simultaneous connection attempts, which can trigger intrusion detection systems, cause account lockouts, or crash the target service. Using fewer threads is slower but stealthier and less likely to disrupt the target or alert defenders.

  1. What makes the password "qwerty" a poor choice for a system administrator account?
Reveal Answer

"Qwerty" is the sequence of the first six letters on a standard keyboard. It appears in every common password list and would be one of the first candidates tested in any brute-force or dictionary attack. An administrative account with such a password can be compromised in seconds.

  1. How would you improve your wordlist if the first attack failed?
Reveal Answer

You could expand the list by adding organization-specific terms from FinanceCorp's website, appending numbers and special characters to existing entries, including seasonal patterns like "Winter2026," and incorporating passwords from known credential leaks. Tools like CeWL, Mentalist, or Hashcat rules can generate these variations automatically.

  1. What defensive measures could prevent this attack from succeeding?
Reveal Answer

Account lockout policies that disable the account after a set number of failures, rate limiting on the SSH service, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and intrusion detection rules that flag rapid failed login attempts would all reduce the effectiveness of brute-force attacks.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A targeted wordlist built from reconnaissance is more effective than a generic dictionary
  • Hydra's -f flag prevents unnecessary noise by stopping after the first successful login
  • Thread count should be balanced between speed and stealth
  • Always document discovered credentials immediately; they may be needed in later exercises
  • In Exercise 5.5, you will use authenticated access to execute commands and enumerate the target system

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercises 5.1 through 5.4 covered the reconnaissance and access phases of the attack chain. You scanned for the service, enumerated its configuration, tested credentials, and brute-forced a password. Now you move into the post-exploitation phase, where authenticated access becomes a platform for deeper system enumeration.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your FinanceCorp penetration test has reached a critical milestone. You have valid credentials for the target host's remote management service. The project lead wants you to demonstrate the impact of unauthorized remote access by enumerating the system; gathering information about users, permissions, network configuration, and installed software. The goal is to show FinanceCorp's leadership exactly what an attacker could learn from a single compromised account.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Establish a remote session on the target using valid credentials
  • Enumerate the current user's identity and privileges
  • Gather system and network information from the target
  • Search the filesystem for sensitive files
  • Document the scope of information accessible through remote management

docs.title: Background: Post-Authentication Enumeration
docs.text:
Gaining access to a host is only the beginning of a penetration test. Once authenticated, an attacker needs to understand the environment before taking further action. Post-authentication enumeration answers critical questions: Who am I on this system? What privileges do I have? What else is on the network? Where is the sensitive data?

On a Linux host, a set of standard commands provides this information. The whoami command reveals the current username. The id command shows the numeric user ID and group memberships, which determine file access permissions. The hostname command identifies the machine, and uname -a provides kernel and operating system details.

On a Windows host accessed through WinRM or Evil-WinRM, equivalent commands include whoami, systeminfo, ipconfig, and net user. The lab environment simulates a Windows target on Linux, so you will use Linux enumeration commands while understanding that the same concepts apply to real Windows targets.

graph LR
    A[Authenticate] --> B[Identify User]
    B --> C[Check Privileges]
    C --> D[Enumerate System]
    D --> E[Search Files]
    E --> F[Document Findings]

docs.title: Tool Primer: System Enumeration Commands
docs.text:
The table below lists the commands you will run on the target after authenticating. Each command reveals a different layer of information about the host.

Command Purpose whoami Display the current username id Show user ID, group ID, and group memberships hostname Print the system's hostname uname -a Display kernel version and system architecture ip addr or ifconfig Show network interface configuration ls -la /home/ List user home directories with permissions find / -name "flag*" 2>/dev/null Search the entire filesystem for flag files cat /etc/passwd List all user accounts on the system

The 2>/dev/null suffix on the find command redirects error messages (like "Permission denied") to nowhere, keeping the output clean and readable.

docs.title: Step 1: Establish a Remote Session
docs.text:
Connect to the target host via SSH using the credentials from earlier labs.

Kali - Connect to the target via SSH

ssh admin@<target_ip>

Enter the password password123 when prompted. You should land in the admin user's home directory.

docs.title: Step 2: Identify the Current User
docs.text:
Run the identity commands to confirm who you are and what groups you belong to.

Target - Check current user and group memberships

whoami
id

The whoami output should show admin. The id output displays your numeric user ID (UID), primary group ID (GID), and any additional group memberships. Group memberships are important because certain groups grant elevated privileges; for example, membership in the sudo or wheel group may allow privilege escalation.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate the System
docs.text:
Gather details about the host itself. Run the following commands one at a time and record each result.

Target - Gather system details

hostname
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release

The hostname command confirms you are on the correct target. The uname -a output reveals the kernel version, architecture (e.g., x86_64), and build date. The /etc/os-release file identifies the specific Linux distribution and version.

docs.title: Step 4: Examine Network Configuration
docs.text:
Understanding the target's network position helps identify pivot opportunities; other hosts you might be able to reach from this machine.

Target - Examine network interfaces and hosts file

ip addr
cat /etc/hosts

The ip addr command lists all network interfaces along with their IP addresses and subnet masks. The /etc/hosts file may contain hardcoded hostnames that point to other internal systems.

docs.title: Step 5: List User Accounts
docs.text:
Enumerate the user accounts on the system to identify other potential targets.

Target - List user accounts and home directories

cat /etc/passwd
ls -la /home/

The /etc/passwd file lists every user account on the system. Each line contains the username, UID, GID, home directory, and default shell. The ls -la /home/ command shows which users have home directories and what permissions are set on them.

docs.title: Step 6: Search for Sensitive Files
docs.text:
Use the find command to search for files that might contain valuable data.

Target - Search for flag files, configs, and logs

find / -name "flag*" 2>/dev/null
find / -name "*.conf" -readable 2>/dev/null | head -20
find / -name "*.log" -readable 2>/dev/null | head -20

The first command searches for any files with names starting with "flag." The second and third commands look for configuration files and log files that your user can read. Configuration files may contain hardcoded credentials, and log files may reveal system activity.

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Read the flag file from the expected location.

Target - Read the flag file

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

Record the flag, then exit the session.

Target - Disconnect from the remote session

exit

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Fill in the system enumeration results below.

Username:
User ID (UID):
Groups:
Hostname:
Kernel version:
OS Distribution:
IP Address(es):
Number of user accounts:
File Search Files Found flag* *.conf *.log

docs.title: Step 8: Record the Flag
docs.text: Write down the flag from /home/admin/flag.txt in the format OCR{<flag_here>}.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is post-authentication enumeration important even when you already have a working shell?
Reveal Answer

A working shell is just the starting point. Enumeration reveals the full scope of what an attacker can access: other users, network connections, sensitive files, and potential privilege escalation paths. Without enumeration, you cannot accurately report the impact of the compromise to the client.

  1. What could an attacker learn from the /etc/passwd file?
Reveal Answer

The /etc/passwd file reveals all usernames on the system, their home directories, and their default shells. An attacker can use this information to target other accounts for brute-force attacks, identify service accounts that may have weak passwords, and map the user landscape of the system.

  1. How does group membership affect what an attacker can do on a compromised host?
Reveal Answer

Group memberships determine file and resource access. A user in the sudo group can execute commands as root. A user in the docker group can interact with Docker containers, which often leads to full root access. Checking group memberships is essential for identifying privilege escalation opportunities.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Post-authentication enumeration is a mandatory phase of every penetration test
  • Identity commands (whoami, id) reveal privilege levels that determine your next steps
  • Network configuration data can expose pivot opportunities to other internal hosts
  • The find command is your primary tool for locating sensitive files across the filesystem
  • In Exercise 5.6, you will focus on finding and retrieving a flag that is hidden outside the expected directory

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 5.5 introduced post-authentication enumeration and the find command for searching the filesystem. In that lab, the flag was in the expected home directory location. Real-world targets are not that convenient. Sensitive files can be stored anywhere on the filesystem; temporary directories, backup folders, web roots, or hidden paths. Knowing how to search effectively is what separates a thorough penetration tester from one who misses critical findings.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: FinanceCorp's incident response team has reported that an employee may have stored sensitive financial data in an unauthorized location on one of the servers. Your job is to locate the file and demonstrate that it is accessible to anyone with remote management credentials. The file is not in the user's home directory, so you will need to search the entire filesystem.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Authenticate to the target using known credentials
  • Search the filesystem systematically for the flag file
  • Demonstrate that sensitive files can be accessed from unexpected locations
  • Retrieve the flag and document the full file path

docs.title: Background: Where Sensitive Files Hide
docs.text:
Administrators and attackers alike store files in locations outside home directories for various reasons. Temporary directories like /tmp and /var/tmp are writable by all users and are often used as staging areas for scripts, backups, and data exports. Because these directories are designed to be ephemeral, security monitoring often overlooks them.

Other common hiding spots include /opt, /var/www, /var/backups, /srv, and custom directories created by applications. Web applications may store uploaded files, database dumps, or configuration backups in locations that are accessible to any authenticated user on the system.

A methodical approach to file retrieval involves three phases: first, check the obvious locations (home directory, desktop, documents). Second, search common temporary and backup directories. Third, perform a full filesystem search using the find command with appropriate filters. Skipping straight to a full filesystem search is tempting but can produce overwhelming output; starting with targeted checks saves time.

graph LR
    A[Check Home Dir] --> B[Check /tmp and /var/tmp]
    B --> C[Check Common Paths]
    C --> D[Full Filesystem Search]
    D --> E[Retrieve Target File]

docs.title: Tool Primer: find Command
docs.text:
The find command searches directory trees based on criteria you specify. The options below are the most useful for file retrieval during a penetration test.

Option Purpose / Start searching from the root of the filesystem -name "pattern" Match files by name (case-sensitive) -iname "pattern" Match files by name (case-insensitive) -type f Only match regular files (not directories) -readable Only match files the current user can read -size +1k Only match files larger than 1 kilobyte 2>/dev/null Suppress "Permission denied" errors

A typical search command combines several of these options to narrow results. The following example finds all readable text files named "flag" anywhere on the system.

find / -type f -name "flag*" -readable 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Step 1: Authenticate to the Target
docs.text:
Connect to the target via SSH using the known credentials.

Kali - Connect to the target via SSH

ssh admin@<target_ip>

Enter the password password123 when prompted.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the Home Directory First
docs.text:
Always start with the most obvious location before searching broadly.

Target - Check the home directory for the flag

ls -la /home/admin/
cat /home/admin/flag.txt 2>/dev/null

In this exercise, the flag is not in the home directory. If the cat command produces no output or an error, the file does not exist at that path. Do not stop here; move on to broader searches.

docs.title: Step 3: Check Common Temporary Directories
docs.text:
Temporary directories are among the most common locations for misplaced or hidden files. Check /tmp and /var/tmp manually.

Target - Check common temporary directories

ls -la /tmp/
ls -la /var/tmp/

Look through the output carefully for any files with "flag" in the name or any files that seem out of place. A flag file among the temporary files is a strong indicator that someone stored sensitive data in an insecure location.

docs.title: Step 4: Search the Full Filesystem
docs.text:
If the targeted checks did not reveal the flag, run a full search from the root directory.

Target - Search the full filesystem for flag files

find / -type f -name "flag*" 2>/dev/null

The command scans every directory on the system and returns the full path of any file whose name starts with "flag." The 2>/dev/null portion suppresses permission-denied errors for directories you cannot access, keeping the output clean.

Review the results. You should see at least one path that does not match the expected home directory location. Note the full path; you will need it for documentation.

docs.title: Step 5: Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Read the flag file using the path discovered in the previous step.

Target - Read the flag from the discovered path

cat /tmp/flag.txt

Record the flag value. The full path /tmp/flag.txt confirms that the sensitive file was stored in a temporary directory accessible to any user on the system.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify File Permissions
docs.text:
Check who owns the file and what permissions are set on it.

Target - Check file ownership and permissions

ls -la /tmp/flag.txt

The permission string (e.g., -rw-r--r--) tells you who can read, write, and execute the file. If the file is world-readable (the last three characters include r), any user on the system can access it regardless of whether they own it.

docs.title: Step 7: Exit the Session
docs.text:
Disconnect from the target cleanly.

Target - Disconnect from the remote session

exit

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the file retrieval process and results below.

Check Location File Found? Home directory /home/admin/ Temp directory /tmp/ Var temp /var/tmp/ Full search find / 
Flag file path:
File owner:
File permissions:
Flag value: OCR{<flag_here>}

docs.title: Step 8: Record the Flag
docs.text: Write down the flag from /tmp/flag.txt in the format OCR{<flag_here>}.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is storing sensitive data in /tmp a security risk?
Reveal Answer

The /tmp directory is typically world-readable and world-writable. Any user on the system can browse its contents and read files stored there. Sensitive data in /tmp is exposed to every account on the machine, and many backup or cleanup processes skip /tmp entirely, meaning the files may persist longer than expected.

  1. Why should a penetration tester search beyond the home directory when looking for sensitive files?
Reveal Answer

Users and applications store files throughout the filesystem, in temporary directories, web roots, backup folders, and log directories. Limiting your search to home directories means missing data that may be stored in shared or misconfigured locations. A thorough search of the full filesystem ensures no sensitive data is overlooked.

  1. What does the -readable flag do in the find command, and when should you use it?
Reveal Answer

The -readable flag filters results to only include files that the current user has permission to read. Using it reduces noise by excluding files you cannot access, but it may also hide the existence of sensitive files that require elevated privileges. Running find both with and without -readable gives you a complete picture: one showing what you can access now, and one showing what you could access after privilege escalation.

  1. How would you search for files containing specific content rather than matching by filename?
Reveal Answer

The grep command searches inside files for text patterns. Running grep -r "password" /etc/ 2>/dev/null would search all readable files under /etc/ for lines containing the word "password." Combining find for file location with grep for content matching covers both name-based and content-based searches.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Sensitive files can exist anywhere on the filesystem, not just in home directories
  • Always check /tmp, /var/tmp, and other common writable directories during post-exploitation
  • The find command with 2>/dev/null is your most powerful tool for filesystem searches
  • File permissions determine who can access a file; always check and document them
  • Completing all six labs gives you a full WinRM attack chain from detection through data retrieval; review your findings in the Chapter Review

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Over the course of six labs, you executed a complete attack chain against a WinRM-enabled host in the FinanceCorp environment. The progression followed the same methodology that professional penetration testers use in real engagements.

Here is a summary of each phase and the core skill it developed.

Exercise Phase Core Skill 5.1 Service Detection Port scanning with nmap to identify WinRM on ports 5985/5986 5.2 Configuration Enumeration HTTP header analysis to discover authentication methods 5.3 Manual Authentication Credential testing against WinRM and SSH services 5.4 Brute Force Automated password attacks using Hydra with custom wordlists 5.5 Command Execution Post-authentication system enumeration 5.6 File Retrieval Filesystem searching to locate sensitive data outside expected paths

The attack chain follows a logical order: you cannot enumerate what you have not found, you cannot authenticate without understanding the configuration, and you cannot execute commands without valid credentials. Each lab depended on skills from the one before it.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Questions
docs.text:
Answer each question in the space provided. Try to answer from memory before checking your notes.

1. What two ports does WinRM use by default, and what transport does each use?

2. What server header value indicates a WinRM service in nmap and curl output?

3. Name three authentication methods that WinRM supports.

4. What Hydra flag stops the attack after finding the first valid password?

5. What command searches the entire filesystem for files named "flag" while suppressing permission errors?

6. Why is Basic authentication over HTTP (port 5985) considered insecure?

7. What information does the id command reveal about the current user?

8. Why should you check /tmp and /var/tmp during post-exploitation?

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
The table below collects every key command from this chapter into a single reference. Bookmark or print this page for quick access during future engagements.

Command Purpose Exercise nmap -p 5985,5986 -sV <target_ip> Scan for WinRM services with version detection 5.1 nmap -p 5985 -sC -sV <target_ip> Run default scripts against WinRM port 5.1 curl -I http://<target_ip>:5985 Fetch HTTP response headers from WinRM 5.2 curl -v http://<target_ip>:5985 Verbose HTTP request showing full exchange 5.2 nmap -p 5985 --script http-headers <target_ip> Enumerate HTTP headers via nmap script 5.2 curl -u user:pass http://<target_ip>:5985/wsman Test Basic authentication against WinRM 5.3 ssh admin@<target_ip> Connect to target via SSH 5.3 evil-winrm -i <target_ip> -u user -p pass Connect to WinRM (real Windows targets) 5.3 hydra -l admin -P wordlist.txt -t 4 -V -f ssh://<target_ip> Brute-force SSH credentials 5.4 whoami Display current username 5.5 id Show UID, GID, and group memberships 5.5 hostname Print the system hostname 5.5 uname -a Display kernel and OS information 5.5 cat /etc/passwd List all user accounts 5.5 find / -type f -name "flag*" 2>/dev/null Search filesystem for flag files 5.6 find / -name "*.conf" -readable 2>/dev/null Find readable configuration files 5.6

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text:
WinRM is one of several remote management and database services that penetration testers encounter in Windows environments. In Chapter 6, you will shift focus to MSSQL (Microsoft SQL Server), another high-value target in enterprise networks.

MSSQL often runs alongside WinRM on the same hosts. The skills you developed here; service detection, credential attacks, and post-authentication enumeration; apply directly to database exploitation. The key difference is that MSSQL provides access to stored data (tables, records, and stored procedures) rather than operating system commands, though certain MSSQL features like xp_cmdshell can bridge that gap.

Consider how the credentials you discovered in this chapter might be reused on MSSQL services. Password reuse across services is one of the most common vulnerabilities in enterprise environments, and it is exactly the kind of finding that FinanceCorp's leadership needs to hear about.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
Review your answers above against the following.

1. Port 5985 uses HTTP (unencrypted) and port 5986 uses HTTPS (encrypted with TLS).

2. The server header value is "Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0," which indicates the Windows HTTP Server API that WinRM is built on.

3. WinRM supports Basic, Negotiate (NTLM/Kerberos), Kerberos, Certificate-based, and CredSSP authentication. Any three of these are acceptable.

4. The -f flag tells Hydra to stop immediately after discovering the first valid set of credentials.

5. find / -type f -name "flag*" 2>/dev/null: the 2>/dev/null portion redirects "Permission denied" errors to keep the output clean.

6. Basic authentication encodes credentials in base64, which is trivially reversible. Over unencrypted HTTP, anyone on the network path can capture and decode the username and password.

7. The id command shows the user's numeric UID (User ID), primary GID (Group ID), and all supplementary group memberships. Group memberships determine what files and resources the user can access.

8. The /tmp and /var/tmp directories are world-writable and often overlooked by security monitoring. Users and applications frequently store sensitive data, scripts, backups, and temporary files in these locations, making them high-value targets during post-exploitation.

docs.title: Final Checklist
docs.text:
Before moving to Chapter 6, confirm that you have completed every item below.

  • Captured and recorded the flag from Exercise 5.1
  • Captured and recorded the flag from Exercise 5.2
  • Captured and recorded the flag from Exercise 5.3
  • Captured and recorded the flag from Exercise 5.4
  • Captured and recorded the flag from Exercise 5.5
  • Captured and recorded the flag from Exercise 5.6
  • Answered all self-assessment questions from memory
  • Reviewed the command cheat sheet and can explain each command's purpose

Proceed to Chapter 6; MSSQL Exploitation when you are ready.

docs.title: Why Database Services Matter
docs.text:
Every web application, internal tool, and enterprise platform stores its data somewhere. In most corporate environments, that somewhere is a database server. When a penetration tester finds a database port open on the network, they have found a direct path to the organization's most sensitive information; financial records, customer data, credentials, and internal secrets. Unlike file shares or remote desktop, a database server is designed to accept structured queries and return precise results, making it an extraordinarily powerful target once access is gained.

FinanceCorp, like many organizations, runs database servers that hold the keys to their critical operations. Your job in this chapter is to find those servers, identify what they are running, authenticate to them, and demonstrate exactly how much damage an attacker could cause with access to the database layer.

docs.title: What Is MS-SQL?
docs.text:
Microsoft SQL Server (MS-SQL) is a relational database management system (RDBMS) developed by Microsoft. Production MS-SQL instances typically listen on TCP port 1433 and use the Tabular Data Stream (TDS) protocol for client-server communication. MS-SQL is one of the most widely deployed database engines in enterprise Windows environments, often backing Active Directory, SharePoint, and custom line-of-business applications.

The account structure in MS-SQL follows a specific hierarchy. The sa (system administrator) account is the built-in superuser with unrestricted access to every database, every table, and every configuration setting on the server. Gaining access to the sa account is the equivalent of obtaining root on a Linux system; it represents total control over the database engine and, potentially, the underlying operating system.

One of the most dangerous features in MS-SQL is xp_cmdshell, a built-in extended stored procedure that allows database administrators to execute operating system commands directly from a SQL query. When an attacker gains access to an MS-SQL instance with xp_cmdshell enabled (or the privileges to enable it), they can pivot from database access to full operating system control. A single SQL statement like EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami' bridges the gap between the database layer and the operating system layer.

Lab environment note: The OpenCyberRange lab environment uses MySQL on port 3306 as a stand-in for MS-SQL. The conceptual teaching in this chapter covers MS-SQL features like xp_cmdshell and TDS authentication, but the practical commands use the mysql client and MySQL syntax. The database user follows the MS-SQL convention of sa (system administrator). The mapping between concepts and commands is called out in each exercise so you always know what you are doing and why.

docs.title: How Database Attacks Differ from Other Services
docs.text:
In Chapters 2 and 3, you attacked file sharing services where the goal was to access shared folders and download files. In Chapter 5, the goal was to obtain a remote shell. Database exploitation is different because the database itself is both the tool and the target. Once authenticated, you do not need to download files or spawn shells; you query the data directly. The database gives you a structured query interface that lets you search, filter, and extract exactly the information you want.

The risk escalation path for database attacks is also steeper. With file shares, access gives you files. With a database, access gives you data, configuration details, and; if file privileges are enabled; the ability to read and write files on the underlying operating system. Each lab in this chapter moves one step further along that escalation path, from "I found the port" to "I can read any file on the server."

docs.title: What Will You Learn?
docs.text:
The seven labs in this chapter build from passive service detection to full file system access through a database connection. By the end, you will be able to:

  • Detect database services on a network using Nmap port scans
  • Enumerate database version information with NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine) scripts
  • Authenticate to a database server with known credentials
  • Brute force database credentials using Hydra
  • Execute SQL queries to enumerate databases, tables, and sensitive data
  • Read files from the target file system using database functions (the MySQL equivalent of xp_cmdshell)
  • Demonstrate complete file system access through a database connection

docs.title: Key Terminology
docs.text:
Several terms appear repeatedly throughout the chapter. Familiarizing yourself with them now will make the walkthroughs easier to follow.

Term Definition RDBMS Relational Database Management System; software that stores and manages data in structured tables sa System Administrator; the highest-privilege built-in account in MS-SQL xp_cmdshell An MS-SQL stored procedure that executes operating system commands from SQL LOAD_FILE() A MySQL function that reads a file from the server's file system and returns it as a string NSE Nmap Scripting Engine; the scripting framework built into Nmap for advanced enumeration secure_file_priv A MySQL configuration variable that controls whether file read/write operations are allowed TDS Tabular Data Stream; the network protocol used by MS-SQL for client-server communication

docs.title: Lab Progression
docs.text:
Each lab adds a new capability to your database exploitation toolkit. The progression mirrors a real-world attack: find the service, learn about it, get in, and then expand your access.

Exercise Title Skill Introduced 6.1 MS-SQL Service Detection Port scanning for database services 6.2 MS-SQL Version and Instance Enumeration NSE script enumeration 6.3 MS-SQL Manual Authentication Connecting with known credentials 6.4 MS-SQL Credential Brute Force Automated password attacks with Hydra 6.5 MS-SQL Basic Query Execution SQL queries for data extraction 6.6 MS-SQL xp_cmdshell Activation File reading via LOAD_FILE() 6.7 MS-SQL File System Access via xp_cmdshell Complete file system exploration

docs.title: The Attack Path
docs.text:
The seven labs follow a logical attack chain, where each phase depends on the results of the previous one.

graph LR
    A["6.1 Detect"] --> B["6.2 Enumerate"]
    B --> C["6.3 Authenticate"]
    C --> D["6.4 Brute Force"]
    D --> E["6.5 Query"]
    E --> F["6.6 File Read"]
    F --> G["6.7 Full Access"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style G fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Make sure the following prerequisites are in place before beginning Exercise 6.1. Skipping these checks often leads to confusion during the walkthroughs.

  • You have completed Chapters 1 through 5 (or are comfortable with Nmap, credential attacks, and basic exploitation concepts)
  • Your VPN connection to the OpenCyberRange environment is active
  • You have a Kali Linux terminal open and ready
  • You can ping the target or confirm network connectivity
  • The nmap tool is available (pre-installed on Kali)
  • The mysql client is installed (sudo apt install default-mysql-client if missing)
  • The hydra tool is available (pre-installed on Kali)
  • You understand basic SQL concepts (SELECT, FROM, WHERE) or are willing to learn them in Exercise 6.5

If any of the earlier chapter concepts feel unclear; especially Nmap scanning from Chapter 1 and brute force methodology from Chapter 3; review those labs before proceeding. The techniques in this chapter assume you are comfortable with port scanning, service enumeration, and automated credential testing.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Before you can exploit a database, you need to find it. Most penetration tests begin with a broad port scan, but once you suspect a database server exists on the network, a targeted scan against the known database port is faster and more reliable. In this exercise, you will scan for a database service on the FinanceCorp target and confirm that the port is open and accepting connections.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: FinanceCorp has engaged your team to assess the security of their internal infrastructure. James Mitchell, the CISO, has hinted that several internal applications rely on a centralized database server. Your first task is to determine whether a database service is exposed on the network. If it is, you need to document what port it runs on and what service banner it presents.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Scan the target for database services on port 3306
  • Identify the service name and version from the scan output
  • Confirm the database is accepting connections
  • Connect to the database and retrieve the flag
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Database Port Scanning
docs.text:
Database servers listen on well-known ports that make them easy to detect with a port scanner. Microsoft SQL Server typically uses TCP port 1433, while MySQL uses TCP port 3306. PostgreSQL listens on 5432, and Oracle on 1521. A penetration tester who knows these defaults can quickly determine which database engines are present on a network by scanning just a handful of ports.

Port scanning for database services is different from scanning for web servers or file shares because database ports are often firewalled from external networks but left wide open on internal segments. Organizations assume that internal users need fast, unfiltered access to the database, so they rarely apply network-level access controls between application servers and database servers. When a penetration tester lands on the internal network, these database ports become prime targets.

graph LR
    A["Attacker"] -->|"nmap -p 3306"| B["Target:3306"]
    B -->|"Service Banner"| A
    A -->|"mysql -h target"| B
    B -->|"Query Results"| A

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#d94a4a,color:#fff

Lab environment note: The lab target runs MySQL on port 3306. In a real MS-SQL environment, you would scan port 1433 instead. The scanning technique is identical; only the port number changes.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap Service Detection
docs.text:
Nmap can do more than just check whether a port is open. The -sV flag activates service version detection, which sends probes to the open port and analyzes the response to identify the software and version running behind it.

The basic syntax for a targeted service version scan is shown below.

nmap -p <port> -sV <target_ip>
Flag Purpose -p 3306 Scan only port 3306 (MySQL default) -sV Probe open ports to determine service name and version -Pn Skip host discovery (assume the host is up) --open Show only open ports in the output

Sample output from a successful service detection scan looks like the following.

PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
3306/tcp open  mysql   MySQL 5.7.42

The SERVICE column tells you what protocol Nmap detected, and the VERSION column shows the specific software and build number. Both pieces of information are valuable; the service type tells you which client tool to use, and the version may reveal known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the OpenCyberRange platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises and select MS-SQL Exploitation then Level 1
  • Click Launch on "MS-SQL Service Detection"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Scan for the Database Service
docs.text:
Run a targeted Nmap scan against port 3306 with service version detection enabled.

Kali - Scan for MySQL service on port 3306

nmap -p 3306 -sV <target_ip>

You should see output similar to the following.

PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
3306/tcp open  mysql   MySQL 5.7.42

The port is open and Nmap has identified the service as MySQL. Record the version number; you will need it for your findings.

docs.title: Step 3: Verify Connectivity with the MySQL Client
docs.text:
A port scan confirms the service is listening, but you should also verify that you can establish a client connection. Attempt to connect with known credentials.

Kali - Verify connectivity with the MySQL client

mysql --ssl-verify-server-cert=0 -h <target_ip> -u sa -p'password' -e "SELECT 'Connection successful';"

If the connection succeeds, you will see a small result table with the text "Connection successful." If it fails, check that the lab environment is fully running and that you have the correct target IP.

docs.title: Step 4: Retrieve the Flag from the Database
docs.text:
Now that you have confirmed connectivity and valid credentials, query the database for the flag.

Kali - Query the secrets table for the flag

mysql --ssl-verify-server-cert=0 -h <target_ip> -u sa -p'password' -e "SELECT * FROM target_db.secrets;"

The query returns the contents of the secrets table in the target_db database. Record the flag value from the output.

docs.title: Step 5: Verify the Flag on the File System
docs.text:
The flag is also stored in a file on the target. Read it using the MySQL LOAD_FILE() function to confirm both sources match.

Kali - Read the flag from the file system via LOAD_FILE

mysql --ssl-verify-server-cert=0 -h <target_ip> -u sa -p'password' -e "SELECT LOAD_FILE('/tmp/flag.txt');"

Both the database query and the file read should return the same flag value. Record both results.

(paste the full nmap output here)

(paste the version string here)

(paste the flag here)
