docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Chapters 1 through 8 taught you to scan, enumerate, and attack individual services one at a time. Exercise 9.1 combines those techniques into a single assessment workflow; scanning all ports, enumerating every discovered service, and extracting data from misconfigurations. Make sure your VPN is connected and your Kali terminal is ready before launching the lab.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: You are conducting the final phase of a penetration test for FinanceCorp. The engagement lead, James Mitchell, wants a thorough network assessment of a Windows server that combines all the techniques you have learned. Your goal is to identify every exposed service, enumerate access controls, and demonstrate data extraction from any misconfigured service. No credentials have been provided; everything you find must come from anonymous or guest-level access.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Run a full port scan to identify all services on the target
  • Enumerate SMB shares using anonymous and guest access
  • Map share permissions to identify accessible resources
  • Retrieve the flag from the HTTP service running on the target

docs.title: Background: Network Assessment Methodology
docs.text:
A network assessment follows a structured sequence of phases, each building on the findings of the previous one. Skipping a phase or testing services in random order leads to missed findings. The methodology ensures completeness and produces documentation that supports every conclusion in the final report.

The standard assessment phases are reconnaissance, enumeration, vulnerability identification, exploitation, and documentation. Reconnaissance identifies open ports and running services. Enumeration extracts detailed information from each service; versions, configurations, access controls, and exposed data. Vulnerability identification maps the enumerated information against known weaknesses. Exploitation confirms that the vulnerabilities are real by demonstrating impact. Documentation captures every step so the findings are reproducible.

graph LR
    A["Reconnaissance"] --> B["Enumeration"]
    B --> C["Vulnerability<br/>Identification"]
    C --> D["Exploitation"]
    D --> E["Documentation"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

In Exercise 9.1, you will practice the first four phases. The target exposes three services: SMB on port 445, RDP on port 3389, and an nginx HTTP server on port 80. Guest access is enabled on the SMB service, and the HTTP server hosts a file containing the flag. No credentials are required for any step; guest and anonymous access are the vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Anonymous SMB Access
docs.text:
SMB supports several authentication modes, and two of them require no credentials at all. A null session sends an empty username and password. A guest session authenticates as the built-in guest account. Both methods bypass normal access controls when the server is misconfigured to allow them.

List shares with a null session

A null session sends an empty username and password. Replace <target_ip> with the target shown in the Active Lab View.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N
Flag Purpose -L List available shares on the target -N Use a null session (no password prompt)

A list of share names confirms the server accepts unauthenticated connections.

List shares as the guest user

A guest session authenticates as the built-in guest account when the server is misconfigured to allow it.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -U guest -N
Flag Purpose -U guest Authenticate as the guest user -N Suppress the password prompt

If the share list returns, guest access is enabled and is a reportable finding.

Map share permissions with smbmap

The smbmap tool connects to the target and reports the access level for every share.

smbmap -H <target_ip>

The tool reports the access level (READ, WRITE, or NO ACCESS) for every share. When guest access is enabled, smbmap shows which shares an unauthenticated user can read or write to; a critical finding in any assessment.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises then Windows then Level 2
  • Click Launch on "Windows Network Assessment"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Run a Full Service Scan
docs.text:
Full service and script scan

Start with a full service version scan to discover every open port and identify the software behind each service. The -sV flag probes each open port to determine the service name and version. The -sC flag runs Nmap's default NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine) scripts, which extract additional information like SMB share names, HTTP page titles, and protocol-specific metadata.

nmap -sV -sC <target_ip>

You should see three services in the output:

PORT     STATE SERVICE       VERSION
80/tcp   open  http          nginx
445/tcp  open  microsoft-ds  ...
3389/tcp open  ms-wbt-server ...

Record every open port, service name, and version string. The scan results form the foundation for all subsequent enumeration.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate SMB Shares Anonymously
docs.text:
Enumerate SMB shares anonymously

Use smbclient with a null session to list all available shares on the target.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N

The output lists every share name and its type. Look for non-default shares; names like public, data, or files indicate shares that administrators created and may have misconfigured. Default shares like IPC$ and ADMIN$ are present on every Windows SMB server and typically require authentication.

docs.title: Step 4: Map Share Permissions
docs.text:
Map share access levels

Run smbmap to determine your access level on each share.

smbmap -H <target_ip>

The output shows READ, WRITE, or NO ACCESS next to each share name. Any share showing READ or WRITE access without credentials is a significant finding. In a real assessment, you would document every accessible share and its permission level.

docs.title: Step 5: Access the Public Share
docs.text:
Connect to the public share

Connect to the accessible share and explore its contents.

smbclient //<target_ip>/public -N

Once connected, use ls to list files and get <filename> to download anything interesting. Guest-accessible shares often contain configuration files, internal documentation, or credentials stored in plaintext. Examine every file you find.

docs.title: Step 6: Run Full SMB Enumeration
docs.text:
Run full SMB enumeration

Use enum4linux to perform a thorough enumeration of the SMB service. The tool combines multiple SMB and RPC (Remote Procedure Call) queries into a single pass.

enum4linux <target_ip>

The output includes user accounts, group memberships, share listings, password policies, and OS (Operating System) information. Review the output for usernames, share details, and any configuration information that could support further attacks.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Nmap scan output:

(paste your nmap -sV -sC output here)

Open ports and services:

Port Service Version

SMB shares discovered:

Share Name Access Level

Files found on accessible shares:

(list files here)

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: _________

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve the Flag via HTTP
docs.text:
Retrieve the flag over HTTP

The Nmap scan revealed an nginx web server on port 80. Use curl to retrieve the flag file directly from the HTTP service. The command sends an HTTP GET request and prints the response body to your terminal.

curl http://<target_ip>/flag.txt

The flag is stored in flag.txt at the web root. Copy the flag value in OCR{...} format and submit it on the platform.

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review everything you have gathered and consider the full picture. The target exposes three services to the network. SMB allows guest access to at least one share. The HTTP server hosts sensitive files without any authentication. RDP is listening but has not been tested yet because no credentials are available.

In a professional assessment, each of these findings would be documented separately with a severity rating. Guest SMB access is a medium-to-high finding because it allows unauthenticated file access. An HTTP server hosting sensitive files without authentication is a high finding. The combination of multiple unauthenticated access paths elevates the overall risk rating for the target.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is guest access to SMB shares considered a critical misconfiguration?

Reveal Answer

Guest access allows anyone on the network to read (and potentially write to) shared files without providing any credentials. Attackers can extract sensitive data, upload malicious files, or use the share as a staging area. The misconfiguration is especially dangerous because many organizations do not monitor guest-level SMB access, making it difficult to detect.

2. How does retrieving the flag via HTTP complement the SMB enumeration findings?

Reveal Answer

Discovering sensitive data on both SMB and HTTP demonstrates that the target has multiple unauthenticated access paths. The SMB finding shows a file-sharing misconfiguration, while the HTTP finding shows a web server misconfiguration. Together, they prove that the target lacks a consistent access control policy; the problem is systemic, not isolated to one service.

3. Based on your findings, what would you recommend to FinanceCorp?

Reveal Answer

Disable guest access on all SMB shares and require authentication for every connection. Remove sensitive files from the HTTP server's web root or place them behind authentication. Review the RDP configuration to ensure it requires strong credentials and Network Level Authentication (NLA). Implement network segmentation to limit which systems can reach these services.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Guest access on SMB shares allows unauthenticated users to list, read, and potentially write files; a critical misconfiguration that appears frequently in real environments
  • Full-service scanning with nmap -sV -sC reveals all exposed services and their configurations in a single pass
  • Multiple unauthenticated access paths (SMB guest access and HTTP without authentication) compound the risk; each finding alone is significant, but together they indicate systemic access control failures
  • No credentials were needed to extract sensitive data from the target; misconfigurations can be as dangerous as weak passwords
  • The next exercise, Exercise 9.2, introduces credential-based attacks against multiple services using CrackMapExec to test known credentials across SMB, RDP, and SSH

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 9.1 demonstrated what an attacker can achieve without any credentials at all. Exercise 9.2 shifts to authenticated attacks; testing known credentials against every service on the target to determine the full scope of access. Make sure you are comfortable with CrackMapExec (CME) from Chapter 8 before proceeding. Your VPN must be connected and your Kali terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: You are continuing the FinanceCorp penetration test. During the previous phase, you discovered guest-accessible shares and an exposed HTTP service. James Mitchell, the engagement lead, now wants to see how an attacker with a single set of credentials can exploit multiple services on the same host. You have obtained the credentials admin:password123 through a previous phase of the assessment. Your task is to determine which services accept these credentials and demonstrate the maximum impact of credential reuse.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Scan the target to identify all exposed services
  • Test the credentials admin:password123 against SMB, SSH, and RDP using CrackMapExec
  • Enumerate SMB shares using the authenticated session
  • Connect via SSH and retrieve the flag from the target

docs.title: Background: Multi-Service Exploitation
docs.text:
Multi-service exploitation combines network assessment methodology with credential reuse techniques. Rather than testing one service and moving on, the approach systematically validates credentials against every protocol the target exposes. The goal is to determine the full blast radius of a single compromised credential set; how many doors does one key open?

When an attacker discovers working credentials on one service, the next step is to test those credentials everywhere else. SMB access allows file share browsing and data exfiltration. RDP access provides a full graphical desktop session. SSH access grants a command-line shell capable of running arbitrary commands. Each service provides a different level of access, and an effective penetration tester documents all of them.

CrackMapExec automates credential validation across multiple protocols. A single CME command can test a username and password against SMB, SSH, or RDP and immediately report whether authentication succeeded. The tool also supports command execution through authenticated sessions, making it possible to both validate credentials and demonstrate impact in one step.

graph TD
    A["Known Credentials"] --> B["Test SMB"]
    A --> C["Test SSH"]
    A --> D["Test RDP"]
    B --> E{"Access?"}
    C --> F{"Access?"}
    D --> G{"Access?"}
    E -->|"Yes"| H["File Share Access"]
    F -->|"Yes"| I["Command Shell"]
    G -->|"Yes"| J["Desktop Session"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style H fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style I fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style J fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style E fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style G fill:#e8a735,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: CrackMapExec Multi-Protocol Testing
docs.text:
CrackMapExec accepts a protocol name as its first argument, followed by the target and credentials. The same credential pair can be tested against different services by changing the protocol keyword.

Test credentials against SMB

Pass the protocol keyword smb to validate the known credentials on the file-sharing service.

crackmapexec smb <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result confirms SMB authentication succeeded.

Test credentials against SSH

Swap the keyword to ssh to test the same credential pair on the shell service.

crackmapexec ssh <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result confirms SSH authentication succeeded.

Test credentials against RDP

Swap the keyword to rdp to test the credentials on the remote desktop service.

crackmapexec rdp <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result confirms RDP authentication succeeded.

Flag Purpose -u Username to test -p Password to test -x Execute a command on the target after successful authentication

CME output indicators:

Symbol Meaning [+] Authentication succeeded [-] Authentication failed (Pwn3d!) The account has administrative privileges on the target

The (Pwn3d!) marker in CME output is especially significant. When CME reports Pwn3d! after an SMB authentication, the account has local administrator rights, which means the attacker can execute commands, dump credentials, and fully control the system.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises then Windows then Level 2
  • Click Launch on "Multi-Service Exploitation"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Run a Full Service Scan
docs.text:
Full service and script scan

Start with a full Nmap scan to identify all open ports and services.

nmap -sV -sC <target_ip>

You should see three services in the output: SMB on port 445, SSH on port 22, and RDP on port 3389. Record every port, service, and version string. The scan confirms which protocols are available for credential testing.

docs.title: Step 3: Test Credentials on SMB
docs.text:
Validate credentials on SMB

Use CrackMapExec to test the known credentials against the SMB service.

crackmapexec smb <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result confirms that the admin account authenticates successfully on SMB. Look for the (Pwn3d!) indicator, which signals administrative-level access. Record the result; authenticated SMB access allows share enumeration and file retrieval.

docs.title: Step 4: Test Credentials on SSH
docs.text:
Validate credentials on SSH

Test the same credentials against the SSH service.

crackmapexec ssh <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result means the credentials work on SSH as well. SSH access is often the most valuable finding because it provides a full command-line shell. An attacker with SSH access can browse the file system, read configuration files, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

docs.title: Step 5: Test Credentials on RDP
docs.text:
Validate credentials on RDP

Complete the credential sweep by testing against RDP.

crackmapexec rdp <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result proves the same credentials work on all three services. Document how many services accept the same username and password; credential reuse across three protocols is a critical finding.

docs.title: Step 6: Enumerate Authenticated SMB Shares
docs.text:
Enumerate authenticated SMB shares

Now that you have confirmed SMB authentication works, enumerate the available shares with your authenticated session. The -U admin%password123 flag passes the username and password inline.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -U admin%password123

Authenticated share listings often reveal additional shares that were not visible during anonymous enumeration. Look for shares named private, confidential, or similar; these typically contain sensitive data.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Nmap scan output:

(paste your nmap -sV -sC output here)

Open ports and services:

Port Service Version

CrackMapExec results:

Protocol Result Admin Access? SMB SSH RDP

Authenticated SMB shares:

Share Name Type

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: _________

docs.title: Step 7: Connect via SSH and Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Open an SSH session to the target

SSH provides the most direct path to the flag. Connect to the target using the validated credentials.

ssh admin@<target_ip>

Enter the password password123 when prompted. A shell prompt confirms you are now logged in on the target host.

Read the flag file

Once connected, navigate to the flag location and read its contents from the target host.

cat /tmp/private/flag.txt

The flag is displayed in OCR{...} format. Copy the value and submit it on the platform.

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the full scope of access that a single set of credentials provided. The admin:password123 credentials worked on SMB, SSH, and RDP; three different protocols providing three different types of access. SMB grants file share access. SSH grants command-line control. RDP grants a full graphical desktop.

The credential reuse finding is critical because it means compromising one service compromises all three. An attacker only needs to discover the password once; through a brute force attack, a phishing campaign, or a leaked credential database; and every service on the target is accessible. The remediation requires unique passwords for each service, or better yet, centralized authentication with multi-factor authentication (MFA).

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why should a penetration tester test all services even after one credential test succeeds?

Reveal Answer

Each service provides different capabilities. SMB gives file access, SSH gives command execution, and RDP gives a graphical desktop. Testing all services documents the full scope of compromise, which affects the severity rating in the final report. A finding that says "credentials work on SMB" is less impactful than "credentials work on SMB, SSH, and RDP, granting full administrative access through three independent attack paths."

2. Which service provides the most direct path to data extraction, and why?

Reveal Answer

SSH provides the most direct path because it grants an interactive command-line shell. From an SSH session, the attacker can browse the entire file system, read arbitrary files, execute commands, and transfer data; all without needing a graphical interface or specialized tools. RDP provides similar access but requires a GUI client. SMB limits access to shared directories only.

3. How would you document multi-service credential reuse findings in a penetration test report?

Reveal Answer

The finding should list every service that accepted the same credentials, the access level granted by each service, and the impact of each access path. A recommended format includes the credential pair tested, a table of services with results, evidence screenshots from each service, and a combined risk rating that reflects the aggregate impact. The remediation section should address both the credential reuse itself and the underlying password policy.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Credential reuse across multiple services is one of the most common and highest-impact findings in penetration testing
  • CrackMapExec enables rapid multi-protocol credential testing with a single tool; switching between SMB, SSH, and RDP requires only changing the protocol keyword
  • SSH access provides the most direct path to command execution and data extraction, making it the preferred post-exploitation channel
  • Multiple attack paths compound the severity; one working password across three services creates three independent ways to compromise the target
  • The next exercise, Exercise 9.3, combines unauthenticated enumeration with authenticated exploitation in a complete penetration test methodology

Exercise 9.3 brings everything together into a complete penetration test; starting with zero knowledge, discovering information through null sessions, testing credentials across all services, and documenting the full attack chain. Make sure you are comfortable with enum4linux, smbclient, smbmap, CrackMapExec (CME), and SSH from previous labs. Your VPN must be connected and your Kali terminal ready.

James Mitchell, the engagement lead, wants a complete penetration test that demonstrates the full attack chain; from initial reconnaissance through exploitation and evidence collection. You are starting with no credentials and no prior knowledge of the target. Your job is to enumerate the target, discover access paths, exploit weaknesses, and retrieve the flag.

docs.title: Background: Penetration Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A penetration test follows six distinct phases, each producing outputs that feed into the next. Skipping phases or testing out of order leads to incomplete findings and unreliable conclusions. The methodology exists to ensure reproducibility; another tester following the same steps should arrive at the same results.

The six phases are:

  1. Reconnaissance: Identify open ports, running services, and software versions
  2. Enumeration: Extract detailed information from each service (users, shares, configurations)
  3. Vulnerability Identification: Map findings against known weaknesses and misconfigurations
  4. Exploitation: Confirm vulnerabilities by demonstrating access or data extraction
  5. Post-Exploitation: Expand access, collect evidence, and determine full impact
  6. Reporting: Document every finding with evidence, severity ratings, and remediation guidance
graph LR
    A["1. Recon"] --> B["2. Enumerate"]
    B --> C["3. Vuln ID"]
    C --> D["4. Exploit"]
    D --> E["5. Post-Exploit"]
    E --> F["6. Report"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

Exercise 9.3 targets a Windows server configured with map to guest = Bad User in its SMB (Server Message Block) configuration. The map to guest = Bad User setting means that any authentication attempt with an invalid username is silently mapped to the guest account instead of being rejected. An attacker can exploit this behavior by connecting with any username and receiving guest-level access; the server never reports an authentication failure. Null session and anonymous connections succeed because the server treats unknown users as guests rather than blocking them.

docs.title: Tool Primer: enum4linux Comprehensive Enumeration
docs.text:
The enum4linux tool wraps several SMB and RPC (Remote Procedure Call) queries into a single command. Running it with the -a flag performs all available enumeration checks and produces a consolidated report covering users, shares, groups, password policies, and OS (Operating System) information.

Run full enumeration with enum4linux

Running enum4linux with the -a flag performs all available enumeration checks in one pass.

enum4linux -a <target_ip>

The output is a consolidated report covering users, shares, groups, password policies, and OS information.

Flag Purpose -a Run all enumeration checks (users, shares, groups, policies, OS info) -U Enumerate users only -S Enumerate shares only -G Enumerate groups only -P Enumerate password policies only

Key output sections to review:

Section What It Reveals OS Information Windows version, domain/workgroup name User Enumeration Local and domain user accounts Share Enumeration All SMB shares and their types Group Enumeration Local and domain groups with memberships Password Policy Lockout thresholds, password complexity requirements

The output from enum4linux -a is lengthy. Focus on user accounts (potential targets for credential attacks), share names (potential data access paths), and password policy (determines whether brute force is viable without triggering lockouts).

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises then Windows then Level 2
  • Click Launch on "Complete Windows Penetration Test"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Conduct Full Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Full reconnaissance scan

Begin with a full Nmap scan to identify every open port and service on the target. The -sV flag performs service version detection, and -sC runs default NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine) scripts for additional enumeration.

nmap -sV -sC <target_ip>

You should see three services: SMB on port 445, RDP on port 3389, and SSH on port 22. Record every port, service name, and version string. The default scripts may also reveal the target's hostname, domain membership, and SMB signing configuration.

docs.title: Step 3: Perform Null Session Enumeration
docs.text:
Null session enumeration

Run enum4linux with the -a flag to extract as much information as possible without credentials.

enum4linux -a <target_ip>

The tool attempts null session connections and queries the target for user accounts, share listings, group memberships, and password policies. Because the target is configured with map to guest = Bad User, these queries succeed even though you have not provided credentials. Review the output carefully and record any usernames, share names, and policy details.

docs.title: Step 4: List Shares Anonymously
docs.text:
List shares anonymously

Confirm the share listings from enum4linux by using smbclient with a null session. The -N flag suppresses the password prompt, sending a null session request.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N

Compare the share list against the enum4linux output to verify consistency. Look for non-default shares like private, public, or data: these are administrator-created shares that may contain sensitive files.

docs.title: Step 5: Test Credentials on All Services
docs.text:
Test common credentials against every exposed service using CrackMapExec, one protocol at a time.

Test credentials on SMB

Start the sweep with the SMB protocol keyword.

crackmapexec smb <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result, and especially the (Pwn3d!) marker, confirms administrative SMB access.

Test credentials on SSH

Repeat the test with the SSH protocol keyword.

crackmapexec ssh <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

A [+] result confirms the same credentials open a shell service.

Test credentials on RDP

Finish the sweep with the RDP protocol keyword.

crackmapexec rdp <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

Record which services return [+] (success) and which return [-] (failure). Credential reuse across all three services is a critical finding.

docs.title: Step 6: Enumerate Authenticated SMB Shares
docs.text:
List shares with credentials

With confirmed credentials, enumerate shares using an authenticated session to reveal any shares hidden from anonymous access.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -U admin%password123

Authenticated listings often reveal shares that did not appear during anonymous enumeration.

Map authenticated share permissions

Map permissions on every share using smbmap with the validated credentials.

smbmap -H <target_ip> -u admin -p password123

Compare the authenticated share list against the anonymous listing from Step 4. Authenticated access often reveals additional shares or elevated permissions on shares that were read-only during anonymous enumeration.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Nmap scan output:

(paste your nmap -sV -sC output here)

Open ports and services:

Port Service Version

enum4linux findings:

Category Details Users Shares Groups OS Info

CrackMapExec results:

Protocol Result Admin Access? SMB SSH RDP

Authenticated share permissions (smbmap):

Share Name Access Level

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: _________

docs.title: Step 7: Connect via SSH and Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Open an SSH session to the target

SSH provides the most direct path to command execution. Connect to the target using the validated credentials.

ssh admin@<target_ip>

Enter the password password123 when prompted. A shell prompt confirms you are logged in on the target host.

Read the flag file

Navigate to the flag location and read its contents from the target host.

cat /tmp/private/flag.txt

The flag is displayed in OCR{...} format. Copy the value and submit it on the platform.

docs.title: Step 8: Document Your Findings
docs.text:
A complete penetration test ends with structured documentation. Review everything you discovered and organize the findings by severity:

Finding Severity Evidence Null session enumeration succeeds High enum4linux -a output shows users and shares Guest mapping enabled (map to guest = Bad User) High Anonymous SMB connections succeed without valid credentials Credential reuse across SMB, SSH, and RDP Critical CME shows [+] on all three protocols with admin:password123 Weak password on admin account Critical Password password123 is trivially guessable Sensitive data accessible via SSH High Flag file readable at /tmp/private/flag.txt

Each finding should include the tool used, the exact command, the output received, and a remediation recommendation. The documentation phase transforms raw tool output into a professional deliverable.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why should a penetration tester start with null session enumeration before attempting credential attacks?

Reveal Answer

Null session enumeration gathers information without triggering authentication failure alerts. The user accounts, share names, and password policies discovered through null sessions help the tester build a targeted credential attack plan. Starting with credentials first risks account lockouts and generates logs that alert defenders. Null sessions reveal the attack surface while remaining as quiet as possible.

2. What does the "map to guest = Bad User" setting reveal about the server's security configuration?

Reveal Answer

The map to guest = Bad User setting means the server maps authentication attempts with invalid usernames to the guest account instead of rejecting them. The server never returns an "access denied" error for unknown users; it silently grants guest-level access. The configuration effectively disables username validation, allowing anyone to connect with any username and receive guest permissions. The setting is a significant misconfiguration because it masks failed authentication attempts and grants unintended access.

3. How would you structure a penetration test report for the findings in this exercise?

Reveal Answer

A professional report follows a standard structure: executive summary (non-technical overview for leadership), methodology (phases followed and tools used), findings (each vulnerability with severity, evidence, and remediation), and appendices (raw tool output). Each finding should include a description, risk rating, proof-of-concept steps, screenshots or command output, business impact, and specific remediation steps. The findings should be ordered by severity, with critical credential reuse and null session vulnerabilities listed first.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Null session enumeration is the first step in any Windows penetration test; the information gathered guides every subsequent attack
  • map to guest = Bad User is a common SMB misconfiguration that grants guest access to any connection, regardless of the username provided
  • Credential reuse across SMB, SSH, and RDP with the same admin:password123 credentials demonstrates the catastrophic impact of weak, reused passwords
  • Structured methodology ensures completeness; following the six phases (recon, enumeration, vulnerability identification, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting) prevents missed findings
  • Documentation transforms raw tool output into actionable intelligence; a penetration test without a report is just unauthorized access
  • Exercise 9.3 is the capstone of the Windows assessment track, combining every technique from Chapters 1 through 9 into a single end-to-end penetration test

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Over three labs, you progressed from anonymous network enumeration to a complete penetration test methodology. Exercise 9.1 demonstrated that guest access and HTTP misconfigurations allow data extraction without any credentials. Exercise 9.2 showed how a single set of credentials can compromise multiple services through credential reuse testing with CrackMapExec. Exercise 9.3 combined null session enumeration, credential attacks, and structured documentation into a full penetration test that mirrors professional engagements.

The chapter brought together every technique from the Windows track; port scanning, service enumeration, SMB reconnaissance, credential testing, and multi-protocol exploitation; into a repeatable assessment methodology. The progression from unauthenticated access to authenticated exploitation to complete penetration testing reflects how real-world assessments escalate from initial reconnaissance to full compromise.

docs.title: The Progression You Followed
docs.text:
Each lab added complexity and new techniques while building on the skills from the previous exercise:

graph LR
    A["9.1 Windows Network<br/>Assessment"] --> B["9.2 Multi-Service<br/>Exploitation"]
    B --> C["9.3 Complete<br/>Penetration Test"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
Exercise What You Practiced Key Skill Added 9.1 Guest SMB access, HTTP flag retrieval Unauthenticated assessment; no credentials needed 9.2 Credential testing across SMB, SSH, RDP Multi-protocol exploitation with CrackMapExec 9.3 Null sessions, credential reuse, full methodology Complete penetration test from recon to reporting

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer the following questions without looking back at the walkthroughs. If you get stuck on a question, revisit that lab before moving on.

1. What Nmap flags would you use to perform a full service scan with default scripts?

2. How do you list SMB shares using a null session with smbclient?

3. What CrackMapExec command tests the credentials admin:password123 against SSH on a target?

4. What does the (Pwn3d!) indicator mean in CrackMapExec output?

5. What does the SMB configuration map to guest = Bad User do, and why is it a security risk?

6. Name the six phases of a penetration testing methodology in order.

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Keep the following reference handy for assessments and future labs.

Command What It Does nmap -sV -sC <target> Full port scan with version detection and default scripts smbclient -L //<target> -N List SMB shares using a null session smbclient //<target>/<share> -N Connect to a share using a null session smbclient -L //<target> -U user%pass List shares with authenticated credentials smbmap -H <target> Map share permissions (anonymous) smbmap -H <target> -u user -p pass Map share permissions (authenticated) enum4linux -a <target> Full SMB/RPC enumeration (users, shares, groups, policies) crackmapexec smb <target> -u user -p pass Test credentials against SMB crackmapexec ssh <target> -u user -p pass Test credentials against SSH crackmapexec rdp <target> -u user -p pass Test credentials against RDP curl http://<target>/flag.txt Retrieve a file from an HTTP server ssh user@<target> Connect to target via SSH

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text:
You have completed the Windows assessment track. Over nine chapters, you progressed from scanning a single port to executing a complete penetration test across multiple services. The skills you built; port scanning, service enumeration, SMB (Server Message Block) reconnaissance, credential attacks, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) enumeration, RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) exploitation, WinRM (Windows Remote Management) access, credential reuse, and structured assessment methodology; form the foundation for every penetration test you will perform.

The Linux track applies similar methodology to Linux-specific services. SSH (Secure Shell) enumeration, authentication attacks, and post-exploitation techniques use many of the same tools you already know (Nmap, CrackMapExec, SSH) but target different service configurations and file system layouts. The Web track introduces HTTP-based vulnerabilities like directory traversal, command injection, and insecure API endpoints. The Network track covers traffic analysis using packet capture tools like tcpdump and Wireshark.

Each track builds on the same core methodology: scan, enumerate, identify vulnerabilities, exploit, and document. The tools and protocols change, but the approach stays the same.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. nmap -sV -sC <target>: the -sV flag enables service version detection and -sC runs Nmap's default NSE scripts for additional enumeration.

2. smbclient -L //<target> -N: the -L flag lists shares and -N sends a null session (no password).

3. crackmapexec ssh <target> -u admin -p password123: the ssh keyword tells CME to test against the SSH service on port 22.

4. The (Pwn3d!) indicator means the authenticated account has local administrator privileges on the target. Administrative access allows command execution, credential dumping, and full system control.

5. The map to guest = Bad User setting maps authentication attempts with invalid usernames to the guest account instead of rejecting them. The server never returns an authentication failure for unknown users; it silently grants guest-level access. The setting is a security risk because it allows anyone to connect with any username and receive guest permissions, effectively disabling username validation.

6. The six phases are: (1) Reconnaissance, (2) Enumeration, (3) Vulnerability Identification, (4) Exploitation, (5) Post-Exploitation, (6) Reporting. Each phase produces outputs that feed into the next, and skipping phases leads to incomplete findings.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Active Directory is the identity backbone of nearly every enterprise Windows environment in the world. Before you attack it, you must learn to read it. Exercise 1 gives you a single low-privileged credential and asks you to produce an organized inventory of the domain. No exploitation. No clever tricks. Just a clean, methodical first pass with the standard tools every consultant carries.

You will work entirely from your Kali workstation. The target is a single Windows Server 2022 domain controller running corp.nordport.local plus one member file server. Both are reachable from your VPN.

Tools required: rpcclient, ldapsearch, netexec (the modern fork of crackmapexec), smbclient, nmap. All are pre-installed on your Kali workstation.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are a junior consultant at Tidewater Security. Nordport Industries hired the firm to assess their Active Directory after a phishing-driven incident last quarter. Your senior consultant, Marcus Bell, has staged you on the Nordport corporate network with one set of credentials.

Marcus's instructions are short: build a baseline picture before doing anything else. He wants to see your enumeration notes before you touch any further attack work. The flag for this exercise is concealed in the description field of one user account. Marcus is not going to tell you which user. Reading the directory thoroughly is the entire point.

Credentials:

Username Password Purpose j.chen Welcome2026# Standard low-privileged domain user (IT Help Desk)

Domain: corp.nordport.local Domain controller hostname: corp-dc01

docs.title: Lab Topology
docs.text:
The picture below shows what is on the wire when you launch this exercise. You attack from Kali; everything in the dashed box belongs to Nordport.

flowchart LR
    Kali["Kali Workstation<br/>(your VPN IP)"]
    subgraph Nordport["corp.nordport.local"]
        DC["corp-dc01<br/>Domain Controller<br/>53, 88, 135, 389, 445, 636, 3268, 5985"]
        FS["file01<br/>Member File Server<br/>445, 5985"]
    end
    Kali -- LDAP/SMB --> DC
    Kali -- SMB/WinRM --> FS
    DC -. replicates AD .- FS

docs.title: Where Your Data Lives
docs.text:
LDAP serves a hierarchical tree. Every account, group, and computer is a leaf or container under the domain root. The diagram below maps the directory you are about to read.

flowchart TD
    Root["DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local"]
    Root --> Users["CN=Users<br/>(default container)"]
    Root --> Computers["CN=Computers"]
    Root --> IT["OU=IT"]
    Root --> Eng["OU=Engineering"]
    Root --> Fin["OU=Finance"]
    Root --> Svc["OU=ServiceAccounts"]
    Users --> DA["CN=Domain Admins (group)"]
    IT --> JC["CN=Jason Chen (user)<br/>sAMAccountName=j.chen"]

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Authenticate to the domain as j.chen
  • Enumerate users, groups, organizational units, and computers
  • Read user attributes thoroughly (description, info, extensionAttribute1)
  • Find the flag in a single user's description field
  • Save your enumeration output for use in later exercises

docs.title: Background: How LDAP and AD Talk to You
docs.text:
Active Directory exposes its data over the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). Every user, group, computer, organizational unit, and policy object is an LDAP entry under a hierarchical tree rooted at the distinguished name of the domain.

For corp.nordport.local, the root DN is:

DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local

Every object has a fully qualified distinguished name (DN) that traces its location, for example:

CN=Jason Chen,OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local

Some attributes you will care about constantly:

Attribute Meaning sAMAccountName The classic short username (e.g., j.chen) userPrincipalName The email-style logon name (e.g., j.chen@corp.nordport.local) description Free-form one-liner. Operators frequently leak credentials and notes here. info Free-form multi-line notes field. Often used internally by IT teams. userAccountControl Bit-flag integer that encodes account state (disabled, no preauth, password never expires, etc.). memberOf The groups this object belongs to. pwdLastSet Last password change time. Old timestamps signal stale accounts. lastLogonTimestamp Approximate last successful logon. Helps identify dormant accounts. servicePrincipalName List of SPNs registered against this account. Crucial for Kerberoasting.

You do not need to memorize every attribute. You do need to know that all of this is readable by any authenticated domain user by default. That is a feature of AD, not a bug, and it is the foundation of every offensive recon technique in this track.

docs.title: Authentication shortcuts
docs.text:
Most enumeration tools accept credentials in one of three forms:

DOMAIN\username           -- NetBIOS-style
username@DOMAIN.tld       -- UPN-style
domain.tld/username       -- Impacket-style

When in doubt, try j.chen@corp.nordport.local. It is the most universally accepted form.

docs.title: rpcclient
docs.text:
A Samba utility that speaks the same Microsoft RPC interfaces the Windows tools use. You authenticate once, then issue interactive commands.

rpcclient -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" <dc_ip>

The -U "DOMAIN\user%password" form bundles the credential inline. At the prompt, useful commands:

Command Effect enumdomusers List all domain users with their RIDs enumdomgroups List all domain groups queryuser <rid> Detailed user info by RID querygroup <rid> Group details lsaenumsid Enumerate domain SIDs srvinfo Server info

docs.title: ldapsearch
docs.text:
A pure LDAP client that returns raw attributes. Verbose, but it shows you exactly what is in the directory.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName description info
Flag Effect -x simple bind (over plaintext or TLS, not SASL) -H LDAP server URL -D bind DN (the user authenticating); DOMAIN\user works for AD -w password (use -W to be prompted instead) -b search base (the root of where the search starts) - The query (objectClass=user) returns user objects - The trailing attribute names limit the output to those fields

docs.title: netexec
docs.text:
The modern, maintained fork of crackmapexec. It speaks SMB, LDAP, MSSQL, WinRM, RDP, FTP, SSH and presents results in clean tables.

netexec ldap <dc_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --users

Useful flags for this exercise:

Flag Effect --users List all domain users in a clean table --groups List all groups --computers List all domain-joined computers --shares (over SMB) list shares --pass-pol Domain password policy

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
Old-school SMB client. Not strictly an LDAP tool, but useful for listing shares and reading files.

smbclient -L //<dc_ip>/ -U "j.chen%Welcome2026#"

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the OpenCyberRange platform in your browser, navigate to the AD Penetration Track, and launch First Contact. Wait for the status to flip to Running. The Active Lab View shows two target IPs labeled corp-dc01 (DC) and file01.

Note both IPs. For the rest of the walkthrough, replace <dc_ip> and <fileserver_ip> with the values shown.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm the Targets Are Up
docs.text:
Before authenticating, prove the targets respond and the expected services are listening. If port 389 (LDAP) or 445 (SMB) is closed, every other tool you reach for in this exercise will hang or refuse; better to find out now than after typing a 200-character ldapsearch command.

We use nmap because it gives us four pieces of information per probe in one pass: is the port reachable, is something listening, what does the service banner look like, and how does the host respond to malformed packets.

Kali - Verify domain controller services

nmap -Pn -p 53,88,135,389,445,636,3268,5985 <dc_ip>

What each option does:

  • -Pn skip ICMP host-discovery and assume the host is up. Required because most production firewalls drop ICMP, and even some lab nets do. Without -Pn, nmap silently skips hosts it cannot ping.
  • -p 53,88,135,389,445,636,3268,5985 scan ONLY these eight ports rather than the default 1000. Faster, and these are exactly the ports a Windows DC is supposed to expose: DNS (53), Kerberos (88), RPC endpoint mapper (135), LDAP (389), SMB (445), LDAPS (636), Global Catalog (3268), WinRM-HTTP (5985).
  • <dc_ip> target IP shown in the lab dashboard.

Read the output line by line. Each port should show STATE open. The presence of port 88 + 389 together is the canonical "this is an Active Directory Domain Controller" fingerprint; no other Windows role co-exposes both. WinRM (5985) confirms remote-management is enabled, which we will use in later exercises.

Kali - Verify file server

nmap -Pn -p 445,5985 <fileserver_ip>

Same flags. Smaller port list because file01 is a member server, not a DC; only SMB and WinRM are expected to be open.

docs.title: Step 3: First Authenticated Touch
docs.text:
Before pulling thousands of LDAP records, prove the credential actually works. A bad password against AD will silently lock the account if you exceed the lockout threshold (5 failures in 15 min on this domain). Validating once with netexec gives you a definitive yes/no without burning attempts in a heavier tool.

Kali - Validate the j.chen credential against SMB

netexec smb <dc_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local

What each option does:

  • smb the protocol module. netexec ships modules for smb, ldap, winrm, mssql, rdp, ftp, ssh, vnc. Each speaks the protocol natively and surfaces clean tabular output.
  • <dc_ip> target IP. netexec accepts a single IP, a CIDR range (10.0.0.0/24), or a file (-t hosts.txt).
  • -u j.chen username (no domain prefix; the -d flag adds it).
  • -p 'Welcome2026#' password. Quote it so # (a shell comment marker) and ! (history expansion) do not get eaten by bash.
  • -d corp.nordport.local domain realm. Required for Kerberos-aware operations and for proper user-principal-name construction.

What the output tells you:

  • [+] prefix on the line means authentication succeeded. [-] means failed.
  • (name:DOCKERW-...) is the host's NetBIOS name.
  • (domain:corp.nordport.local) is the FQDN.
  • (signing:True) is the SMB signing requirement: the server demands signed messages. Important to know; it affects whether NTLM relay attacks work later.
  • (SMBv1:None); SMBv1 is disabled (modern best practice).
  • (Null Auth:True); anonymous (null-session) bind is allowed for SOME operations. Doesn't mean every share is reachable anonymously, just that the protocol negotiation succeeds.

If you see [-] STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE: wrong password. If you see [-] STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT: the account is locked from prior failed attempts; wait 30 min for the policy to reset.

docs.title: Step 4: Enumerate Domain Users
docs.text: Three tools, three different views of the same directory. They are not redundant; each surfaces something the others hide. Run all three and compare.

docs.title: 4a. rpcclient interactive; RPC view
docs.text:
rpcclient is a Samba utility that speaks the same MS-RPC interfaces Windows tools use. It connects once, then accepts interactive commands at a rpcclient $> prompt. RPC enumeration was the original way Windows administrators listed users before LDAP became dominant; many old Microsoft tools (and some still-used third-party AV products) still hit these RPC endpoints.

Kali - rpcclient interactive enumeration

rpcclient -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" <dc_ip>

What each option does:

  • -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" bundles credentials in DOMAIN\user%password form. The \ is escaped to bash; PowerShell-style \\ not needed because we're in a quoted string. Alternative form: -U j.chen%Welcome2026# -W CORP.
  • <dc_ip> target. rpcclient uses port 445 (SMB) to negotiate the RPC interface.

Once you see the rpcclient $> prompt, issue commands one at a time:

enumdomusers
enumdomgroups
querydominfo
exit

What each does:

  • enumdomusers; calls SAMR EnumDomainUsers. Returns a numeric RID (relative ID, the last segment of the user's SID) and the sAMAccountName for every user in the domain. The RID is a stable handle that survives renames; useful when you need to reference a user by its SID later.
  • enumdomgroups; calls SAMR EnumDomainGroups. Same idea for groups.
  • querydominfo; returns domain-wide metadata: domain SID, role of the host you connected to (DC vs. member), domain server type flags. The domain SID prefix (S-1-5-21-XXXX-YYYY-ZZZZ) is what every per-user/per-group SID is derived from; copy it down for later.
  • exit; quit the prompt cleanly.

Common gotcha: the ? command at the prompt lists all available rpcclient subcommands (~150 of them). Unix-style commands like ls do NOT work here; this is rpcclient's own tiny shell.

docs.title: 4b. ldapsearch for full attributes; the canonical view
docs.text:
ldapsearch is a pure LDAP client that returns raw attributes. Verbose output, but it shows you exactly what the directory holds. As a raw client, ldapsearch hides nothing; every other AD tool is a wrapper around this same protocol.

Kali - Pull every user's description and info via LDAP

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName description info \
  > users_attrs.txt

What each option does:

  • -x use simple bind (username + password over the wire) instead of SASL (which would require a Kerberos ticket). Simple is fine over LDAP-over-TLS or inside a trusted lab; in production prefer SASL/GSSAPI.
  • -LLL strip LDIF format noise: no version line, no comments, no blank trailing line. Stripping the noise makes the output easy to grep. The flag is literally three Ls.
  • -H ldap://<dc_ip> LDAP URL. Use ldaps:// for the encrypted variant on port 636.
  • -D "CORP\j.chen" bind DN, the identity authenticating. AD accepts both DOMAIN\user and full DN syntax (CN=Jason Chen,OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local); the short form is friendlier.
  • -w 'Welcome2026#' password literal. Use -W instead to be prompted (more secure if anyone is shoulder-surfing).
  • -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" search base; the root of the subtree to search. The pattern DC=x,DC=y,DC=z mirrors the dotted FQDN x.y.z reversed.
  • "(objectClass=user)" LDAP search filter. Returns only objects whose objectClass includes user (which means User AND Computer accounts; computers also have objectClass: user for legacy reasons).
  • sAMAccountName description info attribute list. Without this, ldapsearch returns ALL attributes per object (~50+ each) which makes the dump enormous. Listing specific attributes keeps the output tight.
  • > users_attrs.txt redirect output to a file so you can grep without re-running the query.

Once the file is written, search for the flag pattern. We filter to description: lines specifically because for Exercise 1.1 the flag lives there:

Kali - Search the LDAP dump for the flag pattern in description

grep -B1 -E '^description:.*OCR\{' users_attrs.txt

What each option does:

  • -B1 print one line of context BEFORE each match. Because LDIF orders attributes and the sAMAccountName for an entry comes immediately before its description, this lets you see WHICH user the flag belongs to.
  • -E interpret the pattern as extended regex (so \{ is a literal brace).
  • '^description:.*OCR\{' match lines that start with description: and contain OCR{ somewhere. The ^ anchors to start-of-line so we ignore description appearing as substring elsewhere.

The grep returns the user whose description field contains this exercise's OCR{...} flag. Take note of both the username (the matching sAMAccountName line above) and the flag itself.

Note on multiple flags: as you enumerate the directory you may encounter OCR{...} strings in other attributes (e.g. info) on different user objects. Those belong to LATER exercises and the platform will reject them here. The 1.1 flag lives ONLY in the description field of a user account. The flag value itself encodes the exercise theme (something like OCR{<welcome>_<to>_<the>_<domain>} in leetspeak, clearly orientation-related) so you can sanity-check before submitting.

docs.title: 4c. netexec for tabular output; the operator's friend
docs.text:
netexec is the modern fork of crackmapexec (which itself replaced the older cme). Same data as ldapsearch, formatted as a clean table you can scroll. Use it as a sanity check after the LDAP dump and as your daily driver for ad-hoc enumeration.

Kali - Tabular user list with netexec

netexec ldap <dc_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --users \
  | tee users_table.txt

What each option does:

  • ldap protocol module; netexec also has SMB, WinRM, MSSQL etc. Choosing ldap connects on port 389/636 and uses LDAP-native enumeration paths.
  • <dc_ip> target.
  • -u/-p/-d same meaning as the SMB call earlier.
  • --users request the user list. Other useful flags on the LDAP module: --groups, --computers, --pass-pol (domain password policy), --asreproast (find DONT_REQ_PREAUTH users), --kerberoasting (find SPN-bearing accounts).
  • | tee users_table.txt pipe stdout to both the terminal AND a file. tee lets you watch progress live while preserving the output for later reuse.

What the columns mean:

  • sAMAccountName; the short username.
  • pwdLastSet; when the password was last changed. Old timestamps signal stale or service accounts.
  • lastLogon; last successful authentication. Empty or very old means dormant accounts (high-value spray targets in Level 3).
  • memberOf (with --groups modifier); what groups the user is in.

Save the file. The full user list is the foundation for later password-spray exercises (Level 3.4) and for BloodHound's SharpHound collector (Level 1.2).

docs.title: Step 5: Enumerate Groups
docs.text:
Groups in AD govern privileges. Knowing the group landscape now will save you hours later when BloodHound asks you to interpret an attack path.

Kali - List all groups

netexec ldap <dc_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --groups

Same flags as before; --groups swaps the LDAP filter that netexec sends from (objectClass=user) to (objectClass=group) and prints results in a tabular format.

What to look for in the output:

  • Anything ending in Admins; these grant elevated rights somewhere. Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins are the obvious Tier-0 prizes.
  • Anything starting with Tier; Microsoft's own tiered-administration model uses Tier0_Admins, Tier1_Admins, Tier2_Admins. Mature shops follow this convention.
  • The built-ins: Schema Admins, Backup Operators, Server Operators, Account Operators. These are sleeper paths to Domain Admin equivalence; non-empty membership is suspicious.
  • Any group with a name suffix like _<token> (e.g. Backup_Operators_j001). Those are per-student per-exercise groups; you will see them in later levels.

To see who belongs to a specific group, use a custom LDAP filter. The interesting bit here is the OID:

Kali - Members of Domain Admins (transitive)

netexec ldap <dc_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local \
  --query "(memberof:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local)" \
  sAMAccountName

What each piece of the query does:

  • --query "..." send a custom LDAP filter rather than netexec's built-in shortcut.
  • (memberof:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=...) the matching rule. The OID 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941 is LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_IN_CHAIN, more commonly called the "transitive membership" matching rule. Without this OID, the memberof attribute returns only DIRECT members of the group; with it, you also get members of nested groups.
  • The right-hand side after := is the full DN of the target group. Domain Admins lives in CN=Users (the legacy Users container, not an OU) so the DN is CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local.
  • sAMAccountName trailing argument restricts the returned attributes to just the username.

Why memorize this OID: every time you ask "is X transitively a member of group Y?" in AD, this is the answer. Real engagements hit it multiple times per day. There are exactly two AD matching-rule OIDs worth remembering: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941 (in chain) and 1.2.840.113556.1.4.803 (bitwise AND, used for userAccountControl flag tests in later exercises).

docs.title: Step 6: Enumerate Organizational Units
docs.text:
OUs are the organizational containers AD uses to group objects for delegation, GPO targeting, and audit scope. Knowing the OU layout tells you where the high-value populations live (admins, service accounts, HR data) before you spend time enumerating every user.

Kali - List OUs

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" name distinguishedName

What changed from the user query:

  • "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)"; different filter, same syntax. Returns only OU objects.
  • name distinguishedName; we want only the name and the full DN per OU. The DN reveals the nesting (e.g. OU=Engineering,DC=corp,... is top-level; OU=Build,OU=Engineering,DC=corp,... would be nested under Engineering).

Read the output and sketch the tree on paper. Nordport's OU structure mirrors the company org chart: Engineering, Finance, HR, Operations, IT, ServiceAccounts. Each OU has different account types and different threat models. ServiceAccounts is where the noisy crackable accounts live; IT is where the privileged humans live.

docs.title: Step 7: Enumerate Computers
docs.text:
Computer objects in AD represent every domain-joined machine; workstations, member servers, DCs themselves. Each computer has a machine account with a 240-byte random password that rotates every 30 days. From an offensive perspective, computer enumeration tells you where to focus reconnaissance after the initial directory dump: which hosts run interesting services, which are running old or unusual OSes, which look like servers vs workstations.

Kali - List domain computers

netexec ldap <dc_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --computers

--computers swaps the filter to (objectClass=computer) and includes the OS string in the output.

What the columns mean:

  • Hostname; short NetBIOS name of the machine.
  • operatingSystem; version string. Server 2008 / Windows 7 / etc. surface here. Old OS versions are over-represented in pwnage statistics because they lack modern memory protections, secure boot, and recent security patches.
  • operatingSystemVersion; build number (e.g. 10.0 (20348) for Server 2022 21H2).
  • dnsHostName; the FQDN. Use this rather than the short name when crafting Kerberos service tickets later.

Save the output. The list of domain-joined hosts becomes your target inventory for everything from RDP testing to LAPS retrieval to RBCD targeting in Level 4.

docs.title: Step 8: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Take the OCR{...} value you discovered in Step 4b and paste it into the Submit Flag form on the platform.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Authenticated LDAP enumeration is hard to detect because it looks like normal directory traffic. Defenders rely on volume thresholds and on flagging atypical attribute patterns rather than blocking the queries outright. The table below maps each tool you ran to the events a SOC analyst could pivot on.

Activity Windows event Log location LDAP bind from j.chen 4624 (logon type 3), 4662 DC Security log Bulk SAMR enumeration via rpcclient 4661 (handle to SAM), 4662 DC Security log Wide LDAP queries ((objectClass=user)) LDAP Diagnostic event 1644 DC Directory Services log netexec SMB probe 4624, 4625, 5140 DC and member-server Security log

What gets noticed first

SOC tooling does not usually alert on individual reads, but BloodHound-style collection lights up Microsoft Defender for Identity ("Reconnaissance using directory services queries") within seconds because the collector pulls thousands of attributes back to back. Pacing your queries lower and using attribute-scoped filters (the way ldapsearch ... sAMAccountName description info does) tends to stay under behavioral baselines.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
Defenders rarely block authenticated reads because doing so breaks legitimate clients, but they can shrink the blast radius. A reasonable hardening checklist includes the points below.

Practical mitigations

  • Set dsHeuristics bit 0 to 1 to disable anonymous LDAP bind on the forest root.
  • Audit and clear all description, info, and extensionAttribute* fields for embedded credentials with a scheduled scan.
  • Add deny ACEs on the Authenticated Users principal for sensitive OUs (e.g., Tier 0 admin OU) so low-privileged enumeration cannot read them.
  • Enable Microsoft Defender for Identity on every domain controller; it baselines normal LDAP volumes per identity and pages on outliers.
  • Send DC Security logs and event 1644 to your SIEM with retention long enough to catch slow-burn recon (30+ days).

docs.text:

(paste the total number of user accounts here)
