docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does any authenticated domain user have read access to so many attributes on every other user, group, and computer in the domain?

Reveal Answer

Active Directory is designed as an identity service. By default, every authenticated user can read most of the directory because the directory itself is what tells clients where to find services, who is in what group, and how to authenticate. If reads required elevated privilege, ordinary domain logon would not work. The default ACLs on AD objects grant Authenticated Users read on most attributes, including description, memberOf, userAccountControl, and servicePrincipalName. That permissive default is why offensive enumeration is so productive in default-configured AD environments. Locking down read access is possible (delegated OUs, custom ACLs) but rarely done because it breaks legitimate tooling.

2. You found a credential leaked in a description field. What other attributes commonly leak similar information, and where else in AD do operators historically leak credentials?

Reveal Answer

Common attribute-level leaks: description, info, comment, and the extensionAttribute1 through extensionAttribute15 fields used by some HRIS sync products. The userParameters and userPassword (legacy) fields are also worth searching. Outside of attributes, the classic leak locations are: SYSVOL Groups.xml (GPP cpassword); SYSVOL scripts (logon scripts hardcoding service account credentials); SMB shares (especially anything called IT-Tools, Helpdesk, or Onboarding); the WSUS configuration on management servers; LAPS attributes if the requesting account has the wrong delegations; and machine account passwords in restored backups. The pattern: any place where humans wrote text that machines read.

3. The userAccountControl attribute is a 32-bit integer that encodes a dozen account flags. Which two flags would make your day if you saw them set on a user?

Reveal Answer

DONT_REQ_PREAUTH (0x400000, decimal 4194304) means the account does not require Kerberos pre-authentication, which makes it ASREPRoastable from any unauthenticated context. TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION (0x80000, decimal 524288) means the account is configured for unconstrained delegation; if you can compromise that account, you can capture TGTs of any user who authenticates to it. Both are findable with one LDAP query each: (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304) for ASREPRoast candidates, (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288) for unconstrained delegation. Memorize these two queries; you will run them on every engagement.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Authenticated domain users can read most of the directory by default. Enumeration is the highest-leverage activity at the start of any AD engagement.
  • rpcclient, ldapsearch, and netexec give you three different views of the same data; use all three.
  • The description, info, and extensionAttribute* fields are common credential-leak surfaces.
  • The transitive group membership LDAP OID (1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941) returns nested members, not just direct ones.
  • The root DN format DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local mirrors the dotted FQDN; you will write this string a lot, so commit it to muscle memory.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The five commands below cover most first-touch enumeration on any engagement. Pin this card; you will reuse it on every box from Level 1 through the capstones.

Goal Command Validate creds and probe SMB netexec smb <dc> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> Tabular user list netexec ldap <dc> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --users Raw user attributes (descriptions, info) ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -D "<DOMAIN>\<user>" -w '<pw>' -b "<DN>" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName description info Members of Domain Admins (transitive) netexec ldap <dc> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --query "(memberof:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,<DN>)" sAMAccountName Find ASREPRoast candidates netexec ldap <dc> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --query "(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304)" sAMAccountName

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: Domain User LDAP Bind

Q: Write the full ldapsearch command to authenticate to corp.local at 10.10.10.10 as j.smith with password Pass123# and return every user's sAMAccountName and description.

Answer 
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://10.10.10.10 \
  -D "CORP\j.smith" -w 'Pass123#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName description

The -x flag forces simple bind. -LLL strips LDIF version noise. The bind DN can also be the UPN form j.smith@corp.local.

Card 2: rpcclient User Enumeration

Q: After rpcclient -U "CORP\user%pass" 10.10.10.10 succeeds, name three commands that produce useful enumeration output.

Answer

enumdomusers lists every domain user with RID. enumdomgroups lists every group. querydominfo returns domain metadata including the SID and the role of the host you are talking to. Bonus: lsaenumsid enumerates SIDs of all object types.

Card 3: Transitive Group Membership Filter

Q: What is the LDAP OID that converts a memberof filter into a transitive (nested) match, and what is the full filter to find every user who is transitively in Domain Admins of corp.local?

Answer

OID: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941. Filter: (memberof:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=local). Without the OID, you only get direct members; with it, you get members of nested groups too.

Card 4: Two userAccountControl Flags Worth Memorizing

Q: Name the two userAccountControl flag values most worth searching for, what they enable, and the LDAP filter for each.

Answer

4194304 (DONT_REQ_PREAUTH) makes the account ASREPRoastable. Filter: (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304). 524288 (TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION) makes the account configured for unconstrained delegation. Filter: (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288). The OID 1.2.840.113556.1.4.803 is the bitwise-AND match operator.

Card 5: netexec One-Liner User List

Q: Write the netexec command that produces a clean tabular list of all domain users for corp.local at 10.10.10.10 using credentials j.smith / Pass123#.

Answer 
netexec ldap 10.10.10.10 -u j.smith -p 'Pass123#' -d corp.local --users

Swap --users for --groups, --computers, or --pass-pol for the matching enumerations.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1 introduced raw LDAP queries. They scale poorly. Five queries are fine; five hundred is a chore. BloodHound turns the same data into a graph and lets you ask "who has a path to Domain Admins?" in one Cypher query rather than thirty manual joins.

In this exercise you will collect data with SharpHound, ingest it into BloodHound CE, and answer four targeted questions about Nordport's privileged group structure. Submit the SHA-1 of the four answers concatenated to retrieve the flag.

Tools required: bloodhound-python (collector), BloodHound CE GUI, neo4j, a working Cypher console. All are pre-installed on your Kali workstation. Neo4j and BloodHound start automatically when you open the BloodHound shortcut.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell, your senior consultant, hands you a four-question pop quiz. Each question is something a senior pentester answers from a BloodHound collection in under a minute. He wants to see you do the same.

The questions:

  1. How many users have a path to Domain Admins (any path, any length, transitive)?
  2. Who is the manager of the manager of the manager of the user priya.ramanathan?
  3. Which user is a member of the most groups (counted transitively)?
  4. Which non-DA user is in the most groups that have local administrator on at least one computer?

Concatenate the four answers in order. Take the SHA-1 of the resulting string. Submit the hash to the scoring API on this exercise's network. The scorer returns the flag if all four answers are correct.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Run SharpHound (bloodhound-python) against corp.nordport.local
  • Ingest the JSON collection into BloodHound CE
  • Use the GUI and Cypher console to answer the four questions
  • Compute the SHA-1 of the concatenation
  • Submit the hash to the scoring API and retrieve the flag

docs.title: Lab Topology
docs.text:
You attack from Kali, run BloodHound CE locally, collect from the DC, and submit answers to a small scorer service inside the lab network. The diagram below maps the data flow.

flowchart LR
    Kali["Kali Workstation<br/>BloodHound CE @ localhost:8080"]
    DC["corp-dc01<br/>LDAP/SMB"]
    Scorer["Scorer Service<br/>:8080/submit"]
    Kali -- "1. bloodhound-python collect" --> DC
    DC -- "2. JSON zip" --> Kali
    Kali -- "3. ingest into Neo4j" --> Kali
    Kali -- "4. POST 4 answers" --> Scorer
    Scorer -- "5. flag (if all correct)" --> Kali

docs.title: Background: What BloodHound Actually Is
docs.text: BloodHound is a graph-database visualization of Active Directory. The collector (SharpHound, or bloodhound-python for the Linux version) reads AD over the same LDAP and SMB interfaces you used in Exercise 1.1. The collected data is loaded into a Neo4j graph database, then a web UI lets you query the graph visually or with Cypher (Neo4j's query language).

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
Each AD object is a node in the graph. Common types:

Node type What it is User A domain user account Group A security or distribution group Computer A domain-joined computer OU An organizational unit GPO A Group Policy Object Domain A domain or trust target

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
Each relationship between objects is an edge. Common edges relevant to attack paths:

Edge Meaning MemberOf The source is a member of the target group AdminTo The source has local admin on the target computer CanRDP The source can RDP to the target computer GenericAll The source has full control on the target GenericWrite The source can write any property on the target WriteDACL The source can change the target's permissions WriteOwner The source can take ownership of the target ForceChangePassword The source can reset the target's password without knowing it AddMember The source can add members to the target group AllowedToDelegate The source is configured to delegate to the target AllowedToAct The source is in the target's RBCD list HasSession The source user has an active session on the target computer

The power of the graph is composition: an attacker walks edges from a starting node (j.chen) to a goal node (Domain Admins) regardless of how many hops are required. BloodHound does the path search; you read off the answer.

docs.title: A Path is a Chain of Edges
docs.text:
The diagram below shows what a typical attack path looks like inside the graph. Reading left to right, each arrow is a single privilege you abuse to take the next hop.

flowchart LR
    JC["User: j.chen<br/>(your foothold)"]
    G1["Group: HelpDesk-Admins"]
    SVC["User: svc-sql<br/>(Kerberoastable)"]
    SQL["Computer: sql01<br/>(local admin)"]
    DA["Group: Domain Admins"]
    JC -->|MemberOf| G1
    G1 -->|ForceChangePassword| SVC
    SVC -->|AdminTo| SQL
    SQL -->|HasSession| DA

A few seconds of Cypher gives you the same answer as an hour of LDAP filtering plus mental graph composition. That speed multiplier is why every modern AD assessment starts with BloodHound.

docs.title: bloodhound-python (the collector)
docs.text:
bloodhound-python -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -d corp.nordport.local -ns <dc_ip> \
  -c All --zip
Flag Effect -u / -p credentials -d domain -ns nameserver to resolve hosts (point at the DC) -c All collect every method (Group, LocalAdmin, Session, Trusts, ACL, Container, RDP, ObjectProps, LoggedOn, DCOM, PSRemote) --zip bundle the resulting JSON files into a single zip ready for ingest

The collection produces a zip file in the current directory.

docs.title: BloodHound CE GUI
docs.text:
Launch with the desktop shortcut BloodHound CE on your Kali. The first run wizard creates an admin account on the embedded Neo4j; remember the password. The web interface opens at http://localhost:8080.

To ingest your collection, click Upload Files and select the zip from bloodhound-python. The dashboard updates within seconds.

docs.title: Cypher
docs.text:
The Neo4j query language. Examples (run from the Cypher tab in the BloodHound UI):

// All users in the domain
MATCH (u:User) RETURN u.name LIMIT 25

// All users transitively in Domain Admins (canonical BloodHound CE form)
MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(m:Group) WHERE m.name = 'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' RETURN u

// Path from j.chen to Domain Admins (canonical form)
MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group)) WHERE n.name = 'J.CHEN@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' AND m.name = 'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' RETURN p

A note on case: BloodHound stores names UPPERCASE with the domain in UPN form. j.chen becomes J.CHEN@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL and Domain Admins becomes DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL in the graph. The official BloodHound CE Cypher form (mirrored above and in every Privilege Zones rule) uses WHERE <var>.name = '...' rather than embedding the name in the node pattern.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Launch Reading the Org Chart in the platform. Note the DC IP and the scorer URL displayed in the Active Lab View. The scorer is a small HTTP service running on the same lab network.

docs.title: Step 2: Pre-flight DNS Sanity Check
docs.text:
bloodhound-python reads the DC's dnsHostName attribute and then attempts to resolve that name to an IP. If resolution fails the collector aborts with AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'extend'. A 30-second sanity check now saves a confused traceback later.

Get the DC IP from your Active Lab View (typically shown as corp-dc01: 10.100.X.10 where X varies per spawn). Substitute it into DC_IP= below. Auto-derivation from Kali's interfaces is unreliable because Kali may sit on a routed lab-management subnet rather than directly on the lab subnet itself.

Kali - Confirm the DC's FQDN resolves

DC_IP=10.100.2.10   # <-- REPLACE with your DC IP from Active Lab View

DC_FQDN=$(ldapsearch -x -LLL -H "ldap://$DC_IP" -s base "(objectClass=*)" dnsHostName 2>/dev/null | awk '/dnsHostName:/{print $2; exit}')
echo "DC reports FQDN: $DC_FQDN"
getent hosts "$DC_FQDN" >/dev/null && echo "Resolves OK" || { echo "Resolution failed; adding /etc/hosts entry as fallback"; echo "$DC_IP $DC_FQDN ${DC_FQDN%%.*}" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts; }
Token Effect DC_IP=10.100.2.10 The DC IP from the Active Lab View. Edit this value before pasting. ldapsearch ... -s base "(objectClass=*)" dnsHostName Read the rootDSE attribute that names the DC's FQDN. awk '/dnsHostName:/{print $2; exit}' Extract the value from LDIF output. getent hosts "$DC_FQDN" Check whether the system resolver knows the name. Conditional sudo tee -a /etc/hosts Add a fallback mapping when the DC's own DNS does not have an A record for itself.

On a properly built lab the DC's DNS already has the matching A record and the script reports Resolves OK. If the lab was built before the DNS-fix patch (2026-04-26), you will see the /etc/hosts fallback fire once.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the Collector
docs.text:
The SharpHound family of collectors enumerates AD objects, ACLs, sessions, and trusts via LDAP and SMB, packages the result as a set of JSON files, and zips them for ingestion. We use the Linux-native variant (bloodhound-python) because we are operating from Kali; the Windows variant (SharpHound.exe) is only useful when you have a Windows foothold.

Kali - Run bloodhound-python

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-1-02 && cd ~/work/adpt-1-02
bloodhound-python -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -d corp.nordport.local -ns <dc_ip> \
  -c All --zip

What each option does:

  • -u j.chen username for the LDAP/SMB binds. The collector authenticates once and reuses the session for every object.
  • -p 'Welcome2026#' password. Quote it so shell special characters do not break it.
  • -d corp.nordport.local domain (and Kerberos realm).
  • -ns <dc_ip> nameserver. The collector resolves hostnames during enumeration; pointing at the DC ensures every internal name resolves correctly.
  • -c All collection methods. Equivalent to -c Group,LocalAdmin,Session,Trusts,ACL,Container,RDP,ObjectProps,LoggedOn,DCOM,PSRemote. Each method exercises a different AD primitive: Group reads memberships, ACL reads object DACLs, Session and LoggedOn enumerate active user sessions on remote hosts, Trusts reads domain trust objects, etc.
  • --zip bundle the resulting JSON files into a single timestamped .zip. The zip is what BloodHound CE wants to ingest.

What the output looks like (per object class):

INFO: Found AD domain: corp.nordport.local
INFO: Connecting to LDAP server: corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local
INFO: Found 1 domains
INFO: Found 1 domains in the forest
INFO: Found 87 users
INFO: Found 42 groups
INFO: Found 4 computers
INFO: Connecting to GC LDAP server...
INFO: Done in 00M 28S

Common gotchas:

  • If Connecting to LDAP server hangs, the -ns value is wrong (DNS resolution is failing). Try the DC's IP literally instead of corp-dc01.
  • -c LoggedOn is the noisiest collection method (it queries every reachable host's session list) and triggers ITDR products like Microsoft Defender for Identity. For stealth, use -c Group,LocalAdmin,Session,Trusts,ACL,Container,RDP,ObjectProps (drop LoggedOn and DCOM).

docs.title: Step 4: Start BloodHound and Ingest
docs.text:
The collector's zip contains data; BloodHound CE is the graph database + visualization that makes the data useful. The Kali distribution ships BloodHound CE pre-installed but not started by default.

Kali - Start BloodHound CE

sudo bloodhound cli start

What this does:

  • Starts the embedded Postgres (BloodHound metadata store), Neo4j (graph database holding the AD model), and the BloodHound API + UI containers via docker-compose under the hood.
  • The first startup creates the local user and admin password; copy these from the terminal output (you will not see them again unless you sudo bloodhound cli reset-admin-password).
  • sudo is required because BloodHound CE manages docker containers in the system docker socket.

Wait for the line BloodHound CE is ready at http://localhost:8080. Open that URL in Firefox.

Once the UI is up, ingest your zip. Click the gear icon at the top right, then File Ingest, then UPLOAD FILE(S) (the explicit upload button is more reliable than drag-and-drop in some Firefox builds). Pick the *_bloodhound.zip from your work directory and click START. Wait for the file's status to progress Ready -> Running -> Complete (60-90 seconds). The dashboard cards at the top of the Explore page (Users, Computers, Groups, OUs) only populate after the ingest reaches Complete. If the tiles still show 0, the ingest has not finished and every Cypher query and every curated rule under Privilege Zones will return "No results match your criteria".

docs.title: Step 5: Answer Question 1 (Paths to Domain Admins)
docs.text:
BloodHound CE ships a curated library of attack-path detection rules under Privilege Zones -> All Rules -> Default Routes. Each rule is a pre-saved Cypher query that runs against the loaded graph and returns matching paths. Browse the rules to see what BloodHound's authors consider high-value attack patterns; run any of them to populate the graph view.

For an exact COUNT (rather than the visual graph), paste a custom query into the Cypher box on the Explore page.

Confirm ingest before querying

Both the curated rules AND any custom Cypher return "No results match your criteria" when the graph is empty. After uploading the zip, check the four dashboard tiles at the top of the Explore page (Users / Computers / Groups / OUs). If they all show 0, the ingest has not completed: gear icon -> File Ingest -> UPLOAD FILE(S) -> select the zip -> wait for Ready -> Running -> Complete (60-90s).

First, confirm the Domain Admins group node exists in the graph by SID. Domain Admins always has a Relative Identifier (RID) of 512, regardless of domain name or BloodHound version. The query below finds it without depending on case-sensitive name matching:

BloodHound CE Cypher - paths from any user to Domain Admins

MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group)) WHERE m.name = 'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' RETURN p

This is the canonical form from the official BloodHound CE docs (https://bloodhound.specterops.io/analyze-data/bloodhound-gui/cypher-search). It returns every shortest path from any User to the Domain Admins group, regardless of edge type, with no depth cap.

What each piece of the query does:

  • MATCH p=shortestPath(...) one MATCH that binds the path to variable p and uses Cypher's built-in shortestPath() function. BHCE renders the path in the graph view.
  • (n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group) the path pattern. (n:User) is any User; (m:Group) is any Group; [*1..] means "1 or more hops via any edge type, no upper bound" (BHCE's planner handles the unbounded case efficiently for this idiom).
  • WHERE m.name = 'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' restricts m to the Domain Admins group by exact name. BloodHound stores group names as <UPPERCASE NAME>@<UPPERCASE DOMAIN>; this string must match exactly.
  • RETURN p returns the path. The graph view renders the result; the result count above the canvas is the integer answer to Question 1.

Look at the result indicator above the graph (typically "X paths" or "X results"). That number is your Question 1 answer. Save it for the SHA-1 calculation in Step 9.

BloodHound CE Cypher quirks

BHCE 5.x+'s Cypher parser is stricter than Neo4j Browser, AND its result panel does not render scalar columns. Two rules cover almost every failure mode:

  • Always return paths or nodes, never scalars. RETURN p, RETURN u, or UNWIND ... RETURN path draws on the canvas. RETURN COUNT(...) or RETURN u.name, COUNT(g) returns numbers and strings the canvas cannot draw, and the GUI shows "No results match your criteria" with no visible result panel. Aggregate inside a WITH clause and return the resulting NODE or PATH.
  • shortestPath() on a single line, one MATCH per query. Line breaks inside shortestPath(), or chaining a second MATCH without an intervening WITH, produce no viable alternative at input errors. Paste each query as a single logical line.

docs.title: Step 6: Answer Question 2 (Manager-of-the-manager-of-the-manager)
docs.text:
The Manager attribute lives on each user object in AD as the LDAP manager attribute (a DN pointing at the next user up the chain). BloodHound CE 5.x represents this as a HasManager edge ONLY when collected by SharpHound CE (Windows-only). The Linux bloodhound-python collector that Kali ships does NOT surface manager as a graph edge, so a [:HasManager] Cypher query returns nothing on this lab.

The data is on the DC regardless of what BloodHound captured. Walk the chain via LDAP directly.

PASTE THIS IN YOUR KALI TERMINAL, NOT BLOODHOUND

The script below is bash (#!/bin/bash-style), not Cypher. Open your Kali shell terminal, not the BloodHound web UI's Cypher box. If you paste bash into BloodHound you will see errors like mismatched input 'DC_IP', token recognition error at: '\j', etc.

Kali shell (NOT BloodHound) - walk Priya's manager chain via LDAP

Set DC_IP to the value shown in your Active Lab View. Each statement is one short line with ; separators - no \ continuations to break on paste:

DC_IP=10.100.2.10   # <-- REPLACE with your DC IP from Active Lab View
CRED='CORP\j.chen'; PASS='Welcome2026#'; BASE='DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local'

walk_manager() { ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H "ldap://$DC_IP" -D "$CRED" -w "$PASS" -b "$1" -s base manager 2>/dev/null | awk '/^manager: /{sub(/^manager: /,""); print; exit}'; }

PRIYA_DN=$(ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H "ldap://$DC_IP" -D "$CRED" -w "$PASS" -b "$BASE" "(sAMAccountName=priya.ramanathan)" dn 2>/dev/null | awk '/^dn: /{sub(/^dn: /,""); print; exit}')
echo "Priya DN: $PRIYA_DN"

M1=$(walk_manager "$PRIYA_DN"); echo "Priya -> $M1"
M2=$(walk_manager "$M1");        echo "       -> $M2"
M3=$(walk_manager "$M2");        echo "       -> $M3"

ldapsearch -x -LLL -o ldif-wrap=no -H "ldap://$DC_IP" -D "$CRED" -w "$PASS" -b "$M3" -s base sAMAccountName 2>/dev/null | awk '/^sAMAccountName: /{sub(/^sAMAccountName: /,""); print "Q2 answer: "$0; exit}'
Token Effect DC_IP=10.100.2.10 The DC IP from the Active Lab View. Edit before pasting; auto-derivation is unreliable because Kali may sit on a routed lab-management subnet rather than the lab subnet itself. -o ldif-wrap=no Tell ldapsearch not to wrap long DN values across lines. Without this, AD users with long full names get DNs split mid-string and the awk truncates. walk_manager() Helper that takes a DN and returns the value of its manager attribute. ldapsearch -b "$1" -s base manager Read the manager attribute on the object whose DN is $1. awk '/^manager: /{sub(/^manager: /,""); print; exit}' Strip the manager: prefix and print the rest of the line. The naive print $2 form takes only the first whitespace-separated field, which truncates DNs that contain spaces (e.g., CN=Priya Ramanathan,... becomes CN=Priya).

The script prints each intermediate DN as it walks up Priya's manager chain, then resolves the third-hop DN to its sAMAccountName. The Q2 answer: line is what you submit (lowercased, before @). Expect: r.kowalski.

If Derived DC IP is empty or wrong

Hardcode it from the Active Lab View. Replace the first line with:

DC_IP=<the value you see in the Active Lab View>; CRED='CORP\j.chen'; PASS='Welcome2026#'; BASE='DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local'

Other failure modes:

  • Can't contact LDAP server (-1) - DC IP is wrong (use Active Lab View) or LDAP/389 is firewalled.
  • Bind succeeds but Priya DN empty - the user account priya.ramanathan may have a different SAM in your seed; run ldapsearch -x -LLL -H "ldap://$DC_IP" -D "$CRED" -w "$PASS" -b "$BASE" "(sAMAccountName=priya*)" sAMAccountName dn to find the actual SAM.
  • Output shows command not found on filter strings - the \ continuations from a hand-edited copy got partially preserved. Paste the verbatim version above; every command sits on one logical line.
Why not BloodHound for this question?

SharpHound CE (the new Windows-only collector for BHCE 5.x) emits HasManager edges via the ObjectProps collection method. The Linux bloodhound-python Kali ships does not. To see manager edges in BHCE you would need to run SharpHound from a Windows host; LDAP is faster and works on the credential you already have.

docs.title: Step 7: Answer Question 3 (User with the Most Groups, Transitive)
docs.text:
Group nesting (a group that contains other groups as members) is what makes counting "transitive" memberships interesting. A user might be DIRECTLY in 3 groups but TRANSITIVELY in 30 because of nesting. Cypher's *1.. syntax does the chain traversal natively.

In BHCE 5.x+, scalar Cypher returns (RETURN u.name, COUNT(g)) do not render in the graph canvas. The query below uses the canonical "find the winner, then return its membership paths as a graph" pattern: aggregate to find who has the most groups, then UNWIND the collected paths so the canvas draws the user node and all its group connections. Read the answer off the single User node label.

BloodHound Cypher - top user by transitive group memberships, rendered as a graph

Paste as one logical line in the Cypher search box.

MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group) WHERE u.enabled = true WITH u, COUNT(DISTINCT g) AS gc ORDER BY gc DESC LIMIT 1 MATCH p=(u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(:Group) RETURN p

What each piece does:

  • MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group) walk every user-to-group membership chain. *1.. traverses the full nesting chain.
  • WITH u, COUNT(DISTINCT g) AS gc ORDER BY gc DESC LIMIT 1 aggregate to find the user with the highest distinct-group count, then narrow the working set to just that one user.
  • MATCH p=(u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(:Group) RETURN p re-walk the paths from the winning user and return them as graph data so the canvas draws them.

The canvas draws ONE central User node fanning out into the group hierarchy. The user's sAMAccountName (lowercased, no @DOMAIN suffix) is your Question 3 answer.

Why two MATCH clauses? BHCE's Cypher REST serialization will not return RETURN p correctly when p was collected and unwound through an aggregation. Aggregating to find the winner with WITH ... LIMIT 1, then re-matching the paths from that single bound user, is the idiom that draws on the canvas reliably.

docs.title: Step 8: Answer Question 4 (Non-DA user with the most ACL-based control over other principals)
docs.text:
In modern AD, the most dangerous unprivileged accounts are usually NOT the ones with AdminTo edges to workstations. They're the ones who, via group membership, hold rewritable ACLs (GenericAll, WriteOwner, WriteDacl, ForceChangePassword, GenericWrite, AddSelf) over other users, groups, or computers. Those edges let an attacker pivot ownership of a target object without needing local admin on any host. BloodHound surfaces them as colored edges between principals.

Question 4 finds the non-Domain-Admin user whose group memberships transitively grant control over the most distinct target principals.

BloodHound Cypher - non-DA user with the most ACL reach, rendered as a graph

Paste as one logical line.

MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)-[:GenericAll|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ForceChangePassword|GenericWrite|AddSelf|AllowedToDelegate]->(target) WHERE u.enabled = true AND NOT (u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(:Group {name:'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL'}) WITH u, COUNT(DISTINCT target) AS reach ORDER BY reach DESC LIMIT 1 MATCH p=(u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(:Group)-[:GenericAll|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ForceChangePassword|GenericWrite|AddSelf|AllowedToDelegate]->() RETURN p

What this query does:

  • First MATCH walks every user-to-group-to-target ACL chain.
  • WHERE u.enabled = true AND NOT (u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(:Group {name:'DOMAIN ADMINS@...'}) excludes disabled accounts and anyone transitively in Domain Admins.
  • WITH u, COUNT(DISTINCT target) AS reach ORDER BY reach DESC LIMIT 1 aggregates to find the single user with the largest ACL reach.
  • Second MATCH re-walks the paths from that one user and returns them as graph data so the canvas draws everything.

The canvas draws ONE central User node, the group(s) they're in, and the targets those groups can take over. The user's sAMAccountName is your Question 4 answer.

Why this matters operationally: a single mis-scoped helpdesk group with WriteOwner on three sensitive accounts gives every member of that group a path to compromise those accounts. Find the user with the largest such fan-out and you've found the most leveraged unprivileged identity in the domain.

docs.title: Step 9: Compute the SHA-1 Hash
docs.text:
The scoring API expects the SHA-1 of your four answers concatenated in Q1+Q2+Q3+Q4 order. Producing a hash (rather than four free-text answers) means the API can validate without revealing the right answers in error messages.

Kali - Compute the SHA-1

Q1='27'                    # replace with your number
Q2='domain admins'         # replace
Q3='j.chen'                # replace
Q4='j.chen'                # replace
echo -n "${Q1}${Q2}${Q3}${Q4}" | sha1sum | awk '{print $1}'

What each piece does:

  • Q1='27' etc.: shell variables holding your answers as strings. Variable assignments must have no spaces around =.
  • echo -n "..." print the concatenation WITHOUT a trailing newline. The -n matters: SHA-1 of the same string with vs. without a newline produces totally different hashes; the scoring API computes its hash without the newline, so you must too.
  • ${Q1}${Q2}${Q3}${Q4} parameter expansion concatenated with no separator. The order matters; the scorer assumes Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 in that exact order.
  • | sha1sum pipe to the SHA-1 hasher. Output looks like <40-hex-chars> - (the trailing dash means "stdin").
  • | awk '{print $1}' keep only the first whitespace-separated field (the hash), drop the dash.

Final output is a 40-character hex string. Copy it for Step 9.

docs.title: Step 10: Submit to the Scorer
docs.text:
The scorer is a small HTTP service running on the same lab network as your Kali. Its IP is shown in the Active Lab View. The /submit endpoint validates your four answers and returns the flag if all match.

Kali - Submit answers to the scorer

curl -s -X POST http://<scorer_ip>:8080/submit \
  -d "q1=${Q1}" -d "q2=${Q2}" -d "q3=${Q3}" -d "q4=${Q4}"

What each option does:

  • -s silent. Suppresses curl's progress meter so the response prints cleanly. Useful when piping the output to jq or saving to a file.
  • -X POST use the HTTP POST method (curl defaults to GET). The scorer expects POST.
  • http://<scorer_ip>:8080/submit the scoring endpoint. Replace <scorer_ip> with the IP from the Active Lab View.
  • -d "q1=${Q1}" form data field. Each -d adds one URL-encoded form field. Multiple -d flags concatenate with & automatically. Equivalent: -d "q1=...&q2=...&q3=...&q4=..." as one big string.

On success the response JSON includes a flag key holding the OCR{...} value to submit to the platform. On failure the JSON lists which answer numbers were wrong (e.g. {"correct":[true,true,false,true]}).

Submit the flag to the OpenCyberRange platform.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) treats SharpHound-style collection as a top-priority signal. Once a single account starts pulling object properties, ACLs, sessions, and group membership across the entire forest in a few seconds, MDI fires the canonical "Reconnaissance using directory services queries" alert. The detection pivots are listed below.

Activity Signal Bulk LDAP property reads MDI alert: "Reconnaissance using directory services queries" Session enumeration via SAMR/NetSessionEnum MDI alert: "User and IP address reconnaissance (SMB)" Cross-DC kerberoast of every SPN Event 4769 spike on each DC Wide LDAP queries Diagnostic event 1644 with high searchSize

What collectors look like to a SOC

SharpHound finishes a small domain in under a minute and emits a recognizable burst pattern: a few hundred 4624 logon events, thousands of 4662 directory-access events, and a tail of 5145 (network share access) on every DC. Splitting the collection into multiple sessions across hours can reduce the burst signature, but defenders running MDI on the DC catch the pattern even when the collection is paced.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
You cannot kill BloodHound without breaking AD itself; defenders settle for raising the cost of the collection and shrinking the resulting graph. The list below is the hardening menu most blue teams reach for.

Mitigations that change BloodHound output

  • Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity on every DC. Detection accuracy is high and the SOC sees the collector immediately.
  • Disable anonymous SAMR (Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM GPO). Forces collectors to authenticate to enumerate sessions.
  • Remove Authenticated Users read on Tier 0 OUs so privileged accounts do not appear in the graph at all.
  • Audit and prune nested group membership; the longer the path, the more rope BloodHound finds for an attacker.
  • Set dsHeuristics bit 0 to 1 to disable anonymous LDAP bind.
  • Ship DC Security and Directory Services logs to a SIEM with high-cardinality query alerts on event 1644.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Question 1: (integer)

Question 2: (sAMAccountName)

Question 3: (sAMAccountName)

Question 4: (sAMAccountName)

Concatenation:

(Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4)

SHA-1:

(40-char hex)

(OCR{...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The collection methods passed to SharpHound differ in noise level. Session collects active user sessions, which requires admin SMB access to remote hosts. Why does collecting Session matter for offensive planning, and what is the noisier alternative?

Reveal Answer

Session populates HasSession edges between users and computers. Knowing where a Domain Admin currently has an active session is the difference between a clean attack path (kerberoast a service account that DA logs into) and a broken one (the DA never logs into anything reachable). The noisier alternative is LoggedOn, which queries each remote host for its session list via SAMR/NetSessionEnum. LoggedOn finds users who do not currently have an active session but have logged on recently, but it makes a connection to every computer in the collection set, which is loud. Operators usually run Session on the first pass and only escalate to LoggedOn when the path search needs more data.

2. Why does BloodHound store object names UPPERCASE in the graph, and what gotcha does that introduce when writing Cypher queries?

Reveal Answer

BloodHound normalizes names to UPPERCASE with the domain in UPN form for case-insensitive matching: AD itself treats j.chen and J.CHEN as the same identity, but Neo4j is case-sensitive by default. By forcing UPPERCASE during ingest, BloodHound side-steps this. The gotcha: when you copy a username from another tool (rpcclient, ldapsearch) and paste it into a Cypher query, you must uppercase it and append @DOMAIN or your query returns no results. A common mistake is searching for 'j.chen' instead of 'J.CHEN@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' and concluding the user does not exist. Use the BloodHound search bar to find the canonical name first, then copy it into Cypher.

3. The official BloodHound CE docs use [*1..] (unbounded depth) in shortestPath(). Why is that safe in BHCE when unbounded path searches are notorious memory hogs?

Reveal Answer

Cypher's shortestPath() function is special-cased in the planner: it terminates as soon as the first matching path is found, even with unbounded depth. The unbounded [*1..] does NOT mean "search every possible path"; it means "find the shortest one, however many hops it takes". Because shortestPath() is bounded by the actual minimum, BHCE's planner explores at most the diameter of the reachable graph rather than every possible path. That makes [*1..] perfectly safe for shortestPath(). Bounded depth ([*1..15]) is only useful for allShortestPaths() or unbounded path enumeration, not for finding a single shortest path. The BHCE Privilege Zones rules all use [*1..] for this reason.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• BloodHound turns LDAP enumeration into a graph. The collector reads the same data ldapsearch reads; the visualization is the difference.
  • Names in the BloodHound graph are stored UPPERCASE with @DOMAIN.TLD; raw lowercase usernames will not match in Cypher.
  • BloodHound CE's curated rule library lives under Privilege Zones -> All Rules -> Default Routes; each rule is a pre-saved Cypher query.
  • Canonical BHCE Cypher pattern (per the official docs): MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group)) WHERE m.name = '<NAME>@<DOMAIN>' RETURN p is the workhorse for any attack-path question.
  • [*1..] (unbounded) is safe inside shortestPath(); the planner returns at the first match. Avoid chaining MATCH clauses without WITH; keep shortestPath() on a single line; scalar RETURN values only show in the Table view tab.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover the BloodHound workflow from collection to first attack-path read. Memorize the shapes; the specifics change per engagement.

Step Command / Query Collect bloodhound-python -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> -ns <dc> -c All --zip Start GUI sudo bloodhound cli start then open http://localhost:8080 Path to DA (visual) Privilege Zones -> All Rules -> Default Routes; or paste Cypher directly on Explore tab Path to DA (Cypher) MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group)) WHERE m.name = 'DOMAIN ADMINS@<DOMAIN>' RETURN p

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: SharpHound Linux Collection

Q: Write the bloodhound-python command to collect every method against corp.local at DC 10.10.10.10 as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
bloodhound-python -u j.smith -p 'Pass#' \
  -d corp.local -ns 10.10.10.10 \
  -c All --zip

-c All enables Group, LocalAdmin, Session, Trusts, ACL, Container, RDP, ObjectProps, LoggedOn, DCOM, PSRemote. --zip bundles the JSON outputs.

Card 2: BloodHound Path Cypher

Q: Write the Cypher query to find the shortest path from user j.smith@corp.local to the Domain Admins group at corp.local.

Answer 
MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group)) WHERE n.name = 'J.SMITH@CORP.LOCAL' AND m.name = 'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.LOCAL' RETURN p

Canonical BloodHound CE form (matches the official docs at bloodhound.specterops.io/analyze-data/bloodhound-gui/cypher-search). Single MATCH, single WHERE with AND, RETURN p so the graph view renders it. Names are UPPERCASE with @DOMAIN.TLD suffix. Keep the entire query on one logical line; pasted line wraps inside the WHERE string literal break the comparison.

Card 3: BloodHound Edges to Memorize

Q: Name five BloodHound edge types that represent direct privilege grants and explain what each enables.

Answer

GenericAll; full control over the target (you can do anything to it). GenericWrite; write any property (set SPNs, change membership). WriteDACL; modify the target's ACL (add your own grant). WriteOwner; take ownership, then grant yourself further rights. ForceChangePassword; reset the target user's password without knowing the old one. Honorable mention: AddMember (add yourself to a group) and AllowedToAct (RBCD trust).

Card 4: Why Sessions Matter

Q: A BloodHound collection without Session data is missing what attack signal, and how does that change planning?

Answer

Session populates HasSession edges showing which users currently have an active session on which computer. Without it, you cannot tell where a Domain Admin currently is, which means kerberoast / overpass-the-hash plans cannot prioritize accounts whose tickets are sitting in memory on reachable hosts. Operators who skip Session end up with attack paths that look great on paper but require waiting for the right user to log on to the right host before they execute.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
The least glamorous attack in offensive AD is reading files. Operators leak credentials, network diagrams, deploy scripts, and configuration files onto SMB shares constantly. Defenders almost never audit them. Exercise 1.3 asks you to do what every senior pentester does in the first hour of an engagement: tour every reachable share, classify what is in it, and find the document with your scope token in its filename.

Tools required: netexec, smbclient, manspider, plus optional GUI helper smbmap. All are pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "Half of the breaches I have done in the last five years started by reading a file someone left on a share. Engineering at Nordport keeps a quarterly handover folder that everyone forgets to clean up. Find the document with your scope token in its filename. Open it. Submit the flag inside."

Your scope token is a four-character lowercase hex string assigned to you by the platform. You see it on the lab dashboard ("Your scope: a7f3") and your Kali workstation has it set as the environment variable OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate shares on corp-dc01 and corp-dc01
  • Identify shares with read access for j.chen
  • Recursively spider the readable shares
  • Locate the handover document whose filename contains your scope token
  • Read the file, extract the flag, and submit it

docs.title: Lab Topology
docs.text:
All shares for this exercise live on corp-dc01. You attack from Kali; the DC exposes both replicated shares (SYSVOL, NETLOGON) and the department shares (Engineering, Public, Backup-Old).

flowchart LR
    Kali["Kali Workstation"]
    DC["corp-dc01<br/>SYSVOL, NETLOGON, Engineering, Public, Backup-Old"]
    Kali -- "SMB :445" --> DC

docs.title: How Effective Access is Computed
docs.text:
Two ACLs gate every share read. The effective answer is the AND of both. The flowchart below mirrors the decision the file server makes for every request.

flowchart TD
    Q["SMB request from j.chen"]
    Q --> S{"Share-level ACL<br/>permits action?"}
    S -- "No" --> D1["Deny<br/>NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED"]
    S -- "Yes" --> N{"NTFS ACL on<br/>file/folder permits?"}
    N -- "No" --> D2["Deny<br/>NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED"]
    N -- "Yes" --> A["Allow<br/>read returns data"]

docs.title: Background: SMB Shares and Access Masks
docs.text:
A share is a named directory exposed over SMB. Every share has two layers of permissions:

  1. Share-level permissions (configured on the share itself: Full, Change, Read, None)
  2. NTFS permissions on the underlying directory (the file-system ACLs)

The effective permission is the most restrictive of the two. If the share grants Full but NTFS only allows Read, you get Read.

For enumeration, you mostly care about whether you have any read access at all. netexec --shares reports the share-level masks; smbclient will fail with NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED if NTFS denies you regardless of share permission.

docs.title: Common share names and meanings
docs.text: Share name Meaning ADMIN$ Hidden admin share, mapped to C:\Windows. Requires admin to access. C$, D$, etc. Hidden drive shares. Admin-only. IPC$ Inter-process communication endpoint. Always present, used for null sessions. NETLOGON Replicated logon scripts. Read-only to domain users. Often readable. SYSVOL Replicated GPOs and scripts. Read-only to domain users. Often readable. Public, Common, Departmental Custom org shares. Usually readable by Domain Users. Backup-Old, Archives, Legacy Stale shares. Most credential leaks live here.

docs.title: The pattern: read everything once, filter forever
docs.text: The first sweep should pull every readable file to local disk. Once everything is local, grep and pattern-matching make finding interesting strings near-instant. Reading files individually over SMB is slow and rate-limited.

docs.title: netexec for share inventory
docs.text:
netexec smb <host> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --shares

Output shows a table:

SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     [+] corp.nordport.local\j.chen:Welcome2026#
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     [*] Enumerated shares
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     Share         Permissions     Remark
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     -----         -----------     ------
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     ADMIN$                        Remote Admin
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     C$                            Default share
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     IPC$          READ            Remote IPC
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     Engineering   READ            Engineering team share
SMB    10.x.x.10    445   CORP-DC01     Public        READ            Company-wide bulletin board

A blank Permissions column means access denied. READ means you can list and download. READ,WRITE means you can also drop files (rare on production shares but huge if you find it).

docs.title: smbclient interactive mode
docs.text:
smbclient //corp-dc01/Engineering -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#"

At the smb: \> prompt:

Command Effect ls List current directory cd <path> Change directory recurse on Toggle recursive operations prompt off Disable per-file confirmation mget * Download all files in current directory get <file> Download a single file more <file> View a file inline exit Quit

The combination recurse on; prompt off; mget * mirrors a share to your current local directory.

docs.title: manspider for content scanning
docs.text:
manspider recursively spiders shares and greps file contents for arbitrary patterns. Useful for hunting credentials at scale.

manspider <host> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local \
  --content "OCR\{" -e txt,docx,xml,ini,xls,xlsx
Flag Effect --content "OCR\{" regex to match in file contents -e txt,docx,xml,ini,xls,xlsx only search these file extensions -d domain - Hits print the file path and the matching line

docs.title: Step 1: Note Your Scope Token
docs.text:
The platform injects your scope token into your Kali container's environment as OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN. Workbook commands reference ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} directly so the same paste works for any student. Confirm the variable is set before you start so a missing token does not waste 20 minutes of attempts.

Kali - Print scope token

echo "$OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN"

What this does:

  • echo prints its arguments. With variable expansion (the $VAR form), bash substitutes the value before echo sees it.
  • Quoted with double-quotes so an empty variable produces an empty (but visible) output rather than a parse error.

The output should be a four-character lowercase string (example: a7f3, j001, or fsat). If the variable is empty, find your token in the lab dashboard banner ("Your scope: ...") and export it manually with export OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN=<your_token>.

docs.title: Step 2: Inventory Shares on Both Hosts
docs.text:
SMB share enumeration is the first step of any share-credential hunt. The goal is a list of every reachable share with the access mask the authenticating user has on each. netexec --shares gets you the table in one call.

Kali - Enumerate shares on the DC

netexec smb <dc_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --shares

What each option does:

Flag Effect smb Module: speaks SMB on port 445. <dc_ip> Target. Accepts a single IP, a CIDR (10.0.0.0/24), or a host file (-t hosts.txt). -u j.chen Username for the bind. -p 'Welcome2026#' Password. Quote so # and ! survive bash. -d corp.nordport.local Domain realm. --shares Issue an SRVSVC NetShareEnumAll RPC and parse the results.

What the columns mean in the output:

  • Share: the share name as registered on the host (e.g. IPC$, Engineering, Public).
  • Permissions: what the authenticated user can do on the share. Possible values: blank (denied), READ, READ,WRITE, or Admin (rare, only for service accounts that are local admin).
  • Remark: the description set by the share's creator. Sometimes useful (helpdesk staff put notes here).

Note every share where Permissions is non-blank. Skip the standard hidden shares (ADMIN$, C$, D$, IPC$) unless the access shows you have unexpected rights on them.

Kali - Enumerate shares on corp-dc01

netexec smb <fileserver_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --shares

Same flags, different host. The DC and corp-dc01 expose different share sets because the DC has SYSVOL and NETLOGON (replicated GPO content) while corp-dc01 has the actual user-accessible department shares like Engineering, Finance, IT-Tools, and Public. The Engineering share on corp-dc01 is the target for this exercise.

docs.title: Step 3: Walk the Engineering Share
docs.text:
netexec told us WHICH shares are reachable; smbclient lets us browse them interactively. The interactive shell is faster than running 20 separate commands when you are exploring a directory tree.

Kali - Browse the Engineering share

smbclient //corp-dc01/Engineering -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#"

What each piece does:

  • //corp-dc01/Engineering UNC path: //<host>/<share>. NetBIOS name resolution comes from the lab's DNS (the DC), so corp-dc01 resolves to the right IP if your /etc/resolv.conf points at it; otherwise use the literal IP.
  • -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" credential bundle. Format: DOMAIN\user%password. The backslash needs no escaping inside double quotes for bash.

Once connected, you land at the smb: \> prompt. Useful built-in commands:

Command Effect ls List the current directory. cd <path> Change directory. Use forward slashes; backslashes work too. recurse on Toggle recursive operations for subsequent ls/mget. prompt off Disable per-file confirmation on bulk operations. mget * Download every file in current directory to local CWD. more <file> Page a file inline without downloading. exit or quit Leave the prompt.

Walk the directory tree:

ls
cd Handovers
ls

The Handovers directory holds the per-quarter notes engineering teams typically forget to clean up. One file in there has your token in its filename.

docs.title: Step 4: Filter to Your Token
docs.text:
Walking the entire directory tree by hand is fine for a small share. For a real engagement with hundreds of files, use the non-interactive form of smbclient and let glob matching do the filtering.

Kali - Find your file with one smbclient command

smbclient //corp-dc01/Engineering -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "cd Handovers; ls *${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}*"

What is new on this invocation:

  • -c "..." non-interactive command string. smbclient runs the semicolon-separated commands and exits, instead of dropping into the interactive prompt. Same shell built-ins as the interactive mode work.
  • ls *${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}* shell-glob filter. The * wildcards match any chars; the variable is expanded by BASH (not by smbclient) before the command is sent. So if your token is j001, the literal command sent is ls *j001*.

The output shows exactly one matching file: engineering_handover_<token>.txt.

docs.title: Step 5: Download and Read
docs.text:
Same non-interactive smbclient pattern, but this time use get to pull the file to local disk, then cat it.

Kali - Get the file

smbclient //corp-dc01/Engineering -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "cd Handovers; get engineering_handover_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat engineering_handover_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt

What each piece does:

  • get <remote-name> download a file from the share to your current local directory. To save under a different name use get <remote> <local>.
  • The variable expansion happens in the BASH layer, not the SMB layer; if OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN is unset, the path becomes engineering_handover_.txt and get will return NT_STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND.
  • cat is the standard Unix file printer; nothing SMB-specific.

The flag string appears inside the file. Submit it on the platform. The flag has the form OCR{<shares_as_directory_listings_theme>} for this exercise, distinct from any other exercise's flag.

docs.title: Step 6: Try the Mass-Spider Approach (Bonus)
docs.text:
When you do not know the filename pattern (which is the realistic case in a fresh engagement), grep file CONTENTS instead of names. manspider is purpose-built for this: it spiders every reachable share, opens supported file types, and runs your regex against the content.

Kali - Mass content search across the Engineering share

manspider <fileserver_ip> -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local \
  --content "OCR\{smb_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" -e txt

What each option does:

Flag Effect <fileserver_ip> Target host. Accepts CIDR for multi-host sweeps. -u, -p, -d Same credentials as smbclient/netexec. --content "<regex>" Regex to match file contents. Supports the full Python re syntax. -e txt Restrict to .txt extension. Add more with comma: -e txt,docx,xlsx,csv,ini.

Other flags worth knowing:

  • -d corp.nordport.local: the domain (already shown above; included in the comparison only if you confuse it with the manspider -d for "search depth").
  • --depth 5: limit recursion depth. Default is unlimited; for very deep shares this prevents runaway scans.
  • --exclude-shares ADMIN$,C$,IPC$: skip the noisy admin shares. Default behaviour skips IPC$ already.

Manspider returns the file path that contains the matching string. Both approaches (filename glob in step 4, content regex here) reach the same answer; the second one scales when you do not yet know the filename pattern.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Share enumeration and bulk file reads are noisy at the file-server log level even though they look benign on the wire. A SOC pulling the Security log can spot a wide spider in minutes. The mapping below shows what each step lights up.

Activity Event ID Source Connect to share 5140 File server Security log File access (object access auditing) 4663 File server Security log Detailed file access 5145 File server Security log Failed share access 5140 + 4625 File server Security log

Why a manspider sweep stands out

A manspider against a single share generates one 5140 per file plus a 4663 burst. On a healthy share with 5,000 files the audit log gains ~10,000 entries in under a minute, which is the same volume a backup agent generates over four hours. SOCs that baseline events per identity per minute on file servers catch the burst.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
Defenders cannot disable SMB without breaking file services, but they can shrink the attack surface significantly. The list below is the practical checklist.

What would have stopped this exercise

  • Scope Domain Users off the Engineering share; replace with Engineering_All.
  • Enforce Object Access auditing on file servers and ship 4663/5140/5145 to the SIEM.
  • Run quarterly internal manspider against all readable shares with a credential-pattern regex; remove or quarantine matches.
  • Disable SMB1 entirely (Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false).
  • Require SMB signing on all servers and enforce it via Group Policy.
  • Tag stale shares with a 30-day archival lifecycle so Backup-Old and Archives cannot accumulate forever.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Shares with read access on corp-dc01:

Share Permissions

Filename containing your token:

(filename here)

Flag:

(OCR{...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The Engineering share allows read for Domain Users. From a defender's perspective, what makes that configuration risky, and what is the standard mitigation?

Reveal Answer

Granting read on a department share to all Domain Users means every authenticated user in the company, including freshly hired junior staff, contractors, and any compromised account, can read every file. Engineering teams routinely place onboarding docs, deploy scripts, vendor lists, and partial credentials on those shares. The standard mitigation is least-privileged share scoping: each share is restricted to a department-specific group (Engineering_All) rather than Domain Users, NTFS permissions match, and the share contents are audited periodically with tools like manspider against a regex of common credential patterns. A defender who ran manspider --content "password" against their own shares quarterly would catch most of these leaks.

2. manspider matches against file contents, including binary files like .docx and .xlsx. How does it read inside those compressed Office formats?

Reveal Answer

.docx, .xlsx, .pptx are zip archives containing XML files (word/document.xml, xl/sharedStrings.xml, etc.). Manspider unzips each file in memory, concatenates the XML content, and runs the regex against the concatenated text. Older .doc and .xls formats use a binary OLE container, for which manspider relies on a converter (olefile or antiword style libraries). PDFs are extracted with pdftotext under the hood. Encrypted Office documents will not match because the inner XML is encrypted at rest; manspider cannot search them without a known password.

3. You have read access on the IT-Tools share. Name three patterns to grep for that frequently surface credentials.

Reveal Answer

password\s*=, password:\s*, pwd:; match config files and shell scripts. cpassword; the Group Policy Preferences AES-encrypted password attribute (legacy, but still found). connectionString= and DSN=; ODBC and ADO.NET connection strings often embed plaintext passwords. Bonus targets: BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY, aws_secret_access_key, client_secret, Authorization: Basic. Combine with manspider's --content flag in a regex alternation: --content "password\s*=|cpassword|connectionString=|client_secret".

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SMB share enumeration is the highest-yield activity in the first hour of an AD engagement.
  • netexec --shares gives a clean inventory; smbclient browses interactively; manspider greps at scale.
  • Two permission layers (share + NTFS) determine effective access; the most restrictive wins.
  • recurse on; prompt off; mget * is the smbclient idiom to mirror a share to local disk.
  • Tools that grep inside .docx and .xlsx work because those formats are zipped XML.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below are the SMB tour, condensed. Run them on every host that exposes 445 in the first 30 minutes of any AD engagement.

Goal Command Inventory shares with permission masks netexec smb <host> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --shares Browse a share interactively smbclient //<host>/<share> -U "<DOMAIN>\<user>%<pw>" Mirror a share to local disk smbclient //<host>/<share> -U "..." -c "recurse on; prompt off; mget *" Grep file contents at scale manspider <host> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --content "<regex>" -e txt,ini,xml,docx,xlsx

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: netexec Share Enumeration

Q: Write the netexec command to list shares on 10.10.10.10 for corp.local as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
netexec smb 10.10.10.10 -u j.smith -p 'Pass#' -d corp.local --shares

Add --filter-shares READ,WRITE to show only shares with at least read access.

Card 2: smbclient One-Liner Mirror

Q: Write the smbclient command that recursively downloads all files from \\srv01\Backup-Old using corp.local\j.smith / Pass# to your current directory.

Answer 
smbclient //srv01/Backup-Old -U "CORP\j.smith%Pass#" \
  -c "recurse on; prompt off; mget *"

recurse on enables descent into subdirectories. prompt off skips the per-file confirmation. mget * downloads everything in the current remote directory.

Card 3: manspider for Credential Hunt

Q: Write the manspider command to search every reachable share on 10.10.10.10 for the substring "password=" inside .txt, .ini, .xml, and .config files.

Answer 
manspider 10.10.10.10 -u j.smith -p 'Pass#' -d corp.local \
  --content "password=" -e txt,ini,xml,config

Add multiple patterns with |: --content "password=|cpassword|client_secret".

Card 4: Effective Permission Rule

Q: A share grants Full Control to Domain Users but the underlying NTFS permission grants only Read. What can a domain user do?

Answer

Read only. The effective permission is the most restrictive of share and NTFS. The share-level permission gates SMB-layer access; the NTFS permission gates filesystem-layer access. Both must permit an action for it to succeed. Defenders often leave share-level permissions wide (Full Control to Everyone) and rely on NTFS to do the gating, which works but is harder to audit.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Kerberos is the protocol behind nearly every offensive Active Directory attack worth knowing. ASREPRoast attacks the AS-REP message. Kerberoast attacks the TGS-REP message. Golden ticket forges a TGT inside an AS-REP. Silver ticket forges a TGS-REP. None of these attacks make sense until you can name the four messages of the Kerberos exchange and point at which fields they manipulate.

Exercise 1.4 puts the protocol in front of you on the wire. You will run tshark while triggering authentications, decode the AS-REQ, AS-REP, TGS-REQ, and TGS-REP messages, and pull a flag fragment out of three different message fields.

Tools required: tshark, wireshark, smbclient, kinit. All are pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "Every Kerberos attack worth knowing exploits one specific message in the exchange. You cannot abuse what you do not understand. Capture the protocol, read it, name the parts. Three fragments of the flag are split across three Kerberos message fields. Find them all, concatenate them in the order AS-REQ + AS-REP + TGS-REQ, and submit."

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local Domain controller: corp-dc01

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Capture Kerberos AS-REQ and AS-REP exchanges between your Kali and the DC
  • Capture a TGS-REQ and TGS-REP triggered by an SMB connection to a member service
  • Identify the encrypted-timestamp field in the AS-REQ
  • Locate the TGT inside the AS-REP
  • Read the sname field in a TGS-REQ to identify the service requested
  • Concatenate three fragments and submit the assembled flag

docs.title: Background: The Four Messages of Kerberos
docs.text: Kerberos answers two questions: "who are you?" and "what may you talk to?" It separates the two by issuing two different kinds of tickets.

docs.title: Ticket Lifecycle at a Glance
docs.text:
The diagram below collapses an entire authentication-to-service-access flow into one picture. Hold this in your head for the rest of the track; every Kerberos attack twists exactly one arrow on this diagram.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client (Kali / j.chen)
    participant K as KDC (corp-dc01)
    participant S as Service (cifs/file01)

    Note over C,K: Step 1 -- Authentication (AS exchange)
    C->>K: AS-REQ<br/>cname=j.chen, padata=ENC-TIMESTAMP(user_key)
    K-->>C: AS-REP<br/>TGT enc with krbtgt_key + session_key enc with user_key

    Note over C,K: Step 2 -- Authorization (TGS exchange)
    C->>K: TGS-REQ<br/>TGT in padata, sname=cifs/file01
    K-->>C: TGS-REP<br/>service ticket enc with service_key

    Note over C,S: Step 3 -- Service access (AP exchange)
    C->>S: AP-REQ<br/>service ticket presented over SMB
    S-->>C: AP-REP / SMB session established

docs.title: AS-REQ / AS-REP: identity
docs.text:
The Authentication Service exchange proves who you are and gives you a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT).

Client                                                    KDC (DC)
  |                                                          |
  |  AS-REQ  (cname=j.chen, realm=CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL,       |
  |          padata: pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP encrypted with         |
  |          the user's password-derived key)                |
  |--------------------------------------------------------->|
  |                                                          |
  |                                          [KDC verifies   |
  |                                           timestamp can  |
  |                                           be decrypted   |
  |                                           with user key] |
  |                                                          |
  |  AS-REP  (TGT encrypted with krbtgt's key,               |
  |          enc-part with session key encrypted to user)    |
  |<---------------------------------------------------------|

The pre-authentication padata is the security boundary that ASREPRoast attacks. If pre-auth is disabled (DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag), the KDC sends an AS-REP without checking the timestamp first. The encrypted enc-part is then crackable offline because it is encrypted with a derivation of the user's password.

docs.title: TGS-REQ / TGS-REP: authorization
docs.text:
Once you have a TGT you ask the KDC for service tickets, one per service you want to talk to.

Client                                                    KDC
  |                                                          |
  |  TGS-REQ (TGT in padata, sname=cifs/file01, ...)         |
  |--------------------------------------------------------->|
  |                                                          |
  |                                          [KDC validates  |
  |                                           TGT, checks    |
  |                                           that user can  |
  |                                           access target] |
  |                                                          |
  |  TGS-REP (service ticket encrypted with the              |
  |          target service account's key)                   |
  |<---------------------------------------------------------|
  |                                                          |
  |                                                       Service
  |  AP-REQ  (service ticket presented to the service)       |
  |--------------------------------------------------------->|

The service ticket is encrypted with the service account's password-derived key, not the user's. That is the boundary Kerberoast attacks. If the service account password is weak, the encrypted blob can be cracked offline. The TGS-REQ itself is observable on the wire to anyone watching the KDC; that is how SOC tools detect mass enumeration.

docs.title: The four-message map
docs.text:
Message Purpose Encrypted with AS-REQ Request a TGT, prove identity User's key (in pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP) AS-REP TGT issued TGT body: krbtgt key. Enc-part: user key. TGS-REQ Request a service ticket TGT presented as proof TGS-REP Service ticket issued Ticket body: service account key. Enc-part: TGT session key.

Memorize this table. It is the framework every Kerberos attack maps to.

docs.title: Which Attack Touches Which Message
docs.text:
Each major Kerberos attack hijacks exactly one of the four messages. The map below tells you where on the wire each technique lives. Refer back here when you reach Levels 3 through 5 of the track.

flowchart TD
    AS_REQ["AS-REQ<br/>(client to KDC)"]
    AS_REP["AS-REP<br/>(KDC to client)"]
    TGS_REQ["TGS-REQ<br/>(client to KDC)"]
    TGS_REP["TGS-REP<br/>(KDC to client)"]

    AS_REP -- "no preauth -> crackable" --> ASREP["ASREPRoast<br/>(Hashcat 18200)"]
    TGS_REP -- "weak service pw -> crackable" --> KROAST["Kerberoast<br/>(Hashcat 13100)"]
    AS_REP -- "forge TGT body w/ krbtgt key" --> GOLD["Golden Ticket"]
    TGS_REP -- "forge service ticket w/ service key" --> SILV["Silver Ticket"]
    TGS_REQ -- "S4U2self + S4U2proxy" --> DEL["Delegation abuse<br/>(constrained / RBCD)"]

docs.title: tshark
docs.text:
The CLI version of Wireshark. Lighter than the GUI, scriptable, and handles all the same dissectors.

sudo tshark -i any -f "host <dc_ip> and port 88" -w kerb.pcap
Flag Effect -i any capture on any interface -f "..." BPF filter to keep the capture small (port 88 is Kerberos) -w kerb.pcap write to a file you can open in Wireshark later

To analyze a capture file from the CLI:

tshark -r kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 10"   # AS-REQ
tshark -r kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 11"   # AS-REP
tshark -r kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 12"   # TGS-REQ
tshark -r kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 13"   # TGS-REP

Kerberos message types are integers; remember 10/11/12/13.

docs.title: Wireshark Kerberos display filters
docs.text: Filter Matches kerberos All Kerberos packets kerberos.msg_type == 10 AS-REQ kerberos.msg_type == 11 AS-REP kerberos.msg_type == 12 TGS-REQ kerberos.msg_type == 13 TGS-REP kerberos.CNameString == "j.chen" Packets where the cname is j.chen kerberos.SNameString == "cifs" Service tickets for cifs

docs.title: kinit (manual TGT request)
docs.text:
kinit j.chen@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL

kinit performs a clean AS-REQ/AS-REP cycle and stores the resulting TGT in your local credential cache (klist to view). Useful for triggering an isolated AS exchange without the side effects of a full SMB connect.

docs.title: smbclient (TGS triggering)
docs.text:
Once you have a TGT in cache, an SMB connect to a domain-joined host triggers a TGS-REQ for cifs/<host>.

smbclient //corp-dc01/Public -k

The -k flag tells smbclient to use the cached Kerberos credential rather than prompting for a password.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Launch Kerberos Walkthrough from the AD Penetration Track. Note the DC IP from the Active Lab View.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Your Kerberos Realm
docs.text:
Linux Kerberos clients (kinit, klist, kdestroy, anything that speaks GSSAPI) read /etc/krb5.conf to find out which KDC serves which realm and how to talk to it. Without this file every Kerberos call defaults to either no realm at all or whatever Kerberos picks up from DNS SRV records, which is fragile.

Kali - Configure /etc/krb5.conf

sudo tee /etc/krb5.conf >/dev/null <<EOF
[libdefaults]
    default_realm = CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
    dns_lookup_kdc = true
    dns_lookup_realm = false

[realms]
    CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL = {
        kdc = <dc_ip>
        admin_server = <dc_ip>
    }

[domain_realm]
    .corp.nordport.local = CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
    corp.nordport.local = CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
EOF

What each piece does:

  • sudo tee /etc/krb5.conf >/dev/null write standard input to the file as root, redirecting tee's stdout to /dev/null so the heredoc doesn't echo back.
  • <<EOF ... EOF heredoc; the lines between are sent to tee as input.
  • [libdefaults] default_realm = CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL the realm to assume when one is not specified. Kerberos realm names are conventionally the uppercase form of the domain FQDN.
  • dns_lookup_kdc = true if a realm is not in the [realms] block, ask DNS for _kerberos._tcp.<realm> SRV records. AD publishes these by default.
  • dns_lookup_realm = false do NOT trust DNS to map a hostname to a realm; use the explicit [domain_realm] mapping below. Disabling this avoids spoofing risk in untrusted networks.
  • [realms] block: maps each realm name to a list of KDCs. kdc = <dc_ip> says "this IP is a KDC for CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL". admin_server is the host that handles password changes via kpasswd (port 464); same IP for AD.
  • [domain_realm] maps DNS-style hostnames to Kerberos realms. The leading dot form (.corp.nordport.local) matches all subdomains; the bare form matches the realm itself.

Replace <dc_ip> with the IP shown in the lab dashboard. Verify with cat /etc/krb5.conf after writing.

docs.title: Step 3: Start the Capture
docs.text:
Open two terminals: one for tshark to capture packets, one to drive the auth flow. Capturing is read-only; nothing depends on the order between the two terminals other than starting tshark BEFORE the auth so you do not miss the first packets.

Kali - Start tshark capturing all Kerberos traffic

sudo tshark -i any -f "host <dc_ip> and (port 88 or port 445)" \
  -w /tmp/kerb.pcap

What each option does:

Flag Effect sudo Required: only root can put an interface in promiscuous mode and read raw packets. -i any Capture on every available interface. tshark merges packets from all NICs into one stream. Use -i eth0 to limit to one interface. -f "host <dc_ip> and (port 88 or port 445)" BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) capture filter. Applied at kernel level, drops non-matching packets before tshark sees them. Drastically reduces capture file size. -w /tmp/kerb.pcap Write captured packets to a file in pcap format. Without -w, tshark prints to stdout (one line per packet).

The BPF filter explained:

  • host <dc_ip> packets where source OR destination matches the DC IP.
  • port 88 or port 445 Kerberos (88) OR SMB (445). Kerberos rides over both UDP and TCP/88; SMB carries the AP-REQ tickets we want to inspect.
  • The combination: capture every packet to or from the DC on those two ports.

Leave tshark running in this terminal. The pcap grows until you Ctrl-C the process. Open a SECOND terminal for the next steps.

docs.title: Step 4: Trigger the AS Exchange
docs.text:
kinit performs a clean AS-REQ/AS-REP cycle and stores the resulting TGT in the local credential cache. Useful for triggering an isolated AS exchange without the side effects of a full SMB connect.

Kali - Request a TGT for j.chen

echo 'Welcome2026#' | kinit j.chen@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
klist

What each piece does:

  • echo 'Welcome2026#' | kinit ... pipe the password into kinit's stdin. By default kinit prompts interactively; piping skips the prompt.
  • kinit j.chen@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL request a TGT for the principal j.chen in the realm CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL. The realm form is user@REALM (always uppercase realm).
  • klist list cached tickets. After a successful kinit you see one TGT (krbtgt/CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL) with a 10-hour default lifetime.

Common errors:

  • kinit: Clock skew too great while getting initial credentials: your Kali clock differs from the DC's by more than 5 minutes. Fix: sudo ntpdate -u <dc_ip> (uses the DC's clock as the reference) or sudo timedatectl set-ntp true if your network has working NTP.
  • kinit: Pre-authentication failed while getting initial credentials: wrong password.
  • kinit: Cannot find KDC for realm: /etc/krb5.conf is missing or the realm name is wrong.

docs.title: Step 5: Trigger the TGS Exchange
docs.text:
Once you have a TGT cached, the next step in normal Kerberos flow is requesting a service ticket (TGS) for some service. Connecting to SMB on the DC triggers a TGS-REQ for cifs/<host>.

Kali - Trigger a TGS-REQ for cifs/corp-dc01

smbclient //corp-dc01/Public -k -c "ls"

What each option does:

  • //corp-dc01/Public UNC path: SMB connect to the Public share on corp-dc01. Use the FQDN or short name; smbclient resolves it via /etc/hosts, then DNS, then NetBIOS.
  • -k use Kerberos authentication: present the cached TGT to the KDC and exchange it for a TGS for cifs/<host>. WITHOUT -k, smbclient falls back to NTLM and uses the password from -U (no Kerberos exchange happens at all).
  • -c "ls" non-interactive: run ls then exit.

What happens on the wire (visible in the pcap):

  1. Client sends TGS-REQ to KDC, padata contains the TGT-wrapped AP-REQ.
  2. KDC returns TGS-REP with a service ticket encrypted with corp-dc01$'s machine key.
  3. Client opens TCP/445 to corp-dc01 and presents the service ticket inside an AP-REQ.
  4. corp-dc01 decrypts and accepts; SMB session established; share lists.

Once the share lists, stop the capture in the first terminal with Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Step 6: Analyze AS-REQ for Fragment 1
docs.text:
Open the captured pcap and filter to the AS-REQ packets only. tshark in read mode (no -i, just -r) is the same dissector as Wireshark with no GUI overhead.

Kali - Read the AS-REQ packet

tshark -r /tmp/kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 10" | less

What each option does:

Flag Effect -r /tmp/kerb.pcap Read mode: parse this pcap file instead of capturing live. -V Verbose: print the FULL dissector tree (every protocol layer, every field). Without -V, tshark prints a one-line summary per packet. -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 10" Display filter (different from BPF capture filter). Applied AFTER dissection; can reference parsed fields like kerberos.msg_type. The integer 10 is the AS-REQ Kerberos message type. \| less Page the output (verbose dissector trees are tens of lines per packet). Use space/b for next/previous page, q to quit.

Kerberos message types worth memorizing: AS-REQ=10, AS-REP=11, TGS-REQ=12, TGS-REP=13. Every Kerberos attack maps to one of these.

Inside the AS-REQ you will see:

Kerberos
    Pvno: 5
    MSG Type: AS-REQ (10)
    padata: 1 item
        PA-DATA pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP
            padata-type: pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP (2)
            padata-value: <encrypted bytes>
    req-body
        cname: j.chen
        realm: CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
        sname: krbtgt/CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL

The pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP value is the encrypted-timestamp field. Its presence is the proof of pre-authentication; an account with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH would have no such field. Fragment 1 is the literal string kdc; the answer to the question "what acronym is the KDC role?". The hint that this is the right fragment lives in priya.ramanathan's description attribute (your config script seeded it there).

Confirm the hint:

Kali - Confirm Fragment 1 from priya.ramanathan's description

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=priya.ramanathan)" description

The description ends with Kerberos protocol fragment hint: kdc. Fragment 1 = kdc.

docs.title: Step 7: Analyze AS-REP for Fragment 2
docs.text:
