docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The SUID binary passes user input to a system() call. Why is this more dangerous than a binary that simply reads files?

Reveal Answer

A binary that only reads files limits the attacker to information disclosure. A binary that passes user input to system() allows arbitrary command execution as root. The attacker can inject shell commands (;, |, &&, backticks) to run anything: creating new root accounts, installing backdoors, modifying system configuration, or pivoting to other systems. The system() function invokes /bin/sh, so any valid shell syntax is accepted.

2. The cron job runs every minute. How would a defender detect this exploitation after the fact?

Reveal Answer

Defenders should monitor /opt/maintenance/ for new or modified files using file integrity monitoring (AIDE, OSSEC, inotify). Cron execution logs in /var/log/syslog or /var/log/cron.log would show the execution of unexpected scripts. The file /tmp/escalated.txt containing root-owned data is also an indicator. Proactively, the cron entry should reference a specific script rather than a wildcard glob, and the directory should not be world-writable.

3. What is the defensive fix for each vulnerability?

Reveal Answer

SUID binary: Remove the SUID bit (chmod u-s /usr/local/bin/firmware-check), rewrite the binary to validate and sanitize input (reject characters like ;, |, &, backticks), or eliminate the system() call entirely in favor of direct file I/O with path whitelisting. Better yet, remove the binary if it is not essential.

Cron job: Change /opt/maintenance/ permissions to 700 (root only) or 755 (root-writable, others read/execute). Replace the wildcard glob with a specific script path. Use run-parts with --lsbsysinit which enforces naming conventions and ignores files not matching the pattern. Audit all root cron entries quarterly.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SUID binaries are high-value targets: find / -perm -4000 is one of the first commands to run after gaining a shell
  • Custom SUID binaries are especially dangerous: unlike well-audited system binaries, custom tools often lack input validation
  • Cron jobs with writable paths are trivial to exploit: if root runs scripts from a directory you can write to, you have a root shell on a timer
  • Wildcard globs in cron amplify risk: *.sh means any new script is automatically picked up on the next cycle
  • Privilege escalation completes the kill chain: foothold access becomes full compromise when escalation vectors exist
  • Defense requires least privilege at every layer: file permissions, SUID bits, cron configurations, and directory ownership all contribute to or prevent escalation

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Previous exercises placed you in the attacker's role: scanning, enumerating, exploiting, escalating. The perspective flips here. A security incident has already occurred at the Bean & Byte Cafe. Your job is to figure out what happened by analyzing a packet capture.

Make sure you have:

  • VPN connected and verified
  • SSH client available
  • Familiarity with strings, grep, base64 commands
  • Credentials: analyst:An4lyst_2026#

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text: [Reconnaissance] → [Enumeration] → [Exploitation] → [Credential Access] → [Privilege Escalation] → >> Detection & Forensics <<

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A Bean & Byte Cafe customer reported unauthorized transactions on their bank account shortly after using the cafe WiFi. Management retained your firm to investigate. A network tap captured traffic during the suspected incident window.

The packet capture resides on an analyst workstation. SSH in, examine the evidence, and reconstruct the attack chain. Determine what the attacker did, what they stole, and how they did it.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Access the analyst workstation
  • Analyze the PCAP file for attack evidence
  • Identify the attack method (ARP spoofing, DNS hijacking)
  • Extract stolen credentials from HTTP traffic
  • Decode exfiltrated data to find the flag

docs.title: Background: Network Forensics
docs.text: Network forensics examines captured traffic to reconstruct events, identify attackers, and determine the scope of a compromise. The primary evidence format is the PCAP (packet capture) file.

docs.title: Common Attack Indicators in PCAP Data
docs.text: Attack What to Look For ARP Spoofing Multiple ARP replies for the same IP from different MACs DNS Hijacking DNS responses resolving legitimate domains to unexpected IPs Credential Theft HTTP POST requests containing usernames and passwords in cleartext Data Exfiltration Outbound connections to unfamiliar hosts carrying encoded payloads

docs.title: Forensic Tools
docs.text: Tool Use Case strings Extract readable text from binary files: fast first pass tcpdump -r Parse and display PCAP packets with protocol detail grep Filter output for specific patterns (IPs, keywords, credentials) base64 -d Decode base64-encoded data found in packet payloads xxd Hex dump for examining raw packet bytes

docs.title: Step 1: Access the Analyst Workstation
docs.text:
SSH to the analyst workstation

Connect to the analyst workstation from Kali. Replace <target_ip> with the address shown in the Active Lab View.

ssh analyst@<target_ip>

Password: An4lyst_2026#

A successful login drops you into the analyst's shell where the evidence lives.

docs.title: Step 2: Examine Available Evidence
docs.text:
List the evidence and read the brief

Run these on the analyst workstation. The directory listing shows the available files, and the incident brief explains what management already knows.

ls -la ~/
cat ~/INCIDENT_BRIEF.txt

Read the incident brief. Note the PCAP file at /home/analyst/incident.pcap.

docs.title: Step 3: Initial Triage with strings
docs.text:
Triage the PCAP with strings

Run a broad extraction of readable strings from the PCAP on the analyst workstation. strings pulls printable text out of the binary capture for a fast first look.

strings /home/analyst/incident.pcap

Scan the output. You should see HTTP headers, hostnames, and other protocol data embedded in the packets. The result provides a fast overview of what the capture contains without needing a full protocol parser.

docs.title: Step 4: Identify the Attacker
docs.text:
Filter for attacker indicators

Look for MAC addresses and suspicious network indicators. Piping strings into grep -i narrows the output to host and server references.

strings /home/analyst/incident.pcap | grep -i 'host\|server\|evil'

Note any references to external or suspicious hostnames. The MAC address AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF appears repeatedly: that address belongs to the attacker's interface.

docs.title: Step 5: Find Stolen Credentials
docs.text:
Search for stolen credentials

Search for HTTP authentication data. The grep filter surfaces the cleartext login fields captured in the traffic.

strings /home/analyst/incident.pcap | grep -i 'password\|username\|login'

You should find an HTTP POST containing form-encoded credentials. The victim submitted their banking login through a hijacked connection. Record the username and password.

docs.title: Step 6: Identify DNS Hijacking
docs.text:
Spot the DNS hijack

Look for DNS-related anomalies. The grep terms pull the forged banking domain and the attacker-controlled IP out of the capture.

strings /home/analyst/incident.pcap | grep -i 'banking\|HIJACK\|192.168.99'

The attacker redirected banking.example.com to 192.168.99.1: an IP under their control. Combined with the ARP spoofing evidence, the data confirms a man-in-the-middle attack chain.

docs.title: Step 7: Decode Exfiltrated Data
docs.text:
Find the exfiltration payload

Search for the outbound upload that carries the encoded data. The attacker POSTed the stolen records to an external server in a data= form field, so the base64 blob sits behind a data= prefix rather than alone on its own line.

strings /home/analyst/incident.pcap | grep 'data='

The matching line is the exfiltration payload: a long base64 string immediately after data=. A whole-line anchored regex would miss it because the data= prefix sits on the same line, so target the data= field directly.

Extract and decode the payload

Pull out the data= field, strip the data= prefix, and decode the remaining base64. grep -oE prints only the matched data=... portion, sed removes the prefix, and base64 -d reverses the encoding.

strings /home/analyst/incident.pcap | grep -oE 'data=[A-Za-z0-9+/=]+' | head -1 | sed 's/^data=//' | base64 -d

The decoded output reveals the exfiltrated data, including the flag in the form OCR{...}. Record the full flag exactly as it appears.

docs.title: Step 8: Record the Flag
docs.text: The flag appears in the decoded exfiltration payload.

docs.title: Step 9: Exit
docs.text:
Close the analyst session

Leave the analyst workstation once you have recorded the flag and findings.

exit

The session returns you to your Kali terminal.

docs.text:

Timestamp Event Evidence T+0 ARP spoofing begins T+5s DNS hijacking T+15s Victim visits fake banking site T+20s Credentials stolen T+30s Data exfiltrated

Attacker Identification:

Item Value Attacker MAC Method Exfiltration destination

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The attacker used ARP spoofing before DNS hijacking. Why was that sequence necessary?

Reveal Answer

ARP spoofing redirects the victim's traffic through the attacker's machine at Layer 2. Without this, the attacker cannot intercept or modify the victim's DNS queries. The ARP spoof positions the attacker as a man-in-the-middle, which then enables the DNS hijack (returning a forged DNS response pointing banking.example.com to an attacker-controlled IP). The sequence is: ARP spoof to become the gateway, then DNS hijack to redirect specific domains, then serve a fake login page to harvest credentials.

2. The credentials were transmitted in cleartext HTTP. What would have prevented this?

Reveal Answer

HTTPS with proper certificate validation would have prevented credential theft. If the banking site enforced HTTPS and the victim's browser validated the TLS certificate, the attacker's fake site would have triggered a certificate warning (the attacker cannot produce a valid certificate for banking.example.com). HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) preload lists provide additional protection by preventing the browser from ever making an HTTP connection to known HTTPS-only domains.

3. How could the cafe network have detected or prevented the ARP spoofing attack?

Reveal Answer

Prevention: 802.1X port-based authentication, Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches, static ARP entries for critical infrastructure like the gateway. Detection: ARP monitoring tools (arpwatch, XArp) that alert on MAC-IP binding changes, IDS rules that flag gratuitous ARP replies, and network segmentation that isolates customer WiFi from internal systems. The cafe's flat network with no monitoring made the attack trivial.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The attacks you learned to execute are visible in traffic captures: ARP spoofing, DNS hijacking, and credential theft all leave forensic evidence
  • strings is the fastest first-pass forensic tool: extracting readable text from binary captures reveals hostnames, credentials, and payloads without protocol parsing
  • Base64 encoding is not encryption: exfiltrated data encoded in base64 is trivially decoded by any analyst
  • Attack chains follow a logical sequence: ARP spoof enables man-in-the-middle, which enables DNS hijack, which enables credential theft, which enables data exfiltration
  • Defenders analyze what attackers create: every technique from Exercises 1-8 produces artifacts that forensic analysis can uncover
  • Cleartext protocols are forensic goldmines: HTTP, DNS, and ARP operate without encryption: everything is visible in the capture

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client: Bean & Byte Cafe Role: Security Auditor Phase: Reconnaissance Service Enumeration Exploitation Detection Hardening Verification

What you know so far:

  • You mapped the entire cafe network (9 devices, flat subnet, zero segmentation)
  • You exploited default SNMP community strings, DVR default passwords, POS debug endpoints, thermostat command injection, NAS default credentials, printer JetDirect, barista workstation cron escalation, and more
  • You captured traffic, performed credential pivots, wrote IDS rules, and delivered a full audit report
  • The cafe owner hired an IT consultant to remediate the findings

Your task: The consultant claims the worst vulnerabilities are fixed. Verify the remediation independently. Find what's actually been secured, what hasn't, and collect the flag parts from the remaining vulnerable services. Flag tokens in service responses are prefixed with OCR-SN:: use only the value after the prefix when assembling the flag.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Re-test the partially hardened Bean & Byte Cafe environment. Systematically verify each previously exploited attack path. Determine which vulnerabilities have been remediated and which remain. Extract flag parts from the services that are still exploitable.

Difficulty: Advanced Estimated time: 75 minutes

docs.title: Background: Why Verification Matters
docs.text:
Remediation without verification is theater. An IT consultant says "I fixed SNMP" -- what does that actually mean? Did they change the community string? Disable the service entirely? Restrict it to a management VLAN? You don't know until you test.

Partial hardening is arguably worse than no hardening at all. It creates a false sense of security. The cafe owner thinks the problems are solved. Meanwhile, half the attack surface is exactly where you left it.

Your job is to produce a verification matrix -- a device-by-device, vulnerability-by-vulnerability accounting of what changed and what didn't.

docs.title: The Verification Methodology
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Previous Finding] --> B{Re-test Exploit}
    B -->|Fails| C[Remediated]
    B -->|Succeeds| D[Still Vulnerable]
    C --> E[Document Fix Method]
    D --> F[Document Remaining Risk]
    E --> G[Verification Report]
    F --> G

docs.title: Flag Progress
docs.text:
The flag has 2 parts. Both come from services that remain vulnerable despite the consultant's work.

Part Source Token Found? 1 Smart thermostat command injection ________ 2 NAS default SSH credentials ________

docs.title: What the Consultant Claims to Have Fixed
docs.text:
According to the remediation report you received:

  1. Gateway SNMP -- Community string changed from public to a non-default value
  2. DVR default password -- Admin password changed from 123456 to a strong password

docs.title: Phase 1: Verify Claimed Remediations
docs.text: Start by confirming the three fixes the consultant reported.

docs.title: SNMP Community String
docs.text:
Test the gateway SNMP community string

Test whether the gateway still responds to public. Replace <gateway_ip> with the gateway address from your prior recon.

timeout 5 snmpget -v2c -c public <gateway_ip> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0

A real fix causes the command to timeout or return "No Response." A successful data response means the community string was never changed.

docs.title: DVR Default Password
docs.text:
Re-test the DVR login with the old password

Send the previously working credentials to the DVR login endpoint. Replace <dvr_ip> with the DVR address.

curl -s -X POST http://<dvr_ip>/login -d 'user=admin&pass=123456'

A real fix returns an authentication failure. Check the HTTP response code and body.

Browse to the DVR login

Open http://<dvr_ip>/ to see the login form you are testing. The web console is still exposed to the whole subnet, so even if the password changed, the form remains a brute-force target you note in the verification matrix.

The HikVision DVR login console. The consultant claims the default password was changed; the form is still reachable from the entire flat subnet.

docs.title: POS Debug Endpoint
docs.text:
Probe the POS debug route

Request the debug route and read only the HTTP status code. Replace <pos_ip> with the POS terminal address.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<pos_ip>:8080/debug

A real fix returns 404.

docs.title: Phase 2: Re-test Remaining Attack Surface
docs.text: Now test everything else. The consultant's report only mentioned three fixes. What about the rest?

docs.title: Smart Thermostat: Command Injection
docs.text:
Re-test thermostat command injection

The /diagnostics endpoint was vulnerable to command injection. Inject id after a benign host value to verify whether the vulnerability persists. Replace <thermo_ip> with the thermostat address.

curl -s http://<thermo_ip>:8080/diagnostics -d 'host=127.0.0.1;id'

If the output includes uid=0(root), the vulnerability is still live. Go deeper.

Browse to the thermostat console

Open http://<thermo_ip>:8080/ to see the operator UI and the "Network Diagnostics" link at the bottom. That link reaches the /diagnostics endpoint you just abused, confirming the injectable feature is still wired into the live interface.

The CafeTherm CT-200 console. The "Network Diagnostics" link drives the `/diagnostics` endpoint that is still vulnerable to command injection, the source of flag part 1.

docs.title: NAS Backup: Default SSH Credentials
docs.text:
Re-test NAS default SSH credentials

The NAS accepted admin:password via SSH. Attempt the same login and run whoami on it. Replace <nas_ip> with the NAS address.

sshpass -p 'password' ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no admin@<nas_ip> 'whoami'

If you get admin back, nothing has changed.

Browse to the NAS File Station

Open https://<nas_ip>:8443/ (accept the self-signed certificate). The console lands straight on File Station with the default account, exposing the /backups share of POS database dumps, WiFi logs, and employee records. Default credentials over SSH and the same default exposure through the web UI are the same unfixed finding.

The CafeNAS File Station reached with the unchanged default account. The backup share holds the sensitive data, and the NAS is the source of flag part 2.

docs.title: Printer: JetDirect
docs.text:
Query the printer over JetDirect

Send a PJL information request to the raw print port and read the response. Replace <printer_ip> with the printer address.

echo '@PJL INFO ID' | nc -w 5 <printer_ip> 9100

Still responding without authentication? Note it.

docs.title: Barista Workstation: Cron Escalation
docs.text:
Re-check the barista maintenance directory

Log in as the barista user and list the maintenance directory permissions. Replace <barista_ip> with the workstation address.

sshpass -p 'C0ff33_Br3w#' ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no barista@<barista_ip> 'ls -la /opt/maintenance/'

If /opt/maintenance/ is still world-writable, the cron escalation path is still open.

Read the thermostat flag part via command injection

docs.title: Phase 4: Suricata Rule Development
docs.text: A hardened environment needs monitoring. Write Suricata rules to detect exploitation attempts against both the fixed and unfixed vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Provided Example Rules
docs.text:
These two rules are provided as a starting point:

alert udp any any -> $HOME_NET 161 (msg:"SNMP Community String Brute Force"; content:"public"; sid:1000001; rev:1;)
alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 9100 (msg:"Unauthenticated PJL Access"; content:"@PJL"; sid:1000002; rev:1;)

docs.title: Your Rules
docs.text:
Write Suricata rules for the following detection scenarios. Consider what network traffic each attack generates.

Rule 1: Thermostat Command Injection Detection

The /diagnostics endpoint receives POST data with a host parameter. Command injection payloads typically contain shell metacharacters (;, |, `, $() after the hostname.

# Write your rule here
# Hint: alert on POST requests to port 8080 containing both "diagnostics" and shell metacharacters

Rule 2: NAS Default Credential SSH Login

Detecting default credential use over SSH is harder at the network level because SSH is encrypted. Think about what you can detect: repeated SSH connection attempts to the NAS from non-management IPs, or successful SSH sessions from unexpected sources.

# Write your rule here
# Hint: alert on SSH connections to the NAS IP from any source outside the management range

Rule 3: DVR Brute Force Detection

Even though the password was changed, the login form is still exposed. Detect brute force attempts.

# Write your rule here
# Hint: alert on repeated POST requests to /login on port 80 within a short time window

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations: Complete Hardening
docs.text:
The consultant fixed three things. Here is what complete hardening looks like:

Category Remediation Priority Network Architecture Implement VLANs: POS, IoT, Staff, Guest, Management Critical SNMP Disable SNMP or restrict to SNMPv3 with authentication; bind to management VLAN only High SSH Disable password authentication; use key-based auth only; restrict to management VLAN High IoT Devices Isolate thermostat, cameras, menu display on dedicated IoT VLAN with no internet egress High Web Applications Input validation on all endpoints; parameterized queries; remove debug interfaces Critical Default Credentials Audit and change ALL default passwords across every device Critical Printer Require authentication for PJL/management; restrict JetDirect to print VLAN Medium Cron Jobs Audit file permissions on all scheduled task directories; principle of least privilege Medium Monitoring Deploy IDS/IPS (Suricata) with rules for all known attack patterns High Certificate Management Replace self-signed certificates with CA-signed; enforce HTTPS everywhere Medium Firmware Update all device firmware; establish patch management schedule High

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Assuming fixed means secure

The SNMP community string was changed, but SNMP still runs on the gateway and remains accessible from the entire subnet. Changing the string is a band-aid, not a fix. The real fix is network segmentation plus SNMPv3.

Testing only what was reported

The consultant fixed three things. If you only tested those three, you missed six other vulnerabilities that are still wide open. Always re-test the full attack surface.

Forgetting the cron escalation

The barista workstation cron job is subtle. The world-writable maintenance directory means any user with SSH access can escalate to root. The consultant never addressed it.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
What You Learned

  1. Verification is a separate discipline from remediation. The person who fixes a vulnerability should not be the person who verifies the fix. Independent verification catches gaps.

  2. Partial hardening creates false confidence. Three fixes out of eleven vulnerabilities is a 27% remediation rate. The cafe owner believes the network is secure. It is not.

  3. Defense in depth requires completeness. Changing a password doesn't help if the service is still exposed to the entire network. Removing a debug endpoint doesn't help if the admin login is still injectable. Each fix must be evaluated in context.

  4. Monitoring fills the gap. While remediation catches up, detection rules (Suricata, log analysis) provide visibility into exploitation attempts. You can't fix everything overnight, but you can watch for attacks.

  5. Documentation drives accountability. The verification matrix is a professional deliverable. It tells the client exactly what was fixed, what wasn't, and what the remaining risk is. No ambiguity.

docs.title: Course Complete
docs.text:
You have completed all 10 exercises in the Bean & Byte Cafe engagement series.

Over the course of this series, you progressed through the full lifecycle of a security engagement:

Week Exercise Skill 1 Network Discovery Host enumeration, service fingerprinting, protocol queries 1 Traffic Analysis Passive reconnaissance, packet capture, protocol identification 2 Service Exploitation Default credentials, SNMP enumeration, unauthenticated APIs 2 Web Application Testing SQL injection, command injection, debug endpoints 3 Credential Pivoting Password reuse, lateral movement, privilege escalation 3 Data Exfiltration Sensitive data identification, backup analysis, evidence collection 4 IoT Exploitation Telnet default credentials, firmware analysis, command injection 4 IDS/Detection Suricata rule writing, alert tuning, detection engineering 5 Full Penetration Test End-to-end attack chain, report writing, risk assessment 5 Hardening Verification Remediation validation, verification matrices, gap analysis

You started by not knowing what was on the network. You ended by verifying which fixes actually work and writing detection rules for the gaps. That is the full arc of a security professional's engagement with a real-world environment.

The skills from this series map directly to the CompTIA Security+ objectives: network reconnaissance, vulnerability assessment, penetration testing methodology, incident detection, and security operations. Every tool you used (nmap, curl, sshpass, snmpget, smbclient, Suricata) is a tool you will use in production environments.

The cafe is still not fully secure. It never will be if the owner keeps treating security as a one-time project instead of an ongoing process. That's the final lesson: security is a practice, not a product.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
You will perform Layer 2 reconnaissance using the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP). You will map MAC addresses to IP addresses, observe ARP broadcast behavior, and build a baseline of the cafe network's Layer 2 identity bindings. The baseline you create here is essential for detecting ARP spoofing attacks in later exercises.

Make sure you have:

  • VPN connected and verified
  • Access to the lab network (attacker machine)
  • Familiarity with basic networking concepts (IP, MAC, broadcast)

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text: >> ARP Reconnaissance << → [ARP Spoofing] → [Man-in-the-Middle] → [Detection & Defense]

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You've already mapped the Bean & Byte Cafe network at Layers 3 and 4: IP addresses, open ports, running services. But there's a layer beneath all of that: Layer 2, where MAC addresses live. ARP is the protocol that translates between IP addresses and MAC addresses, and it operates on blind trust. Any device can claim any MAC-to-IP binding, and the network will believe it.

Before you can detect ARP-based attacks, you need to know what "normal" looks like. Your task is to build a complete ARP baseline of the cafe network: every device's MAC address, its IP binding, and its ARP broadcast behavior.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Discover all 5 devices and their MAC addresses using arp-scan
  • Verify individual MAC-to-IP bindings with arping
  • Capture live ARP traffic with tcpdump and identify broadcast patterns
  • Build a baseline ARP table documenting MAC, IP, and vendor OUI for every device
  • Identify which devices send gratuitous ARPs and explain why

docs.title: What is ARP?
docs.text: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) operates at Layer 2 of the OSI model. When a device needs to communicate with another device on the same subnet, it knows the destination IP address but needs the destination MAC address to construct an Ethernet frame. ARP solves this by broadcasting a question to the entire network: "Who has IP x.x.x.x? Tell me your MAC address."

docs.title: How ARP Works
docs.text: Step Action Packet Type 1 Source broadcasts "Who has 10.100.2.42?" ARP Request (broadcast) 2 Target responds "10.100.2.42 is at AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF" ARP Reply (unicast) 3 Source caches the binding in its ARP table (no packet)

docs.title: ARP Request vs. ARP Reply
docs.text:
• ARP Request: Broadcast to all devices on the subnet (destination MAC = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff). Contains the sender's MAC and IP, and the target IP being queried.
  • ARP Reply: Unicast response from the target device. Contains the target's MAC address, confirming the binding.

docs.title: Gratuitous ARP
docs.text: A gratuitous ARP is an ARP reply sent without a preceding request. A device sends a gratuitous ARP to announce its own MAC-to-IP binding, typically after booting up, changing IP addresses, or for redundancy failover. While legitimate, gratuitous ARPs are also the mechanism exploited in ARP spoofing attacks.

docs.title: Why ARP is Insecure
docs.text: ARP has no authentication. Any device can send an ARP reply claiming any MAC-to-IP binding, and other devices will accept it without verification. The lack of authentication is the fundamental vulnerability that enables ARP spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks.

docs.title: OUI: Organizationally Unique Identifier
docs.text:
The first three octets (24 bits) of a MAC address identify the manufacturer. The first three octets form the OUI. For example:

OUI Vendor 00:1A:2B Cisco Systems DC:A6:32 Raspberry Pi Foundation B8:27:EB Raspberry Pi Foundation (older)

Tools like arp-scan automatically look up OUI vendor strings, which helps identify device types on the network.

docs.title: Tools You'll Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose arp-scan Discover devices by sending ARP requests to every IP on the subnet arping Send ARP requests to a specific IP and observe the reply tcpdump Capture and display raw network traffic, including ARP packets arp View and manage the local ARP cache table ip neigh Modern alternative to arp for viewing neighbor (ARP) table

docs.title: Flag Progress
docs.text:
Token Source Found? Part 1 Discovered via arp-scan: examine the vendor strings Part 2 Investigate the printer's services after mapping it Part 3 Connect to the thermostat's management interface

Flag tokens are prefixed with OCR-SN: to help you identify them. When assembling the flag, use only the token value after the prefix.

Flag format: OCR{________}

docs.title: Step 0: SSH into the Network Tap
docs.text:
ARP operates at Layer 2: you must be on the same broadcast domain as the target devices. Your Kali machine connects through a VPN (Layer 3), so ARP tools won't work from there. Blackridge Security has placed a network tap on the cafe's switch. SSH into it to get Layer 2 access.

SSH into the network tap

From your Kali terminal, open an SSH session to the tap. Once connected, the prompt is a shell on the tap that sits on the same broadcast domain as the cafe devices.

ssh pentest@10.100.2.250

Authenticate with password Security1#. All ARP commands in this walkthrough run from inside the tap, not from your Kali terminal.

docs.title: Step 1: Discover All Devices with arp-scan
docs.text:
Discover all devices with arp-scan

arp-scan sends ARP requests to every IP address on the local subnet and reports which ones reply. Unlike nmap -sn (which uses ICMP and TCP), arp-scan operates purely at Layer 2 and will find devices that block ping. The -l flag tells arp-scan to scan the local network, auto-detecting the subnet from the interface configuration.

arp-scan -I eth0 -l

Expected output (your IPs will match, MACs are fixed):

Interface: eth0, type: EN10MB, MAC: b6:a1:50:24:4c:af, IPv4: 10.100.2.250
Starting arp-scan 1.9.7 with 256 hosts (https://github.com/royhills/arp-scan)
10.100.2.1      00:18:f8:10:01:01       ???????????? Linksys WRT54G Wireless Router
10.100.2.17     00:17:c5:10:11:17       2Wire Inc POS Terminal Controller
10.100.2.23     d4:be:d9:10:17:23       Dell Inc Barista Workstation
10.100.2.42     3c:2a:f4:10:2a:42       HP Inc LaserJet Pro M404dn
10.100.2.51     b4:75:0e:10:33:51       Belkin IoT Smart Thermostat v3.1
10.100.2.254    6e:3c:1d:f1:08:15       (Unknown: locally administered)

7 packets received by filter, 0 packets dropped by kernel
Ending arp-scan 1.9.7: 256 hosts scanned in 1.824 seconds (140.35 hosts/sec). 7 responded

Notice that five devices responded with real vendor OUI identifiers, plus the host bridge at .254. One of the vendor strings contains something unusual: examine each one carefully.

Flag Token 1

Look at the vendor string for the gateway (IP ending in .1). The OUI vendor field contains the first flag token prefixed with OCR-SN:.

Record every device in your baseline table:

IP Address MAC Address Vendor (OUI) Device Role x.x.x.1 Gateway x.x.x.17 POS Terminal x.x.x.23 Barista Workstation x.x.x.42 Printer x.x.x.51 Smart Thermostat

docs.title: Step 2: Verify MAC-to-IP Bindings with arping
docs.text:
Verify the gateway binding with arping

arping sends ARP requests to a specific host and reports each reply. The response confirms whether a specific IP address maps to the expected MAC address. The -c 3 flag sends exactly 3 ARP requests. Replace <gateway_ip> with the gateway IP from your arp-scan results.

arping -I eth0 -c 3 <gateway_ip>

Expected output:

ARPING 10.100.2.1 from 10.100.2.250 eth0
Unicast reply from 10.100.2.1 [00:18:f8:10:01:01]  0.847ms
Unicast reply from 10.100.2.1 [00:18:f8:10:01:01]  0.652ms
Unicast reply from 10.100.2.1 [00:18:f8:10:01:01]  0.714ms
Sent 3 probes (1 broadcast(s))
Received 3 response(s)

Key observations:

  • The MAC address in each reply should be identical: if it changes between replies, something is wrong (possible ARP spoofing).
  • The response time gives you a rough latency baseline.

Verify every other device

Repeat the targeted verification for each remaining device, substituting its IP from your arp-scan results.

arping -I eth0 -c 3 <pos_terminal_ip>
arping -I eth0 -c 3 <barista_ip>
arping -I eth0 -c 3 <printer_ip>
arping -I eth0 -c 3 <thermostat_ip>

Compare the MAC address returned by arping against what arp-scan reported. They should match exactly. If they don't, the ARP cache may have been poisoned.

docs.title: Step 3: View the ARP Cache
docs.text:
Inspect the local ARP cache

After scanning and pinging, the tap has built an ARP cache: a local table of known MAC-to-IP bindings. ip neigh reads that neighbor table for the chosen interface.

ip neigh show dev eth0

Expected output:

10.100.2.1 dev eth0 lladdr 00:18:f8:10:01:01 REACHABLE
10.100.2.17 dev eth0 lladdr 00:17:c5:10:11:17 REACHABLE
10.100.2.23 dev eth0 lladdr d4:be:d9:10:17:23 STALE
10.100.2.42 dev eth0 lladdr 3c:2a:f4:10:2a:42 REACHABLE
10.100.2.51 dev eth0 lladdr b4:75:0e:10:33:51 REACHABLE

The state field tells you how fresh each entry is, as summarized below.

State Meaning REACHABLE Recently confirmed: binding is trusted STALE Not recently confirmed: will be re-verified on next use DELAY Re-verification in progress FAILED ARP request sent but no reply received

docs.title: Step 4: Capture ARP Traffic with tcpdump
docs.text:
Capture live ARP traffic with tcpdump

Observe ARP traffic flowing across the network in real time. The -e flag shows Ethernet (Layer 2) headers including MAC addresses, and -nn disables hostname and port-name resolution so you see raw IPs and numbers. Let this run for 30-60 seconds to observe the patterns.

tcpdump -i eth0 -enn arp

Expected output:

12:34:56.789 00:18:f8:10:01:01 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ARP, Request who-has 10.100.2.17 tell 10.100.2.1, length 28
12:34:56.790 00:17:c5:10:11:17 > 00:18:f8:10:01:01, ARP, Reply 10.100.2.17 is-at 00:17:c5:10:11:17, length 28
12:34:57.123 b4:75:0e:10:33:51 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ARP, Reply 10.100.2.51 is-at b4:75:0e:10:33:51, length 28

The third packet above is a gratuitous ARP: an ARP Reply sent to the broadcast address (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) without a preceding Request. The thermostat is announcing its own binding. Press Ctrl+C to stop the capture.

docs.title: Step 5: Isolate Gratuitous ARPs
docs.text:
Filter for ARP replies only

Filter the capture to ARP replies to surface gratuitous ARPs. The filter arp[6:2] = 2 matches ARP operation code 2 (Reply). Gratuitous ARPs are replies sent to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, the broadcast address.

tcpdump -i eth0 -enn 'arp and arp[6:2] = 2'

Each line is a reply. Watch for replies sent to the broadcast MAC, which are the gratuitous announcements.

Capture a bounded set of gratuitous ARPs

Capture a fixed number of reply packets so the command exits on its own. The -c 10 flag captures exactly 10 matching packets, then stops.

tcpdump -i eth0 -enn -c 10 'arp and arp[6:2] = 2'

Review the 10 captured replies and note which devices announce their own binding unprompted.

docs.title: Step 6: Investigate Discovered Services
docs.text:
Your ARP baseline tells you which devices are on the network and their MAC addresses. Now use that information to investigate the services running on those devices. In a real assessment, mapping Layer 2 is just the first step: the value comes from what you discover on each host.

Return to your Kali terminal

Exit the SSH session so the remaining steps run from your own machine using standard network tools.

exit

The prompt returns to your Kali shell, which reaches the printer and thermostat over the VPN at Layer 3.

Query the printer's CUPS web interface:

Query the printer's CUPS interface

Your arp-scan revealed the printer at offset .42 with an HP OUI. From earlier exercises, you know printers often run web management interfaces. The printer has CUPS on port 631. Replace <printer_ip> with the printer IP from your baseline.

curl -s http://<printer_ip>:631

Read the HTML output carefully. Look for any fields containing the OCR-SN: prefix.

Flag Token 2

The printer's CUPS status page contains an Asset Tag field with the second token prefixed with OCR-SN:.

Connect to the thermostat's telnet interface:

Connect to the thermostat's telnet interface

Your arp-scan identified the thermostat at offset .51 with a Belkin IoT OUI. IoT devices frequently expose telnet management interfaces. Connect to port 23, replacing <thermostat_ip> with the thermostat IP from your baseline.

telnet <thermostat_ip>

Pay attention to the banner text that appears before the login prompt: IoT devices often print serial numbers and diagnostic information on connection.

Flag Token 3

The thermostat's telnet banner displays a serial number field containing the third token prefixed with OCR-SN:.

docs.text:
Combine all three tokens:

docs.text:
Complete the baseline table with all information gathered:

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the thermostat send gratuitous ARPs, and how could an attacker exploit this?

Reveal Answer The thermostat sends gratuitous ARPs to announce or refresh its MAC-to-IP binding on the network. IoT devices commonly do this after waking from sleep mode or reconnecting to the network. An attacker could exploit this by sending their own gratuitous ARPs with the thermostat's IP but the attacker's MAC address: all other devices would update their ARP caches to point the thermostat's IP to the attacker. Since gratuitous ARPs are accepted without verification, this is trivial to execute.

2. What is the difference between the ARP cache states REACHABLE and STALE? Why does it matter for security?

Reveal Answer REACHABLE means the binding was recently confirmed via a successful ARP exchange and is trusted by the kernel. STALE means the entry exists but hasn't been reconfirmed recently: the kernel will re-verify it (send a new ARP request) the next time it's needed. For security, STALE entries are vulnerable: if an attacker sends a spoofed ARP reply before the legitimate device responds to the re-verification, the attacker's binding will be cached as REACHABLE. Monitoring for unexpected state transitions can indicate ARP spoofing.

3. You used arp-scan (broadcast) and arping (targeted). When would you use one versus the other?

Reveal Answer `arp-scan -I eth0 -l` is a discovery tool, use it when you need to find all devices on a subnet. It sends ARP requests to every possible IP and reports all responders. `arping` is a verification tool, use it when you already know a specific IP and want to confirm its MAC binding, measure response time, or detect if multiple devices claim the same IP (which would indicate ARP spoofing). In an incident response scenario, you'd use `arp-scan` first for situational awareness, then `arping` to verify suspicious bindings.

4. How could you detect ARP spoofing using only the tools from this exercise?

Reveal Answer Compare your baseline against live observations. Run `arp-scan -I eth0 -l` periodically and compare MAC-to-IP bindings against your documented baseline. If a MAC address changes for a given IP, spoofing may be occurring. Use `arping` to send targeted ARP requests: if you get replies from two different MAC addresses for the same IP, one of them is an attacker. Monitor `tcpdump -i eth0 -enn arp` for an unusual volume of gratuitous ARPs or ARP replies for IPs that weren't queried. The baseline you built today is the reference point for all of these checks.

5. Why does arp-scan find devices that nmap -sn sometimes misses?

Reveal Answer `nmap -sn` uses a combination of ICMP echo requests, TCP SYN packets, and ARP requests (when scanning the local subnet). Some devices have firewalls that block ICMP and TCP probes but cannot block ARP, because ARP is required for basic network communication. A device that drops all ICMP pings will still respond to ARP requests, because without ARP it cannot communicate on the Ethernet network at all. `arp-scan` operates exclusively at Layer 2, bypassing any Layer 3/4 firewall rules.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
Based on your ARP reconnaissance findings:

  1. Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches to validate ARP packets against a trusted DHCP snooping database
  2. Configure static ARP entries for critical infrastructure (gateway, POS terminal) to prevent their bindings from being spoofed
  3. Deploy ARP monitoring (e.g., arpwatch) to alert on MAC-to-IP binding changes
  4. Segment the network: IoT devices (thermostat) should not share a broadcast domain with payment systems (POS terminal)
  5. Disable gratuitous ARP acceptance on critical servers where possible (/proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/*/arp_accept)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ARP operates on trust: There is no authentication mechanism in ARP: any device can claim any MAC-to-IP binding
  • A baseline is your first defense: Without documenting normal MAC-to-IP bindings, you cannot detect when they change
  • Gratuitous ARPs are both useful and dangerous: Legitimate devices use them for announcements, but attackers use the same mechanism for spoofing
  • Layer 2 reconnaissance precedes Layer 2 attacks: The mapping you did today is exactly what an attacker does before launching ARP spoofing
  • arp-scan, arping, and tcpdump are complementary: Discovery, verification, and live monitoring form a complete ARP reconnaissance toolkit
  • OUI lookup reveals device identity: The vendor portion of a MAC address helps classify unknown devices on the network

docs.text:
The Bean & Byte Cafe has more than one network segment. You've baselined the core infrastructure: gateway, POS, barista workstation, printer, and thermostat. Now a different set of devices needs the same treatment: the security camera DVR, digital menu display, NAS backup server, and a customer laptop, along with the gateway.

Map this segment. Build the baseline. Find the flag. No walkthrough this time.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
You already know how ARP works from Exercise 11. Here's what's different about this segment:

Device IP Offset What to Expect Cafe Gateway 1 Same gateway, shared across segments Security Camera DVR 67 Embedded Linux device, RTSP streaming Digital Menu Display 89 Lightweight IoT, HTTP-based NAS Backup 127 Storage appliance, multiple services Customer Laptop 200 Transient device, may have different ARP behavior

docs.title: Tools Available
docs.text: Tool Reminder arp-scan Subnet-wide Layer 2 discovery (vendor OUI resolution) arping Targeted MAC-to-IP verification tcpdump Live traffic capture and analysis arp / ip neigh Local ARP cache inspection snmpget / snmpwalk Query the gateway's SNMP system description smbclient List the NAS backup server's SMB shares and read its server string

docs.title: Flag
docs.text:
The flag follows the same format as Exercise 11: three tokens assembled from your ARP reconnaissance results.

Flag format: OCR{________}

Hint: Each token is prefixed with OCR-SN:, and the token is the part after the prefix. The three sources are:

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. How does the customer laptop's ARP behavior differ from the always-on infrastructure devices? Why?

Reveal Answer Transient devices like the customer laptop generate more ARP requests because they need to discover the gateway and other resources each time they connect. They may also send gratuitous ARPs upon joining the network to announce their presence. Infrastructure devices that have been running continuously will have stable, cached ARP entries and generate fewer requests. The customer laptop's ARP cache state is more likely to be STALE or DELAY compared to the REACHABLE state of long-running devices.

2. The NAS backup server has three services (SSH, SMB, HTTPS). Does having multiple services affect its ARP behavior?

Reveal Answer No. ARP operates at Layer 2 and maps IP addresses to MAC addresses regardless of what services run on the host. A device with one service and a device with fifty services generate the same ARP traffic: one MAC address, one IP address, one ARP binding. The number of services matters at Layers 3-7 (TCP/UDP ports, protocol behavior), but ARP only cares about the network interface's MAC and IP assignment.

3. You now have baselines for two cafe network segments. How would you use them together to detect a rogue device?

Reveal Answer A rogue device would appear as an unknown MAC address in your arp-scan results: one that doesn't match any entry in either baseline table. Cross-referencing both baselines also helps detect MAC spoofing: if a MAC address from Segment A suddenly appears on Segment B claiming a different IP, that's suspicious. Regular automated scans compared against the combined baseline can alert on new devices, changed bindings, or MAC addresses appearing on unexpected segments.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
Consider these additional recommendations based on the devices in this segment:

  1. Isolate IoT devices (DVR, menu display) from storage systems (NAS) using VLANs: a compromised camera should not be able to ARP-spoof the backup server
  2. Implement 802.1X port authentication for the customer WiFi segment to prevent unauthorized devices from joining
  3. Monitor for MAC address duplication across segments: the gateway appears on both segments and its MAC should be consistent
  4. Set shorter ARP cache timeouts on critical devices to force more frequent re-verification of bindings

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Independence validates learning: If you can map a new segment without a walkthrough, you've internalized the methodology
  • Different device types, same protocol: IoT cameras, storage appliances, and laptops all use ARP identically: the reconnaissance approach is universal
  • Transient devices create noise: Customer devices connecting and disconnecting generate ARP traffic that can mask malicious activity
  • Baselines are living documents: Each new segment needs its own baseline, and all baselines should be maintained and compared over time
  • Layer 2 visibility is often neglected: Most network monitoring focuses on Layers 3-7: ARP baselines fill a critical gap in network visibility

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
You will perform a bidirectional ARP spoofing attack to position yourself between two devices on the Bean & Byte Cafe network. Once you sit in the middle of their conversation, you will capture the cleartext HTTP traffic flowing between them and recover the flag tokens hidden in a payment transaction. The exercise builds directly on the ARP reconnaissance baseline you assembled earlier: now you exploit the same lack of authentication you documented before.

Make sure you have:

  • VPN connected and verified
  • The tap IP from the Active Lab View (the .250 host on your segment)
  • Completed Exercise 6A so you understand ARP request and reply behavior
