The file contains customer card numbers and transaction details. Right now, anyone who accesses the machine, or captures it over the network, can read it all.

docs.title: Step 4: Generate a Random AES Key
docs.text:
Before you can encrypt, you need a key. AES-128 uses a 128-bit key, which is 16 bytes:

openssl rand -out my_aes_key 16

What this does:

Part Meaning openssl rand Generate cryptographically random bytes -out my_aes_key Save the random bytes to a file called my_aes_key 16 Generate 16 bytes (128 bits): the key size for AES-128

Why 16 bytes?

AES comes in three flavors: AES-128 (16-byte key), AES-192 (24-byte key), and AES-256 (32-byte key). The number refers to the key length in bits. Longer keys are harder to brute-force. AES-128 is considered secure for most purposes: brute-forcing it would take longer than the age of the universe with current technology.

You can verify the key file exists:

ls -la my_aes_key
Expected Output 
-rw------- 1 crypto crypto 16 Mar 19 12:00 my_aes_key

The file is exactly 16 bytes: your AES-128 encryption key. The key file contains raw binary data, so cat would show garbled characters.

docs.title: Step 5: Encrypt the File
docs.text:
Now encrypt the customer data using AES-128-CBC:

openssl enc -aes-128-cbc -base64 -e -kfile my_aes_key -in /data/customer_data.txt -out customer_encrypted.enc

What every flag means:

Flag Meaning openssl enc Use OpenSSL's symmetric encryption tool -aes-128-cbc Algorithm: AES with 128-bit key in CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode -base64 Encode the output as Base64 text (readable characters instead of raw binary) -e Encrypt (as opposed to -d for decrypt) -kfile my_aes_key Read the encryption key from the file my_aes_key -in /data/customer_data.txt Input file: the plaintext to encrypt -out customer_encrypted.enc Output file: where to write the ciphertext

What is CBC mode?

CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) is a mode of operation for block ciphers. AES encrypts data in 16-byte blocks. In CBC mode, each block of plaintext is XORed with the previous block's ciphertext before being encrypted. The chaining means identical plaintext blocks produce different ciphertext blocks, making pattern analysis much harder for an attacker.

docs.title: Step 6: Try to Read the Encrypted File
docs.text:
Now look at what an attacker would see if they captured this file:

cat customer_encrypted.enc
Expected Output 
U2FsdGVkX19kYmR3bHpwZ3J4dGtscnF2...
aW5nIHRoZSBCZWFuICYgQnl0ZSBDYWZl...
MjAyNi0wMy0xMCAwNzoxMiAgTGF0dGUg...
...
(several lines of Base64-encoded ciphertext)

Encrypted data looks like random gibberish. The original transaction records, card numbers, amounts, everything, are now completely unreadable. An attacker running a MITM attack would capture this gibberish and have no way to recover the original data without your key.

docs.title: Step 7: Decrypt the File
docs.text:
Now prove you can recover the original data:

openssl enc -aes-128-cbc -base64 -d -kfile my_aes_key -in customer_encrypted.enc -out customer_decrypted.txt

Notice the only change from the encrypt command: -d (decrypt) instead of -e (encrypt). Everything else stays the same: same algorithm, same key, same base64 encoding.

docs.title: Step 8: Verify the Decryption
docs.text:
Compare the decrypted file to the original:

diff /data/customer_data.txt customer_decrypted.txt
Expected Output 
(no output)

No output from diff means the files are identical. Your decryption perfectly recovered the original plaintext.

You can also view the decrypted file to confirm:

cat customer_decrypted.txt

You should see the exact same POS transaction log you started with.

docs.title: The Key Distribution Problem
docs.text:
You encrypted a file and decrypted it with the same key. But consider the following scenario:

The cafe owner wants to send the encrypted POS backup to the NAS for safe storage. The NAS needs the AES key to decrypt it. How do you send the key?

  • Option 1: Send the key over the network. But if an attacker is watching (like your MITM from Phase 7), they capture the key, and now they can decrypt everything.
  • Option 2: Walk the key over on a USB drive. Secure, but impractical for automated systems.
  • Option 3: Use asymmetric encryption to securely transmit the key. Asymmetric encryption is the solution.

The key distribution problem is exactly why cryptographers developed asymmetric encryption.

docs.title: Section 3: Asymmetric Encryption with OpenSSL
docs.text: Asymmetric encryption uses two keys: a public key that anyone can have, and a private key that must be kept secret. What one key encrypts, only the other can decrypt.

docs.title: The Mailbox Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a mailbox on the street:

  • The mail slot is the public key: anyone can drop a letter in
  • The mailbox door key is the private key: only the owner can open it and read the letters
  • You can tell the whole world where your mailbox is (share your public key) without worrying: all they can do is put letters in, not take them out

docs.title: Step 1: Generate an RSA Keypair
docs.text:
Generate a 4096-bit RSA private key:

openssl genrsa -out private_key.pem 4096

What this does:

Part Meaning openssl genrsa Generate an RSA private key -out private_key.pem Save the private key to this file 4096 Key size in bits: 4096 is very secure Expected Output 
Generating RSA private key, 4096 bit long modulus (2 primes)
.......++++
.........................................++++
e is 65537 (0x010001)

What does 4096 bits mean?

The key size determines how hard it is to break the encryption. A 4096-bit RSA key means the mathematical problem an attacker would need to solve involves a number with over 1,200 digits. With current technology, brute-forcing a 4096-bit RSA key would take billions of years. For comparison, a 512-bit RSA key was broken in 1999.

docs.title: Step 2: Extract the Public Key
docs.text:
The private key file actually contains both keys. Extract only the public key:

openssl rsa -in private_key.pem -pubout -out public_key.pem
Part Meaning openssl rsa RSA key management tool -in private_key.pem Read from the private key file -pubout Output only the public key -out public_key.pem Save the public key to this file Expected Output 
writing RSA key

docs.title: Step 3: Examine Both Keys
docs.text:
Look at the public key:

cat public_key.pem
Expected Output 
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MIICIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAg8AMIICCgKCAgEA...
(several lines of Base64-encoded data)
...
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----

Now look at the private key:

cat private_key.pem
Expected Output 
-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
MIIJQwIBADANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAASCCS0wggkpAgEA...
(many more lines -- the private key is much longer)
...
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----

Notice that the private key is much larger than the public key. The private key contains the mathematical components needed for both encryption and decryption, while the public key only contains what's needed for encryption.

Critical Security Rule

The public key can be shared with anyone: post it on a website, email it, print it on a business card. It can only encrypt, never decrypt.

The private key must NEVER be shared. Anyone with the private key can decrypt everything encrypted with the corresponding public key. Treat it like a password.

docs.title: Step 4: Encrypt a File with the Public Key
docs.text:
Encrypt the employee schedule using the public key:

openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -inkey public_key.pem -pubin -in /data/employee_schedule.txt -out schedule_encrypted.enc
Flag Meaning openssl pkeyutl Public key utility: RSA encrypt/decrypt operations -encrypt Perform encryption -inkey public_key.pem Use this key for the operation -pubin The key file is a public key (not a private key) -in /data/employee_schedule.txt Input file to encrypt -out schedule_encrypted.enc Output encrypted file

Note about pkeyutl vs rsautl

Older tutorials may show openssl rsautl. The rsautl command is deprecated in newer versions of OpenSSL. The modern replacement is openssl pkeyutl, which works with RSA and other key types. Both do the same thing for RSA operations.

docs.title: Step 5: Decrypt with the Private Key
docs.text:
Now decrypt using the private key: the only key that can reverse this:

openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey private_key.pem -in schedule_encrypted.enc -out schedule_decrypted.txt

Notice: no -pubin flag this time, because we're using the private key.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify
docs.text:
diff /data/employee_schedule.txt schedule_decrypted.txt
Expected Output 
(no output -- files are identical)

The decryption perfectly recovered the original schedule.

docs.title: RSA's Size Limitation
docs.text:
Try encrypting the larger customer data file with RSA:

openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -inkey public_key.pem -pubin -in /data/customer_data.txt -out customer_rsa_encrypted.enc
Expected Output 
Public Key operation error
...
pkeyutl: Error in encrypt operation

The command fails because RSA can only encrypt data smaller than the key size. A 4096-bit key can encrypt at most ~470 bytes of data. The customer data file is much larger than that.

A fundamental limitation of asymmetric encryption: it works great for small pieces of data (like keys), but cannot handle large files.

docs.title: Section 4: Why We Use Both: The Hybrid Approach
docs.text:
You've now seen both types of encryption:

Type Speed Size Limit Key Distribution Symmetric (AES) Very fast No limit Problematic: how to share the key? Asymmetric (RSA) Slow ~470 bytes for RSA-4096 Solved: public key can be shared openly

Each has a critical weakness. But together, they cover each other's gaps.

docs.title: The Real-World Solution: Hybrid Encryption
docs.text:
Here's how real systems combine both:

  1. Generate a random AES key (only 16 or 32 bytes: tiny)
  2. Encrypt the DATA with AES (fast, no size limit)
  3. Encrypt the AES KEY with RSA (the key is tiny enough for RSA)
  4. Send both the encrypted data and the encrypted key

The recipient uses their RSA private key to decrypt the AES key, then uses the AES key to decrypt the data.

docs.title: Walk Through It
docs.text:
Walk through it step by step:

Step 1: Generate a fresh AES key:

openssl rand -out hybrid_aes_key 16

Step 2: Encrypt the large customer data file with AES:

openssl enc -aes-128-cbc -base64 -e -kfile hybrid_aes_key -in /data/customer_data.txt -out hybrid_data.enc

Step 3: Encrypt the tiny AES key with RSA:

openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -inkey public_key.pem -pubin -in hybrid_aes_key -out hybrid_key.enc

The AES key is only 16 bytes: well within RSA's size limit.

Step 4: Now you could safely send hybrid_data.enc and hybrid_key.enc over the network. An attacker who captures both files has:

  • hybrid_data.enc: AES-encrypted data, unreadable without the AES key
  • hybrid_key.enc: the AES key, RSA-encrypted, unreadable without the private key

Without the RSA private key, the attacker is stuck.

Step 5: The recipient decrypts the chain:

openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey private_key.pem -in hybrid_key.enc -out recovered_aes_key

openssl enc -aes-128-cbc -base64 -d -kfile recovered_aes_key -in hybrid_data.enc -out recovered_data.txt

Step 6: Verify:

diff /data/customer_data.txt recovered_data.txt

No output means perfect recovery through the entire hybrid chain.

docs.title: This Is How TLS/HTTPS Works
docs.text:
Every time you visit a website with https://, your browser performs this exact hybrid approach:

  1. Your browser gets the server's public key (from the TLS certificate)
  2. Your browser generates a random session key (like an AES key)
  3. Your browser encrypts the session key with the server's public key and sends it
  4. Both sides now have the session key and use it for fast symmetric encryption of all data

The entire process happens in milliseconds, every time, for every HTTPS connection. The concepts you practiced by hand are running billions of times per second across the internet.

docs.title: Section 5: The Flag: Decrypt the Secret Report
docs.text: Put your skills to work. A hidden encrypted file on the crypto-station contains the flag.

docs.title: Step 1: Find the Hidden Files
docs.text:
Look for hidden files in the data directory:

ls -la /data/
Expected Output 
total 20
drwxr-xr-x 2 crypto crypto 4096 Mar 19 12:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 1 root   root   4096 Mar 19 12:00 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 crypto crypto  ... .report_key
-rw-r--r-- 1 crypto crypto  ... .secret_report.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 crypto crypto  ... README.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 crypto crypto  ... customer_data.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 crypto crypto  ... employee_schedule.txt

Two hidden files:

  • .secret_report.txt: an AES-encrypted file
  • .report_key: the AES key used to encrypt it

docs.title: Step 2: Try to Read the Encrypted Report
docs.text:
cat /data/.secret_report.txt

The output is Base64-encoded ciphertext: unreadable.

docs.title: Step 3: Decrypt It
docs.text:
You know from Section 2 that AES decryption needs the same algorithm, the key file, and the -d flag:

openssl enc -aes-128-cbc -base64 -d -kfile /data/.report_key -in /data/.secret_report.txt -out secret.txt

docs.title: Step 4: Read the Flag
docs.text:
cat secret.txt
Expected Output

The decrypted file contains the flag. The token within the flag was originally prefixed with OCR-SN: in service responses. 

OCR{_____}

Your flag, recovered using the symmetric decryption skills from Section 2.

Flag: OCR{_____}

Submit this flag to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Section 6: Analysis Questions
docs.text: Answer these questions in your lab report. Each one connects what you practiced to real-world security concepts.

docs.title: Question 1: The MITM Scenario
docs.text:
You encrypted customer_data.txt with AES-128. Imagine an attacker running the same MITM attack from Phase 7: they're ARP spoofing the crypto-station and capturing all its traffic. They intercept the encrypted file customer_encrypted.enc as it's being sent to the NAS.

  • Can the attacker read the transaction data? Why or why not?
  • What specific piece of information would the attacker need to decrypt it?
  • If the AES key were also sent over the network in plaintext, would the encryption still protect the data?

docs.title: Question 2: RSA Key Strength
docs.text:
You generated a 4096-bit RSA key. RSA security depends on the difficulty of factoring large numbers: specifically, the product of two large prime numbers.

  • Why is a 4096-bit RSA key considered secure today?
  • The largest RSA key ever publicly factored was 829 bits (RSA-250) in 2020, using a cluster of computers over several years. How many bits is your key, and roughly how much harder is it to factor?
  • Quantum computers threaten RSA encryption. Research: what key size would be needed to resist quantum attacks? (Hint: the answer might surprise you.)

docs.title: Question 3: The Trade-offs
docs.text:
The cafe owner asks: "If encryption is so good, why isn't everything encrypted? Why don't we encrypt every file on every computer?"

Write a response addressing:

  • Performance cost: Encryption requires CPU time. What impact would encrypting everything have on the cafe's POS system during a rush?
  • Key management: If every file is encrypted, where do you store all the keys? What happens if a key is lost?
  • Usability: How would employees access encrypted files? What training would they need?
  • The practical answer: What files SHOULD the cafe encrypt, and what can remain in plaintext?

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text:
In Exercise C11.2 ("Protect the Backup"), you'll face a real-world scenario: the NAS has a backup file encrypted using the hybrid approach (AES + RSA). The private key is hidden somewhere on the barista workstation. You'll need to find it, decrypt the chain, and recover the backup: independently, with no step-by-step guidance.

The skills you practiced here, symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption, and the hybrid approach, are exactly what you'll need.

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client: Bean & Byte Cafe Role: Security Auditor Phase: Reconnaissance Service Enumeration Exploitation Detection Defense Encryption

What you know so far:

  • You've completed Exercise C11.1 and understand symmetric (AES) and asymmetric (RSA) encryption
  • You know the hybrid approach: AES encrypts the data, RSA encrypts the AES key
  • You've practiced encryption and decryption with OpenSSL on the command line
  • The cafe recently implemented an encryption policy for all POS backup files on the NAS

Your task: The NAS has an encrypted backup that the cafe owner needs urgently. The IT admin who set up the encryption is unreachable. Find the decryption key, reverse the hybrid encryption chain, and recover the backup contents.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Independently decrypt a hybrid-encrypted backup file on the NAS. The backup was encrypted using AES-256-CBC, and the AES key was encrypted using RSA. You must locate the RSA private key, decrypt the AES key, then use it to decrypt the backup file and recover the flag.

Difficulty: Beginner Estimated time: 45 minutes

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The Bean & Byte Cafe implemented your encryption recommendations from Phase 11. All POS backup files on the NAS are now encrypted using the hybrid approach:

  1. A random AES-256 key encrypts the backup data
  2. The AES key is encrypted with an RSA public key
  3. Only the corresponding RSA private key can reverse the chain

The cafe owner needs the latest POS revenue report for a tax filing deadline. The IT admin who configured the encryption left for a two-week vacation and isn't answering their phone.

The encrypted backup is on the NAS. The decryption key is somewhere on the network. The cafe owner is counting on you.

docs.title: See the Encrypted Backup on the NAS
docs.text:
The NAS runs a web File Station you can open in a browser before you touch the command line. Seeing the encrypted files listed makes the task concrete: you are looking at the exact .enc files you will decrypt. The NAS serves this console over HTTPS on port 8443. Substitute your own subnet base for <NAS_IP>.

Open the NAS File Station

From a browser on your Kali machine, open the NAS File Station. It uses a self-signed certificate, so accept the browser certificate warning the first time.

https://<NAS_IP>:8443/

The /backups view lists the cafe files. Two of them appear in red: pos_backup_encrypted.enc and backup_key.enc. The status line at the bottom reads Encryption policy active since March 2026. Those two red files are your target: the encrypted backup data and the RSA-encrypted AES key that protects it.

The File Station only shows you that the files exist; it does not decrypt them. To recover the backup you still need the RSA private key from the barista workstation and the OpenSSL chain below. Note the two .enc filenames now, because you will pull them off the NAS over SSH in the next steps.

docs.title: Network Topology
docs.text:
Device IP Offset Hostname Role Cafe Gateway .1 cafe-gateway Default route, NAT Barista Workstation .23 barista-pc Staff workstation, IT admin's primary machine NAS Backup .127 cafe-nas File storage, contains encrypted backups

Known credentials:

Device Username Password Barista Workstation barista C0ff33_Br3w# NAS Backup admin password

docs.title: Objectives Checklist
docs.text:
Complete all items to successfully recover the backup:

  • Connect to the NAS and examine the encrypted backup files
  • Read the README to understand the encryption scheme used
  • Locate the RSA private key on the barista workstation
  • Copy the encrypted files to a machine where you can work with them
  • Decrypt the RSA-encrypted AES key using the private key
  • Decrypt the AES-256-CBC encrypted backup using the recovered key
  • Read the decrypted backup and find the flag
  • Submit the flag

docs.title: Tools and Concepts
docs.text:
You have everything you need from Exercise C11.1. Here's a reminder of the relevant tools: no commands provided this time:

Tool What It Does openssl enc Symmetric encryption and decryption (AES) openssl pkeyutl Asymmetric encryption and decryption (RSA) ssh / scp Connect to remote machines and copy files between them cat View file contents ls -la List files including hidden ones find Search for files by name or pattern

Key concepts to apply:

  • The hybrid decryption chain has two steps: order matters
  • The AES key must be decrypted first (with RSA), then used to decrypt the data
  • The RSA private key might not be in an obvious location: IT admins often store keys in config directories
  • Hidden files start with a dot (.) and don't appear in a regular ls listing
  • scp can copy files between machines: scp user@host:/path/to/file ./local_destination

docs.title: Flag
docs.text:
The flag is embedded in the decrypted backup file.

Flag format: OCR{_____________}

What to look for

Once you successfully decrypt the backup, the flag will be clearly visible in the file contents. You do not need to search for hidden text: read the decrypted output. If tokens appear with the OCR-SN: prefix, strip the prefix when assembling the flag.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• The backup was encrypted with AES-256-CBC (not AES-128-CBC). Make sure your decryption command uses the correct algorithm.
  • The AES key was encrypted with RSA. You need the corresponding RSA private key.
  • The -base64 flag was used during encryption, so you'll need it during decryption too.
  • Check the NAS README carefully: it tells you exactly what encryption was used.

docs.title: Report Template
docs.text:
After recovering the backup, write a brief incident response report:

Paragraph 1: What Happened: Describe the situation: what was encrypted, what encryption scheme was used, and why access was needed urgently.

Paragraph 2: What You Did: Walk through the steps you took to recover the backup. What did you find, where did you find it, and how did you use it?

Paragraph 3: Recommendations: What should the cafe do differently? Consider:

  • Key escrow: should a backup copy of the private key exist? Where should it be stored?
  • Documentation: was the encryption setup documented? How would a new employee know how to access backups?
  • Single point of failure: what happens if the IT admin's workstation is compromised or destroyed? Is the private key backed up?
  • Separation of duties: should the same person who encrypts the backups also hold the only copy of the private key?

This report is not graded

The report is a professional development exercise. In real security consulting, documenting your findings and making actionable recommendations is as important as the technical work itself.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Using the wrong AES variant (AES-128 vs AES-256): the error message may be cryptic
  • Forgetting the -base64 flag during decryption: results in a garbled output or error
  • Looking for the private key on the NAS instead of the barista workstation
  • Trying to decrypt the backup directly with the RSA key (you must decrypt the AES key first)
  • Not checking hidden files and directories (use ls -la and explore .config/ directories)

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text:
With Exercises C11.1 and C11.2 complete, you understand the encryption fundamentals that protect data at rest and in transit. You can now:

  • Encrypt files using symmetric (AES) and asymmetric (RSA) encryption
  • Decrypt files using the corresponding keys
  • Understand the hybrid approach that powers TLS/HTTPS and modern file encryption
  • Apply encryption concepts to real-world scenarios independently

These skills are foundational for understanding certificate-based authentication, TLS inspection, VPN tunnels, and disk encryption: all topics you'll encounter in advanced security work.

docs.title: Exercise 12A: HTTP vs HTTPS: See the Difference
Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client: Bean & Byte Cafe Role: Security Auditor Phase: Reconnaissance Service Enumeration Exploitation ARP Encryption in Transit

What you know so far:

  • You have mapped the cafe network and identified every device.
  • You have performed ARP reconnaissance and spoofing attacks.
  • You have learned about encryption concepts (symmetric, asymmetric, hybrid).
  • The cafe is mid-upgrade: the old POS terminal still answers on plain HTTP, while a new secure portal answers on HTTPS.

Your task: Read a destination-side packet capture from two cafe services, the POS terminal on HTTP and the secure portal on HTTPS, then compare what each one reveals. The HTTP capture exposes a staff login in plain text, flag and all. The HTTPS capture protects the same kind of login behind TLS so it never appears on the wire in readable form.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Compare an HTTP service against an HTTPS service using real captured traffic. Read the cleartext credentials from the HTTP capture, confirm that the HTTPS service exposes nothing readable, and explain why that single difference, TLS, decides whether a password is private or public. Extract the flag from the plaintext HTTP traffic.

Difficulty: Beginner Estimated time: 45 minutes

docs.title: The Padlock in Your Browser
docs.text:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) is encryption for network traffic. When the padlock icon shows in a browser address bar, TLS is protecting the data in transit. Every value sent between the browser and the server, passwords, card numbers, personal messages, is encrypted before it leaves the machine and decrypted only after it arrives.

HTTP has no such protection. An HTTP request travels as readable ASCII text. Anyone positioned to read the traffic, a destination host, a tapped switch port, a compromised router, sees the request exactly as the sender typed it.

docs.title: A Brief History: SSL to TLS
docs.text:
Version Year Status SSL 2.0 1995 Deprecated (insecure) SSL 3.0 1996 Deprecated (POODLE attack) TLS 1.0 1999 Deprecated TLS 1.1 2006 Deprecated TLS 1.2 2008 Widely supported standard TLS 1.3 2018 Latest and fastest

SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) was the original protocol from the 1990s. The IETF renamed it to TLS when development moved over. People still say "SSL" out of habit, but every modern secure connection uses TLS. When someone says "SSL certificate," they mean a TLS certificate.

docs.title: Why the Difference Matters Here
docs.text:
A login is a login. The POS staff login and the secure portal login carry the same kind of data: a username and a password. The only thing that changes between the two services is the transport:

  • The POS terminal answers on HTTP, port 8080. The login POST crosses the wire as plain text.
  • The secure portal answers on HTTPS, port 443. The same login POST crosses the wire as TLS ciphertext.

By the end of this exercise you will have read both captures with your own eyes and seen that one hands you the password and the other hands you nothing.

docs.title: Section 2: How the Capture Reaches You
A Note on Where Captures Come From
docs.text:
A passive third host on a switched or bridged network cannot simply sniff another pair of hosts talking. The switch forwards frames only to the port that owns the destination MAC, so traffic between the login simulator and the POS never reaches an uninvolved listener.

The destination host, on the other hand, receives every byte addressed to it. In this lab each plaintext-HTTP service runs a packet capture on its own interface and publishes that capture over a small read endpoint. The POS terminal serves its running capture at http://<POS_IP>:8080/tap. You read it from the network tap, so you are looking at genuine captured packets, not a contrived text file.

The secure portal does no such thing, and it does not need to. Its traffic is already TLS ciphertext on the wire, so there is nothing readable to publish.

docs.title: Network Layout
docs.text:
Device Hostname IP Offset Port Transport Cafe Gateway cafe-gateway .1 80/443 mixed POS Terminal cafe-pos .17 8080 HTTP Secure Portal cafe-secure-portal .180 443 HTTPS Login Simulator cafe-login-sim .190 none client Network Tap nettap .250 22 SSH

The placeholders <SUBNET>, <POS_IP>, and <PORTAL_IP> stand in for values from your lab page. If your subnet base is 10.100.121, then the POS is 10.100.121.17, the portal is 10.100.121.180, and the tap is 10.100.121.250. The transcripts below use those exact addresses.

docs.title: See Both Services in a Browser First
docs.text:
Before reading a single capture, open the two services in a browser so the difference between them is something you have looked at, not just something you have been told. Both pages handle a staff login. Only one of them protects it on the wire.

Browse the plain-HTTP POS terminal

From a browser on your Kali machine, open the POS register over plain HTTP. Substitute your own subnet base for <POS_IP>.

http://<POS_IP>:8080/

The address bar shows http:// with no padlock. The POS register loads in the clear: live transaction log, card numbers, revenue totals, and a Manager Login tab. Every byte of this page, and every credential typed into that login, crosses the wire as readable text.

Browse the HTTPS secure portal

Now open the secure portal over HTTPS in the same browser. Substitute your own subnet base for <PORTAL_IP>.

https://<PORTAL_IP>/

The portal uses a self-signed certificate, so the browser shows a certificate warning the first time; accept it to continue. The page is the cafe employee login, and it states Connection secured with TLS with a padlock. The login form looks the same as the POS, but the transport underneath it is TLS ciphertext, not cleartext.

Hold the two pages side by side. The POS on the left is http:// and exposes its data in the open; the portal on the right is https:// and wraps the identical kind of login in TLS. The rest of this exercise proves, from the captures, that the page you just loaded over HTTP hands its password to anyone on the wire while the HTTPS page hands over nothing readable.

docs.title: Step 0: SSH into the Network Tap
docs.text:
Start "Bean & Byte Cafe: HTTP vs HTTPS" from the Coffee Shop labs and wait for Running. Note the subnet on the lab page. All capture reading happens from the tap device, an on-subnet jump box, because you must be on the same broadcast domain as the cafe traffic.

Connect to the tap over SSH

From your Kali machine, SSH into the tap at offset .250. The password is Security1#. Replace the address with your subnet if it differs.

ssh pentest@<SUBNET>.250

Once connected, the prompt changes to pentest@nettap. Everything from here runs on the tap.

docs.title: Step 1: Read the HTTP Capture from the POS
docs.text:
The POS terminal publishes its running capture at /tap. The login simulator sends a staff login every few seconds, so within a few seconds of the lab starting there is captured traffic to read.

Pull the POS capture and find the login POST

From the tap, read the served capture and isolate the login request. The first command shows the IP header line so you can see who is talking to whom; the second pulls the line that carries the credential token.

curl -s http://<POS_IP>:8080/tap | grep -a -B1 'POST /login' | head -2
curl -s http://<POS_IP>:8080/tap | grep -a 'OCR-SN'

The captured output looks like the screenshot below. The IP header line shows the login simulator at 10.100.121.190 sending to the POS at 10.100.121.17 on port 8080. The body line carries the username, the password, and the flag token, all in clear text.

Read the body line carefully:

username=barista&password=C0ff33_OCR-SN:<TOKEN>&token=OCR-SN:<TOKEN>

The username is barista. The password and a token both carry the marker OCR-SN:, and the value after that marker is the flag content. Nothing here is hashed, masked, or encrypted. The wire carried the password as plainly as if it were printed on a receipt.

docs.title: Step 2: See the Whole Request, Not Just the Body
docs.text:
The credential is not an isolated leak. The entire HTTP request is readable, headers and all, which means an observer learns the target host, the content type, the exact field names, and the values.

Read the full HTTP request from the capture

Pull a few lines of context around the POST so you can see the complete request as it crossed the wire.

curl -s http://<POS_IP>:8080/tap | grep -a -A6 'POST /login' | head -8

A defender reading this should feel the weight of it. Anyone on the path, a malicious destination, a switch-port tap, a router admin, reconstructs the entire login with no effort and no cracking. HTTP made the password public the moment it was sent.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm the Secure Portal Protects the Same Data
docs.text:
Now look at the HTTPS service. The secure portal carries the same kind of staff login, but over TLS. Test three things: that the portal answers over a real TLS connection, that it offers no plaintext capture to read, and that the HTTPS credential never appears anywhere in the clear.

Probe the HTTPS portal and prove the data is protected

The -k flag tells curl to accept the portal self-signed certificate. The verbose probe prints the negotiated TLS version and the certificate subject. The last two commands show that the portal has no capture feed and that the HTTPS password is absent from the POS capture.

curl -ks https://<PORTAL_IP>/ | grep -i title
curl -ksv https://<PORTAL_IP>/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'SSL connection|subject:'
curl -ks -o /dev/null -w 'GET /tap -> HTTP %{http_code}\n' https://<PORTAL_IP>/tap
curl -s http://<POS_IP>:8080/tap | grep -c 'S3cur3_N0t_V1s1bl3'

Read the four results together:

  • The portal returns its application page, so the service is live and working.
  • The connection negotiated TLSv1.3 with an AES-256-GCM cipher, and the certificate identifies cafe-secure-portal. The traffic on the wire is genuine TLS ciphertext.
  • The portal has no /tap feed, so the request returns HTTP 404. There is no plaintext capture to read, because there is no plaintext.
  • The portal login password S3cur3_N0t_V1s1bl3 appears 0 times in the POS capture. Even when the same simulator sends an HTTPS login every cycle, that credential never shows up in readable form anywhere on the network.

Same login pattern, same kind of secret, opposite outcome. TLS is the only thing that changed.

docs.title: Step 4: Submit the Flag
docs.text:
Assemble the flag

The token you read from the POS capture sits after the OCR-SN: marker in the cleartext password and token fields. Its value expresses exactly what happened: a cleartext credential exposed on the wire.

Wrap the token in the flag format and submit it:

OCR{ ... }

Place the token you captured inside the OCR{} wrapper and submit it on the lab page.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
A password is only as private as the transport carrying it. In this exercise the POS and the portal handled the same kind of staff login, but only one of them kept it secret. HTTP put the username, the password, and a token into readable ASCII that any host on the path could lift without cracking anything. HTTPS wrapped the identical exchange in TLS, so the wire carried only ciphertext and a 404 where the plaintext capture would have been.

The lesson is not that the cafe staff chose weak passwords. The lesson is that on plain HTTP the strength of the password does not matter, because the attacker never has to guess it. TLS is what turns a readable credential into a string of random bytes. Every service that handles a login, a session cookie, a card number, or any private value belongs on HTTPS for exactly this reason. A service still answering on plain HTTP, like the cafe POS, is handing its secrets to anyone who can read its traffic.

When you audit a network, treat every plain-HTTP service that accepts sensitive input as already breached. The fix is not a stronger password. The fix is TLS.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• HTTP traffic crosses the wire as readable text; a destination-side capture exposes the full request, credentials included.
  • HTTPS wraps the same request in TLS, so the wire carries ciphertext and an observer sees nothing useful.
  • A TLS handshake is visible (version and cipher negotiation), but the application data after it is not.
  • Password strength is irrelevant on plain HTTP, because the credential is captured rather than cracked.
  • Any service accepting sensitive input over HTTP should be treated as exposed until it is moved to HTTPS.

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client: Bean & Byte Cafe Role: Security Auditor Phase: Reconnaissance Service Enumeration Exploitation ARP Encryption in Transit

What you know so far:

  • You have observed the difference between HTTP and HTTPS traffic firsthand.
  • You know how to read a destination-side capture from the network tap.
  • The cafe has expanded: several services now run, some on HTTP and some on HTTPS.
  • A login simulator sends credentials to each of them on a loop.

Your task: Survey the expanded cafe network on your own, classify every service as protected (HTTPS) or unprotected (HTTP), and recover the flag that the unprotected services leak. The flag is split into two halves, one in each HTTP service capture.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Work the network independently. Classify four services by transport security, read the cleartext POST bodies that the two HTTP services expose, and assemble the flag from the two tokens. Confirm that the two HTTPS services protect their credentials so nothing readable reaches the wire. Produce a short service security report for the cafe owner.

Difficulty: Beginner Estimated time: 30 minutes

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
The previous exercise walked you through a single HTTP service against a single HTTPS service. Here the cafe runs four services at once, and the flag is deliberately split so you have to find and read more than one capture.

Two of the four services answer on plain HTTP. Each one runs a destination-side packet capture on its own interface and serves that capture over a small read endpoint, the same model you used on the POS terminal. The other two answer on HTTPS, so their traffic is TLS ciphertext and there is nothing readable to publish.

Your job is to decide which is which by evidence, not by assumption, and to lift the flag from the services that fail to protect it.

docs.title: Network Layout
docs.text:
Device Hostname IP Offset Port Capture endpoint Security Camera DVR cafe-dvr .67 80 /tap Menu Display cafe-menu .89 80 /tap NAS Backup cafe-nas .127 8443 none (HTTPS) Secure Portal cafe-secure-portal .180 443 none (HTTPS) Login Simulator cafe-login-sim .190 none client Network Tap nettap .250 22 SSH

The placeholders <SUBNET> and the per-host addresses stand in for values from your lab page. If your subnet base is 10.100.121, then the DVR is 10.100.121.67, the menu display is 10.100.121.89, the NAS is 10.100.121.127, and the portal is 10.100.121.180. The transcripts below use those exact addresses.

docs.title: Browse the Four Services First
docs.text:
Before you classify anything from a capture, open all four services in a browser and let the address bar tell you the first part of the story. Two of them load over http:// with no padlock; two of them load over https:// and present a TLS connection. Substitute your own subnet base for each placeholder.

Open the two plain-HTTP services

From a browser on your Kali machine, open the DVR console and the menu display. Both answer on plain HTTP, port 80.

http://<DVR_IP>/
http://<MENU_IP>/

The DVR serves an admin login console (admin username pre-filled), and the menu display serves the public cafe menu board. Neither shows a padlock, because neither uses TLS. The login the DVR accepts crosses the wire in the clear, which is exactly why a capture of its traffic will hand you a credential.

Open the two HTTPS services

Now open the NAS File Station and the management portal over HTTPS. The NAS answers on port 8443, the portal on 443. Both use self-signed certificates, so accept the browser certificate warning the first time.

https://<NAS_IP>:8443/
https://<PORTAL_IP>/

The NAS File Station lists the cafe backup files, and the portal presents a login that states Encrypted connection (TLS) with a padlock. Both run real TLS underneath, so their traffic on the wire is ciphertext rather than readable text.

You have now seen the split with your own eyes: two http:// services on the left exposing their pages in the open, two https:// services on the right wrapped in TLS. The rest of this exercise proves it from the captures, recovers the flag the two HTTP services leak, and confirms the two HTTPS services leak nothing.

docs.title: Step 0: SSH into the Network Tap
docs.text:
Start "Bean & Byte Cafe: What's Protected?" from the Coffee Shop labs and wait for Running. Note the subnet on the lab page. All capture reading happens from the tap, an on-subnet jump box, because you must sit on the same broadcast domain as the cafe traffic.

Connect to the tap over SSH

From your Kali machine, SSH into the tap at offset .250. The password is Security1#. Replace the address with your subnet if it differs.

ssh pentest@<SUBNET>.250

The prompt becomes pentest@nettap. Everything below runs from the tap.

docs.title: Step 1: Classify Each Service by Transport
docs.text:
Before reading any captures, decide which services are HTTP and which are HTTPS. A plain HTTP service answers an http:// request; an HTTPS service answers https:// and negotiates a TLS connection. Probe all four and note which scheme each one accepts.

Probe every service and record its transport

The -k flag accepts the self-signed certificates on the HTTPS hosts. A 200 against http:// means the service is unprotected; a 200 against https:// means it speaks TLS.

curl -ks -o /dev/null -w 'http://<DVR_IP>:80 -> %{http_code}\n'      http://<DVR_IP>:80/
curl -ks -o /dev/null -w 'http://<MENU_IP>:80 -> %{http_code}\n'     http://<MENU_IP>:80/
curl -ks -o /dev/null -w 'https://<NAS_IP>:8443 -> %{http_code}\n'   https://<NAS_IP>:8443/
curl -ks -o /dev/null -w 'https://<PORTAL_IP>:443 -> %{http_code}\n' https://<PORTAL_IP>:443/

The DVR and the menu display answer over plain HTTP. The NAS and the secure portal answer over HTTPS. The two HTTP services are the ones that will leak.

docs.title: Step 2: Read the Two HTTP Captures and Recover Both Flag Halves
docs.text:
Each HTTP service publishes its running capture at /tap. The login simulator sends a credentialed POST to each one on its cycle, so both captures contain a plaintext login. Read both and pull the line carrying the OCR-SN: marker.

Pull the cleartext tokens from both HTTP services

Read each capture and grep for the credential marker. The DVR carries the first half of the flag; the menu display carries the second.

curl -s http://<DVR_IP>/tap  | grep -a 'OCR-SN'
curl -s http://<MENU_IP>/tap | grep -a 'OCR-SN'

Read both bodies:

username=admin&password=OCR-SN:<TOKEN>&session=cam_review_01
username=manager&password=OCR-SN:<TOKEN>&content=daily_specials

Strip the OCR-SN: prefix from each password to read the token. The first token is the DVR password value after its prefix; the second token is the menu display password value after its prefix. Both crossed the wire as plain text, captured at the destination with no cracking required.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm the HTTPS Services Protect Their Credentials
docs.text:
The NAS and the secure portal carry their own logins, but over TLS. Verify that each negotiates a real TLS connection, that neither offers a plaintext capture endpoint, and that neither HTTPS password ever appears in the HTTP captures you just read.

Prove the HTTPS services leak nothing

The verbose probe prints the negotiated TLS version and certificate subject. The /tap probe shows there is no capture feed to read. The two grep counts show the HTTPS passwords are absent from the HTTP captures.

curl -ksv https://<NAS_IP>:8443/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'SSL connection|subject:'
curl -ks -o /dev/null -w 'NAS /tap -> HTTP %{http_code}\n' https://<NAS_IP>:8443/tap
curl -s http://<DVR_IP>/tap  | grep -c 'N4S_Pr0t3ct3d_S3cr3t'
curl -s http://<MENU_IP>/tap | grep -c 'P0rt4l_Encryp73d_S4f3'

Read the results together:

  • The NAS negotiates TLSv1.3 with an AES-256-GCM cipher and presents a certificate for CafeNAS. The secure portal does the same under cafe-secure-portal. The traffic to both is genuine TLS ciphertext.
  • The NAS has no /tap feed and returns HTTP 404. There is no plaintext capture, because there is no plaintext to capture.
  • The NAS password N4S_Pr0t3ct3d_S3cr3t and the portal password P0rt4l_Encryp73d_S4f3 each appear 0 times in the HTTP captures. The same simulator sends those logins every cycle, yet neither one ever surfaces in readable form.

docs.title: Step 4: Write the Service Security Report
docs.text:
You now have everything for the cafe owner report. Classify each service and flag the unprotected ones for remediation.

Service Transport Status Exposure Security Camera DVR HTTP Unprotected Credentials and token in clear Menu Display HTTP Unprotected Credentials and token in clear NAS Backup HTTPS Protected TLS 1.3, nothing readable on wire Secure Portal HTTPS Protected TLS 1.3, nothing readable on wire

The recommendation writes itself: move the DVR and the menu display to HTTPS, because right now both hand their admin credentials to anyone who can read their traffic.

docs.title: Step 5: Submit the Flag
docs.text:
Assemble the flag from both halves

The first token comes from the DVR password; the second fragment comes from the menu display password. Joined with an underscore they spell out the lesson: HTTP needs TLS.

Combine the two halves inside the OCR{} wrapper and submit it:

OCR{ ... }

Join the two halves you captured with an underscore, wrap the result in OCR{}, and submit it on the lab page.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
The cafe did not run a single insecure service by accident; it ran several, side by side with secure ones, and could not tell them apart. That is the real situation an auditor walks into. Some services were moved to HTTPS, the NAS and the portal, and they held the line: TLS 1.3 turned each login into ciphertext, and nothing readable reached the wire. The DVR and the menu display were left on plain HTTP, and both leaked their admin credentials and a flag token to any host that could read their traffic.

The split flag drives the point home. One insecure service is enough to lose a secret, and the cafe had two. An audit that stops at the first finding misses the rest, so the discipline is to classify every service by evidence and treat each plain-HTTP service that accepts sensitive input as already breached.

The remediation is the same as last time and just as simple to state: HTTP needs TLS. Every service handling a credential, a session, or any private value belongs on HTTPS, and the ones that are not belong at the top of the fix list.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Classify services by evidence: probe each one and confirm whether it answers over HTTP or HTTPS before drawing conclusions.
  • A single plain-HTTP service is enough to leak a credential; an expanded network multiplies the exposure.
  • HTTP captures hand over the full login at the destination with no cracking; HTTPS captures yield only ciphertext and a 404 where a plaintext feed would be.
  • A self-signed certificate still provides real TLS encryption on the wire; the -k flag only bypasses trust validation, not the encryption itself.
  • The fix for an exposed HTTP service is TLS, not a stronger password.

docs.title: Why Reconnaissance Matters
docs.text:
Every penetration test begins with reconnaissance. Before launching a single exploit, an assessor must understand what the target exposes: its pages, forms, technologies, and configuration details. Skipping reconnaissance means attacking blind, wasting time on defenses that do not exist and missing vulnerabilities hidden in plain sight. The two exercises in this chapter teach systematic web reconnaissance against a realistic fintech trading platform.

CapitalFlow Markets is a fictional financial technology company preparing to launch a public trading platform. The company retained your firm to assess its web presence before going live. The platform serves a homepage, authentication forms, API endpoints, and supporting documentation. Your job across both exercises is to map the entire attack surface and identify every piece of information that could aid an attacker.

docs.title: Chapter Exercises
docs.text:
Chapter CF01 contains two exercises that build on each other in sequence.

Exercise Title Core Skill Tools CF1.1 Basic Web Enumeration Page discovery, source analysis, form identification curl, browser, gobuster CF1.2 Technology Fingerprinting Server/framework identification, header analysis curl -I, whatweb

Exercise CF1.1 covers manual exploration: browsing pages, reading HTML source, checking comments, inspecting forms, and enumerating directories. Exercise CF1.2 shifts to technology identification: extracting server versions, framework signatures, and JavaScript library details from HTTP headers and page content.

docs.title: Progression
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["CF1.1<br/>Web Enumeration"] --> B["CF1.2<br/>Tech Fingerprinting"]
    B --> C["CF2.1<br/>Login Bruteforce"]
    C --> D["CF2.2-2.5<br/>Auth Attacks"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style D fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

The reconnaissance phase feeds directly into the authentication attack exercises in Chapter 2. Information gathered here (login endpoints, form field names, technology versions, hidden directories) becomes the foundation for brute-force, session hijacking, SQL injection, IDOR, and XSS attacks.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Confirm each item below before starting Exercise CF1.1.

  • Platform account is active and approved
  • VPN tunnel is connected (test with ping to a lab IP)
  • Terminal application is open (Linux terminal, macOS Terminal, or Windows WSL)
  • You can access the Exercises page on the platform
  • You have a web browser available for manual inspection

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have read the Chapter 1 Introduction, which explains the CapitalFlow Markets scenario and the progression through both reconnaissance exercises. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before continuing. No prior web exploitation experience is required; every step is explained in full.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
CapitalFlow Markets is a fintech startup preparing to launch a public trading platform. Sarah Chen (CTO) has retained your firm, Blackridge Security, to perform a pre-launch security assessment. The first phase focuses entirely on reconnaissance: mapping the web application's pages, forms, inputs, and any information leaked through HTML source code, comments, or configuration files.

Sarah provided the following brief: "We pushed the trading platform to our staging environment last week. The development team says everything is production-ready, but I want an independent review of what the site exposes before we open registration. Focus on what an unauthenticated visitor can discover."

Target: capitalflow.lab (port 80)

No credentials are provided for this exercise. You are assessing the application as an unauthenticated visitor.

The CapitalFlow Markets landing page is your starting point. Every navigation link, button, and section here is a lead to follow, and the HTML behind it may hold comments the rendered page never shows.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Browse every accessible page on the CapitalFlow Markets website
  • Examine HTML source code for hidden comments, hardcoded values, and developer notes
  • Identify all forms and input fields, recording their field names and submission endpoints
  • Check HTTP response headers for information leakage
  • Discover hidden or unlisted directories using automated enumeration
  • Find and submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Why Source Code Matters
docs.text: Every web page a browser renders is built from HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), CSS (Cascading Style Sheets), and JavaScript files delivered by the server. The browser interprets these files to display the visual page, but the raw source code often contains more than what appears on screen. Developers leave comments in the HTML to communicate with teammates, embed version strings for debugging, include references to internal API endpoints, and sometimes hardcode credentials or tokens during development. Viewing the page source reveals all of this information.

docs.title: Forms and Input Fields
docs.text: HTML forms collect user input and submit it to the server. Each form contains <input> elements with name attributes that define the parameter names sent in the HTTP request. Knowing the exact field names and the form's action URL (where data is submitted) is essential for later testing phases. A login form with fields named email and password submitting to /api/auth/login tells an attacker exactly where to send brute-force attempts.

docs.title: robots.txt and Directory Enumeration
docs.text:
The robots.txt file instructs search engine crawlers which paths to avoid indexing. Security testers read this file because it often lists directories the organization considers sensitive. Directory enumeration tools like gobuster take this further by testing thousands of common path names against the server and reporting which ones return valid responses.

graph TD
    A["Browse homepage<br/>and visible pages"] --> B["View HTML source<br/>for comments/tokens"]
    A --> C["Check robots.txt<br/>for hidden paths"]
    A --> D["Inspect HTTP headers<br/>for server info"]
    B --> E["Record forms,<br/>inputs, endpoints"]
    C --> F["Run gobuster<br/>for directory scan"]
    D --> E
    F --> E
    E --> G["Complete attack<br/>surface map"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style E fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style G fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

The diagram above shows the reconnaissance workflow. Manual browsing, source inspection, and header analysis happen in parallel, all feeding into a comprehensive map of the application's attack surface.

docs.title: curl for Web Requests
docs.text:
curl is a command-line tool for sending HTTP requests and viewing raw responses. Penetration testers use curl because it shows the exact HTML, headers, and status codes without browser rendering getting in the way.

Basic GET request:

curl -s http://<target>/

View response headers only:

curl -I http://<target>/

Verbose mode (request and response headers):

curl -v http://<target>/
Flag Purpose -s Silent mode; hides the progress bar -I Fetch headers only (HEAD request) -v Verbose; show full request and response headers -L Follow redirects automatically -o /dev/null Discard response body

docs.title: gobuster for Directory Enumeration
docs.text:
Gobuster sends HTTP requests for each entry in a wordlist and reports which paths return valid responses.

gobuster dir -u http://<target> -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt
Flag Purpose dir Directory brute-forcing mode -u Target URL -w Path to wordlist -t Number of threads (default 10) -x File extensions to test (e.g., -x html,txt,php)

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the CapitalFlow Markets track
  • Find Basic Web Enumeration and click Launch
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Browse the Homepage
docs.text:
Begin by visiting the CapitalFlow Markets homepage. Read the visible content and get a sense of what the application presents to visitors.

Kali - Fetch the homepage

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/

Read through the HTML output. Look for navigation links, page sections, and any references to other pages or endpoints. Note every URL you find in href attributes, as each one is a page worth visiting. Pay attention to links pointing to login pages, about pages, documentation, or API references.

docs.title: Step 3: Examine the HTML Source for Comments and Hidden Content
docs.text:
Developers embed comments in HTML using <!-- --> tags. These comments are invisible in the browser but fully visible in the source code. Search the homepage source for any comments that contain credentials, internal notes, version strings, or references to hidden functionality.

Kali - Search for HTML comments on the homepage

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/ | grep -i "<!--"

Review each comment you find. Developer notes sometimes include TODO items referencing unfinished security features, hardcoded test credentials left from development, or internal endpoint paths. Record everything, even comments that seem harmless, because they may become relevant in later exercises.

docs.title: Step 4: Visit All Linked Pages
docs.text:
Follow every link you discovered on the homepage. Each page may contain additional forms, comments, or information not present on the landing page.

Kali - Fetch the login page

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/login

Kali - Fetch the about page

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/about

Kali - Fetch the contact or support page

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/contact

For each page, read the HTML output and search for <form> elements, <input> fields, comments, and links to additional resources. Login and registration forms are especially important; record the form action URL, the HTTP method (GET or POST), and every name attribute on the input fields.

docs.title: Step 5: Inspect Login Form Fields
docs.text:
The login page contains the form you will target in Chapter 2. Document its structure completely.

Kali - Extract form fields from the login page

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/login | grep -i "input\|form\|action\|method"

Record the form action (e.g., /api/auth/login), the method (POST), and the input field names (e.g., email, password). Knowing these details is essential for crafting authentication attacks in later exercises.

The sign-in form is the authentication entry point you will attack in Chapter 2. Document its action URL, method, and the email and password field names exactly as they appear in the source.

docs.title: Step 6: Check HTTP Response Headers
docs.text:
HTTP headers sent by the server can reveal the web server software, application framework, caching policies, and security configurations. Many servers include a Server header identifying the software and version.

Kali - Fetch HTTP response headers

curl -I http://capitalflow.lab/

Look for these headers in the response:

  • Server: Identifies the web server (e.g., nginx, Apache)
  • X-Powered-By: Reveals the backend framework (e.g., Express, PHP)
  • X-Frame-Options: Indicates clickjacking protection
  • Content-Security-Policy: Shows what resources the page can load
  • Set-Cookie: Reveals session management details and cookie flags

Each header provides intelligence. A Server: nginx/1.24.0 header tells you the exact version, which you can cross-reference with CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) databases. A missing X-Frame-Options header means the site may be vulnerable to clickjacking.

docs.title: Step 7: Check robots.txt
docs.text:
The robots.txt file often reveals paths the organization wants to keep out of search engines. Retrieve and review it.

Kali - Fetch robots.txt

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/robots.txt

Look for Disallow entries listing directory paths. Each path listed is a directory worth visiting manually. Developers sometimes list admin panels, backup directories, or staging endpoints here, thinking that search engine exclusion equals access control.

docs.title: Step 8: Enumerate Directories with gobuster
docs.text:
Manual browsing only finds pages that are linked from other pages. Directory enumeration tests thousands of common path names to find unlisted content.

Kali - Run gobuster with the common wordlist

gobuster dir -u http://capitalflow.lab -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Wait for the scan to complete. Review each result, paying attention to the HTTP status codes:

  • 200: The path exists and returned content
  • 301/302: The path exists and redirected (usually a valid directory)
  • 403: The path exists but access is denied (worth noting for later)
  • 404: The path does not exist

Visit any paths that returned 200 or 301/302 and examine their content. Hidden administrative panels, API documentation, or backup files may appear in the results.

Kali - Visit a discovered directory

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/<discovered-path>/

Replace <discovered-path> with each interesting path from the gobuster output. Look for tokens, credentials, or references to internal systems.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document everything you discovered during the reconnaissance phase.

Pages discovered:

URL Path Description Notable Content / Homepage /login Login page

HTML comments found:

(paste any comments here)

Form fields identified:

Form Location Action URL Method Field Names /login

HTTP headers of interest:

Header Value Server X-Powered-By

robots.txt entries:

(paste output here)

gobuster results:

(paste output here)

Flag:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider each question carefully before reading the answer. These questions connect the reconnaissance techniques to real-world security implications.

1. Why should developers remove HTML comments before deploying a web application to production?

Reveal Answer

HTML comments are delivered to every visitor's browser as part of the page source. Any information embedded in comments, such as internal API paths, developer names, TODO notes about unfinished security features, or hardcoded credentials, becomes visible to anyone who views the source. Stripping comments during the build process (using tools like HTMLMinifier or a CI/CD pipeline step) eliminates this information leakage without affecting the user experience.

2. A gobuster scan returns a path with a 403 Forbidden status. Does a 403 response mean the path is inaccessible? What should a tester do next?

Reveal Answer

A 403 response confirms the path exists but the server is denying access with the current request. The path is not necessarily inaccessible. A tester should try different HTTP methods (POST, PUT, OPTIONS), add authentication headers, test for path traversal variations (adding trailing slashes, encoding characters), and check whether the restriction applies only to certain user agents. A 403 is often more interesting than a 404 because it confirms something worth protecting lives at that path.

3. The Server header reveals the exact version of the web server software. How would an attacker use that information, and what can the organization do to reduce the risk?

Reveal Answer

An attacker cross-references the server version against public vulnerability databases (CVE, NVD, Exploit-DB) to find known exploits for that exact version. For example, a specific nginx version might have a known buffer overflow or request smuggling vulnerability. The organization can configure the web server to suppress or generalize the Server header (e.g., returning just "nginx" instead of "nginx/1.24.0") and ensure the software is patched to the latest stable release. Hiding the version slows attackers but is not a substitute for patching.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Manual browsing reveals the visible attack surface, but HTML source code, HTTP headers, and robots.txt expose information that never appears in the rendered page
  • HTML comments left by developers during the build process can leak credentials, internal paths, version strings, and TODO notes about unfinished security controls
  • HTTP response headers like Server and X-Powered-By reveal the exact technology stack, enabling attackers to search for version-specific vulnerabilities
  • Directory enumeration with tools like gobuster discovers unlisted pages, admin panels, and backup files that manual browsing would miss entirely
  • Form field documentation (action URLs, field names, HTTP methods) is the essential input for authentication attacks in Chapter 2

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have completed Exercise CF1.1 (Basic Web Enumeration), where you mapped the CapitalFlow Markets website, documented its pages and forms, and discovered hidden directories. The skills from CF1.1 carry forward here, as you will build on the attack surface map by identifying the exact technologies powering the application. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Sarah Chen (CTO of CapitalFlow Markets) reviewed your initial reconnaissance findings and wants a deeper analysis. She asked: "You found the pages and forms. Now tell me exactly what software stack we are running, down to the version numbers. If any component has a known vulnerability, I want to know before we go live."

Phase 2 of the assessment focuses on technology fingerprinting: identifying the web server, backend framework, frontend libraries, and any other software components from their signatures in HTTP headers, HTML markup, and JavaScript files.

Target: capitalflow.lab (port 80)

No credentials are provided. All fingerprinting is performed as an unauthenticated visitor.

The same CapitalFlow Markets homepage, viewed now as a fingerprinting target. The rendered page looks ordinary, but the response that delivered it carries a Server header, cookie names, and markup signatures that name the exact software stack behind it.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Extract web server identification from HTTP response headers
  • Identify the backend framework from X-Powered-By and other custom headers
  • Analyze HTML source for frontend framework signatures and meta tags
  • Inspect JavaScript files for library names and version strings
  • Run an automated fingerprinting scan with whatweb
  • Find and submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Why Technology Identification Matters
docs.text: Every piece of software has a history of vulnerabilities. Knowing that a server runs nginx 1.24.0 narrows the search to CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) affecting that exact version. Knowing the frontend uses jQuery 3.6.0 reveals whether the application is susceptible to known prototype pollution or XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) vectors in that library. Technology fingerprinting transforms a generic target into a specific list of software components, each with its own vulnerability profile.

docs.title: Where Technology Signatures Hide
docs.text:
Web applications leak technology information through multiple channels:

Source What It Reveals Example Server header Web server name and version nginx/1.24.0 X-Powered-By header Backend framework Express, PHP/8.2 HTML <meta> tags CMS or generator <meta name="generator" content="WordPress 6.4"> JavaScript <script> tags Frontend libraries jquery-3.6.0.min.js CSS class naming CSS framework class="btn btn-primary" (Bootstrap) Cookie names Session framework PHPSESSID (PHP), connect.sid (Express) Error pages Server/framework defaults Default nginx 404 or Express error handler

docs.title: Automated Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Manual inspection catches obvious signatures, but automated tools combine hundreds of detection rules to identify technologies that leave subtle traces. Tools like whatweb, Wappalyzer, and BuiltWith test for specific patterns across headers, HTML, cookies, and JavaScript.

graph TD
    A["Target web server"] --> B["HTTP Headers<br/>Server, X-Powered-By"]
    A --> C["HTML Source<br/>meta tags, scripts"]
    A --> D["JavaScript Files<br/>library versions"]
    A --> E["CSS Classes<br/>framework patterns"]
    A --> F["Cookie Names<br/>session technology"]
    B --> G["Technology<br/>Profile"]
    C --> G
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H["CVE Lookup<br/>per component"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style G fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style H fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

The diagram shows how multiple information sources feed into a complete technology profile, which then drives vulnerability research.

docs.title: curl -I for Header Inspection
docs.text:
The -I flag sends an HTTP HEAD request and displays only the response headers. Headers contain server identification, caching policy, security controls, and session management details.

curl -I http://<target>/

Sample output:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx/1.24.0
X-Powered-By: Express
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Set-Cookie: connect.sid=abc123; Path=/; HttpOnly

Each header line provides a data point for the technology profile.

docs.title: whatweb for Automated Fingerprinting
docs.text:
WhatWeb identifies web technologies by testing for known signatures across headers, HTML content, cookies, and JavaScript. The tool comes pre-installed on Kali Linux.

whatweb http://<target>/

Verbosity levels:

Flag Level Output Detail (default) Brief One-line summary of detected technologies -v Verbose Detailed breakdown of each detection -a 3 Aggressive Sends additional requests to confirm detections

Sample output:

http://example.com [200 OK] Bootstrap, Country[US], HTML5, HTTPServer[nginx/1.24.0],
JQuery[3.6.0], Script, Title[Example Site], X-Powered-By[Express]

WhatWeb lists every technology it detects along with version numbers where available.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the CapitalFlow Markets track
  • Find Technology Fingerprinting and click Launch
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Fetch HTTP Response Headers
docs.text:
Start by requesting the response headers from the main page. The headers are the fastest source of technology information.

Kali - Fetch response headers from the homepage

curl -I http://capitalflow.lab/

Examine each header line in the response. Look for:

  • Server: The web server software and version (e.g., nginx/1.24.0)
  • X-Powered-By: The backend framework (e.g., Express, PHP/8.2)
  • Set-Cookie: The cookie name reveals the session framework (connect.sid means Express/Node.js, PHPSESSID means PHP, JSESSIONID means Java)
  • X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security: Security headers (or their absence)

Record every header and its value. Missing security headers are findings too; they indicate gaps in the server's defensive configuration.

docs.title: Step 3: Inspect Headers on Additional Endpoints
docs.text:
Different pages may return different headers. The login endpoint, API paths, and error pages can reveal additional technology details.

Kali - Fetch headers from the login endpoint

curl -I http://capitalflow.lab/login

Kali - Fetch headers from an API endpoint

curl -I http://capitalflow.lab/api/

Kali - Trigger a 404 error page and examine its headers

curl -I http://capitalflow.lab/nonexistent-page-12345

Compare the headers across all three responses. Error pages sometimes reveal framework-specific default error handlers. API endpoints may return different Content-Type headers or additional custom headers that the main page does not include.

docs.title: Step 4: Analyze HTML Source for Framework Signatures
docs.text:
Frontend frameworks leave distinctive patterns in the HTML markup. Bootstrap uses specific CSS class names, React injects a data-reactroot attribute, and content management systems embed generator meta tags.

Kali - Search for meta generator tags

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/ | grep -i "meta.*generator\|meta.*version"

Kali - Search for CSS framework signatures

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/ | grep -i "bootstrap\|tailwind\|bulma\|foundation"

Kali - Search for frontend framework markers

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/ | grep -i "react\|angular\|vue\|data-reactroot\|ng-app\|v-app"

Each match narrows down the technology stack. A class="navbar navbar-expand-lg" pattern indicates Bootstrap. A <div id="app"> with v-cloak attributes indicates Vue.js. Record every framework indicator you find.

docs.title: Step 5: Inspect JavaScript Files for Library Versions
docs.text:
JavaScript files loaded by the page often contain version strings in their filenames or within the file content itself.

Kali - List all JavaScript files loaded by the homepage

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/ | grep -oi 'src="[^"]*\.js[^"]*"'

Look at the filenames in the output. A reference to jquery-3.6.0.min.js immediately identifies jQuery 3.6.0. Framework bundles like app.bundle.js or vendor.js may contain version strings inside the file.

Kali - Fetch a JavaScript file and search for version strings

curl -s http://capitalflow.lab/js/app.js | grep -i "version\|@license\|jQuery v\|React v\|Vue v"

Library files typically include a license header at the top with the exact version number. These headers survive minification in many build configurations.

docs.title: Step 6: Run whatweb for Automated Detection
docs.text:
Manual inspection catches the obvious signatures, but whatweb combines hundreds of detection rules to find technologies you might miss.

Kali - Run whatweb in verbose mode

whatweb -v http://capitalflow.lab/

Review the output section by section. WhatWeb reports each detected technology with a confidence level and the evidence that triggered the detection. Pay attention to:

  • Technologies you already identified manually (confirmation)
  • Technologies you missed (new findings)
  • Version numbers you could not determine from headers alone

Kali - Run whatweb in aggressive mode for deeper detection

whatweb -a 3 http://capitalflow.lab/

Aggressive mode sends additional requests to probe for technologies that require specific pages or paths to detect. Compare the aggressive results with the verbose results to see if additional components appear.

docs.title: Step 7: Compile the Technology Profile
docs.text: Combine all findings from headers, HTML source, JavaScript files, and whatweb into a single technology profile. The profile should list every identified component with its version number (where known).

docs.text:
Compile your complete technology profile below.

Header Value What It Reveals Server X-Powered-By Set-Cookie

Frontend technologies:

Technology Version Evidence Source

Backend technologies:

Technology Version Evidence Source

(paste output here)

Flag:

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. A web server returns the header Server: nginx without a version number. Does the absence of a version number mean the server is secure? What should a tester do next?

Reveal Answer

The absence of a version number means the administrator configured nginx to suppress version information (using server_tokens off). The server may still run a vulnerable version. A tester should look for other fingerprinting vectors: error page formatting, specific response behaviors, timing differences, and tools like nmap's HTTP fingerprinting scripts (http-server-header, http-headers) that can sometimes infer the version from behavioral patterns rather than explicit headers.

2. Why is identifying JavaScript library versions important for a security assessment, even when the libraries run in the browser rather than on the server?

Reveal Answer

Client-side JavaScript libraries with known vulnerabilities can be exploited through XSS attacks. For example, older jQuery versions are vulnerable to selector-based XSS, and outdated Angular versions have template injection flaws. An attacker who identifies a vulnerable library version can craft payloads tailored to that library's specific weaknesses. Additionally, library versions sometimes correlate with the overall application age and maintenance level; a site running jQuery 2.x is likely to have other outdated components as well.

3. An application sets a cookie named connect.sid. What does the cookie name tell you about the backend technology, and how does that knowledge help an attacker?

Reveal Answer

The connect.sid cookie name is the default for the express-session middleware in Node.js/Express applications. Knowing the backend framework helps an attacker in several ways: searching for Express-specific vulnerabilities, understanding the session management implementation (e.g., how tokens are generated and stored), and crafting payloads that target Node.js behaviors (such as prototype pollution or type coercion). Framework identification narrows the attack surface from "all possible technologies" to a specific set of known issues.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• HTTP response headers are the fastest source of technology information, often revealing the web server, backend framework, and session management approach in a single request
  • HTML source code contains framework signatures through CSS class naming conventions, meta tags, and data attributes that identify frontend libraries
  • JavaScript files include version strings in filenames and license headers that survive minification, revealing exact library versions for CVE research
  • Automated tools like whatweb combine hundreds of detection rules to catch subtle technology indicators that manual inspection would miss
  • Technology profiles feed directly into vulnerability research; every identified component with a version number becomes a search query against CVE databases and exploit repositories

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
The two exercises in this chapter covered the complete web reconnaissance workflow against the CapitalFlow Markets trading platform. Exercise CF1.1 focused on manual exploration: browsing pages, reading HTML source code, identifying forms and input fields, checking robots.txt, and running gobuster to discover hidden directories. Exercise CF1.2 shifted to technology fingerprinting: extracting server versions from HTTP headers, identifying frontend frameworks from HTML signatures, inspecting JavaScript files for library versions, and running whatweb for automated detection.

Together, these exercises produced a comprehensive attack surface map and technology profile for the CapitalFlow Markets application. Every finding from this chapter feeds directly into the authentication attack exercises in Chapter 2.
