A successful login drops you into a shell on the target as the developer user.

After logging in, confirm your identity and check your privileges.

Confirm your identity on the target

Run these on the target shell you just opened to verify the account and its group memberships.

whoami
id

The whoami command should return developer, and the id command will show your user ID (UID), group ID (GID), and group memberships. Note that you are a standard user with no special group memberships; you cannot run sudo or access /root/ directly.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate SUID Binaries with find
docs.text:
Now that you have confirmed your access level, search the filesystem for binaries with the SUID bit set. SUID enumeration is one of the first checks in any Linux privilege escalation methodology.

Enumerate SUID binaries

Run the SUID search on the target. The 2>/dev/null suppresses permission-denied noise so only the file paths print.

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Review the output carefully. You will see a list of file paths, each representing a binary that runs with its owner's permissions. Write down every binary in the list; you will need to compare them against what is normal in the next step.

docs.title: Step 4: Identify the Misconfigured Binary
docs.text:
Compare the SUID binaries you found against the set of programs that normally carry the SUID bit. Standard SUID binaries include passwd, su, mount, umount, chfn, chsh, and newgrp. Any binary outside that expected set deserves investigation.

You should notice that /usr/bin/find has the SUID bit set. Verify the permissions and owner.

Verify the find binary permissions

Inspect the binary on the target to confirm the SUID bit and its owner.

ls -la /usr/bin/find

The output will look similar to:

-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 320160 ... /usr/bin/find

The s in the owner's execute position confirms the SUID bit is active, and the file is owned by root. The find command includes an -exec flag that can run arbitrary commands; and because of the SUID bit, those commands will execute with root privileges.

docs.title: Step 5: Exploit SUID find to Get a Root Shell
docs.text:
The find binary's -exec flag runs a specified command for each file matched. By combining -exec with a shell invocation, you can spawn a shell that inherits the elevated effective UID (User ID). The -p flag on /bin/sh preserves the effective UID instead of dropping it.

Spawn a root shell through SUID find

Run this on the target. The -exec flag launches /bin/sh -p, and because find is SUID root the shell keeps root's effective UID.

find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit

Breaking down the command:

  • find .: search the current directory (the search target does not matter here)
  • -exec /bin/sh -p \;: for each matched file, execute /bin/sh with the -p flag
  • -quit: stop after the first match so only one shell is spawned

After running the command, verify that you now have root privileges.

Confirm root privileges

Check your effective identity in the new shell.

whoami
id

The whoami command should return root, and the id output should show euid=0(root), confirming that you are operating with root-level permissions.

docs.title: Step 6: Read the Flag
docs.text:
With root privileges, you now have access to the /root/ directory. Read the flag file stored there.

Read the root flag

Print the flag file from the root home directory, now readable thanks to your root shell.

cat /root/flag.txt

The flag follows the OCR{...} format. Copy the entire string exactly as it appears; you will need it for submission.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the steps you took and the evidence you collected during the privilege escalation.

My SUID enumeration output:

(paste your find / -perm -4000 output here)

Misconfigured binary I found:

Binary Path Owner Why It Should Not Have SUID

Root shell confirmation:

(paste your whoami and id output here)

Flag value:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Step 7: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review what you accomplished and why each step mattered. The enumeration phase revealed that /usr/bin/find had the SUID bit set, which is not part of the default configuration on most Linux distributions.

The find binary is dangerous with SUID because it includes the -exec flag, allowing execution of arbitrary commands. When find runs as root (due to SUID), every command launched through -exec also runs as root. A single misconfigured permission turned a routine file-search utility into a full root-access vector.

In a real engagement, you would document the exact binary path, its permissions, the exploit command, and a remediation recommendation. Riley Park asked for precisely that information so the Meridian Data Corp team can remove the SUID bit from /usr/bin/find and audit the rest of their servers.

Flag Format

The flag is a single token found in the root flag file:

OCR{token}

docs.title: Step 8: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Return to the platform in your browser. Paste the flag value from /root/flag.txt into the Submit Flag form and click Submit. The flag follows the OCR{...} format.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider the following questions to deepen your understanding of SUID-based privilege escalation. Each answer appears directly below the question.

1. Why does the -p flag matter when spawning a shell through a SUID binary?

Reveal Answer

Without -p, most modern shells (including bash and sh) will drop the effective UID back to the real UID as a security measure. The -p flag tells the shell to preserve the effective UID, which means the root privileges inherited from the SUID binary remain active. Omitting -p would result in a shell running as the developer user, defeating the escalation.

2. An administrator removes the SUID bit from /usr/bin/find but does not check the rest of the system. Why is that response incomplete?

Reveal Answer

Other binaries on the system may also have inappropriate SUID permissions. A thorough remediation requires auditing every SUID binary against a known-good baseline and removing the bit from anything that does not require it. Automated tools like linpeas or manual find sweeps should be run on every server in the environment, not just the one that was exploited.

3. Name two other common Linux binaries that, if given the SUID bit, could be exploited for privilege escalation.

Reveal Answer

Common examples include vim (which can spawn a shell from within the editor using :!sh), python (which can execute arbitrary code including os.system("/bin/sh")), cp (which can overwrite sensitive files like /etc/shadow), and bash (which can be invoked with -p to preserve elevated privileges). GTFOBins documents escalation techniques for dozens of binaries.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The SUID bit allows a binary to run with its owner's privileges, which means a root-owned SUID program gives any user root-level execution
  • SUID enumeration with find / -perm -4000 is one of the first checks in any Linux privilege escalation workflow; always compare results against a known-good baseline
  • GTFOBins is an essential reference for determining whether a SUID binary can be exploited, and it provides ready-made escalation commands for common utilities
  • A single misconfigured permission on one binary can undermine an otherwise well-secured system; regular auditing is the primary defense
  • Remediation requires more than fixing the one binary you found; a full audit across all servers in the environment is necessary to prevent similar misconfigurations elsewhere
  • Week 8 builds on the post-exploitation theme by exploring additional privilege escalation vectors beyond SUID, including cron jobs and writable scripts

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Week 7 introduced SUID (Set User ID) escalation, where a misconfigured binary gave you root-level execution on a target. The lab you are about to start takes privilege escalation in a different direction: cracking password hashes recovered from backup files. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready before you proceed.

Password attacks target the credentials themselves rather than a specific binary or service. When an attacker obtains hashed passwords from a system file, the attacker can run an offline cracking tool against those hashes without triggering any account lockout or generating login alerts on the target.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Ironforge Systems, a managed hosting provider in Denver, recently lost its senior sysadmin. The former employee's backup scripts are still running on a production server, and management suspects the scripts may be copying sensitive files to insecure locations. Rachel Kim, Ironforge's Security Manager, has asked you to conduct an internal assessment.

Rachel has given you low-privilege SSH (Secure Shell) access as the "technician" account. Your goal is to find exposed password hashes, crack them offline, and demonstrate how a weak password leads to full privilege escalation. Rachel's words: "Our sysadmin left last month. I know his backup scripts were sloppy, but I want to see exactly how bad it is. Show me the worst case."

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Discover exposed password hash files through filesystem enumeration
  • Identify the hash type and select an appropriate cracking tool
  • Use John the Ripper to crack weak password hashes with a dictionary attack
  • Escalate privileges using cracked credentials
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Password Hashes and Offline Cracking
docs.text:
Linux systems store user passwords in /etc/shadow, a file readable only by root. Each line in the shadow file contains a username, a hashed password, and several fields related to password aging. The password field uses a structured format that identifies the hashing algorithm.

A typical shadow entry looks like the following:

sysadmin:$6$randomsalt$longhashvalue:19500:0:99999:7:::

The $6$ prefix indicates SHA-512 hashing. Other common prefixes include $1$ for MD5 and $5$ for SHA-256. The salt (the value between the second and third $ signs) makes each hash unique even when two users choose the same password.

Offline cracking works by hashing every word in a dictionary with the same algorithm and salt, then comparing the result to the stolen hash. When a match occurs, the tool has recovered the plaintext password. Weak passwords like common dictionary words, pet names, or short numeric strings crack in seconds because they appear early in standard wordlists. Strong passwords with length, complexity, and randomness resist dictionary attacks because no wordlist entry will match.

graph LR
    A["Attacker finds<br/>shadow.bak"] --> B["Copy hashes<br/>to local machine"]
    B --> C["Run John<br/>with wordlist"]
    C --> D{"Hash matches<br/>a word?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Password<br/>cracked"]
    D -->|"No"| F["Try next word<br/>in wordlist"]
    F --> C

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#888,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e8a735,color:#fff

The diagram above illustrates why offline cracking is dangerous: the attacker works entirely on their own machine, at their own speed, with no failed-login alerts reaching the target. The only defense is strong passwords and proper file permissions on /etc/shadow.

docs.title: Tool Primer: John the Ripper
docs.text:
John the Ripper (commonly called "john") is an open-source password cracking tool that supports many hash formats, including Linux shadow file hashes. The tool reads a hash file, detects the algorithm automatically, and tests candidate passwords from a wordlist.

The basic syntax for cracking a shadow-format file is shown below.

Crack a shadow-format hash file with John

Run John against the hash file using a dictionary. The rockyou.txt wordlist is the standard first choice because it holds millions of real leaked passwords.

john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt <hash_file>

John loads the hashes, auto-detects the algorithm, and prints each cracked password next to its account as it finds a match.

  • --wordlist= specifies the dictionary file to use. The rockyou.txt wordlist contains over 14 million real passwords leaked from a 2009 breach, making it the standard first choice for dictionary attacks.
  • <hash_file> is the path to the file containing the hashes you want to crack. John expects the file to follow the /etc/shadow line format.

Reading the output:

Loaded 2 password hashes with 2 different salts (sha512crypt [SHA512 256/256 AVX2 4x])
Press 'q' or Ctrl-C to abort, almost any other key for status
dragon           (sysadmin)
1g 0:00:00:03 DONE (2026-03-05 10:15) 0.3125g/s 1200p/s 1200c/s 1200C/s

The line dragon (sysadmin) shows that John found a match: the sysadmin account's password hashes to the dictionary word shown. The timing line shows how long the attack took and the cracking speed.

To display previously cracked passwords without re-running the attack, use the --show flag.

Display already-cracked passwords

Use --show to reprint results from John's pot file without repeating the attack.

john --show <hash_file>

The output lists each cracked account and its recovered password in username:password format.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. The target containers must be running before you can connect.

  • Navigate to Exercises and select the Linux track
  • Find Exercise 8; Password Hash Cracking under Week 8
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Connect via SSH as the Technician
docs.text:
Your initial access uses the low-privilege technician account. SSH provides a remote terminal session on the target server.

Open your terminal and connect.

SSH into the target as technician

Replace <target_ip> with the IP address shown in the Active Lab View. Enter the technician credential when prompted.

ssh technician@<target_ip>

When prompted for a password, enter:

Ir0nf0rg3_T3ch#

A shell prompt indicates you are logged in as technician on the target.

Confirm your identity

Check the account and group memberships on the target shell.

whoami
id

The whoami output should read technician, and id shows your group memberships; note that you have no special privileges yet.

docs.title: Step 3: Discover the Exposed Shadow Backup
docs.text:
The former sysadmin's backup scripts may have copied sensitive files to world-readable locations. Common backup directories include /opt, /var/backups, /tmp, and user home directories. Your goal is to find any copies of the shadow file.

Explore the filesystem.

Browse the backup directory tree

Walk down through the /opt tree on the target to locate the backup directory the scripts wrote to.

ls -la /opt/
ls -la /opt/ironforge/
ls -la /opt/ironforge/backups/

You should find a file named shadow.bak in /opt/ironforge/backups/.

Check the backup file permissions

Inspect the permissions on the shadow backup to confirm it is exposed.

ls -la /opt/ironforge/backups/shadow.bak

The file is world-readable; any user on the system can read it. A properly secured shadow file has permissions 640 and is owned by root. The backup script copied the file without preserving these restrictive permissions, creating the vulnerability Rachel suspected.

View the shadow backup contents

Print the backup so you can pick out the crackable hashes.

cat /opt/ironforge/backups/shadow.bak

Look for lines that contain a $6$ hash in the second field. These are accounts with SHA-512 hashed passwords that you can attempt to crack.

docs.title: Step 4: Extract the Assessment Token
docs.text:
The backup directory contains more than the shadow file. Look for an assessment token that forms part of your final flag.

Read the assessment token

List the backup directory again and print the token file it contains.

ls -la /opt/ironforge/backups/
cat /opt/ironforge/backups/assessment_token.txt

Record the token value you find. You will combine the token from the backup directory with a second piece found later to form the complete flag in OCR{...} format.

docs.title: Step 5: Crack the Hashes with John the Ripper
docs.text:
All tools needed for this step are pre-installed on the target. Copy both the passwd and shadow backups to a working location. John the Ripper needs the passwd file combined with the shadow file to correctly parse the hashes. The unshadow utility merges the two files into a format that John can process.

Merge the backups with unshadow

Copy both backups to /tmp and combine them so John can map each hash to a username.

cp /opt/ironforge/backups/shadow.bak /tmp/shadow.bak
cp /opt/ironforge/backups/passwd.bak /tmp/passwd.bak
unshadow /tmp/passwd.bak /tmp/shadow.bak > /tmp/hashes.txt

The merged file at /tmp/hashes.txt now pairs each user with the hash John needs to crack.

Run John against the merged hashes

Launch John with the rockyou wordlist against the combined file.

john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt /tmp/hashes.txt

John will load the hashes, detect the SHA-512 algorithm, and begin testing candidates from the wordlist. Watch the output for cracked passwords; weak passwords will appear within seconds.

Display the cracked passwords

Reprint the results once the run finishes.

john --show /tmp/hashes.txt

Note which accounts cracked and what their passwords are. The sysadmin account's password should appear in the output.

docs.title: Step 6: Escalate Privileges with the Cracked Password
docs.text:
Now that you have the sysadmin password, use su (substitute user) to switch to that account. The su command starts a new shell running as the specified user.

Switch to the sysadmin account

Run su on the target and enter the cracked password when prompted.

su sysadmin

A new shell opens running as sysadmin once the password is accepted.

Confirm the new identity

Verify the account switch took effect.

whoami
id

You should now be operating as sysadmin with elevated privileges on the system.

docs.title: Step 7: Read the Flag
docs.text:
The sysadmin's home directory contains the second piece of the flag. Navigate there and read the flag file.

Read the sysadmin flag

Print the flag file from the sysadmin home directory, now readable as the sysadmin user.

cat /home/sysadmin/flag.txt

Combine the token from Step 4 with the value from the flag file to assemble the complete flag in OCR{...} format.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Record the evidence you gathered during the assessment. In a real engagement, these notes become part of your penetration testing report.

Shadow backup location and permissions:

(paste the output of ls -la /opt/ironforge/backups/shadow.bak here)

Shadow file contents (hash entries):

(paste the relevant shadow.bak lines here)

John the Ripper output:

(paste your john cracking output here)

Cracked credentials:

Username Password

Complete flag:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review what you discovered and consider the full attack chain. You started with low-privilege technician access and ended with sysadmin credentials; all because of two failures.

The first failure was insecure file permissions on the backup. The backup script copied /etc/shadow to a world-readable directory, exposing password hashes to every user on the system. A properly written script would preserve the original file permissions or store backups in a root-only directory.

The second failure was a weak password. The sysadmin account used a common dictionary word that appears near the top of the rockyou.txt wordlist. A strong password; long, random, and not based on any dictionary word; would have resisted the cracking attempt entirely.

Together, these two failures created a privilege escalation path: exposed hashes plus a weak password equals compromised accounts.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{________}

Where token1 is from the backup assessment token file, and token2 is from the user flag after cracking the password.

docs.title: Step 9: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Paste the complete OCR{...} flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit. The platform will validate your submission and mark the lab as complete.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider the following questions to deepen your understanding of password hash cracking and its implications.

1. Why is offline cracking more dangerous than an online brute-force attack against a login prompt?

Reveal Answer

An offline attack runs entirely on the attacker's machine, so there are no failed-login alerts, no account lockouts, and no rate limiting. The attacker can test millions of candidates per second without the target system ever knowing. An online brute-force attack, by contrast, generates log entries for every attempt and can be stopped by lockout policies after a few failures.

2. The sysadmin password cracked in seconds. What characteristics would make a password resistant to a dictionary attack using rockyou.txt?

Reveal Answer

A resistant password would be long (12 or more characters), contain a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters, and would not be based on any real word, name, or common pattern. Randomly generated passphrases or password manager output resist dictionary attacks because no wordlist entry will match the exact combination.

3. Beyond fixing file permissions on the backup, what other controls could prevent the attack chain you demonstrated?

Reveal Answer

The organization could enforce password complexity policies to prevent weak passwords, use multi-factor authentication (MFA) so that a cracked password alone is not sufficient, restrict su access to specific groups, monitor for unauthorized file access in sensitive directories, and rotate passwords regularly. Encrypting backups would also prevent hash extraction even if the backup file were accessible.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Offline password cracking allows an attacker to test millions of password candidates per second without triggering any alerts on the target system
  • File permissions on sensitive files like /etc/shadow are a critical security control; a single misconfigured backup script can expose every password hash on the system
  • Weak passwords based on dictionary words crack in seconds regardless of the hashing algorithm; password strength is the last line of defense after hashes are exposed
  • Privilege escalation through credential reuse demonstrates why each account should have a unique, strong password; one cracked password can unlock access to higher-privilege accounts
  • John the Ripper with the rockyou.txt wordlist is a standard first step in any password audit; Week 9 will combine hash cracking with earlier techniques in a multi-stage assessment

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Weeks 1 through 8 introduced individual penetration testing skills in isolation; port scanning, service enumeration, web exploitation, credential discovery, lateral movement, and privilege escalation. Exercise 9 requires you to chain every one of those skills together against a multi-server environment. You will not receive step-by-step guidance at the same level of detail as previous labs; the walkthrough provides direction, but you are expected to recognize which tool and technique to apply at each stage.

Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before continuing. Review your notes from Exercises 1 through 8, because every major concept from those weeks appears somewhere in the attack chain.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Nexus Dynamics is a growing SaaS (Software as a Service) company based in Atlanta, Georgia. The company has hired your firm for a full-scope penetration test before their Series B funding round. The board of directors wants assurance that the company's infrastructure is secure before investors commit.

Your point of contact is Andrea Walsh, VP of Security: "We have a perimeter web server that runs our marketing site and customer API. Behind that is our core application server that handles the heavy lifting. The web server is the only thing exposed to the internet; the core server should be completely unreachable from outside."

Two target servers make up the engagement scope: a perimeter web server exposed on port 80, and a core application server running SSH (Secure Shell) on port 22. Three assessment markers are distributed across the infrastructure. Your job is to retrieve all three markers and assemble them into the final flag, proving complete compromise of the environment.

A few important notes about the lab structure: the difficulty level is Advanced, and the time limit is 90 minutes. Hints are locked for the first 20 minutes; the platform will not display any hint text until that delay has passed. Use the first 20 minutes to work independently and apply your skills from the course so far.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The following list outlines what you need to accomplish during the assessment. Each objective maps to one or more walkthrough phases below.

  • Enumerate services across both target systems using port scanning
  • Identify and exploit a web application vulnerability for initial access to the perimeter server
  • Discover credentials stored in application configuration files on the perimeter server
  • Pivot laterally to the core server using discovered credentials
  • Escalate privileges on the core server to achieve root access
  • Collect all three assessment markers and assemble the final flag
  • Submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Background: Attack Chaining Methodology
docs.text:
Real-world penetration tests rarely involve a single exploit that grants immediate access to the target. Most engagements follow a kill chain: a sequence of stages where each successful step provides the foothold needed for the next. Understanding the kill chain helps you approach complex environments methodically rather than attempting random attacks.

The five phases of the attack chain you will execute in this exercise map directly to skills you learned in previous weeks:

  1. Reconnaissance (Week 1); Scan the target environment to discover hosts, open ports, and running services. Port scanning reveals the attack surface and tells you where to focus.
  2. Initial Access (Weeks 5-6); Exploit a vulnerability in an exposed service to gain a foothold. In web applications, command injection and other input validation flaws often provide the first way in.
  3. Credential Discovery (Weeks 2-3); Search the compromised system for credentials, configuration files, and secrets that grant access to additional systems. Developers frequently store passwords in plaintext configuration files.
  4. Lateral Movement (Week 4); Use discovered credentials to move from the initial foothold to other systems in the environment. SSH connections between servers are a common lateral movement path.
  5. Privilege Escalation (Week 7); Elevate from a standard user account to root on the target system. Misconfigured permissions, SUID (Set User ID) binaries, and weak sudo rules are the most common escalation vectors on Linux.

The following diagram illustrates the full kill chain for the Nexus Dynamics engagement:

graph LR
    A["Phase 1<br/>Reconnaissance"] -->|"Discover services"| B["Phase 2<br/>Initial Access"]
    B -->|"Exploit web vuln"| C["Phase 3<br/>Credential Discovery"]
    C -->|"Extract SSH creds"| D["Phase 4<br/>Lateral Movement"]
    D -->|"SSH to core"| E["Phase 5<br/>Priv Escalation"]
    E -->|"SUID exploit"| F["Root Access<br/>Flag Captured"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

Each phase builds on the one before it. You cannot pivot to the core server without credentials, and you cannot find credentials without command execution on the perimeter server. Skipping a phase or attempting them out of order will not work; the attack chain must be followed sequentially.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Combining Your Arsenal
docs.text:
Previous labs introduced each tool in isolation. Exercise 9 requires you to use multiple tools in sequence, where the output of one tool feeds directly into the next. The table below summarizes the core tools and how they connect across phases.

Tool Purpose Phase nmap Discover open ports and services on both servers Reconnaissance curl Interact with web applications and send POST requests with injection payloads Initial Access, Credential Discovery ssh Connect to remote servers using discovered credentials Lateral Movement find Search for files, enumerate SUID binaries, and exploit SUID misconfigurations Privilege Escalation cat Read file contents; flags, configuration files, markers All Phases

The chaining pattern works like a pipeline. Nmap output tells you which ports are open, which tells you to investigate the web application on port 80. Curl lets you interact with the web application, discover injectable endpoints, and execute commands on the perimeter server. Command execution lets you read configuration files containing SSH credentials. SSH gets you onto the core server. The find command on the core server reveals SUID binaries, and exploiting a SUID binary gives you root. Each tool's output is the input for the next decision.

A key difference from earlier labs: nobody will tell you which tool to use at each step. The scenario provides the context, and you must recognize which tool fits the situation. When you reach a new server or discover a new service, pause and ask yourself: "What did I learn in previous weeks that applies here?"

docs.title: Phase 1: Reconnaissance
docs.text: The engagement begins with reconnaissance. Before you can exploit anything, you need to know what is running and where.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Note Both Target IPs
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. The Nexus Dynamics lab deploys two servers, so you will see two IP addresses in the Active Lab View rather than the single IP you are used to from previous labs.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate Nexus Dynamics: Full Penetration Test
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note both target IPs displayed in the Active Lab View; one for the perimeter server and one for the core server
  • Record both IPs before proceeding; you will need both throughout the assessment

The perimeter server is the externally facing system that Andrea Walsh described. The core server is the internal system that "should be completely unreachable from outside." Your attack path starts at the perimeter and works inward.

docs.title: Step 2: Scan the Perimeter Server
docs.text:
Begin with a port scan of the perimeter server to identify exposed services. The perimeter server handles web traffic, so you should expect to find HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) services.

Scan the perimeter server

Replace <perimeter_ip> with the first target IP from the Active Lab View. Nmap reports the open ports and services that define the perimeter attack surface.

nmap <perimeter_ip>

Review the output and identify every open port and service. You should see port 80 open with an HTTP service; the web application that Andrea Walsh mentioned.

Scan the core server

Replace <core_ip> with the second target IP from the Active Lab View. Scan the internal host to learn which services it exposes.

nmap <core_ip>

The core server should show port 22 open with an SSH service. Record both scan results, because they define your attack surface for the rest of the assessment.

Comparing the two scans tells you the engagement layout: the perimeter server has a web application you can reach over HTTP, and the core server has SSH that you will need credentials to access. The attack path is clear; start with the web application, find credentials, then move to SSH.

docs.title: Phase 2: Initial Access
docs.text: With reconnaissance complete, you know the perimeter server runs a web application on port 80. Your next task is to explore the application, identify injectable inputs, and achieve command execution.

docs.title: Step 3: Identify the Web Application on the Perimeter Server
docs.text:
Load the perimeter web application in your browser or use curl to examine it from the command line. Start by requesting the root page to see what the application offers.

Request the perimeter root page

Fetch the root page of the perimeter web application to see what it exposes.

curl http://<perimeter_ip>/

Examine the response for clues about the application's functionality. Look for links, endpoints, API routes, or references to diagnostic features. Nexus Dynamics runs a marketing site and customer API; the application may expose administrative or operational endpoints beyond the public-facing pages.

docs.title: Step 4: Discover the /healthcheck Endpoint
docs.text:
Web applications often include health-check or diagnostic endpoints that system administrators use for monitoring. These endpoints sometimes accept user input to perform network tests like ping or DNS lookups, making them potential targets for command injection.

Probe the /healthcheck endpoint to see how it responds.

Probe the healthcheck endpoint

Send a plain GET request to learn what the diagnostic endpoint returns.

curl http://<perimeter_ip>/healthcheck

A GET request to /healthcheck may return usage information or a status page. The important detail is how the endpoint behaves when it receives POST data; diagnostic features typically accept a hostname or IP address as input to test connectivity.

Send a baseline healthcheck POST

Post a host value to exercise the diagnostic feature with legitimate input.

curl -X POST http://<perimeter_ip>/healthcheck -d 'host=127.0.0.1'

The response should contain network diagnostic output (such as ping results) for the IP address you provided. The application accepted your input and passed it to a system command; the same pattern you saw in Exercise 6 with the CloudPing diagnostic tool.

docs.title: Step 5: Exploit Command Injection on the /healthcheck Endpoint
docs.text:
The /healthcheck endpoint accepts a host parameter and passes it to a system command. Test whether the application sanitizes the input by appending a shell metacharacter and a second command. The semicolon (;) tells the shell to execute an additional command after the first one completes.

Start with a basic injection test using the id command.

Inject the id command

Append ;id to the host value so the shell runs id after the diagnostic command.

curl -X POST http://<perimeter_ip>/healthcheck -d 'host=127.0.0.1;id'

If the application is vulnerable, the response will contain the normal diagnostic output followed by the output of the id command; a line showing uid=, gid=, and groups=. The presence of the id output confirms that the server executes your injected commands without filtering.

With command injection confirmed, you can run any command the web server process has permission to execute. Test reading a file to verify filesystem access.

Verify filesystem access

Inject a cat of /etc/hostname to confirm you can read files on the perimeter server.

curl -X POST http://<perimeter_ip>/healthcheck -d 'host=127.0.0.1;cat /etc/hostname'

The response should include the server's hostname, confirming that you have arbitrary command execution on the perimeter server.

The first assessment marker is located on the perimeter server. Use your command injection access to read it.

Read the first marker

Inject a cat command that prints the marker file from the assessment directory.

curl -X POST http://<perimeter_ip>/healthcheck -d 'host=127.0.0.1;cat /opt/nexus/assessment/marker1.txt'

Record the marker value; you will need it to assemble the final flag.

docs.title: Phase 3: Credential Discovery
docs.text: You now have command execution on the perimeter server. The next objective is to find credentials that grant access to the core server. Developers frequently store database passwords, API keys, and SSH credentials in environment files and configuration files within the application directory.

docs.title: Step 6: Extract SSH Credentials from the Application Configuration
docs.text:
The Nexus Dynamics web application lives in /var/www/nexus-app/. Environment files (commonly named .env) are a standard location for storing application secrets such as database connection strings, API tokens, and service credentials. Use your command injection to read the .env file.

Read the application .env file

Inject a cat of the application's environment file to harvest any stored secrets.

curl -X POST http://<perimeter_ip>/healthcheck -d 'host=127.0.0.1;cat /var/www/nexus-app/.env'

Examine the output for variables containing SSH credentials. You should find entries that specify a username and password for the core server, formatted as environment variables:

CORE_SSH_USER=deploy
CORE_SSH_PASS=N3xus_D3pl0y#

These credentials belong to the deploy account on the core application server. Record both values; the username and the password; because you will use them in the next phase to establish an SSH connection. Credential storage in plaintext .env files is a common finding in web application penetration tests, and it represents a significant security risk when an attacker gains filesystem access through any vulnerability.

docs.title: Phase 4: Lateral Movement
docs.text: With valid SSH credentials for the core server, you can now move laterally from the perimeter to the internal infrastructure. Lateral movement is the point where a perimeter breach becomes a full internal compromise.

docs.title: Step 7: SSH to the Core Server
docs.text:
Use the credentials discovered in Step 6 to connect to the core server over SSH. The core server exposes port 22, which your Nmap scan confirmed in Step 2.

SSH to the core server

Replace <core_ip> with the second target IP from the Active Lab View. When prompted for a password, enter the credential you extracted from the .env file.

ssh deploy@<core_ip>

A successful login drops you into a shell on the core server as the deploy user.

After logging in, confirm your identity and assess your current privilege level.

Confirm your foothold on the core server

Check your account and privileges on the core server shell.

whoami
id

The whoami command should return deploy, and the id output should show a standard user account with no special group memberships. You are now on the core server, but you do not yet have root access.

Read the second assessment marker, which is accessible to the deploy user.

Read the second marker

Print the marker file from the deploy user's home directory.

cat /home/deploy/marker2.txt

Record the marker value alongside the first one from the perimeter server.

docs.title: Phase 5: Privilege Escalation
docs.text: You have user-level access on the core server, but the final assessment marker is in /root/, which requires root privileges to read. Apply the privilege escalation techniques you learned in Week 7 to elevate from the deploy user to root.

docs.title: Step 8: Enumerate SUID Binaries on the Core Server
docs.text:
SUID enumeration is one of the first checks in any Linux privilege escalation methodology. Search the filesystem for binaries with the SUID bit set.

Enumerate SUID binaries on the core server

Run the SUID search on the core server. The 2>/dev/null suppresses permission-denied noise so only the file paths print.

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Review the output and compare it against the standard set of SUID binaries you learned about in Exercise 7. Expected SUID binaries include passwd, su, mount, umount, chfn, chsh, and newgrp. Any binary outside that expected set is a potential escalation vector. Look for /usr/bin/find in the results; its -exec flag allows execution of arbitrary commands, so when it carries the SUID bit and is owned by root, every command run through -exec runs as root.

Verify the permissions on the suspicious binary.

Verify the find binary permissions

Inspect the binary to confirm the SUID bit and owner.

ls -la /usr/bin/find

The output should show -rwsr-xr-x with root as the owner; the s in the owner's execute position confirms the SUID bit is active.

docs.title: Step 9: Exploit SUID find to Escalate to Root
docs.text:
Use the same technique from Exercise 7 to spawn a root shell through the SUID find binary. The -exec flag runs a command for each matched file, and the -p flag on /bin/sh preserves the elevated effective UID (User ID) instead of dropping it.

Spawn a root shell through SUID find

Run this on the core server. Because find is SUID root, the /bin/sh -p it launches keeps root's effective UID.

find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit

Breaking down the command:

  • find .: search the current directory (the search target does not matter; you need find to execute, not to find files)
  • -exec /bin/sh -p \;: for each matched file, execute /bin/sh with the -p flag to preserve root privileges
  • -quit: stop after the first match so only one shell is spawned

Verify that the escalation succeeded.

Confirm root on the core server

Check your effective identity in the new shell.

whoami
id

The whoami command should return root, and the id output should show euid=0(root). You now have full root-level access on the core server.

docs.title: Step 10: Read the Final Assessment Marker
docs.text:
With root privileges, you can access the /root/ directory. Read the third and final assessment marker.

Read the final marker

Print the last marker file from the root home directory, now readable thanks to your root shell.

cat /root/marker3.txt

Record the marker value. You now have all three assessment markers from across the infrastructure:

  • Marker 1: from /opt/nexus/assessment/marker1.txt on the perimeter server
  • Marker 2: from /home/deploy/marker2.txt on the core server
  • Marker 3: from /root/marker3.txt on the core server

Assemble the three markers into the final flag using the OCR{...} format as indicated by the lab instructions.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The following questions ask you to reflect on the methodology you applied across the full assessment. Each answer appears directly below the question.

1. The Nexus Dynamics engagement required five distinct phases to achieve full compromise. Why is it important to follow the kill chain sequentially rather than attempting random exploits against each server?

Reveal Answer

Each phase produces information required by the next phase. Without reconnaissance, you would not know which ports are open or which services to target. Without initial access on the perimeter server, you could not read the .env file containing SSH credentials. Without those credentials, you could not log into the core server. Random exploitation skips the information-gathering steps that make each subsequent attack possible, wasting time on attacks that lack the necessary context to succeed.

2. Andrea Walsh stated that the core server "should be completely unreachable from outside." Your Nmap scan showed port 22 open on the core server. Does the fact that you could scan port 22 contradict her statement, and what does it tell you about the network architecture?

Reveal Answer

The network architecture in the lab environment allows direct connectivity to both servers for practical purposes. In a production environment, the core server would sit behind a firewall that blocks external access to port 22. Andrea's statement reflects the intended architecture, but network segmentation must be enforced through firewall rules and access control lists; not assumed. The engagement proved that even if the core server were properly segmented, an attacker who compromises the perimeter server can pivot internally, bypassing perimeter-only defenses.

3. The SSH credentials were stored in plaintext in a .env file on the perimeter server. Name two alternative approaches that would prevent an attacker with filesystem access from extracting usable credentials.

Reveal Answer

The application could retrieve credentials at runtime from a secrets management system such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault. Secrets managers store credentials in an encrypted backend and provide them to the application through authenticated API calls; even if an attacker reads the .env file, it would contain only a reference to the secret, not the secret itself. The second approach is to eliminate shared credentials entirely by using SSH key-based authentication with keys stored in a hardware security module (HSM) or a secrets manager, removing passwords from the filesystem altogether.

4. You exploited the same SUID find binary technique from Exercise 7 to escalate privileges on the core server. If an administrator removed the SUID bit from find but left the deploy user's SSH credentials unchanged, would the system be secure? Explain your reasoning.

Reveal Answer

Removing the SUID bit from find eliminates one escalation path but does not address the root cause. The deploy account still has valid SSH access to the core server, and the credentials are still stored in plaintext on the perimeter server. An attacker could still pivot to the core server and then search for alternative escalation vectors; writable cron jobs, sudo misconfigurations, kernel vulnerabilities, or other SUID binaries. Thorough remediation requires fixing every link in the chain: sanitizing the web application input, removing plaintext credentials, rotating the compromised password, auditing all SUID binaries, and implementing network segmentation.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Attack chaining is the core methodology of penetration testing; real engagements require linking multiple vulnerabilities across different systems to achieve full compromise, not relying on a single exploit
  • Reconnaissance drives every decision in the kill chain; without accurate enumeration of services and ports, you cannot identify which attack techniques to apply at each stage
  • Credential storage in plaintext configuration files (.env, config.ini, settings.py) remains one of the most common findings in web application assessments, and it frequently enables lateral movement to internal systems
  • Lateral movement transforms a perimeter-only breach into a full internal compromise; network segmentation and credential isolation are the primary defenses against pivoting
  • Privilege escalation through SUID misconfigurations demonstrates that a single misconfigured permission can undermine an otherwise well-secured system; regular auditing of SUID binaries is essential
  • Week 10 builds on this exercise by introducing reporting and remediation planning, where you will learn to translate technical findings into actionable recommendations for stakeholders like Andrea Walsh and the Nexus Dynamics board

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
NovaTech Solutions is a mid-size software development consultancy based in Austin, Texas. The company recently launched a redesigned corporate website and hired your firm, Blackridge Security, to perform a web application assessment before a SOC 2 (Service Organization Control Type 2) compliance audit next quarter.

Your point of contact, Devon Harris (VP of Engineering), provided the following brief: "We pushed the new site to production last week. The dev team assures me everything is locked down, but I want a second opinion. We are particularly concerned about any leftover development or staging interfaces that might have been accidentally deployed. The site should be a marketing page; nothing interactive."

The engagement scope covers the web application on the target host and any backend services you discover on the subnet. Devon mentioned that the team runs a MySQL database somewhere on the network but insisted it is "not internet-facing." A security token has been placed on each system as part of the assessment scope. Collect all three tokens and combine them as OCR{...} to complete the engagement.

The NovaTech public site is the marketing page Devon described. Nothing here links to a login, so the staff portal you are about to find is reachable only through enumeration.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Perform directory enumeration against the web application to discover hidden endpoints
  • Analyze discovered pages for sensitive information and credentials
  • Authenticate to a hidden staff portal using discovered default credentials
  • Identify and connect to a backend database using leaked connection details
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Directory Enumeration and Default Credentials
docs.text: Web applications often contain more than what is visible from the homepage. Developers frequently deploy administrative panels, staging pages, and internal tools alongside the public-facing site. When these hidden paths are not properly secured, an attacker can discover them through systematic enumeration.

docs.title: robots.txt and Hidden Paths
docs.text: The file robots.txt sits in the root directory of a web server and tells search engine crawlers which paths they should not index. While the file is intended for search engine etiquette, security testers read it because it often lists the exact directories the site owners want to keep out of public search results. A robots.txt entry does not block access; it is a polite request, not an access control mechanism.

docs.title: Directory Brute-Forcing
docs.text: Directory brute-forcing works by sending HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests for thousands of common directory and file names and watching the response codes. A 200 OK response means the path exists and returned content. A 301 or 302 means the server redirected you, which usually indicates a valid directory. A 404 Not Found means nothing is there. Tools like gobuster automate sending these requests using a wordlist; a text file containing one directory name per line.

docs.title: Why Hidden Admin Panels Exist
docs.text:
Development teams often build internal dashboards, configuration pages, and staff portals during the development cycle. When the application moves to production, these interfaces sometimes remain accessible because no one removed them or placed them behind authentication. The risk compounds when these panels ship with default credentials; factory-set usernames and passwords that the team never changed. An attacker who discovers both the hidden panel and the default credentials gains authenticated access without any exploitation.

    C --> D
    D --> E["View HTML source<br/>find token 1"]

docs.title: Tool Primer: gobuster
docs.text:
Gobuster is a command-line tool that brute-forces directories and files on web servers. You provide a target URL and a wordlist, and gobuster requests each entry from the list and reports which paths return valid responses.

Basic syntax:

gobuster dir -u http://<target_ip> -w <wordlist_path>

Common flags:

Flag Purpose dir Directory/file brute-forcing mode -u Target URL (include the scheme, e.g., http://) -w Path to the wordlist file -t Number of concurrent threads (default 10) -x File extensions to append (e.g., -x php,html) -s Status codes to treat as valid (default: 200, 204, 301, 302, 307)

Wordlist location on the lab VM:

The most commonly used wordlist for directory enumeration is located at:

/usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Sample output:

===============================================================
Gobuster v3.6
===============================================================
[+] Url:            http://10.100.5.23
[+] Wordlist:       /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt
[+] Threads:        10
===============================================================
/index.html           (Status: 200) [Size: 4532]
/robots.txt           (Status: 200) [Size: 87]
/staff-portal         (Status: 301) [Size: 0] [--> /staff-portal/]
===============================================================

Each result line shows the discovered path, the HTTP status code, and the response size. A 301 redirect often indicates a directory; gobuster shows where the redirect points.

docs.title: MySQL CLI Basics
docs.text:
MySQL provides a command-line client for connecting to database servers. You will use it later in the lab to query a backend database once you discover the connection credentials.

Connection syntax:

mysql --skip-ssl -h <db_ip> -u <username> -p'<password>' <database_name>
Flag Purpose -h Hostname or IP of the database server -u Username to authenticate with -p Password (no space between -p and the password) -e Execute a single SQL query and exit

Example; run a query without entering the interactive shell:

mysql --skip-ssl -h 10.100.5.41 -u myuser -p'mypass' mydb -e "SELECT * FROM my_table"

The -e flag is useful when you need to run one query and capture the output directly in the terminal.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. You need the containers running before any web requests will succeed.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Web track
  • Find Hidden Login Discovery and click Launch
  • Wait for the status to change to Running

docs.title: Step 2: Browse the Main Site and Check robots.txt
docs.text:
Start by visiting the target website in your browser to see what is publicly visible. Open a second tab (or use curl) to check whether the site has a robots.txt file, since developers often list hidden directories there.

Browse the main page

Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View. The -s flag runs curl in silent mode so progress meters do not clutter the output.

curl -s http://<target_ip>/

The response is the public marketing page HTML. Scan it for any links or comments that hint at additional paths.

Check for robots.txt

A robots.txt file lists directories the site owners want crawlers to skip. Request it directly from the web root.

curl -s http://<target_ip>/robots.txt

Review the output carefully. Look for any Disallow entries; these paths are directories the site owners asked search engines not to index. Note each path you find; you will visit them in a later step.

docs.title: Step 3: Run gobuster with the common.txt Wordlist
docs.text:
While robots.txt may reveal some paths, a full directory scan can uncover additional endpoints that the file does not mention. Run gobuster against the target using the standard common wordlist.

Brute-force directories with gobuster

Gobuster requests every entry in the wordlist and reports paths that return valid responses. Replace <target_ip> with the target address before running it.

gobuster dir -u http://<target_ip> -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Wait for the scan to complete. Compare the gobuster results with the paths you found in robots.txt. You should see a /staff-portal entry among the results; a path that strongly suggests an internal login page.

docs.title: Step 4: Access the Staff Portal and Examine the HTML Source
docs.text:
Navigate to the staff portal path discovered in the previous steps. The login page itself may contain useful information embedded in the HTML source code; developers sometimes leave build tags, version numbers, or debug comments in the markup.

Fetch the staff portal HTML source

Request the staff portal page so the raw HTML lands in your terminal where you can read the markup, including comments a browser would hide.

curl -s http://<target_ip>/staff-portal/

Read the HTML output carefully. Look for HTML comments (lines wrapped in <!-- -->) that might contain version strings, build identifiers, or tokens. One of the assessment tokens is embedded as a build tag comment in the login page source. Record the token value you find; it is token 1.

The hidden NovaTech staff portal, reachable only after directory enumeration revealed `/staff-portal/`. A plain username and password form with no link from the public site.

docs.title: Step 5: Login with Default Credentials
docs.text:
The staff portal presents a login form. Many internal applications ship with default credentials that the development team sets during initial deployment and never changes. For a company-branded portal, the default username is often admin and the password follows a predictable pattern combining the company name with a year.

Log in with the following credentials:

  • Username: admin
  • Password: NovaTech2024#

You can authenticate using curl or through your browser:

Authenticate with default credentials

Submit the discovered username and password to the login endpoint. The -c flag saves session cookies to a file so you can make authenticated requests afterward, and -L follows the post-login redirect.

curl -s -c /tmp/nova-cookies \
  http://<target_ip>/staff-portal/login \
  -d 'username=admin&password=NovaTech2024#' -L

Review the response; you should land on a dashboard page that displays the second assessment token.

docs.title: Step 6: Explore the Dashboard and Extract Database Credentials
docs.text:
With authenticated access to the staff dashboard, explore the available pages. Configuration pages in internal tools frequently expose backend connection details, including database hostnames, usernames, and passwords.

Pull the authenticated dashboard

The -b flag sends the saved session cookies from your earlier login, proving you are authenticated. Request the dashboard so its content prints to the terminal.

curl -s -b /tmp/nova-cookies http://<target_ip>/staff-portal/dashboard

Read through the dashboard content and look for database connection strings. You should find a MySQL hostname (or IP), a database username, and a password. Record all three values; you will need them in the next step.

The post-login staff dashboard. The Auth Token Prefix value is redacted to keep the flag hidden, but the Application Configuration panel leaks the live MySQL host, user, and password, the pivot you use to reach the backend database.

docs.title: Step 7: Connect to MySQL and Query for the Token
docs.text:
Use the database credentials you extracted from the dashboard to connect to the MySQL server. The database server runs on a separate host within the lab subnet.

Query the MySQL audit_tokens table

Connect to the remote database with the leaked credentials and run a single query using the -e flag, which executes the statement and exits without dropping into the interactive shell.

mysql --skip-ssl -h <db_ip> -u novatech_app -p'Pr0d_DB_2024#' novatech \
  -e "SELECT * FROM audit_tokens"

Replace <db_ip> with the database server IP shown in the lab topology or discovered from the dashboard configuration page. The query targets the audit_tokens table in the novatech database. The result contains the third and final assessment token.

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the three tokens you collected and consider what each one represents in the context of a real-world assessment.

  • Token 1 (HTML source comment): Sensitive information left in client-facing code. Any visitor who views the page source can see comments, build tags, and debug output. Production deployments should strip all development comments before release.
  • Token 2 (staff dashboard): Accessible because the portal used default credentials. An attacker who guesses or brute-forces the login gains access to everything behind the authentication wall. Changing default credentials before deployment is a baseline security requirement.
  • Token 3 (MySQL database): Reachable because the dashboard leaked connection strings and the database accepted remote connections. Storing plaintext credentials in a web interface and exposing a database port to the network creates a direct path from web access to data exfiltration.

Each token maps to a common vulnerability category: information disclosure, weak authentication, and insecure backend configuration.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<htmlsource_token>_<dashboard_token>_<database_token>}

Where <htmlsource_token> is the value from the staff portal HTML comment, <dashboard_token> is from the login dashboard response, and <database_token> is from the MySQL audit_tokens table.

docs.title: Step 9: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Combine the three tokens you collected into a single flag using the OCR{...} format. Separate each token with an underscore. Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider each question carefully before checking the answer. These questions connect the lab techniques to broader security concepts.

1. An entry in robots.txt does not prevent access to a directory. Why do organizations still use the file, and why is it valuable to a penetration tester?

Reveal Answer

Organizations use robots.txt to prevent search engines from indexing pages that are not meant for public discovery; staging environments, admin panels, or internal tools. The file does not enforce access control; it relies on crawlers voluntarily obeying the directives. For a penetration tester, robots.txt is valuable precisely because it acts as a directory of paths the organization considers sensitive. Reading it provides enumeration results without sending a single brute-force request.

2. The staff portal used the credentials admin / NovaTech2024#; a pattern combining a generic username with the company name and year. What makes default credentials particularly dangerous compared to weak passwords?

Reveal Answer

Default credentials are dangerous because they are predictable and widely known. A weak password might be short or simple, but an attacker still needs to guess or crack it. Default credentials follow documented patterns; vendor manuals, setup guides, and public databases list them. An attacker who recognizes the software or vendor can look up the default login without any brute-forcing. The combination of a generic username like "admin" with a company-themed password is especially common in internal tools that teams deploy quickly and forget to harden.

3. The MySQL database was accessible from your attacker machine on port 3306. Devon Harris stated the database was "not internet-facing." What network segmentation failure does the lab demonstrate?

Reveal Answer

The database server accepted connections from any host on the subnet, not only from the web application server. In a properly segmented network, the database would sit in a restricted network zone with firewall rules allowing connections only from the application tier. The lab demonstrates that "not internet-facing" does not mean "not accessible"; a host on the same internal network (or VPN) can still reach the database if no firewall rules enforce segmentation between zones.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Directory enumeration using tools like gobuster and passive sources like robots.txt reveals web application paths that developers intended to keep hidden but failed to protect with access controls
  • Default credentials remain one of the most common entry points into internal applications; changing factory-set usernames and passwords before production deployment is a non-negotiable security step
  • HTML source code can leak sensitive information through comments, build tags, and debug output that developers leave in place during the transition from development to production
  • Backend database exposure occurs when connection credentials are displayed in web interfaces and the database server accepts connections from hosts outside the application tier; proper network segmentation and credential management prevent both issues
  • Chaining low-severity findings (a robots.txt entry, a default login, a leaked connection string) can produce high-impact access; Week 11 builds on these chaining techniques with more complex multi-stage assessments

docs.text: Week 10 focused on web application exploitation, where you probed a target through its exposed HTTP services. The skills you built there; reading source code, understanding application logic, and connecting to remote services; carry forward into a new domain: lateral movement. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Crestline Financial Services, a regional investment firm based in Charlotte, North Carolina, engaged your team at Apex Red Team for an internal network penetration test. Phase 1 is complete; your team gained initial access to the company's front-end web server through a vulnerability in their customer portal.

You now have SSH (Secure Shell) access to the web server as the "webdev" service account. Your objective for Phase 2 is lateral movement: find a way to reach other systems on the internal network. Crestline's IT manager, Nathan Cole, mentioned during the scoping call that the web application connects to an internal database server that "only the app can reach." He is confident the database credentials are properly secured.

Prove him wrong. Find the database credentials, pivot to the internal server, and extract the assessment marker to demonstrate the risk. Document the full attack chain for the final report.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The engagement scope covers two internal servers. Your goals for Phase 2 are well-defined and mirror a real-world penetration test report structure.

  • Enumerate the compromised web server for stored credentials and configuration files
  • Identify hardcoded database credentials in application configuration
  • Use discovered credentials to pivot laterally to an internal server
  • Extract evidence from the database server to complete the assessment
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Lateral Movement Through Credential Reuse
docs.text:
Lateral movement is the process of moving from one compromised system to another within a network. Attackers who gain access to a single machine rarely stop there; they search the filesystem for credentials, tokens, and connection strings that let them reach additional systems. A single set of reused credentials can turn a minor foothold into full network compromise.

Web applications frequently store database connection details in plaintext configuration files. Developers need the application to connect to backend databases automatically, so they place hostnames, usernames, and passwords in files such as .env, config.php, database.yml, or files within a config/ directory. These files often live alongside the application code under /var/www/ or similar web root directories. The credentials stored in these files are rarely rotated and often grant broad access to the database server.

The danger is compounded when administrators reuse the same credentials for SSH access, database logins, or other services. An attacker who finds a database password in a .env file can try that same password against SSH on the database host; and succeed far more often than organizations expect.

The following diagram shows the pivot path for the Crestline engagement:

graph LR

    C -->|"SSH as dbadmin"| D["Database Server<br/>PostgreSQL"]
    D -->|"Extract flag"| E["Assessment<br/>Complete"]

    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: Searching for Credentials
docs.text:
Credential hunting on a Linux system relies on a small set of commands you already know: find, grep, and cat. The key is knowing where to look and what patterns to search for. The following commands are the most useful for locating credentials in application directories.

Locating configuration files with find:

find /var/www/ -name "*.env" -o -name "*.conf" -o -name "*.cfg" -o -name "*.ini"

The find command searches a directory tree for files matching the given name patterns. The -o flag means "or," so the command above looks for any file ending in .env, .conf, .cfg, or .ini under the /var/www/ directory.

Searching file contents with grep:

grep -ri "password\|pass\|secret\|key\|token" /var/www/

The -r flag tells grep to search recursively through all files in the directory. The -i flag makes the search case-insensitive. The \| syntax separates multiple search terms so grep matches any of them. Sensitive keywords like "password," "secret," and "token" frequently appear near hardcoded credentials.

Reading a specific file with cat:

cat /var/www/crestline-portal/.env

Once you identify a promising file, cat prints its full contents to the terminal. Environment files (.env) follow a KEY=VALUE format, making credentials visible at a glance.

docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. You need running containers before any connection will work.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Week 11 lab: Credential Pivot Attack
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
