docs.title: Step 2: Connect to the Web Server
docs.text:
Your team obtained SSH credentials for the web server during Phase 1. Use them now to establish your initial foothold on the Crestline network.

SSH into the web server

Open an SSH session to the compromised web server using the webdev service account recovered in Phase 1. Replace <web_server_ip> with the IP address shown in the Active Lab View.

ssh webdev@<web_server_ip>

When prompted for the password, enter:

Cr3st_W3b_2024#

After a successful login, your prompt should change to reflect the webdev user on the web server.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore the Web Application Directory
docs.text:
Web applications store their files under a web root directory, typically /var/www/. The Crestline customer portal lives in a subdirectory there. Start by listing the contents of the application directory.

List the web application directory

Run this on the web server you just logged into. The -a flag reveals hidden dotfiles, and -l shows ownership and permissions.

ls -la /var/www/crestline-portal/

Look for configuration files and directories in the output. Files named .env are hidden by default (the leading dot hides them from a plain ls), which is why the -a flag is important. You should also look for a config/ directory, which applications commonly use to store connection parameters.

docs.title: Step 4: Read Configuration Files and Discover Database Credentials
docs.text:
The application directory should contain both a .env file and a config/ directory. Read them both to build a complete picture of the application's backend connections.

Read the .env file

Print the environment file on the web server. Environment files follow a KEY=VALUE format, so credentials are visible at a glance.

cat /var/www/crestline-portal/.env

Look for lines starting with DB_HOST, DB_USER, and DB_PASS. These values tell you where the database server lives, what account the application uses, and the password for that account.

List the config directory

Configuration backups and API key files sometimes hold additional credentials or assessment tokens. List the directory contents first.

ls -la /var/www/crestline-portal/config/

Read any files you find there.

Read a config file

Replace <filename> with each file you found in the previous listing and print its contents.

cat /var/www/crestline-portal/config/<filename>

From the .env file, you should find the following connection details:

  • DB_HOST: the hostname of the database server (dbserver)
  • DB_USER: the database account username (dbadmin)
  • DB_PASS: the database account password

Record all of these values. You will use them in Step 6 to pivot to the database server.

docs.title: Step 5: Find the Assessment Token on the Web Server
docs.text:
The config directory may contain a file with an assessment token. Look for files with names that suggest backup or key storage, and search for lines containing "assessment_token" or similar markers.

Search config files for the assessment token

Recursively grep the config directory on the web server for the marker string so you do not have to open every file by hand.

grep -r "assessment_token" /var/www/crestline-portal/config/

Record the token value you find. The complete flag is assembled from pieces found on both servers, so you will need to combine the values from the web server and the database server.

docs.title: Step 6: Pivot to the Database Server
docs.text:
Using the credentials you discovered in Step 4, connect to the database server via SSH. The lateral movement happens here; you are using credentials harvested from the web server to access a completely separate system.

Pivot to the database server over SSH

From the web server shell, SSH onward to the internal database host using the harvested dbadmin credentials. The hostname dbserver resolves on the internal network.

ssh dbadmin@dbserver

When prompted for the password, enter the DB_PASS value you found in the .env file:

F1n4nc3_DB_Pr0d#

A successful login confirms the core finding of the engagement: credentials stored in plaintext application configuration files can be used to access other systems on the network.

docs.title: Step 7: Find the Flag Token on the Database Server
docs.text:
The database server contains the second piece of the assessment marker. Check the dbadmin home directory and any subdirectories for files related to the assessment.

List the dbadmin home directory

Now on the database server, list the home directory to spot maintenance folders or token files.

ls -la /home/dbadmin/

Look for a maintenance/ directory or similar location.

Read the assessment token file

Print the token file from the maintenance directory on the database server.

cat /home/dbadmin/maintenance/assessment_token.txt

Record the value you find. Combine the token from Step 5 with the token from the database server to assemble the complete flag in OCR{...} format.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the full attack chain from initial access through lateral movement. A penetration test report requires evidence at every stage.

Web server credentials used:

Username:
Password:

Database credentials discovered in .env:

Field Value DB_HOST DB_USER DB_PASS

Assessment token from web server:

(paste the token value here)

Assessment token from database server:

(paste the token value here)

Assembled flag:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the attack chain you documented. The engagement followed a clear sequence that penetration testers encounter regularly in corporate environments.

You started with a low-privilege service account on the web server. That account had read access to application configuration files; a normal requirement for the web application to function. Inside those configuration files, you found plaintext database credentials. Because the database server accepted SSH connections with the same credentials, you were able to move laterally from one system to another without exploiting any software vulnerability. The entire pivot relied on credential reuse and plaintext credential storage.

Nathan Cole believed the database was protected because "only the app can reach" it. The database server's PostgreSQL port (5432) may indeed be firewalled from external access, but SSH (port 22) was not restricted in the same way. Layered security; restricting both the credentials and the network access; would have made the pivot significantly harder.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<webserver_token>_<pivottarget_token>}

Where <webserver_token> is the value from the web config API keys backup, and <pivottarget_token> is from the pivot target assessment token on the database server.

docs.title: Step 9: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Combine the two token values you collected into the OCR{...} format. Navigate to the Submit Flag form on the platform and paste the assembled flag. Click Submit to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The following questions ask you to think beyond the steps you performed and consider the broader security implications. Take a moment to reason through each one before reading the answer.

1. Why do developers store database credentials in plaintext configuration files, and what alternatives exist?

Reveal Answer

Applications need credentials at runtime to connect to backend databases. Developers store them in .env files or config directories because the approach is fast and compatible with most frameworks. Safer alternatives include environment variable injection at deploy time (so credentials never touch disk), secrets management tools like HashiCorp Vault, and cloud provider secret stores such as AWS Secrets Manager. Each approach removes the plaintext file from the server's filesystem.

2. The database server accepted SSH connections with the same credentials used for the database. What security principle does credential reuse violate, and how would you fix it?

Reveal Answer

Credential reuse violates the principle of least privilege: each service should have its own unique credentials scoped to the minimum access required. The SSH account and the database account should use separate passwords. Better yet, SSH access to the database server should require key-based authentication with no password login allowed, and database access should be restricted to connections from the web server's IP address only.

3. If the web server had been configured so the webdev account could not read the .env file, would the attack still succeed? Why or why not?

Reveal Answer

Restricting file permissions on .env so that only the application process (running as a different user) can read it would block the credential discovery step entirely. The webdev account would see the file in a directory listing but could not read its contents. Proper file ownership and permissions (e.g., chmod 600 owned by the application user) are a low-cost defense that many organizations overlook.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Lateral movement is the process of moving from one compromised system to another within a network, and credential reuse in configuration files is one of the most common paths attackers exploit
  • Plaintext credentials in .env files and config directories are a top finding in penetration test reports; applications need database access, but storing passwords in readable files creates unnecessary risk
  • Credential reuse across services (using the same password for SSH and database access) multiplies the impact of a single credential leak
  • File permissions on configuration files are a critical but frequently neglected control; the application user should be the only account that can read sensitive configs
  • Defense in depth requires securing both the credentials (unique passwords, secrets management) and the network path (firewall rules, IP allowlists); Week 12 will explore how defenders detect and respond to lateral movement attempts

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Week 11 focused on lateral movement; pivoting from one compromised system to another within a network. The lab you are about to start shifts from movement to impact: you already have root-level access on the target, and your task is to demonstrate what an attacker can do with that access. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready before you proceed.

Post-exploitation is the phase that turns a technical compromise into a business-level finding. Executives rarely care that you obtained root; they care about what data you could reach once you had it.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Redwood Analytics, a business intelligence firm in Portland, has been compromised. Your red team achieved root access on their primary analytics server through a chain of vulnerabilities documented in earlier engagement phases.

Your team lead, Daniel Park, wants a thorough data harvest: "We have root on the analytics box. I need you to demonstrate the real-world impact. Find database backups, extract credentials, locate any hidden data stores. Document everything; the executive summary needs to show them why the compromise matters."

You have SSH (Secure Shell) access as the operator account with full sudo privileges, simulating the root-level access your team obtained during the exploitation phase. Three assessment markers have been hidden across the server using different concealment techniques: compression, encoding, and hidden files. Your job is to find all three.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Search a compromised server for sensitive data across multiple locations
  • Extract and decompress archived backup files to recover embedded tokens
  • Decode base64-encoded credentials from application log files
  • Discover hidden files and directories using filesystem enumeration
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Post-Exploitation and Data Collection
docs.text:
Post-exploitation is the phase of a penetration test where the assessor demonstrates the real-world consequences of a compromise. Gaining access to a system proves a vulnerability exists, but harvesting data from that system proves the vulnerability has business impact. Reports that include specific data findings; database records, credentials, confidential files; are far more persuasive to decision-makers than reports that stop at "we got root."

Linux servers store sensitive data in predictable locations. Database backups often appear in /var/backups/ or custom directories under /opt/. Application logs in /var/log/ frequently contain credentials, session tokens, or API (Application Programming Interface) keys that developers embedded for debugging and never removed. Hidden files; those whose names begin with a dot (.); do not appear in standard ls output, making them a common location for configuration secrets and cached credentials.

Attackers and assessors use three common techniques to locate concealed data. Compressed archives (.tar.gz, .zip) bundle files together and require extraction before inspection. Base64 encoding converts binary or sensitive strings into printable ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) characters, which blends into log output and avoids detection by simple keyword searches. Hidden dotfiles require the -a flag with ls or a targeted find command to reveal.

graph TD
    A["Root access<br/>obtained"] --> B["Search backups<br/>and archives"]
    A --> C["Inspect logs<br/>for credentials"]
    A --> D["Find hidden<br/>dotfiles"]
    B --> E["Extract and<br/>read contents"]
    C --> F["Decode base64<br/>tokens"]
    D --> G["Read hidden<br/>file contents"]
    E --> H["Document<br/>findings"]
    F --> H
    G --> H

    style A fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style E fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style G fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style H fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

The diagram above shows the three parallel data-collection paths you will follow during the lab. Each path uses a different technique to reveal concealed information, and all three converge on the documentation step that ties your findings together.

docs.title: Tool Primer: tar, base64, and find
docs.text:
Three command-line tools form the core of the data-harvesting workflow in the lab. Each one addresses a different concealment technique that defenders and developers commonly use on Linux servers.

tar; Archive extraction

The tar command creates and extracts compressed archive files. The name stands for "tape archive," a holdover from when backups were written to magnetic tape. The flags you need for extraction are:

tar xzf <archive_file> -C <destination_directory>
  • x: extract files from the archive
  • z: decompress using gzip (required for .tar.gz files)
  • f: the next argument is the archive filename
  • -C: change to the specified directory before extracting

Sample output after extraction:

$ tar xzf /var/backups/redwood-db-latest.tar.gz -C /tmp
$ ls /tmp/
redwood_dump.sql

The extracted file appears in the destination directory. You can then search its contents with grep or read it with cat.

base64; Decode encoded strings

The base64 command encodes and decodes Base64 data. Base64 encoding represents binary data using 64 printable characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /), often with trailing = signs as padding. Developers frequently use Base64 to embed tokens or credentials in log files and configuration strings.

echo "c2Vuc2l0aXZlX3Rva2Vu" | base64 -d
  • -d: decode the input (without the flag, base64 encodes instead)

Sample output:

$ echo "c2Vuc2l0aXZlX3Rva2Vu" | base64 -d
sensitive_token

You can also pipe output from grep directly into base64 -d to extract and decode in a single command chain.

find; Locate hidden files

The find command searches the filesystem based on name patterns, file types, permissions, and other criteria. Hidden files on Linux begin with a dot (.) and do not appear in default ls output.

find /opt -name ".marker*" -type f 2>/dev/null
  • /opt: the starting directory for the search
  • -name ".marker*": match filenames beginning with .marker
  • -type f: match only regular files, not directories
  • 2>/dev/null: suppress "Permission denied" errors for directories you cannot read

Sample output:

$ find /opt -name ".marker*" -type f 2>/dev/null
/opt/redwood/.marker_cache

The command returns the full path to each matching file, which you can then read with cat.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect via SSH and Verify Sudo Access
docs.text:
Your access uses the operator account, which has full sudo privileges on the target. SSH provides a remote terminal session on the analytics server.

Open your terminal and connect:

SSH into the analytics server

Open an SSH session to the compromised analytics server using the operator account. Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View.

ssh operator@<target_ip>

When prompted for a password, enter:

R3dw00d_0ps#

You should see a shell prompt indicating you are logged in as operator.

Verify your privilege level

Run these on the analytics server to confirm the account and its sudo access before harvesting data.

whoami
sudo whoami

The first command should return operator. The second should return root, confirming that the operator account has full administrative privileges through sudo. If sudo whoami prompts for a password, enter the same password you used for SSH.

docs.title: Step 3: Search /var/backups/ for Compressed Archives
docs.text:
Database backups are a high-value target during post-exploitation because they often contain full copies of application data, user records, and credentials. The /var/backups/ directory is a standard location for automated backup scripts on Linux.

List the contents of the backup directory:

List the backups directory

On the analytics server, list /var/backups/ to spot archived database dumps left by automated backup scripts.

ls -la /var/backups/

Look for archive files with the .tar.gz extension. You should find a file named redwood-db-latest.tar.gz: a compressed backup of the Redwood Analytics database. Note the file size, ownership, and permissions. On a real engagement, these details go into your report to demonstrate that the backup was accessible from the compromised account.

docs.title: Step 4: Extract the Archive and Find the Token
docs.text:
Compressed archives must be extracted before you can inspect their contents. The tar command handles both decompression and extraction in a single step.

Extract the backup archive to /tmp:

Extract the backup archive

On the analytics server, extract the gzip archive into /tmp. The x flag extracts, z decompresses gzip, f names the file, and -C sets the destination.

sudo tar xzf /var/backups/redwood-db-latest.tar.gz -C /tmp

List the extracted files

Confirm what the archive unpacked into /tmp.

ls -la /tmp/

You should see a file named redwood_dump.sql or similar.

Search the dump for a marker

Grep the extracted SQL dump for the assessment marker string.

grep marker /tmp/redwood_dump.sql

The output should contain a line with a marker value. Record the value; you will need all three markers to assemble the complete flag.

docs.title: Step 5: Decode a Base64-Encoded Token from Application Logs
docs.text:
Application logs often contain sensitive data that developers intended for debugging but never cleaned up. The Redwood Analytics application writes session tokens to its log file using Base64 encoding, which obscures the value from casual inspection but does not provide real security.

Search the application log for Base64-encoded session tokens:

Find session tokens in the app log

On the analytics server, grep the application log for lines holding session tokens.

grep session_token /var/log/redwood/app.log

The output should show one or more log entries containing session_token= followed by a Base64-encoded string.

Extract and decode the token

Pull the encoded value out of the log and decode it in a single pipeline. The decoded output is the second marker.

grep -oP 'session_token=\K[A-Za-z0-9+/=]+' /var/log/redwood/app.log | head -1 | base64 -d
  • grep -oP uses Perl-compatible regular expressions and outputs only the matching portion
  • \K resets the match start, so session_token= is matched but not included in the output
  • head -1 takes the first match if multiple entries exist
  • base64 -d decodes the extracted string

Record the decoded value as the second marker.

docs.title: Step 6: Find Hidden Files in /opt
docs.text:
Hidden files on Linux have names that begin with a dot. Standard ls output does not show them, which makes dotfiles a common place for developers and administrators to store configuration data, cache files, and credentials. The find command locates these files regardless of their hidden status.

Search the /opt directory for hidden marker files:

Find hidden marker files

On the analytics server, search /opt for dotfiles whose names start with .marker. The 2>/dev/null redirect suppresses permission-denied noise.

find /opt -name ".marker*" -type f 2>/dev/null

The output should show a path like /opt/redwood/.marker_cache.

Read the hidden marker file

Print the contents of the hidden file the search returned.

cat /opt/redwood/.marker_cache

The file contents reveal the third marker. Record the value.

docs.text:
Record the evidence you gathered from each data source. In a real engagement, these notes become the evidence section of your penetration testing report.

Archive extraction output:

(paste the output of grep marker /tmp/redwood_dump.sql here)

Decoded session token from logs:

(paste the decoded base64 output here)

Hidden file discovery:

(paste the output of find /opt -name ".marker*" here)

Hidden file contents:

(paste the contents of the hidden marker file here)

All three markers:

Source Marker Value Compressed archive Base64 log token Hidden dotfile

Complete flag:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Step 7: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the three data sources you exploited and consider what each one represents in a real-world breach.

The compressed archive in /var/backups/ contained a full database dump. On a production server, a file like redwood_dump.sql could hold customer records, financial data, or internal credentials. The backup was stored in a standard system directory with no encryption, meaning any user with root access could read it immediately.

The Base64-encoded session token in the application log demonstrates a common developer mistake. Encoding is not encryption; Base64 is a reversible transformation, not a security control. Any attacker who can read the log file can decode the tokens in seconds. Application logs should never contain credentials or session tokens, even in encoded form.

The hidden dotfile under /opt shows that "hidden" on Linux means "not shown by default," not "protected." The find command bypasses the visual concealment of dotfiles without any special privileges. Sensitive data stored in hidden files is accessible to anyone with read permissions on the parent directory.

Together, these three findings demonstrate the breadth of impact that root access enables. A thorough post-exploitation assessment covers all three concealment categories; compressed, encoded, and hidden; to give the client a complete picture of their exposure.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<archive_token>_<logdecode_token>_<dotfile_token>}

Where <archive_token> is the value from the tar backup extraction, <logdecode_token> is from the base64 decoded app.log token, and <dotfile_token> is from the hidden file in .marker_cache.

docs.title: Step 8: Submit the Flag
docs.text:
Combine the three marker values you collected into a single flag using the OCR{...} format. The markers join together with underscores between them.

Paste the complete flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit. The platform will validate your submission and mark the lab as complete.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider the following questions to deepen your understanding of post-exploitation data harvesting and its implications for defensive security.

1. Why is post-exploitation documentation more valuable to a client than a report that stops at "we obtained root access"?

Reveal Answer

Root access alone tells the client they have a vulnerability, but not what the vulnerability means for their business. Documented data harvesting shows the client exactly which sensitive files, credentials, and databases an attacker could reach. Executive decision-makers allocate remediation budgets based on business risk, and specific data findings; "we extracted your full customer database"; communicate risk far more effectively than abstract technical achievements.

2. Base64 encoding obscured the session token in the application log. Why does encoding fail as a security control?

Reveal Answer

Base64 is a reversible transformation, not an encryption algorithm. Any observer who recognizes the character pattern can decode the value using a standard command-line tool or even a web-based decoder. Encoding changes the representation of data but does not restrict access to it. Encryption, by contrast, requires a secret key to reverse the transformation, making the data unreadable to anyone without the key.

3. What defensive measures could Redwood Analytics implement to reduce the impact of a root-level compromise?

Reveal Answer

Encrypting database backups at rest would prevent an attacker from reading the contents even with root access to the filesystem. Removing credentials and tokens from application logs; or configuring the logging framework to redact sensitive fields; would eliminate the encoded token exposure. Implementing file integrity monitoring (FIM) on sensitive directories would alert the security team when files are read or modified. Network segmentation could limit what a compromised analytics server can reach, reducing lateral movement opportunities. Regular access audits would identify unnecessary sudo privileges before an attacker can exploit them.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Post-exploitation proves business impact by demonstrating what data an attacker can access after gaining a foothold, turning a technical finding into an executive-level risk statement
  • Compressed archives in backup directories are high-value targets because they often contain full database dumps, configuration files, and credentials bundled together without encryption
  • Base64 encoding is not a security control: reversing the encoding requires no key and takes a single command; sensitive data in logs must be encrypted or removed entirely
  • Hidden dotfiles are invisible to default ls output but trivially discoverable with find; "hidden" on Linux means "not displayed," not "protected"
  • Systematic enumeration across multiple data sources; backups, logs, and hidden files; ensures a thorough assessment; Week 13 will build on these post-exploitation skills with evidence packaging and reporting techniques

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Over the past three weeks (Weeks 10-12), you have been building skills in credential discovery, lateral movement, and multi-stage attack chains. Week 13 marks a shift from offensive techniques to defensive analysis: instead of attacking a target, you will examine evidence left behind by an attacker. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready for SSH access to the analysis workstation.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Avalon Biotech, a pharmaceutical research company in San Diego, California, has flagged suspicious network activity on their internal network. Their SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system triggered alerts for unusual outbound connections from a workstation in the R&D department (10.20.1.105) to multiple external IP addresses over the past 48 hours.

The incident response team captured a 5-minute segment of the workstation's network traffic before the employee; Mark Sullivan, Research Associate; was informed. The capture has been placed on an analysis workstation for your review.

Dr. Priya Sharma (CISO) needs your analysis: "We need to know exactly what happened. What data was accessed? What credentials were used? How was the data moved out? If Mark is exfiltrating our proprietary drug trial data, we need evidence for legal. Pull everything you can from that capture."

Your job is to analyze the PCAP (Packet Capture) file at /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap, extract three indicators of compromise (IOCs), and reconstruct the attack timeline.

Credentials

Analysis Workstation SSH: analyst / Av4l0n_S0C#

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The evidence file contains traffic from three distinct attack vectors. You will need to find each one and extract the associated IOC marker.

  • Analyze a network packet capture using command-line tools (tcpdump, tshark)
  • Identify suspicious HTTP traffic and extract leaked credentials from POST requests
  • Reconstruct FTP (File Transfer Protocol) sessions to discover data exfiltration activity
  • Detect DNS (Domain Name System)-based data exfiltration techniques
  • Assemble the IOC markers and capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Network Forensics and Packet Analysis
docs.text:
Network forensics is the practice of capturing, recording, and analyzing network traffic to detect intrusions, reconstruct incidents, and gather evidence. Every packet that crosses a network carries metadata; source and destination addresses, protocol information, timestamps; and often carries payload data such as login credentials, file contents, or command sequences. When an attacker moves data across a network, that activity leaves traces in the captured traffic.

A PCAP file is the standard format for storing captured network traffic. Tools like tcpdump and Wireshark write PCAP files, and analysts can replay them later to examine every packet in detail. Each packet in a PCAP contains the full protocol stack: Ethernet frame headers, IP headers, transport-layer headers (TCP or UDP), and the application-layer payload (HTTP requests, FTP commands, DNS queries, and so on).

Network traffic is evidence because attackers cannot avoid generating packets. Whether they are logging into a web application, transferring files, or tunneling data through DNS, the packets record what happened. Your role as an analyst is to filter, decode, and interpret those packets to build a picture of the incident.

graph LR
    A["Capture Traffic<br/>(PCAP file)"] --> B["Filter by<br/>Protocol"]
    B --> C["Extract<br/>Payloads"]
    C --> D["Identify IOCs<br/>and Evidence"]
    D --> E["Reconstruct<br/>Attack Timeline"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style E fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: tshark and tcpdump
docs.text:
Two command-line tools dominate PCAP analysis on Linux: tcpdump and tshark. Both can read PCAP files and apply filters, but they differ in their strengths. tcpdump excels at quick, raw packet inspection, while tshark (the terminal version of Wireshark) provides powerful protocol dissection and field extraction.

Reading a PCAP with tcpdump:

tcpdump -r capture.pcap -n | head -50
  • -r capture.pcap: read from a file instead of a live interface
  • -n: do not resolve hostnames (show raw IP addresses)
  • | head -50: display only the first 50 packets for a quick overview

Reading a PCAP with tshark:

tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z conv,ip
  • -r capture.pcap: read from a file
  • -q: quiet mode (suppress per-packet output)
  • -z conv,ip: show a summary table of IP conversations

Filtering by protocol; HTTP traffic:

tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "http.request.method==POST" -T fields -e http.file_data

The -Y flag applies a display filter. The -T fields -e flags extract specific protocol fields from matching packets.

Filtering by protocol; FTP commands:

tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "ftp.request.command==PASS" -T fields -e ftp.request.arg

FTP sends credentials in plaintext. The PASS command carries the password, and tshark can extract the argument directly.

Filtering by protocol; DNS queries:

tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "dns.qry.type==16" -T fields -e dns.qry.name

DNS TXT record queries (type 16) are a common channel for data exfiltration. Attackers encode stolen data as subdomain labels and send DNS lookups to a server they control.

Alternative tcpdump approach; searching for strings:

tcpdump -r capture.pcap -A port 80 | grep token=

The -A flag prints packet payloads in ASCII, making it possible to search for specific strings with grep.
