SSH into the analysis workstation

Open an SSH session to the forensics workstation as the analyst user. Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View.

ssh analyst@<target_ip>

When prompted for a password, enter:

Av4l0n_S0C#

A successful login places you in the analyst's home directory on the analysis workstation.

docs.title: Step 3: Verify the PCAP File
docs.text:
Before running any analysis, confirm that the evidence file exists and is readable. A missing or corrupted file would waste your time troubleshooting tool errors.

Verify the evidence file

On the analysis workstation, list the capture file with -lh so you see a human-readable size and the permissions.

ls -lh /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap

You should see the file listed with its size and permissions. The file path is /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap: all subsequent commands reference it there.

docs.title: Step 4: Get an Overview of the Capture
docs.text:
Start with a broad view of the traffic before diving into specific protocols. Understanding the volume, duration, and protocol distribution helps you know where to focus.

Run a conversation summary to see which IP addresses are communicating:

Summarize IP conversations

On the analysis workstation, ask tshark for a conversation table. The -q flag suppresses per-packet output and -z conv,ip prints the summary.

tshark -r /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap -q -z conv,ip

Look for connections from the suspect workstation (10.20.1.105) to external IP addresses.

Preview the first 50 packets

Get a raw look at the traffic with tcpdump. The -n flag skips name resolution so you see raw IPs.

tcpdump -r /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap -n | head -50

Note which protocols appear; HTTP, FTP, and DNS are the three you need to investigate.

docs.title: Step 5: Extract HTTP POST Data
docs.text:
HTTP POST requests carry form data in their body, which can include usernames, passwords, and session tokens. An attacker who submits credentials to an external server leaves that data visible in the PCAP.

Filter the capture for HTTP POST requests and extract the body content:

Extract HTTP POST bodies with tshark

Apply a display filter for POST requests and pull the body field. The -Y flag is the display filter and -T fields -e extracts a single named field.

tshark -r /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap -Y "http.request.method==POST" -T fields -e http.file_data

Grep POST traffic with tcpdump

Alternatively, dump port 80 payloads in ASCII and search for the field name directly.

tcpdump -r /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap -A port 80 | grep token=

Look for a token= field in the POST body. The value after token= is your first IOC marker. Record it before moving on.

docs.title: Step 6: Extract FTP Credentials
docs.text:
FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transmits everything in cleartext, including usernames and passwords. The PASS command contains the password sent during authentication. An FTP session to an external IP from the suspect workstation is strong evidence of data exfiltration.

Extract the FTP PASS command from the capture:

Extract the FTP PASS argument

Filter for the FTP PASS command and extract its argument, which is the cleartext password the attacker sent.

tshark -r /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap -Y "ftp.request.command==PASS" -T fields -e ftp.request.arg

Grep FTP traffic with tcpdump

Alternatively, dump port 21 payloads and search for the PASS line.

tcpdump -r /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap -A port 21 | grep PASS

The password value is your second IOC marker. Record it alongside the first.

docs.title: Step 7: Analyze DNS Queries for Data Exfiltration
docs.text:
DNS-based data exfiltration is a technique where an attacker encodes stolen data into subdomain labels and sends DNS queries to a command-and-control (C2) server. Because DNS traffic is rarely blocked or inspected, attackers use it to bypass firewalls and data loss prevention systems.

For example, a query to encoded-data.data.evil-c2.net hides the stolen content in the subdomain encoded-data. The attacker's DNS server receives the query and logs the subdomain as exfiltrated data.

Filter the capture for DNS TXT record queries (query type 16):

Extract DNS TXT query names

Filter for DNS TXT queries (type 16) and print the query names, which carry the encoded exfiltration data in their subdomain labels.

tshark -r /home/analyst/evidence/capture.pcap -Y "dns.qry.type==16" -T fields -e dns.qry.name

Look for queries directed at a suspicious domain. Among the exfiltration traffic, one query has a subdomain prefixed with token_. The value after token_ (before the first dot) is your third IOC marker. Record it with the other two.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Record the three IOC markers you extracted from the packet capture. You will combine them to form the flag.

IOC 1; HTTP POST token value:

(paste your finding here)

IOC 2; FTP PASS value:

(paste your finding here)

IOC 3; DNS exfiltration subdomain:

(paste your finding here)

Assembled flag:

OCR{_____________________________}

Attack timeline summary:

Order Protocol External IP Activity

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Now that you have extracted all three IOC markers, step back and reconstruct the full attack timeline. Understanding the sequence of events matters as much as finding the individual artifacts.

The suspect workstation (10.20.1.105) made outbound connections using three different protocols:

  • HTTP POST to an external server (198.51.100.47): the attacker submitted credentials or tokens to a remote web endpoint. The POST body contained the first IOC marker, suggesting the attacker authenticated to an external service or exfiltrated authentication tokens.
  • FTP session to another external server (203.0.113.22): the attacker connected to an FTP server and authenticated with a password containing the second IOC marker. FTP is commonly used to transfer files in bulk, pointing to data exfiltration of larger assets.
  • DNS TXT queries to a C2 domain: the attacker sent multiple DNS queries to a C2 domain, encoding exfiltrated data as subdomain labels. One of those queries is tagged with a token_ prefix, marking it as the third IOC. DNS exfiltration is a covert channel; most organizations do not inspect DNS query content, making it an effective way to smuggle small amounts of data past security controls.

The three markers combine to form the flag in OCR{...} format, with underscores separating each marker.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<httptoken>_<ftptoken>_<dnstoken>}

Where httptoken is from the HTTP POST token= parameter, ftptoken is from the FTP PASS command, and dnstoken is the value after token_ in the DNS TXT query subdomain.

docs.title: Step 9: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Combine the three IOC markers you extracted into the flag format: OCR{...}. The markers are joined with underscores in the order you found them (HTTP, FTP, DNS). Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Take a moment to think through these questions. They build on what you observed in the packet capture and connect to broader network security concepts.

1. Why is FTP considered a security risk compared to protocols like SFTP or SCP?

Reveal Answer

FTP transmits all data in cleartext, including usernames and passwords. Anyone with access to the network path; whether through a packet capture, a man-in-the-middle position, or a compromised switch; can read every credential and file transferred. SFTP and SCP encrypt the entire session, making captured packets unreadable without the encryption keys.

2. How does DNS-based data exfiltration bypass traditional security controls, and what defenses can detect it?

Reveal Answer

Most firewalls allow DNS traffic (port 53) outbound without inspection because DNS is essential for normal network operations. Attackers exploit that permissiveness by encoding data in subdomain labels. Defenses include DNS query logging and analysis, monitoring for unusually long subdomain labels, tracking query volume per domain, and deploying DNS-aware security tools that inspect query content for encoded or anomalous patterns.

3. An analyst finds HTTP POST traffic to an external IP but the POST body is encrypted with TLS. How does TLS change the analyst's ability to reconstruct the incident?

Reveal Answer

TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts the HTTP payload, so the analyst would see the connection metadata (source IP, destination IP, destination port, timing) but not the POST body content. Reconstructing the incident would require access to the TLS session keys (sometimes logged by endpoint agents), a TLS-intercepting proxy that decrypts and re-encrypts traffic, or endpoint forensic artifacts like browser history and process memory. Without decryption, the analyst can prove a connection occurred but cannot determine what data was sent.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• PCAP files are the foundation of network forensics; they record every packet and allow analysts to reconstruct exactly what happened on the wire
  • Protocol-specific filters in tshark and tcpdump let you isolate HTTP, FTP, DNS, and other traffic types from large captures, turning thousands of packets into targeted evidence
  • Cleartext protocols like HTTP and FTP expose credentials and data to anyone who captures the traffic; encrypted alternatives (HTTPS, SFTP) prevent that exposure
  • DNS exfiltration is a covert channel that abuses the ubiquity of DNS to smuggle data past firewalls and security controls, making DNS query analysis an essential defensive skill
  • Attack timeline reconstruction ties individual artifacts together into a coherent narrative, which is the deliverable that incident response teams and legal counsel need; Week 14 builds on these forensic skills with log analysis and correlation techniques

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Week 13 introduced offline traffic analysis using PCAP (Packet Capture) files; you examined pre-recorded network data for signs of malicious activity. Week 14 shifts from post-incident analysis to real-time detection. The attack is happening now, and your job is to write rules that catch it as packets cross the wire.

Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open. You should be comfortable with basic Linux command-line navigation and have a working understanding of HTTP request structure from previous labs.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Sentinel Defense Corp, a boutique cybersecurity consulting firm based in Arlington, Virginia, has detected anomalous network traffic on their DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) segment. The Network Operations Center flagged repeated connections from an unidentified source targeting multiple hosts in the 10.100.x.0/24 range. Initial triage suggests automated reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

You are a junior SOC (Security Operations Center) analyst pulling the night shift. Your supervisor, Marcus Chen (Senior Threat Hunter), left you a voicemail before signing off:

"We've got active probing hitting the DMZ. The IDS sensor is online but we never deployed custom detection rules; it's running blind. I need you to analyze the traffic, write Suricata rules that catch the specific attack signatures, and pull the IOCs from the captured payloads. Also check the web portal; I think the attacker got some hits there. Extract everything you can. I'll review your findings in the morning."

Your toolkit includes SSH access to the IDS sensor (running Suricata and tcpdump) and the corporate web portal (running nginx). The attack is ongoing; new malicious requests arrive every few seconds. The clock is ticking.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The following list outlines what you need to accomplish in the lab environment. Each objective maps to one or more walkthrough steps below.

  • Observe live attack traffic on the IDS sensor using packet capture tools
  • Identify distinct attack signatures in the traffic (SQL injection, command injection)
  • Write custom Suricata IDS rules to detect each attack vector
  • Extract indicators of compromise (IOCs) from Suricata alert payloads
  • Investigate the target web server's logs for additional forensic evidence
  • Assemble the flag parts and submit the completed flag

docs.title: Background: Intrusion Detection Systems and Suricata
docs.text:
An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) is a network security tool that monitors traffic for suspicious patterns and generates alerts when it finds a match. An IDS differs from an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) in one critical way: an IDS observes and alerts, while an IPS can actively block or drop malicious packets. Think of an IDS as a security camera and an IPS as a security guard; one watches, the other intervenes.

Most IDS engines rely on signature-based detection, where the system compares each packet against a database of known attack patterns. Each pattern is expressed as a rule that describes what to look for; a specific string in the URL, a byte sequence in the payload, or a combination of header values. When a packet matches a rule, the engine writes an alert to its log file with details about the match.

Suricata is an open-source, high-performance IDS/IPS engine maintained by the Open Information Security Foundation (OISF). Suricata inspects network traffic in real time, applies rules against each packet or reassembled stream, and logs alerts in a structured JSON format called Eve (Extensible eVent Engine) JSON. Security analysts use Eve JSON logs to investigate alerts, correlate events, and extract IOCs.

The following diagram illustrates how traffic flows through a Suricata IDS sensor:

graph LR
    A["Network Traffic<br/>(HTTP, DNS, etc.)"] --> B["Suricata<br/>IDS Engine"]
    B --> C{"Rule<br/>Match?"}
    C -->|"Yes"| D["Alert Written<br/>to Eve JSON"]
    C -->|"No"| E["Traffic Passes<br/>Unlogged"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#888,color:#fff
  • Network Traffic arrives at the sensor's network interface
  • Suricata reassembles streams and inspects content against loaded rules
  • Rule Match: if a signature matches, an alert record is written to the Eve JSON log
  • No Match: traffic that does not trigger any rule passes without generating an alert

The distinction between IDS and IPS matters for your work tonight. The Sentinel Defense Corp sensor is configured in IDS mode; it will detect and log, but it will not block. Your rules need to be precise enough to flag the real attacks without generating noise from normal traffic.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Writing Suricata Rules
docs.text: Suricata rules follow a structured syntax that tells the engine what traffic to inspect and what conditions trigger an alert. Understanding the rule format is essential before you write your own detection signatures.

docs.title: Rule Structure
docs.text:
Every Suricata rule has two parts: a header and an options section. The header specifies the action, protocol, source, destination, and direction. The options section (in parentheses) contains the detection logic and metadata.

alert http <src_ip> <src_port> -> <dst_ip> <dst_port> (options;)

Here is a concrete example that detects the string "UNION SELECT" in an HTTP URI:

alert http any any -> any any (msg:"SQLi Detected"; content:"UNION SELECT"; nocase; http_uri; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

Breaking down each component:

Component Value Meaning Action alert Generate an alert when matched Protocol http Inspect HTTP traffic only Source any any Any source IP and port Direction -> Traffic flowing to the destination Destination any any Any destination IP and port msg "SQLi Detected" Human-readable alert message content "UNION SELECT" Byte string to match nocase ; Case-insensitive matching http_uri ; Match only within the HTTP URI sid 1000001 Signature ID (unique per rule) rev 1 Rule revision number

docs.title: Key Content Modifiers
docs.text:
Suricata provides several modifiers that control where content matching occurs within a packet or stream:

  • http_uri: match within the request URI (the path and query string)
  • http_client_body: match within the POST body sent by the client
  • http_header: match within HTTP headers
  • nocase: ignore capitalization when matching the content string

docs.title: Eve JSON Log Format
docs.text:
When a rule fires, Suricata writes a JSON record to /var/log/suricata/eve.json. Each alert record contains the signature name, signature ID, source and destination IPs, and protocol-specific fields like the HTTP URL and payload.

A typical alert entry looks like the following (simplified for readability):

{
  "timestamp": "2024-11-15T03:22:41.123456+0000",
  "event_type": "alert",
  "src_ip": "10.100.5.31",
  "dest_ip": "10.100.5.47",
  "alert": {
    "signature": "SQLi Detected",
    "signature_id": 1000001
  },
  "http": {
    "url": "/search?q=1'+UNION+SELECT+...&campaign=REDACTED"
  }
}

docs.title: Parsing Eve JSON with jq
docs.text:
The jq command-line tool filters and formats JSON data. You will use it to extract alert records from the Eve log and pull specific fields from matching entries.

Filter only alert events from the log:

jq 'select(.alert != null)' /var/log/suricata/eve.json

Extract only the alert signature and HTTP URL from alert events:

jq 'select(.alert != null) | {sig: .alert.signature, url: .http.url}' /var/log/suricata/eve.json

Filter alerts by a specific signature ID:

jq 'select(.alert != null) | select(.alert.signature_id == 1000001)' /var/log/suricata/eve.json

These jq patterns will be essential for extracting IOCs from your Suricata alerts during the walkthrough.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
The lab environment provisions two servers: an IDS sensor running Suricata and a web portal running nginx. Both machines must be running before you begin your investigation.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Week 14 lab: Sentinel Defense Corp; Live IDS Detection
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the IP addresses for both the IDS Sensor and the Web Portal displayed in the Active Lab View

The IDS sensor sits between the attacker and the web portal on the DMZ network. Automated attack traffic is already flowing; your containers begin receiving malicious requests as soon as the lab starts.

docs.title: Step 2: SSH to the IDS Sensor
docs.text:
You will perform most of your work on the IDS sensor, where Suricata is running. Connect using the analyst credentials provided for the engagement.

SSH into the IDS sensor

Open an SSH session to the Suricata IDS sensor as the analyst user. Replace <ids_sensor_ip> with the IDS Sensor IP shown in the Active Lab View.

ssh analyst@<ids_sensor_ip>

When prompted for the password, enter:

S3nt1n3l_S0C#

After logging in, you should see a standard Linux shell prompt. Confirm you are on the correct machine by checking the hostname; it should indicate the IDS sensor role.

docs.title: Step 3: Verify Suricata Is Running
docs.text:
Before writing detection rules, confirm that the Suricata process is active and listening on the network interface. A stopped engine cannot detect anything, and writing rules for a dead process wastes time.

Confirm Suricata is running

On the IDS sensor, ask for the Suricata process ID. A numeric result means the engine is active.

pidof suricata

A numeric process ID in the output confirms Suricata is running. If the command returns nothing, the engine is not active; contact your lab platform support before proceeding.

Note that pgrep -x suricata does not reliably detect a running Suricata. When Suricata runs in daemon mode, its main thread renames itself (for example, to Suricata-Main), so the exact-match flag (-x) misses it. Use pidof suricata or pgrep -f suricata instead.

You can also check the Suricata service status for more detail:

Inspect the Suricata process line

Print the full process listing and filter for suricata to see which interface and config file it loaded.

ps aux | grep suricata

Look for a process line showing suricata with flags indicating which interface and configuration file it is using. The presence of the process means the engine is ready to accept rules and begin generating alerts.

docs.title: Step 4: Observe Live Attack Traffic
docs.text:
Before writing rules, you need to understand what the attack looks like on the wire. Watching raw traffic with tcpdump reveals the attack patterns, which you will then translate into Suricata signatures.

Run the following command to capture HTTP traffic on port 80 and display the ASCII content of each packet:

Watch live HTTP traffic with tcpdump

On the IDS sensor, sniff port 80 on eth0. The -A flag prints payloads in ASCII so you can read the request lines.

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 | head -100

Watch the output for 15-20 seconds. You should see HTTP requests arriving at regular intervals. Pay close attention to two distinct patterns:

Pattern 1; SQL Injection (SQLi) via GET requests:

Look for GET requests where the URL query string contains SQL syntax. The attacker is injecting UNION SELECT statements into search parameters. A typical request URI looks something like:

GET /search?q=1'+UNION+SELECT+username,password+FROM+users--&campaign=SOMETHING

The UNION SELECT keyword combination is a hallmark of SQL injection; the attacker is attempting to append their own database query to a legitimate search.

Pattern 2; Command Injection (CMDi) via POST requests:

Look for POST requests where the body contains operating system commands. The attacker is injecting system commands like cat /etc/passwd into form fields. A typical POST body looks something like:

cmd=;cat /etc/passwd&exfil=SOMETHING

The cat /etc pattern reveals command injection; the attacker is attempting to execute arbitrary commands on the server and read sensitive system files.

Note both patterns carefully. Each one will require its own Suricata rule.

docs.title: Step 5: Write Suricata Rules for SQLi and CMDi Detection
docs.text:
Now that you have identified the two attack vectors, write Suricata rules that detect each pattern. The rules file for custom signatures on the IDS sensor is located at /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules.

Open the file in a text editor:

Open the local rules file

On the IDS sensor, open the custom rules file with nano under sudo so you can save it.

sudo nano /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules

Add the two rules shown below to the file.

Add the following two rules to the file:

Rule 1; SQL Injection Detection:

alert http any any -> any any (msg:"SQLi Attack Detected"; content:"UNION SELECT"; nocase; http_uri; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

The first rule matches any HTTP traffic containing the string UNION SELECT (case-insensitive) in the request URI. The http_uri modifier restricts the match to the URL path and query string, avoiding false positives from response bodies.

Rule 2; Command Injection Detection:

alert http any any -> any any (msg:"Command Injection Detected"; content:"cat /etc"; nocase; http_client_body; sid:1000002; rev:1;)

The second rule matches HTTP traffic containing cat /etc in the POST body. The http_client_body modifier limits the search to data sent by the client (the attacker), ensuring the rule fires on inbound exploitation attempts.

Save the file and exit the editor (in nano: Ctrl+O to write, Enter to confirm, Ctrl+X to exit).

docs.title: Step 6: Reload Suricata Rules
docs.text:
Suricata does not automatically pick up changes to rule files. You must signal the running process to reload its rule set. The USR2 signal tells Suricata to re-read all configured rule files without restarting the engine or dropping monitored traffic.

Signal Suricata to reload rules

On the IDS sensor, send the USR2 signal to the Suricata process so it re-reads the rule files without restarting.

sudo kill -USR2 $(pidof suricata)

No output from the command means the signal was delivered successfully. Suricata will parse the updated rule files in the background. Wait approximately 5 seconds for the reload to complete before proceeding.

If you instead see kill print its usage help (kill [options] <pid> [...]), that means the command inside $(...) returned no PID and kill had nothing to signal. The empty result comes from the same daemon-mode issue from Step 3; pgrep suricata misses the renamed main thread. Use pidof suricata (shown above), or read the PID directly from Suricata's PID file:

Reload using the PID file

If pidof returned nothing, read the PID straight from Suricata's PID file and signal that instead.

sudo kill -USR2 $(sudo cat /var/run/suricata/suricata.pid)

docs.title: Step 7: Verify Alerts Are Firing in Eve JSON
docs.text:
With rules loaded and attack traffic still flowing, Suricata should begin generating alerts within 15-20 seconds (the interval between attack cycles). Check the Eve JSON log for alert records.

Read alert records from the Eve log

On the IDS sensor, filter the Eve JSON log for records that contain an alert object.

jq 'select(.alert != null)' /var/log/suricata/eve.json

You should see JSON objects containing your alert signatures. If the output is empty, wait another 15 seconds and try again; the next wave of attack traffic has not yet arrived. If no alerts appear after 30 seconds, revisit Step 5 and verify your rule syntax.

To see only the signature names from your alerts:

List unique alert signatures

Extract just the signature names and deduplicate them so you can confirm both rules fired.

jq -r 'select(.alert != null) | .alert.signature' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | sort -u

Successful output shows both SQLi Attack Detected and Command Injection Detected in the list. Seeing both signatures confirms your rules are working against the live traffic.

docs.title: Step 8: Extract the SQLi Indicator (Campaign Tag)
docs.text:
The attacker's SQL injection requests contain a campaign parameter in the query string. Suricata captured the full URL in the Eve JSON alert record, and you can extract the campaign value using jq and grep.

Extract the SQLi campaign tag

On the IDS sensor, pull the captured URL from the SQLi alerts (signature ID 1000001) and grep out the campaign parameter value.

jq -r 'select(.alert != null) | select(.alert.signature_id == 1000001) | .http.url' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | grep -oP 'campaign=\K[^&]+' | head -1

Record the value returned; the campaign tag is the first part of the flag. Write it down before moving on.

docs.title: Step 9: Extract the CMDi Indicator (Exfil Tag)
docs.text:
The attacker's command injection POST requests contain an exfil parameter in the request body. Suricata captured the printable payload content, and you can extract the exfil value from the alert records.

Extract the CMDi exfil tag

On the IDS sensor, pull the printable payload from the CMDi alerts (signature ID 1000002) and grep out the exfil parameter value.

jq -r 'select(.alert != null) | select(.alert.signature_id == 1000002) | .payload_printable' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | grep -oP 'exfil=\K[^& \r\n]+' | head -1

Record the value returned; the exfil tag is the second part of the flag.

docs.title: Step 10: Investigate the Web Portal Access Logs
docs.text:
Marcus mentioned the attacker may have hit the web portal too. SSH to the web portal server to examine the nginx access logs for additional forensic evidence.

Open a new terminal window (or exit the IDS sensor session) and connect to the web portal:

SSH into the web portal

From a fresh terminal, open an SSH session to the nginx web portal as webadmin. Replace <web_portal_ip> with the Web Portal IP shown in the Active Lab View.

ssh webadmin@<web_portal_ip>

When prompted for the password, enter:

Dmz_Adm1n_2024#

Read the nginx access log

On the web portal, print the access log and scan the User-Agent strings. Normal browsers report Mozilla/5.0 ...; the attacker's tool stands out.

cat /var/log/nginx/access.log

Look for a User-Agent containing SentinelBreaker/ followed by a value.

Extract the attacker User-Agent value

Grep the access log for the custom User-Agent and print only the value that follows SentinelBreaker/.

grep -oP 'SentinelBreaker/\K[^ "]+' /var/log/nginx/access.log | head -1

Record the value returned; the User-Agent tag is the third and final part of the flag.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Use the sections below to document each piece of evidence you collected during the investigation.

SQLi Campaign Tag (from Step 8):

(paste your campaign value here)

CMDi Exfil Tag (from Step 9):

(paste your exfil value here)

Attacker User-Agent Value (from Step 10):

(paste your User-Agent value here)

Assembled Flag:

OCR{___________}

Suricata Rules I Wrote:

(paste your two rules from local.rules here)

Alert Evidence (sample jq output):

(paste one or two sample alert JSON records here)

docs.title: Step 11: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the three IOCs you extracted and consider what they reveal about the attacker's operation.

The campaign tag embedded in the SQL injection requests is a label the attacker uses to track which exploitation campaign generated the data. Attackers often tag their payloads with internal identifiers so they can correlate stolen data back to specific targets or timeframes. Finding the tag confirms the attack is organized, not random.

The exfil tag in the command injection POST requests serves a similar purpose; it labels the data exfiltration channel. The presence of both a campaign tag and an exfil tag suggests the attacker is running multiple concurrent operations and uses tagging to keep them organized.

The custom User-Agent on the web portal confirms that the same attacker (or the same tool) targeted both the IDS sensor and the web portal. Automated attack tools frequently use distinctive User-Agent strings, either by accident or by design. Correlating the User-Agent across both servers links the two attack streams to a single source.

Assemble the three values into the flag format: OCR{________}, where each part is separated by an underscore.

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<sqlitoken>_<cmditoken>_<useragenttoken>}

Where sqlitoken is from the Suricata SQLi alert campaign payload, cmditoken is from the Suricata CMDi alert exfil payload, and useragenttoken is from the Nginx access log User-Agent string.

docs.title: Step 12: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Navigate back to the lab platform in your browser. Paste the assembled flag in OCR{...} format into the Submit Flag field and click Submit. The platform will confirm whether your flag is correct. If the submission is rejected, double-check each extracted value and ensure the parts are joined with underscores in the correct order.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The following questions ask you to think beyond the mechanics of writing rules. Consider each one before reading the answer.

1. Why does the http_uri modifier matter in the SQLi rule? What would happen if you omitted it and matched content:"UNION SELECT" against all traffic?

Reveal Answer

Without http_uri, Suricata matches the string against the entire packet payload, including response bodies. A web page that discusses SQL injection (such as a security tutorial) could contain the words "UNION SELECT" in its HTML content, triggering a false positive. The modifier constrains matching to the request URI, where the string indicates an actual injection attempt rather than benign content.

2. The attacker embedded campaign and exfil tags directly in the HTTP requests. Why would a real-world attacker include metadata in their payloads, and what risk does it create for them?

Reveal Answer

Attackers tag payloads to organize multi-target campaigns; the metadata helps them sort incoming stolen data by victim, timeframe, or method. However, embedding identifiers in cleartext HTTP creates a significant operational security risk. Defenders who capture the traffic (as you did) can use those tags to link different attack streams, attribute activity to a specific campaign, and potentially track the attacker across multiple targets or incidents.

3. The IDS sensor was running in detection mode, not prevention mode. If the sensor had been configured as an IPS, how would the outcome differ?

Reveal Answer

In IPS mode, Suricata can drop or reject packets that match a rule instead of only logging them. The SQL injection and command injection requests would have been blocked before reaching the target application, preventing exploitation entirely. However, IPS mode carries risk; a poorly written rule can block legitimate traffic. Organizations often start with IDS mode to validate rules before switching to inline prevention.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Signature-based IDS detection works by matching traffic against predefined rules; the rules are only as good as the analyst who writes them, and an IDS with no custom rules is effectively blind to targeted attacks.
  • Suricata rules follow a structured format with an action, protocol, addressing, and options section; content modifiers like http_uri and http_client_body control exactly where matching occurs to reduce false positives.
  • Eve JSON logs provide structured, machine-readable alert data that analysts can parse with tools like jq to extract specific fields, filter by signature ID, and correlate events across time.
  • IOC extraction from captured payloads turns raw alerts into actionable intelligence; campaign tags, exfiltration labels, and custom User-Agents all serve as forensic evidence linking attack activity.
  • Correlating evidence across multiple servers (the IDS sensor and the web portal) provides a fuller picture of an attacker's operation than any single data source alone. Week 15 builds on these skills in the capstone exercise, where you will combine enumeration, exploitation, and detection techniques across a multi-host environment.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Over the past fourteen weeks, you have progressed from running your first port scan to chaining exploits across multi-server environments. Every technique you practiced; enumeration, web exploitation, credential discovery, lateral movement, privilege escalation, and database extraction; appears somewhere in the attack path ahead. Exercise 15 is the final assessment for the course, and it requires you to identify which skill applies at each stage without being told.

Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before you proceed. Review your notes from Exercises 1 through 14, because the engagement draws on concepts from every prior week. One important difference from previous labs: hints are locked for the first 30 minutes. The platform will not display any hint text until that delay has passed. Use those 30 minutes to work independently and demonstrate the methodology you have built over the semester.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Zenith Global Corp is a multinational logistics company headquartered in Chicago. The company has engaged your elite red team for a full-scope penetration test as part of their annual security program. Everything you have learned across the entire course comes together in the engagement ahead.

Your briefing comes from Diane Holloway, CISO (Chief Information Security Officer): "We have three tiers of infrastructure. The web frontend handles customer tracking and order management. Behind that, our application server runs the business logic. And at the core, our database server holds everything; customer data, financial records, shipping manifests. I want you to demonstrate whether an external attacker can reach our data. Our architecture team says it's impossible without insider access."

Prove them wrong. Three target servers make up the engagement scope: a web frontend running an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) API on port 80, an application server running SSH (Secure Shell) on port 22, and a database server running MySQL on port 3306. Assessment markers are distributed across all three tiers. Your job is to chain vulnerabilities across the full infrastructure, moving from the externally facing web frontend all the way to the backend database. The difficulty level is Advanced, the time limit is 120 minutes, and hints remain locked for the first 30 minutes.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The following list outlines what you need to accomplish during the engagement. Each objective maps to one or more walkthrough phases below.

  • Perform thorough reconnaissance across all three target systems
  • Exploit an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) vulnerability in the web frontend API to discover internal credentials
  • Identify broken access control on an administrative API endpoint to extract a marker token
  • Use discovered credentials to pivot laterally to the application server via SSH
  • Escalate privileges on the application server by exploiting a SUID (Set User ID) binary
  • Extract database credentials from the compromised application server
  • Connect to the backend MySQL database and query for the final assessment marker
  • Assemble and submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Background: Red Team Engagement Methodology
docs.text:
A red team engagement differs from a standard penetration test in scope and approach. A penetration test typically focuses on finding as many vulnerabilities as possible within a defined target set. A red team engagement, by contrast, simulates a real adversary attempting to achieve a specific objective; usually proving that an attacker can reach sensitive data or critical systems. The red team operates with a defined goal and chains together whatever vulnerabilities are necessary to reach it.

Full-scope assessments like the Zenith Global engagement test the entire defensive posture of an organization, not individual components in isolation. The web frontend may have its own vulnerabilities, the application server may have misconfigurations, and the database may have weak access controls; but the real finding is whether an attacker can chain all three weaknesses together to move from external access to complete data compromise. Defenders often test each tier independently and miss the compounding risk that emerges when flaws exist across multiple layers.

Multi-tier architecture attacks follow a predictable pattern: gain a foothold on the outermost tier, discover credentials or pivot paths to the next tier, and repeat until you reach the core data. The Zenith Global infrastructure follows a classic three-tier model where the web frontend is publicly accessible, the application server sits behind it, and the database server holds the sensitive records at the core.

The diagram below shows the three-tier target architecture and the attack path you will follow from external reconnaissance to full database compromise:

graph LR
    ATK["Attacker<br/>(You)"] -->|"HTTP :80"| WEB["Web Frontend<br/>Flask API"]
    WEB -->|"IDOR + Config"| CREDS["Credentials<br/>Discovered"]
    CREDS -->|"SSH :22"| APP["App Server<br/>OpenSSH"]
    APP -->|"SUID python3"| ROOT["Root Access<br/>Achieved"]
    ROOT -->|"Read db.conf"| DBCRED["DB Credentials<br/>Extracted"]
    DBCRED -->|"MySQL :3306"| DB["Database<br/>Flag Captured"]

    style ATK fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style WEB fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style CREDS fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style APP fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style ROOT fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style DBCRED fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style DB fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

Each node in the diagram represents a stage of the engagement. You cannot reach the database without first escalating privileges on the application server, and you cannot reach the application server without first extracting credentials from the web frontend. The attack chain must be followed in sequence.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Combining Everything
docs.text:
The capstone engagement uses four core tools, each mapped to a specific phase of the attack. You have practiced each of these tools in previous labs, so the primer below focuses on how they connect rather than introducing them from scratch.

Tool Phase Purpose curl Web Reconnaissance + API Exploitation Send HTTP requests to the web frontend, enumerate API endpoints, and extract JSON responses containing credentials and tokens ssh Lateral Movement Connect to the application server using credentials discovered during the web exploitation phase python3 Privilege Escalation Exploit the SUID bit on the python3 binary to escalate from a standard user to root on the application server mysql Database Extraction Connect to the MySQL database server and query tables for the final assessment marker

The chaining pattern works as a pipeline. Curl discovers credentials in the web API, which feeds into an SSH connection to the application server. Privilege escalation on the application server reveals database credentials stored in a configuration file. Those database credentials feed into a MySQL connection that retrieves the final marker. Each tool's output becomes the input for the next stage.

curl; HTTP request syntax:

curl -s http://<target>/api/endpoint

The -s flag silences the progress bar, producing clean JSON output that you can read or pipe into other tools.

ssh; Remote connection syntax:

ssh <username>@<target>

You will be prompted for a password. Use the credentials discovered during the web exploitation phase.

python3; SUID escalation technique:

When python3 has the SUID bit set and is owned by root, calling os.setuid(0) switches the effective user to root. The os.system() function then spawns a shell or executes a command with root privileges.

python3 -c "import os; os.setuid(0); os.system('/bin/sh')"

mysql; Database query syntax:

mysql --skip-ssl -h <db_host> -u <username> -p'<password>' <database_name> -e "SELECT * FROM <table>"

The -h flag specifies the remote host, -u sets the username, -p provides the password (with no space between -p and the password), and -e executes a query without entering the interactive MySQL shell.

docs.title: Phase 1: Web Reconnaissance
docs.text: The engagement begins with the externally facing web frontend. Before you can exploit anything, you need to understand what is running and how the API is structured.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Note All Three Target IPs
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. The Zenith Global lab deploys three servers, so you will see three IP addresses in the Active Lab View rather than the one or two IPs from previous labs.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate Exercise 15; Capstone CTF
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note all three target IPs displayed in the Active Lab View:
  • Web Frontend: serves the customer-facing API on port 80
  • App Server: runs SSH on port 22
  • Database: runs MySQL on port 3306
  • Record all three IPs before proceeding; you will need each one at different phases of the engagement

The web frontend is the only externally facing service described in Diane Holloway's briefing. Your attack path starts there and works inward toward the database.

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate the Web Frontend
docs.text:
Confirm that the web frontend is responding and explore its API surface.

Request the web frontend root

Send a basic HTTP request to the root URL of the web frontend.

curl -s http://<webfront_ip>/

Replace <webfront_ip> with the web frontend IP from the Active Lab View. You should receive a response confirming the application is running; look for JSON output or an HTML page that references the Zenith Global order management system.

Probe for an API endpoint

Now probe for API endpoints. Web applications built with Flask (a Python web framework) commonly expose their functionality through /api/ routes. Test whether an API exists by requesting a known path pattern.

curl -s http://<webfront_ip>/api/orders/1

A successful response containing order data confirms that the API endpoint exists and is returning records. The response format will be JSON (JavaScript Object Notation); a structured data format using key-value pairs enclosed in curly braces.

docs.title: Step 3: Discover the IDOR Vulnerability
docs.text:
An IDOR vulnerability occurs when an application exposes internal object references (like order IDs) in the URL and does not verify that the requesting user is authorized to view the requested record. If the API returns order data for /api/orders/1, test whether it returns data for other order IDs as well; even those that would belong to different users.

Enumerate order IDs to confirm IDOR

Enumerate orders 1 through 10 by changing the ID number in the URL.

curl -s http://<webfront_ip>/api/orders/1
curl -s http://<webfront_ip>/api/orders/2
curl -s http://<webfront_ip>/api/orders/3

Continue through /api/orders/10. A different response per ID confirms the API serves any order without an authorization check.

Automate the order enumeration with a loop

You can also use a bash loop to automate the enumeration across all ten IDs in one command.

for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  echo "=== Order $i ==="
  curl -s http://<webfront_ip>/api/orders/$i
  echo ""
done

The loop prints each order in turn so you can scan them together.

Read each response carefully. Most orders will contain standard logistics data; tracking numbers, addresses, shipment details. One order contains something different: internal notes with system credentials. Look for fields labeled notes, internal_notes, comments, or similar keys that contain usernames and passwords rather than shipping information.

Expected finding: Order #7 contains internal notes that include SSH credentials for the application server. Record the username and password; you will need them in Phase 3.

docs.title: Phase 2: API Exploitation
docs.text: With the IDOR vulnerability confirmed and credentials extracted, there is still more to gather from the web frontend before moving on. Broken access control vulnerabilities often expose administrative endpoints that should be restricted.

docs.title: Step 4: Record the SSH Credentials from Order #7
docs.text:
Examine the full JSON response from order #7. The response contains a field with credentials for the application server. The format will resemble:

{
  "order_id": 7,
  "notes": "Internal: appserver credentials; appuser / <password>"
}

The exact field names may vary, but the critical information is a username and password pair intended for SSH access to the application server. Write down or copy both values; you will use them during the lateral movement phase.

docs.title: Step 5: Access the Config Endpoint and Extract the First Marker
docs.text:
Many web applications have configuration or status endpoints that developers create during development and forget to restrict in production.

Access the unprotected config endpoint

Test whether the Zenith Global frontend exposes a configuration endpoint that should be restricted.

curl -s http://<webfront_ip>/api/config

A successful response indicates broken access control; the /api/config endpoint should require authentication but does not. The response contains internal application configuration data, including a marker token that proves you accessed the administrative configuration.

Expected output: The JSON response includes a field like "marker" with a value that forms part of your final flag assembly. Record the marker value from the config endpoint.

The combination of IDOR on the orders API and broken access control on the config endpoint demonstrates two distinct vulnerability classes on the web frontend. Both stem from missing authorization checks; the application serves data to anyone who requests it, regardless of whether they should have access.

docs.title: Phase 3: Lateral Movement
docs.text: With credentials in hand from the web frontend, pivot to the application server. Lateral movement is the process of using access on one system to reach another system in the environment.

docs.title: Step 6: SSH to the Application Server
docs.text:
SSH to the application server

Use the username and password discovered in order #7 to connect to the application server via SSH.

ssh appuser@<appserver_ip>

Replace <appserver_ip> with the application server IP from the Active Lab View. When prompted, enter the password you extracted from the API response. A successful login places you on the application server with a standard user shell.

Confirm your identity on the application server

Confirm your identity and orientation on the new system now that you have a shell on the target.

whoami
hostname
pwd

The whoami command should return appuser, confirming you are logged in as the account whose credentials were exposed through the IDOR vulnerability. You now have a foothold on the second tier of the infrastructure; the application server that Diane Holloway's architecture team said was "impossible to reach without insider access."

docs.title: Phase 4: Privilege Escalation
docs.text: Standard user access on the application server is not sufficient to reach all files and configurations. Root-level access is needed to read sensitive configuration files that may contain database credentials. A common privilege escalation vector on Linux systems is the SUID bit; a file permission that allows a program to run with the privileges of its owner rather than the user who executed it.

docs.title: Step 7: Discover the SUID python3 Binary
docs.text:
Search the filesystem for binaries with the SUID bit set.

Search for SUID binaries

The find command with the -perm flag locates files that have specific permission bits enabled. Run it on the application server where you now have a shell.

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

The -perm -4000 flag matches files where the SUID bit is set. The 2>/dev/null portion redirects error messages (from directories you cannot access) to /dev/null so they do not clutter your output. The output includes /usr/bin/python3 (or a similar path) in the list of SUID binaries. Python3 with the SUID bit set is a critical misconfiguration; the Python interpreter can execute arbitrary system calls, and the SUID bit means those calls run as root.

Confirm the SUID bit on python3

Confirm the finding by checking the permissions on the python3 binary.

ls -la $(which python3)

Look for the s character in the permission string (e.g., -rwsr-xr-x). The s in the owner's execute position confirms the SUID bit is active.

docs.title: Step 8: Exploit SUID python3 to Escalate to Root
docs.text:
Python3 with SUID can escalate privileges because the os.setuid(0) call switches the effective user ID to 0 (root), and that call succeeds when the binary has the SUID bit set and is owned by root.

Spawn a root shell via SUID python3

Execute the following command on the application server to spawn a root shell.

python3 -c "import os; os.setuid(0); os.system('/bin/sh')"

Breaking down the command:

  • import os: loads the Python operating system module
  • os.setuid(0): sets the effective user ID to 0 (root); succeeds because of SUID
  • os.system('/bin/sh'): spawns an interactive shell, which inherits the root privilege

Confirm root on the application server

After execution, you should have a root shell. Confirm your effective user.

whoami

The output should read root. You now have full administrative access to the application server.

Read the privilege escalation marker

With root access, check for a marker file in the root home directory.

cat /root/marker.txt

Record the marker value. The content of the marker file proves you achieved privilege escalation on the application server.

docs.title: Phase 5: Database Extraction
docs.text: Root access on the application server opens the path to the final tier: the database. Application servers commonly store database connection credentials in configuration files, because the application needs those credentials to communicate with the backend.

docs.title: Step 9: Read Database Credentials from the Configuration File
docs.text:
Read the database configuration file

Search for database configuration files on the application server. The Zenith Global application stores its configuration under /opt/zenith/.

cat /opt/zenith/db.conf

The configuration file contains database connection parameters; a hostname or IP, a username, a password, and a database name. The format will resemble:

DB_HOST=<datastore_ip>
DB_USER=zenith_app
DB_PASS=<password>
DB_NAME=zenith

Record the database hostname (or IP), username, password, and database name. You will need all four values to connect to the MySQL server in the next step.

docs.title: Step 10: Connect to MySQL and Query for the Final Flag
docs.text:
Query the MySQL database for the final flag

Use the MySQL command-line client from the compromised application server to connect to the database server and query for the assessment marker. Replace the placeholders with the values from db.conf.

mysql --skip-ssl -h <datastore_ip> -u zenith_app -p'<password>' zenith -e "SELECT * FROM flags"

The query returns one or more rows from the flags table. Look for a row with a name column of assessment and a value column containing the final marker.

Breaking down the command:

  • -h <datastore_ip>: the database server's IP address (from the Active Lab View or from db.conf)
  • -u zenith_app: the database username from the configuration file
  • -p'<password>': the database password, with no space between -p and the password string
  • zenith: the database name
  • -e "SELECT * FROM flags": executes the SQL query and returns the results without entering the interactive MySQL prompt

Expected output: The query returns one or more rows from the flags table. Look for a row with a name column of assessment and a value column containing the final marker.

Record the value from the flags table. Combined with the markers from the web frontend config endpoint and the root marker on the application server, you now have all the pieces needed to assemble the final flag.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the results of each engagement phase below. Complete records demonstrate the full attack chain from external access to database compromise.

Assembled flag:

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

Where apitoken is from the API IDOR/config endpoint, privesctoken is from the SUID privilege escalation marker in /root/marker.txt, and dbtoken is from the MySQL flags table query.

docs.title: Step 11: Assemble and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The three markers you collected across the infrastructure tiers combine to form the final flag. The flag follows the OCR{...} format, with the markers assembled in the order you discovered them across the three tiers.

Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form on the platform and click Submit. A correct submission confirms that you successfully compromised all three tiers of the Zenith Global infrastructure; from the externally facing web frontend through the application server to the backend database.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The following questions ask you to reflect on the strategy and methodology behind the engagement, not the specific commands you typed. Think through each one before reading the answer.

1. Why is the IDOR vulnerability on the orders API more dangerous than it might appear at first glance? What makes the exposure of order #7 different from a typical data leak?

Reveal Answer

A standard IDOR vulnerability exposes data belonging to other users; order details, personal information, or financial records. The Zenith Global IDOR goes further because order #7 contains internal system credentials. The leaked data is not customer information but an authentication secret that grants access to a different tier of the infrastructure. A single missing authorization check on the web frontend created a pivot path to the application server, which means the IDOR is not an isolated finding; it is the entry point for a full infrastructure compromise.

2. The /api/config endpoint had no authentication requirement. How does broken access control differ from an IDOR, and why do both matter in the same application?

Reveal Answer

An IDOR vulnerability exposes data by manipulating object references (like order IDs) within an endpoint that does perform some level of access control; the endpoint exists for legitimate users, but it fails to verify that the requesting user owns the specific record. Broken access control on the config endpoint is a different class: the entire endpoint should be restricted to administrators, but no access control exists at all. Finding both in the same application indicates a systemic authorization weakness; the development team likely did not implement a consistent access control framework, which means other endpoints may have similar gaps.

3. Python3 had the SUID bit set on the application server. Why is SUID on an interpreter (like python3, perl, or bash) more dangerous than SUID on a purpose-built utility?

Reveal Answer

A purpose-built SUID utility (like passwd or ping) performs a narrow, well-defined function and then exits. An interpreter with SUID can execute any code the user provides, which means the entire programming language runs with root privileges. Python3 with SUID allows the attacker to call os.setuid(0) and spawn a root shell; turning arbitrary code execution into full privilege escalation. System administrators should never set the SUID bit on interpreters, because doing so grants unrestricted root access to anyone who can execute the binary.

4. Trace the full attack chain from the first curl command to the final MySQL query. At which single point could Zenith Global have broken the chain most effectively?

Reveal Answer

Removing the IDOR vulnerability on the orders API would have been the most effective single fix. Without the credentials leaked through order #7, the attacker has no path from the web frontend to the application server. The config endpoint leak and the SUID python3 misconfiguration are both serious findings, but neither one is reachable without the initial credential exposure. Fixing the earliest link in the chain denies the attacker every subsequent step; the SUID binary and the database credentials become irrelevant if the attacker never reaches the application server.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
The capstone engagement brings together every technique from the fourteen weeks that preceded it. The following points summarize the core lessons from the full course journey.

  • Attack chains are greater than the sum of their parts. Individual vulnerabilities that seem moderate in isolation; an IDOR, a missing access control check, a SUID misconfiguration; combine into a complete infrastructure compromise when they exist across connected systems. Defenders must evaluate risk across tiers, not within them.

  • Reconnaissance determines everything that follows. The entire engagement depended on methodical enumeration of the web frontend API. Skipping orders or failing to test the config endpoint would have left critical credentials and markers undiscovered. Thorough reconnaissance is the foundation of every successful assessment.

  • Credentials are the most valuable discovery in any engagement. Passwords, API keys, and database connection strings found during one phase unlock access to the next phase. The SSH password in order #7 and the database password in db.conf were the two pivots that moved the attack from tier to tier.

  • SUID binaries on interpreters are a critical misconfiguration. Setting the SUID bit on python3, perl, bash, or any general-purpose interpreter grants unrestricted root access to any user who can run the binary. Regular SUID audits using find / -perm -4000 should be part of every system hardening checklist.

  • Broken access control is a systemic problem, not an isolated bug. The Zenith Global web frontend had both IDOR and unauthenticated admin endpoints, indicating a missing authorization framework. Organizations that find one access control flaw should audit every endpoint for the same pattern.

  • Post-exploitation proves business impact. Reaching the database and extracting records from the flags table demonstrates that an external attacker can access Zenith Global's core data; the exact scenario Diane Holloway's architecture team said was impossible. The technical chain matters, but the finding that resonates with executives is the data at the end of it.

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Over 15 weeks, you built a complete offensive security skill set; starting from basic TCP port scanning in Week 1 and ending with a multi-server red team engagement in Week 15. The course followed a deliberate progression: each week introduced one new technique while requiring you to recall and apply techniques from previous weeks. By Week 9, you had already combined enumeration, web exploitation, and privilege escalation into a single attack chain.

The first four weeks focused on enumeration; the art of discovering what exists on a target network before attempting any exploitation. You learned to scan TCP and UDP ports, enumerate SMB (Server Message Block) shares, extract data through SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) community strings, and exploit directory traversal vulnerabilities. These reconnaissance skills formed the foundation for every engagement that followed.

Weeks 5 through 8 shifted to active exploitation and privilege escalation. You attacked insecure API (Application Programming Interface) endpoints, injected operating system commands through web applications, abused SUID binaries to escalate from a low-privilege user to root, and cracked password hashes offline using John the Ripper. The full penetration test in Week 9 tested whether you could chain all of these skills together without step-by-step guidance.

The second half of the course expanded into lateral movement, post-exploitation, and defensive analysis. You discovered hidden login pages, pivoted between servers using credentials found in configuration files, harvested encoded data from compromised systems, analyzed packet captures for attack indicators, and wrote IDS (Intrusion Detection System) rules to detect the very attacks you had learned to perform. The capstone in Week 15 combined all three phases into a full red team exercise spanning three servers.

docs.title: Skills Progression Table
docs.text:
Each week introduced one core skill while reinforcing techniques from earlier labs. The table below summarizes the full 15-week progression and explains why each skill matters in a real penetration testing engagement.

Week Skill Added Why It Matters 1 TCP port scanning and service interaction Identifies open ports and running services; the starting point for every engagement 2 SMB share enumeration and anonymous access Exposes misconfigured file shares that often contain credentials, backups, or sensitive documents 3 UDP scanning and SNMP enumeration Reveals services that TCP-only scans miss, including SNMP agents that leak system configuration data 4 Path traversal exploitation Demonstrates how improper input validation allows attackers to read files outside the web root 5 API enumeration and broken access control Targets the authentication and authorization gaps that plague modern web applications 6 OS command injection via web applications Grants direct shell access to the server, turning a web vulnerability into full system compromise 7 SUID binary discovery and privilege escalation Converts low-privilege access into root-level control through misconfigured file permissions 8 Password hash extraction and offline cracking Breaks weak passwords without triggering account lockouts or generating login alerts 9 Multi-phase attack chaining Tests the ability to combine enumeration, exploitation, and escalation without guided steps 9A/9B Investigation and evidence collection Applies systematic data investigation across web/database breach assessment and encrypted data recovery 10 Directory brute-forcing and database access Finds hidden administrative interfaces and extracts credentials from backend databases 11 Lateral movement via configuration files Extends access from one compromised server to others using credentials stored in config files 12 Data extraction, encoding, and hidden file discovery Recovers obfuscated or archived data that attackers and defenders commonly encounter 13 Network traffic capture and forensic analysis Identifies attack patterns in packet captures; a core defensive and investigative skill 14 IDS rule writing and alert analysis Detects known attack signatures in live traffic using Suricata rules 15 Full red team across multiple servers (capstone) Chains every technique from the course into a realistic multi-server engagement

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer the following questions without looking back at the walkthroughs. If you cannot answer a question confidently, revisit the corresponding week before moving on.

1. What are the key differences between TCP and UDP port scanning, and why does UDP scanning take longer?

2. Why is anonymous SMB access dangerous, and what types of data can an attacker obtain through misconfigured shares?

3. What makes SNMP community strings a security risk, and how does the default "public" community string contribute to that risk?

4. How does a path traversal attack bypass file access controls, and what is the role of ../ sequences in the exploit?

5. What is the difference between authentication and authorization in the context of API security?

6. Why is command injection generally more dangerous than cross-site scripting (XSS)?

7. How does the SUID bit on a binary enable privilege escalation, and what command finds SUID files on a Linux system?

8. Why is offline password cracking effective against weak passwords, and what makes it harder to detect than online brute-force attacks?

9. How does lateral movement extend an attacker's reach after the initial compromise of a single system?

10. How do IDS rules complement penetration testing skills, and why should offensive security professionals understand detection techniques?

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
The commands below represent the core toolkit you built across all 15 weeks. Keep a copy of the table accessible during future labs and assessments.

Command Purpose Week nmap -sV -sC <target> Scan TCP ports with version detection and default scripts 1 nmap -p- <target> Scan all 65,535 TCP ports 1 smbclient -L //<target> -N List SMB shares using anonymous (null session) access 2 enum4linux -a <target> Enumerate SMB users, shares, groups, and OS information 2 nmap -sU -p 161 <target> Scan for SNMP on UDP port 161 3 snmpwalk -v2c -c public <target> Walk the SNMP MIB tree using the "public" community string 3 curl http://<target>/../../etc/passwd Test for path traversal by requesting files outside the web root 4 curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://<target>/api/ Send authenticated API requests with a bearer token 5 curl -d "ip=;id" http://<target>/ping Test for command injection by appending a shell command 6 find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null Search the file system for SUID binaries 7 john --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt Crack password hashes offline using a wordlist 8 gobuster dir -u http://<target> -w wordlist.txt Brute-force directory and file paths on a web server 10 mysql -u <user> -p -h <target> Connect to a remote MySQL database server 10 tar -xzf archive.tar.gz Extract a compressed tar archive 12 base64 -d encoded.txt Decode base64-encoded content 12 tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "http" Filter and display HTTP traffic from a packet capture 13 tcpdump -r capture.pcap -n Read and display packets from a capture file 13 alert http any any -> any any (msg:".."; content:".."; sid:1;) Suricata IDS rule syntax for detecting HTTP-based attacks 14

docs.title: Connect the Dots
docs.text:
Real penetration tests never rely on a single technique. Every engagement follows a pattern: enumerate the target, identify a vulnerability, exploit it, escalate privileges, and then move laterally to reach the actual objective. The 15 weeks of the course mirror exactly the pattern that professional red teams follow on every assessment.

Consider how the full penetration test in Week 9 demonstrated the power of chaining. You started with an Nmap scan to find open services, identified a vulnerable web application, used command injection or path traversal to gain initial access, and then escalated privileges through SUID abuse or hash cracking. No single technique would have been enough; the attack succeeded because each step provided the information or access needed for the next step.

The capstone in Week 15 raised the complexity by spanning three servers. Credentials discovered on the first server unlocked access to the second, and data harvested from the second server revealed the path to the third. Lateral movement and post-exploitation skills from Weeks 11 and 12 proved essential, as did the enumeration fundamentals from Weeks 1 through 3. Attackers who can only perform one technique hit a dead end quickly; attackers who can chain techniques reach objectives that defenders assumed were protected by network segmentation.

Defensive skills from Weeks 13 and 14 complete the picture. Understanding how IDS rules detect command injection, path traversal, and credential reuse helps penetration testers anticipate which actions will trigger alerts. Professional red teams modify their techniques to avoid detection, and that awareness only comes from studying both sides; the attack and the defense. The full course progression, from a basic Nmap scan to writing Suricata rules, gives you the foundation for both offensive and defensive security work.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. TCP scanning uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to reliably determine whether a port is open, closed, or filtered. UDP scanning is slower because UDP is connectionless; there is no handshake, so Nmap must wait for ICMP "port unreachable" responses (or a lack of any response) to infer port state, and retransmissions add significant delay.

2. Anonymous SMB access allows anyone on the network to browse shared folders without providing credentials. Misconfigured shares often contain sensitive documents, backup files, configuration files with embedded passwords, and internal network information that an attacker can use to deepen the compromise.

3. SNMP community strings act as passwords for reading device configuration data, yet many devices ship with the default string "public" and administrators never change it. An attacker who guesses or discovers the community string can extract system details, network interface information, running processes, and installed software; all without authentication.

4. Path traversal uses ../ sequences in a URL or input field to navigate up the directory tree beyond the intended web root. The web server resolves the relative path and returns files like /etc/passwd or application configuration files that the developer never intended to expose to users.

5. Authentication verifies who the user is; confirming identity through credentials such as a username and password or an API token. Authorization determines what that authenticated user is allowed to do; an API that authenticates a user but fails to check whether that user has permission to access a specific resource has a broken access control vulnerability.

6. Command injection gives the attacker direct access to the server's operating system, allowing arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the web application process. XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) executes code in a victim's browser, which limits the attacker to the user's session context rather than granting server-level access.

7. The SUID (Set User ID) bit causes a binary to execute with the file owner's privileges rather than the privileges of the user who runs it. When a root-owned SUID binary can be manipulated to spawn a shell or read arbitrary files, the attacker gains root-level access. The command find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null searches the entire file system for files with the SUID bit set.

8. Offline cracking works against a copy of the password hash file, so the attacker can make billions of guesses per second without any network communication or account lockout mechanism interfering. Weak passwords using common words, short lengths, or predictable patterns fall within minutes because tools like John the Ripper test dictionary words and common mutations first.

9. Lateral movement allows an attacker to pivot from a compromised system to other systems on the network, often by reusing credentials found in configuration files, databases, or memory. A single compromised web server might seem low-impact on its own, but lateral movement can turn that foothold into access to database servers, domain controllers, or other high-value targets.

10. IDS rules detect specific attack patterns in network traffic, such as path traversal sequences, SQL injection strings, or command injection payloads. Penetration testers who understand detection logic can anticipate which techniques will trigger alerts and modify their approach to test whether defenses actually catch real-world attacks; making both the testing and the defensive posture stronger.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Challenge 1B is an unguided reinforcement exercise that builds on the skills from Challenge 1 (Network Discovery). You should have completed that exercise before attempting this one. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Vanguard Logistics, a freight management company in Memphis, Tennessee, has reported suspicious activity on their network segment. Three servers are active on the subnet, but the IT team is unsure which ones are legitimate production systems and which might be rogue or misconfigured.

Your firm has been engaged to identify the real Vanguard Logistics server among the three hosts. The other two are either decommissioned machines that should have been powered off or unauthorized devices that appeared after a recent office move. Your contact, Derek Huang (Network Operations Manager), needs a definitive answer: "Which of these three boxes is actually ours, and what is it running?"

Three assessment tokens are hidden on the real target. The decoy servers have open ports but contain no useful information. You must scan all three hosts, correlate the findings to identify the legitimate server, and extract the tokens.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Scan the entire subnet to discover all active hosts
  • Enumerate services on each host to identify the legitimate Vanguard Logistics server
  • Distinguish real services from decoys by examining banners, content, and behavior
  • Interact with the correct services in the right order to extract all three tokens
  • Assemble and submit the flag

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What characteristics helped you distinguish the real Vanguard Logistics server from the decoys?

2. If an attacker encountered the same three hosts during a real engagement, how would decoy servers affect their reconnaissance timeline?

3. What is the security benefit and risk of running honeypot or decoy servers on a production network?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Service banners reveal organizational identity when servers are not hardened; this helps both defenders and attackers identify legitimate assets.
  • Decoy identification requires comparing content and behavior across multiple hosts, not just checking whether ports are open.
  • Subnet scanning with nmap -sn or a full port scan across a CIDR range reveals all active hosts, which is the mandatory first step in any multi-host engagement.
  • Methodical triage: scanning first, documenting second, exploiting third; prevents wasted time on dead ends.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Challenge 2B is an unguided reinforcement exercise that builds on Challenge 2 (SMB Share Enumeration). Complete that exercise first. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Hargrove Medical Group, a regional healthcare provider in Nashville, Tennessee, recently migrated their file server infrastructure. During the transition, the IT contractor responsible for configuring Samba shares left several misconfigurations in place.

Your firm has been engaged for a focused assessment of the file server. Diana Reeves (Compliance Officer) is concerned: "We store patient-adjacent data on that server. If any of it is accessible without proper credentials, we have a HIPAA exposure. Find out what is open, what credentials you can discover, and how far they take you."

Two assessment tokens are distributed across the shares. One is accessible through anonymous enumeration. The second requires credentials that you must discover during the assessment; they are not provided to you.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate all SMB shares on the target
  • Access shares that allow anonymous or guest connections
  • Discover credentials hidden in accessible files
  • Use discovered credentials to access restricted shares
  • Assemble and submit the flag
