docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is storing credentials in plaintext configuration files on a shared drive a critical risk, even if the share requires authentication?

2. How does null session enumeration differ from anonymous share access in terms of what information each reveals?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Credential reuse across services is a common finding; credentials discovered on one share often unlock access to others.
  • Configuration files (.env, .ini, .conf, .bak) are high-value targets during post-exploitation because developers frequently embed plaintext passwords.
  • Layered share access means a single anonymous foothold can cascade into authenticated access when credentials are exposed in accessible files.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Challenge 3B is an unguided reinforcement exercise that builds on Challenge 3 (SNMP Community Strings). Complete that exercise first. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Ridgeline Power Systems operates a hydroelectric monitoring station in rural Montana. Their operational technology (OT) network uses SNMP to manage an Industrial Control System (ICS) gateway. A routine vendor audit flagged the gateway as "potentially over-exposing management data."

Your assessment covers the SNMP service and any other services running on the gateway. Kyle Brennan (OT Security Manager) provided a single directive: "The vendor says we might have more than one community string active. We should only have 'public' for read-only monitoring. If there is another one, find it, and tell me exactly what it exposes. Also check if the SNMP data leaks any credentials for other services on the box."

No credentials are provided. You must discover everything through SNMP enumeration and use what you find to access additional services on the target.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Discover the SNMP service using UDP port scanning
  • Enumerate system information with the default community string
  • Identify a non-default community string hidden in the SNMP data
  • Use the second community string to discover additional sensitive information
  • Access another service on the target using credentials found via SNMP
  • Capture the flag

docs.text:
1. Why is using a non-default SNMP community string insufficient as a security control by itself?

2. How does the risk profile change when SNMP data exposes credentials for other services on the same host?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SNMP community strings function as passwords; a "secret" community string discovered through one MIB walk can unlock entirely different data subtrees.
  • Cross-protocol chaining (SNMP to SSH in this case) demonstrates how a single misconfigured service can compromise an entire host.
  • OT/ICS environments often have weaker security controls than corporate IT, making SNMP enumeration a high-value technique during industrial assessments.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Challenge 4B is an unguided reinforcement exercise that builds on Challenge 4 (Directory Traversal). Complete that exercise first. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Cascade Digital Media, a content distribution company in Seattle, Washington, runs a media management platform with multiple download endpoints. Each endpoint serves a different type of content; media assets, documentation, and API-generated reports.

Your firm has been engaged to test the platform for path traversal vulnerabilities. Priya Mehta (Security Lead) suspects that more than one endpoint may be vulnerable: "Our junior developer reused the same file-serving code across three different features. If one is vulnerable, they might all be. We need to know the full extent of the exposure."

Three assessment tokens have been placed at different filesystem locations on the server. Each token is reachable through a different vulnerable endpoint. You must discover all three endpoints, craft traversal payloads for each, and extract the tokens.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Explore the web application to discover all file download endpoints
  • Identify which endpoints are vulnerable to path traversal
  • Craft traversal payloads of varying depth for each endpoint
  • Extract all three tokens from different filesystem locations
  • Assemble and submit the flag

2. What is the difference between absolute path injection (/etc/passwd) and relative path traversal (../../../etc/passwd), and which is more commonly exploitable?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Multiple endpoints sharing the same vulnerable code pattern means a single root cause can create several independent attack vectors.
  • Traversal depth varies depending on where the application's working directory sits in the filesystem hierarchy; deeper paths require more ../ sequences.
  • Automated scanning tools like gobuster or ffuf can discover download endpoints, but understanding the parameter structure requires manual analysis.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Challenge 5B is an unguided reinforcement exercise that builds on Challenge 5 (Insecure API Endpoints). Complete that exercise first. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Stonebridge Capital, a wealth management firm in Boston, Massachusetts, launched a client-facing REST API for portfolio tracking. The development team shipped version 2 of the API alongside the documented version 1; but forgot to apply the same access controls.

Your point of contact, Marcus Webb (CTO), authorized the assessment: "We documented our v1 API and put authentication on every endpoint. But I just learned the team deployed a v2 internally for mobile app development. I need to know if v2 is exposed and what it leaks."

The assessment spans the API server and a backend database. Tokens are distributed across both systems. You must discover the unprotected API version, extract authentication tokens, use them to access administrative endpoints, and connect to the database to retrieve the final token.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate API versions and discover unprotected endpoints
  • Extract authentication tokens from user profile data
  • Use discovered tokens to access administrative API endpoints
  • Discover database credentials from the admin configuration
  • Connect to the backend database and extract the assessment token
  • Assemble and submit the flag

1. Why is API versioning a common source of security vulnerabilities in production environments?

2. How does an authorization token extracted from one endpoint enable access to others, and what OWASP category does this fall under?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• API version enumeration (/v1/, /v2/, /v3/) is a standard reconnaissance technique; legacy or internal API versions frequently lack production security controls.
  • Bearer token reuse across endpoints means a single leaked token can unlock administrative functionality.
  • Database credential exposure through API configuration endpoints bridges web application compromise to direct database access.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Challenge 6B is an unguided reinforcement exercise that builds on Challenge 6 (Command Injection). Complete that exercise first. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
TrueNorth Hosting, a managed DNS provider in Toronto, Ontario, offers a web-based DNS lookup tool. After a previous security audit flagged command injection, the development team added input filtering to strip dangerous characters. They are confident the fix is sufficient.

Your firm has been engaged to verify the remediation. Alex Tran (VP of Engineering) is direct: "We strip semicolons, pipes, and ampersands from all input. Our pen test last quarter said we were clean. Prove us wrong; or prove us right."

Two assessment tokens are placed on the server. Reaching them requires bypassing the input filter to execute arbitrary commands. The filter blocks common injection characters but has a gap that allows an alternative injection technique.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Test the DNS lookup tool with normal input to understand its behavior
  • Attempt standard command injection techniques and observe the filtering
  • Identify which characters are filtered and which are not
  • Discover a bypass technique that the filter does not catch
  • Use the bypass to execute commands and extract assessment tokens
  • Assemble and submit the flag

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is input filtering (blocklist approach) generally less secure than input validation (allowlist approach) for preventing command injection?

2. What alternative to shell=True could the developer use to eliminate command injection entirely, regardless of filtering?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Blocklist-based filtering (stripping specific characters) is inherently incomplete; attackers will find characters or encodings the developer did not anticipate.
  • Newline injection (%0a) is a frequently overlooked bypass because newlines are not traditionally considered "dangerous" characters, yet the shell interprets them as command separators.
  • Defense in depth requires using parameterized command execution (e.g., subprocess.run(["nslookup", user_input]) without shell=True) rather than relying on input sanitization alone.

Your team obtained initial SSH access as the "operator" account. Your objective is to demonstrate a credential relay chain: find exposed password hashes, crack them to access a second account, then use information in that account to access a third account where the final assessment token resides.

Vanessa Ortiz (Security Director) wants the full chain documented: "Show me every link in the chain; from the backup misconfiguration to the final account compromise. I want to understand how one sloppy backup script can cascade into total server compromise."

2. What filesystem permission would prevent the initial exposure of the shadow backup file?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Credential relay chains demonstrate how a single misconfiguration cascades; each compromised account reveals access to the next, compounding the damage.
  • Weak passwords in /etc/shadow are trivially cracked with dictionary attacks, making password policy enforcement critical.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 9A walked you through a full penetration test with detailed guidance at every step. Challenge 9B uses the same multi-phase attack methodology but removes the safety net. You will face a different target environment, a different vulnerability class, and a different company, but the kill chain structure is identical: reconnaissance, initial access, credential discovery, lateral movement, and privilege escalation.

Your VPN must be connected and your terminal open before continuing. Challenge 9B has a 90-minute time limit and hints are locked for the first 30 minutes. Use the first 30 minutes to work independently using the skills you have built over Weeks 1 through 9.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Apex Meridian Group is a mid-size management consulting firm headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina. They are preparing for a federal contract bid and require an independent security assessment of their infrastructure before submission. Your firm has been engaged for a black-box penetration test.

Your point of contact is Daniel Reeves, Director of IT: "We have a public-facing web server that hosts our corporate site and a document download portal. Behind that sits our backend application server that handles internal processing. The backend should only be reachable by our operations team: not from the outside."

Two target servers make up the engagement scope: a web server exposed on port 80, and a backend application server running SSH on port 22. Three assessment markers are distributed across the infrastructure. Retrieve all three and assemble the final flag to demonstrate complete compromise.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate services across both target systems using port scanning
  • Identify and exploit a directory traversal vulnerability in the web application's file download feature
  • Discover sensitive configuration files containing backend credentials
  • Retrieve the first assessment marker from the web server
  • Pivot laterally to the backend server using discovered SSH credentials
  • Retrieve the second assessment marker from the backend server
  • Escalate privileges on the backend server to achieve root access
  • Retrieve the third assessment marker and assemble the complete flag
  • Submit the flag in OCR{...} format

docs.title: Background: Directory Traversal Attacks
docs.text:
Exercise 9A exploited command injection: a vulnerability where the server executes attacker-supplied input as an operating system command. Challenge 9B introduces a different vulnerability class: directory traversal (also called path traversal).

Directory traversal occurs when a web application accepts a filename or path as user input and uses it to read files from the filesystem without properly validating the input. If the application does not restrict the input to a specific directory, an attacker can use ../ sequences to navigate up the directory tree and read files outside the intended folder.

Consider a file download endpoint that works like this:

http://example.com/download?file=report.pdf

The server reads /var/www/documents/report.pdf and returns it. But if the application does not sanitize the file parameter, an attacker can request:

http://example.com/download?file=../../../etc/passwd

The server resolves the path as /var/www/documents/../../../etc/passwd, which simplifies to /etc/passwd, and returns the system's password file. The ../ sequences climb out of the documents directory one level at a time until reaching the filesystem root.

Directory traversal is particularly dangerous because it provides read access to any file the web server process can read. Configuration files, environment files, SSH keys, and application source code are all potential targets. While command injection gives you the ability to execute commands, directory traversal gives you the ability to read files, and files often contain credentials that enable the next phase of the attack.

The following diagram compares the two attack types:

graph TD
    A["User Input"] --> B{"Vulnerability Type"}
    B -->|"Command Injection"| C["Server executes input<br/>as OS command"]
    B -->|"Directory Traversal"| D["Server reads file<br/>at attacker-chosen path"]
    C --> E["Arbitrary command execution"]
    D --> F["Arbitrary file read"]
    E --> G["Direct system access"]
    F --> H["Credential extraction<br/>→ System access"]

    style C fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style G fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style H fill:#e8a735,color:#fff

Both vulnerabilities result from the same root cause: trusting user input without validation. The difference is what the application does with that input: passes it to a shell (command injection) or passes it to a file-read function (directory traversal).

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Note Both Target IPs
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. Like Exercise 9A, this lab deploys two servers, so you will see two IP addresses in the Active Lab View.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate Apex Meridian Group: Blind Penetration Test
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note both target IPs displayed in the Active Lab View: one for the web server and one for the backend server
  • Record both IPs before proceeding

Daniel Reeves described a public-facing web server and an internal backend server. Your attack path starts at the web server and works inward: the same pattern as Exercise 9A, but with a different vulnerability to exploit.

docs.title: Step 2: Scan Both Servers
docs.text:
Begin with port scans to identify exposed services on each server.

Scan the web server

Scan the web server first to confirm the exposed HTTP service.

nmap <webserver_ip>

You should see port 80 open with an HTTP service: the corporate site and document download portal that Daniel mentioned.

Scan the backend server

Now scan the backend server to find its remote access service.

nmap <backend_ip>

The backend server should show port 22 open with an SSH service. The engagement layout mirrors Exercise 9A: a web application as the entry point and SSH as the lateral movement path.

Record both scan results. The attack surface is clear: exploit the web application on port 80 to find credentials, then use those credentials to SSH into the backend on port 22.

docs.title: Phase 2: Initial Access via Directory Traversal
docs.text: With reconnaissance complete, you know the web server hosts a web application on port 80. Your next task is to explore the application, identify file-handling functionality, and test for directory traversal.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore the Web Application
docs.text:
Load the web application

Load the web application in your browser or use curl to examine it from the command line.

curl http://<webserver_ip>/

Examine the response for clues about the application's functionality. Daniel Reeves mentioned a "document download portal": look for links, endpoints, or references to file download features. Web applications that serve files to users are prime candidates for directory traversal if they pass filenames through URL parameters.

docs.title: Step 4: Identify the Download Endpoint
docs.text:
Explore the application to find the file download feature. Look for URLs that include a file parameter or similar: these indicate the server reads a file based on user input.

Probe the download endpoint

Test the /download endpoint to confirm it reads a file based on the file parameter.

curl http://<webserver_ip>/download?file=test

The response should indicate that the endpoint expects a valid filename. The file parameter is the input you will manipulate: if the server does not validate it, you can traverse outside the intended directory.

docs.title: Step 5: Test for Directory Traversal
docs.text:
Test for directory traversal with /etc/passwd

Test whether the application sanitizes the file parameter by using ../ sequences to climb out of the document directory. Start with a well-known file that exists on every Linux system.

curl "http://<webserver_ip>/download?file=../../../../etc/passwd"

If the application is vulnerable, the response will contain the contents of /etc/passwd: a list of user accounts on the web server. The presence of this file in the response confirms that the server reads files at whatever path you specify, without restricting access to the documents directory.

How many ../ sequences do you need?

The number of ../ sequences depends on how deep the documents directory is in the filesystem. Using more ../ than necessary is harmless: once you reach the filesystem root (/), additional ../ sequences have no effect. If three levels does not work, add another ../ and try again. Four levels is typically enough for most web application layouts.

docs.title: Phase 3: Credential Discovery
docs.text: You now have arbitrary file read access on the web server through the directory traversal vulnerability. The next objective is to find credentials that grant access to the backend server. Think about where applications store their configuration: environment files, config directories, and application settings are common locations.

docs.title: Step 6: Locate Configuration Files
docs.text:
Web applications typically store their configuration in files within or adjacent to the application directory. Common locations include:

  • .env files (environment variables)
  • config/ directories (application configuration)
  • settings.py, config.ini, app.env (framework-specific config files)

Use the directory traversal to explore the web server's filesystem. Since the documents directory is likely inside the application directory, you may only need to traverse up one or two levels to reach configuration files.

Read the application config via traversal

Try reading configuration files relative to the document root.

curl "http://<webserver_ip>/download?file=../config/app.env"

Examine the output for variables containing SSH credentials for the backend server. You should find a username and password pair formatted as environment variables.

Think like a developer

Developers store secrets in configuration files because it is convenient. Environment files (.env, app.env) are the most common location for database passwords, API keys, and SSH credentials. When you gain file read access to a server, configuration directories are always the first place to check.

Examine the output for variables containing SSH credentials for the backend server. You should find entries that specify a username and password, formatted as environment variables with names that reference the backend system.

Record both the username and password: you will use them in the next phase to establish an SSH connection to the backend server.

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve the First Assessment Marker
docs.text:
Retrieve the first marker via traversal

The first assessment marker is also stored on the web server in a location accessible through the directory traversal. Look for marker or assessment files in the same area where you found the configuration.

curl "http://<webserver_ip>/download?file=../config/assessment_marker.txt"

Record the marker value: this is the first of three tokens you need to assemble the final flag.

docs.title: Phase 4: Lateral Movement
docs.text: With valid SSH credentials for the backend server, you can now pivot from the web server to the internal infrastructure: exactly as you did in Exercise 9A.

docs.title: Step 8: SSH to the Backend Server
docs.text:
SSH to the backend server

Use the credentials discovered in Step 6 to connect to the backend server over SSH.

ssh <username>@<backend_ip>

Replace <username> with the SSH user from the configuration file, and <backend_ip> with the second target IP from the Active Lab View. When prompted, enter the password you extracted.

Confirm your privilege level on the backend

After logging in, confirm your identity and assess your privilege level on the backend server.

whoami
id

The whoami command should return the username you logged in with, and the id output should show a standard user account. You are on the backend server, but you do not yet have root access.

docs.title: Step 9: Retrieve the Second Assessment Marker
docs.text:
Read the second marker from the home directory

The second marker is accessible to the user you logged in as. Check the user's home directory on the backend server.

ls -la ~
cat ~/marker.txt

Record the marker value alongside the first one from the web server.

docs.title: Phase 5: Privilege Escalation
docs.text: You have user-level access on the backend server, but the final assessment marker requires root privileges. Apply the same privilege escalation methodology from Exercise 9A.

docs.title: Step 10: Enumerate SUID Binaries
docs.text:
Enumerate SUID binaries on the backend

Search the filesystem for binaries with the SUID bit set: the same technique you used in Exercise 9A and learned in Week 7.

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Review the output and compare it against the standard set of SUID binaries. Look for anything unusual: a binary that does not normally have the SUID bit set is your escalation vector.

Verify the suspicious binary permissions

Verify the permissions on any suspicious binary you spotted.

ls -la /usr/bin/<suspicious_binary>

The -rwsr-xr-x permission string with root as the owner confirms the SUID bit is active. The s in the owner's execute position means this binary runs with root privileges regardless of who invokes it.

docs.title: Step 11: Exploit the SUID Binary to Escalate to Root
docs.text:
Exploit the SUID binary for a root shell

If you find the same SUID binary from Exercise 9A, the same exploitation technique applies. Use the -exec flag to spawn a root shell, and remember the -p flag to preserve the elevated privileges.

find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit

The -p flag prevents the shell from dropping the inherited root privilege.

Verify the root escalation

Verify the escalation succeeded.

whoami
id

The whoami command should return root, and the id output should show euid=0(root).

docs.title: Step 12: Retrieve the Final Assessment Marker
docs.text:
Read the final root-owned marker

With root privileges, read the third and final marker.

cat /root/flag.txt

Record the marker value. You now have all three assessment markers:

  • Marker 1: from the web server's configuration directory (via directory traversal)
  • Marker 2: from the user's home directory on the backend server
  • Marker 3: from /root/flag.txt on the backend server (requires root)

Assemble the three markers into the final flag using the OCR{...} format as indicated by the lab instructions.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document your complete attack chain. Recording evidence at each phase builds the habit of maintaining a penetration test report.

Phase 1: Reconnaissance:

Web server scan output:

(paste your nmap output here)

Backend server scan output:

(paste your nmap output here)
Server Open Ports Services Web Server Backend

Phase 2: Initial Access:

Directory traversal proof (/etc/passwd):

(paste your output here)

Phase 3: Credential Discovery:

Credentials found in configuration file:

Variable Value SSH User SSH Pass

Marker 1 value:

(paste marker 1 here)

Phase 4: Lateral Movement:

SSH login confirmation (whoami / id output):

(paste your output here)

Marker 2 value:

(paste marker 2 here)

Phase 5: Privilege Escalation:

SUID enumeration output:

(paste your find / -perm -4000 output here)

Misconfigured binary:

Binary Path Owner Permissions Why Dangerous

Root shell confirmation:

(paste your whoami and id output here)

Marker 3 value:

(paste marker 3 here)

Assembled flag:

Component Value Marker 1 Marker 2 Marker 3 Full flag OCR{...}

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<token1>_<token2>_<token3>}

Where <token1> is from the web server's configuration directory via directory traversal, <token2> is from the user's home directory on the backend server, and <token3> is from the root directory after privilege escalation.

docs.title: Step 13: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Return to the platform in your browser. Paste the assembled flag into the Submit Flag form and click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Exercise 9A used command injection for initial access, while Challenge 9B used directory traversal. Both gave you access to sensitive information on the web server. Compare the two vulnerability types: which one gives the attacker more capability, and why might directory traversal still be considered equally dangerous in practice?

Reveal Answer

Command injection gives the attacker more raw capability because it allows execution of arbitrary commands, reading files, writing files, starting reverse shells, and modifying system configuration. Directory traversal is limited to reading files that the web server process has permission to access. However, directory traversal is equally dangerous in practice because the files it exposes (credentials, SSH keys, configuration secrets) frequently enable the attacker to gain full command execution through other means, such as SSH login with discovered credentials. The end result, full system compromise, is the same; the path is just different.

2. Daniel Reeves stated that the backend server "should only be reachable by our operations team." Your assessment proved that an external attacker can reach it by pivoting through the web server. Propose two architectural changes that would prevent the lateral movement you performed, even if the web server is fully compromised.

Reveal Answer

First, implement network segmentation with firewall rules that prevent the web server from initiating SSH connections to the backend server. The web server should only communicate with the backend through a tightly scoped API, not through general-purpose protocols like SSH. Second, replace password-based SSH authentication with certificate-based authentication managed through a bastion host with multi-factor authentication. Even if an attacker discovers a password in a configuration file, it would be useless without the corresponding SSH certificate and access to the bastion host.

3. You exploited the same SUID binary escalation technique from Exercise 9A. If this were a real engagement and you reported this finding, the client might fix only the specific SUID binary you exploited. Explain why this response would be insufficient and what a thorough remediation plan should include.

Reveal Answer

Fixing one SUID binary addresses a single symptom, not the root cause. A thorough remediation plan should include: (1) a full audit of all SUID and SGID binaries across every server, removing the SUID bit from any binary that does not require it; (2) implementing a regular audit schedule to detect new SUID binaries introduced by software updates or misconfigurations; (3) deploying a file integrity monitoring solution to alert on permission changes; and (4) applying the principle of least privilege to service accounts so that even if an attacker gains access as the deploy user, the account has minimal capabilities beyond its intended function.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Directory traversal exploits applications that pass user-controlled filenames to file-read operations without validation: the ../ sequence lets an attacker navigate the filesystem and read any file the server process can access
  • Blind assessments test your ability to select the right technique at each phase without guidance: recognizing vulnerability types from application behavior is a core penetration testing skill
  • Configuration files are high-value targets in any file-read vulnerability: .env, app.env, and config/ directories frequently contain plaintext credentials that enable lateral movement
  • The same privilege escalation vectors appear across different environments: SUID binary exploitation is a transferable skill that applies to any Linux system with misconfigured permissions
  • Attack chain documentation (reconnaissance → exploitation → lateral movement → escalation) is the standard structure for penetration test reports and should be practiced in every engagement

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 10A introduced directory enumeration, hidden portals, default credentials, and database pivoting. Those skills carry forward into this exercise, but the entry point is different. Instead of logging in with a default password, you will bypass the login entirely by exploiting a SQL injection vulnerability in the authentication form.

SQL injection is one of the most impactful web application vulnerabilities. It has appeared in the OWASP Top 10 every year since the list was created, and it remains a leading cause of data breaches. Exercise 10B teaches you how SQL injection works, how to identify it, and how to exploit it using UNION-based techniques to extract data from a backend database.

Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Vertex Healthcare is a regional healthcare technology company headquartered in Denver, Colorado. They provide electronic health record (EHR) integration services to over 40 clinics and hospitals across the western United States.

Your firm, Blackridge Security, has been engaged to perform a web application penetration test ahead of their upcoming HIPAA compliance review. Your point of contact, Rachel Nguyen (Director of IT Security), shared the following brief: "We recently deployed a new patient portal for provider authentication. The development team says it is production-ready, but I want your team to verify before we open it to all partner clinics. The portal should not be publicly accessible; it is supposed to be behind our VPN."

The engagement scope covers the web application on the target host and any backend services you discover on the subnet. Rachel mentioned they run a MySQL database on a separate server for the portal backend.

An assessment token has been split across the environment. Collect both parts and combine them as OCR{________} to complete the engagement.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate the web application and discover hidden paths via robots.txt and directory brute-forcing
  • Identify a login form vulnerable to SQL injection
  • Craft a UNION-based SQL injection payload to bypass authentication
  • Extract database credentials from the authenticated dashboard
  • Connect directly to the backend MySQL database and retrieve the assessment flag

docs.title: Network Layout
docs.text:
The lab environment contains two target servers on the same subnet:

Server Role Port IP Offset Web Application Nginx + Flask patient portal 80 .16 Database Server MySQL 8.0 backend 3306 .37

Both servers are reachable from your attacker machine. The web application connects to the database internally, but the database also accepts direct connections from the subnet; a segmentation failure you will exploit in the final phase.

docs.title: Why SQL Injection Exists
docs.text:
Web applications store data in databases. When a user submits a login form, searches for a product, or updates their profile, the application translates that action into a SQL query and sends it to the database. The vulnerability arises when developers build these queries by pasting user input directly into the SQL string rather than using safe mechanisms that keep data separate from code.

The pattern is not a rare oversight. SQL injection was first documented in 1998 and remains in the OWASP Top 10 over twenty-five years later (currently A03:2021: Injection). It persists because the vulnerable pattern is the simplest way to write database queries, and developers under deadline pressure often ship it without realizing the risk.

docs.title: How a Login Query Works
docs.text:
When you submit a username and password to a login form, the application typically runs a query like this:

SELECT id, username, password, email FROM users
WHERE username='alice' AND password='secretpass'

The database checks whether any row matches both the username and password. If a row is returned, the application considers the login successful. If no rows match, the login fails.

The vulnerability arises when the application builds this query using string formatting:

# VULNERABLE -- user input inserted directly into the query string
query = f"SELECT id, username, password, email FROM users WHERE username='{username}' AND password='{password}'"

Whatever the user types in the username field gets pasted directly into the SQL statement. If the user types a normal username, the query works as intended. But if the user types SQL syntax, the query structure changes, and the database executes the modified query without question.

Compare this to the safe approach:

# SAFE -- parameterized query keeps data separate from code
cursor.execute(
    "SELECT id, username, password, email FROM users WHERE username=%s AND password=%s",
    (username, password)
)

With parameterized queries, the database treats the username and password as data values, never as part of the SQL syntax. Even if the user submits SQL commands, they are interpreted as a literal string to search for.

docs.title: Detecting SQL Injection: The Single Quote Test
docs.text:
The simplest test for SQL injection is typing a single quote (') into an input field. If the application is vulnerable, the single quote closes the string delimiter early and breaks the SQL syntax:

SELECT id, username, password, email FROM users
WHERE username=''' AND password='anything'

The three consecutive quotes create a parsing error. Depending on how the application handles errors, you may see:

  • A database error message displayed on the page (most obvious sign)
  • A different response compared to a normal failed login (the page looks different, returns a different status code, or takes noticeably longer)
  • The application crashes or returns a 500 error
  • A generic error page that differs from the normal "invalid credentials" response

Any change in behavior compared to submitting a normal username suggests the input is reaching the SQL query unsanitized.

docs.title: Classic Bypass: ' OR 1=1-- -
docs.text:
Once you confirm the field is injectable, the next step is attempting an authentication bypass. The most common payload is ' OR 1=1-- -. Here is what happens when this is submitted as the username:

SELECT id, username, password, email FROM users
WHERE username='' OR 1=1-- -' AND password='anything'

Breaking this down piece by piece:

Fragment Purpose ' Closes the username string that the application opened OR 1=1 Adds a condition that is always true: every row in the table matches -- - SQL comment syntax that discards everything after it, including the AND password= check

The query now returns every row in the users table. The application sees a result and logs the attacker in as the first user returned, usually the admin account. The bypass works because many login forms only check whether the query returned a row: the entire authentication decision lives inside the SQL WHERE clause, and the injection just made it always true.

The ' OR 1=1-- - technique is effective but blunt: it returns every user in the table and logs you in as whichever row comes back first. You have no control over which account you land on. For more precision, UNION-based injection is the better tool.

docs.title: UNION-Based Injection
docs.text:
UNION-based injection is more powerful. Instead of manipulating the WHERE clause to return existing rows, it appends an entirely new SELECT statement that returns data the attacker fabricates:

SELECT id, username, password, email FROM users
WHERE username='' UNION SELECT 1,'admin','x','admin@test.com'-- -'
AND password='anything'

Here is what happens step by step:

  1. The original query searches for a user with an empty username: no rows match
  2. The UNION SELECT appends a second result set containing one fabricated row
  3. The -- - comments out the remaining original query (the password check)
  4. The database returns the fabricated row as the query result
  5. The application sees a row was returned and considers the login successful

Critical rule: the UNION SELECT must return the same number of columns as the original query. If the original SELECT retrieves four columns (id, username, password, email), your UNION must also provide exactly four values. If the column count does not match, the database returns an error like "The used SELECT statements have a different number of columns."

The values in the fabricated row can be anything: the application just checks whether a row was returned. The attacker controls every field: the username that appears in the session, the email, everything. Full control over the returned row is what makes UNION injection powerful beyond simple authentication bypass.

docs.title: Determining the Column Count
docs.text:
In a real assessment, you will not always know how many columns the original query selects. Two techniques help you discover the count:

ORDER BY method: inject ' ORDER BY 1-- -, then ' ORDER BY 2-- -, incrementing until the application returns an error. If ORDER BY 4 works but ORDER BY 5 fails, the query has four columns.

NULL method: inject ' UNION SELECT NULL-- -, then ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- -, adding NULLs until the query succeeds. NULL is compatible with any column type, so this avoids type mismatch errors.

In this exercise, the column count is provided in the hints, but knowing these techniques prepares you for real-world assessments where you must discover it yourself.

docs.title: The Full Attack Flow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the complete path from initial reconnaissance to flag capture in this exercise. Notice that the first three steps (enumeration, robots.txt, hidden portal) are identical to Exercise 10A. The divergence begins at the login form, where SQL injection replaces default credentials as the entry technique.

graph TD
    A["Scan target website"] --> B["Check robots.txt<br/>for hidden paths"]
    A --> C["Run gobuster with<br/>common wordlist"]
    B --> D["Discover<br/>/portal/"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["Access login form"]
    E --> F["Test for SQL injection<br/>(single quote test)"]
    F --> G["Craft UNION SELECT<br/>payload (4 columns)"]
    G --> H["Bypass authentication<br/>access dashboard"]
    H --> I["Collect Token 1<br/>from dashboard"]
    I --> J["Extract DB credentials<br/>from config panel"]
    J --> K["Connect to MySQL<br/>query audit_flags"]
    K --> L["Collect Token 2<br/>assemble flag"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style E fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style G fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style H fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style I fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style J fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style K fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style L fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

Color key: Blue = reconnaissance, Orange = discovery, Red = exploitation (SQL injection), Green = post-exploitation and data extraction.

docs.title: Exercise 10A vs 10B: Two Paths Past the Login Form
docs.text:
Both exercises follow the same structure: enumerate hidden paths, find a login form, get past it, extract data from the dashboard and database. The difference is how you get past the login.

graph LR
    A["Hidden Portal<br/>Discovered"] --> B{"Login Form"}
    B -->|"Exercise 10A"| C["Default credentials<br/>(admin / CompanyYear#)"]
    B -->|"Exercise 10B"| D["SQL injection<br/>(UNION SELECT)"]
    C --> E["Dashboard<br/>→ DB Credentials<br/>→ Flag"]
    D --> E

    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

In 10A, the developers left default credentials in place, a configuration error. In 10B, the developers wrote vulnerable code, a programming error. Both are common in the real world, and a penetration tester needs to recognize and exploit both.

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl for Form Submission
docs.text:
You used curl in Exercise 10A to send GET requests and POST login forms. SQL injection testing uses the same POST technique, but the payloads in the form data contain SQL syntax instead of normal credentials.

Sending a POST request with form data:

curl -s http://<target>/portal/login \
  -d 'username=testuser&password=testpass'

The -d flag automatically sets the request method to POST: you do not need -X POST. In fact, using -X POST explicitly can cause problems: when combined with -L (follow redirects), curl will re-send the POST to the redirect target. Most login forms redirect to a dashboard via GET after success, so the dashboard route rejects the unexpected POST with a 405 Method Not Allowed error. By omitting -X POST and relying on -d to imply it, curl correctly switches to GET when following the redirect.

Common flags:

Flag Purpose -d Form data (URL-encoded key=value pairs separated by &); implies POST -c <file> Save cookies from the response to a file -b <file> Send cookies from a file with the request -L Follow redirects (login forms typically redirect after success) -s Silent mode (suppress progress output)

Saving and reusing session cookies:

After a successful login (whether through default credentials or SQL injection), the server sets a session cookie. You must save this cookie and send it with subsequent requests to access authenticated pages.

# Login and save session cookie
curl -s -c /tmp/cookies http://<target>/portal/login \
  -d 'username=admin&password=pass' -L

# Access authenticated page using saved cookie
curl -s -b /tmp/cookies http://<target>/portal/dashboard

The -c flag writes cookies to a file after the response. The -b flag reads cookies from that file and includes them in the next request. Without the cookie, the dashboard will redirect you back to the login page.

docs.title: MySQL CLI (Review from Exercise 10A)
docs.text:
You will use the MySQL command-line client again in the final phase to query the backend database directly.

mysql --skip-ssl -h <db_ip> -u <username> -p'<password>' <database_name> \
  -e "SELECT * FROM table_name"
Flag Purpose -h Hostname or IP of the database server -u Username to authenticate with -p Password (no space between -p and the password) -e Execute a single SQL query and exit

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment. Wait for all containers to reach the Running state before proceeding.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate the Web track
  • Find SQL Injection to Shell and click Launch
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP addresses displayed in the Active Lab View; the web application and database server run on separate hosts

docs.title: Step 2: Browse the Main Site and Check robots.txt
docs.text:
Start the same way you did in Exercise 10A: visit the target website to see what is publicly visible, then check for a robots.txt file. The browse-then-robots.txt sequence is the same reconnaissance workflow you will use on every web application assessment.

Browse the main site

Browse to the main page first to see what is publicly visible.

curl -s http://<target_ip>/

The main site is a corporate healthcare landing page for Vertex Healthcare. The navigation links (Home, About, Services, Contact) are standard marketing pages. Nothing interactive is visible.

Check robots.txt for hidden paths

Now check robots.txt for paths the developers excluded from search indexes.

curl -s http://<target_ip>/robots.txt

Review the output carefully. You should see Disallow entries listing paths the developers wanted to keep out of search engine indexes. One of those paths points to a portal. Note each path you find; you will visit them in a later step.

docs.title: Step 3: Run gobuster to Confirm Hidden Paths
docs.text:
Reinforce your directory enumeration skills from Exercise 10A. While robots.txt reveals paths the developers intentionally listed, gobuster may uncover additional endpoints that the file does not mention.

Brute-force directories with gobuster

Run gobuster against the target with a common wordlist to discover endpoints robots.txt does not list.

gobuster dir -u http://<target_ip> -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Wait for the scan to complete. Compare the gobuster results with the paths you found in robots.txt. You should see a /portal entry among the results; a path that strongly suggests an internal login page. Additional entries like /api/internal/ and /backups/ may appear: you can investigate these, but the portal is the primary target.

docs.title: Step 4: Access the Hidden Portal
docs.text:
Access the hidden portal

Navigate to the portal path you discovered with gobuster and robots.txt.

curl -s http://<target_ip>/portal/

You should see a login form for the Vertex Provider Portal. Unlike Exercise 10A where the NovaTech staff portal had a build tag comment in the HTML source (token 1), the Vertex portal login page does not contain any comments, tokens, or embedded credentials. The HTML is clean.

The Vertex Provider Portal login form. The HTML source is clean, with no leaked credentials, so SQL injection becomes the way past this gate.

The clean HTML means you cannot extract information from the page source, and you do not have any known credentials to try. You need a different approach to get past the login form.

docs.title: Step 5: Test for SQL Injection
docs.text:
With no known credentials and no information leakage in the HTML source, test whether the login form is vulnerable to SQL injection.

Send the single quote test

Start with the single quote test described in the background section to see whether input reaches the query.

curl -s http://<target_ip>/portal/login \
  -d "username='&password=test"

Observe the response. The application redirects you back to the login page with an error parameter: its generic "invalid credentials" response. A single quote alone does not give you access, but importantly, the application did not return a database error or block your request with a WAF (Web Application Firewall). The input reached the query.

Attempt the classic OR 1=1 bypass

Now test the classic authentication bypass payload.

curl -s -c /tmp/vtx-cookies http://<target_ip>/portal/login \
  -d "username=' OR 1=1-- -&password=anything" -L

Check the response. If you see dashboard HTML instead of a login form, the bypass worked: the application only checks whether the SQL query returned a row, and OR 1=1 makes every row match. The -c flag saved your session cookie. You can skip ahead to Step 7 to access the dashboard.

If you want more control over the injection, or if you want to practice the more precise technique, proceed to the UNION-based approach below.

docs.title: Step 6: Craft a UNION-Based SQL Injection Payload
docs.text:
The ' OR 1=1-- - bypass returns every user in the table and logs you in as whichever account comes back first. The UNION technique gives you more precision: you fabricate an exact row so the application receives only the data you choose.

The login query selects four columns: id, username, password, and email. Your UNION SELECT must provide exactly four values to match. The values themselves can be anything: the application only cares that a row was returned.

Username field: 

' UNION SELECT 1,'admin','x','admin@vertex.com'-- -

Password field: 

anything

Here is what the database sees after the application pastes your input into the query:

SELECT id, username, password, email FROM users
WHERE username='' UNION SELECT 1,'admin','x','admin@vertex.com'-- -'
AND password='anything'

Walking through it:

  1. username='': the original WHERE clause searches for an empty username and finds nothing
  2. UNION SELECT 1,'admin','x','admin@vertex.com': appends your fabricated row with four values matching the four columns
  3. -- -: comments out the rest of the query, including the AND password='anything' check
  4. The database returns one row: your fabricated data
  5. The application sees a row was returned and logs you in

Submit the UNION injection

Submit the UNION payload through the login form to fabricate a matching row.

curl -s -c /tmp/vtx-cookies http://<target_ip>/portal/login \
  -d "username=' UNION SELECT 1,'admin','x','admin@vertex.com'-- -&password=anything" -L

The -c flag saves the session cookie so you can access authenticated pages. The -L flag follows the redirect to the dashboard. If the response contains dashboard HTML rather than a login form, the injection succeeded.

docs.title: Step 7: Access the Dashboard and Collect Token 1
docs.text:
After a successful injection, the application sets a session cookie and redirects you to the provider dashboard. If the dashboard content appeared in the Step 5 or Step 6 response, you already have it.

Access the dashboard with the saved cookie

Access the dashboard explicitly using the session cookie you saved during the injection.

curl -s -b /tmp/vtx-cookies http://<target_ip>/portal/dashboard

Read through the dashboard HTML carefully. The System Status table lists several application components and their values. Look for the Assessment Token row: its value column contains the first token: sql1_un10n.

Record this value. Token 1 represents the fact that you bypassed authentication through SQL injection. In a real assessment, reaching an authenticated dashboard without valid credentials is a critical finding.

The provider dashboard reached without any valid credentials. The Assessment Token value is redacted to keep the flag hidden, but the Application Configuration panel exposes the backend MySQL host, user, and password.

docs.title: Step 8: Extract Database Credentials from the Dashboard
docs.text:
Continue reading the dashboard output. Below the system status table and quick links section, an Application Configuration panel displays environment variables in a monospace block. The exposed configuration panel repeats the same pattern you saw in Exercise 10A's NovaTech dashboard: developers exposing backend configuration in a web interface.

Look for these fields:

Variable Meaning DB_HOST Database server hostname DB_PORT Database port (3306 for MySQL) DB_NAME Database name DB_USER Database admin username DB_PASS Database admin password

Record all the database connection values. These credentials give you direct access to the backend database, bypassing the web application entirely. Notice the DB_USER here is an admin-level account (not the limited application account the web app uses internally): this is a common mistake where dashboards expose higher-privilege credentials than necessary.

docs.title: Step 9: Connect to MySQL and Retrieve Token 2
docs.text:
Query the MySQL backend directly

Use the database credentials from the dashboard to connect to the MySQL server. The database server's IP address is shown in the lab topology (the .37 offset on the subnet).

mysql --skip-ssl -h <db_ip> -u vtx_admin -p'Vtx_DB_R00t#' vertex_portal \
  -e "SELECT * FROM audit_flags"

The audit_flags table contains several rows including health checks, backup verifications, and schema versions. Look for the row where the name column is assessment; its value column contains the second token: 3xtr4ct.

Record this value. Token 2 represents the fact that you pivoted from the web application layer to the database layer using leaked credentials: the same technique from Exercise 10A, but this time you reached the dashboard through SQL injection rather than default credentials.

A direct MySQL session opened with the leaked dashboard credentials, dumping the `audit_flags` table. The `assessment` row value is masked so the flag stays hidden; the point is that web-layer credentials pivoted straight into the database.

docs.title: Step 10: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the two tokens you collected and consider what each one represents in the context of a real-world assessment.

  • Token 1 (dashboard via SQL injection): The patient portal's login form was vulnerable to SQL injection because the developers used string concatenation to build the SQL query. An attacker with no credentials at all could bypass authentication and access the full provider dashboard. In a healthcare context, this dashboard could expose patient records, clinical data, and system configurations. Authentication bypass of this kind is a critical finding under both OWASP and HIPAA frameworks.

  • Token 2 (MySQL database via leaked credentials): The dashboard's configuration panel exposed database admin credentials in plaintext. Combined with the fact that the database server accepted connections from any host on the subnet, an attacker can query the database directly. Direct database access bypasses any application-level access controls and exposes every table the admin account can read. In a real healthcare environment, this could include patient health information (PHI) protected under HIPAA.

The two tokens together demonstrate a chained attack: SQL injection provided the initial foothold (dashboard access), and information disclosure on the dashboard enabled lateral movement to the database layer. Neither vulnerability alone would be as damaging, but together they create a path from zero access to full database compromise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Consider each question carefully before checking the answer. These questions connect the lab techniques to broader security concepts.

1. What is the difference between a UNION-based SQL injection and a blind SQL injection, and which is more efficient for data extraction?

Reveal Answer

A UNION-based injection appends a second SELECT statement to the original query, allowing the attacker to directly read the results in the application's response. A blind SQL injection occurs when the application does not display query results; the attacker must infer data by observing differences in the application's behavior (boolean-based) or response timing (time-based). UNION-based injection is far more efficient because the data appears directly in the response. Blind injection requires sending many requests to extract data one character at a time: for example, extracting a 32-character password hash via boolean-based blind injection would require hundreds of requests.

2. How do parameterized queries (prepared statements) prevent SQL injection, even when user input contains SQL syntax?

Reveal Answer

Parameterized queries separate the query structure from the data. The application sends the SQL template to the database first (e.g., SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?), and then sends the user input as separate parameters. The database engine treats the parameters strictly as data values, not as part of the SQL syntax. Even if a user submits ' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4-- -, the database interprets the entire string as a literal username to search for, not as SQL commands. The query structure is fixed at compile time and cannot be altered by user input. Fixing the structure at compile time is why parameterized queries are considered the definitive defense against SQL injection.

3. Why does the UNION injection payload in this exercise require exactly four values? What happens if you provide three or five instead?

Reveal Answer

The UNION operator in SQL requires that both SELECT statements return the same number of columns. The original query in this application selects four columns: id, username, password, and email. If the UNION SELECT provides fewer or more columns, the database returns an error like "The used SELECT statements have a different number of columns." In a real assessment, determining the column count is a necessary step before building a UNION payload. Two common techniques: (1) inject ORDER BY N with increasing N until an error occurs: if ORDER BY 4 works but ORDER BY 5 fails, there are four columns; (2) inject UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,... adding NULLs until the query succeeds, since NULL is type-compatible with any column.

4. In Exercise 10A, the entry point was default credentials. In Exercise 10B, it was SQL injection. From a defender's perspective, which vulnerability is easier to prevent, and why?

Reveal Answer

Both are straightforward to prevent, but they require different types of discipline. Default credentials are a configuration problem, the fix is an organizational process that requires changing all default passwords before deployment and auditing for them regularly. SQL injection is a code problem, the fix is using parameterized queries consistently across the entire codebase. In practice, SQL injection is arguably harder to eliminate completely because it requires every developer on the team to follow the secure coding pattern for every query they write. A single missed query in thousands of lines of code creates a vulnerability. Default credentials, by contrast, can be caught with a single automated scan. Both, however, are considered "solved problems" that should not exist in production systems.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SQL injection remains one of the most critical web vulnerabilities (OWASP A03:2021) because it bypasses authentication entirely and grants direct access to the database layer; it exists whenever developers use string concatenation instead of parameterized queries to build SQL statements
  • UNION-based injection allows an attacker to append arbitrary SELECT queries to the original, returning fabricated data that the application trusts; the technique requires matching the exact column count of the original query, which can be discovered through ORDER BY or NULL-based probing
  • The single quote test (' in an input field) is the fastest way to check whether an input is reaching a SQL query unsanitized; any change in application behavior compared to normal input suggests the field is injectable
  • Parameterized queries (prepared statements) are the definitive defense; they keep user input separate from SQL syntax at the database level, making injection impossible regardless of what the user submits
  • Chaining vulnerabilities continues to be the pattern in real-world assessments: directory enumeration (Exercise 10A) finds the portal, SQL injection (this exercise) bypasses the login, and credential leakage on the dashboard enables database pivoting (Exercise 10A technique); Exercise 6 will combine these with lateral movement and privilege escalation from Week 9

If you have not completed those exercises, go back and finish them before attempting this challenge.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Exercise 6 chains five distinct vulnerability classes into a single attack path. If MedCore could fix only one vulnerability to break the entire chain, which one should they prioritize and why?

2. The database server stored SSH credentials for the internal processing server in a configuration table. What is the security principle this violates, and what alternative approach should MedCore use for service-to-service authentication?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Multi-phase attack chains reflect real-world penetration tests where each finding enables the next; a single low-severity vulnerability in isolation can become critical when it links to a chain that achieves full compromise
  • Web-to-infrastructure pivoting is a common pattern: a web application vulnerability provides an initial foothold, leaked credentials bridge to backend systems, and misconfigurations on internal servers grant root access
  • Defense in depth means no single layer can be relied upon; even if the SQL injection is fixed, credentials should not be stored in dashboard configuration panels, SSH passwords should not be stored in database tables, and SUID binaries should be audited regularly
  • Skill integration is the core competency being tested: recognizing which tool and technique to apply at each phase, adapting when one approach fails, and maintaining a methodical kill chain from initial reconnaissance through full compromise
