docs.title: Challenge 14B: Brute Force Detection and Response
Before You Begin
docs.text:
Challenge 14 taught you how to write Suricata rules against two classic web attacks (SQL injection and command injection) where each attack fires on a single packet. Challenge 14B widens the lens to a credential-stuffing campaign: the same attacker, sending hundreds of login attempts in a row, mostly failures with one success buried in the flood. Your detection task is to catch the bulk pattern, catch the successful one, and extract the IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) the attacker tool left behind.

Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready. You should be comfortable with SSH, basic Linux navigation, and the Suricata rule-writing workflow from Challenge 14. If you have not completed Challenge 14 yet, do that first; the syntax background is assumed here.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Aegis Security Corp, a managed security services provider headquartered in Denver, Colorado, has observed a sustained brute-force attack against their client-facing authentication portal. The Security Operations Center detected a high volume of HTTP POST requests to the login endpoint originating from a single source, with hundreds of different username and password combinations attempted over a short period. Worse, their access logs show one entry where the POST got a 200 OK back; the attacker appears to have guessed a valid credential.

You are an analyst on the incident response team. Your team lead, Sarah Nguyen (Principal Threat Analyst), sent you this message:

"We have an active credential stuffing campaign hitting our auth gateway. The IDS sensor is deployed inline but has no custom rules, so it's not catching anything. I need you to write Suricata detection rules for the brute-force POST traffic, find the campaign identifier the attacker is using (they embed tracking tags in their payloads), and check the web portal logs. I suspect the same actor is hitting that too with a custom tool. Pull every IOC you can find. Brief me by end of shift."

Your toolkit includes SSH access to the Aegis IDS sensor (Suricata and tcpdump) and the corporate web portal (nginx). The brute-force attack is ongoing; new login attempts arrive every few seconds.

Credentials

  • IDS Sensor SSH: analyst / A3g1s_S0C_2024#
  • Web Portal SSH: webadmin / A3g1s_Adm1n#

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Credential stuffing is the single most common attack against public-facing auth endpoints today, and the attacker's economics are in their favor: password reuse means a list of millions of stolen credentials from one breach yields thousands of valid logins somewhere else. Detecting the volume signature early is what separates a contained incident from a breach disclosure call to Aegis's entire client base.

  • Aegis's clients include financial and healthcare firms. Every valid credential the attacker finds risks a downstream incident at a customer, escalating contractually to breach notification under SLAs and regulatory scope (GLBA, HIPAA).
  • Sarah has to brief the CEO in the morning on whether the SOC caught the attack or whether customers saw it first. Rule evidence with timestamps is the artifact she needs; a vague "we saw something" is not enough.
  • The rate limiting on the auth gateway is an application-layer control; the IDS is your layer-7 visibility for traffic that never reaches the application. Without the rule, the attacker can iterate for hours before anyone notices.
  • Campaign identifiers embedded by the attacker tool are forensic gold: they let the SOC pivot across time to find every prior attempt from the same campaign, and they support threat-intel sharing with peer SOCs.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The following list outlines what you need to accomplish in the lab environment. Each objective maps to one or more walkthrough steps below.

  • Observe live brute-force POST traffic on the IDS sensor with packet capture
  • Identify the repeated-login pattern and the single successful-login marker
  • Write two Suricata rules: one for any brute-force POST, one for the campaign marker
  • Reload Suricata and verify the rules loaded
  • Extract the campaign and exfil tokens from the alert payloads
  • Investigate the patient portal nginx log for the attacker's tool fingerprint
  • Assemble the flag parts and submit the completed flag

docs.title: Background: Brute Force and Credential Stuffing
docs.text:
A brute-force login attack tries many username and password combinations against an authentication endpoint until one succeeds. A credential-stuffing attack is a narrower form: instead of guessing passwords, the attacker reuses known-valid (username, password) pairs stolen from other breaches, relying on password reuse across sites. The network signature is similar; the defender's detection task is the same.

Three properties of brute-force traffic make it detectable even when each individual request looks valid:

  1. Volume: hundreds of POST requests to the same endpoint in a short window
  2. Shape: each request carries a password (or similar) field in the body
  3. Repetition: the attacker's tool uses the same User-Agent, the same Content-Type, and often the same request structure across every attempt

Detection can hit any of these properties. A threshold rule counts requests per source; a content rule matches the shape of the POST; a User-Agent rule flags the attacker's tool directly. For Challenge 14B you will write two content rules that fire on every POST body carrying a password field, and a tighter one that fires on the one POST body carrying a specific campaign tracking tag the attacker embedded.

The following diagram illustrates the traffic flow:

graph LR
    A["Attacker tool<br/>(AegisCracker)"] -->|"POST /login<br/>username+password<br/>exfil=TOKEN"| B["Aegis IDS sensor<br/>(Suricata + nginx honeypot)"]
    A -->|"GET /admin, /api<br/>recon probes<br/>User-Agent: AegisCracker/TOKEN"| C["Aegis Web Portal<br/>(nginx access log)"]
    B -->|"alert records"| D["/var/log/suricata/eve.json"]
    C -->|"request records"| E["/var/log/nginx/access.log"]

    style A fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#0a6e8a,color:#fff
    style E fill:#0a6e8a,color:#fff
  • Attacker tool sends POSTs to the IDS sensor and reconnaissance GETs to the portal
  • IDS sensor runs Suricata; your rules turn raw traffic into alert records
  • Web portal logs each request to nginx access.log; the attacker's User-Agent is the fingerprint to extract

docs.title: Tool Primer: Suricata Rule Options for POST Traffic
docs.text: Suricata's rule syntax was covered in Challenge 14; this primer extends it to the POST-specific options you need for brute-force detection.

docs.title: Matching HTTP methods
docs.text: The content:"POST"; http_method; pair tells Suricata to match the literal string POST against the parsed HTTP method field, not against the raw packet bytes. Using the parsed field avoids a false positive on any random request whose body happens to contain the characters POST (for example a POST request describing a blog post).

docs.title: Matching POST bodies
docs.text:
The http_client_body modifier, applied to a content: keyword, tells Suricata to match only inside the client-sent request body. For a login POST the body looks like:

username=alice&password=Winter2024&campaign=brut3&exfil=d3t3ct

A rule with content:"password"; http_client_body; fires when the word password appears in that body. It does not fire when password appears in a response body from the server, or in an HTTP header, or in the URL.

docs.title: Flow direction
docs.text: The flow:to_server,established; keyword pair restricts matching to packets traveling from the client toward the server on an already-established TCP connection. For brute-force detection you never want to match server-to-client traffic (responses), so always include the flow keyword on POST-inspection rules. It also cuts processing cost by skipping packets that cannot be attacks.

docs.title: The full rule shape
docs.text:
Putting the pieces together:

alert http any any -> any any (
    msg:"Brute Force Login Attempt";
    flow:to_server,established;
    content:"POST"; http_method;
    content:"password"; http_client_body;
    sid:1000001; rev:1;
)

In plain English: alert on HTTP traffic in either direction (address-wise), arriving on an established connection in the client-to-server direction, where the method is POST and the word password appears in the client body. That one rule catches every brute-force attempt even when the username and password values themselves are unique.

docs.title: Parsing eve.json alerts
docs.text:
When the rules above match, Suricata writes an alert record to /var/log/suricata/eve.json. The payload_printable field holds the raw request body (the place where the campaign and exfil tokens live). The jq filter pattern you need is:

jq -r 'select(.alert != null) | select(.alert.signature_id == 1000001) | .payload_printable' /var/log/suricata/eve.json

Use head -1 to stop after the first match once you have confirmed the extraction works.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
The lab provisions three containers: the attacker, the Aegis IDS sensor, and the web portal. All three must be running before the walkthrough makes sense.

  • Open the Network Security course view and find Aegis Security Corp: Brute Force Detection
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Open the Exercise Network panel and read the three IP addresses. The panel shows per-node IPs; record them in the table below

Record the IPs and note which tool or credential you will use against each one. All three nodes sit on the same /24 subnet; only the last octet changes between roles:

Role (Exercise Network label) Last octet Port you will use What you do here Web Portal .19 TCP 22 (SSH) SSH as webadmin to read the nginx access log for the attacker User-Agent Unknown Attacker .35 n/a Source of the brute-force POST traffic; you do not log in here IDS Sensor .44 TCP 22 (SSH) SSH as analyst to run tcpdump, write Suricata rules, reload the engine, parse eve.json

Attack traffic begins flowing automatically within about twenty seconds of launch. The attacker sends a POST to the sensor's login endpoint roughly every three seconds.

docs.title: Step 2: SSH to the IDS Sensor
docs.text:
All of the detection work runs on the sensor.

SSH to the IDS sensor

Open a terminal on your Kali and connect with the analyst credentials.

ssh analyst@<ids_sensor_ip>

When prompted for the password, enter:

A3g1s_S0C_2024#

Confirm the shell prompt and the hostname; you should be on the Aegis sensor.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm Suricata Is Running
docs.text:
Writing rules against a dead engine wastes your shift.

Confirm Suricata is running

Check that Suricata is running on the sensor before touching the rules file.

pidof suricata

A numeric process ID in the output means the engine is up. An empty response means Suricata is not running; re-check that the lab finished launching.

Note that pgrep -x suricata does not reliably detect Suricata in daemon mode; the main thread renames itself to Suricata-Main, so the exact-match flag misses it. Use pidof suricata or pgrep -f suricata.

docs.title: Step 4: Observe Live Brute-Force Traffic
docs.text:
Before writing rules, you need to see what the attacker is sending.

Capture live brute-force traffic with tcpdump

Run tcpdump on port 80 on the sensor and filter for POST to focus on the login requests.

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 | grep -A 5 "POST /login" | head -40

Let the capture run for fifteen to twenty seconds, then stop it with Ctrl+C. Look for three details in the output:

Field What to look for Why it matters Request method and URL POST /login HTTP/1.1 Confirms the brute-force target Request body username=<varied>&password=<varied>&exfil=d3t3ct The exfil= parameter is the same on every attempt; that is a content signature Successful request body username=<valid>&password=<valid>&campaign=brut3 The campaign=brut3 parameter only appears on the successful login; that is a second content signature worth catching separately

Two patterns jump out: every brute-force POST body contains the literal word password, and one specific POST body contains campaign=brut3. Each becomes its own Suricata rule.

docs.title: Step 5: Write Two Suricata Rules
docs.text:
Custom signatures live in /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules on the sensor. The image is a stripped-down Ubuntu build with no interactive editor installed (production IDS appliances are minimal for the same reason), so write the file with a heredoc through sudo tee. The single-quoted 'EOF' marker tells bash to pass every character through verbatim, which preserves the double quotes inside the rule bodies.

Rule 1: Brute-force POST detection. The rule fires on every POST carrying a password field, which covers the entire flood. The flow:to_server,established; limit keeps the rule from inspecting server responses.

Write the brute-force detection rule

Write the first rule on the sensor, overwriting any existing contents of the file.

sudo tee /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules > /dev/null <<'EOF'
alert http any any -> any any (msg:"Brute Force Login Attempt"; flow:to_server,established; content:"POST"; http_method; content:"password"; http_client_body; sid:1000001; rev:1;)
EOF

The redirect to /dev/null discards the echoed rule text so the terminal stays clean.

Rule 2: Campaign marker detection. The rule fires only on the single POST that carries the attacker's tracking tag campaign=brut3. Pairing a high-noise rule with a narrow rule is a standard SOC pattern: the narrow rule tells you when the "interesting" event happened inside the volume pattern.

Append the campaign marker rule

Append the second rule. The -a flag tells tee to append rather than overwrite, which keeps Rule 1 in place.

sudo tee -a /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules > /dev/null <<'EOF'
alert http any any -> any any (msg:"Campaign Marker Detected"; flow:to_server,established; content:"POST"; http_method; content:"campaign=brut3"; http_client_body; sid:1000002; rev:1;)
EOF

The narrow rule fires only on the single POST carrying the attacker's tracking tag.

Confirm both rules landed in the file

Confirm both rules landed in the file before reloading; a missing newline or stray quote at this stage is the most common reason the reload in Step 6 reports zero loaded rules.

cat /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules

Expected output: two alert http any any lines, one ending in sid:1000001; rev:1;) and the other in sid:1000002; rev:1;).

docs.title: Step 6: Reload Suricata Without Restarting
docs.text:
Suricata does not watch the rules file for changes.

Reload Suricata with the USR2 signal

Send Suricata the USR2 signal to re-read every configured rule file without dropping monitored traffic.

sudo kill -USR2 $(pidof suricata)

No output from the command means the signal was delivered. Suricata takes a few seconds to parse the new rules. If you instead see the kill usage help print, the $(...) expansion returned nothing; re-check Step 3.

docs.title: Confirm the reload actually loaded your rules
docs.text:
The most common failure in this exercise is that the USR2 was delivered but Suricata ended up with zero rules loaded (bad path, bad syntax, stale process). A silent reload looks identical to a bad reload, so always verify.

Verify the ruleset loaded

Query Suricata's command socket for ruleset statistics to confirm both rules are active.

sudo suricatasc -c ruleset-stats /var/run/suricata/suricata-command.socket

Read rules_loaded and rules_failed from the JSON; you want rules_loaded to be 2 and rules_failed to be 0.

Expected output:

{"message": [{"id": 0, "rules_loaded": 2, "rules_failed": 0}], "return": "OK"}

Interpret the result:

rules_loaded rules_failed Meaning What to do 2 0 Both rules active Move on to Step 7 0 0 Rules file empty, unreadable, or reload never reached Suricata Re-check Step 5, re-run the USR2 1 with rules_failed > 0 nonzero One rule has a syntax error and was skipped Tail /var/log/suricata/suricata.log for an Error parsing signature line, fix the broken rule, re-run the USR2

Do not move on to Step 7 until rules_loaded is 2. Alerts will not fire and you will waste time looking for IOCs that do not exist yet.

docs.title: Step 7: Verify Alerts Are Firing
docs.text:
With both rules loaded and the attack traffic still flowing, Suricata should begin writing alert records within fifteen to twenty seconds (one attack cycle).

List the firing alert signatures

Check the eve.json log on the sensor for the distinct alert signatures that have fired.

jq 'select(.alert != null) | .alert.signature' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | sort -u

Expected output:

"Brute Force Login Attempt"
"Campaign Marker Detected"

If only one signature shows, one of your rules is not matching. Re-open local.rules and double-check syntax, then re-run Step 6. If both signatures show, you have working detection and can move on to IOC extraction.

Count alerts per signature

To get a feel for the rate, count how many alerts have fired so far per signature.

jq -r 'select(.alert != null) | .alert.signature' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | sort | uniq -c

In a typical five-minute window you will see dozens of Brute Force alerts (one per attack cycle) and a much smaller count of Campaign Marker alerts (one per full attack loop).

docs.title: Step 8: Extract Token 1 from the Campaign Marker Alert
docs.text:
The campaign=brut3 parameter is the attacker's tracking tag for the successful-login POST. Suricata captured the full POST body in the alert's payload_printable field.

Extract the campaign token

Pull the campaign value from the Campaign Marker alert with jq and grep.

jq -r 'select(.alert != null) | select(.alert.signature_id == 1000002) | .payload_printable' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | grep -oP 'campaign=\K[^& \r\n]+' | head -1

Record the value returned as flag part 1.

What the filter does, step by step:

Fragment Purpose select(.alert != null) Keep only alert records, not HTTP metadata events select(.alert.signature_id == 1000002) Keep only Campaign Marker alerts (sid of Rule 2) .payload_printable Emit the raw POST body as a string grep -oP 'campaign=\K[^& \r\n]+' Match campaign=... and emit only the value head -1 Stop after the first match

Record the value returned as flag part 1.

docs.title: Step 9: Extract Token 2 from the Brute-Force Alerts
docs.text:
The exfil=d3t3ct parameter rides on every failed-login POST body. It is the attacker's outbound-data tag: every credential the tool tests gets shipped back with this label.

Extract the exfil token

Pull the exfil value from a Brute Force alert the same way you pulled the campaign token.

jq -r 'select(.alert != null) | select(.alert.signature_id == 1000001) | .payload_printable' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | grep -oP 'exfil=\K[^& \r\n]+' | head -1

The only difference from Step 8 is the signature_id filter (1000001 is your Brute Force rule) and the parameter name (exfil instead of campaign). Record the value returned as flag part 2.

Record the value returned as flag part 2.

docs.title: Step 10: Correlate with the Web Portal nginx Log
docs.text:
Sarah mentioned the attacker probably hit the portal too. SSH to the web portal with the portaladmin credentials and grep the nginx access log for the attacker's tool fingerprint.

SSH to the web portal

Open a second terminal (or exit the sensor session) and connect to the portal with the webadmin credentials.

ssh webadmin@<web_portal_ip>

When prompted, enter:

A3g1s_Adm1n#

A successful login places you on the portal host where the nginx access log lives.

The attacker's custom tool identifies itself with a distinctive User-Agent beginning with AegisCracker/. Normal browsers use Mozilla/5.0 ...; this attacker uses a tool-build string that stands out immediately.

Extract the User-Agent token from nginx logs

Grep the nginx access log on the portal for the attacker's tool fingerprint.

grep -oP 'AegisCracker/\K[^ "]+' /var/log/nginx/access.log | head -1

The value after the slash is flag part 3.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document each piece of evidence you collected during detection.

Observed attack patterns:

Pattern Where you saw it Why it is distinctive

Suricata rules you wrote:

(paste your two rules from local.rules here)

Ruleset-stats output after reload:

(paste the one-line JSON from Step 6's verification here)

Extracted tokens:

Token Value Source sid (or source file) 1 (campaign) Suricata payload_printable 1000002 2 (exfil) Suricata payload_printable 1000001 3 (User-Agent) nginx access.log /var/log/nginx/access.log

Assembled flag:

OCR{___________}

docs.title: Step 11: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review the three IOCs and what they say about the attacker's operation.

The campaign marker campaign=brut3 rode on the single successful-login POST. Attackers use campaign markers to link a successful hit back to the specific wordlist, target list, or customer job that produced it. In a credential-stuffing-as-a-service operation the marker tells the operator which customer to bill; in an independent attack the marker tells the attacker which campaign's tooling was most efficient. For you, the marker is a pivot point: every prior alert carrying campaign=brut3 is part of the same operation.

The exfil tag exfil=d3t3ct appeared on every failed-login POST. The tag labels the outbound-data channel; the attacker ships every tested credential back to themselves under this label, regardless of whether the login succeeded. The tag is therefore a volume indicator: a spike of traffic carrying exfil=d3t3ct is a spike of this attacker's activity, and it decouples "attacker tool" from "attacker identity" (the same tool can run several concurrent exfil channels).

The AegisCracker User-Agent on the portal ties the recon probing to the same adversary (or the same tool) that ran the brute-force against the sensor. Custom User-Agent strings are lazy OpSec but strong IOCs: they link attack streams across hosts, support WAF blocking, and travel with the tool even when the source IP rotates.

Assemble the three values with underscores between them: OCR{________}.

Flag Format

Use the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<campaigntoken>_<exfiltoken>_<useragenttoken>}

Where campaigntoken is from the Campaign Marker alert payload, exfiltoken is from the Brute Force alert payload, and useragenttoken is from the nginx access log User-Agent string.

docs.title: Step 12: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Return to the Network Security course view, open the Aegis Security Corp lab, and paste the assembled flag in OCR{...} format into the Submit Flag field. The platform confirms or rejects the submission. If it rejects, double-check each extracted value and confirm the _ characters appear between parts in the right order.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The questions below ask you to generalize beyond the mechanics of the exercise. Consider each one before reading the answer.

1. Your brute-force rule fires on every POST that contains the word password. In a real production auth gateway, why would a rule written that loosely generate too much noise, and what would you add to tighten it?

Reveal Answer

Every legitimate login request also contains the word password in the POST body, so in production the rule would fire on real users as well as attackers. Real credential-stuffing detection rules add one or more of the following constraints to tighten the match: (a) a threshold keyword that only fires after N matches from the same src_ip within a time window (for example, threshold: type threshold, track by_src, count 20, seconds 60); (b) a dsize constraint on request size; (c) a content filter on the specific User-Agent string of the attacker tool; (d) an anomaly detector that compares request rate per source against a baseline. For lab work the loose rule is pedagogically useful because it reliably fires every three seconds and lets you focus on the extraction workflow, but it would be unshippable to a live SOC.

2. The attacker embedded campaign=brut3 and exfil=d3t3ct in the POST body, both in cleartext. Why would a real attacker leave identifiers like that inline, and what risk does it create for them?

Reveal Answer

Attackers embed campaign and exfil tags for the same reasons any software operator adds tracking identifiers: they need to reconcile billing in credential-stuffing-as-a-service, A/B-test different wordlists or targets against each other, or correlate successful hits back to specific jobs. The OpSec risk is that any defender who captures the traffic can use those tags to cluster otherwise-unrelated attack streams, build a timeline of the same operator's activity, pivot across victims, and supply a high-quality IOC to threat-intel sharing groups. A sophisticated attacker would encode or encrypt the tags, rotate them between campaigns, or embed them in a header the IDS is less likely to log. Seeing them inline in cleartext is either a sign of a lower-skill operator or a sign that the tooling is mature enough that the operator accepts the exposure as the cost of easier internal reconciliation.

3. The campaign-marker rule (sid 1000002) is a subset of the brute-force rule (sid 1000001); every packet that matches the campaign rule also matches the brute-force rule. Why write both instead of just the tighter one, and how does a SOC analyst benefit from the pair?

Reveal Answer

The two rules serve different operational purposes. The wide rule (sid 1000001) measures the volume and shape of the attack: how long the flood lasted, how many attempts per minute, which source IPs participated, when it started and stopped. The narrow rule (sid 1000002) measures the outcome: the single moment the attacker found a valid credential, including the exact payload that succeeded. Writing only the tighter rule means the SOC misses the flood entirely and sees only the success; writing only the wider rule means the SOC buries the success in the noise of the flood. Paired, the two rules let an analyst answer two distinct questions in one query: "how big is the attack" and "did the attacker win". In real deployments this layering is standard: one rule per pattern of interest, regardless of whether one is a subset of another.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Flow and body modifiers together turn a generic content: match into a tight HTTP rule that only fires on client-to-server POST bodies. Always include flow:to_server,established; on POST-inspection rules to cut noise and processing cost.
  • Pair a wide rule with a narrow rule when you care about both the shape of an attack and a specific outcome inside it. The wide rule measures volume; the narrow rule measures success. A SOC that runs only one of the pair has half the picture.
  • Always verify the rule reload with suricatasc -c ruleset-stats .... A silent failed reload looks identical to a successful reload in the terminal, and debugging "why am I not seeing alerts" wastes far more time than the verification takes.
  • Payload tokens in cleartext are IOC gold. Campaign tags, exfil tags, and custom User-Agent strings travel with the attacker tool across targets and over time. Extracting them from a single alert lets the SOC pivot across the rest of the attack surface.
  • Cross-source correlation is more defensible than single-source evidence. IDS payloads plus nginx logs together tell Sarah a story she can brief to the CEO; either alone is a fragment. Week 15 builds on detection and correlation in the capstone CTF.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Challenge 15B is an unguided final assessment. You should have completed all exercises from Weeks 1 through 14 and the Week 15 capstone before attempting this challenge. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

No scenario brief is provided beyond the objective. No hints are available for the first 30 minutes. Treat the target as a black box engagement.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Titan Global Industries. Four servers. Find all flags.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Discover and enumerate all hosts on the target subnet
  • Exploit each server using the appropriate technique
  • Chain credentials and clues across servers to progress
  • Retrieve one flag fragment from each server
  • Assemble all four fragments into the final flag and submit it

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Host inventory:

Host IP Open Ports Services Technique Required

Attack chain:

Server Technique Flag Fragment Credentials/Clues Found

Flag Format

Assemble the flag using the tokens in the order you discovered them:

OCR{<alphatoken>_<bravotoken>_<charlietoken>_<deltatoken>}

Where alphatoken is from server-alpha (SQL injection), bravotoken is from server-bravo (SSH pivot), charlietoken is from server-charlie (SUID find), and deltatoken is from server-delta (PCAP analysis).

Assembled flag:

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Which of the four servers was the most challenging to exploit, and why?

2. Map each server to the week in the course that taught the primary technique required. How effectively did the course progression prepare you for this assessment?

3. If you were writing a penetration test report for Titan Global Industries, what would your top three remediation recommendations be?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Black box assessments test your ability to identify vulnerability classes without prior knowledge; the right technique for each target must be selected based on enumeration results.
  • Multi-server CTFs require methodical documentation; tracking discovered credentials, clues, and flag fragments across hosts prevents rework and missed connections.
  • Technique diversity (SQL injection, credential pivoting, privilege escalation, traffic analysis) reflects real-world engagements where no two systems are vulnerable to the same attack.
  • Course integration: every technique used in this assessment was introduced in an earlier weekly challenge. Mastery comes from repetition and independent application.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 9A combines web application enumeration with backend database analysis to investigate a potential data breach. You should have completed Exercises 1 through 8 before attempting this lab. The skills from Exercise 4 (directory traversal) and Exercise 10's preview of database interaction are both relevant here. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Financial Group is a mid-size investment advisory firm headquartered in Raleigh, North Carolina. The firm has engaged your team at Ironwood Security Consulting for a data protection assessment. The engagement was triggered by an internal audit that flagged "potential data exposure," but the scope and severity are unknown.

Your point of contact is James Park, IT Director: "We migrated our internal systems last quarter and stood up a new employee intranet. The development team assures me everything is locked down, but our compliance officer noticed some anomalies in the access logs. I need your team to investigate the intranet and our backend database to determine if any sensitive data was exposed during the migration."

James shares that the intranet runs on one server and the company database runs on a separate host. He believes the database is only accessible to authenticated application users. Your task is to assess both systems, identify any data protection failures, and locate the compliance finding that documents the breach.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate the corporate intranet to discover all available pages and directories
  • Identify exposed backup files containing sensitive data
  • Extract database credentials from backup artifacts
  • Connect to the backend database and enumerate schemas and tables
  • Locate the compliance finding that documents the data breach
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Data Breach Investigation Methodology
docs.text: Data breach assessments follow a structured investigation process. Unlike a penetration test where the goal is to break in, a breach assessment asks "what was already exposed, and how bad is the damage?" The methodology involves four stages: asset discovery, exposure mapping, data classification, and impact assessment.

docs.title: Asset Discovery
docs.text: The first step is identifying what systems and data stores exist. In a corporate environment, web servers, databases, file shares, and backup archives form the data landscape. Each asset may store, process, or transmit sensitive information, and each one needs to be examined for misconfiguration.

docs.title: Exposure Mapping
docs.text: Once assets are identified, you determine which ones are accessible without proper authorization. Common exposures include world-readable backup directories, unprotected database ports, and configuration files left in web-accessible locations. The gap between "what should be accessible" and "what actually is accessible" defines the breach surface.

docs.title: Data Classification
docs.text: Not all exposed data carries the same risk. Data classification assigns sensitivity levels, public, internal, confidential, and PII (Personally Identifiable Information), to each piece of exposed data. A marketing brochure left in an open directory is low-impact; a SQL dump containing customer records is critical.

docs.title: Impact Assessment
docs.text:
The final stage documents the findings in terms of regulatory and business impact. Compliance frameworks like SOC 2, HIPAA, and PCI DSS define specific requirements for data protection. A breach assessment maps each finding to the relevant compliance requirement and assigns a severity level.

graph LR
    A["Asset<br/>Discovery"] --> B["Exposure<br/>Mapping"]
    B --> C["Data<br/>Classification"]
    C --> D["Impact<br/>Assessment"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl and mysql
docs.text:
Two tools drive this exercise. You have used curl since Week 1 for HTTP requests; here you will use it for web enumeration and file retrieval. The mysql command-line client is new; it connects directly to a MySQL database server and lets you run SQL queries interactively.

curl for directory probing:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<target>/path/

The flags work together: -s suppresses progress output, -o /dev/null discards the response body, and -w '%{http_code}' prints only the HTTP status code. A 200 means the path exists and is accessible. A 403 means the path exists but access is denied. A 404 means the path does not exist. Probing with the status code alone lets you map directories quickly without reading their full content.

mysql client for database interaction:

mysql --skip-ssl -h <db_host> -u <username> -p'<password>'

The --skip-ssl flag prevents Kali's MariaDB client from rejecting MySQL 8.0's self-signed SSL certificate. The -h flag specifies the database server's IP address. The -u flag provides the username, and -p provides the password (with no space between -p and the password value).

The -p flag has no space

Write -p'MyPassword': not -p 'MyPassword'. If you put a space after -p, MySQL interprets the next word as a database name instead of a password, and the connection will fail with an "Access denied" error.

Once connected, your terminal prompt changes to MariaDB [(none)]>: this means you are inside the MySQL client and the server is waiting for SQL commands. Everything you type from this point forward is SQL, not bash. Here are the essential commands:

Command Purpose SHOW DATABASES; List all databases the user can see USE <database>; Switch to a specific database (prompt changes to show the database name) SHOW TABLES; List all tables in the current database DESCRIBE <table>; Show the column names and data types of a table SELECT * FROM <table>; Display all rows from a table SELECT * FROM <table> WHERE <column> = '<value>'; Filter rows by a condition EXIT; or quit Leave the MySQL client and return to your bash shell

Important SQL syntax rules:

  • Every SQL command must end with a semicolon (;). If you press Enter without a semicolon, MySQL shows a -> continuation prompt: it is waiting for you to finish the command. Type ; and press Enter to execute it.
  • SQL keywords like SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and SHOW are case-insensitive: show databases; works the same as SHOW DATABASES;. However, database names, table names, and column values are case-sensitive on Linux systems.
  • If a table returns too many columns and the output wraps awkwardly, you can select specific columns instead of using *: SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name;

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Note Both Target IPs
docs.text:
Exercise 9A deploys two servers: a web server hosting the corporate intranet and a database server running MySQL. Both IP addresses appear in the Active Lab View.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate Exercise 9A; Data Breach Assessment
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note both target IPs: one for the intranet web server and one for the database server

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate the Corporate Intranet
docs.text:
Retrieve the intranet homepage

Start by retrieving the intranet homepage and examining its content for navigation links, references to internal pages, or clues about the site structure.

curl http://<webserver_ip>/

The homepage should contain links to internal pages. Follow each link to understand what the intranet offers. Common corporate intranet sections include staff directories, internal notices, policies, and contact pages.

Follow the internal page links

Retrieve the staff and notices pages to understand the intranet structure.

curl http://<webserver_ip>/staff/
curl http://<webserver_ip>/notices/

Read the content of each page carefully. The IT notices page is particularly important; look for any references to system migrations, backup procedures, or infrastructure changes. A notice mentioning a "backup migration" is a strong indicator that backup files may still be accessible on the web server.

docs.title: Step 3: Probe for Backup Directories
docs.text:
Corporate web servers sometimes host backup directories that should have been removed or access-restricted after a migration.

Probe for a backups directory by status code

Test whether a /backups/ directory exists on the web server by reading the HTTP status code alone.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<webserver_ip>/backups/

A 403 Forbidden response means the directory exists but the root path is access-restricted. However, subdirectories within a restricted parent may have different permissions.

Test backup subdirectory names

Common backup subdirectory names include legacy, old, archive, and temp. Test variations against the restricted parent.

curl http://<webserver_ip>/backups/legacy/

If the legacy subdirectory is accessible, it will return a directory listing showing the files inside. Look for SQL dump files, configuration backups, and migration notes; any of these could contain sensitive information.

docs.title: Step 4: Extract Credentials from the SQL Dump
docs.text:
Download the SQL dump file

Download and examine the SQL dump file found in the backup directory. SQL dump files are database exports that contain table definitions, data, and sometimes user credentials embedded in GRANT statements or INSERT commands.

curl http://<webserver_ip>/backups/legacy/meridian_dump.sql

The dump may be large; the next command narrows it to the lines that matter.

Grep the dump for credentials

Search the output for credential-related keywords so you do not have to read the whole dump.

curl -s http://<webserver_ip>/backups/legacy/meridian_dump.sql | grep -i -E "grant|password|identified"

The dump file should contain a MySQL GRANT statement that reveals a database username and password. Record these credentials; they provide access to the backend database server.

docs.title: Step 5: Connect to the Backend Database
docs.text:
Connect to the backend database

Use the credentials extracted from the SQL dump to connect to the MySQL database server. The database server listens on port 3306, which is the default MySQL port.

mysql --skip-ssl -h <dbserver_ip> \
  -u meridian_app -p'M3r1d14n_App_2024#'

Replace <dbserver_ip> with the second target IP from the Active Lab View.

If the connection succeeds, your terminal prompt will change from the normal Kali prompt to something like:

MariaDB [(none)]>

The (none) means you are connected to the MySQL server but have not selected a database yet. If you see an "Access denied" error instead, double-check that you copied the username and password exactly as they appeared in the SQL dump: including special characters like #, !, and @.

Stuck at the -> prompt?

If you accidentally pressed Enter without a semicolon, MySQL shows a -> continuation prompt. It is waiting for you to finish the command. Simply type ; and press Enter to execute whatever you have typed so far. If you want to cancel the current command entirely, type \c and press Enter.

docs.title: Step 6: Explore the Available Databases
docs.text:
List the visible databases

Now that you are inside the MySQL client, start by listing all databases your account can see.

SHOW DATABASES;

The output will show a table of database names. You should see several databases listed. Not all of them will be accessible.

Test access to a restricted database

Try switching to the HR database to see whether your account can reach it.

USE meridian_hr;

If the account does not have permission, MySQL will return an error like ERROR 1044 (42000): Access denied for user 'meridian_app'@'%' to database 'meridian_hr'. The denial is expected and demonstrates the principle of least privilege: the application service account was granted access only to the databases it needs, not to all data in the system.

Switch to the compliance database

Try switching to the compliance database, which the service account should be able to reach.

USE meridian_compliance;

If this succeeds, the prompt will change to MariaDB [meridian_compliance]>, confirming you are now working inside that database.

docs.title: Step 7: Enumerate Tables and Understand the Schema
docs.text:
List tables in the compliance database

With a database selected, list its tables.

SHOW TABLES;

The SHOW TABLES statement returns a list of table names.

Inspect the data_classifications schema

Before querying a table, it helps to understand its structure: what columns it has and what type of data each column holds. Use DESCRIBE to inspect a table's schema.

DESCRIBE data_classifications;

The output shows each column name, its data type (VARCHAR, INT, TEXT, etc.), and whether it allows NULL values. The schema tells you what columns are available to query before you run any SELECT statements.

Query all data classifications

Now query the data classifications to understand the scope of the breach.

SELECT * FROM data_classifications;

The SELECT * query returns all rows and all columns.

Filter for PII records

If the output is too wide for your terminal, you can select specific columns and filter for the most sensitive category instead.

SELECT classification, record_name
FROM data_classifications
WHERE classification = 'PII';

The WHERE clause filters the results to show only PII (Personally Identifiable Information) records: the most sensitive category. Any exposure of PII data triggers regulatory notification requirements under frameworks like GDPR, CCPA, and HIPAA.

docs.title: Step 8: Locate the Critical Finding and Capture the Flag
docs.text:
Inspect the compliance_findings schema

Now examine the compliance findings table. Start by checking its structure.

DESCRIBE compliance_findings;

The schema shows which column holds the severity and which holds the finding detail.

Query for the critical finding

Then query for critical-severity entries to locate the documented breach.

SELECT finding_id, severity, finding_detail
FROM compliance_findings
WHERE severity = 'CRITICAL';

The critical finding contains the flag in OCR{...} format. Record the flag.

Exit the MySQL client

When you are finished exploring, exit the MySQL client and return to your bash shell.

EXIT;

Your prompt returns to the normal Kali shell.

Flag Format

The flag is a single token retrieved from the database:

OCR{token}

Return to the platform in your browser and submit the flag.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document your investigation at each stage. Breach assessments require detailed evidence logs because findings may need to be presented to compliance officers, legal teams, or regulators.

Web Enumeration:

Pages discovered on the intranet:

Path Content Summary

Backup directory probe results:

Path HTTP Status Accessible? /backups/ /backups/legacy/

Credentials extracted from SQL dump:

Username Password Source File

Database Enumeration:

Databases visible to the service account:

Database Accessible?

PII records found:

Classification Record Name

Critical finding:

(paste the finding detail here)

Assembled flag:

OCR{...}

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The /backups/ directory returned a 403 Forbidden status, but /backups/legacy/ was accessible. Why does restricting access to a parent directory not automatically protect its subdirectories?

Reveal Answer

Web server access controls are configured per-directory. A Deny or Require directive on /backups/ applies only to that specific path unless the configuration explicitly includes subdirectories. If /backups/legacy/ has its own configuration block (or no configuration at all), it inherits the server's default permissions, which may allow directory listing. Inherited defaults are a common misconfiguration: administrators assume that blocking the parent path protects everything beneath it, but web servers evaluate each directory independently unless configured otherwise with recursive rules.

2. The meridian_app database account could access meridian_compliance but not meridian_hr or meridian_finance. How does this demonstrate the principle of least privilege, and why is it still insufficient to prevent the breach?

Reveal Answer

Least privilege means granting each account only the minimum permissions required for its function. The meridian_app account was correctly restricted to the compliance database because the application only needs compliance data. However, least privilege at the database layer does not compensate for failures at other layers. The breach occurred because the web server exposed backup files containing the credentials in the first place. Even with perfect database permissions, an attacker who obtains any valid credential can query whatever that credential allows. Defense in depth requires security controls at every layer: web server access controls, encrypted backups, credential rotation, and network segmentation, not just database permissions.

3. The SQL dump file contained credentials in plaintext. What steps should the migration team have taken before placing the dump file on the web server?

Reveal Answer

The migration team should have: (1) stripped all credential-related statements (GRANT, CREATE USER, SET PASSWORD) from the dump before transferring it; (2) stored the dump in a location outside the web server's document root so it could never be served over HTTP; (3) encrypted the dump file at rest using a tool like gpg or openssl so that even if the file were accessed, its contents would be unreadable without the decryption key; (4) deleted the dump file from the web server after the migration was complete. Leaving credentials in a web-accessible backup file is one of the most common and preventable data exposure findings in security assessments.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Backup files on web servers are a frequent source of data breaches; SQL dumps, configuration backups, and archive files often contain credentials, schema details, and sensitive data that developers assume are protected by obscurity
  • HTTP status codes reveal directory structure even when access is denied; a 403 confirms the path exists, which guides further enumeration of subdirectories
  • Database least privilege limits the blast radius of a credential compromise but does not prevent the compromise itself; defense in depth requires securing every layer independently
  • Data classification helps prioritize investigation findings; PII exposure carries regulatory consequences that internal-only data exposure does not
  • Breach assessments follow a structured methodology: discover assets, map exposures, classify data, and assess impact; each stage informs the next and builds the evidence needed for compliance reporting

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 9B builds on the investigative skills from Exercise 9A by challenging you to recover encrypted data from a shared workstation using a corporate encryption policy. Where Exercise 9A investigated a web-accessible data breach across two servers, this exercise focuses on local forensic investigation on a single host. The skills you practiced in earlier exercises, reading file contents, examining configurations, and piecing together clues, all apply here. Your VPN must be connected and your terminal ready.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
CryptoVault Solutions is a cybersecurity consulting firm based in Austin, Texas. A senior consultant, Marcus Webb, departed the company abruptly two weeks ago. His laptop has been reimaged, but his encrypted backups remain on the shared analyst workstation.

Your manager, Diana Reeves (Director of Operations), explains: "Marcus was working on a sensitive internal audit before he left. The audit report is in one of his encrypted backup files, but we can't access it. Our company has a standard recovery procedure for encrypted data: the passphrase format is documented in our internal policy. I need you to follow the recovery process, decrypt the correct file, and retrieve the audit report."

Diana provides SSH credentials for the analyst workstation. She reminds you that company policy dictates the passphrase construction method: you should not need to brute force anything. "Everything you need is on that workstation."

SSH credentials: analyst / CV_4n4lyst_2024#

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Connect to the analyst workstation via SSH
  • Enumerate the departed employee's files and directories
  • Identify the encryption method from shell history artifacts
  • Locate and interpret the company encryption recovery policy
  • Reconstruct the passphrase using policy format, employee records, and contextual clues
  • Decrypt the correct file and retrieve the assessment finding
  • Assemble and submit the flag

docs.title: Background: Digital Forensics and Data Recovery
docs.text: When an employee leaves an organization, encrypted files may remain on shared systems. Recovering that data without the employee's cooperation requires a structured forensic approach: identify what encryption was used, find the key material or recovery policy, and apply it to the correct file. The recovery operation in this exercise is controlled and policy-driven, not a brute force attack.

docs.title: Shell History as a Forensic Artifact
docs.text: Linux systems record commands in history files (typically ~/.bash_history). These files persist after user sessions end and can reveal exactly which tools, options, and file paths a user worked with. In forensic investigations, shell history is one of the first artifacts examined because it provides a timeline of user activity without requiring access to the data itself.

docs.title: Encryption Tool Identification
docs.text: Different encryption tools use different formats, algorithms, and key derivation methods. A file encrypted with openssl cannot be decrypted with gpg, and vice versa. Before attempting decryption, an investigator must identify which tool was used. Misidentifying the tool wastes time and produces misleading error messages rather than plaintext.

docs.title: Policy-Based Key Recovery
docs.text:
Many organizations implement passphrase construction policies that allow authorized personnel to reconstruct encryption keys from employee records. The passphrase follows a documented format combining company identifiers, employee IDs, and date components. While convenient for business continuity, this approach creates a recoverable, and potentially predictable, key derivation method.

graph LR
    A["Shell History<br/>Analysis"] --> B["Encryption Tool<br/>Identification"]
    B --> C["Policy<br/>Lookup"]
    C --> D["Passphrase<br/>Reconstruction"]
    D --> E["File<br/>Decryption"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: SSH, openssl, and Common Forensic Commands
docs.text:
SSH for remote access:

ssh <username>@<target_ip>

You have used SSH in previous exercises. The -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no flag can be added if the host key prompt interferes with your connection.

openssl for symmetric decryption:

openssl enc -<algorithm> -d -pbkdf2 -in <encrypted_file> -pass pass:<passphrase>
Flag Purpose enc Use the symmetric encryption subcommand -aes-256-cbc Algorithm (AES-256 in CBC mode) -d Decrypt (instead of encrypt) -pbkdf2 Use PBKDF2 key derivation (modern standard) -in Input file path -pass pass: Supply passphrase on the command line (no space after pass:)

File exploration commands:

Command Purpose ls -la /home/ List all home directories with permissions ls -la /home/<user>/ List a specific user's files including hidden files cat <file> Read file contents cat ~/.bash_history Read a user's command history find /home/<user>/ -type f List all files recursively under a directory file <filename> Identify file type (text, encrypted data, etc.)

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Connect via SSH
docs.text:
Exercise 9B deploys a single workstation. Only one IP address appears in the Active Lab View.

  • Navigate to Exercises and locate Exercise 9B; CryptoVault Recovery Operation
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

Connect to the analyst workstation over SSH

Connect to the analyst workstation using the credentials provided in the scenario. Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View.

ssh analyst@<target_ip>

When prompted for the password, enter CV_4n4lyst_2024#. You should see a shell prompt on the workstation.

docs.title: Step 2: Read the Analyst's README
docs.text:
Read the analyst README on the workstation

Check your home directory for any briefing documents left by management. Run this in the SSH session you just opened on the workstation.

cat ~/README.txt

The README.txt file provides context about the recovery operation and confirms your objectives. Read it carefully: it reinforces what Diana Reeves told you in the scenario briefing.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate the Departed Employee's Home Directory
docs.text:
List home directories on the workstation

Determine what user accounts exist on the workstation by listing home directories.

ls -la /home/

You should see your own home directory (analyst) and the departed employee's directory.

List the departed employee's files including hidden ones

Navigate to the departed employee's home directory and list all files, including hidden ones.

ls -la /home/mwebb/

Note the files and subdirectories present. Hidden files (those starting with .) are often the most forensically interesting because they include configuration files and shell history.

docs.title: Step 4: Examine the Shell History
docs.text:
Read the departed employee's shell history

The .bash_history file records commands the departed employee ran. The history is your primary clue for identifying the encryption method.

cat /home/mwebb/.bash_history

Read the history carefully. Look for commands that reference encryption tools (openssl, gpg, zip), specific algorithms, and file names. One entry should reveal exactly which tool and algorithm was used to create the encrypted backup, including the input filename and output filename.

Record the encryption command you found: you will need the tool name, algorithm, and any flags to construct your decryption command later.

docs.title: Step 5: Examine the Employee Record
docs.text:
Read the employee record file

Look for personnel files that contain identifying information about the departed employee.

cat /home/mwebb/employee-record.txt

The employee-record.txt file contains the employee's full name, employee ID, role, and separation date. Record the employee ID: it follows a specific format that will be needed for passphrase reconstruction.

docs.title: Step 6: Explore Desktop and Documents
docs.text:
List the Desktop and Documents directories

Check the departed employee's Desktop and Documents directories for additional clues.

ls -la /home/mwebb/Desktop/
ls -la /home/mwebb/Documents/

Read any files you find. One file in particular contains a note that points you toward the company's encryption standard policy. The note is the breadcrumb trail: the employee left a reference to where the passphrase construction rules are documented.

Read the sticky note left on the Desktop

Open the note the employee left behind. It points to where the passphrase construction rules are documented.

cat /home/mwebb/Desktop/sticky_note.txt

docs.title: Step 7: Locate and Read the Company Encryption Policy
docs.text:
Read the company encryption policy

The sticky note referenced a company policy location. Navigate to that path and read the encryption standard.

cat /etc/company-policy/encryption-standard.txt

The encryption-standard policy document is the key to the entire exercise. It defines:

  • Which encryption tools the company uses and for what purpose
  • The exact passphrase format for internal backups
  • What each component of the passphrase represents
  • Where to find each component value

Read the policy thoroughly. The passphrase format uses a template with multiple fields that you need to fill in from the evidence you have already gathered.

docs.title: Step 8: Reconstruct the Passphrase
docs.text:
Using the policy's passphrase format, substitute the values you found:

  • Company Prefix: Stated directly in the policy (case-sensitive)
  • Employee ID: From the employee record file (Step 5)
  • Year: The four-digit year when the backup was created: determine this from the evidence you have collected (shell history timestamps, employee record dates, file dates)

Common Mistake: Wrong Year

Students frequently use the current year or the employee's separation year. Think carefully about when the backup was created, not when the employee left. Look at the evidence for date clues: the bash history entry, the employee record dates, and the file modification times all provide context.

Assemble the passphrase by combining all three components in the format specified by the policy, with the correct separators. Once you have it, plug it into the decryption command.

Decrypt the audit backup with openssl

Run the decryption on the workstation where the encrypted file lives. The -pass pass: flag is how you supply a passphrase to openssl on the command line. There is no space between pass: and the passphrase value.

openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -d -pbkdf2 \
  -in /home/mwebb/audit_backup.enc \
  -pass pass:<YOUR_PASSPHRASE>

Replace <YOUR_PASSPHRASE> with the passphrase you just assembled: the three components joined with the correct separators. A correct passphrase prints the decrypted audit report to your terminal; a wrong one prints a bad decrypt error.

Flag Format

The flag is a single token revealed by decrypting the backup file:

OCR{token}

docs.title: Step 9: Decrypt and Capture the Flag
docs.text:
Run the command you constructed above. If the passphrase is correct, the decrypted content will print to your terminal and contain the assessment flag in OCR{...} format.

If you see bad decrypt errors, double-check:

  • Is the company prefix exactly as written in the policy (case-sensitive)?
  • Is the employee ID in the correct format?
  • Is the year correct (creation year, not separation year)?
  • Are the separators correct (dashes, not underscores)?

docs.title: Step 10: Avoid the Red Herrings
docs.text:
The workstation contains additional encrypted files in /opt/recovery/ that are not the target. These decoy files use different encryption methods (GPG, password-protected ZIP) and random passphrases that do not follow the company policy. They exist to test whether you follow the evidence trail methodically or waste time on files that do not match the investigation objective.

If you explored /opt/recovery/ and tried to decrypt files there, that is okay: recognizing that those files use different encryption methods is part of the forensic process. The key insight is that the bash history pointed to a specific file encrypted with a specific tool, and the company policy only covers that tool's passphrase format.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Departed employee's home directory contents:

(paste ls -la output here)

Shell history: encryption command found:

Tool Algorithm Input File Output File

Employee record details:

Field Value Full Name Employee ID Role Separation Date

Company passphrase policy:

Policy Field Value Format template Company Prefix Employee ID source Year determination

Reconstructed passphrase:

(write your assembled passphrase here)

Decryption command used:

(paste your full command here)

Assembled flag:

OCR{_____}

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The company's passphrase recovery policy uses a predictable format: {Prefix}-{ID}-{Year}. Why is a predictable passphrase construction method a security weakness, even when the policy is stored internally?

Reveal Answer

A predictable passphrase format reduces the key space from billions of possible combinations to a small, enumerable set. Anyone who reads the policy, current employees, contractors, attackers who compromise the intranet, can reconstruct passphrases for any employee's encrypted files. The security of the encrypted data depends entirely on the secrecy of the policy document rather than the strength of the passphrase itself. Relying on a secret construction rule violates Kerckhoffs's principle: a cryptographic system should be secure even if everything about the system except the key is public knowledge. A better approach would use randomly generated passphrases stored in a centralized key management system with access controls and audit logging.

2. Marcus's .bash_history revealed the exact encryption command he used. Several other files on the workstation used GPG with random passphrases. Why does identifying the correct encryption tool matter, and what would happen if you tried to decrypt an openssl file with GPG?

Reveal Answer

OpenSSL and GPG use fundamentally different file formats, key derivation methods, and encryption wrappers. An openssl-encrypted file starts with a Salted__ header and uses PBKDF2 (or the older EVP_BytesToKey) to derive the encryption key from the passphrase. A GPG-encrypted file uses the OpenPGP format with its own key derivation and packet structure. Attempting to decrypt an openssl file with gpg produces an error like "gpg: no valid OpenPGP data found" because GPG cannot parse the openssl format. Identifying the correct tool is a prerequisite for successful decryption: no amount of correct passphrases will work if you are using the wrong tool.

3. The analyst account could read Marcus's home directory and files despite being a different user. What file permission setting would have prevented this cross-user access, and why is it important during employee offboarding?

Reveal Answer

Setting the home directory to chmod 700 (owner read/write/execute only) would prevent any other non-root user from listing or reading files inside it. The default permissions on many Linux distributions allow group or world read access to home directories (755 or 750), which means any user on the system can browse another user's files. During employee offboarding, this is critical because the departing employee's files may contain sensitive data, credentials, encryption keys, or proprietary information. Best practice is to restrict home directory permissions to 700 at account creation and to either archive or securely delete the departing employee's files as part of the offboarding checklist, rather than leaving them accessible on shared systems.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Shell history (.bash_history) is a forensic artifact that reveals exactly which commands a user ran, including encryption tools, algorithms, and file paths: it is one of the first files an investigator should examine
  • Policy-based passphrase construction creates a recoverable but predictable key derivation method; convenient for business continuity but exploitable by anyone who reads the policy
  • Encryption tool identification is essential before attempting decryption; openssl and GPG use different formats, key derivation methods, and command syntax, and using the wrong tool produces errors rather than plaintext
  • Red herrings (GPG files, unrelated encrypted archives) test whether you follow evidence methodically or waste time on files that do not match the investigation objective
  • Cross-user file access on shared workstations is a common misconfiguration; restrictive home directory permissions (chmod 700) prevent one user from reading another's files, which is critical during offboarding when departing employees may leave sensitive data behind

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Earlier Week 14 exercises had you write Suricata rules and read alerts straight from eve.json at the terminal. Exercise 14.3 adds the missing layer a working SOC relies on: live alert triage in a browser-based console. You will still write Suricata rules, but instead of grepping JSON, you will work the alerts the way a Tier 1 analyst does on shift, from a SIEM dashboard that shows new events as they arrive.

Your VPN must be connected and both your terminal and web browser open. You should be comfortable with SSH login, basic Linux navigation, and the HTTP request structure from earlier exercises.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Aurora Medical Group, a regional healthcare network headquartered in Portland, Oregon, runs a public-facing patient portal in its DMZ (Demilitarized Zone). Overnight, the SOC (Security Operations Center) pulse board lit up with anomalous HTTP traffic targeting the corporate subnet. The traffic looks like active scanning and exploitation, not background noise.

You are the Tier 1 SOC analyst on the night shift. The CISO (Chief Information Security Officer), Dr. Priya Sharma, messages you on the ops bridge before logging off:

"The Suricata sensor is running but it has no custom rules loaded. Spin up detection for what you're seeing, then use the EveBox console to triage the alerts; I don't want you grepping eve.json at 3am. Pull every IOC you can out of the payloads. The HIPAA notification clock starts the moment we confirm PHI exposure, so we need clean evidence, not guesses."

Your toolkit includes SSH access to the Aurora IDS sensor (Suricata and tcpdump), SSH access to the patient portal web host, and an EveBox web console that live-tails the sensor's eve.json file. Attack traffic is ongoing; new requests arrive every few seconds.

Credentials:

  • IDS Sensor SSH: tier1 / Aur0r4_S0C#
  • Patient Portal SSH: portaladmin / P4t13nt_P0rt4l#
  • EveBox Web Console: http://<evebox_ip>:5636 (no login required in lab mode)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Aurora's overnight shift gets paged by hundreds of low-severity alerts every week. The difference between a Tier 1 analyst who spots a real intrusion and one who misses it is often not the detection rule; it is the time the analyst spends in a triage tool. A SOC running without a console means every investigation begins with jq and grep, which is fine for a researcher but does not scale during a live incident with a breach disclosure deadline.

  • HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) requires patient notification within 60 days, and the clock starts at discovery. Audit-ready evidence tied to a triage timeline beats a scratchpad of copy-pasted terminal output.
  • The CISO presents a post-incident report to the hospital board. Screenshots from a SIEM console carry more weight than terminal scrollback.
  • Cyber insurance carriers often require SIEM dashboards as a coverage precondition. A claim filed without SIEM-sourced evidence may be denied or reduced.
  • The next shift inherits whatever you leave behind. Alerts marked "reviewed" in a shared console carry forward; a terminal session does not.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Observe live attack traffic on the Aurora IDS sensor using packet capture
  • Write Suricata rules that detect SQL injection and command injection
  • Triage the resulting alerts in the EveBox web console
  • Extract IOCs (indicators of compromise) from the alert drill-down view
  • Investigate the patient portal nginx access log for attacker tooling fingerprints
  • Assemble the flag parts and submit the completed flag

docs.title: Background: Alert Triage in a SIEM Console
docs.text:
A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) console sits on top of raw detection output and organizes events for a human analyst. Suricata produces the raw alerts; a tool like EveBox reads that stream and presents each alert as a clickable row with filters, drill-down panels, and archive state. Analysts call this workflow "triage": sorting a queue of alerts by priority, investigating the ones that matter, and marking the rest as handled.

A common industry pattern pairs Suricata (detection) with a dashboard (triage) and a longer-term store (search and analytics). Wazuh, SELKS, and the Elastic stack all fill the same slot as EveBox; they differ in weight, storage backend, and feature depth, not in concept. What matters for your shift is that the dashboard shows new alerts as they arrive, exposes the captured payload for each alert, and lets you export evidence without hand-rolling shell pipelines.

The following diagram illustrates the data flow on the Aurora sensor:

graph LR
    A["Network Traffic<br/>(attacker HTTP)"] --> B["Suricata<br/>IDS Engine"]
    B --> C{"Rule<br/>Match?"}
    C -->|"Yes"| D["Alert appended<br/>to eve.json"]
    C -->|"No"| E["Packet passes<br/>unlogged"]
    D --> F["EveBox tails<br/>eve.json"]
    F --> G["Analyst opens<br/>console in browser"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#888,color:#fff
    style F fill:#0a6e8a,color:#fff
    style G fill:#0f8a7f,color:#fff
  • Network traffic arrives at the sensor's network interface
  • Suricata inspects each packet against its loaded rules
  • Rule match: an alert record is appended to /var/log/suricata/eve.json
  • EveBox tails the file as new records land and writes them into its own SQLite store
  • Analyst opens the web console and works the queue

For Aurora's sensor the eve.json file lives on a shared Docker volume that both the Suricata container and the EveBox container can see, so an alert written by Suricata shows up in the console within a second or two.

docs.title: Tool Primer: EveBox
docs.text:
EveBox is an open-source web front end for Suricata alerts. The lab runs it with an embedded SQLite store, no-auth lab mode, and plain HTTP on port 5636.

Key views you will use tonight:

View Purpose Inbox Queue of unhandled alerts, newest first Alert detail Full JSON record for the selected alert, including URL, payload, source IP Events All eve.json events (flows, HTTP metadata, DNS), not only alerts Archived Alerts you have marked as triaged

Keyboard shortcuts worth remembering:

Key Action j / k Next / previous alert in the list o Open selected alert F Toggle filter bar ? Full shortcut reference

EveBox groups duplicate alerts in the Inbox by default: when the same rule fires ten times in a row for the same source and destination, you see one row with a count, not ten rows. The grouping is deliberate; you triage the group, not each packet. Use the Events view if you need to see every individual record.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
The lab provisions four containers: the attacker, the Aurora IDS sensor, the patient portal, and the EveBox console. All four must be running before you begin triage work.

  • Open the Network Security course view and find Aurora Medical Group: SOC Triage with EveBox
  • Click Launch and wait for the status to change to Running
  • Open the Exercise Network panel. It lists four IPs, each tied to a role you will use in this walkthrough

Record the IPs from the panel and note which tool or credential you will use against each one. Every node in this lab sits on the same /24 subnet; only the last octet (the IP offset) changes between roles. Keep this table open in a second tab while you work:

Role (Exercise Network label) Last octet Port you will use What you do here Patient Portal .17 TCP 22 (SSH) SSH as portaladmin to read the nginx access log for the attacker User-Agent Unknown Attacker .31 n/a Source of the automated attack traffic; you do not log in here Aurora IDS Sensor .47 TCP 22 (SSH) SSH as tier1 to run tcpdump, write Suricata rules, reload the engine EveBox SOC Console .53 TCP 5636 (HTTP) Open in a browser, no login, to triage alerts and pull IOCs from payloads

Attack traffic begins flowing automatically within about twenty seconds of launch. Your sensor starts receiving malicious HTTP requests immediately after that.

Where to find each IP

The four IPs are all shown in the Exercise Network panel on the lab page, one row per node. The IDS sensor and patient portal are the SSH targets; EveBox is the one you open in the browser. If you spawn the lab more than once, the IPs change between runs, so read them from the panel each session rather than saving them from a previous attempt.

docs.title: Step 2: SSH to the Aurora IDS Sensor
docs.text:
SSH to the Aurora IDS sensor

Most of the detection work runs on the sensor. Open a terminal on your Kali and connect with the Tier 1 analyst credentials from the scenario block. Replace <ids_sensor_ip> with the sensor IP from the Exercise Network panel.

ssh tier1@<ids_sensor_ip>

When prompted for the password, enter:

Aur0r4_S0C#

The hostname in your shell prompt should read aurora-sensor. That confirms you landed on the right host.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm Suricata Is Running
docs.text:
Confirm Suricata is running on the sensor

Writing rules against a dead engine wastes your shift. Check the Suricata process before touching the rules file. Run this in the sensor SSH session.

pidof suricata

A numeric process ID in the output means the engine is up. An empty response means Suricata is not running; re-check that the lab finished launching.

Note that pgrep -x suricata does not reliably detect Suricata in daemon mode. The main thread renames itself to Suricata-Main, so the exact-match flag misses it. Use pidof suricata or pgrep -f suricata instead.

docs.title: Step 4: Watch Live Attack Traffic
docs.text:
Capture live attack traffic with tcpdump

Before writing rules, you need to see what the attacker is sending. Raw capture on port 80 reveals the two distinct HTTP payloads you will translate into signatures.

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 | head -80

Let the capture run for ten to fifteen seconds, then stop it with Ctrl+C. Two patterns should stand out in the output.

Pattern 1: SQL injection in GET requests. A URL query string containing UNION SELECT is not normal user input. The attacker is trying to append a malicious SELECT clause to a legitimate search query. A typical URI looks like:

GET /search?q=1'+UNION+SELECT+username,password+FROM+credentials--&campaign=TOKEN

Pattern 2: Command injection in POST bodies. A form body containing shell syntax such as ;cat /etc/shadow is not valid form input. The attacker is trying to break out of the server-side handler and read system files. A typical POST body looks like:

host=10.200.0.1;cat /etc/shadow&exfil=TOKEN

Note both patterns carefully. Each one becomes a Suricata rule.

docs.title: Step 5: Write Suricata Rules for the Two Attack Vectors
docs.text:
Open the local rules file on the sensor

Custom signatures live in /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules on the sensor. Open the file in nano.

sudo nano /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules

The editor opens an empty or near-empty file ready for your two signatures.

Add the two rules below, one per line.

Rule 1: SQL injection detection. The content:"UNION SELECT" check is scoped to the HTTP URI, so response bodies and log viewers that happen to contain those words do not fire the rule. The classtype:web-application-attack keyword tags the alert with a category that Suricata's classification file maps to severity 1 (high). Without a classtype the alert lands with an empty category and severity 3, and the EveBox Alerts view hides or buries it.

alert http any any -> any any (msg:"SQLi Attack Detected"; content:"UNION SELECT"; nocase; http_uri; classtype:web-application-attack; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

Rule 2: Command injection detection. The http_client_body modifier limits the match to the request body the client sent, so response bodies from any file server do not create false positives. The same classtype is used so both rules share a category in the console.

alert http any any -> any any (msg:"Command Injection Detected"; content:"cat /etc"; nocase; http_client_body; classtype:web-application-attack; sid:1000002; rev:1;)

Save and exit nano with Ctrl+O, Enter, then Ctrl+X.

Why classtype matters for triage

A Suricata alert written without classtype fires correctly and shows up under the Events view in EveBox, because every alert is also an event. It does not reliably appear under Alerts or the Inbox, because those views filter and group by category and severity. Classification mappings live in /etc/suricata/classification.config; run grep web-application /etc/suricata/classification.config on the sensor to see which severity each category maps to.

docs.title: Step 6: Reload Suricata Without Restarting
docs.text:
Reload Suricata rules with a USR2 signal

Suricata does not watch the rules file for changes. Send the USR2 signal to the running engine and it re-reads every configured rule file without dropping monitored traffic.

sudo kill -USR2 $(pidof suricata)

No output from the command means the signal was delivered. Suricata takes a few seconds to parse the new rules. If instead you see the kill usage help print, that means the $(...) expansion returned nothing; re-check Step 3.

docs.title: Confirm the reload actually loaded your rules
docs.text:
