docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Security assessment is a structured process. Frameworks like NIST CSF and IEC 62443 turn ad hoc findings into systematic, actionable reports.

  • Risk ratings must account for physical safety. A "medium" IT vulnerability becomes "critical" when it enables manipulation of a physical process at a petroleum terminal.

  • The Purdue Model is not optional. Network segmentation is the single most effective control. A flat network is indefensible regardless of how well individual applications are hardened.

  • Defense-in-depth means overlapping controls. Segmentation stops lateral movement, firewalls restrict protocols, authentication blocks unauthorized commands, monitoring detects anomalies, and incident response limits impact.

  • IT and OT security must collaborate. Neither team alone can secure an ICS environment. Effective security requires both perspectives working with a shared framework.

  • Course complete. You have progressed from network discovery through protocol analysis, exploitation, attack chaining, and defense analysis: the core skills of an ICS security professional.

docs.title: Why Windows Forensics Matters
docs.text:
Windows dominates the enterprise landscape. Over 75% of corporate desktops and a significant share of servers run some version of Windows, making it the primary operating system that incident responders encounter during investigations. When an organization suffers a breach, the compromised endpoints are almost always Windows machines. Understanding how Windows stores evidence; in event logs, the registry, scheduled tasks, file system artifacts, and PowerShell history; is not optional for a security professional. It is foundational.

Attackers know this landscape intimately. They exploit Windows-specific services like SMB and RDP, create persistence through scheduled tasks and registry Run keys, and hide their tracks by clearing event logs. A defender who cannot navigate these artifacts will miss critical indicators of compromise. These three labs take you from external reconnaissance of a Windows target through SMB enumeration and credential discovery to a full incident investigation on a compromised machine ; the same progression you would follow in a real engagement.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
Three labs in this chapter build your Windows forensics skillset. You will:

  • Perform network reconnaissance against a live Windows 10 target using nmap
  • Identify Windows-specific services (SMB, RPC, RDP, WinRM) and understand their security implications
  • Enumerate SMB shares and discover exposed credentials through null session access
  • Use discovered credentials to access restricted file shares
  • Investigate a simulated breach using Windows Event Viewer, scheduled tasks, registry keys, and PowerShell history
  • Decode Base64-encoded attacker payloads
  • Reconstruct an attack timeline from forensic artifacts
  • Assemble a multi-part flag from evidence scattered across the system

docs.title: How the Labs Work
docs.text:
These labs target a shared live Windows 10 machine. Unlike container-based labs where each student gets an isolated environment, all students interact with the same Windows target. The target IP address is displayed in the Active Lab panel when you start the exercise. Exercises 1.1 and 1.2 are performed entirely from your Kali machine using command-line tools (nmap, smbclient, enum4linux). Exercise 1.3 requires an RDP session to the Windows machine for hands-on forensic investigation using native Windows tools.

Note: These labs target a real Windows 10 machine running on the range. The machine has been deliberately configured with security weaknesses and simulated attack artifacts for educational purposes. Do not attempt to modify the target system configuration, create new user accounts, or delete files; this will disrupt the lab for other students.

docs.title: Connection Details
docs.text:
Field Value Target IP Shown in the Active Lab panel when you start the exercise RDP Username LabUser (Exercise 1.3 only) RDP Password Password123# (Exercise 1.3 only) Network Your Kali machine must be connected via VPN or through a RangeBox session
  • Exercises 1.1-1.2: All commands run from your Kali terminal. Replace <target-ip> in each command with the IP shown in the Active Lab panel
  • Exercise 1.3: RDP connection using xfreerdp /v:<target-ip> /u:LabUser /p:Password123# /cert:ignore

docs.title: Lab Progression
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["1.1 Reconnaissance"] --> B["1.2 Enumeration"]
    B --> C["1.3 Incident Investigation"]
    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

Each lab builds directly on the previous one. In Exercise 1.1, you discover what services are running. In Exercise 1.2, you use that knowledge to enumerate shares and find credentials. In Exercise 1.3, you use those credentials (along with provided RDP access) to investigate a breach from the inside.

docs.title: Lab Overview
docs.text: Exercise Title Focus Key Tools Duration 1.1 Windows Reconnaissance Service discovery and OS fingerprinting nmap, nmap scripts 30 min 1.2 Remote Enumeration & Data Discovery SMB share enumeration and credential hunting smbclient, enum4linux 45 min 1.3 Incident Investigation Host-based forensic analysis of a compromised machine Event Viewer, schtasks, reg query, PowerShell 60-90 min

docs.title: The Meridian Technologies Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Technologies is a mid-sized financial services firm with 2,000 employees across three offices. Their IT environment runs primarily on Windows; Active Directory for authentication, Windows 10 desktops, Windows Server 2019 for file shares and applications. After a series of phishing attempts targeting their finance department, Meridian's CISO has engaged your security team to perform a thorough assessment.

Your engagement begins with external reconnaissance: what can you learn about their Windows infrastructure from the network? You then move to enumeration, probing SMB shares for misconfigurations and exposed data. Finally, Meridian's SOC detects signs of an active breach on one of their workstations, and you pivot from assessment to incident response; investigating the compromised machine to determine what the attacker did, how they persisted, and what data they accessed.

Over three exercises, you progress from passive observation to active investigation, building the skills that define a competent Windows incident responder.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following before beginning any lab in this chapter:

  • Your Kali machine is connected to the lab network (VPN active or RangeBox session running)
  • You have terminal access on your Kali machine
  • Target IP noted from the Active Lab panel
  • nmap is installed: nmap --version
  • smbclient is installed: smbclient --version
  • enum4linux is installed: enum4linux (shows usage)
  • xfreerdp is installed: xfreerdp --version (needed for Exercise 1.3)

Proceed to Exercise 1.1; Windows Reconnaissance when you are ready.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1 is the first exercise in Chapter F1 (Windows Forensics). You will use nmap from your Kali machine to scan a live Windows 10 target and identify the services it exposes. No credentials are needed for this exercise; everything is performed remotely from the network. If you have completed the enumeration chapters (CH01-CH07), the nmap commands will be familiar. this exercise focuses specifically on interpreting scan results in a Windows context.

Make sure you have:

  • Your Kali machine connected to the lab network (VPN active or RangeBox session running)
  • Terminal access on your Kali machine
  • nmap installed (nmap --version)
  • Target IP noted from the Active Lab panel; replace <target-ip> in the commands below with this address

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Meridian Technologies has engaged your team to assess their Windows infrastructure. Before testing any credentials or accessing any systems, your first task is pure reconnaissance: identify what services the target Windows workstation exposes to the network. The exposed services determine your attack surface and guide the next phase of the assessment. A single Windows machine can expose a dozen services by default; your job is to find them all and understand what each one means.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Verify network connectivity to the Windows target
  • Perform a SYN scan to identify open ports
  • Run service version detection to fingerprint each service
  • Use OS fingerprinting to confirm the target operating system
  • Extract NetBIOS information (hostname, workgroup, MAC address)
  • Use SMB scripts to discover OS-level details and retrieve the flag

docs.title: Background: Windows Network Services
docs.text:
A default Windows installation exposes significantly more network services than a typical Linux server. Understanding what each service does; and why it exists; is essential for both attackers and defenders.

Port Service Protocol What It Does 135 RPC Endpoint Mapper MSRPC Microsoft's inter-process communication broker. Maps RPC services to dynamic high ports. Required for DCOM, WMI, and many Windows management tools. 139 NetBIOS Session NetBIOS/SMB Legacy Windows networking. Provides name resolution, session management, and datagram services. Predates DNS-based Windows networking. 445 SMB Direct SMB/CIFS File and printer sharing over TCP. The primary protocol for Windows file access, Active Directory communication, and lateral movement. 3389 RDP RDP Remote Desktop Protocol. Provides full graphical remote access to the Windows desktop. Frequently targeted by brute-force attacks. 5985 WinRM HTTP/SOAP Windows Remote Management. Allows remote PowerShell execution and system management over HTTP. The modern replacement for WMI-over-DCOM.

docs.title: Why This Matters for Security
docs.text:
Windows exposes these services because enterprise environments depend on them. SMB enables file sharing and Group Policy distribution. RPC underpins Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI). RDP provides remote administration. But each open port is an attack vector.

SMB has a particularly notorious history. The EternalBlue exploit (MS17-010), leaked from the NSA in 2017, targeted a vulnerability in SMBv1 and powered the WannaCry ransomware outbreak that crippled hospitals, shipping companies, and government agencies worldwide. Port 445 open on a Windows machine is the single most important finding in any Windows reconnaissance scan.

RDP is the second most-targeted service. Attackers routinely brute-force RDP credentials, and once they have a valid login, they have full interactive access to the machine; no malware required. The BlueKeep vulnerability (CVE-2019-0708) demonstrated that RDP itself can be exploited for remote code execution without any credentials at all.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap for Windows Targets
docs.text:
The table below lists the nmap options you will use in this exercise. Each flag is explained in the context of scanning Windows systems.

Flag / Option What It Does -sS SYN scan (stealth scan). Sends SYN packets and analyzes responses without completing the TCP handshake. Fast and reliable. Requires root/sudo. -sV Service version detection. Probes open ports to determine the service name and version. Essential for identifying Windows-specific services. -O OS fingerprinting. Analyzes TCP/IP stack behavior to guess the operating system. Requires root/sudo. -p Specify ports to scan. Use -p 135,139,445,3389,5985 to target Windows services directly. --script nbstat Runs the NetBIOS statistics script. Extracts the hostname, workgroup/domain, and MAC address from the target. --script smb-os-discovery Queries SMB to determine the OS version, computer name, domain, and workgroup. Often reveals details that -O alone misses. -Pn Skip host discovery (treat host as online). Useful when ICMP is blocked by Windows Firewall.

docs.title: Step 1: Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Confirm the target is reachable

Before scanning, confirm that the target is reachable from your Kali machine. Use the target IP shown in the Active Lab panel. The -c 3 flag sends three ICMP echo requests.

ping -c 3 <target-ip>

You should receive three replies. If ICMP is blocked (request timed out), the target may still be accessible; Windows Firewall sometimes blocks ping while allowing other traffic. In that case, proceed with the scan using the -Pn flag.

Record Your Findings

  • Ping successful (yes/no): ___
  • Round-trip time (avg): ___

docs.title: Step 2: SYN Scan (Top 1000 Ports)
docs.text:
Run a SYN scan of the top 1000 ports

Run a SYN scan against the default top 1000 ports to get a broad view of the target's attack surface. The -sS flag performs a stealth scan that does not complete the TCP handshake and requires sudo.

sudo nmap -sS <target-ip>

Review the output carefully. On a Windows 10 machine, you should expect to see several ports open; typically 135, 139, 445, 3389, and 5985. Compare this to a typical Linux server, which might only show port 22 (SSH) and port 80 (HTTP). Windows exposes more services by default because its networking model is built around SMB, RPC, and remote management.

Note any additional open ports beyond the five listed above. Windows machines in enterprise environments often run additional services; MSSQL (1433), IIS (80/443), or LDAP (389/636); depending on their role.

Record Your Findings

Port State Service
  • Total open ports: ___
  • Any unexpected ports? ___

docs.title: Step 3: Service Version Detection
docs.text:
Fingerprint the service versions

Now probe the open ports to identify the exact service versions running behind them. The -sV flag triggers version detection, and -p restricts the probe to the five Windows ports.

nmap -sV -p 135,139,445,3389,5985 <target-ip>

The output shows the service name and version for each port. For Windows services, you will typically see entries like:

  • 135/tcp: Microsoft Windows RPC
  • 139/tcp: Microsoft Windows netbios-ssn
  • 445/tcp: microsoft-ds (Microsoft Directory Services, i.e., SMB)
  • 3389/tcp: ms-wbt-server (Microsoft Windows-Based Terminal, i.e., RDP)
  • 5985/tcp: Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0 (WinRM running on HTTP.sys)

The version strings confirm that this is a Windows system. The microsoft-ds label on port 445 is particularly important; it tells you SMB is available for enumeration, which is the focus of the next exercise.

Record Your Findings

Port Service Version String 135 139 445 3389 5985

docs.title: Step 4: OS Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Fingerprint the operating system

Use nmap's OS detection to confirm the exact Windows version. The -O flag analyzes TCP/IP stack behavior and requires sudo.

sudo nmap -O <target-ip>

The output includes several important fields:

  • OS CPE: A standardized identifier like cpe:/o:microsoft:windows_10 that uniquely identifies the operating system
  • OS guesses: One or more guesses with confidence percentages, such as Microsoft Windows 10 1709 - 1909 (93%)
  • Network Distance: The number of hops to the target

OS fingerprinting works by analyzing subtle differences in how operating systems implement the TCP/IP stack; window sizes, TTL values, TCP options, and response patterns to unusual packets. Different Windows versions have distinct fingerprints.

Record Your Findings

  • OS CPE: ___
  • Best OS guess: ___
  • Confidence: ___%
  • Network distance: ___ hops

docs.title: Step 5: NetBIOS Information
docs.text:
Extract NetBIOS information

Extract the target's NetBIOS name, workgroup, and MAC address using nmap's nbstat script. The --script nbstat option runs the NetBIOS statistics NSE script against the host.

nmap --script nbstat <target-ip>

The output reveals:

  • NetBIOS name: The computer's hostname as registered on the network
  • NetBIOS user: The currently logged-in user (if available)
  • Workgroup/Domain: Whether the machine belongs to a workgroup or Active Directory domain
  • MAC address: The physical network adapter address and its vendor

The NetBIOS data is valuable for mapping the target environment. The hostname often reveals the machine's purpose (e.g., FINANCE-WS01, DC01, FILESERVER). The workgroup or domain name tells you about the network architecture. The MAC address vendor can identify the hardware manufacturer or virtualization platform.

Record Your Findings

  • NetBIOS name: ___
  • Workgroup/Domain: ___
  • MAC address: ___
  • MAC vendor: ___

docs.title: Step 6: SMB OS Discovery (Find the Flag)
docs.text:
Query SMB for OS details and the flag

Run the SMB OS discovery script to extract detailed operating system information directly from the SMB service. The --script smb-os-discovery option queries SMB and often reveals more detail than OS fingerprinting alone.

nmap --script smb-os-discovery <target-ip>

Examine the output carefully. The script returns:

  • OS: The full Windows version string
  • Computer name: The NetBIOS and DNS hostname
  • Domain/Workgroup: Active Directory domain or workgroup membership
  • System time: The target's current date and time
  • Computer description: A free-text field set by the administrator

The computer description field contains the flag for this exercise, in the form:

OCR{...}

Administrators often set computer descriptions for asset management purposes, but they rarely realize this field is readable by anyone who can reach port 445. In a real assessment, this field sometimes contains internal documentation, IP addresses of other systems, or administrator notes; all of which is useful for further reconnaissance.

Record Your Findings

  • OS version: ___
  • Computer name: ___
  • Domain/Workgroup: ___
  • Computer description: ___
  • Flag: ___

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. How does a Windows scan profile differ from a typical Linux scan profile?

Reveal Answer

A default Windows machine typically exposes 5 or more services (RPC on 135, NetBIOS on 139, SMB on 445, RDP on 3389, WinRM on 5985), while a hardened Linux server often shows only SSH (22) and the application port (80 or 443). Windows exposes more services because its networking model depends on RPC for management, SMB for file sharing and Group Policy, and RDP for remote administration. Each additional open port increases the attack surface. The expanded surface is why Windows hardening guides emphasize disabling unnecessary services and using host-based firewalls to restrict access to essential ports only.

2. What is the security significance of port 445 (SMB)?

Reveal Answer

Port 445 is the most security-critical port on any Windows machine. SMB has been the target of devastating exploits, most notably EternalBlue (MS17-010), which was exploited by the WannaCry and NotPetya ransomware campaigns in 2017. Beyond remote code execution vulnerabilities, SMB also enables null session enumeration (listing shares, users, and groups without credentials), credential relay attacks (NTLM relay), and lateral movement using tools like PsExec and Impacket. If port 445 is open and accessible, the machine is exposed to a wide range of attacks. Best practice is to block SMB at the perimeter firewall and restrict internal SMB access to only the systems that require it.

3. Why does Windows expose RPC (port 135) and dynamically assigned high-numbered RPC ports?

Port 135 is the RPC Endpoint Mapper, a directory service that tells clients which high-numbered port a specific RPC service is listening on. When a client wants to use DCOM (Distributed Component Object Model) or WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation), it first queries port 135 to find the dynamic port assigned to that service, then connects to that port directly. The endpoint-mapper design means that blocking port 135 breaks many Windows management tools, but leaving it open exposes the RPC service directory to anyone on the network. Attackers use RPC enumeration to discover available services, identify the OS version, and find additional attack vectors. In segmented networks, RPC traffic should be restricted to management VLANs.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Windows machines expose significantly more network services by default than Linux systems, creating a larger attack surface that must be understood and managed
  • The five core Windows ports (135, 139, 445, 3389, 5985) each serve a distinct function in the Windows networking model, and each represents a potential attack vector
  • SMB (port 445) is the highest-priority finding in any Windows scan due to its history of critical vulnerabilities and its central role in lateral movement
  • Nmap scripts like nbstat and smb-os-discovery extract valuable metadata (hostname, domain, OS version, description) without requiring any credentials
  • OS fingerprinting, service version detection, and NSE scripts provide complementary information; use all three together for the most complete picture of the target

Next: Exercise 1.2; Remote Enumeration & Data Discovery

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
this exercise builds directly on Exercise 1.1. You identified SMB (port 445) as an open service on the Windows target. Now you will probe that service to enumerate shares, discover user accounts, and search for exposed credentials. All commands run from your Kali machine; you do not need RDP access for this exercise.

Make sure you have:

  • Completed Exercise 1.1 (Windows Reconnaissance)
  • Your Kali machine connected to the lab network (VPN active or RangeBox session running)
  • smbclient installed (smbclient --version)
  • enum4linux installed (enum4linux shows usage)
  • Target IP noted from the Active Lab panel; replace <target-ip> in the commands below

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your reconnaissance in Exercise 1.1 confirmed that the Meridian Technologies workstation exposes SMB on port 445. The assessment lead wants you to determine what data is accessible through SMB; both anonymously and with any credentials you can discover. In enterprise environments, misconfigured SMB shares are one of the most common sources of data exposure. Sensitive files; credentials, network diagrams, configuration backups; are routinely left on shares with overly permissive access controls. Your task is to find out exactly what Meridian has exposed.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• List all SMB shares available on the target
  • Enumerate local user accounts using null session access
  • Access publicly readable shares and examine their contents
  • Discover exposed credentials in accessible files
  • Use found credentials to access restricted shares
  • Retrieve the flag from a protected share

docs.title: Background: SMB Protocol and Share Permissions
docs.text: SMB (Server Message Block) is the protocol Windows uses for file and printer sharing. When you open \\server\share in Windows Explorer, you are using SMB. The protocol handles authentication, authorization, and data transfer.

docs.title: Null Sessions
docs.text:
A null session is an unauthenticated SMB connection; the client connects without providing a username or password. On older or misconfigured Windows systems, null sessions can enumerate shares, list user accounts, and even read certain shares. Null session access persists because of a legacy Windows feature that allowed anonymous access to IPC$ (Inter-Process Communication) for network browsing.

Modern Windows versions (10/11, Server 2016+) restrict null sessions by default, but administrators often relax these restrictions for compatibility with legacy applications, monitoring tools, or backup systems.

docs.title: Share Types
docs.text: Share Type Example Description Custom shares Public, IT_Docs Created by administrators for specific purposes. Permissions vary widely. Administrative shares ADMIN$, C$ Hidden shares that map to system directories. Require administrator credentials. The $ suffix hides them from casual browsing. IPC$ IPC$ Inter-Process Communication share. Used for null sessions, named pipes, and RPC. Not a file share; you cannot browse files on IPC$.

docs.title: How Credentials Flow
docs.text:
When you connect to an SMB share, Windows uses NTLM or Kerberos authentication. The client sends credentials (or a null session request), the server validates them against its local Security Account Manager (SAM) database or Active Directory, and grants or denies access based on the share permissions and NTFS permissions combined.

The weakest link in this chain is almost always the share permissions. Administrators set NTFS permissions carefully but forget that the share itself also has a permission layer. A share set to "Everyone: Full Control" with restrictive NTFS permissions still allows enumeration of the share contents; and if the NTFS permissions are also misconfigured, full read/write access.

docs.title: Tool Primer: SMB Enumeration Tools
docs.text:
Tool Purpose Key Options smbclient Interactive SMB client (like FTP for SMB). Lists shares, browses directories, downloads files. -N (null session, no password), -L (list shares), -U user%pass (authenticate) enum4linux Automated Windows/SMB enumeration. Extracts users, groups, shares, password policy, and OS info from null sessions. -U (users), -S (shares), -a (all), -r (RID cycling for users) smbmap Maps SMB share permissions. Shows read/write access for each share at a glance. -H (host), -u/-p (credentials), --no-banner crackmapexec Multi-protocol offensive tool. Tests credentials across multiple hosts, enumerates shares, and executes commands. smb (protocol), --shares (list shares), -u/-p (credentials)

For this exercise, you will primarily use smbclient and enum4linux. These tools are pre-installed on most penetration testing distributions including Kali Linux.

docs.title: Step 1: List Available Shares
docs.text:
List SMB shares via null session

Use smbclient to list all SMB shares on the target using a null session (no credentials). The -N flag uses a null session with no password prompt, and -L requests a share listing.

smbclient -N -L //<target-ip>

Review the output, which should show both custom and default shares:

Share Type Description Public Disk Public file share IT_Docs Disk IT documentation Backups Disk System backups IPC$ IPC IPC Service ADMIN$ Disk Remote Admin C$ Disk Default share

The custom shares (Public, IT_Docs, Backups) are the ones worth investigating. The administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$) require administrator credentials and will be inaccessible with null or low-privilege sessions. IPC$ is not a file share but confirms that null session access is allowed, which means other enumeration tools will also work.

Record Your Findings

  • Total shares listed: ___
  • Custom shares found: ___
  • Administrative shares: ___
  • Null session to IPC$ allowed (yes/no): ___

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate User Accounts
docs.text:
Enumerate local user accounts

Use enum4linux to extract the list of local user accounts via null session. The -U flag requests user enumeration; enum4linux queries the target's SAM database through the IPC$ null session and returns a list of local accounts.

enum4linux -U <target-ip>

You should see output similar to:

user:[Administrator] rid:[0x1f4]
user:[LabUser] rid:[0x3e8]
user:[admin.backup] rid:[0x3e9]
user:[svc_scanner] rid:[0x3ea]
user:[svc_updater] rid:[0x3eb]

Analyze the account names:

  • Administrator: Built-in admin account. Expected on every Windows system.
  • LabUser: The standard lab account. You will use this account for RDP in Exercise 1.3.
  • admin.backup: Naming convention suggests a backup administrator account. Service accounts with "admin" in the name often have elevated privileges.
  • svc_scanner: A service account, likely for a vulnerability scanner or monitoring tool.
  • svc_updater: Another service account. Service accounts are frequently targeted because they often have weak passwords and broad permissions.

In a real assessment, this user list would feed directly into a password attack. Knowing valid usernames eliminates half the guesswork in a brute-force attempt.

Record Your Findings

  • Number of accounts discovered: ___
  • Account names: ___
  • Which accounts appear to be service accounts? ___
  • Which account names suggest elevated privileges? ___

docs.title: Step 3: Access the Public Share
docs.text:
Browse the Public share

Connect to the Public share using a null session and explore its contents. The -N flag keeps the session anonymous.

smbclient //<target-ip>/Public -N

You are now in an interactive SMB session. Use standard commands to list and download files:

smb: \> ls
smb: \> get readme.txt
smb: \> get network_diagram.txt
smb: \> exit

The get commands copy each file to your Kali working directory before you exit the session.

Read the downloaded files

After downloading the files, examine their contents on your Kali machine.

cat readme.txt
cat network_diagram.txt

The readme.txt file contains a welcome message and basic instructions for Meridian employees. The network_diagram.txt contains an ASCII network diagram showing internal subnets, server names, and IP addresses. In a real engagement, network diagrams found on public shares are extremely valuable; they map the entire internal environment without any scanning.

Record Your Findings

  • Files found on Public share: ___
  • Useful information in readme.txt: ___
  • Network information discovered in network_diagram.txt: ___

docs.title: Step 4: Access the IT_Docs Share
docs.text:
Browse the IT_Docs share

Connect to the IT_Docs share using a null session, then list and download any files you find.

smbclient //<target-ip>/IT_Docs -N

From the interactive prompt, pull down the documents:

smb: \> ls
smb: \> get old_credentials.txt
smb: \> exit

The old_credentials.txt filename is an immediate red flag; credentials stored on a readable share are a common real-world exposure.

Read the exposed credential file

Examine the downloaded file on your Kali machine.

cat old_credentials.txt

The file old_credentials.txt contains credentials for the admin.backup account:

admin.backup / B@ckup2024#

The admin.backup credential is a critical finding. An IT documentation share accessible via null session contains plaintext credentials for a backup administrator account. Credential exposure of this kind is alarmingly common in real environments; IT teams store passwords in text files on shared drives for convenience, and those shares are often readable by far more people (or systems) than intended.

The account name admin.backup combined with a password containing "Backup" and the current year follows a predictable pattern. In a real assessment, you would test these credentials against every service that accepts authentication: SMB, RDP, WinRM, and any web applications.

Record Your Findings

  • Files found on IT_Docs share: ___
  • Credentials discovered: ___
  • Account name: ___
  • Password: ___

docs.title: Step 5: Access the Restricted Share with Found Credentials
docs.text:
Access the Backups share with found credentials

The Backups share was listed in Step 1 but likely requires authentication. Test the credentials you discovered in Step 4. The -U user%password syntax provides credentials inline.

smbclient //<target-ip>/Backups -U admin.backup%'B@ckup2024#'

If authentication succeeds, you will see the smb: \> prompt. Browse and download the flag:

smb: \> ls
smb: \> get flag-part.txt
smb: \> exit

Reaching the prompt confirms the discovered credentials are valid against the protected share.

Read the flag file

Read the flag on your Kali machine.

cat flag-part.txt

The file contains a token in the form:

OCR{...}

The flag confirms that you successfully progressed from anonymous share listing to credential discovery to authenticated access; the exact attack chain that real adversaries follow when targeting Windows file shares.

Record Your Findings

  • Authentication to Backups share succeeded (yes/no): ___
  • Files found on Backups share: ___
  • Flag: ___
  • What other files were on the Backups share? ___

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What is a null session, and why is it dangerous?

Reveal Answer

A null session is an unauthenticated SMB connection where the client provides no username and no password. It exploits the IPC$ share, which Windows uses for inter-process communication. When null sessions are allowed, an attacker can enumerate share names, user accounts, group memberships, and password policies ; all without any credentials. The enumerated data feeds directly into targeted attacks: knowing valid usernames enables password spraying, knowing share names reveals where sensitive data is stored, and knowing the password policy tells the attacker exactly what complexity requirements they need to meet. Null sessions should be disabled on all modern Windows systems by setting RestrictAnonymous = 1 in the registry.

2. How could Meridian have prevented the credential exposure you discovered?

Reveal Answer

Multiple layers of defense were missing. First, the IT_Docs share should not have been accessible via null session; requiring authentication would have prevented anonymous access. Second, plaintext credentials should never be stored in files on network shares. Password managers or vault solutions (like CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault, or even KeePass) should be used instead. Third, the admin.backup account password should follow a strong, unique pattern rather than a predictable format like B@ckup2024#. Finally, regular access reviews and file audits would identify sensitive files stored in inappropriate locations before an attacker finds them.

3. You found credentials on one share and used them to access another. How does this reflect real-world attacks?

This is a textbook example of credential reuse and privilege escalation through information gathering. Real attackers routinely chain together small findings ; a username from one source, a password from another, a share name from a third ; to build access incrementally. The MITRE ATT&CK framework catalogs this under T1552 (Unsecured Credentials) and T1021.002 (Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares). In many real breaches, the initial foothold comes not from a sophisticated exploit but from credentials found in a readable file share, a wiki page, a code repository, or a sticky note in a screenshot. Defending against this requires treating credential storage as a security-critical function, not a convenience shortcut.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SMB null sessions can expose share listings, user accounts, group memberships, and password policies without any authentication; always test for null session access during a Windows assessment
  • Credential exposure on file shares is one of the most common and impactful findings in real penetration tests; IT teams routinely store passwords in plaintext on network shares
  • The progression from anonymous enumeration to credential discovery to authenticated access is a realistic attack chain that defenders must anticipate
  • Tools like smbclient and enum4linux make SMB enumeration straightforward, but understanding what the results mean is more important than knowing the commands
  • Every user account discovered is a potential target for password attacks; service accounts (svc_*) and backup accounts (admin.backup) are high-value targets because they often have weak passwords and elevated privileges

Next: Exercise 1.3; Incident Investigation

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.3 is the capstone lab of Chapter F1 and the longest exercise in this chapter. You will connect to the Windows target via RDP and conduct a hands-on forensic investigation of a simulated breach. Unlike Exercises 1.1 and 1.2 where you worked from your Kali machine, this exercise requires you to work directly on the Windows desktop using native Windows tools: Event Viewer, the command prompt, and PowerShell.

The flag for this exercise is split into three parts hidden across different forensic artifacts. You must investigate the system thoroughly to find all three parts and assemble the complete flag.

Connection Details

Field Value RDP Command xfreerdp /v:<target-ip> /u:LabUser /p:Password123# /cert:ignore Username LabUser Password Password123#

Estimated time: 60-90 minutes. this exercise involves significant investigation. Keep a text file open on the Windows desktop to organize your notes as you work through each step.

Make sure you have:

  • Completed Exercises 1.1 and 1.2
  • xfreerdp installed on your Kali machine (xfreerdp --version)
  • Target IP noted from the Active Lab panel; replace <target-ip> below
  • Credentials ready: LabUser / Password123#

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Technologies' SOC has detected suspicious activity on the workstation you assessed in Exercises 1.1 and 1.2. Their SIEM flagged a series of failed login attempts from IP address 10.150.0.99: an address that does not belong to any known Meridian system; followed by a successful authentication. Shortly after, an unauthorized user account appeared in the local Administrators group, and anomalous scheduled tasks were registered on the system.

The SOC has preserved the machine in its current state and granted your team RDP access for investigation. Your task is to determine what the attacker did, how they maintained persistence, and what indicators of compromise (IOCs) they left behind. The engagement is no longer an assessment; it is incident response.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Connect to the target via RDP and orient yourself on the Windows desktop
  • Examine Windows Event Logs to identify the brute-force attack pattern
  • Identify unauthorized user accounts and group membership changes
  • Investigate suspicious scheduled tasks and decode encoded payloads
  • Check registry persistence mechanisms (Run keys)
  • Explore file system artifacts left by the attacker
  • Review PowerShell command history for attacker activity
  • Assemble the three-part flag from evidence found across the system
  • Construct a complete attack timeline

docs.title: Background: Windows Forensic Artifacts
docs.text: Windows maintains an extensive collection of artifacts that record system activity. During an incident investigation, these artifacts tell the story of what happened, when it happened, and often who did it. Understanding where to look is half the battle.

docs.title: Windows Event Logs
docs.text:
Windows Event Logs are the primary source of security telemetry on a Windows system. They are stored in .evtx files under C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\ and are accessed through Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) or PowerShell (Get-WinEvent). The three most important logs for incident response are:

  • Security Log: Authentication events, privilege use, policy changes
  • System Log: Service starts/stops, driver loading, system errors
  • Application Log: Application-specific events, including custom logging

The following Event IDs are critical for detecting unauthorized access and persistence:

Event ID Log What It Records 4624 Security Successful logon. Includes logon type, source IP, and account name. 4625 Security Failed logon. Same fields as 4624; critical for detecting brute force. 4720 Security User account created. Records the new account name and who created it. 4732 Security Member added to a security-enabled local group. Key for detecting privilege escalation. 1102 Security Audit log was cleared. Strong indicator of anti-forensic activity. 4688 Security A new process was created. When enabled, records every command executed. 7045 System A new service was installed. Used to detect persistence via service creation.

docs.title: Persistence Mechanisms
docs.text:
Attackers who gain access to a system want to maintain that access even if the machine reboots or the user logs out. Common Windows persistence mechanisms include:

  • Scheduled Tasks: Windows Task Scheduler can execute programs on a schedule or at system events (logon, startup). Attackers create scheduled tasks that run their malware automatically. Investigate with schtasks /query /fo LIST /v.

  • Registry Run Keys: The registry keys HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and the corresponding HKCU key execute programs every time a user logs on. These are among the oldest and most common persistence mechanisms. Check with reg query.

  • Services: Windows services run in the background with SYSTEM privileges. Attackers create malicious services that start automatically. Event ID 7045 records new service installations.

docs.title: PowerShell Artifacts
docs.text:
PowerShell is the attacker's tool of choice on Windows. It provides full access to the .NET framework, Windows APIs, and system management functions; all from a command line that can be scripted and obfuscated.

Key PowerShell artifacts:

  • ConsoleHost_history.txt: PowerShell records every command typed in an interactive session to C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt. This file persists across sessions and is rarely cleaned by attackers.

  • Script Block Logging: When enabled, records the full text of every PowerShell script that executes, including decoded versions of obfuscated scripts. Stored in the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational event log.

  • Base64 Encoding: Attackers frequently encode PowerShell commands in Base64 using the -EncodedCommand parameter. The encoding evades simple string-based detection but is trivially decoded with [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String('...')).

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text: Tool / Command What It Does eventvwr.msc Opens Event Viewer GUI. Navigate to Windows Logs > Security/System/Application. net user Lists all local user accounts. net user <username> Shows detailed information about a specific account (creation date, group membership, last logon). net localgroup Administrators Lists members of the local Administrators group. schtasks /query /fo LIST /v Lists all scheduled tasks with full details (trigger, command, author). reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" Shows programs that auto-run at user logon (machine-wide). reg query "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" Shows programs that auto-run at logon (current user only). powershell -c "[System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String('...'))" Decodes a Base64-encoded Unicode string.

docs.title: Step 1: Connect via RDP
docs.text:
Open an RDP session to the target

From your Kali terminal, initiate an RDP session to the Windows target. The /cert:ignore flag bypasses the self-signed certificate warning.

xfreerdp /v:<target-ip> /u:LabUser /p:Password123# /cert:ignore

Once connected, you should see the Windows 10 desktop. Open a Command Prompt (cmd.exe); you will use it extensively throughout this investigation.

Take a moment to orient yourself. Note the computer name in the system properties, the current date/time, and any unusual icons or files on the desktop. Investigators always document the initial state of the system before making any changes.

docs.title: Step 2: Examine Event Viewer
docs.text:
Open Event Viewer by typing eventvwr.msc in the Start menu search or Run dialog.

Navigate to Windows Logs > Application. In the Application log, look for events from a source called SecuritySimulation. These events record the simulated attack activity. To filter for them:

  1. In Event Viewer, click Filter Current Log in the right panel
  2. In the Event sources dropdown, type or select SecuritySimulation
  3. Click OK to apply the filter

Review the filtered events chronologically (oldest first). You will see a pattern that tells the story of the attack:

  • Eight failed login attempts from IP 10.150.0.99: the attacker tried multiple passwords against the local accounts
  • One successful login: the attacker found valid credentials
  • Account creation and privilege escalation events: the attacker established persistence

Look carefully at the description field of the event that records the successful brute force completion. It contains Flag Part 1:

Flag Part 1: 1nc1d3nt

Write this down. You will need all three parts to assemble the complete flag at the end of the investigation.

Record Your Findings

  • Number of failed login events: ___
  • Source IP of the attacker: ___
  • Which account was successfully compromised? ___
  • Flag Part 1: ___
  • Timestamp of the first failed attempt: ___
  • Timestamp of the successful login: ___

docs.title: Step 3: Identify Unauthorized Accounts
docs.text:
List local user accounts on the target

In the Command Prompt on the Windows desktop, list all local user accounts.

net user

Compare this list to the accounts you discovered remotely in Exercise 1.2. Look for any account that was not present before or that seems out of place.

Check the Administrators group

Still on the Windows host, check who belongs to the local Administrators group.

net localgroup Administrators

You should find that the svc_updater account is a member of the local Administrators group. In Exercise 1.2, you enumerated this account, but now you need to determine whether it is legitimate. The name suggests a Windows Update service account, but legitimate Windows Update does not use a local user account; it runs as the built-in SYSTEM account.

Record Your Findings

  • Accounts listed by net user: ___
  • Members of the Administrators group: ___
  • Which account appears unauthorized? ___

docs.title: Step 4: Examine the Backdoor Account
docs.text:
Inspect the suspicious account

On the Windows host, get detailed information about the suspicious account.

net user svc_updater

Review the output carefully:

  • Full Name: May be blank or contain a misleading name
  • Comment/Description: Look for Windows Update Service or similar. A label like that is a social engineering tactic; the attacker named the account to look legitimate at a glance
  • Account active: Should show Yes
  • Last logon: When was this account last used?
  • Password last set: When was it created?
  • Local Group Memberships: Confirms Administrators group membership

The description field saying "Windows Update Service" is a red flag. Real Windows services run under built-in accounts (SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE), not under custom local accounts. An attacker created this account to blend in with legitimate services; a common persistence technique.

Record Your Findings

  • Account description: ___
  • Account active: ___
  • Last logon time: ___
  • Group memberships: ___
  • Why is this account suspicious? ___

docs.title: Step 5: Investigate Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Query scheduled tasks for persistence

Attackers use scheduled tasks to maintain persistence and execute commands automatically. On the Windows host, query all scheduled tasks and filter for the task name, the command, and the author.

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr /i "task\|command\|author"

Scroll through the output and look for tasks that:

  • Have unusual names that mimic legitimate Windows tasks
  • Execute PowerShell with encoded commands
  • Were authored by an unexpected user account
  • Trigger at logon or system startup

You should find a task named WindowsUpdateCheck that stands out. Note its properties:

  • Task Name: \WindowsUpdateCheck
  • Trigger: At logon (runs every time any user logs in)
  • Action: Executes powershell.exe with a -EncodedCommand parameter
  • Author: The compromised or attacker-created account

A legitimate Windows Update task would be authored by Microsoft and would not use encoded PowerShell commands. The task is attacker-created persistence.

Record Your Findings

  • Suspicious task name: ___
  • Trigger type: ___
  • Command executed: ___
  • Author: ___
  • Base64-encoded payload: ___

docs.title: Step 6: Decode the Base64 Payload
docs.text:
The scheduled task from Step 5 runs a Base64-encoded PowerShell command. Decode it to reveal the attacker's payload.

Decode the Base64 PowerShell payload

Open PowerShell on the Windows host (type powershell in the Command Prompt) and run the decoder. The one-liner converts the Base64 string from Unicode bytes back to readable text.

powershell -c "[System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String('UABpAG4AZwAgADEAMAAuADEANQAwAC4AMAAuADkAOQA='))"

The decoded output is:

Ping 10.150.0.99

The ping is a callback to the attacker's IP address (10.150.0.99). Every time a user logs in, the scheduled task pings the attacker's machine; a basic heartbeat mechanism that tells the attacker the compromised system is online. In a real attack, this would be replaced with a reverse shell or C2 beacon, but the principle is identical: the persistence mechanism phones home automatically.

Now examine the full encoded command from the scheduled task. The complete payload contains a comment with Flag Part 2. Decode the full Base64 string found in the task definition:

Flag Part 2: r3sp0ns3

Record Your Findings

  • Decoded command: ___
  • Attacker callback IP: ___
  • Purpose of the scheduled task: ___
  • Flag Part 2: ___

docs.title: Step 7: Check Registry Persistence
docs.text:
Check the machine-wide Run key

Attackers frequently add entries to the Windows Run registry keys so their tools execute automatically at logon. On the Windows host, check the machine-wide Run key.

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

A non-standard entry here runs for every user on the machine, which makes the HKLM key a high-value persistence location.

Check the current-user Run key

Now check the current user Run key for entries scoped to the logged-in account.

reg query "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

In the HKLM Run key, you should find an entry named WindowsUpdateHelper that points to a PowerShell script:

WindowsUpdateHelper    REG_SZ    powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\update_helper.ps1

Analyze this entry:

  • -WindowStyle Hidden: The PowerShell window is invisible to the user
  • -ExecutionPolicy Bypass: Script execution restrictions are overridden
  • -File C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\update_helper.ps1: The script runs from a temporary directory, not a legitimate Program Files location

Every element of this command is a red flag. Legitimate software installs to C:\Program Files, does not bypass execution policies, and does not hide its windows. The registry key ensures the attacker's script runs silently every time the system starts.

Record Your Findings

  • Registry key path: ___
  • Entry name: ___
  • Command value: ___
  • Script location: ___
  • Why is this suspicious? ___

docs.title: Step 8: Explore File System Artifacts
docs.text:
List the attacker's tool directory

Based on the registry entry from Step 7, the attacker stored tools in C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\. On the Windows host, list this directory.

dir C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\

You should find several attacker files:

File Contents dump.txt Credential hashes dumped from the local SAM database recon.txt Network reconnaissance output; IP ranges, hostnames, open ports update_helper.ps1 The PowerShell script from the registry Run key; contains a reverse shell or callback mechanism

Read the attacker's dropped files

Display the contents of each file the attacker left behind.

type C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\dump.txt
type C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\recon.txt
type C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\update_helper.ps1

The dump.txt file contains NTLM hashes; evidence that the attacker ran a credential dumping tool (like Mimikatz or secretsdump) to harvest passwords from the local Security Account Manager. The recon.txt file shows the attacker was mapping the internal network for lateral movement targets. The update_helper.ps1 script contains the persistence payload.

Read the PowerShell command history

Next, check the PowerShell command history. The history file records every command the attacker typed in an interactive PowerShell session.

type C:\Users\LabUser\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

Review the history for commands that reveal the attacker's methodology; account creation, scheduled task registration, credential dumping, and network reconnaissance. The history file is often the most revealing artifact in a Windows investigation because it captures the attacker's exact sequence of actions in chronological order.

Record Your Findings

  • Files found in svc_tools directory: ___
  • What credentials were dumped (hash type): ___
  • What network ranges were scanned: ___
  • What does update_helper.ps1 do? ___
  • Key commands from PowerShell history: ___

docs.title: Step 9: Retrieve Flag Part 3
docs.text:
Retrieve the final flag part

The final piece of the flag has been placed in a forensic evidence directory. On the Windows host, read it.

type C:\forensic_evidence\flag.txt

The file contains:

Flag Part 3: c0mpl3t3

Record Your Findings

  • Flag Part 3: ___
  • Location of the flag file: ___

docs.title: Step 10: Assemble the Complete Flag
docs.text:
You have collected all three flag parts from different forensic artifacts across the system. Combine them to form the complete flag:

Part Source Value Part 1 Event Viewer (Application log, SecuritySimulation) <part1> Part 2 Scheduled Task (Base64-decoded payload comment) <part2> Part 3 File system (C:\forensic_evidence\flag.txt) <part3>

Complete flag:

OCR{<part1>_<part2>_<part3>}

The flag parts were deliberately scattered across different artifact categories to reinforce the principle that a thorough investigation examines all available evidence sources; logs, accounts, tasks, registry, file system, and command history. Checking only one category misses parts of the story.

docs.title: Attack Timeline
docs.text:
Assemble your findings into a chronological timeline of the attack. The timeline is the deliverable you would present to Meridian's incident response team.

Time Event ID / Source Source IP Action Evidence Location T+0 4625 (Security) 10.150.0.99 First failed login attempt; brute force begins Event Viewer > Application > SecuritySimulation T+2 min 4625 (Security) 10.150.0.99 Failed login attempts continue (8 total) Event Viewer > Application > SecuritySimulation T+5 min 4624 (Security) 10.150.0.99 Successful login; attacker gains access Event Viewer > Application > SecuritySimulation T+7 min 4720 (Security) Local svc_updater account created net user svc_updater T+8 min 4732 (Security) Local svc_updater added to Administrators group net localgroup Administrators T+10 min Task created Local WindowsUpdateCheck scheduled task registered schtasks /query T+12 min Registry modified Local WindowsUpdateHelper Run key added reg query HKLM\...\Run T+15 min File creation Local Attacker tools deployed to C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\ dir C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\ T+20 min Credential dump Local SAM database hashes extracted C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\dump.txt T+25 min Network recon Local Internal network scanned for lateral movement C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\recon.txt

The timeline shows that the attacker moved from initial brute force to full persistence and credential harvesting in approximately 25 minutes. Every stage left evidence in a different artifact category, and every stage represented a detection opportunity that was missed.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The attacker created a scheduled task and a registry Run key for persistence. Why use two different mechanisms?

Redundancy. If a defender discovers and removes the scheduled task, the registry Run key still executes the attacker's payload at next logon. If they find and clean the registry key, the scheduled task still fires. Sophisticated attackers install multiple persistence mechanisms so that removing one does not evict them from the system. During remediation, incident responders must identify and remove ALL persistence mechanisms; missing even one means the attacker retains access.

2. What indicators of compromise (IOCs) would you extract from this investigation for your threat intelligence team?

IP address: 10.150.0.99 (attacker source). Account name: svc_updater (backdoor account). Scheduled task name: WindowsUpdateCheck. Registry value: WindowsUpdateHelper. File paths: C:\Windows\Temp\svc_tools\*. PowerShell command patterns: Base64-encoded commands with -WindowStyle Hidden and -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. These IOCs should be searched across all systems in the environment to determine if the attacker compromised other machines using the same tools and techniques.

3. The attacker used the account name svc_updater with the description "Windows Update Service." How does this demonstrate social engineering at the system level?

The attacker chose an account name and description that mimic a legitimate Windows service to avoid detection during casual review. An administrator running net user or viewing the account in Computer Management might glance at "svc_updater" and assume it belongs to a legitimate update service. The deception is social engineering applied to system artifacts rather than humans. Defenders should maintain an authoritative list of approved service accounts and alert on any new account creation, especially accounts added to the Administrators group.

4. Why is the PowerShell ConsoleHost_history.txt file so valuable for forensic investigation?

ConsoleHost_history.txt records every command typed in an interactive PowerShell session, in chronological order, across all sessions. Unlike event logs which may be cleared (Event ID 1102), many attackers forget that this file exists. It provides a complete record of the attacker's manual activity; account creation commands, tool execution, credential dumping, reconnaissance; in the exact order they were performed. The file is often the single most informative artifact on a compromised Windows system.

5. The scheduled task payload decoded to Ping 10.150.0.99. In a real attack, what would this likely be replaced with?

A real attacker would replace the simple ping with a reverse shell (connecting back to their command-and-control server), a PowerShell download cradle (fetching and executing a remote payload), or a C2 beacon (such as Cobalt Strike, Sliver, or Metasploit). The ping serves the same conceptual purpose; it contacts the attacker's infrastructure; but a real payload would establish an interactive command channel. The Base64 encoding technique is identical in both cases, making this exercise exercise directly applicable to real-world investigations.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Windows Event Logs are the first place to look in any incident investigation ; Event IDs 4624/4625 (logon success/failure), 4720 (account creation), and 4732 (group membership change) tell the authentication story
  • Attackers create accounts that mimic legitimate services to blend in; always verify new accounts against an approved service account list
  • Scheduled tasks and registry Run keys are the two most common persistence mechanisms on Windows; check both during every investigation
  • Base64-encoded PowerShell commands are trivially decoded; the encoding evades casual inspection but not forensic analysis
  • The PowerShell ConsoleHost_history.txt file is an often-overlooked artifact that records the attacker's exact command sequence
  • Attacker tools and outputs (credential dumps, recon data) are frequently left on disk in temporary directories; always check C:\Windows\Temp\ and user profile temp directories
  • A complete investigation examines all artifact categories (logs, accounts, tasks, registry, file system, command history); checking only one category misses critical evidence

Next: Chapter F1; Review

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Over three labs, you built a complete Windows forensics workflow; from external network reconnaissance through SMB credential discovery to full incident investigation on a compromised host. You can now scan Windows targets, enumerate shares and users, connect via RDP, and investigate a breach using native Windows forensic artifacts.

Each lab introduced new tools and techniques, but the investigative methodology stayed consistent:

  1. Identify what is exposed; services, shares, accounts.
  2. Determine what is accessible; null sessions, weak permissions, found credentials.
  3. Investigate what happened; event logs, persistence mechanisms, attacker artifacts.
  4. Document everything; timelines, IOCs, evidence locations.

By the final lab, you were applying all four steps simultaneously across multiple artifact categories in a single investigation.

docs.title: The Progression You Followed
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["1.1 Reconnaissance"] --> B["1.2 Enumeration"]
    B --> C["1.3 Incident Investigation"]
    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
Exercise Focus What You Detected 1.1 Network Reconnaissance Open Windows services (SMB, RPC, RDP, WinRM), OS version, hostname 1.2 SMB Enumeration Null session access, exposed credentials, restricted share access 1.3 Incident Investigation Brute-force attack, backdoor account, persistence mechanisms, attacker tools

Each lab built directly on the previous one:

  • Exercise 1.1 taught you to identify Windows services from the network using nmap, nmap scripts, and OS fingerprinting.
  • Exercise 1.2 used the SMB service discovered in Exercise 1.1 to enumerate shares, discover user accounts, find exposed credentials, and access restricted data.
  • Exercise 1.3 pivoted from external assessment to internal investigation, using Windows Event Viewer, scheduled tasks, registry keys, and PowerShell history to reconstruct a complete attack timeline.

docs.title: Windows Forensic Investigation Checklist
docs.text: Use this checklist as a step-by-step guide when investigating any compromised Windows system. The checklist generalizes the methodology you practiced in Exercise 1.3 for any incident.

docs.title: Phase 1: Initial Assessment
docs.text:
• Document the date, time, and reason for investigation
  • Record the system hostname, IP address, and OS version
  • Note the current logged-in users
  • Take a screenshot of the desktop for documentation

docs.title: Phase 2: Event Log Analysis
docs.text:
• Open Event Viewer and review the Security log
  • Filter for Event ID 4625 (failed logons); look for brute-force patterns
  • Filter for Event ID 4624 (successful logons); identify suspicious sessions
  • Filter for Event ID 4720 (account creation); find unauthorized accounts
  • Filter for Event ID 4732 (group membership changes); detect privilege escalation
  • Check for Event ID 1102 (log cleared); anti-forensic activity
  • Review the System log for Event ID 7045 (new services installed)
  • Check the Application log for custom or unusual event sources

docs.title: Phase 3: Account Investigation
docs.text:
• Run net user and compare against known-good account list
  • Run net localgroup Administrators: verify every member is authorized
  • For each suspicious account: net user <name>: check creation date, description, last logon
  • Look for accounts mimicking service names (svc_, admin., backup*)

docs.title: Phase 4: Persistence Mechanisms
docs.text:
• Check scheduled tasks: schtasks /query /fo LIST /v
  • Check HKLM Run key: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
  • Check HKCU Run key: reg query "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
  • Check services: sc query type= all state= all (look for unusual entries)
  • Check startup folders: dir "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
  • Decode any Base64-encoded payloads found in tasks or registry values

docs.title: Phase 5: File System Artifacts
docs.text:
• Check C:\Windows\Temp\ for attacker tools and output files
  • Check user profile temp directories: C:\Users\*\AppData\Local\Temp\
  • Review PowerShell history: ConsoleHost_history.txt in each user profile
  • Look for recently modified files in unusual locations
  • Check the Recycle Bin for deleted evidence

docs.title: Phase 6: Documentation
docs.text:
• Construct a complete attack timeline with timestamps
  • List all IOCs (IPs, domains, filenames, account names, hashes)
  • Document all persistence mechanisms found
  • Record all evidence locations and file paths
  • Recommend remediation actions

docs.title: Critical Windows Event IDs
docs.text:
Reference table of the most important Event IDs for incident response. These cover authentication, account management, privilege use, and anti-forensic activity.

Event ID Log Category What It Records 4624 Security Logon Successful logon (includes logon type, source IP, account) 4625 Security Logon Failed logon (same fields; critical for brute-force detection) 4634 Security Logon Account logoff 4648 Security Logon Logon using explicit credentials (runas, network logon) 4672 Security Logon Special privileges assigned to new logon (admin logon) 4688 Security Process New process created (requires audit policy configuration) 4689 Security Process Process exited 4720 Security Account User account created 4722 Security Account User account enabled 4724 Security Account Password reset attempted 4725 Security Account User account disabled 4726 Security Account User account deleted 4732 Security Group Member added to security-enabled local group 4733 Security Group Member removed from security-enabled local group 4735 Security Group Security-enabled local group was changed 1102 Security Audit Audit log was cleared (strong anti-forensic indicator) 7045 System Service New service installed (persistence mechanism) 7036 System Service Service started or stopped 4697 Security Service A service was installed in the system

docs.text: Logon Type Name Description 2 Interactive Local keyboard/console logon 3 Network SMB, mapped drive, or other network logon 7 Unlock Workstation unlocked 10 RemoteInteractive RDP logon 11 CachedInteractive Logon with cached domain credentials (offline)

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer these questions without looking at the answer key below. If you can answer all six confidently, you have internalized the core skills of this chapter.

  1. You run nmap -sS against a Windows machine and see ports 135, 139, 445, 3389, and 5985 open. What service runs on each port? (Exercise 1.1)

  2. What is a null session, and what information can you extract through one? (Exercise 1.2)

  3. You find a file called old_credentials.txt on a public SMB share. What should you do with the credentials inside? (Exercise 1.2)

  4. Event ID 4625 appears 50 times in 2 minutes from the same source IP. What attack is this? (Exercise 1.3)

  5. You find a scheduled task that runs powershell.exe -EncodedCommand <base64>. How do you decode it? (Exercise 1.3)

  6. Why should you check both scheduled tasks AND registry Run keys during an investigation? (Exercise 1.3)

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. Port 135 is RPC Endpoint Mapper, 139 is NetBIOS Session Service, 445 is SMB (file sharing), 3389 is RDP (Remote Desktop), and 5985 is WinRM (remote PowerShell management). Together, these form the standard Windows service profile visible from the network.

  2. A null session is an unauthenticated SMB connection to IPC$. Through null sessions, you can enumerate share names, user accounts, group memberships, and password policies without providing any credentials. Anonymous access works because of legacy Windows compatibility settings that allow unauthenticated connections to the IPC$ share.

  3. Test them against every authenticated service on the target: SMB, RDP, WinRM, and any web applications. Credentials found on one system often work on others due to password reuse. In this exercise, the credentials from IT_Docs granted access to the restricted Backups share.

  4. A brute-force attack. Fifty failed logon attempts in two minutes from a single source IP is a clear pattern of automated password guessing. Filter for Event ID 4624 from the same source to determine if any attempt eventually succeeded.

  5. Use PowerShell: [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String('<base64_string>')). The -EncodedCommand parameter accepts UTF-16LE-encoded Base64 strings, so you must decode using Unicode (UTF-16LE), not ASCII or UTF-8.

  6. Attackers use multiple persistence mechanisms for redundancy. If you find and remove a scheduled task but miss the registry Run key, the attacker's payload still executes at next logon. A thorough investigation checks all known persistence locations; scheduled tasks, Run keys, services, startup folders, and WMI event subscriptions; to ensure complete remediation.

docs.text:
