docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Plant 3 uses two completely different protocols (CIP and DNP3). What challenge does that create for an OT IDS deployment?

Reveal answer

Each protocol requires its own set of IDS dissectors and signature rules. A CIP-aware IDS cannot parse DNP3 frames and vice versa. Plant 3 needs either two specialized IDS deployments or a single platform (Zeek, Nozomi, Claroty) that ships with both CIP and DNP3 parsers. Signature tuning, baseline traffic models, and alert thresholds must be configured independently for each protocol. The operational cost of multi-protocol monitoring is roughly proportional to the number of distinct protocols on the segment.

2. The packaging PLC uses CIP (name-based tags) and the RTU uses DNP3 (group/index addressing). Which approach gives an attacker more information from the wire?

Reveal answer

CIP name-based tags are self-documenting. An attacker who enumerates the tag list learns ConveyorSpeed, PalletCount, and LineState without any external documentation. DNP3 group and index numbers (Group 1 index 0, Group 30 index 2) are meaningful only if the attacker has the outstation's point map. CIP therefore leaks more operational context to an unauthenticated network observer. The trade-off is that DNP3's obscurity is not a security control; it merely raises the effort required for the attacker to understand what each data point controls.

3. The flag format requires exact counts. Why is precision important in an OT asset inventory?

Reveal answer

An OT asset inventory is a security baseline. If the inventory says the PLC has 9 tags and a later audit finds 10, the 10th tag is either a new legitimate addition or an injected artifact (as in Exercise 5.2). Imprecise counts ("about 9" or "several") make change detection impossible. Every data point in the inventory must have an exact count, an exact name, and an exact data type so that deviations are detectable in future audits.

4. An assessor could scan Plant 3 with nmap before enumerating protocols. What additional information would a port scan provide beyond what Exercises 5.1 and 5.3 already revealed?

Reveal answer

A port scan (nmap -n -sS plc-packaging.masa.local dnp3-rtu.masa.local) would confirm which TCP ports are open and whether any unexpected services are listening (HTTP management interfaces, Telnet, FTP, or SNMP). Exercises 5.1 and 5.3 assumed the ports and protocols. A scan removes that assumption and may reveal additional attack surface that the protocol-specific exercises did not cover. In a real engagement, the port scan comes first.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Plant 3 runs two unauthenticated protocols (CIP and DNP3) on the same OT LAN Critical Segment CIP and DNP3 traffic into separate VLANs with a firewall between them, limiting lateral movement from one protocol domain to the other No unified OT asset inventory exists for Plant 3 High Establish a configuration management database (CMDB) that records every CIP tag and every DNP3 data point, with quarterly reconciliation audits Multi-protocol monitoring requires two distinct IDS rulesets Medium Deploy a multi-protocol OT monitoring platform (Nozomi, Claroty, or Dragos) that covers both CIP and DNP3 from a single sensor CIP tag names expose process semantics that DNP3 indexes do not Medium Restrict CIP network access more aggressively than DNP3 access because CIP leaks more actionable intelligence to an attacker

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A real OT assessment covers multiple protocols on the same network segment. Plant 3 uses CIP (TCP/44818) and DNP3 (TCP/20000)
  • CIP tag enumeration and DNP3 integrity polling are complementary skills. Both produce structured data point inventories
  • Exact counts matter. An asset report that says "9 CIP tags and 4 binary inputs" is useful. A report that says "some tags and some inputs" is not
  • Multi-protocol environments require multi-protocol monitoring. A CIP IDS cannot detect DNP3 anomalies
  • The assessor's job is to unify data from different protocols into a single coherent asset inventory that the plant manager can act on

docs.title: Why this matters

Detection engineering is where offensive skills become defensive value. Every attack you executed in Levels 1 through 5 left a network signature. A Modbus FC 6 from an unexpected source IP, an S7 write from outside the HMI subnet, a CIP Write Tag from an unauthorized host: each of these is a pattern a Snort rule can match. Writing those rules is the single most impactful defensive action Reyna can take before the next budget cycle, because it turns the existing Snort sensors (already deployed, already licensed) into ICS-aware monitors at zero additional cost.

The professional skill Exercise 6.1 builds is translating attack knowledge into detection logic. Penetration testers who can write the detection rules for their own findings are worth more to the client than testers who only write findings.

docs.title: Background: Snort Rule Syntax for ICS Protocols
docs.text:
Snort rules follow a consistent structure. Every rule has a header (action, protocol, source, destination) and an options block (content matches, metadata, SID).

action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options)

A concrete example for generic TCP traffic:

alert tcp any any -> any 502 (msg:"Modbus write from any source"; sid:999999; rev:1;)

docs.title: Key options for ICS detection
docs.text: Option Purpose Example msg Human-readable alert description msg:"Modbus FC6 from non-HMI"; content Byte pattern match in payload content:"\|00 06\|"; offset Start matching at byte N offset:7; depth Match within N bytes from offset depth:1; sid Unique signature ID sid:1000001; rev Rule revision number rev:1;

docs.title: Modbus over TCP frame structure
docs.text: Modbus TCP wraps the function code at byte offset 7 of the TCP payload (after the 7-byte MBAP header). Function Code 6 (Write Single Register) is the byte \x06 at offset 7. The legitimate HMI address ends in .5; any write from another source (such as .99) is suspicious.

docs.title: S7comm frame structure
docs.text: S7comm runs inside TPKT/COTP on TCP port 102. A Write PDU contains the S7 function byte \x05 (Write Var) in the S7 header. The exact offset varies by COTP negotiation, but the content match on \x05 combined with port 102 and a non-HMI source IP is sufficient for a first-pass rule.

docs.title: CIP frame structure
docs.text: CIP runs on TCP port 44818. The Write Tag service uses service code \x4D. Matching that byte in the CIP payload, combined with port 44818 and a non-HMI source IP, produces a targeted detection rule.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose curl Download PCAPs from the evidence server tcpdump or tshark Inspect PCAP contents and identify attack patterns snort Validate rules against PCAPs Text editor (nano, vim) Write the rules file

docs.title: Stage 1: Download All PCAPs
docs.text:
The evidence server hosts four files. Download all of them into a working directory so you can inspect them locally.

Kali

mkdir -p ~/icspt-detection && cd ~/icspt-detection
curl -O http://pcap-evidence.masa.local:8080/benign_baseline.pcap
curl -O http://pcap-evidence.masa.local:8080/plant1_modbus_attack.pcap
curl -O http://pcap-evidence.masa.local:8080/plant2_s7_attack.pcap
curl -O http://pcap-evidence.masa.local:8080/plant3_cip_attack.pcap
ls -lh *.pcap
Expected output 
-rw-r--r-- 1 kali kali  ...  benign_baseline.pcap
-rw-r--r-- 1 kali kali  ...  plant1_modbus_attack.pcap
-rw-r--r-- 1 kali kali  ...  plant2_s7_attack.pcap
-rw-r--r-- 1 kali kali  ...  plant3_cip_attack.pcap

All four files should be present and non-empty.

docs.title: Stage 2: Analyze the Plant 1 Attack PCAP (Modbus)
docs.text:
Before writing any rule, examine the attack traffic to confirm the detection-worthy pattern. The Plant 1 attack uses Modbus Function Code 6 (Write Single Register) from a source IP ending in .99 rather than the legitimate HMI at .5.

Kali

cd ~/icspt-detection
tcpdump -r plant1_modbus_attack.pcap -nn 'tcp port 502' | head -20

Look for packets from a .99 source address destined for port 502. Each Modbus TCP frame carries the function code at byte 7 of the payload. You can use tshark to extract the function code field directly.

Kali

tshark -r plant1_modbus_attack.pcap -Y "modbus.func_code == 6" -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e modbus.func_code
Expected output 
10.x.x.99    10.x.x.10    6

The source address .99 is not the authorized HMI (.5). Function code 6 means Write Single Register. Both facts together form the detection signature.

docs.title: Stage 3: Analyze the Plant 2 Attack PCAP (S7comm)
docs.text:
The Plant 2 attack sends an S7comm Write PDU on port 102 from a non-HMI source. Examine the capture to confirm.

Kali

tshark -r plant2_s7_attack.pcap -Y "s7comm" -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e s7comm.param.func
Expected output 
10.x.x.99    10.x.x.10    0x05

The S7 function 0x05 is Write Var. Any S7 write from a non-HMI source on port 102 is the detection pattern.

docs.title: Stage 4: Analyze the Plant 3 Attack PCAP (CIP)
docs.text:
The Plant 3 attack sends a CIP Write Tag (service code 0x4D) on port 44818 from a non-HMI source.

Kali

tshark -r plant3_cip_attack.pcap -Y "cip" -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e cip.service
Expected output 
10.x.x.99    10.x.x.10    0x4d

Service code 0x4D is CIP Write Tag. Combined with port 44818 and a non-HMI source, the pattern is clear.

docs.title: Stage 5: Write the Snort Rules
docs.text:
Now that you have confirmed all three attack patterns, write a rules file with three signatures. Each rule matches the protocol, the target port, and a content byte that identifies the write operation. The source IP is set to any rather than hardcoding .99 because the next attacker will use a different address. The key detection logic is "write operation from anything other than the HMI."

Create the rules file with the following three rules.

Kali

cat > ~/icspt-detection/masa_ics.rules << 'EOF'
# Plant 1: Modbus FC 6 (Write Single Register) from any source to port 502
# Byte \x06 at offset 7 in TCP payload (after 7-byte MBAP header)
alert tcp any any -> any 502 (msg:"MASA Modbus FC6 Write Single Register from non-HMI"; content:"|06|"; offset:7; depth:1; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

# Plant 2: S7comm Write Var (function 0x05) on port 102 from any source
alert tcp any any -> any 102 (msg:"MASA S7comm Write Var from non-HMI"; content:"|05|"; sid:1000002; rev:1;)

# Plant 3: CIP Write Tag (service 0x4D) on port 44818 from any source
alert tcp any any -> any 44818 (msg:"MASA CIP Write Tag from non-HMI"; content:"|4d|"; sid:1000003; rev:1;)
EOF
cat ~/icspt-detection/masa_ics.rules

Each rule targets the destination port for its protocol (502, 102, 44818) and matches the single byte that identifies the write operation. The msg field describes what the rule detects in plain language.

docs.title: Stage 6: Validate Against Attack PCAPs (True Positives)
docs.text:
Run Snort in packet-logging mode against each attack PCAP to confirm the corresponding rule fires. Each command below should produce at least one alert.

Kali

cd ~/icspt-detection
snort -r plant1_modbus_attack.pcap -c /dev/null -R masa_ics.rules -A console -q 2>&1 | grep "1000001"
Expected output 
... [1:1000001:1] MASA Modbus FC6 Write Single Register from non-HMI ...

Repeat for Plant 2 and Plant 3 to verify SIDs 1000002 and 1000003 fire on their respective PCAPs.

Kali

snort -r plant2_s7_attack.pcap -c /dev/null -R masa_ics.rules -A console -q 2>&1 | grep "1000002"
snort -r plant3_cip_attack.pcap -c /dev/null -R masa_ics.rules -A console -q 2>&1 | grep "1000003"

Both commands should return alert lines containing their respective SIDs.

docs.title: Stage 7: Validate Against Benign Baseline (False Positives)
docs.text:
Run all three rules against the benign baseline PCAP. No alerts should fire because the benign capture contains only legitimate HMI traffic with no write operations from unauthorized sources.

Kali

snort -r benign_baseline.pcap -c /dev/null -R masa_ics.rules -A console -q 2>&1 | grep -c "Priority"
Expected output 
0

A count of zero confirms no false positives. If you see alerts, review the benign PCAP to determine whether legitimate traffic is matching your content patterns and tighten the rule (add offset and depth constraints, or narrow the source IP range).

docs.title: Stage 8: Submit the Flag
docs.text:
All three SIDs validated. The flag encodes the three SIDs in order.

Kali

OCR{________}

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• An alert line from Snort includes the SID, the message, the source IP, and the destination IP. Confirm the SID matches the rule you expect and the source IP is the attacker (.99), not the HMI (.5)
  • A false positive on the benign baseline means your content match is too broad. Adding offset and depth constraints narrows the match to the exact byte position of the function code rather than matching anywhere in the payload
  • If Snort exits with a parse error, check the rules file for missing semicolons inside the options block. Every option must end with a semicolon, and the options block must be enclosed in parentheses
  • If Snort produces zero alerts on an attack PCAP, verify the content byte is correct by re-examining the PCAP with tshark and checking the exact hex value at the expected offset

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The three rules use any as the source IP instead of hardcoding the attacker address 10.x.x.99. Why is that the better detection strategy?

Reveal answer

Hardcoding the attacker's IP creates a signature that only catches one specific attacker. The next attacker will use a different source address. The detection-worthy event is "a write operation from any host that is not the authorized HMI," not "a write operation from 10.x.x.99 specifically." Using any as the source catches all unauthorized writes regardless of the attacker's IP. In a production deployment, you would further refine the rule with a ! negation on the HMI IP (e.g., !10.x.x.5) to allow legitimate HMI writes through while alerting on everything else.

2. The Plant 2 rule (SID 1000002) matches the byte \x05 without an offset constraint. What is the risk of that approach?

Reveal answer

Without offset and depth, Snort will match the byte \x05 anywhere in the TCP payload, not just in the S7 function code field. A benign packet that happens to contain \x05 in its data payload (a setpoint value, a string character, a length field) could trigger a false positive. A production-quality rule would constrain the match to the exact byte position of the S7 function field within the TPKT/COTP/S7 header stack. The exercise uses the simpler form to demonstrate the concept, but a SOC deployment must add positional constraints.

3. Snort is a signature-based IDS. What category of ICS attacks would these three rules completely miss?

Reveal answer

Signature-based rules match known byte patterns. Attacks that use legitimate function codes with legitimate-looking values from legitimate-looking sources will not trigger any of these rules. For example, an attacker who compromises the actual HMI and sends writes from the HMI's IP address using the correct function code will bypass all three rules. Process-anomaly detection (monitoring for out-of-range setpoint values rather than unauthorized sources) requires a different detection approach, typically a behavioral or model-based IDS that understands normal operating ranges.

4. Reyna asks you to reduce false positives on the Modbus rule without reducing true positives. What single change would you make?

Reveal answer

Replace any any on the source side with !10.x.x.5 any (negating the legitimate HMI address). Legitimate Modbus writes from the HMI are expected and should not alert. Writes from any other source are suspicious. The negation preserves full detection coverage for unauthorized writes while eliminating alerts on normal HMI operations. In a plant with multiple authorized HMI stations, use a variable like $HMI_HOSTS and negate the entire group.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation No ICS-specific Snort rules deployed on plant-floor sensors Critical Deploy the three rules from Exercise 6.1 (SIDs 1000001 through 1000003) on all plant-floor Snort sensors immediately Rules use any source, which will alert on legitimate HMI writes Medium Refine each rule with !$HMI_HOSTS source negation after documenting all authorized HMI addresses per plant Signature-based detection cannot catch compromised-HMI attacks High Supplement Snort with a process-anomaly IDS that monitors setpoint values against safe operating ranges No rule management process exists for OT Snort sensors Medium Establish a quarterly rule review cycle where the OT security team updates SIDs based on new threat intelligence and plant topology changes

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Detection engineering translates offensive findings into defensive value. Every attack you executed in Levels 1 through 5 has a network signature that Snort can match
  • Snort rules follow the pattern: action, protocol, source, destination, then options with content matches, offsets, and a unique SID
  • Validation requires both true-positive testing (rule fires on attack traffic) and false-positive testing (rule does not fire on benign traffic)
  • Positional constraints (offset and depth) reduce false positives by matching bytes at the exact protocol field rather than anywhere in the payload
  • Signature-based detection is a starting point, not an endpoint. Process-anomaly and behavioral detection are necessary complements for ICS environments

docs.text:
Client Masa Foods, Inc. (fictional) Role OT Security Engineer, All Plants Phase Discovery Detection Rules Defense (segmentation design) Capstone

What you know so far: Exercise 6.1 produced detection rules for the three attack patterns you exploited across Levels 1 through 5. Detection is reactive. Reyna Alvarado now wants a proactive defense: a network segmentation proposal that would have prevented lateral movement between plants in the first place. Exercise 6.2 is an independent exercise with no step-by-step walkthrough. You write the proposal, submit it to the rubric checker, and iterate until it passes.

Kali

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Penetration test reports identify vulnerabilities. Segmentation proposals fix them. Every OT security engagement ends with a recommendation section, and the most common recommendation in ICS environments is network segmentation. Writing a segmentation proposal that references the Purdue model, specifies per-plant firewall rules, and addresses authentication gaps is a core deliverable for any OT security consultant. The rubric checker simulates a demanding client who rejects vague recommendations and requires specifics.

The professional skill Exercise 6.2 builds is translating technical findings into an actionable architectural document. A proposal that says "segment the network" is useless. A proposal that says "deploy a firewall between the Plant 1 Modbus segment (10.1.x.0/24) and the corporate LAN, permitting only TCP/502 from the authorized HMI at 10.1.x.5" is useful.

docs.title: Background: The Purdue Model and OT Segmentation
docs.text:
The Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture (PERA) divides an industrial network into six levels. Segmentation proposals for ICS environments reference these levels to establish trust boundaries.

Level Name Masa Foods Examples 0 Physical Process Ovens, conveyors, water treatment tanks, packaging lines 1 Basic Control PLCs (Modbus, S7, CIP controllers) 2 Area Supervisory HMIs, SCADA servers, historians 3 Site Operations Engineering workstations, patch servers 3.5 DMZ Jump servers, data diodes, file transfer servers 4-5 Enterprise Corporate IT, email, ERP, internet access

The critical segmentation boundary is between Level 3 and Level 4 (the IT/OT DMZ at Level 3.5). A second critical boundary separates each plant's Level 1/2 network from every other plant. The attacks you executed in Levels 1 through 5 all crossed at least one of these boundaries.

docs.title: What the rubric checker looks for
docs.text:
The rubric checker at rubric.masa.local:8080 evaluates your proposal against specific criteria. Retrieve the full list with GET /rubric. Common requirements include:

  • Plant-specific firewall rules (not generic "add a firewall" statements)
  • Explicit Purdue model references with level assignments for Masa assets
  • Authentication controls for OT protocol access (Modbus, S7, CIP)
  • Monitoring and logging recommendations per plant
  • Firmware update and patch management strategy

docs.title: Submission format
docs.text: The rubric checker accepts a plain-text proposal via POST /check. Submit the proposal as the request body. The response includes a score, pass/fail status, and feedback on missing criteria.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose curl Retrieve rubric and submit proposals Text editor (nano, vim) Write the proposal document jq (optional) Format JSON responses from the rubric checker

docs.title: Suggested Methodology
docs.text: Exercise 6.2 is an independent exercise. No step-by-step walkthrough is provided. Instead, here are the stages a methodical assessor would follow.

docs.title: Stage 1: Retrieve the Rubric
docs.text:
Query the rubric endpoint to understand exactly what the checker expects. Read every requirement carefully before writing a single line of the proposal. Missing even one required section will cause a rejection.

Kali

curl -s http://rubric.masa.local:8080/rubric | jq .

Record each requirement as a checklist item. Your proposal must address every item on the list.

docs.title: Stage 2: Draft the Proposal
docs.text:
Create a plain-text file that addresses each rubric requirement. Structure the proposal with clear section headers so the rubric checker can find each required element. A recommended structure:

  1. Executive Summary: One paragraph stating the purpose and scope
  2. Current State: Brief description of the flat network and the risks you identified
  3. Purdue Model Mapping: Assign each Masa asset to a Purdue level
  4. Plant-Specific Firewall Rules: Separate subsection per plant with source, destination, port, and action
  5. Authentication Controls: Per-protocol authentication recommendations
  6. Monitoring and Logging: IDS placement, log collection, alerting
  7. Firmware and Patch Management: Update cadence and change control

Be specific. Name protocols (Modbus TCP/502, S7comm TCP/102, CIP TCP/44818), name assets (Plant 1 oven PLC, Plant 2 water treatment PLCs, Plant 3 packaging PLC and warehouse RTU), and name Purdue levels.

docs.title: Stage 3: Submit and Review Feedback
docs.text:
Submit the proposal to the rubric checker and examine the response. The checker returns structured feedback indicating which criteria passed and which are missing.

Kali

curl -s -X POST http://rubric.masa.local:8080/check \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  --data-binary @proposal.txt | jq .

Read every feedback item. Each missing criterion tells you exactly what to add or revise.

docs.title: Stage 4: Iterate Until Accepted
docs.text: Revise the proposal based on the feedback, resubmit, and repeat until the checker returns a passing score and the flag. Most proposals require two to three iterations. Focus on the specific feedback rather than rewriting the entire document.

docs.title: Stage 5: Record the Flag
docs.text: When the rubric checker accepts the proposal, the response includes the flag. Record it and submit.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A response with "pass": false includes a feedback array listing every missing criterion. Address each one before resubmitting
  • A response with "pass": true includes the flag in the response body
  • If the checker rejects your proposal for "missing plant-specific firewall rules," verify that each plant section includes explicit source IP, destination IP, port, and allow/deny action
  • If the checker rejects for "missing Purdue model reference," verify that you explicitly assign Masa assets to numbered Purdue levels (Level 0 through Level 5), not just mention the Purdue model in passing
  • A connection refused error means the rubric server container is not running. Return to the Environment Checklist

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The rubric requires plant-specific firewall rules rather than a single global policy. Why is per-plant segmentation necessary?

Reveal answer

Each Masa Foods plant runs a different ICS protocol (Modbus, S7comm, CIP) with different authorized endpoints, different port numbers, and different traffic patterns. A global firewall policy that permits TCP/502 everywhere would leave Plant 2 and Plant 3 unprotected against unauthorized Modbus traffic on their segments. Per-plant rules ensure that only the correct protocol is permitted on each segment and only from authorized sources. The attacks in Levels 1 through 5 demonstrated that an attacker on one plant's network could reach other plants precisely because no per-plant boundaries existed.

2. Where does the IT/OT DMZ (Purdue Level 3.5) sit in the Masa Foods network, and what devices belong there?

Reveal answer

The DMZ sits between the corporate IT network (Levels 4 and 5) and the plant operations network (Levels 0 through 3). Devices that belong in the DMZ include jump servers (for remote access to OT systems), historians that replicate data from Level 2 to the enterprise, patch distribution servers, and any file transfer mechanisms. The DMZ should permit no direct connections from Level 4/5 to Level 1/2. All cross-boundary traffic must pass through a DMZ intermediary. The attacker in Exercise 3.1 pivoted from the corporate web server directly into the OT network because no DMZ existed.

3. The Purdue model was published in the 1990s. Is it still relevant for modern ICS environments that include cloud connectivity and remote access?

Reveal answer

The Purdue model's core principle (hierarchical trust zones with strict boundary enforcement) remains relevant even in cloud-connected environments. Modern extensions like IEC 62443 build on the same zone-and-conduit architecture. Cloud connectivity adds a new trust boundary above Level 5 that requires its own set of controls (encrypted tunnels, identity federation, API gateways). The model does not mandate physical separation at every level; logical segmentation via VLANs and firewalls satisfies the architecture. The model's value is the structured thinking it enforces, not the specific technology it prescribes.

4. Your proposal includes authentication recommendations for Modbus, S7, and CIP. Which of these three protocols has the weakest native authentication support?

Reveal answer

Modbus TCP has no native authentication at all. The protocol specification includes no mechanism for the server to verify the identity of a client. Any device that can reach TCP/502 can read and write registers without credentials. S7comm has protection levels (as explored in Exercises 4.5 and 4.6) that provide varying degrees of write protection. CIP supports CIP Security (TLS-based authentication) on newer devices. Modbus environments must rely entirely on network-layer controls (firewalls, segmentation) because the protocol itself offers nothing.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Flat network allows lateral movement between all three plants Critical Implement per-plant VLANs with inter-plant firewalls permitting only documented, protocol-specific traffic No IT/OT DMZ exists between corporate and plant networks Critical Deploy a Level 3.5 DMZ with jump servers for all remote OT access and historians for data replication Modbus, S7, and CIP endpoints accept connections from any source High Restrict each protocol port to authorized HMI and engineering workstation IPs via firewall rules No firmware update or patch management process for PLCs and RTUs High Establish a quarterly firmware review cycle with change control documentation and rollback procedures

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A segmentation proposal is the highest-value deliverable from an OT penetration test because it directly addresses the root cause of lateral movement
  • The Purdue model provides a standard vocabulary (Levels 0 through 5, DMZ at 3.5) that makes proposals readable by both IT and OT teams
  • Per-plant firewall rules must specify source, destination, port, and action. Generic statements like "add a firewall" are not actionable
  • Iterative submission against a rubric checker mirrors the real consulting workflow where clients review, reject, and request revisions on deliverables
  • Modbus has zero native authentication, making network segmentation the only effective access control for Plant 1

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
On February 14, 2025 at 14:30 UTC, the Masa Foods SOC received alerts from all three plants within a 20-minute window. Plant 1 reported an oven temperature exceedance. Plant 2's Safety Instrumented System (SIS) tripped on a caustic dosing anomaly. Plant 3's packaging line reported phantom pallet counts. Reyna Alvarado has preserved the following evidence artifacts for your investigation:

Evidence server (evidence.masa.local:8080):

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Incident investigation in OT environments is harder than in IT because the evidence spans two domains: traditional IT logs (web server access logs, SSH authentication, bash history) and OT artifacts (PCAPs with ICS protocol traffic, historian time-series data). An effective OT incident responder must correlate timestamps across both domains to reconstruct how an attacker moved from IT initial access to OT impact. Exercise 6.3 builds exactly that skill.

The professional habit Exercise 6.3 develops is independent analysis before reading the official report. In a real incident, the official timeline is written by the responder, not handed to them. Reconstructing the kill chain from raw evidence and then comparing your findings to the summary teaches you to trust evidence over narrative.

docs.title: The incident at a glance
docs.text:
The attacker (source IP: 10.100.1.99) exploited a Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability on the corporate web server to steal OT credentials. Using those credentials, the attacker SSH-pivoted through the jump server into the OT network and attacked all three plants:

  • Plant 1: Oven setpoint written to 500 degrees F via Modbus (normal operating range: 350 to 400 degrees F)
  • Plant 2: Caustic dosing rate set to 200 ml/min via S7comm, triggering the SIS trip threshold at 120 ml/min
  • Plant 3: PalletCount set to 9999 via CIP, causing phantom pallet counts on the packaging line

docs.title: Background: OT Incident Kill Chain
docs.text:
ICS-targeted attacks follow a recognizable kill chain that spans IT and OT domains. The MITRE ATT&CK for ICS framework documents the common stages:

Stage IT/OT Domain Masa Foods Incident Initial Access IT LFI on corporate web server Credential Access IT OT credentials stolen from server config files Lateral Movement IT to OT SSH pivot through jump server Discovery OT Protocol enumeration on plant networks Impact OT Process variable manipulation on all three plants

docs.title: Evidence correlation methodology
docs.text:
The key to reconstructing a cross-domain kill chain is timestamp correlation. Each evidence artifact covers a different part of the attack:

  1. Web access logs reveal the initial access vector and the exact time the attacker first touched the corporate perimeter
  2. SSH auth logs reveal when the attacker pivoted from IT to OT and which credentials were used
  3. Bash history reveals the commands the attacker ran on the jump server (protocol tools, network scans, attack scripts)
  4. PCAPs reveal the exact protocol commands sent to each plant's PLCs
  5. Historian time-series reveals the process impact (temperature exceedances, dosing anomalies, phantom counts)

Read the artifacts in that order. Each artifact builds context for the next.

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose curl Download evidence artifacts jq Parse JSON artifacts (historian data, incident summary) tshark or tcpdump Analyze attack PCAPs grep, awk Filter and correlate log files Text editor Record your kill chain timeline

docs.title: Suggested Methodology
docs.text: Exercise 6.3 is an independent exercise. No step-by-step walkthrough is provided. Instead, here are the stages a methodical incident responder would follow.

docs.title: Stage 1: Collect All Evidence
docs.text: Download every artifact from both servers into a working directory. Verify file sizes to confirm complete downloads. Do not read the incident_summary.json yet. Save it for Stage 5.

docs.title: Stage 2: Analyze IT-Side Evidence
docs.text:
Start with the corporate web server access log. Search for requests from the attacker IP (10.100.1.99) and identify the LFI pattern. LFI requests typically contain path traversal sequences (../) in URL parameters. Note the timestamp of the first malicious request.

Move to the jump server authentication log. Search for successful SSH logins from 10.100.1.99 or from the corporate web server's IP. Note the timestamp and the username used. Compare the credentials to the ones stolen via LFI.

Review the bash history from the jump server session. The commands reveal what the attacker did after gaining OT network access: scanning, protocol tool usage, and attack execution.

docs.title: Stage 3: Analyze OT-Side Evidence
docs.text:
Examine the attack PCAPs (reuse the Plant 1, 2, and 3 captures from Exercise 6.1). For each PCAP, identify the exact protocol command that caused the process impact:

  • Plant 1: Look for Modbus FC 6 writing an oven setpoint value of 500
  • Plant 2: Look for S7comm Write Var setting a caustic dosing rate to 200
  • Plant 3: Look for CIP Write Tag setting PalletCount to 9999

Cross-reference the PCAP timestamps with the historian time-series data to confirm when each plant's process variables deviated from normal.

docs.title: Stage 4: Build the Kill Chain Timeline
docs.text:
Assemble a chronological timeline that links every artifact to a kill chain stage. A complete timeline should include at minimum:

  1. First LFI request on the corporate web server (timestamp, URL, source IP)
  2. Credential theft (which file was read via LFI, what credentials were extracted)
  3. SSH login to the jump server (timestamp, username, source IP)
  4. OT network reconnaissance (commands from bash history)
  5. Plant 1 attack (Modbus write, timestamp, setpoint value)
  6. Plant 2 attack (S7 write, timestamp, dosing rate)
  7. Plant 3 attack (CIP write, timestamp, pallet count)
  8. Process impact detection (SIS trip on Plant 2, temperature alarm on Plant 1, phantom pallets on Plant 3)

docs.title: Stage 5: Validate Against the Official Summary
docs.text: Now read incident_summary.json. Compare the official timeline, attacker IP, initial access vector, and per-plant impact against your reconstruction. Note any discrepancies. In a real incident, discrepancies mean either your analysis missed evidence or the official summary is incomplete.

docs.title: Stage 6: Assemble and Submit the Flag
docs.text: The flag encodes the three plant impacts: the oven setpoint (500), the SIS trip, and the phantom pallet count (9999). Combine them into the flag format and submit.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The web access log should show LFI attempts with path traversal sequences targeting configuration files that contain OT credentials
  • The SSH auth log should show a successful login using the plant_op account from an unexpected source (the corporate web server or the attacker's IP)
  • The bash history should reveal ICS protocol tools (Python scripts, nmap scans targeting OT ports) that match the attack PCAPs
  • Historian time-series data should show sharp deviations at timestamps matching the PCAP attack packets: oven temperature spiking, caustic dosing rate jumping, pallet count leaping to 9999
  • If timestamps between logs and PCAPs do not align, check for timezone differences. The exercise uses UTC throughout, but verify the log format headers

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The attacker used LFI on the corporate web server as initial access. What single control would have prevented the pivot from IT to OT?

Reveal answer

An IT/OT DMZ (Purdue Level 3.5) with a jump server that requires multi-factor authentication would have blocked the pivot. The attacker stole a username and password via LFI, but MFA on the jump server would have rendered the stolen credentials insufficient for SSH access. Even without MFA, network segmentation that blocks direct SSH from the corporate web server to the OT jump server would have forced the attacker to find another pivot path.

2. The attacker hit all three plants within a 20-minute window. What does that speed suggest about the attacker's preparation?

Reveal answer

A 20-minute window across three different ICS protocols (Modbus, S7comm, CIP) suggests the attacker had pre-written attack scripts for each protocol and had already performed reconnaissance on the plant network topology. An unprepared attacker would need hours to learn each protocol, identify the target PLCs, and craft the correct write commands. The speed indicates prior access (possibly from an earlier undetected intrusion) or detailed knowledge of Masa Foods' OT environment from insider information or public disclosures.

3. Plant 2's SIS tripped and shut down the caustic dosing process. From an incident response perspective, is the SIS trip a success or a failure?

Reveal answer

The SIS trip is a safety success and a security failure. The Safety Instrumented System performed exactly as designed: it detected an out-of-range process variable (200 ml/min exceeds the 120 ml/min threshold) and shut down the process to prevent physical harm. The security failure is that the attacker reached the SIS trip point at all. A properly segmented network with authenticated S7comm access would have prevented the unauthorized write before the SIS needed to act. In the ideal defense-in-depth model, the SIS should never be the first line of defense against a cyber attack.

4. You reconstructed the kill chain before reading the official incident summary. Why is that order important in real incident response?

Reveal answer

Reading the summary first introduces confirmation bias. An investigator who reads the conclusion before examining the evidence will unconsciously seek evidence that confirms the narrative and dismiss evidence that contradicts it. Independent reconstruction forces the investigator to follow the evidence wherever it leads, which may reveal attack stages or secondary compromises that the original summary missed. In a real incident, the first summary is always incomplete. The investigator's job is to find what the summary missed, not to confirm what it already says.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Corporate web server vulnerable to LFI, providing access to OT credentials Critical Patch the LFI vulnerability immediately; move OT credentials out of web-accessible configuration files; rotate all OT passwords Single-factor SSH authentication on the OT jump server Critical Enforce multi-factor authentication for all jump server access; restrict SSH source IPs to authorized management stations Attacker pivoted from IT to OT with no detection until process impact occurred High Deploy network monitoring at the IT/OT boundary that alerts on new SSH sessions from unexpected sources All three plants attacked within 20 minutes, suggesting pre-staged scripts High Implement rate limiting and anomaly detection on OT protocol writes; alert on multiple write commands from a single source within a short window

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• OT incident investigation requires correlating evidence across IT logs (web access, SSH auth, bash history) and OT artifacts (PCAPs, historian data)
  • Timestamp correlation is the primary technique for linking kill chain stages across domains
  • Independent analysis before reading the official summary prevents confirmation bias and reveals gaps in the existing narrative
  • The SIS is a safety system, not a security control. Defense-in-depth should prevent attackers from reaching the SIS trip threshold
  • A 20-minute multi-plant attack window indicates pre-staged scripts and prior reconnaissance, pointing to a sophisticated or insider-informed adversary

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Masa Foods, Inc. (fictional) Role OT Security Engineer, All Plants Phase Discovery Incident Response Capstone (board-level report) Engagement Complete

What you know so far: Exercise 6.3 gave you a complete kill chain reconstruction of the February 14, 2025 cross-site incident. You know the initial access vector (LFI), the pivot mechanism (SSH with stolen credentials), and the per-plant impact (oven setpoint, SIS trip, phantom pallets). Exercise 6.4 is the capstone: translate your technical findings into a board-level incident report that a non-technical audience can act on. The rubric checker scores your report against executive communication standards.

docs.title: Environment Checklist
docs.text:
Exercise 6.4 uses both the evidence server (for reference data) and the rubric checker (for submission scoring). Verify connectivity to each.

Kali

curl -s http://evidence.masa.local:8080/ | head -10
curl -s http://rubric.masa.local:8080/rubric | head -30

Both servers should respond. The evidence server provides the incident artifacts you analyzed in Exercise 6.3. The rubric server scores your board report.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: The Masa Foods board of directors has called an emergency session following the February 14 incident. Reyna Alvarado has been asked to present a written incident report suitable for board members who have no technical background. The report must explain what happened, quantify the business impact, attribute the attack using industry-standard frameworks, and propose prioritized remediation. Reyna has delegated the writing to you. A rubric checker at rubric.masa.local:8080 scores your report against the board's expectations.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Most cybersecurity professionals can write a technical incident report. Very few can write a board report. The difference is audience: board members do not understand Modbus function codes, S7 protection levels, or CIP service bytes. Board members understand production downtime, food safety risk, regulatory exposure, and dollars. A board report that says "the attacker sent Modbus FC 6 with value 500 to DB1 offset 0" is useless to a director. A board report that says "the attacker remotely raised an industrial oven to 500 degrees F, exceeding the safe operating range and creating a fire and food safety hazard" is actionable.

The professional skill Exercise 6.4 builds is the ability to translate deep technical knowledge into business language without losing accuracy. Every sentence in the report must be technically correct, but no sentence should require ICS protocol knowledge to understand. Board reports are the deliverable that justifies security budgets, and security budgets are the mechanism that funds the controls you recommended in Exercises 6.1 and 6.2.

docs.title: What makes a good board report
docs.text:
A board-level incident report has several characteristics that distinguish it from a technical report:

  1. Non-technical language throughout. Replace protocol names with plain descriptions. "Modbus Function Code 6" becomes "a remote command to change the oven temperature." "S7comm Write Var" becomes "a remote command to increase chemical dosing."
  2. Business impact focus. Quantify downtime in hours, food safety risk in regulatory terms (FDA, FSMA), and financial exposure in dollars or production batches lost.
  3. Timeline with cause and effect. Board members need to see the sequence: how did the attacker get in, what did they do, and what was the consequence at each step?
  4. MITRE ATT&CK ICS references. The board's external auditors and insurance carrier expect standardized attack technique references. Use technique IDs (T0855 for Unauthorized Command Message, T0836 for Modify Parameter) alongside plain-language descriptions.
  5. Prioritized recommendations. Rank remediation actions by risk reduction and cost. The board approves budgets, so recommendations must be sequenced by priority with rough cost categories (low, medium, high).
Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Plant operator (reference) plant_op masa_op_2025 Referenced in the incident narrative

  • Write a board-level incident report for the February 14, 2025 attack
  • Submit the report to the rubric checker and iterate based on feedback

Detail Value Difficulty Advanced Estimated Time 60 to 90 minutes Prerequisites Exercise 6.3 (incident investigation) Flag Source Found? OCR{...} Rubric checker response on accepted report

docs.title: Background: Board Communication for Cyber Incidents
MITRE ATT&CK for ICS Techniques
docs.text:
The February 14 incident maps to several MITRE ATT&CK for ICS techniques. The rubric checker expects at least two of these:

Technique ID Name Masa Foods Mapping T0855 Unauthorized Command Message Attacker sent write commands to PLCs across all three plants without authorization T0836 Modify Parameter Attacker changed oven setpoint (Plant 1), caustic dosing rate (Plant 2), and pallet count (Plant 3) T0859 Valid Accounts Attacker used stolen OT credentials (plant_op) to authenticate to the jump server T0886 Remote Services Attacker used SSH to pivot from the corporate network to the OT jump server

docs.title: Translating technical findings to business language
docs.text: Technical Finding Board Language Modbus FC 6 wrote oven setpoint to 500 degrees F An unauthorized party remotely raised Plant 1 oven temperature to 500 degrees F, exceeding the safe operating limit and creating fire and food safety hazards S7comm Write Var set caustic dosing to 200 ml/min, SIS tripped An unauthorized party increased chemical dosing in Plant 2 water treatment to dangerous levels, triggering an automatic safety shutdown that halted production CIP Write Tag set PalletCount to 9999 An unauthorized party injected false inventory data into Plant 3 packaging, causing the system to report 9999 phantom pallets and disrupting shipping logistics LFI on corporate web server The attacker exploited a software vulnerability on a public-facing web application to steal internal credentials SSH pivot through jump server The attacker used stolen credentials to access the industrial control network through a remote access gateway

docs.title: Report structure the rubric expects
docs.text:
Based on the rubric checker requirements, the board report should include:

  1. Executive Summary: 3 to 5 sentences covering what happened, when, and the overall business impact
  2. Incident Timeline: Chronological sequence of attacker actions from initial access to process impact
  3. Per-Plant Impact: Separate subsection for each plant describing the physical consequence in business terms
  4. Initial Access and Pivot: How the attacker entered the network and reached the OT environment
  5. MITRE ATT&CK ICS Mapping: At minimum T0855 and T0836 with plain-language explanations
  6. Remediation Recommendations: Prioritized list with cost categories
  7. Detection Improvements: Specific monitoring and alerting changes to catch similar attacks in the future
  8. Authentication and Access Control: Recommendations for credential management and access restrictions

docs.title: Tools You Will Need
docs.text: Tool Purpose curl Retrieve rubric and submit the report jq (optional) Format JSON responses from the rubric checker Text editor (nano, vim) Write the board report Evidence artifacts from Exercise 6.3 Reference data for the incident narrative

docs.title: Suggested Methodology
docs.text: Exercise 6.4 is an independent exercise. No step-by-step walkthrough is provided. Instead, here are the stages a methodical report author would follow.

docs.title: Stage 1: Retrieve the Rubric
docs.text:
Query the rubric endpoint to understand the exact scoring criteria. Each criterion maps to a section of the board report.

Kali

curl -s http://rubric.masa.local:8080/rubric | jq .

Record every criterion. Your report must address all of them to pass.

docs.title: Stage 2: Gather Your Evidence
docs.text: Review the kill chain timeline you built in Exercise 6.3. Pull up the incident summary, historian data, and PCAPs as reference. You do not need to re-analyze the evidence, but you do need to translate every technical finding into business language for the board.

docs.title: Stage 3: Draft the Report
docs.text:
Write the board report as a plain-text document. Follow the structure from the Background section. For each section, ask yourself: "Would a board member with no cybersecurity background understand every sentence?" If the answer is no, rewrite the sentence in plainer language.

Key writing principles for board reports:

  • Lead with impact, not with method. "Plant 1 oven temperature was raised to dangerous levels" before "the attacker used Modbus Function Code 6."
  • Quantify wherever possible. Hours of downtime, batches of product at risk, regulatory standards potentially violated.
  • Use MITRE ATT&CK ICS technique IDs as parenthetical references, not as the primary description. Write "unauthorized remote commands (MITRE T0855)" rather than "T0855 was observed."
  • Prioritize recommendations by risk reduction. The most impactful, lowest-cost fix comes first.

docs.title: Stage 4: Submit and Iterate
docs.text:
Submit the report to the rubric checker and review the feedback. The checker evaluates each required section independently, so partial credit is possible. Focus revisions on the sections that failed.

Kali

curl -s -X POST http://rubric.masa.local:8080/check \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  --data-binary @board_report.txt | jq .

Most reports require two to four iterations. Common rejection reasons include: missing MITRE technique IDs, technical jargon without plain-language explanation, missing per-plant impact sections, or recommendations without prioritization.

docs.title: Stage 5: Record the Flag
docs.text: When the rubric checker accepts the report, the response includes the flag. Record it and submit.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A response with "pass": false lists every failing criterion. Address each one specifically rather than rewriting the entire report
  • The rubric checker evaluates text content, not formatting. Plain text with clear section headers is sufficient
  • If the checker rejects for "missing executive summary," ensure your report opens with a standalone paragraph that a board member could read in 30 seconds and understand the full situation
  • If the checker rejects for "missing MITRE ATT&CK ICS," verify you included at least T0855 (Unauthorized Command Message) and T0836 (Modify Parameter) with their technique IDs
  • If the checker rejects for "missing authentication recommendations," verify you addressed credential rotation, multi-factor authentication for OT access, and the elimination of shared accounts

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The board report must avoid technical jargon, but it also must be technically accurate. How do you handle the tension between accessibility and precision?

Reveal answer

Use layered language. The primary sentence uses plain business terms ("the attacker remotely raised the oven temperature to dangerous levels"). A parenthetical or footnote provides the technical detail for the security team and auditors ("via Modbus Function Code 6, writing value 500 to the oven setpoint register"). Board members read the sentence. Auditors read the parenthetical. Both audiences are served without compromising accuracy or accessibility.

2. The rubric requires MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique references. Why do board reports include framework references that board members will not understand?

Reveal answer

Board reports are read by more than just board members. The company's cyber insurance carrier, external auditors, legal counsel, and regulatory bodies all review incident reports. These stakeholders expect standardized technique references because they use them to assess coverage, liability, and compliance. MITRE ATT&CK ICS is the industry-standard taxonomy. Including technique IDs signals professional rigor and makes the report defensible in regulatory and legal contexts. The board members themselves may skip the IDs, but the IDs serve the broader audience of the document.

3. Your remediation recommendations must be prioritized. What criteria determine the priority order?

Reveal answer

Priority is determined by the intersection of risk reduction and implementation cost. The highest-priority recommendation reduces the most risk at the lowest cost. For the Masa Foods incident, patching the LFI vulnerability and rotating stolen credentials are highest priority because they close the exact attack path used, and both are low-cost actions. Deploying an IT/OT DMZ with multi-factor authentication is high priority and medium cost. Implementing a full ICS-aware monitoring platform is high priority but also high cost, so it ranks lower despite its importance. The board approves budgets sequentially, so the order determines what gets funded first.

4. The February 14 attacker hit all three plants. Should the board report recommend separate remediation for each plant or a unified platform-wide approach?

Reveal answer

Both. The report should recommend immediate per-plant fixes (credential rotation, firewall rules specific to each protocol) and a unified long-term architecture (centralized IT/OT DMZ, enterprise-wide MFA, cross-plant monitoring). Per-plant fixes are fast and address the specific vulnerabilities exploited. The unified approach prevents the next attacker from finding a different path to the same targets. Board members understand the distinction between "stop the bleeding" (per-plant) and "prevent recurrence" (platform-wide), so framing recommendations in those two categories makes the prioritization intuitive.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Masa
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation No board-level incident reporting process existed before this attack High Establish a documented incident reporting template that the CISO completes within 48 hours of any OT security event Technical incident reports are not translated for non-technical stakeholders Medium Require every incident report to include a board-ready executive summary written in business language MITRE ATT&CK ICS framework not previously used in Masa incident documentation Medium Adopt MITRE ATT&CK for ICS as the standard taxonomy for all future incident reports, enabling consistent communication with insurance carriers and auditors Remediation recommendations in past reports were not prioritized by cost and risk High Require all future remediation sections to rank actions by risk reduction and include cost categories (low, medium, high) so the board can make informed funding decisions

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Board reports translate technical findings into business language. Every sentence must be understandable by a reader with no cybersecurity background
  • Lead with business impact (downtime, safety risk, regulatory exposure), not with protocol details. Method is supporting evidence, not the headline
  • MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique IDs (T0855, T0836) serve auditors, insurers, and regulators even when board members do not read them directly
  • Prioritized remediation recommendations are the actionable output of the report. The board funds fixes in the order you present them
  • Writing a board report is the final step in the OT security engagement lifecycle: discovery, exploitation, detection, defense design, incident response, and executive communication

docs.title: Why Linux Enumeration Comes First
docs.text:
Every penetration test begins with a question: what is running on the target? Before you can exploit a vulnerability, bypass authentication, or escalate privileges, you need to know which services are listening and what software is behind them. Linux servers power the majority of internet-facing infrastructure; web servers, file transfer services, remote administration tools, and databases all run on Linux. Learning to enumerate these services is the foundation of every assessment that follows.

Service enumeration is not a single step. A basic port scan tells you a door exists. Version detection tells you what is behind the door. Script-based enumeration and direct interaction reveal details that surface-level scans miss entirely. Across six labs, you will build from a single-port scan to full service analysis, learning why each layer of depth matters.

In a real engagement, incomplete enumeration leads to missed vulnerabilities. A server running an outdated FTP daemon on a non-standard port will not appear in a default scan. A custom banner containing credentials will not show up in version detection output. The progression in this chapter ensures you never stop at the surface.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
The six labs in this chapter progress from simple to thorough:

  • Detect a single SSH service using targeted port scanning
  • Discover multiple services running on the same host
  • Interact directly with services to extract information that scanners miss
  • Scan the full port range to find services hidden on non-standard ports
  • Enumerate service details using Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) scripts
  • Identify vulnerable software versions and research known exploits

By the end of this chapter, you will have a repeatable methodology for enumerating any Linux host; from the first SYN packet to a vulnerability report.

docs.title: What Are Linux Services?
docs.text:
A service is a program that listens on a network port, waiting for connections. Each service speaks a specific protocol and serves a specific purpose. When a client connects to the correct port, the service responds according to its protocol; an HTTP server returns web pages, an SSH server initiates an encrypted session, and an FTP server begins a file transfer negotiation.

The table below lists the services you will encounter most often during Linux assessments.

Port Protocol Service Purpose 21 TCP FTP File Transfer Protocol 22 TCP SSH Secure Shell remote access 80 TCP HTTP Web server (unencrypted) 443 TCP HTTPS Web server (encrypted) 3306 TCP MySQL Database server 139 TCP NetBIOS Legacy file/printer sharing 445 TCP SMB Server Message Block file shares 8080 TCP HTTP-Alt Alternate web server / proxy

These port assignments are defaults defined by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). Administrators can; and often do; move services to non-standard ports. Your enumeration must account for that possibility, which is why Exercise L1.4 teaches full-range scanning.

docs.title: What Is Nmap?
docs.text:
Nmap (Network Mapper) is an open-source tool for network discovery and security auditing. If you completed the Windows track, you already used Nmap to scan Windows services. The same tool works against Linux targets; the commands are identical, but the services you discover will differ. Linux hosts typically expose SSH instead of Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), Apache or Nginx instead of Internet Information Services (IIS), and vsftpd instead of Windows FTP.

Nmap runs on Linux, Windows, and macOS. Throughout this chapter, you will run Nmap from your Kali Linux attack machine, but the syntax is the same on any platform. Beyond port scanning, Nmap includes the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE); a library of scripts that perform targeted enumeration tasks like retrieving SSH host keys or listing supported authentication methods. You will use NSE in Exercise L1.5.

Nmap is pre-installed on Kali Linux. You can verify your installation at any time:

nmap --version

docs.title: The Nmap Commands You Will Use
docs.text:
Each lab builds on the previous one, adding a new Nmap capability:

graph LR
    A[L1.1 Targeted Scan]
    B[L1.2 Multi-Port]
    C[L1.3 Direct Connect]
    D[L1.4 Full Range]
    E[L1.5 NSE Scripts]
    F[L1.6 Vuln Research]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F
Lab Core Command What It Adds L1.1 nmap -p 22 -sV Single-port version detection L1.2 nmap -sV Default top-port scanning L1.3 ftp <target> Direct service interaction L1.4 nmap -p- Full 65535-port range scan L1.5 nmap --script NSE script enumeration L1.6 nmap -sV + searchsploit Version-to-vulnerability lookup

Notice the progression: each exercise asks a deeper question about the same types of services. By the final lab, you will chain version detection with vulnerability research to produce actionable findings.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following before launching your first exercise:

  • VPN connection to the lab environment is active
  • Terminal open and ready for commands
  • Nmap installed and accessible (type nmap --version to confirm)
  • FTP client available (type ftp --help to confirm)
  • Netcat installed (type nc -h to confirm)
  • Web browser available for HTTP interaction
  • Notebook or text editor ready for recording findings
  • Access to the OCR platform at the provided URL

Each lab takes approximately 15 to 30 minutes. Work through them in order; later exercises assume familiarity with the tools and techniques from earlier ones.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
• Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach the lab network.
  • No credentials are needed for scanning; you will observe the service from the outside.
  • You should be comfortable running commands in a Linux terminal.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: TechStart Inc, a growing SaaS startup, has hired your security team to audit their Linux infrastructure. Your project lead, Dana Reeves, wants to start simple: confirm whether a Secure Shell (SSH) service is running on one of the company's development servers. SSH is how the engineering team manages servers remotely, so verifying its presence and version is the first step in the assessment.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Launch the lab environment and note the target IP address
  • Run a targeted Nmap scan against port 22
  • Identify the SSH service version running on the target
  • Understand the difference between port state and service version
  • Record your findings and submit the flag

docs.title: Background: How SSH Works
docs.text:
SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote access to a system. When an SSH server starts, it binds to a port (default 22) and waits for incoming connections. During the initial handshake, the server announces its version string; a banner that identifies the software and protocol version.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Your Machine
    participant S as SSH Server (port 22)
    C->>S: TCP SYN (connection request)
    S->>C: TCP SYN-ACK
    C->>S: TCP ACK
    S->>C: SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_8.9p1 (banner)
    C->>S: SSH-2.0-client_version
    Note over C,S: Key exchange begins

That version banner is exactly what Nmap reads during a version scan. The server volunteers the information; no authentication required. The banner follows a standard format: the protocol version (SSH-2.0), a hyphen, and the software identifier (OpenSSH_8.9p1).

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap Version Scan
docs.text:
The -sV flag tells Nmap to probe open ports and identify the service and version running behind them. Combined with -p, you can target a specific port.

Version scan syntax

The general form of the version scan is shown below. You will fill in the port and the target IP from your own lab session in the steps that follow.

nmap -p <port> -sV <target_ip>

Key flags:

Flag Purpose -p Specify port(s) to scan -sV Probe open ports for service/version info -v Increase verbosity (optional but helpful) -oN Save output to a normal text file

Sample output:

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu0.1

The output tells you the port number, its state, the service name, and the exact version string. Each field provides a different piece of the puzzle.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Navigate to Exercises then Linux then Level 1, click Launch, wait for Running, note target IP.

Write down the IP address. You will use it in every command that follows.

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Verify connectivity to the target

Before scanning, confirm you can reach the target. The -c 3 flag sends three ICMP echo requests and then stops.

ping -c 3 <target_ip>

You should see replies indicating the host is reachable. If the ping times out, check your VPN connection.

docs.title: Step 3: Run a Targeted SSH Scan
docs.text:
Scan port 22 for the SSH version

Open your terminal and run a version scan against port 22. The -p 22 flag limits the scan to a single port, and -sV probes that port for the service banner.

nmap -p 22 -sV <target_ip>

Replace <target_ip> with the IP address from Step 1. A line reading 22/tcp open ssh confirms the service is reachable, and the VERSION column reveals the exact OpenSSH build.

docs.title: Step 4: Read the Output
docs.text:
Your output should look similar to the following:

Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org )
Nmap scan report for <target_ip>
Host is up (0.023s latency).

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu0.1

Service detection performed.
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 2.31 seconds

Break down what each column means:

  • PORT: The port number and protocol (22/tcp)
  • STATE: Whether the port is open, closed, or filtered
  • SERVICE: The type of service Nmap identified (ssh)
  • VERSION: The exact software version (OpenSSH 8.9p1)

docs.title: Step 5: Understand What Happened
docs.text:
Nmap completed three actions during the scan:

  1. Sent a TCP SYN packet to port 22 to check if the port is open
  2. Completed the TCP handshake when the port responded
  3. Read the SSH version banner the server sent back

No password or authentication was needed. The SSH server freely shares its version with any client that connects. Understanding why is important: the SSH protocol specification requires version exchange before the encrypted channel is established.

docs.title: Step 6: Save Your Output (Optional)
docs.text:
Save the scan results to a file

For documentation, you can save the scan results to a file. The -oN flag mirrors the normal console output into the named text file.

nmap -p 22 -sV -oN ssh_scan.txt <target_ip>

The command writes ssh_scan.txt in your current directory. Building a habit of saving scan results now will serve you well in later exercises and real engagements.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Target IP: ___

Field Your Finding Port ___ State ___ Service ___ Version ___ Flag OCR{_______________}

docs.title: Step 7: Record the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is:

OCR{________}

Submit the flag on the OCR platform to mark the lab complete.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does an SSH server reveal its version to unauthenticated clients?

Reveal Answer

The SSH protocol requires both sides to exchange version strings before the encrypted session begins. The server sends its banner immediately after the TCP handshake, before any authentication occurs. Protocol compatibility depends on this exchange.

2. What risk does version disclosure create for a server administrator?

Reveal Answer

An attacker can match the exact version string against public vulnerability databases. If the version has known flaws, the attacker gains a starting point for exploitation without ever logging in.

3. Could an administrator hide the SSH version, and would that help?

Reveal Answer

Some SSH configurations allow modifying or obscuring the banner, but the protocol still requires a version exchange. Changing the banner provides minimal protection; fingerprinting techniques can often identify the true version regardless. Defense should focus on patching, not hiding.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Version scanning (-sV) reads banners that services send during connection setup
  • SSH announces its version before authentication, making it visible to any scanner
  • A single targeted port scan runs faster than a broad scan when you know what to look for
  • Port state matters: open means accessible, closed means rejected, filtered means blocked by a firewall
  • Saving scan output with -oN creates a record for documentation and comparison
  • Version strings map to vulnerabilities: you will use this relationship throughout the chapter

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
• Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach the lab network.
  • You should have completed Exercise L1.1 and be comfortable reading Nmap output.
  • You will need a terminal, an FTP client, and a web browser (or curl).

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Dana Reeves at TechStart Inc is satisfied that SSH was found on the first server. Now she wants a broader picture. A second development server is suspected to run multiple services; not just SSH. Your job is to scan the host, discover every service on the default port range, and interact with each one to gather information. The flag for this exercise is split across two services, so scanning alone will not be enough.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Scan the target to discover all services on common ports
  • Identify FTP, SSH, and HTTP services and their versions
  • Connect to the FTP service using anonymous login
  • Inspect the HTTP service to find hidden information in the page source
  • Combine the flag halves from FTP and HTTP

docs.title: Background: Multiple Services on One Host
docs.text:
Production servers often run several services simultaneously. A single Linux host might serve web pages on port 80, accept file uploads on port 21, and allow remote administration on port 22. Each service binds to its own port and operates independently.

graph TD
    A[Linux Host]
    A --> B[Port 21 - FTP]
    A --> C[Port 22 - SSH]
    A --> D[Port 80 - HTTP]
    B --> E[File transfers]
    C --> F[Remote shell access]
    D --> G[Web pages]

Discovering all active services is essential. A forgotten FTP server or a test web application can become the weakest link in an otherwise secure system.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap Default Scan and FTP Client
docs.text:
Nmap default service scan:

Run a default service scan

When you run nmap -sV without specifying ports, Nmap scans the top 1,000 most common ports. For most initial assessments, the default range catches standard services.

nmap -sV <target_ip>

The output lists each open port with its detected service and version string.

FTP anonymous login:

Connect to the FTP service

Many FTP servers allow anonymous access; a guest account that requires no real credentials. The username is anonymous and any email address works as the password.

ftp <target_ip>

A successful connection drops you at an ftp> prompt after the login exchange.

Curl for HTTP inspection:

Fetch the web page

Use curl to retrieve the raw HTML served on port 80 without a browser.

curl http://<target_ip>

The raw HTML, including any HTML comments, prints to your terminal.

Tool Command Purpose nmap nmap -sV Scan top 1000 ports with version ftp ftp <target_ip> Connect to FTP service curl curl <url> Fetch web page content

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Navigate to Exercises then Linux then Level 1, click Launch, wait for Running, note target IP.

docs.title: Step 2: Run a Broad Service Scan
docs.text:
Run a broad service scan

Scan the target without specifying ports to let Nmap check its default top-1000 list:

nmap -sV <target_ip>

Nmap reports every open port in the top-1000 range along with the detected service and version.

docs.title: Step 3: Review the Results
docs.text:
You should see three services:

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
21/tcp open  ftp     vsftpd 3.0.5
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.9p1
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.54

Three open ports means three attack surfaces to investigate. Note each service and version.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect to FTP with Anonymous Login
docs.text:
Connect to FTP and list files

Connect to the FTP service:

ftp <target_ip>

When prompted, enter anonymous as the username and press Enter for the password (or type any email address). Once logged in, list the files:

ls

Look for a text file. Download it:

get <filename>
bye

The get command saves the file to your current local directory, and bye closes the FTP session.

Read the downloaded file

Read the downloaded file on your local machine:

cat <filename>

The file contains the first half of the flag.

docs.title: Step 5: Inspect the HTTP Service
docs.text:
Inspect the HTTP service

Open a web browser and navigate to http://<target_ip>, or use curl from the terminal:

curl http://<target_ip>

The page may look ordinary at first glance. View the page source (right-click, "View Page Source" in a browser, or read the raw curl output). Look for an HTML comment containing the second half of the flag. HTML comments follow the format <!-- comment -->.

docs.title: Step 6: Combine the Flag
docs.text: The two halves you found; one from FTP, one from the HTTP page source; form the complete flag when joined together.
