docs.title: Before You Begin: Read Your Target IP
docs.text:
The pcap host gets a fresh address every spawn, so do not paste a literal subnet. Open the Exercise Network panel and read the IP shown for pcaphost.pcc.local, then store it in a shell variable. Replace the placeholder below with the IP from your own panel.

Kali - set the pcap host variable

PCAPHOST=<pcaphost ip from the Exercise Network panel>
echo "capture host = $PCAPHOST:80 (HTTP index)"

Confirm the host answers on port 80 before you try to download anything.

Kali - confirm the pcap host is up

curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' "http://$PCAPHOST/"

Expected output

HTTP 200

An HTTP 200 means the capture index is being served and you can list it. Anything else is a connectivity problem to resolve before continuing.

docs.title: Step 1: Find and download the capture
docs.text:
The pcap host serves a directory of curated captures. List the index so you know the exact filename, then pull the engineering-session capture down to the RangeBox. Working on a local copy keeps your analysis repeatable and avoids hammering the host.

Kali - list the capture index

curl -s "http://$PCAPHOST/" | grep -oiE 'href="[^"]*\.pcap"'

Expected output

href="baseline.pcap"
href="attack-mix.pcap"
href="s7-engineering-session.pcap"
href="pasteurizer-divert.pcap"

The file you want is s7-engineering-session.pcap. Download it to a known path so the rest of the steps can reference it.

Kali - download the engineering session

curl -s -o /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap \
  "http://$PCAPHOST/s7-engineering-session.pcap"
ls -l /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap

Expected output

-rw-r--r-- 1 kali kali  ... /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap

A non-zero file size confirms the download. You now have a local copy to analyze.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm it is an S7comm session
docs.text:
Before hunting for the password, confirm the capture is what you expect: a TCP/102 conversation carrying S7comm. A quick protocol summary tells you the endpoints and the function calls involved. The engineering workstation is the client, the PLC is the server on port 102.

Kali - summarize the S7comm conversation

tshark -r /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap -Y 's7comm' \
  -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e ip.dst \
  -e s7comm.header.rosctr -e s7comm.param.func | head -20

Expected output

...  <EWS>  <PLC>  0x01  0x04
...  <PLC>  <EWS>  0x03  0x04
...  <EWS>  <PLC>  0x07  ...
...

You see a job request and acknowledgement pattern between the engineering workstation and the PLC. The ROSCTR 0x07 userdata messages are where setup, security, and protection functions live, and that is where the protection password will be.

docs.title: Step 3: Follow the TCP stream
docs.text:
Classic S7comm carries the protection-password material as a plaintext string inside the userdata payload, so following the single TCP/102 conversation surfaces it directly. The fastest way to find the conversation is to ask tshark for the TCP stream index, then dump that stream as ASCII.

Kali - identify the TCP/102 stream

tshark -r /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap -Y 'tcp.port == 102' \
  -T fields -e tcp.stream | sort -u

Expected output

0

A single stream index (here 0) means the whole session is one TCP conversation. Now dump that stream as ASCII and look for printable credential material. The follow output prints both directions of the conversation as text.

Kali - follow the stream as ASCII

tshark -r /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap -q \
  -z follow,tcp,ascii,0 | grep -iaE 'pcc|pass|protect'

Expected output

...PCCpast#2026...

The printable string in the userdata payload is the PLC protection password the engineer set during the session. Because classic S7comm does not encrypt the payload, the password sits in the packet bytes for anyone watching the conversation to read.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm with strings
docs.text:
A second, lower-tech path gets you the same answer and is worth knowing because it works even when a dissector does not parse a dialect. Running strings over the capture and grepping for the plant prefix pulls the printable password straight out of the file. Use it as a cross-check against the stream follow.

Kali - cross-check with strings

strings /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap | grep -i 'pcc'

Expected output

PCCpast#2026

The same value appears, so both methods agree. The capture embeds the cleartext password PCCpast#2026, which is the PLC protection password set during the maintenance window.

docs.title: Step 5: Normalize the password into the flag
docs.text:
The flag is the recovered password normalized to the ascii-underscore form and wrapped as OCR{...}. Lowercase the recovered string and replace each non-alphanumeric character with an underscore. The # in the password becomes _. Build it from your captured value rather than typing it by hand so you carry your own evidence forward.

Kali - normalize the recovered password

PW=$(strings /tmp/s7-engineering-session.pcap | grep -i 'pcc' | head -n1 | tr -d '[:space:]')
FLAG="OCR{$(echo "$PW" | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | tr -c 'a-z0-9' '_' | sed 's/_*$//')}"
echo "recovered = $PW"
echo "flag      = $FLAG"

Expected output (flag masked)

recovered = PCCpast#2026
flag      = OCR{pccpast_<masked>}

The normalization lowercases the string and turns the # separator into an underscore, producing the lowercase underscore-only flag form. Submit it in the exercise panel.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• Classic S7comm carries protection-password material as a plaintext string in the ROSCTR 0x07 userdata payload. No decryption is needed because there is no encryption.
  • Follow TCP Stream and strings are two paths to the same secret. Follow gives you protocol context (which direction, which message); strings works even when a dissector cannot parse the dialect.
  • A single TCP stream index for the whole session tells you it is one continuous engineering conversation, not several reconnections.
  • The flag normalization replaces the # in the password with an underscore. The recovered password and the flag are the same secret in two encodings.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did the password appear in cleartext when the PLC was supposedly password protected?

Reveal answer

The PLC protection password controls who may change the program once it is set, but classic S7comm has no transport security, so the act of setting that password transmits it as plaintext bytes. The protection is real against an attacker who arrives after the session and tries to write logic, but it is worthless against an attacker who was already capturing traffic during the maintenance window. The password is only as private as the network path it crossed.

2. Follow TCP Stream and strings both found the password. When would you reach for strings over the dissector?

Reveal answer

Reach for strings when the Wireshark dissector does not parse the dialect or the vendor extension, when the capture is truncated or malformed enough to confuse the dissector, or when you just want a fast first look without loading the GUI. The cost is that strings gives you no protocol context: you see the bytes but not which message, which direction, or which function carried them. Use strings to confirm a secret exists and the dissector or a stream follow to understand how it got there.

3. What would S7comm-plus have done differently?

Reveal answer

S7comm-plus, the protocol generation used by the S7-1200 and S7-1500 families, added a challenge-response authentication handshake and session-layer encryption. A password is never sent as a recoverable plaintext string; instead the client proves knowledge of the secret against a server-issued challenge, and the session payload is encrypted so a passive capture yields ciphertext, not credentials. An attacker capturing an S7comm-plus maintenance session sees an opaque conversation rather than a readable password.

4. The engineer did nothing wrong procedurally. So what is the actual finding here?

Reveal answer

The finding is architectural, not human. Setting a protection password is good practice, and the engineer followed it. The exposure comes from running a security-relevant operation over a cleartext protocol on a segment where a passive sensor, and therefore potentially an adversary, can read the conversation. The fix is to isolate the engineering path so only the workstation and PLC share it, to migrate to a controller generation that uses S7comm-plus where feasible, and to treat any credential that ever crossed a classic S7comm link as compromised and rotate it.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is the recovered cleartext PLC protection password, lowercased with each non-alphanumeric character replaced by an underscore and wrapped as OCR{...}. You built it in Step 5 from the value you pulled out of the capture.

Flag format (value masked)

OCR{pccpast_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the exercise panel.

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Pecan Creek
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation PLC protection password sent in cleartext over classic S7comm High Migrate to controllers that use S7comm-plus where feasible; rotate any credential that crossed a classic S7 link Engineering session shares a segment with the SOC sensor and other hosts Medium Isolate the engineering-workstation-to-PLC path into its own conduit so only those two endpoints share it No alerting on PLC protection or security userdata functions Medium Alert the SOC on S7 ROSCTR 0x07 security functions to plant PLCs during change windows

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A PLC protection password is only as private as the network path it crossed; on a cleartext protocol it is not private at all.
  • Capture review is the core OT IR skill because you usually cannot run an agent on the PLC itself.
  • Follow TCP Stream gives protocol context; strings is the dissector-independent fallback. Use both.
  • The defensible answer to a cleartext-protocol exposure is segmentation plus migration to an authenticated protocol generation, and rotation of any exposed credential.

docs.title: Exercise OTSOC-2.3: Freezer Tags and Warehouse Telemetry
Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Pecan Creek Creamery (fictional) Role OT SOC Analyst, Cold Side Phase Visibility Protocol Analysis Detection Priority order Safety, then Integrity, then Availability, then Confidentiality

What you know so far: You can now read Modbus and S7comm and tell a read from a write. The cold side of the plant speaks two newer protocols: the continuous freezer is an EtherNet/IP CIP controller and the cold storage and switchgear are a DNP3 outstation. Both express the same read-versus-command distinction you already know, but with different vocabulary, and this exercise teaches you to recognize it in each.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are an OT SOC analyst at Pecan Creek Creamery. The modern supervisory layer on the cold side runs two protocols. The continuous freezer freeze.pcc.local is an EtherNet/IP CIP controller on port 44818, and the cold storage and switchgear cold.pcc.local are a DNP3 outstation on port 20000. Your job is to read both well enough to tell a steady telemetry report from a control command.

For the freezer you will enumerate the CIP tag list and the controller identity (barrel temperature, dasher speed, overrun, carton count, product code, and serial number) and contrast the steady stream of tag reads with a write to the barrel setpoint. For the cold storage you will issue a DNP3 class 0 integrity poll, read the binary inputs (door and breaker states) and analog inputs (room temperatures), and learn why a lone operate without a matching select is the suspicious pattern in DNP3. You are reading and enumerating only. No write or control command touches either device.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The cold side is where a cyber action turns directly into spoiled inventory or a tripped breaker, and the two protocols here encode their commands in ways an analyst must recognize on sight.

Three concrete reasons the skill matters. First, EtherNet/IP CIP exposes named tags rather than numbered registers, which is friendlier to read but means an attacker can enumerate the entire control program by name. Knowing how to pull the tag list and the CIP identity is both your asset-inventory tool and your early warning that someone else is enumerating the same controller. Second, DNP3 was built for the electric utility world and carries a safety feature most protocols lack: select-before-operate. A control like opening a breaker is supposed to arrive as a select message followed by a matching operate. A lone operate with no preceding select is the signature of an attacker replaying or forging a command, and recognizing that two-step pattern is the core DNP3 detection skill. Third, the report-versus-command distinction is what keeps the cold chain intact. A DNP3 class 0 poll that returns door states and room temperatures is telemetry; a CROB (control relay output block) operate on a feeder breaker is a command that can drop power to a freezer full of product. Your detections live or die on telling those apart.

The freezer serial you recover is a training artifact. The skill of enumerating CIP identity and reasoning about DNP3 select-before-operate is permanent.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Operator HMI operator PecanCreek#2026 Reference only; CIP and DNP3 reads require no login

docs.title: The operator cockpit
docs.text:
The cold side runs a live operator cockpit for the continuous freezer. Open it in a browser at the address shown for ophmi in the Exercise Network panel (HTTP, port 80). The cockpit shows the freezer barrel, the dasher and overrun gauges, the carton conveyor, and the cold-chain integrity panel in real time, so you can watch the barrel hold its band while the same CIP tags you enumerate by hand update on screen.

Normal operation: the continuous freezer barrel holds -5.0 C, the dasher and overrun gauges sit in band, and the cold-chain integrity panel reads nominal. The barrel-temperature gauge runs a negative scale, so a reading that climbs toward warm is the alarm side, not the cold side.

Flip the cockpit into its Engineering view and every element is labelled with the live CIP tag behind it, so the barrel temperature reads BarrelTempC and the setpoint reads BarrelSetpoint straight off the HMI. The same named tag list you are about to enumerate by hand sits one click away on the operator console.

The Engineering X-ray binds the freezer barrel to `BarrelTempC` and the setpoint to `BarrelSetpoint`, the exact tags you read in Part 1, and exposes the full CIP tag list as a live register map.

docs.title: Before You Begin: Read Your Target IPs
docs.text:
The cold-side hosts get fresh addresses every spawn. Open the Exercise Network panel and read the IPs for freeze.pcc.local and cold.pcc.local into shell variables. Replace the placeholders below with the values from your own panel.

The passive sensor on this segment does not sniff the live wire. A switched control network hides unicast from a SPAN-less sniffer, so the sensor serves a recorded capture of the cold-side plant network taken earlier. In that recorded capture the plant hosts appear on the control-network addressing as 10.100.4.6 for the freezer and 10.100.4.7 for the cold-storage RTU. Your live Exercise Network panel hands out its own session subnet, so a captured host and its live panel device line up by their shared last octet. The freezer is the panel IP ending in .6 and the cold RTU is the panel IP ending in .7. You read the live devices by their panel IPs below, then cross-check them against the recorded capture in Part 3.

Kali - set target variables

FREEZE=<freeze ip from the Exercise Network panel>
COLD=<cold ip from the Exercise Network panel>
echo "freezer       = $FREEZE:44818 (EtherNet/IP CIP)"
echo "cold storage  = $COLD:20000 (DNP3)"

Confirm both answer before decoding. EtherNet/IP listens on 44818 and DNP3 on 20000.

Kali - confirm reachability

nc -zv "$FREEZE" 44818
nc -zv "$COLD" 20000

Expected output

Connection to <FREEZE> 44818 port [tcp/*] succeeded!
Connection to <COLD> 20000 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

Two succeeded! lines confirm both control links are up. Fix connectivity first if either fails.

docs.title: Part 1: Enumerate the Freezer over EtherNet/IP CIP
Step 1: Pull the CIP tag list
docs.text:
EtherNet/IP CIP controllers expose a named tag database rather than numbered registers. The pycomm3 LogixDriver speaks CIP and can list every tag the controller publishes. Enumerating the tag list is your asset-inventory step and shows you exactly what process values the freezer exposes.

Kali - enumerate the CIP tag list

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver
with LogixDriver(os.environ["FREEZE"]) as plc:
    tags = plc.get_tag_list()
    for t in tags:
        print(t["tag_name"], "::", t["data_type"])
PYEOF

Expected output

BarrelTempC    :: REAL
BarrelSetpoint :: REAL
DasherSpeed    :: INT
Overrun        :: INT
LineState      :: INT
CartonCount    :: DINT
ProductCode    :: DINT
SerialNumber   :: STRING
FlagBlock      :: STRING

The tag list is the freezer's published control surface: barrel temperature and setpoint, dasher speed, overrun (a product-quality variable), line state, carton count, product code, and a serial number. Any host that can reach port 44818 can read this list, which is convenient for you and equally convenient for an attacker doing reconnaissance.

docs.title: Step 2: Read the controller identity and recover the serial
docs.text:
The CIP identity, plus the named tags, fingerprint the controller. Read the process tags to see a steady freezer (barrel near -5 C, carton count climbing) and pull the SerialNumber tag, which carries the controller serial you need for the flag.

Kali - read freezer tags and the serial

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver
with LogixDriver(os.environ["FREEZE"]) as plc:
    for name in ["BarrelTempC", "DasherSpeed", "Overrun",
                 "CartonCount", "ProductCode", "SerialNumber"]:
        r = plc.read(name)
        print(f"{name:14} = {r.value}")
PYEOF

Expected output

BarrelTempC    = -5.0
DasherSpeed    = 70
Overrun        = 100
CartonCount    = ...
ProductCode    = 30815
SerialNumber   = <freezer controller serial>

The barrel sits at -5.0 C with the dasher near 70 and overrun near 100, the signature of a freezer running normally. The carton count climbs over time. The SerialNumber tag reads the controller serial you will normalize into the flag. It is a short PCC-FRZ- asset tag; read the live value yourself rather than copying it from here.

docs.title: Step 3: Pull the CIP identity object
docs.text:
Named tags are the program's data; the CIP identity object is the device's own nameplate. Reading it gives you vendor, product type, and a device serial that an attacker would use to look up known vulnerabilities. pycomm3 exposes it through get_module_info.

Kali - read the CIP identity object

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver
with LogixDriver(os.environ["FREEZE"]) as plc:
    info = plc.get_module_info(0)
    print("vendor       :", info.get("vendor"))
    print("product_name :", info.get("product_name"))
    print("serial       :", hex(info.get("serial")) if info.get("serial") else None)
PYEOF

Expected output

vendor       : Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley
product_name : 1756-L83E/B LOGIX5583E
serial       : 0x6f8ee06

The identity names a ControlLogix-class controller. The device serial in the identity object is distinct from the application SerialNumber tag you read in Step 2: the identity serial is the silicon nameplate, while the tag is a string the program author chose. The flag comes from the application SerialNumber tag.

docs.title: Step 4: Tell a read from a write in CIP
docs.text:
You have been reading. A write looks different on the wire, and recognizing it is the detection skill. The point of this step is awareness, not action: you will inspect what a CIP write to the barrel setpoint would look like without sending one. Capture a few seconds of normal CIP traffic and inspect the service codes.

Kali - capture and classify CIP services

sudo tshark -i any -f "tcp port 44818 and host $FREEZE" -a duration:8 \
  -Y 'cip' -T fields -e frame.number -e cip.sc 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c

Expected output

 12  0x4c
  8  0x4d

CIP service 0x4c is Read Tag and 0x4d is Write Tag (the read-modify-write variant 0x4e also exists). In a healthy freezer dominated by HMI polling you see mostly Read Tag. A Write Tag to BarrelSetpoint is the command you alert on, because raising the freezer setpoint slowly is exactly how a patient attacker spoils product without tripping an obvious alarm. You will hunt that drift in Level 3.

Why CIP service codes matter for detection

EtherNet/IP wraps CIP, and CIP carries the actual operation in a one-byte service code. Read Tag (0x4c) is the normal polling service; Write Tag (0x4d) changes a tag value. A detection that alerts on cip.sc == 0x4d targeting BarrelSetpoint catches setpoint tampering while ignoring the flood of reads. Same idea as Modbus function 6 and S7 Write Var, different vocabulary.

A single Write Tag that raises BarrelSetpoint from -5.0 C toward warm is enough to break the cold chain. On the operator cockpit the change is loud: the barrel glows warm, the temperature crosses to the alarm side of the negative scale, and the spoilage banner fires.

The moment a CIP Write Tag pushes the setpoint warm: the barrel reads 3.1 C, the BARREL OVER-TEMP - PRODUCT SPOILAGE banner fires, and the cold-chain integrity panel drops to a critical spoilage alarm. A patient attacker raises the setpoint a fraction at a time to land here without ever tripping a hard threshold, which is the silent drift you hunt in Level 3.

docs.title: Part 2: Read the Cold Storage over DNP3
Step 5: Issue a class 0 integrity poll
docs.text:
DNP3 organizes data into classes. A class 0 integrity poll asks the outstation for the current value of every static point: binary inputs, analog inputs, and counters. The outstation here is address 10 and the master is address 1. Issuing the poll is how a DNP3 master gets a full snapshot, and it is the read you build your baseline from.

Kali - class 0 integrity poll

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os, time
from pydnp3 import opendnp3, asiodnp3, asiopal, openpal

# Minimal DNP3 master: connect, integrity poll, print, exit.
# The cold outstation is link address 10; this master is link address 1.
print(f"polling DNP3 outstation 10 at {os.environ['COLD']}:20000 ...")
# (Run your class-0 integrity poll with your DNP3 master of choice.)
PYEOF

Expected output

polling DNP3 outstation 10 at <COLD>:20000 ...

A class 0 poll returns every static point in one response. If your environment ships a DNP3 master CLI rather than a Python binding, the same integrity poll is available there; the concept is identical. The values you care about are the binary inputs and analog inputs you read next.

docs.title: Step 6: Read binary inputs (doors and breakers)
docs.text:
DNP3 group 1 holds binary inputs: door contacts and breaker positions for the cold storage and switchgear. Reading them tells you the physical state of the warehouse: which doors are open and which feeders are energized. A door that opens off-hours or a breaker that trips is a physical event your telemetry must show.

Kali - decode binary input states

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
# Map of DNP3 group 1 (binary input) indices for the cold outstation.
labels = {
    0: "freezer_door", 1: "cooler_door", 2: "dock_door",
    3: "main_breaker", 4: "freezer_feeder_brkr", 5: "cooler_feeder_brkr",
}
# Normal packed byte across indices 0-5 is 0x38 (breakers closed, doors shut).
packed = 0x38
for idx, name in labels.items():
    print(f"BI[{idx}] {name:20} = {(packed >> idx) & 1}")
PYEOF

Expected output

BI[0] freezer_door         = 0
BI[1] cooler_door          = 0
BI[2] dock_door            = 0
BI[3] main_breaker         = 1
BI[4] freezer_feeder_brkr  = 1
BI[5] cooler_feeder_brkr   = 1

All three doors read closed (0) and all three breakers read closed/energized (1), the normal packed byte 0x38. A 1 on a door index or a 0 on a breaker index is a physical change worth a second look.

docs.title: Step 7: Read analog inputs (room temperatures)
docs.text:
DNP3 group 30 holds analog inputs: the room temperatures scaled by 100. The freezer room is the spoilage-critical point, held in a tight band. Reading these is how the cold chain proves itself, and a freezer-room temperature drifting out of band is the headline cold-chain alarm.

Kali - decode analog input temperatures

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
labels = {0: "freezer_room", 1: "cooler_room", 2: "dock", 3: "ambient"}
# Group 30 analog inputs are degC * 100. Example normal snapshot:
raw = {0: -2500, 1: 350, 2: 750, 3: 2100}
for idx, name in labels.items():
    print(f"AI[{idx}] {name:14} = {raw[idx]/100:.2f} C")
PYEOF

Expected output

AI[0] freezer_room   = -25.00 C
AI[1] cooler_room    = 3.50 C
AI[2] dock           = 7.50 C
AI[3] ambient        = 21.00 C

The freezer room sits at -25.00 C, inside the spoilage-critical band of roughly -26 to -24 C. The cooler, dock, and ambient readings are normal for a warehouse. A freezer room climbing past -24 C is the cold-chain alarm that puts product at risk.

docs.title: Step 8: Understand select-before-operate
docs.text:
DNP3 controls (CROB, control relay output block) are supposed to use select-before-operate: a select message names the point and parameters, and a matching operate executes it, like arming then firing. A lone operate with no preceding select is the suspicious pattern, because it means a command arrived without the handshake a legitimate master performs. You will not send a control; you will learn to spot the pattern in a capture.

Kali - classify DNP3 control function codes in a capture

sudo tshark -i any -f "tcp port 20000 and host $COLD" -a duration:8 \
  -Y 'dnp3' -T fields -e frame.number -e dnp3.al.func 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c

Expected output

 10  0x01
  6  0x81

Application function 0x01 is Read and 0x81 is Response, the normal poll-and-respond pattern of healthy telemetry. The control functions are 0x03 SELECT, 0x04 OPERATE, and 0x05 DIRECT_OPERATE. A legitimate breaker control is a SELECT (0x03) immediately followed by a matching OPERATE (0x04) on the same point. An OPERATE with no preceding SELECT, or a DIRECT_OPERATE on a feeder breaker, is the signature you alert on.

Why select-before-operate is a detection gift

The two-step handshake means a forged or replayed control usually shows up as a half-pattern: an operate with no matching select, or a select that never operates. A detection that pairs SELECT and OPERATE by point and time, and alerts when an OPERATE arrives unpaired, catches command injection on breakers without flagging normal telemetry. DNP3 hands you a built-in invariant most OT protocols lack; use it.

docs.title: Part 3: Cross-Check Against the Sensor
docs.text:
Your passive sensor sensor.pcc.local runs Zeek with ICSNPP and serves a recorded capture of the cold-side plant network, writing enip.log, cip.log, and dnp3.log. Because the logs come from that recorded capture, the plant hosts show up on the control-network addressing as 10.100.4.6 (the freezer) and 10.100.4.7 (the cold RTU), which line up with the live panel devices ending in .6 and .7. Cross-checking your hand decode against the sensor builds the habit of trusting, and verifying, the SOC's own telemetry. Read the sensor IP from the Exercise Network panel.

Kali - pull the Zeek cold-side logs

SENSOR=<sensor ip from the Exercise Network panel>
curl -s "http://$SENSOR:8000/cip.log"  | zeek-cut id.resp_h cip_service_code 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c | head
curl -s "http://$SENSOR:8000/dnp3.log" | zeek-cut id.resp_h fc_request fc_reply 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c | head

Expected output

   1104 10.100.4.6  0x4c
    276 10.100.4.6  0x01
     23 10.100.4.7  READ  RESPONSE

The Zeek cip.log confirms the freezer traffic is dominated by CIP service 0x4c (Read Tag) to the freezer, with the odd 0x01 (Get Attributes All) from the operator poller enumerating the tag list, and dnp3.log confirms the cold-storage traffic is READ and RESPONSE. This ICSNPP build names only the generic CIP services, so the Rockwell Logix Read Tag shows as its raw service code 0x4c in the cip_service_code field rather than a friendly name. The addresses read as 10.100.4.6 and 10.100.4.7 because the sensor is replaying the recorded plant capture. They map to your live freezer and cold RTU by the shared last octet, .6 and .7. When the sensor and your manual analysis agree, you can trust the sensor for volume and reserve hand decoding for what looks wrong.

The sensor's recorded-capture logs at a glance: cip.log shows a stream of Read Tag operations to the freezer at 10.100.4.6, and dnp3.log shows READ requests answered by RESPONSE from the cold RTU at 10.100.4.7. Both hosts line up with your live panel devices by their shared last octet, .6 and .7.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• CIP exposes named tags, not numbered registers. The tag list is both your inventory and an attacker's reconnaissance surface.
  • CIP service 0x4c is Read Tag, 0x4d is Write Tag. The application SerialNumber tag is a program string, distinct from the CIP identity object's silicon serial.
  • A DNP3 class 0 integrity poll returns every static point: binary inputs (group 1), analog inputs (group 30), and counters (group 20).
  • The freezer room band of roughly -26 to -24 C is spoilage-critical; a climb past -24 C is the cold-chain alarm.
  • DNP3 controls use select-before-operate. A lone OPERATE with no matching SELECT, or a DIRECT_OPERATE on a breaker, is the suspicious pattern.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The freezer publishes a named tag list any host can read. Is that a vulnerability?

Reveal answer

The tag list itself is a design feature of EtherNet/IP CIP, not a bug. The vulnerability is the lack of access control around it: any host that can reach port 44818 can enumerate the entire control program, including setpoint tags it could then write. The fix is not to hide tags but to segment the network so only the HMI and engineering workstation reach the controller, and to monitor for tag enumeration from unexpected sources.

2. You read a CIP identity serial and an application SerialNumber tag and they differ. Which is which?

Reveal answer

The CIP identity object's serial is the device nameplate burned in by the manufacturer; it identifies the physical controller and is what you would use to check for known vulnerabilities by model and revision. The application SerialNumber tag is a string a program author defined inside the controller logic, so it can be anything the integrator chose, often a plant asset tag. They serve different purposes and will not match.

3. Why is a lone DNP3 OPERATE more suspicious than an OPERATE that follows a SELECT?

Reveal answer

A legitimate DNP3 master performs select-before-operate: it sends a SELECT naming the point and the intended action, the outstation echoes it back to confirm, and only then does the master send a matching OPERATE. An OPERATE with no preceding SELECT skips the confirmation handshake, which is what a replayed or forged control looks like. Pairing SELECT and OPERATE by point and time and alerting on unpaired OPERATEs is a high-signal detection because legitimate masters almost never produce a lone OPERATE.

4. The freezer room reads -25 C and the cold chain is fine. What single change would put product at risk, and how would you see it first?

Reveal answer

A slow upward drift of the CIP BarrelSetpoint (or the freezer-room temperature climbing past -24 C) puts product at risk while staying under obvious alarm thresholds. You would see it first in the analog input trend, not in a single reading, which is why you baseline the band and watch for drift rather than waiting for a hard alarm. A patient attacker raises the setpoint a fraction at a time precisely to stay below the alarm, so trending and rate-of-change detection beat threshold alarms here.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is the freezer controller serial number recovered from the CIP identity in Step 2, normalized to lowercase with each non-alphanumeric character replaced by an underscore and wrapped as OCR{...}. Build it from the SerialNumber tag value you read rather than typing it by hand.

Kali - normalize the serial into the flag

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os, re
from pycomm3 import LogixDriver
with LogixDriver(os.environ["FREEZE"]) as plc:
    serial = plc.read("SerialNumber").value
norm = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "_", serial.lower()).strip("_")
print("serial =", serial)
print("flag   = OCR{cip_freezer_serial_" + norm + "}")
PYEOF

Expected output (flag masked)

serial = <freezer controller serial>
flag   = OCR{cip_freezer_serial_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the exercise panel.

Flag format (value masked)

OCR{cip_freezer_serial_<masked>}

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Pecan Creek
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation Unauthenticated CIP tag enumeration on the freezer Medium Restrict TCP/44818 to the HMI and engineering workstation; alert on tag enumeration from new sources No alerting on CIP Write Tag to BarrelSetpoint High Alert the SOC on cip.sc == 0x4d targeting setpoint tags and watch setpoint rate-of-change DNP3 controls accepted without SELECT/OPERATE pairing review High Pair SELECT and OPERATE by point and time; alert on unpaired OPERATE or DIRECT_OPERATE on breakers

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• EtherNet/IP CIP names its data as tags; DNP3 numbers its data as points in groups. Both still carry the report-versus-command distinction you already know.
  • CIP service 0x4d (Write Tag) and DNP3 OPERATE are the commands you alert on; reads and class 0 polls are normal telemetry.
  • DNP3 select-before-operate is a built-in invariant: a lone OPERATE is high-signal evidence of a forged or replayed control.
  • The freezer-room temperature band is the cold chain's vital sign; trend it and watch for drift rather than waiting for a hard alarm.

docs.title: Exercise OTSOC-2.4: The Anonymous OPC-UA Server
Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Pecan Creek Creamery (fictional) Role OT SOC Analyst, Supervisory Layer Phase Visibility Protocol Analysis Detection Priority order Safety, then Integrity, then Availability, then Confidentiality

What you know so far: You have read the legacy plant protocols (Modbus, S7comm) and the modern cold-side protocols (CIP, DNP3). The newest layer is an OPC-UA supervisory server the plant added last year. OPC-UA was designed with security in mind, which makes its most common real-world finding instructive: a server deployed with all the security turned off.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are an OT SOC analyst at Pecan Creek Creamery. The plant added a modern OPC-UA supervisory server last year. The vendor left it with SecurityPolicy None (no signing, no encryption) and Anonymous access allowed, which is the single most common OPC-UA finding in the field. The target is opcua.pcc.local on port 4840, endpoint opc.tcp://opcua.pcc.local:4840/pcc/supervisory/, namespace http://pecancreek.local/plant/.

You will connect as an anonymous client with the asyncua library, confirm the endpoint advertises SecurityPolicy None and Anonymous, then browse the address space under Objects/PecanCreek. The tree mirrors a handful of plant tags (Mix, Pasteurizer, Freezer, Ammonia) plus a Commissioning object. You will read the Commissioning/CommissioningToken node, which is readable only because anonymous access is enabled, and that read is the proof of the misconfiguration. You are demonstrating the finding, not exploiting anything. Then you document it the way an architecture review expects: what is exposed, why None plus Anonymous is a problem, and what the secure configuration would be.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
OPC-UA is the protocol the OT industry chose to fix the sins of the legacy dialects: it has authentication, signing, and encryption built into the standard. The catch is that those protections are configurable, and a server shipped with them off is no safer than classic Modbus, while everyone assumes it is safe because it is the modern protocol.

Three concrete reasons the skill matters. First, recognizing the None-plus-Anonymous misconfiguration is the highest-value OPC-UA finding you will report. A server in that state lets any host on the segment connect with no credentials and read the entire address space, which on a supervisory server can include recipes, batch records, and commissioning material. The finding is common precisely because the secure setup requires certificate management that vendors skip during commissioning. Second, browsing an OPC-UA address space is a transferable enumeration skill. The tree of objects and variables maps directly to the plant's process model, so an analyst who can browse it understands what the supervisory layer knows, which is the same understanding an attacker would build before manipulating it. Third, knowing the secure configuration turns the finding into a fundable recommendation. Saying "OPC-UA is insecure" is wrong and useless; saying "the endpoint advertises only SecurityPolicy None with Anonymous, and it should advertise Basic256Sha256 with certificate or username authentication" is a finding a plant can act on.

The commissioning token you read is a training artifact. The skill of confirming an endpoint's security policy and browsing its namespace is permanent.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Operator HMI operator PecanCreek#2026 Reference only; anonymous access is the whole point here

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Connect to the OPC-UA endpoint as an anonymous client with asyncua
  • Confirm the endpoint advertises SecurityPolicy None and Anonymous access
  • Browse the address space under Objects/PecanCreek and enumerate the namespace
  • Read the CommissioningToken marker node exposed by anonymous access
  • Write a defensible finding stating the problem and the secure configuration
Detail Value Difficulty Beginner Estimated Time 40 minutes Prerequisites Exercises 2.1 through 2.3 Flag Source Found? OCR{<commissioning_token_value>} CommissioningToken node, readable only because anonymous is allowed

docs.title: Before You Begin: Read Your Target IP
docs.text:
The OPC-UA server gets a fresh address every spawn. Open the Exercise Network panel and read the IP for opcua.pcc.local into a shell variable. Replace the placeholder below with the value from your own panel.

Kali - set the OPC-UA target variable

OPCUA=<opcua ip from the Exercise Network panel>
echo "opc-ua server = $OPCUA:4840"
echo "endpoint      = opc.tcp://$OPCUA:4840/pcc/supervisory/"

Confirm the server answers on port 4840 before you try to connect.

Kali - confirm the OPC-UA port is open

nc -zv "$OPCUA" 4840

Expected output

Connection to <OPCUA> 4840 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

A succeeded! line confirms the supervisory server is listening. Fix connectivity first if it fails.

docs.title: Step 1: Enumerate the advertised endpoints
docs.text:
Before connecting, ask the server what security it offers. OPC-UA exposes a get_endpoints call that lists every endpoint with its SecurityPolicy and the token types it accepts, and you can read it without authenticating. The presence of a None policy with an Anonymous token type is the misconfiguration in plain sight.

Kali - list endpoints and their security policies

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os, asyncio
from asyncua import Client

async def main():
    url = f"opc.tcp://{os.environ['OPCUA']}:4840/pcc/supervisory/"
    c = Client(url)
    eps = await c.connect_and_get_server_endpoints()
    for ep in eps:
        policy = ep.SecurityPolicyURI.split("#")[-1]
        modes = [t.TokenType.name for t in ep.UserIdentityTokens]
        print(f"policy={policy:16} mode={ep.SecurityMode.name:12} tokens={modes}")

asyncio.run(main())
PYEOF

Expected output

policy=None             mode=None_        tokens=['Anonymous']

The only advertised policy is None with security mode None and an Anonymous user-identity token. No signing, no encryption, and no credential required. An endpoint list that offers a real policy such as Basic256Sha256 alongside None would be a partial finding; a server that offers only None is fully exposed.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect anonymously
docs.text:
Confirming the policy is one thing; demonstrating that you can connect with no credentials makes the finding undeniable. Connect to the endpoint with no username, password, or certificate. A clean session proves anonymous access is live.

Kali - connect as an anonymous client

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os, asyncio
from asyncua import Client

async def main():
    url = f"opc.tcp://{os.environ['OPCUA']}:4840/pcc/supervisory/"
    async with Client(url) as c:           # no credentials supplied
        srv = await c.nodes.server.read_browse_name()
        print("connected anonymously; server node browse name =", srv.Name)

asyncio.run(main())
PYEOF

Expected output

connected anonymously; server node browse name = Server

The session opened with no credentials at all, which confirms the Anonymous token type the endpoint advertised. Any host that can reach port 4840 can do the same.

docs.title: Step 3: Browse the address space
docs.text:
OPC-UA organizes data as a tree of nodes under Objects. Browsing that tree is your enumeration step: it shows you exactly what the supervisory server publishes, which mirrors the plant's process model. Resolve the plant namespace index first, then walk the tree under PecanCreek.

Kali - browse the PecanCreek object tree

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os, asyncio
from asyncua import Client

async def main():
    url = f"opc.tcp://{os.environ['OPCUA']}:4840/pcc/supervisory/"
    async with Client(url) as c:
        idx = await c.get_namespace_index("http://pecancreek.local/plant/")
        root = await c.nodes.objects.get_child(f"{idx}:PecanCreek")
        for child in await root.get_children():
            bn = await child.read_browse_name()
            print(f"{idx}:{bn.Name}")
            for leaf in await child.get_children():
                lbn = await leaf.read_browse_name()
                print(f"    {idx}:{lbn.Name}")

asyncio.run(main())
PYEOF

Expected output

2:Mix
    2:RecipeId
    2:SugarPct
2:Pasteurizer
    2:HoldTempC
2:Freezer
    2:BarrelTempC
2:Ammonia
    2:SuctionPsig
2:Commissioning
    2:CommissioningToken

The tree mirrors the plant: Mix, Pasteurizer, Freezer, and Ammonia each expose a few process variables, and a Commissioning object holds a CommissioningToken node. An anonymous reader sees the entire supervisory model of the plant, which is exactly the reconnaissance an attacker would perform.

docs.title: Step 4: Read the commissioning token
docs.text:
The CommissioningToken node is readable only because anonymous access is enabled. Reading it is the proof of the misconfiguration and the source of the flag. On a properly secured server this read would fail with a credential or security error. Navigate to the node and read its value.

Kali - read the CommissioningToken node

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os, asyncio
from asyncua import Client

async def main():
    url = f"opc.tcp://{os.environ['OPCUA']}:4840/pcc/supervisory/"
    async with Client(url) as c:
        idx = await c.get_namespace_index("http://pecancreek.local/plant/")
        node = await c.nodes.objects.get_child(
            [f"{idx}:PecanCreek", f"{idx}:Commissioning", f"{idx}:CommissioningToken"])
        print("CommissioningToken =", await node.read_value())

asyncio.run(main())
PYEOF

Expected output (value masked)

CommissioningToken = pcc_opcua_anon_<masked>

The token value reads back over an unauthenticated session. On a server configured with a signed-and-encrypted policy and certificate or username authentication, this read returns an access-denied or security error instead. The fact that it succeeds anonymously is the finding.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• get_endpoints lets you read a server's advertised SecurityPolicy and token types before connecting. A server that advertises only None with Anonymous is fully exposed.
  • Connecting with no credentials proves the Anonymous token type is live, not merely advertised.
  • The OPC-UA address space is a tree under Objects; browsing it mirrors the plant's process model and is the core enumeration skill.
  • The CommissioningToken reads back only because anonymous access is enabled. On a secured server the same read fails, which is what makes the successful read the proof of the misconfiguration.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. OPC-UA was designed to be secure. Why is None-plus-Anonymous so common in the field?

Reveal answer

The secure configuration requires certificate management: the server and each client need certificates, and an administrator must establish trust between them. During commissioning, integrators under time pressure frequently turn security off to get the system talking, intending to harden it later, and "later" never arrives. The result is a modern protocol running with no signing, no encryption, and no authentication, which is no safer than the legacy dialects it was meant to replace. The protocol is not the problem; the deployment is.

2. You connected with no credentials and read the whole tree. What is the realistic worst case on a real supervisory server?

Reveal answer

A real supervisory OPC-UA server aggregates data from across the plant: recipes, batch records, production counts, setpoints, and sometimes write access to those setpoints. An anonymous reader gets the entire production picture for reconnaissance, and if the server also allows anonymous writes, an attacker can change setpoints from a single unauthenticated session. Even read-only exposure leaks proprietary recipes and batch data, which is a confidentiality and competitive loss on top of the security risk.

3. What is the secure configuration you would recommend, specifically?

Reveal answer

Disable the None security policy and the Anonymous identity token entirely. Configure the endpoint to advertise a signed-and-encrypted policy such as Basic256Sha256 with security mode SignAndEncrypt, and require either certificate-based or username-and-password authentication for client identity. Establish a certificate trust list so only known clients (the HMI, the historian, the engineering workstation) can connect, and place the server in a conduit reachable only from those hosts. Name the specific policy and mode in the finding so the plant can verify the change.

4. How would your SOC detect an attacker abusing this server, given it is misconfigured?

Reveal answer

Until the server is hardened, the detection is connection-based: alert on any OPC-UA session from a source that is not the known HMI, historian, or engineering workstation, because a legitimate plant has a small, fixed set of clients. Watch for browse and read activity that walks the whole address space quickly, which is enumeration rather than the targeted polling a real client does. The durable fix is to require authentication so unknown clients cannot connect at all, but until then, a tight allowlist on the session source is your best signal.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is the CommissioningToken node value you read in Step 4, wrapped as OCR{...}. The node is readable only because anonymous access is enabled, so recovering it is itself the demonstration of the misconfiguration. Build the flag from the value you read rather than typing it by hand.

Kali - assemble the flag from the token

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import os, asyncio
from asyncua import Client

async def main():
    url = f"opc.tcp://{os.environ['OPCUA']}:4840/pcc/supervisory/"
    async with Client(url) as c:
        idx = await c.get_namespace_index("http://pecancreek.local/plant/")
        node = await c.nodes.objects.get_child(
            [f"{idx}:PecanCreek", f"{idx}:Commissioning", f"{idx}:CommissioningToken"])
        token = await node.read_value()
        print("flag = OCR{" + token + "}")

asyncio.run(main())
PYEOF

Expected output (flag masked)

flag = OCR{pcc_opcua_anon_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the exercise panel.

Flag format (value masked)

OCR{pcc_opcua_anon_<masked>}

docs.title: Defensive Recommendations to Pecan Creek
docs.text: Finding Risk Mitigation OPC-UA endpoint advertises only SecurityPolicy None with Anonymous High Advertise Basic256Sha256 with SignAndEncrypt; require certificate or username authentication Entire supervisory address space readable without credentials High Restrict TCP/4840 to the HMI, historian, and engineering workstation via a conduit No alerting on OPC-UA sessions from unexpected sources Medium Allowlist known OPC-UA clients and alert the SOC on any session from a new source

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• OPC-UA ships with authentication, signing, and encryption, but they are configurable, and a server with them off is no safer than classic Modbus.
  • get_endpoints reveals a server's security posture before you connect; an endpoint offering only None with Anonymous is the highest-value OPC-UA finding.
  • Browsing the address space mirrors the plant's process model and is the enumeration skill an attacker uses first.
  • A defensible finding names the specific secure policy (Basic256Sha256, SignAndEncrypt, certificate or username auth), not just "turn on security."

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Pecan Creek Creamery (fictional) Role OT SOC Analyst, Plant Floor Phase Reconstruction Detection Engineering Threat Hunting

What you know so far: Last shift, a rogue host on the OT segment reached the blend tank, swept its Modbus holding registers, then wrote new setpoints. The attack is already over. Your job is not to attack anything; it is to reconstruct what happened and translate it into a shared vocabulary the whole team can defend against.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Pecan Creek Creamery ran an unauthorized intrusion against the blend tank and freezer lines last shift. A rogue host at 172.31.4.66 swept the Modbus holding registers on the blend tank, then issued function code 6 writes that flipped the recipe and the agitator setpoint. The plant sensor and the pcap host preserved the evidence. The blend tank PLC is mix.pcc.local, a Pecan Creek Controls PCCK-300 on Modbus/TCP port 502.

Your role is the SOC analyst on the day-after. The adversary already acted. You walk the capture and the Zeek logs, list each action in order, and translate raw packets into MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique IDs. The deliverable is a coverage table you submit to the plant rubric grader at rubric.pcc.local, which scores your mapping against a canonical checklist and releases the flag once your coverage clears the pass threshold.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A pile of packets is not an incident report. Until you can name what the adversary did in a vocabulary your detection engineers, your management, and your peers at other plants all recognize, the capture is just noise on a disk. MITRE ATT&CK for ICS is that vocabulary. Mapping a real intrusion to technique IDs is the bridge between "something weird happened" and "here is the detection we are building so it never happens silently again."

Mapping also forces honesty about coverage. When you write down that the rogue host ran a register sweep (T0846 Remote System Discovery) and you realize no sensor rule would have caught it, you have just found a detection gap before the next adversary does. The coverage table you hand the grader is the same artifact a real OT SOC hands its detection-engineering backlog: each row is a technique observed, the data source that revealed it, and the rule you owe.

docs.title: Before You Begin: Read the Network Panel
docs.text:
After the lab shows Running, the Exercise Network panel on the track page lists every target with its IP. Two hosts matter here: the PCAP evidence host and the rubric grader. Copy their IPs into shell variables so the walkthrough commands work without hardcoding any subnet octets.

Kali - set target variables from the Exercise Network panel

# Replace each value with the IP shown in the Exercise Network panel.
PCAP=<pcaphost-ip-from-panel>     # pcaphost.pcc.local, HTTP/80
RUBRIC=<rubric-ip-from-panel>     # rubric.pcc.local, HTTP/80
echo "pcap=$PCAP rubric=$RUBRIC"

A quick reachability check confirms both hosts answer before you invest time in analysis. A succeeded! on each line means you are wired into the plant network.

Kali - confirm both evidence hosts are reachable

nc -zv "$PCAP" 80
nc -zv "$RUBRIC" 80

If either probe hangs or reports No route to host, the lab is not fully Running yet, or your VPN tunnel dropped. Fix connectivity before continuing.

docs.title: Step 1: Pull the Capture Index
docs.text:
The pcap host serves a small library of curated captures over plain HTTP. List them first so you know which file holds the blend tank intrusion. The index is a simple directory page.

Kali - list the available captures

curl -s "http://$PCAP/" | grep -oE '[a-z-]+\.pcap'

You should see four captures: baseline.pcap, attack-mix.pcap, pasteurizer-divert.pcap, and ammonia-trip.pcap. The blend tank intrusion lives in attack-mix.pcap. The baseline.pcap is your benign reference: the HMI polling the freezer with read-only function code 3 every couple of seconds, nothing writing.

docs.title: Step 2: Download the Attack Capture
docs.text:
Pull attack-mix.pcap to your Kali so you can analyze it offline with Zeek and Wireshark. Saving to /tmp keeps it as scratch you can re-parse.

Kali - download the blend tank attack capture

curl -s "http://$PCAP/attack-mix.pcap" -o /tmp/attack-mix.pcap
ls -l /tmp/attack-mix.pcap

A non-zero file size confirms the download. If the file is empty, re-check that attack-mix.pcap appeared in the Step 1 listing and that $PCAP holds the right IP.

docs.title: Step 3: Run Zeek to Extract the Modbus Conversation
docs.text:
Wireshark is fine for a visual pass, but Zeek with the ICSNPP Modbus analyzer turns the capture into a flat modbus.log you can grep and reason about. Run Zeek against the pcap in a scratch directory so the log files land somewhere tidy.

Kali - parse the capture with Zeek

mkdir -p /tmp/zeek-mix && cd /tmp/zeek-mix
zeek -C -r /tmp/attack-mix.pcap
ls

Zeek writes conn.log, modbus.log, and possibly modbus_detailed.log. The -C flag tells Zeek to ignore TCP checksum errors that are common in curated captures. If zeek is not on your Kali, the same analysis works in Wireshark by filtering on modbus.

docs.title: Step 4: Identify the Read Sweep
docs.text:
Open modbus.log and look at the function codes the rogue host issued. The attack always starts with reconnaissance: a sweep of read requests across the holding-register bands to learn the tank's layout before touching anything. In Modbus, that is function code 3 (read holding registers).

Kali - list every Modbus request with its source and function

zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h func < modbus.log | head -40

Watch the id.orig_h column. The legitimate poller appears repeatedly with READ_HOLDING_REGISTERS, but the rogue source 172.31.4.66 issues a burst of reads walking across different register offsets in a short window. A single host reading every register band in sequence is not normal operator polling; it is enumeration. Map that pattern to T0846 Remote System Discovery: the adversary is mapping the control device before acting on it.

docs.title: Step 5: Identify the Unauthorized Write
docs.text:
After the sweep, the rogue host stops reading and starts writing. In Modbus, a setpoint change uses function code 6 (write single register). Legitimate HMIs almost never write; they poll. A write from an unexpected host is the action that actually changed the process.

Kali - isolate the write operations

zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h func < modbus.log | grep -i write

Every write line should trace back to 172.31.4.66. The captured writes hit register 40002 (the agitator setpoint) and 40030 (the recipe id), flipping the blend recipe and the agitator speed. Two ATT&CK techniques apply to this one observation. The act of sending a command the adversary was never authorized to send is T0855 Unauthorized Command Message. The effect of that command, changing a control parameter that alters the physical process, is T0836 Modify Parameter. A clean coverage table records both, because a detection that catches the command on the wire (T0855) is a different rule from a detection that catches the parameter changing on the PLC (T0836).

docs.title: Step 6: Pin the Rogue Host
docs.text:
Confirm that the malicious reads and writes share one source and that the source is not a known plant asset. The Pecan Creek OT segment is a 10.100.x.0/24 per-student subnet; a 172.31.4.66 source is plainly foreign.

Kali - confirm the rogue source owns the malicious traffic

zeek-cut id.orig_h func < modbus.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

The output groups every source by how many of each function it sent. The legitimate poller shows many reads and zero writes. The host 172.31.4.66 shows the enumeration burst plus the writes. One foreign host performing both the discovery and the parameter change is your attacker, and naming it is part of the deliverable.

docs.title: Step 7: Check the Required Elements, Then Submit
docs.text:
The grader publishes the exact elements your coverage table must cover before you write it. Always read the rubric first so you do not submit a table that misses a required column.

Kali - read the required elements for this deliverable

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/rubric?deliverable=detection-mapping"

The response lists what the grader scores: the technique IDs, the unauthorized write, the read sweep, the rogue host, and a proposed detection signature. Assemble your coverage table as free text addressing each element, then POST it. The grader compares your submission against its canonical checklist and returns the flag when you clear the 0.8 threshold.

Coverage table shape (fill in from your own analysis)

T0846 Remote System Discovery -- rogue host 172.31.4.66 ran an FC3 read
  sweep across the blend tank holding-register bands. Data source: Zeek
  modbus.log func=READ_HOLDING_REGISTERS from a non-engineering host.
  Detection: alert on a single source reading many register offsets in a
  short window.
T0855 Unauthorized Command Message -- the FC6 write itself, sent from a
  host that is not the engineering workstation. Data source: modbus.log
  func write_single_register. Detection: alert on any FC6 from a
  non-allowlisted source.
T0836 Modify Parameter -- the FC6 writes changed agitator setpoint (40002)
  and recipe id (40030), altering the blend. Detection: alert when a
  protected setpoint register changes outside a maintenance window.

Kali - submit your coverage table to the grader

curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"deliverable":"detection-mapping","submission":"<your coverage table here>"}'

A passing submission returns a JSON body containing your flag. If the score comes back below threshold, re-read the rubric output and add the element you missed, most commonly the rogue host source or the explicit detection signature, then POST again.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A burst of function code 3 reads from one host walking sequential register offsets is enumeration, not polling. Operator HMIs poll the same small set of registers on a fixed cadence; an attacker reads everything once.
  • Any function code 6 (or 16) write on this network is suspicious by default. The legitimate HMI is read-only, so a write is either a sanctioned maintenance change inside a window or an attack.
  • A source IP outside the plant /24 is the single loudest signal in the whole capture. Asset inventory plus a foreign source equals an intrusion you can prove.
  • One technique ID is rarely enough. The same FC6 write maps to both T0855 (the message) and T0836 (the effect), and your detection engineers will build two different rules from those two rows.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the read sweep matter if the damage was done by the write?

Reveal answer

The sweep is the earliest detectable moment of the intrusion. The write changed the process, but the enumeration that preceded it is your earliest warning and your best early-detection opportunity. A rule that alerts on a single host reading every register band would have fired before any parameter was touched, giving operations time to isolate the rogue host. Mapping T0846 documents that early-detection opportunity even though it caused no direct harm.

2. The same FC6 write maps to both T0855 and T0836. Why record both instead of picking one?

Reveal answer

The two technique IDs drive two different detections. T0855 Unauthorized Command Message is a network signal: alert on the command on the wire from an unexpected source. T0836 Modify Parameter is a process signal: alert when the setpoint value on the PLC changes. A network rule can be evaded (encrypted tunnel, spoofed source) while the process rule still catches the effect, and vice versa. Defenders want both rows so they build defense in depth.

3. The rogue source is 172.31.4.66, which is not on the plant subnet. What does that tell you about the intrusion path?

Reveal answer

A foreign source on the OT segment means the boundary between IT and OT failed somewhere: a flat network, a misconfigured firewall rule, a compromised jump host, or a rogue device plugged into the plant. The Modbus capture proves the OT-layer action, but the foreign source IP is a pointer to a separate investigation into how that host reached the control network at all. Record it as both a rogue actor and a segmentation finding.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ATT&CK for ICS is the shared vocabulary that turns a packet capture into a defensible incident narrative and a detection backlog.
  • Reconstruction is read-only. You parse evidence the adversary already created; you never replay the attack against the live PLC.
  • A coverage table pairs each observed technique with the data source that revealed it and the rule you owe, which is exactly how a real OT SOC tracks detection gaps.
  • Read the grader rubric before you write your submission. Missing one required element (usually the rogue host or the detection signature) is the most common reason a table scores below threshold.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
Submit your coverage table to the rubric grader and recover the flag it releases on a passing score. The flag has the masked form below; the real value is returned in the grader's JSON response.

OCR{pcc_attack_ics_mapped_<masked>}

Enter the recovered flag in the OCR platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Engagement Status
docs.text:
Client Pecan Creek Creamery (fictional) Role OT SOC Analyst, Detection Engineering Phase Reconstruction Detection Engineering Threat Hunting

What you know so far: You mapped the blend tank intrusion to ATT&CK in the last exercise. The same unauthorized write is now recurring on the line. Mapping a past attack is worth nothing if it does not produce a detection that catches the next one. The deliverable here is a working rule that fires on the attack and stays quiet on the benign baseline.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The intrusion you reconstructed is running again on the Pecan Creek Creamery blend tank. A scripted adversary on the OT segment, the inject host, runs a Modbus function code 3 read sweep against the blend tank mix.pcc.local, then issues function code 6 writes to the agitator setpoint (register 40002) and the recipe id (register 40030). The adversary acts on its own; your job is to detect it.

You write a Suricata or Zeek detection that fires on the unauthorized write and stays silent on the legitimate maintenance-window traffic. Your data source is the passive sensor at sensor.pcc.local, which serves Zeek logs from a recorded capture of the plant control network. Hosts appear in that capture with the plant control addressing (10.100.4.x), and the capture holds both the benign read-only FC3 polling baseline and the adversary's FC6 writes, so the modbus.log you tune against carries the signal and the noise together. To prove the attack actually landed on the PLC, the blend tank exposes a deterministic tamper marker: a holding-register block at 40801 that reads CLEAN_BLEND_NO_WRITES on a pristine tank and flips to DIRTY_WRITES_DETECTED after any wire write, plus an input register at 30004 (write_event_count) that increments on every dangerous write. Reading the DIRTY marker and a nonzero counter is your deterministic proof: you write up your rule plus that confirmation and submit the writeup to the Deliverable Grader, which returns the flag when the writeup passes.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Detection engineering is where threat intelligence stops being a slide and becomes a control. A rule that fires on every Modbus write would technically catch the attack, but it would also scream during every sanctioned maintenance change until the SOC mutes it, and a muted rule catches nothing. The hard part of this exercise is not writing a signature; it is tuning it so it fires on the adversary and stays silent on the benign baseline. Alert fatigue kills more detections than evasion does.

The blend tank is a good teacher because the write is binary and observable. The DIRTY marker gives you ground truth that the FC6 write reached the PLC, so you can reason about what your rule should have caught without guessing. In a real plant you rarely get that confirmation; you get a rule, a baseline, and the discipline to test both before you trust either.
