docs.title: Background: The Impact Counter
docs.text:
The pasteurizer datablock carries a counter that rises every tick the FDV forwards mix while the hold temperature is below the legal floor. The counter is the impact number a recall decision rests on.

DB / offset Name Meaning DB1 offset 2 cut_in_sp_c cut-in setpoint, 7900 normal, lowered to 6800 (68 C) by the attack DB1 offset 16 fdv_state 0 = DIVERT, 1 = FORWARD DB1 offset 22 under_temp_fwd count of under-temperature forwards, the impact figure DB300 offset 0 cut_in_legal_floor 7900, read-only legal floor

0x44 in the capture is 68 C

The capture shows the cut-in written to 0x44. As a temperature in C times 100 the attack drove the setpoint to 6800, which is 68.00 C, well below the 79.00 C legal floor. A cut-in at 68 C lets mix that never reached the kill temperature count as legal and forward to filling.

docs.title: Before You Begin: Populate Variables From the Panel
docs.text:
After the lab reaches Running, the Exercise Network panel lists past.pcc.local and pcaphost.pcc.local. Read both IPs into variables.

Kali - capture the target IPs into variables

# Replace the example IPs with the values from the Exercise Network panel.
PAST=10.0.0.0       # past.pcc.local
PCAPHOST=10.0.0.0   # pcaphost.pcc.local
nc -zv "$PAST" 102
nc -zv "$PCAPHOST" 80

Two succeeded! lines mean the pasteurizer and the capture archive are reachable and the variables are set for the session.

docs.title: Step 1: Identify the Defeat Path From the Live State
docs.text:
Read the live cut-in setpoint at DB1 offset 2 and compare it against the read-only legal floor at DB300 offset 0, then read the FDV state at offset 16. The scripted attack may still be acting, so read the cut-in in a short loop until it settles below the floor.

Kali - read the cut-in setpoint, the legal floor, and the FDV state

python3 - "$PAST" <<'PY'
import sys, struct, time, snap7
c = snap7.client.Client()
c.connect(sys.argv[1], 0, 1, tcpport=102)
floor = struct.unpack(">H", c.db_read(300, 0, 2))[0]   # legal floor
cut_in = None
for _ in range(30):
    cut_in = struct.unpack(">H", c.db_read(1, 2, 2))[0] # cut_in_sp_c
    if cut_in < floor:
        break
    time.sleep(2)
fdv = struct.unpack(">H", c.db_read(1, 16, 2))[0]       # fdv_state
print(f"legal floor: {floor/100:.2f} C")
print(f"cut-in setpoint: {cut_in/100:.2f} C")
print(f"fdv_state: {fdv}  ({'FORWARD' if fdv==1 else 'DIVERT'})")
print("below floor:", cut_in < floor)
c.disconnect()
PY

A cut-in of 6800 (68.00 C) sitting below the 7900 legal floor while fdv_state reads FORWARD is the lowered-cut-in path, defeat path 1 from the previous exercise. The bar was lowered so under-processed mix counts as legal and forwards. The FDV is doing exactly what its logic says, but its logic was tampered.

docs.title: Step 2: Quantify the Impact
docs.text:
Read the under_temp_fwd counter at DB1 offset 22. The counter rises every tick the FDV forwards while the hold temperature is below the legal floor, so its value is the number of under-temperature forwards: the batches that should have diverted but shipped instead. Read it twice a few seconds apart to confirm it is still climbing.

Kali - read and confirm the under-temperature forward counter

python3 - "$PAST" <<'PY'
import sys, struct, time, snap7
c = snap7.client.Client()
c.connect(sys.argv[1], 0, 1, tcpport=102)
a = struct.unpack(">H", c.db_read(1, 22, 2))[0]  # under_temp_fwd
time.sleep(5)
b = struct.unpack(">H", c.db_read(1, 22, 2))[0]
print(f"under_temp_fwd first read: {a}")
print(f"under_temp_fwd after 5s:   {b}")
print("rising:", b > a)
c.disconnect()
PY

A non-zero counter that is still climbing confirms the FDV is actively forwarding under-temperature mix right now. The value is your impact figure: every count is an under-processed batch forwarded to filling. A rising counter also tells the responder the attack is ongoing, not historical, which sharpens the urgency of the stop call.

The food-safety failure on the cockpit: with the cut-in driven below the legal floor and the flow-diversion valve forwarding, under-temperature mix is going to packaging. The certificate banner reads FOOD SAFETY FAILURE, the flow-diversion valve drops to its failure state, and the cockpit declares the public-health hazard the under-temperature forward count is now quantifying. The same numbers your scripts read are what the night-shift operator would have seen on this screen.

docs.title: Step 3: Corroborate With the Capture
docs.text:
The live state tells you what is true now. The pasteurizer-divert.pcap capture on the archive tells you how it got there: the S7 engineering-workstation write that set the cut-in to 0x44 (68 C). Pull the capture index and confirm the file is present, then note it as your evidence source.

Kali - list the capture archive and locate the evidence

curl -s "http://$PCAPHOST/" | grep -o 'pasteurizer-divert.pcap'

A line echoing pasteurizer-divert.pcap confirms the evidence file is in the archive. Download it and inspect the S7 write that lowered the cut-in:

Kali - download the capture and find the cut-in write

curl -s "http://$PCAPHOST/pasteurizer-divert.pcap" -o /tmp/divert.pcap
tshark -r /tmp/divert.pcap -Y 's7comm' -T fields \
  -e frame.number -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e s7comm.param.func 2>/dev/null | head

The S7comm frames from the engineering-workstation source show the write-request function that carried the lowered cut-in value to DB1. Pairing the capture (the write on the wire) with the live state from Steps 1 and 2 (the cut-in below the floor and the rising counter) gives an evidenced timeline: the attacker lowered the bar, and the pasteurizer has been forwarding under-temperature mix since. Cite the pcap filename in your report as the source for the engineering-workstation write.

docs.title: Step 4: Make the Recall and Notification Call
docs.text:
You now hold the defeat path (lowered cut-in to 68 C, below the 79 C floor), the impact figure (the under_temp_fwd count), and the evidence source (pasteurizer-divert.pcap). The inverted triad orders the response. Under-processed dairy forwarded to filling is recall-triggering, and Safety outranks Availability, so containment and notification come before any concern about restarting the line.

Defender response to record

Finding:   Cut-in setpoint lowered to 68 C, below the 79 C legal floor,
           while the FDV forwarded. under_temp_fwd counter rising.
Defeat:    Path 1 - lowered cut-in (DB1 offset 2 below DB300 floor).
Evidence:  pasteurizer-divert.pcap - S7 engineering-workstation write
           set cut-in to 0x44 (68 C). Live state corroborates.
Impact:    under_temp_fwd batches forwarded under temperature (still rising).
Priority:  Safety > Integrity > Availability > Confidentiality.
Action:    1. Stop the line and quarantine the affected batches now.
           2. Initiate recall of forwarded under-temperature product.
           3. Notify food-safety lead and the relevant public-health
              authority; preserve the pcap and PLC state as evidence.
           4. Restore the cut-in to 79 C under change control.
           5. Restart production only after the FDV is verified clean.

The ordered call plus the reconstruction is the deliverable you submit to the grader: contain the public-health risk and notify first, restore and restart last. When your writeup passes the rubric, the grader returns the flag.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A cut-in of 68 C below the 79 C legal floor while the FDV forwards is the lowered-cut-in defeat path; the bar was moved, not removed.
  • A non-zero, rising under_temp_fwd counter is the impact figure and proof the attack is ongoing, not historical.
  • The pcap supplies the on-the-wire engineering-workstation write that set the cut-in; the live state corroborates it. Two sources beat one.
  • Once under-processed product has forwarded, the call is public health: recall and notify first, restore and restart last, ordered Safety before Availability.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The cut-in reads 68 C and the FDV is forwarding. Which defeat path is this, and how do you know?

Reveal answer

Defeat path 1, the lowered-cut-in path. The cut-in setpoint at DB1 offset 2 was driven to 6800 (68 C), below the read-only legal floor of 7900 (79 C) at DB300. The FDV logic itself is untouched; it correctly forwards mix that reads above its setpoint, but the setpoint was lowered so under-processed mix now qualifies. The force-forward path would instead leave the cut-in alone and override the FDV state directly.

2. Why is the under_temp_fwd counter, not the cut-in value, the figure a recall rests on?

Reveal answer

The cut-in value tells you the protection was defeated; the under_temp_fwd counter tells you how many batches actually forwarded under temperature, which is the quantity of product at risk. A recall has to be scoped to real impact, not to the existence of a tamper. The counter turns a known compromise into a numbered batch count that the recall and the notification can be built on.

3. The capture and the live PLC state agree. Why cite both rather than just the live read?

Reveal answer

The live read shows the current state but not how it got there; an operator could argue it was a legitimate retune. The pcap shows the actual engineering-workstation write on the wire that lowered the cut-in, with source and timing. Together they form an evidenced timeline that survives scrutiny: the attacker wrote the setpoint down, and the pasteurizer has been forwarding under-temperature mix since. A recall and a regulatory notification need that defensible chain.

4. The line is still producing salable-looking product. Why stop it before worrying about uptime?

Reveal answer

The inverted triad puts Safety above Availability, and here Safety is public health. Every minute the line runs with the cut-in below the floor forwards more under-processed dairy that may carry pathogens. Lost production is recoverable; product that reaches and harms customers is not. The correct order is stop and quarantine, recall and notify, then restore and restart.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A cut-in setpoint below the read-only legal floor while the FDV forwards is the lowered-cut-in defeat path.
  • The under_temp_fwd counter quantifies impact: each count is an under-processed batch forwarded, and a rising counter means the attack is live.
  • Corroborate the live PLC state with pasteurizer-divert.pcap, which carries the engineering-workstation write; cite the pcap as the evidence source.
  • Under-processed dairy forwarded to filling is recall-triggering with a notification obligation.
  • The inverted triad orders the response: contain and notify under Safety first, restore and restart for Availability last.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
Reconstruct the under-temperature forwarding event on past.pcc.local: confirm the cut-in below the 79 C legal floor, quantify the under_temp_fwd count, and corroborate with pasteurizer-divert.pcap. The reconstruction is not the answer by itself; it is the deliverable you submit. Write up the defeat path (the lowered cut-in at 6800, below the 7900 legal floor), the impact count from under_temp_fwd, the evidence (pasteurizer-divert.pcap), and the ordered recall and notification call, then POST that writeup to the Deliverable Grader shown in the Exercise Network panel (HTTP, port 80).

Check the rubric first so you know what the grader scores. A GET against /rubric returns the checklist your submission is measured against, with no flag attached.

Kali - read the grader rubric for this deliverable

GRADER=<grader-ip-from-panel>   # rubric host, HTTP 80
curl -s "http://$GRADER/rubric?deliverable=under-temp-notify"

With the reconstruction in hand, assemble the recall notification writeup and POST it to the grader. Cover the defeat path, the impact count, the pcap evidence, and the safety-first ordering under the inverted triad in the submission field.

Kali - submit your recall notification to the grader

curl -s -X POST "http://$GRADER/check" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"deliverable":"under-temp-notify","submission":"<your notification: lowered cut-in defeat path (6800 below the 7900 legal floor), the under_temp_fwd count, pasteurizer-divert.pcap as evidence, the recall and notification call, and safety-first ordering under the inverted triad>"}'

A passing writeup returns {"passed": true, "score": ..., "total": ..., "flag": "OCR{pasteurizer_under_temp...}"}. Copy that returned flag into the OCR platform to complete the exercise. A submission that misses rubric items comes back with "passed": false and no flag field, so revise the writeup and POST it again until it passes.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A freezer line at Pecan Creek Creamery is drifting warm. The creamery historian shows the real barrel temperature climbing while the operator HMI keeps painting a normal minus 5 C. You are the on-call OT incident lead, and you have one hour before the next shift change to run the first hour of this incident without making it worse.

You are a defender. You do not attack, scan, or write to any plant device. Your tools are curl, jq, and python3 on your Kali-based RangeBox, and you use them to read the historian trend, the adversary truth feed, and the staged incident evidence package, then to submit a written decision log to the deliverable grader. Every reachable host in this exercise speaks plain HTTP, so reading them is a safe, passive act.

The hosts in scope for the first hour:

Host Role in this incident freeze.pcc.local (EtherNet/IP CIP 44818) The drifting freezer PLC historian.pcc.local (HTTP 3000) Creamery trends, shows the truth hmi.pcc.local (HTTP 80) Operator SCADA, replaying a normal value inject.pcc.local (HTTP 8080) Adversary control and ground-truth feed evidence.pcc.local (HTTP 80) The incident evidence package rubric.pcc.local (HTTP 80) The decision-log grader

The read-only HMI kiosk account is operator / PecanCreek#2026 if you want to cross-reference the operator view. You do not need it to finish the exercise.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The first hour of an OT incident is where IT muscle memory gets people hurt. An IT analyst who sees a compromised host reaches for the same three moves every time: isolate it, image it, wipe and rebuild it. Run those moves on a live controller and you can drop a safety function, halt a process unsafely, or destroy the only volatile evidence of what the attacker did. OT incident response inverts the IT priority order. Where IT optimizes for confidentiality, integrity, then availability, OT optimizes for safety first, then availability of the process, then integrity of data, with confidentiality last. Safety leads because the consequence of a wrong move is not a data breach, it is ammonia in a packaging hall or a freezer dumping spoiled product into the food supply.

The discipline you build here is the Safe Cyber Position: the minimal set of actions that stops the harm while keeping the process in a known-safe state. A Safe Cyber Position blocks the rogue source path and freezes further engineering writes rather than pulling the PLC or wiping the HMI. The deliverable that matters to the plant is the decision log you write, a defensible record that an after-action review and a regulator can read. The flag you recover at the end is only proof that your reasoning held together.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Operator HMI kiosk operator PecanCreek#2026 Optional read-only cross-reference at hmi.pcc.local

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Every command in the OTSOC track runs on your analysis workstation, a Kali-based RangeBox. You are the incident lead sitting at that workstation; the plant hosts are systems you read across the network. Nothing here runs on a plant device.

After the lab transitions to Running, the Exercise Network panel on the track page lists every target with its IP. These labs set show_target_ips, so you get the exact per-host address instead of just the /24. Read the IPs off the panel rather than hardcoding them, because every student gets a different /24. Capture the hosts you need into shell variables now, then call the variables for the rest of the exercise.

Kali - capture the target IPs from the panel

# Replace each example octet with the matching IP from the Exercise Network panel.
HIST=10.100.42.9
INJECT=10.100.42.12
HMI=10.100.42.10
EVID=10.100.42.21
RUBRIC=10.100.42.22
echo "historian=$HIST inject=$INJECT hmi=$HMI evidence=$EVID rubric=$RUBRIC"

Confirm the historian answers before you go further, and make it your first triage view. Open the plantwide historian trends dashboard in your browser using the historian IP from the Exercise Network panel on port 3000. The dashboard renders the real freezer barrel-temperature trend, so if it paints, the lab is wired and you are on the network.

Kali - open the historian dashboard in the browser

In your browser address bar, enter the historian IP from the panel on port 3000, for example http://HIST_IP:3000/.

The dashboard is your ground truth: the freezer barrel-temperature trend climbs above its normal minus 5 C while the operator station stays calm. A dashboard that renders with live trends means you are on the network and looking at the real process. A blank page or a hang means the lab is not Running yet, so wait for the panel to show all targets, then reload.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Scope the incident from the historian trend and the adversary truth feed
  • Confirm the HMI is replaying a normal value while the process drifts warm
  • Evaluate three proposed containment actions against the inverted OT triad
  • Reject containment actions that halt production unsafely or destroy evidence
  • Select a Safe Cyber Position and justify keeping the PLC and HMI in place
  • Submit the decision log to the ir-decision grader and recover the flag

docs.title: Background: The Inverted Triad and the Safe Cyber Position
docs.text:
IT security ranks the CIA triad as Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. OT flips it to Safety, then Availability of the process, then Integrity of data, then Confidentiality. The reordering changes which containment actions are acceptable.

Priority IT default OT inversion What it means for containment 1 Confidentiality Safety Never take an action that drops a safety function or moves the process toward an unsafe state 2 Integrity Availability Keep the process running, or bring it to a known-safe hold, rather than halting it unsafely 3 Availability Integrity Preserve evidence and trust in the data; do not destroy volatile state 4 (Safety implicit) Confidentiality Lowest priority during an active OT incident

A Safe Cyber Position is the OT containment goal: stop the harm while holding the process in a known-safe state. For this freezer incident the Safe Cyber Position is to block the rogue source path, freeze further engineering writes to the freezer PLC, and hold the line rather than pull the controller or wipe the HMI.

Why wipe-and-rebuild is the wrong instinct here

Pulling the freezer PLC drops control of a running process and destroys the volatile parameter state that proves the attack. Wiping the HMI erases the replay configuration that is itself evidence. Both are correct in an IT SOC and wrong in a plant. The OT-safe move contains the attacker without touching the controller or the operator station.

docs.title: Step 1: Scope the incident from the truth and the lie
docs.text:
Scoping means answering two questions: what is affected, and what is not. The historian polls the real freezer and reports the true barrel temperature. The adversary truth feed at inject.pcc.local exposes its own ground-truth JSON, which tells you which attack is running. Read both and compare them against the HMI, which is showing a replayed normal value.

You already opened the historian dashboard in the browser, so you have seen the real barrel temperature climbing above its normal minus 5 C. Confirm that reading programmatically by pulling the same latest values as JSON, which is the right place for the command line: a machine-readable copy of what the trend already showed you.

Kali - cross-check the historian reading from the command line

curl -s "http://$HIST:3000/api/latest" | jq '.'

The JSON echoes the dashboard: the barrel-temperature tag reads warm, above its normal minus 5 C. Note the value; it is the truth, and the dashboard and the JSON agree on it.

Now read the adversary truth feed and its status. The truth feed names the running attack and reports the same warm barrel.

Kali - read the adversary ground-truth feed

curl -s "http://$INJECT:8080/status" | jq '.'
curl -s "http://$INJECT:8080/truth"  | jq '.'

Expected shape of the status feed

{
  "attack": "freeze-slow-drift",
  "running": true
}

The running attack is freeze-slow-drift: a slow, sub-threshold raise of the freezer barrel setpoint that warms product while staying under coarse alarm limits. The /truth feed confirms the real barrel temperature matches what the historian sees.

Finally, see what the operator is being shown, the way the operator sees it. Open the operator HMI board in your browser using the HMI IP from the Exercise Network panel on port 80. The board is the false-normal view: the freezer tile the operator is trusting while the barrel drifts warm.

Kali - open the operator HMI in the browser

In your browser address bar, enter the HMI IP from the panel on port 80, for example http://HMI_IP/.

The operator sees a calm freezer: the CONTINUOUS FREEZER tile reads BARREL TEMP minus 5 C with LINE STATE RUNNING, the reassuring value that hides the drift. The tell is the REPLAY badge on the tile: the number is not being read live, it is being replayed, which is exactly the deception the historian just contradicted. The other subsystem tiles read COMMS FAIL because this lab runs only the freezer cell, so ignore them and keep your eye on the freezer.

With the operator's view in front of you, confirm the replay flag programmatically, the right job for the command line. Read the HMI freeze state as JSON and check the replay field the board renders.

Kali - cross-check the replay flag from the command line

curl -s "http://$HMI/api/state" | jq '.freeze'

The JSON reports a steady minus 5 C with the replay indicator set and a climbing carton count: the lie, confirmed on the wire. The HMI says normal, the historian and the truth feed say warm. The gap between them is the manipulation, and it scopes the incident to the freezer line. The ammonia refrigeration, the pasteurizer, and the cold storage show nothing anomalous, so they are out of scope for containment.

docs.title: Step 2: Pull the incident evidence package
docs.text:
The IR evidence package documents the incident with an id and a MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique. Read the incident summary so your decision log references the right identifiers.

Kali - read the incident summary

curl -s "http://$EVID/incident_summary.json" | jq '.'

Key fields in the summary

{
  "incident_id": "PCC-IR-2026-014",
  "classification": "OT intrusion with product-quality impact",
  "impacts": [ { "asset": "freeze.pcc.local", "mitre_technique": "T0836", ... } ],
  "attacker_source_ip": "10.100.4.66"
}

The incident id is PCC-IR-2026-014, the technique is T0836 (Modify Parameter), and the attacker reached the controller from a single source. The source IP listed here is evidence read out of the file, not a target you connect to. You now have everything a decision log needs: the scope, the running attack, and the identifiers.

docs.title: Step 3: Evaluate three containment actions against the inverted triad
docs.text:
Three actions are on the table. Judge each one against safety first, then availability, then integrity. Write down the verdict and the reason for each, because the grader checks that you evaluated three options against the inverted order.

Proposed action Safety Availability Integrity Verdict A. Pull the freezer PLC off the network Drops control of a running process toward an unsafe state Halts the freezer line Destroys volatile controller state and write history Reject B. Wipe and rebuild the operator HMI No direct safety gain Blinds the operator during an active incident Erases the replay configuration, which is evidence Reject C. Block the rogue source path and freeze engineering writes, hold the process Keeps safety functions intact Holds the line in a known-safe state Preserves the PLC and HMI for forensics Select

Option A and Option B are the IT instincts: isolate the box, rebuild the box. Applying safety before availability rejects both, because each drops a function or destroys evidence while delivering no safety benefit. Option C is the Safe Cyber Position.

docs.title: Step 4: Select the Safe Cyber Position and read the rubric
docs.text:
Before you write the decision log, read the required elements the grader expects. The grader matches keywords, so knowing the elements tells you what your log must literally state.

Kali - list the required elements of the decision log

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/rubric?deliverable=ir-decision" | jq '.'

Required elements returned

{
  "deliverable": "ir-decision",
  "threshold": 1.0,
  "required": [
    {"name": "scope of the affected process"},
    {"name": "three containment actions evaluated"},
    {"name": "inverted triad applied (safety before availability)"},
    {"name": "Safe Cyber Position selected"},
    {"name": "evidence and PLC preserved (no wipe)"}
  ]
}

The threshold is 1.0, so every element must be present. Your decision log has to state the scope, evaluate three containment actions, apply the inverted triad with safety before availability, select the Safe Cyber Position, and confirm that evidence and the PLC are preserved with no wipe.

docs.title: Step 5: Write and submit the decision log
docs.text:
Write the log the way an IR lead writes for an after-action review: scope, options considered, the reasoning that rejected the IT moves, the position selected, and the evidence stance. Compose it into a shell variable so you can submit it cleanly, then POST it to the grader.

Kali - compose the first-hour decision log

LOG="Pecan Creek Creamery first-hour decision log, incident PCC-IR-2026-014. \
Scope: the affected process is the freezer line only; ammonia, pasteurizer and \
cold storage are not impacted. I evaluated three containment actions against the \
inverted triad, safety first then availability. Option A pull the freezer PLC, \
Option B wipe the HMI, Option C block the rogue source and freeze engineering \
writes. Applying safety before availability I reject A and B because they drop a \
safety function and destroy volatile evidence. I select the Safe Cyber Position, \
holding the process in a known-safe state. Evidence preserved, no wipe, the PLC \
preserved for forensics."
echo "$LOG" | head -c 120; echo " ..."

Now submit the log. The grader scores the keyword coverage and returns a flag when every element is present.

Kali - submit the decision log to the grader

curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "$(jq -nc --arg s "$LOG" '{deliverable:"ir-decision", submission:$s}')" \
  | jq '.'

A passing response

{
  "deliverable": "ir-decision",
  "passed": true,
  "score": 5,
  "total": 5,
  "threshold": 1.0,
  "flag": "OCR{pcc_safe_cyber_<masked>}"
}

A passed of true with score equal to total means every required element registered. The flag field carries your submission. If passed is false, read the feedback array: any element with found set to false names exactly which keyword your log is missing, so add it and resubmit.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The historian and the truth feed agree on a warm barrel; the HMI disagrees. The disagreement is the evidence of a replay, and it scopes the incident to the freezer line
  • freeze-slow-drift is a deliberately quiet attack: it stays under coarse alarm limits, which is why a passive trend comparison, not an alarm, is what catches it
  • A decision log that evaluates only one action fails the grader; the inverted triad is a reasoning method, and the grader checks that you reasoned through the alternatives you rejected
  • The attacker source IP in the evidence is a finding to record, not a host to probe; you read it, you do not connect to it

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does pulling the freezer PLC fail the inverted triad even though it would stop the attacker's writes?

Reveal answer

Pulling the PLC drops control of a running process, which is a safety risk, and it halts the freezer line, which is an availability loss. It also destroys the volatile controller state that proves the attack, an integrity loss. The Safe Cyber Position achieves the same containment goal, stopping further malicious writes, without surrendering safety, availability, or evidence. Safety leads, so an action that trades a safety function for a containment win is rejected.

2. The HMI shows minus 5 C and the historian shows a warm barrel. Which do you trust, and why?

Reveal answer

Trust the historian. It polls the real freezer over the live protocol and reports ground truth. The HMI is replaying a pinned normal value while still emitting normal-looking read traffic, the same deception pattern Stuxnet used to hide centrifuge speed from operators. In OT, an instrument that disagrees with the historian is the alarm; the value the operator sees is not automatically the value the process is at.

3. What is the difference between an IT isolate-and-wipe and an OT Safe Cyber Position?

Reveal answer

Isolate-and-wipe assumes the asset is disposable and that availability can be sacrificed to guarantee integrity. A Safe Cyber Position assumes the asset is a live controller whose loss has physical and safety consequences, so it contains the attacker by the least invasive means, blocking the source path and freezing writes, while holding the process in a known-safe state and preserving everything for forensics.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is released by the ir-decision grader only when your decision log contains all five required elements at threshold 1.0: the scope of the affected process, three containment actions evaluated, the inverted triad applied with safety before availability, the Safe Cyber Position selected, and evidence and the PLC preserved with no wipe. Submit the log from Step 5; the grader returns the flag in the flag field of the response. The flag names what your first hour achieved, a Safe Cyber Position held instead of a wipe-and-rebuild.

Flag format: OCR{pcc_safe_cyber_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The freezer incident at Pecan Creek Creamery is being worked, and the plant engineer wants to reboot the affected freezer PLC to clear the warm drift and get production back. A reboot is reasonable from an operations point of view and a disaster from a forensics point of view: it wipes the volatile controller state, the running parameter export, and any in-memory write history. You have fifteen minutes of scenario time before that reboot to preserve the evidence that proves what the attacker did.

You are the OT incident responder. Everything has been staged in a read-only evidence package so you can practice the prioritization and the evidentiary reasoning without touching production. You pull each artifact with curl and inspect it with jq on your Kali-based RangeBox.

Host Role evidence.pcc.local (HTTP 80) The IR evidence package

The package holds the controller running export, the known-good baseline, the corporate web access log, the jump-host auth log and shell history, the historian time series, and an incident summary. One of those artifacts is destroyed by the reboot. Your job is to collect in the right order and to recover the attacker's last logic change before the controller state is gone.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Order of volatility is an IT forensics idea that matters even more in OT, because the most valuable OT artifact is also the most fragile. In an IT breach you race to capture RAM before the host is powered off. In an OT breach you race to capture the controller's running parameters before an engineer reboots the PLC to restore production, and the operational pressure to reboot is enormous: every minute the line is down costs product. The running parameter export holds the attacker's last write, the register, the value, and the source, and a reboot clears it from controller memory with no copy anywhere else. The logs on the engineering workstation and the jump host are written to disk and survive a controller reboot, so they are lower in the collection order. Getting the order wrong means you reboot, restore production, and then discover the one artifact that proved the attack is gone.

The reasoning you practice here is what separates an OT responder from an IT responder dropped into a plant. The IT responder pulls the logs first because that is the IT habit. The OT responder grabs the volatile controller state first, because the controller is about to be rebooted and the disk-based logs are not going anywhere. The flag is encoded in the controller artifact, so recovering it proves you preserved the right thing first.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Every command runs on your Kali-based RangeBox. After the lab transitions to Running, read the evidence host IP from the Exercise Network panel and capture it into a shell variable, because every student gets a different /24.

Kali - capture the evidence host IP from the panel

# Replace the example octet with the evidence IP from the Exercise Network panel.
EVID=10.100.42.21
echo "evidence=$EVID"

Confirm the package answers by reading its index.

Kali - prove the evidence package is reachable

curl -s "http://$EVID/" | head -20

A directory index listing JSON and log files means the package is up. An empty reply or a hang means the lab is not Running yet.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Prioritize OT forensic evidence by order of volatility under a reboot deadline
  • Identify the controller running export as the highest-priority, reboot-volatile artifact
  • Collect each artifact from the package and state its evidentiary value
  • Recover the attacker's last logic change from the controller export
  • Assemble the flag from the last write register and value

docs.title: Background: Order of Volatility in OT
docs.text:
Order of volatility ranks evidence by how quickly it disappears, so you collect the most perishable first. The ranking for this incident, most volatile at the top:

Rank Artifact Why it ranks here Survives a PLC reboot? 1 Controller running parameter export Lives in controller memory; cleared by the reboot No 2 Engineering workstation / jump-host auth log Written to disk on the jump host Yes 3 Jump-host shell history On-disk file on the jump host Yes 4 Corporate web access log On-disk Apache log on the IT/OT boundary Yes 5 Historian time series Persisted on the historian database Yes

The single artifact that the reboot destroys is the controller running export, so it is collected first regardless of how easy the disk-based logs are to grab. Everything below it can wait until after the line is restored.

The OT inversion of the IT habit

An IT responder grabs the logs first. In OT the controller running state is more volatile than any disk log and carries the proof of the manipulation, so it leads the collection order. Train the habit: in a plant, the controller memory is your RAM capture, and a pending reboot is your power-off clock.

docs.title: Step 1: Inventory the package
docs.text:
List every staged artifact so you can plan the collection order before the clock runs out. Read the index, then note which file is the controller running state.

Kali - list the staged artifacts

curl -s "http://$EVID/" | grep -oE 'href="[^"]+"' | sed 's/href="//; s/"//'

Artifacts in the package

freezer_plc_running.json
freezer_plc_baseline.json
corpweb_access.log
jumphost_auth.log
jumphost_shell_history.txt
historian_timeseries.json
incident_summary.json

The file named freezer_plc_running.json is the controller running export. It is the only artifact a PLC reboot would destroy, so it is first in the collection order.

docs.title: Step 2: Collect the highest-priority artifact first
docs.text:
Collect the controller running export before anything else. Saving a local copy is your preservation step: once it is on your workstation, the reboot can no longer take it.

Kali - preserve the controller running export

curl -s "http://$EVID/freezer_plc_running.json" -o running.json
jq '.' running.json

The running export

{
  "controller": "freeze.pcc.local",
  "label": "running parameters at time of incident",
  "parameters": {
    "barrel_temp_pv_c": 1.8,
    "barrel_temp_sp_c": 2.5,
    "run_state": 1,
    "last_write_register": 11,
    "last_write_value_raw": 25,
    "last_write_source_ip": "10.100.4.66"
  }
}

The parameters object carries the live state at the time of impact: a barrel process value of 1.8 C against a setpoint of 2.5 C, far above the normal minus 5 C. The three last_write_* fields are the attacker's last logic change, the register written, the raw value, and the source. None of that survives the reboot, which is why you grabbed it first.

docs.title: Step 3: Collect the surviving artifacts and note what each proves
docs.text:
With the volatile artifact safe, collect the disk-based evidence. Each one corroborates a different stage of the intrusion. Read the jump-host auth log and shell history to establish the access path.

Kali - collect the jump-host evidence

curl -s "http://$EVID/jumphost_auth.log"
echo "----"
curl -s "http://$EVID/jumphost_shell_history.txt"

What the jump-host evidence shows

jump01 sshd[4811]: Accepted password for ot_contractor from 10.100.4.66 ...
...
nmap -n -p 502,102,44818,20000,4840 10.100.4.6 ...
python3 -c "...c.write_register(11, 25, slave=1)..."
history -c

The auth log proves the ot_contractor account logged in from the same source IP the controller recorded, and the shell history shows the register enumeration, the write_register(11, 25) that set the warm drift, and the history -c the attacker ran to cover the tracks. The history -c cleared the in-memory history, but the on-disk copy you just collected survived.

Now collect the boundary log and the historian trend to round out the timeline.

Kali - collect the boundary log and the historian trend

curl -s "http://$EVID/corpweb_access.log" | grep -i 'portal.php?page=../'
echo "----"
curl -s "http://$EVID/historian_timeseries.json" | jq '.[-4:]'

The corporate access log shows the LFI requests that pulled the remote-access profile from the IT/OT boundary, the attacker's initial access. The historian trend shows the freezer barrel temperature climbing across the anomaly window, the physical effect of the write. Together they bracket the intrusion from initial access to physical impact.

docs.title: Step 4: Recover the attacker's last logic change
docs.text:
The flag is built from the controller's last logic change: the register that was written and the raw value. Read both fields out of the running export you preserved.

Kali - extract the last write register and value

jq '{register: .parameters.last_write_register, value: .parameters.last_write_value_raw, source: .parameters.last_write_source_ip}' running.json

The last logic change

{
  "register": 11,
  "value": 25,
  "source": "10.100.4.66"
}

The attacker wrote register 11 with a raw value of 25. On the CIP setpoint scale, a raw 25 corresponds to a barrel setpoint of plus 2.5 C, the warm drift that spoils product while staying under the coarse alarm limit. The register and value are the two tokens the flag encodes. The source IP is a finding you record in the timeline; it is read from the artifact, not a host you connect to.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The controller running export was the only artifact at risk from the reboot, so collecting it first was the whole point of the exercise; the disk-based logs were never going to disappear
  • last_write_register and last_write_value_raw are the controller's own record of the manipulation, which is stronger evidence than the shell history because it lives on the device that was changed
  • The history -c in the shell history is an anti-forensics step, but the on-disk history file the responder collected predates the in-memory clear, so the attacker's commands survived
  • A raw register value of 25 is not 25 degrees; it is the raw integer on the controller's setpoint scale, which decodes to plus 2.5 C. Reading raw values without decoding them is a common analyst error

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The engineer wants to reboot the PLC immediately. What do you collect before you let that happen, and why only that?

Reveal answer

Collect the controller running parameter export, freezer_plc_running.json, because it is the only artifact the reboot destroys. The auth log, shell history, web access log, and historian trend are all written to disk on hosts that are not being rebooted, so they can be collected after production is restored. Order of volatility says you spend your fifteen minutes on the one thing that is about to vanish, not on the logs that will still be there in an hour.

2. The shell history ends with history -c. Does that mean the attacker's commands are gone?

Reveal answer

No. history -c clears the current shell's in-memory history list, but the responder collected the on-disk history file that was written before the clear ran, so the enumeration and the write_register(11, 25) are still recoverable. Anti-forensics that targets in-memory state often misses the on-disk copy, which is why preserving the file early matters.

3. Why is the controller's last_write_register field stronger evidence than the jump-host shell history showing the same write?

Reveal answer

The shell history shows what the attacker typed on the jump host; the controller's running export shows what the controller actually received and applied. The shell history could be incomplete or tampered, but the controller recording its own last write is the device's first-party record of the change. Corroborating the two together, the typed command and the applied change, is the strongest evidentiary position.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is built from the attacker's last logic change recorded in freezer_plc_running.json: the register that was written and the raw value. From Step 4, the register is the last_write_register field and the value is the last_write_value_raw field. Assemble them into the flag format below using the two integers you recovered. The flag names the engineering-workstation artifact and the last write it preserved.

Flag format: OCR{ews_last_write_<masked>}

The masked tokens are the register and value you read out of the controller running export. Assemble the flag and submit it in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The freezer incident at Pecan Creek Creamery is contained and the volatile evidence is preserved. Now you have to prove the root cause. The plant kept a known-good baseline parameter export from seven days before the incident, and the incident response team captured the running parameters at the time of impact. Diff the two exports, find the single changed setpoint, reconstruct what the attacker did, and build a timeline mapped to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS.

You are the OT incident responder writing the root-cause section of the report. Both exports are staged in the read-only evidence package. You pull them with curl, diff them with jq and python3 on your Kali-based RangeBox, and cross-reference the auth log and the historian trend to fix the access path and the change time.

Host Role evidence.pcc.local (HTTP 80) The IR evidence package

The two controller exports you need:

File What it is freezer_plc_baseline.json Known-good baseline, captured seven days before the incident freezer_plc_running.json Running parameters at the time of impact

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Containment stops the bleeding; root cause stops it from happening again. An OT incident report that says the freezer got warm is useless to a plant manager who has to decide whether to change a credential, a firewall rule, or a controller protection setting. A root cause that names the exact parameter that changed, the value it changed from and to, and the access path that delivered the change tells the manager precisely what to fix. The cleanest way to prove root cause on a controller is a baseline diff: compare the running parameters against a known-good export and let the single difference fall out. Every other parameter matching the baseline is itself evidence, because it rules out a broad reconfiguration and pins the incident to one deliberate write.

Mapping the reconstructed change to ATT&CK for ICS turns a one-off finding into a defensible narrative. T0836, Modify Parameter, is the technique an unauthorized setpoint write falls under, and naming it lets a SOC compare this incident against known adversary behavior and build a detection that catches the next one. The flag is derived from the changed setpoint, so reconstructing the diff correctly is what earns it.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Every command runs on your Kali-based RangeBox. Read the evidence host IP from the Exercise Network panel and capture it into a variable, because every student gets a different /24.

Kali - capture the evidence host IP from the panel

# Replace the example octet with the evidence IP from the Exercise Network panel.
EVID=10.100.42.21
echo "evidence=$EVID"

Confirm the package answers before you diff anything.

Kali - prove the evidence package is reachable

curl -s "http://$EVID/" | head -10

A directory index means the package is up. An empty reply or a hang means the lab is not Running yet.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Diff the running freezer PLC export against the known-good baseline
  • Identify the single changed parameter and read its before and after values
  • Correlate the change with the last-write metadata and the access path
  • Build an incident timeline mapped to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS
  • State the root cause in one executive sentence and derive the flag

docs.title: Background: Baseline Diff as Root-Cause Proof
docs.text:
A baseline diff compares a known-good controller configuration against the configuration at the time of impact. In OT it is the most reliable root-cause method for a parameter attack, because controllers hold a small, stable set of setpoints, and a single changed value stands out against an otherwise identical baseline.

Concept Meaning here Baseline The export captured seven days before, labeled known-good Running The export captured at the time of impact Single-difference principle If only one parameter differs, the incident is one deliberate change, not a broad reconfiguration ATT&CK for ICS T0836 Modify Parameter: an adversary alters a control setpoint or parameter to affect the process

Why the unchanged parameters matter too

A diff that shows only one changed parameter is a strong finding. It rules out a sweeping reconfiguration, a firmware swap, or a logic download, and pins the incident to a single setpoint write. The parameters that match the baseline are not noise; they are the control that proves the change was surgical.

docs.title: Step 1: Pull both controller exports
docs.text:
Collect the baseline and the running export so you can compare their parameter sets. Save local copies so the diff is repeatable.

Kali - pull the baseline and the running export

curl -s "http://$EVID/freezer_plc_baseline.json" -o baseline.json
curl -s "http://$EVID/freezer_plc_running.json"  -o running.json
jq '{label: .label, params: .parameters}' baseline.json
jq '{label: .label, params: .parameters}' running.json

The baseline is labeled known-good and the running export is labeled as the parameters at the time of the incident. The running export carries a few extra fields the baseline lacks, the last_write_* metadata, which you will use to pin the access path.

docs.title: Step 2: Diff the parameter sets
docs.text:
Compare the two parameters objects key by key. A small Python diff lists every key whose value changed between the baseline and the running export, so you do not have to eyeball two JSON blobs.

Kali - diff the parameter sets

python3 - <<'PY'
import json
base = json.load(open("baseline.json"))["parameters"]
run  = json.load(open("running.json"))["parameters"]
for k in sorted(set(base) & set(run)):
    if base[k] != run[k]:
        print(f"CHANGED  {k}: {base[k]}  ->  {run[k]}")
PY

The diff output

CHANGED  barrel_temp_pv_c: -5.0  ->  1.8
CHANGED  barrel_temp_sp_c: -5.0  ->  2.5

Two values differ, but only one is a commanded change. The barrel_temp_pv_c is the process value, the measured temperature, and it moved because the setpoint moved. The barrel_temp_sp_c is the setpoint, the commanded target, and it is the parameter the attacker actually wrote. The setpoint changed from minus 5.0 C to plus 2.5 C; the process value followed. Every other parameter matched the baseline, which confirms a single surgical change.

docs.title: Step 3: Correlate the change with the access path
docs.text:
A changed setpoint is the what. The last_write_* metadata in the running export plus the auth log give you the who and the how. Read the metadata, then confirm it against the jump-host auth log.

Kali - read the last-write metadata

jq '.parameters | {last_write_register, last_write_value_raw, last_write_source_ip}' running.json

The write metadata

{
  "last_write_register": 11,
  "last_write_value_raw": 25,
  "last_write_source_ip": "10.100.4.66"
}

The controller recorded that register 11 was written with a raw value of 25, the integer that decodes to plus 2.5 C on the setpoint scale, from a single source. Now confirm that source reached the OT network through the jump host.

Kali - confirm the access path in the auth log

curl -s "http://$EVID/jumphost_auth.log" | grep -i 'Accepted'

The auth log shows the ot_contractor account accepted from the same source IP the controller recorded. The access path is now fixed: a stolen contractor credential, a jump-host login, and a single Modbus-style write to the freezer setpoint register.

docs.title: Step 4: Build the timeline mapped to ATT&CK for ICS
docs.text:
Assemble the corroborated facts into an ordered timeline and tag each step with its ATT&CK for ICS technique. The historian trend and the corporate access log give you the bracketing events; the controller export gives you the impact.

Kali - confirm the physical effect in the historian trend

curl -s "http://$EVID/historian_timeseries.json" \
  | jq '[.[] | select(.tag=="freezer_barrel_temp_c")] | .[-3:]'

The trend shows the barrel temperature climbing across the anomaly window, the physical confirmation that the setpoint write took effect. With that, build the timeline:

Incident timeline (PCC-IR-2026-014):

Order Event Evidence source ATT&CK for ICS 1 LFI on the IT/OT boundary portal pulled the remote-access profile corpweb_access.log Initial access via IT/OT boundary 2 Contractor credential used to log into the jump host jumphost_auth.log Valid Accounts 3 Freezer registers enumerated, then setpoint register written jumphost_shell_history.txt T0836 Modify Parameter 4 Barrel setpoint changed from minus 5.0 C to plus 2.5 C freezer_plc_running.json diff T0836 Modify Parameter 5 Barrel temperature drifted warm across the window historian_timeseries.json Impact: product spoilage

docs.title: Step 5: State the root cause
docs.text:
Write the root cause in one sentence a manager can act on. Name the parameter, the before and after values, and the consequence.

Root cause: An unauthorized engineering write moved the freezer barrel setpoint from minus 5 C to plus 2.5 C, warming product below the alarm threshold while the process kept running.

That sentence tells the plant exactly what to fix: control who can write to the freezer setpoint register, and add a detection for an out-of-band setpoint change.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• Two values changed in the diff, but only the setpoint is a commanded change; the process value moved because the setpoint moved, so report the setpoint as the attack and the process value as the effect
  • Every unchanged parameter is evidence that the attack was a single surgical write, not a broad reconfiguration, which narrows the remediation to one register and one access path
  • A raw register value of 25 decodes to plus 2.5 C on the controller scale; reporting the raw integer without decoding it would understate the impact to a reader who reads it as 25 degrees
  • The historian trend is the independent confirmation that the setpoint write reached the physical process; a setpoint change with no corresponding temperature drift would suggest the write was blocked or rolled back

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The diff shows two changed values. Why do you report only one of them as the root cause?

Reveal answer

Only barrel_temp_sp_c, the setpoint, is a commanded change. barrel_temp_pv_c, the process value, is the measured temperature, and it moved because the controller drove the barrel toward the new setpoint. Reporting both as separate attacks would misrepresent a single write as two events. The setpoint is the cause; the process value is the effect.

2. Why does it matter that every other parameter matched the baseline?

Reveal answer

Matching parameters rule out a sweeping reconfiguration, a firmware change, or a logic download, and pin the incident to one deliberate setpoint write. That narrows remediation to controlling write access to a single register and confirms the attacker's goal was a quiet quality attack, not a destructive one. The unchanged parameters are the control that gives the diff its evidentiary weight.

3. Which ATT&CK for ICS technique covers the setpoint write, and why is naming it useful?

Reveal answer

T0836, Modify Parameter, covers an adversary altering a control setpoint or parameter to affect the process. Naming the technique lets the SOC map this incident against known adversary behavior, write a detection that generalizes beyond this one register, and communicate the incident in a vocabulary that other defenders and regulators already share.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is derived from the changed setpoint you found in the diff: the baseline value and the running value. From Step 2, the baseline barrel_temp_sp_c is minus 5.0 C and the running value is plus 2.5 C. To stay ASCII-safe the flag spells a minus sign as the word minus and a decimal point as an underscore, so the baseline value minus 5.0 becomes the token minus5 and the running value plus 2.5 becomes the token 2_5. Join your two tokens with the literal _to_ (underscore, the word to, underscore) to form OCR{barrel_sp_changed_<baseline-token>_to_<running-token>}. Worked example with different numbers: a baseline of minus 8.0 and a running of plus 1.5 would read OCR{barrel_sp_changed_minus8_to_1_5}. The flag names the parameter that changed and the values it changed between.

Flag format: OCR{barrel_sp_changed_<masked>}

The masked part encodes the baseline setpoint and the running setpoint you read out of the diff. Assemble the flag and submit it in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The Pecan Creek Creamery freezer incident is contained and the root cause is known: an unauthorized engineering write moved the freezer barrel setpoint from minus 5 C to plus 2.5 C, a warm drift that spoiled product while staying under the coarse alarm limits. The attacker reached the controller through the IT/OT boundary using a stolen contractor credential, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS T0836, Modify Parameter. Containment, forensics, and root cause are done. What is left is the part many responders skip and regulators do not: the notification.

You are the incident lead writing the mandated report. You write a CIP-008 style incident notification and an internal executive brief, then submit them to the deliverable grader, which checks for every required element and releases a flag only when the report is complete. You read the required elements and submit the report with curl, jq, and python3 on your Kali-based RangeBox.

Host Role rubric.pcc.local (HTTP 80) The incident-report deliverable grader

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A technically perfect incident response that produces no report is an incomplete response. NERC CIP-008 governs cyber security incident reporting and response for the bulk electric system, and the same structure is the de facto standard for OT incident notification across critical-infrastructure sectors. The point of a mandated report is not paperwork; it is that the next defender, the regulator, and the information-sharing community all get a complete, comparable picture of what happened. A report that omits the safety impact, or the severity justification, or the remediation, leaves the reader unable to judge whether the response was adequate or whether the same attack is hitting them right now.

The seven elements the grader checks are the irreducible minimum of an OT incident notification: what happened, affected systems, safety impact, containment, root cause, remediation, and severity classification. Writing them in plain language a regulator and an executive can both read is a skill, and the discipline of severity classification is the part responders get wrong most often. A warm-drift product-spoilage event with a contained safety impact and no loss of life is not the same severity as an ammonia release, and your report has to say why. The flag is released only when every element is present, so a complete report is the deliverable.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Every command runs on your Kali-based RangeBox. Read the grader host IP from the Exercise Network panel and capture it into a variable, because every student gets a different /24.

Kali - capture the grader host IP from the panel

# Replace the example octet with the rubric IP from the Exercise Network panel.
RUBRIC=10.100.42.22
echo "rubric=$RUBRIC"

Confirm the grader answers with a health check.

Kali - prove the grader is reachable

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/health"

A JSON status of ok means the grader is up. An empty reply or a hang means the lab is not Running yet.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• List the required elements of the CIP-008 style report from the grader
  • Write the regulator notification and the internal executive brief
  • Cover what happened, affected systems, safety impact, containment, root cause, and remediation
  • Decide and justify the severity classification
  • Submit the report and pass at threshold 1.0, then recover the flag

docs.title: Background: CIP-008 Style Incident Reporting
docs.text:
CIP-008 structures an incident notification so that any reader can reconstruct the event and judge the response. The grader encodes the seven required elements; every one must be present to pass.

Element What it answers What it must literally state What happened The narrative A summary of events Affected systems The scope The affected or impacted assets Safety impact The consequence The food-safety consequence assessment Containment The response How it was contained, the Safe Cyber Position Root cause The cause The one-sentence root cause Remediation The recovery Corrective action and recovery steps Severity classification The judgment The severity or priority and its justification

Severity is a judgment you justify, not a label you pick

A severity classification with no justification fails the purpose of the element. State the severity and then say why: a contained warm-drift spoilage event with no safety-system trip and no loss of life sits below a release event in any OT severity scale. The justification is what lets a regulator agree or push back.

docs.title: Step 1: List the required elements from the grader
docs.text:
Read the required elements before you write, so your report covers every one. The grader returns the element names, weights, and the pass threshold.

Kali - list the required elements

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/rubric?deliverable=incident-report" | jq '.'

Required elements returned

{
  "deliverable": "incident-report",
  "threshold": 1.0,
  "required": [
    {"name": "what happened"},
    {"name": "affected systems"},
    {"name": "safety impact assessment"},
    {"name": "containment actions"},
    {"name": "root cause"},
    {"name": "remediation steps"},
    {"name": "severity classification"}
  ]
}

The threshold is 1.0, so all seven elements must be present. The grader matches on keywords, which means your report has to literally name each element: a summary of events, the affected systems, the safety impact, the containment and Safe Cyber Position, the root cause, the remediation, and the severity classification.

docs.title: Step 2: Draft the report covering every element
docs.text:
Write the report in plain language a regulator and an executive can both read, and make sure each of the seven elements appears explicitly. Compose it into a shell variable so you can submit it without quoting headaches. Build it element by element so nothing is missed.

Kali - draft the CIP-008 style report

REPORT="Pecan Creek Creamery incident notification, PCC-IR-2026-014.

What happened: summary of events. An unauthorized engineering write changed the
continuous freezer barrel setpoint, producing a slow warm drift that spoiled
product while staying under coarse alarm limits.

Affected systems: the affected assets are the continuous freezer PLC and the
freezer production line. Ammonia refrigeration, the pasteurizer, and cold storage
were not impacted.

Safety impact: the food safety consequence was a quantity of product warmed below
the cold-chain threshold. The independent ammonia safety function did not trip and
there was no release and no loss of life.

Containment: the incident was contained with a Safe Cyber Position that blocked the
rogue source path and froze further engineering writes while holding the process in
a known-safe state, without pulling the PLC or wiping the HMI.

Root cause: an unauthorized parameter write moved the freezer barrel setpoint from
minus 5 C to plus 2.5 C, warming product below the alarm threshold.

Remediation: corrective action restored the baseline setpoint, revoked the abused
contractor credential, and added a detection for out-of-band setpoint writes;
recovery of the line is complete.

Severity classification: moderate priority. Justification: a contained product
spoilage event with no safety-system trip, no release, and no loss of life ranks
below an ammonia release event on the plant severity scale."
echo "$REPORT" | head -c 160; echo " ..."

Each paragraph names one required element with the keyword the grader looks for. Drafting element by element is how you guarantee threshold 1.0; skipping any one paragraph drops you below passing.

docs.title: Step 3: Submit the report and read the score
docs.text:
POST the report to the grader. The response reports passed, the score against the total, per-element feedback, and the flag when you pass.

Kali - submit the report to the grader

curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "$(jq -nc --arg s "$REPORT" '{deliverable:"incident-report", submission:$s}')" \
  | jq '.'

A passing response

{
  "deliverable": "incident-report",
  "passed": true,
  "score": 7,
  "total": 7,
  "threshold": 1.0,
  "flag": "OCR{pcc_cip008_<masked>}"
}

A passed of true with score equal to total means all seven elements registered. The flag field carries your submission.

docs.title: Step 4: Fix any missing element
docs.text:
If passed is false, the feedback array names exactly which element did not register. Filter for the gaps, add the missing wording, and resubmit.

Kali - show only the elements the grader did not find

curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "$(jq -nc --arg s "$REPORT" '{deliverable:"incident-report", submission:$s}')" \
  | jq '[.feedback[] | select(.found==false)]'

An empty array means nothing is missing. Any entry names an element whose keyword your report lacks; add a sentence that states it plainly and resubmit. A common miss is the severity justification, where the word severity appears but the reason it is moderate rather than critical does not.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The grader is a keyword check, so the report has to literally state each element; a report that implies the safety impact without naming it fails the safety element even if a human reader would infer it
  • Threshold 1.0 means there is no partial credit; six of seven elements is a fail, which mirrors a real regulator returning an incomplete notification
  • The severity element is the one most often missed, because responders state a severity without justifying it; the justification is what the element actually grades
  • A passing score is the deliverable, but the value to the plant is the report itself, a record the regulator, the insurer, and the next defender can all read

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is severity classified as moderate here rather than critical, and how do you justify it?

Reveal answer

The incident was a contained product-spoilage event: the independent ammonia safety function never tripped, there was no release, and there was no loss of life. Severity in OT is driven by consequence, and a quality impact that was caught and contained ranks below a safety-system event such as an ammonia release. The justification names the absence of a safety trip, a release, and casualties as the reasons the classification is moderate and not critical.

2. The grader matches keywords. Why is that a reasonable model for an incident-report exercise?

Reveal answer

A CIP-008 style notification is judged on whether it contains the mandated elements, and a keyword check is a fair proxy for completeness: it confirms the report names what happened, the affected systems, the safety impact, the containment, the root cause, the remediation, and the severity. It does not grade prose quality, which a human reviewer would, but for the completeness gate that a regulator applies first, presence of every element is exactly the right check.

3. Which element would a technically strong responder most likely omit, and why does omitting it fail the report?

Reveal answer

The severity justification. A responder who solved the technical incident often states a severity label and moves on, treating the justification as obvious. The report fails because severity drives the regulator's and the insurer's response, and an unjustified severity gives them nothing to agree with or challenge. The element grades the reasoning, not the label.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The flag is released by the incident-report grader only when your report contains all seven required elements at threshold 1.0: what happened, affected systems, safety impact, containment, root cause, remediation, and severity classification with its justification. Submit the report from Step 3; the grader returns the flag in the flag field. The flag names the completed CIP-008 style report.

Flag format: OCR{pcc_cip008_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Exercise OTSOC-6.1: Draw the Zones and Conduits
Scenario
docs.text:
Pecan Creek Creamery runs a flat OT network. Every controller, the supervisory layer, the historian, and the corporate web portal share one broadcast domain with no internal boundary. A blend-tank PLC, an ammonia safety controller, and an internet-facing portal all sit in the same Layer 2 segment, which means a foothold anywhere is a foothold everywhere.

The insurer's OT security questionnaire has landed on the SOC desk, and the first deliverable it demands is a zone-and-conduit architecture drawn to IEC 62443-3-2. Your job in this exercise is the partition itself: group the plant assets into security zones, define the conduits that connect them, and isolate the ammonia safety instrumented system in its own safety zone. The plant is attached read-only so you can build the partition from the real asset inventory rather than from a guess. When the model is complete you POST it to the architecture rubric grader, which releases the flag once the safety zone is isolated and the required conduits are present.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
IEC 62443-3-2 is the standard the insurer's questionnaire is written against, and its ZCR (Zone and Conduit Requirements) workflow is the first thing an underwriter looks for: can the plant even describe its own segmentation. A zone is a grouping of assets that share the same security requirement and the same worst-case consequence. A conduit is the controlled communication path between zones, and every conduit is a place you can put a firewall, an ACL, or a data diode.

The single most important call in the whole partition is the ammonia safety system. A safety instrumented function that an attacker can defeat is a worker-safety event, an ammonia release, not a spoiled batch. IEC 61511 and 62443 both demand that the SIS not share a failure domain with the basic process control it protects. Putting the ammonia SIS in its own safety zone, separate from the ammonia BPCS, is the move that keeps a compromise of the refrigeration controller from also disabling the trip that protects the people on the floor. The flag is only proof of submission; the partition you draw is the artifact the insurer actually buys.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Operator HMI kiosk operator PecanCreek#2026 Read-only cross-reference (optional)
