docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Define the system under consideration and its boundary per ZCR1
  • Enumerate the live plant so the partition reflects the real assets
  • Group assets into zones by shared security requirement and consequence
  • Isolate the ammonia SIS in its own safety zone, separate from the BPCS
  • Define the conduits, including the IT-to-OT boundary and the historian replication path
  • Submit the zone-and-conduit model to the architecture rubric and retrieve the flag

docs.title: Background: The IEC 62443-3-2 ZCR Workflow
docs.text:
IEC 62443-3-2 partitions a plant in a fixed order. The first three Zone and Conduit Requirements are the ones you exercise here.

Step Name What you produce ZCR1 Define the system under consideration (SUC) A boundary: which assets are in scope, which are out ZCR2 Initial high-level risk assessment The worst-case consequence per asset group ZCR3 Partition into zones and conduits The zones grouped by shared requirement, the conduits between them

A zone groups assets that share a security requirement and a consequence. A conduit is the controlled path between two zones, and it is the only sanctioned way traffic crosses a zone boundary. The discipline of 62443 is that you justify every zone against the consequence model from ZCR2: the higher the worst-case harm, the more isolation the zone earns.

Why the SIS gets its own zone

A basic process control system (BPCS) runs the process. A safety instrumented system (SIS) exists only to trip the process to a safe state when the BPCS fails. If the SIS shares a network and a failure domain with the BPCS, a single compromise can disable both the control and the protection at once, which is exactly the TRITON attack pattern. IEC 62443 and IEC 61511 require the SIS to be independent, so it earns its own safety zone with the tightest conduit rules in the plant.

docs.title: Step 1: Define the system under consideration (ZCR1)
docs.text:
Start by drawing the boundary. Enumerate the live plant so your partition is built from observed assets, not from the inherited spreadsheet. The plantwide historian at port 3000 serves a real operator dashboard, and its "About this historian" panel lists every source it polls with the protocol behind each one, which is the asset inventory you map into zones. Open the dashboard in your browser and read the source list off the About panel first, because seeing the assets and their protocols in one view is how a defender grounds the partition.

Kali - open the historian dashboard in the browser

Read the historian IP off the Exercise Network panel and open it in your browser on port 3000, for example http://HIST_IP:3000/. Scroll to the "About this historian" panel and read the polled-source inventory: each source name paired with the protocol it speaks.

Interpret the About panel one source at a time: each row is an asset you place in a zone, and the protocol next to it tells you what kind of controller it is. The blend tank, the ammonia BPCS, and the ammonia SIS answer on Modbus, the freezer answers on CIP, and the cold-storage RTU answers on DNP3. Anything the historian polls is inside your system under consideration; the corporate portal is outside the OT boundary but touches it, so it belongs in the IT zone with a conduit into the plant.

For analysts who want the same inventory as machine-readable JSON, the historian exposes the source list at /api/sources. Pulling it programmatically is a legitimate cross-check that the dashboard and the API agree, and it hands you a list you can paste straight into your notes.

Kali (optional) - cross-check the source list as JSON

# Read the historian IP off the Exercise Network panel.
HIST=10.100.42.9
curl -s "http://$HIST:3000/api/sources"

The JSON returns the same list of control devices the About panel showed, which confirms the blend tank, the ammonia controllers, the freezer, and the cold-storage RTU are live. The API and the dashboard agreeing is your evidence the inventory is real and complete before you draw a single zone.

The system under consideration for this partition is the OT estate of the creamery: every control and supervisory device, plus the conduit to the corporate IT zone. The boundary excludes the broader enterprise network but explicitly includes the one IT asset that reaches into the plant, the corporate portal.

docs.title: Step 2: Rank the assets by worst-case consequence (ZCR2)
docs.text:
Before you draw a single zone, rank the consequence of each asset group. The ranking drives the partition: the highest-consequence assets earn the most isolation. Order them by the harm a successful attacker causes, not by how the network happens to be wired today.

Asset group Worst-case consequence Rank Ammonia SIS (sis.pcc.local) Defeated ammonia trip, toxic release, worker-safety event 1 (highest) Pasteurizer (past.pcc.local) Under-processed milk shipped, public-health food-safety event 2 Ammonia BPCS (ammonia.pcc.local) Refrigeration loss, process upset (annunciation only, no trip authority) 3 Blend tank, freezer (mix, freeze) Off-spec or ruined product, lost batch 4 Cold storage (cold.pcc.local) Cold-chain spoilage if telemetry goes stale 5 Supervisory and historian (opcua, historian) Loss of view, degraded monitoring 6

The ammonia safety zone and the pasteurizer food-safety zone rank above the cold-storage telemetry zone. That ordering is the spine of the whole deliverable and reappears in every later Level 6 exercise.

docs.title: Step 3: Partition into zones and conduits (ZCR3)
docs.text:
Now group the ranked assets into zones by shared security requirement and consequence, and draw the conduits between them. The ammonia SIS goes in its own safety zone, fenced off from the ammonia BPCS even though both speak Modbus on 502. The diagram below is the target partition.

flowchart TB
    subgraph IT["IT Zone (Level 4)"]
        CORP["corpweb.pcc.local<br/>corporate portal"]
    end
    subgraph IDMZ["Industrial DMZ (Level 3.5)"]
        JUMP["brokered jump host"]
        HISTREP["replicated historian"]
    end
    subgraph SUP["Supervisory Zone (Level 2/3)"]
        OPCUA["opcua.pcc.local"]
        HIST["historian.pcc.local"]
        HMI["hmi.pcc.local"]
    end
    subgraph CTRL["Control Zone (Level 1)"]
        MIX["mix.pcc.local"]
        PAST["past.pcc.local"]
        FREEZE["freeze.pcc.local"]
        COLD["cold.pcc.local"]
        AMMON["ammonia.pcc.local BPCS"]
    end
    subgraph SAFE["Safety Zone (SIS, isolated)"]
        SIS["sis.pcc.local<br/>ammonia trip authority"]
    end
    CORP -->|"C1: IT-to-OT boundary conduit"| IDMZ
    IDMZ -->|"C2: brokered access"| SUP
    SUP -->|"C3: supervisory poll"| CTRL
    HIST -->|"C4: historian replication path"| HISTREP
    AMMON -.->|"C5: hardwired status only, no trip"| SAFE

Walk the zones in the diagram:

  • Safety zone. The ammonia SIS alone. It holds the trip setpoints and the trip authority. No engineering workstation, no historian, and no BPCS shares its segment. The only crossing is a tightly controlled status conduit, ideally hardwired, never a writable network path.
  • Control zone (Level 1). The blend tank, pasteurizer, freezer, cold-storage RTU, and the ammonia BPCS. The BPCS lives here, not in the safety zone, because it only annunciates ammonia status and has no trip authority.
  • Supervisory zone (Level 2/3). The OPC-UA server, the historian, and the operator HMI.
  • Industrial DMZ (Level 3.5). The brokered jump host and the replicated historian. You design this fully in Exercise 6.3; here you only need to name it as the buffer between IT and OT.
  • IT zone (Level 4). The corporate portal, outside the OT boundary but connected by a single conduit.

The required conduits are: C1 the IT-to-OT boundary conduit, C4 the historian replication path out of the control and supervisory zones into the DMZ, and the safety conduit C5 that carries status only. Every conduit is a deny-by-default control point.

docs.title: Step 4: Write the submission
docs.text:
The grader is keyword based, so your submission must name the zones, the conduits, the safety zone or SIS, and the IT-to-OT boundary explicitly. Read the required elements first so you know exactly what the grader checks for.

Kali - read the required elements for the architecture deliverable

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/rubric?deliverable=architecture" | python3 -m json.tool

The JSON lists the required keywords: the grader wants to see the ZCR workflow named, the zones, the conduits, the isolated safety zone, the IT-to-OT boundary, and the consequence ordering. Compose a single submission string that covers every element. Build it in a file so you can iterate without retyping.

Kali - write the zone-and-conduit deliverable to a file

cat > /tmp/architecture.txt <<'EOF'
Pecan Creek Creamery zone and conduit architecture per IEC 62443-3-2.
ZCR1: the system under consideration is the OT estate; boundary defined to
include every control and supervisory device plus the conduit to the IT zone.
ZCR2: initial high-level risk assessment ranks assets by worst-case consequence.
ZCR3: assets partitioned into zones by shared security requirement and consequence.
Safety zone: the ammonia SIS (sis.pcc.local) is a safety instrumented system
isolated in its own safety zone, separate from the ammonia BPCS, because a
defeated trip is a worker-safety event and the SIS must not share a failure domain.
Control zone (Level 1): blend tank, pasteurizer, freezer, cold storage, ammonia BPCS.
Supervisory zone (Level 2/3): opcua and historian and the operator HMI.
Industrial DMZ (iDMZ) sits between the IT zone and the OT zones at Level 3.5.
Conduits: deny by default with a firewall and ACL between every zone, including
the IT-to-OT boundary conduit and the historian replication path out of the
control zones into the DMZ, and a status-only safety conduit to the SIS.
Security level targets SL-T are assigned per zone by worst-case consequence,
ammonia safety highest. Remediation is prioritized by consequence, safety first.
EOF
wc -l /tmp/architecture.txt

The wc -l confirms the file was written. Read it back once to be sure every required element is present before you submit.

docs.title: Step 5: Submit to the rubric and retrieve the flag
docs.text:
POST the file as the submission field with deliverable set to architecture. Use jq to build the JSON body so the multi-line text is escaped correctly, then read the flag field of the response.

Kali - POST the deliverable to the architecture rubric

jq -n --rawfile s /tmp/architecture.txt \
   '{deliverable:"architecture", submission:$s}' \
  | curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- \
  | python3 -m json.tool

Expected output (flag value masked)

{
    "deliverable": "architecture",
    "score": 1.0,
    "passed": true,
    "flag": "OCR{pcc_zones_conduits_<masked>}"
}

A passed of true and a score at or above the threshold means the partition met every required element. The flag field is your submission. If passed is false, read the missing or score field in the response, add the missing element to /tmp/architecture.txt, and POST again. The grader is idempotent, so iterate until it passes.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The grader scores on keyword coverage, so a partition that is correct in your head but silent on the page fails; name every zone, conduit, and the SIS explicitly
  • A score below the threshold with passed false tells you an element is missing, not that your architecture is wrong; compare your text against the /rubric element list
  • The ammonia BPCS and the ammonia SIS both speak Modbus on 502 but land in different zones; treating them as one asset is the single most common partition error
  • The IT-to-OT boundary conduit and the historian replication path are the two conduits the grader specifically checks, because they are where a flat network leaks the worst

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the ammonia SIS earn its own safety zone instead of joining the ammonia BPCS in the control zone?

Reveal answer

The BPCS runs the refrigeration loop; the SIS exists only to trip the process to a safe state when the BPCS fails. If they share a zone and a failure domain, one compromise disables both control and protection at once, which is the TRITON pattern. IEC 62443 and IEC 61511 require the SIS to be independent, so it gets the most isolated zone with a status-only conduit and no writable network path.

2. What is the difference between a zone and a conduit, and why does every conduit matter to the insurer?

Reveal answer

A zone groups assets that share a security requirement and consequence. A conduit is the controlled communication path between zones and is the only sanctioned way traffic crosses a boundary. Each conduit is a place to enforce a control: a firewall, an ACL, or a data diode. The insurer cares because conduits are where segmentation either holds or fails; a plant with named zones but undefined conduits has drawn a map with no doors.

3. ZCR2 ranks assets by worst-case consequence. Why does that ranking drive the partition rather than the current network layout?

Reveal answer

The current flat layout is the problem you were hired to fix, so it cannot define the target. Consequence drives isolation: the higher the worst-case harm, the tighter the zone. Ranking the ammonia safety and pasteurizer food-safety zones above the cold-storage telemetry zone tells you where to spend segmentation budget first and sets up the SL-T assignment in the next exercise.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The architecture rubric grader releases the flag when your zone-and-conduit model isolates the ammonia SIS in its own safety zone and names the required conduits, including the IT-to-OT boundary. You earn it by submitting a correct partition, not by touching the plant. The flag describes what you accomplished: the zones and conduits with their SL targets.

Flag format: OCR{pcc_zones_conduits_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Exercise OTSOC-6.2: Assign the Security Levels
Scenario
docs.text:
You drew the zones in the previous exercise. Now you put a number on each one. The insurer's questionnaire does not stop at a partition: it asks what protection each zone is supposed to deliver, and IEC 62443-3-3 answers that question with a security-level target. A security-level target (SL-T) is not a single grade for a zone. It is a vector of seven values, one per Foundational Requirement, set by the worst-case consequence of compromising that zone.

Your job in this exercise is to assign a per-FR SL-T vector to every zone you defined, drive each value from the consequence model, then find the one place where the target you set exceeds what the plant can actually deliver. That gap lives on the IT-to-OT boundary conduit, where the flat network delivers no real protection while the target demands SL 2 or higher. You name the compensating control that closes it, then POST the SL vectors and the gap analysis to the security-levels rubric, which releases the flag once the per-FR vectors, the consequence ranking, and the SL-T versus SL-C gap are all present.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
An SL-T vector is how 62443 turns "this zone is important" into something an engineer can procure and an insurer can audit. IEC 62443-3-3 defines four security levels: SL 1 protects against casual or coincidental violation, SL 2 against intentional violation using simple means, SL 3 against sophisticated means with moderate resources, and SL 4 against sophisticated means with extended resources. Assigning a vector forces you to reason per requirement: a zone might need strong authentication (FR1) and integrity (FR3) but tolerate weak confidentiality (FR4), and a single overall grade would hide that.

The gap analysis is where the deliverable earns its keep. SL-T is the target. SL-C is the capability the installed equipment and current architecture can actually achieve. When SL-T exceeds SL-C you have three choices: buy better equipment, change the architecture, or add a compensating control. On a flat creamery network the IT-to-OT boundary has an SL-C near zero and an SL-T of 2 or higher, and the compensating control that closes the gap is the industrial DMZ you design next. Naming the gap and its control is the language an underwriter and a plant manager both understand.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
After the lab transitions to Running, the Exercise Network panel lists the rubric grader with its IP. Read the IP off the panel and capture it into a shell variable, since every submission goes to it. Every student gets a different subnet, so do not hardcode the octet.

Kali - capture the rubric IP from the panel

RUBRIC=10.100.42.22
echo "Rubric grader is $RUBRIC"

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Assign a per-FR SL-T vector to every zone defined in the partition
  • Drive each SL-T value from worst-case consequence and justify it per FR
  • Rank the ammonia safety and pasteurizer zones above the cold-storage zone
  • Identify where the IT-to-OT boundary conduit SL-T exceeds the current SL-C
  • Name the compensating control that closes the SL-T versus SL-C gap
  • Submit the SL vectors and gap analysis to the security-levels rubric and retrieve the flag

docs.title: Background: The Seven Foundational Requirements
docs.text:
IEC 62443-3-3 organizes every security capability into seven Foundational Requirements. An SL-T vector assigns one security level to each.

FR Name What it covers FR1 Identification and Authentication Control (IAC) Who and what is allowed to connect FR2 Use Control (UC) What an authenticated identity is permitted to do FR3 System Integrity (SI) Protection of code, configuration, and data from tampering FR4 Data Confidentiality (DC) Protection of information from disclosure FR5 Restricted Data Flow (RDF) Segmentation and conduit enforcement between zones FR6 Timely Response to Events (TRE) Logging, alerting, and the ability to react FR7 Resource Availability (RA) Keeping the process running under stress or attack

Why a vector and not a single number

A safety zone may demand SL 3 on authentication (FR1) and integrity (FR3) because a defeated trip kills people, yet only SL 1 on confidentiality (FR4) because the trip setpoints are not secret. A single overall SL would force you to either over-build confidentiality or under-build integrity. The vector lets each requirement carry the level its consequence actually warrants.

docs.title: Step 1: Map consequence to a per-FR vector
docs.text:
Carry forward the consequence ranking from Exercise 6.1. The higher a zone's worst-case harm, the higher its SL-T on the requirements that defend against that harm. Reason one zone at a time. The ammonia safety zone is the worst case: a defeated trip is a toxic release. An attacker reaching the SIS must be stopped at authentication (FR1), the trip setpoints must be tamper-proof (FR3), and the SIS must be unreachable from the rest of the plant (FR5). Those three earn SL 3. Confidentiality (FR4) is low because the setpoints are not secret.

Work the same logic down the consequence ranking and you get the target table below. The numbers are defensible targets, not the only correct answer; what the grader checks is that the safety and food-safety zones outrank the telemetry zone and that you justify each value.

Zone FR1 IAC FR2 UC FR3 SI FR4 DC FR5 RDF FR6 TRE FR7 RA Driver Safety (ammonia SIS) 3 3 3 1 3 3 3 Defeated trip is a worker-safety event Pasteurizer (food safety) 3 3 3 1 3 2 2 Under-processed milk shipped, public-health event Control (mix, freeze, ammonia BPCS) 2 2 2 1 2 2 3 Lost batch, process upset Cold-storage telemetry 2 1 2 1 2 2 2 Spoilage if telemetry goes stale, lower consequence Supervisory (opcua, historian) 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 Loss of view, degraded monitoring IT-to-OT boundary conduit 3 3 3 2 3 3 2 Sole path from IT to every control zone

The safety zone and the pasteurizer zone sit at the top, the cold-storage telemetry zone sits lower, and the IT-to-OT conduit carries a high target because it is the one path that touches everything.

docs.title: Step 2: Justify the safety-zone vector per FR
docs.text: The grader wants the per-FR reasoning written down, not just the numbers. Spell out why the safety zone earns SL 3 on the requirements that matter. FR1 at SL 3 means no casual or simple-means actor can authenticate to the SIS; only a sophisticated attacker with moderate resources should even reach the authentication boundary. FR3 at SL 3 means the trip setpoints cannot be altered without detection, which directly answers the attack where 40010 and 40011 are weakened. FR5 at SL 3 means the SIS sits behind a conduit that blocks all but the status path, so a compromise of the ammonia BPCS cannot pivot into the safety zone.

docs.title: Step 3: Find the SL-T versus SL-C gap on the boundary
docs.text:
Now compare target against capability on the IT-to-OT boundary conduit. The target you assigned is SL 3 on FR5 (restricted data flow). The capability the current plant delivers is the flat network: no firewall, no ACL, no conduit, so the SL-C on FR5 is effectively SL 0. The gap is the distance between them.

Conduit FR5 SL-T (target) FR5 SL-C (current) Gap IT-to-OT boundary 3 0 3 levels, target far exceeds capability

A gap this wide is exactly what the insurer is looking for: it quantifies how exposed the plant is today. The corpweb LFI from the next exercise is the proof that SL-C is near zero, since an internet-facing portal bug reaches a control-network credential with nothing in the way.

docs.title: Step 4: Name the compensating control
docs.text:
When SL-T exceeds SL-C you close the gap by buying equipment, changing the architecture, or adding a compensating control. Here the answer is architectural: an industrial DMZ at Level 3.5 with a deny-by-default boundary firewall and a brokered jump host. Map the control to the requirements it satisfies, so the underwriter can trace the fix back to the gap.

Compensating control FR raised How it closes the gap Industrial DMZ with deny-by-default firewall FR5 RDF Replaces the flat segment with an enforced conduit Brokered jump host with MFA FR1 IAC, FR2 UC No direct IT credential reaches the control zone Conduit logging and alerting FR6 TRE Boundary crossings become visible and auditable

docs.title: Step 5: Write and submit the deliverable
docs.text:
Read the required elements first so your text names every keyword the grader checks: the SL-T vectors, the per-FR justification, the consequence ranking, and the SL-T versus SL-C gap.

Kali - read the required elements for the security-levels deliverable

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/rubric?deliverable=security-levels" | python3 -m json.tool

Compose the deliverable in a file so you can iterate. Cover the vectors, the ranking, the gap, and the compensating control in one submission.

Kali - write the SL-vector deliverable to a file

cat > /tmp/security-levels.txt <<'EOF'
Pecan Creek Creamery security level target assignment per IEC 62443-3-3.
For each zone and conduit in the partition a per-FR SL-T vector is assigned by
worst-case consequence, one value per foundational requirement FR1 through FR7.
Safety zone: the ammonia SIS safety instrumented system is ranked highest on
FR1, FR3, and FR5 because a defeated trip is a worker-safety event; each value
is justified per FR. Pasteurizer food-safety zone ranks next. The cold-storage
telemetry zone is lower consequence with a lower SL-T security level target.
Consequence ranking: safety and food safety above telemetry.
Boundary gap: on the IT-to-OT conduit the target SL-T exceeds the current
capability SL-C, a clear capability gap where target exceeds capability, because
the flat network delivers no restricted data flow. The compensating control is
an industrial dmz (iDMZ) with a deny by default boundary firewall and ACL and a
brokered jump host, mapped to FR1, FR2, FR5, and FR6.
EOF
wc -l /tmp/security-levels.txt

POST the file with deliverable set to security-levels and read the flag field.

Kali - POST the deliverable to the security-levels rubric

jq -n --rawfile s /tmp/security-levels.txt \
   '{deliverable:"security-levels", submission:$s}' \
  | curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- \
  | python3 -m json.tool

Expected output (flag value masked)

{
    "deliverable": "security-levels",
    "score": 1.0,
    "passed": true,
    "flag": "OCR{pcc_sl_vectors_<masked>}"
}

A passed of true means the vectors, the ranking, and the gap analysis were all present. If passed is false, the response tells you which element is missing; add it to the file and POST again until it passes.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• A single overall SL hides the per-FR trade-off; the grader and the standard both expect a vector, so a submission that gives one number per zone will read as incomplete
  • The consequence ranking is load-bearing: if the cold-storage zone outranks the safety zone in your text, the deliverable contradicts the partition and the score drops
  • The SL-T versus SL-C gap is the element students miss most; the grader checks for the words target, capability, and gap, because that triplet is what an insurer audits
  • The compensating control must map to the requirements it raises (FR1, FR2, FR5, FR6), otherwise it reads as a vague recommendation rather than a closed gap

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is an SL-T a vector of seven values instead of a single security level for the zone?

Reveal answer

Different Foundational Requirements carry different consequences in the same zone. A safety zone needs SL 3 authentication and integrity because a defeated trip kills people, but only SL 1 confidentiality because the setpoints are not secret. A single number would force over-building one requirement or under-building another. The vector lets each requirement carry the level its own consequence warrants, which is also how equipment is actually certified.

2. What is the difference between SL-T and SL-C, and what do you do when SL-T exceeds SL-C?

Reveal answer

SL-T is the target you assign from consequence. SL-C is the capability the installed equipment and current architecture can actually achieve. When the target exceeds the capability you have a gap, and you close it by procuring better equipment, changing the architecture, or adding a compensating control. On the flat creamery network the IT-to-OT conduit has an SL-C near zero against an SL-T of 3, and the compensating control is the industrial DMZ.

3. Why does the IT-to-OT boundary conduit carry a higher SL-T than most of the individual zones?

Reveal answer

The boundary conduit is the single path through which IT traffic can reach every control zone, so its compromise inherits the consequence of everything behind it, including the safety zone. A conduit that touches the highest-consequence zone must be protected to at least that zone's level on restricted data flow and authentication. The flat network gives it none of that today, which is why the gap on this conduit is the widest in the plant.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The security-levels rubric grader releases the flag when your deliverable carries the per-FR SL-T vectors, the consequence ranking with safety and food safety on top, and the SL-T versus SL-C gap on the IT-to-OT boundary with its compensating control. You earn it by submitting a complete vector analysis. The flag describes what you accomplished: the SL vectors assigned across the plant.

Flag format: OCR{pcc_sl_vectors_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Exercise OTSOC-6.3: Design the IT/OT Boundary
Scenario
docs.text:
Pecan Creek Creamery has a corporate web portal sitting on the same flat network as the plant. The portal carries a Local File Inclusion bug, and through it an attacker reaches an OT VPN profile that hands out a working control-network credential. The boundary that should stop that pivot does not exist, so a web bug on a marketing portal becomes a path to the ammonia controllers.

Your job in this exercise is to design the Level 3.5 industrial DMZ that closes the gap. You reproduce the LFI first so the exposure is concrete, then you design the iDMZ: which services move into it, what the brokered jump host enforces, and the replicated-historian pattern that keeps IT consumers out of the control zones. You write the deny-by-default boundary firewall rule set, mapping each control to its Foundational Requirement, and you prove that no direct IT-to-OT path survives. The boundary design goes to the boundary-design rubric, which releases the flag once every direct path is eliminated and the rule set is deny-by-default with justifications.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The IT/OT boundary is the single most scrutinized control in any OT insurance questionnaire, because it is where the overwhelming majority of real intrusions cross from the enterprise into the plant. A Level 3.5 industrial DMZ is the 62443 answer: a buffer segment between IT (Level 4) and OT (Levels 0 to 3) where the only assets are brokers and replicas. IT consumers talk to the DMZ; OT devices talk to the DMZ; nothing talks straight through.

The corpweb LFI you reproduce is the textbook failure mode. A vulnerability on an IT-reachable asset leaks a credential, and on a flat network that credential reaches a PLC with nothing in the way. The fix is not to patch the LFI alone, because the next bug will leak the next credential. The fix is architectural: a brokered jump host that demands MFA and records sessions, a replicated historian so IT reads a copy instead of reaching into the control zone, and a deny-by-default firewall where every allow is explicit, minimal, and justified. Each control maps to a Foundational Requirement, which is how the underwriter ties your design back to the SL-T vectors from Exercise 6.2.

Credentials in scope Username Password Where it is used Leaked OT contractor account ot_contractor PecanCreek#2026 Leaked by the corpweb LFI; the credential your design must neutralize Operator HMI kiosk operator PecanCreek#2026 Read-only cross-reference (optional)

RUBRIC=10.100.42.22
CORP=10.100.42.30

echo "Rubric $RUBRIC, corpweb $CORP, historian $HIST"

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Reproduce the corpweb LFI and confirm the leaked OT contractor credential
  • Identify every current direct IT-to-OT path, including the portal pivot
  • Design the Level 3.5 iDMZ with a brokered MFA jump host and replicated historian
  • Write deny-by-default boundary firewall rules with per-rule justification
  • Map each control to its Foundational Requirement (FR1, FR2, FR3, FR5, FR6)
  • Submit the boundary design to the boundary-design rubric and retrieve the flag

docs.title: Step 1: Reproduce the LFI and confirm the exposure
docs.text:
Before you design the fix, see the exposure for yourself. The corporate portal includes a page parameter that reads a file off disk with no path validation, the classic Local File Inclusion. Point it at the OT VPN profile and the remote-access document and read what leaks. Confirming the bug yourself is read-only against an IT asset; you touch no plant device.

Kali - reach the OT VPN profile through the LFI

curl -s "http://$CORP/portal.php?page=config/ot_vpn_profile.ovpn"

Expected output (abridged)

# Pecan Creek Creamery OT remote access profile
remote jump01.pcc.local 1194
# contractor login
auth-user-pass
# username ot_contractor
# password PecanCreek#2026
...

The profile leaks the credential ot_contractor / PecanCreek#2026 and points at the jump host jump01.pcc.local. Pull the remote-access document too, since it names the assets the contractor was expected to reach.

Kali - read the remote-access document through the same bug

curl -s "http://$CORP/portal.php?page=config/remote_access.pdf" | strings | head -20

The document confirms the contractor account is meant to reach control-network devices. On the current flat network nothing stops that credential from reaching the PLCs directly, so a web bug on the portal is a straight line to the ammonia controllers. That line is what your design eliminates.

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate every direct IT-to-OT path
docs.text:
List the paths that exist today. Each one is a finding the boundary design must close. The LFI pivot is the headline, but it is not the only path.

Direct IT-to-OT path today Why it is dangerous corpweb LFI to OT VPN profile to PLCs A web bug leaks a credential that reaches control devices Flat segment: any IT host can ARP the control zone No segmentation between Level 4 and Level 1 IT consumers read the historian inside the control area A read path into OT is also a potential write path Contractor VPN lands directly on the OT subnet No brokered hop, no MFA, no session recording

Every row resolves to the same root cause: there is no boundary. The design in the next steps replaces all four with conduits through a single DMZ.

docs.title: Step 3: Design the Level 3.5 industrial DMZ
docs.text:
The target architecture puts a buffer segment between IT and OT. IT talks to the DMZ, OT talks to the DMZ, and the firewall denies everything else. The diagram below is the target boundary.

flowchart LR
    subgraph IT["IT Zone (Level 4)"]
        CORP["corpweb portal"]
        ITUSER["IT consumers"]
    end
    subgraph IDMZ["Industrial DMZ (Level 3.5)"]
        JUMP["jump01: brokered jump host<br/>MFA, session recording"]
        HISTREP["replicated historian<br/>read-only copy"]
    end
    subgraph OT["OT Zones (Levels 1 to 3)"]
        HIST["historian.pcc.local"]
        CTRL["control + supervisory devices"]
        SIS["ammonia SIS (safety zone)"]
    end
    ITUSER -->|"MFA, brokered"| JUMP
    JUMP -->|"explicit allow only"| CTRL
    HIST -->|"one-way replication"| HISTREP
    ITUSER -->|"read the replica"| HISTREP
    CORP -.->|"DENY: no path to OT"| OT

The DMZ holds two assets. The brokered jump host, jump01, is the only way an IT identity reaches OT: it demands MFA, it brokers the connection rather than passing the credential through, and it records every session. The replicated historian is a read-only copy of the plant historian; IT consumers read the replica in the DMZ and never reach into the control zone for live data. The corpweb portal stays in IT with no path into OT at all, so even if the LFI is exploited again, the leaked credential lands on a segment that cannot reach a PLC.

docs.title: Step 4: Write the deny-by-default firewall rule set
docs.text:
The boundary firewall denies everything by default. Every allow is a single explicit rule naming a source, a destination, a protocol or port, and a justification. The implicit final rule is deny-all-log. Write the rules as a table the grader and an auditor can both read.

# Source Destination Proto/Port Action Justification 1 IT consumers jump01 (DMZ) TCP 443 + MFA ALLOW Sole brokered entry into OT; MFA enforced 2 jump01 (DMZ) control zone named mgmt ports ALLOW Engineering access, brokered and recorded only 3 plant historian replicated historian (DMZ) one-way replication ALLOW Historian copy; replication is push-only 4 IT consumers replicated historian (DMZ) TCP 3000 read ALLOW IT reads the replica, never the live plant 5 corpweb / any IT any OT zone any DENY (log) No direct IT-to-OT path survives 6 any ammonia safety zone any except status DENY (log) SIS isolated; status conduit only 7 any any any DENY (log) Default deny, everything else dropped and logged

Rules 5 through 7 are the ones the grader checks hardest: rule 5 kills the LFI pivot, rule 6 protects the safety zone, and rule 7 is the deny-by-default backstop. Every allow above it is minimal and justified.

docs.title: Step 5: Map each control to its Foundational Requirement
docs.text:
Tie the design back to the SL-T vectors from Exercise 6.2 by mapping each control to the requirement it satisfies. The mapping is how the underwriter traces the fix to the gap.

Control Foundational Requirement MFA on the jump host FR1 Identification and Authentication Control Brokered access, no pass-through credential FR2 Use Control Integrity monitoring on the conduit FR3 System Integrity Segmentation, no direct IT-to-OT path FR5 Restricted Data Flow Session recording and conduit logging FR6 Timely Response to Events

docs.title: Step 6: Write and submit the deliverable
docs.text:
Read the required elements first so your text names every keyword the grader checks: the iDMZ, the deny-by-default rules, the replicated historian, and the elimination of every direct path.

Kali - read the required elements for the boundary-design deliverable

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/rubric?deliverable=boundary-design" | python3 -m json.tool

Compose the deliverable in a file so you can iterate, covering the current paths, the iDMZ, the rule set, and the FR mapping.

Kali - write the boundary-design deliverable to a file

cat > /tmp/boundary-design.txt <<'EOF'
Pecan Creek Creamery IT-to-OT boundary design, Level 3.5 industrial dmz.
Current direct IT-to-OT paths: the corpweb portal LFI leaks the ot_contractor
credential and reaches jump01 and the PLCs on the flat network; IT consumers
read the live historian; the contractor VPN lands directly on the OT subnet.
Target: an industrial dmz (iDMZ) between the IT and OT zones. Services moved to
the dmz are a brokered jump host (jump01) enforcing MFA and session recording,
and a replicated historian so IT reads the replica and never reaches the control
zone. Deny by default boundary firewall rules: every allow is explicit with a
source, a destination, a protocol or port, and a justification, with an ACL on
the conduit; no direct IT-to-OT path survives and the corpweb-to-OT path is
denied. Conduit rules enforce zone separation between zones, and the ammonia
safety zone takes a status-only conduit. Controls map to foundational
requirements: MFA to FR1, brokered access to FR2, integrity monitoring to FR3,
segmentation to FR5, logging to FR6.
EOF
wc -l /tmp/boundary-design.txt

POST the file with deliverable set to boundary-design and read the flag field.

Kali - POST the deliverable to the boundary-design rubric

jq -n --rawfile s /tmp/boundary-design.txt \
   '{deliverable:"boundary-design", submission:$s}' \
  | curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- \
  | python3 -m json.tool

Expected output (flag value masked)

{
    "deliverable": "boundary-design",
    "score": 1.0,
    "passed": true,
    "flag": "OCR{pcc_idmz_boundary_<masked>}"
}

A passed of true means no direct IT-to-OT path remained and the rule set was deny-by-default with justifications. If passed is false, the response names the missing element; add it and POST again until it passes.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The LFI is the motivation, not the fix; a submission that only patches the portal and leaves the flat network fails, because the grader checks that no direct IT-to-OT path survives
  • Deny-by-default is a specific structure: the grader looks for an explicit default-deny plus minimal justified allows, not a list of blocks
  • The replicated historian is the element students forget; without it, IT still reads into the control zone and a direct path remains
  • The FR mapping is what ties this design to the SL-T gap from Exercise 6.2; an unmapped control reads as a recommendation, not a closed requirement

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is patching the corpweb LFI not a sufficient fix for the IT/OT boundary?

Reveal answer

The LFI is one instance of a class. The next web bug, misconfiguration, or stolen laptop will leak the next credential, and on a flat network that credential reaches a PLC just as easily. The durable fix is architectural: an industrial DMZ where no IT asset has a direct path to OT, so a leaked credential lands on a segment that cannot reach the control zone regardless of how it leaked.

2. What does a brokered jump host give you that a plain VPN into the OT subnet does not?

Reveal answer

A plain VPN drops the user directly onto the control network with whatever credential they hold. A brokered jump host terminates the IT session in the DMZ, demands MFA, opens a separate controlled connection to OT, and records the whole session. The IT credential never reaches the plant, the access is logged, and a single broker is far easier to monitor and revoke than a flat VPN landing zone.

3. Why does the design replicate the historian into the DMZ instead of letting IT read the plant historian directly?

Reveal answer

Any read path from IT into the control zone is also a potential write path and a reconnaissance channel, and it keeps an IT-to-OT conduit open. A one-way push of historian data to a read-only replica in the DMZ lets IT consumers get the trends they need while the live plant historian stays unreachable from IT. The replication is push-only, so the control zone initiates the flow and IT never reaches in.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The boundary-design rubric grader releases the flag when your design eliminates every direct IT-to-OT path and presents a deny-by-default firewall rule set with per-rule justifications, a brokered MFA jump host, and a replicated historian. You earn it by submitting a complete boundary design. The flag describes what you accomplished: the iDMZ boundary, designed.

Flag format: OCR{pcc_idmz_boundary_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Exercise OTSOC-6.4: Capstone, The Insurer Report
Scenario
docs.text:
The insurer's OT security questionnaire is due. Pecan Creek Creamery cannot renew its cyber policy until the SOC delivers a full architecture and risk package, and you are the analyst who owns it. Everything you built across the track feeds this one deliverable: the zone-and-conduit diagram from Exercise 6.1, the SL-T vectors from Exercise 6.2, the iDMZ and boundary design from Exercise 6.3, and the consequence model you have carried since the first level. The capstone is the synthesis.

The full plant runs live for reference, including the operator HMI and the corporate portal, so you can confirm the asset inventory and ground every claim in a real device. You produce the integrated package: the partition with the ammonia SIS in its own safety zone, the per-FR security-level targets, the Level 3.5 DMZ with no direct IT-to-OT path, a remediation roadmap ordered by consequence, and a one-page executive summary for the insurer and the board. The package goes to the insurer rubric, which scores it against every required element and against the consequence model, and releases the flag once the deliverable is complete and the roadmap is ordered safety-first.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
An insurer questionnaire is the moment an OT program is forced to prove it can describe and defend itself in one document. The underwriter is not a control engineer; the executive summary has to land in one page for a board, while the architecture, SL vectors, and rule set have to survive review by a technical assessor. Producing both registers in one package is the skill this capstone certifies.

The ordering of the remediation roadmap is the single most consequential editorial choice. OT inverts the IT CIA triad: safety and integrity come before confidentiality, because a defeated ammonia trip injures people and under-processed milk reaches the public, while a leaked portal file is a lower-consequence loss. A roadmap that fixes the corpweb LFI before it isolates the ammonia SIS, because the LFI is easier, is a roadmap that an OT assessor rejects. Ordering by consequence, safety first, then food safety, then availability, then confidentiality, is what tells the insurer the SOC understands what it is actually protecting.

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm the asset inventory against the live plant
docs.text:
Ground the package in the real plant before you write a word. The historian polls every control device, so its plantwide trends dashboard is the fastest way to confirm the inventory you carry from the earlier levels is still accurate. Open the dashboard in your browser using the historian IP from the Exercise Network panel on port 3000.

Kali - open the historian dashboard in the browser

In your browser address bar, enter the historian IP from the panel on port 3000, for example http://HIST_IP:3000/.

The dashboard trends the whole plant, and its About panel enumerates every polled source and the protocol behind each one: the blend tank, pasteurizer, ammonia BPCS, freezer, and cold-storage RTU. That source inventory and its protocol list are exactly what the insurer report's asset and exposure picture is built from, because each polled endpoint is an asset to name and each protocol is an exposure to assess. If you want the same list programmatically to paste into the package, the historian exposes it as JSON as an optional cross-check.

Kali (optional) - cross-check the source inventory as JSON

curl -s "http://$HIST:3000/api/sources" | python3 -m json.tool

Cross-check the operator HMI next to confirm the supervisory layer is live and the plant is at a normal state. Open the operator board in your browser using the HMI IP from the panel on port 80; the kiosk account is read-only.

Kali - open the operator HMI in the browser

In your browser address bar, enter the HMI IP from the panel on port 80, for example http://HMI_IP/, and sign in read-only as operator / PecanCreek#2026 if prompted.

The operator board shows the plant running as a whole: the blend tank online with its agitator turning and its recipe loaded, the ammonia refrigeration compressor running at pressure, and the freezer tile present. Reading the supervisory layer off the board confirms the control assets you name in the package are live and calm, which is what the insurer expects: claims tied to a real operator view, not to a stale spreadsheet. For analysts who want the same state as raw fields, the HMI exposes it as JSON as an optional programmatic cross-check.

Kali (optional) - cross-check the supervisory state as JSON

curl -s -u operator:PecanCreek#2026 "http://$HMI/api/state" | python3 -m json.tool | head -30

docs.title: Step 2: Assemble the four technical sections
docs.text:
The capstone integrates the three earlier deliverables plus the consequence model. Lay the sections out before you write the prose so nothing is dropped.

Section Source The one thing the grader checks Zone-and-conduit diagram Exercise 6.1 Ammonia SIS isolated in its own safety zone SL-T vectors Exercise 6.2 Per-FR vectors ordered by consequence, safety highest iDMZ and boundary design Exercise 6.3 Deny-by-default, no direct IT-to-OT path Remediation roadmap This exercise Ordered by consequence, safety first

docs.title: Step 3: Order the remediation roadmap by consequence
docs.text:
The roadmap is where the capstone is won or lost. Order the fixes by the harm they prevent, not by how easy they are. The inverted CIA triad puts safety and integrity ahead of confidentiality.

Priority Remediation Consequence class 1 Isolate the ammonia SIS; restore tamper-evident trip setpoints; status-only conduit Safety: a defeated trip is a toxic release 2 Protect the pasteurizer FDV and cut-in setpoints from unauthorized writes Food safety: under-processed milk shipped 3 Harden the control zone; restrict writes on blend, freezer, ammonia BPCS Process integrity: lost batch, refrigeration upset 4 Build the iDMZ; replicate the historian; segment the cold-chain telemetry Availability: cold-chain spoilage, loss of view 5 Patch the corpweb LFI; rotate the leaked contractor credential Confidentiality: leaked file and credential

The corpweb LFI is the easiest fix and the lowest consequence, so it sits last. Sequencing it ahead of the ammonia SIS would invert the safety ordering and the grader penalizes that.

docs.title: Step 4: Write the one-page executive summary
docs.text: The summary speaks to the board and the underwriter, not the engineer. Keep it to one page: state the top risk in plain language (a flat network lets a web bug reach the ammonia safety controller), state the worst-case consequence (a worker-safety event), name the fix (zones and conduits, an SL-target program, and an industrial DMZ), and state the sequence (safety first). Avoid protocol jargon; the technical sections carry the detail.

docs.title: Step 5: Compose and submit the package
docs.text:
Read the required elements first so your package names every keyword the insurer rubric checks: the zone-and-conduit diagram, the SL-T vectors, the iDMZ, the prioritized roadmap, the executive summary, and the consequence ordering.

Kali - read the required elements for the capstone deliverable

curl -s "http://$RUBRIC/rubric?deliverable=capstone" | python3 -m json.tool

Compose the full package in a file so you can iterate. Pull every section together in one submission, ending with the consequence-ordered roadmap.

Kali - write the capstone package to a file

cat > /tmp/capstone.txt <<'EOF'
Pecan Creek Creamery insurer architecture and risk package per IEC 62443.
Asset inventory confirmed against the live plant.
Zone and conduit diagram: assets partitioned into zones with conduit rules
between them, the ammonia SIS safety instrumented system isolated in its own
safety zone separate from the BPCS, with the IT-to-OT boundary conduit named.
Security level target SL-T vectors assigned per FR ordered by consequence,
ammonia safety highest, with the SL-T versus SL-C boundary gap identified.
Industrial dmz (iDMZ) boundary design at Level 3.5 between IT and OT with a
brokered MFA jump host and a replicated historian, no direct IT-to-OT path.
Boundary firewall deny by default with conduit rules and ACL, every allow
justified.
Prioritized remediation roadmap ordered by consequence: ammonia safety trips and
the pasteurizer food safety FDV first, then cold-chain availability, then the
corpweb confidentiality LFI fix. Roadmap ordered by consequence, safety first.
One-page executive summary for the insurer and the board in plain language.
EOF
wc -l /tmp/capstone.txt

POST the file with deliverable set to capstone and read the flag field.

Kali - POST the package to the insurer rubric

jq -n --rawfile s /tmp/capstone.txt \
   '{deliverable:"capstone", submission:$s}' \
  | curl -s -X POST "http://$RUBRIC/check" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- \
  | python3 -m json.tool

Expected output (flag value masked)

{
    "deliverable": "capstone",
    "score": 1.0,
    "passed": true,
    "flag": "OCR{pcc_otsoc_capstone_<masked>}"
}

A passed of true means every required element was present and the roadmap was consequence-ordered. The insurer rubric is the strictest grader on the track, so if passed is false, read the response carefully: it names the missing element or flags the roadmap order. Add or reorder, then POST again. Iterate until passed is true.

docs.title: Output Interpretation
docs.text:
• The capstone grader checks for all four technical sections plus the executive summary; a package strong on architecture but missing the roadmap or the summary fails on completeness, not on quality
  • Roadmap order is scored explicitly: the words safety first and the safety-before-confidentiality sequence are what the grader reads, so state the ordering in plain language, do not leave it implied
  • The executive summary is the element most often written like a technical section; the grader and the board both want plain-language consequence, not protocol detail
  • Because this deliverable integrates the three earlier ones, a missing element usually traces back to a section you can lift directly from your 6.1, 6.2, or 6.3 submission

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the remediation roadmap fix the ammonia SIS before the corpweb LFI, when the LFI is far easier to patch?

Reveal answer

OT inverts the CIA triad to safety and integrity first, confidentiality last. A defeated ammonia trip is a toxic release that injures people; the LFI leaks a file. Ordering by ease would put the low-consequence fix first and leave the worker-safety risk open longest, which an OT assessor rejects. The roadmap is ordered by the harm each fix prevents, so safety leads regardless of effort.

2. The executive summary and the technical sections target two different readers. How should that change how you write each?

Reveal answer

The technical sections target an assessor who needs the zones, the SL vectors, the rule set, and the FR mapping in full detail. The executive summary targets a board and an underwriter who need the top risk, its worst-case consequence, the fix, and the sequence in one page of plain language. Putting protocol detail in the summary loses the board; putting hand-waving in the technical sections loses the assessor. Write each to its reader.

3. The capstone integrates three earlier deliverables. Why does the insurer want them synthesized into one package rather than as three separate documents?

Reveal answer

The underwriter is pricing a single policy against a single plant, so they need one coherent picture: the partition, the targets it implies, the boundary that enforces them, and the sequence in which the gaps close. Three disconnected documents force the assessor to reconcile them and leave room for contradictions, such as a roadmap that does not match the SL gaps. A synthesized package proves the SOC reasons about the plant as one system, which is what the insurer is actually buying.

docs.title: Capture the Flag
docs.text:
The insurer rubric grader releases the flag when your package carries every required element, the zone-and-conduit diagram with the isolated safety zone, the per-FR SL-T vectors, the iDMZ boundary with no direct IT-to-OT path, the one-page executive summary, and a remediation roadmap ordered by consequence with safety first. You earn it by submitting the complete, consequence-ordered package. The flag marks the capstone of the OT SOC track, complete.

Flag format: OCR{pcc_otsoc_capstone_<masked>}

Submit the assembled flag in the OCR platform.

docs.title: Why Web Reconnaissance Comes First
docs.text:
Every web application penetration test begins with the same question: what is the target exposing? Before you can test for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, or authentication flaws, you need a map of the application's attack surface. Web reconnaissance builds that map, directory by directory, header by header, subdomain by subdomain.

Reconnaissance is not a single scan. A directory enumeration reveals hidden paths. Technology identification tells you what software powers the application. HTTP method testing uncovers API misconfigurations. Header analysis exposes information leaks and missing security controls. Subdomain discovery reveals forgotten services that no one remembered to lock down. Across six labs, you will build from a single gobuster scan to a complete reconnaissance methodology, learning why each layer of investigation matters.

In a real engagement, incomplete reconnaissance leads to missed vulnerabilities. An admin panel hidden behind an unlinked directory will not appear in a casual browse. A staging subdomain with debug mode enabled will not show up unless you enumerate it. The progression in this chapter ensures you never stop at the surface.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
The six labs in this chapter progress from targeted to comprehensive:

  • Enumerate hidden directories and files using wordlist-based brute forcing
  • Identify the technology stack powering a web application through headers and fingerprinting
  • Test HTTP methods to find dangerous API misconfigurations
  • Analyze HTTP headers for security weaknesses and information disclosure
  • Discover subdomains to map the full attack surface beyond the main application
  • Combine all techniques into a complete reconnaissance workflow

By the end of this chapter, you will have a repeatable methodology for assessing any web application, from the first directory scan to a comprehensive attack surface report.

docs.title: What Is Web Reconnaissance?
docs.text:
Web reconnaissance (also called web enumeration or web footprinting) is the process of gathering information about a web application and its infrastructure. Unlike network scanning, which focuses on open ports and services, web reconnaissance targets the application layer: the directories, technologies, headers, and domains that define what an attacker can reach.

The table below lists the reconnaissance techniques you will use in this chapter.

Technique What It Reveals Primary Tool Directory enumeration Hidden paths, admin panels, backup files gobuster Technology ID Web server, framework, CMS, language versions curl, whatweb HTTP method testing Allowed methods, dangerous API configurations curl Header analysis Security headers, information disclosure curl Subdomain discovery Additional hosts, staging environments, APIs gobuster (DNS) Combined assessment Complete attack surface map All tools

Each technique answers a different question about the target. Together, they produce the complete picture that later testing phases (authentication attacks, injection testing, and exploitation) depend on.

docs.title: What Is Gobuster?
docs.text:
Gobuster is an open-source tool for brute-forcing URIs (directories and files), DNS subdomains, and virtual host names. It works by testing entries from a wordlist against a target, reporting which entries return valid responses.

Gobuster operates in two modes relevant to this chapter:

  • Directory mode (dir): tests directory and file names against a web server
  • DNS mode (dns): tests subdomain names against a domain's DNS records

Gobuster is fast, multi-threaded, and widely used in penetration testing. Combined with curl for header inspection and whatweb for technology fingerprinting, it forms the core toolkit for web reconnaissance.

Gobuster is pre-installed on Kali Linux. You can verify your installation at any time:

gobuster --help

docs.title: The Reconnaissance Workflow
docs.text:
Each lab builds on the previous one, adding a new reconnaissance capability:

graph LR
    A[W1.1 Directories]
    B[W1.2 Technologies]
    C[W1.3 HTTP Methods]
    D[W1.4 Headers]
    E[W1.5 Subdomains]
    F[W1.6 Combined]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F
Lab Core Technique What It Adds W1.1 gobuster dir Directory and file discovery W1.2 curl -I, whatweb Technology stack identification W1.3 curl -X OPTIONS HTTP method enumeration W1.4 curl -v Security header analysis W1.5 gobuster dns Subdomain enumeration W1.6 All tools combined Complete reconnaissance workflow

Notice the progression: each lab asks a different question about the same type of target. By the final lab, you will chain every technique into a systematic assessment that covers the full attack surface.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following before launching your first lab:

  • VPN connection to the lab environment is active
  • Terminal open and ready for commands
  • Gobuster installed and accessible (type gobuster --help to confirm)
  • curl installed and accessible (type curl --version to confirm)
  • whatweb installed and accessible (type whatweb --version to confirm)
  • Web browser available for inspecting pages and source code
  • Notebook or text editor ready for recording findings
  • Access to the OCR platform at the provided URL

Each lab takes approximately 20 to 40 minutes. Work through them in order: later labs assume familiarity with the tools and techniques from earlier ones.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
• Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach the lab network.
  • No credentials are needed: you will discover publicly accessible directories.
  • You should be comfortable running commands in a Linux terminal.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
TechStart Inc, a rapidly growing tech startup, has hired your security team to assess their web application before its public launch. Your contact, Sarah Chen (CTO), has heard rumours from the development team about exposed directories and wants to understand what information is publicly accessible beyond the main page.

Your initial briefing indicates the application is hosted at recon.lab. TechStart wants a comprehensive security assessment, starting with reconnaissance. Your first task is to discover hidden directories, exposed files, and any information that could aid an attacker.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Launch the lab environment and note the target hostname
  • Use gobuster to discover hidden directories on the web server
  • Identify common web directories (admin panels, backups, configuration files)
  • Investigate discovered directories for sensitive information and files
  • Record your findings and submit the flag

docs.title: Background: What Is Directory Enumeration?
docs.text:
Web applications serve content from directories on the server's file system. The main page is just the front door; behind it, the server may host administrative panels, backup files, configuration directories, and development resources that are not linked from any visible page. Directory enumeration systematically tests for these hidden paths.

graph TD
    A["http://recon.lab/"]
    A --> B["/admin"]
    A --> C["/backup"]
    A --> D["/config"]
    B --> E["Admin panel\nMay contain sensitive files"]
    C --> F["Backup data\nDatabase dumps, old files"]
    D --> G["Configuration files\nCredentials, settings"]

The technique works by sending HTTP requests for directory names drawn from a wordlist. If the server returns a successful response (200 OK) or a redirect (301/302), the directory exists. A 404 Not Found means it does not. A 403 Forbidden means the directory exists but access is denied, which is still valuable information.

Common findings during directory enumeration include:

Discovery Type Examples Risk Admin panels /admin, /administrator Unauthorized management access Backup files /backup, /old, .bak files Source code or database exposure Configuration files /config, .env, web.config Credentials, API keys Development paths /dev, /test, /staging Debug information, test accounts

docs.title: Tool Primer: Gobuster Directory Mode
docs.text:
Gobuster's dir mode tests directory and file names from a wordlist against a target URL. It is fast, multi-threaded, and reports HTTP status codes for each match.

Syntax:

gobuster dir -u <url> -w <wordlist>

Key flags:

Flag Purpose -u <url> Target URL (required) -w <wordlist> Path to wordlist file (required) -t <threads> Number of concurrent threads (default: 10) -x <ext> File extensions to search (e.g., -x php,txt) -o <file> Save output to a file -s <codes> Show only specific status codes

Common wordlists on Kali Linux:

Wordlist Size Use Case /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt ~4,600 Quick general scan /usr/share/wordlists/dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt ~220,000 Thorough scan /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt ~4,700 General purpose

For beginner labs, the smaller common.txt wordlist is sufficient and much faster than the medium list.

Sample output:

===============================================================
Gobuster v3.6
===============================================================
[+] Url:            http://recon.lab
[+] Wordlist:       /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt
[+] Threads:        10
===============================================================
/admin                (Status: 200) [Size: 1234]
/backup               (Status: 301) [Size: 312] [--> http://recon.lab/backup/]
/config               (Status: 301) [Size: 312] [--> http://recon.lab/config/]
===============================================================

Each line shows a discovered path, its HTTP status code, and the response size. Status 200 means the content is directly accessible. Status 301 means the server redirected to the directory with a trailing slash.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab
docs.text:
Navigate to Learning Paths then Web then Level 1, click Launch, wait for Running, note the target hostname (recon.lab).

Write down the hostname. You will use it in every command that follows.

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Before scanning, confirm you can reach the target.

Check that the target web server responds

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://recon.lab

You should see 200, indicating the web server is responding. If you get no response, check your VPN connection.

Open http://recon.lab in a web browser. You should see a welcome page for recon.lab, a basic web server set up for directory enumeration practice. The main page does not link to any other directories. Everything beyond this page must be discovered through enumeration.

docs.title: Step 3: Run a Directory Scan
docs.text:
Open your terminal and run gobuster in directory mode.

Run a gobuster directory scan against the target

gobuster dir -u http://recon.lab -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Gobuster will test each entry from the wordlist against the target. The scan may take one to two minutes depending on thread count and network speed.

docs.title: Step 4: Read the Output
docs.text:
Your output should show several discovered directories with status codes 200, 301, 302, or 403. You are looking for directories like /admin, /backup, and /config, exactly the kind of paths that should not be publicly accessible on a production server.

Record every result, noting the status code for each:

Understanding status codes:

  • 200: the page exists and is directly accessible
  • 301/302: the directory exists and the server redirected (usually adding a trailing slash)
  • 403: the directory exists but the server denied access (still confirms existence)
  • 404: not found (gobuster does not show these by default)

docs.title: Step 5: Investigate Discovered Directories
docs.text:
Visit each discovered directory in your browser or with curl. Start with the most interesting: an admin directory on a web server is always a high-priority finding.

Fetch each discovered directory with curl

curl http://recon.lab/admin
curl http://recon.lab/backup
curl http://recon.lab/config

Browse the contents carefully. Some directories may display a file listing. Look at every file available. If you see a directory index, check each file it contains.

docs.title: Step 6: Look Inside Directories for Files
docs.text:
When you find an interesting directory, look deeper. Directories often contain files that are not listed on the page itself. Try common file names inside discovered directories.

Request a common file name inside the admin directory

curl http://recon.lab/admin/flag.txt

The /admin directory is the most sensitive path you discovered. An admin panel that is publicly accessible without authentication is a critical finding. Examine its contents thoroughly: check for any text files, configuration files, or data that has been left exposed.

docs.title: Step 7: Scan with File Extensions
docs.text:
Some sensitive files have specific extensions. Run a second scan targeting common file types.

Rescan with common file extensions appended

gobuster dir -u http://recon.lab -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x txt,php,html,bak

The -x flag appends each extension to every wordlist entry, testing paths like /admin/flag.txt, /config.bak, and /backup.sql in addition to the base directory names. The extension scan confirms files within the directories you already found.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Target Hostname: ___

Directory Status Code Contents / Notes /admin /backup /config

Files found inside directories:

File Path Contents

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: OCR{_______________}

docs.title: Step 8: Record the Flag
docs.text: The flag is located in a text file within one of the discovered directories. Enter the flag in the format OCR{________} on the lab submission page.

docs.title: Step 9: Clean Up
docs.text: Close any browser tabs open to the target. You have completed the directory enumeration phase.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do web applications have directories that are not linked from the main page?

Web applications accumulate directories over time: admin panels for management, backup directories from maintenance, development paths from testing, and configuration directories from deployment. Developers and administrators create these for operational reasons. Without a deliberate cleanup process, they persist on production servers even when they are no longer needed.

2. What is the difference between a 403 and a 404 response during directory enumeration?

A 403 Forbidden response confirms the directory exists but access is denied. A 404 Not Found response means the path does not exist on the server. From an attacker's perspective, 403 is more valuable: it confirms a target that may be accessible through other means (credential discovery, parameter manipulation, or misconfiguration exploitation).

3. Why should you scan with file extensions in addition to directory names?

Directory scans alone miss files within discovered directories. A file like flag.txt inside /admin/ will not appear in a directory-only scan. Adding extensions with -x tests for files at every path level, catching sensitive documents that directory enumeration alone overlooks.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Directory enumeration reveals paths that are invisible from the main page
  • Gobuster tests wordlist entries against a target and reports valid responses
  • Status codes tell you whether a path exists (200, 301) or is blocked (403)
  • Wordlist selection balances speed against coverage: start small, escalate if needed
  • File extension scanning catches individual files (like .txt or .bak) within discovered directories
  • Admin directories are high-priority findings: always investigate their contents thoroughly
  • Every discovered path is a potential entry point that requires further investigation

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
• Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach the lab network.
  • You should have completed Lab W1.1 and be comfortable using curl from the command line.
  • No credentials are needed: all information is gathered from public responses.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Continuing your assessment of TechStart Inc, Sarah Chen wants to understand what technologies power the company's web application. Your directory enumeration in the previous lab revealed several paths, but Sarah needs to know the full technology stack (web server software, programming languages, frameworks, and content management systems) so her team can evaluate whether any components have known vulnerabilities.

The application is accessible at target.lab. Your job is to fingerprint every technology in use and document version numbers wherever possible.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Use curl to inspect HTTP response headers for server and framework information
  • Run whatweb to perform comprehensive technology fingerprinting
  • Identify the web server, programming language, framework, and CMS in use
  • Explore CMS-specific directories and files that confirm the platform
  • Document all version numbers discovered
  • Record your findings and submit the flag

docs.title: Background: Why Technology Identification Matters
docs.text:
Every piece of software in a web application's stack introduces its own set of potential vulnerabilities. An Apache web server has different weaknesses than Nginx. A PHP application faces different threats than one built on Node.js. A WordPress site has an entirely different attack surface from a custom-built application. Knowing the exact technology stack transforms a generic web application into a set of specific software targets, each with its own CVE history.

graph TD
    A["Web Application"]
    A --> B["Web Server\nApache, Nginx, IIS"]
    A --> C["Language\nPHP, Python, Node.js"]
    A --> D["CMS Platform\nWordPress, Drupal, Joomla"]
    A --> E["CMS Directories\n/wp-admin, /wp-content,\n/wp-includes"]
    B --> F["Version-specific CVEs"]
    C --> F
    D --> F
    E --> G["Admin panels,\ntheme files,\nplugin vulnerabilities"]

Technology identification (also called fingerprinting) collects this information through several channels:

Source What It Reveals Example Server header Web server software and version Apache/2.4.54 X-Powered-By Backend language or framework PHP/8.1.0 Custom headers CMS or framework identity X-Framework: WordPress/6.2.0 HTML source Meta tags, script references <meta name="generator" content="WordPress 6.2"> Known file paths CMS structure confirmation /wp-admin/, /readme.html robots.txt Directory structure, CMS directories Disallow: /wp-admin/

When you identify a CMS like WordPress, the attack surface expands dramatically. WordPress has its own admin panel (/wp-admin), a plugin ecosystem with known vulnerabilities, theme files that may leak information, and configuration files like readme.html that disclose the exact version.

docs.title: Tool Primer: curl and whatweb
docs.text:
curl is a command-line tool for transferring data with URLs. For reconnaissance, its most useful feature is fetching HTTP headers.

curl -I <url>          # Fetch headers only (HEAD request)
curl -v <url>          # Verbose output showing full request and response
curl -s <url>          # Silent mode (suppress progress bar)

Key curl flags for reconnaissance:

Flag Purpose -I Send HEAD request, show response headers only -v Show complete HTTP exchange (verbose) -s Suppress progress meter -L Follow redirects -A <agent> Set custom User-Agent string

whatweb is a web application fingerprinting tool that identifies technologies by matching response patterns against a database of known signatures.

whatweb <url>           # Basic fingerprinting
whatweb -v <url>        # Verbose output with details
whatweb -a 3 <url>      # Aggressive mode (more requests, more detail)

whatweb checks HTTP headers, HTML content, JavaScript files, cookies, and URL patterns to build a comprehensive technology profile.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab
docs.text: Navigate to Learning Paths then Web then Level 1, click Launch, wait for Running, note the target hostname (target.lab).

docs.title: Step 2: Fetch Response Headers with curl
docs.text:
Start by examining the HTTP response headers.

Fetch the response headers with curl

curl -I http://target.lab

The output will show headers returned by the server. Pay close attention to three headers:

  • Server: identifies the web server software and version (e.g., Apache/2.4.54)
  • X-Powered-By: reveals the backend programming language (e.g., PHP/8.1.0)
  • X-Framework: a custom header that may identify the CMS or framework

Record every header value. In this lab, the server is intentionally configured with ServerTokens Full, meaning it discloses maximum version information. In production, administrators should suppress these details.

docs.title: Step 3: Run whatweb
docs.text:
Use whatweb for comprehensive fingerprinting.

Fingerprint the web stack with whatweb

whatweb http://target.lab

whatweb produces a compact summary identifying technologies. For more detail.

Run whatweb in verbose mode

whatweb -v http://target.lab

The verbose output breaks down each identified technology with the evidence that matched. Look for CMS identification: whatweb may detect a content management system by recognising its characteristic file structure, meta tags, or response patterns.

docs.title: Step 4: Inspect the HTML Source
docs.text:
Fetch the full page and look for technology clues in the HTML.

Retrieve the HTML source with curl

curl -s http://target.lab

Look for:

  • Meta generator tags: a <meta name="generator"> tag often identifies the CMS and version
  • Script tags: <script src="/wp-includes/js/..."> paths reveal WordPress
  • CSS references: /wp-content/themes/ paths confirm WordPress theming
  • HTML comments: developers sometimes leave framework-specific comments

If the page references paths like /wp-content/, /wp-includes/, or /wp-admin/, the application is running WordPress or simulating its structure.

docs.title: Step 5: Explore CMS-Specific Paths
docs.text:
Once you identify the CMS, check its known file paths. WordPress has several predictable locations.

Probe the WordPress file paths

curl http://target.lab/readme.html
curl http://target.lab/robots.txt
curl http://target.lab/wp-admin/
curl http://target.lab/wp-content/
curl http://target.lab/wp-includes/
  • readme.html: WordPress ships with a readme file that often includes the version number
  • robots.txt: may list WordPress-specific directories that the site owner wants hidden from search engines
  • /wp-admin/: the WordPress administration panel; check if it is accessible and what it contains

Investigate each path. The flag for this lab is located within one of these CMS-specific directories.

docs.title: Step 6: Check the Admin Directory
docs.text:
Navigate into the WordPress admin directory and look for exposed files.

Check the admin directory for the flag file

curl http://target.lab/wp-admin/
curl http://target.lab/wp-admin/flag.txt

WordPress admin directories sometimes contain configuration files, backup scripts, or in this case, a flag file that should not be publicly accessible. The fact that you can reach it without authentication is the vulnerability.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Target Hostname: ___

Technology Stack:

Component Identified Value Source (header/page/path) Web Server Language CMS / Framework CMS Version

CMS Directories Found:

Path Accessible? Contents /wp-admin/ /wp-content/ /wp-includes/ /readme.html

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: OCR{_______________}

docs.title: Step 7: Record the Flag
docs.text: Enter the flag discovered during technology identification in the format OCR{________} on the lab submission page.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do web servers include version information in the Server header by default?

The HTTP specification defines the Server header as a way for servers to identify themselves. Most web server software includes the version by default for interoperability and debugging purposes. From a security perspective, this is information disclosure: administrators should configure their servers to suppress or minimise version details in production (e.g., ServerTokens Prod in Apache).

2. Why is identifying a CMS like WordPress more valuable than identifying just the web server?

A CMS identification opens a much larger attack surface. WordPress has known admin panel paths (/wp-admin), a plugin ecosystem with frequent vulnerabilities, theme files that may leak information, and predictable file structures. Knowing the CMS version maps to specific CVEs and known exploits. The web server alone tells you far less about the application's vulnerabilities.

3. Why should readme.html and similar default files be removed from production WordPress installations?

Default files like readme.html disclose the exact WordPress version, which maps directly to known vulnerabilities. An attacker who reads the readme file can immediately search for exploits targeting that specific version.
