The domain name is corp.ocr-range.lab. The DC hosts DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, SMB, and other standard AD services. No credentials are required for any exercise in this chapter; all techniques rely on unauthenticated protocol queries.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following before beginning Exercise WS-1.1.

  • VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range is active
  • You can resolve dc01 from your Kali Linux attack box (run ping -c 1 dc01)
  • The tools nmap, dig, smbclient, and ldapsearch are installed (all are included in the default Kali image)
  • You have a terminal window open and a text file or note-taking application ready to record findings
  • You understand that all scanning is confined to the lab environment; never run these commands against systems you do not have authorization to test

docs.title: Exercise WS-1.1: Domain Controller Port Discovery
Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise WS-1.1 is the first exercise in the Windows Server track. No prior exercise results are needed, but you should confirm that your VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range is active and that your Kali Linux attack box can reach the target host dc01.

Prerequisites:

  • Active VPN connection to the lab environment
  • Terminal access on your Kali Linux attack box
  • The nmap and dig commands available in your PATH

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: You are a junior penetration tester at CyberShield Consulting. Your team has been engaged to assess a corporate Active Directory (AD) environment. Your first task is to perform initial reconnaissance against a suspected Domain Controller (DC) at hostname dc01. You need to identify the services running on the host and confirm whether the machine is functioning as a DC.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
1. Perform a targeted TCP port scan against dc01 to identify AD-related services
  2. Identify AD-specific ports: 88 (Kerberos), 389 (LDAP), 636 (LDAPS), 3268 (Global Catalog)
  3. Run DNS queries to confirm the DC role
  4. Retrieve the flag from a DNS TXT record

docs.title: Background: Domain Controller Port Signatures
docs.text:
A Domain Controller is the most service-dense host in any Windows domain. Because the DC must handle authentication, name resolution, directory queries, file replication, and group policy distribution, the server listens on a predictable set of TCP ports. Recognizing the pattern of open ports is often the fastest way to confirm that a host is a DC.

The signature that distinguishes a Domain Controller from a regular Windows server is the combination of Kerberos (port 88), LDAP (port 389), and Global Catalog (port 3268). A member server might run DNS or SMB (Server Message Block), but only a DC exposes Kerberos and the Global Catalog service. When you see ports 88, 389, 636, and 3268 open alongside DNS (53) and SMB (445), you can be confident the target is a Domain Controller.

flowchart TB
    DC["Domain Controller<br/>dc01"]:::blue

    DC --> DNS["Port 53<br/>DNS"]:::green
    DC --> KRB["Port 88<br/>Kerberos"]:::green
    DC --> RPC["Port 135<br/>RPC"]:::gray
    DC --> NB["Port 139<br/>NetBIOS"]:::gray
    DC --> LDAP["Port 389<br/>LDAP"]:::green
    DC --> SMB["Port 445<br/>SMB"]:::green
    DC --> LDAPS["Port 636<br/>LDAPS"]:::green
    DC --> GC["Port 3268<br/>Global Catalog"]:::green
    DC --> RDP["Port 3389<br/>RDP"]:::gray
    DC --> WINRM["Port 5985<br/>WinRM"]:::gray

    classDef blue fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2a6ab9,color:#fff
    classDef green fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#4a8a44,color:#fff
    classDef gray fill:#888,stroke:#666,color:#fff

The green nodes above represent the ports most critical to Active Directory operations. The gray nodes are common Windows services that may or may not be present depending on server configuration.

docs.title: Tool Primer: nmap
docs.text:
Nmap is the standard network scanner for discovering hosts and services on a network. The command syntax for a targeted service-version scan is shown below.

nmap -sV -p <port-list> <target>

The flags break down as follows:

Flag Purpose -sV Probe open ports to determine service name and version -p Specify a comma-separated list of ports to scan

Nmap outputs a table with four columns for each scanned port: the port number, its state (open, closed, or filtered), the service name, and the detected version. A sample output line looks like the following:

88/tcp   open  kerberos-sec  Microsoft Windows Kerberos

When scanning a known target with a specific port list, the scan completes in seconds. Scanning all 65,535 ports is unnecessary when you already know which services to look for on a DC.

docs.title: Tool Primer: dig
docs.text:
The dig command (Domain Information Groper) queries DNS servers directly. You will use dig to query specific record types against the target DC.

dig <record-type> <name> @<server>
Parameter Purpose <record-type> The DNS record type: A, AAAA, TXT, MX, AXFR, PTR, etc. <name> The fully qualified domain name to query @<server> The DNS server to query (the DC in these exercises)

A TXT record query returns arbitrary text strings stored in DNS. Administrators sometimes use TXT records for SPF (Sender Policy Framework) entries, domain verification tokens, and other metadata.

docs.title: Step 1: Run a Targeted Port Scan
docs.text:
Scan the DC for AD service ports

Open a terminal on your Kali attack box and run the following Nmap command. The port list covers the standard AD services plus RDP and WinRM (Windows Remote Management).

nmap -sV -p 53,88,135,139,389,445,636,3268,3389,5985 dc01

Nmap will take a few seconds to probe each port and attempt service-version detection. Watch the output for the STATE column; you are looking for ports reported as open.

docs.title: Step 2: Read the Scan Results
docs.text:
Review the Nmap output carefully. You should see a results table similar to the following (version strings may vary):

PORT     STATE SERVICE       VERSION
53/tcp   open  domain        Simple DNS Plus
88/tcp   open  kerberos-sec  Microsoft Windows Kerberos
389/tcp  open  ldap          Microsoft Windows Active Directory LDAP
...
(additional ports omitted; check your own output)

Focus on the AD-critical ports. Port 88 (Kerberos), port 389 (LDAP), port 636 (LDAPS; LDAP over TLS), and port 3268 (Global Catalog) together confirm that dc01 is a Domain Controller, not a regular member server.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm the DC Role with a DNS Query
docs.text:
Query the Kerberos SRV record

A Domain Controller that also runs a DNS server registers special SRV (Service Locator) records in the domain's DNS zone. Query for the Kerberos SRV record to confirm the DC role.

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The response should include a record pointing to dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab on port 88. The presence of the Kerberos SRV record is definitive proof that the DNS server knows about an AD domain named corp.ocr-range.lab and that dc01 is registered as a Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) for that domain.

docs.title: Step 4: Query for DNS TXT Records
docs.text:
Query the flag TXT record

DNS TXT records can hold arbitrary text. Query for a TXT record at _flag.corp.ocr-range.lab to check for useful information.

dig TXT _flag.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

Examine the ANSWER SECTION of the dig output. TXT record values are enclosed in double quotes in the response.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Record the information you gathered in the tables below. Filling in these tables now will make later exercises faster, since each exercise builds on the previous exercise's discoveries.

Open Ports on dc01:

Port Service Version 53 88 135 139 389 445 636 3268 3389 5985

Domain Name (from SRV query): _________

DC Hostname (from SRV query): _________

TXT Record Value: _________

docs.title: Step 5: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review your findings table and answer the following questions for yourself before moving on:

  • Which ports confirmed that dc01 is a Domain Controller rather than a standard Windows server?
  • What domain name did the SRV record reveal?
  • Why would a penetration tester scan a specific port list rather than scanning all 65,535 ports during initial AD reconnaissance?

Port 88 (Kerberos) and port 3268 (Global Catalog) are the two most distinctive indicators of a Domain Controller. Member servers do not run Kerberos KDC services or host the Global Catalog. The combination of these ports with LDAP (389) and DNS (53) forms a fingerprint that is unique to a DC.

docs.title: Step 6: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The DNS TXT record query in Step 4 returned the flag for this exercise. The flag value is stored in the TXT record at _flag.corp.ocr-range.lab. Enter the flag value in the format OCR{...} on the submission page.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a Domain Controller expose more services than a typical Windows member server?

Reveal Answer

A Domain Controller must handle authentication (Kerberos on port 88), directory queries (LDAP on port 389 and LDAPS on port 636), forest-wide lookups (Global Catalog on port 3268), name resolution (DNS on port 53), and file-based policy distribution (SMB on port 445). A member server only needs to consume these services; not host them; so the member server does not open the corresponding listener ports.

2. If you saw ports 53, 135, 139, and 445 open but ports 88, 389, and 3268 closed, what could you conclude about the target host?

Reveal Answer

The host is likely a Windows member server or workstation, not a Domain Controller. DNS (53) can run on any server configured as a DNS server, and SMB (445), RPC (135), and NetBIOS (139) are standard on all Windows machines. The absence of Kerberos, LDAP, and Global Catalog rules out the DC role.

3. What is the advantage of using the -sV flag in Nmap rather than performing a basic port scan without version detection?

Reveal Answer

The -sV flag instructs Nmap to send protocol-specific probes to each open port and match the response against its signature database. The version information helps you distinguish between services that share the same port number on different platforms. For example, port 389 could host OpenLDAP on a Linux server or Microsoft Active Directory LDAP on a Windows DC; version detection tells you which one you are dealing with.

4. Why would a penetration tester query DNS SRV records early in the reconnaissance phase?

Reveal Answer

SRV records published by Active Directory reveal the domain name, the hostnames of all Domain Controllers, and the services each DC provides (Kerberos KDC, LDAP, Global Catalog). A single SRV query can map the entire DC infrastructure of a domain without triggering authentication events or account lockouts.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Domain Controllers expose a distinctive set of ports: 53 (DNS), 88 (Kerberos), 389 (LDAP), 636 (LDAPS), and 3268 (Global Catalog). Recognizing the pattern lets you confirm a DC in seconds.
  • Nmap with -sV provides service-version details that help you distinguish AD-specific services from generic listeners on the same port numbers.
  • DNS SRV records (_kerberos._tcp, _ldap._tcp) are registered automatically by AD and confirm both the domain name and the DC hostname.
  • TXT records in DNS can hold arbitrary data. Penetration testers routinely check for TXT records because administrators and applications store metadata there that may be useful during an engagement.
  • The open ports you discovered in this exercise; especially DNS (53), SMB (445), and LDAP (389); are the entry points for the remaining exercises in this chapter. Exercise WS-1.2 will target the DNS service you confirmed here.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise WS-1.1 confirmed that dc01 is a Domain Controller running DNS on port 53. Exercise WS-1.2 builds directly on that finding by querying the DNS service for a full inventory of records in the corp.ocr-range.lab zone.

Prerequisites:

  • Exercise WS-1.1 completed (you know dc01 is a DC with DNS on port 53)
  • Active VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range
  • The dig command available on your Kali Linux attack box

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Having confirmed that dc01 is a Domain Controller running DNS, your next step as a penetration tester at CyberShield Consulting is to enumerate the DNS zone. A misconfigured DNS server may allow zone transfers, which would reveal every record in the domain's forward lookup zone; hostnames, IP addresses, mail servers, service locators, and text records; in a single query.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
1. Attempt an AXFR (full zone transfer) against corp.ocr-range.lab
  2. Enumerate DNS records returned in the zone transfer
  3. Identify TXT records that may contain useful information
  4. Retrieve the flag from a DNS TXT record

docs.title: Background: DNS Zones and Zone Transfers
docs.text:
DNS organizes records into zones. A forward lookup zone maps hostnames to IP addresses (A and AAAA records), while a reverse lookup zone maps IP addresses back to hostnames (PTR records). Active Directory Integrated DNS zones also contain SRV records that advertise domain services, TXT records for various metadata, and other record types that support AD operations.

A zone transfer (AXFR) is a mechanism designed to let secondary DNS servers replicate the full contents of a zone from a primary server. When a secondary server requests an AXFR, the primary server sends every record in the zone. The problem arises when the DNS server does not restrict which hosts can request a transfer. An unrestricted AXFR allows any client; including an attacker; to download the complete zone file.

In a properly hardened environment, zone transfers are restricted to specific IP addresses (the secondary DNS servers). In lab and poorly configured production environments, zone transfers are sometimes left open to all clients. Penetration testers always check for unrestricted AXFR because the payoff; a complete map of the domain's DNS records; is enormous for minimal effort.

flowchart LR
    ATK["Attacker<br/>Kali Linux"]:::red
    DC["dc01<br/>DNS Server"]:::blue
    ZONE["Zone File<br/>corp.ocr-range.lab"]:::green

    ATK -->|"AXFR Request"| DC
    DC -->|"All Records"| ATK
    DC --- ZONE

    classDef red fill:#d9534f,stroke:#b9342f,color:#fff
    classDef blue fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2a6ab9,color:#fff
    classDef green fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#4a8a44,color:#fff

The diagram above shows the AXFR flow. The attacker sends a single AXFR request, and the DNS server responds with the entire contents of the zone.

docs.title: Tool Primer: dig for Zone Transfers
docs.text:
The dig command supports zone transfers with the AXFR query type. The syntax is as follows:

dig AXFR <zone-name> @<dns-server>
Parameter Purpose AXFR Request a full zone transfer (all records in the zone) <zone-name> The DNS zone to transfer, e.g., corp.ocr-range.lab @<dns-server> The DNS server to query

When a zone transfer succeeds, dig prints every record in the zone. The output begins and ends with an SOA (Start of Authority) record, and all other records appear between those two SOA entries. A failed transfer returns a Transfer failed message or a REFUSED status code.

You can also query for specific record types within a zone without a full transfer:

dig TXT <name> @<dns-server>

The TXT query returns only the text records associated with the specified name.

docs.title: Step 1: Attempt a Zone Transfer
docs.text:
Attempt a full zone transfer

Run the following command to request a full zone transfer of the corp.ocr-range.lab zone from dc01.

dig AXFR corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The output will be long if the transfer succeeds. Scroll through the results and look for the following record types:

  • SOA: Start of Authority, marks the beginning and end of the zone data
  • A: Hostname-to-IP mappings
  • SRV: Service locator records (AD uses these heavily)
  • TXT: Text records that may contain metadata, flags, or configuration data
  • NS: Name server records identifying the authoritative DNS servers

If the transfer fails with Transfer failed or ;; connection timed out, the server is configured to deny AXFR requests from unauthorized clients.

docs.title: Step 2: Analyze the Zone Transfer Output
docs.text:
A successful zone transfer reveals the full structure of the domain's DNS namespace. Review the output and look for patterns that help you understand the environment.

Pay attention to the hostnames in A records; each one represents a host registered in DNS. Count the number of unique hostnames to estimate the size of the environment. Note any hostnames that suggest specific roles, such as dc01, web01, sql01, or file01.

SRV records in the zone follow a naming convention that reveals AD services. Records under _tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab advertise Kerberos, LDAP, and Global Catalog (GC) endpoints. These records confirm the DC infrastructure you identified in Exercise WS-1.1.

docs.title: Step 3: Identify TXT Records in the Zone
docs.text:
Scan the zone transfer output for lines containing TXT. TXT records stand out because their data is enclosed in double quotes. Some TXT records are standard (SPF records for email validation, for example), while others may contain custom data placed by administrators or applications.

Filter the zone transfer for TXT records

If you want to isolate TXT records from the zone transfer output, you can pipe the results through grep:

dig AXFR corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01 | grep TXT

The grep filter reduces the output to only lines containing the string "TXT," making flag-related records easier to spot among hundreds of zone entries.

docs.title: Step 4: Query the Flag TXT Record Directly
docs.text:
Query the flag TXT record directly

Based on the TXT records you found in the zone transfer, query the specific record that contains the flag.

dig TXT _zone-flag.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

Examine the ANSWER SECTION of the response. The TXT record value appears in double quotes and contains the flag for this exercise.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the results of your zone transfer in the spaces below. The information gathered here will be used in Exercise WS-1.3 (DNS Reverse Lookup Mapping).

Zone Transfer Status: Succeeded / Failed (circle one)

Hostnames Discovered (A Records):

Hostname IP Address

SRV Records Found:

Service Target Host Port

TXT Records Found:

Record Name Value

Reverse Lookup Zones Referenced: _________

Flag Value: _________

docs.title: Step 5: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
The zone transfer gave you a complete view of the domain's DNS structure. Consider what the results tell you about the target environment:

  • How many hosts are registered in the forward zone?
  • Are there any hostnames that suggest high-value targets (database servers, web applications, file servers)?
  • Did the zone transfer reveal any reverse lookup zones? The presence of reverse zones means PTR (Pointer) records exist, which you will explore in Exercise WS-1.3.
  • What does a successful zone transfer tell you about the DNS server's security configuration?

A successful AXFR against a production DNS server is a significant finding. The administrator has failed to restrict zone transfers to authorized secondary DNS servers. In a real engagement, you would document the unrestricted zone transfer as a vulnerability in your report and recommend configuring transfer restrictions.

docs.title: Step 6: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The TXT record query in Step 4 returned the flag for this exercise. The flag is stored in the DNS TXT record at _zone-flag.corp.ocr-range.lab. Enter the flag value in the format OCR{...} on the submission page.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why are unrestricted zone transfers considered a security vulnerability?

Reveal Answer

An unrestricted zone transfer exposes every DNS record in the zone to any client that requests one. The attacker gains a complete map of hostnames, IP addresses, service locations, and metadata; information that would otherwise require many individual queries or brute-force enumeration to collect. Restricting AXFR to authorized secondary DNS server addresses prevents unauthenticated information disclosure.

2. What is the difference between a forward lookup zone and a reverse lookup zone?

Reveal Answer

A forward lookup zone maps hostnames to IP addresses using A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6). A reverse lookup zone maps IP addresses back to hostnames using PTR records. Both zone types can be stored in Active Directory Integrated DNS. Forward zones are organized by domain name (corp.ocr-range.lab), while reverse zones are organized by IP network in reverse notation (e.g., 250.100.10.in-addr.arpa for the 10.100.250.0/24 subnet).

3. If the zone transfer had failed, what alternative techniques could you use to enumerate DNS records?

Reveal Answer

When AXFR is blocked, you can enumerate DNS records through brute-force subdomain enumeration using wordlists (tools like dnsrecon, dnsenum, or fierce automate the process). You can also query for known AD SRV record patterns (_ldap._tcp, _kerberos._tcp, _gc._tcp) to discover DCs and services. Reverse DNS sweeps across known IP ranges (covered in Exercise WS-1.3) provide another path to hostname discovery without relying on zone transfers.

4. Why do Active Directory environments rely heavily on DNS SRV records?

Reveal Answer

Active Directory uses DNS SRV records to advertise the location of domain services to clients. When a workstation needs to find a Kerberos KDC, an LDAP server, or a Global Catalog server, the workstation queries DNS for the appropriate SRV record rather than relying on a hardcoded server list. SRV records enable automatic DC discovery, site-aware authentication, and failover when a DC goes offline.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Zone transfers (AXFR) dump the entire contents of a DNS zone in a single query. When unrestricted, AXFR gives an attacker a complete map of the domain's DNS namespace.
  • Active Directory Integrated DNS stores zone data within the AD database itself, and zone transfers follow the same permissioning model as standard DNS; if not locked down, anyone can request a copy.
  • TXT records in DNS can hold arbitrary strings. Penetration testers check TXT records because administrators and applications store metadata, verification tokens, and configuration data there.
  • SRV records reveal the service infrastructure of the domain: which hosts serve as Kerberos KDCs, LDAP servers, and Global Catalog servers.
  • The zone transfer may have revealed a reverse lookup zone for the network. Exercise WS-1.3 will use reverse DNS lookups to map IP addresses to hostnames across an entire subnet.

docs.title: Exercise WS-1.3: DNS Reverse Lookup Mapping
Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise WS-1.2 revealed the forward lookup zone contents through a zone transfer. The zone data referenced a reverse lookup zone for the 10.100.0.0/16 network. Exercise WS-1.3 uses reverse DNS queries to map IP addresses to hostnames across a specific subnet within that range.

Prerequisites:

  • Exercises WS-1.1 and WS-1.2 completed (you know dc01 hosts DNS and have seen the forward zone)
  • Active VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range
  • The dig command available on your Kali Linux attack box
  • Basic familiarity with shell scripting (for loops in Bash)

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your zone enumeration in Exercise WS-1.2 revealed that a reverse lookup zone exists for the 10.100.0.0/16 network. Your team lead asks you to scan the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope subnet; 10.100.250.0/24; for PTR (Pointer) records. Reverse lookups map IP addresses back to hostnames, and sweeping an entire subnet reveals which addresses are in use and what the associated hosts are named.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
1. Understand how PTR records work in reverse DNS zones
  2. Perform reverse lookups across the 10.100.250.0/24 subnet to discover active hosts
  3. Map discovered IP addresses to their hostnames
  4. Locate and retrieve the flag hidden in a reverse DNS entry

docs.title: Background: Reverse DNS and PTR Records
docs.text:
Forward DNS maps names to addresses: you ask "What is the IP for dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab?" and get back an A record with the IP address. Reverse DNS works in the opposite direction: you provide an IP address and ask "What hostname is associated with 10.100.250.10?" The answer comes back as a PTR record.

Reverse DNS zones are structured using the special in-addr.arpa domain. The octets of the IP address are reversed and appended to in-addr.arpa. For example, the reverse lookup for 10.100.250.10 queries the name 10.250.100.10.in-addr.arpa. Active Directory environments typically maintain reverse lookup zones so that PTR records are created automatically when hosts register their A records.

Penetration testers use reverse DNS sweeps when they know a network range but do not have a complete list of hostnames. Sweeping a /24 subnet (256 addresses) takes only a few seconds and reveals every host that has a PTR record. Hosts without PTR records will return an empty response, so the sweep also shows which IP addresses are unused or unregistered in DNS.

flowchart LR
    IP["IP Address<br/>10.100.250.10"]:::blue
    REV["Reverse Query<br/>10.250.100.10<br/>.in-addr.arpa"]:::amber
    PTR["PTR Record<br/>host.corp<br/>.ocr-range.lab"]:::green

    IP -->|"Reverse Octets"| REV
    REV -->|"DNS Lookup"| PTR

    classDef blue fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2a6ab9,color:#fff
    classDef amber fill:#e8a735,stroke:#c88715,color:#fff
    classDef green fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#4a8a44,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: dig for Reverse Lookups
docs.text:
The dig command supports reverse lookups with the -x flag. The -x flag automatically converts the IP address into the in-addr.arpa format and queries for a PTR record.

dig +short -x <ip-address> @<dns-server>
Flag Purpose +short Print only the answer (hostname), not the full DNS response -x Perform a reverse lookup (PTR query) for the given IP @<dns-server> The DNS server to query

When a PTR record exists, dig +short -x returns the hostname. When no PTR record exists, the command returns nothing (empty output). The +short flag is valuable when scripting because the output is a single line; the hostname; with no headers or extra sections.

Wrap reverse lookups in a sweep loop

To sweep a range of addresses, you can wrap the dig command in a Bash for loop:

for i in $(seq 1 254); do
    result=$(dig +short -x 10.100.250.$i @dc01)
    if [ -n "$result" ]; then
        echo "10.100.250.$i -> $result"
    fi
done

The loop iterates through addresses 10.100.250.1 to 10.100.250.254, performs a reverse lookup for each one, and prints only the addresses that have PTR records. The if [ -n "$result" ] test filters out empty responses so the output contains only live entries.

docs.title: Step 1: Test a Single Reverse Lookup
docs.text:
Test a single reverse lookup

Before sweeping the entire subnet, confirm that reverse DNS is working by querying a known address. The DC itself should have a PTR record.

dig +short -x 10.100.250.10 @dc01

Replace 10.100.250.10 with the IP address of dc01 if you recorded a different address in Exercise WS-1.1. A successful response returns the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of the host, such as dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab. (note the trailing dot, which is standard in DNS responses).

If the query returns nothing, verify that you are using the correct IP address and that your VPN connection is active.

docs.title: Step 2: Sweep the Subnet
docs.text:
Sweep the subnet for PTR records

Run the following loop to perform reverse lookups across the entire 10.100.250.0/24 subnet. The loop scans addresses 1 through 100 in the DHCP scope range.

for i in $(seq 1 100); do
    result=$(dig +short -x 10.100.250.$i @dc01)
    if [ -n "$result" ]; then
        echo "10.100.250.$i -> $result"
    fi
done

The sweep takes approximately 30-60 seconds depending on network latency. Each address with a PTR record will produce a line of output showing the IP-to-hostname mapping. Addresses without PTR records are silently skipped.

Watch the output as the loop runs. Record every IP-to-hostname mapping you see; the complete list gives you a network map of the subnet.

docs.title: Step 3: Review the Sweep Results
docs.text:
After the loop completes, review the list of discovered hosts. Look for patterns in the hostnames that suggest specific server roles or naming conventions. Note any hostnames that seem unusual or do not follow the standard naming pattern.

Look through your results for any entry whose hostname suggests it might be significant or related to a flag.

If you missed the entry during the live sweep, re-examine your sweep output carefully. You can also re-run the sweep and watch for hostnames that stand out from the standard naming pattern.

docs.title: Step 4: Query the Flag Hostname for a TXT Record
docs.text:
Query the flag hostname for a TXT record

The reverse lookup revealed a hostname that looks like a flag marker. Query that hostname for a TXT record to retrieve the actual flag value.

dig +short TXT flag-r3v3rs3.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The TXT record associated with the flag hostname contains the lab flag. The value appears in double quotes in the dig output.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the reverse DNS sweep results below. The IP-to-hostname map you build here will help you understand the lab network layout for the remaining exercises.

Reverse DNS Sweep; 10.100.250.0/24:

IP Address Hostname

Total PTR records found: _____

Flag hostname (from PTR at 10.100.250.53): _________

Flag TXT record value: _________

docs.title: Step 5: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
The reverse DNS sweep turned IP addresses into a readable network map. Consider the following as you review your findings:

  • How many hosts are active in the 10.100.250.0/24 subnet?
  • Do the hostnames follow a consistent naming convention?
  • Which hosts appear to be servers versus workstations based on their names?
  • Why might the flag have been placed at a PTR record pointing to IP address 10.100.250.53 specifically? (Port 53 is the well-known port for DNS.)

Reverse DNS sweeps are a reliable technique even when forward zone transfers are blocked. Administrators often forget to lock down reverse zones because the information disclosure risk is less obvious; but a complete IP-to-hostname map is valuable for an attacker planning lateral movement.

docs.title: Step 6: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The TXT record query in Step 4 returned the flag for this exercise. The flag was found by following the chain: reverse lookup of 10.100.250.53 yielded the hostname flag-r3v3rs3.corp.ocr-range.lab, and a TXT query against that hostname returned the flag. Enter the value in OCR{...} format on the submission page.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do penetration testers perform reverse DNS sweeps even when they already have forward zone data from a zone transfer?

Reveal Answer

Forward zone transfers and reverse DNS sweeps can reveal different sets of hosts. Some hosts may have A records without corresponding PTR records, and vice versa. Running both techniques provides a more complete picture. Reverse sweeps also confirm which IP addresses are actively registered in DNS, helping the tester identify live hosts in a specific subnet.

2. What does the in-addr.arpa domain do, and why are the IP octets reversed?

Reveal Answer

The in-addr.arpa domain is the DNS namespace designated for reverse lookups. The octets are reversed so that the DNS delegation hierarchy matches the IP address hierarchy. IP addresses are allocated from left to right (the leftmost octets identify the network), but DNS delegates from right to left (the rightmost labels are the top-level domain). Reversing the octets aligns the two hierarchies, allowing reverse DNS zones to be delegated along network boundaries.

3. How could an administrator prevent the reverse DNS sweep performed in this exercise?

Reveal Answer

The administrator could restrict reverse zone queries by configuring DNS access control lists (ACLs) to limit which clients can query the reverse zone, or by removing the reverse lookup zone entirely if reverse DNS is not needed. In Active Directory environments, limiting DNS query access is more complex because domain-joined machines rely on DNS for service discovery. A more practical mitigation is to monitor DNS query logs for sweep patterns; hundreds of sequential PTR queries from a single source in a short time period.

4. Why might some IP addresses in the subnet have no PTR record?

Reveal Answer

Hosts that are powered off, that use static IPs without DNS registration, or that were recently decommissioned may lack PTR records. DHCP-assigned addresses only have PTR records if the DHCP server or the client is configured to register reverse DNS entries. Devices outside the Windows domain (printers, network appliances, Linux hosts) may not register PTR records automatically.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• PTR records map IP addresses to hostnames and are stored in reverse lookup zones under the in-addr.arpa domain.
  • Reverse DNS sweeps across a subnet reveal which IP addresses are in use and what the associated hosts are named, even when forward zone transfers are blocked.
  • The dig -x flag automates the conversion of an IP address into in-addr.arpa format for reverse lookups.
  • Bash for loops combined with dig +short allow you to sweep an entire /24 subnet in under a minute from the command line.
  • The reconnaissance picture is growing: you now have open ports (Exercise WS-1.1), forward DNS records (Exercise WS-1.2), and reverse DNS mappings (Exercise WS-1.3). Exercise WS-1.4 will probe the SMB service on port 445 to extract domain information and discover file shares.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercises WS-1.1 through WS-1.3 focused on DNS-based reconnaissance. Exercise WS-1.4 shifts to a different protocol; SMB (Server Message Block) on port 445; which your port scan in Exercise WS-1.1 confirmed is open on dc01. SMB can reveal domain information and file shares without requiring credentials.

Prerequisites:

  • Exercises WS-1.1 through WS-1.3 completed (you have a network map and know dc01's services)
  • Active VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range
  • The smbclient command available on your Kali Linux attack box

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your port scan in Exercise WS-1.1 revealed that SMB (port 445) is open on dc01. SMB is the protocol Windows uses for file sharing, printer sharing, and inter-process communication. When queried without credentials (a "null session"), SMB can still reveal the domain name, the computer name, and sometimes a list of available file shares. Your task is to extract as much information as possible from the SMB service using anonymous access.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
1. Use SMB to identify the domain name and the DC hostname
  2. List all SMB shares available on dc01
  3. Access the Public share anonymously and examine its contents
  4. Retrieve the flag from a file on the Public share

docs.title: Background: SMB and Null Sessions
docs.text:
SMB is a network file-sharing protocol that runs on port 445 in modern Windows environments. Beyond file sharing, SMB is also the transport for named pipes used in Remote Procedure Calls (RPC), Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), and other administrative interfaces. On a Domain Controller, SMB hosts the SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares that distribute Group Policy Objects (GPOs) and logon scripts to domain-joined machines.

A null session occurs when a client connects to SMB without providing a username or password. Older versions of Windows allowed extensive enumeration through null sessions; listing users, groups, shares, and policies. Modern Windows Server versions (2016 and later) restrict null session access significantly, but share listing and access to explicitly shared folders may still be permitted depending on the server's configuration.

Even when null sessions are restricted, the SMB protocol's negotiation phase reveals the server's NetBIOS name (computer name) and domain name in cleartext. These values are part of the protocol handshake and cannot be hidden without disabling SMB entirely.

flowchart TB
    CLIENT["Attacker<br/>smbclient"]:::red
    SMB["SMB Service<br/>Port 445"]:::blue
    INFO["Protocol Info<br/>Domain + Hostname"]:::amber
    SHARES["Share List<br/>SYSVOL, NETLOGON,<br/>Public, etc."]:::green
    FILES["File Access<br/>flag.txt"]:::green

    CLIENT -->|"Null Session"| SMB
    SMB --> INFO
    SMB --> SHARES
    SHARES --> FILES

    classDef red fill:#d9534f,stroke:#b9342f,color:#fff
    classDef blue fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2a6ab9,color:#fff
    classDef amber fill:#e8a735,stroke:#c88715,color:#fff
    classDef green fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#4a8a44,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: smbclient
docs.text:
The smbclient tool is part of the Samba suite and provides an FTP-like interface for interacting with SMB shares. The tool supports listing shares, connecting to shares, browsing directories, and downloading files.

Listing shares on a server (null session):

smbclient -L <target> -N
Flag Purpose -L List available shares on the target -N Use a null session (no username or password)

Connecting to a specific share:

smbclient //<target>/<share> -N

Once connected, you have an interactive prompt similar to FTP. Common commands include:

Command Purpose ls List files and directories in the current location cd <dir> Change to a different directory get <file> Download a file to your local machine get <file> - Download a file and print its contents to the terminal exit Disconnect from the share

You can also pass commands directly on the command line using the -c flag, which avoids entering the interactive prompt:

smbclient //<target>/<share> -N -c 'ls'

The -c flag is useful for scripting and for performing quick lookups without entering the interactive session.

docs.title: Step 1: List Available Shares
docs.text:
List SMB shares with a null session

Run the following command to list all SMB shares on dc01 using a null session.

smbclient -L dc01 -N

The output contains two sections of information. The first section (the header) shows the protocol negotiation results, including the server's name and domain. The second section lists the available shares with their type (Disk, IPC, or Printer) and an optional comment.

Review the share list carefully. You should see standard DC shares like SYSVOL and NETLOGON, along with any custom shares the administrator has created. Look for a share named Public: shares with generic names like "Public" or "Shared" are often configured to allow anonymous access.

A typical share listing looks similar to the following:

    Sharename       Type      Comment
    ---------       ----      -------
    NETLOGON        Disk      Logon server share
    SYSVOL          Disk      Logon server share
    ...
(additional shares may be listed; check your own output)

docs.title: Step 2: Note the Domain and Server Information
docs.text:
Examine the output header from the smbclient -L command. The SMB negotiation phase reveals the following information:

  • Server name: The NetBIOS name of the host (e.g., DC01)
  • Domain name: The NetBIOS domain name (e.g., CORP)

These values appear in the protocol negotiation output even when the null session cannot enumerate additional information. Record both values; the domain name confirms the AD domain you identified through DNS in earlier labs.

docs.title: Step 3: Access the Public Share
docs.text:
Access the Public share and list its contents

Connect to the Public share using a null session and list its contents.

smbclient //dc01/Public -N -c 'ls'

The ls output shows files and directories on the share, along with their size and modification date. Look for any files that might contain useful information; text files, configuration files, scripts, or documents.

Examine the files listed on the share for anything that might contain the flag.

docs.title: Step 4: Retrieve the Flag File
docs.text:
Retrieve the flag file to the terminal

Download the contents of flag.txt directly to your terminal.

smbclient //dc01/Public -N -c 'get flag.txt -'

The get flag.txt - command downloads the file and prints its contents to standard output (the terminal) instead of saving the file to disk. The output contains the flag for this exercise.

Save the flag file to disk instead

If you prefer to save the file locally instead, you can omit the trailing dash:

smbclient //dc01/Public -N -c 'get flag.txt'

The file will be saved to your current working directory.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Document the SMB enumeration results below.

Server Name (NetBIOS): _________

Domain Name (NetBIOS): _________

SMB Shares Discovered:

Share Name Type Comment Anonymous Access?

Files Found on Public Share:

File Name Size

Flag Value (from flag.txt): _________

docs.title: Step 5: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review your SMB findings and consider the following:

  • The domain name obtained via SMB should match what you found through DNS in Exercises WS-1.1 and WS-1.2. Cross-referencing information from multiple protocols increases your confidence in the findings.
  • The SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares are standard on every Domain Controller. Authenticated users can access SYSVOL to read Group Policy settings, which can contain credentials, scripts, and configuration details. Anonymous access to SYSVOL is blocked by default, but the share's presence confirms the DC role.
  • A Public share with anonymous access is a misconfiguration. Any files placed on an anonymously accessible share are available to every user on the network, including attackers with no credentials.

docs.title: Step 6: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise was in flag.txt on the Public share. Enter the flag value in OCR{...} format on the submission page.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What is a null session, and why is anonymous SMB access a security concern?

Reveal Answer

A null session is an SMB connection established without providing a username or password. Anonymous SMB access is a security concern because the attacker can enumerate share names, access files on poorly configured shares, and extract the domain name and server name from the protocol negotiation. On older Windows versions, null sessions could also enumerate user accounts and group memberships. Even on modern systems, any data exposed through null sessions is available to unauthenticated attackers.

2. Why do the SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares exist on a Domain Controller, and what risks do they present?

Reveal Answer

SYSVOL stores Group Policy Objects (GPOs), logon scripts, and other domain configuration data that must be accessible to all authenticated domain members. NETLOGON hosts scripts that run during user logon. These shares present a risk because GPOs in SYSVOL can contain embedded credentials (such as passwords set through Group Policy Preferences, a well-known misconfiguration), and logon scripts may reference internal server paths, database connection strings, or service account names. Authenticated attackers routinely search SYSVOL for credential artifacts.

3. How does the information gained from SMB complement the DNS reconnaissance performed in Exercises WS-1.1 through WS-1.3?

Reveal Answer

DNS reveals hostnames, IP addresses, and service locations. SMB adds the NetBIOS domain name, the server's NetBIOS hostname, the list of shared folders, and access to any files on anonymously accessible shares. Together, the two protocols provide a complete view: DNS maps the network infrastructure, while SMB reveals the server's identity within the Windows domain and any data exposed through file shares.

4. An attacker finds the ADMIN$ and C$ shares listed but cannot connect to them with a null session. Why do those shares still appear in the listing?

Reveal Answer

ADMIN$ and C$ are default administrative shares that Windows creates automatically. The server includes them in the share listing because the listing operation and the access control check are separate actions. The server lists all shares that exist, but enforces access permissions when a client attempts to connect. Administrative shares require local administrator credentials, so null session connections are denied at the access control stage.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SMB protocol negotiation reveals the server's NetBIOS hostname and domain name automatically, even when null session enumeration is restricted.
  • Null sessions (smbclient -N) allow share listing and, when misconfigured, file access without any credentials.
  • SYSVOL and NETLOGON are standard DC shares that hold Group Policy and logon script data; high-value targets for authenticated attackers.
  • Anonymously accessible shares are a misconfiguration. Any data on these shares should be considered public to all network users.
  • The smbclient -c flag allows you to run commands without entering an interactive session, which is useful for quick lookups and scripting.
  • You have now confirmed the DC through port scanning (Exercise WS-1.1), mapped DNS forward and reverse records (Exercises WS-1.2 and WS-1.3), and extracted domain information via SMB (Exercise WS-1.4). Exercise WS-1.5 will query the final unauthenticated protocol: LDAP on port 389.

docs.title: Exercise WS-1.5: LDAP Anonymous Bind Reconnaissance
Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercises WS-1.1 through WS-1.4 established the DC's identity through port scanning, DNS enumeration, and SMB queries. Exercise WS-1.5 completes the unauthenticated reconnaissance phase by querying LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) on port 389; the protocol that provides direct access to the Active Directory database.

Prerequisites:

  • Exercises WS-1.1 through WS-1.4 completed
  • Active VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range
  • The ldapsearch command available on your Kali Linux attack box (part of the ldap-utils package)

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your reconnaissance has revealed that LDAP (port 389) is open on dc01. LDAP is the primary protocol for querying Active Directory. If anonymous binds are permitted, an attacker can extract the directory structure; including the base Distinguished Name (DN), naming contexts, and domain-level attributes; without providing any credentials. Your task is to determine whether anonymous LDAP access is allowed and to extract as much directory information as possible.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
1. Perform an anonymous LDAP bind against dc01
  2. Extract the Root DSE (Directory Server Agent-Specific Entry) to discover the base DN and naming contexts
  3. Query domain-level attributes for additional information
  4. Retrieve the flag from an LDAP attribute on the domain root object

docs.title: Background: LDAP and the Active Directory Database
docs.text:
Active Directory stores its data in a hierarchical database accessed primarily through LDAP. Every object in the directory; users, computers, groups, organizational units; has a Distinguished Name (DN) that specifies its location in the hierarchy. For example, a user named "jsmith" in the "Users" container of the corp.ocr-range.lab domain has the DN:

CN=jsmith,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab

The base of the hierarchy is the domain's root DN, which is derived from the domain name. For corp.ocr-range.lab, the root DN is DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab. Every LDAP query starts from a base DN and searches downward through the tree.

An anonymous bind connects to the LDAP server without authentication. By default, Windows Server 2003 and later restrict anonymous LDAP queries to the Root DSE (also called the rootDSE); a special entry at the top of the directory that describes the server's capabilities. The rootDSE contains the base DN, the naming contexts (the top-level partitions of the directory), the LDAP version supported, and other metadata.

When anonymous binds are configured more permissively (a misconfiguration), the attacker can query beyond the rootDSE and enumerate user accounts, group memberships, computer objects, and other directory data without credentials.

flowchart TB
    ANON["Anonymous Bind<br/>No Credentials"]:::red
    ROOTDSE["Root DSE<br/>Base DN, Naming<br/>Contexts, Metadata"]:::amber
    DOMAIN["Domain Root<br/>DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,<br/>DC=lab"]:::blue
    USERS["User Objects"]:::green
    COMPUTERS["Computer Objects"]:::green
    GROUPS["Group Objects"]:::green

    ANON -->|"Always Allowed"| ROOTDSE
    ANON -.->|"If Misconfigured"| DOMAIN
    DOMAIN --> USERS
    DOMAIN --> COMPUTERS
    DOMAIN --> GROUPS

    classDef red fill:#d9534f,stroke:#b9342f,color:#fff
    classDef amber fill:#e8a735,stroke:#c88715,color:#fff
    classDef blue fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2a6ab9,color:#fff
    classDef green fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#4a8a44,color:#fff

The solid arrow from the anonymous bind to the rootDSE shows the default permitted access. The dashed arrow to the domain root shows access that requires a misconfiguration.

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch
docs.text:
The ldapsearch command queries LDAP directories from the command line. The tool is part of the OpenLDAP utilities (ldap-utils package on Debian/Kali).

Basic syntax for an anonymous query:

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<target> -b "<base-dn>" -s <scope> "<filter>" [attributes]
Flag Purpose -x Use simple authentication (required for anonymous binds) -H ldap://<target> The LDAP server URI -b "<base-dn>" The base DN to start the search from -s <scope> Search scope: base (single object), one (immediate children), sub (entire subtree) "<filter>" LDAP search filter (e.g., "objectClass=*" matches everything) [attributes] Optional list of specific attributes to return

To query the rootDSE, use an empty base DN (-b "") with base scope (-s base):

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "" -s base "objectClass=*"

The rootDSE response includes several important attributes:

Attribute What It Reveals defaultNamingContext The domain's base DN (e.g., DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab) rootDomainNamingContext The forest root domain's base DN configurationNamingContext The configuration partition DN schemaNamingContext The schema partition DN namingContexts All naming contexts (partitions) in the directory dnsHostName The FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name) of the DC ldapServiceName The Kerberos service principal name

docs.title: Step 1: Query the Root DSE
docs.text:
Query the Root DSE with an anonymous bind

Run the following command to perform an anonymous bind and retrieve the rootDSE from dc01.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "" -s base "objectClass=*"

The output contains the server's metadata attributes. Look for defaultNamingContext, namingContexts, and dnsHostName in the response. The defaultNamingContext value is the base DN you will need for all subsequent LDAP queries in this exercise and in future labs.

A typical rootDSE response includes lines similar to the following:

defaultNamingContext: DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
configurationNamingContext: DC=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
dnsHostName: dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab
...
(additional attributes omitted; review your own output for the full list)

docs.title: Step 2: Request Only the Naming Contexts
docs.text:
Request only the naming contexts

You can request specific attributes to reduce the output. Run the following command to retrieve only the naming contexts.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "" -s base "objectClass=*" namingContexts

The output should list all five naming contexts. Each naming context represents a separate partition of the Active Directory database:

  • Domain partition (DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab); Contains users, groups, computers, and OUs (Organizational Units)
  • Configuration partition: Contains site topology, service connection points, and replication settings
  • Schema partition: Defines the classes and attributes available in the directory
  • DomainDnsZones: Holds DNS zone data for the domain
  • ForestDnsZones: Holds DNS zone data replicated across the entire forest

docs.title: Step 3: Query the Domain Root Object
docs.text:
Query the domain root object

Use the base DN from Step 1 to query the domain root object. The domain root is the top-level object in the domain partition and contains domain-wide attributes.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s base "objectClass=*"

The output shows all attributes of the domain root object. Look for attributes like distinguishedName, objectClass, whenCreated, and any custom attributes that may have been set by the administrator.

docs.title: Step 4: Query for the adminDescription Attribute
docs.text:
Query the adminDescription attribute

The adminDescription attribute on the domain root object is a free-text field that administrators sometimes use for documentation. Query the attribute specifically.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s base "objectClass=*" adminDescription

The output should include the adminDescription attribute with its value. The flag for this exercise is stored in the adminDescription attribute of the domain root object.

docs.title: Step 5: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
The LDAP queries you performed reveal the internal structure of the Active Directory database. Consider the following as you review your findings:

  • The defaultNamingContext is the starting point for all directory queries. Every search for users, groups, or computers in the domain begins at the base DN: DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab.
  • The five naming contexts represent the partitions of the AD database. Each partition replicates independently, and some partitions (Configuration, Schema) replicate across the entire forest, not a single domain.
  • The dnsHostName attribute confirms the FQDN of the DC, matching the information you obtained from DNS in earlier labs. Cross-referencing data from multiple protocols strengthens your confidence in the findings.
  • The fact that the adminDescription attribute was readable through an anonymous bind is a misconfiguration. In a hardened environment, anonymous binds should be limited to the rootDSE only.

docs.title: Step 6: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The adminDescription attribute query in Step 4 returned the flag for this exercise. Enter the value in OCR{...} format on the submission page.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What is the Root DSE, and why is it always accessible through an anonymous bind?

Reveal Answer

The Root DSE (rootDSE) is a special LDAP entry with an empty DN that describes the capabilities and configuration of the LDAP server. Microsoft's implementation of LDAP in Active Directory exposes the rootDSE to anonymous clients by design because client applications need the information to construct proper LDAP queries; specifically the base DN and supported LDAP versions. Without rootDSE access, a client would need to know the base DN in advance, which limits interoperability.

2. What is the difference between the defaultNamingContext and the configurationNamingContext?

Reveal Answer

The defaultNamingContext points to the domain partition, which contains the domain's user accounts, computer accounts, groups, organizational units, and Group Policy Objects. The configurationNamingContext points to the configuration partition, which contains forest-wide settings: site definitions, subnet-to-site mappings, replication topology, and service connection points. The domain partition is unique to each domain, while the configuration partition is replicated across every DC in the forest.

3. How could a defender detect anonymous LDAP enumeration?

Reveal Answer

Defenders can enable LDAP diagnostic logging on the Domain Controller (Event IDs 2889 and 2887 in the Directory Services event log track unsigned and unencrypted LDAP binds, including anonymous ones). Network monitoring tools can flag LDAP traffic from non-domain-joined IP addresses. Configuring the DC to require LDAP signing (LDAPServerIntegrity = 2) forces clients to authenticate, although the rootDSE remains accessible. Disabling anonymous LDAP access beyond the rootDSE is the most direct mitigation.

4. Why is the base DN (DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab) derived from the domain's DNS name?

Reveal Answer

Active Directory tightly integrates with DNS. When a new AD domain is created, the installer converts the DNS domain name into LDAP naming components by splitting the name at each dot and prefixing each component with DC=. The domain corp.ocr-range.lab becomes DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab. The consistent naming convention means an attacker who knows the DNS domain name can immediately construct the LDAP base DN without querying the rootDSE first.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Anonymous LDAP binds are permitted against the rootDSE by default on all Active Directory Domain Controllers. The rootDSE reveals the base DN, naming contexts, and server capabilities.
  • The base DN (DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab) is the starting point for all LDAP queries against the domain partition. Knowing the base DN is a prerequisite for user and group enumeration in later exercises.
  • Five naming contexts exist in a standard AD forest: domain, configuration, schema, DomainDnsZones, and ForestDnsZones. Each partition serves a different purpose and replicates independently.
  • Misconfigured anonymous access can expose domain-level attributes (like adminDescription) that should require authentication. Defenders should restrict anonymous LDAP queries to the rootDSE.
  • ldapsearch is the standard command-line tool for LDAP queries. The -x flag enables simple (anonymous) authentication, -b sets the search base, and -s base restricts the query to a single object.
  • Exercise WS-1.5 completes the unauthenticated reconnaissance phase. You have surveyed the DC from five angles: port scanning, forward DNS, reverse DNS, SMB, and LDAP. Chapter WS02 will build on this foundation with authenticated enumeration techniques.

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Over five labs, you performed a complete unauthenticated reconnaissance sweep against a Windows Server 2022 Domain Controller. Starting with nothing but a hostname (dc01), you built a detailed picture of the target: its open ports, DNS records, reverse DNS mappings, SMB shares, and LDAP directory structure. Every technique in this chapter works without credentials; the information was obtained purely through protocol-level queries that the DC responded to by design or by misconfiguration.

The central lesson of this chapter is that Active Directory Domain Controllers are information-rich targets. Each protocol exposed by a DC reveals a different slice of the domain, and layering those slices together produces a complete map that feeds directly into the next phase of an engagement.

docs.text:
The following table summarizes every command used across the five labs in this chapter. Keep the table as a quick reference for future engagements.

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text:
Chapter WS01 covered unauthenticated reconnaissance; what you can learn about an AD environment with no credentials at all. The findings from this chapter provide the foundation for everything that follows.

Chapter WS02 will introduce authenticated enumeration. With a set of valid domain credentials (obtained through password spraying, credential harvesting, or provided as part of the engagement scope), you can query LDAP for user accounts, group memberships, and computer objects. The base DN you extracted in Exercise WS-1.5 (DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab) will be the starting point for those queries. The domain name confirmed through DNS and SMB will be required when constructing authenticated LDAP binds and Kerberos authentication requests.

The progression from unauthenticated to authenticated reconnaissance mirrors the real-world attack lifecycle: gather what you can without credentials, use that information to target credential acquisition, then use credentials to enumerate the environment in depth.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. Which combination of open ports distinguishes a Domain Controller from a regular Windows member server?

Ports 88 (Kerberos), 389 (LDAP), 636 (LDAPS), and 3268 (Global Catalog) are unique to Domain Controllers. Member servers do not run the Kerberos KDC or Global Catalog services. DNS (53) and SMB (445) can appear on member servers, but the full combination with Kerberos and Global Catalog is exclusive to DCs.

2. What does the AXFR query type request from a DNS server?

AXFR requests a full zone transfer; a complete copy of every DNS record in the specified zone. The mechanism exists so secondary DNS servers can replicate zone data from a primary server, but unrestricted AXFR allows any client to download the entire zone.

3. What is the in-addr.arpa domain used for, and why are the IP address octets reversed?

The in-addr.arpa domain is the DNS namespace for reverse lookups (IP-to-hostname mappings via PTR records). The octets are reversed so that the DNS delegation hierarchy (which reads right to left) aligns with the IP address hierarchy (which allocates from left to right), enabling reverse zones to be delegated along network boundaries.

4. What two pieces of information does the SMB protocol negotiation reveal even when a null session has limited permissions?

The server's NetBIOS hostname and the NetBIOS domain name. These values are part of the SMB protocol handshake and are transmitted before access control decisions are made.

5. What is the Root DSE in LDAP, and what is the most important attribute it contains for an attacker?

The Root DSE (rootDSE) is a special LDAP entry with an empty DN that describes the LDAP server's capabilities. The most important attribute for an attacker is defaultNamingContext, which provides the base DN needed to construct queries against the domain partition.

6. What is the base DN for the corp.ocr-range.lab domain, and how is it derived from the DNS name?

The base DN is DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab. Active Directory derives the base DN by splitting the DNS domain name at each dot and prefixing each component with DC=.

7. Name two mitigations that would prevent the techniques used in Exercises WS-1.2 (zone transfer) and WS-1.5 (anonymous LDAP beyond rootDSE).

For zone transfers: configure the DNS server to restrict AXFR to authorized secondary DNS server IP addresses only. For anonymous LDAP: configure the Domain Controller to limit anonymous LDAP access to the rootDSE (the default on Windows Server 2003 and later, but verify the dsHeuristics attribute and the "Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares" policy).

8. Why do penetration testers cross-reference findings from multiple protocols (DNS, SMB, LDAP) rather than relying on a single source?

Different protocols reveal different information, and some protocols may be restricted while others remain open. Cross-referencing confirms findings (the domain name from DNS, SMB, and LDAP should match) and fills gaps (DNS provides hostnames and IPs, SMB reveals share data, LDAP exposes directory structure). Relying on a single protocol risks missing information that another protocol would have disclosed.

docs.title: Why Directory Enumeration Matters
docs.text:
Active Directory (AD) is the backbone of most enterprise Windows networks. Every user account, computer, group, and organizational boundary lives inside the AD directory, and the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is the primary protocol applications and administrators use to query that directory. When an attacker gains even limited read access to LDAP, the directory becomes an open book; revealing the organization's structure, its privileged accounts, and the policies that govern credential security.

In Chapter WS01 you confirmed that anonymous LDAP binds are allowed against the domain controller. That single finding unlocked the door to a wealth of reconnaissance data. Chapter WS02 walks through that door systematically, querying LDAP to extract Organizational Units (OUs), user accounts, group memberships, computer objects, and password policies. Each query builds on the last, steadily assembling a picture of the target domain that will inform every later attack path.

Understanding directory enumeration also matters on the defensive side. Blue-team analysts who know exactly what LDAP exposes can audit permissions, restrict anonymous access, and monitor for the telltale query patterns that signal reconnaissance in progress. Whether you sit on offense or defense, mastering LDAP enumeration is a foundational skill for Windows-domain security work.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
The five exercises in Chapter WS02 follow a deliberate progression: start with the containers that organize the directory (OUs), then enumerate the objects inside those containers (users, groups, computers), and finish by extracting the domain-wide password policy that governs credential strength. Each exercise introduces new LDAP search filters and attributes while reinforcing the core ldapsearch workflow you will use throughout the Windows Server track.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

  • Query LDAP for every Organizational Unit and interpret OU attributes such as description
  • Enumerate all domain user accounts and distinguish regular users from service and administrative accounts
  • Map security-group memberships to identify users with elevated privileges
  • Discover every domain-joined computer and extract operating-system metadata
  • Retrieve the domain password policy, including minimum length, complexity, and lockout thresholds
  • Combine the results of multiple LDAP queries to build a coherent map of the target domain

docs.title: Understanding LDAP and Active Directory Structure
docs.text:
LDAP is a client-server protocol designed for reading and writing directory data. In an AD environment the domain controller hosts the LDAP service (TCP port 389 for plaintext, 636 for LDAPS). Clients send search requests that specify a base DN (the starting point in the directory tree), a scope (how deep to search), a filter (which objects to match), and a list of attributes to return.

Active Directory organizes objects in a hierarchical tree rooted at the domain's Distinguished Name (DN). For the lab domain corp.ocr-range.lab, the root DN is DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab. Below the root sit Organizational Units: container objects that group related accounts and computers much like folders group files. Inside OUs you find leaf objects: users, groups, computers, and other directory entries. Every object has a set of attributes; key-value pairs such as sAMAccountName, description, memberOf, and operatingSystem: that store the object's metadata.

A critical concept is the objectClass attribute. Every directory object carries one or more object classes that define which attributes the object may (or must) have. Filtering on objectClass is the primary way to select a specific type of object. For example, (objectClass=organizationalUnit) returns only OUs, while (objectClass=user) returns user accounts. Mastering these filters lets you slice the directory precisely and extract only the data you need.

docs.title: How LDAP Search Scopes Work
docs.text:
Every LDAP search operates within a defined scope that controls how far below the base DN the server looks for matching objects. Three scope levels exist, and choosing the right one determines whether your query returns a single object, a shallow list, or a deep recursive result.

flowchart TD
    R["DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab"]:::blue
    R --> O1["OU=IT"]:::green
    R --> O2["OU=HR"]:::green
    R --> O3["OU=Finance"]:::green
    O1 --> U1["CN=jsmith"]:::gray
    O1 --> U2["CN=svc_backup"]:::gray
    O2 --> U3["CN=agarcia"]:::gray

    classDef blue fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    classDef green fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    classDef gray fill:#888,stroke:#333,color:#fff

The subtree scope (the default when no -s flag is specified) searches the base DN and every object beneath it at any depth. The one-level scope (-s one) returns only the immediate children of the base DN, ignoring grandchildren and deeper objects. The base scope (-s base) returns only the single object at the base DN itself, which is how Exercise WS-2.5 extracts password policy attributes stored directly on the domain object. Understanding these scopes lets you control query breadth; broad searches for discovery, narrow searches for targeted extraction.

docs.title: Key Terminology Reference
docs.text:
The following terms appear throughout the chapter. Refer back to this list whenever you encounter an unfamiliar abbreviation or concept.

Term Definition LDAP Lightweight Directory Access Protocol; the protocol used to query and modify directory data AD Active Directory; Microsoft's directory service for Windows domain networks DN Distinguished Name; the full path to an object in the directory tree RDN Relative Distinguished Name; the leftmost component of a DN, identifying the object within its parent container OU Organizational Unit; a container object used to group and organize directory objects objectClass An attribute that defines the type of a directory object and which attributes it may carry Base DN The starting point in the directory tree for an LDAP search Scope The depth of an LDAP search: base (single object), one-level (immediate children), or subtree (all descendants) Anonymous bind An LDAP connection that provides no credentials, relying on the server to permit unauthenticated reads sAMAccountName The pre-Windows 2000 logon name; the short username used for authentication
