docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following items before beginning Exercise 2.1.

  • VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range is active
  • Kali Linux attack machine has network connectivity to the lab environment
  • You can ping dc01 (the domain controller at corp.ocr-range.lab)
  • The ldapsearch command is available on your Kali system (installed via the ldap-utils package)
  • Chapter WS01 is complete; you have confirmed that anonymous LDAP binds succeed against dc01
  • You have a note-taking document or terminal logging enabled to capture command output

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Chapter WS01 confirmed that the domain controller dc01 accepts anonymous LDAP binds on port 389. Exercise WS-2.1 puts that access to work by querying for the directory containers that organize every other object in the domain. You should have ldapsearch installed on your Kali machine and a working VPN connection to the lab environment.

Prerequisites

  • Chapter WS01 completed (anonymous LDAP access confirmed)
  • VPN active and dc01 reachable
  • ldapsearch available (ldap-utils package)

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: With anonymous LDAP access confirmed, your next task is to map the organization's Organizational Unit (OU) structure. OUs often mirror an organization's departmental layout; Human Resources, Finance, IT, and so on. Enumerating OUs early in reconnaissance reveals how the directory is partitioned, which guides where to look for high-value accounts and sensitive resources in later queries.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate all OUs in the domain using an LDAP search filter
  • Understand the hierarchical directory structure by reading OU Distinguished Names (DNs)
  • Examine OU attributes; especially description: for hidden or overlooked information
  • Locate a hidden OU whose description attribute contains the lab flag

docs.title: Background: Organizational Units in Active Directory
docs.text:
An Organizational Unit is a container object inside Active Directory that groups related objects such as users, computers, and groups. Administrators create OUs to reflect organizational structure, delegate administrative control, and apply Group Policy Objects (GPOs) to specific subsets of the directory. A company with offices in multiple cities might create OUs named OU=NewYork, OU=London, and OU=Tokyo, each containing the user and computer accounts for that location.

Every OU has a Distinguished Name that encodes its position in the directory tree. The DN OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab tells you the OU named "IT" sits directly under the domain root. Nested OUs work the same way: OU=Servers,OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab describes a "Servers" OU inside the "IT" OU. Reading DNs from right to left reveals the path from the root down to the object.

OUs also carry optional attributes. The description attribute is a free-text field that administrators sometimes use for internal notes; and occasionally for information they assume no one outside the admin team will ever read. During enumeration, always request the description attribute because careless notes, temporary passwords, or references to sensitive systems sometimes appear there.

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch
docs.text:
The ldapsearch command-line tool sends LDAP search requests and prints the results to standard output. Below is the anatomy of the command you will run in this exercise.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" dn description

Each flag and argument serves a specific purpose.

Component Meaning -x Use simple authentication (anonymous bind; no credentials) -H ldap://dc01 Connect to the LDAP server at hostname dc01 on port 389 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" Set the search base to the domain root "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" Filter: return only objects whose class is organizationalUnit dn description Request only the DN and description attributes

When ldapsearch returns results, each matching object is printed as a block of attribute-value pairs separated by a blank line. A typical entry looks like the following.

# IT, corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
description: Information Technology department

The first line (starting with #) is a comment showing the object's Relative Distinguished Name (RDN) and domain. The dn: line gives the full path. Any requested attributes that have values follow on subsequent lines. If an attribute has no value set, the line is omitted entirely.

docs.title: Step 1: Verify LDAP Connectivity
docs.text:
Verify anonymous LDAP connectivity

Before running a targeted query, confirm that ldapsearch can reach dc01 and that anonymous access still works. Run a minimal query that returns the root DSE (Directory Service Agent-Specific Entry), which every LDAP server exposes without authentication.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "" -s base "(objectClass=*)" namingContexts

The output should include a namingContexts attribute listing the directory partitions. Look for DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab in the results. If the command times out or returns an error, verify your VPN connection and confirm that port 389 is open on dc01.

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate All Organizational Units
docs.text:
Enumerate all Organizational Units

Run the primary OU enumeration command. The filter (objectClass=organizationalUnit) matches every OU in the directory, and requesting dn and description keeps the output concise.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" dn description

Scroll through the output and note every OU that appears. Pay attention to the DN of each entry; the OU names and their nesting reveal the directory's organizational layout. Some OUs sit directly under the domain root while others are nested inside parent OUs.

docs.title: Step 3: Count the Results
docs.text:
The final line of ldapsearch output reports how many entries matched the filter. Look for a line like the following.

# numEntries: X

Record the total count. Knowing how many OUs exist helps you confirm that you have captured the full list and gives you a baseline for comparison if you run the query again later.

docs.title: Step 4: Map the OU Hierarchy
docs.text:
Using the DN values from Step 2, sketch the OU hierarchy on paper or in a text file. Start with the domain root at the top and draw each OU as a branch. Nested OUs should appear as children of their parent OU. The hierarchy will resemble a directory tree.

DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
├── OU=IT
├── OU=HR
├── OU=Finance
├── OU=...
│   └── OU=NestedExample
└── OU=...

Replace the placeholder names with the actual OUs you discovered. The goal is a visual map you can reference throughout the rest of this chapter.

docs.title: Step 5: Inspect OU Descriptions
docs.text:
Review each OU entry in the output and look for the description attribute. Some OUs will have a description value; others will not (the line will be absent). Read every description carefully. Administrators sometimes leave internal notes, temporary references, or metadata in description fields that they expect only fellow admins to see.

Page OU descriptions through less

If the output from Step 2 scrolled past your terminal buffer, re-run the command and pipe it through less for easier navigation.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" dn description | less

Use the / key inside less to search for specific strings. Try searching for "hidden", "secret", "flag", or "OCR" to locate noteworthy descriptions quickly.

docs.title: Step 6: Look for Unusual or Hidden OUs
docs.text:
Not every OU will have an obvious departmental name. Some organizations create OUs for staging, testing, decommissioned accounts, or security-sensitive purposes and give them nondescript or misleading names. Compare your OU list against what you would expect from a typical corporate directory. Any OU whose name does not match a standard department warrants closer inspection.

When you find an OU with an unexpected name, examine its description attribute carefully. The flag for this exercise is stored in the description attribute of a hidden OU.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Total OUs discovered: __

OU hierarchy (paste your tree sketch):

OUs with description values:

OU Name Description

Hidden or unusual OUs identified: __

docs.title: Step 7: Interpret the Results
docs.text: Review the hierarchy you mapped and the descriptions you collected. Consider what the OU structure tells you about the organization. Departments like IT and Finance suggest where to look for privileged accounts and sensitive data in later exercises. Nested OUs may indicate sub-teams or role-based separation. Hidden or unusually named OUs may contain objects the administrators wanted to keep out of casual view.

docs.title: Step 8: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
One of the OUs you discovered has a description attribute containing the flag. The flag follows the format OCR{...} and is located on a hidden OU; one whose name does not correspond to a standard corporate department. Copy the flag exactly as it appears in the LDAP output and submit it.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do administrators create Organizational Units rather than placing all objects directly under the domain root?

Reveal Answer

OUs allow administrators to delegate control over subsets of the directory, apply Group Policy Objects to specific groups of objects, and maintain a logical structure that mirrors the organization. Placing all objects at the root would make delegation and policy targeting far more difficult.

2. An OU's description field contained sensitive information in this exercise. What defensive step would prevent that exposure?

Reveal Answer

Disabling anonymous LDAP binds would prevent unauthenticated users from reading any directory attributes. Administrators should also audit description fields across all OUs and objects to remove sensitive notes, and apply access-control entries that restrict read access to the description attribute where needed.

3. How does the -b (search base) flag affect the scope of your query, and when might you change it?

Reveal Answer

The -b flag sets the starting point in the directory tree. Searching from the domain root returns objects across the entire domain. Narrowing the base to a specific OU; for example, -b "OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab": limits results to that OU and its children, which is useful when you want to focus on a particular department.

4. What LDAP scope option would you use if you only wanted OUs directly under the domain root, not nested OUs?

Reveal Answer

The -s one (one-level) scope restricts results to objects that are immediate children of the search base. Combined with the domain root as the base, the query ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s one "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" dn returns only top-level OUs.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Organizational Units are the directory's structural framework; enumerating them first gives you a roadmap for every subsequent query.
  • The description attribute on any object type can contain notes, references, or data that administrators did not intend to be publicly visible.
  • Anonymous LDAP access exposes the entire directory tree unless the administrator has explicitly restricted it, making OU enumeration trivial when it is allowed.
  • Reading Distinguished Names from right to left reveals the hierarchical path from the domain root down to the object.
  • With the OU map in hand, Exercise WS-2.2 will enumerate the user accounts that live inside these containers, expanding your understanding of the domain's population.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise WS-2.1 mapped the Organizational Unit structure of the corp.ocr-range.lab domain, revealing which departments and divisions exist in the directory. Exercise WS-2.2 builds on that map by enumerating the user accounts that populate those OUs. You will need the same ldapsearch setup; a Kali Linux machine with VPN access and anonymous LDAP connectivity to dc01.

Prerequisites

  • Exercise WS-2.1 completed (OU structure mapped)
  • VPN active and dc01 reachable
  • ldapsearch available (ldap-utils package)
  • Your OU hierarchy notes from Exercise WS-2.1

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: With the OU structure mapped, your next objective is to enumerate user accounts across the domain. Active Directory (AD) stores detailed information about every user; display names, descriptions, group memberships, and freeform info fields. Enumerating these accounts reveals who works in which department, which accounts have administrative roles, and whether any accounts carry sensitive notes that administrators left in public-facing attributes.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• List all user accounts in the domain using an LDAP search filter
  • Identify key attributes for each account: sAMAccountName, displayName, description, info, and memberOf
  • Distinguish between regular user accounts, service accounts, and administrative accounts based on naming conventions and group membership
  • Locate the lab flag hidden in a user's info attribute field

docs.title: Background: User Objects in Active Directory
docs.text:
Every person, service, or application that authenticates to an AD domain has a user object stored in the directory. User objects belong to the user objectClass and carry dozens of attributes that describe the account. Some attributes; like sAMAccountName (the pre-Windows 2000 logon name) and userPrincipalName: are required for authentication. Others; like displayName, description, title, and info: are optional metadata fields that administrators and HR provisioning systems populate during account creation.

From a reconnaissance perspective, user objects are among the most valuable targets in the directory. The sAMAccountName gives you a valid logon name you can test against authentication services. The memberOf attribute lists every group the user belongs to, immediately flagging accounts with elevated privileges. The description and info fields are freeform text that administrators sometimes use to store temporary passwords, account purpose notes, or system references that were never meant for external eyes.

Service accounts deserve special attention during enumeration. Organizations often create dedicated user objects for applications and automated tasks; names like svc_backup, sql_service, or app_monitor are common patterns. Service accounts frequently hold elevated privileges and may have weaker password policies or passwords that rarely change, making them prime targets in later attack phases.

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch for User Enumeration
docs.text:
The command below queries every user object in the domain and returns the five most informative attributes for reconnaissance.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName displayName description info memberOf

The filter (objectClass=user) matches all user objects. Note that in AD, computer accounts also inherit from the user class, but they are more specifically classified under computer. The query may return a small number of built-in system accounts (like krbtgt) alongside the regular user accounts.

A typical user entry in the output looks like the following.

# jsmith, Users, corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: CN=John Smith,OU=HR,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
sAMAccountName: jsmith
displayName: John Smith
description: HR department analyst
memberOf: CN=HR-Staff,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab

Attributes that have no value; for example, an empty info field; are omitted from the output. When you spot an attribute that most users lack but one user has, pay close attention to its contents.

Attribute What It Reveals sAMAccountName Logon username; usable for authentication attempts displayName Full name; helps identify the person behind the account description Admin-written notes; may contain passwords or sensitive info info Freeform text field; rarely audited, sometimes misused for notes memberOf Group memberships; reveals privilege level at a glance

docs.title: Step 1: Run the User Enumeration Query
docs.text:
Enumerate all domain user accounts

Execute the full user enumeration command against dc01. The output will contain one block per user object, separated by blank lines.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName displayName description info memberOf

The result set may be large. Pipe the output to a file so you can search and sort it without losing data to terminal scrollback limits.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName displayName description info memberOf > /tmp/users.ldif

docs.title: Step 2: Count the User Accounts
docs.text:
Count the user accounts

Check the summary line at the end of the output to see how many user entries the query returned. You can also count entries in the saved file.

grep -c "^dn:" /tmp/users.ldif

Record the total number of user accounts. Compare this number against what you would expect for an organization with the OU structure you mapped in Exercise WS-2.1.

docs.title: Step 3: Identify Account Types
docs.text:
Review the saved output and categorize each account into one of three types based on naming conventions and attributes.

Regular user accounts typically have names that follow a firstname.lastname or flastname pattern, carry a displayName matching a person's real name, and belong to departmental groups.

Service accounts often start with a prefix like svc_, svc-, app_, or sql_. Their description fields usually state the service or application they support. Service accounts may belong to privileged groups that grant access to specific resources.

Administrative accounts may follow patterns like admin_jsmith or belong to groups such as Domain Admins, Administrators, or custom admin groups. The memberOf attribute is the fastest way to spot these.

Create a table in your notes with columns for username, account type, and notable attributes.

docs.title: Step 4: Examine the memberOf Attribute
docs.text:
The memberOf attribute lists the Distinguished Names of every group the user belongs to. Scan the output for users who are members of high-privilege groups. Look for group names containing keywords like "Admin", "Domain Admins", "Enterprise Admins", "Administrators", or custom elevated groups discovered during OU enumeration.

Find users in administrative groups

The next filter pulls every user whose memberOf value references an Admin group.

grep -B5 "memberOf.*Admin" /tmp/users.ldif

The -B5 flag shows the five lines before each match, which should include the user's sAMAccountName and displayName. Record every user that appears in an administrative group.

docs.title: Step 5: Search the description and info Fields
docs.text:
Search description and info fields

The description and info attributes are freeform text fields that warrant careful inspection. Search the saved output for any description or info lines that contain interesting data.

grep -i "^description:\|^info:" /tmp/users.ldif

Most entries will have brief, routine descriptions. Focus on entries that stand out; passwords, flags, internal references, or anything that looks like it was not intended for public consumption. The flag for this exercise is stored in the info attribute of a user account in the IT department.

docs.title: Step 6: Narrow the Search to IT Department Users
docs.text:
Narrow the search to IT department users

Using the OU structure from Exercise WS-2.1, you know which OU holds IT department accounts. Run a targeted query with a narrower search base to isolate IT users and their info fields.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName displayName info

Review the output for any user whose info attribute contains the flag. The info field is rarely populated, so any entry that has a value is worth examining.

docs.title: Step 7: Extract a Complete User List
docs.text:
Extract a complete username list

For reference in later exercises, generate a clean list of all sAMAccountName values in the domain. The following command extracts usernames and sorts them alphabetically.

grep "^sAMAccountName:" /tmp/users.ldif | awk '{print $2}' | sort

Save the sorted list to a file for future use.

grep "^sAMAccountName:" /tmp/users.ldif | awk '{print $2}' | sort > /tmp/usernames.txt

The username list will be valuable for credential-testing and password-spraying exercises in later chapters.

docs.text:

Account classification:

sAMAccountName Type (Regular/Service/Admin) Notable Attributes

Users in administrative groups:

Username Group Membership

Interesting description or info field values:

Username Field Value

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review your account classification table and group membership findings. Consider what the user inventory reveals about the organization. A large number of users in administrative groups may indicate poor privilege separation. Service accounts with broad group memberships may represent overly permissive configurations. Users with notes in description or info fields highlight a pattern of storing sensitive data in publicly readable attributes.

Cross-reference the user locations (the OU portion of each DN) with the OU hierarchy from Exercise WS-2.1. Confirm that users appear in the OUs you would expect based on their department and role.

docs.title: Step 9: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is stored in the info attribute of a user account located in the IT department OU. If you followed Steps 5 and 6, you should have already identified the entry. The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Copy it exactly as it appears in the LDAP output.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is the info attribute particularly risky from a security standpoint?

Reveal Answer

The info attribute is a freeform text field with no enforced structure or validation. Administrators and help-desk staff sometimes use it to store temporary notes, including passwords or sensitive references. Because the field is rarely audited and is readable by anyone with LDAP access, sensitive data stored there can persist indefinitely without detection.

2. What distinguishes a service account from a regular user account in Active Directory, and why do attackers target service accounts?

Reveal Answer

Service accounts are user objects created to run applications or automated tasks rather than to represent a person. They are often identifiable by naming conventions (prefixes like svc_) and by their group memberships. Attackers target service accounts because they frequently hold elevated privileges, may have passwords that rarely rotate, and are less likely to trigger suspicious-logon alerts than interactive user accounts.

3. How could an administrator reduce the information exposed by anonymous LDAP user enumeration?

Reveal Answer

The most effective measure is to disable anonymous LDAP binds entirely, requiring authentication before any query can return results. Administrators can also apply granular access-control entries to sensitive attributes (like description and info) so that only authorized principals can read them. Removing unnecessary data from user attributes during provisioning further limits exposure.

4. You saved the user list to /tmp/usernames.txt. How might an attacker use that list in a later phase?

Reveal Answer

A list of valid usernames enables password-spraying attacks, where the attacker tries a small number of common passwords against every account. Valid usernames also support Kerberos-based attacks like AS-REP roasting (targeting accounts that do not require pre-authentication). Having confirmed usernames eliminates guesswork and reduces the number of failed authentication attempts, helping the attacker stay below lockout thresholds.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• User objects are the richest source of reconnaissance data in Active Directory; every account carries a logon name, group memberships, and optional freeform fields.
  • The sAMAccountName attribute provides valid logon names that can be used in authentication attacks during later phases.
  • Freeform attributes like description and info are frequently overlooked during security audits but are fully readable through LDAP, making them a common hiding place for sensitive data.
  • Categorizing accounts into regular, service, and administrative types helps prioritize targets and understand the organization's privilege model.
  • With users enumerated, Exercise WS-2.3 will map group memberships in detail to build a complete picture of who has access to what.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise WS-2.2 enumerated user accounts across the domain, revealing logon names, freeform attributes, and preliminary group memberships through the memberOf attribute on each user object. Exercise WS-2.3 approaches group membership from the opposite direction; querying group objects directly to extract their member lists. You will need the same Kali Linux machine with anonymous Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) access to dc01.

Prerequisites

  • Exercise WS-2.2 completed (user accounts enumerated)
  • VPN active and dc01 reachable
  • ldapsearch available (ldap-utils package)
  • Your user account list from Exercise WS-2.2

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: User enumeration in Exercise WS-2.2 revealed interesting accounts, including some that appeared in administrative groups. Exercise WS-2.3 takes the next logical step: map every security group and its members to understand who holds elevated access. In Active Directory (AD), permissions are primarily assigned through group membership rather than directly to individual users, so a complete group map is the key to understanding the domain's access model.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Enumerate all security groups in the domain using an LDAP search filter
  • Map group memberships by reading the member attribute on each group object
  • Identify the Domain Admins group and other high-privilege groups
  • Locate the lab flag hidden in the description attribute of a specific group

docs.title: Background: Security Groups and Privilege in Active Directory
docs.text:
Active Directory uses two categories of groups: security groups and distribution groups. Security groups are the ones that matter for access control; they can be assigned permissions on files, shares, services, and other resources. Distribution groups exist only for email distribution lists and carry no security permissions. Both types share the group objectClass, but security groups have a groupType attribute value that includes a flag marking them as security-enabled.

The member attribute on a group object lists the Distinguished Names (DNs) of every object that belongs to that group. Reading the member attribute on the Domain Admins group, for example, gives you the DN of every user (or nested group) with full administrative control over the domain. Groups can also be members of other groups; a pattern called nested group membership: which means a user can inherit privileges from groups they do not directly belong to.

Several built-in groups carry significant default privileges. Domain Admins members have unrestricted access to every domain-joined machine. Enterprise Admins members control the entire AD forest. Account Operators can create and modify user accounts. Server Operators can log on to domain controllers. Identifying which accounts belong to these groups is one of the highest-priority tasks during directory enumeration.

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch for Group Objects
docs.text:
The command below queries every group object in the domain and returns the group's common name, description, and member list.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=group)" cn description member

A typical group entry in the output looks like the following.

# Domain Admins, Users, corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
cn: Domain Admins
description: Designated administrators of the domain
member: CN=Administrator,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
member: CN=Admin User,OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab

Each member: line lists one member's full DN. Groups with many members will have many member: lines. Groups with no members will omit the member attribute entirely.

Attribute What It Reveals cn The group's common name; its display name in the directory description Admin-written notes about the group's purpose member Full DN of every direct member (user, computer, or nested group)

docs.title: Step 1: Enumerate All Groups
docs.text:
Enumerate all security groups

Run the group enumeration query and save the results to a file for analysis. The domain may contain dozens of groups, including both custom groups created by administrators and built-in default groups.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=group)" cn description member > /tmp/groups.ldif

Check the entry count at the end of the output or count the DN lines.

grep -c "^dn:" /tmp/groups.ldif

Record the total number of groups discovered.

docs.title: Step 2: Identify High-Privilege Built-in Groups
docs.text:
Identify high-privilege built-in groups

Search the saved output for groups with well-known names that carry elevated privileges. The following command highlights the most critical built-in groups.

grep -A2 "^cn: Domain Admins\|^cn: Enterprise Admins\|^cn: Administrators\|^cn: Account Operators\|^cn: Server Operators\|^cn: Backup Operators" /tmp/groups.ldif

The -A2 flag shows two lines after each match, which often includes the first member: line. For a complete view of any group's membership, search for the group's DN block and read all member: lines.

docs.title: Step 3: Extract Domain Admins Membership
docs.text:
Extract Domain Admins membership

The Domain Admins group is the single most important group to audit. Extract its full entry from the saved output.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s base "(objectClass=*)" member

The -s base scope flag tells ldapsearch to return only the object at the exact DN specified, without searching below it. Record every member DN that appears. Cross-reference these DNs with the user accounts you enumerated in Exercise WS-2.2 to match usernames to their Domain Admin membership.

docs.title: Step 4: Identify Custom Administrative Groups
docs.text:
Identify custom administrative groups

Organizations frequently create custom groups to manage access for specific teams; names like IT-Admins, Server-Admins, DB-Admins, or HelpDesk-Elevated are common patterns. Search the group list for names that suggest administrative or elevated access.

grep -i "^cn:.*admin\|^cn:.*elevated\|^cn:.*privileged\|^cn:.*operator" /tmp/groups.ldif

For each custom admin group you find, extract its members using the same approach as Step 3; query the group's DN directly and read the member attribute.

docs.title: Step 5: Build a Group Membership Map
docs.text:
Using the data from Steps 2 through 4, create a membership map that links groups to their members. The map should highlight which users appear in multiple privileged groups, as those accounts represent the highest-value targets.

Domain Admins
├── Administrator
└── [admin username]

IT-Admins
├── [username]
├── [username]
└── [username]

[Other groups...]

Fill in actual usernames by extracting the Common Name (CN) portion from each member's DN. The CN appears as the first component; for example, CN=John Smith,OU=IT,... has a CN of "John Smith."

docs.title: Step 6: Examine Group Descriptions
docs.text:
Examine group descriptions

Search the saved output for all description values on group objects. Group descriptions often state the group's purpose and intended scope, providing context that helps you understand the access model.

grep -B1 "^description:" /tmp/groups.ldif

The -B1 flag shows the line before each match, which is typically the cn: line, letting you pair each description with its group name. Read every description carefully. The flag for this exercise is stored in the description attribute of the IT-Admins group.

docs.title: Step 7: Check for Empty Groups
docs.text:
Groups with no members appear in the output without any member: lines. Empty security groups are worth noting because they may represent groups that were created for a future purpose, groups whose members were removed during a cleanup, or staging groups that will gain members during a migration.

To find groups that have no members, look for group blocks that jump from description: (or cn:) directly to the next entry's comment line without any member: lines in between.

docs.text:

High-privilege group membership:

Group descriptions of interest:

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review your membership map with an eye toward attack paths. Users who belong to Domain Admins or multiple privileged groups represent the shortest path to full domain compromise; if an attacker can obtain their credentials, the entire domain is controlled. Service accounts in administrative groups are particularly concerning because they may authenticate non-interactively and have credentials stored in configuration files or scripts.

Consider the defensive perspective as well. Are there more Domain Admins than necessary? Do custom admin groups follow the principle of least privilege, or do they grant broad access? Empty groups that were intended to restrict membership may indicate an incomplete security configuration.

docs.title: Step 9: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is located in the description attribute of the IT-Admins group. If you completed Step 6, you should have already spotted the flag while reviewing group descriptions. The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do organizations assign permissions through groups rather than directly to individual user accounts?

Reveal Answer

Group-based permissions are far easier to manage at scale. When an employee changes roles, an administrator updates their group memberships rather than modifying permissions on every resource. Groups also make auditing clearer; reviewing a group's member list shows at a glance who has access, rather than checking each resource's access-control list individually.

2. What risk does nested group membership create, and how can it complicate auditing?

Reveal Answer

Nested groups allow a user to inherit privileges indirectly. If Group A is a member of Group B, every member of Group A gains Group B's permissions without appearing directly in Group B's member list. An auditor reviewing Group B may not realize that an entire set of users has inherited access through the nested group. Attackers can exploit these hidden trust paths to escalate privileges.

3. You found the flag in a group's description attribute. How is finding sensitive data in a group description similar to the finding in Exercise WS-2.1?

Reveal Answer

Both findings demonstrate the same pattern: administrators storing information in freeform text attributes that are readable via anonymous LDAP. In Exercise WS-2.1 the data was in an OU description; in Exercise WS-2.3 the data was in a group description. The lesson is consistent; any attribute exposed through LDAP should be treated as publicly readable and audited regularly.

4. An attacker discovers a service account in the Domain Admins group. Why is that finding more dangerous than a regular user in Domain Admins?

Reveal Answer

Service accounts often have passwords that are set once and rarely changed, sometimes stored in scripts or configuration files in plaintext. Unlike interactive user accounts, service accounts may not trigger the same monitoring alerts when accessed from unexpected locations. An attacker who compromises a service account in Domain Admins gains persistent, high-privilege access that is harder for defenders to detect and remediate.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Security groups are the mechanism through which Active Directory assigns permissions, making group enumeration essential for understanding the domain's access model.
  • The member attribute on group objects provides a complete roster of direct members, while nested groups can hide indirect membership from casual inspection.
  • Domain Admins and other built-in privileged groups should have minimal membership; a large number of members indicates poor privilege hygiene.
  • Group descriptions, like OU and user descriptions, are readable through LDAP and may contain sensitive notes or metadata.
  • With group memberships mapped, Exercise WS-2.4 will enumerate computer accounts to catalog the infrastructure and identify potential targets for lateral movement.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise WS-2.3 mapped security groups and their members, identifying which users hold elevated privileges across the domain. Exercise WS-2.4 shifts focus from people to machines; querying the directory for computer objects that represent every domain-joined system. You will need the same Kali Linux machine with anonymous Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) access to dc01.

Prerequisites

  • Exercise WS-2.3 completed (group memberships mapped)
  • VPN active and dc01 reachable
  • ldapsearch available (ldap-utils package)
  • Your user and group membership notes from Exercises WS-2.2 and WS-2.3

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Computer accounts represent every domain-joined machine in the corp.ocr-range.lab environment. Each computer object stores the machine's operating system version, DNS hostname, last logon timestamp, and optional metadata in its attributes. Enumerating computer accounts lets you map the organization's infrastructure, identify the domain controller's computer object, and spot systems running older or potentially vulnerable operating systems.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Query LDAP for all computer objects in the domain
  • Extract operating system information, DNS hostnames, and descriptions for each machine
  • Identify the domain controller's computer object and confirm its role
  • Locate the lab flag stored in the description attribute of the domain controller's computer account

docs.title: Background: Computer Objects in Active Directory
docs.text:
When a Windows machine joins an Active Directory (AD) domain, the join process creates a computer object in the directory. The computer object stores machine-specific attributes that the domain uses for authentication, policy application, and management. Computer objects belong to the computer objectClass, which is a subclass of the user objectClass; meaning computer accounts inherit many of the same attributes that user accounts have, including description, memberOf, and password-related fields.

Several attributes on computer objects are especially valuable for reconnaissance. The operatingSystem attribute records the OS name (for example, "Windows Server 2022 Standard"), and operatingSystemVersion stores the build number. Together these attributes let you identify machines running outdated or unpatched operating systems. The dNSHostName attribute contains the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of the machine, which you can use for direct network targeting. The description attribute, like the description on user and group objects, is a freeform field that may contain administrator notes.

Domain controllers are particularly easy to spot among computer objects. Their Distinguished Names (DNs) typically place them in the OU=Domain Controllers container, and their operatingSystem attribute identifies a server-class OS. Confirming which computer object belongs to the domain controller validates the targeting information you gathered during Chapter WS01's port scans and DNS enumeration.

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch for Computer Objects
docs.text:
The command below queries every computer object in the domain and returns the attributes most relevant to infrastructure mapping.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=computer)" cn operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion description dNSHostName

A typical computer entry in the output looks like the following.

# WKS01, Computers, corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: CN=WKS01,OU=Computers,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
cn: WKS01
operatingSystem: <operating system>
operatingSystemVersion: <version>
dNSHostName: wks01.corp.ocr-range.lab
description: <description if set>

Note: The example above uses placeholder values. Your lab output will show the actual machines, operating systems, and descriptions present in the environment.

Each attribute line reports a single value. Computer objects that lack a particular attribute will omit that line from the output.

Attribute What It Reveals cn The machine's NetBIOS name (hostname) operatingSystem Full OS name; reveals server vs. workstation, edition, and major version operatingSystemVersion Build number; useful for identifying patch level description Freeform notes set by administrators dNSHostName The machine's FQDN; directly usable for network access

docs.title: Step 1: Enumerate All Computer Objects
docs.text:
Enumerate all computer objects

Run the computer enumeration query and save the results for analysis. Even in a small lab environment, capturing the output to a file prevents loss of data if the terminal buffer wraps.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=computer)" cn operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion description dNSHostName > /tmp/computers.ldif

Count the returned entries to determine how many domain-joined machines exist.

grep -c "^dn:" /tmp/computers.ldif

Record the total count. In the lab environment, expect a modest number of machines; the domain controller, one or more member servers, and possibly workstations.

docs.title: Step 2: Catalog Operating Systems
docs.text:
Catalog operating systems

Extract the operatingSystem attribute from each entry to build an OS inventory. The following command lists every unique operating system string in the results.

grep "^operatingSystem:" /tmp/computers.ldif | sort -u

For each unique OS, note how many machines run it. Server operating systems indicate infrastructure servers; workstation operating systems (like "Windows 10 Enterprise" or "Windows 11 Pro") indicate end-user machines.

grep "^operatingSystem:" /tmp/computers.ldif | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

An OS inventory helps you prioritize targets. Machines running older operating systems or server editions that have reached end of life are more likely to have unpatched vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Step 3: Identify the Domain Controller's Computer Object
docs.text:
Identify the domain controller computer object

The domain controller's computer object typically resides in the OU=Domain Controllers container. Search for entries whose DN includes that OU.

grep -A5 "OU=Domain Controllers" /tmp/computers.ldif

Confirm that the cn value matches DC01 and that the operatingSystem shows a Windows Server edition. The dNSHostName should match the hostname you have been using throughout the chapter. Record the full set of attributes for the domain controller's computer object.

docs.title: Step 4: Extract DNS Hostnames
docs.text:
Extract DNS hostnames

Build a list of all machine FQDNs from the dNSHostName attribute. The FQDN list is a target inventory for later phases where you will connect directly to specific machines.

grep "^dNSHostName:" /tmp/computers.ldif | awk '{print $2}'

Save the hostname list to a file for future reference.

grep "^dNSHostName:" /tmp/computers.ldif | awk '{print $2}' > /tmp/computer_hostnames.txt

docs.title: Step 5: Review Computer Descriptions
docs.text:
Review computer descriptions

Search the saved output for description attributes on computer objects. Administrators sometimes annotate computer accounts with location information, purpose notes, or configuration details.

grep -B3 "^description:" /tmp/computers.ldif

The -B3 flag shows the three lines before each match, which should include the cn and dn values. Read every description carefully. The flag for this exercise is stored in the description attribute of the domain controller's computer object.

docs.title: Step 6: Check for OS Version Details
docs.text:
Check for OS version details

The operatingSystemVersion attribute provides the Windows build number, which maps to a specific release and patch level. Extract these values and pair them with the machine names.

grep -B2 "^operatingSystemVersion:" /tmp/computers.ldif

For Windows Server 2022, the build number 10.0 (20348) is expected. Older build numbers on other machines may indicate systems that have not been updated. Cross-reference build numbers with Microsoft's published build history to determine approximate patch status.

docs.title: Step 7: Build an Infrastructure Map
docs.text:
Combine the data from the previous steps into an infrastructure summary. The map should include each machine's hostname, OS, build version, OU location, and any description content. A table format works well for this summary.

| Hostname | OS                        | Build      | OU                  | Description         |
|----------|---------------------------|------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| DC01     | Windows Server 2022 Std   | 10.0(20348)| Domain Controllers  | [from output]       |
| ...      | ...                       | ...        | ...                 | ...                 |

Fill in the table with the actual values from your enumeration. The infrastructure map, combined with the user and group data from earlier labs, provides a complete view of the domain.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Total computer accounts discovered: __

Operating system inventory:

Operating System Count

Infrastructure map:

Hostname OS Build Version OU Description

Domain controller computer object DN: __

Saved hostname list location: /tmp/computer_hostnames.txt

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Review your infrastructure map and consider what the computer inventory reveals about the environment. The number and types of machines give you a sense of the organization's scale and technology choices. Machines running older operating systems represent higher-risk targets due to the likelihood of unpatched vulnerabilities. The domain controller's computer object confirms the server you have been querying throughout the chapter and anchors your infrastructure map.

Combine the computer data with your earlier findings. You now know the OU structure (Exercise WS-2.1), the users (Exercise WS-2.2), the group memberships (Exercise WS-2.3), and the machines (Exercise WS-2.4). The remaining piece; the domain password policy; will complete your reconnaissance picture in Exercise WS-2.5.

docs.title: Step 9: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is located in the description attribute of the domain controller's computer object. If you followed Step 5, you should have already identified it. The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do computer accounts in Active Directory inherit from the user objectClass, and what security implication does that create?

Reveal Answer

AD's schema defines the computer class as a subclass of user, meaning computer accounts have passwords, can authenticate to Kerberos, and carry attributes like description and memberOf. The security implication is that computer accounts can be targeted with many of the same attacks used against user accounts; for example, an attacker can request a Kerberos ticket for a computer account or read its publicly accessible attributes.

2. An attacker discovers a computer object with operatingSystem: Windows Server 2012 R2. Why is that finding significant?

Reveal Answer

Windows Server 2012 R2 reached end of extended support in October 2023 and no longer receives security patches. A machine running an unsupported OS is likely to have multiple unpatched vulnerabilities that an attacker can exploit for initial access or lateral movement.

3. How does the dNSHostName attribute differ from the cn attribute, and when would you use each?

Reveal Answer

The cn attribute holds the machine's NetBIOS name (short hostname), while dNSHostName holds the Fully Qualified Domain Name including the domain suffix. The FQDN is needed for DNS-based connections and for protocols that validate hostnames during authentication (such as Kerberos). The short name may suffice for WINS or NetBIOS-based connections within the same network segment.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Computer objects are created automatically when a machine joins the domain, and they store operating system metadata, DNS names, and freeform attributes readable through LDAP.
  • The operatingSystem and operatingSystemVersion attributes provide an instant infrastructure audit, revealing which machines may be running outdated or unsupported software.
  • Domain controller computer objects reside in the OU=Domain Controllers container and can be confirmed by matching their hostname and OS to the server you have been querying.
  • The description attribute pattern continues; for the fourth time in this chapter, a freeform text field has contained data that administrators did not expect to be publicly accessible.
  • With users, groups, and computers mapped, Exercise WS-2.5 will extract the domain password policy; the final piece needed to plan credential attacks and assess the organization's security posture.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercises WS-2.1 through WS-2.4 systematically enumerated the directory's structure, user accounts, group memberships, and computer objects. Exercise WS-2.5 completes the reconnaissance picture by extracting the domain-wide password policy; the set of rules that govern credential strength, history, and lockout behavior. You will need the same Kali Linux machine with anonymous Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) access to dc01.

Prerequisites

  • Exercises WS-2.1 through WS-2.4 completed
  • VPN active and dc01 reachable
  • ldapsearch available (ldap-utils package)
  • Your user list and group membership notes from earlier labs

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Before launching any credential attacks against the domain, a careful attacker checks the password policy. The policy dictates the minimum password length, complexity requirements, lockout thresholds, and lockout duration. Attempting too many incorrect passwords without knowing the lockout threshold risks locking out accounts and alerting defenders. Extracting the policy first lets you calibrate your approach; choosing password candidates that meet the minimum length and complexity, and staying below the lockout threshold to avoid detection.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Query the domain object for password policy attributes using a base-scope LDAP search
  • Extract the minimum password length and understand its impact on credential attacks
  • Determine the account lockout threshold and lockout duration
  • Derive the lab flag from the extracted policy values

docs.title: Background: Domain Password Policy in Active Directory
docs.text:
Active Directory (AD) stores the default password policy as a set of attributes on the domain object itself; the root entry at DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab. Unlike OUs, users, and groups, the password policy is not a separate object; the attributes live directly on the domain's top-level entry. Reading the policy requires a base-scope search (-s base) targeting the domain DN, which returns only the domain object and its attributes without descending into child containers.

Five attributes define the core password policy.

Attribute Meaning minPwdLength Minimum number of characters a password must contain maxPwdAge Maximum time a password can be used before it must be changed (stored in 100-nanosecond intervals as a negative value) lockoutThreshold Number of consecutive failed logon attempts before the account is locked lockoutDuration How long a locked account remains locked (stored in 100-nanosecond intervals as a negative value) pwdHistoryLength Number of previous passwords the system remembers, preventing reuse

The maxPwdAge and lockoutDuration values use a format unique to AD: they are stored as negative 64-bit integers representing intervals of 100 nanoseconds. For example, a maxPwdAge of -36288000000000 equals 42 days. Converting these values to human-readable durations requires dividing the absolute value by 10,000,000 (to get seconds) and then converting seconds to days, hours, or minutes.

The lockoutThreshold deserves special attention. A threshold of 0 means account lockout is disabled; an attacker can make unlimited password guesses without triggering a lockout. Any non-zero threshold defines the number of failed attempts allowed within the observation window before the account locks. Staying one or two attempts below that threshold is a standard technique during password-spraying attacks.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Base-Scope LDAP Search
docs.text:
The command below retrieves password policy attributes from the domain object using a base-scope search.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s base minPwdLength maxPwdAge lockoutThreshold lockoutDuration pwdHistoryLength

The -s base flag is the key difference from the queries in earlier labs. Instead of searching an entire subtree for matching objects, a base-scope search returns only the single object at the specified base DN. Because the password policy attributes live on the domain object, the base DN and the target object are the same.

Sample output from a base-scope policy query looks like the following.

# corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
minPwdLength: <value>
maxPwdAge: <value>
lockoutThreshold: <value>
lockoutDuration: <value>
pwdHistoryLength: <value>

Note: Your lab values will differ from any examples shown in this walkthrough.

Each attribute appears on its own line with its value. The minPwdLength and lockoutThreshold values are plain integers. The maxPwdAge and lockoutDuration values require conversion from 100-nanosecond intervals to human-readable time periods.

docs.title: Step 1: Query the Domain Password Policy
docs.text:
Query the domain password policy

Execute the base-scope search against the domain object to retrieve all five password policy attributes.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s base minPwdLength maxPwdAge lockoutThreshold lockoutDuration pwdHistoryLength

Save the output to a file for reference.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s base minPwdLength maxPwdAge lockoutThreshold lockoutDuration pwdHistoryLength > /tmp/policy.ldif

Confirm that all five attributes appear in the output. If any attribute is missing, the domain may not have that policy configured, or the attribute name may have a typo.

docs.title: Step 2: Read the Minimum Password Length
docs.text:
Read the minimum password length

Locate the minPwdLength line in the output. The value is a plain integer specifying the minimum number of characters.

grep "^minPwdLength:" /tmp/policy.ldif

The minPwdLength value tells you the minimum number of characters every password in the domain must contain. When preparing a password list for spraying or brute-force attacks, you would exclude any candidate shorter than the minimum; they cannot be valid.

Record the minimum password length value. You will need it to construct the flag.

docs.title: Step 3: Determine the Lockout Threshold
docs.text:
Determine the lockout threshold

Locate the lockoutThreshold line.

grep "^lockoutThreshold:" /tmp/policy.ldif

The lockoutThreshold value tells you how many consecutive failed logon attempts are allowed before an account locks. A value of 0 would mean lockout is disabled entirely. Record the lockout threshold value; you will need it for the flag and for calibrating any future credential attacks.

When planning a password-spraying attack, the standard approach is to attempt no more than lockoutThreshold - 2 guesses per account within the observation window. Subtract 2 from the threshold you found to determine your safe maximum; this constraint shapes the attack strategy.

docs.title: Step 4: Convert the Maximum Password Age
docs.text:
Read the maximum password age

Locate the maxPwdAge line. The value will be a large negative number in 100-nanosecond intervals.

grep "^maxPwdAge:" /tmp/policy.ldif

Convert the absolute value to days using the following formula.

days = absolute_value / 10,000,000 / 60 / 60 / 24

For example, if maxPwdAge were -25920000000000 (substitute your actual value):

25920000000000 / 10,000,000 = 2,592,000 seconds
2,592,000 / 60 = 43,200 minutes
43,200 / 60 = 720 hours
720 / 24 = 30 days

Apply this same conversion to the maxPwdAge value from your output and record the result in days.

docs.title: Step 5: Convert the Lockout Duration
docs.text:
Read the lockout duration

Locate the lockoutDuration line and apply the same conversion.

grep "^lockoutDuration:" /tmp/policy.ldif

Convert the absolute value to minutes.

minutes = absolute_value / 10,000,000 / 60

For example, if lockoutDuration were -12000000000 (substitute your actual value):

12000000000 / 10,000,000 = 1,200 seconds
1,200 / 60 = 20 minutes

Apply this same conversion to the lockoutDuration value from your output and record the result in minutes.

docs.title: Step 6: Read the Password History Length
docs.text:
Read the password history length

Locate the pwdHistoryLength line.

grep "^pwdHistoryLength:" /tmp/policy.ldif

The password history length specifies how many previous passwords the system remembers. A value of 24 means a user cannot reuse any of their last 24 passwords. The higher the history length, the harder it is for users to cycle back to a familiar password, which generally improves security.

docs.title: Step 7: Summarize the Policy
docs.text:
Compile all five values into a single policy summary table. Convert the raw AD time values to human-readable formats. The summary should look similar to the following.

Policy Attribute Raw Value Human-Readable Value Minimum Password Length [integer] [integer] characters Maximum Password Age [negative integer] [X] days Lockout Threshold [integer] [integer] attempts Lockout Duration [negative integer] [X] minutes Password History Length [integer] [integer] passwords remembered

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Password policy summary:

Policy Attribute Raw Value Human-Readable minPwdLength maxPwdAge lockoutThreshold lockoutDuration pwdHistoryLength

Safe password-spray limit (threshold - 2): __

Minimum candidate password length: __

docs.title: Step 8: Interpret the Results
docs.text:
Consider what the password policy tells you about the organization's security posture. Compare the minimum password length against modern guidance from NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology), which recommends a minimum of 8 characters, with many organizations requiring 12 or more. Evaluate whether the lockout threshold provides meaningful protection against brute-force attacks or still allows a window for careful password spraying.

The combination of policy values shapes your attack strategy. The minPwdLength value you found determines the shortest viable password candidate. Subtracting 2 from the lockoutThreshold value gives you the safe number of guesses per account per lockout window. The lockout duration you calculated tells you how long to wait before resuming attempts after a lockout expires.

docs.title: Step 9: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is derived from two policy values: the minimum password length and the lockout threshold. The format is OCR{p0l1cy_3xtr4ct3d_<minPwdLength>_<lockoutThreshold>}. Using the values you extracted, construct the flag.

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does extracting the password policy matter before attempting credential attacks?

Reveal Answer

Knowing the minimum password length allows an attacker to filter their wordlist to exclude candidates that are too short, improving efficiency. Knowing the lockout threshold prevents the attacker from accidentally locking accounts, which would alert defenders and deny access to legitimate users. Together, the policy values let the attacker calibrate their approach for maximum effectiveness with minimum risk of detection.

2. The maxPwdAge and lockoutDuration values are stored as negative 100-nanosecond intervals. Why does Active Directory use this format?

Reveal Answer

AD inherited its time format from Windows NT, which represents time intervals as 64-bit integers in 100-nanosecond units. Negative values indicate relative durations (how long from now) rather than absolute timestamps. While the format is unintuitive for humans, it provides high precision and is consistent with how the Windows kernel tracks time internally.

3. A domain has a lockoutThreshold of 0. What does that mean for an attacker, and what does it mean for the defender?

Reveal Answer

A threshold of 0 means account lockout is disabled. An attacker can make unlimited password guesses against any account without triggering a lockout. For the defender, the lack of lockout means brute-force and password-spraying attacks face no automatic barrier, making strong passwords and monitoring for high volumes of failed logon events critical compensating controls.

4. How would a Fine-Grained Password Policy (FGPP) change the results of this exercise?

Reveal Answer

Fine-Grained Password Policies allow administrators to define different password policies for different groups of users within the same domain. The default domain policy returned by a base-scope search may not apply to all accounts; privileged accounts might have stricter requirements (longer minimum length, lower lockout threshold). To discover FGPPs, an attacker would need to query the CN=Password Settings Container,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab container for msDS-PasswordSettings objects.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The domain password policy is stored as attributes on the domain object itself and is readable through a base-scope LDAP search.
  • minPwdLength and lockoutThreshold are the two most operationally relevant values for planning credential attacks; they define the minimum viable password length and the safe number of guesses.
  • AD stores time-based policy values in 100-nanosecond intervals as negative integers; converting them to days, hours, or minutes requires dividing by 10,000,000 and then by the appropriate time factor.
  • A lockout threshold of 0 disables account lockout entirely, removing an important braking mechanism against brute-force attacks.
  • With all five labs complete, you have a complete map of the corp.ocr-range.lab domain: OUs, users, groups, computers, and password policy. The Chapter Review consolidates these findings and prepares you for Chapter WS03.

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Chapter WS02 took the anonymous Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) access confirmed in Chapter WS01 and used it to systematically enumerate every major category of Active Directory (AD) object. Across five labs you queried the domain controller dc01 for Organizational Units (OUs), user accounts, security groups, computer objects, and the domain password policy. Each lab added a new layer to your understanding of the corp.ocr-range.lab domain.

The chapter reinforced a single tool; ldapsearch: applied with different filters, scopes, and attribute lists to extract distinct types of information. You learned that LDAP filters select objects by objectClass, that the -s base scope retrieves attributes from a single object, and that freeform text attributes like description and info frequently contain data that administrators did not intend to be publicly visible. You also built practical artifacts; an OU hierarchy, a username list, a group membership map, an infrastructure inventory, and a password policy summary; that feed directly into later attack phases.

docs.text:
The five labs formed a deliberate pipeline, each query providing context that informed the next. The diagram below shows the progression and what each exercise contributed to the overall reconnaissance picture.

The table below summarizes each exercise's filter, key findings, and flag.

Exercise LDAP Filter / Scope Key Finding Flag 2.1; OU Discovery (objectClass=organizationalUnit) Directory structure mapped; hidden OU found OCR{...} 2.2; User Enumeration (objectClass=user) User accounts cataloged; sensitive data in info field OCR{...} 2.3; Group Membership (objectClass=group) Privilege map built; admin groups identified OCR{...} 2.4; Computer Accounts (objectClass=computer) Infrastructure inventoried; DC object confirmed OCR{...} 2.5; Password Policy -s base on domain DN Policy extracted; spray limits determined OCR{...}

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer each question below to test your retention. Write your answers in the spaces provided, then check them against the answer key at the bottom of this file.

1. What ldapsearch flag enables anonymous (simple) authentication?

2. What LDAP filter returns only Organizational Unit objects?

3. Name two freeform text attributes on user objects that may contain sensitive information left by administrators.

4. What attribute on a group object lists the Distinguished Names of its direct members?

5. Which built-in OU typically contains the domain controller's computer object?

6. What does a lockoutThreshold value of 0 mean for the domain's security?

7. How do you convert an AD time value stored in 100-nanosecond intervals to seconds?

8. What -s scope value retrieves attributes from a single object at the specified base DN without searching child objects?

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
The table below collects every ldapsearch command used across the five labs. Each row shows the lab, the full command, and a brief description of its purpose.

Exercise Command Purpose 2.1 ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" dn description Enumerate all OUs and their descriptions 2.2 ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName displayName description info memberOf List all user accounts with key attributes 2.3 ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=group)" cn description member Enumerate all groups and their members 2.4 ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=computer)" cn operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion description dNSHostName Discover all computer objects and OS info 2.5 ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" -s base minPwdLength maxPwdAge lockoutThreshold lockoutDuration pwdHistoryLength Extract the domain password policy

Useful modifiers:

Modifier Example Purpose Save output to file ldapsearch ... > /tmp/output.ldif Preserve results for searching and analysis Base-scope search -s base Return only the object at the specified DN One-level scope -s one Return only immediate children of the base DN Specific base DN -b "OU=IT,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" Narrow search to a specific OU

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text:
Chapter WS02 gave you a complete read-only view of the domain through anonymous LDAP queries. You mapped the organizational structure, identified users and their privilege levels, cataloged the infrastructure, and extracted the password policy. The data you collected; especially the username list and the password policy constraints; sets the stage for active credential attacks.

Chapter WS03 will shift from passive enumeration to authenticated and targeted techniques. Expect to use the artifacts you built in WS02 (username lists, group membership maps, and the password policy) as direct inputs to tools that test for weak credentials, misconfigured service accounts, and exploitable trust relationships. The transition from "what can I read?" to "what can I access?" begins in the next chapter.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. The -x flag enables simple (anonymous) authentication.

2. (objectClass=organizationalUnit) returns only OU objects.

3. The description and info attributes are freeform text fields that may contain sensitive data such as temporary passwords or internal notes.

4. The member attribute on a group object lists the DNs of its direct members.

5. The OU=Domain Controllers container typically holds the domain controller's computer object.

6. A lockoutThreshold of 0 means account lockout is disabled; an attacker can make unlimited password guesses without triggering a lockout.

7. Divide the absolute value by 10,000,000 (ten million) to convert 100-nanosecond intervals to seconds.

8. The -s base scope returns attributes from only the single object at the specified base DN.

docs.title: Why Network Service Mapping Matters
docs.text:
Active Directory (AD) environments depend on a web of interconnected services to function. Domain Name System (DNS) records advertise where Domain Controllers (DCs), Kerberos servers, and Global Catalog (GC) servers live. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) scopes define network addressing. Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) stores computer objects that represent every machine joined to the domain. A penetration tester who examines only one of these sources sees a fragment of the picture. Correlating all three reveals the full network topology; subnets, trust relationships, and services that administrators may not realize are exposed.

Chapters WS01 and WS02 introduced you to DNS queries and LDAP enumeration as isolated skills. WS03 raises the bar by combining those skills with new techniques; SRV record analysis, conditional forwarder detection, and DHCP scope reconnaissance; to map infrastructure that no single tool can uncover alone. The exercises in this chapter do not require credentials for DNS and DHCP work. You will perform unauthenticated queries against dc01 and correlate results across protocols.

In real engagements, incomplete mapping leads to missed attack paths. A conditional forwarder pointing to a partner domain reveals a trust relationship. A non-standard SRV record exposes an undocumented service. A DHCP option containing a Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD) URL creates a man-in-the-middle opportunity. The four exercises ahead teach you to find all of these.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
The four exercises in this chapter progress from DNS-specific techniques to full network correlation:

  • Discover SRV records that AD uses to advertise services, including non-standard entries that reveal hidden infrastructure
  • Detect DNS conditional forwarders that expose trust relationships and partner domain resolution paths
  • Enumerate DHCP scopes to extract network addressing, gateway assignments, and custom options like WPAD
  • Correlate DNS, DHCP, and LDAP data to build a complete network topology map

By the end of this chapter, you will have a repeatable methodology for mapping any Windows Server environment from the network layer up.

docs.title: How AD Services Interconnect
docs.text:
Active Directory does not function through a single protocol. Domain-joined clients rely on DNS to locate services, DHCP to obtain addressing, and LDAP to query the directory. Understanding how these protocols interact is essential to mapping the environment.

graph TD
    A["Client Machine"]
    B["DNS Server<br/>(dc01)"]
    C["DHCP Server<br/>(dc01)"]
    D["LDAP / AD<br/>(dc01)"]
    E["Partner Domain<br/>(partner.local)"]

    A -->|"SRV queries"| B
    A -->|"DHCP request"| C
    A -->|"LDAP bind"| D
    B -->|"Conditional<br/>forwarder"| E

    style A fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style D fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff

The diagram above shows dc01 serving three roles simultaneously; DNS, DHCP, and LDAP. A conditional forwarder on dc01 points DNS queries for partner.local to an external domain, exposing a trust relationship that Exercises WS-3.2 and WS-3.4 will investigate.

docs.title: The Tools You Will Use
docs.text:
Each exercise introduces or builds on a specific tool. The table below summarizes what you need.

Exercise Primary Tool Purpose WS-3.1 dig Query DNS SRV and TXT records WS-3.2 dig Zone transfer attempts and forwarder detection WS-3.3 nmap (NSE) DHCP service discovery and option enumeration WS-3.4 dig, ldapsearch Cross-protocol correlation and topology mapping

The dig command is a DNS lookup tool pre-installed on Kali Linux. Nmap's DHCP discovery scripts send crafted UDP packets to enumerate DHCP responses. The ldapsearch command queries LDAP directories. All three tools are available on your Kali attack machine without additional installation.

You can verify each tool is ready:

dig -v
nmap --version
ldapsearch -VV

docs.title: The Progression Across Labs
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["WS-3.1<br/>SRV Records"]
    B["WS-3.2<br/>Cond. Forwarders"]
    C["WS-3.3<br/>DHCP Scopes"]
    D["WS-3.4<br/>Topology Map"]

    A --> B --> C --> D

    style A fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,stroke:#333,color:#fff
