Each lab adds a new data source to your understanding of the network. Exercise WS-3.4 ties everything together by requiring you to combine findings from DNS, DHCP, and LDAP into a single topology view.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following before launching your first exercise:

  • VPN connection to the lab environment is active
  • Terminal open and ready for commands
  • dig installed and accessible (type dig -v to confirm)
  • Nmap installed and accessible (type nmap --version to confirm)
  • ldapsearch available (type ldapsearch -VV to confirm)
  • Notebook or text editor ready for recording findings
  • Access to the OCR platform at the provided URL

Each lab takes approximately 45 minutes. Work through them in order; Exercise WS-3.4 requires data gathered in the earlier labs.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Active Directory relies on DNS more than any other service. If you completed the WS01 DNS labs, you already know how to query A records and basic zone data. Exercise WS-3.1 goes deeper by querying SRV (Service) records; the mechanism AD uses to advertise Domain Controllers, Kerberos servers, and Global Catalog endpoints.

  • Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach dc01.
  • No credentials are needed for DNS queries; all SRV records are publicly resolvable within the domain.
  • You should be comfortable running dig commands from a Linux terminal.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your security team is assessing the corp.ocr-range.lab Active Directory (AD) environment. The domain controller dc01 runs Windows Server 2022 and hosts the primary DNS zone. AD-integrated DNS contains SRV (Service Location) records that domain-joined clients query to locate critical infrastructure; Kerberos Key Distribution Centers (KDCs), Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) servers, and Global Catalog (GC) endpoints. Your task is to enumerate these standard SRV records and determine whether any non-standard SRV entries exist that might reveal undocumented services.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Query standard AD SRV records for Kerberos, LDAP, and Global Catalog services
  • Understand the SRV record format and what each field communicates
  • Discover non-standard SRV records that may expose hidden services
  • Follow the chain from a non-standard SRV entry to retrieve the flag

docs.title: Background: SRV Records in Active Directory
docs.text:
DNS SRV records define the location of servers for specific services. Unlike A records that map hostnames to IP addresses, SRV records map a service name to a host, port, priority, and weight. Every AD domain creates SRV records automatically when a Domain Controller is promoted. Without these records, domain-joined clients cannot locate the services they need to authenticate and function.

The SRV record format follows a specific naming convention:

_service._protocol.domain.  TTL  IN  SRV  priority  weight  port  target

Each field serves a distinct purpose. The _service label identifies what the record advertises (such as _kerberos or _ldap). The _protocol label specifies TCP or UDP. Priority and weight allow administrators to control failover and load balancing when multiple servers provide the same service. The target field contains the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of the server hosting that service.

AD creates several well-known SRV records during domain controller promotion. The three most significant categories are Kerberos authentication (_kerberos._tcp), LDAP directory services (_ldap._tcp), and Global Catalog lookups (_gc._tcp). Querying these records reveals every DC in the domain, including DCs in child domains or sites. Penetration testers use SRV enumeration to build a list of high-value targets without scanning a single port.

Non-standard SRV records present a different opportunity. Administrators sometimes create custom SRV entries for internal applications, monitoring systems, or services that need automated discovery. These records may not appear in documentation, but they are visible to anyone who can query DNS. A non-standard SRV record is a signpost pointing to infrastructure the organization may have forgotten about.

docs.title: Tool Primer: dig for SRV Queries
docs.text:
The dig (Domain Information Groper) command is a DNS lookup tool that supports all standard record types. Querying SRV records requires specifying the record type explicitly.

Syntax for SRV queries:

dig SRV _service._protocol.domain @nameserver

Key flags and options:

Option Purpose SRV Specifies the query type as SRV TXT Specifies the query type as TXT (text records) @nameserver Directs the query to a specific DNS server +short Returns only the answer, no extra sections +noall +answer Shows only the answer section with full detail

Sample SRV output:

;; ANSWER SECTION:
_kerberos._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab. 600 IN SRV 0 100 88 dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab.

Reading left to right: the service is Kerberos over TCP in the corp.ocr-range.lab domain. The Time to Live (TTL) is 600 seconds. The priority is 0 (highest), the weight is 100, the port is 88, and the target server is dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab. Kerberos uses port 88 by default, so the SRV record confirms dc01 is the KDC for the domain.

Sample TXT output:

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.corp.ocr-range.lab. 600 IN TXT "some text value here"

TXT records store arbitrary text strings. Administrators use them for SPF records, domain verification, and occasionally for storing metadata. In a lab context, TXT records may contain flags or clues.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab and Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 3, and launch Exercise WS-3.1. Wait for the environment status to show Running and note the target information. The target for all DNS queries is dc01 at corp.ocr-range.lab.

Verify DNS connectivity to dc01

Verify you can reach the DNS server with a simple A record lookup. The +short flag trims the output to just the answer so you can confirm resolution at a glance.

dig +short A dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

You should receive an IP address in response. If the query times out, check your VPN connection before proceeding.

docs.title: Step 2: Query Kerberos SRV Records
docs.text:
Kerberos is the primary authentication protocol for AD. Every DC runs a Kerberos KDC on port 88. Querying the _kerberos._tcp SRV record reveals which servers handle authentication for the domain.

Query Kerberos SRV records

Run the following query to ask dc01 which servers advertise the Kerberos service. The _kerberos._tcp label is the well-known SRV name every DC registers when it is promoted.

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

Examine the ANSWER SECTION of the output. You should see one or more SRV records listing dc01 as the Kerberos server. Note the priority, weight, and port values.

The port field should show 88; the standard Kerberos port. If multiple DCs existed in the domain, each would appear as a separate SRV record with its own priority and weight values, allowing clients to select the best server.

docs.title: Step 3: Query LDAP SRV Records
docs.text:
LDAP is how domain-joined machines locate directory services. Clients query _ldap._tcp to find DCs that accept LDAP connections on port 389.

Query LDAP SRV records

Run the following query to find the DCs that accept LDAP connections. Domain-joined machines resolve this record to locate directory services on port 389.

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The output should show dc01 advertising LDAP on port 389. Compare the priority and weight values with the Kerberos SRV record from Step 2; in a single-DC environment, they are typically identical.

Query LDAPS SRV records

You can also query for LDAP over Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) on port 636. The presence of an _ldaps record signals that the DC accepts encrypted LDAP.

dig SRV _ldaps._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The presence or absence of an _ldaps SRV record tells you whether the DC is configured for encrypted LDAP connections. Not all environments configure LDAPS.

docs.title: Step 4: Query Global Catalog SRV Records
docs.text:
The Global Catalog (GC) is a read-only copy of all objects across an AD forest, served on port 3268. Multi-domain forests rely on the GC for cross-domain searches.

Query Global Catalog SRV records

Query the GC SRV record to find the servers that answer forest-wide searches. The Global Catalog listens on port 3268, distinct from the LDAP port.

dig SRV _gc._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The target should again be dc01, but the port field should show 3268 instead of 389. The GC contains a partial attribute set for every object in the forest, making it a high-value target for enumeration.

docs.title: Step 5: Compile Standard SRV Records
docs.text:
At this point you have queried three standard AD SRV record types. Compiling the results into a single view provides a baseline map of AD infrastructure.

Compile all standard SRV records

You can query all three at once using short output for a quick summary. The +short flag collapses each answer to one line so the three results read as a compact baseline.

dig +short SRV _kerberos._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01
dig +short SRV _ldap._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01
dig +short SRV _gc._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

Record the server names, ports, and priorities. In larger environments, you would see multiple DCs here, each with different site affiliations and priority values.

graph TD
    A["dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab"]
    B["Kerberos<br/>Port 88"]
    C["LDAP<br/>Port 389"]
    D["Global Catalog<br/>Port 3268"]

    A --- B
    A --- C
    A --- D

    style A fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style D fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff

docs.title: Step 6: Discover Non-Standard SRV Records
docs.text:
Standard SRV records reveal the expected AD infrastructure. Non-standard records reveal what administrators have added beyond the defaults. Querying for custom service names can uncover applications, monitoring systems, or test entries.

Probe for non-standard SRV records

If the zone transfer from Step 2 succeeded, review the output for SRV records with non-standard service names; entries that do not match the well-known AD services (_kerberos, _ldap, _gc, etc.). If the zone transfer was denied, try querying common non-standard service names such as _http, _sip, or other short keywords that an administrator might use for custom services. Replace <service_name> with each candidate keyword.

dig SRV _<service_name>._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

When you find a non-standard SRV record, the ANSWER SECTION will contain an entry pointing to a hostname you have not seen before. Note the target hostname; the SRV record functions as a pointer, directing you to the server that hosts that service.

Non-standard SRV records like this one would not appear in a port scan. Only DNS enumeration reveals them, which is why SRV record discovery is a required step in any AD assessment.

docs.title: Step 7: Follow the SRV Record to the Flag
docs.text:
The non-standard SRV record from Step 6 points to a hostname. That hostname holds additional DNS records containing the flag. SRV records often serve as the first link in a chain; the record tells you where to look, and further queries at that location reveal the data.

Query the TXT record at the SRV target

Query the TXT record at the hostname referenced by the SRV entry you discovered in Step 6. Replace <target_hostname> with the target from the non-standard SRV record.

dig TXT <target_hostname> @dc01

The TXT record in the ANSWER SECTION contains the flag value. Read the quoted string in the response.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Target DNS Server: dc01

Query Target Host Port _kerberos._tcp ___ ______ _ldap._tcp ___ ______ _gc._tcp ___ ______ _secret._tcp ___ ______

Non-standard SRV target hostname: ___

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: OCR{_______________}

docs.title: Step 8: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for Exercise WS-3.1 is contained in the TXT record you queried in Step 7. The flag value is:

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does Active Directory create SRV records automatically during DC promotion?

Reveal Answer

Domain-joined clients need a way to locate DCs, Kerberos KDCs, and GC servers without hardcoding IP addresses. SRV records provide a standard DNS mechanism for service discovery. When a DC is promoted, the Netlogon service registers SRV records so clients can find the DC through standard DNS queries.

2. What is the security risk of non-standard SRV records in a production AD environment?

Reveal Answer

Non-standard SRV records expose the existence and location of services that may not be documented or monitored. An attacker who discovers a custom SRV entry gains knowledge of infrastructure that might be overlooked during security reviews. The SRV record itself does not grant access, but it directs the attacker to a target they would not have found through port scanning alone.

3. How do priority and weight values affect client behavior when multiple SRV records exist for the same service?

Reveal Answer

Clients prefer SRV records with lower priority values. When multiple records share the same priority, the weight value determines how traffic is distributed; higher-weight records receive more connections. Administrators use these fields to implement failover (priority) and load balancing (weight) across multiple servers.

4. What other non-standard SRV record names might an attacker look for in an AD environment?

Reveal Answer

Attackers commonly query for _sip._tcp (Voice over IP), _xmpp._tcp (messaging), _http._tcp (internal web apps), _ntp._udp (time servers), and any application-specific service names. Automated tools can brute-force common service names against the DNS server to build a full list.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SRV records map services to hosts: they provide the service name, protocol, port, priority, weight, and target server in a single DNS entry
  • Standard AD SRV records for _kerberos, _ldap, and _gc reveal every DC in the domain without port scanning
  • Non-standard SRV records expose custom or undocumented services that administrators may have forgotten about
  • SRV records can form chains: one record points to a hostname where additional records (TXT, A, CNAME) contain further information
  • DNS enumeration is prerequisite to network mapping: later exercises in this chapter build on the DNS data gathered here

docs.title: Exercise WS-3.2: DNS Conditional Forwarder Detection
Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise WS-3.1 demonstrated how SRV records reveal the internal services that Active Directory (AD) advertises. Exercise WS-3.2 shifts focus from internal service discovery to external relationships. DNS conditional forwarders are configured when an organization needs to resolve domain names belonging to a partner, subsidiary, or trusted domain. Detecting these forwarders exposes business relationships and potential trust paths that extend beyond the primary domain.

  • Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach dc01.
  • No credentials are needed; all queries in this exercise are unauthenticated DNS lookups.
  • You should be comfortable with dig syntax from Exercise WS-3.1.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your assessment of corp.ocr-range.lab continues. During SRV record enumeration, you mapped the internal AD services. Now your team lead wants to know whether dc01 resolves names for any domains outside corp.ocr-range.lab. Conditional forwarders configured on a Domain Controller (DC) indicate that the organization has a relationship with another domain; possibly a business partner, acquired company, or federated identity provider. Your task is to identify any conditional forwarders on dc01, query the forwarded zone, and determine what information the partner domain exposes.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Attempt a DNS zone transfer to enumerate all records in the corp.ocr-range.lab zone
  • Identify references to additional DNS zones that suggest conditional forwarders
  • Query the forwarded zone to confirm resolution through dc01
  • Retrieve the flag from a TXT record in the partner domain

docs.title: Background: DNS Conditional Forwarders
docs.text:
A standard DNS forwarder sends all unresolvable queries to a designated upstream server; typically an Internet Service Provider (ISP) or public DNS resolver. A conditional forwarder is more specific: it forwards queries for a particular domain to a designated DNS server, while all other queries follow the normal resolution path. Windows Server administrators configure conditional forwarders through the DNS Manager console or PowerShell.

Conditional forwarders serve a practical purpose. When two organizations establish a trust relationship, each domain needs to resolve the other's hostnames. Rather than creating a secondary zone or replicating DNS data, the administrator configures a conditional forwarder that sends queries for partner.local to the partner's DNS server. From the client's perspective, the resolution is transparent; they query their own DC, and the DC silently forwards the request.

From a security assessment perspective, conditional forwarders are valuable intelligence. Each forwarder reveals a domain that the organization communicates with. The forwarded domain may host shared applications, federated authentication endpoints, or trust relationships that extend access across organizational boundaries. An attacker who discovers a conditional forwarder gains a new target domain to investigate, and the forwarder itself may resolve records that the partner never intended to expose externally.

graph LR
    A["Client"]
    B["dc01<br/>(corp.ocr-range.lab)"]
    C["Partner DNS<br/>(partner.local)"]

    A -->|"Query:<br/>flag.partner.local?"| B
    B -->|"Conditional<br/>forward"| C
    C -->|"Answer:<br/>TXT record"| B
    B -->|"Response"| A

    style A fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff

The diagram shows the resolution flow. The client asks dc01 for a record in partner.local. Because dc01 has a conditional forwarder configured for that domain, dc01 queries the partner's DNS server and returns the result to the client. The client never communicates directly with the partner DNS server.

docs.title: Tool Primer: dig for Zone Transfers and Multi-Type Queries
docs.text:
Zone transfers replicate an entire DNS zone from server to client. The AXFR query type requests a full zone transfer. While many production DNS servers deny zone transfers to unauthorized clients, attempting one is a standard enumeration step because misconfigured servers will return every record in the zone.

Zone transfer syntax:

dig AXFR domain @nameserver

ANY query syntax:

The ANY query type asks the DNS server to return all record types for a given name. Some servers restrict ANY queries, but many respond with the full set of records.

dig ANY name @nameserver

Key flags for this exercise:

Option Purpose AXFR Request a full zone transfer ANY Request all record types for a name TXT Request TXT (text) records specifically +short Display only the answer data without extra sections +tcp Force DNS query over TCP (required for AXFR)

Sample zone transfer output (truncated):

corp.ocr-range.lab.     600  IN  SOA   dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab. ...
corp.ocr-range.lab.     600  IN  NS    dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab.
dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab. 600 IN  A     <dc01_ip>
_kerberos._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab. 600 IN SRV 0 100 88 dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab.

A successful zone transfer returns the Start of Authority (SOA) record, Name Server (NS) records, A records, SRV records, and any other entries in the zone. Look for hostnames or TXT records that reference other domains; these hints suggest conditional forwarders.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab and Verify DNS Access
docs.text:
Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 3, and launch Exercise WS-3.2. Wait for the environment status to show Running.

Confirm DNS access with an SOA query

Confirm you can query dc01's DNS service by asking for the zone's Start of Authority record. The +short flag keeps the response to a single line.

dig +short SOA corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The SOA record confirms dc01 is authoritative for the corp.ocr-range.lab zone. If the query returns no answer or times out, verify your VPN connection.

docs.title: Step 2: Attempt a Zone Transfer
docs.text:
A zone transfer returns every DNS record in a zone at once. Attempting an AXFR query against dc01 may or may not succeed; Windows DNS servers can be configured to allow or deny transfers. The attempt is worth making because a successful transfer provides a complete inventory of the zone.

Attempt a full zone transfer

Run the zone transfer. The AXFR query type requests every record in the zone at once, which a misconfigured server will return in full.

dig AXFR corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

If the transfer succeeds, you will see a list of all records in the corp.ocr-range.lab zone. Scan the output for any references to domains other than corp.ocr-range.lab. Hostnames, TXT records, or CNAME records that mention a different domain name are indicators of cross-domain relationships.

If the transfer fails with a "Transfer failed" message, dc01 is configured to deny AXFR requests. Proceed to Step 3 to use alternative discovery methods.

docs.title: Step 3: Probe for the Partner Domain
docs.text:
Conditional forwarders are not stored as DNS records within the primary zone; they are server-level configurations. However, references to the forwarded domain sometimes appear in TXT records, CNAME aliases, or documentation entries within the primary zone.

Probe for the forwarded partner domain

Examine the zone transfer output from Step 2 for any references to domains other than corp.ocr-range.lab; look for TXT records, CNAME aliases, or hostnames that mention a different domain name. If the zone transfer was denied, try probing common trust-related naming patterns such as partner, trust, or subsidiary-style domains (e.g., .local suffixes). Query any candidate domain through dc01 and replace <candidate_domain> with each guess.

dig ANY <candidate_domain> @dc01

If dc01 has a conditional forwarder configured for that domain, the query will succeed and return records from the forwarded zone. If no forwarder exists, the query will return NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) or SERVFAIL.

A successful response confirms the conditional forwarder. Note the record types and values returned; they reveal what the partner domain exposes through the forwarder.

docs.title: Step 4: Enumerate the Partner Domain
docs.text:
Now that you have confirmed the conditional forwarder, enumerate the partner domain further. Query specific record types to understand what the partner zone contains.

Identify the partner's authoritative server

Start with the SOA record to identify the partner's authoritative server. The query travels through dc01's conditional forwarder to the partner's DNS infrastructure.

dig +short SOA partner.local @dc01

The SOA answer names the partner's primary name server and confirms the forwarder is resolving the partner zone.

List the partner's name servers

Query for NS records to see which name servers the partner domain uses.

dig +short NS partner.local @dc01

These queries flow through dc01's conditional forwarder. Every response you receive is data from the partner's DNS infrastructure, resolved transparently through the forwarder. In a real engagement, the partner organization may not realize their DNS data is accessible through the trust relationship.

docs.title: Step 5: Understand the Security Implications
docs.text:
Conditional forwarders create a resolution path between two organizations. The security implications depend on what the partner domain exposes through DNS.

Consider the following scenarios that conditional forwarders enable:

graph TD
    A["Conditional Forwarder<br/>Detected"]
    B["Trust Relationship<br/>Exists"]
    C["Partner DNS Records<br/>Accessible"]
    D["Cross-Domain<br/>Enumeration"]
    E["Potential Lateral<br/>Movement Path"]

    A --> B
    A --> C
    C --> D
    B --> E

    style A fill:#e8a735,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style D fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff

A forwarder by itself does not grant authentication access. However, the existence of a forwarder strongly suggests a trust relationship; and trust relationships allow credential delegation across domain boundaries. The DNS path you discovered in Steps 3-4 may parallel an AD trust path that allows authentication from corp.ocr-range.lab to partner.local.

docs.title: Step 6: Query for Specific Records in the Partner Zone
docs.text:
With the conditional forwarder confirmed, search the partner domain for records that contain assessment-relevant data. TXT records are a common location for metadata, verification strings, and in lab environments, flags.

Query TXT records in the partner zone

Enumerate TXT records in the discovered partner zone. Try querying for common hostnames such as flag, info, or test within the partner domain, or attempt a zone transfer against the partner zone through dc01 to list all available records. Replace <hostname> and <partner_domain> with your candidates.

dig TXT <hostname>.<partner_domain> @dc01

The response should contain a TXT record with a quoted string value. Read the value carefully; the flag is embedded in the TXT record data.

Verify the TXT record with short output

You can also verify the record using the short output format, which is easier to copy.

dig +short TXT <hostname>.<partner_domain> @dc01

The short format strips away the extra sections and displays only the answer, making the TXT string easier to read.

docs.title: Step 7: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for Exercise WS-3.2 is contained in the TXT record at flag.partner.local, resolved through dc01's conditional forwarder. The flag value is:

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a standard DNS forwarder and a conditional forwarder?

Reveal Answer

A standard forwarder sends all unresolvable queries to a single upstream DNS server, regardless of domain. A conditional forwarder routes queries for a specific domain to a designated DNS server. Standard forwarders handle general resolution; conditional forwarders target specific domains based on organizational relationships.

2. Why would discovering a conditional forwarder matter during a penetration test?

Reveal Answer

A conditional forwarder reveals that the target organization has a relationship with another domain. The forwarded domain may be a business partner, subsidiary, or acquired company. The trust relationship behind the forwarder could allow cross-domain authentication, making the partner domain a potential lateral movement target. The forwarder also grants DNS-level visibility into the partner's infrastructure.

3. Can a conditional forwarder exist without an AD trust relationship?

Reveal Answer

Yes. A conditional forwarder only configures DNS name resolution; it does not create an AD trust. Administrators sometimes configure conditional forwarders for name resolution without establishing a trust. However, in practice, environments that need to resolve a partner domain often also need cross-domain authentication, so a trust relationship frequently accompanies the forwarder.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Zone transfers (AXFR) attempt to retrieve all records from a DNS zone and should always be tested during an assessment
  • Conditional forwarders route DNS queries for specific domains to designated servers, revealing cross-organizational relationships
  • Forwarders indicate trust paths: the DNS resolution path often parallels an AD trust relationship that enables cross-domain authentication
  • Partner domain records become accessible through the forwarder, exposing the partner's DNS data to anyone who can query the forwarding server
  • TXT records in forwarded zones may contain sensitive metadata, verification tokens, or configuration details that administrators assume are private

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercises WS-3.1 and WS-3.2 focused on DNS; querying SRV records and detecting conditional forwarders. Exercise WS-3.3 shifts to a different protocol: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP). While DNS tells you what services exist and where they live, DHCP reveals how the network itself is structured; address ranges, gateways, DNS servers, and custom options that administrators configure for client machines. Combining DHCP data with DNS findings produces a much richer picture of the environment.

  • Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach dc01.
  • No credentials are needed; DHCP discovery uses broadcast packets that any client on the network can send.
  • You should be comfortable running Nmap from a Linux terminal.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your team has mapped the DNS infrastructure of corp.ocr-range.lab across Exercises WS-3.1 and WS-3.2. The next task is to understand the network addressing layer. The Domain Controller dc01 also runs the DHCP server role; a common configuration in Windows Server environments. DHCP scopes define which IP ranges are assigned to clients, which gateways and DNS servers clients receive, and what custom options are pushed. Your objective is to enumerate the DHCP scope on dc01, identify its configuration, and examine custom DHCP options; particularly option 252, the Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD) URL, which has a well-documented history of abuse in man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Discover DHCP services running on dc01
  • Enumerate DHCP scope details including address range, subnet mask, gateway, and DNS servers
  • Identify custom DHCP options, particularly option 252 (WPAD)
  • Understand the security implications of WPAD in enterprise environments
  • Extract the flag from DHCP response data

docs.title: Background: DHCP in Active Directory Environments
docs.text:
DHCP assigns IP addresses and network configuration to clients automatically. When a client connects to a network, it sends a DHCP Discover broadcast. A DHCP server responds with an Offer containing an available IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, and any custom options the administrator has configured. The client then requests the offered configuration, and the server acknowledges the assignment.

In many AD environments, the Domain Controller runs the DHCP server role alongside DNS and AD Directory Services (AD DS). Hosting DHCP on the DC centralizes management but also means that the DC responds to DHCP queries from any client on the network segment. A penetration tester can send a DHCP Discover packet and receive the full scope configuration without authentication.

DHCP options extend the base configuration with additional parameters. Each option has a numeric code and a value. Some common options include:

Option Name Purpose 1 Subnet Mask Defines the network mask for the assigned IP 3 Router Default gateway address 6 DNS Servers DNS server addresses for name resolution 15 Domain Name DNS domain suffix for the client 252 WPAD URL URL for proxy auto-configuration script

Option 252 deserves special attention. WPAD allows clients to automatically discover a web proxy by fetching a configuration file from a URL pushed by DHCP. Attackers who can inject a malicious WPAD URL; through DHCP spoofing or DNS poisoning; can redirect all HTTP traffic through a proxy they control. Even when configured legitimately, the WPAD option reveals internal proxy infrastructure that may be vulnerable to attack.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Kali (Attacker)
    participant S as dc01 (DHCP Server)

    C->>S: DHCP Discover (broadcast)
    S->>C: DHCP Offer
    Note over C: Reads scope config:<br/>IP range, gateway,<br/>DNS, WPAD URL
    C->>S: DHCP Request
    S->>C: DHCP Acknowledge

The discovery process does not require the client to be domain-joined or authenticated. Any device on the network segment can send a DHCP Discover and receive the full scope configuration.

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap DHCP Discovery Scripts
docs.text:
Nmap includes Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) scripts specifically designed for DHCP enumeration. Two scripts are relevant for this exercise.

dhcp-discover script:

The dhcp-discover script sends a DHCP Discover packet to a specific host and displays the response, including all DHCP options.

nmap --script dhcp-discover -sU -p 67 <target>

broadcast-dhcp-discover script:

The broadcast-dhcp-discover script sends a broadcast DHCP Discover packet. Any DHCP server on the network segment will respond, making this useful for discovering unknown DHCP servers.

nmap --script broadcast-dhcp-discover

Key flags:

Flag Purpose --script dhcp-discover Targeted DHCP query to a specific server --script broadcast-dhcp-discover Broadcast DHCP discovery on the local segment -sU UDP scan (DHCP uses UDP) -p 67 Target DHCP server port (67/UDP)

Sample output:

PORT   STATE SERVICE
67/udp open  dhcps
| dhcp-discover:
|   DHCP Message Type: DHCPACK
|   Server Identifier: <dc01_ip>
|   IP Address Lease Time: 8d00h00m00s
|   Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0
|   Router: <gateway_ip>
|   Domain Name Server: <dc01_ip>
|   Domain Name: corp.ocr-range.lab
|   WPAD: http://wpad.corp.ocr-range.lab/wpad.dat

The output reveals the full DHCP configuration in a readable format. Each line corresponds to a DHCP option and its value. The WPAD entry shows the proxy auto-configuration URL pushed to all clients.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab and Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 3, and launch Exercise WS-3.3. Wait for the environment status to show Running.

Verify connectivity to dc01

Verify you can reach dc01 with a short ping. The -c 3 flag sends three packets and then exits.

ping -c 3 dc01

You should see replies confirming network connectivity. If the ping times out, check your VPN connection.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm DHCP Service on dc01
docs.text:
Before enumerating DHCP options, confirm that dc01 is running a DHCP server. DHCP servers listen on UDP port 67. A targeted UDP scan reveals whether the port is open.

Scan for the DHCP port on dc01

Run a UDP scan against port 67 to confirm dc01 is listening for DHCP. The -sU flag selects a UDP scan and -p 67 limits it to the DHCP server port.

nmap -sU -p 67 dc01

The output should show port 67/udp as open. UDP scanning is inherently less reliable than TCP scanning because UDP does not use a three-way handshake; an open port may appear as open|filtered if no response is received. The DHCP discovery scripts in the next steps will confirm the service definitively by eliciting an actual DHCP response.

docs.title: Step 3: Run DHCP Discovery Against dc01
docs.text:
With the DHCP port confirmed, run the dhcp-discover NSE script to retrieve the full scope configuration from dc01.

Run targeted DHCP discovery against dc01

Execute the targeted DHCP discovery. The dhcp-discover NSE script sends a DHCP Discover packet to dc01 and prints every option the server returns.

nmap --script dhcp-discover -sU -p 67 dc01

Examine the output carefully. The script sends a DHCP Discover packet directly to dc01 and displays the server's response. Look for the following fields in the output:

  • Server Identifier: The IP address of the DHCP server (should match dc01)
  • Subnet Mask: Defines the size of the network (e.g., 255.255.255.0 for a /24)
  • Router: The default gateway clients will use
  • Domain Name Server: The DNS server(s) pushed to clients
  • Domain Name: The DNS suffix for the domain
  • WPAD: The Web Proxy Auto-Discovery URL (option 252)

Record each value. Together, these fields describe the network architecture that every client on the subnet receives automatically.

docs.title: Step 4: Run Broadcast DHCP Discovery
docs.text:
The broadcast method discovers all DHCP servers on the network segment, not a single target. Running both targeted and broadcast discovery ensures you do not miss rogue DHCP servers.

Run broadcast DHCP discovery

Execute the broadcast discovery. The broadcast-dhcp-discover script sends its DHCP Discover to the whole segment, so any DHCP server present replies.

nmap --script broadcast-dhcp-discover

Compare the results with the targeted discovery from Step 3. The responding server should be dc01. If additional DHCP servers respond, note their IP addresses; rogue DHCP servers are a serious security concern in any network.

The broadcast script does not require a target IP because the DHCP Discover packet is sent to the broadcast address (255.255.255.255). Every DHCP server on the local segment will respond.

docs.title: Step 5: Analyze the WPAD Option
docs.text:
Option 252 (WPAD) pushes a URL to clients that points to a Proxy Auto-Configuration (PAC) file. When a client receives the WPAD URL through DHCP, the operating system's proxy settings automatically fetch the PAC file and configure web traffic routing.

Review the WPAD value from your DHCP discovery output. The URL typically follows the format:

http://wpad.corp.ocr-range.lab/wpad.dat

The security implications of WPAD are significant:

graph TD
    A["DHCP Pushes<br/>WPAD URL"]
    B["Client Fetches<br/>wpad.dat"]
    C["Legitimate Proxy<br/>Configured"]
    D["Attacker Spoofs<br/>WPAD URL"]
    E["Traffic Routed<br/>Through Attacker"]

    A --> B
    B --> C
    D --> B
    B --> E

    style A fill:#e8a735,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff

An attacker who can respond to DHCP requests (through ARP spoofing or a rogue DHCP server) can push a malicious WPAD URL. Clients that trust the DHCP response will route their HTTP traffic through the attacker's proxy, enabling credential interception and content manipulation. Tools like Responder exploit WPAD poisoning as a primary attack vector in Windows networks.

docs.title: Step 6: Map the Network from DHCP Data
docs.text:
The DHCP response provides enough information to sketch the network topology for the subnet. Combine the scope data into a network summary.

Use the values from your DHCP discovery to fill in the network map:

graph TD
    A["Network Subnet<br/>(from DHCP scope)"]
    B["Gateway"]
    C["DNS / DHCP / DC<br/>dc01"]
    D["Client Range<br/>(from DHCP scope)"]
    E["WPAD Proxy<br/>(from option 252)"]

    A --- B
    A --- C
    A --- D
    C --- E

    style A fill:#888,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff

The gateway address, DNS server, and DHCP server identify the core infrastructure. The client range defines where workstations and other devices receive addresses. The WPAD URL identifies proxy infrastructure. All of this data was obtained without credentials.

docs.title: Step 7: Examine the Flag in the DHCP Response
docs.text:
The flag for Exercise WS-3.3 is embedded in the DHCP response data. Review your output from Step 3 carefully. The flag value appears in the DHCP options; look at the WPAD option (option 252) or other custom options in the response.

Re-run discovery to inspect the flag

If you need to see the raw DHCP response again, rerun the discovery and read every option value the server returns.

nmap --script dhcp-discover -sU -p 67 dc01

Scan all option values in the output. The flag follows the OCR{...} format and appears as a value within one of the DHCP options.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is hosting DHCP on the Domain Controller a common but risky configuration?

Reveal Answer

Hosting DHCP on the DC centralizes network management and reduces the number of servers to maintain. The risk is that a compromise of the DC also compromises DHCP, allowing the attacker to push malicious configurations; rogue DNS servers, WPAD URLs, or incorrect gateways; to every client on the network. Separating roles limits the blast radius of a single server compromise.

2. How can an attacker abuse the WPAD option in a DHCP response?

Reveal Answer

An attacker who controls DHCP responses (through a rogue server or spoofing) can push a WPAD URL pointing to a malicious PAC file. Clients that auto-configure proxy settings will route HTTP traffic through the attacker's proxy. The attacker can then intercept credentials transmitted over HTTP, inject content into web pages, or redirect users to phishing sites. Tools like Responder automate WPAD poisoning in Windows environments.

3. What defenses can an organization deploy against DHCP-based attacks?

Reveal Answer

DHCP snooping on network switches restricts DHCP responses to trusted ports, preventing rogue servers from responding. Disabling WPAD through Group Policy removes the auto-configuration vector. 802.1X port-based authentication ensures only authorized devices receive network access. Monitoring DHCP logs for unexpected scope changes or option modifications provides detection capability.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• DHCP scopes reveal network architecture: address ranges, gateways, DNS servers, and domain suffixes are all visible without authentication
  • Nmap NSE scripts for DHCP discovery (dhcp-discover and broadcast-dhcp-discover) extract the full scope configuration from a DHCP server
  • Option 252 (WPAD) pushes proxy auto-configuration URLs to clients and is a well-known vector for MITM attacks
  • Broadcast DHCP discovery detects rogue DHCP servers that targeted scans would miss
  • DHCP data complements DNS findings: combining scope information with SRV records and conditional forwarders builds a complete network map

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercises WS-3.1 through WS-3.3 each focused on a single protocol; DNS SRV records, conditional forwarders, and DHCP scopes. Exercise WS-3.4 brings these data sources together. Network topology mapping is the practice of correlating findings from multiple protocols to build a complete picture of an environment. A DNS record alone tells you a hostname exists. A DHCP scope alone tells you an address range is in use. Combined with Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) computer objects, these fragments form a map that reveals the full network architecture.

  • Confirm your VPN connection is active and you can reach dc01.
  • LDAP anonymous bind must be available on dc01 for the user attribute query in the second half of this exercise.
  • You should be comfortable with dig, nmap, and ldapsearch from previous exercises.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Your assessment of corp.ocr-range.lab is nearing completion. You have enumerated DNS SRV records, discovered a conditional forwarder to partner.local, and extracted DHCP scope data. Your team lead wants a consolidated network topology that correlates all findings. The final deliverable requires combining DNS hostnames, DHCP addressing, and LDAP computer objects into a single view. A two-part flag validates your work: the first part comes from a DNS TXT record, and the second part comes from an LDAP user attribute. Assembling the complete flag demonstrates your ability to correlate data across protocols.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Correlate DNS records with LDAP computer objects to identify all hosts in the domain
  • Map the DHCP scope to the discovered hosts
  • Build a network topology diagram from combined data sources
  • Retrieve Part 1 of the flag from a DNS TXT record
  • Retrieve Part 2 of the flag from an LDAP user attribute
  • Assemble the complete multi-part flag

docs.title: Background: Cross-Protocol Correlation
docs.text:
No single protocol provides a complete view of an Active Directory (AD) environment. DNS contains SRV records and hostname-to-IP mappings, but DNS does not know which machines are domain-joined or what roles they serve. LDAP stores computer objects with attributes like operating system, organizational unit (OU) placement, and service principal names (SPNs), but LDAP does not reveal network addressing. DHCP defines address ranges and network parameters, but DHCP does not know hostnames or domain roles.

Effective network mapping requires layering these data sources. Start with DNS to build a list of hostnames and their IP addresses. Add LDAP computer objects to confirm which machines are domain-joined and what operating systems they run. Overlay the DHCP scope to understand which addresses are dynamically assigned versus statically configured. The result is a topology that shows what exists and how the network is organized.

In penetration testing, cross-protocol correlation reveals inconsistencies that attackers exploit. A computer object in LDAP with no corresponding DNS record may be a decommissioned machine that was never removed from the directory. A DHCP reservation for a hostname not found in DNS may indicate a device that bypasses normal name resolution. A DNS A record pointing to an address outside the DHCP scope may be a server with a static IP that the DHCP scope does not manage. Each inconsistency is a potential finding worth investigating.

graph TD
    A["DNS Records"]
    B["LDAP Objects"]
    C["DHCP Scope"]
    D["Correlated<br/>Topology Map"]

    A -->|"Hostnames<br/>+ IPs"| D
    B -->|"Computer Objects<br/>+ OS Info"| D
    C -->|"Address Ranges<br/>+ Options"| D

    style A fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style D fill:#888,stroke:#333,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch for Computer and User Queries
docs.text:
The ldapsearch command queries LDAP directories from the command line. For topology mapping, you will query both computer objects and user objects. Computer objects live in the default CN=Computers container or in custom OUs. User objects used for flag storage may reside in a dedicated Flags OU.

Syntax for computer enumeration:

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=computer)" cn operatingSystem dNSHostName

Syntax for user attribute query:

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(cn=topo.flag)" info

Key flags:

Flag Purpose -x Use simple authentication (anonymous bind) -H Specify the LDAP server URI -b Set the search base Distinguished Name (DN) (filter) LDAP search filter to match specific objects

Sample computer object output:

dn: CN=DC01,OU=Domain Controllers,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
cn: DC01
operatingSystem: Windows Server 2022 Standard
dNSHostName: dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab

Each computer object contains the hostname (cn), operating system, and DNS hostname. Cross-referencing dNSHostName with DNS A records confirms the machine's IP address.

Sample user attribute output:

dn: CN=topo.flag,OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
cn: topo.flag
info: <flag_part>

The info attribute on user objects stores a freeform string. In this exercise, the Flags OU contains a user object whose info attribute holds the second part of the flag.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab and Verify Access
docs.text:
Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 3, and launch Exercise WS-3.4. Wait for the environment status to show Running.

Verify DNS, LDAP, and network access

Verify all three data sources respond before you start mapping. The three commands confirm DNS resolution, anonymous LDAP bind, and basic reachability in turn.

dig +short A dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "" -s base namingContexts
ping -c 2 dc01

The dig query should return dc01's IP address. The ldapsearch query should return the naming contexts, confirming anonymous LDAP access. The ping confirms basic connectivity. If any of these fail, check your VPN connection before continuing.

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate DNS A Records
docs.text:
DNS A records map hostnames to IP addresses. Querying for A records across the corp.ocr-range.lab zone builds the hostname layer of your topology.

Attempt a zone transfer for all A records

Attempt a zone transfer to get all records at once. The AXFR query type returns the entire zone when the server permits it.

dig AXFR corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

If the zone transfer succeeds, extract all A records from the output.

Query individual A records if the transfer is denied

If the transfer is denied, query for known hostnames individually and repeat for each name you suspect exists.

dig +short A dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

Record every hostname-to-IP mapping you discover. These become the nodes in your topology diagram.

docs.title: Step 3: Enumerate LDAP Computer Objects
docs.text:
LDAP computer objects represent domain-joined machines. Querying for all computer objects reveals machines that DNS may not list; such as workstations that were joined to the domain but never received a DNS A record.

Enumerate LDAP computer objects

Run the computer object query. The -x flag uses an anonymous bind, and the (objectClass=computer) filter returns only machine accounts.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=computer)" cn operatingSystem dNSHostName

The output lists every computer object in the domain. For each entry, note the cn (common name), operatingSystem, and dNSHostName attributes. Compare the dNSHostName values with the DNS A records from Step 2.

Machines that appear in LDAP but not in DNS may have been removed from DNS but not from the directory. Machines in DNS but not in LDAP may be non-domain-joined devices with static DNS entries.

docs.title: Step 4: Review DHCP Scope Data
docs.text:
Retrieve the DHCP scope data

If you completed Exercise WS-3.3, you already have the DHCP scope data. Retrieve it again if needed with the same dhcp-discover NSE script.

nmap --script dhcp-discover -sU -p 67 dc01

From the DHCP response, record:

  • Subnet and mask: defines the address range for the network segment
  • Gateway: the default route for all clients
  • DNS server: should match dc01's IP address
  • Domain name: should match corp.ocr-range.lab

Compare the DHCP address range with the IP addresses you found in DNS A records. Addresses within the DHCP scope are likely dynamically assigned to workstations. Addresses outside the scope (but within the same subnet) are likely statically assigned to servers.

docs.title: Step 5: Build the Correlated Topology
docs.text:
Combine your findings from DNS, LDAP, and DHCP into a single topology view. The goal is a map that shows every discovered host, its IP address, its role, and whether it uses static or dynamic addressing.

Use the following template to organize your data:

Hostname IP Address Source(s) OS / Role Addressing dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab ____ DNS, LDAP, DHCP Windows Server 2022 DC Static (additional hosts) ____ _____ _____ ____

Hosts that appear in all three sources are well-documented infrastructure. Hosts that appear in only one source are anomalies worth investigating.

graph TD
    subgraph Network ["corp.ocr-range.lab"]
        A["dc01<br/>DNS + LDAP + DHCP<br/>Windows Server 2022"]
        B["Gateway<br/>(from DHCP)"]
        C["DHCP Client Range<br/>(dynamic addresses)"]
        D["Partner Domain<br/>(conditional fwd)"]
    end

    B --- A
    A --- C
    A -.->|"DNS forwarder"| D

    style A fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,stroke:#333,color:#fff

The topology above is a simplified example. Your version should include every host you discovered, with connections showing which services each host provides.

docs.title: Step 6: Retrieve Flag Part 1 from DNS
docs.text:
Query the topology TXT record

The first part of the flag is stored in a DNS TXT record. TXT records often contain metadata, verification strings, or documentation notes. Search for topology-related TXT records by reviewing the zone transfer output from Step 2 for TXT entries, or probe common naming patterns related to topology (e.g., prefixes like _topo, _map, or _net). Replace <record_name> with each candidate.

dig TXT <record_name>.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The ANSWER SECTION contains a quoted string. Record the value; the string is the first half of the flag.

Confirm the TXT value with short output

You can also use the short format for a cleaner view of the same record.

dig +short TXT _topo1.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The response should return a quoted string value. Note the exact value including any special characters.

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve Flag Part 2 from LDAP
docs.text:
The second part of the flag is stored in an LDAP user object's info attribute. The user topo.flag exists in the Flags OU within the domain directory. Querying this user object requires an LDAP search with the correct base DN and filter.

Enumerate the Flags OU for user objects

Enumerate the Flags OU in the domain directory and look for user objects with interesting attributes. Start by listing all user objects in the Flags OU, requesting the cn and info attributes.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=user)" cn info

Review the results for user objects whose names relate to topology or mapping. Once you identify the relevant user object, examine its info attribute; the second half of the flag lives there.

Broaden the search to the whole domain

If the query returns no results, broaden the search base to the entire domain rather than a single OU.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=user)" cn info

The broader search base looks across the entire domain rather than a specific OU. The info attribute should return the second part of the flag.

docs.title: Step 8: Assemble the Complete Flag
docs.text:
The full flag combines Part 1 (from DNS) and Part 2 (from LDAP). Concatenate the two values inside the OCR{...} wrapper.

  • Part 1 (DNS TXT): The value from the TXT record query in Step 6
  • Part 2 (LDAP info): The value from the LDAP query in Step 7
  • Complete flag: OCR{<part1><part2>}

The multi-part flag structure demonstrates the core principle of this exercise: no single protocol provides the complete answer. Correlating DNS and LDAP data produces information that neither source contains alone.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
DNS Hosts Discovered: | Hostname | IP Address | |----------|------------| | _ | _ | | _ | _ |

LDAP Computer Objects: | CN | Operating System | dNSHostName | |----------|---------------------|-------------| | _ | ___ | ___ | | _ | ___ | ___ |

DHCP Scope Summary: | Field | Value | |---------------|--------------| | Subnet | __ | | Gateway | _ | | DNS Server | ___ | | Domain | ______ |

Hosts in DNS but not LDAP: ___

Hosts in LDAP but not DNS: ___

Flag Part 1 (DNS): ___

Flag Part 2 (LDAP): ___

Complete Flag: OCR{_______________}

docs.title: Step 9: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
The complete flag for Exercise WS-3.4, assembled from DNS and LDAP sources, is:

The flag follows the standard OCR{...} format. Submit it on the platform to complete the exercise.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is cross-protocol correlation more valuable than querying a single data source?

Reveal Answer

Each protocol reveals different aspects of the environment. DNS provides hostname-to-IP mappings and service locations. LDAP provides computer object details, OS versions, and organizational structure. DHCP provides network addressing and configuration. Correlating all three produces a topology that no single source can provide alone. Inconsistencies between sources; such as a computer in LDAP with no DNS record; often point to misconfigurations or decommissioned systems that were not fully cleaned up.

2. What does a computer object in LDAP without a corresponding DNS A record suggest?

Reveal Answer

The computer account may belong to a machine that was decommissioned but never removed from the directory. Stale computer accounts retain their passwords and SPNs in AD. An attacker who can reset or impersonate a stale computer account may gain access to the domain with that machine's identity. AD hygiene policies should regularly audit and remove inactive computer accounts.

3. How would you extend this methodology to a multi-site AD environment?

Reveal Answer

Multi-site AD environments contain site-specific SRV records under _tcp.<site-name>._sites. subdomains. Querying these reveals which DCs serve each site. DHCP scopes differ per subnet, so each site has its own address range and gateway. LDAP site objects under CN=Sites,CN=Configuration describe the site topology and subnet-to-site mappings. Correlating all of these across sites produces a complete enterprise topology.

4. What LDAP attributes on computer objects are most useful for topology mapping?

Reveal Answer

The dNSHostName attribute links the LDAP object to its DNS name. The operatingSystem and operatingSystemVersion attributes identify the OS. The servicePrincipalName (SPN) attribute reveals what services the machine hosts (e.g., HTTP, MSSQL, Exchange). The whenCreated and lastLogonTimestamp attributes indicate whether the machine is active. The managedBy attribute may link the machine to a responsible user or group.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Cross-protocol correlation combines DNS, LDAP, and DHCP data into a topology that no single source can provide
  • Inconsistencies between sources reveal decommissioned systems, misconfigurations, and shadow IT that attackers exploit
  • DNS provides hostnames and service locations, LDAP provides computer objects and organizational context, and DHCP provides network addressing
  • Multi-part flags mirror real-world assessments where complete findings require data from multiple sources
  • Topology mapping is a deliverable: clients expect penetration test reports to include network diagrams built from correlated evidence, not assumptions

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Across four labs, you built a network service mapping methodology that goes beyond individual protocol queries to produce a correlated view of an Active Directory (AD) environment. Each lab added a new data source and a new perspective on the corp.ocr-range.lab infrastructure.

You started by querying DNS SRV records to discover the standard services AD advertises; Kerberos, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), and Global Catalog (GC). Following a non-standard SRV record to its target revealed infrastructure that port scanning would never find. Conditional forwarder detection exposed a trust relationship with a partner domain, showing that DNS configuration leaks organizational relationships. DHCP scope enumeration revealed network addressing, gateways, and the WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) option that creates man-in-the-middle attack opportunities. The final lab tied everything together by correlating DNS, DHCP, and LDAP data into a topology map. Thorough assessment requires multi-protocol analysis.

The corp.ocr-range.lab assessment demonstrated a methodology that applies to any Windows Server environment. Real penetration tests follow the same progression: enumerate DNS infrastructure, check for cross-domain relationships, profile network addressing, and correlate findings across protocols. The tools change as environments grow in complexity, but the approach remains consistent.

docs.text:
graph LR

    B["WS-3.2<br/>Cond. Forwarders"]

docs.title: Key Concepts Revisited
docs.text:
• SRV records: DNS Service Location records that map a service name to a host, port, priority, and weight. AD creates SRV records automatically for Kerberos, LDAP, and GC. Non-standard SRV records reveal custom or undocumented services.
  • Conditional forwarders: DNS server configurations that route queries for a specific domain to a designated external DNS server. Each forwarder indicates an organizational relationship and a potential trust path.
  • Zone transfers (AXFR): Requests for a complete copy of a DNS zone. Successful transfers provide every record in the zone. Denied transfers indicate the server restricts replication to authorized recipients.
  • DHCP scopes: Address ranges and configuration options that a DHCP server distributes to clients. Scopes reveal subnets, gateways, DNS servers, and custom options like WPAD.
  • WPAD (option 252): A DHCP option that pushes a proxy auto-configuration URL to clients. Historically abused for man-in-the-middle attacks through DHCP spoofing or DNS poisoning.
  • Cross-protocol correlation: Combining data from DNS, LDAP, and DHCP to build a topology map. Inconsistencies between sources reveal misconfigurations, stale objects, and shadow infrastructure.

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer each question from memory before checking the answer key at the bottom of the page.

1. What three standard SRV record types does Active Directory create for every Domain Controller?

2. What DNS query type requests a full copy of all records in a zone?

3. What is the difference between a standard DNS forwarder and a conditional forwarder?

4. What UDP port does the DHCP server listen on?

5. What DHCP option number corresponds to the WPAD URL?

6. Name the two Nmap NSE scripts used for DHCP enumeration in Exercise WS-3.3.

7. What LDAP attribute on a computer object links it to its DNS hostname?

8. Why is a computer object in LDAP with no corresponding DNS A record a security concern?

9. What dig flag displays only the answer data without extra sections?

10. What ldapsearch flag enables anonymous bind (simple authentication)?

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
The following table summarizes the key commands used across all four labs in this chapter. Use it as a quick reference during assessments or when reviewing for exams.

Command Purpose dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.domain @ns Query Kerberos SRV records dig SRV _ldap._tcp.domain @ns Query LDAP SRV records dig SRV _gc._tcp.domain @ns Query Global Catalog SRV records dig AXFR domain @ns Attempt a full DNS zone transfer dig ANY name @ns Query all record types for a name dig TXT name @ns Query TXT records for a name dig +short TXT name @ns Query TXT records (answer only) nmap -sU -p 67 target Scan for DHCP server on UDP port 67 nmap --script dhcp-discover -sU -p 67 target Targeted DHCP scope enumeration nmap --script broadcast-dhcp-discover Broadcast DHCP discovery on local segment ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc -b "base" "(filter)" attrs LDAP query with anonymous bind ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc -b "base" "(objectClass=computer)" cn dNSHostName Enumerate computer objects

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text:
You now know how to map network infrastructure by correlating DNS, DHCP, and LDAP data. The next chapter; CH_WS04: builds on this foundation by moving from passive mapping to active exploitation of the services you discovered. Understanding where services live and how the network is structured is the prerequisite for targeting those services effectively.

The DNS SRV records you enumerated in WS-3.1 point to the exact hosts and ports where Kerberos and LDAP accept connections. The conditional forwarder you discovered in WS-3.2 identifies a trust path to a partner domain. The DHCP scope from WS-3.3 defines the network addressing that every client receives. All of this data becomes targeting information when you shift from reconnaissance to exploitation.

Consider reviewing the command cheat sheet above until you can recall each command and its purpose without looking. Fluency with network mapping tools allows you to focus on analysis rather than syntax during time-limited assessments.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. Active Directory creates SRV records for _kerberos._tcp (Kerberos authentication on port 88), _ldap._tcp (LDAP directory services on port 389), and _gc._tcp (Global Catalog on port 3268).

2. The AXFR query type requests a full zone transfer, returning every record in the DNS zone.

3. A standard forwarder sends all unresolvable queries to a single upstream DNS server. A conditional forwarder routes queries for a specific domain to a designated server, leaving other queries to follow the normal resolution path.

4. The DHCP server listens on UDP port 67. DHCP clients send requests from UDP port 68.

5. Option 252 is the WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) URL that pushes a proxy auto-configuration script to clients.

6. The dhcp-discover script sends a targeted DHCP query to a specific server. The broadcast-dhcp-discover script sends a broadcast to discover all DHCP servers on the local network segment.

7. The dNSHostName attribute on a computer object contains the fully qualified DNS hostname, linking the LDAP object to its DNS A record.

8. A computer object without a DNS A record may represent a decommissioned machine that was never removed from the directory. Stale computer accounts retain passwords and Service Principal Names (SPNs) in AD. An attacker who can impersonate or reset a stale account may gain domain access with that machine's identity.

9. The +short flag causes dig to display only the answer data without the question, authority, or additional sections.

10. The -x flag enables simple authentication, which allows anonymous bind when no credentials are provided.

docs.title: The Shift from Anonymous to Authenticated Access
docs.text:
Previous chapters focused on what an unauthenticated attacker can see: open ports, DNS records, anonymous LDAP queries, and null-session SMB shares. Those techniques reveal the outline of an Active Directory (AD) environment, but they leave most of the directory hidden behind authentication barriers. Authenticated enumeration changes the equation entirely.

A single set of low-privilege domain credentials unlocks a vast amount of information that anonymous access cannot reach. Domain users can list every share on a file server, read Group Policy Object (GPO) templates stored on SYSVOL, query Service Principal Names (SPNs) registered in the directory, and inspect Discretionary Access Control Lists (DACLs) on AD objects. None of these actions require administrative privileges; any authenticated domain user can perform them by default.

docs.title: Why Low-Privilege Credentials Matter
docs.text:
In real-world engagements, attackers obtain low-privilege credentials through many paths: password spraying, credential stuffing, phishing, or discovering hardcoded passwords in scripts and configuration files. The guest.user account used throughout this chapter represents exactly that scenario; a basic domain account with no special group memberships or administrative rights.

The power of authenticated enumeration lies in what Active Directory shares with every domain member by design. Microsoft built AD to be readable by authenticated users so that workstations, applications, and services can function properly. Group policies must be readable so machines can apply them. SPNs must be queryable so Kerberos authentication works. DACLs must be accessible so the operating system can enforce permissions. Penetration testers and attackers take advantage of these design decisions to map the entire domain from a single compromised account.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Authenticate to SMB shares using domain credentials and compare results against anonymous access
  • Navigate the SYSVOL share to read GPO templates, scripts, and policy settings
  • Query LDAP for accounts with registered SPNs and assess Kerberoasting attack surface
  • Analyze AD object permissions to identify weak DACLs that create privilege escalation paths

docs.title: Credentials for All Exercises
docs.text:
Every exercise in this chapter uses the same domain account. The guest.user account was discovered through LDAP enumeration in earlier chapters and represents a low-privilege foothold in the corp.ocr-range.lab domain.

Field Value Username guest.user Password Guest2024# Domain corp.ocr-range.lab Target DC dc01

docs.text:
The four exercises in this chapter follow a logical progression through authenticated AD enumeration techniques. Each exercise builds on the access established by the credentials above, exploring a different category of information that domain authentication unlocks.

docs.text:
Authenticated enumeration sits between initial access and privilege escalation in a typical penetration test. The diagram below shows where this chapter fits within the broader Windows Server attack path.

graph TD

    B --> C["Credential Discovery"]
