The information gathered in this chapter directly feeds later attack stages. Share contents may reveal credentials or sensitive data. GPO templates may contain scheduled task passwords or logon scripts worth hijacking. SPN accounts become Kerberoasting targets whose password hashes can be cracked offline. Weak DACLs become privilege escalation paths that let a low-privilege user modify high-value objects.

docs.title: Exercise Progression
docs.text:
Each exercise targets dc01 in the corp.ocr-range.lab domain and uses the guest.user credentials above. The exercises are designed to be completed in order, though each can stand alone.

Exercise Title Duration Focus WS-4.1 Authenticated Share Enumeration 45 min SMB shares visible only to domain users WS-4.2 Group Policy Object Enumeration 60 min SYSVOL, GPO templates, and policy settings WS-4.3 Service Principal Name Discovery 45 min SPN accounts and Kerberoasting surface WS-4.4 AD ACL Weak Permission Discovery 60 min DACLs, object permissions, and escalation paths

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
The exercises in this chapter rely on tools already installed on your Kali Linux attack machine. No additional software installation is required.

Tool Purpose smbclient SMB share listing, file browsing, and file retrieval ldapsearch LDAP queries for GPOs, SPNs, and ACL-related objects

Both tools support authenticated access using the -U 'user%password' syntax (smbclient) or -D "user@domain" -w "password" syntax (ldapsearch). You will see these authentication flags in every command throughout the chapter.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: In previous chapters, you explored Server Message Block (SMB) shares using anonymous and null-session access. Those techniques revealed publicly accessible shares, but many shares on a domain controller are hidden from unauthenticated users. Authenticated share enumeration uses valid domain credentials to reveal the full list of shares and access files that require domain membership.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: During earlier LDAP enumeration of the corp.ocr-range.lab domain, you discovered the guest.user account. You have confirmed the password Guest2024# through credential testing. Your task is to authenticate to the domain controller dc01 and enumerate all available SMB shares. Comparing authenticated results against anonymous results will demonstrate the gap between what unauthenticated attackers see and what a domain user can access.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Authenticate to SMB on dc01 using the guest.user domain credentials
  • List all shares visible to an authenticated domain user, including hidden administrative shares
  • Compare the authenticated share list against an anonymous (unauthenticated) share list
  • Browse and retrieve files from shares that require domain authentication
  • Locate and submit the flag from a restricted share

docs.title: Background: Anonymous vs. Authenticated SMB Access
docs.text:
SMB share visibility depends on the caller's authentication level. Windows Server exposes different sets of shares depending on whether the connection is anonymous, authenticated as a regular user, or authenticated as an administrator. Understanding these access tiers is essential for thorough SMB enumeration.

The table below summarizes what each access level typically reveals on a Windows domain controller:

Access Level Shares Visible File Access Anonymous (no creds) IPC$, sometimes a few public shares Minimal; usually limited to IPC$ Authenticated (domain user) NETLOGON, SYSVOL, all custom shares, hidden shares Full read access to non-admin shares Administrative (Domain Admin) All shares including C$, ADMIN$ Full read/write to everything

Hidden shares are shares whose names end with a dollar sign ($). Windows creates several hidden administrative shares by default (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$). Administrators can also create custom hidden shares. Anonymous connections typically cannot even see these shares in a listing, but authenticated users can see them and may have read access depending on the share permissions.

The NETLOGON and SYSVOL shares are special shares that exist on every domain controller. NETLOGON stores logon scripts, and SYSVOL stores Group Policy templates. Both are readable by any authenticated domain user; a design requirement for domain-joined machines to function.

graph TD
    A["SMB Connection"] --> B{"Authenticated?"}
    B -->|"No"| C["Anonymous Share List<br/>IPC$, limited shares"]
    B -->|"Yes"| D{"Admin Privileges?"}
    D -->|"No"| E["Domain User Share List<br/>NETLOGON, SYSVOL,<br/>custom shares"]
    D -->|"Yes"| F["Full Share List<br/>C$, ADMIN$, all shares"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#888,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style E fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e8a735,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: smbclient with Authentication
docs.text:
The smbclient tool supports authenticated connections through the -U flag. Credentials can be supplied in username%password format to avoid interactive password prompts, which is useful for scripting and documentation.

Authenticated share listing:

smbclient -L dc01 -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#'

Anonymous share listing (for comparison):

smbclient -L dc01 -N

Connecting to a specific share:

smbclient //dc01/ShareName -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#'

Running a single command without entering the interactive shell:

smbclient //dc01/ShareName -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'ls'

The key flags used in this exercise serve the following purposes:

Flag Purpose -L List shares on the specified host -U 'user%pass' Authenticate with the given username and password -N Suppress password prompt (anonymous/null session) -c 'command' Execute a single command and exit

When using the -c flag, you can chain multiple commands separated by semicolons. Common smbclient commands include ls (list files), cd (change directory), get (download a file), and cat (display file contents). The special syntax get filename - prints file contents to standard output instead of saving to disk.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab
docs.text:
Open the Open Cyber Range platform in your browser and start the lab environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 4
  • Click Launch on "Authenticated Share Enumeration"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: List Shares with Anonymous Access
docs.text:
List shares with anonymous access

Before using credentials, establish a baseline by listing shares without authentication. The -N flag suppresses the password prompt so the connection runs as a null session.

smbclient -L dc01 -N

Record the shares that appear in the output. Pay attention to which shares are listed and note any "ACCESS_DENIED" or "NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED" messages. Anonymous access on a hardened domain controller typically shows very few shares.

Expected output (approximate):

Anonymous login successful

    Sharename       Type      Comment
    ---------       ----      -------
    IPC$            IPC       Remote IPC

The anonymous listing may show only IPC$ or a small set of public shares. Keep this result for comparison in the next step.

docs.title: Step 3: List Shares with Authenticated Access
docs.text:
List shares with authenticated access

Now authenticate as guest.user and list shares again. The -U 'user%pass' syntax supplies the domain credentials inline so no interactive prompt appears.

smbclient -L dc01 -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#'

The authenticated listing should return significantly more shares than the anonymous listing. Compare the two results side by side.

Expected output (approximate):

    Sharename       Type      Comment
    ---------       ----      -------
    ADMIN$          Disk      Remote Admin
    C$              Disk      Default share
    IPC$            IPC       Remote IPC
    IT-Tools        Disk
    NETLOGON        Disk      Logon server share
    SYSVOL          Disk      Logon server share

Several shares that were invisible to the anonymous connection now appear. The NETLOGON, SYSVOL, and custom shares like IT-Tools become visible because the server recognizes guest.user as a valid domain member.

docs.title: Step 4: Identify the Differences
docs.text:
Document the gap between anonymous and authenticated share listings. The difference demonstrates why credential-based enumeration is a critical step in any Active Directory assessment.

Shares that appear only with authentication typically include:

  • NETLOGON: logon scripts and domain-wide configuration files
  • SYSVOL: Group Policy templates (explored in detail in Exercise WS-4.2)
  • Custom shares: department-specific file shares created by administrators
  • Administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$); visible in the listing but accessible only to administrators

The IT-Tools share is particularly interesting because custom shares often contain operational scripts, configuration files, and internal documentation that administrators did not intend to expose to every domain user.

docs.title: Step 5: Browse the IT-Tools Share
docs.text:
Browse the IT-Tools share

List the contents of the IT-Tools share to see what files are available to your authenticated session. The -c 'ls' flag runs a single directory listing and exits without entering the interactive shell.

smbclient //dc01/IT-Tools -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'ls'

Examine the directory listing for files and subdirectories. Note file names, sizes, and timestamps. Files in IT-related shares frequently contain scripts, tools, documentation, and configuration files that reveal infrastructure details.

docs.title: Step 6: Retrieve Files from the Share
docs.text:
Download files of interest from the IT-Tools share. The get command with - as the destination prints file contents to your terminal instead of saving to disk:

Print a file to the terminal

Use the get command with - as the destination to print a file's contents to your terminal. Download the file you identified in the previous step and review its content for the lab flag. Replace <filename> with the file you found in Step 5.

smbclient //dc01/IT-Tools -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'get <filename> -'

The get <filename> - syntax retrieves the specified file and writes its contents to standard output. Review the output for the lab flag.

Save a file to disk instead

If you want to save the file locally instead, omit the trailing dash so smbclient writes it to disk.

smbclient //dc01/IT-Tools -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'get <filename>'

The file will be saved to your current working directory on the Kali machine.

docs.title: Step 7: Test Access to Administrative Shares
docs.text:
Test access to an administrative share

Verify that your low-privilege account cannot access administrative shares. Attempt to list the contents of C$, the hidden share that maps the server's system drive.

smbclient //dc01/C$ -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'ls'

The expected result is an NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED error. Administrative shares require membership in the Domain Admins group or equivalent privileges. Confirming that access is denied validates the privilege boundary between a standard domain user and an administrator.

docs.title: Step 8: Browse NETLOGON
docs.text:
Browse the NETLOGON share

Check the NETLOGON share for logon scripts and configuration files. Any authenticated domain user can read this share by design.

smbclient //dc01/NETLOGON -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'ls'

The NETLOGON share contains scripts that run when users log on to domain-joined machines. Logon scripts may contain mapped drive letters, server names, file paths, and occasionally hardcoded credentials. Record any files you find for analysis in later exercises.

docs.text:

Contents of IT-Tools share: _________

Contents of NETLOGON share: _________

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: _________

docs.title: Step 9: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text: The flag for this exercise is stored in a file on the IT-Tools share. Retrieve the file contents using the command from Step 6. The flag follows the OCR{...} format. Copy the flag value and paste it into the Submit Flag form on the platform, then click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does Windows expose more shares to authenticated users than to anonymous connections?

Reveal Answer

Windows Server is designed to support domain operations. Shares like NETLOGON and SYSVOL must be readable by every domain-joined machine so those machines can apply logon scripts and Group Policy settings. Anonymous access restrictions exist to prevent information leakage to external attackers, but once an attacker obtains even a single low-privilege domain account, those protections no longer apply. The design assumes that domain membership implies a baseline level of trust.

2. What is the security risk of custom shares like IT-Tools being readable by all domain users?

Reveal Answer

Administrators often create departmental shares and assign broad read permissions for convenience. Shares intended for IT staff may contain deployment scripts with hardcoded credentials, network diagrams, configuration files with internal IP addresses, or administrative tools that reveal infrastructure details. When every domain user can read these shares, a compromised low-privilege account gains access to information that should be restricted to specific teams.

3. How does comparing anonymous and authenticated share listings help during a penetration test?

Reveal Answer

The comparison quantifies what an attacker gains from obtaining domain credentials. A small set of anonymous shares tells you the organization has restricted unauthenticated access, but a much larger set of authenticated shares shows the post-compromise attack surface. The delta between the two listings helps prioritize credential-focused attacks: if authenticated access reveals many sensitive shares, investing time in password spraying or phishing becomes a high-value strategy.

4. You confirmed that C$ is visible but not accessible. What does that tell you about administrative share security?

Reveal Answer

The visibility of C$ in the share listing confirms that the server advertises administrative shares to authenticated users, but access control enforcement prevents non-administrators from connecting. The share-level permissions and NTFS permissions on C$ restrict access to Domain Admins and equivalent groups. Seeing the share in the listing without being able to access it confirms that privilege boundaries are functioning, and it identifies a target for privilege escalation; if you can obtain Domain Admin credentials, full file system access through C$ becomes available.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Authenticated SMB enumeration reveals significantly more shares than anonymous access
  • Domain user credentials unlock access to NETLOGON, SYSVOL, and custom shares by design
  • Custom shares created by administrators often contain sensitive operational data
  • The -U 'user%password' syntax provides non-interactive authentication for scripting
  • Comparing anonymous and authenticated results quantifies the value of compromised credentials
  • Administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$) are visible but not accessible to standard domain users
  • Exercise WS-4.2 explores the SYSVOL share in depth, examining Group Policy templates and their security implications

docs.title: Exercise WS-4.2: Group Policy Object Enumeration
Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise WS-4.1 demonstrated that authenticated domain users can access shares hidden from anonymous connections. One of those shares; SYSVOL; is especially valuable because it stores Group Policy Object (GPO) templates that define security settings, software deployment rules, and logon scripts for the entire domain. Any authenticated user can read SYSVOL by design, making GPO enumeration a standard post-compromise reconnaissance technique.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: You have authenticated SMB access to dc01 using the guest.user account. The engagement lead has asked you to examine the domain's Group Policy infrastructure for sensitive information. GPOs may contain password policies, drive mapping configurations, scheduled task definitions, startup scripts, and occasionally hardcoded credentials. Your task is to navigate the SYSVOL share, identify GPO folders, and use Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) queries to extract GPO metadata including names and descriptions.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Access the SYSVOL share on dc01 using authenticated credentials
  • Navigate the GPO folder structure within SYSVOL
  • Identify individual GPO folders by their Globally Unique Identifier (GUID) names
  • Read GPO settings files and scripts stored in the GPO template directories
  • Use LDAP to query GPO metadata (display names, descriptions) from Active Directory (AD)
  • Locate and submit the flag hidden in a GPO description

docs.title: Background: Group Policy Objects and SYSVOL
docs.text:
Group Policy is the primary configuration management system in Windows Active Directory environments. Administrators create GPOs that define settings for users and computers; password complexity requirements, firewall rules, software installation packages, logon scripts, drive mappings, and hundreds of other configuration options. GPOs are linked to Organizational Units (OUs), sites, or the domain itself, and they apply automatically to all objects within their scope.

Every GPO consists of two parts stored in different locations:

Component Location Contains Group Policy Container (GPC) Active Directory (LDAP) GPO metadata: name, description, version, link information Group Policy Template (GPT) SYSVOL share on domain controllers GPO files: scripts, settings, registry policies, software packages

The SYSVOL share is replicated across all domain controllers to ensure every DC has an identical copy of the policy templates. The share path follows a standard structure:

\\dc01\SYSVOL\corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies\{GPO-GUID}\

Each GPO folder is named with the GPO's GUID; a long hexadecimal identifier enclosed in curly braces. Inside each GPO folder, you find a Machine directory (computer settings) and a User directory (user settings), along with a GPT.INI file that tracks the GPO version number.

graph TD
    A["SYSVOL"] --> B["corp.ocr-range.lab"]
    B --> C["Policies"]
    C --> D["{GPO-GUID-1}"]
    C --> E["{GPO-GUID-2}"]
    D --> F["Machine"]
    D --> G["User"]
    D --> H["GPT.INI"]
    F --> I["Scripts"]
    F --> J["Preferences"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style D fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style E fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style F fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style G fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style H fill:#888,color:#fff
    style I fill:#888,color:#fff
    style J fill:#888,color:#fff

The security-sensitive files within GPO templates include:

Path Contains Machine\Scripts\Startup\ Scripts that run when computers boot User\Scripts\Logon\ Scripts that run when users log on Machine\Preferences\Groups\Groups.xml Local group membership changes (may contain passwords) Machine\Preferences\ScheduledTasks\ Scheduled task definitions Machine\Preferences\Services\ Service configuration changes Machine\Preferences\DataSources\ ODBC data source configurations (may contain credentials)

Historically, Microsoft's Group Policy Preferences (GPP) stored encrypted passwords in XML files within SYSVOL. The encryption key was published by Microsoft, making those passwords trivially recoverable. Microsoft patched the ability to set new GPP passwords in MS14-025, but legacy passwords from before the patch may still exist in SYSVOL.

docs.title: Tool Primer: smbclient for SYSVOL Navigation and ldapsearch for GPO Metadata
docs.text:
Two tools work together for thorough GPO enumeration. The smbclient tool provides file-level access to the SYSVOL share, while ldapsearch queries Active Directory for GPO metadata that maps GUID folder names to human-readable policy names.

List the SYSVOL share root

Authenticate to SYSVOL with the guest.user credentials and list the top-level contents in one non-interactive command.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'ls'

A successful listing confirms your account can read SYSVOL and shows the domain-named folder at the root.

Navigate into subdirectories

Chain cd and ls inside the -c argument to drill into the Policies directory without opening an interactive session.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' \
  -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies; ls'

The result lists one folder per GPO, each named with a GUID.

Read a file from SYSVOL

Use the get command with - as the destination to print a file directly to your terminal instead of saving it to disk.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' \
  -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies\{GPO-GUID}; get GPT.INI -'

The file contents stream to stdout so you can inspect scripts and settings inline.

Query GPO metadata via LDAP

Run an LDAP query against the Policies container to map each GPO GUID to its human-readable display name and description.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=groupPolicyContainer)" \
  displayName description

Each returned entry pairs a GUID with a display name, letting you prioritize which GPO folders to inspect.

The LDAP query targets the CN=Policies,CN=System container, which holds all Group Policy Container objects. The filter (objectClass=groupPolicyContainer) matches GPO entries. The attributes displayName and description provide the human-readable name and any description the administrator set for each GPO.

Parameter Purpose -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" Bind DN; authenticate as guest.user using UPN format -w "Guest2024#" Password for the bind account -H ldap://dc01 LDAP server URI -b "CN=Policies,CN=System,..." Search base; the Policies container in AD "(objectClass=groupPolicyContainer)" Filter for GPO objects only displayName description Return only these attributes

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab
docs.text:
Open the Open Cyber Range platform in your browser and start the lab environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 4
  • Click Launch on "Group Policy Object Enumeration"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Access the SYSVOL Share
docs.text:
Connect to the SYSVOL share

Connect to the SYSVOL share on dc01 and list its top-level contents.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'ls'

The top-level directory should contain a folder named after the domain (corp.ocr-range.lab). SYSVOL follows a rigid structure that is consistent across all Windows AD environments.

docs.title: Step 3: Navigate to the Policies Directory
docs.text:
Navigate to the Policies directory

Drill into the domain folder and then into the Policies subdirectory.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' \
  -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies; ls'

The Policies directory contains one subdirectory for each GPO in the domain. Each subdirectory is named with a GUID in curly braces (e.g., {31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}). Two GUIDs are present on every domain by default:

GUID GPO Name {31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9} Default Domain Policy {6AC1786C-016F-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9} Default Domain Controllers Policy

Any additional GUIDs represent custom GPOs created by the domain administrators. Record all GUIDs you find.

docs.title: Step 4: Explore a GPO Template Directory
docs.text:
Explore a GPO template directory

Pick one of the GPO GUIDs from the listing and examine its internal structure.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' \
  -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}; ls'

The standard GPO template structure contains Machine and User directories along with a GPT.INI file. Explore both the Machine and User directories to look for scripts, preferences, and configuration files.

docs.title: Step 5: Read GPT.INI Files
docs.text:
Read GPT.INI files

The GPT.INI file inside each GPO folder tracks the GPO version. Reading it confirms the GPO is active and tells you how many times the policy has been modified.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' \
  -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}; get GPT.INI -'

A GPT.INI file with a version number greater than zero indicates the GPO has been configured with custom settings. A version of zero means the GPO exists but has no custom configuration applied.

docs.title: Step 6: Search for Scripts and Preferences
docs.text:
Search for scripts and preferences

Check the Machine and User script directories within each GPO for startup, shutdown, logon, and logoff scripts. Run the Machine listing first, then the User listing.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' \
  -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}\Machine\Scripts; ls'

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' \
  -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}\User\Scripts; ls'

Look for .bat, .ps1, .vbs, or .cmd files in the script directories. Read any scripts you find; they may contain server names, file paths, credentials, or other operationally sensitive information.

docs.title: Step 7: Map GUIDs to GPO Names via LDAP
docs.text:
Map GUIDs to GPO names via LDAP

The GUID folder names in SYSVOL are not human-readable. Use an LDAP query to retrieve the display names and descriptions of all GPOs in the domain.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=groupPolicyContainer)" \
  displayName description

The output maps each GPO's Distinguished Name (DN); which contains the GUID; to its displayName attribute. Cross-reference the GUIDs from your SYSVOL listing with the display names from the LDAP query to identify which policy is stored in which folder. Expected output (approximate):

# {31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}, Policies, System, corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: CN={31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
displayName: Default Domain Policy

# {6AC1786C-016F-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}, Policies, System, corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: CN={6AC1786C-016F-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
displayName: Default Domain Controllers Policy

Review the description field on each GPO entry. Administrators sometimes store notes, configuration details, or other metadata in the description attribute.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
GPO GUIDs found in SYSVOL:

GUID Display Name Description

Scripts found in GPO templates:

GPO GUID Script Path Script Name

GPT.INI version numbers:

GPO GUID Version

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: _________

docs.title: Step 8: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text: The flag for this exercise is embedded in the description attribute of a GPO object in Active Directory. Run the LDAP query from Step 7 and examine the description field on each GPO entry. The flag follows the OCR{...} format. Copy the flag value and paste it into the Submit Flag form on the platform, then click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is SYSVOL readable by all authenticated domain users?

Reveal Answer

Domain-joined computers must read GPO templates from SYSVOL to apply Group Policy settings during startup and logon. If SYSVOL were restricted, machines could not apply security policies, software deployment rules, or logon scripts. Microsoft designed SYSVOL with broad read access as a functional requirement. Attackers benefit from the same access that machines need for normal operations.

2. What types of sensitive information might a penetration tester find inside GPO template directories?

Reveal Answer

GPO templates can contain logon/startup scripts with hardcoded credentials, Group Policy Preferences XML files with encrypted passwords (decryptable using the published Microsoft key), scheduled task definitions revealing service accounts, registry policy files showing security configurations, and drive mapping settings exposing internal file server names and share paths. Any of these can provide footholds for deeper compromise.

3. Why is mapping GUIDs to display names an important step in GPO enumeration?

Reveal Answer

SYSVOL stores GPO templates in folders named by GUIDs, which are meaningless without context. Mapping GUIDs to display names lets you prioritize which GPOs to examine. A GPO named "Deploy SQL Credentials" warrants immediate inspection, while "Desktop Wallpaper Policy" is low priority. The LDAP query provides this mapping and may also reveal sensitive information in the description field, as demonstrated by the flag in this exercise.

4. What was the MS14-025 vulnerability, and why might it still be relevant today?

Reveal Answer

MS14-025 addressed a design flaw in Group Policy Preferences where administrators could set local account passwords through GPP. The passwords were stored in XML files in SYSVOL, encrypted with a symmetric AES key that Microsoft published in MSDN documentation. Any authenticated user could read these files and decrypt the passwords. Microsoft's patch prevented creation of new GPP passwords but did not remove existing ones. Organizations that used GPP passwords before the patch may still have decryptable credentials sitting in their SYSVOL share, accessible to any domain user.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SYSVOL is a domain controller share readable by all authenticated domain users by design
  • GPO templates stored in SYSVOL may contain scripts, credentials, and configuration details
  • GPO folders are named by GUIDs that require an LDAP query to map to human-readable names
  • The groupPolicyContainer LDAP object class stores GPO metadata including names and descriptions
  • Combining SMB file access with LDAP metadata queries provides a complete picture of domain Group Policy
  • GPO enumeration feeds directly into later attack stages: credential harvesting, privilege escalation, and lateral movement
  • Exercise WS-4.3 shifts focus to Service Principal Names, another category of AD information accessible to any authenticated user

docs.title: Exercise WS-4.3: Service Principal Name Discovery
Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercises WS-4.1 and WS-4.2 demonstrated that authenticated domain users can read SMB shares and GPO templates that are invisible to anonymous connections. Service Principal Name (SPN) discovery takes authenticated enumeration in a different direction; querying Active Directory (AD) directly for accounts that run services. SPN-registered accounts are high-value targets because any authenticated user can request a Kerberos service ticket for them, and that ticket can be cracked offline to recover the account's password.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: You continue your assessment of the corp.ocr-range.lab domain using the guest.user credentials. The engagement lead wants you to identify all accounts with registered SPNs, document the services they provide, and assess the Kerberoasting attack surface. Service accounts frequently run with elevated privileges and use passwords that are weaker than expected because administrators set them once and rarely rotate them. Your task is to query Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) for all SPN-bearing user accounts and analyze what you find.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Query the AD directory for all user accounts that have a servicePrincipalName attribute
  • Identify what services each account provides based on its SPN values
  • Understand how SPN discovery enables the Kerberoasting attack
  • Document the Kerberoasting attack surface for the domain
  • Locate and submit the flag from a service account description

docs.title: Background: Service Principal Names and Kerberoasting
docs.text:
A Service Principal Name is a unique identifier that associates a service instance with a logon account in Active Directory. When a client application needs to authenticate to a service (such as a SQL Server database or a web application), Kerberos uses the SPN to locate the correct service account and issue a service ticket. SPNs follow a structured format that encodes the service type, hostname, and optional port number.

SPN format:

serviceclass/hostname:port

Common SPN examples:

SPN Service Typical Account MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.ocr-range.lab:1433 Microsoft SQL Server svc-sql HTTP/web01.corp.ocr-range.lab Web application (IIS/HTTP) svc-web CIFS/fileserver.corp.ocr-range.lab SMB file sharing Machine account exchangeMDB/mail01.corp.ocr-range.lab Exchange mailbox service svc-exchange ldap/dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab LDAP directory service Machine account

SPNs registered to machine accounts (accounts ending with $) are not useful for Kerberoasting because machine account passwords are 120+ character random strings that cannot be cracked. SPNs registered to user accounts (standard sAMAccountName entries) are the targets, because human-set passwords are typically much weaker and susceptible to offline cracking.

docs.title: The Kerberoasting Attack
docs.text:
Kerberoasting exploits a fundamental design feature of Kerberos authentication. When any authenticated user requests a service ticket (TGS) for an SPN, the Key Distribution Center (KDC) encrypts part of that ticket using the service account's password hash. The user receives the ticket regardless of whether they actually have permission to access the service.

The attack proceeds in four steps:

graph LR
    A["Enumerate SPNs<br/>via LDAP"] --> B["Request TGS<br/>Tickets"]
    B --> C["Extract Encrypted<br/>Ticket Data"]
    C --> D["Crack Password<br/>Offline"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
  1. Enumerate SPNs: Query LDAP for user accounts with servicePrincipalName attributes (the focus of this exercise)
  2. Request service tickets: Ask the KDC for a TGS ticket for each SPN
  3. Extract ticket data: Pull the encrypted portion from the ticket
  4. Crack offline: Use a tool like Hashcat or John the Ripper to brute-force the service account password

The critical security implication is that steps 2 and 3 require no special privileges; any authenticated domain user can perform them. The KDC does not check whether the requesting user has access to the service. SPN discovery (step 1) is therefore the reconnaissance phase that identifies which accounts to target.

docs.title: Why Service Accounts Are Vulnerable
docs.text:
Service accounts often have characteristics that make their passwords easier to crack than regular user passwords:

Factor Risk Passwords set once, rarely changed Old passwords may predate current complexity requirements Created by administrators, not users May use predictable patterns (e.g., ServiceName2020!) Password never expires flag Often set to prevent service outages from password rotation Elevated privileges Service accounts frequently hold admin rights on multiple servers

A cracked service account password provides the attacker with that account's full set of permissions, which often includes local administrator access on the servers running the service.

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch for SPN Enumeration
docs.text:
The ldapsearch tool can query AD for all user accounts that have an SPN registered. The key is combining an LDAP filter that matches user objects with a presence test for the servicePrincipalName attribute.

Enumerate user accounts with SPNs

Combine an objectClass=user filter with a presence test for servicePrincipalName to return only user accounts that have an SPN registered.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(&(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))" \
  sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName description

Each result block is one Kerberoasting candidate; record the sAMAccountName, every servicePrincipalName, and any description text.

The filter components work together to narrow the results:

Filter Component Purpose (objectClass=user) Match user account objects (not groups, OUs, or containers) (servicePrincipalName=*) Match entries that have at least one SPN attribute & Boolean AND; both conditions must be true

The requested attributes provide the information needed for attack planning:

Attribute Purpose sAMAccountName The account's logon name (used in Kerberoasting tools) servicePrincipalName The registered SPN values (identifies which services the account runs) description Administrator-written notes (may reveal account purpose or credentials)

Expected output (approximate):

# svc-sql, Users, corp.ocr-range.lab
dn: CN=svc-sql,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
sAMAccountName: svc-sql
servicePrincipalName: MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.ocr-range.lab:1433
description: SQL Server service account

Each result block shows one account that could be targeted for Kerberoasting. Multiple servicePrincipalName lines on a single entry indicate the account serves multiple hosts or ports.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab
docs.text:
Open the Open Cyber Range platform in your browser and start the lab environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 4
  • Click Launch on "Service Principal Name Discovery"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Query for All SPN-Bearing User Accounts
docs.text:
Query for all SPN-bearing user accounts

Run the LDAP query that searches the entire domain for user accounts with registered SPNs.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(&(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))" \
  sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName description

Examine the output carefully. Each result block represents one account that the Kerberos KDC will issue service tickets for. Note the sAMAccountName, all servicePrincipalName values, and any description text.

docs.title: Step 3: Analyze the SPN Values
docs.text:
For each account returned in Step 2, break down the SPN values to understand what services are running and where. Parse the SPN format to extract the service class, hostname, and port.

Example analysis:

SPN Value Service Class Hostname Port MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.ocr-range.lab:1433 MSSQLSvc sql01 1433 HTTP/web01.corp.ocr-range.lab HTTP web01 (default)

The service class tells you what application the account supports. The hostname reveals which server runs the service. The port confirms the listening port, which is useful for direct service enumeration.

docs.title: Step 4: Filter Out Machine Accounts
docs.text:
Compare against machine accounts

Machine accounts (computer objects) also have SPNs, but they are not useful for Kerberoasting. Verify that your filter targets user objects by running an unfiltered presence query and comparing the results.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(servicePrincipalName=*)" \
  sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName objectClass

The unfiltered query returns both user and computer accounts with SPNs. Machine accounts have objectClass: computer and their sAMAccountName ends with a $ character. Comparing the two result sets confirms that the filtered query from Step 2 correctly targets only user accounts; the ones vulnerable to Kerberoasting.

docs.title: Step 5: Check Account Descriptions
docs.text:
Check account descriptions

Service account descriptions frequently contain useful information that administrators leave as internal documentation. Query for all user accounts with SPNs and pay close attention to the description attribute.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(&(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))" \
  sAMAccountName description

Administrators sometimes store password hints, creation dates, responsible teams, or operational notes in the description field. Any of this information helps profile the account for targeted password guessing or social engineering.

docs.title: Step 6: Assess the Kerberoasting Attack Surface
docs.text:
Document the complete Kerberoasting attack surface based on your findings. For each SPN-bearing user account, record the account name, the services it provides, and any notes from the description field. An account running with elevated privileges or a critical service warrants higher priority in an actual Kerberoasting attack.

Consider the following questions for each account:

  • What service does the account run? (SQL, web, file services)
  • Does the account likely have elevated privileges?
  • How old might the password be based on description or naming patterns?
  • Are multiple services registered to a single account (broader blast radius if compromised)?

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
SPN-bearing user accounts discovered:

sAMAccountName SPN Values Description

Total user accounts with SPNs (Kerberoasting targets): _________

Total machine accounts with SPNs (not Kerberoastable): _________

Highest-value target account and reasoning: _________

How to submit: enter the flag on the exercise page exactly as you recovered it, keeping the OCR{...} wrapper.

Flag: _________

docs.title: Step 7: Find and Submit the Flag
docs.text: The flag for this exercise is stored in the description attribute of one of the service accounts with a registered SPN. Review the LDAP output from Steps 2 and 5. The flag follows the OCR{...} format. Copy the flag value and paste it into the Submit Flag form on the platform, then click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why can any authenticated domain user request a Kerberos service ticket for any SPN?

Reveal Answer

Kerberos was designed so that authentication happens before authorization. When a client requests a service ticket, the KDC verifies the client's identity (authentication) and issues the ticket without checking whether the client has permission to use the service (authorization). Authorization is the service's responsibility; the service checks the ticket and decides whether to grant access. The KDC's willingness to issue tickets to any authenticated user is what makes Kerberoasting possible.

2. Why are SPNs registered to user accounts vulnerable but SPNs registered to machine accounts are not?

Reveal Answer

Machine account passwords are automatically generated by Windows as 120+ character random strings that change every 30 days by default. Cracking a password of that length and complexity is computationally infeasible with current hardware. User account passwords, by contrast, are set by humans (typically administrators) and are subject to human password-selection habits; shorter, less random, and often unchanged for years. The difference in password strength makes user-account SPNs practical targets for offline cracking.

3. How does SPN discovery fit into a broader attack chain against Active Directory?

Reveal Answer

SPN discovery is a reconnaissance step that identifies Kerberoasting targets. If the attacker cracks a service account password, they gain that account's permissions; often local administrator access on one or more servers. From there, the attacker can move laterally to other systems, extract additional credentials from memory, and work toward domain administrator access. SPN discovery turns a low-privilege domain account into a path toward high-privilege compromise without exploiting any software vulnerability.

4. What defenses can an organization implement to reduce Kerberoasting risk?

Reveal Answer

Organizations can defend against Kerberoasting through several measures: use long (25+ character) random passwords for all service accounts, use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) that rotate passwords automatically, monitor for anomalous TGS ticket requests (a spike in SPN ticket requests from a single user is suspicious), implement the "Protected Users" group for sensitive accounts, and audit SPN registrations to remove unnecessary entries. Reducing the number of user accounts with SPNs directly shrinks the attack surface.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Any authenticated domain user can query LDAP for all accounts with registered SPNs
  • SPNs registered to user accounts (not machine accounts) are targets for Kerberoasting
  • Kerberoasting allows offline password cracking of service account credentials without triggering account lockout
  • Service account descriptions may contain operational details that help profile the account
  • The LDAP filter (&(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*)) isolates user accounts with SPNs
  • SPN discovery requires no special tools or privileges; standard ldapsearch is sufficient
  • Exercise WS-4.4 examines another category of AD information accessible to authenticated users: object permissions and DACLs

docs.title: Exercise WS-4.4: AD ACL Weak Permission Discovery
Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercises WS-4.1 through WS-4.3 focused on reading data that Active Directory (AD) exposes to authenticated users: SMB shares, Group Policy Object (GPO) templates, and Service Principal Names (SPNs). AD Access Control List (ACL) analysis takes a fundamentally different approach; instead of reading data, you examine who has permission to modify data. Weak ACLs on AD objects create privilege escalation paths that let low-privilege users perform high-privilege actions like resetting passwords, modifying group memberships, or writing attributes on sensitive accounts.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: You continue your assessment of the corp.ocr-range.lab domain with the guest.user credentials. The engagement lead suspects that AD object permissions have not been properly audited and that some objects may have overly permissive Discretionary Access Control Lists (DACLs). Your task is to enumerate Organizational Units (OUs) and user accounts in the domain, identify objects where guest.user has unexpected write access, and document the privilege escalation paths that weak permissions create.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand how AD DACLs control access to directory objects
  • Enumerate OUs and objects in the domain using authenticated Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) queries
  • Discover the Flags OU and analyze its contents
  • Identify objects where guest.user has been granted excessive permissions
  • Locate and submit the flag from a misconfigured object's description

docs.title: Background: Active Directory Access Control
docs.text:
Every object in Active Directory; users, groups, OUs, computers, GPOs; has a security descriptor that controls who can read, modify, or delete the object. The security descriptor contains a DACL, which is a list of Access Control Entries (ACEs). Each ACE grants or denies a specific permission to a specific security principal (user, group, or computer).

AD permissions are more granular than file system permissions. Instead of basic read/write/execute, AD supports object-specific permissions that control access at the attribute level.

Common AD permissions and their attack value:

Permission What It Allows Attack Potential GenericAll Full control over the object Reset passwords, modify group membership, write any attribute GenericWrite Write any attribute on the object Modify descriptions, write SPNs, change logon scripts WriteDacl Modify the object's ACL Grant yourself additional permissions WriteOwner Change the object's owner Take ownership, then modify the ACL ForceChangePassword Reset the target's password Take over the target account without knowing the current password AddMember Add members to a group Add yourself to privileged groups WriteProperty (specific) Write to a specific attribute Depends on the target attribute

docs.title: How Weak ACLs Create Attack Paths
docs.text:
In a properly secured environment, low-privilege users can read most AD objects but cannot modify them. Misconfigurations occur when administrators grant excessive permissions; often during troubleshooting, delegation, or automated provisioning; and forget to remove them. A low-privilege user with GenericAll on a high-privilege group can add themselves to that group, instantly escalating to administrative access.

graph TD
    A["guest.user<br/>Low Privilege"] -->|"GenericAll"| B["Target OU<br/>or Account"]
    B --> C["Read Attributes"]
    B --> D["Write Attributes"]
    B --> E["Reset Password"]
    B --> F["Modify Group<br/>Membership"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style F fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

ACL-based attack paths are among the most common findings in AD security assessments. Tools like BloodHound map these paths across an entire domain, but the underlying technique starts with the same LDAP queries you will use in this exercise.

docs.title: Permission Inheritance
docs.text:
AD permissions can be inherited from parent objects. An OU with a misconfigured ACL passes those permissions down to every object inside it. Granting guest.user GenericAll on the Flags OU means guest.user has full control over every user, group, and computer object within that OU; including the ability to read and write any attribute on those objects.

graph TD
    A["Domain Root"] --> B["Flags OU<br/>GenericAll: guest.user"]
    B --> C["flag.account<br/>Inherits GenericAll"]
    B --> D["Other Objects<br/>Inherit GenericAll"]

    style A fill:#888,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: ldapsearch for ACL-Related Object Discovery
docs.text:
Directly reading DACLs via ldapsearch requires parsing binary security descriptor data, which is complex. In a full engagement, tools like BloodHound, PowerView, or dacledit.py from Impacket handle DACL parsing. For this exercise, you will use ldapsearch to discover objects that your account has access to and read their attributes; the readable attributes themselves reveal what permissions you hold.

Enumerate OUs in the domain

Filter on objectClass=organizationalUnit to map every OU container in the directory tree.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" \
  dn description

The returned DNs reveal the organizational structure; watch for any OU with an unusual name or description.

List objects in a specific OU

Set the search base to a single OU and match all object types to see what accounts and resources it contains.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=*)" \
  dn description

Results are limited to objects inside the named OU, so the listing stays focused.

Query a specific account

Match a single account by its sAMAccountName to read its attributes directly.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(sAMAccountName=flag.account)" \
  description

The fact that your low-privilege account can read these attributes is itself evidence of the permission delegation.

The search base (-b) parameter controls where in the directory tree the search begins. Setting the base to a specific OU limits results to objects within that OU. The filter (objectClass=*) matches all object types, while (objectClass=organizationalUnit) matches only OUs.

Parameter Purpose -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" Search only within the Flags OU "(objectClass=*)" Match all objects regardless of type "(sAMAccountName=flag.account)" Match a specific account by logon name dn description Return the Distinguished Name and description attribute

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Lab
docs.text:
Open the Open Cyber Range platform in your browser and start the lab environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises, then Windows Server, then Level 4
  • Click Launch on "AD ACL Weak Permission Discovery"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Enumerate All Organizational Units
docs.text:
Enumerate all Organizational Units

Begin by mapping the OU structure of the domain. OUs are the organizational containers that hold users, groups, and computers, and each OU can have its own set of delegated permissions.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" \
  dn description

Review the list of OUs in the output. Standard AD deployments include OUs like Domain Controllers, but custom OUs created by administrators reveal organizational structure. Look for any OU with an unusual name or an interesting description.

docs.title: Step 3: Discover the Flags OU
docs.text:
Discover the Flags OU

The OU listing from Step 2 should reveal an OU named Flags. Enumerate all objects within the Flags OU to see what accounts and resources it contains.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=*)" \
  dn description

The search base is set to the Flags OU, so results are limited to objects within that container. Record the Distinguished Names (DNs) of all objects returned. The DN tells you the object's name, type, and location in the directory tree.

docs.title: Step 4: Examine Objects in the Flags OU
docs.text:
Examine objects in the Flags OU

For each object found in Step 3, query its full set of attributes to understand what information is stored on it.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=*)" \
  dn objectClass sAMAccountName description memberOf

The additional attributes reveal each object's type (objectClass), account name (sAMAccountName), description, and group memberships (memberOf). Pay attention to the description field; administrators and lab designers store metadata there.

docs.title: Step 5: Query Objects Discovered in the Flags OU
docs.text:
Query objects discovered in the Flags OU

Based on the results from Steps 3 and 4, query the user objects you discovered in the Flags OU directly to read their attributes. Use the sAMAccountName values returned in the previous steps to confirm the targets.

ldapsearch -D "guest.user@corp.ocr-range.lab" -w "Guest2024#" \
  -H ldap://dc01 \
  -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" \
  "(objectClass=user)" \
  sAMAccountName description

Examine the description attribute on each account returned. The fact that guest.user can read these attributes is itself evidence of the permission delegation; in this case, guest.user has GenericAll on the Flags OU, which grants full control (including read and write) over every object inside it.

docs.title: Step 6: Understand the Permission Implication
docs.text:
The guest.user account has GenericAll permissions on the Flags OU. GenericAll is the most powerful AD permission; equivalent to full control. In a real environment, GenericAll on an OU grants the following capabilities over every object within that OU:

  • Read all attributes on any object in the OU
  • Write all attributes on any object in the OU (modify descriptions, phone numbers, logon scripts)
  • Reset passwords for any user account in the OU (without knowing the current password)
  • Modify group membership for any group in the OU
  • Delete objects from the OU
  • Create new objects in the OU

A penetration tester who discovers GenericAll on an OU containing privileged accounts could reset an administrator's password, log in as that administrator, and gain full domain control; all from a low-privilege starting point.

docs.title: Step 7: Map the Attack Path
docs.text:
Document the privilege escalation path that the weak ACL creates. Consider the following chain:

graph LR
    A["guest.user<br/>Domain User"] -->|"GenericAll on<br/>Flags OU"| B["flag.account"]
    B -->|"Reset Password"| C["Compromised<br/>flag.account"]
    C -->|"Check Group<br/>Memberships"| D["Potential Further<br/>Access"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style C fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style D fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

In a real engagement, you would next check what groups flag.account belongs to and what access those groups provide. Each link in the chain multiplies the attacker's reach. AD ACL abuse paths often chain through multiple objects before reaching Domain Admin.

docs.text: The flag for this exercise is stored in the description attribute of flag.account within the Flags OU. Run the LDAP query from Step 5 to retrieve the description. The flag follows the OCR{...} format. Copy the flag value and paste it into the Submit Flag form on the platform, then click Submit.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why are ACL misconfigurations considered one of the most dangerous AD security issues?

Reveal Answer

ACL misconfigurations create invisible privilege escalation paths. Unlike a missing patch or a weak password, a misconfigured ACL does not generate alerts, does not appear in vulnerability scans, and persists until someone explicitly audits and corrects the permissions. An attacker who discovers a GenericAll permission on a privileged group can escalate to Domain Admin in seconds. Organizations with complex delegation models; where permissions are granted for helpdesk operations, provisioning workflows, or third-party integrations; are especially prone to ACL drift over time.

2. How does permission inheritance amplify the risk of a single misconfigured ACL?

Reveal Answer

Permissions set on a parent OU propagate to every child object within it unless inheritance is explicitly blocked. A single GenericAll ACE on a top-level OU grants full control over potentially hundreds of user accounts, groups, and computer objects. The attacker does not need separate permissions on each object; the inherited permission covers them all. Auditing individual object ACLs without considering inheritance misses these cascading grants entirely.

3. What tools do professional penetration testers use to map AD ACL attack paths at scale?

Reveal Answer

BloodHound is the primary tool for mapping AD ACL attack paths. BloodHound uses an ingestor (SharpHound or BloodHound.py) to collect ACL data, group memberships, session data, and trust relationships from AD. The collected data is loaded into a Neo4j graph database, and BloodHound's query engine identifies shortest paths from any compromised account to high-value targets like Domain Admins. PowerView (part of PowerSploit) and Impacket's dacledit.py provide command-line alternatives for querying and modifying AD ACLs.

4. The guest.user account has GenericAll on the Flags OU. In a real engagement, what would your next steps be?

Reveal Answer

The next steps follow the attack chain: first, enumerate all objects in the Flags OU and identify which accounts have elevated privileges or interesting group memberships. For any user account in the OU, you could reset the password (using GenericAll's ForceChangePassword capability) and log in as that user. You would check whether the compromised account has access to additional systems, is a member of privileged groups, or has its own ACL-based permissions on other objects. Each compromised account becomes a new starting point for further enumeration and escalation.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Every AD object has a DACL that controls who can read, modify, or delete the object
  • GenericAll grants full control, including the ability to reset passwords and modify group membership
  • Permission inheritance means a misconfigured OU ACL affects every object inside that OU
  • Low-privilege users with unexpected write access represent the most common AD attack paths
  • LDAP queries can discover objects and read attributes, revealing what permissions your account holds
  • Professional tools like BloodHound automate ACL analysis at domain-wide scale
  • ACL-based attacks do not exploit software vulnerabilities; they abuse legitimate AD features that have been misconfigured
  • Authenticated enumeration across all four labs in this chapter demonstrates the massive information gap between anonymous and authenticated access in Active Directory

docs.title: What You Accomplished
docs.text:
Chapter WS04 shifted the attack perspective from anonymous reconnaissance to authenticated enumeration. Using a single set of low-privilege domain credentials (guest.user / Guest2024#), you accessed information that anonymous connections cannot reach. The four labs demonstrated four distinct categories of data that any authenticated domain user can extract from Active Directory (AD).

Each lab built on the same credential set while exploring a different attack surface:

Exercise Technique Key Finding WS-4.1 Authenticated SMB share listing Custom shares (IT-Tools) and domain shares (NETLOGON, SYSVOL) hidden from anonymous access WS-4.2 GPO template and metadata enumeration SYSVOL file structure, GPO display names, and descriptions via LDAP WS-4.3 SPN discovery via LDAP Service accounts vulnerable to Kerberoasting WS-4.4 AD ACL analysis Weak DACL granting GenericAll to a low-privilege user

docs.title: Anonymous vs. Authenticated Access
docs.text:
The central theme of this chapter is the information gap between unauthenticated and authenticated access. Anonymous enumeration in previous chapters revealed ports, DNS records, and limited Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) data. Authenticated enumeration exposed the full share inventory, Group Policy infrastructure, service account landscape, and object-level permissions; all from the same low-privilege account.

Active Directory is designed to be readable by authenticated users. Domain-joined machines need to read Group Policy Object (GPO) templates from SYSVOL, query Service Principal Names (SPNs) for Kerberos ticket requests, and evaluate Discretionary Access Control Lists (DACLs) for permission enforcement. Penetration testers and attackers take advantage of these design requirements.

docs.title: The Value of a Low-Privilege Account
docs.text:
The guest.user account used throughout this chapter holds no special group memberships and no administrative rights. Despite that limited standing, the account provided access to:

  • All non-administrative SMB shares on the domain controller
  • Every GPO template and its LDAP metadata
  • All SPN registrations in the domain
  • Object attributes on any AD object where permissions allow read access

Defending against authenticated enumeration requires rethinking the default AD permission model, not patching software vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Key Terminology
docs.text:
The following terms were introduced or used extensively in this chapter. Each definition reflects the term's meaning in the context of AD security assessments.

Term Definition ACE Access Control Entry; a single permission grant or denial within a DACL ACL Access Control List; the complete set of permission entries on an AD object DACL Discretionary Access Control List; the portion of the security descriptor that defines who can access the object GenericAll Full control permission in AD; allows reading, writing, deleting, and modifying permissions GPO Group Policy Object; a policy configuration applied to users and computers in AD GPP Group Policy Preferences; an extension of GPOs that historically stored encrypted (and recoverable) passwords GUID Globally Unique Identifier; a hexadecimal string that uniquely names a GPO folder in SYSVOL Kerberoasting An attack that requests Kerberos service tickets and cracks them offline to recover service account passwords OU Organizational Unit; a container in AD used to organize objects and delegate permissions SPN Service Principal Name; an identifier linking a service instance to a logon account for Kerberos authentication SYSVOL A domain controller share that stores GPO templates, scripts, and policy files TGS Ticket Granting Service; the Kerberos component that issues service tickets
