docs.title: Self-Assessment Questions
docs.text:
Test your understanding of the concepts covered in this chapter. Answer each question before reading the provided explanation.

1. A colleague says "We found a low-privilege domain account, but there is nothing useful we can do with it." How would you respond?

A low-privilege domain account grants access to far more information than anonymous access. Authenticated users can enumerate all SMB shares (including custom and hidden shares), read SYSVOL for GPO templates and scripts, query LDAP for SPNs (enabling Kerberoasting), and discover ACL misconfigurations that create privilege escalation paths. Every one of these techniques was demonstrated in this chapter using credentials with no special group memberships.

2. Explain the relationship between SYSVOL, GPOs, and LDAP in three sentences.

GPOs consist of two components: a Group Policy Container stored in AD (queryable via LDAP) and a Group Policy Template stored on the SYSVOL share. LDAP provides the metadata; the GPO's display name, description, version, and link information; while SYSVOL provides the files: scripts, preference XML files, and registry policy definitions. Complete GPO enumeration requires querying both sources and cross-referencing the GUID-based folder names with the LDAP display names.

3. Why is Kerberoasting considered a low-risk, high-reward attack technique?

Kerberoasting is low-risk because the service ticket request is a normal Kerberos operation that generates no failed logon events and triggers no account lockouts. The password cracking happens offline on the attacker's own hardware, completely invisible to the target organization's monitoring. The reward is potentially high because service accounts often run with elevated privileges and use passwords that are weaker and older than regular user passwords, making them more susceptible to offline cracking.

4. How does GenericAll on an OU differ from GenericAll on a single user object?

GenericAll on a single user object grants full control over that one account; the ability to reset its password, modify its attributes, and change its group memberships. GenericAll on an OU grants those same capabilities over every object inside the OU through permission inheritance. A single misconfigured ACL on an OU can compromise dozens or hundreds of accounts, making OU-level permissions far more dangerous than individual object permissions.

docs.title: What Comes Next
docs.text: The authenticated enumeration techniques in this chapter provide the reconnaissance foundation for active exploitation. Kerberoasting targets identified through SPN discovery can be attacked to obtain service account passwords. Weak DACLs can be exploited to reset passwords and escalate privileges. Files discovered in SMB shares and SYSVOL may contain credentials that unlock additional systems. The progression from passive enumeration to active exploitation is the next phase of the Windows Server attack path.

docs.title: The Capstone Assessment
docs.text:
Active Directory (AD) reconnaissance is not a single technique; it is a discipline that weaves together DNS (Domain Name System) queries, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) enumeration, SMB (Server Message Block) share access, and Group Policy Object (GPO) analysis into a coherent picture of a domain environment. Chapters WS01 through WS04 introduced each of these techniques individually, building your skills one protocol at a time. Chapter WS05 asks you to combine everything into a single thorough assessment against a live AD environment.

A capstone assessment differs from a guided exercise in one critical way: you decide the methodology. No step-by-step instructions tell you which tool to run next or which flag to look for first. Instead, you receive a target domain, a set of credentials, and a mission; find all three parts of a split flag hidden across different AD data sources. The techniques you need are the same ones you practiced in previous chapters, but the order, the troubleshooting, and the analysis are entirely up to you.

The flag for the assessment is split into three parts, each stored in a different data source. You will need to query DNS records, search LDAP attributes, and access SMB shares to recover all three parts and assemble the complete flag. The split-flag design mirrors real-world scenarios where intelligence about a target is scattered across multiple protocols and services.

docs.title: What You Learned in Chapters WS01-WS04
docs.text:
Each previous chapter focused on a specific reconnaissance technique. The table below summarizes the core skills from each chapter that you will need during the assessment.

Chapter Focus Area Key Skills WS01 Initial Reconnaissance Port scanning, DNS forward lookups, DNS reverse lookups, anonymous SMB listing, anonymous LDAP queries WS02 LDAP Deep Dive Organizational Unit (OU) enumeration, user and group discovery, computer object listing, password policy extraction WS03 DNS Infrastructure SRV record queries, conditional forwarder discovery, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope analysis, network topology mapping WS04 Authenticated Analysis Authenticated SMB access, GPO enumeration, Service Principal Name (SPN) discovery, Access Control List (ACL) analysis

The assessment draws on techniques from every chapter. DNS queries from WS01 and WS03 reveal infrastructure details and hidden records. LDAP searches from WS01 and WS02 expose user attributes and organizational structure. SMB access from WS01 and WS04 grants file retrieval from shares. GPO review from WS04 provides configuration and policy context.

docs.title: How the Multi-Part Flag Works
docs.text:
The assessment flag follows the standard OCR{...} format, but the content is split into three segments stored in three different locations. Each segment is a standalone string that makes no sense on its own; only when you concatenate all three parts in the correct order does the complete flag emerge.

graph TD
    DNS["DNS TXT Record<br/>Part 1"]
    LDAP["LDAP User Attribute<br/>Part 2"]
    SMB["SMB Share File<br/>Part 3"]
    FLAG["Complete Flag<br/>OCR{part1+part2+part3}"]

    DNS --> FLAG
    LDAP --> FLAG
    SMB --> FLAG

    style DNS fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style LDAP fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style SMB fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style FLAG fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

You do not need to find the parts in any specific order. Each part is independent, stored in a different protocol's data, and retrievable with a different tool. The assessment tests whether you can identify which tool and technique to use for each data source.

docs.title: The Four Pillars of AD Reconnaissance
docs.text:
The assessment covers four core reconnaissance techniques. Each technique targets a different layer of the AD infrastructure, and together they provide full visibility into the domain environment.

graph LR
    A["DNS Recon"] --> E["Complete<br/>AD Assessment"]
    B["LDAP Enum"] --> E
    C["SMB Analysis"] --> E
    D["GPO Review"] --> E

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8a735,color:#fff
    style D fill:#888,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

DNS Reconnaissance reveals the naming infrastructure of the domain; hostnames, IP addresses, service locations, and custom records that administrators may have created. Forward lookups resolve names to addresses, reverse lookups map addresses back to names, SRV records identify domain controllers and key services, and TXT records sometimes contain metadata or configuration strings.

LDAP Enumeration exposes the directory structure; users, groups, computers, OUs, and the attributes attached to each object. Every AD object has dozens of attributes, and administrators sometimes store sensitive information in fields like description, info, or comment that are readable by authenticated users.

SMB Share Analysis provides access to files stored on domain-joined systems. Anonymous shares may expose public documents, while authenticated shares can contain internal tools, scripts, configuration files, and assessment data. Both access levels are worth testing.

GPO Review reveals the policies applied across the domain; password requirements, software restrictions, logon scripts, and security configurations. The SYSVOL share on domain controllers stores GPO templates and scripts that are readable by any authenticated domain user.

docs.title: Assessment Methodology Checklist
docs.text:
The checklist below outlines the reconnaissance areas you should cover during the assessment. The checklist is not a step-by-step guide; you decide the order and the specific commands based on what you discover along the way.

DNS Reconnaissance:

DNS reconnaissance covers the discovery of hostnames, IP addresses, service records, and any custom TXT entries within the target domain. These queries form the foundation of the assessment by revealing the naming infrastructure and service topology.

  • Perform forward lookups for key hostnames in the domain
  • Perform reverse lookups for discovered IP addresses
  • Query SRV records for domain controller and service locations
  • Check for TXT records on assessment-related subdomains
  • Document all discovered DNS entries

LDAP Enumeration:

  • Query the base Distinguished Name (DN) and domain structure
  • Enumerate OUs for any assessment-specific containers
  • Search for user objects and examine non-standard attributes
  • List group memberships and computer objects
  • Review password policy settings

SMB Share Analysis:

SMB share analysis tests both anonymous and authenticated access to file shares on domain-joined systems. The goal is to discover accessible shares, map permission levels, and retrieve any files that contain assessment data or sensitive information.

  • Test anonymous access to all discovered shares
  • Test authenticated access using provided credentials
  • List and retrieve files from accessible shares
  • Review file contents for flag data and configuration details

GPO and SYSVOL Review:

GPO and SYSVOL review examines the group policy configurations and supporting files stored on the domain controller. The review uncovers security policies, logon scripts, and configuration templates that reveal how the domain is managed and secured.

  • Access the SYSVOL share on the domain controller
  • Enumerate GPO names and settings
  • Review logon scripts and policy templates
  • Document any security-relevant configurations

Flag Assembly:

After completing all reconnaissance phases, assemble the flag parts collected from each data source. Verify that each part is recorded accurately and that the final assembled flag conforms to the expected format.

  • Record each flag part with its source
  • Concatenate all parts in order
  • Verify the complete flag matches the OCR{...} format
  • Submit the flag on the platform

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Make sure the following prerequisites are met before beginning the assessment.

  • You have completed Chapters WS01 through WS04 and are comfortable with DNS, LDAP, SMB, and GPO techniques
  • You understand how to use dig, nslookup, ldapsearch, smbclient, and smbmap
  • You have the assessment credentials: guest.user / Guest2024#
  • Your VPN connection to the Open Cyber Range is active
  • You can resolve dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab from your Kali terminal
  • You have a text editor or notes file open to record findings as you go
  • You have reviewed the methodology checklist above and have a plan for your approach

The assessment has a suggested duration of 90 minutes. Allocate roughly 20 minutes for DNS reconnaissance, 25 minutes for LDAP enumeration, 20 minutes for SMB analysis, and 25 minutes for GPO review and flag assembly. Adjust the time allocation based on your comfort level with each technique.

If you get stuck during the assessment, a detailed walkthrough is available in the exercise file. Try to complete as much as you can independently before consulting the walkthrough; the goal is to test your ability to apply techniques without step-by-step guidance.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
The previous four chapters each focused on a single reconnaissance discipline; DNS (Domain Name System) queries, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) enumeration, SMB (Server Message Block) share analysis, and GPO (Group Policy Object) review. Exercise WS-5.1 is the capstone assessment for the Windows Server track. You will apply all four disciplines against a live Active Directory (AD) domain to locate three flag parts hidden in different data sources.

Read the scenario and objectives carefully before you begin. The assessment is designed to be completed independently using the methodology checklist from the chapter introduction.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Meridian Technologies has contracted your security team to perform a thorough AD reconnaissance assessment against their primary domain controller. The engagement scope covers DNS infrastructure, directory services, file shares, and group policy configurations. Your point of contact, Aisha Patel, has provided a low-privilege domain account for authenticated testing. The domain runs on a Windows Server environment with standard AD services.

Your mission is to demonstrate full reconnaissance capability by recovering three assessment markers (flag parts) that the Meridian IT team has placed across different AD data sources. Each marker is stored in a different protocol layer; DNS, LDAP, and SMB; and requires a different reconnaissance technique to retrieve. Recovering all three markers and assembling the complete flag proves that your team can extract intelligence from every layer of the AD infrastructure.

docs.title: Lab Details
docs.text:
The following connection details and credentials apply to the assessment.

Parameter Value Target dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab Domain corp.ocr-range.lab Username guest.user Password Guest2024# Difficulty Advanced Duration 90 minutes

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
The assessment requires you to demonstrate proficiency across all four reconnaissance disciplines covered in the Windows Server track.

  • Perform thorough DNS reconnaissance including forward lookups, reverse lookups, SRV record queries, and TXT record discovery
  • Enumerate AD objects via LDAP including users, groups, Organizational Units (OUs), and computer objects
  • Access and analyze SMB shares using both anonymous and authenticated connections
  • Review GPO configurations and SYSVOL contents for policy and security information
  • Locate all three flag parts across the different data sources
  • Assemble the complete flag from the three parts and submit the result

docs.title: Suggested Approach
docs.text: The guidance below provides a general methodology for approaching the assessment. Specific commands and exact syntax are not included; the assessment tests your ability to select the right tool and construct the right query based on what you learned in Chapters WS01 through WS04.

docs.title: Phase 1: DNS Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Start with DNS because the results inform every subsequent phase. DNS records reveal hostnames, IP addresses, and service locations that you will need when querying LDAP and connecting to SMB shares.

Begin by performing forward lookups for the domain controller hostname and the domain itself. Check whether the DNS server responds to queries for the corp.ocr-range.lab zone. Query SRV records to confirm domain controller locations and identify any additional services registered in DNS.

Look beyond standard records. TXT records are often used for SPF (Sender Policy Framework) configurations, domain verification tokens, and sometimes custom metadata. Administrators may have created TXT records on specific subdomains; consider what subdomain names might be relevant to an assessment scenario. The dig tool supports querying specific record types on specific hostnames.

Record every DNS finding in your worksheet. Pay attention to any records that contain strings or codes that look like flag fragments.

docs.title: Phase 2: LDAP Enumeration
docs.text:
LDAP enumeration reveals the directory structure and the attributes attached to every AD object. Start by confirming the base Distinguished Name (DN) for the domain, then work your way through the directory tree.

Enumerate OUs first; they organize the directory and may contain assessment-specific containers. Search for user objects within each OU, paying close attention to attributes beyond the common ones. Standard attributes like sAMAccountName and displayName contain expected values, but attributes like info, description, and comment sometimes hold data that administrators did not intend to be widely visible.

Look for user accounts with names related to the assessment scenario. The ldapsearch tool supports filters that match specific attribute values or patterns. Once you find a relevant user object, dump all of its attributes to see the complete picture.

Record every LDAP finding; OUs, users, groups, and any unusual attribute values; in your worksheet.

docs.title: Phase 3: SMB Share Analysis
docs.text:
SMB analysis provides access to files stored on the domain controller. Test both anonymous and authenticated access to discover all available shares and their permission levels.

Start with anonymous enumeration to establish a baseline. Then connect using the provided credentials to see which additional shares become available. Authenticated access typically reveals more shares and higher permission levels than anonymous connections.

Once you identify accessible shares, list their contents and examine any files that relate to the assessment. Look for text files, notes, configuration files, and any documents that might contain flag data. The smbclient tool supports inline commands for listing directory contents and retrieving files without entering an interactive session.

Record every share name, permission level, and file listing in your worksheet.

docs.title: Phase 4: GPO and SYSVOL Review
docs.text:
GPO review provides insight into the domain's security configuration and policy enforcement. The SYSVOL share on every domain controller contains GPO templates, logon scripts, and policy definitions that are readable by any authenticated domain user.

Access the SYSVOL share using authenticated credentials and browse the policy directories. Look for GPO names, script files, and configuration templates. While the GPO review may not contain a flag part directly, the information supports the assessment report and demonstrates thorough methodology.

Document the GPO names, any scripts you find, and notable policy settings in your worksheet.

docs.title: Phase 5: Flag Assembly
docs.text:
After completing all four phases, review your worksheet for the three flag parts. Each part is a string fragment found in a different data source. Concatenate the parts in order (Part 1 from DNS, Part 2 from LDAP, Part 3 from SMB) and wrap them in the OCR{...} format.

Verify that the assembled flag looks syntactically correct before submitting. The complete flag should be a single continuous string inside the braces with no spaces.

docs.title: Detailed Walkthrough
docs.text: The walkthrough below provides the exact commands and expected output for each phase of the assessment. Use the walkthrough only after attempting the assessment independently; the learning value comes from figuring out the approach on your own.

docs.title: Launch the Lab
docs.text:
Open the platform and start the assessment environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises then Windows Server then Level 5
  • Click Launch on "AD Reconnaissance Assessment"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target information displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 1: DNS Forward Lookups
docs.text:
Resolve the domain controller hostname

Begin by resolving the domain controller hostname to confirm connectivity and identify the target IP address.

dig A dc01.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The dig command queries the DNS server at dc01 for the A record (IPv4 address) of the domain controller hostname. The response should contain a single A record with the IP address of dc01. Record the IP address; you will need it for reverse lookups and as a fallback if hostname resolution fails during later steps.

Resolve the domain name

Next, resolve the domain name itself to check for any additional addresses.

dig A corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The domain name may resolve to the same IP as the domain controller, or it may return multiple addresses if there are additional DCs (Domain Controllers) in the environment.

docs.title: Step 2: DNS Reverse Lookup
docs.text:
Reverse-lookup the domain controller IP

Perform a reverse lookup on the IP address you discovered in Step 1 to verify that forward and reverse DNS are consistent. Replace <dc01_ip> with the address from Step 1.

dig -x <dc01_ip> @dc01

The -x flag tells dig to perform a PTR (Pointer) record lookup, which maps an IP address back to a hostname. Consistent forward and reverse records confirm that the DNS infrastructure is properly maintained. Inconsistencies can indicate stale records or split-horizon DNS configurations.

docs.title: Step 3: SRV Record Queries
docs.text:
Query SRV records for domain services

Query SRV records to discover domain services registered in DNS. SRV records identify the hostname and port for specific services within the domain. Run each query in turn.

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

dig SRV _gc._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

Each SRV query returns the hostname, port, priority, and weight for the specified service. The _ldap._tcp record identifies LDAP servers (domain controllers). The _kerberos._tcp record identifies Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) servers. The _gc._tcp record identifies Global Catalog servers. All three are standard AD DNS records.

docs.title: Step 4: DNS TXT Record Discovery (Flag Part 1)
docs.text:
Discover the TXT record flag part

Query TXT records for assessment-related subdomains. The assessment scenario indicates that a flag part is stored in a DNS TXT record on a specific subdomain.

dig TXT _assess1.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01

The response should contain a TXT record with a string value. The value is the first part of the assessment flag. Expected output fragment:

_assess1.corp.ocr-range.lab.  IN  TXT  "<flag_part_1>"

Record the value returned by the TXT query as Flag Part 1 in your worksheet.

docs.title: Step 5: LDAP Base DN Discovery
docs.text:
Discover the LDAP base DN

Query the LDAP root DSE (Directory System Agent Entry) to discover the base DN for the domain.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -s base namingContexts

The output reveals the base DN, typically DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab for the corp.ocr-range.lab domain. Record the base DN; every subsequent LDAP query needs it.

Flag Purpose -x Use simple authentication instead of SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) -H ldap://dc01 Connect to the LDAP server on dc01 -s base Search only the root entry (base scope) namingContexts Request the naming context attributes

docs.title: Step 6: LDAP OU Enumeration
docs.text:
Enumerate all OUs

Enumerate all OUs in the domain to find assessment-related containers.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" dn

The filter (objectClass=organizationalUnit) returns only OU objects. The dn at the end limits the output to Distinguished Names, making the results easier to scan. Look for OUs with names related to the assessment; an OU named "Flags" or "Assessment" is a strong indicator of where flag data is stored.

docs.title: Step 7: LDAP User Search (Flag Part 2)
docs.text:
Search for user objects in the Flags OU

Search for user objects within the Flags OU and examine their attributes.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=user)"

The query returns all user objects within the Flags OU along with their readable attributes. Look for a user account named assess.flag or similar. Once you identify the relevant user, examine the info attribute; AD stores freeform text in the info field, and administrators sometimes use the field for notes or metadata.

Dump all attributes for the flag user

To search specifically for the assessment flag user and retrieve all attributes, target it by sAMAccountName and request every attribute with *.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(sAMAccountName=assess.flag)" "*"

The info attribute holds Flag Part 2. Expected output fragment:

dn: CN=assess.flag,OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab
sAMAccountName: assess.flag
info: <flag_part_2>

Record the info attribute value as Flag Part 2 in your worksheet.

docs.title: Step 8: LDAP Group and Computer Enumeration
docs.text:
Enumerate groups and computers

Perform additional LDAP enumeration to demonstrate full coverage. Query group objects and then computer objects within the domain.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=group)" cn description

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=computer)" cn operatingSystem

The group query returns group names and descriptions. The computer query returns computer names and their operating system versions. Record the results in your worksheet; full enumeration demonstrates thoroughness even when specific objects do not contain flag data.

docs.title: Step 9: Anonymous SMB Enumeration
docs.text:
List shares with a null session

Test anonymous access to SMB shares on the domain controller.

smbclient -L //dc01 -N

The -N flag suppresses the password prompt, sending a null session. The output lists all shares visible to anonymous users, along with their type (Disk, IPC, or Printer). Record every share name and type.

Map anonymous share permissions

Next, map permissions for anonymous access.

smbmap -H dc01

The smbmap output shows READ, WRITE, or NO ACCESS for each share. Any share granting anonymous read or write access is a significant finding. Document the results even if anonymous access is limited; the contrast between anonymous and authenticated access levels is itself a useful finding.

docs.title: Step 10: Authenticated SMB Access (Flag Part 3)
docs.text:
List shares with authenticated credentials

Connect to shares using the provided credentials to discover additional accessible resources.

smbclient -L //dc01 -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#'

Compare the authenticated share list with the anonymous results from Step 9. Authenticated access typically reveals additional shares or higher permission levels on existing shares.

Retrieve the assessment notes file

Access the IT-Tools share and retrieve the assessment notes file.

smbclient //dc01/IT-Tools -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'get assessment-notes.txt -'

The file contents include the third flag part. Record the value from the file as Flag Part 3 in your worksheet.

Flag Purpose //dc01/IT-Tools Connect to the IT-Tools share on dc01 -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' Authenticate with the provided credentials -c 'get assessment-notes.txt -' Execute the get command to retrieve the file, printing to stdout (-)

docs.title: Step 11: Authenticated SMB Permission Mapping
docs.text:
Map authenticated share permissions

Map share permissions with authenticated credentials to complete the SMB analysis.

smbmap -H dc01 -u guest.user -p 'Guest2024#'

Compare the authenticated permission map with the anonymous results. Document which shares are accessible only with credentials and what permission level each share grants. The difference between anonymous and authenticated access demonstrates the value of credential-based testing.

docs.title: Step 12: SYSVOL and GPO Review
docs.text:
Recursively list SYSVOL

Access the SYSVOL share to review GPO configurations and scripts.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'recurse ON; ls'

The recurse ON; ls command sequence enables recursive directory listing and then lists all files and directories within the SYSVOL share. The output includes GPO template directories, logon scripts, and policy definition files. Each GPO is stored in a directory named with its GUID (Globally Unique Identifier).

Browse the GPO policy directories

Browse the GPO directories to find policy files.

smbclient //dc01/SYSVOL -U 'guest.user%Guest2024#' -c 'cd corp.ocr-range.lab\Policies; ls'

Record the GPO GUIDs and any scripts or configuration files you discover. While the GPO data may not contain a flag part, the review demonstrates thorough assessment methodology.

docs.title: Step 13: Assemble the Complete Flag
docs.text:
Gather the three flag parts from your worksheet and concatenate them in order.

Part Source Value Part 1 DNS TXT record on _assess1.corp.ocr-range.lab (your Part 1) Part 2 LDAP info attribute on user assess.flag (your Part 2) Part 3 SMB file assessment-notes.txt on IT-Tools share (your Part 3)

Concatenate the three parts to form the complete flag:

Complete flag: OCR{<part1><part2><part3>}

Submit the complete flag on the platform to confirm your assessment is successful.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
The questions below go beyond individual techniques and ask you to evaluate the assessment as a whole. Consider the relationships between the four reconnaissance disciplines and the real-world implications of the findings.

1. Why is combining multiple reconnaissance techniques more effective than relying on a single protocol?

Reveal Answer

Each protocol exposes a different layer of the AD infrastructure. DNS reveals naming and service locations but not user details. LDAP exposes directory objects and attributes but not file contents. SMB provides file access but not directory structure. GPO shows security policies but not individual user data. An attacker who queries only one protocol sees a partial picture; combining all four produces a full map of the environment that reveals relationships and misconfigurations invisible from any single vantage point.

2. What does the presence of sensitive data in the LDAP info attribute suggest about the organization's directory hygiene?

Reveal Answer

The info attribute is readable by any authenticated domain user by default. Storing sensitive data in the info field means that every user in the domain can retrieve the information with a basic LDAP query. The finding suggests that the organization does not audit non-standard LDAP attributes for sensitive content and has not applied restrictive ACLs (Access Control Lists) to limit attribute visibility. In a real environment, password hints, internal notes, and configuration details stored in readable attributes represent a significant information disclosure risk.

3. How would you prioritize the remediation of findings from this assessment for a real client?

Reveal Answer

The highest priority is restricting anonymous and low-privilege access to sensitive data. The TXT record containing assessment data should be removed or restricted. The LDAP info attribute should be cleared and ACLs tightened to prevent low-privilege users from reading sensitive attributes. The SMB share should enforce least-privilege access so that general-purpose accounts cannot retrieve internal files. GPO configurations should be reviewed to ensure SYSVOL permissions follow the principle of least privilege. Each finding should be documented with business impact and a specific remediation action.

4. An attacker has compromised a low-privilege domain account. Based on this assessment, what information could they extract without escalating privileges?

Reveal Answer

With a low-privilege account, an attacker could query DNS for all registered services and hostnames, enumerate the full directory tree via LDAP including user accounts and group memberships, access authenticated SMB shares to retrieve files, and browse SYSVOL for GPO scripts and policy configurations. The assessment demonstrates that low-privilege access is sufficient to map the entire AD infrastructure, identify high-value targets, and extract data from misconfigured shares and attributes. Privilege escalation is not required to cause significant damage when basic access controls are weak.

5. How would the methodology change if you had no credentials at all?

Reveal Answer

Without credentials, LDAP enumeration would be limited to anonymous bind capabilities; some domains allow anonymous base DN queries but restrict object enumeration. SMB access would be limited to null sessions and guest access, which typically expose fewer shares. DNS reconnaissance would be unaffected because DNS queries do not require domain authentication. GPO review would be unavailable because SYSVOL requires authentication. The overall coverage would be significantly reduced. Even low-privilege credentials are valuable for thorough reconnaissance.

docs.title: Key Takeaways: Windows Server Track Summary
docs.text:
The five chapters of the Windows Server track built a complete AD reconnaissance methodology from the ground up. Each takeaway below connects a technique to the broader assessment discipline.

  • DNS is the foundation of AD reconnaissance. Forward lookups, reverse lookups, SRV records, and TXT records reveal the naming infrastructure, service locations, and sometimes hidden metadata. Every assessment should start with thorough DNS queries because the results inform every subsequent phase.

  • LDAP exposes the directory tree to any authenticated user. OUs, users, groups, computers, and their attributes are all queryable with basic credentials. Non-standard attributes like info, description, and comment frequently contain data that administrators did not intend to expose. Always enumerate beyond the obvious fields.

  • SMB share access depends on both the share permissions and the NTFS (New Technology File System) permissions. Anonymous access reveals misconfigurations at the share level, while authenticated access tests NTFS-level controls. The difference between the two access levels is itself a finding worth documenting.

  • GPO configurations and SYSVOL contents are readable by every authenticated domain user. Policy settings, logon scripts, and configuration templates stored in SYSVOL provide insight into the domain's security posture. Reviewing GPO data completes the picture that DNS, LDAP, and SMB began.

  • Multi-source intelligence is more valuable than any single finding. The split-flag design in the assessment mirrors real-world scenarios where important information is scattered across protocols. A thorough methodology that covers all four disciplines produces findings that no single-protocol approach could achieve.

  • Low-privilege access is sufficient for thorough reconnaissance. The entire assessment was completed with a guest-level domain account. Organizations that focus exclusively on preventing privilege escalation while neglecting basic access controls leave their AD infrastructure exposed to thorough enumeration by any authenticated user.

docs.title: Windows Server Track Complete
docs.text:
Over five chapters and nineteen labs, you progressed from basic port scanning and DNS lookups to a full Active Directory (AD) reconnaissance assessment. Each chapter introduced a new discipline; initial discovery, directory enumeration, DNS infrastructure analysis, authenticated service analysis, and finally the capstone that combined all four. The Windows Server track has equipped you with a repeatable methodology for mapping AD environments using only standard reconnaissance tools.

The progression followed a deliberate learning curve. Early labs provided exact commands and expected output. Later labs required you to select the right tool and construct queries based on your findings. The capstone assessment removed step-by-step guidance entirely, testing whether you could apply the full methodology independently.

docs.title: What You Learned at Each Level
docs.text:
Level 1; Initial Reconnaissance (WS01) introduced the foundational tools and techniques. You learned to scan ports with Nmap, resolve hostnames with dig, perform reverse DNS (Domain Name System) lookups, list SMB (Server Message Block) shares anonymously, and query LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) without credentials. Every technique in Levels 2 through 5 builds on the skills from Level 1.

Level 2; LDAP Deep Dive (WS02) explored the AD directory structure in depth. You enumerated Organizational Units (OUs), discovered user accounts and their attributes, mapped group memberships, listed computer objects, and extracted password policy settings. Level 2 demonstrated that LDAP exposes the full directory tree to any user who can bind to the service.

Level 3; DNS Infrastructure (WS03) moved beyond basic lookups into infrastructure-level DNS analysis. You queried SRV records to locate domain controllers and services, discovered conditional forwarders that reveal trust relationships, analyzed DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scopes for network layout, and mapped the network topology from DNS data alone. Level 3 showed that DNS is not merely a name resolution service; it is an infrastructure map.

Level 4; Authenticated Analysis (WS04) introduced credential-based techniques. You accessed SMB shares that require authentication, enumerated Group Policy Objects (GPOs) and their settings, discovered Service Principal Names (SPNs) that identify service accounts, and analyzed Access Control Lists (ACLs) to understand permission structures. Level 4 demonstrated the gap between anonymous and authenticated access.

Level 5; Capstone Assessment (WS05) combined all four disciplines into a single assessment. You applied DNS, LDAP, SMB, and GPO techniques independently to locate flag parts scattered across different data sources. The capstone tested technical skill and methodology alike; the ability to plan, execute, and document a thorough assessment without step-by-step guidance.

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer the following questions without referring back to the walkthroughs. The questions span all five levels of the Windows Server track. If any question feels unfamiliar, revisit the corresponding chapter before considering the track complete.

1. What dig command queries the SRV record for LDAP services in the corp.ocr-range.lab domain?

2. How do you perform an anonymous LDAP search for all OUs in a domain with base DN DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab?

3. What is the difference between a null session and a guest session when connecting to SMB?

4. How would you use ldapsearch to retrieve the info attribute of a specific user named assess.flag in the Flags OU?

5. What does an SRV record for _kerberos._tcp tell you about the domain environment?

6. How do you list files on an authenticated SMB share without entering an interactive session?

7. Why is the SYSVOL share readable by all authenticated domain users, and what security risk does that create?

8. What LDAP attribute stores freeform text that administrators sometimes use for notes, and why is the attribute a security concern?

9. Name three types of DNS records that are useful for AD reconnaissance and explain what each reveals.

10. Describe a complete AD reconnaissance methodology in four phases, naming the primary tool for each phase.

docs.text: The table below covers every key command used across the five chapters of the Windows Server track. Keep the reference available during future assessments and engagements.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. dig SRV _ldap._tcp.corp.ocr-range.lab @dc01: the SRV record type is specified after dig, and the service name follows the _service._protocol.domain convention.

2. ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(objectClass=organizationalUnit)" dn: the -x flag uses simple authentication (anonymous bind), -b sets the search base, and the filter matches only OU objects.

3. A null session sends an empty username and empty password to the SMB server. A guest session authenticates as the built-in guest account. Both bypass normal credential requirements, but they rely on different server-side configurations; null sessions require anonymous access to be enabled, while guest sessions require the guest account to be active or the map to guest setting to redirect failed logins.

4. ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01 -b "OU=Flags,DC=corp,DC=ocr-range,DC=lab" "(sAMAccountName=assess.flag)" info: the search base is narrowed to the Flags OU, the filter matches the specific user, and info limits the output to that attribute.

5. The _kerberos._tcp SRV record identifies the hostname and port of the Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) in the domain. The KDC handles authentication ticket requests for domain-joined systems. The record confirms that Kerberos authentication is active and reveals which server handles authentication; information that is valuable for both reconnaissance and later attack phases like Kerberoasting.

6. smbclient //<host>/<share> -U 'user%pass' -c 'ls': the -c flag passes a command to smbclient for non-interactive execution. The ls command lists directory contents and smbclient exits after completing the command.

7. SYSVOL is readable by all authenticated domain users because domain-joined computers need to download GPO settings and logon scripts during startup and login. The security risk is that any authenticated user; including compromised low-privilege accounts; can browse GPO templates, read logon scripts (which may contain hardcoded credentials), and examine policy settings that reveal the domain's security configuration.

8. The info attribute stores freeform text and is readable by default by all authenticated users. Administrators sometimes use the field for internal notes, password hints, or configuration details without realizing that the content is visible to every domain user. The attribute is a security concern because no default ACL restricts read access, making it a common source of information disclosure in AD environments.

9. Three useful DNS record types for AD reconnaissance: (1) A records map hostnames to IP addresses, revealing the network location of servers. (2) SRV records identify specific services and the servers hosting them, exposing domain controllers, KDCs, and Global Catalog servers. (3) TXT records contain freeform text strings, sometimes holding SPF configurations, domain verification tokens, or custom metadata that reveals organizational details.

10. A complete AD reconnaissance methodology: (1) DNS Reconnaissance using dig: discover hostnames, IP addresses, SRV records, and service locations. (2) LDAP Enumeration using ldapsearch: map the directory tree including OUs, users, groups, computers, and attributes. (3) SMB Analysis using smbclient and smbmap: test anonymous and authenticated share access, retrieve files, and map permissions. (4) GPO Review using smbclient against SYSVOL; examine group policy configurations, scripts, and security settings.

docs.title: What Comes Next
docs.text: The Windows Server track has given you a complete methodology for AD reconnaissance. The skills you built translate directly into several professional paths and certification objectives.

docs.title: Real-World Applications
docs.text:
Penetration Testing Engagements follow the same methodology you practiced in the capstone assessment. Professional pentesters begin every internal engagement with DNS reconnaissance, LDAP enumeration, and SMB analysis before attempting exploitation. The tools and techniques from the Windows Server track; dig, ldapsearch, smbclient, smbmap: appear in virtually every internal network assessment.

Security Auditing and Compliance requires the same enumeration techniques applied defensively. Security teams use LDAP queries to audit user attributes for sensitive data, SMB permission mapping to verify share access controls, and GPO review to confirm that security policies are applied correctly. The difference between an attacker and an auditor is intent; the techniques are identical.

Incident Response benefits from rapid AD enumeration during containment. When a domain account is compromised, responders need to quickly determine what the account can access; which shares, which systems, which group memberships. The LDAP and SMB techniques from the track enable fast scoping of a compromised account's reach.

docs.title: Further Study
docs.text:
Active Directory attack paths extend beyond reconnaissance into exploitation techniques like Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, delegation abuse, and credential relay attacks. The SPN discovery skills from WS04 provide the foundation for Kerberoasting; the next logical step after reconnaissance.

BloodHound and SharpHound automate AD relationship mapping by collecting user, group, computer, and ACL data into a graph database. The manual enumeration techniques from the track help you understand what BloodHound collects and how to interpret its output.

PowerShell-based AD enumeration using modules like ActiveDirectory and PowerView provides Windows-native alternatives to the Linux tools used in the track. Many professional engagements require both Linux and Windows tooling, and understanding both approaches makes you effective in any environment.

Cloud and hybrid environments extend AD into Azure AD (now Entra ID), where directory enumeration techniques adapt to REST APIs and OAuth tokens rather than LDAP and SMB. The conceptual framework; enumerate users, groups, permissions, and policies; remains the same even when the protocols change.
